together with the root, root and branch, Soph., Ar.; αὐτ. τι διδόναι to give in absolute possession, Aesch.
in one's own person, without a mask, Luc.
seeing oneself, an eyewitness, Hdt.
selling one's own goods or products, Plat.
= αὐτοπώλης: ἡ -κη (sc. τέχνη), the trade of an αὐτοπώλης, Plat.
roots and all; poet. αὐτόριζος, Babr.
self-rooted, self-founded, Eur.
self-flowing, flowing unbidden, Anth.
thither, to the very place, Lat. illuc, Hdt., Thuc.
of sheer iron, with stroke of sword, Eur.
self, Lat. ipse:— in the oblique cases simply for the personal Pron., him, her, it:— with the Artic. ὁ αὐτός, ἡ αὐτή, τὸ αὐτό (or ταὐτόν), etc., the very one, the same.
self, myself, thyself, etc., acc. to the person of the Verb., Hom., etc.:

oneself, one's true self, the soul, not the body, Od.; or opp. to others, as king to subjects, parent to children, man to wife, etc., Hom.; hence absol. for the master, τίς οὗτος;—Αὐτός, i. e. Socrates, Ar.; similarly in neut. αὐτὸ δείξει the result will shew, Eur.
of oneself, of one's own accord, Lat. sponte, Hom., Soph.
by oneself, alone, αὐτός περ ἐών although alone, Il.; αὐτοί ἐσμεν we are by ourselves, i. e. among friends, Ar.
in Plat., τὸ δίκαιον αὐτό right in itself, the idea of right, etc.; cf. αὐτοάνθρωπος.
in dat. with Subst., together with, ἀνόρουσεν αὐτῆι σὺν φόρμιγγι he sprang up lyre in hand, Il.; αὐτῆι σὺν πήληκι helmet and all, Id.; and without σύν, αὐτοῖς ἀνδράσι men and all, Hdt., etc.
added to ordinal Numbers, e. g. πέμπτος αὐτός himself the fifth, i.e. himself with four others, Thuc.

in connexion with the person. Pron., ἐγὼ αὐτός, ἐμέθεν αὐτῆς, σὲ αὐτόν, etc., Hom.; in Hdt. and attic it coalesces with oblique cases of Pron., ἐμαυτοῦ, σε-αυτοῦ, ἑ-αυτοῦ:— it is joined with these reflexive Pronouns to add force, αὐτὸς καθ’ αὑτοῦ, αὐτοὶ ὑφ’ αὑτῶν Aesch., etc.
gen. αὐτοῦ is used with the possessive Pron., πατρὸς κλέος ἠδ’ ἐμὸν αὐτοῦ Il.
αὐτὸς ἑαυτοῦ is also used with comp. and Sup. adj. to express something unusual, αὐτὸς ἑωυτοῦ πολλῶι ὑποδεέστερος Hdt.
he, she, it, for the simple Pron. of 3 person, only in oblique cases, and never at the beginning of a sentence, Hom., attic: cf. ἑαυτοῦ.

with Article ὁ αὐτός, ἡ αὐτή, τὸ αὐτό, and attic contr. αὑτός, αὑτή, ταὐτό and ταὐτόν, gen. ταὐτοῦ, dat. ταὐτῶι, pl. neut. ταὐτά: ionic ὡὐτός, τὠυτό:— the very one, the same, Lat. idem, Hom., Hdt., attic:—it freq. takes a dat., like ὅμοιος, to denote sameness, τὠυτὸ ἂν ὑμῖν ἐπρήσσομεν we should fare the same as you, Hdt.; also, ὁ αὐτὸς καί, cf. Lat. simul ac, Id.
αὐτο- in Compos.:
of itself, i. e. natural, native, not made, as in αὐτόκτιτος.
of mere . . , of nothing but . . , as in αὐτόξυλος.
of oneself, self-, as in αὐτοδίδακτος, αὐτόματος: and so independently, as in αὐτόνομος.
just, exactly, as in αὐτόδεκα.
with reflex. sense of αὑτοῦ and ἀλλήλων, as αὐθέντης, αὐτοκτονέω.
together with, as in αὐτόπρεμνος, αὐτόρριζος.
self-sped, Aesch.
a stand-up fight, close fight, ἔν γ’ αὐτοσταδίηι Il.
self-sent, going or acting of oneself, Soph., Anth.
lamenting by or for oneself, Aesch.
slain by oneself or by kinsmen, Soph., Eur.
to act or speak off-hand, Xen.
c. acc. to devise off-hand, extemporise, Thuc., Xen.
in bad sense, to act, speak, or think unadvisedly, try rash experiments, Plat.
an impromptu, Arist.
one who acts or speaks offhand: a raw hand, bungler, Lat. tiro, Xen.
hand to hand, αὐτοσχεδίηι (sc. μάχηι) in close fight, in the fray, Il.: αὐτοσχεδίην as adv., = αὐτοσχεδόν, Hom.
off-hand, of an improvisatore, Hhymn.
near at hand, hand to hand, Lat. cominus, of close fight, Hom.
self-accomplished, spontaneous, Anth.
ending in itself, complete in itself, supporting oneself, ἱππεῖς Luc.
（τέλος IV) taxing oneself, self-taxed, Thuc.
young and all, Aesch.
arrant tragic, Dem.
to turn straightway, Hhymn.

properly gen. of αὐτός, at the very place, just here, just there, Lat. illico, Hom., Hdt., attic; with the place added, αὐτοῦ ἐνὶ Τροίηι Il.; αὐτοῦ τῶιδ’ ἐνὶ χώρωι Od.; αὐτοῦ ταύτηι exactly here, Hdt., etc.
to work with one's own hand, Luc.
self-wrought, rudely wrought, Anth.
a working on oneself, i. e. self-murder or the murder of one's own kin, Aesch.
personal labour, opp. to slave-labour, Plut.
self-working, Soph.

as Subst., one who works his land himself (not by slaves), a husbandman, poor farmer, Eur.; of the Peloponnesians, Thuc.:—metaph., αὐτουργὸς τῆς φιλοσοφίας one that has worked at philosophy by himself, without a teacher, Xen.
pass. self-wrought, simple, native, Anth.
epic gen. and dat. sg. and pl. of αὐτός Hom.; ἀπ. αὐτόφιν, παρ’ αὐτόφιν or -φι, from the very spot, Il.; ἐπ’ αὐτόφιν on the spot, Id.
with the bark on, Theocr.
self-murdering, murdering those of one's own family, Aesch.
a murderer, Eur.
bearing one's own baggage, Aesch.
cargo and all, ναῦς Plut.
self-grown, Plat.:— of home growth, Xen.
natural, opp. to artificial, Hes., Thuc.; κορύνα αὐτοφυής rough as it came from the tree, Theocr.
τὸ αὐτοφυές, one's own nature, Plat.
self-caused, ἕλκεα Pind.
natural, αὐτ. ἐργασία, = αὐτουργία, i. e. agriculture, Arist.
self-sounding, χρησμὸς αὐτ. an oracle delivered by the god himself, Luc.

self-detected, caught in the act of theft, Soph.; ἐπ’ αὐτοφώρωι λαμβάνειν to catch in the act, Eur., Dem.; ἐπ’ αὐτοφώρωι ἁλῶναι Hdt.: in a more general sense, ἐπ’ αὐτοφώρωι καταλαμβάνειν τινα ἀμαθέστερον ὄντα to detect him point blank of ignorance, Plat.; ἐπ’ αὐτ. εἴλημμαι πλουσιώτατος ὤν Xen.
murder perpetrated by one's own hand, Plat.: dat. αὐτοχειρίαι, ionic -ίηι, with one's own hand, αὐτ. κτείνειν Hdt., etc.
with one's own hand, Aesch., Soph., etc.: c. gen. the very doer or author of a thing, Id., Dem.
absol., like αὐθέντης, one who kills himself or one of his kin, Soph.: then, simply, a murderer, homicide, Id., Dem.; in full, τὸν αὐτ. τοῦ φόνου the perpetrator of . . , Soph.
as adj. murderous, Eur.; πληγέντες αὐτόχειρι μιάσματι of brothers smitten by mutual slaughter, Soph.
country and all, Aesch.
sprung from the land itself, Lat. terrigena: αὐτόχθονες, οἱ, like Lat. Indigenae, aborigines, natives, Hdt., Thuc.; of the Athenians, Eur., Ar., etc.
as adj. indigenous, Hdt.
angry at oneself, Anth.
rudely cast, massive, of a lump of iron used as a quoit, Il.
in very deed, really and truly, Ar.
just, exactly, Luc.
a seeing with one's own eyes, Luc.
in this very manner, even so, just so, as it is, γυμνὸν ἐόντα, αὔτως—ὥστε γυναῖκα, unarmed just as I am— like a woman, Il.
in a contemptuous sense, just so, no better, τί σὺ κήδεαι αὔτως ἀνδρῶν; why take you no better care? Id.; νήπιος αὔτως a mere child, Id.; αὔτως ἄχθος ἀρούρης Od.
in reference to the past, still so, just as before, as it was, Hom.; λευκὸν ἔτ’ αὔτως still white as when new, Il.
in vain, without effect, οὐκ αὔτως μυθήσομαι Od.
to cut the throat of a person, behead, c. acc., Soph.
of the neck, Od.
like καυχάομαι, to boast, plume oneself, Hdt., Eur.; τινι or ἐπί τινι on a thing, Id., Anth.
c. acc. et inf. to boast or declare loudly that, protest that, Hdt., Thuc., Eur.:—c. inf. only, Aesch.; οὐ γάρ ποτ’ ηὔχουν μεθέξειν I never thought that . . , Id.
braggart, proud, Anth.
a thing boasted of, a pride, boast, Soph.: cause for boasting, glory, Id., Thuc.
boasting, self-confidence, Id.
the neck, throat, of men and beasts, Hom., etc.
metaph. any narrow passage, a neck of land, isthmus, Hdt., Xen.
a narrow sea, strait, Hdt., Aesch.; of the point at which the Danube spreads into several branches, Hdt.
a narrow mountain-pass, defile, Id.
boasting, exultation, Thuc.
to be squalid or unwashed, Lat. squaleo, Od., Ar., Plat.
dry, dusty, rough, squalid, Eur., Plat.; esp. of hair, Eur.
drought, Hdt., Thuc.
the effects of drought, squalor, Plat.
looking dry, squalid, κόμη Eur.: τὸ αὐχμῶδες drought, Hdt.

entry.etym: Akin to εὕω: hence αὐαίνω, αὐχμός.
entry.sense: to burn, light a fire, get a light, Od.

entry.etym: The Root is ΑϜ, akin to ἄημι: hence ἀϋτή.
entry.sense: to shout out, shout, call aloud, Hom.; αὖε δ’ Ἀθήνη, μακρὸν ἄϋσε, etc., Id.: —also in Trag.; c. acc. cogn. to utter, στεναγμόν, αὐδάν Eur.
c. acc. pers. to call upon, Hom.
rarely of things, to ring, ἀσπὶς ἄϋσεν Il.; cf. αὖος.
to purify:— Mid. to purify oneself by offerings, τοῖς θεοῖς to the gods, Eur.
a taking away, carrying off, Plat.
one must take away, Plat.
ἀφαιρετέος, έα, έον, to be taken away, Id.
to be taken away, separable, Plat.

to take from, take away from a person, τί τινι Od., etc.; also τί τινος, Ar., Xen.; and τί τινα Aesch., Soph.:—c. acc. solo, ἀπελὼν τὰ ἄχθεα having taken them off, Hdt.; ὀργὴν ἀφ. to remove it, Eur.; ἀφ. χωρίς separate, set aside, Plat.
Mid., fut. ἀφαιρήσομαι, and later ἀφελοῦμαι: aor2 ἀφειλόμην:— to take away for oneself, take away, in sense and construction much like Act., Hom., etc.
followed by μή c. inf. to prevent, hinder from doing, Soph., Eur.
ἀφαιρεῖσθαί τινα εἰς ἐλευθερίαν, Lat. vindicare in libertatem, to set a man free, Plat., Dem.
Pass., fut. -αιρεθήσομαι: aor1 ἀφηιρέθην: perf. ἀφῄρημαι, ionic ἀπαραίρημαι:— to be robbed or deprived of a thing, to have it taken from one, τι Hdt., attic
Hephaestus , Doric for Ἥφαιστος.
to spring off or from, ἐκ νεώς Aesch.; ἀφήλατο jumped off, Ar.
to rebound, glance off, Anth.
without the φάλος or boss, in which the plume was fixed, Il.
to miss one's mark, c. gen., Il., Xen.
to be deprived of what one has, Il.
random-talking, Il.
to displease, not to please, Od., Hdt., Soph.
obscurity, ἀξιώματος ἀφ. want of illustrious birth, Thuc.
disappearance, utter destruction, Aesch.
unseen, invisible, viewless, of the nether world, Aesch.: χάσμα ἀφ. a blind pit, Hdt.; ἡ ἀφ. θεός, of Proserpine, Soph.
ἀφ. γίγνεσθαι = ἀφανίζεσθαι, to disappear, be missing, Hdt., Eur.:— of soldiers missing after a battle, Thuc.: cf. ἀφανίζω.
unseen, unnoticed, secret, Solon, Thuc.: —c. part., ἀφ. εἰμι ποιῶν τι I do it without being noticed, Xen.
unknown, uncertain, obscure, Hdt., attic: of future events, τὸ ἀφανές uncertainty, Hdt.:—adv. ἀφανῶς, Thuc.; so ἐκ τοῦ ἀφανοῦς as adv., Id.; and neut. pl. ἀφανῆ, Eur.
of persons, unnoticed, obscure, Id., Thuc.
ἀφανὴς οὐσία personal property, as money, which can be made away with, opp. to φανερά (real), as land, Oratt.
to make unseen, hide from sight, Xen., Thuc., etc.

to do away with, remove, ἄχος Soph.; ἀφ. τινὰ πόλεος to carry off one from the city, Eur.; ἀφ. αὑτὸν εἰς τὸν νεών to disappear into the temple, Ar.:—of state criminals, to remove from sight, make away with, Hdt., Xen.: Pass. to be concealed or suppressed, Thuc.
to destroy utterly, rase to the ground, erase writing, Id., Dem.: to obliterate traces, Xen.
to obliterate, tarnish one's good name, Thuc., Plat.:—but in good sense, ἀφ. ἀγαθῶι κακόν to wipe out ill deeds by good, Thuc.; δύσκλειαν Id.
to disfigure, ἀφ. τὰ πρόσωπα, of hypocritical sadness, NTest.
to make away with property, Aeschin., Dem.
Pass. to become unseen, to disappear, Hdt., Soph.; of persons buried by a sand-storm, Hdt.; or, lost at sea, Thuc., Xen.
a getting rid of, τῆς δίκης Ar.
(from Pass.) disappearance, Hdt.
to be suppressed, Isocr.
made invisible, blotted out, forgotten, Il.: hidden, Aesch., Soph.; ἀφ. βῆναι, οἴχεσθαι, ἔρρειν, = ἀφανισθῆναι, to disappear, Trag.
in secret, Pind.
obscure, Id.
to fasten from or upon, ἅμματα ἀφ. to tie knots on a string, Hdt.:—Pass. to be hung on, hang on, perf. part. ἀπαμμένος (ionic for ἀφημμένος), Hdt.; ἀφημμένος ἔκ τινος Theocr.
to tear off or from, c. gen., Il.; to snatch away, steal from, τί τινος Ar.: c. acc. only, to snatch eagerly, Soph., Eur.
straightway, forthwith, at once, quickly, presently, Hom., Trag.
thereupon, after that, Hom.
in Theogn. as adj. swift, fleet (cf. ἀφάρτερος).
more fleet, Il.
speechlessness, Eur., Plat.
to handle, feel, c. acc., Hdt.
not uttered, nameless, Hes.
untold, unutterable, ineffable, extraordinary, Hdt., Soph.; ἄφατον ὡς there's no saying how, i. e. marvellously, immensely, Ar.
feeble, powerless, παιδὸς ἀφαυροῦ Il.; mostly in comp. and Sup., Hom., Hes.:—adv. -ρῶς, Anth.
to dry up, parch, Ar.
to handle, rub, polish, Il.
without light, φῶς ἀφ. a light that is no light (i. e. to the blind), Soph.; νυκτὸς ἀφεγγὲς βλέφαρον, of the moon, as opp. to the sun, Eur.
obscure, dim, faint, Aesch.
metaph., ill-starred, unlucky, Soph.
a privy, NTest.
to be unsparing or lavish of, ψυχῆς Soph.; ἑαυτοῦ Thuc.:—absol. ἀφειδήσας (sub. ἑαυτοῦ) recklessly, Eur.; but
ἀφειδεῖν πόνου to be careless of it, i. e. neglect, avoid, labour, Soph.
unsparing or lavish of a thing, c. gen., Aesch.
of actions, done without regard to cost or risk, Thuc.
adv. -δῶς, ionic -δέως, freely, lavishly Hdt., Dem.:—also sparing no pains, with all zeal, Id.
unsparingly, without mercy, Hdt.; comp. -έστερον, Sup. -έστατα, Xen.
profuseness, Plat.
harsh treatment, neglect, NTest.
one must abstain from, τινός Xen.
without a stone, even, smooth, Ar.: metaph. of persons, simple, plain, blunt, Dem., Luc.:—adv. ἀφελῶς, simply, roughly, Theogn.
to drag away suppliants, ἐκ τοῦ ἱροῦ Hdt., etc.; to drag or tow ships away, Thuc.:— to draw aside, ἐπί τι Xen.
to draw off liquor, drink up, Aesch.
Mid. to draw off for oneself, Ar.
simplicity, NTest.

entry.etym: From same Root as Lat. opes.
entry.sense: riches, wealth, plenty, Il., Theogn.
shut out from a place, Aesch.
to interpret, expound, Plat.
to creep off, steal away, retire, Soph.
insufferable, intolerable, Aesch.
a letting go, dismissal, Philipp. ap. Dem.:— a quittance or discharge from a bond, Id.: exemption from service, Plut.: a divorce, Id.

a letting go (Lat. missio) of horses from the starting-post, and then the starting-post itself, ἰσώσας τἀφέσει τὰ τέρματα having made the winning-post one with the starting-post, i. e. having come back to the starting-post, Soph.

entry.etym: old Attic future formed from ἀφέστηκα fut pf. of ἀφίστημι
entry.sense: I shall be absent, away from, τινός Plat., Xen.
one must dismiss, Plat.
to be let go, Id.
for letting go or starting for a race: ἀφ. Διόσκουροι whose statues stood at the starting place, Anth.
let loose, at large, ranging at will, of sacred flocks that were free from work, Aesch., Plat.: metaph. of person, dedicated to a god, Eur.: τὸ ἄφετον, freedom from restraint, Luc.
to singe off, Ar.
to fry, toast, Id.
to refine by boiling off the refuse, to boil down, Hdt.:—esp. to boil free of dirt and dross, to refine, χρυσίον Id.: to boil young again, Ar.:—Pass., ὕδωρ ἀπεψημένον Hdt.
Dep.
to lead from a point, and so, generally, to lead the way, go first, οἱ ἀφηγούμενοι the van, Xen.
to tell or relate in full, explain, Hdt.: perf. in pass. sense, τὸ ἀπηγημένον what has been told, Id.
a tale, narrative, Hdt.
a telling, narrating, ἄξιον ἀπηγήσιος worth telling, Hdt.
a guide, Anth.
to sweeten, Plut., Luc.
to arrive at, Plat.
beyond youth, elderly, mostly in comp. ἀπηλικέστερος, Hdt.
to sit apart.
a lighting, kindling, περὶ λύχνων ἁφάς about lamp- lighting time, Hdt.
（ἅπτομαι) a touching, touch, Aesch.: the sense of touch, Plat., etc.
the archer, of Apollo, Il.
incorruption, NTest.
uncorrupted, incorruptible, Arist., etc.
voiceless, Aesch., Anth.
of places, where none may speak, Soph.
pass. unspeakable, Plat.
not liable to perish, imperishable, Hom., Trag.: of persons, immortal, Hhymn.
voiceless, speechless, Hdt., Aesch., etc.
unenvied, Aesch.
freedom from envy or grudging, readiness, Plat.
of things, plenty, abundance, Pind., Plat.
without envy:
act. free from envy, Hdt., Plat.
ungrudging, bounteous, Lat. benignus, Trag.
pass. not grudged, bounteously given, plentiful, abundant, Hdt., attic; ἐν ἀφθόνοις βιοτεύειν to live in plenty, Xen.
unenvied, provoking no envy, ὄλβος Aesch.
irreg. comp. -έστερος, Sup. -έστατος, Plat.; but -ώτερος, -ώτατος, Xen.
adv. in abundance, ἀφθ. ἔχειν τινός to have enough of it, Plat.
incorruption, NTest.
uncorrupt, of young persons, Anth.
to remove to another settlement: Mid. to cause to be transported, Eur.
to purify, hallow: Pass., perf. ταῦτ’ ἀφιερώμεθα I have had these expiatory rites performed, Aesch.

entry.etym: ι short in epic, except in augm. tenses: ῑ attic
entry.sense: to send forth, discharge, Lat. emittere, of missiles, Hom., etc.:—hence to let loose, utter, give vent to words, Hdt., Trag.
to let fall, Il.
to send forth an expedition, dispatch it, Hdt.: Pass., of troops, Id.
to give up or hand over to, τινι τί Id., attic:—Pass., ἡ Ἀττικὴ ἀπεῖτο ἤδη Hdt.

to send away, let go, loose, set free, Il., attic:—c. acc. pers. et gen. rei, to set free from a thing, let off from, Hdt.: in legal sense to release from an engagement, accusation, etc., ἀφ. τινὰ φόνου Dem.
to dissolve, disband, break up an army, Hdt.:— to dismiss the council or law-courts, Ar.
to put away, divorce, Hdt.
to let go as an ἄφετος, consecrate, Xen.
of things, to get rid of, δίψαν Il.; to shed its blossoms, of plants, Od.; to slacken its force, of a dart, Il.
ἀφ. πλοῖον ἐς . . to loose ship for a place, Hdt.
in legal sense, c. dat. pers. et acc. rei, ἀφ. τινὶ αἰτίην to remit him a charge or a fine, Hdt., Dem.
to leave alone, give up, let pass, neglect, Hdt., attic; foll. by a predicate, ἀφύλακτον ἀφ. to leave unguarded.
c. acc. et inf., ἀφ. τι δημόσιον εἶναι to give up to be public property, Thuc.; ἀφ. τὸ πλοῖον φέρεσθαι to let the boat be carried away, Hdt.
c. acc. pers. et inf. to let, suffer, permit one to do a thing, Id., Plat., etc.
seemingly intr. (sub. στρατόν, ναῦς, etc.), to break up, march, sail, etc., Hdt.
Mid. to send forth from oneself, send forth, attic
δειρῆς ἀφίετο πήχεε she loosed her arms from off my neck.
c. gen. only, τέκνων ἀφοῦ let go hold of the children, Soph., Thuc.
to arrive at, to have come to, c. acc., Hom.

to come to one place from another, to arrive at, reach: c. acc. loci, Hom.; or ἀφ. ἐς . . , ἐπί . . , κατά . . , πρός . . , Id., attic (in Prose the prep. is seldom omitted); absol. to arrive, Od.:—Hom. also puts the person reached in acc., μνηστῆρας ἀφ. came up to them, Od.; so, to come up to a throw (of the quoit), Id.:— ἀφ. ἐπὶ or εἰς πάντα to try every means, Soph., Eur.
to come into a certain condition, ἀπ. ἐς πᾶν κακόν or κακοῦ, ἐς ἀπορίην, etc., Hdt., attic
ἀπ. τινι ἐς λόγους to hold converse with one, Hdt.; so, ἐς ἔριν, ἐς ἔχθεα ἀφ. τινι Id.; διὰ μάχης, δι’ ἔχθρας ἀπ. τινί to come to battle, or into enmity with one, Id.; διὰ λόγων τινί Eur.
ἐς τόξευμα ἀφ. to come within shot, Xen.
not loving the good, NTest.
not loving money, NTest.
unloved, Soph.
unphilosophic, Plat.
without friends, friendless, Trag.
unfriendly, hateful, Id.—adv. ἀφίλως in unfriendly manner, Aesch.
without ears of corn, starving, Anth.
want of due ambition, Arist.
without due ambition, Isae., Arist.
contempt for riches, Plut.
an arrival, Hdt., Dem.
departure, NTest.
Dep. to ride off or away, Plut.
to ride off, away, or back, Xen.
awkwardness in riding, Xen.
unsuited for cavalry, χώρα Xen.
of persons, unused to riding, Plat.

Causal in pres. and imperf., in fut. ἀποστήσω, aor1 ἀπέστησα, as also in aor1 mid.:— to put away, remove, c. acc., Aesch., etc.; ἀφ. τινὰ λόγου to hinder from speech, Eur.; ἀφ. τὴν ἐπιβουλήν to frustrate it, Thuc.; ἀφ. τὸν ἄρχοντα to depose him, Xen.; so in aor1 mid., δόρυ πυλῶν ἀπεστήσασθε removed war from your own gates, Eur.
to make to revolt, move to revolt, Hdt., Thuc.
to weigh out, Xen.:—aor1 mid., ἀποστήσασθαι χρεῖος to weigh out or pay the debt in full, Il.; ἀποστήσασθαι τὸν χαλκόν to have the money weighed out to one, Dem.

intr., in Pass., as also in aor2 act. ἀπέστην, imperat. ἀπόστηθι, ἀπόστα, perf. ἀφέστηκα in pres. sense, syncop. pl. ἀφέσταμεν, -στατε, -στᾶσι, inf. ἀφεστάναι, part. ἀφεστώς, -ῶσα, -ός or -ώς: fut. mid. ἀποστήσομαι: aor1 ἀπεστάθην [α]:— to stand away or aloof from, keep far from, c. gen., Hom., attic; μακρὰν τόποις καὶ χρόνοις ἀφ. Diod.; ἀφεστάναι φρενῶν to lose one's wits, Soph.; ἀφ. πραγμάτων to withdraw from business, Dem., etc.
in Prose, to revolt from, τινος or ἀπό τινος, Hdt., attic: absol. to revolt, Hdt.
ἀφ. τινός τινι to give up a thing to another, Dem.; hence, ἀφ. τινι to make way for him, give way to him, Eur.; c. inf. to shrink from doing, Id.
absol. to stand aloof, Il., attic
Lat. aplustre, the curved stern of a ship with its ornaments, Il., Hdt.
unburnt, unconsumed by fire, πέλανοι Eur.
without bark, Epigr. ap. Plut.
of an angry man, spluttering or perh. foaming, Il.
rich, wealthy, Il.; c. gen., ἀφνειὸς βιότοιο rich in substance, Hom.; c. acc., Hes.; c. dat., Theocr.
unforeseen, sudden, Aesch., Thuc.:—adv. -ίως, Id.; also -ιον, Plut.
unawares, of a sudden, Eur., Thuc.; cf. ἐξ-αίφνης.
without fear of, δίκης Soph.: absol. fearless, Anth.
fearlessness, Plat.
without fear:
fearless, intrepid, dauntless, Pind., Soph.:—adv. -βως, Xen.
causing no fear, free from fear, Aesch.
ἄφοβοι θῆρες beasts which no one fears, i. e. cattle, Soph.
fearless of heart, Ar.
a going away, departure, Hdt., Xen.
a going or coming back, return, Id.
uncleansed, unclean, Aesch.
to make like, τί τινί Plat.: to compare, τι Id.:—Pass. to be or become like, τινι Id.
c. acc. rei only, to pourtray, copy, Id., Xen.
a resemblance, copy, Plat.
to strip of arms, τινά τινος Luc.: to disarm, τινά Anth.:—Mid., ἀφοπλίζεσθαι ἔντεα to put off one's armour, Il.
to look away from all others at one, to have in full view, to look at, τι or πρός τι Thuc.; also in Mid., Ar.
to view from a place, ἀπὸ δενδρέου Hdt.
to look away, have the back turned, Xen.
intolerable, insufferable, Hdt., Thuc.
a not bearing:
non-production, dearth, καρπῶν Xen.
barrenness, sterility of land: metaph., ἀφ. φρενῶν Id.
to mark off by boundaries, Dem.: —Mid. to mark off for oneself, appropriate, Eur.
to distinguish, determine, define, Plat.
c. acc. pers.,
to banish, Eur.
to set apart, separate, NTest.: then,
to cast out, excommunicate, Id.
to set apart for some office, to appoint, ordain, Id.
one must put aside, Arist.
to make to start from a place:— Pass. to go forth, start, depart from a place, c. gen., Hom., attic
intr. in same sense as Pass., Eur., Thuc.: of lightning, to break forth, Soph.; c. acc. cogn., ἀφορμᾶν πεῖραν to begin an enterprise. Id.
a starting-point, esp. in war, a base of operations, Thuc.:—also a place of safety, Eur.
generally, a starting-point, the origin, occasion or pretext of a thing, Id.; ἀφορμὴν παρέχειν, διδόναι to give occasion, Dem.
the means with which one begins a thing, resources, Xen., Dem.; ἀφ. ἔργων means for undertaking works, Xen.
the capital of a banker, Id., Dem.
without the lyre, Aesch.
departing from a place, c. gen., Soph.
not bearing, barren, Hdt., Xen.
causing barrenness, blighting, Aesch.
unspotted, unstained, Anth.
to purify from guilt or pollution, τὴν πόλιν Plat.
Mid. to purify oneself from sins of negligence, Id.; ἀφοσιοῦσθαι τῆι θεῶι to make expiatory offerings to the goddess, Hdt.
c. acc. rei, to acquit oneself of an obligation, ἀποσιοῦσθαι τὴν ἐξόρκωσιν to quit oneself of one's oath, Id.; ἀπ. λόγιον quitting oneself of the orders of an oracle, Id.
expiation: ἀφοσιώσεως ἕνεκα for form's sake, Plut.
to be senseless, act thoughtlessly, Hom.
insensate, reckless, Od.; of the dead, senseless, lifeless, Id. adv. ἀφραδέως, senselessly, recklessly, Il.
folly, thoughtlessness, mostly in epic dat. pl., ἀφραδίηισι Hom.; δι’ ἀφραδίας Od.
= ἀφραδής, without sense, Hhymn.
to be silly, senseless, Hom.
unfenced, unfortified, unguarded, Thuc.; c. gen., ἄφρ. φίλων by friends, Soph.; c. dat., ἄφρ. ὅρκοις Eur.
not to be kept in, irrepressible, Aesch.
unguarded, off one's guard, Thuc.
unutterable, inexpressible, Hhymn., Aesch., Soph.
（φράζομαι) not perceived or thought of, Aesch.; τὸ ἀφραστότατον χωρίον the place least likely to be thought of, Hdt.:—adv. -τως, beyond thought, Soph.
to befoam, cover with foam, ἵπποι ἄφρεον στήθεα Il.
gathering froth, skimming, τινός Anth.
the foamer, of a dolphin, Anth.
without brotherhood (φράτρα), i. e. bound by no social tie, Il.
to foam, Soph.
foamy, Anth.
foam-born, of Aphrodite, Hes.: fem. Ἀφρο-γένεια, Mosch.
to indulge lust, Plat., Xen.
sacred to Aphrodite, name of an island, Hdt.
belonging to Aphrodite, Plat.
Ἀφροδίσια, τά, sexual pleasures, Xen.
a festival of Aphrodite, Id.
Ἀφροδίσιον, ου, τό, the temple of Aphrodite, Id.
Aphrodite, Lat. Venus, goddess of love, said to be born from the sea-foam, Hhymn., Hes.
as appellat. love, pleasure, Od.: —Ἀφρ. κακῶν enjoyment, Eur.
attractive beauty, grace, Lat. venustas, Aesch., Luc;. cf. Lat. venus.
to be silly, act foolishly, only in part., Il., Anth.
to have no care of, pay no heed to a thing, c. gen., Xen.
thoughtless, heedless, taking no care, Lat. securus, Xen., Theocr.:—adv. -τως, inconsiderately, Soph.; ἀφρ. ἔχειν to be heedless, Xen.; also to be senseless, demented, Soph.
pass. unthought of, unexpected, Aesch.
foam, of the sea, Il.: of an angry lion, foam, froth, Id.; ἀπ’ ἀνθρώπων ἀφρόν frothy blood, Aesch.
folly, thoughtlessness, senselessness, in sg. and pl., Hom., Soph., Thuc.
unguarded, unwatched, Plat.
foam-producing, Anth.
foamy, Eur.
without sense, of statues, Xen.:— crazed, frantic, or silly, foolish, Hom., attic: τὸ ἄφρον = ἀφροσύνη, Thuc. adv. ἀφρόνως, senselessly, Soph.
to give loose to passion, Plut.
to wash clean from dirt:—Mid., aor1 -υδρηνάμην, to wash oneself clean, bathe, Eur.
a sort of anchovy or sardine, Ar.
without natural talent, witless, dull, Plat.; ἀφυὴς πρός τι naturally unsuited to a thing, Id., Xen.
simple, unschooled, Soph.
not to be shunned, from which none escape, Aesch., Soph.; of an arrow, unerring, Id., Eur.; of a question, admitting no escape, inevitable, Plat.
act. unable to escape, Ar.
to be off one's guard, Xen.: c. gen. to be careless about, Id.
unguarded, unwatched, Hdt., Thuc.
（φυλάσσομαι) unguarded, off one's guard, Id.; ἀφύλακτον εὕδειν to sleep securely, Aesch.; ἀφ. τινα λαμβάνειν to catch one off his guard, Xen.; τὸ ἀφ. want of precaution, Thuc.:—adv. -τως, Xen.
not to be guarded against, inevitable, Arist.
to strain off, Anth.
leafless, of dry wood, Il.; ἄφ. στόμα words not seconded by the suppliant's olivebranch, Eur.
act. stripping off the leaves, blighting, Aesch.
to wake one from sleep, Eur., Plut.
to wake from sleep, Anth.
to fall asleep, NTest.
the mud and filth which a stream carries with it, rubbish, Il.

to draw liquids, esp. from a larger vessel with a smaller, οἶνον ἐν ἀμφιφορεῦσιν ἠφύσαμεν Od.:—Pass., πίθων ἠφύσσετο οἶνος was drawn from the wine-jars, Id.:—metaph., πλοῦτον ἀφύξειν to draw full draughts of wealth, i. e. heap it up, τινί for another, Il.
Mid. to draw for oneself, οἶνον Id.; ῥοάς Eur.:—metaph., φύλλα ἠφυσάμην I heaped me up a bed of leaves, Od.
voiceless, speechless, Soph.
voiceless, speechless, dumb, silent, Theogn., Hdt., Dem.: c. gen., ἄφωνος ἀρᾶς unable to utter a curse, Soph.:—adv. -νως, without speaking, Id.; neut. pl. as adv., Aesch.
ἄφωνα (sc. γράμματα), consonants, opp. to φωνοῦντα or φωνήεντα (vowels), Eur., Plat.
Achaia in Peloponnese, Thuc.
name of Demeter in Attica, Hdt.
of or for the Achaians, Achaian, Aesch., Eur.
the Achaian land, with or without γαῖα, Il.
(sub. γυνή) an Achaian woman, Id.
with single points to his horns, a young deer, Babr.
Achaian, Lat. Achivus, Hom.:— Ἀχαιοί, οἱ, the Achaians or Greeks generally, Id.
unbridled, Eur., Ar., etc.
without bridle, Xen.
penniless, Anth.
not forged of metal, Aesch.
to be penniless, Anth.
without brass, ἄχαλκος ἀσπίδων, i. e. ἄνευ ἀσπίδων χαλκείων, Soph.
not brasened; without money, Anth.
a Persian measure, = 45 μέδιμνοι, Ar.
not opening the mouth, Luc.
（α euphon. ) yawning, wide, Plut., Anth.
not palisaded, Plut.
without grace or charms, graceless, Theogn.
unpleasant, disagreeable, οὐδὲν ἄχαρι παθέειν Hdt.; as euphem. for grievous, ἄχ. συμφορή Id.
ungracious, thankless, Id.; χάρις ἄχαρις a graceless grace, thankless favour, Aesch., Eur.
to be thankless, shew ingratitude, Xen.
= οὐ χαρίζομαι, to discourage, τινί Plat.;
thanklessness, ingratitude, Xen., Dem.
ungraciousness, Plat.
ungracious, unpleasant, unpleasing, Od.; irreg. comp., δόρπου ἀχαρίστερον (for -ιστότερον) Id.: without grace or charms, Xen.
of persons, ungracious, unfavourable, Theogn.
ungrateful, thankless, Hdt., attic; τινι Eur.; πρός τινα Xen.
adv. -τως, with an ill-will, Id.; ἀχαρίστως ἔχει μοι thanks are wanting to me, Id.
= ἀχάριστος or ἄχαρις, Hdt.
ungrateful, thankless, Id.; χάρις ἀχ., like χάρις ἄχαρις, Eur.
Acharnae, a demos of Attica, Thuc.
an inhabitant of Acharnae, pl. Ἀχαρνεῖς, poet. Ἀχαρνηΐδαι Ar.
belonging to or of Acharnae, Ar.
not vexed by storms, Alcae.
not wrought by hands, NTest.
without hands: τὰ ἄχειρα of the hinder parts of the body, Xen.
untamed, unconquered, Thuc.
not planted by man's hand, Soph.
sc. νῆσοι, islands at the mouth of the Achelous, Aesch.
Achelous, name of several rivers; the best known ran through Aetolia and Acarnania, Il., Hes.
any stream, or, generally, water, Eur.
a wild prickly shrub, a wild pear, Od., Soph.; masc. in Theocr.
of Acheron, Eur.
the white poplar, said to have been brought by Hercules from the banks of Acheron, Il.
Acheron, river of woe (cf. Κωκυτός), one of the rivers of the world below, Od.
in pres. part. grieving, sorrowing, mourning, Hom.
from the same Root ΑΧ, came also
aor2 in Causal sense, to grieve, vex, annoy, distress, Hom.: so also, redupl. fut. ἀκαχήσω, epic aor1 ἀκάχησα, Id.; and a pres. ἀκαχίζω
pass. to be grieved, distressed, Hom.; c. gen. causae, to grieve for a person, Id.; rarely c. dat. to grieve at a person's death, Od.; the cause of grief also in partic., μή τι θανὼν ἀκαχίζεο Id.
later c. acc. to lament, Soph.

entry.etym: old form for ἰαχέω, Hhymn., Eur.

entry.sense: need, want, χρημάτων Aesch.; ὀμμάτων ἀχηνίαις in the eyes blank gaze, Id.
poor, needy, Theocr.
burdensome, oppressive, wearisome, Lat. molestus, of persons, Eur., Xen.:—adv. -νῶς, unwillingly, Id.
a weight, burden, Aesch.
metaph. grievance, distress, vexation, annoyance, Thuc., Plat.; δι’ ἀχθηδόνα for the sake of teasing, Thuc. (From ἄχθος, as ἀλγηδών from ἄλγος.）
to load, Babr.
to be loaded, νηῦς ἤχθετο Od.

of mental oppression, to be weighed down, vexed, annoyed, grieved, Hom.; τινι at a thing, or with a person, Hdt., etc.; so, ἐπί τινι Xen.; περί τινος Hdt.; ὑπέρ τινος Plat.:—also c. acc., ἄχθομαι ἕλκος Il.;—also c. part., either of subject, as ἄχθομαι ἰδών Soph.; or of object, ἤχθετο δαμναμένους at their being conquered, Il.; but the object is also in gen., οὐδὲν ἤχθετο αὐτῶν πολεμούντων he had no objection to going to war, Xen.
a weight, burden, load, Hom.; ἄχθος ἀρούρης a dead weight on earth, cumberers of the ground, Id.
a load of grief, grief, trouble, distress, sorrow, Trag.
to bear burdens, Plut.
to bear as a burden, τι Anth.
bearing burdens, Hdt.
of Achilles, Hdt., Eur.
Ἀχιλλείη κριθή Achilles-barley, a fine kind: hence Ἀχίλλειαι (μᾶζαι) cakes of fine barley, Ar.

entry.etym: From ἄχος, the grief of the hero being the subject of the Il., cf. Ὀδυσσεύς
entry.sense: Achilles, son of Peleus and Thetis, prince of the Myrmidons.
without tunic, i. e. wearing the ἱμάτιον only, of Socrates, Xen.
want of a cloak or mantle, Eur.
without cloak or mantle, Simon.
without herbage, Eur.
gloomy, Simon. ap. Hdt.
a mist, Lat. caligo, Od.; a mist over the eyes of one dying, Il.; or of a person deprived of the power of knowing others, Id.—metaph. gloom, trouble, Aesch.
to be or grow dark, Od.
anything that comes off the surface:
foam, froth, of the sea, Od.; of wine, Eur.; ἄχνη οὐρανία the dew of heaven, Soph.; δακρύων ἄχνη dewy tears, Id.
of solids, the chaff that flies off in winnowing, in pl., Il.; the down on fruits, Anth.
ἄχνην in acc. as adv., a morsel, the least bit, Ar.
without down, Anth.
allaying bile or anger, Od.
not attended with the dance, joyless, melancholy, Soph., Eur.
without the dance, of death, Soph.: melancholy, Eur.
pain, distress, Hom., Pind., attic Poets.
undefiled, immaculate, Plat.
useless, unprofitable, good for nothing, Hes., Soph., etc.
esp. unserviceable, unfit for war, Hdt.; τὸ ἄχρ. τοῦ στρατοῦ the unserviceable part of an army, Id., Thuc., etc.

in Hom. neut. ἀχρεῖον as adv., ἀχρεῖον ἰδών giving a helpless look, looking foolish, of Thersites after being beaten, Il.; ἀχρεῖον ἐγέλασσε laughing without cause or meaning, laughed with a forced laugh, Od.; so, ἀχρεῖον κλάζειν to bark without cause, Theocr.
want of money, Thuc.
without money or means, Hdt., Aesch.
want of money, Od., Theogn.
without money, poor, needy, Solon, Eur.
uselessness, Plat.
the non-usance of a thing, Id.
useless, unprofitable, unserviceable, Hdt., Thuc.: of an oracle, without effect, Eur.:— ἄχρ. ἔς or πρός τι unfit for a thing, Hdt.; ἄχρ. τινι useless to a person, Id., Eur.
like ἀχρεῖος, of useless, do-nothing persons, Oratt.
act. making no use of, c. dat., Eur.
（χρηστός) unkind, cruel, Hdt.
adv. to the uttermost, utterly, Il.
after Hom., before Preps., ἄχρι εἰς . . ἄχρι πρὸς . . , Lat. usque ad . . , Xen., Luc.
prep. with gen. even to, as far as:
of Time, until, ἄχρι μάλα κνέφαος until deep in the night, Od.; ἄχρι τῆς ἡμέρας Dem.
of Space, as far as, even to, ἄχρι τῆς ἐσόδου Hdt.
of Degree, ἄχρι τούτου up to this point, Dem.; ἄχρι τοῦ μὴ πεινᾶν Xen.
as Conj., ἄχρι οὗ or ἄχρι alone:
of Time, Lat donec, until, so long as, ἄχρι οὗ ὅδε ὁ λόγος ἐγράφετο Id.; ἄχρι ἄν with Subj., ἄχρι ἂν σχολάσηι till he should be at leisure, Id.
of Space, so far as, Id., Luc.
colourless, Plat.
colourless, Plat.
untouched, χερῶν ἐμῶν by my hands, Eur.
a heap of chaff, Il., Anth.
mostly in pl. ἄχυρα, husks, chaff, bran, Hdt.; metaph., ἄχυρα τῶν ἀστῶν Ar.
a chaff-heap, Ar.; but ἀχυρμός is prob. the true form.
threshing out the husks, Anth.
not parted, not divided, Plat.
（χῶρος) with no place assigned one, Xen.
untouched, not to be touched, sacred, Thuc.
act. not touching a thing, c. gen., Soph.
unblamed, blameless, Soph.
truthfulness, Plat.
not to lie, to speak truth, πρός τινα Soph., Plat.
without lie and deceit, truthful, sincere, trusty, Hes., Hdt., etc.:—adv. -δέως, attic -δῶς, really and truly, Id.
not having voted, Ar.
Pass. to be encircled, Anth.
satisfied with touching, i. e. fastidious, dainty, Plat.:— τὸ ἁψ. fastidiousness, Plut., Luc.
to skirmish with an enemy, lead on to fight, Plut.
a skirmishing, Aeschin.
skirmishing.
wormwood, Xen.
wormwood.
a juncture, loop, mesh, such as form a net, Il.
the felloe or felly of a wheel, the wheel itself, Hes., Hdt., Eur.
any circle or disk, of the sun, Id.
an arch or vault, Plat., Luc.
backflowing, refluent, of Ocean, regarded as a stream encircling the earth and flowing back into itself, Hom.
going back, backwards, Il., Soph.:—neut. ἄψορρον as adv., backward, back again, Il., Aesch., Soph.
a joint, Od.
noiseless; c. gen., ἀψ. κωκυμάτων without sound of wailings, Soph.
of Place, backwards, back, back again, Hom.
of actions, again, in return, Id.; so, ἂψ αὖτις, ἂψ πάλιν, yet again, Il.
not capable of being cooled, Plat.
want of life: want of spirit, faint-heartedness, Aesch., Eur.
lifeless, inanimate, Simon., Eur., Plat.
ἄψ. βορά non-animal food, Eur.
spiritless, faint-hearted, Aesch.
= ἄημι, to blow.
= ἰαύω, to sleep, used only in aor1 ἄεσα, epic ἄεσσα Od.; also 1st pl. contr. ἄσαμεν, Id.
to hurt, contr. from ἀάω.
trans. to satiate, αἵματος ἆσαι Ἀρῆα to give him his fill of blood, Il.
intr. to take one's fill of a thing, c. gen., χροὸς ἄμεναι, χροὸς ἆσαι Ib; so in Mid., ἄσεσθε κλαυθμοῖο, ποτῆτος ἄσασθαι Id.
a wrong time: acc. as adv., ἀωρίαν ἥκειν to have come too late, Ar.; ἀωρίαι at an unseasonable time, so late, Luc.
Adv. of ἄωρος, at an untimely hour, too early, Luc., Anth.; ἀωρὶ τῆς νυκτός at dead of night, Antipho, Theocr.
at midnight, Aesch.
untimely, unseasonable, Lat. intempestivus, Aesch., Eur.:—c. gen., γήρως ἀωρότερα things unbecoming old age, Plut.
unripe, ἄωρος πρὸς γάμον Id.
without youthful freshness, ugly, Xen., Plat.
pendulous, waving about, of the πλεκτάναι or polypus-like legs of Scylla, Od.
to sleep well, Hom.
fine wool, flock, οἰὸς ἄωτον, or without οἰός, the sheep's finest wool, Hom.; λίνοιο λεπτὸν ἄωτον the delicate flock of flax, i. e. the finest linen, Il.
metaph. the finest, best of its kind, the flower of a thing, ἄωτος ζωᾶς the flower of life, Pind.; Χαρίτων ἄωτος their choisest gift, Id.
Lat. papae! exclamation of surprise, bless me! Eur., Ar.

entry.etym: Lacon. for γέφυρα, Arist. ap. Plut.

entry.sense: a speech, Aesch.
step by step, Lat. pedetentim, Il.; in marching step, Hdt.; β. ταχύ at quick step, Xen.
gradually, more and more, Ar.
walking, marching, opp. to riding, driving, sailing, Aesch.
to go slowly, to walk, Lat. ambulare, Hhymn., Xen.: to go, march, of horsemen, Id.: to go by land, Dem.:—c. acc. cogn., βάδον, ὁδὸν β. Ar., Xen.
generally, ἐπ’ οἰκίας βαδ. to enter houses, Dem.: to proceed (in argument), Id.:—of things, αἱ τιμαὶ ἐπ’ ἔλαττον ἐβάδιζον prices were getting lower, Id.
a walking, going, Ar.; of hares, Xen.
walk, gait, Xen., Dem.
one must walk or go, Soph.:—so pl. βαδιστέα, Ar.
a goer, ταχὺς βαδ. a quick runner, Eur.
good at walking, Ar.
a walk, βάδον βαδίζειν Ar.

to speak, say, Hom.; βάζειν τί τινα to say somewhat to a man, Il.; also, τί τινί Aesch.; c. dat. modi, χαλεποῖς βάζειν ἐπέεσσι to address with sharp words, Hes.:—Pass., ἔπος βέβακται a word has been spoken, Od.
a step, Anth.
a step: metaph. a step, degree, NTest.

depth or height, acc. as measured up or down, Lat. altitudo, Ταρτάρου βάθη Aesch.; αἰθέρος βάθος Eur.: in military sense, the depth of a line of battle, Thuc., Xen.:— β. τριχῶν depth, i. e. thickness or length, of hair, Hdt.:—in NTest., τὸ βάθος the deep water.
metaph., κακῶν βάθος Aesch.; πλούτου βάθος Soph.
that on which anything stands:
a base, pedestal, Hdt., Aesch.
a stage or scaffold, Hdt.
generally solid ground, Σαλαμῖνος β. Soph.; ὦ πατρῶιον ἑστίας βάθρον i. e. house of my father, Id.:—in pl. foundations, Eur.; ἐν βάθροις εἶναι to stand firm, Id.
a step, Soph.; the round of a ladder, Eur.
a bench, seat, Soph., Dem.
metaph., κινδύνου βάθρα the verge of danger, Eur.
with deep dells, Anth.
deep-counselling, Aesch.
with deep soil, productive, Hdt.
in great old age, decrepit, Anth.
deep-eddying, Il., Hes.
deep-girded, i. e. girded not close under the breast, but over the hips, so that the gown fell over the girdle in folds (cf. βαθύκολπος), Hom.
of sheep, with thick wool, Hhymn.
strongly curved, Anth.
deep yawning, of the sea, Theogn.
illustrious, Anth.
with dress falling in deep folds (cf. βαθύζωνος), of Trojan women, Il.
with deep, full breasts, deep-bosomed, Aesch.; of the earth, Pind.: cf. βαθύστερνος.
with high cliffs, ἅλς Pind.; β. ἀκταί deep and rugged headlands, Id.
with great possessions, plenteous, Anth.
with deep, rich meadows, Il.
with deep crop, very fruitful, Il.
of deep mind, Anth.
to deepen, hollow out, of a torrent, Il.: to dig deep, NTest.
as military term, to deepen, τὴν φάλαγγα Xen.
with deep wood, Eur.
thick-soled, Anth.
exceeding rich, Aesch.
plunged deep in war, Pind.
with thick wool, Anth.
deep-rooted, Soph.
deep-flowing, brimming, Il., Soph.
deep-dug, Soph.
deep-shaded, Hhymn., Theocr.

deep or high, acc. to one's position, like Lat. altus, Hom., etc.; βαθέης αὐλῆς from high-fenced court, Il.; ἠιόνος προπάροιθε βαθείης the deep, i. e. wide, shore, Id.; in Prose, of a line of battle, Xen.
deep or thick in substance, of a mist, Hom.; of ploughed land, opp. to stony ground, Il., Eur.:— deep, thick, of woods, corn, clouds, Il., Hdt., etc.; of hair, Xen.
violent, of a storm, Il.
generally, large, copious, abundant, κλέος, κλῆρος Pind.; βαθεῖα τέρψις Soph.; βαθὺς ἀνήρ a rich man, Xen.; β. ὕπνος deep sleep, Theocr.
of the mind, deep, Il., Aesch.; βαθύτερα ἤθεα Hdt.
of Time, far-advanced, late, βαθὺς ὄρθρος (v. ὄρθρος); βαθὺ τῆς ἡλικίας Ar.; β. γῆρας Anth.
adv. βαθέως, Theocr.
deep-sown, fruitful, Eur.
deep-chested, λέων Pind., cf. βαθύκολπος.
with deep, full robe, Anth.
deep-strewn, well-covered, Babr.
deep-grown with rushes, Il.
= βάθος, depth, Luc.
thick-leafed, Mosch.
with deep, thick hair, Hes.
in most forms,

intr. to walk, step, properly of motion on foot, ποσσὶ or ποσὶ βαίνειν Hom., etc.; c. inf. in Hom., βῆ ἰέναι, βῆ ἰέμεν set out to go, went his way, Il.; βῆ θέειν started to run, Id.; βῆ δ’ ἐλάαν, Id., etc.:—c. acc. loci, Soph.; and with all Preps. implying motion, as, ἐπὶ νηὸς ἔβαινεν was going on board ship, Od.; ἐφ’ ἵππων βάντες having mounted the chariot, Id.; βαίνειν δι’ αἵματος to wade through blood, Eur., etc.

in perf. to stand or be in a place, χῶρος ἐν ὧι βεβήκαμεν Soph.; often almost= εἰμί (sum), εὖ βεβηκώς on a good footing, well established, prosperous, Hdt., etc.; so, οἱ ἐν τέλει βεβῶτες they who are in office, Id., Soph.; cf. ξυρόν.
to go, go away, depart, Il., Soph.; βέβηκα euphem. for τέθνηκα, Aesch., Soph.:—of things, ἐννέα ἐνιαυτοὶ βεβάασι nine years have come and gone, Il.
to come, τίπτε βέβηκας; Id.: to arrive, Soph.
to go on, advance, ἐς τόδε τόλμης, ἐς τοσοῦτον ἐλπίδων Id.
c. acc. to mount, Hom. only in aor1 mid., βήσασθαι δίφρον:— Pass., ἵπποι βαινόμεναι brood mares, Hdt.
χρέος ἔβα με debts came on me, Ar.
in Poets, with acc. of the instrument of motion, which is simply pleonastic, βαίνειν πόδα to advance the foot, step on, Eur., etc.
Causal, in fut. βήσω, aor1 ἔβησα:— to make to go, βῆσεν ἀφ’ ἵππον, ἐξ ἵππων βῆσε brought them down from the chariot, Il. The pres. in this sense is βιβάζω.

little, small, scanty, and of number, few, Pind., Aesch., Soph.; ἐχώρει βαιός he was going with scanty escort, i. e. alone, Id.: of condition, low, mean, humble, Id.: of time, short, Solon, Soph.:— neut. βαιόν, as adv. a little, Id.; so pl. βαιά, Ar. Cf. ἠβαιός.
a palm-branch, NTest.
a shepherd's or peasant's coat of skins, Hdt., Theocr.
an eunuch in the service of Cybele, Anth., Luc.
to prophesy like Bacis, Ar.
an old Boeotian prophet, Hdt.
Lat. baculum, a stick, Aesop.
a staff, cane, Ar., Thuc.: borne as a badge of office by the δικασταί, Dem.
a staff, βακτρεύματα ποδός support lent to one's foot, Eur.
to lean on a staff.
Lat. baculus, a staff, stick, cudgel, Aesch., Eur.
going about begging with a staff, of a Cynic, Anth.
= βάκλον: pl. = Lat. fasces, Plut.
to be in Bacchic frenzy, to rave, Aesch.
βακχέβακχον ἆισαι, to sing the song Βάκχε Βάκχε! Ar.
the feast of Bacchus, Bacchic frenzy, revelry, Aesch., Eur.: generally, frenzy, Plat.:—in pl. Bacchic orgies, Eur.
the temple of Bacchus, Ar.
Bacchic revelry, Eur.:—in pl. Bacchic orgies, Ar.; also Βάκχια, Eur.
Bacchic, of or belonging to Bacchus and his rites, Eur., Xen.; frenzied, frenzy-stricken, Hdt., Soph.; τὸν B. ἄνακτα, of Aeschylus, Ar.
as Subst., Βάκχιος, ὁ, = Βάκχος, Soph., Eur.
= οἶνος, Id.
Βάκχειος (sc. πούς), a foot of three syllables, ˘ ˘ ¯ opp. to antibacchius.
in pl. Bacchic revelries, Eur., Plut.
Bacchanalian, frenzied, Eur.
Bacchic revelry, Eur.
a Bacchanal: as adj. Bacchanalian, Anth.
disposed to Bacchic revels, Arist.
to keep the feast of Bacchus, celebrate his mysteries, Hdt.
to speak or act like one frantic, Lat. bacchari, Soph., Eur.
Causal, to inspire with frenzy, Id.:—Pass., Id.
a Bacchante, Aesch., Soph., etc.:—generally, Βάκχη Ἅιδου frantic handmaid of Hades, Eur.; β. νεκύων Id.

entry.etym: The Root seems to be ϜΑΧ, so that Βάκχος represents ϝάκχος; and Ἴακχος is for ϝίϝακχος; prob. from ἰάχω, = ϝιϝάχω, to shout
entry.sense: Bacchus, a later name of Dionysus, Soph., etc.: called Διόνυσος Βάκχειος and ὁ Βάκχειος in Hdt.
as appellat. wine, Eur., etc.
a Bacchanal, any one inspired, frantic, Id., Plat.
a key or hook for pulling out the doorpin, Hdt., Xen.
Lat. balineum, balneum, a bath or bathing-room, Ar.; in pl., Id.
a bath-man, Lat. balneator .
to wait upon a person at the bath, β. ἑαυτῶι to be one's own bath-man, Ar.
acorn-eating, Orac. ap. Hdt.
bearing dates, Hdt.
βαλανίζω δρῦν, to shake acorns from the oak: as a proverb. answer to beggars, ἄλλην δρῦν βαλάνιζε Anth.
a bathing-woman, Anth.
the socket in a door-post to receive the βάλανος (II).
an acorn, Lat. glans, the fruit of the φηγός, given to swine, Od.:— any similar fruit, the date, Hdt., Xen.

from similarity of shape, an iron peg, a bolt-pin, Lat. pessulus, passed through the wooden bar (μοχλός) into the door-post, so that the bar could not be removed till the pin was taken out with a hook (βαλανάγρα), Ar., Thuc.
to fasten with a bolt-pin (βάλανος II), βεβαλάνωκε τὴν θύραν Ar.:—Pass., βεβαλανωμένος, η, ον, shut close, secured, Id.

properly, the rope drawn across the race-course: mostly in pl., Lat. carceres, the posts marking the line whence the racers started, and to which they returned, Ar.:—then, any starting point, Eur., Ar.; metaph., πρὸς βαλβῖδα βίου Eur.
also any point to be gained, as the battlements (by one scaling a wall), Soph.
parox. Βαλίος, one of the horses of Achilles, dapple, Il.
spotted, dappled, Eur.
a bag, pouch, purse, Simon., Ar.
to cut purses, Plat., Xen.
a cut-purse, Ar., Plat.
βαλληνάδε βλέπειν, a pun between βάλλω and the Attic deme Παλλήνη, Ar.
a king, Aesch.
Act. to throw:

with acc. of person or thing aimed at, to throw so as to hit, to hit one with a missile, opp. to striking (τύπτω, οὐτάω), βλήμενος ἠὲ τυπείς Il.; c. dupl. acc. pers. et partis, μιν βάλε μηρὸν ὀϊστῶι Id.: c. acc. cogn. added, ἕλκος, τό μιν βάλε the wound which he gave him, Id.:—also, βάλε κατ’ ἀσπίδα smote upon it, Id.
of things, ἡνίοχον ῥαθάμιγγες ἔβαλλον Id.; of the Sun, ἀκτῖσιν ἔβαλλεν [χθόνα] Od.: to strike the senses, of sound, κτύπος οὔατα βάλλει Il.
metaph., β. τινὰ κακοῖς to smite with reproaches, Soph., etc.; φθόνος βάλλει τινά Aesch.

with acc. of the weapon thrown, to throw, cast, hurl, βαλὼν βέλος Il; ἐν νηυσὶν πῦρ βάλλειν Id.:—with dat. of the weapon, to throw or shoot with a thing, χερμαδίοισι Id.; βέλεσι β. τινα Hom.; β. ἐπί τινα to throw at one, Thuc.; ἐπὶ σκοπόν or σκοποῦ Xen.

generally of anything thrown, εἰς ἅλα λύματ’ ἔβαλλον Il., etc.:—of persons, β. τινὰ ἐν κονίηισιν, ἐν δαπέδωι Hom., etc.; metaph., ἐς κακὸν β. τινά Od.; β. τινὰ ἐς φόβον Eur.; also, ἐν αἰτίαι or αἰτία β. τινά Soph.
to let fall, ἑτέρωσε κάρη βάλεν Il.; β. ἀπὸ δάκρυ παρειῶν Od.
of the eyes, ἑτέρωσε βάλ’ ὄμματα cast them the other way, Id., etc.

in a loose sense, to throw, to put, place, ἐν στήθεσσι μένος βάλε Il.; ὅπως φιλότητα μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισι βάλωμεν may put frienship between them, Id.; β. τί τινι ἐν θυμῶι Od.; ἐς θυμὸν β. to lay to heart, Soph.
to put round, ἀμφ’ ὀχέεσσι βάλε κύκλα Il.; and of clothes or arms, ἀμφὶ δ’ Ἀθήνη ὤμοις βάλ’ αἰγίδα Id.
βαλών is sometimes added, like λαβών or ἔχων, at the end of a sentence, almost as an expletive, with, Soph.
intr., ποταμὸς εἰς ἅλα βάλλων falling, Il.; ἐν πέδωι βαλῶ (sc. ἐμαυτήν) Aesch.
so in familiar language, βάλλ’ ἐς κόρακας away with you! be hanged! Lat. pasce corvos! abi in malam rem! Ar.
Mid. to put for oneself, ἐνὶ θυμῶι βάλλευ lay it to heart, Od.; ἐς θυμὸν βάλλεσθαί τι Hdt.; ἐφ’ ἑωυτοῦ βαλόμενος on one's own judgment, of oneself, Id.
τόξα or ξίφος ἀμφ’ ὤμοις βάλλεσθαι to throw about one's shoulder, Il.
ἐς γαστέρα βάλλεσθαι, of a woman, to conceive, Hdt.
to lay the foundations of, begin to form, οἰκοδομίαν, στρατόπεδον, Plat., etc.; β. ἄγκυραν to cast anchor, Hdt.
rarely, χρόα βάλλεσθαι λουτροῖς to dash one's flesh with water, bathe, Hhymn.
to chatter with the teeth, Il.: to stammer, Bion.
that in which a thing is dipped, dye, Plat., v. βάπτω I. 3.
handicraft, the practice of a mere mechanical art, Hdt.
of or for mechanics: τέχνη β. a mere mechanical art, Lat. ars sellularia, Xen.
mechanical, and as Subst. a mechanic, Arist.
τέχνη βάναυσος a mere mechanical art, a base, ignoble art, Soph., Plat.
handicraft, Plut.
a saying, esp. an oracular saying, like φήμη, Aesch., Soph.
a report, rumour, Theogn., Soph., Eur.; ἁλώσιμος β. tidings of the capture, Aesch.
to dip in or under water; metaph., βεβαπτισμένοι soaked in wine, Plat.; ὀφλήμασι βεβ. over head and ears in debt, Plut.
to baptize, τινά NTest.:—Pass., βαπτίζεσθαι εἰς μετάνοιαν, εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν Id.:—Mid. to get oneself baptized, Id.
baptism, NTest.
a dipping in water, ablution, NTest.
one that dips: a baptizer, ὁ B. the baptist, NTest.
dipped, dyed, bright-coloured, Ar.
for dyeing, χρώματα Plat.
of water, drawn by dipping vessels (cf. βάπτω I. 3), Eur.
trans. to dip in water, Lat. immergere, Od., Plat.:—of slaughter, ἐν σφαγαῖσι βάψασα ξίφος Aesch.; ἔβαψας ἔγχος Soph.; φάσγανον εἴσω σαρκὸς ἔβαψεν Eur.
to dip in poison, ἰούς, χιτῶνα Soph.
to dip in dye, to dye, Hdt., Aesch.:—Comic, βάπτειν τινὰ βάμμα Σαρδιανικόν to dye one in the [red] dye of Sardis, i. e. give him a bloody coxcomb, Ar.
to draw water by dipping a vessel, Theocr.; βάψασα ἁλός (sc. τὸ τεῦχος) having dipped it so as to draw water from the sea, Eur.
intr., ναῦς ἔβαψεν the ship dipped, sank, Id.
king! Aesch.
a gulf, pit:— at Athens a cleft behind the Acropolis, into which criminals were thrown, Hdt., Ar.
metaph. ruin, perdition, Dem.
to behave like a barbarian, speak like one, Hdt.: to speak broken Greek, speak gibberish, Plat.
to hold with the barbarians, i. e. the Persians, Xen.
barbaric, foreign, like a foreigner, opp. to Ἑλληνικός, Simon.; τὸ βαρβαρικόν, = οἱ βάρβαροι, Thuc.; esp. of the Persians, Xen.:—adv., βαρβαρικῶς καὶ Ἑλληνικῶς i. e. both in Persian and Greek, Id.
barbarism, Arist.
Pass. to become barbarous, Eur.; βεβαρβαρωμένος of barbarous or outlandish sound, Soph.

barbarous, i. e. not Greek, foreign, known to Hom., as appears from the word βαρβαρόφωνος in Il.:—as Subst. βάρβαροι, οἱ, originally all that were not Greeks, specially the Medes and Persians, Hdt., attic: so the Hebrews called the rest of mankind Gentiles. From the Augustan age however the name was given by the Romans to all tribes which had no Greek or Roman accomplishments.
after the Persian war the word took the sense of outlandish, ἀμαθὴς καὶ βάρβαρος Ar.; βαρβαρώτατος Id., Thuc.
speaking a foreign tongue, Κᾶρες Il.
a musical instrument of many strings (πολύχορδος Theocr.), like the lyre, and often used for the lyre itself, Anacr., Eur., etc.

entry.etym: by epic metath. for βράδιστος, Sup.of βραδύς, Il.

entry.sense: to weigh down, depress, Luc.
intr. in epic perf. part. βεβαρηώς, weighed down, heavy, οἴνωι βεβαρηότες Od.: later in part. pass. βεβαρημένος, Theocr., Anth., etc.
a flat-bottomed boat, used in Egypt, Hdt., Aesch.
weight, Hdt., etc.
a weight, burden, load, Aesch., etc.
metaph. a heavy weight, πημονῆς, συμφορᾶς β. Soph.; then alone for grief, misery, Aesch.; βάρος ἔχειν Arist.
abundance, πλούτου, ὄλβου Eur.
very grievous, Soph.
heavy with woe, Soph.
loud-thundering, Soph.
loud-roaring, loud-sounding, Eur.
gnawing, corroding, Soph.
heavy-kneed, lazy, Call.
weighing down the limbs, wearisome, Anth.
to be grievously unlucky, Ar.
pressed by a heavy fate, luckless, Eur.
weeping grievously, Anth.
taking heavy vengeance, Aesch.
giver of ill gifts, Aesch.
loud-sounding, Mosch.
exceeding jealous, Anth.
deep-voiced, Ar.
deep or loud-sounding, Mosch.
to be weighed down: to be heavy at heart: in Mid., Plut.
sullenness, Plut.
heavy in spirit: indignant, sullen, Eur.
to be weighed down, Il., Hes.
to be heavy, Anth.
heavy in wrath, Aesch.
heavy-sounding, loud-thundering, Hhymn., Hes.
heavy in wrath, exceeding wrathful, Aesch.
largely paid, Anth.
very toilsome, painful, Anth.

to weigh down, oppress by weight, depress, Hom.:—Pass., γυῖα βαρύνεται he is heavy, i. e. weary, in limb, Il.; χεῖρα βαρυνθείς disabled in hand, Id.; βαρύνεταί τινι τὸ σκέλος Ar.; ὄμμα β., of one dying, Eur.
metaph. to oppress, weary, τοὺς δικαστάς Xen.:—Pass. to be oppressed, distressed, Lat. gravari, Aesch., Soph.
exceeding angry, Anth.
heavy-handed, Pind.
causing grievous woe, Anth.
mourning heavily, Anth.
heavy-falling, Aesch.
of persons, Soph.; of sufferings, grievous, Id.
heavy at the end, Anth.
heavy with iron, Plut.

entry.etym: poet. gen. pl. fem. βαρεῶν for βαρειῶν
entry.sense: heavy in weight, opp. to κοῦφος, Hdt., etc.: in Hom. mostly with a notion of strength and force, χεῖρα βαρεῖαν Il., etc.: also, heavy with age or suffering, γήραι, νόσωι Soph.

heavy to bear, grievous, Hom.; βαρὺ or βαρέα στενάχειν to sob heavily, Id.:—in attic, burdensome, grievous, oppressive:— adv., βαρέως φέρειν τι to take a thing ill, Lat. graviter ferre, Hdt., etc.; βαρέως ἀκούειν to hear with disgust, Xen.
violent, Theocr., Plat., etc.
weighty, impressive, NTest.
of persons, severe, stern, Aesch., Soph.:—also, wearisome, oppressive, Eur., Dem.: in good sense, grave, dignified, Arist.
of soldiers, heavy-armed, Xen.
of impressions on the senses,
of sound, strong, deep, bass, Od., Aesch., Soph.
of smell, strong, offensive, Hdt., Soph.
weighing heavy, Ar.
groaning heavily, bellowing, Dem.:—adv. -νως, Aesch.
of things, heavily lamented, grievous, Soph.
loud-thundering, Pind.
weight, heaviness, Thuc.
of men, importunity, disagreeableness, Dem., Plut.
in good sense, gravity, dignity, Arist., Plut.
of sound, strength, depth, Plat.
very costly, NTest.
bearing a heavy weight, Anth.
pass. ill to bear, Id.
deep-sounding, Xen.
loud-sounding, roaring, Hhymn.
gloominess, indignation, Plut.
weighty of purpose, grave-minded, Theocr.
thick-lipped, Anth.
deep-toned, Anth.
heavy of soul, dejected, Soph.
to rub gold upon the touch-stone (βάσανος), Plat.: hence, to try the genuineness of a thing, to put to the test, make proof of, Id.
of persons, to examine closely, cross-question, Hdt., Ar.
to question by applying torture, to torture, Id.:—Pass. to be put to the torture, for the purpose of extorting confession, Thuc.: to be tormented by disease or storm, NTest.
to be put to the proof, Plat.
βασανιστέον one must put to the torture, τινά Id., Dem.
questioner, torturer, tormentor, Dem., NTest.
an examiner, Ar.
the touch-stone, Lat. lapis Lydius, a dark-coloured stone on which pure gold, when rubbed, leaves a peculiar mark, Theogn.: hence.
generally, a test, trial whether a thing be genuine or real, Hdt., Soph.
inquiry by torture, the "question, " torture, used to extort evidence from slaves, Oratt.
torture of disease, NTest.
a queen, princess, Od., Aesch.
a kingdom, dominion, Hdt.: hereditary monarchy, opp. to τυραννίς, Thuc., etc.
a petty king, Plut.
a kingly dwelling, palace, Xen. mostly in pl., Hdt., etc.
the royal treasury, Id.
of the king, kingly, royal, Hdt., etc.

a king, chief, Hom.: later it was an hereditary king, opp. to τύραννος, Hdt., attic; ἄναξ β. lord king, Aesch.: c. gen., β. νεῶν Id.; οἰωνῶν β., of the eagle, Id.:—Hom. has a comp. βασιλεύτερος more of a king, more kingly, Sup. βασιλεύτατος most kingly.
of the king's son, prince, or any one sharing in the government, Od.
generally, a lord, master, householder, Il., Pind.
at Athens, the second of the nine Archons was called βασιλεύς; he had charge of the public worship, and the conduct of criminal processes, Plat., etc.
after the Persian war, the king of Persia was called βασιλεύς (without the Art.), Hdt., attic; more rarely ὁ βασιλεύς, or ὁ μέγας βας. Hdt.

to be king, to rule, reign, Hom., etc.; of a woman, to be queen, Id.; c. gen. to be king of, Od.; also, ὄφρ’ Ἰθάκης κατὰ δῆμον βασιλεύοι Id.; in aor. to have become king, Hdt.; c. dat. to be king among others, Od.:—Pass. to be governed by a king, Plat.: to submit to the king, Plut.
to be master of a thing, c. gen., Theocr.
royal, Il., Eur.
to be of the king's party, Plut.
royal, kingly, Hdt., attic
like a king, kingly, princely, βασιλικώτατος Xen.:—adv., βασιλικῶς as a king, with kingly authority, Id.
as Subst.,
βασιλική (sub. στοά), a colonnade at Athens, Plat.; v. στοά.
βασιλικός, ὁ, king's officer, NTest.
a queen, princess, Soph., Eur., etc.
as adj. royal, Id.
passable, accessible, Dem., Plut.
a stepping, step, and collectively steps, Aesch., Soph., etc.; οὐκ ἔχων βάσιν power to step, Id.; τροχῶν βάσεις the rolling of the wheels, Id.
that with which one steps, a foot, Eur., NTest.
that whereon one stands, a base, Plat.
c. acc. to slander, malign, belie, disparage, Dem.
c. dat. to envy, grudge, Id.
to bewitch, by means of spells: Pass., ὡς μὴ βασκανθῶ (aor1 subj.) that I be not bewitched, Theocr.
slander, envy, malice, Plat., Dem.
slanderous, envious, malignant, Ar., Dem.
as Subst. a slanderer, Id.
a sorcerer, Id.
a kind of duck, Ar.

entry.etym: akin to βαίνω, cf. χάσκω, χαίνω
entry.sense: βάσκ’ ἴθι speed thee! away! Il.; also come! Aesch.
a fox.
a Thracian bacchanal, Anth.
a little fox, Hdt.
that which is borne, a burden, Eur.
to lift, lift up, raise, Od., Soph., Eur.: to bear, carry, support, Aesch., Soph.
to hold in one's hands, Id.
βαστάζειν ἐν γνώμηι to bear in mind, consider, weigh, make proof of, Aesch.
to carry off, take away, NTest.
attic also = ψηλαφάω, to touch, Aesch.
to be borne, Anth.
a nickname given to Demosthenes, from his stuttering, Aeschin.
to tread, cover, of animals, Theocr.
κλῖμαξ β. a mounting ladder, Anth.
looking after skates, Ar.
a flat fish, perhaps the skate, Ar.
pulling berries off, Hhymn.
a bramble-bush or wild raspberry, Od.
the Hebrew measure bath, = attic μετρητής, NTest.
passable, Xen.
of or belonging to a frog: βατράχεια (sc. χρώματα), frog-colour, pale-green, Ar.
a frog-green coat, Ar.

sense.gloss: the battle of the frogs and mice

entry.sense: a frog, Batr., Hdt., etc.
to stutter, Luc.
to speak stammeringly, say the same thing over and over again, NTest.
stammerer, name of a king of Cyrene, Hdt.
to cry βαά βαά, to bark, Theocr.: of angry persons, to snarl, yelp, Aesch.; trans. to shriek aloud for, τινά Id.
a wine-cooler, Anth.
a paltry braggart, Arist.
prudish.
a dipping of red-hot iron in water, the temper produced thereby, Arist.
a dipping in dye, dyeing, dye, Aesch., Plat., etc.; κρόκου βαφαί the saffron- dyed robe, Aesch.; βαφαὶ ὕδρας the robe dipped in the hydra's blood, Eur.
χαλκοῦ βαφαί, in Aesch., is prob. the art of tempering brass, to express something which no woman could know.
in Soph. Aj., βαφῆι σίδηρος ὥς must be construed not with ἐθηλύνθην, but with the preceding words καρτερὸς γενόμενος, for iron becomes harder, not softer, by being dipped.
fit for dyeing, Luc.
to milk cows, Plat.: to suck, Arist.
a leech, Hdt., Theocr.
an abomination, i. e. an idol, NTest.
nausea, disgust, Xen.
disgusting, abominable, NTest.
Dep. to behave in a brutal manner, Dem.
brutal conduct, want of shame and decency, brutality, Oratt.
loathsome, disgusting, brutal, Ar., Oratt.; Sup. -ώτατος, Dem.
to feel nausea, to be sick, Ar.
c. acc. to feel a loathing at, to loath, Id.
to be loathsome: οἱ ἐβδελυγμένοι the abominable (in ref. to βδέλυγμα), NTest.
to break wind, Ar.
Lat. oppedere, to insult grossly, τινά Ar.
to be afraid of, Id.
firm, steady, steadfast, sure, certain, Aesch., etc.; βεβαιότερος κίνδυνος a surer game, Thuc.
of persons, steadfast, steady sure, constant, Aesch., etc.; c. inf., βεβαιότεροι μηδὲν νεωτεριεῖν more certain to make no change, Thuc.
τὸ βέβαιον certainty, firmness, resolution, Hdt., Thuc.
adv. -ως, Aesch., etc.; comp. -ότερον, Thuc.; Sup. -ότατα, Id.
firmness, steadfastness, stability, assurance, certainty, Thuc., Plat.
to make firm, confirm, establish, secure, warrant, make good, Plat., Xen.; ἔργωι βεβαιούμενα things warranted by fact, opp. to ἀκοῆι λεγόμενα, Thuc.
β. τί τινι to secure one the possession of a thing, Id.:—Mid. to establish for oneself, to confirm, secure, Id.
Mid. also to secure one's ground in argument, to asseverate, maintain, make good, Plat.
to guarantee a title, Isae.
confirmation, Thuc., Aeschin.

entry.etym: βηλός, with βε- as a redupl.
entry.sense: allowable to be trodden, permitted to human use, Lat. profanus, Soph., Eur.; ἐν βεβήλωι Thuc.
of persons, unhallowed, impure, Id., Plat.: c. gen. uninitiated in rites, Anth.
to profane, NTest.
to be stricken with grief, Hom.; βεβολήατο epic 3rd pl. plup.
advisedly, designedly, Dem.

entry.etym: A word coined from the story about βέκος in Hdt. 2. 2, and the Arcadian claim of being προσέληνοι.
entry.sense: superannuated, doting, Ar.
bread, a Phrygian word, Hdt.
bearing darts, Anth.
poet. for βέλος, a dart, javelin, Il., Aesch.
in darts, Anth.
any sharp point, a needle, Batr., Aeschin.
a needle-seller, Ar.

entry.etym: βάλλω, as Lat. jaculum from jacio
entry.sense: a missile, esp. an arrow, dart, bolt, Hom.; of the rock hurled by the Cyclops, Od.; of the ox's leg thrown at Ulysses, Id.; ὑπὲκ βελέων out of the reach of darts, out of shot, Il.; so ἔξω βελῶν Xen.
like ἔγχος, used of any weapon, as a sword, Ar.: an axe, Eur.
the ἀγανὰ βέλεα of Apollo and Artemis in Hom. always denote the sudden, easy death of men and women respectively.

after Hom. of anything swift-darting, Ζηνὸς βέλη the bolts of Zeus, thunderbolts, Aesch.; πύρπνουν β. Id.; βέλη πάγων the piercing frosts, Soph.:—metaph., ὀμμάτων βέλος the glance of the eye, Aesch.; ἱμέρου βέλος the shaft of love, Id.; of arguments, πᾶν τετόξευται βέλος Id.
a dart wrapped with pitch and tow, and thrown while on fire, Plut.

entry.etym: Prob. from same Root as βούλομαι.
poet. comp. and superl. of ἀγαθός
entry.sense: better, more excellent, βέλτερόν [ἐστι] it is better, c. inf., Hom.; in Theogn., Aesch., etc.

best, Ar., Plat., etc.:— ὦ βέλτιστε or βέλτιστε, a common mode of address, my good friend, Ar., etc.:— τὸ βέλτιστον the best, what is best, Aesch., Plat.:— οἱ βέλτιστοι or τὸ βέλτιστον the aristocracy, Lat. optimates, Xen.
better, ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον χωρεῖν to improve, advance, Thuc.
to spin like a top, Ar.
to set a spinning, Ar.
Lat. turbo, a top spun by whipping, Ar.
the festival of Bendis, Plat.
the temple of Bendis, Xen.
the Thracian Artemis, Luc.

entry.etym: poet. for βάθος, as πένθος for πάθος
entry.sense: the depth of the sea, Hom.; also in pl., θαλάσσης βένθεα, ἐν βένθεσσιν ἁλός Il., Hom.:—also of a wood, βένθεσιν ὕλης Od.

entry.etym: Homeric fut. with no pres. in use
entry.sense: I shall live (akin to βιόω):— others regard it epic fut. of βαίνω.
a booby, Ar.
that on which one treads, the threshold, Lat. limen, Il., Aesch.
a step, pace, stride, Hhymn., Aesch., Eur.; Διὸς εὔφρονι βήματι under the kindly guidance of Zeus, Soph.
= βάθρον, a step, seat, Id.:— a raised place or tribune to speak from in a public assembly or law-court, Thuc., Oratt.
a cough, Thuc.
baa, the cry of sheep, Cratin.
a wooded comb or glen, Hom., Soph.
of or like a glen, wooded, Hes.
to cough, Hdt.
Β, β, , indecl., second letter of the Gr. alphabet: hence as numeral, βʹ = δύο, δεύτερος, ͵β = 2000.
β is the medial labial mute, between tenuis τ and asp. θ. The dialectic variations of β seem to be mostly due to uncertainties of pronunciation:
for γ, as βλήχων γληχών, βλέφαρον doric γλέφαρον, βουνός γουνός· βεμβράς for μεμβράς, βροτός for μορτός (mortalis).
β is sometimes inserted between μλ, μρ to give a fuller sound, as in ἄμβροτος, μεσημβρία, γαμβρός, μέμβλεται.
a dancer, Od.

to constrain, Od.:—Pass., aor1 ἐβιάσθην, perf. βεβίασμαι:— to be hard pressed or overpowered, Il.; βιάζομαι τάδε I suffer violence herein, Soph.; βιασθείς Id.; ἐπεὶ ἐβιάσθη Thuc.; βεβιασμένοι forcibly made slaves, Xen.:—of things, τοὔνειδος βιασθέν forced from one, Soph.

Mid. βιάζομαι, with aor1 mid. ἐβιασάμην, perf. βεβίασμαι:— to overpower by force, press hard, Hom.; βιάζεσθαι νόμους to do them violence, Thuc.;— β. αὑτόν to lay violent hands on oneself, Plat.:— β. τινα, c. inf., to force one to do, Xen.; and inf. omitted, β. τὰ σφάγια to force the victims [to be favourable], Hdt.
c. acc. rei, βιάζεσθαι τὸν ἔκπλουν to force the entrance, Thuc.
absol. to use force, struggle, Aesch., Soph., etc.: to force one's way, Thuc., Xen.; c. inf., β. πρὸς τὸν λόφον ἐλθεῖν Thuc.: of a famine, to increase in violence, Hdt.
fighting violently, Anth.

forcible, violent, ἔργα βίαια Od.; β. θάνατος a violent death, Hdt., Plat., etc.; ὁ πόλεμος β. διδάσκαλος is a teacher of violence, Thuc.:—adv., βιαίως by force, perforce, Od., Aesch., etc.; so, πρὸς τὸ βίαιον Id.
pass. constrained, compulsory, Plat.
bodily strength, force, power, might, Hom., etc.; periphr. βίη Ἡρακληείη the strength of Hercules, i. e. the strong Hercules, Il.; βίη Διομήδεος Id.; Τυδέως βία, Πολυνείκους β. Aesch., etc.
of the mind, Il.

force, an act of violence, Od.; in pl., Id.; in attic, βίαι τινός against one's will, in spite of him, Aesch., Thuc., etc.; βίαι φρενῶν Aesch.; also βίαι alone as an adv., perforce, Od., etc.; so, πρὸς βίαν τινός and πρὸς βίαν alone, Aesch.
supplying the necessaries of life, Anth.
one must do violence to, Eur.
one who uses force, a violent man, NTest.
to constrain, Il.:— Pass. to be forcibly driven, of fire, Hdt.; θανάτωι βιηθείς overpowered, Id.

as Dep. in act. sense, to constrain, press hard, overpower, Hom.; βιήσατο κῦμ’ ἐπὶ χέρσου it forced me upon land, Od.; νῶϊ βιήσατο μισθόν he did us wrong in respect of our wages, Il.:— to force or urge on, Aesch.
Causal of βαίνω, to make to mount, to lift up, exalt, Soph.
striding, Il.
to stride, πέλωρα βιβᾶι he takes huge strides, Hhymn.; ἐβίβασκε, 3rd sg. ionic imperf., Id.; elsewhere in part., μακρὰ βιβῶντα, μακρὰ βιβῶσα Hom.
to stride, only in part., μακρὰ βιβάς Il.
βίβλινος, οἶνος , Biblian wine, from Biblis in Thrace, Hes., Theocr.: βύβλινος in Eur.
a dealer in books, Luc.
a paper, scroll, letter, Hdt., Ar., etc.; often written βυβλίον.
the inner bark of the papyrus (βύβλος): generally, bark, Plat.
a book, of which the leaves were made of this bark, Dem.

entry.etym: The Root is ΒΟΡ, v. βορά, Lat. voro.
entry.sense: to eat, eat up, βεβρωκὼς κακὰ φάρμακ’ Il.: c. gen. to eat of a thing, βεβρωκὼς βοός Od.:—Pass. to be eaten, χρήματα βεβρώσεται will be devoured, Id.
Oriental word for a wine-jar, Hdt., Xen.
coire, of illicit intercourse, Ar.
giver of life or food, Plat.
life-giving, Poeta ap. Plat., Soph.
lively, strong, hale, Hhymn.
supporting the life, Ar.
a bow, Il.
life, i. e. not animal life (ζωή), but a course of life, manner of living, Lat. vita, Od., etc.; in pl., τίνες καὶ πόσοι εἰσὶ βίοι; Plat.
in Poets = ζωή, βίον ἐκπνεῖν Aesch.; ἀποψύχειν Soph.
life-time, Hdt., Plat.
a living, livelihood, means of living, substance, Lat. victus, Hes., Soph., etc.; τὸν βίον ποιεῖσθαι ἀπό τινος to make one's living of a thing, Thuc., etc.
a life, biography, as those of Plut.
reft of the means of life, Soph.
a way of life, Xen.
to live, Eur.
to get food, Thuc.: to live by or off a thing, ἀπὸ πολέμου Xen.
= βίοτος, βίος, Od., attic Poets.
a living, sustenance, Soph., Ar.
a scant living, Ar.
life, Il., Trag.
= βίος II, means of living, substance, Lat. victus, Hom.
the world, mankind, Anth.
penurious, Anth.

to live, pass one's life (whereas ζάω properly means to live, exist), Il., etc.; ἀπ’ αὐτῶν ὧν αὐτὸς βεβίωκεν from the very actions of his own life, Dem.; hence in Pass., τὰ σοὶ κἀμοὶ βεβιωμένα the actions of our life, Id.; impers., βεβίωταί μοι I have lived, Lat. vixi, Id.:—Mid. in act. sense, Hdt.
to be lived, worth living, Eur.; οὐ βιώσιμόν ἐστί τινι ’tis not meet for him to live, Hdt., Soph.
manner of life, NTest.
to quicken, make or keep alive, Od.
one must live, Plat.
of or pertaining to life, NTest.
to be lived, worth living, Soph., Ar., etc.
hurtful, noxious, disadvantageous, Hes., Xen.

hurt, harm, damage, opp. to wilful wrong (ἀδίκημα), Aesch., etc.:— βλ. τινός damage to a person or thing, φορτίων Ar.; but, βλάβη θεοῦ mischief from a god, Eur.:—of a person, ἡ πᾶσα βλάβη who is naught but mischief, Soph.
βλάβης δίκη an action for damage done, Dem., etc.
having the knees bent inwards, bandylegged, Lat. valgus, Batr., Xen.:—generally, twisted, crooked, Anth.
distortion, retortion, Arist.
laziness, stupidity, Xen., Plat.
only in pres., to be slack, lazy, Xen.
c. acc. to lose or waste through laziness, Luc.
lazy, stupid, Plat.: adv. -κῶς, Ar.
lazy-like, lazy, Xen.
slack in body and mind, stupid, a dolt, Plat., Xen.:—Sup. βλακίστατος.

to disable, hinder, stop Hom.:—βλ. πόδας to disable the feet, to lame them, Od.:—Pass., ὄζωι ἔνι βλαφθέντε [the horses] caught in a branch, Il.; βλάβεν ἅρματα were stopped, Id.; Διόθεν βλαφθέντα βέλεμνα stopped, made frustrate by Zeus, Id.
c. gen. to hinder from, βλάπτουσι κελεύθου Od.:—Pass., βλαβέντα λοισθίων δρόμων arrested in its last course, Aesch.
of the mind, to distract, delude, deceive, mislead, of the Gods, Hom.; βλαφθείς, Lat. mente captus, Il.
after Hom. to damage, hurt, mar, opp. to wilful wrong (ἀδικεῖν), Aesch., etc.
to bud, sprout, grow, of plants, Aesch., etc.
metaph. to shoot forth, come to light, of men; ἀνθρώπου φύσιν βλαστών born in man's nature, Soph.; βλαστάνει ἀπιστία Id.
entry.etym: The Root is ΒΛΑΣΤ, v. βλαστεῖν, βλαστή.

entry.sense: late form of βλαστάνω, often introduced by Copyist for the aor2 forms βλαστεῖν, βλαστών.
= βλάστη I, Eur.
metaph. offspring, an offshoot, Aesch., Eur.
an eruption on the skin, Aretae.
= βλαστός, Plat., etc.; πετραία βλ. the growing rock, Soph.
of children, βλάσται πατρός, birth from a father, Id.; παιδὸς βλάσται its growth, Id.
a sprout, shoot, sucker, Lat. germen, Hdt.
to drop evil or profane words, speak lightly or amiss of sacred things, βλ. εἰς θεούς Plat.: to utter ominous words, Aeschin.
to speak ill or to the prejudice of one, to speak slander, περί τινος Dem.; εἴς τινα Id.:—also, βλ. τινα Babr., NTest.:—Pass. to have evil spoken of one, Id.
to speak impiously or irreverently of God, to blaspheme, Id.
a profane speech, opp. to εὐφημία, Eur., Plat.
defamation, evil-speaking, slander, Dem.
impious and irreverent speech against God, blasphemy, NTest.; τοῦ πνεύματος against the Spirit, Id.; πρός τινα Id.

entry.etym: The origin of βλας is uncertain: βλάξ and βλάπτω have both been suggested.
entry.sense: evil-speaking: of words, slanderous, Dem.
speaking blasphemy, blasphemous, and as Subst. a blasphemer, NTest.
a kind of slipper worn by fops, Plat.
a harming, damage, Plat.
mad, Aesch.
to look fiercely, glare around, Il.
a look, glance, Eur., Ar.
a look, Ar.
one must look, Plat.
of or for sight, Anth.
to be seen, worth seeing, Soph.
to see, have the power of sight, Soph.; μὴ βλέπηι ὁ μάντις lest he see too clearly, Id.

to look, εἴς τινα or τι, Aesch., etc.; πῶς βλέπων; with what face? Soph.;—with an adv., ἐχθρῶς βλ. πρός τινα Xen.:—foll. by a noun, φόβον βλ. to look terror, i. e. to look terrible, Aesch.; ἔβλεψε νᾶπυ looked mustard, Ar.; πυρρίχην βλέπων looking like a war-dancer, Id.; πεφροντικὸς βλέπειν to look thoughtful, Eur.
to look to some one from whom help is expected, Soph.; εἴς τινα Id., etc.:— of places, οἰκία πρὸς μεσημβρίαν βλέπουσα looking towards the south, Xen.
to look longingly, expect eagerly, c. inf., Ar.
to look to, ἑαυτούς NTest.; also, βλ. ἀπό τινος to beware of . . , Id.; βλ. ἵνα .. to see that . . , Id.

trans. to see, behold, c. acc., Trag.: βλ. φάος, φῶς ἡλίου to see the light of day, to live, Aesch., Eur.; and, without φάος, to be alive, live, Aesch., etc.; of things, βλέποντα actually existing, Id.
an eyelash, in pl. eyelashes, Lat. cilia, Ar., Xen., etc.

entry.etym: γλέφαρον is variously listed as Doric and Aeolic.
entry.sense: mostly in pl. the eyelids, Hom.
the eyes, Trag.: ἁμέρας βλέφαρον, νυκτὸς βλέφαρον, i. e. the sun, the moon, Soph., Eur.
sight, Plut.
a throw, cast, of dice, Eur.
a shot, wound, Hdt.
a coverlet, Anth.
one must put, NTest.
a fastening, a band or rivet, Il.
Dep. to bleat, of sheep and goats, Ar.; of infants, Id.
a bleating, οἰῶν Od.: the wailing of children, Eur.
weak, faint, slight, Plut.: cf. ἀ-βληχρός.
bleating, sheepish, Babr.
prepared with pennyroyal, Ar.
pennyroyal, Ar., Theocr.
honey-taking, Anth.
a booby, Ar.

entry.etym: The Root is ΒΛΙΤ of μέλιτος, gen. of μέλι, β being in place of μ, cf. βλώσκω for μλώσκω).
entry.sense: to cut out the comb of bees, take the honey, Plat.:—metaph., βλ. τὸν δῆμον to rob the people of their honey, Ar.:—Pass., μέλι βλίττεται Plat.
grim, fierce, Il.: terrible, Aesch.: bluff, burly, valiant, Plat.
grim-looking, Γοργώ Il.
gush forth; c. dat., βλ. Λυαίωι with wine, Anth.
a bubbling up, Anth.
tall, stately, of trees, Hom.

entry.etym: The Root is ΜΟΛ, so that βλώσκω is for μολώσκω, μλώσκω; cf. θρώσκω from ΘΟΡ.
entry.sense: to go or come, Hom., Trag.
a shield of wild bull's hide, Il.
a wild bull.
a shriek, cry, Aesch.
an ox-stall, Theocr.

entry.etym: a later form βοάσω in Eur. is aor1 subj
entry.sense: to cry aloud, to shout, Hom., Aesch.; οἱ βοησόμενοι men ready to shout (in the ἐκκλησία), Dem.
of things, to sound, resound, roar, howl, as the wind and waves, Il., Aesch.; αὐτὸ βοᾶι it proclaims itself, Ar.
c. acc. pers. to call to one, call on, Eur., Xen.
to call for, shout out for, Soph.
c. acc. cogn., β. βοάν, μέλος, etc., Ar., Soph.
to noise abroad, βεβωμένα ἀνὰ Ἰωνίην Hdt.; ἐβώσθησαν ἀνὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα Id.
c. inf. to cry aloud or command in a loud voice to do a thing, Soph., Eur., Xen.
sc.βοείη δορή, an ox-hide, ox-hide shield, Hom.; gen. pl. βοῶν, contr. for βοέων, Il.
of or for oxen, ζεύγη β. wagons drawn by oxen, Thuc., Xen.
of an ox or oxen, esp. of ox-hide, Hom.; βόεα κρέα Hdt.; γάλα βόειον cows milk, Eur.; metaph., βόεια ῥήματα great bull- words (cf. βούπαις, etc.), Ar.
a rope of ox-hide, Od.
born of an ox, of bees, Anth.
to run to a cry for aid, haste to help, Eur.
games in memory of the succour given by Theseus against the Amazons, Dem., Plut.
the third Attic month, in which the Βοηδρόμια were celebrated, answering nearly to our September, Dem.
running to a cry for aid, giving succour, a helper, Eur.: cf. βοηθόος.
help, aid, rescue, support, Thuc., etc.
medical aid, cure, Plut.
an auxiliary force, βοήθεια Thuc., Xen.
to come to aid, to succour, assist, aid, c. dat. pers., Hdt., Eur., etc.; πρός τινα Xen.
absol. to give aid, come to the rescue, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
one must help, Xen., Dem.
hasting to the battle-shout, hasting to battle, Il.; cf. βοηδρόμος.
aiding, helping, Pind.; and as Subst. an assistant, Theocr.
assisting, auxiliary, Thuc.; and as Subst. an assistant, Hdt., Plat.
a driving of oxen, cattle-lifting, Il.
a cattle-run, Anth.
one that drives away oxen, a cattle-lifter, Anth.
ox-driving, Id.
of or for cattle-driving:— ἡ βοηλατική (sc. τέχνη) the herdsman's art, Plat.

a loud cry, shout, Hom., etc.:— a battle-cry, βοὴν ἀγαθός good at the battle-cry, Il.; βοᾶς μηδ’ ὄνομ’ ἔστω let there be not even the name of war, Theocr.:—also of the roar of the sea, Od.; of the sound of musical instruments, Il., Pind.; the cry of birds or beasts, Soph., Eur.;— ὅσον ἀπὸ βοῆς ἕνεκεν as far as sound went, only in appearance, Thuc., Xen.
= βοήθεια, aid called for, succour, Aesch., Soph.
clamorous:— doric fem. βοᾶτις Aesch.
a shouting, clamour, Od.

entry.etym: Prob. from the same Root as βαθύς: cp. also Lat. fodio.
entry.sense: any hole or pit dug in the ground, Lat. puteus, Hom.: a natural trough for washing clothes in, Od.:— a hole, such as a fire makes in the snow, Xen.
like αἰβοῖ, exclam. of disgust, Ar.
to be a Boeotarch, Thuc.
a Boeotarch, one of the chief magistrates at Thebes, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
the office of Boeotarch, Plut.
to play the Boeotian, speak Boeotian, side with the Boeotians, Xen.
Boeotia, so called from its cattle-pastures, Hes.
Boeotian: the Boeotians were proverbially clownish, whence the saying ὗς Βοιωτία.
of Boeotian work, Xen.
a Boeotian, Il., etc.
violent, Trag. ap. Plut.
the Lat. vulva, Anth.
a bulb: in Theocr. a truffle?
a throw, the stroke or wound of a missile, opp. to πληγή (stroke of sword or pike), Od., Eur., Thuc.: βολαῖς σφόγγος ὤλεσεν γραφήν by its stroke or touch, Aesch.
metaph., like βέλος, a glance from the eyes, Od.
βολαὶ κεραύνιοι thunder- bolts, Aesch.; βολαὶ ἡλίου sun- beams, Soph.; βολὴ χιόνος a snow- shower, Eur.
to heave the lead, take soundings, NTest.
a javelin, Plut.
a cast of the dice, a die, Anth.
of cow-dung, Ar.
cow-dung, mostly in pl., Ar.
the rattling of the dice, Anth.
a throw with a casting-net, a cast, Orac. ap. Hdt., Theocr.: metaph., εἰς βόλον καθίστασθαι to fall within the cast of the net, Eur.
the thing caught, a draft of fish, Aesch., Id.
a bagpiper, with a play on βομβυλιός, Ar.

to make a booming, humming noise, to sound deep or hollow, Hom.; βόμβησαν κατὰ ῥόον the oars fell with a loud noise down into the tide, Od.; βόμβησεν λίθος the stone flew humming through the air, Id.:—of bees, to hum, Theocr.; of mosquitoes, to buzz, Ar.
humming, buzzing, Anth.
a hummer, buzzer, Anth.
a booming, humming, Plat.
an insect that hums or buzzes, a bumble-bee, Ar.
slaughter of oxen, Anth.
eatage, meat, properly of carnivorous beasts, Trag.; of cannibal-like feast, Hdt., Trag.:—rarely of simple food, Aesch., Soph.
muddy-minded, Ar.
mudcoucher, name of a frog, Batr.
mud, mire, Lat. coenum, Aesch., Ar., etc.
a mud-stirrer, mudlark, Ar.
muddy, miry, Plat.

entry.etym: Prob. from ὄρος, ϝόρος, wind from the mountains.
entry.sense: the North wind, Lat. Aquilo, Od.; πρὸς βορῆν ἄνεμον towards the North, Hdt.; πρὸς βορέαν τινός northward of a place, Thuc.
from the quarter of the North wind, northern, Hdt.; ἀκτὰ β. exposed to the north, Soph.
a Boread, daughter of Boreas, Soph.
devouring, gluttonous, Ar.
unknown Libyan animals, Hdt.; cf. ὄρυες.
an inhabitant of the banks of the Borysthenes, Hdt
the Borysthenes or Dnieper, a river of Scythia, Hdt.
food, Il.
that which is fed or fatted: in pl. fatted beasts, cattle, Soph., etc.; of sheep, Eur.; of horses, Id.; of pigs, Ar.
food, Aesch.
fodder, food, Aesch., Eur.
one must feed, Ar.
a herdsman, Anth.
of the herdsman, to feed, tend, Lat. pasco, Od.
generally, to feed, nourish, support, of earth, Id.; of the Sun, Soph.; of soldiers, to maintain, Hdt., Thuc.: metaph., β. νόσον Soph.; πράγματα β. to feed up troubles, i. e. children, Ar.
Pass., of cattle, to feed, graze, Lat. pascor, Hom., c. acc.:— to feed on, Aesch.
metaph. to be fed or nurtured, Trag.; β. τινί or περί τι to run riot in athing, Anth. (The Root appears to be ΒΟΤ, cf. βοτήρ, βοτός, βοτάνη.）
ox-ford, name of several straits, of which the Thracian and Cimmerian are best known, Hdt.; also of the Hellespont, Aesch., Soph.
like curls, Luc.
a curl or lock of hair, Aesch., etc.
anything twisted or wreathed, πυρὸς β., of a flash of lightning, Id.
pastures, meadows, Thuc.
grass, fodder, Il., Plat.; ἐκ βοτάνης from feeding, from pasture, Theocr.
of or for a herdsman, Plut., Anth.
a herdsman, herd, Od.; οἰωνῶν β. a soothsayer, Aesch.; κύων βοτήρ a herdsman's dog, Soph.
a beast, Aesch., Soph.: mostly in pl. grazing beasts, Il., Trag., etc.; but of birds, Ar.
like a bunch of grapes, in clusters, Il.
of grapes, Anth.
grape-producing, Ar.
clustering, Anth.
grape-born, child of the grape, Anth.
act. bearing grapes, Theocr.
with clustering hair, Anth.
a cluster or bunch of grapes, Il., attic
= βόστρυχος, Anth.
like curls, curly, Eur.
like a bunch of grapes, Eur.
an African species of antelope, prob. the hartbeeste, Hdt.
grazed by cattle, Od.
eating enormously: metaph. grinding poverty or misery, Il.
to suffer from swellings in the groin, Ar.
the groin, Lat. inguen, Il.
a great bully or braggart, voc. βουγάϊε Hom.
flaying oxen, Hes.
as Subst. a knife for flaying, Babr.
affording summer-pasture, Soph.
beef-eater, Anth.
a sacrifice of oxen, Anth.
to slay or sacrifice oxen, Soph., Eur.: generally to sacrifice any animals, Ar.
of or belonging to sacrifices, esp. of oxen, Aesch., Eur.
on which oxen are offered, sacrificial, Trag., Ar.
cowherd, Theocr.
horned like an ox or cow, Hdt., Aesch.
the horse of Alexander the Great, Plut.
bull-headed, epith. of Thessalian horses, Ar.
to tend cattle, Il.:—Pass. of cattle, to range the fields, graze, Id.
of persons, to tend, serve, worship, Ar.: Mid., τόνδε βουκολούμενος πόνον being constantly engaged in this toil, Aesch.
metaph. to delude, beguile, Id.; Mid., ἐλπίσι βουκολοῦμαι I feed myself on hopes, cheat myself with them, Eur.
a beguilement, τῆς λύπης Babr.
Dep. to sing or write pastorals, Theocr.
a herd of cattle, Hhymn., Hes.
a byre, ox-stall, Hdt.
a pastoral poet, Theocr.
pastoral, Theocr.
a herd of cattle, Hdt., Theocr.
a means of beguiling, Anth.

entry.etym: -kolos is prob. an altered form of -πολος, cf. αἰπόλος.
entry.sense: a cowherd, herdsman, Hom., Plat.
of the council: βουλαία, a name of Vesta, as having a statue in the Senate House, Aeschin.
to be a βούλαρχος, Arist.
chief of the senate.
adviser of a plan, Lat. auctor consilii, Aesch.
a deliberate resolution, purpose, design, plan, Hdt., attic
deliberation, Arist.
the wrongful enrolment of a person among the public debtors, Dem.
one must take counsel, Aesch., Soph., Thuc.
a council-chamber, senate-house, Lat. curia, Hdt., attic
the council or senate itself: and poet. a counsellor, Eur.
advising, Aesch.
