a councillor, senator, Il., Hdt., etc.;—at Athens, one of the 500, Oratt.
of or for the council or the councillors, Xen., Dem.
able to advise or deliberate, Plat., etc.
as Subst., βουλευτικόν, in the Athen. theatre, the seats next the orchestra, reserved for the Council, Ar.
the senatorial order, Plut.
devised, plotted, Aesch.
to take counsel, deliberate, concert measures, and in past tenses to have considered and so to determine, resolve:

absol., οἷος ἔην βουλευέμεν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι such as he was in council and in battle, Od.; ἔς γε μίαν βουλεύσομεν [sc. βουλήν] we shall agree to one plan, Id.:—in Prose, this sense belongs chiefly to the Mid.

c. acc. rei, to deliberate on, plan, devise, Od., Hdt., attic:—Pass. with fut. mid., aor1 ἐβουλεύθην: perf. βεβούλευμαι:— to be determined or resolved on, Aesch., etc.; τὰ βεβουλευμένα = βουλεύματα, Hdt.
c. inf. to resolve to do, Od., Hdt.
to give counsel, τὰ λῷστα β. Aesch.; c. dat. pers. to advise, Il., Aesch.
in polit. writers, to be a member of Council, Hdt.; esp. of the Council of 500 at Athens, Plat., Xen., etc.
Mid., fut. -εύσομαι: aor1 ἐβουλευσάμην, epic βουλ or in pass. form ἐβουλεύθην: perf. βεβούλευμαι:
absol. to take counsel with oneself, deliberate, Hdt., attic
c. acc. rei, to determine with oneself, resolve on, Il., Hdt.
c. inf. to resolve to do, Id., Plat.; β. ὅπως . . , Xen.
of good counsel, Solon.
will, determination, Lat. consilium, esp. of the gods, Il., etc.
a counsel, piece of advice, plan, design, Id., Hdt., attic:—in pl. counsels, Aesch.
a Council of the elders or chiefs, a Senate, Hom., Aesch.:—at Athens, the Council of 500 created by Cleisthenes, Hdt., Ar., etc.:— βουλῆς εἶναι to be of the Council, a member of it, Thuc.
a willing: one's will, intention, purpose, Eur., Thuc., etc.
the purpose or meaning of a poem, Plat.
that is or should be willed: —τὸ β. the object of the will, Plat., Arist.
counselling, advising, Il.; c. gen. a counsellor, Id.
ravenous hunger, a disease, Arist.
to suffer from βουλιμία, Ar., Xen.
sage, Aesch.

entry.etym: The Root is ΒΟΛ, which appears in epic βόλομαι, Lat.volo: hence βουλή.
entry.sense: Dep.

to will, wish, be willing, Hom., etc.:—mostly c. inf. or c. acc. et inf., Id., etc.: when βούλομαι is foll. by acc. only, an inf. may be supplied, Τρώεσσιν ἐβούλετο νίκην he willed victory to the Trojans, or Τρώεσσιν ἐβούλετο κῦδος ὀρέξαι, — both in Il.
attic usages:
βούλει or βούλεσθε foll. by subj., adds force to the demand, βούλει λάβωμαι would you have me take hold, Soph.
εἰ βούλει, a courteous phrase, like Lat. sis (si vis), if you please, Id.
ὁ βουλόμενος, Lat. quivis, the first that offers, Hdt., attic
βουλομένωι μοί ἐστι, nobis volentibus est, c. inf., it is according to my wish that . . , Thuc.
to mean so and so, τί βούλεται εἶναι; quid sibi vult haec res? Plat.:—hence, βούλεται εἶναι professes or pretends to be, would fain be, Id.
followed by ἤ, to prefer, for βούλομαι μᾶλλον, βούλομ’ ἐγὼ λαὸν σόον ἔμμεναι, ἢ ἀπολέσθαι I had rather the people were saved than lost, Il.
strife-desiring, Ar.
towards even, at eventide, Hom.
the time for unyoking oxen, evening, Ar.
cow-milking, Anth.
a dweller on the hills, Anth.
to walk the hills, Anth.
hilly, Plut.
grazed by cattle, Soph.
ἀγέλαι βουνόμοι (parox.) herds of oxen at pasture, Id.
a hill, mound, Hdt.
a big boy, Ar.
（βοῦς, παῖς) child of the ox, of bees, in allusion to their fabulous origin, Anth.
like Bupalus, i. e. stupid, Anth.
wrestling like a bull, i. e. hard-struggling, Anth.
rich in cattle, Anth.
cow-modeller, of the sculptor Myron, Anth.
goading oxen, Anth.
an ox-goad, Lat. stimulus, Il.
an axe for felling an ox, Anth.
a herdsman, Anth.
ox-piercing, βουπ. ὀβελός a spit large enough to spit an ox, Hdt., Eur.
with the face of an ox, Soph.
prefix often used in compos. to express something huge and monstrous, e. g. βούπαις, βουγάϊος.
Lat. bos (bov-is), a bullock, bull, ox, or a cow, in pl. oxen or kine, cattle, Hom., etc.
= βοείη or βοέη (always fem.), an ox-hide shield, Il.
proverb., βοῦς ἐπὶ γλώσσηι βέβηκε, βοῦς ἐπὶ γλώσσης ἐπιβαίνει, of people who keep silence from some weighty reason, from the notion of a heavy body keeping down the tongue, Theogn., Aesch.
an ox-stall, Eur.
ox-guiding, and as Subst. an ox-goad, Anth.
to slaughter oxen, Eur.
a herdsman, Aesch., Eur., Theocr.
as adj., βούτ. φόνος the slaughter of kine, Eur.
butomus, the flowering rush, Ar., Theocr.
ox-eating, Anth.
to slaughter oxen, Il.
sc. βουφόνια ἱερά a festival with sacrifices of oxen, Ar.
ox-slaying, ox-offering, Hhymn.
at or for which steers are slain, Aesch.
to tend cattle, Eur.
a herd of oxen, Eur.
ox-feeding, and as Subst. a herdsman, Eur., Plat.
holding a whole ox, Anth.
at Athens, an officer who bought oxen for the sacrifices, Dem.
ox-eyed, i. e. having large, full eyes, mostly of Hera, Hom.
to plough, Hes.
a ploughman, Babr.
the name given to the constellation Arcturus, Od.; v. ἄρκτος II.
arbitration, judgment, Eur.
a prize in the games, NTest.
the judge who assigned the prizes at the games, Lat. arbiter, Soph., Plat.
generally, an arbitrator, umpire, judge, Eur.: then a chief, leader, Aesch.: an author, Eur.
to act as a judge or umpire, Isocr.
c. acc. to arbitrate, decide on, τὰ δίκαια Dem.:— to direct, arrange, control, Anth.
a wild plum, Theocr.
hoarse, Anth.
hoarseness, or sore throat causing hoarseness, Thuc.
trans. to make slow, delay:— Pass. to be delayed, Soph.
intr. to be long, to loiter, delay, Id.: so in Mid., Aesch.
slow to believe, Anth.
to sail slowly, NTest.
slow of foot, slow, Eur.
slow of leg, Anth.
slow, Hom., etc.:—c. inf., ἵπποι βάρδιστοι θείειν slowest at running, Il.; β. λέγειν Eur.:—adv., βραδέως χωρεῖν Thuc.
of the mind, like Lat. tardus, Il.; c. inf., προνοῆσαι βραδεῖς Thuc.; τὸ βραδύ slowness, Id.:—adv., βραδέως βουλεύεσθαι Id.
of Time, tardy, late, Soph., Thuc.
slowness, Il., attic
of the mind, Plat.
a rich woman's-garment, Theocr.
to shake violently, throw up, of the sea, Anth.
to winnow grain, Plat.

entry.etym: as if from a nom. βράχος, or βραχέα (neut. pl. of βραχύς）
entry.sense: shallows, Lat. brevia, Hdt., Thuc.

entry.etym: found only in 3rdc sing. epic aor2 ἔβραχε or βράχε
entry.sense: to rattle, clash, ring, of arms; of a torrent, to roar; of an axle, to creak; of one wounded, to shriek or roar, — all in Il.
an armlet, Plut.
the arm, Lat. brachium, Il.; πρυμνὸς βραχίων the shoulder, Id.
short-lived, Plat.
with small or few clods, Anth.
of small understanding, Xen.
running a short way, Xen.
with short limbs or ends, Strab.
consisting of short clauses, περίοδοι Arist.
brevity in speech or writing, Plat.
short in speech, of few words, Plat.
fut. υνῶ, to shorten, to use as a short syllable, Plut.
with a short passage, Plat.
with narrow passage, Plut.
short, Lat. brevis:
of Space and Time, Hdt., attic; ἐν βραχεῖ (ionic βραχέϊ) in a short time, briefly, Hdt., etc.; διὰ βραχέος Thuc.:—adv. βραχέως, scantily, seldom, Id.
of Size, short, small, little, Pind., Soph.; βρ. τεῖχος a low wall, Thuc.; κατὰ βραχύ little by little, Id.
of Quantity, few, διὰ βραχέων in few words, Plat.; διὰ βραχυτάτων Dem.:—adv., βραχέως, briefly, in few words, Xen.
of quality, humble, insignificant, Soph.:—of things, small, petty, trifling, Id., etc.:—neut. as adv., βραχὺ φροντίζειν τινός to think lightly of, Dem.
bringing a small contribution, Anth.
shortness, Thuc.
narrowness, deficiency, Id.
reaching but a short way, Plut.
short-necked, Plat.
with few leaves, Anth.
the front part of the head, Lat. sinciput, Batr.
formed to imitate the croaking of frogs, Ar.
to roar, of a wave, Il.; so also in Mid., Id., Soph.
in later Poets, of arms, to clash, ring, Eur.; of men, to shout, rage, Aesch., Eur. to bear oneself haughtily, to hold one's head high, swagger, Ar., Plat.
a wetting, Xen.
a wooden image of a god, Aesch., Eur., Ar.
the babe in the womb, Lat. foetus: of an unborn foal, Il.
the new-born babe, Aesch., Eur.:—of beasts, a foal, whelp, cub, Hdt.:— ἐκ βρέφεος from babyhood, Anth.
the top of the head, Lat. sinciput, Il.

Lat. rigo, to wet, τὸ γόνυ, of men walking through water, Hdt.:—Pass. to be wetted, get wet, βρεχόμενοι πρὸς τὸν ὀμφαλόν Xen.; βρέχεσθαι ἐν ὕδατι to bathe in water, Hdt.: of hard drinkers, βρεχθείς soaked, Eur.
to rain, send rain, NTest.; c. acc. cogn., βρ. πῦρ to rain fire, Id.
impers. βρέχει, like ὕει, Lat. pluit, it rains, Id.
a hundred-handed giant, so called by the gods, but by men Aegaeon, Il.

entry.etym: From same Root as βριθύς, βρίθω, βαρύς.
entry.sense: strong, stout, Il.
to make or to be strong and mighty, Hes. (v. βριαρός.）
to be sleepy, to slumber, nod, Il., Aesch.
loud-shouting, of Ares, Il.
weight, Eur.
weight, heaviness, Il.
grave-minded, thoughtful, Anth.
weighty, heavy, Il, Irreg. comp. βριθύτερος, Aesch.
to be heavy or weighed down with a thing, c. dat., of fruit-trees, Hom.; metaph., ὄλβωι βρίθειν Eur.; ξίφεσι βρ. to visit heavily with the sword, Id.
c. gen. to groan with weight of a thing, σίτου, οἴνου Od.
absol. to be heavy, Il.; rare in attic, βρίθει ὁ ἵππος sinks, Plat.
of men, to outweigh, prevail, ἐέδνοισι by gifts, Od.: absol. to have the preponderance in fight, to be master, prevail, Il.
trans. to weigh down, Aesch.:—Pass. to be laden, καρπῶι βριθομένη laden with fruit, Il.:—c. gen., βρίθεσθαι σταχύων Hes.
Dep. to snort with anger, to be indignant, Ar.
strength, bulk, Hhymn.
chariot-loading, Hes.
of flies, to buzz, Il.
Dep.
as a name of Bacchus, Aesch., Eur.; Βρομίου πῶμα, i. e. wine, Id.
as adj. Βρόμιος, α, ον, Bacchic, Id., Ar.
Lat. fremitus, any loud noise, as the crackling of fire, Il.; roaring of a storm, Aesch.; neighing of horses, Id.
rage, fury, Eur.
to thunder, Od.; metaph. of Pericles, Ar.
impers., βροντᾶι it thunders, Id.
a thunder-clap, Aesch.
thunder, Hom., etc.
the state of one struck with thunder, astonishment, Hdt.
sending thunder and lightning, Ar.
thunderer, one of the three Cyclopes, Hes.
mortal, human, of mortal mould, Trag.
trampling on men, Anth.
with human voice, Anth.
gory, blood-boltered, Il.
to murder men, Aesch.
man-slaying, homicidal, Eur.
plague of man, bane of men, of Ares, Hom.
Pass., to be stained with gore, Od.
taking note of man, Aesch.
blood that has run from a wound, gore, Hom.

entry.etym: The orig. form seems to have been μορτός, cf. ἄμβροτος.
entry.sense: a mortal man, Hom., attic Poets.
hated by men or man-hating, Aesch.
giving light to men, Anth.
man-destroying, Aesch.
a wetting, rain, Anth.
rain, NTest.
the throat, Theocr., Anth.
Dim. of βρόχος, Anth.
（βρέχω) an ink-horn, Id.
a noose or slip-knot, for hanging or strangling, Od., Hdt., Soph.:— a snare for birds, Ar.:— the mesh of a net; metaph., ληφθέντες ἐν ταὐτῶι βρόχωι Aesch.
to gulp down, a Root only found in aor1 ἔβροξα, Anth.:—used by Hom. only in compds.,
ἀναβρόξαι, to swallow again, suck down again, ὅτ’ ἀναβρόξειε ὕδωρ, of Charybdis, Od.; and in aor2 part. pass., ὕδωρ ἀναβροχέν Id.
καταβρόξαι, to gulp down, ὃς τὸ καταβρόξειε whoever swallowed the potion, Id.
to eat with much noise, to eat greedily, Eur., Ar.:—metaph. to tear in pieces, devour, of a gnawing disease, Soph.; so in Pass., βρύκομαι, Id., Anth.
to cry for drink, of children, Ar.
in Ar. βρῦν εἰπεῖν to say bryn, cry for drink.
a kind of mossy sea-weed, Theocr.

Dep., to roar, bellow, Lat. rugire, of a bull, Soph., Ar.; of elephants, Plut.:—in Il. mostly of the death-cry of wounded men, κεῖτο βεβρυχώς; so, βρυχώμενον σπασμοῖσι, of Hercules, Soph.; δεινὰ βρυχηθείς Id.:—in Od. of the roaring of waves. (Formed from the sound.) Hence
with gnashing of teeth, Anth.
bellowing, roaring, of men, Plut.
a bellower, roarer, Anth.

entry.etym: From *βρύξ, of which an acc. βρύχα occurs in late poets; cf. ὑποβρύχιος.
entry.sense: from the depths of the sea, Aesch.; of thunder from the deep, Id.
to be full to bursting:
c. dat. to swell or teem with, βρύει ἄνθεϊ teems with bloom, Il.:—metaph., βρύων μελίτταις καὶ προβάτοις Ar.; of men, θράσει βρύων Aesch.
c. gen. to be full of, βρύων δάφνης, ἐλαίας, ἀμπέλου Soph.: metaph., νόσου βρ. Aesch.
absol. to abound, grow luxuriantly, Soph.: of the earth, to teem with produce, Xen.
c. acc. cogn. to send forth water, NTest. (Akin to βλύω, βλύζω, and perh. to φλύω.）
Dep. to bray, Lat. rudere, βρωμησάμενος Ar.
that which is eaten, food, meat, Thuc., Plat., etc.
the false pleasure of eating made dishes, Anth.
food, Od.
eatable, Aesch.
meat, Od., Thuc., etc.
eating, Plat.
corrosion, rust, NTest.
eating, Aesch.
to be eaten:— βρωτόν, meat, Eur., Xen.
made of byblus, Od., Hdt.
the Egyptian papyrus, the root and triangular stalk of which were eaten by the poor, Hdt.
its fibrous coats, as prepared for ropes, Id.; cf. βύβλινος.
the outer coat of the papyrus, used for writing on, hence in pl. leaves of byblus, Id.
a paper, book, Id.; in this sense more commonly written βίβλος (q. v.):—pl. βύβλα, τά, Anth.
close pressed, closely, Thuc.
to sink a ship: metaph. to sink or ruin men, NTest.
in the deep, sunken, Luc., Anth.
in or of the sea, τὰ βύθια (sc. ζῷα), water-animals, Anth.
metaph. of sound, deep, Plut.
pecul. fem. of βύθιος, Anth.
the depth, esp. of the sea, the deep, Aesch., Soph.
swelling, blustering, βυκτάων ἀνέμων (epic gen.) Od.
to stuff, Ar.
leather-eagle, nickname of Cleon the tanner, Ar.
the skin stripped off, a hide, Batr., Hdt.; βύρσης ὄζειν to smell of leather, Ar.: a drum, Eur.
the skin of a live animal, Theocr.
a tanner, NTest.
a leathern thong, Ar.
to dress or tan hides, Ar.
a tanner, Ar.
made of hides, Plut.
leather-Paphlagonian, nickname of Cleon, Ar.
a leather-seller, Ar.
with skin stretched over it, of a drum, Eur.
made of βύσσος, σινδών β. a fine linen bandage, used for mummy-cloths,, Hdt.; for wounds, Id.; β. πέπλοι Aesch
to build in the deep: metaph. to brood over a thing in the depth of one's soul, ponder deeply, Od.
from the bottom of the sea, Soph.
measuring the deeps, epith. of a fisherman, Anth.
the depth of the sea, the bottom, Il., Hdt.

entry.etym: A foreign word; cf. Hebr. butz.
entry.sense: a fine flax, and the linen made from it, Theocr.
deep-thinking, Aesch.
of nets, which stopped the passage of a shoal of tunnies, Anth.
to stuff,
c. gen. rei, to stuff full of, only in Pass., νήματος βεβυσμένος stuffed full of spun-work or yarn, Od.; τὸ στόμα ἐβέβυστο [sc. χρυσοῦ] Hdt.
c. dat. rei, to stop or bung up with, plug: Pass., σπογγίωι βεβυσμένος Ar.
absol., βεβ. τὰ ὦτα deaf, Luc.
a lump of earth, a clod, Lat. gleba, Od., Soph., Xen.
like Lat. gleba, land, ground, soil, Mosch., Anth.
generally, a lump of anything, a mass, of the sun, Eur.
clod-breaking, Anth.
of an altar, Soph., Eur.
of a suppliant, βωμία at the altar, Id.
a step, Hdt.
like an altar, Plut.
a piece of low flattery, in pl. base flatteries, ribald jests, Ar.
Dep. to use low flattery, indulge in ribaldry, Ar., Isocr.
buffoonery, ribaldry, Plat.
inclined to ribaldry, Luc.
properly one that lurked about the altars for the scraps that could be got there, a half-starved beggar, Luc.
metaph. one who would do any dirty work to get a meal, a lick-spittle, low jester, buffoon, Ar.:—as adj., βωμολόχον τι ἐξευρεῖν to invent some ribald trick, Id.; of vulgar music, Id.
any raised platform, a stand, Lat. suggestus, for chariots, Il.: of a statue, a base, pedestal, Od.
a raised place for sacrificing, an altar, Hom., Trag., etc.
a tomb, cairn, Anth.
to call on, esp. to call to aid, Od., Ar.
man-feeding, nurse of heroes, Il.
a small round net: metaph. a net, δουλείας γ. Aesch.
adv., from Cadiz, Anth.
Γαδειραῖος πορθμός the Straits of Gibraltar, Plut.
Lat. Gades, Cadiz, Hdt.
Lat. gaza, treasure, Theophr.
a treasury, NTest.
a treasurer.
a land, country, Hom., Trag.; φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν to one's dear father land, Hom.
earth, soil, Il.
Γαῖα, as prop. n., Gaia, Tellus, Earth, spouse of Uranus, mother of the Titans, Hes.
sprung from Gaia or Earth, Od.
poet. for γηοῦχος, earth-upholding, of Poseidon, Hom., Trag.
protecting the country, Soph.
on land, Aesch.

entry.etym: The Root was ΓΑΥ, or ΓΑϜ, cf. γαῦρος, Lat. gaudium.
entry.sense: to exult, only in part. κύδεϊ γαίων Il.
sucking, young, tender, Od., Theocr.; γαλαθηνά (sc. πρόβατα), Hdt.
milky, milk-white, Anth.
like curdled milk, Anth.
a milk-drinker, Hdt.
milk-fed, Strab.

entry.etym: The Root seems to be ΓΛΑΚ, or ΓΛΑΓ, cf. gen. γάλακτος, γλάγος, and (with γ dropt) Lat. lac, lactis
entry.sense: milk, Hom., etc.; ὀρνίθων γάλα, proverb. of rare and dainty things, Ar.
a weasel, marten-cat or polecat, Lat. mustela, Hdt., Ar.
cheerful: adv. -ρῶς, Anth.
a spotted lizard, Lat. stellio, Ar.

entry.etym: Deriv. uncertain: perh. akin to γελάω.
entry.sense: stillness of the sea, calm, Od.; λευκὴ γ. Id.; ἐλόωσι γαλήνην will sail the calm sea, i. e. over it, Id.:—metaph., φρόνημα νηνέμου γαλάνας spirit of serenest calm, Aesch.; ἐν γαλήνηι in calm, Soph.
to be calm, epic part. γαληνιόωσα Anth.
calm; γαλήν’ ὁρῶ I see a calm, Eur.; of persons, gentle, Id.
a husband's sister or brother's wife, a sister-in-law, Lat. glos, Il., etc.
any one connected by marriage, Lat. affinis, Aesch.:
a son-in-law, Lat. gener, Hom., Hdt., Eur.
a brother-in-law, a sister's husband, Il., Hdt.; or, a wife's brother Soph.
= πενθερός, a father-in-law, Eur.
doric and aeolic a bridegroom, wooer, suitor, Pind., Theocr.
fem. of γαμέτης a married woman, wife, γυνὴ γαμ. a wedded wife, Hes.
a husband, spouse, Aesch., Eur.; doric gen. γαμέτα, Id.
a wife, Anth.

to marry, i. e. to take to wife, Lat. ducere, of the man, Hom., etc.; ἔγημε θυγατρῶν married one of his daughters, Il.:—c. acc. cogn., γάμον γαμεῖν, Aesch., Eur.:— ἐκ κακοῦ, ἐξ ἀγαθοῦ γῆμαι to marry a wife of mean or noble stock, Theogn.
Mid. to give oneself or one's child in marriage:

of the woman, to give herself in marriage, i. e. to get married, to wed, Lat. nubere, c. dat., Od., Hdt.; γήμασθαι εἰς . . to marry into a family, Eur.:—ironically of a henpecked husband, κεῖνος οὐκ ἔγημεν ἀλλ’ ἐγήματο Anacr.; (cf. Martial, uxori nubere nolo meae); so Medea speaks contemptuously of Jason, as if she were the husband, γαμοῦσα σέ Eur.
of the parents, to get their children married, or betroth them, to get a wife for the son, Πηλεύς μοι γυναῖκα γαμέσσεται Il.
belonging to a wedding, bridal, Aesch., Eur.
γαμηλία (sc. θυσία), a wedding feast, Dem.
the seventh month of the Attic year, from γαμέω, because it was the fashionable time for weddings;— the last half of January and first of February, Arist.
to give in marriage, NTest.
of or for marriage, Plat.; τὰ γαμ. a bridal, wedding, Thuc.
indecl, third letter in Gr. alphabet; as Numeral γʹ = three, third: but ͵γ = 3000.

γ is the medial palatal mute, between tenuis κ and asp. χ. Before the palatals γ, κ, χ and before ξ, pronounced like n in ng, as in ἄγγος, ἄγκος, ἄγχι, ἄγξω: before the same letters ἐν- in compos. becomes ἐγ-.
changes of γ, etc.:
γ is sometimes prefixed, αἶα γαῖα, lac γλάγος, γάλακτος, νοέω γνῶναι, νέφος γνόφος.
sometimes interchanged with β, v. βῆτα I. 1; sometimes with κ, γνάπτω κνάπτω.
adulterous, Anth.
a wedding, wedding-feast, Hom., etc.
marriage, wedlock, Id., etc.; τὸν Οἰνέως γ. marriage with him, Soph.; mostly in pl., like Lat. nuptiae, nuptials, Aesch., etc.
preparing a wedding, Lat. pronuba, epith. of Hera and Aphrodite, Anth.
the jaws of animals; of the lion, Il.; of the horse, Id.; of Typhon, Aesch.: the bill or beak of birds, Eur.
curved: of birds of prey.
with crooked talons, of birds of prey, Hom., Aesch., etc.
to shine, glitter, gleam, of metals, Hom.: then, like Lat. nitere, to look bright, of garden-beds, Od.
brightness, sheen: gladness, joy, pride, Aesch.; of water διόσδοτον γάνος, of refreshing rain, Id.; γ. ἀμπέλον of wine, Id.
to make bright:— Pass. to be made glad, exult, Ar.; part. perf. pass. γεγανωμένος, like Lat. nitidus, glad-looking, joyous, Plat.
to brighten up, γάνυται φρένα he is glad at heart, Il.; c. dat., to be glad at a thing, Hom.; c. gen., Aesch.
to be drunk up by Earth, of libations, Aesch.
to tickle, Lat. titillare, Plat.:—Pass., generally, to feel tickling or irritation, Id.
heaps, lots, plenty; cf. ψαμμακοσιογάργαρα.
for, Lat. enim, and like it, regularly placed after the first word of a sentence: to introduce the reason:

ARGUMENTATIVE, to introduce the reason for a statement, which usually precedes:—when it precedes the statement, it may be rendered since, as, Ἀτρείδη, πολλοὶ γὰρ τεθνᾶσιν Ἀχαιοί, χρὴ πόλεμον παῦσαι Il.

the statement of which γάρ gives the reason may be omitted, οὐ γάρ τί μοι Ζεὺς ἦν ὁ κηρύξας τάδε [yes], for it was not Zeus, etc., Soph.; ἔστι γὰρ οὕτω [yes], for so it is, i. e. yes certainly, Plat.; οἵδ’ οὐκέτ’ εἰσί· τοῦτο γάρ σε δήξεται [I say this], for it will sting thee, Eur.: —in Conditional Propositions, where the Condition is omitted, it may be transl. for otherwise, else, οὐ γὰρ ἄν με ἔπεμπον πάλιν, (sc. εἰ μὴ ἐπίστευον), Xen.

EPEXEGETIC, where γάρ is used to begin a promised narration, λεκτέα ἃ γιγνώσκω· ἔχει γὰρ ἡ χώρα πεδία κάλλιστα I must relate what I know; now, the country has most beautiful plains, Xen.; so, after the introductory forms, σκέψασθε δέ, δῆλον δέ, τεκμήριον δέ, μαρτύριον δέ, μέγιστον δέ, Plat., etc.; τούτου δὲ τεκμήριον· τόδε γάρ . . , Hdt.:—in ἀλλὰ γάρ, a clause must be supplied between ἀλλά and γάρ, as, ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἤκουσα but [say no more], for I heard, Aesch.
STRENGTHENING,
a question, like Lat. nam, Engl. why, what, τίς γάρ σε ἧκεν; why who hath sent thee? Il.; τί γάρ; quid enim? i. e. it must be so, Soph.
a wish, with the opt., κακῶς γὰρ ἐξόλοιο O that you might perish! Eur.; in Hom. mostly αἲ γάρ, attic εἰ or εἴθε γάρ, Lat. utinam, O that! so also πῶς γάρ would that.

the paunch, belly, Lat. venter, Hom., etc.: hence, γ. ἀσπίδος the hollow of a shield, Tyrtae.:—often to express greed or gluttony, γαστέρες οἶον mere bellies, Hes.; γαστρὸς ἐγκρατής master of his belly, γαστρὸς ἥττων a slave to it, Xen.
the paunch stuffed with mince-meat, a black-pudding, sausage, Od., Ar.
the womb, Lat. uterus, γαστέρι φέρειν to be with child, Il.; so, ἐκ γαστρός from the womb, from infancy, Theogn.; ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχειν Hdt.
the lower part of a vessel bulging out like a paunch, Hom.
to punch a man in the belly, Ar.
gluttony, Plat.
a glutton, Ar.
heavy with child, Anth.
paunchlike, round, ναῦς, Plut.
to bear in the belly, of a bottle, Anth.
pot-bellied, Ar.
"fat-guts, " Ar.
cleaving the ground, Anth.
of or for a merchant vessel, Xen.
a milk-pail, Od.: a water-bucket, Hdt.; any round vessel, a bee-hive, Anth.; a drinking-bowl, Theocr.
a round-built Phoenician merchant vessel, opp. to the μακρὰ ναῦς used for war, Hdt.
arrogance, exultation, Plut.

entry.etym: mostly in pres. act. and mid.
entry.sense: to bear oneself proudly, prance, of horses, Plut.; and in Mid., Xen.:—metaph. to pride oneself on a thing, c. dat., Dem.; ἐπί σφισι Theocr.
Pass., like γαυριάω, to exult, Batr.: to pride oneself on a thing, c. dat., Eur.
exulting in a thing, c. dat., Eur.: absol. haughty, disdainful, Ar.; of a calf, skittish, Theocr.:— τὸ γ. = γαυρότης, Eur.
exultation, ferocity, Plut.
a subject for boasting, Eur.
rough cloth, like freeze, Strab.
poet. form for δουπέω, ἐπὶ δ’ ἐγδούπησαν Il.

epic perf. with pres. signf., pluperf. used as impf., to call out so as to be heard, ὅσσον τε γέγωνε βοήσας as far as a man can make himself heard by shouting, Od.:—c. dat. pers. to cry out to, Id.Od.
used in same sense as γέγωνα,Hom.
c. acc. rei, to tell out, proclaim, Aesch., Soph.
to cry aloud, Thuc.
c. acc. rei, to tell out, proclaim, Aesch., Eur.
loud-sounding, Aesch.: loud of voice, Anth.:—comp. γεγωνότερος, Id.
= Hebr. ge-hinnom, i. e. the valley of Hinnom, which represented the place of future punishment, NTest.
a plougher of earth, Anth.
as Pass., only in pres. and imperf., to be born, like γίγνομαι, γεινομένωι at one's birth, Hom.; 1st pl. epic imperf. γεινόμεθα Il.
Causal in aor1 mid., of the father, to beget, Id., Trag.; of the mother, to bring forth, Hom.; ἡ γειναμένη the mother, Hdt., Eur.; and οἱ γεινάμενοι the parents, Hdt., Xen.
of Zeus, to bring men into being, Od.
earth-bearing, Anth.
the projecting part of the roof, the eaves, cornice, coping, Eur.
neighbourhood: the neighbours, Plut.
mostly in pres., to be a neighbour, to border on, c. dat., Ar., Dem.
neighbourhood: a neighbouring place, Plat.
neighbourhood, Plat.
neighbouring, Anth.

one of the same land, a neighbour, Lat. vici-nus (from vicus), Od.; γείτων τινός or τινί one's neighbour, Eur., Xen.:— ἐκ τῶν γειτόνων or ἐκ γειτόνων from or in the neighbourhood, Ar., Plat.; as adj. neighbouring, Aesch., Soph.
to be like to laugh, ready to laugh, Plat.
a laugh, κυμάτων ἀνήριθμον γέλασμα "the many-twinkling smile of Ocean, " Aesch.
a laugher, sneerer, Soph.
inclined to laugh, Luc.
laughable, Od.
absol. to laugh, Hom., etc.; ἐγέλασσεν χείλεσιν, of feigned laughter, Il.:—Pass., ἕνεκα τοῦ γελασθῆναι for the sake of a laugh being raised, Dem.
to laugh at a person, Lat. irrideo, ἐπί τινι Il., Aesch.; also at a thing, Xen.; so c. dat., Soph., etc.; rarely, like καταγελάω, c. gen. pers., Id.
c. acc. to deride, τινά or τι Theocr., Ar.:—Pass. to be derided, Aesch., Soph.
a clove of garlic, Anth.
to write comic songs, Anth.
causing laughter, laughable, Il., Hdt., etc.; γελοῖα jests, Theogn.
of persons, causing laughter, ridiculous, Plat., etc.
fellowship in laughing, Anth.

laughter, γέλωι ἔκθανον they were like to die with laughing, Od.; γέλωτα ποιεῖν, κινεῖν, etc., Xen.;— κατέχειν γέλωτα to restrain one's laughter, Id.; γέλωτα ὀφλεῖν to incur laughter, Eur.; ἐπὶ γέλωτι to provoke laughter, Hdt., Ar.; γέλωτος ἄξια ridiculous, Eur.
occasion of laughter, matter for laughter, γ. γίγνομαί τινι Soph.
to create, make laughter, esp. by buffoonery, Plat., Xen.
buffoonery, Xen.
exciting laughter: as Subst. a jester, buffoon, Xen.
to fill full of, to load or freight with, a cargo of a ship, c. gen., Thuc., etc.; σποδοῦ γ. λέβητας charging the urns with ashes, Aesch.:—Pass. to be laden or freighted, Dem.
later in Pass., c. acc., οἶνον γεμισθείς Anth.
a load, freight, Aesch.
to be full, of a ship, Hdt., Xen.
c. gen. rei, to be full of a thing, Thuc., etc.; metaph., Trag.
to trace by way of pedigree, γεν. γένεσιν Hdt.; γεν. τινα to draw out his pedigree, Id.: —Pass., ταῦτα μέν νυν γεγενηλόγηται Id.; γενεαλογούμενος ἔκ τινος NTest.
the making a pedigree, Plat.
a genealogist.
of the persons in a family.

race, stock, family, Hom., etc.; Πριάμου γ. Il.; ἐκ γενεῆς according to his family, Id.; γενεῆι by birth-right, Od.; γενεὴν Αἰτωλός by descent, Il.:—of horses, a breed, Id.:—generally, γενεήν in kind, Hdt.:—also a tribe, nation, Περσῶν γ. Aesch.
a race, generation, οἵηπερ φύλλων γενεὴ τοιήδε καὶ ἀνδρῶν Il.; δύο γενεαὶ ἀνθρώπων Id.
offspring, Orac. ap. Hdt.; and of a single person, Soph.
of time or place in reference to birth:
a birth-place, γενεὴ ἐπὶ λίμνηι Γυγαίηι Il.; of an eagle's eyrie, Od.
age, time of life, esp. in phrases γενεῆι νεώτατος, πρεσβύτατος youngest, eldest, in age, or by birth, Hom.
time of birth, ἐκ γενεῆς Hdt.; ἀπὸ γ. Xen.
from birth, by descent, Anth.
of persons, race, tock, family, Hom.; of horses, a breed, stock, Il.
race, offspring, Soph.
of place or time, birth-place: metaph., ἀργύρου γ. a silver- mine, Il.
of or for a birthday, Anth.
of or belonging to one's birth, Lat. natalis, γ. δόσις a birthday gift, Aesch.; ἡ γενέθλιος (with or without ἡμέρα) one's birth-day, Inscr.; so τὰ γενέθλια a birthday feast, birthday offerings, Eur.
of one's race or family, esp. of tutelary gods (dii gentiles), Ζεὺς γ. Pind.; γ. θεοί Aesch.:— γενέθλιον αἷμα kindred blood, Eur.; γ. ἀραί a parent's curse, Aesch.
giving birth, γεν. πόρος thy natal stream, Id.; βλάσται γεν. Soph.
= γενέθλη race, descent, Aesch.
= γέννημα, offspring, Id., Soph.
to begin to get a beard, Plat.
a beard, Od., Trag.
in pl. the sides of the face, cheeks, Eur.
bearded, Theocr.
to grow a beard, get a beard, Od., Xen., etc.
the part covered by the beard, the chin, Hom., Trag.:—proverb. of a lean animal, οὐδὲν ἄλλο πλὴν γένειον καὶ κέρατα nothing but chin and horns, Ar.
= γενειάς, the beard, Hdt.
the cheek, Anth.
γενέσια, τά a day kept in memory of the dead, Hdt.; to be distinguished from γενέθλια a birthday-feast, though used for it in NTest.
an origin, source, productive cause, Il.:— a beginning, in dual, τοῖν γενεσίοιν, Plat.
manner of birth, Hdt.: race, descent, Id.; γένεσιν by descent, Soph.
production, generation, opp. to φθορά, Plat., etc.
creation, created things, Id.
a race, kind, family, Id.
a generation, age, Id.
ἐκ γενετῆς from the hour of birth, Hom.
the begetter, father, ancestor, Eur., and in pl. parents, Id.
the begotten, the son, Soph., Eur.
as adj., = γενέθλιοι θεοί, Aesch., Eur.
goddess of one's birth-hour, Ar.
a pickaxe, mattock, Soph.
noble, Lat. generosus, Ar., Plat.
befitting a noble: adv. -πῶς, Ar.
suitable to one's birth or descent, οὔ μοι γενναῖον it fits not my nobility, Il.
of persons, high-born, noble by birth, Lat. generosus, Hdt., Trag.; so of animals, well-bred, Plat., Xen.
noble in mind, high-minded, Hdt., attic: τὸ γ. = γενναιότης, Soph.:—also of actions, noble, Hdt., Trag.
of things, good of their kind, excellent, notable, Xen.: genuine, intense, δύη Soph.
adv. -ως, nobly, Hdt., etc.: comp. -οτέρως, Plat.: Sup. -ότατα, Eur.
nobleness of character, nobility, Eur., Thuc.: of land, fertility, Xen.
descent, birth, Aesch.
offspring, Id.: a generation, Id.
a race, family, Id., Eur.

11), of the father, to beget, engender, Aesch., Soph.; rarely of the mother, to bring forth, Aesch.; οἱ γεννήσαντες the parents, Xen.; τὸ γεννώμενον the child, Hdt.:—like φύω 1. 2, as κἂν σῶμα γεννήσηι μέγα even if he grow, get a large body, i. e. if he be of giant frame, Soph.
metaph. to produce, Plat.
that which is produced or born, a child, Soph.:—any product or work, Plat.
breeding, nature, Soph.
act. a begetting, Aesch.
an engendering, producing, Eur., Plat.: birth, NTest.
a parent, Soph., Plat.
γεννῆται, οἱ,(γέννα) at Athens, heads of families, Plat.
begotten, Plat.; γεννητοὶ γυναικῶν born of women, NTest.
noble, Ar., Plat.

race, stock, family, Hom., etc.; absol. in acc., ἐξ Ἰθάκης γένος εἰμί from Ithaca I am by race, Od.; in attic with the Art., ποδαπὸς τὸ γένος εἶ Ar.; so in dat., γένει πολίτης Dem.; οἱ ἐν γένει = συγγενεῖς, Soph.; opp. to οἱ ἔξω γένους, Id.; γένους εἶναί τινος to be of his race, Id.
offspring, even a single descendant, a child, Lat. genus, σὸν γένος Il.; θεῖον γένος, Id.; so in Trag.
collectively, offspring, posterity, Thuc., Dem.

a race, in regard to number, γ. ἀνδρῶν mankind, Il.; ἡμιόνων, βοῶν γ. Hom., etc.:— a clan or house, Lat. gens, Hdt.; at Athens as a subdivision of the φρατρία, Plat.: — a tribe, as a subdivision of ἔθνος, Hdt.:— a caste, Id., Plat.: of animals, a breed, Hdt.
a race in regard to time, an age, generation, Od.; γ. χρύσειον, Hes.:—hence age, time of life, γένει ὕστερος Il.
sex, Plat.: gender, in grammar, Arist.
a class, sort, kind, Xen.
in Logic, genus, opp. to εἶδος (species), Plat.
he grasped, = ἔλαβεν, found only in this form, Il.:—said to be aeolic for ἕλετο (θέλετο) like ἦνθον for ἦλθον.
syncop. for ἐγένετο, v. γίγνομαι.
the under jaw, Od.; in pl. the jaws, the mouth, Il., Trag.; so in sg., Theogn., Eur.:—generally, the side of the face, cheek, Id.
the edge of an axe, a biting axe, Soph. (Cf. γένειον, γνάθος, Lat. gena.）

Enclitic Particle, serving to call attention to the word or words which it follows, by limiting the sense at least, at any rate, Lat. quidem, saltem, ὧδέ γε so at least, i. e. so and not otherwise, Il.; ὁ γ’ ἐνθάδε λεώς at any rate the people here, Soph.: with negatives, οὐ δύο γε, Lat. ne duo quidem, not even two, Il.; οὐ φθόγγος γε not the least sound, Eur.

with Pronouns:—with Pron. of 1st Pers. so closely joined, that the accent is changed, ἔγωγε, Lat. equidem; also σύγε, ὅγε, κεῖνός γε, τοῦτό γε, etc.; in attic after relat. Pronouns, ὅς γε, οἵ γε, etc., much like Lat. quippe qui, οἵ γέ σου καθύβρισαν Soph.
after Conjunctions of all kinds, πρίν γε, before at least; εἴ γε, ἐάν γε, ἄν γε, Lat. siquidem, if that is to say, if really; etc.
exercising an influence over the whole clause:
namely, that is, Διός γε διδόντος that is if God grant it, Od.; ἀνήρ, ὅστις πινυτός γε any man, — at least any wise man, Id.
in attic dialogue, where something is added to the statement of the previous speaker, as, ἔπεμψέ τίς σοι; Answ. καλῶς γε ποιῶν yes and quite right too, Ar.; so, πάνυ γε, etc., Plat.
implying concession, εἶμί γε well then I will go, Eur.

old, in Hom. and Trag.; of men, with notion of dignity, like signor, Id.; ὁ γεραιός that reverend sire, Il.:—comp. γεραίτερος, Hom.; οἱ γεραίτεροι the elders, senators, Aesch., Xen.; cf. γέρων:— Sup. γεραίτατος, Ar.; rarely = πρεσβύτατος, eldest, Theocr.
of things, ancient, Trag.
with old, wrinkled skin, Anth.
to honour or reward with a gift, τινά τινι Hom., etc.:—Pass. to be so honoured, Eur.
reversely, γ. τινί τι to present as an honorary gift, ap. Dem.
to celebrate, χοροῖσι with dances, Hdt.
a crane, Lat. grus, Il.
of reverend bearing, majestic, Il.
= γεραιός, Aesch.
γεραροί, οἱ, priests, Id.; γεραραί, priestesses, Dem.
honouring, Hhymn.
= γεραρός, honoured, Eur.
a gift of honour, Hom.; τὸ γὰρ γέρας ἐστι θανόντων this is the last honour of the dead, Il.:—any privilege or prerogative conferred on kings or nobles, Hom., Hdt., etc.
to guide an old man, Soph.
a little old man, Ar., Xen.
an old man's master, Plat.
a Council of Elders, Senate, Eur.
= πρεσβεία, Id.
for or befitting the seniors or chiefs, Il.; γ. ὅρκος an oath taken by them, Id.
anything made of wicker-work:
an oblong shield, covered with ox-hide, such as the Persians used, Hdt., Xen.
γέρρα, τά, wattled huts, or booths, used in the Athen. market-place, Dem.
the wicker body of a car, Strab.
a kind of troops that used wicker shields, Xen.
an old man, Hom., etc.
in political sense, γέροντες the Elders, Seniors, or Chiefs, who formed the King's Council, Hom.:—then, like Lat. Patres, the Senators, esp. at Sparta, Hdt.
as adj. old, mostly with a masc. Noun, Theogn., Aesch., etc.; but γέρον σάκος occurs in Od.
a taste, smack of a thing, Eur., Ar.
one must make to taste, τινά τινος Plat.

entry.etym: The Root was prob. ΓΕΥΣ, cf. Lat. gustare.
entry.sense: to give a taste of, τι Hdt.; rarely τινά τι Eur.; or τινά τινος Plat.: cf. γευστέος.
Mid. γεύομαι, with perf. pass., to taste of a thing, c. gen., Od., Thuc.

metaph. to taste, feel, δουρὸς ἀκωκῆς, ὀϊστοῦ γεύσασθαι Hom.; γευσόμεθ’ ἀλλήλων ἐγχείαις let us try one another with the spear, Il.: to taste the sweets of, ἀρχῆς, ἐλευθερίης Hdt.; to have experience of, μόχθων, πένθους Soph., Eur.
a dyke, dam or mound to bar a stream, in pl., Il.; the phrase πολέμοιο γεφύραι seems to mean the ground between two lines of battle, = μεταίχμιον, Id.
a bridge, to cross a stream, Hdt., attic; Hom. also seems to recognise this sense in the Verb γεφυρόω.
to abuse from the bridge: there was a bridge between Athens and Eleusis, and as the people passed it in procession, they had a custom of abusing whom they would: hence to abuse freely, Plut.
a reviler, Id.
bridge-maker, Lat. Pontifex, Plut.

to bridge over, make passable by a bridge, γεφύρωσε δέ μιν (sc. τὸν ποταμὸν ἡ πτελέη) the fallen tree made a bridge over the river, Il.; γ. τὸν ποταμόν to throw a bridge over it, Hdt.; ἐγεφυρώθη ὁ πόρος Id.
to make [a passage] like a bridge, γεφύρωσε κέλευθον he made a bridge- way, Il.
geography, Plut.
a geographer.
earth-like, earthy, Plat.; with deep soil, Xen.
a hill of earth, Strab., Anth.
crested with earth: as Subst., a hill, hillock, Xen.: so γεώλοφον, ου, τό, Theocr.
to measure the earth, to practise or profess geometry, Plat.
to measure, c. acc., Xen.
a land-measurer, geometer, Plat.
geometry, Hdt., Plat.
of or for geometry, geometrical, Plat.: γεωμετρικὴ (sc. τέχνη), geometry, Id.
skilled in geometry, a geometrician, Id.
a portion of land.
= γεωργία, Anth.
poor in land, Hdt.
to till the ground; γᾱπονεῖν Eur.
a husbandman, Anth.; in Babr.
to be a husbandman, farmer, Plat., Xen., etc.
c. acc. to till, plough, cultivate, Thuc., Dem.
metaph. to work at a thing, practise it, Lat. agitare, Id.; γ. ἔκ τινος to draw profit from it, live by it, Id.
tillage, agriculture, farming, Thuc., Plat.
in pl. farms, tilled land, Id.
of or for tillage, agricultural, Ar.; ὁ γ. λέως the country folk, Id.:— ἡ γ. (sc. τέχνη), agriculture, farming, Plat.
skilled in farming; and as Subst. a good farmer, Id.
tilling the ground, Ar.:—as Subst., γεωργός, ὁ, a husbandman, Hdt., Ar., Plat.
to dig in the earth, dig a mine, Hdt.
throwing up the earth, Strab.
cutting the ground, ploughing, Anth.
like αὐτόχθων, earthborn, of the primeval men, Hdt., Plat.
born of Gaia or Tellus, of the Titans and Giants, Aesch., Soph.; —so of things, portentous, furious, Ar.
a piece of land, Ar., Xen.
out of or from the earth, Aesch., Soph.

to rejoice, Hom.; c. acc. rei, τίς ἂν τάδε γηθήσειεν; Il.; c. part., γηθήσει προφανείσα (dual acc.) will rejoice at our appearing, Id.; γέγηθας ζῶν thou rejoicest in living, Soph.; γεγηθέναι ἐπί τινι Id.: part. γεγηθώς, like χαίρων, Lat. impune, Id.
joy, delight, Il.
joyful, glad at a thing, c. dat., Il.; absol., Id.
of earth, Xen., Plat.
a husbandman, Soph.
a hill, Xen.
one who has a share of land, a landowner: οἱ γ., the landowners, landlords, Lat. optimates, Hdt.
to possess land, Hdt.

earth opp. to heaven, or land opp. to sea, Hom., etc.; κατὰ γῆν on land, by land, Thuc.; κατὰ γῆς Xen.:— ἐπὶ γῆς on earth, Soph.; κατὰ γῆς below the earth, Trag.:—the gen. with local adverbs, ἵνα γῆς, ποῦ γῆς, ubi terrarum, where in (in what quarter of) the world, where on earth, Soph., etc.
earth, as an element, opp. to air, water, fire, Plat.
a land, country, Aesch., etc.; γῆν πρὸ γῆς from land to land, Id.
the earth or ground as tilled, Soph., Plat.
a lump of earth, in the phrase γῆν καὶ ὕδωρ αἰτεῖν, γῆν καὶ ὕδωρ διδόναι, in token of submission, Hdt.
a plot of ground, Aesch.
falling or fallen to earth, Eur.
longer form of γεραιός, aged, in old age, Hes., Hdt., Aesch.
to grow old, become old, and in aor. and perf. to be so, Hom., etc.; κηρύσσων γήρασκε grew old in his office of herald, Il.; of things, χρόνος γηράσκων Aesch.; c. acc. cogn., βίον γηράναι Soph.
Causal in aor1 ἐγήρᾱσα, to bring to old age, Aesch., Anth.
old age, Lat. senectus, Hom., etc.
to feed or tend in old age, Eur.: —Pass. to be so cherished, Ar.
feeding or tending in old age, Soph., Eur.
care of the aged,Plut.
tending old age, Hes.

entry.etym: fut. mid. in pass. sense, Dem.

entry.sense: born of sound, of echo, Theocr.
a voice, sound, tone, Aesch.
the three-bodied giant Geryon, i. e. the shouter, Pind.
voice, speech, Il., Soph., Eur.
to sing or say, speak, cry, Trag.; c. acc. cogn. to utter, Eur.
the Mid. is used in the same way, to sing, Hhymn.: c. acc. cogn., Hes., Eur.; τοὶ σκῶπες ἀηδόσι γαρύσαιντο let the owls sing against the nightingales, Theocr.
attic for γήθυον, a leek, Ar.
gigantic, Luc.
giant-killer, Anth.
giant-killing, Eur.
a grape-stone, Simon.: in pl. grapes, Ar.
mostly in pl. Γίγαντες, the Giants, a savage race destroyed by the gods, Od.; the sons of Gaia, Hes.
as adj. mighty, Ζέφυρος γίγας Aesch.
a hinge joint: a joint in a coat of mail, Xen.

entry.etym: γί-γνομαι is syncopated from γι-γένομαι, the Root being ΓΕΝ; cf. aor. 2 γενέσθαι, γένος, etc.; so Lat. gi-gno for gi-geno.
entry.sense: Radical sense, to come into being, Lat. gigni:
of persons, to be born, νέον γεγαώς new born, Od.; γεγονέναι ἔκ τινος Hdt.; more rarely ἀπό τινος Id.; τινος Eur.:—with Numerals, ἔτεα τρία καὶ δέκα γεγονώς, Lat. natus annos tredecim, Hdt., etc.
of things, to be produced, Plat., Xen., etc.:—of sums, ὁ γεγονὼς ἀριθμός the result or amount, Plat.

of events, to take place, come to pass, come on, happen, and in past tenses to be, Hom., etc.:— ὃ μὴ γένοιτο, Lat. quod dii prohibeant, Dem.:—c. dat. et part., γίγνεταί τί μοι βουλομένωι, ἀσμένωι I am glad at its being so, Thuc., etc.:—of sacrifices, omens, etc., to be favourable, Id., Xen.:—in neut. part., τὸ γενόμενον the event, the fact, Thuc.; τὰ γενόμενα the facts, Xen.; τὰ γεγενημένα former events, the past, Id.; τὸ γενησόμενον the future, Thuc.:—of Time, ὡς τρίτη ἡμέρη ἐγένετο arrived, Hdt.

followed by a Predicate, to come into a certain state, to become, Lat. fieri, and (in past tenses), to be so and so, Hom., etc.; πάντα γιγνόμενος turning every way, Od.; so, παντοῖος γ. Hdt.; τί γένωμαι; what am I to become? i. e. what is to become of me? Aesch.; οὐκ ἔχοντες ὅ τι γένωνται Thuc.
with Adverbs, κακῶς ἐγένετό μοι it went ill with me, Hdt.; εὖ, καλῶς, γίγνεται it goes well, etc., Xen.
followed by oblique cases of Nouns,

c. gen., γ. τῶν δικαστέων to become one of the jurymen, Hdt., etc.:— to fall to the share of, belong to, ἡ νίκη γίγνεταί τινος Xen.:— to be master of, ἑαυτοῦ γ. Soph., etc.; γ. ἐντὸς ἑωϋτοῦ Hdt.:—of things, to be at, i. e. to cost, so much, c. gen. pretii, Ar.

with Preps., γ. ἀπὸ, or ἐκ δείπνου to be done supper, Hdt.; γ. εἰς τόπον to be at . . , Id.:—. γ. ἐξ ὀφθαλμῶν τινι to be out of sight, Id.; γ. ἐν τόπωι to be in a place, Id.; also, γ. ἐν ποιήσει to be engaged in poetry, Id., etc.; γ. δι’ ἔχθρας, δι’ ἔριδος γ. τινι to be at enmity with, Ar., etc.:— γ. ἐπί τινι to fall into or be in one's power, Xen.:— γ. μετά τινος to be on his side, Id.:— γ. παρά τινα to come to one, Hdt.:— γ. πρὸς τόπωι to be at or near . . , Plat.: γ. πρός τινι to be engaged in . . , Dem.; πρός τι Plat.:— γ. πρὸ ὁδοῦ to be forward on the way, Il.

entry.etym: γιγνώσκω is redupl. from root ΓΝΩ, cf. γνῶναι, γνωτός, etc.: so Lat. gnosco.
entry.sense: to learn to know, to perceive, mark, learn, and in past tenses, to know, c. acc., Hom., etc.:—also to discern, distinguish, ὡς εὖ γιγνώσκηις ἠμὲν θεὸν ἠδὲ καὶ ἄνδρα that thou mayst discern between gods and men, Il.: c. gen., γνώτην ἀλλήλων were aware of each other, Od.; γνῶ χωομένοιο was aware of his being angry, Il.:—c. part., ἔγνων μιν οἰωνὸν ἐόντα perceived that he was a bird of omen, Od.; ἔγνων ἡττημένος I felt that I was beaten, Ar.:—but c. inf., ἵνα γνῶι τρέφειν that he may learn how to keep, Soph.

to observe, to form a judgment on a matter, to judge or think so and so, Hdt., attic: in dialogue, ἔγνων I understand, Soph.:—Pass. to be pronounced, of a sentence or judgment, Thuc., etc.:— also, to judge, determine, decree that . . , c. acc. et inf., Hdt., etc.
to be milky, juicy, Anth.
full of milk, Anth.
curdling milk, Anth.
poet. for γάλα, milk, Il.
living on milk, Il.
blear-eyed, Ar.
glaring fiercely, of a lion, Il.
gray-eyed, Plat.
in Hom., prob. without any notion of colour, gleaming, silvery, of the sea, Il., Trag.
later, certainly, with a notion of colour, bluish green, gray, Lat. glaucus, of the olive, Soph., Eur.:—esp. of the eyes light blue or gray, Lat. caesius, Hdt., Eur..
in Hom. as epith. of Athena, with gleaming eyes, brighteyed; v. γλαυκός.

the owl, so called from its glaring eyes (v. γλαυκός, and cf. σκώψ); γλαῦκ’ Ἀθήναζε, γλαῦκ’ εἰς Ἀθήνας = "carry coals to Newcastle, " Ar.: Athen. silver coins were called γλαῦκες, because they were stamped with an owl, Id.
smoothness, polish, Plut.
hollow, hollowed, of ships, Hom.; of caves, Id.; of the lyre, Od.; γλ. λιμήν a deep harbour or cove, Id.
polished, finished: of persons, subtle, critical, nice, exact, Ar.:—adv. -ρῶς, and neut. as adv., Luc.
to scrape up the ground, of a lion, Hes.
drinker of new wine, Anth.
Lat. mustum, new wine, Arist.
the pupil of the eye, eyeball, Hom., Soph.
because figures are reflected small in the pupil, a puppet, doll; as a taunt, ἔρρε, κακὴ γλήνη away, slight girl, Il.
in pl. things to stare at, shows, wonders, Il.
greedy-pettifogging-barefaced-knavish, Ar.
glutinous, sticky, clammy, Plat.:—metaph.,
sticking close, importunate, Ar.; γλίσχρως ἐπιθυμεῖν Plat.
greedy, grasping, niggardly, Arist.:—adv., Plat., Xen.; hence, with difficulty, hardly, γλίσχρως καὶ μόλις Dem.
of things, mean, shabby, meagre, Id., Plut.
a niggard, Ar.
to cling to, strive after, long for, a thing, c. gen., Hdt., Plat.; ὡς στρατηγήσεις γλίχεαι art anxious how to become general, Hdt.:—c. inf. to be eager to do, Plat., Dem.
sucking up grease, Anth.
as noun, any glutinous substance, gluten, gum, γλ. ἀπὸ τῆς ὕλης tree- gum, Hdt.
as adj. slippery, knavish, Ar.
the rump, Il.:—pl. the buttocks, Lat. nates, Id., Hdt.
to sweeten:— Pass. to be sweetened, to turn sweet, Mosch.
with sweet skin, Anth.
causing sweet tears, Anth.
with sweet gifts, Anth.
sweet-sounding, Anth.
sweetness of mind: benevolence, Plut.
sweet-minded, sweet of mood, Il.
act. charming the mind, delightful. Ar.
bearing sweet fruit, Theocr.
sweet-apple, as a term of endearment, Theocr.
sweetly winning, Hhymn.
sweet-speaking, Anth.
having a fair offspring, Anth.
a sweet maid, Anth.
sweet, Il., etc.:—metaph. sweet, delightful, Hom., etc.:— γλυκύ ἐστι c. inf., Aesch., etc.
of water, sweet, fresh, opp. to πικρός, Hdt.
after Hom., of persons, sweet, dear, Soph.; ὦ γλυκύτατε my dear fellow, Ar.:—sometimes in bad sense, simple, silly, ὡς γλυκὺς εἶ! Plat.
sweetness, Hdt.
a graving tool, chisel, Anth.
a carver, sculptor, Anth.
carved, Anth.
a tool for carving, knife, chisel, Hhymn., Theocr.; γλ. καλάμου a pen-knife, Anth.
the notched end of the arrow, Hom., Hdt.; πτερωταὶ γλυφίδες the arrow itself, Eur.
to carve, cut out with a knife, Ar.; γλ. σφρηγῖδας to engrave them, Hdt.; of sculptors, Id.
to note down [on tablets], τόκους Anth.
the beard of corn, Hes.
endless talking, wordiness, Eur.
talking till one's tongue aches.
the tongue, Hom., etc.

the tongue, as the organ of speech, γλώσσης χάριν through love of talking, Hes., Aesch.; ἀπὸ γλώσσης by word of mouth, Hdt., Thuc.; οὐκ ἀπὸ γλώσσης not by word of mouth, not from mere hearsay, Aesch.; so, οὐ κατὰ γλῶσσαν Soph.; ἱέναι γλῶσσαν to let loose one's tongue, speak without restraint, Id.; pl., κερτομίοις γλώσσαις, i.e. with blasphemies, Id.:—for βοῦς ἐπὶ γλώσσηι, v. βοῦς.
a tongue, language, Hom., Hdt., etc.
the tongue or mouthpiece of a pipe, Aeschin.
a case for the mouthpiece of a pipe: generally, a case, casket, NTest.
= γλῶσσα 111, the mouth-piece of a pipe , Luc.
any projecting point, hence,
the end of the yoke-strap, Il.
the point of an arrow, Soph., Anth.
the jaw, poet. form of γνάθος, Hom.; also in pl., Od.: metaph., γναθμοὶ φαρμάκων the gnawing of poison, Eur.; for ἀλλοτρίοις γναθμοῖσι, v. ἀλλότριος.
the jaw, properly the lower jaw, ἡ κάτω γν. Hdt.; ἔπαγε γνάθον take your teeth to it! Ar.; oft. in pl., Plat., etc.
metaph. of fire, Aesch.
metaph. also, like Lat. fauces, of a narrow strait, Id., Xen.
the point or edge, as of a wedge, Aesch.
curved, bent, Hom.
supple, pliant, of the limbs of living men, Id.
metaph. to be bent, οὔτε νόημα γναμπτὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσι (of Achilles), Il.
to bend; γν. τινα to bend his will, Aesch.

of or belonging to the race, i. e. lawfully begotten, legitimate, opp. to νόθος, Hom.; φρονεῖν γνήσια to have a noble mind, Eur.; γν. γυναῖκες lawful wives, opp. to παλλακίδες, Xen.; γν. τῆς Ἑλλάδος true sons of Greece, Dem.:—adv. -ίως, lawfully, really, truly, Eur.
with bent knee: γνὺξ ἐριπεῖν to fall on the knee, Il.
a mark, token, like γνώρισμα, Hdt., Soph.
an opinion, judgment, = γνώμη, Aesch., Eur.
to form a judgment of, discern, Plat.
a means of knowing, a mark, token, Theogn.
the organ by which one knows, the mind: hence,

thought, judgment, intelligence, Soph.: acc. absol., γνώμην ἱκανός intelligent, Hdt.; γν. ἀγαθός Soph.; γνώμην ἔχειν to understand, Id.; προσέχειν γνώμην to give heed, be on one's guard:— ἀπὸ γνώμης with a good conscience, Aesch.; but, οὐκ ἀπὸ γν. not without judgment, with good sense, Soph.

one's mind, will, purpose, Aesch., etc.; ἐν γνώμηι γεγονέναι τινί to stand high in his favour, Hdt.; τὴν γν. ἔχειν πρός τινα or τι tohave a mind, be inclined towards . . , Thuc.; ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ γνώμης of his own accord, Id.; ἐκ μιᾶς γν. of one accord, Dem.; so, μιᾶι γνώμηι Thuc.:—in pl., φίλιαι γνῶμαι friendly sentiments, Hdt.

a judgment, opinion, πλεῖστός εἰμι τῆι γνώμηι I incline mostly to the opinion that . . , Hdt.; so, ταύτηι πλεῖστος τὴν γν. or ἡ πλείστη γν. ἐστί μοι Id.; γνώμην ἔχειν, like λόγον ἔχ., to be right, Ar.; κατὰ γν. τὴν ἐμήν mea sententia, Hdt.; absol., γνώμην ἐμήν Ar.; παρὰ γνώμην contrary to general opinion, Thuc.:—of orators, γνώμην ἀποφαίνειν, ἀποδείκνυσθαι to deliver an opinion, Hdt.; τίθεσθαι Soph.; δηλοῦν Thuc.
like Lat. sententia, a proposition, motion, γνώμην εἰσφέρειν Hdt.; εἰπεῖν, προθεῖναι Thuc.; γνώμην νικᾶν to carry a motion, Ar.
γνῶμαι the opinions of wise men, maxims, Lat. sententiae.
a purpose, resolve, intent, Thuc.:— τινά ἔχουσα γνώμην; with what purpose? Hdt.; ἡ ξύμπασα γν. τῶν λεχθέντων the general purport . . , Thuc.
a fancy, Ar.
to speak in maxims, Arist.
a speaking in maxims, Plat.
（γνώμων I) fit to give judgment, Xen.: experienced in a thing, c. gen., Plat.
（γνώμων II) of or for sun-dials, Anth.
prudence, judgment, Solon.
clever at coining maxims, Ar.
maxim-coining, sententious, Ar.
one that knows or examines, a judge, interpreter, Aesch., Thuc., Xen.
the gnomon or index of the sundial, Hdt.
οἱ γνώμονες, the teeth that mark a horse's age, Xen.
a carpenter's rule: metaph. a rule of life, Theogn.
to make known, point out, explain, Aesch.:—Pass. to become known, Plat.
c. acc. pers. to make known, τινά τινι Plut.
to gain knowledge of, discover that a thing is, c. part., Soph., Thuc.
to be acquainted with, make acquaintance with, τινά Plat., Dem.
well-known, familiar, of persons and things, Plat., etc.:—as Subst. an acquaintance, Od., Xen., etc.
known to all, notable, distinguished, οἱ γνώριμοι the notables or wealthy class, opp. to δῆμος, Id.:—Sup., οἱ γνωριμώτατοι Dem.
adv. -μως, intelligibly, Eur.
acquaintance, τινος with another, Plat.: knowledge, Id.
that by which a thing is made known, a mark, token Xen.; γνωρίσματα tokens by which a lost child is recognised, Plut.
one must know, Arist.

ionic Verb, to fight with one's own opinion, i. e. to change one's mind, to recognise one's own fighting power (as compared with the enemy): hence to give way, submit, Hdt., Eur., Ar.; γν. μὴ εἶναι ὁμοῖοι to give way and confess that they are not equal, Hdt.
a knowing, knowledge, Plat., NTest.
acquaintance with a person, πρός τινα ap. Aeschin.
a knowing, recognising, Thuc.
a being known, fame, credit, Luc.
one must know, Plat.
one that knows: a surety, Lat. cognitor, Xen.
one that knows, NTest.
a surety, Plut.
good at knowing: ἡ -κή (sc. δύναμις) the faculty of knowing, Plat.
known, to be known, Aesch., Soph., Xen.
of things, perceived, understood, known, Hom.; γνωτὰ κοὐκ ἄγνωτά μοι Soph.
of persons, well-known, Od.:—as Subst. a kinsman, brother, γνωτοί τε γνωταί τε brothers and sisters, Il.
to wail, groan, weep, Hom.:—c. acc. to bewail, mourn, lament, weep for, Il.; ὑπέρ τινος Mosch.:—so also in Mid., Aesch., Soph.:—Pass., γοᾶται Aesch.
to mutter, murmur, NTest.
round, Ar.
a murmuring, NTest.
a murmurer, NTest.
of things, mournful, lamentable, Aesch., Eur.
of persons, lamenting, Eur.
one who howls out enchantments, a sorcerer, enchanter, Hdt., Eur.; γόησι καταείδοντες charming by means of sorcerers, Hdt.
a juggler, cheat, Plat., Dem.
juggling, cheatery, Plat.
to bewitch, beguile, Plat.
a wailer; or, in adv. sense, of lamentation, Aesch.
bewitching.
γοῖ, γοῖ, to imitate the sound of pigs grunting, Anth.
a ship's freight, burden, tonnage, Hdt., Dem.
a beast's load, Babr.
to load, Babr.
rattling between the teeth, Anth.
a grinder-tooth, Lat. molaris, Hdt., Ar., etc.
fastened with bolts, well-bolted, Ar.
a bolt, for ship-building, Od.; and for other uses, Hes., Aesch.:—generally, any bond or fastening, of the cross-ribs of canoes, Hdt.
to fasten with bolts, of ships:—in Pass., γεγόμφωται σκάφος the ship's hull is ready built, Aesch.
that which is fastened by bolts, frame-work, Plut.
a ship-builder, Anth.
a begetter, father: in pl. γονεῖς, έων, οἱ, the parents, Hes., attic: also, a progenitor, ancestor, Hdt.
produce, offspring, Hom., etc.; so in pl., Soph.
like γενεά, γένος, a race, stock, family, Trag.
a generation, Aesch.
that which engenders, the seed, Hes., Hdt., etc.
the womb, Eur.
of the mother, child-birth, Id., Theocr.
of the child, birth, Soph.
γονίας χειμών, perhaps a violent storm, Aesch.
productive, fruitful: γ. μέλεα a parent's limbs, Eur.
metaph. of persons, genuine, Ar.; γ. ὕδωρ Anth.
like γονή, that which is begotten, offspring, a child, Il., Hdt.; ὁ Πηλέως γ. his son, Soph.
any product, of the silver mines at Laureion, Aesch.; of tribute, Ar.
ἐς ἔρσενα γόνον to any of the male sex, Hdt.
like γένος, one's race, stock, descent, Od.
to fall on the knee, to fall down before one, τινι or τινα NTest.
falling on the knee, ἕδραι γον. a kneeling posture, Eur.

entry.etym: the ionic forms γούνατος, -ατι in Trag., but never γουνός, γουνί
entry.sense: the knee, Lat. genu, Hom., etc.

ἅψασθαι γούνων to clasp the knees as a suppliant, Il.; so ἑλεῖν, λαβεῖν, γούνων Id.; τῶν γουνάτων λαβέσθαι Hdt.; περὶ or ἀμφὶ γούνασί τινος χεῖρας βαλεῖν Od.; ἀμφὶ γόνυ τινὸς πίπτειν Eur.; γούνων λίσσεσθαι to supplicate by [clasping] the knees, Hom.; ἄντεσθαι or λίσσεσθαι πρὸς τῶν γονάτων Eur.

of a sitting posture, γόνυ κάμψειν bend the knee so as to sit down, Il.:— ἐπὶ γούνασι on one's knees, of a child, Id.; πέπλον θεῖναι Ἀθηναίης ἐπὶ γούνασιν to lay it on her lap (as an offering), Id.; metaph., θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται, i. e. rests on their will and pleasure, Hom.
the knees are in Hom. the seat of strength; hence, γούνατά τινος λύειν to weaken, lame, kill him, Il.: also, metaph., ἐς γόνυ βάλλειν to bring down upon the knee, i. e. to humble, conquer, Hdt.
proverb., ἀπωτέρω ἢ γόνυ κνήμη "Charity begins at home, " Theocr.
the knee or joint of grasses, such as the cane, Lat. geniculum, Hdt., Xen.
weeping, wailing, groaning, howling, mourning, lamentation, Hom., Trag.
of the Gorgon, Hom.
of Gorgias, Gorgias-like, Xen.
he of the Gorgon-crest, Ar.; fem. Γοργολόφα, ης, ἡ, Id.
with the Gorgon on it, of a shield, Ar.
Pass. to be hot or spirited, of a horse, Xen.
grim, fierce, terrible, Aesch., Eur.; γοργὸς ἰδεῖν terrible to behold, Xen.; of horses, hot, spirited, Id.
Gorgon-killing: fem. Γοργοφόνη, as a name of Athena, Eur.
fierce-eyed, Aesch., Eur.; γοργῶπις of Athena, Soph.

entry.etym: The regular sg. is Γοργώ, gen. Γοργοῦς, dat. Γοργοῖ : later, cases were formed as if from a nom. Γοργών, sc. gen. Γοργόνος; dat. Γοργόνι:— in pl., Γοργόνες, acc. -ας are the only forms.
entry.sense: the Gorgon, i. e. the grim one (cf. γοργός), Hom.: Hes. speaks of three Gorgons, Euryale, Stheino, Medusa, —the last being the Gorgon; her snaky head was fixed on the aegis of Athena, and all who looked on it became stone, Eur.
to clasp another's knees (v. γόνυ I. 2), and so to implore, entreat, supplicate, Il.; c. inf. to implore one to do a thing, Id.; ὑπέρ τινος in behalf of another, Id.; πρός τινος by another, Od.

entry.etym: Dep. only in pres. and imperf.

entry.sense: cramping the knees, Hes.
thick-kneed, Hes. .
a hill, γ. Ἀθηνάων the hill or citadel of Athens, Od.; ὁ γ. ὁ Σουνιακός the hill of Sunium, Hdt.; ἀνὰ γουνὸν ἀλωῆς up the slope of the threshing floor, Od.

entry.etym: γε οὖν a stronger form of γε
entry.sense: at least then, at any rate, any way, γνώσει ὀψὲ γοῦν τὸ σωφρονεῖν Aesch.; used in quoting an example, Thuc., Xen.; also in answers, yes certainly, τὰς γοῦν Ἀθήνας οἶδα Soph.
an old woman, fem. of γραῦς, γέρων (v. γεραιά), Od., Soph., Eur.; γραῖαι δαίμονες, of the Eumenides, Aesch.
as adj. in the obl. cases, old, withered, Id., Eur.
Γραῖαι, αἱ, daughters of Phorcys and Ceto, with fair faces, but hair gray from their birth, Hes.
an old hag, old woman, Ar., Xen.
Pass. to become an old woman, Anth.
σταφυλὴ γραίη raisins, Anth.
that which is drawn, in pl. the lines of a drawing or picture, Eur., Theocr.: in sg. a drawing, picture, Plat.

that which is written, a written character, letter, Lat. litera, Hdt., etc.; and in pl. letters, Aesch.; hence, the alphabet, Hdt., Plat.; γρ. to have learnt to read, Id.; ἐδίδασκες γράμματα, ἐγὼ δ’ ἐφοίτων you kept school, — I went there, Dem.
a note in music, Anth.
in pl. also, a piece of writing, and, like Lat. literae, a letter, Hdt., Eur.: an inscription, epitaph, Hdt.
papers or documents of any kind, records, accounts, Ar., Oratt.:—in sg. a bill, account, NTest.
a man's writings, i. e. a book, treatise, Xen.:—also, letters, learning, Plat.
the office of the γραμματεύς, Plut.
small tablets, Dem., Plut.
that on which one writes, tablets, Plat., etc.
an account-book, register, Dem.
a secretary, clerk, Lat. scriba, Thuc., etc.
to be secretary, Thuc., etc.; c. gen., γρ. τοῦ συνεδρίου Epigr.
a letter-carrier, Plut.
Dep. to be a grammarian, Anth.
knowing one's letters, well grounded in the rudiments, a grammarian, Xen., etc.:—adv. -κῶς, Plat.:— ἡ -κή (with or without τέχνη) grammar, Id.
= γραμματεύς, Hdt., Plat.
one who teaches γράμματα, a schoolmaster, Xen., Plat.
mother of letters, epith. of ink, Anth.
nickname of a γραμματεύς, a porer over records, Dem.
a puzzle-headed grammarian, Anth.
to carry or deliver letters, Strab.
letter-carrying, Polyb.
a box for keeping records, Plut.
the stroke of a pen, a line, Plat.
= βαλβίς, the line across the course, to mark the starting or winning post, Ar.: metaph. of life, Horace's ultima linea rerum, Eur.
the middle line on a board (like our draught-board), also called ἡ ἱερά, proverb., τὸν ἀπὸ γραμμῆς or ἀφ’ ἱερᾶς κινεῖν λίθον to move one's man from this line, i. e. try one's last chance, Theocr.
ἡ μακρά (sc. γραμμή), the long line, i. e. the line of condemnation drawn by the dicast, Ar.
scaring old women, Ar.
one must describe, Xen.
γραπτέος, η, ον, to be described, Luc.
a writer, Anth.
marked as with letters, ἁ γραπτὰ ὑάκινθος Theocr.
a scratching, tearing, Od.
an old woman, Hom., Aesch.; γρ. παλαιή Od.; γραῦς γυνή Eur.
scum, as of boiled milk, Ar.
a painter, Eur.
= γραμματεύς, Xen.
representation by means of lines:
drawing or delineation, Hdt.; of painting, Id., Plat.
a drawing, painting, picture, ὅσον γραφῆι only in a picture, Hdt.; πρέπουσα ὡς ἐν γραφαῖς Aesch.
writing, the art of writing, Plat.
a writing, Soph.: a letter, Thuc.; so in pl., like γράμματα, Eur.: ψευδεῖς γρ. false statements, Id.
（γράφομαι) as attic law-term, an indictment in a public prosecution, a criminal prosecution undertaken by the state, opp. to δίκη (a private action), Plat., etc.
capable of drawing or painting, Plat.:— ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη), the art of painting, Id.
of things, as if painted, as in painting, Plut.
of or for writing, suited for writing, Arist.: ὑπόθεσις γρ. a subject for description, Plut.: adv. -κῶς, Id.
a stile for writing on waxen tablets, Plat., etc.: a needle for embroidering, Anth.
embroidery, Id.

Orig. sense, to scratch, scrape, graze, αἰχμὴ γράψεν ὀστέον Il.; σήματα γράψας ἐν πίνακι having scratched marks as tokens on a tablet, Id.:—then, to represent by lines drawn, to delineate, draw, paint, Hdt., Aesch.; εἰκὼν γεγραμμένη Ar.: also in Mid., ζῷα γράφεσθαι = ζωγραφεῖν, Hdt.
to express by written characters, to write, τι Id.; γο. τινά to write a person's name, Xen.; γ. ἐπιστολήν, etc., Id.; γρ. τι εἰς διφθέρας Hdt.
to inscribe, like ἐπιγράφω, γρ. εἰς στήλην Eur., Dem.
to write down, γρ. τινὰ αἴτιον to set him down as the cause, Hdt.
to register, enrol, γρ. τινὰ τῶν ἱππευόντων among the cavalry, Xen.; Κρέοντος προστάτου γεγράψομαι, as a dependent of Creon, Soph.

to write down a law to be proposed; hence to propose, move, γνώμην, νόμον Xen.: so, absol., γράφειν (sub. νόμον), Dem.; γρ. πόλεμον, εἰρήνην, etc., Id.; c. inf. to move that . .; ἔγραψα ἀποπλεῖν τοὺς πρέσβεις Id.
Mid. to write for oneself or for one's own use, note down, Hdt., Aesch., etc.

as attic law-term, γράφεσθαί τινα to indict one, τινός for some public offence, Plat., etc.; c. acc. et inf., γρ. τινὰ ἀδικεῖν Id.: absol., οἱ γραψάμενοι the prosecutors, Id.:—also, γράφεσθαί τι denounce as criminal, Dem.:—Pass. to be indicted, Id., etc.; τὰ γεγραμμένα the articles of the indictment, Id.; τὸ γεγραμμένον the penalty named in the indictment, Id.:—but γέγραμμαι usually takes the sense of the Mid., to indict, Id.
like an old woman, Strab., NTest.

entry.etym: late pres., formed from perf. ἐγρήγορα
entry.sense: to be awake or wakeful, NTest.
γρῑπηῒς, τέχνη, ἡ, the art of fishing, Anth.
a fisherman, Anth.
like γρῖπος, a fishing-basket, creel, made of rushes, Plut.
metaph. anything intricate, a dark saying, riddle, Ar.
to say γρῦ, to grunt, grumble, mutter, Ar.
to grunt, of swine, Ar.
a pig, porker, Plut.
a kind of griffin or dragon, Ar.
hook-nosed, with aquiline nose, opp. to σιμός, Xen., Plat.
generally, curved, γρυπὴ γαστήρ a round paunch, Xen.
hookedness, of the nose, opp. to σιμότης, Xen.
a grunt, as of swine: hence οὐδὲ γρῦ ἀποκρίνεσθαι to answer not even with a grunt, Ar.; οὐδὲ γρῦ ἀπαγγέλλειν Dem.
a griffin or dragon, Hdt., Aesch.
a cavern, a hollow vessel, kneading-trough, Anth.
a hollow, as of the cuirass (θώρηξ), which was composed of a back-piece and breast-piece, called γύαλα, joined at the sides by clasps or buckles (πόρπαι, περόναι), Il.
the hollow of a vessel or a hollow vessel, Eur.
the hollow of a rock, Soph.: a cavern, grotto, Eur.
in pl., vales, dales, dells, Hes., Eur.
the piece of wood in a plough, to which the share was fitted, the plough-tree, Lat. buris, Hes.
a piece of land (cf. Lat. juger), Eur.: mostly in pl. lands, fields, Aesch., Soph.:— metaph. of a wife, Id.
weighing down the limbs, Aesch.
gnawing the limbs, Hes.
a limb, Hom., in pl., γυῖα λέλυντο, τρόμος or κάματος λάβε γυῖα, so Trag.; γυῖα ποδῶν the feet, Il.; γυῖα the hands, Theocr.; and γυῖον in sg. the hand, Id.
stiffening the limbs, Anth.
a fetter, Aesch.
lame, Anth.
wasting the limbs, Anth.
pass. with pining limbs, Id.
of brasen limb, Anth.
to lame, Il.; γυιωθείς lame, Hes.
long-necked, scraggy-necked, Ar.
a long-shaped wallet, Ar.

to train naked, train in gymnastic exercise: generally, to train, exercise, Xen.: c. inf. to train or accustom persons to do a thing, Id.; so also, γ. τινά τινι to accustom him to it, Id.:—Mid. to exercise for oneself, practise, γ. τέχνην Plat.:—Pass. to practise gymnastic exercises, Hdt., etc.: generally, to practise, exercise oneself, Thuc., Xen.; γυμνάζεσθαι πρός τι to be trained for a thing, Plat.; περί τι in a thing, Xen.
metaph. to wear out, harass, distress, Aesch.:—Pass., Id.
exercise, NTest.
to be gymnasiarch, at Athens, Oratt.: Mid., Xen.:—Pass. to be supplied with gymnasiarchs, Id.
a gymnasiarch, who superintended the palaestrae, and paid the training masters, Dem., etc.
the office of a gymnasiarch, Xen.
of or for a gymnasiarch, Plut.
in pl. bodily exercises, Hdt., etc.
in sg. the public place where athletic exercises were practised, the gymnastic school, Eur., etc.; ἐκ θἠμετέρου γυμνασίου from our school, Ar.: pl., γ. ἱππόκροτα the hippodrome, Eur.
fem. of γυμνός, naked, Eur.
trained, Id.
one must practise, Xen.
a trainer of professional athletes, Xen., Plat.
fond of athletic exercises, skilled in them, Plat.: ἡ -κή (with or without τέχνη), gymnastics, Id.:—adv. -κῶς, Ar.
a light-armed foot-soldier, slinger, Hdt., Eur., Xen.
to be light-armed, Plut.
as adj. naked, Luc.
the light-armed troops, Thuc.
of or for a light-armed soldier (γυμνής), Xen.
of or for gymnastic exercises, Hdt., Thuc.
to be naked, NTest.
a festival in honour of those who fell at Thyrea, at which boys went through gymnastic exercises, Hdt., Thuc., Xen.
the naked philosophers of India, Plut.
naked, unclad, Od., etc.
unarmed, Il., etc.:— τὰ γυμνά the parts not covered by armour, the exposed parts, Thuc., Xen.: esp. the right side (the left being covered by the shields), Thuc.
of things, γυμνὸν τόξον an uncovered bow, i. e. taken out of the case, Od.
c. gen. stripped of a thing, Hdt., Aesch.
in common language γυμνός meant lightly clad, i. e. in the tunic only (χιτών), without the mantle (ἱμάτιον), Lat. nudus, Hes., Xen.
bare, mere, NTest.
nakedness, NTest.

to strip naked, Soph.; τὰ ὀστέα τῶν κρεῶν γ. to strip the bones of their flesh, Hdt.:—in Pass., of warriors, to be left naked or exposed, Hom.; so, τεῖχος ἐγυμνώθη the wall was left bare, i. e. defenceless, Il.: but also to strip oneself naked or to be stript naked, Od.; c. gen., ἐγυμνώθη ῥακέων he stript himself of his rags, Id.; so later, γυμνωθὲν ξίφος Hdt.
a stripping.
nakedness: ἐξαλλάσσειν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γ. his defenceless side (cf. γυμνός 2), Thuc.
to be stript of, τινός Plat.
of or belonging to women, like women, befitting them, feminine, Lat. muliebris, Od., etc.:— ἡ γ. θεός, the Roman bona dea, Plut.: γ. πόλεμος war with women, Anth.
in bad sense, womanish, effeminate, Plat., etc.
as Subst. ἡ γυναικηΐη = γυναικών, the women's apartments, harem, Hdt.
a weakling, Luc.
devised by a woman, Aesch.
proclaimed by a woman, Aesch.
a woman's nature, Plut.
the dominion of women, Arist., Plut.
aping women, Aesch., Eur.
in woman's shape, Eur.
the office of γυναικονόμος, Arist.
one of a board of magistrates, appointed to maintain good manners among the women, Arist.
full of women, Aesch., Eur.
woman-avenging, Aesch.
woman-loving, Theocr.
the women's apartments in a house, opp. to ἀνδρών (cf. γυναικών), Lys.:— the women of the harem, Plut.
mad for women, Il.
γύναια δῶρα presents made to a woman, Od.
as Subst., little woman, wifey, as a term of endearment, Ar.:— in a contemptuous sense, a weak woman, Dem., etc.

entry.etym: Prob. from same Root as γίγνομαι.
entry.sense: a woman, Lat. femina, opp. to man, Hom., etc.; with a second Subst., γυνὴ ταμίη housekeeper, δέσποινα γ., δμωαὶ γυναῖκες, etc., Id.:—in voc. often as a term of respect, mistress, lady, Theocr.:— πρὸς γυναικός like a woman, Aesch.
a wife, spouse, opp. to παρθένος, Hom., Xen.
a mortal woman, opp to a goddess, Hom.
a womanish man, Theocr.
a nest, cranny, Ar.
a vulture's nest: a hole.
of a vulture, Luc.
to run round in a circle, Strab., Babr.
tracing a circle, Anth.
a tadpole, Plat.
running round in a circle, Anth.
a ring, circle, Polyb.
round, γυρὸς ἐν ὤμοισι round- shouldered, Od.
chalk, Hdt., Plat.
to rub with chalk, chalk over, Hdt.
a vulture, Il.; cf. αἰγυπιός.
a corner, angle, Hdt.
a joiner's square, Plat.
a squaring the angles: ἐπῶν γωνιασμοί the finishing of verses by square and rule, Ar.
angular, Thuc.
a bow-case, quiver, Od.; as fem., Anth.
a wax doll, puppet, Theocr.
used of firewood, Ar.
a torch-feast, Luc.
to hold the office of δαιδοῦχος, to carry a torch, esp. in pageants, Eur.
a torch-bearer, an officer at the mysteries of Eleusinian Demeter, Arist.
to carry torches, Luc.
knowing, experienced in a thing, ἔν τινι Il.; c. gen., Od.:— δαημονέστατος Xen.
a husband's brother, brother, in-law, Lat. levir, answering to the fem. γάλως, Il.
cunningly or curiously wrought, of work in metal or wood, Hom.; of embroidery, Hes., Eur.
cunning, of the artificer's skill, Anth.
to work cunningly, deck or inlay with curious arts, to embellish, Hom.:—Pass., perf. part. δεδαιδαλμένος, Pind.
a work of art, Theocr.
cunningly or curiously wrought, Aesch.: in Hom. only in neut. as Subst., δαίδαλα πάντα all cunning works, Il.; so in sg., Od.
as prop. n., Δαίδαλος, ὁ, Daedalus, i. e. the cunning worker, the artist, from Cnosus in Crete, contemporary with Minos, mentioned in Il. as maker of a χορός for Ariadne.
cunning of hand, Anth.
to cleave asunder, cleave, Hom., Aesch.
to slay, smite, Il., Aesch.
to rend, tear, χερσὶ κόμην ἤισχυνε δαΐζων Il.:—Pass., χαλκῷ δεδαϊγμένος Id.; δεδαϊγμένος ἦτορ through the heart, Id.; δεδαϊγμένον ἦτορ a heart torn by misery, Od.; δαϊχθείς Pind., Eur.
simply, to divide, ἐδαΐζετο θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν his soul was divided within him, i. e. was in doubt, Il.; δαϊζόμενος κατὰ θυμὸν διχθάδια divided or doubting between two opinions, Id.
a slayer:— as adj. heart-rending, Aesch.
to be under the power of a δαίμων, to suffer by a divine visitation, δαιμονᾶν κακοῖς to be plunged in heaven-sent woes, Aesch.; so, δ. ἐν ἄται Id.:— absol. to be possessed, to be mad, Eur., Xen.
Mid. to be possessed by a demon or evil spirit, NTest.
the Deity, Lat. numen, or divine operation, Hdt., Eur., etc.: a fatality, Dem.
an inferior divine being, a demon, Xen., Plat.
a demon, evil spirit, NTest.
of or belonging to a δαίμων:

voc. δαιμόνιε, δαιμονίη, mostly in the way of reproach, thou luckless wight! thou wretch! sirrah! madam! Il.;—more rarely by way of admiration, noble sir! excellent man! Id., Hes.; also by way of pity, poor wretch! so in Hdt., δαιμόνιε ἀνδρῶν; also in an iron. sense, my good fellow! good sir! ὦ δαιμόνι’ ἀνδρῶν, ὦ δαιμόνι’, ὦ δαιμόνι’ ἀνθρώπων Ar., Plat.
anything proceeding from the Deity, heaven-sent, divine, miraculous, Hdt., attic; εἰ μή τι δαιμόνιον εἴη were it not a divine intervention, Xen.; τὰ δαιμόνια visitations of Heaven, Thuc.
of persons, divine, excellent, Plat.
adv. -ως, by Divine power, marvellously, Ar.:—so neut. pl. δαιμόνια Id., Xen.; δαιμονιώτατα most clearly by the hand of the gods, Id.
demoniacal, devilish, NTest.

entry.etym: Perh. from δαίω B, to divide or distribute destinies.
entry.sense: a god, goddess, like θεός, θεά, Hom., Trag., etc.:—in Hom. also deity or divine power (θεός denotes a god in person), Lat. numen; πρὸς δαίμονα against the divine power; σὺν δαίμονι with it, by its favour, Il.:—so, κατὰ δαίμονα, nearly = τύχηι, by chance, Hdt.; ἐν τῶι δ. = θεῶν ἐν γούνασι, Soph.
one's daemon or genius, one's lot or fortune, στυγερὸς δαίμων Od.; δαίμονος αἶσα κακή Id.: absol. good or ill fortune, Trag.; esp. of the evil genius of a family, Aesch.
δαίμονες, in Hes., are the souls of men of the golden age, forming the link between gods and men:—later, of any departed souls, Lat. manes, lemures, Luc.
in NTest. an evil spirit, a demon, devil.
to divide :—to give a banquet or feast, δαίνυ δαῖτα γέρουσι Il.; δ. γάμον to give a marriage-feast, Hom.; δ. τάφον to give a funeral feast, Id.
c. acc. pers. to feast one, Hdt.; ζῶν μὲ δαίσεις thou shalt be my living feast, Aesch.
Mid. to have a feast given one, to feast, Hom., Hdt.
c. acc. to feast on, consume, eat, Id.; μίαν δ. τράπεζαν to eat at a common table, Theocr.:— also of poison, to consume, Soph.

entry.etym: In signf. II from *δάω, δαῆναι: in signf. I perh. from δαΐς battle.
entry.sense: hostile, destructive, dreadful, epith. of πῦρ, burning, consuming, Il., Trag.:— δάϊοι, δᾶιοι enemies, Aesch., Soph.; in sg. an enemy, Ar.; hence as adj. hostile, Id.
unhappy, wretched, Trag.
knowing, cunning, Anth.
unhappy in mind, miserable, Aesch.
colloquial form of δή used after interrogatives, τί δαὶ λέγεις σύ; Ar.; τί δαί; what? how? Id., Plat.
a fire-brand, pine-torch, Lat. taeda, Hom.
as collective noun, pine-wood, such as torches were made of, Thuc., Xen.
war, battle, Hom., Aesch.

entry.etym: δαίω2, to divide a meal, feast, banquet
entry.sense: often in Hom., who calls the usual meal δαὶς ἐΐση, equally divided; Θυέστου δαῖτα παιδείων κρεῶν the feast of Thyestes on the flesh of his children, Aesch.; in pl., Od.
of the meat or food itself, Eur.
a banqueter, feaster, Aesch., Ar.
from a feast, Od., Theocr.
poet. for δαίς, a feast, banquet, Il.
to cut up meat, cut into joints or to carve, Od.: to cut up for distribution among the people, Il.
one's portion, δαιτρὸν πίνειν Il.
one that carves meat, a carver, Od.
the art of carving meat, a helping at table, Od.
one that is entertained, an invited guest, in pl., Hom., Hdt.:—in sg., Plat.; ὁ ξένων δαιτυμών who makes his meal on strangers, Eur.
a meal, Il.

in Il., mostly, of warriors; in Od., of Ulysses. In the first case (from δάϊς battle, φρήν) of warlike mind, warlike;— in the second (from *δάω, φρήν) wise of mind, prudent. Others take *δάω as the Root in all cases, and translate skilful, proved.

entry.etym: The Root is ΔΑϜ, which appears in the perf. pass. part. δεδαυμένος, Semon.
the perfect and pluperfect forms are commonly used with the present and imperfect meanings.
entry.sense: to light up, make to burn, kindle, Lat. accendo, Il., Aesch.:—Pass. to blaze, burn fiercely, Il.; πυρὶ ὄσσε δεδήει blazed with fire, Od.; metaph., πόλεμος, μάχη δέδηε war blazes forth, Il.; ὄσσα δεδήει the report spread like wild-fire, Lat. flagrat rumor, Id.
to burn, burn up, Lat. uro:— Pass., δαισθείς Eur.

to divide; for the Act., δαΐζω is used:— Pass., δαίεται ἦτορ Od.; epic 3rd pl. perf., διχθὰ δεδαίαται are divided in two, Id.:—Mid. to distribute, κρέα Id.—The aor1 ἔδαισα, ἐδαισάμην belong to δαίνυμι; fut. δάσομαι, aor1 ἐδασάμην to δατέομαι.
heart-eating, heart-vexing, Soph.
Dep. : metaph. to be afflicted, mournful, imperat. δακνάζου Aesch.
to bite, of dogs, Il.; στόμιον δ. to champ the bit, Aesch.; χεῖλος ὀδοῦσι δακών, as a mark of determination, Tyrtae.; δ. ἑαυτόν to bite one's lips for fear of laughing, Ar.
metaph. of pungent smoke and dust, to sting or prick the eyes, Ar.
of the mind, to bite or sting, δάκε φρένας μῦθος Il.; ἔδακε ἡ λύπη Hdt.; so in Trag.: —Pass., of love, δηχθεῖσα Eur.; καρδίαν δέδηγμαι I was stung, vexed at heart, Ar.
an animal of which the bite is dangerous, a noxious beast, Aesch.; δάκη θηρῶν ravenous beasts, Eur.
that which is wept for, a subject for tears, Orac. ap. Hdt.
that which is wept, a tear, Aesch., Eur.
of persons, tearful, much-weeping, Hom.; δακρυόεν γελάσαι, as adv., to smile through tears, Il.
of things, tearful, causing tears, πόλεμος, μάχη Id.
a tear, Hom., Hdt., attic, etc.
anything like tears, gum, Hdt.
= δάκρυμα Ι, Anth.
to swim with tears, of a drunkard, Od.
a tear, Lat. lacruma, Hom., Trag.
like δάκρυον, any drop, δ. πεύκινον Eur.
to melt into tears, shed tears, Soph.; ἐπί τινι at a thing, Eur.: of the eyes, to run with tears, Id.
flowing with tears, Eur.
dropping tears, Aesch.
wept over, tearful, Aesch., Anth.
delighting in tears, Anth.
shedding tears, Hom., Aesch.; τινός for a person, Od.
tearful, lamentable, Luc.

intr. to weep, shed tears, Hom., etc.; c. acc. cogn., δ. γόους to lament with tears, Soph.: c. gen. causae, to weep for a thing, Eur.:—also, δ. βλέφαρα to flood them with tears, Id.:—so perf. pass. to be tearful, be all in tears, Il.
of trees (cf. δάκρυον), Luc.
c. acc. to weep for, lament, Aesch., Soph., etc.:—Pass. to be wept for, Aesch., Eur.
a finger-sheath, Xen.
set in a ring, Anth.
the art of cutting gems (for rings), Plat.
engraver of gems, Critias.
a ring, seal-ring, Hdt., Ar.
to point at with the finger, Dem.
pointed at with the finger, Lat. digito monstratus, Aesch.
wearying the fingers by keeping them bent, Anth.
a finger, Lat. digitus, ἐπὶ δακτύλων συμβάλλεσθαι to reckon on the fingers, Hdt.; ὁ μέγας δ. the thumb, Id.
οἱ δ. τῶν ποδῶν the toes, Xen.; and δάκτυλος alone, like Lat. digitus, a toe, Ar.
the shortest Greek measure of length, a finger's breadth, = about 7/10 of an inch, Hdt.
a metrical foot, dactyl, ¯ ˘ ˘, Plat.
worn by fingers, Anth.
a fire-brand, piece of blazing wood, Hom., Aesch.
a thunderbolt, Il.
a burnt-out torch: metaph. of an old man, Anth.
to overpower:
of animals, to tame, break in, to bring under the yoke: Mid. to do so for oneself, Hom., Xen.
of maidens, to make subject to a husband, Il.: Pass. to be forced or seduced, Hom.
to subdue or conquer, Id.: Pass. to be subject to another, Id.: (hence δμώς, δμωή).
to strike dead, kill, Od.
of wine and the like, to overcome, overpower, Hom.: Pass. to be overcome, δεδμημένοι ὕπνωι Il.; οἱ δμαθέντες the dead, Eur.
browsed by heifers, Anth.
a young steer, Anth.
beef-eating, Anth.
poet. form of δαμάζω, to subdue, break in: Mid., Eur.
a heifer, Lat. juvenca, Aesch.
a girl, Anth.
a wife, spouse, Il., Trag.
taming mortals, man-slaying, Simon.
one who tames, Anth.
Il.:—Mid., Hom.:—Pass., ὑφ’ Ἕκτορι δάμνατο Il.
= τὰ δημοσίαι ἀιδόμενα, songs sung in public, Ar.
the sons or descendants of Danaus, Eur.
daughters of Danaus.
the Danaans, subjects of Δάναος, king of Argos; in Il., for the Greeks generally.
to put out money at usury, to lend, Plat., etc.
Mid. to have lent to one, to borrow, Ar.; ἐπὶ μεγάλοις τόκοις at high interest, Dem.
Pass., of the money, to be lent out, Ar., Xen.
a loan, Dem.
a loan, δ. ποιεῖσθαι = δανείζεσθαι (in mid. sense), Thuc.
money-lending, Plat., etc.: metaph., αἵματος δανεισμός Eur.
a money-lender, Plut., NTest.
of or for money-lending, Plut.
money lent, a loan, debt, Anth.
burnt, dry, parched, Od.;Sup., δανότατος, Ar.
a firebrand, torch, Hom.

entry.etym: some pass. tenses are also used in depon. sense, pres., imperf., aor1
entry.sense: to spend, Thuc., etc.; δαπ. εἴς τι to spend upon a thing, Id., Xen.; so also as Dep. to spend, Hdt.; ὅσα δεδαπάνησθε εἰς τὸν πόλεμον Dem.
to expend, consume, use up, Arist.:—metaph. of persons, ὑπὸ νόσου δαπανᾶσθαι Plut.
Causal, τὴν πόλιν δαπανᾶν to put it to expense, Thuc.
money spent, Arist.: in pl. costs, expenses, Xen.
outgoing, cost, expense, expenditure, Hes.; χρημάτων Thuc.; δ. κούφη the cost is little, Eur.:—also in pl., Thuc.
money spent, ἵππων on horses, Pind.; δαπάνην παρέχειν money for spending, Hdt.
extravagance, Aeschin.
of men, lavish, extravagant, Plat., Xen.
of things, expensive, Dem., Arist.:—adv. -ρῶς, Xen.

explained by the Scholl. as Dor. for γῆ, in the phrases δᾶ φεῦ, φεῦ δᾶ Aesch., Eur.; οὐ δᾶν no by earth, Theocr. But it is prob. that δᾶ or Δᾶ is a doric voc. of Δάν = Ζάν (i. e. Ζήν = Ζεύς), and Δᾶν acc. = Ζῆν (i. e. Ζῆνα).
intensive Prefix, = ζα-, as in δά-σκιος, δα-φοινός.

entry.etym: prob. for ζάπεδον, i. e. διάπεδον.
entry.sense: any level surface: the floor of a chamber, Il., Hdt., Xen.; also, γῆς δάπεδον Ar.; and absol. the ground, Od.: pl. plains, Pind., Eur.
a carpet, rug, Ar., Xen.
to devour, as wild beasts, Il.; of fire, Id.; of a spear, to rend, Id.: metaph., δάπτει τὸ μὴ ’νδικον injustice gnaws the heart, Soph.; δάπτομαι κέαρ Aesch.
a son or descendant of Dardanus, Il.
Trojan, Il.
a Trojan woman, Il.
Dardanus, son of Zeus, founder of Troy, Il.:—as adj., Δάρδανος ἀνήρ a Trojan, Id.
Il.: κτήματα δαρδάπτουσιν they devour one's patrimony, Od.
Δᾱρεικὸς στατήρ or Δαρεικός, alone, a Persian gold coin, a Daric, Hdt., etc. These are said to have been first coined by Darius Hystaspes.
born from Darius, Aesch.
Darius, name of several kings of Persia; being a Greek form of Persian dara, a king.
to sleep, Od.
thick-shaded, bushy, Od., Eur.; of a beard, Aesch., Soph.
a distributing, Xen.
to collect as tribute, τι παρά τινος Dem.:—c. acc. pers. exact tribute from him, Isocr.
collection of tribute, Plut.
a tax-gatherer, Strab.
a division, distribution, sharing of spoil, Il., Hhymn.
in attic an impost, tribute, ἀοιδοῦ δ. tribute paid to her, Soph.; δασμὸν τίνειν Id.; δασμὸν φέρειν, ἀποφέρειν, ἀποδιδόναι Xen.
to be subject to tribute, Aesch.: —Pass., δασμοφορεῖταί τινι tribute is paid one, Xen.
paying tribute, tributary, Hdt., Xen.

entry.etym: Perh. from δα, πλήσσω, σ being inserted.
entry.sense: horrid, frightful, Ἐρινύς Od.; of Hecate, Theocr.
thick-haired, hairy, Anth.
bushy-tailed, ἀλώπηξ Theocr.
shaggy-legged, of Pan, Anth.
thick-fleeced, woolly, Od., Eur.
rough-foot, i. e. a hare, Arist.; λαγωὸς ὁ δ. Babr.
opp. to ψιλός in all senses:
thick with hair, hairy, shaggy, rough, Od.; of young hares, downy, Hdt.

thick with leaves, Od.; θρίδαξ δασέα a lettuce with all the leaves on, Hdt.:—of places, thick with bushes or wood, Id.; διὰ τῶν δασέων through the copses, Ar.; δ. ὕληι thick with copse-wood, Hdt., etc.; rarely c. gen., δασὺς δένδρων Xen.:— τὸ δασύ bushy country, Id.
shaggy-breasted, Hes.
shaggy-haired, Anth.

to divide among themselves, τὰ μὲν εὖ δάσσαντο μετὰ σφισίν Il.; ἄνδιχα πάντα δάσασθαι Hom.; μένος Ἄρηος δατέονται they share, i. e. are alike filled with, the spirit of Ares, Il.; of persons at a banquet, κρέα δατεῦντο Od.; διδόναι τινα κυσὶ δάσασθαι to tear in pieces, Il.
[ἡμίονοι] χθόνα ποσσὶ δατεῦντο measured the ground with their feet, Lat. carpebant viam pedibus, Id.
to cut in two, Id.
simply, to divide, to divide or give to others, Hdt.:—perf. in pass. sense, to be divided, Il., Hdt., Eur.
dividing, distributing, Aesch.
a distributer, Aesch.
sc. Δαυλία χώρα Phocis, Soph.
a woman of Daulis, epith. of Philomela, who was changed into the nightingale, Thuc.
a Daulian, Hdt.
Daulis, a city of Phocis, Hom., etc.
the laurel, or rather the bay-tree, Lat. laurus, Od., Hes., etc.; sacred to Apollo, who delivered his oracles ἐκ δάφνης, Hhymn.
to bear a laurel crown, Plut.
