（σύμβολον) affording a good omen, auspicious, Plut.
shrewdness, Arist.
quick of apprehension, Arist.:—adv. -τως, with intelligence, comp. -τώτερον, Thuc.
easily understood, Eur.
well-compounded, Arist.
easily taken in at a glance, seen at once, Aeschin., etc.
with beautiful ankles, Hes., Eur.
adv. -μως, with decency, Eur.
gracefulness, decorum, Xen., Plat.
elegant in figure, mien and bearing, graceful, Plat.; comp. -έστερος; Sup. -έστατος, Id., Xen.
in bad sense, with an outside show of goodness, specious, Eur.
of things, decent, becoming, Id., etc.; τὸ εὔσχημον, Lat. decorum, Plat.:—adv. -μόνως, with grace and dignity, like a gentleman, Ar., Xen.
noble, honourable, in rank, NTest.
easily split, Anth.
to be well-grown, to be strong and lusty, Eur., Ar.
with good felloes (σῶτρα), i. e. with good wheels, Hes.
easy to soften by heat, Luc.
to be orderly, behave well, Thuc., Xen., etc.: of soldiers, to obey discipline, Id.
well-ordered, orderly, Ar.
of soldiers, orderly, well-disciplined, Id., Thuc., etc.
adv. -τως, in order, Aesch., Ar.: comp. -ότερον Dem., -τέρως Xen.
good arrangement, good condition, Xen.
good order, discipline, Thuc.
delicate-footed, Anth.
well-walled, Il.

entry.etym: in Il. the acc. is εὐτείχεα, not εὐτειχέα.

entry.sense: the blessing of children, a breed of goodly children, Eur.
blest with children, Eur., etc.; εὔτ. χρησμός an oracle that gives promise of fair children, Id.; εὔτ. ξυνωρίς a pair of fair children, Id.: —Sup. -ώτατος Id.
cheapness, Hdt.; εἰς εὐτέλειαν cheaply, i. e. vilely, Ar.
thrift, economy, ἐπ’ εὐτελείᾳ economically, Id.; μετ’ εὐτελείας Thuc.; εἰς εὐτ. συντέμνειν to cut down to an economical standard, Id.
easily paid for, cheap, Hdt., Plat., etc.; εὐτελέστερα δὲ τὰ δεινά the danger would be more cheaply met, Thuc.:—adv. -λῶς, at a cheap rate, Xen.
mean, paltry, worthless, Aesch.; εὐτελεστέρα ἄσκησις paltry, requiring no exertion, Xen.
thrifty, frugal, Id.
relat. adv.:
of Time, poet. for ὅτε, when, at the time when:
with Opt., whenever, referring to instances in past time, Hes., Aesch.
with Subj., εὖτ’ ἄν, like ὅταν, whenever, so often as, Od.
Causal, since, seeing that, Soph.
as adv. of Comparison, for ἠΰτε, as, even as, twice in Hom.
delightful, Pind., Anth.
artificially wrought, Anth.
skill in art, Luc., Anth.
ingenious, Anth.
much-enduring, steadfast, Aesch., Eur.
well-cut, of leatherwork, Il.
happy child-birth, Anth.
bringing forth easily, Arist.
courage, boldness, Eur.
brave-spirited, courageous, Aesch., Xen. adv. -μως, Tyrtae., Aesch.
well-strung, vigorous, Plat.:—adv. -νως, vigorously, Ar.
well-turned, rounded, circular, Eur.
hospitable, Aesch.
wit, liveliness, Lat. urbanitas, Arist., Plut.
in bad sense, jesting, ribaldry, NTest.
easily turning or changing, λόγος εὐτρ. a dexterous, ready plea, Ar.:—adv. -λως, dexterously, without awkwardness, Thuc.
ready with an answer, witty, Lat. lepidus, Arist.
in bad sense, jesting, ribald, Isocr.
tricky, dishonest, Pind.
well-fed, well-grown, thriving, fat, Eur., etc.
act. nourishing, Aesch.
readily turning: generally, ready, Eur.; εὐτρεπὲς ποιεῖσθαί τι Id.:—adv., εὐτρεπῶς ἔχειν to be in a state of preparation, Dem.
to make ready, get ready, ξίφος Aesch., Eur., etc.; εὐτρ. τὰ τείχη to restore them, Xen.:—Pass. to be made ready, Eur.:—Mid. to get ready for oneself, or something of one's own, Thuc.
to win over, conciliate, τινά τινι Xen.; so in Mid., Id.; in perf. pass., ἅπαντας ηὐτρέπισται Dem.
easily changing, Plut.
well-fed, Od., Eur.
well-pierced, of ears for earrings, Il.: porous, Anth.
with goodly trident, Pind.
versatile, Arist.
good nurture, thriving condition, Plat.
running well, quick-moving, Anth.
well-rounded, Hes.
well-wheeled, Hom., Eur.
quick-running, running easily, of a running cord, Xen.; εὔτροχος γλῶσσα a ready, glib tongue, Eur.
well-rounded, round, Anth.
Dep. to make ready, Aesch.
ready, Aesch., Theocr.
well-made, well-wrought, Hom.
ready, Hdt.

to be well off, successful, prosperous, Hdt., etc.; c. part. to succeed in doing, Eur., etc.:— εὐτύχει, like Lat. vale, at the close of letters, etc.; so, ἀλλ’ εὐτυχοίης Trag.:—Pass., ἱκανὰ τοῖς πολεμίοις εὐτύχηται (impers.) they have had success enough, Thuc.
of things, to turn out well, prosper, Aesch., Soph., etc.
a piece of good luck, a happy issue, a success, Eur., Xen., etc.
well off, successful, lucky, fortunate, prosperous, Hdt., attic; εὐτ. ἱκέσθαι τινί to come with blessings to him, Soph.:— τὸ εὐτυχές, = εὐτυχία, Thuc.
adv. -χῶς, Pind., Trag., etc.; ionic -χέως, Hdt.: comp. -έστερον, Eur., etc.; Sup. -έστατα, Hdt.
good luck, success, prosperity, Hdt., Trag., etc.; εὐτυχίᾳ χρῆσθαι Plat.:—in pl. successes, Thuc.
well-watered, abounding in water, Pind., Hdt.
of a river, with beautiful water, Eur.
celebrated in hymns, Hhymn.
easily overcome, Arist.
well-woven, Anth.
with beautiful quiver, Soph.
bright, brilliant, Aesch.
to use words of good omen, opp. to δυσφημέω:
to avoid all unlucky words, Horace's male ominatis parcere verbis: hence, to keep a religious silence, Il., Hdt., etc.; Imperat., εὐφήμει, εὐφημεῖτε hush! be still! Lat. favete linguis, Ar., Plat.
to shout in praise or honour of any one, or in triumph, Aesch., Ar.
c. acc. to honour by praise, speak well of, Xen.
to sound triumphantly, Aesch.
the use of words of good omen, opp. to δυσφημία:
abstinence from inauspicious language, religious silence, Trag.; εὐφημίαν ἴσχε = εὐφήμει, Soph.; εὐφημία ’στω, a proclamation of silence before a prayer, Ar.
entry.etym: :dnum [II.] in positive sense, auspiciousness, fairness, Aeschin.:—esp. a fair name for a bad thing, euphemism, Id.
entry.sense: prayer and praise, worship, honour, Eur.; in pl. songs of praise, lauds, Pind.

uttering sounds of good omen, or abstaining from inauspicious words, i. e. religiously silent, opp. to δύσφημος, Aesch., etc.; εὐφήμου στόμα φροντίδος ἱέντες uttering words of religious thought, i. e. keeping a holy silence, Soph.; so, ὑπ’ εὐφήμου βοῆς, i. e. in silence, Id.; εὔφημα φώνει, like εὐφήμει, Id.
in positive sense, auspicious, Aesch., Eur., etc.:—so adv. -μως, with or in words of good omen, Hhymn., Aesch.
well-sounding, cheerful, Theogn., Aesch.
well-loved, Aesch.
act. loving well, c. gen., Id.
well-beloved, Aesch.
the children's darling, of a lion's whelp, Aesch.
ambitious, Arist.
easily set on fire, Xen.
easily borne, endurable, τινι Aesch.
with beautiful lyre or playing beautifully on it, Anth.
well or patiently borne, Pind.
easy to bear or wear, manageable, light, ὅπλα Xen.
spreading rapidly, of diseases, Luc.
act. bearing well; of a breeze, favourable, Xen.
of the body, active, vigorous, Id.
able to endure, patient; adv., εὐφόρως Soph.
well-freighted, well-ballasted, Anth.
well-expressed: adv., εὐφραδέως ἀγορεύειν to speak in set terms, eloquently, Od.

entry.etym: ionic and poet. for εὐφράδεια, Anth.

entry.sense: to cheer, delight, gladden, Hom., Trag., etc.
Pass. to make merry, enjoy oneself, be happy, Od., Hdt.; ἐπί τινι Ar.; ἔν τινι, διά τινος, ἀπό τινος Xen.; c. part., εὐφράνθη ἰδών was rejoiced at seeing, Pind.
easy to speak or utter, Arist.
well-meaning, well-judging, Hom. No Verb εὐφρονέω occurs.
the kindly time, euphem. for νύξ, night, Hes., Hdt., etc.
mirth, merriment, Od.:—of a banquet, good cheer, festivity, Id.:—in pl. glad thoughts, Id.; festivities, Aesch., etc.
adv. -νως, in good cheer, Theogn.
cheerful, gladsome, merry, of persons making merry, Hom., etc.: adv. εὐφρόνως, with good cheer, Pind., etc.
act. cheering, making glad or merry, Il., Aesch., etc.
later, well-minded, favourable, gracious, Pind., Aesch., etc.:—adv., in this sense, Id.
= εὔφημος, Id.
well-grown, shapely, goodly, Il., Eur.
of good natural disposition, Xen.; of horses and dogs, Id.
naturally suited or adapted, εἴς or πρός τι Plat.; c. inf., εὐφυὴς λέγειν Aeschin.:— adv. εὐφυῶς Dem.
of good natural parts, clever, Arist.:—adv. εὐφυῶς, Plat.
natural goodness of shape, shapeliness, Plut.
good natural parts, cleverness, genius, and morally, goodness of disposition, Arist.
easy to keep or guard, Aesch.:— ἐν εὐφυλάκτῳ εἶναι to be on one's guard, Eur.; εὐφυλακτότερα αὐτοῖς ἐγίγνετο it was easier for them to keep a look-out, Thuc.
well-leafed, Pind., Eur.
goodness of voice, Xen.
sweet-voiced, musical, Pind., Aesch.
loud-voiced, of a herald, Xen., Dem.
with beautiful hair: of trees, with beautiful leaves, Anth.
wrought of fine brass or well-wrought in brass, Hom., Aesch.
pleasing, engaging, winning, gracious, popular, Eur., Plat.:— τὸ εὔχαρι popularity, urbanity, Xen.
to be thankful, return thanks, ap. Dem.
thankfulness, gratitude, Decret. ap. Dem.
= εὔχαρις, winning, Xen.: of things, agreeable, pleasant, elegant, Id.:—adv., τελευτᾶν τὸν βίον εὐχαρίστως to die happily, Hdt.
grateful, thankful, Lat. gratus, Id., Xen.
quick or ready of hand, expert, dexterous, Pind., Soph.
easy to master or overcome, Aesch., Xen.
dexterity, Plat., etc.
readiness, proneness, εὐχ. πονηρίας proclivity to evil, Id.
licentiousness, recklessness, Aesch.
easily handled, easy to deal with, easy, εὐχερές ἐστι, c. inf., Batr.; πάντα ταῦτ’ ἐν εὐχερεῖ ἔθου didst make light of them, Soph.:—adv. -ρῶς, Id.
of persons, manageable, accommodating, kind, yielding, Soph.:—adv., εὐχερῶς φέρειν Plat., etc.; comp. -έστερον, Xen.
in bad sense, unscrupulous, reckless, Dem.:—adv. -ρῶς, Id.

entry.etym: only in epic pres. and imperf. εὐχετόωνται, -όωντο, inf. -άασθαι
entry.sense: Dep.
to pray, Il.; to make vows, Hom.
to boast oneself, profess, brag, boast, c. inf., τίνες ἔμμεναι εὐχετόωνται; Od., etc.; ἐπ’ ἀνδράσιν εὐχ. to glory over them, Id.

a prayer, vow, Od., etc.: (but the common Homeric words are εὖχος and εὐχωλή); εὐχὴν ἐπιτελέσαι, Lat. vota persolvere, Hdt.; ἀποδιδόναι Xen.; κατὰ χιλίων εὐχὴν ποιήσασθαι χιμάρων to make a vow of a thousand goats, Ar.
a mere wish, an aspiration, as opp. to reality, εὐχαῖς ὅμοια λέγειν to build castles in the air, Plat.
a prayer for evil, i. e. an imprecation, Aesch., Eur.
of a horse, feeding well, Xen.
rich in goats, Anth.
verdant, Soph.
Dep.:
to pray, offer prayers, pay one's vows, make a vow, Lat. precari, vota facere, θεῶι or θεοῖς Hom., etc.; πρὸς τοὺς θεούς Xen., etc.:—c. dat. commodi, to pray for one, Il.
c. inf. to pray that, Hom., etc.; also, εὔχ. τοὺς θεοὺς δοῦναι to pray them to give, Xen.
c. acc. objecti, to pray for a thing, long or wish for, Pind., attic; εὔχ. τινί τι to pray for something for a person, as Soph.
to vow or promise to do, c. inf., Hom., attic
c. acc. rei, like Lat. vovere, to vow a thing, Aesch., Ar.
to profess loudly, to boast, vaunt, Il.; mostly of something of which one has a right to be proud, πατρὸς ἐξ ἀγαθοῦ γένος εὔχομαι εἶναι Id.
simply to profess or declare, Od.
as a Pass., ἐμοὶ μετρίως εὖκται I have prayed sufficiently, Plat.:—but Soph. uses plup. ηὔγμην in act. sense.
well-strung, Pind.
the thing prayed for, object of prayer, εὖχος δοῦναι, πορεῖν to grant one's prayer, Hom.; εὖχος ἀρέσθαι to obtain it, Il.
a boast, vaunt, Id., Pind.
a vow, votive offering, Anth.
easy to make use of, useful, serviceable, Xen., etc.
well-coloured, of good complexion, fresh-looking, healthy, Xen., etc.:—comp. -οώτερος, Id.
rich in gold, of the Pactolus, Soph.
a prayer, vow, Hom.
a boast, vaunt, Il.: a shout of triumph, Id.
an object of boasting, a boast, glory, κὰδ δέ κεν εὐχωλὴν Πριάμῳ λίποιεν Ἑλένην Id.
bound by a vow, Hdt.
sandy, Anth.
to be of good courage, NTest.
imperat. εὐψύχει farewell, Inscr. on tombs, Anth.
good courage, high spirit, Aesch., etc.
of good courage, stout of heart, courageous, Lat. animosus, Aesch., etc.; τὸ ἐς τὰ ἔργα εὔψυχον Thuc.; εὐψυχότατοι πρὸς τὸ ἐπιέναι Id.:— adv. -χως, Xen.
sweet-smelling, fragrant, Hom., etc.; εὐωδέστατος Hdt.
a sweet smell, Hdt., Xen.
happy as a parent, fruitful, Anth.
fair-armed, Pind., Eur.
of fair price, cheap (Fr. à bon marché）, Xen., Dem., etc.
of good name, honoured, Hes., Pind., etc.
of good omen, prosperous, fortunate, Id., Plat.
euphemistic for ἀριστερός (which was a word of ill omen), left, on the left hand, Hdt., Soph., etc.; ἐξ εὐωνύμου χειρός or ἐξ εὐωνύμου, on the left, Hdt.
to singe, of singeing off swine's bristles, Hom.
fair to look on, Od., Pind.
εὐ. πύλαι friendly gates, Id.
to be negligent, Aesch.
careless, τινος about a thing.
to treat or feed well, entertain sumptuously, Hdt., attic: —Mid. to fare sumptuously, feast, Hdt.; κρέα εὐωχ. to feast upon, enjoy, Xen.; of animals, to eat their fill, Ar., Xen.
metaph., εὐωχεῖν τινα καινῶν λόγων to entertain him with novelties, Theophr.: —Mid. to relish, enjoy, c. gen., τοῦ λόγου Plat.
good cheer, feasting, Ar., etc.:—metaph., λόγων εὐωχίαι feasts of reason, Anth.
fair to look on, Soph.
to perform obsequies over the grave, Soph.
τὰ πάντ’ ἐφαγνίσαι to perform all the obsequies, Soph.
Pass. to be chosen to succeed another, Thuc.

entry.note: 3rd sg. epic aor2 ἐπ-ᾶλτο part. ἐπ-άλμενος part. ἐπι-άλμενος
entry.sense: Dep.:— to spring upon, assail, c. dat., Τρώεσσιν ἐπάλμενος Il.:—also, without hostile sense, c. gen., ἐπιάλμενος ἵππων having leaped upon the chariot, Id.
on the sea, of seaports, Il., Soph.
a match for, equal to, rivalling, ἐφ. γίγνεσθαί τινι Xen.
pass. regarded as an object of rivalry or contention, Dem.
to please, be grateful to, c. dat., ἐμοὶ δ’ ἐπιανδάνει οὕτως Il.; τοῖσιν δ’ ἐπιήνδανε μῦθος Od.
once for all, NTest., etc.
at once, at the same time, Id.
to spread or fold over, Babr.

to bind on or to, λύουσα ἢ ’φάπτουσα undoing or making fast, Soph.; τοὖργον ὡς ἐφάψειεν τόδε that she had made fast (i. e. perpetrated) the deed, Id.:—Pass., 3rd sg. perf. and plup. ἐφῆπται, -το, is or was hung over one, impends over, is fixed as one's doom, c. dat., Τρώεσσι κήδε’ ἐφῆπται Il.
Mid. to lay hold of, grasp, reach, c. gen., Od., Theogn., Soph.
to lay hold of with the mind, attain to, Lat. assequi, c. gen., Plat.
in Pind. also c. dat. (like θιγγάνω, ψαύω) , to apply oneself to.
Hdt. uses part. perf. pass. with gen., εἴδεος ἐπαμμένος possessed of a certain degree of beauty.
to follow, come next, Theocr.
intr. to fit on or to, to fit one, c. dat., Il.
to be adapted to, τινί Arist.
trans. to fit one thing to another, fit on, put on, τί τινι Hes., Theocr.:— Mid. to put on oneself, Anth.
to suit, accommodate, Xen.; πίστιν ἐφαρμόσαι to add fitting assurance, Soph.
one must adapt, τί τινι Luc.
a sitting by or before a place: a siege, blockade, Lat. obsessio, Hdt.
a sitting by, waiting for one's turn, of pugilists, Plat.: a lying in wait, Plut.
to sit upon, rest upon, Eur.
to lie by or near, lie in wait, of an enemy waiting to attack, Thuc.; ἐφ. τινί to keep watch over, Eur.: generally, to watch for, Dem.
to halt, Plut.
poet. for ἐφεδρεύω to sit by, τινί Anth.
sitting or seated upon, c. gen., λεόντων ἔφεδρε, of Cybele, Soph.; ἔφ. ἵππου Eur.
sitting by, at, or near, τῶν πηδαλίων, of a pilot, Plat.; also c. dat., Eur.: absol. close at hand, Soph.
posted in support or reserve, Eur.

lying by, of a third combatant (pugilist or wrestler), who sits by to fight the conqueror, Pind., Ar., Xen.:— μόνος ὢν ἔφεδρος δισσοῖς, i. e. one against two, with no one to take his place if beaten, Aesch.
a successor, Hdt.
Dep.
to sit upon, c. dat., Hom., Ar.;—also c. gen., Pind.; and c. acc., Aesch., Eur.
to sit by or near, Od., Aesch.
containing 1+1/6: τόκος ἔφ. when 1/6 of the principal was paid as interest, = 16 2/3 p. cent., Dem.

entry.note: ionic ἐπ- fut. ἐφέλξω aor1 ἐφείλκυσα
entry.sense: to draw on, drag or trail after one, ἐπ. τὰς οὐράς, of long-tailed sheep, Hdt.; ἵππον ἐκ τοῦ βραχίονος ἐπ. to lead a horse by a rein upon the arm, Id.; ναῦς ὡς ἐφέλξω will take in tow, Eur.
to bring on, bring in its train, Id.
to drink off, Id.

Pass., ἐφελκομένοισι πόδεσσι with feet trailing after him, of one who is dragged lifeless away, Il.; ἐφέλκετο ἔγχος, i. e. sticking in his hand, Id.; ἐπελκόμενος trailing behind, of a boat, Hdt.; οἱ ἐπελκόμενοι the stragglers of an army, Id.
to be attracted, Hhymn., Thuc.
Mid. to draw to oneself, attract, αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐφέλκεται ἄνδρα σίδηρος the very sight of arms attracts men, i. e. tempts them to use it, Od.
to draw or pull over, Plut.; ἐφ. ὀφρῦς to frown, Anth.
to bring on consequences, Eur., Xen.
to assume, Plat., Theocr.
in order, in a row, one after another, Hdt., Eur., Xen.
c. dat. next to, Plat.
in succession, without exception, πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν ἐφ. Xen.; τὴν Ἑλλάδα πᾶσαν ἐφ. Dem.
of Time, τρεῖς ἡμέρας ἐπεξῆς Hdt.; τέσσαρες ἐφ. Ar.
thereupon, after, εὐθὺς ἐφ. Dem.
an excuse, pretext, τοῦ ἔφεξιν; = τίνος χάριν; Ar.

entry.note: imperf. epic ἔφεπον ionic ἐφέπεσκον fut. ἐφέψω aor2 ἐπέσπον inf. ἐπισπεῖν part. ἐπισπών mid ἐφέπομαι imperf.mid -ειπόμην fut. -έψομαι aor2 -εσπόμην imperat. ἐπί-σπου inf. ἐπι-σπέσθαι
entry.sense: to go after, follow, pursue, c. acc., Il.
to drive on, urge on, [ἵππους] ἐφέπων μάστιγι Id.; and c. dat. pers., Πατρόκλῳ ἔφεπε ἵππους drove them against him, Id.
to follow a pursuit, busy oneself about it, c. acc., Hom.; ἐφ. Θήβας to administer, govern it, Aesch.
c. acc. loci, to search, explore, traverse, Lat. obire, Hom., Hes.
to come suddenly upon, encounter, incur, πότμον ἐπισπεῖν Hom.; ὀλέθριον ἦμαρ ἐπ. Il.
Mid. to follow, pursue, c. dat., Od., Hdt., etc.
to follow, accompany, attend, Il., Hdt.; ἐπισπέσθαι ποσίν to follow on foot, i. e. keep up with, Hdt.; εἴ οἱ τύχη ἐπίσποιτο if fortune attend him, Id.:—absol., Thuc.

to obey, attend to, θεοῦ ὀμφῇ Od.; ἐπισπόμενοι μένεϊ σφῷ giving the reins to their passion, Id.; βουλῇ ἐπισπέσθαι πατρός Aesch., etc.:—absol., ὁ ἐπισπόμενος, opp. to ὁ πείσας, Thuc.:—also to agree, approve, in tmesi, ἐπὶ δ’ ἕσπωνται θεοὶ ἄλλοι Od.
to follow an argument, Plat.

entry.note: fut. ψω but the aor1 in use is ἐφείρπῠσα
entry.sense: to creep upon, Ar.
poet. to come on or over, come gradually or stealthily upon, τινά Aesch.; ἐπ’ ὄσσοισι νὺξ ἐφέρπει Eur.
absol. to go forth, proceed, Aesch.; in part. advancing, future, Pind.
the feast of Ephesian Artemis, Thuc.
δίκη, a suit in which there was the right of appeal, Dem.
a throwing or hurling at, a shooting, Plat.
as attic law-term, an appeal to another court, Dem.
（ἐφίεμαι) appetite, desire, Arist.
western, Soph.

at one's own fireside, at home, Od.; ἐφέστιοι ὅσσοι ἔασιν as many as have a home of their own, Il.; ἐφέστιον πῆξαι σκῆπτρον (i. e. ἐπὶ τῇ ἑστίᾳ) Soph.:—of suppliants who claim protection by sitting by the fireside, Hdt.; δόμων ἐφ. an inmate of the temple, Aesch.; also merely of guests, Soph.

generally, of or in the house or family, Lat. domesticus, πόνοι δόμων ἐφέστιοι Aesch.; ἐφ. δόμοι the chambers of the house, Id.:—ionic ἐπίστιον, ου, τό, a household, family, Hdt.: — θεοὶ ἐφ. the household gods, Lat. Lares or Penates, Ζεὺς ἐπίστιος, ἐφέστιος, as presiding over hospitality, Id., Soph.
an upper garment, wrapper, Xen., Plut.
a commander, Aesch.
ἐφέται, οἱ, at Athens, the Ephetae, a court of Eupatridae, created by Draco to try cases of homicide, Plut.
a command, behest, Hom., etc.
an inventor, contriver, NTest.

entry.note: ionic ἐπ- fut. ἐφευρήσω aor2 ἐφηῦρον aor2 ἐφεῦ
entry.sense: to light upon, discover, Od.; with a partic. to find one doing so and so, Hom., Soph.:—so in Pass., μὴ ἐπευρεθῇ πρήσσων Hdt.
to invent or bring in besides, generally to invent, Pind., Eur.
Dep. to mock or scoff at, τινι, Lat. illudere, epic 3rd pl. ἐφεψιόωνται Od.
to come to man's estate, grow up to manhood, Hdt., Aesch., Xen.
puberty, man's estate, Anth.
youthful, Anth.
of or for an ἔφηβος, Theocr.
one arrived at puberty (ἥβη) a youth of 18 years when the Athen. youth underwent his δοκιμασία and was registered as a citizen, Xen., etc.
a throw on the dice, Anth.
the age of an ἔφηβος, puberty, Anth.
Dep. to lead to a place: esp. to lead the magistrate to a house where a criminal lay concealed, Dem.
Pass. to exult over a person, τινι Xen.
to have arrived, Soph., Thuc.
ὅσον ἂν ἡ μόρα ἐφήκῃ so far as the division reaches, so much space as it occupies, Xen.

entry.etym: perf. pass. used as a pres.
entry.sense: to be set or seated on, to sit on, θρόνῳ Od.; also c. gen., θινὸς ἐφήμενος Soph.:— to be seated at or in, δόμοις Aesch.: —also c. acc., βρέτας ἐφήμενος Id.
to act as assessor (cf. ἔφεδρος), Παλλὰς οἵ τ’ ἐφήμενοι Id.
ἐφ’ ἡμέραν, for the daily service of the temple, NTest.
on, for or during the day, the day through, Od.; by day, Pind.
for a day only, for the day, ἐφημέρια φρονέοντες taking thought for the day only, Od.:—often of men, ἐφημέριοι creatures of a day, Aesch., etc.
hired for the day, Theogn.
a diary, journal, such as Caesar's Commentarii, Plut.
living but a day, short-lived, Pind., Eur., etc.
of men, ἐφήμεροι creatures of a day, Pind., Aesch.
for the day, daily, Plut., etc.
φάρμακον ἐφ. killing on the same day, Id.
containing seven halves, i. e. 3 1/2, of the first 3 1/2 feet of a Hexameter or Iambic Trimeter.

entry.note: ἑφθός, ή, όν verb. adj. of ἕψω
entry.sense: boiled, dressed, Hdt., Eur., etc.
ἑφθὸς χρυσός refined gold, Simon.
superficial perspiration, Plut.
to sit at or in a place, c. dat., Il.; ὕπνος ἐπὶ βλεφάροισιν ἐφίζανεν sleep sate upon, Id.
Causal, in epic aor1, to set upon, ἐφέσσαι to set me ashore, Od.:—Mid., γούνασιν οἷσιν ἐφεσσάμενος having set [me] on his knees, Id.; imperat., ἔφεσσαί με νηός set me on board the ship, Id.
intr. in pres. and imperf. ἐφῖζον, ionic ἐφίζεσκον, to sit at or by, Id., Pind., etc.

entry.note: ionic ἐπ- fut. ἐφήσω aor1 ind. ἐφῆκα epic ἐφέηκα aor2 imperat. ἔφες subj. ἐφείω, ῃς attic ἐφῇς part. ἐφείς Mid., part. ἐφιέμενος fut. ἐφήσομαι 3rd sg. imperf. ἐφίει
entry.etym: 3rd sg. imperf. ἐφίει as if from ἐφιέω
entry.sense: to send to one, Il.
c. inf. to set on or incite to do, ἐφέηκε ἀεῖσαι Od.; ἐφ. τινὰ χαλεπῆναι, etc., Il.
of things, to throw or launch at one, ὅς τοι ἐφῆκε βέλος Id., etc.; ἐφ. οἰστὸν ἐπί τινι Eur.; ἐφ. χεῖράς τινι to lay hands on him, Od.
of events, destinies, etc., to send upon one, τοῖσιν πότμον ἐφῆκεν Il., etc.
to send against, in hostile sense, Hdt., etc.:— ἐφ. τὸν ποταμὸν ἐπὶ τὴν χώρην Id.; ἐφῆκας γλῶσσαν did'st let loose, Eur.
to throw into, ἐς λέβητ’ ἐφῆκεν μέλη Id.
to let go, loosen, esp. the rein, Plat.:—hence to give up, yield, Lat. concedere, τινὶ τὴν ἡγεμονίαν Thuc.:—c. inf. to permit, allow, τινὶ ποιεῖν τι Hdt., Soph., etc.
to give up, leave as a prey, Soph.:—then, seemingly, intr. (sub. ἑαυτόν), to give oneself up to, οὐρίᾳ a fair wind, Plat.
to put the male to the female, Hdt.
as law-term, to leave to another to decide, δίκας ἐφ. εἴς τινα Dem.:—and absol. to appeal, εἰς τοὺς δικαστάς Id.
Mid. to lay one's command or behest upon, Hom., Aesch., etc.:—c. inf., ἐφ. τινὶ ποιεῖν τι Soph., Ar.; ἐς Λακεδαίμονα to send orders to L., Thuc.
to allow or permit one to do, Soph., etc.
c. gen. to aim at, Arist.:— to long after, desire, Soph., Eur., etc.; c. inf. to desire to do, Eur.

entry.note: ionic ἐπ- fut. ἐφίξομαι aor 2 ἐφῑκόμην ionic ἐπ
entry.sense: Dep.:— to reach at, aim at, c. gen., Il., Plat., etc.
to reach or extend, ἐφ’ ὅσον μνήμη ἐφ. Xen., etc.
metaph. to hit or touch the right points, Lat. rem acu tangere, τῷ λόγῳ ἐφ. τῶν ἐκεῖ κακῶν Dem.;—so, ἐς τὰ ἄλλα ἐπίκεο Hdt.
to reach, gain, attain to, ἀνδραγαθίας Aeschin., etc.
c. acc. to come upon, εἴ σε μοῖρ’ ἐφίκοιτο Pind.; dupl. acc., ἐπικέσθαι πληγὰς τὸν Ἑλλήσποντον to visit it with blows, Hdt.
easy to reach, accessible, Plut.
c. gen., Anth.
longed for, desired, charming, Hes., Aesch.; c. inf., ἐφ. προσλεύσσειν Soph.
Dep. to ride upon, Luc.
to ride upon, Babr.
for putting on a horse, Xen.:— ἐφίππιον (sc. στρῶμα) a saddle-cloth, Id.
on horseback, riding: ἀνδριὰς ἔφ. an equestrian statue, Plut.
κλύδων ἔφιππος a rushing wave of horses, Soph.
Causal in pres., imperf., fut., and aor1:
to set or place upon, τί τινι Thuc.; τι ἐπί τινι Xen.: metaph., ἐφ. μοῖραν βίῳ Plat.
to set over, Lat. praeficere, ἐφ. τινὰ ὕπαρχόν τισι Hdt., etc.
to set up, establish, institute games, Id.
to set by or near to, ἱππέας ἐπιστήσαντες κύκλῳ τὸ σῆμα ( = περὶ τὸ σ.) Id.
to stop, make halt, Lat. inhibere, Xen.: —absol., ἐπιστήσας (sc. ἑαυτόν, τὸν ἵππον) having halted, Id.
ἐφίστημι τὴν γνώμην κατά τι to fix one's mind upon it, attend to it, and then absol. to give attention, Arist.
c. acc. pers. to arrest the attention of, Plut.
intr. in Mid. and Pass., ἐφίσταμαι, aor1 ἐπεστάθην, with perf., plup. and aor2 act.:— to stand upon, πύργῳ, δίφρῳ, ἐπὶ βηλῷ Il.
to be imposed upon, τινι Soph.
to stand on the top or surface, τὸ ἐπιστάμενον τοῦ γάλακτος, i. e. cream, Hdt.
to be set over, Lat. praeesse, c. dat., Aesch., etc.; also c. gen., Hdt., Eur.:—absol. to be in authority, Hdt., etc.
to stand by or near, ἀλλήλοισι Il., etc.: of dreams or visions, to appear to, εὕδοντι ἐπέστη ὄνειρος Hdt.
in hostile sense, to stand against, oppose, Hom.: to come upon by surprise, Thuc.
of events, to impend, be at hand, Lat. instare, Κῆρες ἐφεστᾶσιν θανάτοιο Il.; πρίν μοι τύχη ἐπέστη Soph.
to halt, stop, as in a march, Xen.:— c. gen., ἐπ. τοῦ πλοῦ Thuc.
to fix one's mind on, give one's attention to, τινι Eur., Dem.
the aor1 mid. is used in causal sense, to set up, τὰς θύρας Xen.: to set, post, φρουρούς Id.
to visit, go the rounds, patrol, Xen.:—Pass., ἐφοδεύεται the rounds are made, Ar.
c. dat. to watch over, ἀγῶσιν Aesch.
to furnish with supplies for a journey, Lat. viaticum dare, Hdt.
Mid., πενταδραχμίαν ἑκάστῳ ἐφοδιασάμενος having seen that five drachms were paid to each, Xen.:—metaph. to maintain, ἀργίαν Plut.
, like Lat. viaticum, supplies for travelling, money and provisions, Hdt., Dem.:—of an ambassador's travelling-allowance, Ar.; sometimes in sg., Thuc., Xen.
generally, ways and means, maintenance, support, ἐφόδια τῷ γήρᾳ Dem.; of public money, μιᾶς ἡμέρας ἐφόδια ἐν τῷ κοινῷ Id.
accessible, Thuc.
one who goes the rounds, Xen.
a way towards, approach, Thuc., Xen.:— access for traffic and intercourse, communication, παρ’ ἀλλήλους Thuc.
importation, Xen.
an onset, attack, assault, Aesch., Thuc., etc.
a rudder, Od.
a tow-boat: metaph an appendage, Anth., Plut.
a burdensome appendage, Eur.
drawing on or towards, enticing, alluring, Thuc.
requiring to be drawn on, a laggard, Ar.
to follow close after, Il.

entry.note: fut. σω epic aor1 inf. ἐφοπλίσσαι
entry.sense: to equip, get ready, prepare, Hom.; so in Mid., δόρπα τ’ ἐφοπλισόμεσθα we will get ready our suppers, Il.
to arm against, τινά τινι, so in Mid., Anth.
fit for overlooking, ἔργων Xen.

entry.note: ionic 3rd sg. ἐπορᾷ 3rd pl. ἐπορέωσι inf. ἐπορᾶν imperf. ἐφεώρων ionic 3rd sg. ἐπώρα fut. ἐπόψομαι epic also ἐπιόψομαι the aor. is ἐπεῖδον
entry.sense: to oversee, observe, survey, of the sun, Hom.:—then of the gods, to watch over, observe, take notice of, Od., Hdt., etc.; of a general going his rounds, Thuc.; to visit the sick, Xen.
simply, to look upon, view, behold, Od., etc.:—Pass., ὅσον ἐφεωρᾶτο τῆς νήσου as much of it as was in view, Thuc.
to look out, choose, ἐπιόψομαι ἥτις ἀρίστη Od., etc.
the ephoralty, Xen.
the court of the ephors, Xen.
= ἐφοράω, c. acc., Aesch.; c. gen., Id.
to be ephor, Thuc., Xen.
of or for the ephori, Xen.
on the border or frontier, ap. Dem.
to rush on, Aesch.
to stir up, rouse against one, Hom.; ἐπορμῆσαι τοὺς λύκους to set them on, Hdt.; ναύτας ἐφορμήσαντα τὸ πλεῖν having urged them on to sail, Soph.
intr. to rush upon, attack, τινί Eur.

Pass. and Mid. to be stirred up; c. inf. to be eager or desire to do, Hom.:—absol. to rush furiously on, ἔγχει ἐφορμᾶσθαι Il.; ἐφορμηθείς Id.; and, without hostile sense, to spring forward, Od.:— c. acc. to rush upon, make a dash at, Il.
to lie moored at or over against a place, to blockade it, λαθὼν τοὺς ἐπορμέοντας having escaped the blockading fleet, Hdt.; ἐφ. τῷ λιμένι Thuc.
generally, to lie by and watch, Soph., Dem.
a way of attack, μία δ’ οἴη γίγνετ’ ἐφορμή only room for one to attack, Od.
an assault, attack, Thuc.
a lying at anchor so as to watch an enemy, blockading, Thuc.: a means of so doing, Id.
to bring a ship to its moorings (ὅρμος): — Mid. and Pass. to come to anchor, Thuc.
intr. in Act. to seek refuge in a place, c. dat., Anth.
at anchor, Thuc.
an overseer, guardian, ruler, Aesch., Soph.
at Sparta, ἔφοροι, οἱ, the Ephors, a body of five magistrates, who controlled even the kings, Hdt., etc.
to insult over one, Il.; c. dat., Soph.; c. acc., in Mid., μὴ ’φυβρίζεσθαι νεκρούς Eur.; ἐφύβριζον ἄλλα τε καὶ εἰ they used insulting language, asking especially whether, Thuc.
to exult maliciously over, Soph.
of the water, Νύμφη Anth.
wet, moist, rainy, of the west wind, Od.
well-watered, Hdt.
to sing or chant after or over, τί τινι Aesch., Soph.
to sing a dirge besides, Soph.
to sing of, descant on, c. acc., Id.
above, atop, above, Hom.:— from above, Od.:—c. gen., Theocr.
to sleep meantime, Aesop.
Ephyra, old name of Corinth, Il.
to come later, τὰ ἐφυστερίζοντα = αἱ ὑστεροῦσαι πόλεις, Thuc.
to rain upon:—perf. pass. part. ἐφυσμένος rained upon, exposed to the rain, Xen.
mature, Anth.

having given or able to give security, trust-worthy, secure, Eur.; ζημία ἐχ. a penalty to be relied on (for the prevention of crime), Thuc.: τὸ ἐχέγγυον security, Hdt.: c. inf. sufficiently strong to do, Plut.
pass. having received a pledge, secured against danger, Soph.
master of one's passion, Od.
to hold one's peace, Luc.
silence, reserve, Plut.
ship-detaining, Aesch., Anth.
Homeric epith. of a dart, bitter, or rather sharp-pointed, piercing, Il.
bringing sorrows, Theocr.
= ὁ ἔχων, a man of substance, Pind.
of or belonging to a ploughhandle, Anth.
to be prudent, Anth.
a plough-handle, Lat. stiva, Hes.
prudence, good sense, Anth.
sensible, prudent, discreet, Hom.
to hate, detest, Hom., Trag.; c. acc. cogn., ἔχθος ἐχθήρας μέγα hating with great hatred, Soph.:—Pass. to be hated, hateful, Trag.; so in fut. mid., ἐχθαρεῖ μὲν ἐξ ἐμοῦ Soph.
to be hated, Soph.
yesterday's, Anth.
yesterday, Ar.; ἀπ’ ἐχθές Anth.; νῦν τε κἀχθές to-day or yesterday, Soph.; cf. πρώην.

entry.note: ἔχθιστος, η, ον irreg. Sup. of ἐχθρός
entry.sense: most hated, most hateful, Il., Trag.
most hostile, Thuc.; c. gen., as if a Subst., οἱ ἐκείνου ἔχθ. his bitterest enemies, Xen.
more hated, more hateful, Trag. adv., ἐχθιόνως ἔχειν to be more hostile, Xen.
in hostility with another, c. dat., Il.
hateful, detestable, Soph., Ar., Plat.
hate, hatred, Hom., etc.; ἔχθος τινός hatred for one, Hdt., Thuc.; ἐς ἔχθος ἀπικέσθαι τινί to incur his hatred or enmity, Hdt.; εἰς ἔχθος ἐλθεῖν τινί Eur.
of persons, ὦ πλεῖστον ἔχθος object of direst hate, Aesch.
to hate, Xen., Plut.

hatred, enmity, Hdt., attic; ἔχθρα τινός hatred for, enmity to one, Thuc.; κατ’ ἔχθραν τινός Ar.; ἔχθρα ἔς τινα Hdt.; ἔχθρα πρός τινα Aesch.; δι’ ἔχθρας ἀφικέσθαι, ἐλθεῖν τινί to be at feud with one, Eur., etc.; ἔχθραν συμβάλλειν, συνάπτειν τινί to engage in hostility with . . , Id.; ἔχθραν λύειν, διαλύεσθαι Id., Thuc.
hated of the gods, Soph.
hostile to guests, inhospitable, Aesch., Eur.
hated, hateful, Hom., etc.; ἐχθρόν μοί ἐστιν, c. inf., 'tis hateful to me to . . , Il.
act. hostile, at enmity with, τινι Thuc., etc.
as Subst., ἐχθρός, ὁ, one's enemy, Hes., etc.; ὁ Διὸς ἐχθρός Aesch.; οἱ ἐμοὶ ἐχθροί Thuc.
the regul. comp. and Sup. ἐχθρότερος, -τατος are rare: the irreg. ἐχθίων, ἔχθιστος being more used.
adv. ἐχθρῶς, Plat., etc.; comp. ἐχθροτέρως, Dem.
to hate, Soph., Eur.:—Pass. to be hated, detested, Hom., Aesch.
of or like a viper, Anth.
an adder, viper, Hdt., Trag., etc.; metaph. of a treacherous wife or friend, Aesch., Soph.
the islands in the Ionian sea, Il., Eur., etc.; commonly called Ἐχινάδες.
a kind of mouse with bristly hair, in Libya, Hdt.
the urchin, hedgehog, Ar., etc.
the sea-urchin, Plat.
the shell of the sea-urchin, often used as a cup: then like Lat. testa, a pot, jug, pitcher, Lat. echinus, Ar., etc.:— the vase in which the notes of evidence were deposited, Dem.
in pl. sharp points at each end of a bit, Xen.
an adder, viper, Plat.; metaph., συκοφάντης καὶ ἔχις τὴν φύσιν Dem.
that which holds; and so,
a hindrance, obstacle, Il.
c. gen. a bulwark, defence against a thing, c. gen., Hhymn.
a hold-fast, stay, ἔχματα πέτρης bands of rock, Il.; ἔχματα πύργων stays of the towers, Id.; ἔχματα νηῶν props for the ships, to keep them upright, Id.
strong, secure, of Places, Thuc., etc.; ἐν ἐχυρῷ εἶναι to be in safety, Id.; ἐν ἐχυρωτάτῳ ποιεῖσθαί τι Xen.
of reasons, etc., trustworthy, Thuc.
adv. -ρῶς, Id.; comp. -ώτερον, Id.

entry.etym: for the poet. form ἔσχεθον v. *σχέθω
the aor2 mid. is also used in pass. sense.
entry.sense: Trans., in two senses, to have or to hold:
to have, possess, Hom., etc.; ὁ ἔχων a wealthy man, Soph.; οἱ οὐκ ἔχοντες the poor, Eur.:—c. gen. partit., μαντικῆς ἔχ. τέχνης Soph.:—Pass. to be possessed by, belong to, τινι Il.
to have charge of, keep, πύλας Id.; φυλακὰς ἔχον kept watch, Id., etc.
c. acc. loci, to dwell in, inhabit, haunt, Hom., etc.
to have to wife, Id., etc.
to have in one's house, to entertain, Od.
the pres. part. is joined with a Verb, ἔχων ἀτίταλλε kept and made much of, i. e. kept with special care, Il.; ὃς ἂν ἥκηι ἔχων στρατόν whoever may have come with an army, Hdt.
of Habits or Conditions, γῆρας ἔχ., periphr. for γηράσκειν, Od.
like Lat. teneo, to know, understand, Il., Aesch.; ἔχεις τι; tenes? d' ye understand? Ar.
to involve, imply, give cause for, ἀγανάκτησιν Thuc.
ἔχειν σταθμόν to weigh so much, Hdt.
to hold, Hom., etc.; ἔχ. ἐν χερσίν Hdt.; μετὰ χερσίν Il.; διὰ χειρός Soph., etc.
to hold fast, ἔχειν τινὰ χειρός, ποδός to hold him by the hand, by the foot, Il.; ἔχειν τινὰ μέσον to grip one by the middle, of wrestlers, Ar.
of a woman, to be pregnant, Lat. utero gestare, Hdt.; ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχειν Id.
to hold out, bear up against, support, sustain an attack, Lat. sustinere; in which sense Hom. uses fut. σχήσω, σχήσομαι.
to hold fast, keep close, as bars do a gate, Il.: to enclose, Hom.

to hold or keep in a certain direction, like ἐπέχω, ὀϊστὸν ἔχε he aimed it, Il.; of horses or ships, to guide, drive, steer, Id.; then absol., τῆι ῥ’ ἔχε that way he held his course, Id.:—also to put in, land, εἰς or πρὸς τόπον Hdt.; δεῦρο νοῦν ἔχε attend to this, Eur.; πρός τι τὸν νοῦν ἔχ. Thuc.
to hold in, stay, keep back, ἵππους Il., etc.; οὐ σχήσει χεῖρας will not withhold his hands, Od.; ὀδύνας ἔχ. to allay, assuage them, Il., etc.
to keep away from, c. gen. rei, τινὰ ἀγοράων, νεῶν Id.:—in attic to stop or hinder from doing, τοῦ μὴ καταδῦναι Xen.; ἔσχον μὴ κατανεῖν Eur.
to keep back, withhold a thing, χρήματα Od., etc.
to hold in guard, keep safe, protect, Il.
c. inf. to have means or power to do, to be able, c. inf., Hom., etc.:—with inf. omitted, οὔπως εἶχε he could not, Il.
after Hom., οὐκ ἔχω ὅπως I know not how, etc., Soph., etc.; οὐκ ἔχω ὅ τι χρὴ λέγειν Xen.

intr. to hold oneself, to keep so and so, ἕξω, ὡς ὅτε τις λίθος . . I will hold fast, as a stone . . , Od.; σχὲς οὗπερ εἶ keep where thou art, Soph.; ἔχειν κατὰ χώραν to keep in one's place, Ar., etc.; διὰ φυλακῆς ἔχειν to keep on one's guard, Thuc.
c. gen. to keep from, πολέμου Id.
c. gen., also, to take part in, have to do with, τέχνης Soph.: to be engaged or busy, ἀμφί τι Aesch.; περί τι Xen.

simply to be, often with Advs. of manner, εὖ ἔχει Od.; καλῶς ἔχει, κακῶς ἔχει, Lat. bene habet, male habet, it is going on well, attic; οὕτως ἔχει so the case stands, Ar., etc.:—a gen. modi is often added, εὖ ἔχειν τινός to be well off for a thing, abound in it, Hdt.; ὡς ποδῶν εἶχον as fast as they could go, Id.; ὥς τις εὐνοίας ἢ μνήμης ἔχοι as each man felt disposed or remembered, Thuc.
to lead towards, ἐπὶ τὸν ποταμόν Hdt.; ἔχ. εἴς τι, to point towards, tend towards, Id.; τὸ ἐς Ἀργείους ἔχον what concerns them, Id.; also, ἔπ’ ὅσον ἔποψις εἶχε so far as the view extended, Id.
ἐπί τινι ἔχειν to have hostile feelings towards . . , Id., Soph.

after Hom., ἔχω is joined with aor. part. of another Verb, κρύψαντες ἔχουσι for κεκρύφασι, Hes.; ἀποκληΐσας ἔχεις for ἀποκέκλεικας, Hdt.;—sometimes it gives a pres. sense to the aor., as, θαυμάσας ἔχω I am in a state of wonderment, Soph.; ὅς σφε νῦν ἀτιμάσας ἔχει who now treats her with dishonour, Eur.
the part. ἔχων, with the pres., adds a notion of duration, as, τί κυπτάζεις ἔχων; why do you keep poking about there? Ar.; φλυαρεῖς, ληρεῖς ἔχων you keep chattering, trifling, Plat.
pleonast., ἐστὶν ἔχον = ἔχει, Hdt.; εστὶν ἀναγκαίως ἔχον = ἔχει ἀναγκαίως, Aesch.
Mid. to hold on by, cling to, c. gen., Hom., etc.
metaph. to cleave or cling to, ἔργου Hdt.; ἐλπίδος Eur.; τῆς αὐτῆς γνώμης Thuc.: to lay claim to a thing, Hdt.; to be zealous for, μάχης Soph.

to come next to, follow closely, Xen.; τῆς πληγῆς ἔχεται follows up the blow, Dem.:—of peoples or places, to be close, touch, border on, τινος Hdt., etc.; οἱ ἐχόμενοι the neighbouring people, Id.: of Time, τὸ ἐχόμενον ἔτος the next year, Thuc.
to depend on, τινος or ἔκ τινος Hom.
to pertain to, τινος Hdt.
to bear or hold for oneself, Hom.
to maintain oneself, hold one's ground, Il.
c. acc. to keep off from oneself, repel, Id.
to stop oneself, stop, Id.:— to keep oneself back, abstain or refrain from, Hom., etc.
cooking men, of Medea, Anth.
anything boiled: pl. vegetables for kitchen use, Plat.
a boiling, Hdt.
a pan for boiling, Anth.
boiled, Xen.: ἑψητοί, ῶν, οἱ, boiled fish, Ar.
Dep. to play with pebbles, generally, to amuse oneself, ἑψιαάσθων (epic 3rd dual imperat.), Od.; ἑψιάασθαι μολπῇ καὶ φόρμιγγι (epic inf.) Id.

Ε, ε, fifth letter of the Gr. alphabet: as numeral εʹ = πέντε and πέμπτος, but ͵ε = 5000. The ancients called this vowel εἶ ( as they called ο, οὖ). When in the archonship of Euclides ( B. C. 403) the Athenians adopted long e (Η η) from the Samian alphabet, the Gramm. gave to short e the name of ἒ ψιλόν, i. e. ε without the aspirate, because Ε had been used for the aspirate. In ionic, ε sometimes stood for ᾰ, βέρεθρον ἔρσην τέσσερες for βάραθρον ἄρσην τέσσαρες, and in contr. Verbs in -άω, as ὁρέω φοιτέω.
to boil, seethe, Hdt., attic: proverb. of useless labour, λίθον ἕψεις Ar.; c. gen. partit., ἥψομεν τοῦ κορκόρου we boiled some pimpernel, Id.:—Pass. to be boiled, Hdt.
of metals, to smelt, refine, Pind.
metaph., γῆρας ἀνώνυμον ἕψειν to cherish an inglorious age, Id.
from morn, i. e. at earliest dawn, early in the morning, Plat.; ἕ. εὐθύς Ar.
αὔριον ἕ. to-morrow early, Xen.; so ἕωθεν alone, Ar.
in the morning, early, Hdt., Ar.: —τὸ ἑωθινόν, as adv., early in the morning, Hdt.; so, ἐξ ἑωθινοῦ = ἕωθεν, Xen.

a mixture of the dregs and heel-taps, with which the drunken were dosed at the end of a revel; metaph., ἑωλοκρασίαν μου τῆς πονηρίας κατασκεδάσας having discharged the stale dregs of his rascality over me, Dem.
a day old, kept till the morrow, stale, Comici; ἕωλος θρυαλλίς a stinking wick (after the lamp has been blown out), Luc.
of actions or events, stale, out of date, Dem.
of men, coming a day too late, Plut.
ἐπεί χ’ ἑῶμεν πολέμοιο when we have enough of war:—but prob. it should be written
to take one's fill of a thing.
in or of the morning, at morn, early, πάχνη ἑῴα the morning rime, Aesch.; ἑῷος ἐξαναστῆναι to get up early, Eur.
eastern, Xen.
collat. form of αἰώρα, a halter, Soph.

until, till, Lat. donec, dum, Hom.:—in Hom. sometimes used = τέως, for a time:—to express a fact, ἕως is foll. by Ind., εἷος φίλον ὤλεσε θυμόν Il.; when the event is uncertain, by the opt., ἕως ὅ γε μιγείη till he should reach, Od.
ἕως ἄν or κε with Subj., relating to an uncertain event in future time, μαχήσομαι, εἵως κε κιχείω till I find, Il.
while, so long as, εἵως πολεμίζομεν Od.; ἕως ἔτι ἐλπίς [ἦν] Thuc.

as adv., Lat. usque, mostly with Advs. of Time, ἕως ὅτε, Lat. usque dum, till the time when, Xen.; so, ἕως οὗ Hdt.; ἕως ὀψέ till late, Thuc.:—c. gen., ἕως τοῦ ἀποτῖσαι till he made payment, ap. Aeschin.
even until, Thuc.
bringer of morn, Lat. Lucifer, the Morning-star.
a reaping-hook or sickle, Lat. falx, Sicilian word for δρέπανον, Thuc. Hence Ζάγκλη, the ancient name for Messana.
strong-blowing, stormy, Hom.
very divine, sacred, Il., etc.
very hot, scorching, Anth.
a temple-servant, being perh. a form of διάκονος, Plut.
exceeding wroth, Il., Theocr.
the surging of the sea, surge, spray, Aesch., Soph., etc.; πύρπνοος ζάλη, of the fiery rain from Aetna, Aesch.:—metaph., ζάλαι storms, distresses, Pind.
to put forth all one's might, Hes.
poet. adj. very strong, mighty, raging, Hhymn., Pind.
insep. Prefix, = δα-, ἀρι-, ἐρι-, very, as in ζά-θεος, ζά-κοτος, ζα-μενής, etc.
very full, ζ. γενειάς a thick beard, Aesch.; ζ. Μούσης στόμα full-sounding, Anth.
very rich, Hdt., Eur. aeolic for διαπρέπω.
very fiery, Aesch.
well-fed, fat, goodly, Hom.
full of fire, of men at their prime, Il.
wanting much: c. gen., ζαχρ. ὁδοῦ one who wants to know the way, Theocr.
attacking violently, furious, raging, Hom.
rich in gold, Eur.

to live, Hom., etc.; ἐλέγχιστε ζωόντων vilest of living men, Od.; ζώειν καὶ ὁρᾶν φάος ἠελίοιο Il.; ῥεῖα ζώοντες living at ease, of the gods, Id.; ζῶν κατακαυθῆναι to be burnt alive, Hdt.:—also, ζῆν ἀπό τινος to live off or on a thing, Theogn., Hdt., etc.:— τὸ ζῆν = ζωή, Aesch., etc.: —in a quasi-trans. sense, ἐκ τῶν ἄλλων ὧν ἔζης ( = ἃ ἐν τῶι βίωι ἔπραττες) from the other acts of your life, Dem.
metaph. to be in full life and strength, to be fresh, be strong, ἄτης θύελλαι ζῶσι Aesch.; ἀεὶ ζῆι ταῦτα [νόμιμα] Soph.; ζῶσα φλόξ living fire, Eur.

entry.etym: without mark of gender, a Libyan word
entry.sense: = βουνοί, a kind of mouse, Hdt.
mostly in pl. ζειαί, a kind of grain, spelt, a coarse wheat, used as fodder for horses, Od.; like ὀλύραι in Il.; and Hdt. expressly asserts their identity.
zea-giving, as epith. of the earth, ζείδωρος ἄρουρα fruitful corn-land, Hom.
a wide upper garment, girded about the loins and falling over the feet, Hdt., Xen.
inseparable Suffix, denoting motion towards:— properly it represents -σδε, as in Ἀθήναζε, θύραζε for Ἀθήνασδε, θύρασδε:—but sometimes found with sg. Nouns, as Ὀλυμπίαζε, Μουνυχίαζε.
Dim. of ζεῦγος, a puny team, Ar.
to drive a yoke of oxen, Xen.
the driver of a yoke of oxen, teamster, Xen.
yoked in pairs, of soldiers, in the same rank, Plut.
ζευγῖται, οἱ the third of Solon.'s four classes of Athenian citizens, so called from their being able to keep a team of oxen, ap. Dem.: cf. πεντακοσιομέδιμνοι.
the strap or loop of the yoke (ζυγόν) through which the beasts' heads were put, so that the ζυγόν had two ζεῦγλαι, Il. Hdt., etc.
the cross-bar of the double rudder, Eur.

that which is used for joining, a band, bond, τὸ ζ. τοῦ λιμένος the barrier of ships moored across the harbour, Thuc.:— a bridge of boats, Anth.:— a platform formed by lashing several vessels together, Plut.
metaph., ζεύγματ’ ἀνάγκης the bonds of necessity, Eur.

entry.etym: from Root ΖΥΓ, as in ζυγῆναι
entry.sense: to yoke, put to, ἵππους Hom., etc.; ζ. ἵππους ὑφ’ ἅρματα, ὑφ’ ἅρμασιν, ὑπ’ ὄχεσφιν, ὑπ’ ἀμάξηισιν Il.;—(so in Mid., ἵππους ζεύγνυσθαι to put to one's horses, Hom.);—also of riding horses, to harness, saddle and bridle, ζεῦξαι Πάγασον Pind.:—of chariots, to put to, get ready, Id., Eur.
to bind, bind fast, Xen.:—Pass., φάρη ἐζευγμέναι having them fastened, Eur.
metaph., πότμωι ζυγείς in the yoke of fate, Pind.; ἀνάγκηι, ὁρκίοις ζυγείς Soph., Eur.
to join together, σανίδες ἐζευγμέναι well-joined, Il.
to join in wedlock, Eur.:—in Mid., of the husband, to wed, Id.:—Pass. to be married, Soph., Eur.
to join opposite banks by bridges, τὸν Ἑλλήσποντον ζεῦξαι Hdt., etc.:—also, γέφυραν ζεῦξαι to form a bridge, Id.
to undergird ships with ropes, Thuc.
a yoke of beasts, a pair of mules, oxen or horses, Il., etc.
the carriage drawn by a pair, a chariot, car, Hdt., etc.
a pair or couple of any things, Id., Aesch.
keeping a yoke of beasts, Plut.
fit for joining or yoking, γέφυραν γαῖν δυοῖν ζ. Aesch.
as Subst., ζευκτήριον, τό, = ζυγόν, a yoke, Id.
a yoking or manner of yoking oxen, Hdt.
a joining, as by a bridge, Id.

entry.etym: the obl. cases formed from Δίς, gen. Διός; dat. Διΐ, Δί [ῑ], acc. Δία
in Poets also, Ζηνός, Ζηνί, Ζῆνα
in later doric Ζάν, Ζανός, etc.:—
entry.sense: Zeus, Lat. Ju-piter, father of gods and men, son of Kronos and Rhea, hence called Κρονίδης, Κρονίων, husband of Hera: —Hom. makes him rule in the lower air (ἀήρ); hence rain and storms come from him, Ζεὺς ὕει, etc.:—in oaths, οὐ μὰ Ζῆνα Hom., attic; so μὰ Δία, νὴ Δία, attic
Ζεὺς καταχθόνιος, Pluto, Il.
sc. πνοή the west wind, Od.
Zephyrus, the west wind, Lat. Favonius, Hom., etc.; westerly wind, often represented as stormy, Od.; but also as clearing, ὁπότε νέφεα Z. στυφελίξῃ Il.
entry.etym: From ζόφος night, the region of darkness, as Εὖρος from ἕως, the morn.

entry.sense: to boil, seethe, of water, Hom.; λέβης ζεῖ the kettle boils, Il.
metaph. to boil or bubble up, of the sea, Hdt.; of passion, like Lat. fervere, Aesch., Soph.
c. gen. to boil up or over with a thing, ζεῖν ὕδατος καὶ πηλοῦ Plat.; also c. dat., ζ. φθειρσί Luc.
Causal, to make to boil, θυμόν Anth.
jealous, Anth.
jealous, Od.
giver of bliss, Anth.
mad with jealousy, Anth.
eager rivalry, zealous imitation, emulation, a noble passion, opp. to φθόνος (envy), Plat., etc.:—but also jealousy, Hes.
c. gen. pers. zeal for one, Soph., Plut.
c. gen. rei, rivalry for a thing, Eur.; ζ. πλούτου Plut., etc.
pass. the object of emulation or desire, happiness, bliss, honour, glory, Soph., Dem.
of style, extravagance, Plut.:—also, fierceness, NTest.
to be jealous of, to emulate, rival, c. acc. pers., Plat.
c. acc. rei, to regard with jealous anger, Aeschin.
to pretend to, ἀρετήν Id.
jealousy, rivalry, Aeschin., Plut.
jealous, Ar., Anth.
c. acc. pers. to rival, vie with, emulate, Lat. aemulari, Soph., Thuc., etc.: —in bad sense, to be jealous of, envy, Hes., Theocr.:— absol, to be jealous, NTest.
to esteem or pronounce happy, admire, praise, τινά τινος one for a thing, Soph., Ar.: ironical, ζηλῶ σε happy in your ignorance! Eur.
c. acc. rei, to desire emulously, strive after, Dem.:—Pass., Plat., etc.
Pass. also of persons, to be impelled by zeal, NTest.
that which is emulated: in pl. high fortunes, Eur.
in pl. also emulous efforts, rivalries, Aeschin., Dem.
emulation, imitation, Thuc.
an emulator, zealous admirer or follower, Plat., etc.
a zealot, used to translate Κανανίτης or Καναναῖος (from the Hebr. qana, to glow, be zealous), NTest.
emulous, Arist.
to be emulated, worthy of imitation, Plat., Dem.
to be deemed happy, to be envied, Theogn., Aesch., etc.
of conditions, enviable, blessed, Eur., Ar.
loss, damage, Lat. damnum, opp. to κέρδος, Plat., etc.; ζημίαν λαβεῖν to sustain loss, Dem.
a penalty in money, a fine, mulct, ζημίην ἀποτίνειν Hdt.; ὀφείλειν Id.; καταβάλλειν Dem.; ζημία ἐπίκειται στατήρ a fine of a stater is imposed, Thuc.
generally a penalty, ζ. ἐπιτιθέναι τινί Hdt.; ζ. πρόσκειταί τινι Xen.; θάνατον ζημίαν ἐπιτίθεσθαι, προτιθέναι, τάττειν to make death the penalty, Thuc., etc.
φανερὰ ζαμία a mere good-for-nothing, a dead loss, Ar.
to cause loss or do damage to any one, τινά Plat., etc.:—Pass., μεγάλα ζημιώσεται will suffer great losses, Thuc.

to fine, amerce, mulct in a sum of money, c. dat. rei, ζ. τινὰ χιλίῃσι δραχμῇσι Hdt.; χρήμασιν Thuc.:— Pass. to be fined or amerced in a thing, c. dat., Plat.; c. acc., τὴν ψυχὴν ζημιώσεαι wilt lose thy life, Hdt.
generally to punish, Id., Thuc.
causing loss, ruinous, Xen.
a penalty, fine, Luc.; τῆς ἀταξίας for their disorder, Xen.
knowing the mind of Zeus, of Apollo, Anth.

Ζ, ζ, ζῆτα, τό, indecl., sixth letter of Gk. Alphabet: as numeral ζʹ = ἑπτά and ἕβδομος (the obsol. ϛʹ, i.e. Ϝ, vau, the digamma, being retained to represent ἕξ, ἕκτος) , but ͵ζ = 7000. Ζ ζ is composed of σ and δ, so that in aeolic it becomes σδ, as Σδεύς κωμάσδω ψιθυρίσδω for Ζεύς κωμάζω ψιθυρίζω:—reversely, in attic, σδ becomes ζ, Ἀθήναζε θύραζε for Ἀθήνασδε θύρασδε. But σ often disappears in aeolic, where ζά = δια, see ζά, ζα-:—so in aeolic and doric, as we have Δεύς Δάν for Ζεύς Ζάν, δορκάς = ζορκάς:—so also ἀρίζηλος for ἀρίδηλος; ἀλαπαδνός from ἀλαπάζω, παιδνός from παίζω:—doric, in the middle of words, it becomes δδ, as θερίδδω for -ίζω, μάδδα for μᾶζα. Zeta, being a double conson., made a short vowel at the end of the foregoing syllable long by position. But Homer used the vowel short before two prop. names, which could not otherwise come into the Hexam., viz. ἄστῠ Ζελείης, ὑλήεσσᾰ Ζάκυνθος.
to seek, seek for, Il., Aesch., etc.; μὴ ζητῶν without seeking, Xen.; τὸ ζητούμενον ἁλωτόν what is sought for may be found, Soph.
to enquire for, Xen.: to ask about a thing, Id.
to search after, search out, Soph., Thuc.
to search or inquire into, investigate, Plat., etc.; ζ. τὰ θεῖα Xen., etc.
to require, demand, παρὰ τοῦ στρατηγοῦ λόγον ζητοῦντες Dem.
to seek after, desire, ἀμήχανα Eur.
c. inf. to seek to do, Hdt., Aesch., etc.
to have to seek, feel the want of, Lat. desidero, Hdt.
that which is sought, οὐ ῥᾴδιον ζ. a thing not easy to find, Eur.
an inquiry, question, Soph., Plat., etc.
a search, μητρός after her, Eur.
to be searched, τὰ ζ. places to be beaten for game, Xen.
a seeking, seeking for, search for a thing, c. gen., Hdt., Soph., etc.
a searching, search, ποιέεσθαι ζήτησιν τῶν νεῶν to search the ships, Hdt.
inquiry, investigation, Plat.
to be sought, Soph.
ζητητέον one must seek, Ar.
a seeker, inquirer, Plat.
in pl. commissioners to inquire into state-offences, Dem.
disposed to search or inquire, searching, inquiring, Plat.
sought for, Soph.
a weed that grows in wheat, prob. Lat. lolium, darnel, in pl., NTest.
dusky, gloomy, Hes., Luc.:— metaph., ζ. φροντίδες Anth.
the gloom of the world below, nether darkness, Hom., Aesch.:—generally, gloom, darkness, Hes., Pind.
the dark quarter, i. e. the west, opposed to ἠώς, Hom.: cf. Ζέφυρος.
to darken:—Pass. to be or become dark, Anth.
a chest or box (of board strongly fastened together), Soph., Xen.
of or for the yoke, ζ. ἵππος a draught-horse, wheeler, Ar.:—c. gen., θηρῶν ζυγίους ζεύξασα σατίνας having yoked cars to teams of beasts, Eur.
a yoke-band, i. e. a band for fastening the yoke to the pole, Il., Plut.
to struggle with one's yoke-fellow, generally, to struggle, Dem.
anything which joins two bodies; and so,

the yoke or cross-bar tied by the ζυγόδεσμον to the end of the pole, and having ζεῦγλαι (collars or loops) at each end, by which two horses, mules or oxen drew the plough or carriage, Hom., etc.:—metaph., τὸ δούλιον ζ. the yoke of slavery, Hdt.; δουλείας, ἀνάγκης ζ. Soph., Eur.; ἐπιτιθέναι τινὶ ζυγὰ τοῦ μὴ . . , so as to prevent . . , Xen.
a pair, Eur.; κατὰ ζυγά in pairs, Theocr.
the cross-bar joining the horns of the φόρμιγξ, along which the strings were fastened, Il.
in pl. the thwarts joining the opposite sides of a ship or boat, the benches, Lat. transtra, Od., Hdt.; in sg., Soph.:—metaph., τὸ πόλεος ζ. Eur.
the middle of the three banks in a trireme; metaph., οἱ ἐπὶ ζυγῷ δορός those on the upper bench, Aesch.
the beam of the balance, Dem.: — the balance itself, Plat.
καρχασίου ζ. the yard-arm at the masthead, Pind.
a rank or line of soldiers, opp. to a file, Thuc.
to weigh by the balance, Luc.

sense.gloss: a public officer, who looked to the weights.

entry.sense: bearing the yoke, Eur.
to yoke together, ζ. κιθάραν to put the cross-bar to the lyre, Luc.
to weigh, examine, Ar.
yoked, Soph.
leaven:—metaph. of corruption, falsehood, NTest.
leavened, Xen.
to leaven, NTest.
reward for life saved, Od., Hdt.; also, like θρεπτήρια, a reward for nursing and rearing one, Il.: c. gen. rei, ζωάγρια μόχθων, νούσων Anth.
for saving life, Babr.: v. ζω-άγρια.
to paint from life, to paint, Plat.
the art of painting, Plat., Xen.
skilled in painting, Plat., Xen.
one who paints from life or from nature, a painter, Hdt., Plat., etc.
to take alive, take captive instead of killing, Il., Hdt., etc.:—Pass., Id.
（ζωή, ἀγείρω) to restore to life, revive, Il.
a taking alive, ζωγρίῃ λαμβάνειν or αἱρέειν = ζωγρεῖν, Hdt.
Dim. of ζῷον II, a small figure, Hdt.
in pl. the signs of the Zodiac, Arist.
a living, i. e. one's means of life, substance, Od.; τὴν ζόην ποιεῖσθαι ἀπό or ἔκ τινος to get one's living by . . , Hdt., etc.
life, existence, Tyrtae., Trag., etc.
a way of life, Hdt.
giving the bloom and freshness of life, Pind.
that which is girded, a girded frock or doublet, Od.
in Il. the lower part of the θώρηξ, round which the ζωστήρ passed, Il.
the drawers worn by athletes, in Prose διάζωμα, Id.
= ζώνη, a woman's girdle, Soph., Anth.
soup, ζωμεύματα put by way of joke for ὑποζώματα νεώς, Ar.
to boil into soup, Ar.
a soup-ladle, Anth.
Dim. of ζωμός, a little sauce, Ar.
Lat. jus, sauce to eat with meat, fish, etc., Ar.; ὁ μέλας ζ. the black broth of Spartans, Plut.
a belt, girdle:
properly the lower girdle worn by women above the hips, (the upper-girdle, the στρόφιον, being worn under the breasts), Hom.

Phrases, λῦσε δὲ παρθενίην ζώνην unloosed her maiden girdle, of the bridegroom, Od.; Mid. of the bride, Anth.:—of men on a march, ζ. λύεσθαι to slacken one's belt, i. e. rest oneself, Hdt.:— of pregnant women, φέρειν ὑπὸ ζώνης, τρέφειν ἐντὸς ζώνης Aesch., Eur.:— εἰς ζώνην δεδόσθαι to be given for girdle-money (as we should say, pin-money), of Oriental queens who had cities given them, Xen.
the man's belt (in Hom. commonly ζωστήρ), Il., Xen., etc.
the part round which the girdle past, the waist, loin, Il.
to gird, esp. to gird round the loins for a pugilistic conflict, Od., Hes.; ζ. γαῖαν, of Ocean, Anth.
Mid. ζώννῦμαι, to gird oneself, gird up one's loins, of wrestlers and pugilists, who in early times wore a linen cloth (ζῶμα, διάζωμα) round their loins.
generally, to gird up one's loins, prepare for battle, Il.; also c. acc., ζωννύσκετο μίτρην girded on his belt, Id.; χαλκὸν ζ. to gird on one's sword, Id.
a sculptor, Anth.
to produce alive, Luc.
to preserve alive, NTest.
producing animals, generative, name of Apollo, Anth.
life-bringing, Id.
to make alive, Anth.
in the shape of an animal, Plut.
a living being, animal, Hdt., Ar., etc.

in painting and sculpture, a figure, image, not necessarily of animals, Hdt.; mostly in pl., ζῷα ἐς τὴν ἐσθῆτα ἐγγράφειν Id., Plat., etc.; ζῷα γράφεσθαι, = ζωγραφεῖν, with a second acc. of the thing painted, ζῷα γράψασθαι τὴν ζεῦξιν τοῦ Βοσπόρου to have the passage of the Bosporus painted, Hdt.
to produce animals, Arist., Luc.
to make alive, NTest.
wise unto life, Anth.
alive, living, Homer, Hdt., etc.; ζωὸν ἑλεῖν τινά to take prisoner, Il.; ζωὸν λαβεῖν Xen.
producing its young alive, viviparous, Theocr.
describing to the life, Anth.
life-giving, Anth.
bearing animals: ὁ ζ. (sc. κύκλος), the zodiac, Anth.
to represent alive, Anth.
to kindle into flame, light up: metaph., ζ. τάρβος Aesch.; νείκη Eur.
a spark, ember, Plat., etc.
to drink sheer wine, Anth.
drinking sheer wine, drunken, Anth.

pure, sheer, properly of wine without water, Anth.; absol., ζωρός (sc. οἶνος) Id.:—comp. in Hom., ζωρότερον δὲ κέραιε mix the wine more pure, i. e. add less water, Il. As the Greeks mixed their wine with water, the phrase ζωρότερον πίνειν came to mean not only, as in Hdt., to drink purer wine than common, but, generally, to drink hard, be a drunkard, like ἀκρατοποτεῖν, Theophr., Luc.
a girdle, in Il. always a warrior's belt or baldric, which passed round the loins and secured the bottom of the θώραξ:—in Od., the belt with which the swineherd girds up his frock.
later, = ζώνη, a woman's girdle.
metaph. of the encircling sea, Anth.
girded, Plut.
a belt, girdle, Od.
full of life, lively, Lat. vivax, Plat.:—adv., ζωτικῶς ἔχειν to be fond of life, Plut.
of works of Art, true to life, τὸ ζωτικὸν φαίνεσθαι πῶς ἐνεργάζῃ τοῖς ἀνδριᾶσιν; how do you produce that look of life in your statues? Xen.
giving life to plants, fertilising, generative, Aesch., Plut.
Conjunction with two chief senses, Disjunctive and Comparative.

DISJUNCTIVE, or, Lat. vel, to subjoin one or more clauses differing from the first, ἤκουσας ἢ οὐκ ἤκουσας ἢ κωφῇ λέγω; Aesch.: —ἤ . . , ἤ . . , either . . , or . . , Lat. aut . . , aut . . , Hom., etc.

in indirect Questions, εἰ . . , ἢ . . , whether . . , or . . , Lat. utrum . . , an . . , εἰδῶμεν εἰ νικῶμεν ἢ νικώμεθα Aesch.:—but in Hom. ἢ . . , ἢ (or ἦ) . . is used for εἰ, Lat. an, εἰπὲ ἢ . . , say whether . . , Od.

COMPARATIVE, than, as, Lat. quam, Hom., etc.: after Adjs. which imply comparison, as ἄλλος, ἕτερος, ἀλλοῖος, διπλάσιος, ἐναντίος, ἴδιος, πολλαπλάσιος, and after the Advs. πρίν, πρόσθεν; so, after Verbs implying comparison, βούλεσθαι ἤ . . to wish rather than . .; φθάνειν ἤ . . to come sooner than . . , etc.
ἤ sometimes joins two Comparatives, when they both refer to the same subject, ἐλαφρότεροι ἢ ἀφνειότεροι to be swifter rather than richer, Od.; ταχύτερα ἢ σοφώτερα Hdt.
rarely after a Sup., πλεῖστα θωυμάσια ἔχει Αἴγυπτος ἢ ἄλλη πᾶσα χώρη Id.
ἤ is often omitted with numerals after πλέων, ἐλάττων, μείων, as, ἔτη πλέω ἑβδομήκοντα Plat. [When ἢ οὐ, ἢ οὐκ come together in a verse, the two coalesce into one syll.]
an exclamation, to call one's attention to a thing, ἤ, ἤ, σιώπα Ar.

little, small, poor, slight, with negat. οὐδέ, οὔ οἱ ἔνι φρένες, οὐδ’ ἠβαιαί no sense is in him, no not the least, Hom.; οὔ οἱ ἔνι τρίχες, οὐδ’ ἠβαιαί no not even a few, Od.:—neut. as adv., οὐδ’ ἠβαιόν not in the least, not at all, Lat. ne tantillum quidem, Hom.; rarely without a negat., ἠβαιὸν ἀπὸ σπείους a little from the cave, Od.
to come to man's estate, come to one's strength, Lat. pubescere, Xen.:—metaph. to be new, ἡβάσκει πενίη Anth.

to be at man's estate, to be in the prime of youth, ἀνὴρ οὐδὲ μάλ’ ἡβῶν not even in the prime and pride of life, Hom.; γυνὴ τέτορ’ ἡβώωσα (sc. ἔτη) i. e. being four years past puberty, Hes.; ἡβῶν when I was young, Ar.; οἱ ἡβῶντες the young, Id.:—of plants, ἡμερὶς ἡβώωσα a young luxuriant vine, Od.
metaph. to be young, ἀεὶ γὰρ ἡβᾶι τοῖς γέρουσιν εὖ μαθεῖν learning is young even for the old, i. e. 'tis never too late to learn, Aesch.; ἡβᾶι δῆμος the people is like a young man, Eur.
from the youth upwards, Hdt.
manhood, youthful prime, youth, Lat. pubertas, νεηνίηι ἀνδρὶ ἐοικώς, τοῦπερ χαριεστάτη ἥβη Od.; ἥβης μέτρον ἱκέσθαι or ἱκάνειν = ἡβάσκειν, Id.
youthful strength, vigour, πειρώμενος ἥβης Il.; ἥβηι πεποίθεα Od.
legally, ἥβη was the time before manhood, at Athens 16 years of age; at Sparta, 18, so that τὰ δέκα ἀφ’ ἥβης were men of 28, τὰ τετταράκοντα ἀφ’ ἥβης men of 58, and so on, Xen.: cf. ἔφηβος.
metaph. youthful cheer, merriment, δαιτὸς ἥβη Eur.: also youthful passion, fire, spirit, Pind.
a body of youth, the youth, Lat. juventus, Aesch.
as femin. prop. n., Ἥβη, Hebe, daughter of Zeus and Hera, wife of Hercules, Hom.
a place where young people meet, to eat and drink, exercise and amuse themselves, Plut.
youthful, at one's prime, Hhymn., Eur.
youthful, Lat. juvenilis, Xen.
to be youngish, Ar.
very divine, most holy, Hom.
a leading: in Eur. ἁγεμόνευμα νεκροῖσι = ἡγεμὼν νεκρῶν.
to be or act as ἡγεμών, to go before, lead the way, Hom.; ὁδὸν ἡγ. Od.; c. dat. pers. to lead the way for him, ῥόον ὕδατι ἡγεμόνευεν made a course for the water, Il.

to lead in war, to rule, command, c. dat., Id.; elsewhere, like most Verbs of ruling, c. gen., Id., Hdt., etc.:—absol. to have or take the command, Hdt., Plat.:—Pass. to be ruled, Thuc.; to be governor, τῆς Συρίας NTest.
a leading the way, going first, Hdt.
chief command, Id., Thuc., etc.; ἡγ. δικαστηρίων authority over them, Aeschin.

the hegemony or sovereignty of one state over a number of subordinates, as of Athens in Attica, Thebes in Boeotia:— the hegemony of Greece was wrested from Sparta by Athens; and the Peloponn. war was a struggle for this hegemony.
= Roman imperium, Plut.: the reign of the Emperor, NTest.
a division of the army, a command, Plut.
ready to lead or guide, Xen.
fit to command, authoritative, leading, Id., etc.
= Rom. Consularis, Plut.
sc. ἱερά , τά, thank-offerings for safe conduct, Xen.
one who leads, Lat. dux: and so,
in Od., a guide to shew the way, so Hdt., etc.; ἡγ. γενέσθαι τινὶ τῆς ὁδοῦ Id.
one who is an authority to others, Lat. dux, auctor, τοῖς νεωτέροις ἡγ. ἠθῶν γίγνεσθαι Plat.; ἡγεμόνα εἶναί τινος to be the cause of a thing, Xen., etc.

in Il., a leader, commander, chief, ἡγεμόνες Δαναῶν, φυλάκων, Il., etc.; ἔχοντες ἡγεμόνας τῶν πάνυ στρατηγῶν having some of the best generals as commanders, Thuc.: a chief, sovereign, Pind., Soph., etc.
= Rom. Emperor, Plut.: also a provincial governor, NTest.
Dep. to go before, lead the way, Hom., etc.:—c. dat. pers. to lead the way for him, guide, conduct, Id.:—also, ὁδὸν ἡγήσασθαι to go before on the way, Lat. praeire viam, Od.
c. dat. pers. et gen. rei, to be one's leader in a thing, ἀοιδὸς ἡμῖν ἡγείσθω ὀρχηθμοῖο Id.; ἡγ. τινι σοφίας, ὠιδῆς Pind., etc.:—and c. gen. rei only, ἡγ. νόμων to lead the song, Id., etc.
c. acc. rei, to lead, conduct, τὰς πομπάς Dem., etc.
to lead an army or fleet, c. dat., Hom., etc.:—c. gen. to be the leader or commander of, Id.
absol., οἱ ἡγούμενοι the rulers, Soph.; ἡγούμενοι ἐν τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς leading men, NTest.
to suppose, believe, hold, Lat. ducere, Hdt., etc.; ἡγ. τι εἶναι Id.
with an attributive word added, ἡγ. τινα βασιλέα to hold or regard as king, Id.; ἡγ. τι περὶ πολλοῦ Id.; περὶ πλείστου Thuc.
ἡγ. θεούς to believe in gods, Eur., etc.; cf. νομίζω II.
ἡγοῦμαι δεῖν, to think it fit, deem it necessary to do, c. inf., Dem.; without δεῖν, παθεῖν μᾶλλον ἡγησάμενοι ἤ . . Thuc.
the perf. is used in pass. sense, τὰ ἁγημένα = τὰ νομιζόμενα, ap. Dem.
epic form of ἀγείρομαι (Pass.) to gather together, assemble, Hom.
entry.etym: only in 3rd pl. pres. and imperf. ἠγερέθονται, ἠγερέθοντο, and inf. ἠγερέθεσθαι.

entry.sense: a leader, Anth.
to guide, lead, Od.; κακὸν μόρον ἡγ. to lead a wretched life, Id.
one must lead, Xen.
one must suppose, Plat.
a guide, Soph.
a commander, Pind.
a leader, commander, chief, Il.
that is to say, or rather, to define a word more correctly, Xen.
and, properly correlative to ἠ-μέν v. sub ἠμέν:— but, often without ἠμέν, just like καί, and, Il.:— ἠδὲ καί conjoined and also, Hom.

entry.etym: adverb of ἡδύς, v. ἡδύς III.
related to νῦν, as Lat. jam to nunc
entry.sense: by this time, before this, already, or of the future, now, presently, forthwith, Hom.; νὺξ ἤδη τελέθει 'tis already night, Il.; ἔτος τόδ’ ἤδη δέκατον Soph.:—so in a local relation, ἀπὸ ταύτης ἤδη Αἴγυπτος directly after this is Egypt, Hdt.
of the future, λέξον ὄφρα κεν ἤδη ταρπώμεθα Il.; στείχοις ἂν ἤδη Soph.
often joined with other words of time, ἤδη νῦν now already, Hom.; νῦν ἤδη Soph., etc.; ἤδη πάλαι Id.; ἐπεὶ ἤδη, Lat. quum jam, Od., etc.
to enjoy oneself, take delight, take one's pleasure, Od., etc.—Construction:
with participle, ἥσατο πίνων Od.; ἥσθη ἀκούσας he was glad to have heard, Hdt., etc.
c. dat., ἥδεσθαί τινι to delight in or at a thing, Id., etc.; ἐπί τινι Xen., etc.;—rarely c. gen., πώματος ἥσθη he enjoyed the draught, Soph.
c. acc. and part., ἥσθην πατέρα τὸν ἀμὸν εὐλογοῦντά σε I was pleased to hear you praising him, Id.
part. as an adj. glad, delighted, Ar.: also, like βουλομένωι, ἀσμένωι, in the phrase ἡδομένωι ἐστί μοί τι I am well pleased at the thing happening, Hdt., Plat.
of ἥδομαι, with joy, gladly, Xen.

delight, enjoyment, pleasure, Lat. voluptas, Hdt., etc.; ἡδονῇ ἡσσᾶσθαι, χαρίζεσθαι to give way to pleasure, Thuc., Plat., etc.:—often with Prepositions in adv. sense, πρὸς or καθ’ ἡδονὴν λέγειν to speak so as to please another, Hdt., attic; καθ’ ἡδονὴν κλύειν, ἀκούειν Soph., Dem.; καθ’ ἡδονήν or πρὸς ἡδ. ἐστί μοι Aesch.; ὃ μέν ἐστι πρὸς ἡδ. that which is agreeable, Dem.; ἐν ἡδονῇ ἐστί τινι it is a pleasure or delight to another, Hdt., etc.
a pleasure, a delight, Soph., Ar.
in pl. pleasures, pleasant lusts, Xen., NTest.
delight, enjoyment, pleasure, δαιτὸς ἦδος pleasure from or in the feast, Hom.; ἀλλὰ τί μοι τῶν ἦδος; what delight have I there from? Il.
sweet-sounding, Eur., Anth.
sweetening marriage, Anth.
sweetly laughing, Hhymn., Anth.
sweet-tongued, Pind.
of pleasant mind, Xen.
sweet-speaking, Il., etc.: sweet-sounding, Pind.:—poet. fem. ἡδυέπεια, Hes.
sweet-strained, Eur.
sweet-speaking, sweet-voiced, Pind., Anth.
of persons, flattering, fawning, Eur.
singing sweetly to the lyre, Anth.
sweet-strained, sweet-singing, Pind.
of honey-sweet voice, Anth.
sweetly-mixed, Anth.
sweet, pleasant, Hhymn.
to sweeten, season, give a flavour or relish to a thing, c. acc., Xen., etc.
producing sweet wine, Xen.:— ἡδύοινοι, οἱ, dealers in sweet wine, Id.
pleasant living, luxury, Xen.
to live pleasantly, enjoy oneself, be luxurious, Xen.
enjoyment, Anth.
sweet-breathing, Eur.; of musical sound, Pind.; of dreams, Soph.
sweet-smelling, fragrant, Anth.
dear to the people, Soph.
fond of drinking, Anth.
sweet to drink, Od.
that which gives a relish or flavour, seasoning, sauce, Ar., Xen., etc.

sweet to the taste or smell, Hom.; to the hearing, Id.; then of any pleasant feeling or state, as sleep, Id.:—c. inf., ἡδὺς δρακεῖν Aesch.; ἡδὺς ἀκοῦσαι λόγος Plat.:— ἡδύ ἐστι or γίγνεται it is pleasant, Hom., etc.:—so, οὔ μοι ἥδιόν ἐστι λέγειν I had rather not say, Hdt.:—neut. as Subst., τὰ ἡδέα pleasures, Thuc.:—neut. as adv., sweetly, Il., etc.
after Hom., of persons, pleasant, welcome, Soph.
well-pleased, glad, Id., Dem.; in addressing a person, ὦ ἥδιστε, Horace's dulcissime rerum, Plat.
like εὐήθης, innocent, simple, ὡς ἡδὺς εἶ Id.

adv. ἡδέως, sweetly, pleasantly, with pleasure, Soph., Eur., etc.; ἡδέως ἂν ἐροίμην I would gladly ask, should like to ask, Dem.;— ἡδ. ἔχειν τι to be pleased or content with, Eur.; ἡδ. ἔχειν πρός τινα or τινί to be kind, well-disposed to one, Dem.:— comp. ἥδιον Plat., etc.:—Sup., ἥδιστα Id.
sweet-shining, Anth.
sweet-minded, Anth.
sweetness of voice or sound, Babr.
sweet-voiced, Sapph..
sweetly joyous, Anth.
of sweet complexion, Anth.

entry.etym: epic for ἀείρομαι, Pass., only found in3 pl. pres. and imperf. ἠερέθονται, -οντο
entry.sense: to hang floating or waving in the air, Il.:—metaph., ὁπλοτέρων ἀνδρῶν φρένες ἠερέθονται young men's minds turn with every wind, Id.
early, with early morn, Il.
in the air, high in air, Anth.
wheeling in mid air, Anth.
of dark and cloudy look, cloud-streaked, of the sea, Od.: generally, dark, murky, Id.:—neut. as adv., in the far distance, dimly, ὅσσον τ’ ἠεροειδὲς ἀνὴρ ἴδεν Il.
hazy, murky, Il.; ἠερόεντα κέλευθα the murky road (i. e. death), Od.
from air, Anth.
walking in darkness, Il.
sounding through air, loud-voiced, Il.
accustomed to a thing, acquainted with it, c. gen., Soph.
absol. accustomed, usual, Eur.: of animals, tame, domestic, Lat. mansuetus, Ar.:—as neut., = ἦθος, τὰ καινά γ’ ἐκ τῶν ἠθάδων ἡδίον’ ἐστί Eur.
trusty, honoured, ἠθεῖε sir, Il.; ἠθείη κεφαλή Id.; ἀλλά μιν ἠθεῖον καλέω I will call him my honoured lord, Od.
to sift, strain:—Pass. to be strained, Plat.
of or for morals, ethical, moral, Arist.; τὰ ἠθικά a treatise on morals, Id.
shewing moral character, expressive thereof, Id.:— adv., ἠθικῶς λέγειν Id.
a strainer, Eur.; of the eyelashes, Xen.
to form manners or character, Plut.
forming character, Plut.
an accustomed place: in pl. the haunts or abodes of animals, Hom., Hdt.
custom, usage, Hes., Hdt.
of man, his disposition, character, Lat. ingenium, mores, Hes., attic; ὦ μιαρὸν ἦθος, addressed to a person, Soph.
in pl., generally, of manners, like Lat. mores, Hes., Hdt., Thuc. rare collat. form of ἠθέω.
provisions for a journey, epic word for ἐφόδια, Lat. viaticum, Hom.:—generally, λύκων ἤια food for wolves, Il.
husks or chaff, Od.
a youth just come to manhood, but not yet married, παρθένος ἠίθεός τε Hom.; χοροὺς παρθένων τε καὶ ἠιθέων Hdt.
rare as fem., ἠιθέη = παρθένος.
with banks, high-banked, Il.
epith. of Phoebus, ἤιε Φοῖβε Il. Prob. from the cry ἤ, ἤ, cf. ἰήϊος, εὔϊος.
a sea-bank, shore, beach, Hdt., etc.; a river-bank, Aesch.
of place or motion, slightly, a little, softly, gently, Hom.
of Sound, stilly, softly, low, Il.
of Sight, softly, smoothly, ἦκα στίλβοντες ἐλαίῳ with oil soft shining, Id.
of Time, by little and little, Anth.
untouched by the goad, of young heifers reserved for sacrifices, Il.
ἤκιστος ἐλαυνέμεν, the gentlest or slowest in driving, Il.

entry.etym: Sup. of the comp. ἥσσων, the Posit. in use being μικρός,
entry.sense: least:—as adv. ἥκιστα, least, Soph., etc.; οὐχ ἥκιστα, ἀλλὰ μάλιστα Hdt.; ὡς ἥκιστα as little as possible, Thuc.
often in reply to a question, nay not so, not at all, Lat. minime, Soph., etc.; ἥκιστά γε minime vero, Id.

to have come, be present, be here, Lat. adesse, properly in a perf. sense, with the imperf. ἧκον as plup., I had come, and fut. ἥξω as fut. perf. I shall have come, directly opp. to οἴχομαι to be gone, while ἔρχομαι to come or go serves as pres. to both, Hom., etc.:—to return, Xen.
to have reached a point, ἐς τοσήνδ’ ὕβριν Soph.; ἐς τοσοῦτον ἀμαθίας Plat.
δι’ ὀργῆς ἥκειν to be angry, Soph.; cf. διά A. IV.

like ἔχω B. II, εὖ ἥκειν τινός to be well off for a thing, have plenty of it, as, εὖ ἡκ.τοῦ βίου Hdt.; καλῶς αὐτοῖς ἧκον βίου as they had come to a good age, Eur.; ὧδε γένους ἡκ. τινί to be this degree of kin to him, Id.:—also, εὖ ἥκειν, absol., to be well off, flourishing, Hdt.:—c. gen. only, σὺ δὲ δυνάμιος ἥκεις μεγάλης thou art in great power, Id.
of things, to be brought, Id., etc.; ἵν’ ἥκει τὰ μαντεύματα what they have come to, Soph.
to concern, relate, or belong to, εἴς ἐμ’ ἥκει τὰ πράγματα Ar.
to depend upon, ἐπί τι Dem.
to wander, stray, Theocr.
the wool on the distaff, Od.
a distaff, Lat. colus, on which the wool is put, Hom., etc.; ἡ ἠλ. τοῦ ἀτράκτου the stalk of the spindle, Plat.
lengthd. form of ἠλάσκω, Il.
c. acc. to flee from, shun, Od.
to wander, stray, roam about, Il.
made of ἤλεκτρον, Luc.

electron, a word sometimes used to denote amber, as prob. in Hom., Hes. and Hdt.;—sometimes pale gold, a compound of 1 part of silver to 4 of gold, Soph., etc.—In Ar. ἐκπιπτουσῶν τῶν ἠλέκτρων, the ἤλεκτροι are prob. the pegs of the lyre made of or inlaid with electron.
amber-gleaming, Eur.
the beaming sun, Il.; as adj., ἠλέκτωρ Ὑπερίων beaming Hyperion, Id.
idle, vain, trifling, Theocr., Anth.
astray, distraught, crazed, Od.; also in apocop. form ἠλέ, Il.: ἠλεά as adv. foolishly, Anth.
act. distracting, crazing, οἶνος Od.
Dep.:— to sit in the court Ἡλιαία, be a Heliast, Ar.
at Athens, a public place or hall, in which the chief law-court was held, Ar.
the supreme court, ap. Dem.
fem. adj. of the sun, ap. Luc.
a juryman of the court ἡλιαία, a Heliast, Ar.
of, for, or like a Heliast, Ar.
high, steep, precipitous, epith. of rocky crags, Hom., Hes., etc.; of the throne of Zeus, Ar.
in Od. 9. 243 ἠλίβατος πέτρη, it seems to mean enormous, huge.
= Lat. altus, deep, profound, Hes., Eur.
enough, sufficiently, Lat. satis, ληὶς ἤλιθα πολλή Il.; δύη ἤλιθα πολλή Od., etc.
to speak or act idly, foolishly, Ar.
idle, vain, random, Pind., Aesch.
of persons, stupid, foolish, silly, like μάταιος, Hdt., Ar., etc. adv. -ίως, Plat.; neut. ἠλίθιον as adv., Ar.
folly, silliness, Plat.
to make foolish, distract, craze, Aesch.
time of life, age, Lat. aetas, Il.;—acc. used absol. in age, νέος ἡλικίην Hdt.; so in dat., ἡλικίᾳ ὢν νέος Thuc.; πόρρω τῆς ἡλ. advanced in years, Plat.

mostly, the flower or prime of life from about 17 to 45, man's estate, manhood, ἐν ἁλικίᾳ πρώτᾳ Pind.; ἐν ἡλικίᾳ εἶναι to be of age, Plat., etc.; so, ἡλικίαν ἔχειν, εἰς ἡλ. ἐλθεῖν Id.; ἡλικίαν ἔχειν, c. inf., to be of fit age for doing, Hdt.; οἱ ἐν ἡλικίᾳ men of serviceable age, Thuc.
youthful heat and passion, ἡλικίῃ ἐπιτρέπειν Hdt.
as collective Noun, = οἱ ἥλικες, those of the same age, fellows, comrades, Il., Thuc.
time, ταῦτα ἡλικίην ἂν εἴη κατὰ Λάϊον about the time of Laius, Hdt.
an age, generation, Lat. saeculum, Dem., etc.
of the body, stature, growth, as a sign of age, Hdt., Plat.
an equal in age, fellow, comrade, Lat. aequalis, Hdt., Ar., etc.
Fem. of ἡλικιώτης, Luc.; ἡλ. ἱστορία contemporary history, Plut.
as big as, Lat. quantus, Ar., Dem.
of age, as old as, Ar., etc.
in expressions of wonder, θαυμάσια ἡλίκα extraordinarily great, as in Lat. mirum quantum, Dem.
of the same age, Od., Pind.: c. gen. of the same age with, Aesch.
as Subst. a fellow, comrade, Hdt., Aesch., etc.
sun-stricken, sun-burnt, Eur.
like the sun, beaming, Plat.
sun-burnt, Theocr.
sun-mad, mad for love of the sun, Ar.
Pass. to live in the sun, Plat.; τὸ ἡλιούμενον a sunny spot, Xen.

the sun, Lat. sol, Hom., etc.; ὁρᾶν φάος ἠελίοιο, i.e. to be alive, Il.—The Sun furnished the earliest mode of determining the points of the heaven, πρὸς ἠῶ τ’ ἠέλιόν τε, i. e. towards the East, opp. to πρὸς ζόφον, Hom.; πρὸς ἠῶ τε καὶ ἡλίου ἀνατολάς, opp. to πρὸς ἑσπέρην, Hdt.
day, a day, like Lat. soles, Pind., Eur.: so in pl. hot sunny days, Thuc.
as prop. n., Helios, the sun-god, Hom.; in later Poets = Apollo, Aesch., etc.
depriving of sun, i. e. shading from the sun, Soph.
sun-trodden, Aesch.
missing the work, failing in one's aim, Anth.
missing the right month, i. e. untimely born, Il.
of the sun, epic ἠελιῶτις Anth.:— οἱ ἡλιῶται the inhabitants of the sun, Luc.
a nail: in Hom. only for ornament, a nail-head or stud.
after Hom. a nail to fasten with, Pind., Xen., etc.
a shadow, shade: metaph., δίκης ἠλύγη the obscurity of a lawsuit, Ar.
the Elysian fields, Lat. Elysium, Od.; in pl., Anth. Hom. places it on the west border of the earth, near to Ocean; Hesiod's Elysium is in the μακάρων νῆσοι.
Elysian, Anth.
a step, Eur.
sandy, Hom.

to be seated, sit, Hom., etc.:— to sit still, sit idle, Il., etc.: of an army, to lie encamped, Id.:—of a spy, to lurk, Id.:— later, of places, to lie, be situated, Hdt.; ἡμένωι ἐν χώρωι = εἱαμενῇ, in a low, sunken place, Theocr.:—rarely c. acc., σέλμα ἧσθαι to be seated on a bench, Aesch.; ἧσθαι Σιμόεντος κοίτας Eur.
that which is thrown, a dart, javelin, Il.
day, Hom.; νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ by night and day, Il.; ἦμαρ by day, Hes.; μέσον ἦμ. mid- day, Il.; δείελον ἦμ. evening, Od.

in Hom. with Adjs. to describe a state or condition, αἴσιμον, ὀλέθριον, μόρσιμον, νηλεὲς ἦμαρ the day of destiny, of death; ἐλεύθερον, δούλιον, ἀναγκαῖον ἦμαρ the day of freedom, of slavery; νόστιμον ἦμαρ, etc.
of the seasons, ἤματ’ ὀπωρινῇ, ἤματι χειμερίῳ Il.

with Preps. ἐπ’ ἤματι day by day, daily, Od.; also, in a day, for a day, Hom.: —so, ἐπ’ ἦμαρ by day, Soph.; for a day, Eur.:— κατ’ ἦμαρ day by day, Lat. quotidie, Soph.; κατ’ ἦμαρ ἀεί Id.; but κατ’ ἦμαρ, also, this day, to-day, Lat. hodie, Id.:— παρ’ ἦμαρ every other day, Pind., Soph.

entry.etym: adverb part. perf. pass. of ἁμαρτάνω,
entry.sense: faultily, Plat.
by day, Od.
day by day, daily, Il.
of our land or country, native, Lat. nostras, Ar.

entry.etym: adverb part. perf. pass. of ἀμελέω,

entry.sense: epic Conjunction, correlative to ἠ-δέ, as well .. , as also . . , Lat. et . . , et . . , but sometimes disjunctive, like Lat. vel . . , vel . . , Hom.
day, Hom., etc.:—phrases for day-break, ἅμα ἡμέρᾳ or ἅμα τῇ ἡμέρᾳ Xen.; ἡμ. διαλάμπει or ἐκλάμπει Ar.; ἡμ. ὑποφαίνεται Xen.; γίγνεται or ἐστὶ πρὸς ἡμέραν Id.
with Adjs. to describe a state or time of life, ἐπίπονος ἡμ. a life of misery, Soph.; λυπρὰν ἄγειν ἡμ. Eur.; αἱ μακραὶ ἡμέραι length of days, Soph.; νέα ἡμ. youth, Eur.
poet. for time, ἡμ. κλίνει τε κἀνάγει πάλιν ἅπαντα τἀνθρώπεια Soph.
absol. usages,
in gen., τριῶν ἡμερέων within three days, Hdt.; ἡμερῶν ὀλίγων within a few days, Thuc.: —also, ἡμέρας by day, Plat.; δὶς τῆς ἡμέρης ἑκάστης twice every day, Hdt.
in dat., τῇδε τῇ ἡμέρᾳ on this day, Soph.; so, τῇδ’ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ Id.
in acc., πᾶσαν ἡμ. all day, Hdt.; τρίτην ἡμ. ἥκων three days after one's arrival, Thuc.; τὰς ἡμέρας in daytime Xen.

with Preps., ἀνὰ πᾶσαν ἡμ. every day, Hdt.:— δι’ ἡμέρης, attic -ρας, the whole day long, Id.; διὰ τρίτης ἡμ. every third day, Lat. tertio quoque die, Id.; δι’ ἡμ. πολλῶν at a distance of many days, Thuc.: — ἐξ ἡμέρας by day, Soph.:— ἐφ’ ἡμέραν sufficient for the day, Hdt., etc.; but, τοὐφ’ ἡμέραν day by day, Eur.:— καθ’ ἡμέραν by day, Aesch.; but commonly day by day, daily, Soph., etc.; τὸ καθ’ ἡμ., absol., every day, Ar., etc.;— μεθ’ ἡμέραν at mid- day, Hdt., etc.
to spend the day, Xen., etc.: —absol. to travel the whole day, Aesch.
to pass one's days, live, Soph.
for the day, by day, ἡμ. φάος light as of the day, Aesch.
a day long, ἡμ. ὁδός a day's journey, Hdt., Plat., etc.
sc. ὥρα, = ἡμέρα, Soph.
of day, Plat.; ἄγγελος ἡμ. a day-messenger, Xen.
for a day, lasting but a day, Soph., Eur.
as Subst., ἡμερίς (sc. ἄμπελος), the cultivated vine, opp. to ἀγριάς, Od.: but distinguished from ἀμπελίς by Ar.
to be an ἡμεροδρόμος, Luc.
as Subst. a courier, Hdt.
sleeping by day, Hes., Eur.
by count of days, Aesch.
to count by days, Hdt.
a calendar, Plut.
watching by day, Aesch., Ar.:—as Subst., a day-watcher, Hdt., Soph., etc.
tame, tamed, reclaimed, Lat. mansuetus, of animals, Od., Plat.; so, τὰ ἥμερα alone, Xen.
of plants and trees, cultivated, Lat. sativus, Hdt., etc.
of men, civilised, gentle, Id., Dem.; so of a lion, Aesch.
tameness:—of men, gentleness, kindness, Plat.
appearing by day, Aesch.
to tame, make tame, of wild beasts, Plat.
of countries, to clear them of robbers and wild beasts, as Hercules and Theseus did, Pind., Aesch.:—also, to tame by conquest, subdue, Hdt.
of men also, to soften, civilise, Plat.
a taming: civilising, Plut.
our, Lat. noster, Hom., etc.; εἰς ἡμέτερον (sc. δῶμα) Od.; so, ἡμέτερόνδε Id.; ἡ ἡμετέρα (sc. χώρα) Thuc.; τὰ ἡμέτερα φρονεῖν to take our part, Xen.
sometimes for ἐμός, Od.
a half-man, Luc.
sodden, Anth.
half-eaten, Xen.
but half-bearded, Theocr.
half-naked, Luc.: so ἡμι-γύναιος, ον, Suid.; ἡμίγυνος, ον, Synes.
half-divided, half-mangled, Anth.
a half-daric, Xen.
wanting half, half-full, Xen., Anth.
a half-slave, Eur.
a half-ἑκτεύς, i. e. 1/12 of a medimnus, Dem.
a half-Greek, Luc.
half-made, half-finished, Luc.
half-boiled, half-cooked, Luc.
half-green, Anth.
half-dead, Anth.
a half-god, demigod, Il., Hes.
half-broken, Eur., Anth.
half the inheritance, Dem.
a semicircle, the front seats in the theatre, Plut.
half-white, Luc.
half-mad, Aeschin., Luc.
half-withered, Luc.
a half-μέδιμνος, Dem.
half-drunk, Anth.
a half-mina, Xen., etc.
half-evil, half a villain, Plat.
half-dry, Anth.
containing one and a half, half as much again, Lat. sesquialter, Plat.:—c. gen. half as large again as, half as much again as, Hdt., Xen.
ἡμιολία ναῦς a ship with one and a half banks of oars, Theophr.
of, belonging to a mule, ἅμαξα ἡμ. a car drawn by mules, Hom.
a half-ass, i. e. a mule, Hom., etc.:— proverb., ἐπεὰν ἡμίονοι τέκωσι, i. e. never, Hdt.
the ἡμ. ἀγροτέρα of Il. 2. 851 is prob. the wild ass.
as adj., βρέφος ἡμίονον a mule-foal, Il.; ἡμ. βασιλεύς a mule-king, half-Mede half-Persian, Orac. ap. Hdt.
half-roasted, Luc.

I say, Lat. inquam, used to repeat something with emphasis, παῖ ἠμί, παῖ boy I say, boy! Ar.:—imperf. ἦν, 3rd sg. ἦ, καὶ σχέθε χεῖρα he spake and held his hand, Il.; in attic, ἦν δ’ ἐγώ said I, Plat.; ἦ δ’ ὅς said he, Ar., Plat.
Insep. Prefix, half-, Lat. semi-.
a half-axe, i. e. a one-edged axe, Il.
half-cooked, Plut.
a half-πλέθρον, Hdt., Xen.
a half-plinth, a brick (two of which formed a plinth), Hdt.
half-breathing, half-alive, Batr.
half-evil, Arist.
half-burnt, Anth.
half-pulled down, Anth.
of half a stadium, Luc.
a half-soldier, Luc.
half-round, Luc.
half, Lat. semis, used both as adj. and Subst.:

as adj., ἡμίσεες λαοί half the people, Hom.; ἥμισυς λόγος half the tale, Aesch., etc.;—c. gen., like a comp., ἥμισυ οὗ διενοεῖτο half of what he intended, Thuc.:— also with its Subst. in gen., τῶν νήσων τὰς ἡμίσεας half of the islands, Hdt.; αἱ ἡμίσειαι τῶν νεῶν Thuc.; ὁ ἥμισυς τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ Plat.
as Subst.,
neut., ἥμισυ τιμῆς, ἐνάρων, ἀρετῆς Hom.; πλέον ἥμισυ παντός, Hes.; mostly with Art., τὸ ἡμ. τοῦ στρατοῦ Thuc., etc.;—also in pl., ἄρτων ἡμίσεα Xen.
fem., ἡ ἡμ. τοῦ τιμήματος Plat.; ἐφ’ ἡμισείᾳ up to one half, Dem.
a half-talent, as a weight, Il.; τρία ἡμιτάλαντα three half-talents, Hdt., but τρίτον ἡμιτάλαντον two talents and a half, Id.
a remission of half the tribute, Luc.
half-finished, Thuc.
half-finished, δόμος ἡμ. a house but half complete, i. e. wanting its lord and master, Il.; ἡμ. ἀνήρ, opp. to τελείως, ἀγαθός, Xen.
a half, Hdt.
half cut through, cut in two, Mosch.
as Subst.,
a stout linen cloth, towel, napkin, Ar. (An Egypt. word.)
half-shining, Anth.
half-bald, Anth.
half-knavish, Luc.
half-burnt, Theocr., Luc.
worth half an obol, Ar.: as large as a half-obol, Xen.
a half-obol, Xen.
at which time, when, Hom.
while, so long as, Soph.
