to bow down, sink, drop, ἑτέρως’ ἤμυσε κάρη his head dropped to one side, Il.; ἤμυσε καρήατι bowed with his head, of a horse, Id.; of a cornfield, ἐπὶ δ’ ἠμύει ἀσταχύεσσι it bows or waves with its ears, Id.: metaph. of cities, to nod to their fall, totter, Id.
a thrower, darter, slinger, Il.
windy, airy, Hom., etc.
of motion, rapid, rushing, Aesch.
reins, Hom., Hes., Pind.
the bridle (in riding), the reins (in driving), like the Homeric ἡνία (τά) mostly in pl., Pind., etc.; πρὸς ἡνίας μάχεσθαι Aesch.; in sg., ἐπισχὼν ἡνίαν Soph.
metaph., χαλάσαι τὰς ἡνίας τοῖς λόγοις to give one's words free reins, Plat.; τῆς Πυκνὸς τὰς ἡνίας παραδοῦναί τινι Id.
as a military term, ἐφ’ ἡνίαν to the left, Plut.

entry.etym: adverb of Time, relat. to τηνίκα
entry.sense: at which time, when, Od., Trag.: also causal, since, Pind., attic
with Opt. in orat. obl., or to denote an uncertain or repeated occurrence in past time, whenever, Soph., etc.
ἡνίκ’ ἄν, like ὅταν, with Subj., of the future, whenever, Id., etc.
a saddler's shop, Xen.
to guide by reins, Aesch., Eur.
one who guides by reins, a charioteer, Soph.
chariot-driving, Plat.
to act as charioteer, Hom.:—metaph. to guide, Anth.
to hold the reins, Xen.
c. acc. to drive, guide, Hdt.: metaph. to direct, Ar.:—Pass. to be guided, Xen.
of or for driving, Plat.: ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) the art of driving, Id.
one who holds the reins, a driver, charioteer, opp. to παραιβάτης (the warrior by his side), Il.
generally a chariot-driver, as in the games, Pind., attic:—in Theogn., a rider.
metaph. a guide, governor, Pind., Ar.
a year old, yearling, Hom.
manhood, Hom.: manly beauty, Il.:—in pl. praises of manhood, Pind.

entry.etym: in Hom., always in phrase ἤνοπι χαλκῷ,
entry.sense: with gleaming, glittering brass.
Interject. see! see there! lo! Lat. en! Ar.:—also ἠνίδε, i. e. ἢν ἴδε, Theocr.

entry.etym: related to εἴπερ, as ἤν (ἐάν) to εἰ, Xen.

entry.sense: the fourth stomach of ruminating animals, a favourite dish at Athens, tripe, Ar.
morning, Ar.:— ἡ ἠοίη (sc. ὥρα), the morning, Od.
toward morning, eastern, Id., Hdt.
αἱ Ἠοῖαι was a poem of Hesiod, in which each sentence began with ἢ οἵη.
on the shore, Anth.
want, Anth.
the liver, Hom., etc.:— ὑφ’ ἥπατος φέρειν, of pregnant women, Eur.:—in Trag. as the seat of the passions, anger, fear, etc., answering therefore to our "heart."
dat. sg. fem. of relat. Pron. ὅς, ἥ, ὁ, Hom.: freq. in adverb. sense
of Place, which way, where, whither, in or at what place, relat. to τῇ, Il., Soph.
of Manner, as, ᾗ καὶ Λοξίας ἐφήμισεν Aesch., Thuc., etc.
wherefore, Lat. quare, Id.
in so far as, Lat. qua, quatenus, Xen.
joined with a Sup., ᾗ ἐδύνατο τάχιστα as quick as he was able, Id.; ᾗ ῥᾷστά τε καὶ ἥδιστα Id.
with two chief senses, Confirmative and Interrogative:

TO CONFIRM an assertion, in truth, truly, verily, of a surety, Hom., etc.; often strengthd. by other Particles, as ἦ ἄρα, ἦ δή, ἦ δή που, ἦ μάλα, etc.;—and to express doubt, ἦ που;—ἦ μήν, ionic and epic ἦ μέν, ἦ μάν, used in protestations and oaths, σὺ μοι ὄμοσσον, ἦ μέν μοι ἀρήξειν Hom., etc.
in INTERROG. sentences, Lat. num? pray? or can it be?— also ἦ οὐκ . . ; Lat. nonne? Particles are often added to this ἦ, ἦ ῥα, ἦ ἄρα δή, etc.
weakly, infirm, halting, Hom.
c. gen. void of a thing, Anth.
born or living in the mainland, Aesch.
to the mainland, Od.
terra-firma, the land, as opp. to the sea, Hom., Hes., etc.; κατ’ ἤπειρον by land, Hdt.; μήτ’ ἐν θαλάττῃ μήτ’ ἐν ἠπείρῳ Ar.:— hence in Od., even an island is called ἤπειρος.
the mainland of Western Greece, opp. to the neighbouring islands (afterwards called Ἤπειρος as n. pr.), Od.:—then, generally, the mainland, Hdt., attic
later, a continent: Asia was esp. called the Continent, Hdt., etc.; also Europe, Aesch.; whence Soph. speaks of δισσαὶ ἤπειροι, i. e. Europe and Asia.
to make into mainland, Anth.:—Pass. to become so, Thuc.
of the mainland, living there, opp. to νησιώτης, Hdt.: αἱ ἠπειρώτιδες πόλιες, opp. to those in islands, Id., etc.; ἠπ. ξυμμαχία alliance with a military power, opp. to ναυτική, Thuc.
of or on the mainland of Asia, Asiatic, Eur.
an Epirote, Luc.
continental, Xen.
of Epirus, Thuc.
a cheat, deceiver, cozener, Od., Anth.
to cheat, cajole, deceive, cozen, Hom.
in the same way as, v. ὅσπερ.
than at all, than even, Hom.

entry.etym: aor1, with no pres. ἠπάομαι in use
entry.sense: to mend, repair, Ar.
a mender, cobbler, Batr., Xen.
to have a fever or ague, Ar.
a fever with shivering, ague, Ar.
= ἐφιάλτης, night-mare, Id.
softly-rolling, Anth.
soothing by gifts, bountiful, Il.
gentle of mood, Anth.
of persons, gentle, mild, kind, πατὴρ δ’ ὣς ἤπιος ἦεν Hom.:—c. dat. pers., Id., Trag.
of sentiments, ἤπια εἰδέναι to have kindly feelings, Hom.; πρὸς τὸ ἠπιώτερον καταστῆσαί τινα to bring him to a milder mood, Thuc.
act. soothing, assuaging, of medicines, Il., etc.
ἤπιον ἦμαρ, c. inf., a day favourable for beginning a thing, Hes.
adv. ἠπίως, Hdt., Soph.
with soothing hand, Anth.
ἤ, που, = ἤ, modified by που, or perhaps, as perhaps, Hom.
or ἦ, που, I suppose, I ween, Il., Soph., etc.: after a negat., much less, Thuc.
to ask a question, is it possible that . . ? can it be that . . ? Od., Aesch.
calling, crying, ἠπύτα κῆρυξ the loud-voiced herald, Il.
to call to, call on, call, Od., Aesch., etc.:—c. dupl. acc., τί με τόδε χρέος ἀπύεις; why callest thou on me for this? Eur.
absol. to call out, shout, Od.; of the wind, to roar, Il.; of the lyre, to sound, Od.
to utter, speak, πατρὸς ὄνομ’ ἀπύεις Aesch.; τί ποτ’ ἀπύσω; Eur.
of Hera: Ἡραῖον (sc. ἱερόν), the temple of Hera, Heraeum, Hdt.
Heracles, Lat. Hercules, son of Zeus and Alcmena, the most famous of the Greek heroes, Hom., etc. (The name signifies Hera's glory, Ἥρας κλέος, from the power she obtained over him at birth.)
the Heraclidae or descendants of Hercules, Hdt.
of Hercules, Lat. Herculeus, βίη Ἡρακληείη, i. e. Hercules himself, Hom.:— Ἡρ. στῆλαι the opposite headlands of Gibraltar and Apes' Hill near Tangier, Hdt.
as Subst., Ἡράκλειον, ionic -ήιον (sc. ἱερόν), the temple of Hercules, Heracleum, Id., etc.
Ἡράκλεια (sc. ἱερά), τά, his festival, Ar.
of Heraclitus, Plat.
Hera, the Lat. Juno, queen of the gods, daughter of Kronos and Rhea, sister and wife of Zeus, Hom., etc.; νὴ τὴν Ἥραν, an oath of Athen. women, Xen.
acceptable gifts, kindnesses, ἦρα φέρειν Hom.
= χάριν, c. gen., on account of, Anth.
still, quiet, gentle, Plat.:—irreg. comp. ἠρεμέστερος, Xen. adv. -αίως, = ἠρέμα, Id.; comp. -εστέρως Id.
stilly, quietly, gently, softly, Ar., Plat.
a little, slightly, Id.
slowly, opp. to τάχιστα, Id.
to keep quiet, be at rest, Xen., Plat.
quietude, Arist.
rest, quietude, ἐπὶ ἠρεμίας ὑμῶν leaving you at rest, Dem.
to make still or quiet, Xen.
intr. = ἠρεμέω, Id.
early-born, child of morn, epith. of Ἠώς, Hom.; also absol., = Ἠώς, Morn, Od.; ἠριγενείας at morn, Theocr.
Eridanus, a river famous in legends, Hes., Hdt.: later authors mostly took it for the Po, as Eur.; others for the Rhone or Rhine, as perh. in Hdt.
of or in spring, Solon., Eur.: —neut. pl. as adv., in spring, Ar.
a mound, barrow, tomb, Il., Theocr.
early, Hom.; ἦρι μάλ’, μάλ’ ἦρι Id.
early-walking: as Subst. the morn, Anth.
of or for a hero, heroic, Plat., etc.
metrically, ἡρ. στίχος the heroic verse, the hexameter, Id.
a heroine, Theocr.; contr. ἡρῴνη, Ar.
= ἡρωίνη, Pind.
as fem. of ἡρωϊκός, Anth.
the temple or chapel of a hero, Hdt., etc.; θἠρῷον, i. e. τὸ ἡρῷον, Ar.
(sub. μέτρον), an hexameter, Plut.
ὁ ἡρ. sc. ῥυθμός the heroic measure, hexameter, Plat., etc.; ποὺς ἡρ. the dactyl, Anth.
a hero, in Hom. used of the Greeks before Troy, then of warriors generally; and then of all free men of the heroic age, as the minstrel Demodocus, the herald Mulius, even the unwarlike Phaeacians.
in Hes. the blessed heroes are the fourth age of men, who fell before Thebes and Troy, and then passed to the Islands of the Blest.

heroes, as objects of worship, demigods or men born from a god and a mortal, as Hercules, Aeneas, Memnon, Hdt., Pind.; then of such as had done great services to mankind, as Daedalus, Triptolemus, Theseus, Anth.
later, the heroes are inferior local deities, patrons of tribes, cities, guilds, founders of cities, etc.; as at Athens, the ἥρωες ἐπώνυμοι were the heroes after whom the φυλαί were named, Hdt.

entry.etym: Note that middle forms such as ἡττήσομαι can have passive sense.
entry.sense: Pass. to be less than another, inferior to him, c. gen. pers., Eur., Xen., etc.; c. gen. rei, ἡ. ῥήματος to yield to the power of a word, Thuc.; ὃ ἡττῶιτο wherein he had proved inferior, Xen.
as a real Pass. to be defeated, discomfited, worsted, beaten, ὑπό τινος Hdt., attic; also c. gen. pers., Eur., etc.;— ἡσσᾶσθαι μάχηι or μάχην Hdt., Dem.
to give way, yield, to be a slave to passion and the like, c. gen., ἡσσημένος ἔρωτος Eur.; τῶν ἡδονῶν Xen.:—also c. dat. to be overcome by, ἡδονῆι ἡσσώμενοι Thuc.
a defeat, discomfiture, opp. to νίκη, Thuc., etc.:—c. gen. rei, a giving way to a thing, ἡδονῶν, ἐπιθυμιῶν Plat.
one must be beaten, γυναικός by a woman, Soph.

entry.etym: (but formed from ἦκα, softly, so that the orig. form was ἡκίων, with Sup. ἥκιστος):
entry.sense: c. gen. pers. less, weaker, less brave, Hom., etc.; c. inf., ἕσσων θεῖν not so good at running, Hdt.; οὐδενὸς ἥσσων γνῶναι "second to none" in judging, Thuc.

absol. of the weaker party, ἥσσους γενέσθαι to have the worst of it, Id.; τὰ τῶν ἡττόνων the fortunes of the vanquished, Xen.; of things, τὸν ἥττω λόγον κρείττω ποιεῖν "to make the worse appear the better reason, " Plat.
c. gen. rei, yielding to a thing, a slave to, ἔρωτος Soph.; κέρδους Ar., etc.: —generally, yielding to, unable to resist, τοῦ πεπρωμένου Eur.
neut. ἧσσον, attic ἧττον, as adv., less, Od., Thuc., etc.:—with a negat., οὐχ ἧσσον, οὐδ’ ἧσσον not the less, just as much, Aesch., etc.

to be still, keep quiet, be at rest, Aesch.; ἡ ἀπορία τοῦ μὴ ἡσυχάζειν the difficulty of finding rest, Thuc.:—often in part., ἡσυχάζων προσμένω Soph.; ἡσυχάσασα by resting from war, Thuc.; τὸ ἡσυχάζον τῆς νυκτός the dead of night, Id.
Causal in aor1, to make still, lay to rest, Plat.

entry.etym: neut. pl. of ἥσυχος, as adv.

entry.sense: stilly, quietly, softly, gently, Pind.; ἔχ’ ἡσυχῆ keep quiet, Plat.; ἡς. γελάσαι Id.
stillness, rest, quiet, Od., Hdt., attic:—c. gen. rest from a thing, Hdt., Plat.

with Preps., δι’ ἡσυχίης εἶναι to keep quiet, Hdt.:— ἐν ἡς. ἔχειν τι to keep it quiet, not speak of it, Id.:— ἐφ’ ἡσυχίας Ar.:— κατ’ ἡσυχίην πολλήν quite at one's ease, Hdt.; καθ’ ἡσυχίαν at leisure, Thuc.:— μεθ’ ἡσυχίας quietly, Eur.
with Verbs, ἡσυχίαν ἄγειν to keep quiet, be at rest, keep silent, Hdt., attic:—so ἡσυχίαν ἔχειν Hdt., attic
solitude, a sequestered place, Hhymn., Xen.
still, quiet, at rest, at ease, Il.; also in Prose, τρόπου ἡσυχίου of a quiet disposition, Hdt.; τὸ ἡσύχιον τῆς εἰρήνης Thuc. adv. -ίως, Hhymn.
still, quiet, at rest, at ease, at leisure, Hes., Hdt., attic; ἡσύχῳ βάσει φρενῶν, i. e. in thought, Aesch.; ἐν ἡσύχῳ quietly, Soph.

quiet, gentle, of character, Aesch., Eur., etc.; τοὺς ἀφ’ ἡσύχου ποδός those of quiet life, Id.; ὀργῇ ὑπόθες ἥσυχον πόδα, i. e. moderate thy anger, Id.; τὸ ξύνηθες ἥσυχον their accustomed quietness, Thuc.
the common attic comp. and Sup. were ἡσυχαίτερος, -αίτατος, but the regular form -ώτερος is also found.
adv. -χως, Eur., etc.: gently, cautiously, Id.:—Sup. ἡσυχαίτατα Plat.—The neut. ἥσυχον, doric ἅσυχον, is also used as adv., Theocr.; and pl. ἅσυχα, Id.

Η, η, ἦτα, τό, indecl., seventh letter of the Gr. alphabet; as numeral ηʹ = ὀκτώ and ὄγδοος, but ͵η = 8000. The uncial form of Eta ( Η) was a double ε and prob. it was pronounced as a long ε, cf. δῆλος (from δέελος). The old Alphabet had only one sign ( Ε) for the ε sound, till the long vowels η and ω were introduced from the Samian Alphabet in the archonship of Euclides, B. C. 403. The sign H, before it was taken to represent the double ε, was used for the spiritus asper, as ΗΟΣ for ὅς, (which remains in the Latin H). When H was taken to represent long e, it was at the same time cut in two, so that †ι† represented the spir.asper, †ο† the spir. lenis; whence came the present signs for the breathings. As to dialectic changes,
the vowel η was much used by the ionic, being in aeolic and doric replaced by ᾱ, as also in attic, but mostly after ρ or a vowel, πρήσσω θώρηξ ἰητρός, attic πράσσω θώραξ ἰατρός.
in attic, ει and ηι were not seldom changed into ῃ, as κλεῖθρα κλῇθρα, Νηρηίδες Νηρῇδες.
doric and aeolic for ει, as τῆνος, κῆνος for κεῖνος.
ἤ τε, or also, Il.
surely, doubtless, Hom.
= ἦ τοι, now surely, truly, verily, Il.; after ἀλλ’ εἰ . . , nevertheless, Id.
= ἤτοι, either in truth, followed by ἤ, or, Hdt., etc.

entry.etym: in Hom. always in nom. or acc.
entry.sense: the heart as a part of the body, Il.:—then, as the seat of life, life, ἦτορ ὀλέσσαι Id.:—as the seat of feeling, the heart, Id., etc.
the warp in a web of cloth, Plat., Theocr.:—in pl. a thin, fine cloth, such that one could see between the threads, Eur.; ἤτρια βύβλων leaves made of strips of papyrus, Anth.
the part below the navel, the abdomen, Plat., Xen., etc.
as, like as, Il., etc.; often in Hom. in similes for ὡς ὅτε.
in Il. 4. 277 after a comp., μελάντερον ἠύτε πίσσα very black, like as pitch, or = ἤ, blacker than pitch.
with fair dances, Anth.
of Hephaestus: Ἡφαιστεῖον or Ἡφαίστειον (sc. ἱερόν), temple of Hephaestus, Hdt., Dem., etc.:— Ἡφαίστεια (sc. ἱερά), τά, his festival, the Lat. Vulcanalia, Xen.
wrought by Hephaestus, Eur.
Hephaestus, Lat. Vulcanus, sonof Zeus and Hera, lame from birth, master of metal working, Hom., etc.
meton. for πῦρ, fire, Il., Soph.
entry.etym: Perh. from ἅπτω, to kindle fire.

entry.sense: wrought by Hephaestus, Soph.
a kind of kettle-drum or gong, Plut.
clear-sounding, musical, Aesch., Eur.:—of the grasshopper, chirping, Hes., Anth.; and ἀχέτας, ου, alone, the chirper, the grasshopper, Ar.
intr. to sound, ring, peal, Hes.; often of metal, ἤχεσκε (ionic imperf.) Hdt.; τὰ χαλκεῖα πληγέντα μακρὸν ἠχεῖ Plat.; of the grasshopper, to chirp, Theocr.
c. acc. cogn., ἀχεῖν ὕμνον to let it sound, Aesch.; κωκυτόν Soph.; χαλκίον ἄχει sound the cymbal, Theocr.:—Pass., ἠχεῖται κτύπος a sound is made, Soph.
sounding, ringing, roaring, Hom.
a sound, sounding, Eur.

a sound or noise of any sort, Hom., attic; of the confused noise of a crowd, the roar of the sea, the groaning of trees in a wind, Il., etc.:—in Trag., like ἰαχή, a cry of sorrow, wail; but, σάλπιγγος ἠχή Eur.:—rarely of articulate sounds, Id.
where, Hom.

entry.etym: later form of ἠχή, Theocr., Mosch.

entry.sense: a sound, but properly of a returned sound, echo, Hhymn., Hes., etc.
generally, a ringing sound, Soph., Trag.; τὴν Βοιωτίην κατεῖχε ἠχὼ ὡς . . Boeotia rang with the news that . . , Hdt.
from morn, i. e. at dawn, at break of day, Hom., etc.; this morning, Od.
at morn, at break of day, Hhymn., Hes.
from the east, eastern, Hdt.

entry.etym: aeolic ἄυως, i. e. ἄϝως, not αὔως
entry.sense: the morning red, daybreak, dawn, Hom., Hdt., etc.:— morning as a time of day, opp. to μέσον ἦμαρ and δείλη, Il.; gen. ἠοῦς at morn, early, Id.; ἠῶ the morning long, Od.:— ἐξ ἠοῦς μέχρι δείλης ὀψίης Hdt.:— ἅμα ἠοῖ at daybreak, Id.; ἅμ’ ἕῳ or ἅμα τῇ ἕῳ Thuc.; epic ἠῶθι πρό Hom.; ἐς ἀῶ to-morrow, Theocr.
since the Greeks counted their days by mornings, ἠώς often denoted a day, Hom.
the East, Id.; ἀπὸ ἠοῦς πρὸς ἑσπέρην Hdt., etc.
as prop. n. Ἠώς, Aurora, the goddess of morn, who rises out of her ocean-bed, Il., Eur.
to sit, Hom.; epic inf. θαασσέμεν Od.

entry.etym: doric for θηέομαι, ionic form of θεάομαι, Pind., Theocr.

entry.sense: a sight, wonder, Theocr.
crasis for τὰ ἱμάτια.
crasis for τὰ ἱματίδια.
the hinge of a door or gate, Il.
to sit, Hdt., Trag.; c. acc. cogn., θακοῦντι παγκρατεῖς ἕδρας sitting on imperial throne, Aesch.: suppliants, Soph., Eur.
a sitting, esp. as a suppliant, Soph.
a seat, Id., Eur.
a sitting, sitting-place, Soph.
a seat, chair, Hom.; θῶκοι ἀμπαυστήριοι seats for resting, Hdt.; θᾶκος κραιπνόσυτος, of a winged car, Aesch., etc.
a chair of office, Ar.
a privy, Theophr.
in Hom. a sitting in council, a council, Od.; θῶκόνδε to the council, Id.; ἐν θώκῳ κατήμενος sitting in council, Hdt.
of or for a θάλαμος, Hes.
a lurking-place, den, hole, cave, Od., Eur.; of the grave, Id.
= θάλαμος III, Luc.
a chamber-maid, waiting maid, Od., Aesch.
a eunuch of the bed chamber, Plut.
rarely, a bridegroom, Soph.
as adj. bridal, Anth.
of or belonging to the θάλαμος:—as Subst.,
θαλαμιός, ὁ, = θαλαμίτης, Thuc.
θαλαμία, ionic -ιή (sub. κώπη), the oar of the θαλαμίτης, Ar.
(sub. ὀπή) the hole in the ship's side, through which this oar worked, διὰ θαλαμιῆς διελεῖν τινα to place a man so that his upper half projected through this hole, Hdt.
one of the rowers on the lowest bench of a trireme, who had the shortest oars and the least pay; cf. ζυγίτης, θρανίτης.
to the bed-chamber, Od.
an inner room or chamber:
generally, the women's apartment, inner part of the house, Hom., Hdt.
a chamber in this part of the house:
a bed-room, Il.:— the bride-chamber, Id., Soph., etc.
a store-room, Hom., Xen.
generally, a chamber, room, Od.
metaph., ὁ παγκοίτας θ. of the grave, Soph.; τυμβήρης θ. of the ark of Danae, Id.; θάλαμοι ὑπὸ γῆς the realms below, Aesch.; θ. Ἀμφιτρίτης of the sea, Soph.; ἀρνῶν θ. their folds or pens, Eur., etc.
the lowest part of the ship, in which the θαλαμῖται sat, the hold.
a shrine, temple, Anth.

the sea, Hom., etc.; when he uses it of a particular sea, he means the Mediterranean, opp. to Ὠκεανός; — Hdt. calls the Mediterranean ἥδε ἡ θάλασσα; so, ἡ παρ’ ἡμῖν θάλ. Plat.; κατὰ θάλασσαν by sea, opp. to πεζῇ by land, Hdt.; to κατὰ γῆς, Thuc.:—metaph., κακῶν θ. a sea of troubles, Aesch.
a well of salt water, said to be produced by a stroke of Poseidon's trident, in the Acropolis at Athens, Hdt.
to be at sea, keep the sea, Thuc.; τὰ θαλαττεύοντα τῆς νεὼς μέρη the parts under water, Plut.

of, in, on or from the sea, belonging to it, Lat. marinus, οὔ σφι θαλάσσια ἔργα μεμήλει, of the Arcadians, Il.; κορῶναι τῇσίν τε θαλ. ἔργα μέμηλεν, i. e. which live by fishing, Od.:— θαλάσσια sea-animals, opp. to χερσαῖα, Hdt.; πεζοί τε καὶ θαλ. landsmen and seamen, Aesch.; θαλ. ἐκρίπτειν τινά to throw one into the sea, Soph.
skilled in the sea, nautical, Hdt., Thuc.
to strike the sea with the oar: metaph. to make a splash, Ar.
to be master of the sea, Hdt., Thuc.
master of the sea, Hdt., Thuc., Xen.
made to wander o'er the sea, sea-tost, Aesch., Eur.
sea-beaten, Aesch.
sea-faring, Anth.
one who works on the sea, a fisherman, seaman, Xen.
to make or change into sea: Mid. to be a sea-faring man, Luc.
good cheer, happy thoughts, θαλέων ἐμπλησάμενος κῆρ Il.
to bloom, flourish, Hom. only in part.; of trees, Od.; of men, Id.; of swine, θαλέθοντες ἀλοιφῇ swelling, wantoning in fat, Il.
fem. adj. blooming, luxuriant, goodly, bounteous, of banquets, θεῶν ἐν δαιτὶ θαλείῃ Od., etc. No masc. θάλυς occurs, θαλερός being used instead.
as prop. n. Θάλεια, ἡ, one of the Muses, the blooming one, Hes.; also Θαλίη, Anth.
blooming, fresh, of young persons, Hom.; θ. γάμος the marriage of a youthful pair, Od.

of the body, fresh, vigorous, Il.; θ. χαίτη luxuriant hair, Id.; θ. ἀλοιφή rich, abundant fat, Od.;—then of other things, θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσα shedding big tears, Il.; θ. γόος the thick and frequent sob, Od.; θαλερὴ φωνή a full, rich voice, Hom.
Thales of Miletus, Hdt.
abundance, plenty, good cheer, Il.; in pl. festivities, Od., Hdt.
a young shoot, young branch, Od., Soph., etc.:—of the young olive-shoot carried by suppliants, Hdt., Trag.; ἱκτὴρ θ. Eur.; also, θαλλοῦ στέφανος the olive- wreath worn at festivals, Aeschin.
carrying young olive-shoots, Ar.

to bloom, abound, to be luxuriant, of fruit-trees, Od., Soph., etc.; often in part. perf. τεθηλώς, epic fem. τεθαλυῖα, as adj., luxuriant, exuberant, Od.; c. acc. cogn., οὐ δένδρε’ ἔθαλλεν χῶρος the place grew no trees, θαλλούσης βίον ἐλαίας Aesch.
of other natural objects, τεθαλυῖα ἐέρση the fresh or copious dew, Od.; τεθαλυῖα ἀλοιφῆι rich with fat, Il.; εἰλαπίνηι τεθαλυίηι at a sumptuous feast, Id.
of men, to bloom, flourish, Hes., Soph., etc.
in bad sense, to be active, νόσος ἀεὶ τέθηλε Soph.; πήματα ἀεὶ θάλλοντα Id.
in metaph. sense of young persons, like ἔρνος (q. v.), φίλον θάλος dear child of mine, Il.; τοιόνδε θάλος so fair a scion of their house, Od.
to be or become warm, εὖ θαλπιόων (epic part.) right warm and comfortable, Od.
warming, fostering, Pind.
warmth, heat, esp. summer heat, Aesch.; θ. θεοῦ the sun's heat, Soph.; μεσημβρινοῖσι θάλπεσιν with the meridian rays (cf. Lat. soles), Aesch.
metaph. a sting, smart, caused by an arrow, Soph., Anth.
warming, Anth.
to heat, soften by heat, Od.:—Pass., ἐτήκετο, κασσίτερος ὣς θαλφθείς Hes.: metaph. to be softened, λόγοις Ar.
to heat, warm, without any notion of softening, καῦμ’ ἔθαλπε (sc. ἡμᾶς) Soph.:—Pass., θάλπεσθαι τοῦ θέρους to be warm in summer, Xen.:—metaph. to be alive, Pind.
to warm at the fire, dry, Soph., Eur.
metaph. of passion, to heat, inflame, Aesch., Soph.
to cherish, comfort, foster, Theocr.
warming: metaph. comfort, consolation, source of hope, Hom.
the firstlings of the harvest, offerings of first fruits, Il., Theocr.
fem. adj. of or for the θαλύσια, Theocr.
often, oft-times, Hom., etc.
to be astonished at, Hhymn.
to be astounded, amazed, Hom., Soph., Eur.
c. acc. to be astonished at, marvel at, Od., Pind.
Causal, to surprise:—Pass., τεθαμβημένος astounded, Plut.
astonishment, amazement, Hom., attic
poet. adj. only in pl., crowded, close-set, thick, Hom.
to come often, Lat. frequentare, Hom., Xen.
to be often or constantly engaged with or in a thing, Od.; οὔτι κομιζόμενός γε θάμιζεν he was not wont to be so cared for, Id.; μινύρεται θαμίζουσα ἀηδών mourns often or constantly, Soph.
frequent, in neut. pl. θαμινά :—asAdv. = θαμά, Pind., attic
a bush, shrub, Lat. arbustum, Hom.; in pl. a copse, thicket, Id., attic
deadly, Trag., etc.
of or belonging to death, θαν. αἷμα (as we say) the life- blood, Aesch.; μέλψασα θ. γόον having sung my death- song, Id.
of persons, near death, Soph., Plat.: subject to death, mortal, Plat.: also dead, Soph.
Desiderat. of θανεῖν, to desire to die, Plat.
death-bringing, mortal, Aesch., Soph., etc.
deadly, θ. δίκη sentence of death, Plut.
deadly, Soph., Eur.
death, Hom., etc.; θ. τινος the death threatened by him, Od.; θάνατόνδε to death, Il., etc.

in attic, θάνατον καταγιγνώσκειν τινός to pass sentence of death on one, Thuc.; θανάτου κρίνεσθαι to be tried for one's life, Id.:—ellipt., τὴν ἐπὶ θανάτῳ κεκοσμημένος (sc. στολήν) Hdt.; δῆσαί τινα τὴν ἐπὶ θανάτου (sc. δέσιν) Id.; τοῖς Ἀθηναίοις ἐπιτρέψαι περὶ σφῶν αὐτῶν πλὴν θανάτου for any penalty short of death, Thuc.
pl. θάνατοι, kinds of death, Od.; or the deaths of several persons or even of one person, Trag.
as prop. n., Θάνατος Death, twin-brother of Sleep, Il.
= νεκρός, Anth.
sc. ἱερά, τά, a feast of the dead, Luc.

entry.etym: fut. mid. in pass. sense θανατώσοιτο Xen.
entry.sense: to put to death, τινά Hdt., attic
metaph. to mortify the flesh, NTest.
to put to death by sentence of law, Plat.:—Pass., Xen.
a putting to death, Thuc.
Dep.
to wonder at, admire, Od.
later, to gaze on, see, 2nd pl. θᾶσθε, Ar.; imperat. θάεο Anth.: doric fut. part. θασόμενος Theocr.; aor1 imperat. θᾶσαι Ar.; inf. θάσασθαι Theocr.
one must bury, Soph.

entry.etym: from Root ΤΑΦ, cf. ταφθῆναι, τάφος
entry.sense: to pay the last dues to a corpse, to honour with funeral rites, i. e. in early times by burning the body, Hom.: then, simply, to bury, inter, Hdt., attic
bold, of good courage, ready, daring, undaunted, Il., attic: —τὸ θαρσαλέον confidence, Thuc.:—so in adv., θαρραλέως ἔχειν to be of good courage, Plat., Xen.
in bad sense, overbold, audacious, Od.
that which may be ventured on, Plat.
boldness, Plut.

to be of good courage, take courage, Il., etc.:—in bad sense, to be over-bold, audacious, Thuc., Plat.; θάρσει, θαρσεῖτε, take courage! cheer up, Hom., etc.; θαρσήσας with good courage, Il.; so, θαρσῶν Hdt., attic:—also, τὸ τεθαρρηκός confidence, Plut.
c. acc., θάρσει τόνδε γ’ ἄεθλον take heart for this struggle, Od.; θ. θάνατον Plat.; θ. μάχην to venture a fight, Xen.:—c. acc. pers. to have confidence in, Id.:—so also, θαρσεῖν τινι Hdt.
c. inf. to believe confidently that, Soph.; also, to make bold or venture to do, Xen.
confidence in a thing, Thuc.
courage, boldness, Hom., attic; θ. τινός courage to do a thing, Aesch., Soph.
that which gives courage, θάρση grounds of confidence, Eur., Plat.
in bad sense, audacity, Il.: cf. θράσος.

entry.etym: adverb from pres. part. of θαρσέω
entry.sense: boldly, courageously, Xen.
c. dat. relying on a thing, Id.
Causal of θαρσέω, to encourage, cheer, θάρσυνον (aor1 imperat.) Il.; θαρσύνεσκε (ionic imperf.) Id.; so Hdt., Thuc., etc.
intr. θάρσυνε be of good courage, Soph.
of or from Thasos, Thasian, οἶνος Ar.:— ἡ Θασία ἅλμη Thasian pickled fish, Id.
quicker, swifter: neut. θᾶσσον as adv., more quickly.
to sit, sit idle;— c. acc. sedis, θάσσειν θρόνον Soph., etc.; c. acc. cogn., θ. δυστήνους ἕδρας to sit in wretched posture, Eur.
to wonder, marvel, be astonied, Il., etc.
c. acc. to look on with wonder and amazement, to wonder at, marvel at, Hom., Hdt., attic
to honour, admire, worship, Lat. admirari, observare, Od., Hdt., attic:—θ. τινά τινος for a thing, Thuc.; ἐπί τινι Xen.
c. gen. to wonder at, marvel at, Thuc., etc.; θ. σοῦ λέγοντος Plat.
c. dat. rei, to wonder at, Thuc.
c. acc. et inf., θ. σε πενθεῖν Eur.
Pass. to be looked at with wonder, Hdt.; θαυμάζεται μὴ παρών, i. e. I keep wondering that he is not present, Soph.
to be admired, Hdt.; τὰ εἰκότα θ. to receive proper marks of respect, Thuc.
to admire, gaze upon, Od., Pind.

of objects, whatever one regards with wonder, a wonder, marvel, Hom., Hes.; θαῦμα, of Polypheme, Od.; θαῦμα βροτοῖσι, of a beautiful woman, Id.; c. inf., θαῦμα ἰδέσθαι or ἰδεῖν a wonder to behold, Id., Eur.; καὶ θαῦμά γ’ οὐδέν and no wonder, Ar.: —θῶμα ποιεῖσθαί τι Hdt.:—in pl., θαύματ’ ἐμοὶ κλύειν Aesch.; θαυμάτων κρείσσονα or πέρα things more than wondrous, Eur.
in pl. also jugglers' tricks, mountebank-gambols, Xen., etc.
of the feeling, wonder, astonishment, Od., etc.; ἐν θώματι εἶναι or γίγνεσθαι to be astonished, Hdt., Thuc.; τινός at a thing, Hdt.

wondrous, wonderful, marvellous, Hes., Hdt.; θαυμάσια wonders, marvels, Hdt., Plat.: θαυμάσιόν [ἐστι], c. inf., Ar.; θαυμάσιος τὸ κάλλος marvellous for beauty, Xen.; θαυμάσιον ὅσον wonderfully much, Plat.; θαυμάσια ἡλίκα Dem.
adv. -ίως, wonderfully, i. e. exceedingly, Ar.; often with ὡς added, θ. ὡς ἄθλιος marvellously wretched, Plat.
admirable, excellent, with slight irony, Id., Dem.; ὦ θαυμασιώτατε ἄνθρωπε, in scorn, Xen.
to work wonders, Xen.
a marvelling, Plut., etc.
to be admired, Plat.
neut. θαυμαστέον, one must admire, Eur.
an admirer, Arist.
inclined to wonder or admire, Arist.

wondrous, wonderful, marvellous, Hhymn., Hdt., attic:—c. acc., θαυμαστὸς τὸ κάλλος Plat.; c. gen., θ. τῆς ἐπιεικείας Plut.; c. dat., πλήθει Id.:—foll. by a Relat., θαυμαστὸν ὅσον, Lat. mirum quantum, Plat., etc.; θαυμαστὸν ἡλίκον Dem.:—adv. -τῶς, θαυμαστῶς ὡς σφόδρα Plat.
admirable, excellent, Pind., Soph.
to work wonders, Luc.
conjuring, juggling, Plat.
wonder-working:—as Subst. a conjuror, juggler, Plat., Dem.
yellow-coloured, yellow, sallow, Ar.
a plant or wood used for dyeing yellow, brought from Thapsos, Theocr.
παρέχουσιν γάλα θῆσθαι they give milk to suck, Od.; aor 1, θήσατο μαζόν he sucked the breast, Il.; part., θησάμενος sucking, Hhymn.
Causal, to suckle a child, Id.
a goddess, Hom.
that which is seen, a sight, show, spectacle, Trag., Thuc., etc.
a spectator, Anth.
Dep.
to look on, gaze at, view, behold, Hom., Hdt., attic; ἐθεᾶτο τὴν θέσιν τῆς πόλεως reconnoitred it, Thuc.
to view as spectators, οἱ θεώμενοι the spectators in a theatre, Ar.:—metaph., θ. τὸν πόλεμον to be spectators of the war, Hdt.
θ. τὸ στράτευμα to review it, Xen.
fem. of θεός, a goddess, Hom.; often with another Subst., θεὰ μήτηρ Il.:— τὰ θεά in dual are Demeter and Persephone (Ceres and Proserpine) Soph.; αἱ σεμναὶ θεαί the Furies, Id.
a seeing, looking at, view, θέης ἄξιος = ἀξιοθέητος, Hdt.; θέαν λαβεῖν to take or get a view, Soph.
aspect, διαπρεπὴς τὴν θέαν Eur.
that which is seen, a sight, spectacle, Trag.
the place for seeing from, a seat in the theatre, Aeschin., Dem.
the place where the θεωροί met, Pind.
to be seen, Plat.
θεατέον, one must see, Id.
one who sees, a spectator, Hdt., Eur., etc.
to be seen, Soph., Plat.
to bring on the stage:— Pass. to be made a show of, a gazing-stock, NTest.
of or for the theatre, theatrical, Arist., Plut.
a place for seeing, esp. a theatre, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
collective for οἱ θεαταί, the people in the theatre, the spectators, "the house, " Hdt., Ar.
= θέαμα, a show, spectacle, θ. γενηθῆναι, = θεατρίζεσθαι, NTest.
divine, Bion.
driven or hunted by a god, Aesch.
sent or caused by a god, Hdt., Soph.; ἔκ τινος θεηλάτου from some destiny, Eur.
built for the gods, like θεόδμητος, Id.
contemplation: a problem, Anth.
to practice divinations, Thuc.
practice of divination, Thuc.
from Thebes, Ar.
at Thebes, Ar.
a sunny spot in the vineyard, on which the grapes were suffered to dry, so as to make raisins, Od.

entry.etym: aor1 ἔθεινα; the other moods are taken from an aor2 ἔθενον which does not occur in ind.
entry.sense: to strike, wound, Hom., Eur.:—Pass., θεινομένου πρὸς οὔδεϊ stricken to earth, Od.
metaph., θείνειν ὀνείδει Aesch.
intr. of ships, θ. ἐπ’ ἀκτᾶς to strike on the shore, Id.
built by gods, Anth.
brimstone, Lat. sulfur, used to fumigate and purify, Hom.; δεινὴ δὲ θεείου γίγνεται ὀδμή, from a thunderbolt, Il.

entry.etym: comp. and Sup. θειότερος, -ότατος, θεώτερος being comp. of θεός
entry.sense: of or from the gods, sent by the gods, issuing from them, divine, Hom., Hdt., attic; θ. νόσος of a whirlwind, Soph.; θείᾳ τινὶ μοίρᾳ by divine intervention, Xen.; so, θείῃ τύχῃ Hdt.:— appointed of God, βασιλῆες Od.
belonging or sacred to a god, in honour of a god, holy, Hom.: under divine protection, δόμος Id.; of heralds and minstrels, Id.

like θεσπέσιος, ἱερός, Lat. divinus, of anything more than human, wondrous: of heroes, divinely strong, great, beautiful, etc., Hom.; and as a mere mark of respect, excellent, θεῖος ὑφορβός Od.; so, θ. πρήγματα marvellous things, Hdt.; ἐν τοῖσι θειότατον one of the most marvellous things, Id.; so, at Sparta, θεῖος (or rather σεῖος) ἀνήρ was a title of distinction, Plat., Arist.
as Subst., θεῖον, ου, τό, the Divine Being, the Divinity, Deity, Hdt., Aesch.
θεῖα, τά, divine things, the acts and attributes of the gods, the course of providence, Soph., Ar., etc.: religious observances, Xen.; ἔρρει τὰ θεῖα religion is out of date, Soph.
adv. θείως, by divine providence, Xen.; θειοτέρως by special providence, Hdt.
one's father's or mother's brother, uncle, Lat. patruus and avunculus, Eur., etc.
divine nature, divinity, Plut.
to smoke with brimstone, fumigate and purify thereby, Od.:—Mid., δῶμα θεειοῦται he fumigates his house, Id.: generally, to purify, hallow, Eur.
soft-speaking, Anth.
a charm or spell, Eur., Luc.

properly, to stroke or touch with magic power, Lat. mulcere, and so to charm, enchant, spell-bind, of Hermes, who with his magic wand ἀνδρῶν ὄμματα θέλγει, lays men in a charmed sleep, Hom.; of the sorceress Circe, Od., etc.
in bad sense, to cheat, cozen, Hom., Soph.
to produce by spells, ἀοιδαὶ θέλξαν νιν (sc. εὐφροσύναν) Pind.; [γαλήνην] θ. ἀνηνεμίην Anth.
will, NTest.
a willing, will, NTest.
a charm, spell, enchantment, of the girdle of Aphrodite, Il.; θεῶν θελκτήριον a means of soothing the gods, Od.; νεκροῖς θελκτήρια, of offerings to the Manes, Eur.
charming, enchanting, soothing, Aesch., Eur.
a soother, charmer, Hhymn.
charming the heart, Anth.
sweetly painful, Anth.

the foundations, lowest part, bottom, ὀφθαλμοῖο θέμεθλα the very bottom, roots of the eye, Il.; Ἄμμωνος θέμ. the place where Ammon stands, i. e. his temple, Pind.; Παγγαίου θέμ. the roots of Mt. Pangaeus, Id.
of or for the foundation, Ar.:—as Subst., θεμέλιος (sub. λίθος) a foundation, οἱ θεμέλιοι the foundations, Thuc.; ἐκ τῶν θεμελίων from the foundations, Id.
to lay the foundation of, found firmly, Xen.:—Pass. to have the foundations laid, NTest.: metaph., βασιλεία καλῶς θεμελιωθεῖσα Diod.; ἡγεμονία κάλλιστα τεθεμελιωμένη Id.; ἐν ἀγαπῇ τεθ. NTest.
of grave and serious aspect, Aesch.
to judge:—Mid., θεμισσάμενοι ὀργάς controlling our wills, Pind.
rightly plaited, θ. στέφανος a well-earned crown, Pind.
seeing to law and order, Pind.
reigning by right, Pind.

that which is laid down or established by custom, Lat. jus or fas, as opp. to lex, θέμις ἐστί 'tis meet and right, Lat. fas est, Hom.; ἣ θέμις ἐστί as 'tis right, as the custom is, Id.; ἣ θέμις ἐστὶ γυναικός as is a woman's custom, Od.; so in attic, ὅ τι θέμις αἰνεῖν what it is right to praise, Aesch., etc.:—also indeclin., θέμις being used as acc., φασὶ θέμις εἶναι Plat., etc.
= δίκη, right, law, Aesch., Soph.
pl. θέμιστες, the decrees of the Gods, oracles, Διὸς θέμιστες Od.; θέμισσιν by oracles, Pind.
rights of the chief, prerogatives, σκῆπτρόν τ’ ἠδὲ θέμιστες Il.
laws or ordinances, οἵτε θέμιστας εἰρύαται who maintain the laws, Id.
claims to be decided by the kings or judges, οἳ σκολιὰς κρίνωσι θέμιστας Id.
as prop. n., gen. Θέμιστος, Θέμιδος, Θέμιτος, voc. Θέμι, Themis, goddess of law and order, Id.
of law and right, θ. σκᾶπτον the sceptre of righteous judgment, Pind.
to declare law and right, Lat. jus dicere, Od.: c. gen. to claim right over, to govern, Id.
to give by way of answer or oracle, Hhymn.:—absol. to deliver oracles, Eur.
ministering law, Hhymn.
like θεμιστός, allowed by the laws of God and men, righteous, Hhymn.; οὐ θεμιτόν [ἐστι], like οὐ θέμις, Pind., Hdt., attic
to drive or bring, νῆα θέμωσε χέροον ἱκέσθαι forced, urged the ship to come to land, or simply, brought it to land, Od.
the palm of the hand, Il.
metaph., θ. βωμοῦ the flat top of the altar, Pind.; ἁλὸς θ. the surface of the sea, Id.
old termin. of the gen., as in ἐμέθεν, σέθεν, Διόθεν, θεόθεν; sometimes after Preps., ἀπὸ Τροίηθεν Od.; ἐξ οὐρανόθεν Il.
as insep. Particle, denoting motion from a place, opp. to -δε, as in ἄλλοθεν, οἴκοθεν, from another place, from home.
madness, blindness, Aeschin.
to offend the Gods, Aesch.
stricken of God, infatuated, Hdt.
begotten of a god, Soph.
with the tongue of a god, Anth.
the generation or genealogy of the gods, Hes., Hdt.
born of God, divine, Eur.
by which the gods are injured, Anth.
taught of God, NTest.
god-built, made or founded by the gods, Il., Pind., etc.
divine of form, Hom., Plat.
godlike, Hom.
old gen. of θεός, used as adv. from the gods, at the hands of the gods, Lat. divinitus, Od.
by the help or favour of the gods, Pind., Aesch., etc.: by the gods, Soph.
the feast of the wine-god, ap. Dem.
to call on the gods, Aesch.; c. acc., Eur.
c. acc. rei, to call aloud, declare, Plut.
calling on the gods, Aesch.
wrought by the gods, Aesch.
judging between gods, Anth.
created by God, Solon.
maddened by the gods, Aesch., Eur.; λύσσα θ. madness caused by the gods, Eur.
one who has a spirit of prophecy, an inspired person, Plat.
to fight against the gods, Eur.
a battle of the gods, as certain books of the Il. were called, Plat.
fighting against God, NTest., Luc.
like the gods in counsel, Aesch.
abominated by the gods, Ar., Plat.
destiny, Anth.
destined by the gods, imparted by them, Pind.
blessed by the gods, Id.
of form divine, Anth.
abominated by the gods, Aesch.
child of the gods, Anth.
sent by the gods, Arist.
inspired of God, NTest.
to make into gods, deify, Luc.
making gods, Anth.
prepared by the gods, Eur.
meet for a god, Pind. adv. -πῶς, Luc.
to prophesy, only in part. masc., θεοπροπέων ἀγορεύεις Hom., Pind., etc.
a prophecy, oracle, Il.; ἐκ θεοπροπίου according to an oracle, Hdt.
foretelling things by a spirit of prophecy, prophetic, Il., Soph.
as Subst. a seer, prophet, diviner, Hom.
a public messenger sent to enquire of the oracle, Il., Hdt., Aesch.
detested by the gods, Aesch.
kindled by the gods, Eur.
sprung from the gods, celestial, Pind., Aesch.
poet. for θεόδοτος, given by the gods, Hes., Pind.
the service or fear of God, religiousness, Xen.
fearing God, religious, Hdt., Soph., etc. adv. -βῶς, Xen.
feared as divine, Ar.
hatred of the gods, Dem.

God, Hom., both in general sense, Θεὸς δώσει God will grant, and in particular sense, θεός τις a god; πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε Hom.:—things are said to happen σὺν θεῷ, σύν γε θεοῖσιν by the will of God, Id., etc.; οὐκ ἄνευ θεοῦ, Lat. non sine diis, Od.; οὐκ ἄνευθε θεοῦ Il.; οὐ θεῶν ἄτερ Pind.;— ἐκ θεόφι Il.;— ὑπὲρ θεόν against his will, Id.;— κατὰ θεόν τινα, Lat. divinitus, Eur.:—as an oath, πρὸς θεῶν by the gods, in God's name, Trag.; θεὸς ἴστω Soph., etc.

θεός as fem. for θεά, θέαινα, a goddess, Hom.; θήλεια θεός Il.; ἡ νερτέρα θ. Proserpine, Soph.; often in oaths, νὴ τὼ θεώ Id.; ναὶ τὼ σιώ, with the Spartans, of Castor and Pollux, Xen.; with the Boeotians, of Amphion and Zethus, Id.
as adj. in comp. θεώτερος, more divine, θύραι θ. doors more used by the gods, Od.
supported by God, Anth.
hated of the gods, Eur.: hated of God, NTest.
sent by the gods, Aesch.
the god-bull, a name for Zeus, Mosch.
walled by gods, of Troy, Anth.
fit for the gods, Anth.
made by God, Anth.
divinity, divine nature, Luc.
honoured by the gods, Tyrtae.
turned or directed by the gods, Aesch.
feeding the gods, Anth.
fearing God, Od.
sc. ἱερά a festival at Delphi, at which the statues of Apollo and other gods were shewn to the people, Hdt.
dear to the gods, highly favoured, Hdt., Pind., attic adv., θεοφιλῶς πράττειν to act as the gods will, Plat.

entry.etym: epic gen. and dat. sg. and pl. of θεός.

entry.sense: to bear God within one: Pass. to be possessed by a god, Luc.
possessed by a god, inspired, Aesch.
inspiration, Anth.
possessed by a god, inspired, θ. δύαι the pains of inspiration, Aesch.
godly-minded, Pind.
inseparable suffix, v. -θεν.
fem. of θεράπων, a waiting maid, handmaid, Hdt., Xen., etc.
a waiting on, service, θ. θεῶν service done to the gods, divine worship, Plat.
service done to gain favour, a courting, paying court, θ. τῶν ἀεὶ προεστώτων Thuc.; ἐν πολλῇ θεραπείᾳ ἔχειν to court one's favour, Id.
of things, a fostering, tending, nurture, care, τοῦ σώματος Plat.
medical treatment, service done to the sick, tending, Thuc., Plat.
of animals or plants, a rearing or bringing up, tendance, Id.
in collective sense, a body of attendants, suite, retinue, Hdt., Xen.
medical treatment, Arist.
one must do service to, τοὺς θεούς Xen.
one must cultivate, τὴν γῆν Plat.
one must cure, Id.
one who serves the gods, a worshipper, Plat.
one who serves a great man, a courtier, Xen.
one who attends to anything, c. gen., Plat.
inclined to serve a person, c. gen., Xen.: inclined to court, Plut.
absol. courteous, courtier-like, obedient, obsequious, Xen., Plut.
that may be fostered, Plat.
to be an attendant, do service, Od.
to do service to the gods, Lat. colere deos, Hes., Hdt., attic:— to do service or honour to one's parents or masters, Eur., Plat.
to serve, court, pay court to, τινά Hdt., Ar., etc.; and in bad sense, to flatter, wheedle, Thuc.: to conciliate, Id.; τὸ θεραπεῦον = οἱ θεραπεύοντες, Id.
of things, to consult, attend to, Lat. inservire, Id.; ἡδονὴν θερ. to indulge one's love of pleasure, Xen.; τὰς θύρας τινὸς θερ. to wait at a great man's door, Id.
to take care of, provide for men, of the gods, Id.
of things, to attend to, provide for, Soph., Thuc., etc.
θερ. τὸ σῶμα to take care of one's person, Lat. cutem curare, Plat.
to treat medically, to heal, cure, Thuc., Xen.
θ. ἡμέρην to observe a day, keep it as a feast, Hdt.; θ. τὰ ἱερά = Lat. sacra procurare, Thuc.
of land, to cultivate, Xen.; δένδρον θερ. to train a tree, Hdt.
a means of cure, Luc.
a handmaid, Hhymn., Eur.
a dwelling, abode, Id.

a waiting-man, attendant, Od., etc.; differing from δοῦλος, as implying free service; and in Hom. a companion in arms, though inferior in rank; as Patroclus is the companion or esquire of Achilles; Meriones of Idomeneus, Il.; so the charioteer is ἡνίοχος θεράπων; kings were Διὸς θεράποντες; warriors θεράποντες Ἄρηος, etc.:—c. dat., οἶκος ξένοισι θεράπων devoted to the service of its guests, Pind.
later, simply, a servant, Hdt.:—in Chios, θεράποντες was the name for their slaves, Thuc.
rare poet. form for θεράπων: nom. pl. θέραπες Eur., Anth.
of summer, in summer:— θερεία, ionic -είη, (sc. ὥρα) = θέρος, summer-time, summer, Hdt.; ταῖς θερείαις Pind.
to do summer-work, to mow, reap, σῖτον, κριθάς, καρπόν Hdt., Ar., etc.:—Mid., καρπὸν Δηοῦς θερίσασθαι Id.
metaph. to cut off, Soph., Eur.
metaph. to reap a good harvest, Ar.
ὁ θερίζων (with or without λόγος) a kind of syllogism, Luc.
intr. to pass the summer, Xen.; cf. ἐαρίζω, χειμάζω.
= θερῐνός: θ. τροπαί the summer solstice, i. e. June 21st, Hdt.
reaping-time, harvest, NTest.
the harvest, crop, Id.
a reaper, harvester, Eur., Xen.
a light summer garment, opp. to χειμάστριον, Theocr., so θέριστρον, ου, τό, Anth.
to warm, heat, Il., Aesch., etc.:—Pass. to be heated, grow hot, Od.

metaph. to heat, ἕως ἐθέρμην’ αὐτὸν φλὸξ οἴνου Eur.; σπλάγχνα θ. Ar.; πολλὰ θ. φρενί to cherish hot feelings, Aesch.:—Pass., θερμαίνεσθαι ἐλπίσι to glow with hope, Soph.; χαρᾶι θ. καρδίαν to have one's heart warm with joy, Eur.
heat, feverish heat, Thuc., etc.
of lupines (θέρμος), Luc.
dyed hot, opp. to ψυχροβαφής, Theophr.
hot-bubbling, Paul_s_therm.
hot-tempered, Eur. ap. Ar.
one who brought the hot water at baths, Lat. caldarius; fem. θερμοδότις, ιδος, Anth.
heated in mind, Aesch.
literally hot-gates, i. e. a narrow gate-like pass, in which were hot springs, name of the famous pass from Thessaly to Locris, the key of Greece, also called simply Πύλαι, Hdt.
hot, warm, θερμὰ λοετρά Hom.; of tears, Id., etc.
metaph. hot, hasty, rash, headlong, like Lat. calidus, Aesch., Ar., etc.
still warm, fresh, ἴχνη Anth.
τὸ θερμόν = θερμότης, heat, Lat. calor, Hdt., Plat., etc.
θερμόν (sc. ὕδωρ), hot water, θερμῷ λοῦσθαι Ar.
τὰ θερμά (sub. χωρία), Hdt.: but (sub. λουτρά), hot baths, Xen.
adv. -μῶς, Plat.
a lupine, Anth.
heat, Lat. calor, Plat.
doing hot and hasty acts, reckless, Xen., Luc.
to heat, make hot, Od., Ar.:—Pass. to be heated, grow hot, Hom.
summer, summertime, χείματος οὐδὲ θέρευς in winter nor in summer, Od.; οὔτ’ ἐν θέρει οὔτ’ ἐν ὀπώρῃ Id.; τὸ θέρος during the summer, Hdt.; θέρους μεσοῦντος about mid summer, Luc.
summer-fruits, harvest, a crop, Aesch., Ar., etc.; metaph., δράκοντος θ. Eur.
Thersites, i. e. the audacious ( from θέρσος, aeolic for θάρσος), Hom.
Pass. to become hot or warm, warm oneself, Od.; πυρός at the fire, Id.; θέρου warm yourself, Ar.
of things, μὴ ἄστυ πυρὸς θέρηται lest the city be burnt by fire, Il.
a setting, placing, arranging, Pind., Plat.; θ. νόμων lawgiving, Dem.
a deposit of money, preparatory to a law-suit, Ar.: money paid in advance, earnest-money, Dem.
position, situation, Lat. situs, of a city, Thuc., etc.
marvellous, wondrous, θέσκελα ἔργα works of wonder, Hom.:—as adv., ἔϊκτο δὲ θέσκελον αὐτῷ 'twas wondrous like him, Il.
according to law, lawful, Pind., Aesch.
θέσμια, τά, as Subst., laws, customs, rites, Hdt., etc.; also in sg., Eur.
to be a θεσμοθέτης, Dem.
a lawgiver:—at Athens, the θεσμοθέται were the six junior archons, who judged causes assigned to no special court, Aeschin., etc.
to make laws, Eur.
like θέμις, that which is laid down and established, a law, ordinance, Lat. institutum, λέκτροιο θεσμὸν ἵκοντο, i. e. they fulfilled the established law of wedlock, Od.; so in Hdt. and attic
at Athens, Draco's laws were called θεσμοί, because each began with the word θεσμός (cf. θεσμοθέτης), while Solon.'s laws were named νόμοι.
an institution, ordinance, as the court of Areopagus, Aesch.; of the great games, Pind.
justice, like δικαιοσύνη, Anth.
to keep the Thesmophoria, Ar., Xen.
the Thesmophoria, an ancient festival held by the Athenian women in honour of Demeter Θεσμοφόρος, Hdt., Ar.
the temple of Demeter Θεσμοφόρος, Ar.
law-giving, an ancient name of Demeter (Ceres), Hdt.; τὼ θεσμοφόρω Ceres and Proserpine, Ar.
guardians of the law, Thuc.
properly of the voice, divinely sounding, divinely sweet, Hom., Pind.
that can be spoken by none but God, i. e. unspeakable, ineffable; hence,
like θεῖος, divine, Hom.; dat. fem. θεσπεσίῃ (sc. βουλῇ) by the will of God, Id.; θ. ὁδός the way of divination, of Cassandra, Aesch.

wondrous, marvellous, portentous, awful, of things, Hom.; θ. χαλκός marvellous fine brass, Od., Il.; θ. ὀδμή a smell divinely sweet, Od.; so in Hdt., θεσπέσιον ὡς ἡδύ:—of human affairs, θ. φόβος Il., etc.
adv. -ίως, θ. ἐφόβηθεν they trembled unspeakably, Id.: so neut. as adv., Theocr.
kindled by a god, θ. πῦρ furious, portentous fire, such as seems more than natural, Hom.
fem. adj. oracular, prophetic, Soph.

entry.etym: ionic inf. θεσπιέειν Hdt.; doric aor1 ἐθέσπιξα
entry.sense: to declare by oracle, prophesy, divine, Hdt., Trag.; Pass., τί δὲ τεθέσπισται; Soph.
in pl., oracular sayings, Hdt., Soph.
having words from God, inspired, Od., Eur.
generally, divine, wondrous, awful, θέσπις ἄελλα Hhymn.
to prophesy, sing in prophetic strain, Aesch., Eur., Ar.
singing in prophetic strain, prophetic, Eur.
caused by prophecy, φόβος Aesch.
a Thessalian, Hdt., etc.; proverb., Θεσσαλὸν σόφισμα a Thessalian trick, from the faithless character of the people, Eur.
Θεσσαλὶς κυνῆ a Thessalian cap, Soph.
to pray, Pind.
prophetic, Aesch.
spoken by God, decreed, ordained, appointed, Lat. fatalis, Aesch., Soph.: θέσφατόν ἐστι it is ordained, Il.; σοὶ δ’ οὐ θ. ἐστι θανέειν 'tis not appointed thee to die, Od.
as Subst., θέσφατα, τά, divine decrees, oracles, Id., Trag., etc.
generally, like θεῖος, divine, Od.
to be laid down, Arist.
θετέον, one must lay down, Xen.
the temple of Thetis, Eur.
of or for adoption, Arist.
Thetis, one of the Nereids, wife of Peleus, mother of Achilles
entry.etym: Hom. uses Θέτῑ for dat. and vocat.; Θέτιν for acc.

entry.sense: taken as one's child, adopted, Pind., Hdt., etc.

entry.etym: the syllables εο, εου remain uncontracted even in attic
the tenses other than present θέω and future θεύσομαι are supplied by τρέχω and *δρέμω
entry.sense: to run, Hom., etc.; θέειν πεδίοιο to run over the plain, Il.: in part. with another Verb, ἦλθε θέων, ἦλθε θέουσα came running, Id.; θέων Αἴαντα κάλεσσον run and call him, Id.
περὶ τρίποδος θεύσεσθαι to run for a tripod, Id.; περὶ ψυχῆς θέον Ἕκτορος they were running for Hector's life, Id.
of other kinds of motion, as,
of birds, θεύσονται δρόμωι Ar.
of ships, ἔθεε κατὰ κῦμα Il.; of a potter's wheel, Id.; of a quoit, ῥίμφα θέων ἀπὸ χειρός flying lightly, Od.

of things which (as we say) run in a continuous line, though not actually in motion, φλὲψ ἀνὰ νῶτα θέουσα Il.; esp. of anything circular, which runs round into itself, ἄντυξ, ἣ πυμάτη θέεν ἀσπίδος Id.
c. acc. loci, to run over, τὰ ὄρη Xen.
to look at, view, behold, Hdt., Aesch., etc.: to inspect or review soldiers, Xen.
of the mind, to contemplate, consider, observe, Plat., etc.
to view the public games, of spectators, θ. τὰ Ὀλύμπια Hdt., etc.; θ. τινά to see him act, Dem.: —absol. to go as a spectator, ἐς τὰ Ἐφέσια Thuc.
to be a θεωρός or state-ambassador to the oracle or at the games, Ar., Thuc.
in θεωρήσασα τοὐμὸν ὄμμα Soph., the acc. ὄμμα may be taken as in βαίνειν πόδα, having beheld with mine eye.
that which is looked at, viewed, a sight, spectacle, Dem., etc.
a principle thereby arrived at, a rule, Lat. praeceptum: in Mathematics, a theorem, Euclid.
a seat in a theatre, Plut.
fond of contemplating a thing, c. gen., Arist.: absol. speculative, Id., Plut., etc.
a looking at, viewing, beholding, θεωρίης εἵνεκεν ἐκδημεῖν to go abroad to see the world, Hdt.; so Thuc., etc.: of the mind, contemplation, speculation, Plat., etc.
pass. = θεώρημα, a sight, show, spectacle, Aesch., Eur., etc.; esp. at a theatre, Ar., Xen.
the being a spectator at the theatre or the public games, Soph., Plat.
the θεωροί or state-ambassadors sentto the office of θεωρός, a mission, Id., Xen.
the office of θεωρός, discharge of that office, Thuc., etc.
of or for θεωρία (signfs. II and III), πεπλώματ’ οὐ θεωρικά no festal robes, Eur.

θεωρικά (sc. χρήματα) τά, the money, which, from the time of Pericles, was given to the poor citizens to pay for seats in the theatre (at 2 obols the seat), but also for other purposes, Dem.: in sg., τὸ θεωρικόν the theatric fund, Id.
a sacred ship, which carried the θεωροί (cf. θεωρός II) to their destination, but was also used for other state-purposes, Hdt., Plat.: metaph. of Charon's bark, Aesch.
(sub. ὁδός) the road by which the θεωροί went.
a spectator, Theogn., Aesch., etc.; θ. εἰκάδων viewing the festivals or present at them, Eur.

an ambassador sent to consult an oracle or to present an offering, Soph., ap. Dem. The Athenians sent θεωροί to Delphi, to Delos, and to the four great games, the Olympian, Pythian, Nemean and Isthmian.
entry.etym: Derived in first sense from θεάομαι; in second perh. from θεός, ὤρα, cura.

entry.sense: more divine: v. θεός.
sprung from Thebes, Theban, Hes.
epith. of Zeus, theTheban, Hdt.
Theban, Hom., etc.; Θηβαϊκός, ή, όν, Hdt.
Thebes, the name of several cities, the most famous being the Egyptian (ἑκατόμπυλοι), and the Boeotian (ἑπτάπυλοι), Hom.
the Thebais, i. e. territory of Thebes (in Egypt), Hdt.; (in Boeotia), Thuc.
to Thebes, Il.
from Thebes, Anth.; aeolic Θείβᾱθεν, Ar.
at Thebes, Hom.; aeolic Θείβᾱθι, Ar.
pointed, sharp, Anth.
act. sharpening, c. gen., Id.
a whetstone, Aesch., Soph.: metaph., αἱματηραὶς θηγάναι incentives to bloodshed, Aesch.
to sharpen, whet, Il.; θήγων λευκὸν ὀδόντα Id.; θ. φάσγανον, ξίφος Aesch., Eur.:—in Mid., δόρυ θηξάσθω let him whet his spear, Il.
metaph. to sharpen, excite, provoke, like Lat. acuere, τὰς ψυχὰς εἰς τὰ πολεμικά Xen.:—Pass., λόγοι τεθηγμένοι sharp, biting words, Aesch.; γλῶσσα τεθηγμένη Soph.
one who gazes at, an admirer, Od.
gazed at, wondrous, admirable, Lat. spectandus, Hes., Pind.
epic for θεῖον, brimstone, Od.
like a chest or coffin, οἴκημα θ. a burial vault, Hdt.
a case to put anything in, a box, chest, Hdt., Eur.
a place for corpses, a grave, tomb, Hdt., Aesch.
a mode of burial, Thuc.
sharpened, Aesch., Eur.
of the mother, to suckle, Lat. lactare, Lys., NTest.
of the young animal, to suck, Lat. lactere; θηλάζων χοῖρος a sucking pig, Theocr.: c. acc., μασδὸν ἐθήλαξεν Id.
a giving suck, suckling, Plut.
to be full of, c. gen., λειμῶνες ἴου ἠδὲ σελίνου θήλεον the meadows were full of violets and parsley, Od.; so c. dat., θάλησε σελίνοις Pind.
absol. to flourish, Anth.
the part of the breast which gives suck, the teat, nipple, Eur., Plat.
of female sex, womanish, Eur.
with woman's tongue, Anth.
a womanish, effeminate person, Hdt., Luc.
swaying women, Aesch.
slaying by woman's hand, Aesch.
singing in soft strain, Anth.
with a woman's head-band, Luc.: fem. θηλυμίτρις, ιδος, Id.
woman-shaped, Eur.
of womanish mind, Aesch.
to make womanish, to enervate, Eur., Xen.: metaph. to soften, Ζέφυρος κῦμα θηλύνει Anth.:—Pass. to become weak and womanish, Soph.: to play the coquet. Bion.
befitting a woman, Anth.
of female kind, Aesch.

of female sex, female, θήλεια θεός a goddess, Il.; θήλειαι ἵπποι mares, Od.; σύες θήλειαι sows, Id.; ὄϊς θῆλυς a ewe, Il.; ἄπαις θήλεος γόνου without female issue, Hdt.:— ἡ θήλεα, attic -εια, the female, Id., Aesch.; χρῆμα θηλειῶν woman-kind, Eur.; τὸ θῆλυ γένος or τὸ θῆλυ the female sex, woman kind, Id.
of or belonging to women, Hdt., Aesch.; θ. φόνος murder by women, Eur.
in Gramm. feminine.
applied to persons and things,
fresh, refreshing, of dew, Hes.

tender, delicate, gentle, θηλύτεραι γυναῖκες, θηλύτεραι θεαί (where the comp. is used much like a Positive), Hom.; θῆλυς ἀπὸ χροιᾶς delicate of skin, Theocr.; of character, soft, yielding, weak, γυνὴ θῆλυς οὖσα Soph.
womanishness, delicacy, effeminacy, Plut.
giving birth to girls, Theocr.
like a woman, Plut., Anth.
with woman's frock, Anth., Luc.
to collect in a heap, shortened from θημωνολογέω, Anth.
a heap, Od.

enclitic Particle, chiefly epic, = δή, expressing strong conviction, surely now, Hom., Theocr.; ironically, λείψετέ θην νέας so then you will leave the ships, Il.; strengthd, ἦ θην in very truth, Id.; οὔ θην surely not, Hom.
a hunter, Eur., Anth.
that which is caught, prey, spoil, booty, Eur., Anth.
a hunting of wild beasts, the chase, Hom., Hdt., etc.
metaph. eager pursuit of anything, Soph.
the beast taken, spoil, booty, prey, game, Od., Aesch., etc; in pl., ὦ πταναὶ θῆραι, of birds, Soph.
to be hunted down or caught, Aesch.
to be hunted after, sought eagerly, Soph., Xen.
θηρατέον one must hunt after, Xen.
a hunter, Il.
one who hunts for words, Ar.

entry.etym: = θηρευτικός: metaph., τὰ θ. τῶν φίλων
entry.sense: the arts for winning friends, Xen.
an instrument of the chase, a net, trap, Xen.
to hunt or chase wild beasts, Soph., Xen.:—of men, to catch, capture, Xen.: metaph. to captivate, Id.:— θ. πόλιν to seek to destroy it, Aesch.
metaph., like Lat. venari, to hunt after a thing, pursue it eagerly, Trag.:—c. inf. to seek or endeavour to do, Eur.; and in Mid., Soph., Eur.
Mid. much like Act. to hunt for, fish for, ἐγχέλεις Ar.; absol., οἱ θηρώμενοι hunters, Xen.
metaph. to cast about for, seek after, Hdt., Eur., etc.
Pass. to be hunted, pursued, Aesch., etc.
of wild beasts, Lat. feri_nus, θήρειον γραφήν the figures of animals worked upon the cloak, Aesch.; θ. δάκος = θήρ, Eur.; θ. βία, periphr. for ὁ θήρ, the centaur, Soph.; θ. κρέα game, Xen.
spoil, prey, Eur.
hunting, the chase, Plat.
a hunter, huntsman, Il.; κυσὶ θηρευτῇσι Id.; also of a fisher, Hdt.
of or for hunting, κύνες θ. hounds, Ar., Xen.; βίος θ. the life of hunters, Arist.
to hunt, go hunting, Od., Hdt.
c. acc. to hunt after, chase, catch, Id., Xen., etc.:—of men, to hunt down, Hdt.; to lay wait for, Xen.:—Pass. to be hunted, Hdt.: to be caught, Aesch.
metaph. to hunt after, Id., Eur., etc.

entry.etym: in form a Dim. of θήρ, but in usage equiv. to it.
entry.sense: a wild animal, beast, of a stag, Od.;—of savage beasts, Hdt., Xen., etc.; but, of a pig, Plat.; of a dog, Theocr.:—in pl. beasts, opp. to men, birds, and fishes, wild animals, game, Hdt., Plat.:—proverb., ἢ θηρίον ἢ θεός, i. e. either below or above the nature of man, Arist.
an animal, Hdt., Plat.
a poisonous animal, reptile, serpent, NTest.
also as real Dim. a little animal, insect, of bees, Theocr.
as a term of reproach, beast! like Lat. bellua, French bete, Ar., Plat.
the nature of a beast, brutality, Arist.

sense.gloss: to make into a wild beast.

entry.sense: full of wild beasts, infested by them, Lat. belluosus, of countries, Hdt.
of men, beast-like, wild, savage, brutal, Lat. bellui_nus, Eur., Plat., etc.:— τὸ θ. the animal nature, Eur.
a turning into a beast, Luc.
to slay wild beasts, Soph.
where wild beasts feed, Anth.
with brutal mind, brutal, Anth.
killing wild beasts, ἐν φοναῖς θηροκτόνοις, i. e. in the chase, Eur.
slayer of beasts, Anth.
slain by beasts, Anth.
half-beast, θηρ. τις ὠρυγή a cry as of beasts, Plut.
tending wild beasts, Anth.
looking out for wild beasts, Hhymn.
the chase, Anth.
producing beasts, ἄλση Anth.
feeding wild beasts, Eur.
proparox. θηρότροφος, feeding on beasts, Id.
killing wild beasts, Eur.
a wild beast, beast of prey, Il., etc.; joined with λέων, Eur.; with λέαινα, Anth.; also of Cerberus, Soph.:—in pl. beasts, as opp. to birds and fishes, Od., etc.
of any animal, as of birds, Ar., etc.
any fabulous monster, as the sphinx, Aesch.; esp. a centaur, Soph. (cf. Φήρ); a satyr, Eur.
to store or treasure up, Hdt., Xen., etc.
a store, treasure, Soph., Eur.
a laying up in store, Arist.
laying up in store, Plat.
a store laid up, treasure, Aesch., Ar.:—metaph., θ. ὕμνων Pind.; Διὸς θ., of fire, Eur.; οἰωνοῖς γλυκὺς θ., of a dead body, Soph.
a store-house, treasure-house, magazine, Hdt.: the treasury of a temple, Id., Xen.
any receptacle for valuables, a chest, casket, Hdt.; θ. βελέεσσιν, of a quiver, Aesch.
sons to Theseus, i. e. the Athenians, Soph.
the temple of Theseus, a sanctuary for criminals and runaway slaves, Ar.
τὰ Θησεῖα, ( sc. ἱερά) the festival of Theseus, Id.
Theseus, the famous ancestral hero of Athens, Il., etc.
entry.etym: From ΘΕ, Root of τίθημι, the settler; cf. θής.

entry.sense: of Theseus, Aesch.
as Subst. the Theseid, a poem on Theseus, Arist.
name of a mode of haircutting, first used by Theseus, Plut.
a serf or villain, bound to till his lord's land, Lat. ascriptus glebae, opp. to a mere slave, θῆτές τε δμῶές τε Od.: also a hired farm-servant or bailiff, Lat. villicus, Hes., Plat.

at Athens, by the constitution of Solon., the θῆτες were the fourth class, (the other three being πεντακοσιομέδιμνοι, ἱππεῖς, ζευγίται) , including all whose property in land was under 150 medimni, Plut.: they were employed as light-armed and seamen.
a poor girl, one obliged to go out for hire, Plut.
as adj. θῆσσα τράπεζα menial fare, Eur.
entry.etym: From ΘΕ, Root of τίθημι, a settler.

entry.sense: fem. of θής, q. v.
Greek form of Lat. thensa, a sacred car, Plut.

Θ, θ, θῆτα, τό, indecl., eighth letter of the Gr. alphabet: as numeral θʹ = ἐννέα, ἔνατος, but ͵θ = 9000. —θ is the aspirated dental mute, related to the tenuis τ and the medial δ. θ is sometimes represented by φ, as θλάω φλάω; so in Lat. θήρ (aeolic φήρ) fera; θύρα fores; byβ, as ἐ-ρυθρός ruber, οὖθαρ uber.
changes of θ in the Gr. dialects:
Lacon., into σ, as σάλασσα σεῖος Ἀσάνα παρσένος for θάλασσα θεῖος Ἀθάνα παρθένος.
aeolic and doric into τ, as αὖτις ἐντεῦθεν for αὖθις ἐντεῦθεν.
when θ was repeated in two foll. syllables, the former became τ, as Ἀτθίς.
hired service, service, Soph.
to be a serf or menial, serve for hire, Hom., Hdt., attic
of or for a hireling, menial, Arist.
τὸ θητικόν, the class of θῆτες, Id.
the leader of a θίασος, Luc.
to bring into the Bacchic company, Eur.:— Pass. to be of the Bacchic company, to be hallowed by Bacchic rites, Id.
a band or company marching through the streets with dance and song, esp. in honour of Bacchus, a band of revellers, Hdt., Eur., etc.
generally, any party, company, troop, Eur., Xen.
the member of a θίασος, Ar., etc.:— c. gen., θιασῶται τοῦ Ἔρωτος followers of Love, Xen.; ὁ ἐμὸς θ. Eur.
of Bacchus, leader of θίασοι, Anth.
to touch, handle, c. gen., Trag.
to take hold of, τινός Soph., etc.; ὠλέναις θ. τινός to embrace, Eur.
to touch, attempt, λόγου γλώσσηι θ. Soph.:—in hostile sense, to attack, θηρός Eur.
metaph. of the feelings, to touch, Id.; ψυχῆς, φρενῶν θ. Id.; πολλὰ θιγγάνει πρὸς ἧπαρ reach to the heart, Aesch.
to reach, gain, win, τινός Pind., etc.:—Pind. uses it in this sense, as he does ψαύω, c. dat.
originally a termin. of the gen., as in Ἰλιόθι πρό, ἠῶθι πρό Il.
insepar. Affix of several Substs., Adjs., and Pronouns, to which it gives an adv. sense, denoting the place at which, οἴκοθι, ἄλλοθι, etc.
a heap, Od., Aesch.:—in pl. sand-heaps, sand-bank, Hdt., etc.
the beach, shore, παρὰ θῖνα θαλάσσης Il.; παρὰ θῖν’ ἁλός Id.; so, ἐπὶ θινί Od.
sand or mud at the bottom of the sea, οἶδμα κυλίνδει βυσσόθεν θῖνα Soph.; metaph., τὸν θῖνά μου ταράττεις you trouble the very bottom of my heart, Ar.
to crush, bruise, Hom.
to press, squeeze, pinch, Ar., Dem.:—Pass. of a person heavy-laden, ὡς θλίβομαι! Ar.:—Mid., πολλῆισι φλιῆισι θλίψεται ὤμους he will rub his shoulders against many doorposts, of a beggar, Od.
to pinch, compress, straiten, Plat.:—Pass. to be compressed, θλιβομένα καλύβα a small, close hut, Theocr.; ὁδὸς τεθλιμμένη a narrow way, NTest.
metaph. to oppress, afflict, distress, Arist.

entry.etym: The Root is ΘΑΝ, found in aor2 θανεῖν, etc.
The form τεθνειώς appears as a variant reading at Iliad 17.161
entry.sense: to die, be dying, in aor2 and perf. to be dead, Hom., etc.; the pres. sometimes takes a perf. sense, θνήσκουσι γάρ, for τεθνήκασι, Soph., Eur.

often used like a pass. Verb, χερσὶν ὑπ’ Αἴαντος θανέειν to fall by his hand, be slain by him, Il., etc.:—note the phrase of Dem., τεθνᾶσι τῶι δέει τοὺς τοιούτους, where τεθνᾶσι τῶι δέει must be taken as a single Verb, are in mortal fear of.
metaph. of things, to die, perish, Aesch., Soph., etc.
of mortal race, Soph., Eur.
of mortal nature, Plat.
liable to death, mortal, Hom., etc.:—as Subst., θνητοί mortals, Od., Trag.
of things, befitting mortals, human, Pind., Eur., etc.
trans. to move quickly, ply rapidly, πτέρυγας Eur.; τίς ὅδ’ ἀγὼν θοάζων σε; what task is thus hurrying thee on? Id.; θοάζω πόνον I urge it on, Id.; θ. σῖτα to dispatch food quickly, Id.
intr. to move quickly, hurry along, rush, dart, Id.
= θάσσω, to sit, τίνας ποθ’ ἕδρας θοάζετε; why sit ye in this suppliant posture? Soph.
a meal, feast, Eur.
lord of the feast, Aesch.
of or for a feast, Xen.
to feast on, eat, ἰχθῦς Hes.
to feast, entertain, φίλους Eur.; τὸ δεῖπνον, τό μιν ἐκεῖνος ἐθοίνησε the feast, which he gave him, Hdt.
Mid. and Pass., fut. ήσομαι and άσομαι [ᾱ]: aor1 ἐθοινήθην and -ησάμην: perf. τεθοίνᾱμαι: — absol. to be feasted, to feast, banquet, Hom., Od., Eur.:—c. acc. to feast on, Eur.; so c. gen., Anth.
a meal, feast, banquet, dinner, Hes., Hdt., attic
muddy, foul, thick, troubled, Lat. turbidus, properly of water, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
metaph. troubled by passion or madness, θολεροὶ λόγοι Aesch.; θολερῷ χειμῶνι with turbid storm of madness, Soph.
a conical hat with a broad brim to keep the sun off, Theocr.
a round building with a conical roof, a vaulted chamber, Od.
at Athens, the Rotunda, in which the Prytanes dined, Plat., etc.
mud, dirt, esp. the thick, dark juice of the cuttle-fish (sepia), which it emits to trouble the water and hide himself, Lat. loligo, Arist.
to make turbid, properly of water: metaph., θ. καρδίαν Eur.

quick, nimble, active, Il.; θοὴ νύξ swift Night, because she drove a car, or came on suddenly, Hom.; θοὴν ἀλεγύνετε δαῖτα prepare a hasty meal, Od., etc.:—adv. θοῶς, quickly, in haste, Hom.; soon, Od.
of the Echinades, islands with sharp-peaks, Id.
to make sharp or pointed, Od.
to Thoricus, Hhymn.
Dep., = θρώσκω II, 3rd pl. subj. θορνύωνται Hdt.
semen genitale, Hdt.
Pass. to be troubled, NTest.
to make a noise or uproar, of a crowd, Ar.
like Lat. acclamare, to shout in token either of approbation or the contrary:
to cheer, applaud, Plat.
to raise clamours against, c. dat., Thuc., Plat., etc.:—Pass. to have clamours raised against one, Soph.
trans. to confuse by noise or tumult, to trouble, throw into confusion, Thuc.:—Pass. to be thrown into confusion, Hdt., etc.
uproarious, turbulent, Ar.
making an uproar, Plut.
a noise, uproar, clamour, Pind., Eur., Thuc., etc.; θόρυβος βοῆς a confused clamour, Soph.
in token of approbation or the contrary:
applause, cheers, Ar., Plat., etc.
groans, murmurs, Soph.
tumult, confusion, Hdt., Thuc.
noisy, uproarious, turbulent, Plat.
causing alarm, Xen.
a Thurian prophet, of Lampon who led the colony to Thurium, Ar.

entry.etym: in attic Poets for θοῦρος, Aesch., etc.

entry.sense: θοῦρις ἀσπίς, the shield with which one rushes to the fight, Il.
rushing, raging, impetuous, furious, Il., Aesch.
speed, as prop. n., Od.
Thrace, Ar., Thuc., etc.: ionic Θρηΐκη, Hdt.; epic contr. Θρῄκη, Il., Trag.; Θρᾴκη in Ar.
Thracian, Thuc., etc.: ionic Θρηΐκῐος, ος, η, ον, Il., Hdt.; contr. Θρῄκιος, Trag.:— Σάμος Θρηϊκίη = Σαμοθρᾴκη, Il.
adv. in Thracian fashion, Theocr.
to be stretched on the tanner's board, to be tanned, Ar.
one of the rowers on the topmost of the three benches in a trireme, who had the longest oars and most work, a top-rower, Ar., Thuc.: —cf. ζυγίτης, θαλαμίτης.
a bench, form, Ar.
a Thracian; ionic Θρηΐξ, ΐκος, pl. Θρηΐκες [ῐ], Il., Hdt., etc.; epic contr. Θρῇξ, Θρῃκός, Il., Trag., etc.
courage, boldness, Il., Soph.; θρ. ἰσχύος confidence in strength, Soph.
in bad sense, over-boldness, daring, rashness, audacity, impudence, attic, Hdt.
a Thracian woman, Soph., etc.
to trouble, disquiet, Aesch., Eur., Plat., etc.
to destroy, ruin, Anth.
bold in counsel, Arist.
strong of limb, Pind.
an impudent coward, Arist.
bold of heart, Il.
bold in battle, Arist.
bravely steadfast (cf. Μέμνων), Hom.
bold of thought or plan, daring, resolute, Pind.
bold in contriving, daring in design, Pind.
bold of speech, saucy, Pind.
= θαρσύνω, to make bold, embolden, encourage, Aesch., Thuc.:—Pass. and Mid., to be bold or ready, take courage, Aesch., Eur., etc.
Pass., in bad sense, to be over-bold, audacious, to speak boldly or insolently, Soph., Ar.
bold or ready at work, Pind.
bold in war, Anth.
bold, spirited, courageous, confident, Hom., Hdt., attic; θρασεῖα τοῦ μέλλοντος full of confidence for the future, Thuc.
in bad sense, over-bold, rash, venturous, Lat. audax, Od., attic
of things, to be ventured, c. inf., θρασύ μοι τόδ’ εἰπεῖν this I am bold to say, Pind.; οὐκ ἆρ’ ἐκείνῳ προσμῖξαι θρασύ; Soph.
adv. -έως: comp. θρασύτερον, too boldly, Thuc.
bold-hearted, Eur. adv. -ως, Aesch.
to be over-bold of tongue, Trag.
insolence, Anth.
bold of tongue, insolent, Aesch.
over-boldness, audacity, Thuc.
bold of hand, Anth.
breaking wheels, Ar.
that which is broken, a fragment, wreck, piece, Aesch.
to break in pieces, shatter, shiver, Hdt., Aesch., Eur.:—Pass. to fly into pieces, Hdt.
metaph., like Lat. frangere, = θρύπτω, to break down, enfeeble, Pind., Eur., etc.
a nursling, creature, of sheep and goats, Xen., Plat.
of men, Soph., etc.
of wild beasts, Id.
as a term of reproach, a creature, θρέμματ’ οὐκ ἀνασχετά Aesch.; ὦ θρέμμ’ ἀναιδές Soph.
ὕδρας θρ., periphr. for ὕδρα, Id.
Dep., to cry aloud, shriek forth, Aesch., Eur.
to be fed, Plat.
θρεπτέον, one must feed, Xen.
from Pass., one must be fed, one must live, Id.
able to feed or rear, feeding, nourishing, Aesch.
πλόκαμος θρ. hair let grow as an offering, Id.
θρεπτήρια, τά, rewards for rearing, Hhymn.; but also, the returns made by children for their rearing, Hes.
= τροφή, nourishment, Soph.
a feeder, rearer, Anth.
promoting growth, Arist.; τὸ θρεπτικόν the principle of growth, Id.
the returns made by children to their parents for their rearing, Il.
a sound imitative of the cithara (as tra lira of the horn), Ar.
in Ar., οὐκ ἔνι μοι τὸ θρέττε, the spirit's not in me; a barbarism for τὸ θράσος.
from Thrace, Il.
to Thrace, Od.
to sing a dirge, to wail, Od., Aesch.:—c. acc. cogn., ἀοιδὴν ἐθρήνεον were singing a dirge, Il.; ὠιδάς, ἐπωιδάς θρ. Soph.:—Pass., ἅλις μοι τεθρήνηται, impers., Id.
c. acc. objecti, to wail for, lament, Aesch., etc.; so also Mid., Id.:—Pass. to be lamented, Soph.
a lament, dirge, Eur.
a mourner, wailer, Aesch.
querulous, Arist.
a funeral-song, dirge, lament, Lat. naenia, Il., Hdt., Trag.; θρῆνος οὑμός for me, Aesch.
a complaint, sad strain, Pind., etc.
a footstool, Hom.
θρ. ἑπταπόδης the seven-foot bench, the seat of the helmsman or the rowers, Il.
to sing a dirge over, τινά Eur.
like a dirge, fit for a dirge, Plat.
lamentation, Plat.
one who sings a dirge, Arist.
religious worship or usage, Hdt.: religion, NTest.; θρ. τῶν ἀγγέλων worshipping of angels, Id.
to hold religious observances, observe religiously, Hdt.
to be a devotee, Plut.
religious, NTest.
of triumphal families, Plut.
to triumph, Plut., etc.; θρ. ἀπό τινος or κατά τινος Lat. triumphare de aliquo, Id.; also, θρ. τινά NTest.
to lead in triumph, τινά Plut.
triumphal, ἀνὴρ θρ. = Lat. vir triumphalis, Plut.
a hymn to Bacchus, Cratin.: also a name for Bacchus, Plut., etc.
used to express the Roman triumphus, Id.
the topmost course of stones in a wall, which projected over the rest, the eaves, cornice, coping, Od., Eur.; θριγκὸς κυάνοιο a cornice of blue metal, Od.
metaph. the coping-stone, culmination, θριγκὸς κακῶν Eur.
a wall, fence of any sort, Id.
to surround with a coping, [αὐλὴν] ἐθρίγκωσεν ἀχέρδῳ he fenced it at top with thornbushes, Od.
to build even to the copingstone: metaph. to put the finishing stroke to a thing, Aesch.; δῶμα κακοῖς θριγκοῦν to bring the house to the height of misery, Eur.
a coping, cornice, Eur.
of lettuce, Luc.
lettuce, Hdt., etc.
an old name of Sicily, from its three promontories, Od., etc.:—in later times, the old form Θρινακίη was altered into Τρινακρία, Lat. Trinacria, as if it were compounded of τρεῖς ἄκραι.
a trident, Ar.
the hair of the head, used by Hom. only in pl.; attic also in sg.; Hom., etc.:—also sheep's wool, Il.; pig's bristles, Hom.; οὐραῖαι τρίχες the hair of a horse's tail, Il.
a single hair, proverb., θρὶξ ἀνὰ μέσσον only a hair's breadth between, Theocr.; ἄξιον τριχός, i. e. good for nothing, Ar.
a fig-leaf, Ar.
a mixture of eggs, milk, lard, flour, honey, and cheese, a kind of omelette, so called because it was wrapped in figleaves, Id.
entry.etym: Prob. from τρίς, from the three lobes of the figleaf.

entry.sense: a wood-worm, Anth.
to cry aloud, Soph.:— to speak, say, utter, Trag.;—and in Mid., Aesch.
to tell out, declare, Id., Soph.
Pass. to be troubled, NTest.
a lump, piece, Lat. grumus, as of asphalt, Hdt.: a clot or gout of blood, Aesch.
like clots, clotted, Soph.
flowers embroidered on cloth, patterns, Il.
flowers or herbs used as drugs and charms, Theocr.
a seat, chair, Hom.: a throne, chair of state, Hdt., attic:—in pl. also, the throne, i. e. the king's estate or dignity, Soph.
the oracular seat of Apollo or the Pythia, Aesch., etc.
the chair of a teacher, Lat. cathedra, Plat.
the enthronement of the newly initiated at the mysteries, Plat.
a noise as of many voices, Il.; of musical sounds, Pind.
the murmuring of a crowd, Thuc.
a report, Lat. rumor, Xen.
a plant which, like our rush, was used for making wicks, a wick, Ar.
to make a confused noise, chatter, babble, Ar., Theocr.
c. acc. rei, to be always talking about a thing, repeat over and over again, Lat. decantare, Eur., Plat., etc.:— Pass., τὸ θρυλούμενον the common talk, what is in every one's mouth, Dem.
to make a false note, Hhymn.
to crush, shiver, smash:— Pass., θρυλίχθη δὲ μέτωπον (epic for ἐθρυλίχθη) Il.
a noise as of many voices, a shouting, murmuring, Batr.
that which is broken off, a piece, bit, Ar., Anth.
a rush, Lat. juncus, Il.
easily broken: metaph. delicate, effeminate, Xen.
to break in pieces, break small, Plat., Theocr.
metaph., like Lat. frangere, to break, crush, enfeeble: Pass., with fut. mid., to be enfeebled, enervated, unmanned, Xen.; τεθρυμμένος Luc.
in Pass. also, to play the coquet, be coy and prudish, give oneself airs, bridle up, Ar., Xen.; θρύπτεσθαι πρός τινα to give oneself airs toward him, Plut.
a breaking in small pieces:—metaph. softness, weakness, debauchery, Xen., Plut., etc.

entry.etym: From Root ΘΟΡ, which appears in fut. and aor2.
entry.sense: to leap, spring, ἐκ δίφροιο, ἀπὸ λέκτροιο Hom.; of arrows, ἀπὸ νευρῆφι θρῶσκον Il.; of the oar, Soph.
foll. by prep. to leap upon, i. e. attack, assault, ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι θόρον Il.: —of a recurring illness, to attack, Soph.
generally, to rush, dart, Pind., Soph.:—metaph., πεδάρσιοι θρώσκουσι leap up into air, i. e. vanish away, Aesch.
trans. to mount, ὁ θρώσκων the sire, Id.
ground rising from the plain, an eminence, Il.
a daughter, Hom., etc.
a daughter's daughter, granddaughter, attic
a daughter's son, grandson, attic; ionic -ιδέος, Hdt.
a mortar, Ar.
a furious storm, hurricane, Hom.; πυρὸς θύελλαι thunderstorms, Od.; ποντία θ. Soph.; metaph., ἄτης θύελλαι Aesch.
of Thyestes, Ar.
receiving incense, Anth.
smoking or smelling with incense, fragrant, Hom., Hes.
the part of the victim that was burnt, the primal offering, mostly in pl., Il., Ar.:—metaph., θυηλὴ Ἄρεος, an offering to Ares, i. e. the blood of the slain, Soph.
to busy oneself with sacrifices, Aesch., Eur.
trans. to sacrifice:—Pass., θυηπολεῖται δ’ ἄστυ is filled with sacrifices, Id.
busy about sacrifices, sacrificial, Aesch.:—as Subst. a diviner, soothsayer, Eur., Ar.
devouring offerings, Aesch.
an African tree with scented wood, a kind of juniper or cedar, Theophr.
a mad or inspired woman, a Bacchante, Aesch.
of the tree θυία, of cedar, NTest.
to be inspired, Hhymn.
a little bag, Hdt., Ar.
a bag, pouch, wallet, Hdt., Ar.; δερῶ σε θύλακον I'll make a bag of your skin, Id.
in pl. the trousers of the Persians, Eur., Ar.
that which is offered; mostly in pl. θυλήματα, cakes, incense, etc., Ar.
to be wroth, angry, Hes., Ar.
heart-grieving, Hom., Hdt.
pass. inly grieving, καρδία Aesch.
a piece of burning wood or charcoal, a hot coal, Ar.
that which is slain or offered, a victim, sacrifice, offering, Trag., Thuc., etc.; πάγκαρπα θ. offerings of all fruits, Soph.
sacrifice, as an act, Id.: metaph., θ. λεύσιμον a sacrifice to be avenged by stoning [the murderers], Aesch.
to be well-pleased, Theocr.
suiting the heart, i. e. well-pleasing, dear, delightful, Hom.:—neut. as adv. in the form θυμῆρες, Od.
a bitter herb, savory, Eupol.
supping on bitter herbs, i. e. living poorly, Ar.
the Tiber, Anth.
eating savory, θυμβροφάγον βλέπειν to look as if one had eaten savory, make a savory or (as we might say) a verjuice face, Ar.
a place for sacrifice, an altar, Aesch., Eur.
θυμέλαι Κυκλώπων, supposed to be the Cyclopian walls at Mycenae, Eur.
in the Athenian theatre, a platform in the orchestra, on the steps of which stood the leader of the chorus, Plut.:— generally, a raised seat or stage, Id.
of or for the thymele, scenic, theatric, Plut.:— οἱ θυμελικοί, i. e. the chorus or musicians, Id.

entry.etym: a part. with no pres. in use
entry.sense: gathering breath, collecting oneself, Od.
well-pleasing, Od., Aesch.
that which is burnt as incense: in pl. fragrant stuffs for burning, Hdt., Soph., etc.
stuff for embalming, Hdt.
a vessel for burning incense, a censer, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
to burn so as to produce smoke, burn, Hdt.:—Pass. to be burnt, 3rd sg. θυμιῆται (ionic for -ᾶται) Id.
high-spirited, passionate, Arist.
flavoured with thyme, Ar.
heavy at heart, Anth.
to gnaw or vex the heart, Hes.
eating the heart, Il.
biting the heart, Od., Anth.
high-spirited, courageous, Lat. animosus, Plat., Xen.
hot-tempered, restive, Id.
lion-hearted, coeur-de-lion, Il.
prophesying from one's own soul (without inspiration, like the θεόμαντις), Aesch.
to fight desperately, NTest., Plut.
thyme, Ar., etc.
a mixture of thyme with honey and vinegar, Id.
wrathful, Aesch.
life-destroying, Il.
like a clever fellow, Ar.
wise from one's own soul, i. e. naturally clever, a man of genius, Ar., Plut.
the soul:

like Lat. anima, the soul, breath, life, θυμὸν ἀπαυρᾶν, ἀφελέσθαι, ἐξελέσθαι, ἐξαίνυσθαι, ὀλέσαι to take away life, Hom.; θυμὸν ἀποπνείειν to expire, Il.; θυμὸν ἀγείρειν to collect oneself, Id., etc.; θυμὸς τείρετο καμάτῳ his spirit was wearied by toil, Id.
like Lat. animus, the soul, heart; and so,

of desire for meat and drink, ἔπιον θ’ ὅσον ἤθελε θυμός Id.:—c. inf., βαλέειν δέ ἑ θυμὸς ἀνώγει his heart bade him shoot, Id.; ἤθελε θυμῷ he wished in his heart or with all his heart, Id.; θυμῷ βουλόμενος wishing with all one's heart, Hdt.; so, ἐκ θυμοῦ φιλέειν Il.:— θυμός ἐστί μοι, θ. γίγνεταί μοι, c. inf., I have a mind to do . . , Id., Xen., etc.:—also as the seat of sorrow or joy, χαῖρε δὲ θυμῷ Il.; ἄχνυτο θυμός Id., etc.

mind, temper, will, θ. πρόφρων, νηλεής, σιδήρεος Hom.; ἕνα θυμὸν ἔχειν to be of one mind, Il.; δόκησε δ’ ἄρα σφίσι θυμὸς ὣς ἔμεν it pleased them to be of this mind, Od.; ἐδαΐζετο θωμός their mind was divided, Il.
spirit, courage, μένος καὶ θυμός Id.; θυμὸν λαμβάνειν to take heart, Od.; παραὶ ποσὶ κάππεσε θυμός Il., etc.
as the seat of anger, νεμεσίζεσθαι ἐνὶ θυμῷ Id.:—hence, anger, wrath, δάμασον θυμόν Id.; θυμὸς μέγας ἐστὶ βασιλῆος Id.
the soul as the agent of thought, ᾔδεε γὰρ κατὰ θυμόν Id.; φράζετο θυμῷ Id.
to torment the soul, break the heart, Soph.
destroying the soul, life-destroying, Od.:— heart-breaking, Id.; of persons, troublesome, annoying, Id.:— θυμοφθόρα πολλά (sc. σήματα) tokens poisoning the king's mind (against Bellerophon), Il.

to make angry:—Mid. and Pass., fut. -ώσομαι; aor1 ἐθυμωσάμην and ἐθυμώθην: perf. inf. τεθυμῶσθαι: — to be wroth or angry, absol., Hdt., Trag.; of animals, to be wild, restive, Soph.; θυμοῦσθαι εἰς κέρας to vent fury with the horns, Virgil's irasci in cornua, Eur.; τὸ θυμούμενον passion, Thuc.: —θυμοῦσθαί τινι to be angry with one, Aesch., etc.; εἴς τινα Hdt.; c. dat. rei, to be angry at a thing, Ar.
wrath, passion, Aesch.
to dart along, Hes.
to spear a tunny-fish, Ar.
of the tunny-fish: τὰ θύννεια (sc. κρέα) its flesh, Ar.
for tunny-fishing, Luc.
tunny-headed, Luc.
to watch for tunnies, Ar.
a tunny-watcher, i. e. one who was posted on a high place, from which he could see the shoals coming, and make a sign to the fisherman to let down their nets, Theocr.
the tunny-fish, a large fish, used for food in the Mediterranean, Orac. ap. Hdt., Aesch., etc.
entry.etym: From θύνω, because of the tuna's quick, darting motion.

entry.sense: to rush or dart along, mostly of warriors in battle, Hom., Pind.
receiving incense, full thereof, odorous, Eur.
laden with incense, odorous, fragrant, Il., Eur.
a tree, the wood of which was burnt as a perfume, Od.
to make burnt-offerings, Aesch.
the sacrificing priest, Hom., Eur.
a sacrifice, offering, Hom., etc.
to fill with sweet smells: perf. pass. part., ἔλαιον τεθυωμένον fragrant oil. Il.
properly θύρασ-δε, out to the door, out of the door, Lat. foras, Hom.
generally, out, Id.; θ. ἐξιέναι to go out of the ship, Il.:—so in attic, ἐκφέρειν θ., ἐξέλκειν τινὰ θ. Ar.; οἱ θ. those outside, Id.
c. gen., ἁλὸς θ. out of the sea, Od.; θ. τῶν νόμων, like ἔξω, Eur.
adv. from outside the door, from without, Eur.
outside the door, outside, θύρηθ’ ἔα was out of the sea, Od.:— οἱ θ. aliens, the enemy, Aesch.
at the door or just outside the door, Aesch., Soph.; θ. οἰχνεῖν to go to the door, go out, Id.; θ. πόλεμος, opp. to civil war, Aesch.
absent, abroad, Id.; from abroad, Eur.; ἄνδρες θυρ. strangers, other men, Id.; θυραῖα φρονήματ’ the thoughts of strangers, Id.
= ἀλλότριος, Lat. alienus, ὄλβος θ. the luck of other men, Aesch.; πῆμα Eur.

a door, Hom., mostly in pl. double or folding doors, in full δικλίδες θύραι Od.: θύρην ἐπιτιθέναι, to put to the door, opp. to ἀνακλίνειν, Il.; so, τὴν θ. προστιθέναι Hdt.; ἐπισπάσαι Xen.; θύραν κόπτειν, πατάσσειν, κρούειν, Lat. januam pulsare, to knock, rap at the door, Ar., Plat.; metaph., ἐπὶ ταῖς θύραις at the door, i. e. close at hand, Xen.

from the Eastern custom of receiving petitions at the gate αἱ τοῦ βασιλέως θύραι became a phrase, βασιλέως θύραις παιδεύονται are educated at court, Id.; αἱ ἐπὶ τὰς θύρας φοιτήσεις dangling after the court, Id.
proverb., γλώσσῃ θύραι οὐκ ἐπίκεινται (cf. ἀθυρόστομος) Theogn.; ἐπὶ θύραις τὴν ὑδρίαν to break the pitcher at the very door, = "there's many a slip 'twixt cup and lip," Arist.
the door of a carriage, Xen.
θύρη καταπακτή a trap-door, Hdt.
a frame of planks, a raft, φραξάμενοι τὴν ἀκρόπολιν θύρῃσί τε καὶ ξύλοις with planks and logs, Id.
generally, an entrance, as to a grotto, Od.
at the door, outside, without, Lat. foris, Ar.
out of doors, abroad, Eur.
to live in the open air, to camp out, Xen., etc.: in war, to keep the field, Arist.
a living out of doors, camping out, Luc.
living out of doors, Hesych.
a large shield, Anth.; cf. θυρεός II.
a stone put against a door to keep it shut, a door-stone, Od.
a large oblong shield (like a door), opp. to ἀσπίς (the round shield), as Lat. scutum to clipeus, ap. Plut.
bearing a shield, Plut.
a door, Hom., etc.

entry.etym: epic dat. of θύρα, used as adv.
entry.sense: outside, Od., Hes.
a little door, wicket, Ar.
a window, Id.
to knock at the door, break it open, Ar.
knocking at the door, begging, Aesch.
to furnish with doors, shut close, Ar.: metaph. to close as with a door, βλεφάροις θυρῶσαι τὴν ὄψιν Xen.
he who raves with the thyrsus, Eur.
the thyrsus or Bacchic wand, being a wand wreathed in ivy and vineleaves with a pine-cone at the top, Eur., Anth.
to assemble or regulate with the thyrsus, Eur.
thyrsus-bearing, Eur., Anth.
delighting in the thyrsus, Anth.
a room with doors to it, a chamber, Hdt.
a door with posts and frame, Thuc., Dem.
the part outside the door, a hall, antechamber, Lat. vestibulum, Soph.
to be a door-keeper, Luc.
a door-keeper, porter, Lat. janitor, Hdt., attic
with a door or aperture, Babr.
tasseled, fringed, of the aegis, Il.
a tassel, in pl. tassels, fringe, Hdt.; of the tufts of the golden fleece, Pind.
