crasis for καὶ αἴκα.
the north-east wind, Ar.
to make new: hence, καί τι καινίζει στέγη and the house has something strange about it, Soph.; καίνισον ζυγόν try on thy new yoke, handsel it, Aesch.; κ. εὐχάς to offer new, strange prayers, Eur.
the New Court, at Athens, Ar.
newly suffered: unheard of, Soph.
newly put together, newmade, Aesch.
new to misery, Aesch.
to make new, to bring about new things, to make changes, innovate, Luc.:—Pass., τί καινοποιηθὲν λέγεις; what new-fangled, strange words art thou using? Soph.
an inventor of new pleasures, Xen.

new, fresh, Lat. recens, novus, καινὰ καὶ παλαιὰ ἔργα Hdt.; καινοὺς λόγους φέρειν to bring news, Aesch.; λέγεταί τι καινόν; Dem.; ἐκ καινῆς (sc. ἀρχῆς) anew, afresh, Lat. de novo, Thuc.:—esp. of dramas produced for the first time, Aeschin., Dem.

newly-invented, new-fangled, novel, Eur., etc.; κ. θεοί strange gods, Plat.; καινά innovations, Xen.; οὐδὲν καινότερον εἰσέφερε τῶν ἄλλων he introduced as little of anything new as others, Id.; τὸ καινὸν τοῦ πολέμου the unforeseen turn which war often takes, Thuc.
κ. ἄνθρωπος = novus homo, Plut.
of a new tomb, Anth.
newness, freshness, Plut.
novelty, Thuc., etc.
to cut fresh into, in mining, to open a new vein, Xen.
metaph. to begin something new, institute anew, Ar.: absol. to make innovations in the state, Lat. res novare, Arist.; also, κ. περὶ τὰ θεῖα Plat.
innovation, Plut.
novelty, Id.
innovating, Arist.
to begin something new, τί καινουργεῖς; what new plan art thou meditating? Eur.; κ. λόγον to speak new, strange words, Id.: to make innovations, Xen.; and
innovation, Isocr.
producing changes: τὸ κ. a novelty, Luc.
to make new, innovate:— Pass., of political changes, Thuc.; καινοῦσθαι τὰς διανοίας to have their minds revolutionised, Id.
= καινίζω, to use for the first time, to handsel, Hdt.
and now perhaps, Hom.

entry.etym: the pluperfect commonly functions as imperf.
entry.sense: to surpass, excel, ἐκαίνυτο φῦλ’ ἀνθρώπων νῆα κυβερνῆσαι he surpassed mankind in steering, Od.; ἐγχείηι δ’ ἐκέκαστο Πανέλληνας he excelled all the Hellenes in throwing the spear, Id.; ὁμηλικίην ἐκέκαστο γνῶναι surpassed them all in knowledge, Id.: esp. in part., δόλοισι κεκασμένε excellent in wiles, Id.: τέχνηισι κεκασμένος Hes.; φρουραῖς κέκασται is well furnished with, Eur.
and now, even now, Hom.
to kill, slay, Trag., Xen.
Conjunction, used in two principal senses, either copulative, to join words and sentences, and, Lat. et; or making a single word or clause emphatic, also, even, Lat. etiam.

copulative, and, merely joining words or sentences, Lat. et, while τε answers to que, Hom., etc.: to combine more closely, τε . . , καὶ . . are used, ἄρκτοι τε καὶ λέοντες both bears and lions, etc.; often to add epithets after πολύς, πολλὰ καὶ ἐσθλά Il.; πολλὰ καὶ μεγάλα Dem., etc.:— θεοὶ καὶ Ζεύς all the gods, and above all Zeus, Aesch.; ἄλλοι τε καί . . , ἄλλως τε καί . . , v. ἄλλος, ἄλλως:—ὀλίγου τινὸς ἄξια καὶ οὐδενός worth little or nothing, Plat.
in questions, to introduce an objection, καὶ πῶς . . ; but how . . ? nay how can it be? Eur., etc.:—also = καίτοι, and yet, Ar.

after words implying sameness or likeness, καί must be rendered by as, like Lat. atque or ac after aeque, perinde, simul, γνώμῃσι ὁμοίῃσι καὶ σύ the same opinion as you, Hdt.; ἴσον or ἴσα καί. . , Soph., etc.: in attic, καί . . , καί . . answer to the Lat. cum, tum, not only, but also, Plat., etc.

influencing single words or clauses, also, even, Lat. etiam, ἔπειτά με καὶ λίποι αἰών then let life also forsake me, i. e. life as well as all other goods, Il.; καὶ αὐτοί they also, they likewise, Xen.; εἴπερ τις καὶ ἄλλος Plat., etc.
although, albeit, mostly with a part., καίπερ πολλὰ παθών Od.; often divided, καὶ οὐκ ἀγαθόν περ ἐόντα Il.; καὶ κρατερός περ ἐών Id.; in Trag., with ὅμως added, καίπερ οὐ στέργων ὅμως Id., etc.
epic, to make a transition, and so, Il.

of Place, in or at the right place, hence of parts of the body, ἐν καιρίῳ, κατὰ καίριον in a vital part, Il.; also, of wounds, πέπληγμαι καιρίαν πληγήν, καιρίας πληγῆς τυχεῖν Aesch.; πληγή is sometimes omitted, Hdt.:— adv. -ίως, mortally, Aesch.
of Time, in season, seasonable, timely, opportune, Hdt., Trag., etc.; τὰ καίρια timely circumstances, opportunities, Thuc.
lasting but for a season, Anth.
adv. -ρίως, in season, seasonably, Aesch.: comp. -ωτέρως Xen.:—so also, πρὸς τὸ καίριον Soph.

a fem. gen. pl. in Od. 7. 107, καιροσέων ὀθονέων ἀπολείβεται ἔλαιον from the close-woven linen trickles off the oil;—i. e. the linen is so well-woven, that oil does not ooze through. It seems to be for καιροεσσέων, epic gen. pl. of an adj. καιρόεις, from καῖρος.
the row of thrums in the loom, to which the threads of the warp are attached, Lat. licia.
due measure, proportion, fitness, Hes., etc.; καιροῦ πέρα beyond measure, unduly, Aesch., etc.; μείζων τοῦ καιροῦ, Lat. justo major, Xen.
of Place, a vital part of the body, like τὸ καίριον, Eur.

of Time, the right point of time, the proper time or season of action, the exact or critical time, Lat. opportunitas, καιρὸς βραχὺ μέτρον ἔχει "time and tide wait for no man," Pind.; καιρὸν παριέναι to let the time go by, Thuc.; καιροῦ τυχεῖν Eur.; καιρὸν λαμβάνειν Thuc.; ἔχειν καιρόν to be in season, Id.:— καιρός ἐστι, c. inf., it is time to do, Hdt., etc.

adverbial usages, εἰς or ἐς καιρόν in season, at the right time, opportune, Hdt., etc.; so, ἐπὶ καιροῦ Dem.;— κατὰ καιρόν Hdt.; πρὸς καιρόν Soph., etc.; and, without Preps., καιρῷ or καιρόν in season, attic;—all these being opp. to ἀπὸ καιροῦ, Plat.; παρὰ καιρόν Eur.; πρὸ καιροῦ prematurely, Aesch.
pl., ἐν τοῖς μεγίστοις κ. at the most critical times, Xen., etc.

advantage, profit, fruit, τινος of or from a thing, Pind.; τί καιρὸς καταλείβειν; what avails it to . . ? Eur.; οὗ κ. εἴη where it was convenient or advantageous, Thuc.; μετὰ μεγίστων καιρῶν with the greatest odds, the most critical results, Id.
to watch for the right time, Dem.:—also, to attend on, Luc.
καί τοι , and indeed, and further, Hom., Eur.
and yet, to mark an objection, καίτοι τί φημι; Aesch.; καίτοι τί φωνῶ; Soph.:—also, strengthd. καίτοι γε Ar.
to light, kindle, πυρὰ πολλά Il.; πῦρ κῆαι Od.; Mid., πῦρ κήαντο they lighted them a fire, Hom.:—Pass. to be lighted, to burn, Il., Hdt., etc.
to set on fire, burn up, burn, Hom.
to burn, scorch, of the sun, Hdt.:—also of extreme cold (as Virg. penetrabile frigus adurit), Xen.
Pass., of fever-heat, to be burnt or parched up, Thuc.: metaph. of passion, Pind., etc.
to burn and destroy (in war), τέμνειν καὶ κ., κ. καὶ πορθεῖν to waste with fire and sword, Xen.
of surgeons, to cauterise, τέμνειν καὶ κάειν to use knife and cautery, Plat., Xen.
bringing ill tidings, Aesch.
caused by ill tidings, Soph.

entry.etym: doric for κακηγόρους, acc. pl. of κακήγορος.

entry.sense: unmanliness, Soph., Eur.
extremely bad, Menand.
to speak ill of, abuse, slander, Plat.
evil-speaking, abuse, slander, Pind., Plat.:— κακηγορίας δίκη an action for defamation, Dem.; also κᾰκηγορίου, δίκη, ap. Dem.
evil-speaking, abusive, slanderous, Pind., Plat.
evil-speaking, Menand.
wickedness, vice, Eur., Ar., etc.
baseness of spirit, cowardice, sloth, Aesch., Eur.
badness in quality, opp. to ἀρετή (excellence), Theogn., Soph.:—pl. κακίαι defects, Luc.
cowardice, sloth, Thuc., Plat.
moral badness, wickedness, vice, Plat., Xen.
ill-repute, Thuc.
evil suffered, NTest.
to abuse, reproach, accuse, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
to make cowardly, Eur.:— Pass. to play the coward, Il., Eur.; κακίζεσθαι τύχῃ to be worsted by fortune alone, Thuc.
one must bring reproach on, τινά Eur.
cacare, Ar.
ordure, dung, Ar.
living ill or poorly, Hdt., Xen.
to be ill-advised, Eur.
ill-advised, Eur., Ar.
κᾰκό-γαμβρος γόος, distress for her wretched brother-in-law, Eur.
κᾰκο-γᾰμίου, δίκη, ἡ, an action for forming an unlawful marriage, Plut.
a bad neighbour or a neighbour to his misery, Soph.
ill-tongued, βοὴ κ. a cry of misery, Eur.
to be tormented by an evil genius, be like one possessed, Ar., Xen., etc.
to be unfortunate, Xen.
unhappiness, misfortune, Hdt., Xen., etc.
possession by a demon, raving madness, Ar., Xen.
possessed by an evil genius, ill-fated, ill-starred, miserable, Eur., Ar.:—adv. -μόνως, Luc.
as Subst. an evil genius, Ar.
to be in bad repute, Xen.
bad repute, infamy, Xen., Plat.
in ill repute: i. e.,
without fame, unknown, Theogn.
infamous, discreditable, Eur., Xen.
ill-clad, Od.
unhappy imitation, affectation, Luc.
badness of disposition, malignity, Plat., etc.
bad manners or habits, Xen.
a malicious deed, Plut.
ill-disposed, malicious, Ar., Dem.
as Subst., τὸ κακόηθες wickedness, an ill habit or itch for doing a thing, Plat.
of diseases, malignant:—adv. -θως, ap. Dem.
disorderliness, Hes.
evil-speaking, slanderous, Soph.
malevolence, Plut.
evil or unhappy Ilium, Od.
base love of gain, Theogn.
weak-legged, thin-legged, Theocr.
a bad judgment, Anth.
to speak ill of, to revile, abuse, Lys., NTest.
evil-speaking, reviling, Hdt., Xen., etc.
evil-speaking, Pind., attic
prophet of ill or evil, Aesch.
to behave ill in fight, Luc.
busied with evil, Aesch.
contriving ill, deceitful, Hhymn.
a practising of base arts, Luc.
mischief plotting, mischievous, baneful, Hom.
imitating ill; adv. -τως, Arist.
ill-fated, Anth.
ill-will, malignity, malice, Xen., Dem.
a bad system of laws and government, a bad constitution, Xen.
with bad laws, ill-governed, Hdt.
ill-disposed, disaffected, Ar., Thuc., etc.:— bearing malice against, τινι Xen.:—Sup. κακονούστατος Dem.
ill-married, of unhappy wedlock, Eur.
as Subst. an ill or unhappy bridegroom, Id.
unfortunate in guests, in irreg. epic comp. κακοξεινώτερος, Od.
unfriendly to strangers, inhospitable, Eur., Anth.
wise for evil, Thuc.
ill plight, distress, Thuc.
to suffer ill, to be in ill plight, be in distress, Thuc., Xen., etc.
suffering ill, in ill plight; adv. -θῶς, miserably, Arist.
unbecoming a maid, Anth.
having a mean father, low-born, Theogn.
exceeding filthy, loathsome, Sup. κακοπινέστατος Soph.
to do ill, play the knave, Ar.: to manage one's affairs ill, Xen.
trans. to do mischief to, maltreat, Id.
evil-doing, injury, Isocr.
ill-doing, mischievous, Pind.
unfit for toil, Arist.
ill-fated, ill-starred, Aesch., Eur.
with bad feet, Xen.
to fare ill, fail in an enterprise, to be in ill plight, Thuc.
misadventure, failure, Thuc.
contrivance of ill, mischievousness, Hom.
telling of ill, ill omened, Aesch.
to speak evil of, abuse, revile, Eur., Ar.
very filthy, Babr.
eating badly, i. e. having no appetite, fastidious, Plat.
with bad legs, Xen.
of a bad, mean body, Anth.
ill-smelling, Ar.
bad, Lat. malus:
of persons,
opp. to καλός, mean, ugly, Il.
opp. to ἀγαθός, ἐσθλός, ill-born, mean, ignoble, Hom., Soph.
craven, cowardly, base, Hom., Hdt., attic

bad of his kind, i. e. worthless, sorry, poor, κ. ἀλήτης a sorry beggar, Od.; κ. ἰατρός Aesch.; κ. ναύτης Eur.; πάντα κακός bad in all things, Od.; κακὸς γνώμην Soph.;— c. inf., κακὸς μανθάνειν bad at learning, Id.
in moral sense, bad, evil, wicked, Od., attic
of death, disease, etc., bad, evil, baneful, Hom., attic; of omens, bad, unlucky, attic; of words, evil, abusive, Soph.; κ. ποιμήν, i. e. the storm, Aesch.

κακόν, and κακά, τά, as Subst. evil, ill, Od., Hdt., etc.; δυοῖν ἀποκρίνας κακοῖν having chosen the least of two evils, Soph.:— κακόν τι ἔρδειν or ῥέζειν τινά to do evil or ill to any one, Il.; κακὸν (or κακὰ) ποιεῖν τινά attic; κακὰ κακῶν = τὰ κάκιστα, Soph.
kaka/, ta/, also evil words, reproaches, Hdt., Trag.
degrees of Comparison:
regul. comp. κακώτερος Od., Theocr.; but never in attic:—irreg. κακίων, ον, [ with ῐ], Hom., [with ῑ], attic
Sup. κάκιστος, Hom., etc.:—but χείρων, χείριστος, and ἥσσων, ἥκιστος, are also used as comp. and Sup.

adv. κακῶς, Lat. male, ill, Il., etc.:— κακῶς ποιεῖν τινα to treat one ill; κακῶς ποιεῖν τινά τι to do one any evil, attic; κακῶς πράσσειν to fare ill, Aesch.; κακῶς πάσχειν Id.; κακῶς γίγνεταί τινι Hdt.; κακῶς ἐκπέφευγα, Lat. vix demum effugi, Dem.:—comp. κάκιον, Hdt., attic: Sup. κάκιστα, Ar., etc.

in Compos., when added to words already signifying something bad, it increases this property, as in κακο-πινής: but added to words signifying something good, it implies too little of this property, as in κακό-δοξος. Once or twice it stands merely as an adj. agreeing with the Subst. with which it is compounded, as Κακοΐλιος for κακὴ Ἴλιος, κακόνυμφος for κακὸς νυμφίος.
faint-hearted, Aesch.
a bad sowing or crop, Anth.
with bad stomach, fastidious, Anth.
to speak evil of, abuse, τινά Soph.
evil-speaking, Eur.
ill-spread, i. e. rugged, Aesch.
ill put together, Luc.
using one's leisure ill, indolent, lazy, Anth.
act., κ. πνοαί winds that wear men out in idleness, Aesch.
to use base arts, act basely or meanly, deal fraudulently, Hdt., Dem.
bad art:
often in pl., forgeries, falsifications, Plat., Dem.
bad, base art, Luc.
using bad arts or evil practices, artful, wily, δόλος Il.:—irreg. comp. -τεχνέστερος, as from κακοτεχνής, Luc.
badness:
of character, baseness, weakness, cowardice, Hom., Thuc.
badness, wickedness, Il., Hdt., attic; κακότητι λειφθῆναι to have been absent by malice prepense, Hdt.
of condition, evil condition, distress, misery, Od., Hdt.
badness of habits, mischievousness, maliciousness, wickedness, Thuc.
to be unfortunate, Thuc.
unfortunate, Eur.
to do evil, work wickedness, deal basely, Eur., etc.; of a horse, to be vicious, Xen.
c. acc. pers. to do evil or mischief to one, to maltreat, Eur., Plat.:— to ravage a country, Thuc.: — to corrupt, falsify, τοὺς νόμους Dem.
an ill deed, fraud, Plat.
the character and conduct of a κακοῦργος, ill-doing, wickedness, villany, malice, Od., Thuc., etc.; of a horse, viciousness, Xen.
in pl. malpractices, Id.
malicious, Arist.
doing ill, mischievous, knavish, villanous, γαστὴρ κακοεργός importunate, Od.; κακοῦργοι κλῶπες Hdt.; ἀνήρ Soph.; κακουργότατος λόγος Dem.
as Subst. a malefactor, criminal, Thuc., etc.: esp. a thief, robber, Dem.
doing harm, hurtful, c. gen., κ. εἶναί τινος to hurt any one, Xen.
ill-treatment, ill-conduct, Plat.; χθονὸς κ. devastation of it, Aesch.
ill-sounding, ill-omened, Aesch.
bad in counsel, Il.
badness of counsel, folly, Hhymn.
to bear ill-will, Aesch.
ill-minded, malicious, malignant, Aesch., Eur.
imprudent, thoughtless, heedless, Soph., Eur.
of bad natural qualities, Plat.
rejoicing in men's ills, Hes.
difficult to live with, Theocr.
malignantly blaming, Theogn.
of persons, to treat ill, maltreat, afflict, distress, Hom., Aesch., etc.:—Pass. to suffer ill, be in ill plight, be distressed, Hom., etc.; κεκακωμένος ἁλμῇ befouled with brine, Od.
of things, to spoil, ruin, Hdt., Thuc.
to damage:—Pass., in moral sense, to become bad, behave badly, act basely, Eur.: of soldiers, to be mutinous, Xen.
Pass. also, to be reproached, Eur.
ill-treatment, τοῦ ἡγεμόνος Xen.: a distressing, harassing, τῶν πληρωμάτων of the crews, Thuc.
in attic law, κακώσεως δίκη an action for ill-usage or neglect of parents, Dem., etc.
damage, misfortune, Thuc.
a vase-shaped basket, Lat. calathus, Ar.
a cooling-vessel, cooler, Virgil
like the κάλαϊς, of changeful hue, of the cock, Anth.
a precious stone of a greenish blue (v. κᾰλάϊνος), the turquoise or chrysolite, Plin.
a kind of grasshopper, Theocr.
a reaper, mower, Theocr.
an angler, Anth.

the stalk or straw of corn: metaph., αἶψα φυλόπιδος πέλεται κόρος, ἧς τε πλείστην μὲν καλάμην χθονὶ χαλκὸς ἔχευεν, ἄμητος δ’ ὀλίγιστος men are soon satiated with battle, where the sword throws much straw on the ground, and there is little harvest, i. e. much slaughter and little profit, Il.; κ. πυρῶν wheat-straw, Hdt.

the stalk without the ear, stubble; metaph. of an old man, καλάμην γέ σ’ ὀΐομαι εἰσορόωντα γιγνώσκειν thou mayst still, I ween, perceive the stubble (i. e. the residue) of former strength, Od.; ἀπὸ τῆς καλάμης τεκμαίρεσθαι to judge from the remains, Luc.
a reaping, Anth.
devouring stalks, i.e. cutting them, Anth.
carrying reeds, Xen.
made of reed, Hdt.
made of cane, Id.
a bit of reed, used as a phial, Ar.
a reed fishing-rod, Anth.
of reed, Eur.
a reed, larger than the δόναξ, Lat. arundo, being used for thatching houses or even for making the walls, Hdt.; for making mats or crates, Id., Thuc.
anything made of reed or cane:
a reed-pipe, flute, Pind., Eur.
a fishing-rod, Theocr.
an arrow, Hor.
collectively, of plants, which are neither bush (ὕλη), nor tree (δένδρον), Xen.
a mat of reeds, Plat.
= καλάμη, the stalk of wheat, Xen.
covered with reed, Batr.
played on a reed, of tunes, Ar.
like reed, full of reeds, Anth.
a shoemaker's last, Plat.
a long garment, with fringe at bottom, Hdt.
the Καλασίριες were a branch of the military caste in Egypt, Id.
a shepherd's staff, which was thrown so as to drive back the cattle to the herd, Il., Anth.
to call, summon, Hom., etc.: Mid. to call to oneself, Id.
to call to a repast, to invite, Od.; κ. ἐπὶ δεῖπνον Hdt., Xen.; κληθέντες πρός τινα invited to his house, Dem.
to call on, invoke, τοὺς θεούς Hdt., attic; so in Mid., Aesch., etc.:—but ἀράς, ἅς σοι καλοῦμαι curses, which I call down on thee, Soph.:—in Pass., of the god, to be invoked, Aesch.
as law-term, of the judge, to cite or summon before the court, Ar., Dem.; πρὶν τὴν ἐμὴν [δίκην] καλεῖσθαι before it is called on, Ar.
of the plaintiff, in Mid., καλεῖσθαί τινα to sue at law, Lat. vocare in jus, Id., etc.

to call by name, to call, name, Il., Trag.:— ὄνομα καλεῖν τινά to call him a name (i. e. by name), Od.; so, without ὄνομα, τί νιν καλοῦσα τύχοιμ’ ἄν; Aesch.:—Pass., τύμβωι δ’ ὄνομα σῶι κεκλήσεται a name shall be given to thy tomb, Eur.

in perf. pass. κέκλημαι, to have received a name, to bear it, often = εἰμί, to be, οὕνεκα σὴ παράκοιτις κέκλημαι because I am thy wife, Il.; πόσις κεκλημένος εἴη were to be my spouse, Od.;—rarely in pres., ἐμὸς γαμβρὸς καλέεσθαι Id.
poet. Ἀλεισίου ἔνθα κολώνη κέκληται where is the hill called the hill of Aleisios, Il.
foll. by a dependent clause, καλεῖ με, πλαστὸς ὡς εἴην πατρί, i. e. καλεῖ με πλαστόν, calls me a supposititious son, Soph.
with fortunate days, Anth.
a crier, Lat. calator, Il.
a wooden dwelling, hut, barn, Hes.: a bird's nest, Theocr.
a hut, Anth.: a chapel, Plut.
Dep., to lie rolling about or wallowing, Lat. volutari, Hdt., Thuc.:— hence, to be constantly engaged in a thing, Lat. versari in aliqua re, Xen., etc.
a cock's comb: pl. κάλλαια, τά, the wattles, Lat. palea, Ar.
with beautiful eyelids, beautiful-eyed, Eur.
beautiful-sounding, Soph., Ar.
beautiful-clustering, Soph.
with fine, rich soil, Eur.
beautiful in calm, Eur.
happy in marriage, Anth.
bearer of a fair offspring, name of Demeter at the Thesmophoria, Ar.
with beautiful bridges, Eur.
with beautiful women, only in the obl. cases, Ἑλλάδα καλλιγύναικα Ἀχαιΐδα κ., Σπάρτην κ. Hom.
beautifully flowing, Eur.
with beautiful chariot, Eur.
with beautiful reeds, Eur.
Mid. to say in fine phrases, Thuc.: to use fine language, Arist.:—Pass., λόγοι κεκαλλιεπημένοι ῥήμασί τε καὶ ὀνόμασι decked out with verbs and nouns, Plat.
to have favourable signs in a sacrifice, to obtain good omens for an undertaking, Lat. litare, perlitare, Xen.; so in Mid., Hdt., etc.
c. acc. to sacrifice with good omens, Theocr.:—so in Mid., Ar.

of the offering, to give good omens, be favourable, καλλιρῆσαι οὐκ ἐδύνατο [τὰ ἱρά] the sacrifices would not give good omens, Hdt.; ὥς σφι ἐκαλλιρέετο [τὰ ἱρά] Id.; also c. inf., οὐκ ἐκαλλίρεε διαβαίνειν μιν the sacrifices were not favourable for his crossing, Id.:—in Mid., ὡς οὐδὲ ταῦτα ἐκαλλιερεῖτο Xen.
beautifully yoked, Eur.
with beautiful girdles, Hom.
with beautiful manes, of horses, Hom.; of sheep, with fine wool, Od.
to offer in auspicious sacrifice, κάπρον Anth.
with beautiful fruit, Aesch., Eur.
with beautiful horns, Anth.
fair-hill, a place near Troy, Il.
beautiful-haired, of women, Hom., Hes., Ar.
with beautiful headband, Od.
Mid. to use specious phrases, Luc.
beautifully shaped or formed, Eur.
beautiful, Od.
beautiful-flowing, Eur.
with glorious victory, κῦδος κ. the glory of noble victory, Pind.: c. gen., τῶν ἐχθρῶν κ. triumphant over one's enemies, Eur.
adorning or ennobling victory, ὕμνος, ᾠδή, μοῦσα Pind., Eur.:— τὸ καλλίνικον the glory of victory, Pind.; so, καλλίνικος (sub. ὕμνος) Id.
neut. of καλλίων, used as adv., v. καλός C.
Calliope, the beautiful-voiced, chief of the nine Muses, the epic Muse, Hes., Hhymn.: also Καλλιόπεια, Anth.
with beautiful children, blessed with fair children, Aesch., Eur.
a beautiful child, Eur.; v. καλλι- 2.
beautiful-cheeked, Hom.
with beautiful nymphs, Eur.; δέρη κ. necks of beauteous maidens, Id.
the first part in compds., where the notion of beautiful is added to the simple notion: καλο- is later and less common.
sometimes like a mere adj. with its Subst., as καλλίπαις = καλὴ παῖς.
with beautiful sandals, Hhymn.
with beautiful robe, Pind., Eur.
with beautiful leaves, Anth.
gen. εως, with beautiful elbow, Eur.
with beautiful locks, Hom., Eur.
adorned with riches, Pind.
fair-city, Plat.
of beautiful rivers, Eur.
with beautiful prow, Eur.:— metaph. with beautiful face, beautiful, Aesch.
with beautiful gates, Anth.
with beautiful towers, Eur.; κ. σοφία high-towering, Ar.
with beautiful steeds, Pind.
beautiful-flowing, Od., Eur.
elegance of language, Luc.
braggart language, Id.

beautiful flowing, Hom., Aesch.:—metaph. of the flute, Pind.— Fem. Καλλιρόη, one of the Oceanids, Hhymn., Hes.:— but Καλλιρρόη, also, a spring at Athens, later Ἐννεάκρουνος (but now again Καλλιρρόη), Thuc.
with a fine race-course, Eur.
the prize of beauty, Eur.
in pl. = ἀριστεῖα, the meed of valour, Soph.
exceeding beauty, Eur.
the first-fruits of beauty or the most beautiful, Id.
to be the most beautiful, Hdt., Eur.; c. gen., καλλιστεύσει πασέων τῶν γυναικῶν Hdt.:—also in Mid., δῶρ’ ἃ καλλιστεύεται Eur.
beautiful-crowned, Hhymn., Eur.

entry.etym: Sup. of καλός: v. καλός B.

entry.sense: most-beautiful, daughter of Lycaon, Eur.
beautiful-ankled, Hom.
with fair children, Plut., Luc.
beauty of workmanship, Plut.
with beautiful bow, Eur.
beautiful-shining, Eur.
beautiful-sounding, Eur.
auspiciously burning, Eur.
beauty of sound, Luc.
with a fine voice, Plat.

entry.etym: I, epic for καλλίχωρος, II from χόρος
entry.sense: with beautiful places, as εὐρύχορος for εὐρύχωρος, epith. of large cities, Od., Pind.
of or for beautiful dances, Eur., Ar.:— ὁ κ. a spring near Eleusis, the fount of goodly dances, Hhymn., Eur.
beautiful in the dance, of Apollo, Eur.

entry.etym: comp. of καλός: v. καλός B.

entry.sense: beauty, Hdt., Eur.
beauty, Hom., etc.:— ἐς κάλλος with an eye to beauty, so as to set off her beauty, Eur.; but, εἰς κ. ζῆν for pleasure, Xen.
of persons, a beauty, Id., Luc.
in pl. also rich garments and stuffs, Aesch., Plat.; κάλλεα κηροῦ beautiful works of wax, i. e. honeycombs, Anth.
an implement for cleaning, broom, Plut.
to beautify: metaph. to gloss over, Soph.
Mid. to pride oneself in a thing, Plat.
properly, to make the face beautiful; hence, to beautify, embellish, Plat.:—Pass., κεκαλλωπισμέναι τὸ χρῶμα, i. e. painted, Xen.
Mid. to adorn oneself, make oneself fine or smart, Plat.: metaph. to pride oneself in or on a thing, τινι or ἐπί τινι Id.:—absol. to make a display, shew off, of a horse, Xen.
to be coy, play the prude, τινι or πρός τινα towards another, Plat.; c. inf., κ. παραιτεῖσθαι to affect to deprecate, Plut.
ornament, embellishment, Plat.
an adorning oneself, making a display, Plat., Xen.
ornamentation, εἰς κ. for ornament, Xen.; καλλωπισμοὶ περὶ τὸ σῶμα Plat.
a teacher of virtue, NTest.
the character and conduct of a καλὸς κἀγαθός, nobleness, goodness, Xen., Dem.
beseeming a καλὸς κἀγαθός, honourable:—adv. -κῶς, Plut.
inclined to καλοκἀγαθία, Id.

entry.etym: in good writers written divisim καλὸς κἀγαθός,
entry.sense: beautiful and good, noble and good, used in earlier times of the nobles or gentlemen, Lat. optimates, Hdt., attic; later, καλὸς κἀγαθός was a perfect man, a man as he should be, also applied to qualities and actions, Plat., Xen.; to an army, Xen., etc.
wood, but only used in pl. κᾶλα, logs for burning (prob. from καίω), Hhymn.: seasoned wood, for joiner's work, καμπύλα κ. Hes.
wooden shoes, used to keep a cow still while milking, Theocr.
to do good, NTest.
beautiful, beauteous, fair, Lat. pulcher, of outward form, Hom., etc.; καλὸς δέμας beautiful of form, Od.; so, εἶδος κάλλιστος Xen.; καλὸς τὸ σῶμα Id.; c. inf., κ. εἰσοράασθαι Hom.
τὸ καλόν, like κάλλος, beauty, Eur., etc.: τὰ καλά the decencies, proprieties, elegancies of life, Hdt., etc.

in reference to use, beautiful, fair, good, κ. λιμήν Od.; καλὸς εἴς τι Xen.; πρός τι Plat.; c. inf., κάλλιστος τρέχειν Xen.;—esp. in the foll. phrases, ἐν καλῷ [τόπῳ] in a good place, Thuc.; ἐν καλῷ τοῦ κόλπου, τῆς πόλεως Xen.; ἐν κ. (sub. χρόνῳ), in good time, in season, Eur.:—so, καλόν ἐστι, c. inf., Soph.
of sacrifices, good, auspicious, Aesch., etc.
in moral sense, beautiful, noble, καλόν [ἐστι] c. inf., Hom., etc.; καλὰ ἔργματα noble deeds, Pind., etc.
τὸ καλόν moral beauty, virtue, opp. to τὸ αἰσχρόν (Cicero's honestum and turpe), Xen., Plat.
in attic not seldom ironically, like Lat. praeclarus, admirable, specious, fair, κ. γὰρ οὑμὸς βίοτος, ὥστε θαυμάσαι Soph.; μετ’ ὀνομάτων καλῶν Thuc.
Degrees of comp.: comp. καλλίων (short ι) ον, Sup. κάλλιστος, η, ον, Hom., etc.
adv.:— καλόν as adv., καλὸν ἀείδειν, etc., Hom.; so καλά Il.; τὸ καλόν Theocr.
regul. adv. καλῶς, mostly in moral sense, well, rightly, Od.; καλῶς ζῆν, τεθνηκέναι, etc., Soph., etc.; οὐ καλῶς ταρβεῖς Id.; often in phrase καλῶς καὶ εὖ, καλῶς τε καὶ εὖ Plat.
of good fortune, well, happily, κ. πράσσειν = εὖ πρ. to fare well, Aesch., etc.; κ. ἔχειν to be well, Id.; κ. ἔχει, c. inf., 'tis well to . . , Xen.
καλῶς = πάνυ, right well, κ. ἔξοιδα Soph.; so in comp., κάλλιον εἰδέναι Plat.; and in Sup. κάλλιστα, Soph., etc.
κ. ποιῶν, as adv., rightly, deservedly, Lat. merito, κ. ποιῶν ἀπόλλυται Ar.

in answers, to approve the words of the former speaker, well said! Lat. euge, Eur., Dem.:—but, also, to decline an offer courteously or ironically, thank you! Lat. benigne, Ar.; and in Sup., κάλλιστ’, ἐπαινῶ Id.
ironically, finely, Lat. belle, Soph., Eur.
Quantity: ᾱ in epic Poets: ᾰ in attic: in later Poets ᾰ or ᾱ, as the verse requires.
a vessel for drawing water, a pitcher or ewer, Od., attic:— an urn for drawing lots or collecting votes, Anth., Luc.: — a cinerary urn, Anth.
Sicil. form of Lat. calceus, a shoe, Plut.
a hut, cabin, cell, Lat. tugurium, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
a cover, screen, Anth.
crowned with flower-buds, Anth.
like a budding flower in face, i. e. blushing, roseate, Hhymn.
a head-covering used by women, a hood or veil, Il.; worn by brides, Aesch.; a covering put over the face of the dead, Soph.
a grave, Anth.
a covering, used only of flowers and fruit:
the shell or pod of plants, Hdt.; κάλυκος ἐν λοχεύμασι, i. e. when the fruit is setting, Aesch.
the calyx of a flower, a bud, a rose-bud, Hhymn., Theocr.
in Il. 18. 401, κάλυκες seem to be earrings like flower-cups.
a veil, Anth.
put round so as to cover, enfolding, enveloping, Soph.
a woman's veil, Hom., Aesch.:—metaph., δνοφερὰ κ. the dark veil of night, Aesch.
of land given to queens as veil-money (cf. ζώνη I. 2), Plat.
the cover or lid of a quiver, Hdt.

entry.etym: lengthd. from Root ΚΑΛΥΒ, v. καλύβη
entry.sense: to cover with a thing, παρδαλέηι μετάφρενον κάλυψεν Il.; νυκτὶ καλύψας Id.: simply, to cover, μέλαν δέ ἑ κῦμα κάλυψεν Id.; πέτρον χεὶρ ἐκάλυψεν his hand covered, grasped a stone, Id.; of death, τέλος θανάτοιο κάλυψεν ὀφθαλμούς Id., etc.; of grief, τὸν δ’ ἄχεος νεφέλη ἐκάλυψε Id.; κ. χθονὶ γυῖα, i. e. to be buried, Pind.; also, χθονί, τάφωι κ. to bury another, Aesch.:—Mid. to cover or veil oneself, Hom.:—Pass., ἀσπίδι κεκαλυμμένος ὤμους Il.; ἐν χλαίνηι κεκαλ. Id., etc.
like κρύπτω, to cover or conceal; κ. καρδίαι τι Soph.; Pass., κεκαλυμμένοι ἵππωι concealed in the horse, Od.
to cover with dishonour, throw a cloud over, σὺ μὴ κάλυπτε Ἀθήνας Soph.
to put over as a covering, Lat. circumdare, οἱ πέπλοιο πτύγμ’ ἐκάλυψεν Il.; οἱ ἄσιν καθύπερθε καλύψω I will put mud over him, Id.; ἀμφὶ Μενοιτιάδηι σάκος εὐρὺ καλύψας Id.
properly, to make purple: metaph. to make dark and troublous like a stormy sea, to ponder deeply, Soph., Eur.
Calchas the Greek seer at Troy, properly the searcher.
the murex or purple limpet.
a small cord, Ar., Thuc.

a reefing rope, reef, Od., where the κάλοι are distinguished from πόδες (sheets) and ὑπέραι (braces); κάλως ἐξῑέναι to let out the reefs, i. e. to set all sail, Eur.; metaph., ἐχθροὶ γὰρ ἐξίασι πάντα δὴ κάλων are letting out every reef, i. e. using every effort, Id.; φόνιον ἐξίει κάλων give a loose to slaughter, Id.; so, πάντα ἐξιέναι κάλων Ar.
generally, a rope, line, κάλων κατιέναι to let down a sounding-line, Hdt.
a cable, Id.; πρυμνήτης κ. a stern cable, Eur.; ἀπὸ κάλω παραπλεῖν to be towed along shore, Thuc.
a rope-maker, Plut.
made of reed or cane, Xen.
a vine-pole, vine-prop, Il., Hes.
the shaft of a spear, Aesch., Eur.
the tiller of the rudder, Luc.
Lat. camera, anything with an arched cover, a covered carriage, Hdt.
a kind of fish, Anth.
toilsome, troublesome, wearisome, Hhymn.:— tiring, exhausting, Luc.
pass. bowed down with toil, broken down, worn out, Hdt.
toil, trouble, labour, Od., Soph., Eur.
the effects of toil, distress, weariness, Hom.; ὕπνῳ καὶ καμάτῳ ἀρημένος (so Hor., ludo fatigatumque somno), Od.
that which is earned by toil, ἡμέτερος κάματος our hard-won earnings, Id.; ἀλλότριος κάματος the earnings of other men's toil, Hes.
the result of labour, a work, a thing wrought by the lathe, Anth.
toilsome, wearisome, Hes., Pind.
a camel, Hdt., etc.; κ. ἀμνός a camel-lamb, i. e. young camel, Ar.
ἡ κ. (like ἡ ἵππος) the camels in an army, as one might say the camelry, camel-brigade, Hdt.
αὐλὸς κ. the pipe of a smith's bellows, Anth.
to heat in a furnace, Arist.
an oven, furnace, kiln, for baking, smelting metals, for burning bricks, Hdt.
a furnace-woman, Od.
the reward of endurance, Il.
subject to destiny, i. e. ill-fated, Od.
trans. to work of smith's work, σκῆπτρον, τὸ μὲν Ἥφαιστος κάμε which he wrought, Il.; κ. νῆας Od.
Mid. to win by toil, τὰς (sc. γυναῖκας) αὐτοὶ καμόμεσθα Il.
to work or till by labour, Od.

intr. to work, labour, Thuc.:—then, to be weary, ἀνδρὶ δὲ κεκμηῶτι μένος οἶνος ἀέξει Il.; οὐδέ τι γυῖα κάμνει nor is he weary in limb, Id.; περὶ δ’ ἔγχεϊ χεῖρα καμεῖται he will have his hand weary in grasping the spear, Id.:—c. part., κάμνει πολεμίζων, ἐλαύνων is weary of fighting, rowing, Id.; οὐκ ἔκαμον τανύων I found no trouble in stringing the bow, i. e. did it without trouble, Od.; οὔτοι καμοῦμαι λέγουσα I shall never be tired of saying, Aesch., etc.
to be sick or ill, suffer under illness, οἱ κάμνοντες the sick, Hdt., etc.; so, κάμνειν νόσον Eur.; κ. τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς Hdt.
generally, to suffer, be distressed or afflicted, στρατοῦ καμόντος Aesch.; οὐ καμεῖ will not have to complain, Soph.; οὐκ ἴσον καμὼν ἐμοὶ λύπης not having borne an equal share of grief with me, Id.
οἱ καμόντες (aor. part.) those who have done their work, Lat. defuncti, i. e. the dead, Hom.; so, κεκμηκότες Eur., Thuc.
a bending, winding, of a river, Hdt.
the turning in a race-course, turning-post, Ar.: metaph., μῦθον ἐς καμπὴν ἄγειν to bring a speech to its middle or turning point, Eur.; καμπὰς ποιεῖσθαι Plat.
bent, turning, Eur.
a bend, an angle, Xen.
the turning-point in the δίαυλος, the goal, Arist.: metaph., κ. πύματος life's last turn or course, Anth.

entry.etym: lengthd. from Root ΚΑΜΠ, v. καμπή
entry.sense: to bend, curve, ὄφρα ἰτὺν κάμψηι that he may bend it into a chariot-rail, Il.; γόνυ κ. to bend the knee so as to sit down and rest, Id.; οὐ κάμπτων γόνυ, i. e. never resting, Aesch.; so, κ. κῶλα Soph.; then, κάμπτειν alone, to sit down, rest, Id.;—also, γόνυ κ. to bend the knee in worship, NTest.

to turn or guide a horse or chariot round the turning-post (καμπή II); hence, of the horse or chariot, κάμψαι διαύλου θάτερον κῶλον πάλιν to double the post (καμπτήρ) and return along the second half of the δίαυλος, Aesch.; κάμπτοντος ἵππου as the horse was turning, Soph.:—metaph., κ. βίον to make the last turn in the course of life, Id.; κ. βίου τέλος Eur.
so also of seamen, to double a headland, ἄκρην κ. Hdt.; also, κ. περὶ ἄκραν Ar.; κ. κόλπον to wind round the bay, Hdt.
absol., πάλιν κ. to turn back, Eur.; ἐγγὺς τῶν ἐμῶν κάμπτεις φρενῶν thou comest near my meaning, Id.
metaph., like Lat. flectere, κάμπτειν τινά to bend or bow one down, Pind.:—Pass. to be bowed down, Aesch., Thuc.; κάμπτομαι I submit, Plat.
bent, crooked, curved, of a bow, Il.; of wheels, Id.; of chariots, Id.
bending the foot, i. e. swift-running, Aesch.
of or for a block-figure, σῶμα κ. a body so lean as to be a mere skeleton, Anth.
a wooden block round which artists moulded wax or clay, a block-figure.
a cane or wicker carriage, Xen.
a dish, epic, Hom.
to ring, clash, clang, of metal, Od.
with a sharp loud noise, of water, Hes.

a sharp sound: the ring or clang of metal, Il., Soph.; kanax6h d' 25hn 3hmi4onoi7in loud rang their tramp, Od.; ὀδόντων καναχή a gnashing of teeth, Il.; καναχὰ αὐλῶν the sound of flutes, Pind. (For Verb κανάσσω v. ἐγ-κανάσσω.）
of water, plashing, Aesch.
to ring, Hom.
a Median cloak with sleeves, Xen.
a basket of reed or cane, a bread-basket, Lat. canistrum, Hom., Hdt., attic; also made of metal, Hom.: —it was used for the sacred barley at sacrifices, ἔχεν οὐλὰς ἐν κανέῳ Od.
a mat of reeds such as the Athen. women took with them when they went out, Lex Solonis ap. Plut.
to carry the sacred basket in procession, Ar.
the office of κανηφόρος, Plat.
carrying a basket:— Κανηφόροι, αἱ, Basket-bearers, at Athens, maidens who carried on their heads baskets containing the sacred things used at the feasts of Demeter, Bacchus and Athena, Ar.
Lat. cantharus, a beetle worshipped in Egypt, Aesch., etc.
a Naxian boat, Ar.
a mark or knot like a beetle, on the tongue of the Egyptian god Apis, Hdt.
Lat. clitellae, a pack-saddle, or the panniers at the sides of a pack-saddle, Ar.
a large sort of ass for carrying burdens, a pack-ass, Xen., Plat., etc.
a pack-ass, Ar., Anth.
hempen, of hemp, like it, Anth.
hemp, Hdt., etc.;—it was burnt, so as to medicate vapour-baths, Id.
a reed, Lat. canna: in pl. a reed-fence, railing, Ar.
for κὰν (i. e. κατὰ) νόμον.
to measure by rule, Longin.: to regulate, square, Arist., Anth.
a ruler, Anth.
crasis for καὶ ἄν or καὶ ἐάν

for καὶ ἄν, Hes., attic; κακὸν δὲ κἂν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ γνοίης μιᾷ Soph.:—later, κἄν came to be used, even when the Verb in apodosi was of a tense that could not be joined with ἄν, as, κἂν εἰ πολλαὶ [αἱ ἀρεταί] εἰσιν, for ὦσι, Plat.
for καὶ ἄν or καὶ ἐάν, and if, even if, although, Soph., Ar., etc.
Canopus, a town in lower Egypt, Hdt., etc.; famed for its temple of Serapis, who was called Κανωβίτης, Anth.:—the Westernmost mouth of the Nile was called the Κανωβικὸν στόμα, Hdt.
any straight rod or bar:
in Hom. the κανόνες of a shield seem to have been two rods running across the hollow of the shield, through which the arm was passed.
a rod used in weaving, the shuttle or quill, by which the threads of the woof (πηνίον) were passed between those of the warp (μίτος), Il.
a rule used by masons or carpenters, Eur., Xen., etc.
a ruler, Anth.
metaph., ἀκτὶς ἡλίου, κανὼν σαφής, Milton's "long-levelled rule of light, " Eur.
the beam or tongue of the balance, Anth.
in pl. the keys or stops of the flute, Id.
metaph., like Lat. regula, norma, a rule, standard of excellence, Eur.;—in Chronology, κανόνες χρονικοί were chief epochs or eras, Plut.
a ditch, trench, Il.:— a hole, grave, Id., Soph.
retail trade, tavern-keeping, Plat.
the shop of a κάπηλος, esp. a tavern, Lat. caupona, Ar.
to be a retail-dealer, Hdt.; δι’ ἀψύχου βορᾶς σίτοις καπήλευ’ drive a trade, chaffer with your vegetable food, Eur.

c. acc. to sell by retail, Hdt.:—metaph., καπηλεύειν μάχην to make a trade of war, Lat. cauponari bellum, Aesch.; καπηλεύουσα τὸν βίον playing tricks with life, corrupting it, Anth.; κ. τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ NTest.
of or for a retail dealer: —ἡ καπηλική (sc. τέχνη) = καπηλεία, Plat.
like a petty trader, knavish, Anth.:—adv., καπηλικῶς ἔχειν to be vamped up for sale, Ar.
Lat. copa, Ar.

a retail-dealer, huckster, hawker, peddlar, higgler, Lat. institor, Hdt., attic; opp. to the merchant (ἔμπορος), Xen., etc.; applied to Darius because of his finance-regulations, Hdt.:— κ. ἀσπίδων, ὅπλων a dealer in . . , Ar.
a tavern-keeper, publican, Lat. caupo, Id., etc.
metaph., κ. πονηρίας a dealer in petty roguery, Dem.
a crib for the food of cattle, manger, Hom.
a measure containing two χοίνικες, Xen.
to make smoke, i. e. to make a fire, Il.
to smoke, blacken with smoke, Dem.
intr. to be black with smoke, Ar.
incense, Anth.
properly, a smoke-receiver, i. e. a hole in the roof for the smoke to pass through, Hdt.
Pass. to be turned into smoke, burnt to ashes, Pind., Eur.
smoke, Hom., etc.; proverb., καπνοῦ σκιά shadow of smoke, of things worth nothing, Soph.; περὶ καπνοῦ στενολεσχεῖν to quibble about smoke, Ar.; γραμμάτων καπνοί learned trifles, Eur.
the Cappadocians, notorious as knaves and cowards, Hdt.
to favour the Cappadocians,Hdt.:—Pass. to play the Cappadocian, Anth.

Κ, κ, κάππα, τό, indecl., tenth letter in Gr. alphabet: as numeral κʹ = 20, but ͵κ = 20,000:— κ is the tenuis guttural mute, related to the medial γ and the aspir. χ. Changes of κ in the Gr. dialects:
ionic κ replaces χ, as κιθών δέκομαι κύθρη for χιτών δέχομαι χύτρα:—it represents π, as κου κοτε κως, etc., for που ποτε πως, etc.; so, ἴσκε = ἔσπεν, ἵππος Lat. equus.
doric κ is interchanged with τ, as ὅκα ἄλλοκα τῆνος for ὅτε ἄλλοτε κεῖνος.
the caper-plant, or its fruit, the caper, Lat. capparis, Arist.
marked with a κάππα, Luc.
to catch, take fire, aor1 part. καππυρίσασα Theocr.
metaph. to be lewd or lecherous, Ar.
a wild boar, Il.; also, σῦς κάπριος Id.
as adj. κάπριος, ον, like a wild boar, Hdt.
the boar, wild boar, Lat. aper, Il., etc.; also, σῦς κάπρος Id.
killing wild boars, Anth.

entry.etym: lengthd. from Root ΚΑΠ, v. κάπη
entry.sense: to gulp down, Ar., etc.: cf. κεκαφηώς.
dried by the air, dry, Theocr.
act. drying, parching, Id.
metaph. of sound, καπυρὸν γελᾶν to laugh loud, Anth.; κ. στόμα a loud, clear-sounding voice, Theocr., Mosch.; κ. συρίζειν to play clearly on the syrinx, Luc.
with the face of a κάραβος, Luc.
the stag-beetle, Arist.
to watch with outstretched head, i. e. to watch eagerly or anxiously, Hdt., Eur., Xen.: —also, κ. εἴς τινα to look eagerly at one, Ar.
a hood, Lat. caracalla, Anth.
beheading, capital, Aesch.
a chief, Xen.
to achieve, Aesch.
the head, Il., etc.
the head or top of anything, as of a mountain, Hes.; the edge or brim of a cup, Soph.
in attic Poets, it is used like κεφαλή, periphr. for a person, Οἰδίπου κάρα, i. e. Οἰδίπους, Soph.; ὦ κασίγνητον κ., for ὦ κασίγνητε, Id., etc.
to cut off the head, behead, Eur.
beheaded, Eur.; κ. ἐρημία νεανίδων, i. e. their slaughter, Id.
cut off from the head, κ. χλιδαί one's shorn locks, Soph.
outlandish, foreign, Aesch.
shoes of undressed leather, brogues, Xen.
a kind of cress, Lat. nasturtium, or its seed, which was eaten like mustard by the Persians, Xen.; in pl. cresses, Ar.;—metaph., βλέπειν κάρδαμα, i. e. look sharp and stinging, Id.

the heart, ἐν στέρνοισι κραδίη πατάσσει Il.; κραδίη ἔξω στήθεος ἐκθρώσκει, of one panic-stricken, Id.; οἰδάνεται κραδίη χόλῳ Id., etc.; ἐκ τῆς καρδίας φιλεῖν Ar.; τἀπὸ καρδίας λέγειν, Lat. ex animo, to speak freely, Eur.
the stomach, Thuc.
knower of hearts, NTest.
gnawing the heart, Aesch.
to draw the heart out of the victim, Luc.
a kneading-trough, Ar.
with hair on the head, long-haired, of the Achaians, who let all their hair grow (whereas the Abantes, who wore theirs long only at the back of the head, were called ὄπιθεν κομόωντες) , Il.
the head, mostly in pl., ἀνδρῶν κάρηνα, periphr. for ἄνδρες, Il.; νεκύων κ., for νέκυες, Od.; βοῶν κ., as we say, so many head of cattle, Il.
metaph. of mountain- peaks, Οὐλύμποιο κ. Id.; and of towns, a citadel, Id.
Carian, Soph.; Κ. αὐλήματα dirges, Ar.
a Carian woman, Phan. ap. Plut.
a shrimp or prawn, Ar.
to quake under the feet of men and horses, Lat. tremere, Il. (Formed from the sound.)
a crab, Lat. cancer, Batr., Ar., Plat.:—proverb., οὔποτε ποιήσεις τὸν καρκίνον ὀρθὰ βαδίζειν Ar.
a pair of tongs, Anth.: καρκίνα compasses, Id.
with crab's claws for hands, Luc.
a festival held in honour of Apollo Κάρνειος by the Spartans, during nine days of the attic month Metageitnion, called by them Καρνεῖος μήν, Eur., Thuc.
Carpathus, an island between Crete and Rhodes, Hom.
a mimic dance of the Thessalians, Xen.
swift, Lat. rapidus, Il.: adv. -μως, swiftly, rapidly, Id.
in Pind., γένυες κ. eager jaws.

a Carian, Il., etc.; fem. Κάειρα, Id.:—the Carians hired themselves out as mercenaries, and were used to spare the lives of the citizen-soldiers; hence, ἐν τῷ Καρὶ κινδυνεύειν to make the risk, not with one's own person, but with a Carian, Lat. experimentum facere in corpore vili, Eur.
hair cut off, a lock of hair, (cf. κείρω, ἀ-καρής), τίω δέ μιν ἐν κᾰρὸς αἴσῃ I value him but at a hair's worth, flocci eum facio, Il.
also = κάρα, κάρη, head, ἐπὶ κάρ head- long, Id.
to make fruitful, fertilise, Eur.

fruit-bearing, fruitful, Aesch., Eur., etc.:— κάρπιμα, τά, fruit-trees or corn-fields, Ar.; κάρπιμα ἀγαθά property that yields a produce, opp. to ἄκαρπα, Arist.:—metaph., τῶν ξένων τοὺς κ. rich foreigners from whom money can be wrung, Ar.
fruit-producing, Anth.
fruit, καρπὸς ἀρούρης, i. e. corn, Il.; so, κ. Δήμητρος Hdt., etc.; of trees, Od., etc.
generally, produce, returns, profits, Hdt., etc.; οἱ καρποὶ ἐκ τῶν ἀγελῶν the produce of the herds, Xen.

of actions, fruit, result, profit, εἰ καρπὸς ἔσται θεσφάτοισι if his oracles shall bear fruit, i. e. be fulfilled, Aesch.; γλώσσης ματαίας κ., i. e. curses, Id.; κ. ἐπέων οὐ κατέφθινε, i. e. poesy, Pind.; κ. φρενῶν wisdom, Id.
the wrist, Hom., etc.
bearing fruit, Anth.
living on fruit, Arist.
spoiling fruit, Anth.
to bear fruit, Xen.
fruit-bearing, fruitful, of trees, Hdt., Xen.; of lands, Pind., Eur.; of Demeter, Ar.
watcher of fruit, Anth.
to bear fruit or bear as fruit, Aesch.
Mid. to get fruit for oneself, i. e.,
to reap crops from land, Hdt., Aesch.: metaph. to exhaust or drain, τὴν Ἑλλάδα Ar.
to enjoy the interest of money, Dem.; so in perf. pass., τὸ ἐργαστήριον κεκαρπωμένος enjoying the profits of the shop, Id.:—absol. to make profit, Ar.
to reap the fruits of, enjoy the free use of, Thuc., etc.: —then,
simply, to enjoy, Soph., Eur., etc.:— sometimes in bad sense, καρποῦσθαι τὴν ἁμαρτίαν Aesch.; πένθη Eur.
use or profit, Xen.
very, very, much, extremely, Lat. valde, admodum.
beyond measure, in good earnest, κ. ἐγχώριος a thorough native, Aesch.; κ. ὢν ἐπώνυμος true to thy name, Id.; κ. δ’ εἰμὶ τοῦ πατρός all on my father's side, Id.
καὶ κάρτα, used to increase the force of a previous statement, really and truly, most certainly, Hdt., Soph.; so, τὸ κάρτα, with iron. sense, in good sooth, with a vengeance, Hdt.

to be steadfast, patient, staunch, Soph., etc.; with a prep., κ. πρός τι to hold up against a thing, Xen., etc.:—with a part. to persevere in doing, Eur.: absol., τὰ δείν’ ἐκαρτέρουν was strangely obdurate or obstinate, Soph.
c. acc. rei, to bear patiently, Eur., Xen.:—Pass., κεκαρτέρηται τἀμά my time for patience is over, Eur.
an act of patience, Plat.
a bearing patiently, patience, Plat.
c. gen. patient endurance of a thing, Id.
patient endurance, patience, opp. to μαλακία, Xen., Plat.
capable of endurance, patient, Xen., Arist.
stout-hearted, Hom., Hes.: generally, strong, mighty, ἄνεμοι Hes.
strong, staunch, stout, sturdy; c. inf., καρτερὸς ἐναίρειν strong to kill, Il.; τὰ καρτερώτατα the strongest, Soph.
c. gen. possessed of a thing, lord or master of it, Theogn., Theocr.
like καρτερικός, steadfast, patient, πρὸς πάντα Xen.: obstinate, Plat.

of things, strong, mighty, potent, ὅρκος Il.; κ. ἔργα deeds of might, Id.; κ. μάχη strongly contested, desperate, Hdt., Thuc.; —τὸ καρτερόν, τόλμης τὸ κ. the extremity of daring, Eur.:— κατὰ τὸ καρτερόν by force, Hdt., Ar., etc.; so, πρὸς τὸ καρτερόν Aesch.; τὸ καρτερόν, absol., Theocr.
of place, like ὀχυρός, strong, Thuc.; τὸ καρτερώτερον τοῦ χωρίου Id.
adv. -ρῶς, strongly, etc., κ. ὑπνοῦσθαι to sleep soundly, Hdt.
the common comp. and Sup. are κρείσσων and κράτιστος (qq. v.): but the regular forms καρτερώτερος, -ώτατος, occur now and then, Pind., attic
strongly, stoutly, Plat.
strong-handed, Hhymn.
strength, vigour, courage, Hom., Hes.
a place in Laconia with a famous temple of Artemis, Thuc.:—hence,
Καρυᾶτις, ἡ, a name of Artemis
to dance the Caryatic dance, Luc.
a Persian dish, composed of blood and rich spices, Luc.
dark-red, Xen.
to make a καρύκη or rich sauce, Ar.
one who sails in a nut-shell, Luc.
any kind of nut, Ar., Xen.; distinguished into various kinds, as κ. βασιλικά or Περσικά, walnuts, also called simply κάρυα, Batr.; κ. κασταναϊκά or κασταναῖα chestnuts, etc.
dry, parched, Od.:—of sound, καρφαλέον ἀσπὶς ἄϋσε the shield rang dry, i. e. hollow, Il.
dry grass, hay, Xen.
of dry straw, Eur.
built of dry straws, Anth.
a dry stalk, Lat. palea, stipula, a chip of wood, Ar.: in pl. the dry sticks of cinnamon, Hdt.; dry twigs, chips, straws, bits of wool, such as birds make nests of, Ar.
to dry up, wither, κάρψω χρόα καλόν I will wither the fair skin, wrinkle it, Od.; ἠέλιος χρόα κάρφει Hes.
rough, δίψῃ καρχαλέοι rough in the throat with thirst, Virgil's siti asper, Il.
with sharp, jagged teeth, of dogs, Il.; applied to Cleon by Ar.
sharp-pointed, jagged, with sharp or jagged teeth, κάρχαρον μειδήσας, of the wolf, Babr.: —metaph. sharp, biting, of language, Luc.
to side with the Carthaginians, Plut.
Carthage, Hdt.:—adj. Καρχηδόνιος, α, ον, Carthaginian, Id.
a drinking-cup narrower in the middle than the top and bottom, Sapph., etc.
the mast-head of a ship, Pind., etc.; in pl., Eur.
to abuse in harlot fashion, Ar.
a courtesan, harlot, Ar.
a carpet or skin to sit upon, a saddle, Xen.
cassia, an Arabian spice like cinnamon, but of inferior quality, Hdt.
a sister, Hom., etc.
a brother, Hom., etc.:—in more general sense, a cousin, Il.
as adj., κασίγνητος, η, ον, brotherly, sisterly, Soph., Eur.
a brother, Aesch., Soph.:— a sister, Eur.
the Cassiterides or tin-islands, prob. the Scilly islands and Cornwall, Hdt.
tin, Lat. stannum, Il. It was melted, and then cast upon χαλκός, hence χεῦμα κασσιτέροιο a plating of tin, Id.
anything stitched, esp. the sole stitched under a shoe or sandal, a shoe-sole, Ar.; metaph., ὑποδύσασθαι ἐχθρῶν παρ’ ἀνδρῶν καττύματα to put on shoes made by an enemy, Id.

entry.etym: prob. for κατα-σύω, though σύω only occurs in Lat. suo
entry.sense: to stitch or sew together like a shoemaker, Plat.
metaph. to stitch up a plot, like Lat. dolos suere, Ar.
the famous spring of the Muses on Mt. Parnassus, Hdt., Soph., etc.
entry.etym: Prob. akin to καθαρός, Lat. castus.

entry.sense: of or for Castor;— τὸ Κ. μέλος, a martial song, set to the flute, used in celebrating victories in the chariot-race (Castor being the inventor of the ξυνωρίς), Pind., Plut.; ὁ Κ. ὕμνος Pind.
a Laconian breed of hounds, first reared by Castor, Anth.: also καστόριαι κύνες Xen.
Castor, son of Zeus (or Tyndareus) and Leda, brother of Pollux, Hom.
the beaver, Hdt.
going down or downstairs: cf. ἀναβάδην.
a descent, name of the steep descent from Nubia to Egypt, Aesch.

entry.note: fut. -βήσομαι perf. -βέβηκα aor2 κατέβην poet. 3rd pl. κατέβαν imperat. κατάβηθι or κατάβα epic 1st pl. subj. καταβείομεν Mid., epic 3rd sg. aor1 κατεβήσετο imperat. καταβήσεο
entry.sense: to step down, go or come down, Lat. descendere, ἐξ ὄρεος from the mountain, Il.; κ. πόλιος to go down from the city, Id.; κ. δίφρου to dismount from the chariot, Id.; c. acc. loci, θάλαμον κατεβήσετο she came down to her chamber, Od.:—but also c. acc., κατέβαιν’ ὑπερώϊα she came down from the upper floor, Id.; κλίμακα κατεβήσετο came down the ladder, Id.; absol. to come down stairs, Ar.; hence in Pass., ἵππος καταβαίνεται the horse is dismounted from, Xen.
to go down from the inland parts to the sea, esp. from central Asia (cf. ἀναβαίνω II. 3), Hdt.; κ. ἐς Πειραιᾶ, Plat.
to come to land, get safe ashore, Pind.
to go down into the arena, κ. ἐπ’ ἄεθλα Hdt.; and absol., like Lat. in certamen descendere, Soph., Xen.
of an orator, to come down from the tribune, κατάβα: —answer, καταβήσομαι Ar.
πόσσω κατέβα τοι ἀφ’ ἵστω; at what price did [the robe] come down from the loom? Theocr.

metaph., καταβαίνειν εἴς τι to come to a thing in the course of speaking, κατέβαινε ἐς λιτάς he ended with prayer, Hdt.; c. part., κατέβαινεν παραιτεόμενος ended in begging, Id.; κ. ἐπὶ τελευτήν Plat.
trans. to bring down, Pind.
Pass. to be full of Bacchic frenzy, καταβακχιοῦσθε δρυὸς κλάδοις in oak-wreath ye rave with Bacchic fury, Eur.
to throw down, overthrow, Hom., etc.; κ. εἰς τὸ μηδέν to bring down to nothing, Hdt.
to strike down with a weapon, to slay, Il., Hdt., etc.
to throw or bring into a certain state, Eur., Plat.
to cast down or away, cast off, reject, Xen.
in milder sense, to let fall, drop down, Hom.; κ. ἱστία to lower sail, Theogn.; τὰς ὀφρῦς κ. Eur.
to lay down, set down, Lat. deponere, Il., Ar.
to bring or carry down, esp. to the sea-coast, Hdt.
to pay down, yield or bring in, Id.:— to pay down, pay, Thuc., etc.:—Mid. to cause to be deposited, Dem.
to put in, render, μαρτυρίαν Id.
to throw down seed, sow, Id.; κ. φάτιν, Lat. spargere voces, Hdt.
to lay down as a foundation, mostly in Mid., Eur.:—Pass., καταβεβλημένος laid down, ordinary, Arist.
to dip down into, Luc.
to weigh down, overload, Luc.
a going down, way down, descent, Hdt., attic; cf. καταίβασις.
the descent from Central Asia, Xen.
one must descend, Ar., Plat.
one must attack, Ar.
to bark at, τινός Anth.
Dep. to affirm strongly, Plut.
Dep.
to constrain, Thuc.
Pass. to be forced, Plut.
Causal of καταβαίνω to make to go down, bring down, bring down, Hdt., Plut.
to bring down by force, Xen.
to be brought down, Plat.
to eat up, devour, Hdt., Plat.

entry.note: fut. ώσομαι aor2 κατεβίων later aor1 -εβίωσα
entry.sense: to bring life to an end, Plat.
to hurt greatly, damage, Hhymn., Plat.
to look down at, Plut.
fit for throwing off horseback, Xen.
Dep. to bleat loudly, Theocr.
to go down through a place, c. acc., Od.
to cry down, cry out against, c. gen., Hdt.; κ. τινῶν ὅτι τὰς σπονδὰς λελυκότες εἶεν Thuc.; c. acc. to bawl down, outcry, Ar.
an outcry against, c. gen., Thuc.
a crying out against, Plut.
a throwing or laying down, NTest.
metaph.,
a foundation, beginning, Pind., NTest.
a paying down, by instalments, Dem.
a periodical attack of illness, a fit, access, Plat.
to feed flocks upon or in a place, Lat. depascere, χὠ τὰν Σαμίαν καταβόσκων the shepherd of Samos, Theocr.
with flowing locks, Eur.
to give judgment against, c. acc., NTest.:—Pass. to have judgment given against one, Dem.
to wet through, drench:—metaph., μέλιτι καταβρέχειν Pind.
intr. to be heavily laden or weighed down by a thing, c. dat., Hes., Theocr.
trans. to weigh down, to outweigh, ὄλβῳ κ. βασιλῆας Theocr.
to gulp down, Ar.
to bite in pieces, eat up, Anth.
to cover quite with hides, Thuc.
proclamation, Luc.
to denounce, betray, Xen.
to declare, πόλεμον Lys.
denounced, betrayed, Thuc.
in or under the earth, underground, subterranean, Hdt., Xen., etc.
Comic name of a supposed town, with a play on the Sicil. Gela, Γέλα καὶ Καταγέλα Ar.
ridiculous, absurd, Hdt., Ar.: adv. -τως, Sup. -τότατα, Plat.
to laugh at, jeer or mock at, c. gen., Hdt., Ar., etc.; also c. dat., Hdt.:—absol. to laugh scornfully, Eur., Ar., etc.
c. acc. to laugh down, deride, Eur.: —Pass. to be derided, Aesch., Ar., etc.

mockery, derision, ridicule, Lat. ludibrium, ἐμαυτοῦ καταγέλωτα τάδε; these ornaments which bring ridicule upon me? Aesch.; κ. πλατύς sheer mockery, Ar.; ὁ κ. τῆς πράξεως the crowning absurdity of the matter, Plat.
to grow old, Lat. senescere, Od., Hdt.
to abide, dwell, ap. Dem.

to remark, discover, esp. something to one's prejudice, οὐκ ἐπιτήδεα κατά τινος κ. having formed unfavourable prejudices against one, Hdt.; καταγνοὺς τοῦ γέροντος τοὺς τρόπους having observed his foibles, Ar.
c. acc. criminis, to lay as a charge against a person, κακίαν, ἀδικίαν κ. τινός Plat.:—Pass., perf. part. κατεγνωσμένος condemned, NTest.
c. gen. criminis, παρανόμων κ. τινός Dem.

c. inf., κ. ἑαυτοῦ ἀδικεῖν to charge oneself with wrong-doing, Aeschin.; so, κ. ἑαυτοῦ μὴ περιέσεσθαι he passed sentence of non-survival against himself, Thuc.: Pass., καταγνωσθεὶς νεώτερα πρήσσειν being suspected of doing, Hdt.
c. acc. poenae, to give as judgment or sentence against a person, κ. τινὸς θάνατον to pass sentence of death on one, Lat. damnare aliquem mortis, Thuc.:—Pass., θάνατός τινος κατέγνωστο ap. Dem.
of a suit, to decide it against one, δίκην Ar.:—Pass. to be decided, Aesch.
to bring down, Od.
to glorify, Anth.
Pass. to be talked down, Ar.
wool drawn or spun out, worsted, Plat.: a flock of wool, Soph.
to bend down, Anth.
to comb away, lacerate, Hdt.

entry.note: inf. -ύναι καταγνύω fut. κατάξω aor1 κατέαξα part. κατάξας Pass., aor2 κατεάγην opt. κατᾱγείην perf. κατέᾱγα ionic κατέηγα
entry.sense: to break in pieces, shatter, shiver, crack, Hom., attic
to break up, weaken, enervate, Eur., Plat.

Pass. with perf. act. to be broken, δόρατα κατεηγότα Hdt.; κατεαγέναι or καταγῆναι τὴν κεφαλήν to have the head broken, Ar., etc.; c. gen., τῆς κεφαλῆς κατέαγε he has got a bit of his head broken, Id.
a thinking ill of, a low or contemptuous opinion of, c. gen., Thuc.
judgment given against one, condemnation, Id., Dem.; τοῦ θανάτου to death, Xen.
one must condemn, τινός Luc.
to enchant, bewitch: to cheat or blind by trickery, τινά Xen.
to buy up, φορτία Dem.
to denounce, τί τινι Ar., Thuc.; τι πρός τινα Xen.
embroidered, Luc.
to scratch away, lacerate, Hdt.
to engrave, inscribe, νόμους Plut.
to paint over, Luc.
to fill tablets with writing Eur.
to write down, register, record, Plat.
to exercise much, discipline, Luc.

entry.note: fut. ξω epic inf. -αξέμεν aor2 κατήγᾰγον perf. καταγήοχα
entry.sense: to lead down, Lat. deducere, Od., etc.; esp. into the nether world, Id.; εἰς Ἀΐδαο Id.
to bring down to the sea-coast, Il., Xen.
to bring down from the high seas to land, Od.; κατ. ναῦν to bring a ship into port, Hdt., attic: —Pass. to come to land, land, opp. to ἀνάγεσθαι, Od., Hdt., attic
κατάγεσθαι παρά τινι to turn in and lodge in a person's house, Lat. deversari apud aliquem, Dem.
to draw down or out, spin, Lat. deducere filum, Plat.
to reduce to a certain state, ἐς κίνδυνον κ. τὴν πόλιν Thuc.
κ. θρίαμβον, Lat. deducere triumphum, Plut.: to escort, like πομπεύω, Id.
κ. γένος to derive a pedigree, Id.
κατ. βοάν to lower the voice, Eur.
to bring back, Lat. reducere, Od.: to bring home, recall, Hdt., attic: generally, to restore, Hdt.:—Pass. to return, Plat., Xen.
a bringing down from the high sea: a landing, landing-place, Thuc.:—generally, a halting-place, inn, Lat. statio, Hdt., Plat.
a place to lodge in, an inn, hotel, Thuc., Xen., etc.
Dep. to struggle against, prevail against, conquer, Luc.: as Pass., καταγωνισθεὶς ὑπό τινος Id.
Dep. to devour, Theocr.
to bite in pieces, Batr., Theocr.
to bewail, τὴν τύχην Xen.: absol. to weep bitterly, Eur.
Mid. to subdue utterly, Thuc.
to squander, lavish, Xen.:— Pass., [τὰ χρήματα] καταδεδαπάνητό σφι Hdt.
to consume entirely, of an army, Xen.
to rend in pieces, devour, Hom.: metaph. in Mid., καταδάπτεται ἦτορ Od.
to fall asleep, in aor. to be asleep, sleep, Od.:—in pres. to be just falling asleep, Plat.; perf. καταδεδαρθηκώς having fallen asleep, Id.
simply to pass the night, κατέδαρθον ἐν ὅπλοις Thuc.
Mid. to divide among themselves, tear and devour, Il.
wanting or failing in, lacking a thing, c. gen., Hdt.: absol., needy, Dem.
comp. καταδεέστερος, weaker, inferior, Id., etc.
adv. -δεῶς, mostly in comp., καταδεεστέρως ἔχειν περί τι to be very ill off in a thing, Id.
impers. there is wanting, v. καταδέω2.
to fear greatly, τι Ar., Thuc.

entry.note: and -ύω fut. δείξω ionic aor1 κατέδεξα Pass., ionic 3rd sg. plup. κατεδέδεκτο
entry.sense: to discover and make known, Hdt., Plat., etc.; c. inf. to give notice that . . , Aeschin.:—Pass., c. part., κατεδέδεκτο ἐοῦσα χρηστή had been proved to be good, Hdt.
to invent and teach, introduce, exhibit, Ar., Plat.; c. inf. to shew how to do, Hdt., Ar.
to shew signs of fear, Xen.
Dep.:— to look down upon, Od., Soph.
a tie, band: a magic knot, Plat.
to wet through, Il., Hes.:—of a river, to water, πεδία Eur.
Dep.
to receive, admit, Plat., etc.
to receive back, take home again, Oratt.: —aor1 pass. καταδεχθῆναι in pass. sense, Luc.

to bind on or to, bind fast, Hom., Hdt.:—Pass., καταδεδεμένος τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς, having his eyes bound, Hdt.; ἐν φόβῳ καταδεθεῖσα Eur.; καταδεῖται ψυχὴ ὑπὸ τοῦ σώματος Plat.:—Mid. to bind to oneself, Eur.
to put in bonds, imprison, Hdt., Thuc., etc.; κ. τὴν ἐπὶ θανάτῳ (sc. δέσιν) to bind him for execution, Hdt.
to convict and condemn of a crime, κ. τινα φῶρα εἶναι Id.
to tie down, stop, check, ἀνέμων κατέδησε κελεύθους Od.; κατέδησε κέλευθα stopped my course, Id.
to want, lack, need, c. gen., esp. of numbers, καταδέει πεντεκαίδεκα σταδίων ὡς μὴ εἶναι πεντακοσίων it wants 15 stadia of being 500, Hdt.
Dep. καταδέομαι to intreat earnestly, Lat. deprecari, c. gen. pers., Plat.
quite manifest, plain, visible, Hdt., Thuc.; κατάδηλον ποιεῖν to make known, discover, Hdt., Soph.; κ. εἶναι to be discovered, Hdt., Plat.
to conquer by the arts of a demagogue:—Pass. to be so conquered, Plut.
to consume publicly, Il.
to decide as arbitrator against, give judgment against c. gen., Dem.: Pass. to be decided against one, Id.
to reconcile again, Ar.
to give away, intr. to open into, ἡ Προποντὶς καταδιδοῖ ἐς τὸν Ἑλλήσποντον Hdt.

entry.note: fut. άσω Pass., aor1 κατεδικάσθην perf. καταδεδίκασμαι
entry.sense: to give judgment against a person, pass sentence upon him, condemn him, opp. to ἀποδικάζω, c. gen. pers. et acc. rei, κ. τινὸς θάνατον to pass sentence of death upon him, Hdt.; c. inf., κ. τινὸς τὰ ἔσχατα παθεῖν to condemn him to suffer extreme penalties, Xen.:—Mid. to get sentence given against one, δίκην καταδικάζεσθαί τινος Thuc.:—Pass., καταδικασθείς condemned, Plat.; c. inf., καταδικάζεται ἀποθανεῖν Luc.; of the sentence, ἀντέλεγον μὴ δικαίως σφῶν καταδεδικάσθαι they contended that judgment had been given against them unjustly, Thuc.
to declare by express judgment, Xen.
judgment given against one: the damages awarded, Thuc.
to pursue closely, Thuc.

to suppose a thing to any one's prejudice, c. inf., κ. τινα ποιεῖν τι to suspect one of doing so and so, Hdt.; κ. σφέας εἶναι κλῶπας to suspect them of being thieves, Id.; also, οὐκ ἄν κοτε κατέδοξα ἔνθεν ἦν should never have guessed whose son he was, Id.
= katadoke/w, Xen.
to reduce to slavery, enslave, Hdt., Thuc.:—Pass., καταδεδούλωντο, κατεδουλώθησαν Hdt.
Mid. to make a slave to oneself, to enslave, Id., Xen.: so in perf. pass., Eur., Plat.
to enslave in mind:—Pass., Xen., Plat.
enslavement, subjugation, Thuc.
to fall with a heavy sound, Anth.
the Cataracts of the Nile, Hdt. (Commonly derived from καταδουπέω, as if downroars.)
to strip off from, τί τινος Hdt.
an inroad, raid, Thuc., etc.:—metaph. a vehement attack, invective, Aeschin.
overrun, wasted, Eur.
a tearing or rending, Eur.
to tear in pieces, rend, Anth.:— Mid., Hes.
to exercise power over, Xen.
a going down into, descent, Luc.
to put to the blush by earnest intreaty, Luc.

entry.note: or -δύνω act. pres. καταδύνω mid. καταδύομαι fut. -δύσομαι aor1 mid. -εδῡσάμην epic 2nd sg. -δύσεο 3rd sg. -δύσετο aor2 act. κατέδυν perf. καταδέδῡκα
entry.sense: intr., in act. pres. καταδύνω and mid. καταδύομαι:— to go down, sink, set, of the sun, ἠέλιος κατέδυ Il.; ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα till sun set, Od.; of ships, to be sunk or rather to be disabled (v. infr. II), Hdt., Thuc.:—of persons, καταδεδυκώς having popped down, Ar.

to go down into, plunge into, c. acc., καταδῦναι ὅμιλον, μάχην, δόμον, πόλιν Hom.; foll. by a prep., καταδυσόμεθ’ εἰς Ἀΐδαο δόμους we will go down into . . , Od., etc.:—with a notion of secresy, to insinuate oneself, steal into, Plat.
to slink away and lie hid, καταδύομαι ὑπὸ τῆς αἰσχύνης Xen.
to get into, put on, τεύχεα Hom.
Causal, to make to sink, Lat. submergere, ἐμὲ καταδύουσι τῷ ἄχει Xen.; mostly in aor1, τοὺς γαυλοὺς καταδύσας Hdt.; καταδῦσαι ναῦν to cut it down to the water's edge, disable it, Id., Thuc.
to sing to, Lat. occinere, and so,
trans. to charm or appease by singing, Luc.; c. dat. to sing a spell or incantation (ἐπῳδή) to another, Hdt.
to deafen by singing, Luc.: Pass. to have another sing before one, Id.
to sing by way of incantation, βάρβαρα μέλη Eur.
to take presents, or bribes, Ar.; so in Mid., Id.

entry.note: καταειμένος, η, ον part. perf. pass. of κατα-έννυμι

entry.etym: only in imperf., aor1 and perf. pass.
entry.sense: to clothe, cover, θριξὶ νέκυν καταείνυσαν Il.:— Pass., ὄρος καταειμένον ὕλῃ Od.
to make quite dry, parch quite up, καταζήνασκε δὲ δαίμων (ionic aor1), Od.
to live on, Eur., Plat.
to yoke together, yoke, Pind.:—Pass. to be united, Plat.
Pass., also, to be straitened, confined, imprisoned, Hdt., Soph.
a yoking together:—opp. to ἀνάζευξις, encamping, Plut.
to gird fast; Mid. to gird for oneself, Eur.
Pass. to be astonished at, c. acc., Plut.
to bury, Il., Aesch.
to embolden or encourage against, τινὰ πρὸς τὸ μέλλον Plut.:—Pass., in form καταθρασύνομαι, Luc.
Dep. to look down upon, watch from above, Xen.:—generally, to contemplate, Id.
to subdue by spells or enchantments, Od.
enchantment, Luc.
to curse, NTest.
to run down, Thuc., Xen.: of ships, to run into port, Xen.
to make inroads, Id.:—c. acc. to overrun a country, Thuc., Xen.
to contemplate from above, Plat.
to sharpen, whet, Anth.
to make womanish, Luc.
to exercise oneself much, ἠθληκότες well-trained, of soldiers, Plut.
to press down, press out: aor. 2 pass. part. καταθλῐβείς, Plut.

entry.note: fut. κατα-θανοῦμαι sync. κατθανοῦμαι aor2 κατέθᾰνον epic κάτθᾰνον perf. -τέθνηκα
entry.sense: to die away, be dying, and in aor2 and perf. to be dead, Il., Trag.
to die away, disappear, Mosch., Bion.
mortal, Il.
to cry down, Plat.
to break in pieces, shatter, Plat.
to bewail, lament, mourn, Eur.
to leap down, Il.; c. acc., κ. τὴν αἱμασιήν to leap down the wall, Hdt.
to be quite cast down, lose all heart, Xen.
in the mind or thoughts, Od.; μηδέ τί τοι θάνατος κατ. ἔστω let not death sit heavy on thy heart, Il.
according to one's mind, satisfactory, Theogn., Hdt.
to sacrifice, Hdt., Xen.
to offer, dedicate, τὴν δεκάτην Xen.
Mid., φίλτροις καταθύσομαι I will compel by magic sacrifices, Theocr.
Pass. to be armed at all points, Xen.
a name of Zeus as descending in thunder and lightning, Ar.:—also of his thunder, descending, hurled down, Aesch.
of Ἀχέρων, that to which one descends, downward, Eur.
θύραι κ. gates by which men descend, downward-leading, Od.
to rush down like a storm, Aesch.:—generally, to be tempestuous, Anth.
Dep. to feel shame or reverence before another, stand in awe of him, Hdt., Soph., etc.: c. inf. to be ashamed to do a thing, Eur.
to burn to ashes, Eur., Ar.:— Pass., [Τροίας] πυρὶ κατῃθαλωμένης Eur.
to wave or float adown, πλόκαμοι νῶτον καταίθυσσον Pind.; Κάστωρ καταιθύσσει ἑστίαν Castor sheds his lustre down upon the hearth, Id.
to burn down, burn to ashes, Aesch., Eur.: —metaph. of love, Theocr.

entry.note: fut. attic ιῶ Pass., perf. κατῄκισμαι
entry.sense: to wound severely, to spoil utterly, Od.; so Mid., Eur.
an agreement: a betrothal, Plut.
to agree to a thing, approve of it, c. acc. rei, Hdt.; also c. dat. rei, Thuc.
to agree or promise to do, c. inf., Pind., Soph.; also, κ. τοῦτον βασιλέα σφίσι εἶναι to agree that he should be king, Hdt.
to grant, promise, Soph.: to promise in marriage, betroth, Eur.
intr. to come down, make a swoop, of birds, Ar.; of persons, Eur., etc.
of ships, to put into port, put in, Thuc.
Dep. to come to full perception of, Soph.
all righteous, Aesch.
a dishonourer, Aesch.

to disgrace, dishonour, put to shame, Od., Hdt., attic; τὴν σὴν οὐ κατ. φύσιν I put not thy nature to shame, i. e. show myself not unworthy of thee, Soph.; ἐμὸν καταίσχυνε χρέος covered me with dishonour in that my debt remained unpaid, Pind.
Mid. to feel shame before, θεούς Soph.; so in aor1 pass., καταισχυνθῆναι, ὅπως μὴ δόξει . . to be ashamed of being thought, Thuc.
Dep. to accuse, arraign, reproach, Hdt., Dem.:—Mid. to accuse one another, Hdt.
c. acc. rei, to lay something to one's charge, impute, ἀμαθίαν Thuc.
part. aor1 pass. καταιτιαθείς is used in pass. sense, an accused person, defendant, Id., Xen.
a low helmet or skull-cap of neat's leather, Il.
Pass. to hang down, κατῃωρεῦντο (ionic imperf.) Hes.
to laugh aloud at, τινός Anth.

entry.note: attic -κάω epic inf. κατακαιέμεν fut. -καύσω aor1 κατέκαυσα epic κατέκηα 1st pl. subj. κατακήομεν 1st pl. subj -κείομεν inf. κατακῆαι syncop. κακκῆαι perf. -κέκαυκα Pass., fut. -καυθήσομαι aor1 κατεκαύθην aor2 κατεκάην perf. -κέκαυμαι
entry.sense: to burn down, burn completely, Hom., Il., Hdt.; κ. τοὺς μάντιας to burn them alive, Hdt.; ζώοντα κατακαυθῆναι Id.
Pass., of fire, in tmesi, κατὰ πῦρ ἐκάη had burnt down, burnt out, Il.
to call down, summon, invite, Thuc.:—Mid., Plut.
to cover up, Il., Hdt., attic:— Mid., in tmesi, κατὰ κρᾶτα καλυψάμενος having covered his head, Od.; so -καλυψάμενος alone, having veiled oneself, Hdt.; and -κεκαλυμμένος Id., Plat.
to bend down, so as to be concave, Plat.:—metaph., μ. ἐλπίδας to bend down, overthrow hopes, Eur.:—Pass. to be bent (by intreaty), Aeschin.
Pass. to wither away, Aesch.
Dep. to boast against one, exult over him, τινος or κατά τινος NTest.: to have no fear of, τινος Id.

entry.note: epic 3rd pl. κατακείαται ionic -κέαται subj. -κέωμαι fut. mid. -κείσομαι
entry.etym: Pass., only in pres. and imperf.
entry.sense: to lie down, lie outstretched, Hom., Ar.; κατακείω used as fut. of κατάκειμαι κατακείετε οἴκαδ’ ἰόντες, Od.; σπείσαντες κατακείομεν (epic for -κείωμεν), Id.; κακκείοντες ἔβαν (epic part.) they went to lie down, Hom.
to lie hid, lurk, Hom.
to lie stored up, Lat. reponi, Il., Hes.
to lie sick, Hdt.:— also to lie idle, Xen.
to recline at meals, Lat. accumbere, πῖνε, κατάκεισο Ar.
of land, to lie sloping to the sea (so Hor. Usticae cubantis), Pind.
to shear off:—Mid., κ. τὰς κεφαλάς to crop their heads close, Hdt.
metaph. to cut away, destroy, squander, Od.
one who cries down, a bawler, Ar.
to command silence, Ar.: generally, to command, c. inf., Plut.
of the κελευστής, to give the time in rowing, Ar.
to make gain of a thing wrongfully, Xen.
to change into small coin: generally, to divide into small parts, to cut up, Plat.
to rail violently, Hdt.
to charm away, Lat. delinire, Soph.
to cover with wax, Hdt.
to proclaim or command by public crier, Xen.
in an auction, κ. τι εἴς τινα to order it to be knocked down to one, Plut.
to bewail loudly, lament, Ar.; so in Mid., Eur.
absol. to wail aloud, Id.

entry.note: imperf. κατέκλων aor1 -έκλᾰσα Pass., aor1 -εκλάσθην perf. -κέκλασμαι
entry.sense: to break down, break short, snap off, Il., Hdt.
metaph. to break down, οὐδένα ὅντινα οὐ κατέκλασε he broke us all down, broke all our hearts, Plat.: Pass., κατεκλάσθη φίλον ἦτορ Od.; φρένας κατεκλάσθη Eur.
an instrument for fastening doors, a key, Ar.

entry.note: ionic -κληΐω old attic -κλῄω fut.Ion. -κληΐσω doric κατακλᾴξω Mid., aor1 κατεκλείσθην ionic doric κατεκλᾳξάμην Pass., aor1 κατεκλείσθην ionic κατεκληΐσθην perf. κατα-κέκλειμαι or -κέκλεισμαι
entry.sense: c. acc. pers. to shut in, inclose a mummy in its case, Hdt.; τοὺς Ἕλληνας ἐς τὴν νῆσον κ. to drive them into the island and shut them up there, Thuc.:—Mid. to shut oneself up, Xen.; κατακλᾴξασθαι to shut up the bride with oneself, Theocr.
metaph., νόμῳ κ. to shut up, i. e. to compel, oblige, Dem.; also, εἰς κίνδυνον μέγιστον κατακεκλεῖσθαι to be reduced, Id.
c. acc. rei, to shut up, close, τὰς πυλίδας Hdt.; τὰ ἱρά Id., etc.
to distribute by lot, NTest.
to obtain by inheritance, Plut.
to portion out:—Mid. to receive as one's portion, Plut.
sloping, Anth.

entry.note: fut. -κλῐνῶ Pass., aor1 κατ-εκλίθην aor2 κατ-εκλίνην part. -κλῐνείς fut. -κλῐνήσομαι
entry.sense: to lay down, [δόρυ] κατακλίνας ἐπὶ γαίῃ, Od.; κατ. τοὺς Πέρσας εἰς λειμῶνα having made them recline (for dinner) in a meadow, Hdt.; κ. τινὰ εἰς Ἀσκληπιοῦ to lay a sick person in the temple of Aesculapius, that he might sleep there and so be cured, Ar.: —Pass. to lie at table, sit at meat, Lat. accumbere, Hdt., Ar., etc.
metaph. to lay prostrate, overthrow, Theogn.
a making one to lie down, seating him at table, Plat.; ἡ κ. τοῦ γάμου the celebration of the marriage feast, Hdt.
(from Pass.) a lying at table, sitting at meat, Plat.
to dash over, flood, deluge, inundate, Hdt., etc.:—metaph. to deluge, overwhelm, Eur., Plat.:—Pass., κύματι κατακλυσθῆν (aor1 inf., poet. for -κλυσθῆναι), Aesch.
to wash down or away, Pind.
to wash out, wash away, Xen.
a deluge, inundation: metaph., Dem.
to scrape away, make away with, Ar.
to pull to pieces, shred small, Luc.
to tickle: Pass. to itch, Ar.
intr. to sleep through, κ. τὴν φυλακήν to sleep out the watch, i. e. sleep all the time of one's watch, Hdt.; so, κατακοιμῆσαι τὴν ἡμέραν Xen.: absol. to go to sleep, Hdt.
in Causal sense, to put to sleep, Soph.:—Pass., aor1 κατακοιμηθῆναι, to go to sleep, sleep, Il., Hdt.
to make one a partaker, Dem.; κ. τὰ τῆς πόλεως to share the public property among themselves, Aeschin.
to follow after, obey, Plut.
to run into a bay, Thuc.
to dive down, Thuc.
a bringing down to the sea-shore for exportation, Thuc.
to bring down, esp. from the inland to the coast, Thuc.
κ. ναῦν to bring it into harbour, Dem.
metaph. to bring into a place of refuge, Id.
with long falling hair, Eur.
destruction, Eur.
to buffet sharply, Aeschin.
to shoot down, Hdt., Dem.
to cut down, cut in pieces, cut up, Hdt., Ar., etc.: Pass., aor2 part. κατακοπείς cut in pieces, Hdt.
to kill, slay, Id., attic
in a military sense, to cut in pieces, "cut up, " Dem.; Pass., aor2 inf. κατακοπῆναι Xen.
generally, to break in pieces, destroy, Dem.
to coin into money, Hdt., Xen.
satiated, glutted: metaph. insatiable, excessive, wearisome, Plat.
adv. -ρως, to excess, intemperately, ap. Dem.
to set in order, arrange, Od. (in Mid.); ἐπὶ νευρῇ κατακόσμει ὀϊστόν was fitting it on the string, Il.
to fit out completely, adorn, Ar., Plat.
to reduce to order, Plut.
to hear and obey, be subject to another, c. dat., Hdt.; c. gen., τινός Dem.
to hearken or give ear to one, Id.
to hear plainly, τι or τινά, Eur., Thuc., etc.; τινός Ar.
to cry down, outdo in crying, Ar.
to prevail over, τινός: absol. to prevail, gain the mastery, Hdt., Aesch.; of a name, to prevail, become current, Hdt.
to hang up, Od., Hdt.
κατακρέμαμαι Pass. to hang down, be suspended, Hdt.
better κατὰ κρῆθεν, v. κράς II.
to throw down a precipice, Dem., Plut.
generally, to throw headlong down, ἐκ τριηρέων Xen.:—Pass. to be so thrown down, Id.
steep and rugged, Batr.
better κατ’ ἄκρης, v. ἄκρα.
condemnation, judgment, NTest.

to give as sentence against, τινός:—Pass., τοῖσι κατακέκρῐται θάνατος sentence of death has been passed upon them, Hdt.; κατακεκριμένων οἱ τούτων when this sentence has been given against him, Id.; impers., ἢν κατακρῐθῇ μοι if sentence be given against me, Xen.
c. acc. pers. to condemn, κατέκρινάν μιν ἔκδοτον ἄγεσθαι Hdt.; κ. τινὰ θανάτῳ NTest.:—Pass. to be condemned, Eur., Xen.
to cover over, hide away, conceal, Hom., etc.
absol. to use concealment, to conceal oneself, of the gods, Od.
concealment: a subterfuge, Soph.
to croak at, croak down, like jackdaws, Ar.
Dep. to get for oneself entirely, gain possession of, and in past tenses, to have in full possession, Soph., etc.

entry.note: fut. -κτενῶ ionic -κτᾰνῶ epic -κτᾰνέω aor1 κατέκτεινα aor2 κατέκτᾰνον epic imperat. κάκτανε poet. κατέκτᾰν poet. κατέκτᾰς poet. κατέκτᾰ epic inf. κακτάμεναι epic inf κατακτέμεν part. κατακτάς perf. κατέκτονα mid fut κατακτανέεσθε aor1 κατεκτάθην 3rd pl. κατεκτάθεν part. mid. κατακτάμενος
entry.etym: fut. mid. in pass. sense κατακτανέεσθε
part. mid. κατακτάμενος in pass. sense
entry.sense: to kill, slay, murder, Hom., Hdt.
to be sunk or let down, Ar.
to lose in dicing:—Pass. to be gambled away, Aeschin.
to encircle; in Mid., Plut.
to roll down:—Pass. to be rolled down or thrown off, Hdt., Xen.
to bend down, stoop, Il.:— bend down and peep into a thing, Luc.
to gain dominion over, c. gen., NTest.
to confirm, ratify, Soph.:—Pass., ψήφῳ θανάτου κατακυρωθείς, = κατακριθείς, condemned to death, Eur.
to hinder from doing, Ar.: to detain, keep back, Xen.:—Pass., c. gen. rei, κατεκωλύθη τοῦ πλοῦ Dem.
to burst riotously in upon, τὸ δαιμόνιον κατεκώμασε δώμασιν Eur.
Dep. to boast or brag largely, Dem.
to talk loudly, to blab, Ar.
evil report, slander, NTest.
a slanderer, NTest.

entry.note: fut. -λήψομαι ionic -λάμψομαι perf. -είληφα ionic plup. -λελαβήκεε Pass., ionic aor1 -ελάμφθην
entry.sense: to seize upon, lay hold of, Lat. occupare, Od., Hdt., attic:—Mid. to seize for oneself, Lat. capesso, Hdt.
to seize, overpower, of death and fatigue, Hom.
to seize with the mind, apprehend, comprehend, Plat.
to catch, overtake, come up with, τοὺς φεύγοντας Hdt.: of mischances, to overtake, befall, Id.
to surprise, catch, find, Lat. deprehendo, with a partic., κ. τινὰ ζῶντα Id.; καταλαμβάνει τοὺς ἄρχοντας ἐξιόντας Dem., etc.
impers., καταλαμβάνει τινά, c. inf., like the attic συμβαίνει, it happens to one, it is one's fortune to do so and so, τοῦτον κατέλαβε κεῖσθαι Hdt.
absol., τὰ καταλαβόντα = τὰ συμβάντα, what happened, the circumstances, Id.; ἢν πόλεμος καταλαβῇ Thuc.

to repress, arrest, check, τὴν δύναμιν Κύρου Hdt.; κ. τὸ πῦρ to get it under, Id.; κ. ἑαυτόν Id.; κ. τὰς διαφοράς to put an end to them, Id.:—Pass., ὁ θάνατος καταλαμφθεὶς ἐσιγήθη inquiries about the death being checked, Id.
to bind, κ. πίστι, ὁρκίοις, Lat. jurejurando adstringere, to bind by oath, Id., Thuc.
to force or compel one to do, c. inf., ἀναγκαίη μιν κ. φαίνειν forces him to bring out the truth, Hdt.:—Pass., καταλαμβανόμενος being constrained, Id.
to be arrested, Hdt.
to shine upon or over, c. gen., Plat.: c. acc., κ. τοὺς στενωπούς to light them, Plut.
absol. to shine, Eur.; so in Mid., Id.
to suffer much, feel sore pain, Soph.
to lay down: Mid. and Pass. to lie down, go to bed, aor1 κατελέξατο Hom.; epic syncop. aor2 pass. κατέλεκτο Il., etc.; part. καταλέγμενος and inf. καταλέχθαι Od.; fut. καταλέξομαι Hes.

to pick out, choose out of many, Hdt.:— to choose as soldiers, to enrol, enlist, Ar., Thuc.; Mid. to choose for himself, Hdt., Thuc., etc.:—Pass. to be enlisted or enrolled, Lat. conscribi, Hdt., etc.
to recount, tell at length or in order, in fut. or aor1, ταῦτα καταλέξω Il.; πᾶσαν ἀληθείην κατάλεξον Id.:—Pass., τούτων δὴ τῶν καταλεχθέντων of those which have been recounted, Hdt.
to reckon up, Od., Hdt., etc.
to pour down; absol. to shed tears, Eur.:- Pass. to drop down, Il., Eur.
anointed, Ar.

entry.note: epic also καλλείπω fut. καλλείψω aor2 κάλλῐπον ionic imperf. καταλείπεσκον fut. καταλειφθήσομαι
entry.sense: to leave behind, Il.; esp. of persons dying or going into a far country, οἷόν μιν Τροίηνδε κιὼν κατέλειπεν Ὀδυσσεύς Od.; κ. τινὰ μόνον Soph., etc.; so in Mid., καταλείπεσθαι παῖδας to leave behind one, Hdt., etc.: —Pass. καταλελειμμένος τοῦ ἄλλου στρατοῦ being part of the army left behind, Id.
to leave as an heritage, Od., attic; καταλείψει οὐδὲ ταφῆναι will leave not enough to be buried with, Ar.
in Mid., simply, to leave in a certain state, Hdt.
to forsake, abandon, leave in the lurch, Hom., attic
to leave remaining, ὀκτὼ μόνον Xen.: Mid. to reserve for oneself, Id.:—Pass., καταλείπεται μάχη yet remains to be fought Id.
to leave alone, Id.
to spend all one's substance in bearing the public burdens (λειτουργίαι), Dem.
a leaving behind, Plat.
to waste in subtle talk, Ar.
to stone to death, Hdt., Ar., etc.
to grind down, Od., Hdt.
to leave off, end, stop, Aesch.; ποῖ καταλήξει; at what point will it cease? Id.:— τὰ καταλήγοντα the limits of a district, Plut.
Dep. to forget utterly, τινός Il.
to be seized or occupied, Plut.
able to keep down or check, c. gen., Ar.
to be achieved, Thuc.
act. seizing suddenly; πένθος θεόθεν καταληπτόν grief that falls on us from the gods, Eur.
a seizing, ἐν καταλήψει within one's grasp, Thuc.:— an assaulting, Ar.
a taking possession, occupation, Plat., Dem., etc.
to stone to death, Dem.
to make into a lake or swamp, Byz.
to entreat earnestly, Luc.
exchange, esp. of money: the profits of the money-changer, Dem.
a change from enmity to friendship, reconciliation, Aesch., etc.
reconciliation of sinners with God, NTest.
easy to reconcile, placable, Arist.
to change money, Plut., etc.; and so in Mid., Dem.:—Mid. to exchange one thing for another Plat.

to change a person from enmity to friendship, reconcile, Hdt., NTest.:— Mid., καταλλάσσεσθαι τὴν ἔχθρην τινί to make up one's enmity with any one, Hdt.:—Pass., esp. in aor1 κατηλλάχθην or aor2 κατηλλάγην [ᾰ], to become reconciled, Soph., Eur., etc.
to crush in pieces, make an end of, Xen., Aeschin.
by way of conversation, in prose, Plat.
Dep. to count up, number, reckon, Xen.; κ. τὸ εὐεργέτημα πρός τινα to put it down to his account, Dem.; καταλογιζέσθω μηδεὶς τοῦθ’ ὑμῖν ἐν ἀρετῇ let no one impute it to you as a virtue, Aeschin.
to count or reckon among, Lat. annumerare, τοὺς ἀχαρίστους ἐν τοῖς ἀδίκοις Xen.
an enrolment, register, list, catalogue, Plat.; κ. νεῶν the catalogue of ships in Il. 2.

at Athens, the register of citizens, Ar., etc.: [ὁπλῖται] ἐκ καταλόγου soldiers on the list for service, Thuc., etc.; οἱ ἐν τῷ καταλόγῳ Xen.; οἱ ἔξω τοῦ κ., or, οἱ ὑπὲρ τὸν κ., the superannuated, Lat. emeriti, Id.; καταλόγοις χρηστοῖς ἐκκριθέν, of picked troops, Thuc.
to cut into furrows, Eur.
Mid. to spend in bathing, καταλόει [metri grat. pro -λούει] Ar.
= κατὰ τὸν λόφον, on the neck, βῆν δὲ καταλοφάδεια φέρων (sc. τὸν ἔλαφον) Od.
to distribute into λόχοι, and generally to distribute, Plut.
distribution into bodies, Plut., Luc.
an inn, lodging, NTest.
Dep. to ruin utterly, destroy, Xen.
to be dissolved or done away, Soph.
a dissolving, dissolution of governments, Thuc., etc.
the dismissal or disbanding of a body of men, στρατιᾶς Xen.; εἰς κατάλυσιν till dismissal, of soldiers at a review, Id.
κ. τοῦ πολέμου an ending of the war, pacification, Thuc., Xen.
generally, an end, termination, Xen.
a resting, lodging, rest, Eur.
= κατάλυμα, a resting-place, guest-chamber, quarters, lodging, καταλύσιες (ionic for -λύσεις), Hdt., Plat.
to put down, destroy, Il., Eur.

of governments, to dissolve, break up, put down, Hdt., Ar., etc.; κ. τύραννον to put down, to depose, Thuc.; κ. τινὰ τῆς ἀρχῆς Xen.:—Pass., τῶν ἄλλων καταλελυμένων στρατηγῶν having been dismissed, Hdt.,
to dissolve, dismiss, disband a body, καταλύειν τὴν βουλήν Id.; τὸ ναυτικόν Dem.
τὴν φυλακὴν κ. to neglect the watch, Ar.
to end, bring to an end, βίοτον Eur.; τὸν βίον Xen.
κ. τὴν εἰρήνην to break the peace, Aeschin.

κ. τὸν πόλεμον to end the war, make peace, Thuc., Xen., etc.; and absol. (sub. τὸν πόλεμον) καταλύειν τινί or πρός τινα to make peace with him, Thuc.:—so in Mid., Id., etc.; καταλύεσθαι τὰς ἔχθρας Hdt.
to unloose, unyoke, ἵππους Od.; τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ἀδελφεοῦ κ. to take it down from the wall, Hdt.

intr. to take up one's quarters, to lodge, παρ’ ἐμοὶ καταλύει he is my guest, Plat.; κ. παρά τινα to go and lodge with him, Thuc.: absol. to take one's rest, Ar.; Mid., θανάτῳ καταλυσαίμαν may I take my rest in the grave, Eur.
to rest from a thing, c. gen., Od.
to bewitch, Luc.
to make soft, or effeminate, Jo_chrys.:—Pass. to be or become so, Xen.
to soften much, Luc.; metaph. to appease, Id.
to observe well, examine closely, Hdt., Xen.
to learn thoroughly, τι Plat., etc.
to perceive, understand, Id., etc.
to discover, find, c. part., καταμαθόντες μιν ἀγοράζοντα Hdt.; κ. τινὰ θύοντα Xen.
to learn thoroughly, and in perf. to have learnt, to be aware, Id.
to consider, τι Id.
Dep. to divine, surmise, Arist.
to be stark mad, Hdt.
to catch, Lat. deprehendo, Il.; esp. to catch one running away, Hom., Pind.
