the Cercopes were a kind of men-monkeys, Hdt.
metaph. a mischievous fellow, knave, Aeschin.
a slice: hence, a small coin, mite, in pl. small coin, small change, Ar.
generally, small wares, Anth.
to cut small, mince, chop up, Plat.
to coin into small money, Anth.
a money-changer, NTest.
κέρνος, a large earthen dish, in which fruits were offered to the Corybantes, borne by a priest or priestess called κερνᾶς, Anth.
horn-footed, hoofed, Ar.
horn-sounding, of a horn flute, Anth.
bound with or made of horn, Eur.
horned, Eur.
of horn, of a flute, Anth.
a rope belonging to the sailyards, Luc.
to butt with the horns:—Pass., of ships in a storm, buffeted, Aesch.
drawn by the horns, pass. of a bow, because tipped with horn, Eur.
to toss the horns, Lat. cornua tollere: metaph. of persons, to toss the head, give oneself airs, Ar.
having horns, horned, Babr.
= κερασφόρος, horned, Eur.
to taunt or sneer at, c. acc. pers., Od., Aesch., Eur.: absol. to sneer, Od.:— Pass. to be scoffed at, Eur.
jeering, mockery, Soph.
= κερτόμησις, jeering, mockery, in pl., κερτομίας ἤδ’ αἴσυλα μυθήσασθαι Il.; κερτομίας καὶ χεῖρας ἀφέξω Od.
heart-cutting, stinging, reproachful, Od.; Δία κερτομίοις ἐπέεσσι Hom.; also, κερτομίοισι (without ἐπέεσσι) Id.; κέρτομα βάζειν Hes.; χοροὶ κέρτομοι abusive, Hdt.
mocking, delusive, κέρτομος χαρά Eur.
a kind of hawk, the kestrel; also
stitched, embroidered, κεστὸς ἱμάς of Aphrodite's charmed girdle, Il.
later, κεστός, οῦ, as Subst., Lat. cestus, Anth., Luc.
a fish held in esteem among the Greeks, Ar.
a hiding place, hole, corner, Od.; κευθμῶνες ὀρέων the hollows of the mountains, Pind., Eur.
of the nether world, the abyss, Hes., Aesch.
in Aesch. Eum. 805 = ἄδυτον, a sanctuary.
ὑπὸ κεύθεσι γαίης in the depths of the earth, Hom.; in sg., κ. νεκύων Soph.; κ. οἴκων the innermost chambers, like μυχός, Eur.

to cover quite up, to cover, hide, of the grave, ὅπου κύθε γαῖα where earth covered him, Od.; so, ὃν οὐδὲ κατθανόντα γαῖα κ. Aesch.; also, ὁπότ’ ἄν σε δόμοι κεκύθωσι, i. e. when thou hast entered the house, Od.: Soph.:—perf. to contain, Hom., Soph.
to conceal, and in perf. to keep concealed, Hom.; οὐκέτι κεύθετε βρωτὺν οὐδὲ ποτῆτα no more can ye disguise your eating and drinking, Od.; κ. τι ἔνδον καρδίας Aesch.; κ. μῆνιν to cherish anger, Eur.
c. dupl. acc., οὐδέ σε κεύσω [ταῦτα] nor will I keep them secret from thee, Od.
in Trag. sometimes intr. to be concealed, lie hidden, esp. in perf., Aesch., Soph.
of the head: metaph., like Lat. capitalis, principal, Ar.
as Subst., κεφάλαιον, ου, τό, the head, Id.
the chief or main point, the sum of the matter, Pind., Thuc., etc.; ἐν κεφαλαίῳ, or ὡς ἐν κ., εἰπεῖν to speak summarily, Xen., etc.; ἐν κεφαλαίοις ὑπομνῆσαι, ἀποδεῖξαι, περιλαβεῖν τι Thuc.
of persons, the head or chief, Luc.
of money, the capital, Lat. caput, Opp. to interest, Plat., etc.: the sum total, Dem.
the crown, completion of a thing, a crowning act of wrong, Id.; κ. ἐπιτιθέναι ἐπί τινι, Lat. corollam imponere rei, Plat.
to bring under heads, sum up, state summarily, Thuc.
to smite on the head, NTest.
capital, principal, chief, Luc.:—adv. -δῶς, summarily, Arist.
the sum total, Hdt.
causing headache, Xen.
head-ache: later κεφαλαλγίη, Luc.

the head of man or beast, Hom., etc.; κατὰ κεφαλῆς, epic κὰκ κεφαλῆς, over the head, Id.; κὰκ κεφαλήν on the head, Il.:— ἐς πόδας ἐκ κεφαλῆς from head to foot, Id.:— ἐπὶ κεφαλήν head foremost, head downwards, headlong, Hdt., Plat., etc.
the head, put for the whole person, Hom.; ἶσον ἐμῇ κεφαλῇ like myself, Il.; φίλη κ., Lat. carum caput, Id.: in bad sense, ὦ κακαὶ κεφαλαί Hdt.; ὦ μιαρὰ κ. Ar.
the head, i. e. the life, παρθέμενοι κεφαλάς setting their heads on the cast, Od.:—in imprecations, ἐς κεφαλὴν τρέποιτ’ ἐμοί on my head be it! Ar., etc.
generally, κ. σκορόδου a head of garlic, Id.: the top or brim of a vessel, Theocr.: the coping of a wall, Xen.:—in pl. the head or source of a river, Hdt.
metaph., like κεφάλαιον, the crown, completion of a thing, Plat.
a sea-fish, = βλεψίας, Dorio ap. Ath.
Dim. of κεφαλή.
part of a shoe, Arist.
a head, chapter, NTest.
Comic word for Ἀθηναῖοι, Gapenians for Athenians, Ar.
separately, Arist.
Ceos, one of the Cyclades, Hdt., etc.: —hence, Κεῖος, ionic Κήϊος, ὁ, a Ceian, Id., etc.; οὐ Χῖος, ἀλλὰ Κεῖος not a (roguish) Chian, but an (honest) Ceian, proverb in Ar.
connexion by marriage, alliance, Lat. affinitas, Eur., Xen.
cared for, dear, beloved, Il.
careful of, or caring for, c. gen., Eur.
of a funeral or tomb, mourning, sepulchral, Aesch., Eur.
care, solicitude, Plat.
provident, careful: adv. -κῶς, Luc.
one who is in charge, esp. for burial, Il.
generally, a protector, guardian, Theogn., Soph., etc.:—also of a female, Soph.
= κηδεστής, Eur., Ar.
given in charge for burial, Il.
a connexion by marriage, Lat. affinis, Xen., etc.: esp. a son-in-law, father-in-law, a step-father, Dem.:— a brother-in-law, Eur.
connexion by marriage, Xen.
connexion or alliance by marriage, Lat. affinitas, Eur.
poet. for κηδεστής, one who is so connected, Soph., Eur.
to take charge of, attend to, tend, Soph., Eur.
esp. to attend to a corpse, close the eyes, bury, mourn, Eur., etc.
to contract a marriage, ally oneself in marriage, Aesch., Eur.; κ. λέχος to marry, Soph.:—Pass. to be so allied, Eur.
c. acc. pers. to make one's kinsman by marriage, Id.
absol., οἱ κηδεύσαντες those who formed the marriage, Id.
most worthy of our care, most cared for, Hom.
nearest allied by marriage, Od.
care for others, c. gen., Od.
trouble, sorrow; mostly in pl. troubles, Hom.
esp. cares for the dead, mourning, Id., Aesch., etc.; also in sg., κᾶδος φθιμένου Pind.; ἅμα κήδεϊ when there is a death in the family, Hdt.; ἐς τὸ κ. ἰέναι to attend the funeral, Id.
an object of care, a care, Aesch.
connexion by marriage, Lat. affinitas, Hdt., attic
anxious, Eur.

entry.etym: κεκαδήσομαι from κήδω, for κεκαδήσω, κέκαδον, v. χάζω II
entry.sense: Act. to trouble, distress, vex, Hom.
Mid. and Pass. to be troubled or distressed for others, c. gen. pers., Il., etc.: also c. gen. rei, τῶν ἀλφίτων Ar.:—absol. in part. κηδόμενος, η, ον, caring for a person, anxious, Il.
a vessel into which the ψῆφοι were cast in voting, Ar.
anything oozing forth, ooze, Aesch.; κ. φόνου oozing blood, Id.; μυδῶσα κ., of the juices drawn by fire from a sacrificial victim, Soph.
the dye made from sap oozing from the gall-nut, Dem.; κ. πορφύρας the dye of the purple-fish, Aesch.
to gush or ooze, Od., Soph.:—Pass., αἱμάς κηκιομένα ἑλκέων Soph. [ι epic; ῑ attic]
burning, Il.:—so κήλειος, Id.
to charm, bewitch, enchant, beguile, fascinate, esp. by music, Lat. mulcere, Eur., Plat.
enchantment, fascination, Od.
a magic charm, spell, Eur.
a tumor, esp. a rupture, Lat. hernia, Anth.
an enchanting, fascination, Plat.
charming, appeasing, Eur.; τὸ κ. = κήλημα, Soph.
one who is ruptured, Anth.
to stain, sully, soil, Eur.
a stain, spot, defilement, esp. of blood, Trag.
metaph. a stain, blemish, dishonour, Soph., Xen.
a shaft, an arrow, Il., Hes.
a swipe or swing-beam, for drawing water, Lat. tolleno:—so, κηλώνειον, ionic κηλωνήιον.
a muzzle, put on a led horse, Xen., Anth.
the funnel-shaped top to the voting urn (κάδος, καδίσκος) in the Athen. law-courts, through which the ballots (ψῆφοι) were dropt, Ar.
to muzzle a horse, Xen.
Lat. census, registration of taxation, NTest.: — the tax itself, Id.
a sea-bird that dashes into the sea to seize its prey, perh. the tern or gannet, Od.
a garden-flower, Ar.
a gardener, Anth.
to rear in a garden, Luc.: metaph. to tend, cherish, freshen, Eur.
Dim. of κῆπος: a parterre: metaph. a decoration, appendage, Thuc.
teaching in a garden, Anth.
a garden, orchard, plantation, Od.:—of any fertile region, Ἀφροδίτης κᾶπος, i. e. Cyrene, Pind.; Διὸς κ., i. e. Libya, Id., etc.:— οἱ Ἀδώνιδος κῆποι, v. Ἄδωνις 2.
of or for gardening, Plat.

sense.gloss: keeper of a garden, a gardener.

entry.sense: to be sick at heart, to be disquieted, anxious, Eur.
urged on by the Κῆρες, Il.
of wax, waxen, Plat.: metaph. pliable as wax (Hor., cereus in vitium flecti), Id.
stealer of honeycombs, Theocr.
a honeycomb, Lat. favus, Hes., Hdt., etc.; also, κηρίον σφηκῶν Hdt.
a wax tablet, Anth.
born to misery, Hes.
wax-bound, μέλι Anth.
in the heart, with all the heart, heartily, Hom., Hes.
Mid. to form for oneself of wax, Anth.
fastened with wax, Anth.
moulded of wax, waxen, Anth.
= κηρόδετος, Aesch.
bees-wax, Lat. cera, Od., Plat.
a modeller in wax, Anacreont.
producing wax, waxen, Anth.
clad in wax, Anth.
to make waxen cells, Anth.

the goddess of death, hence doom, fate, Hom.; in full, Κὴρ Θανάτοιο Od.; Κῆρες Θανάτοιο Il.: generally, bane, ruin, βαρεῖα μὲν κὴρ τὸ μὴ πιθέσθαι grievous ruin it were not to obey, Aesch.; κὴρ οὐ καλή an unseemly calamity, Soph.

entry.etym: contr. from κέαρ, as ἦρ from ἔαρ
entry.sense: the heart, Lat. cor, Hom.; dat. κῆρι as adv., with all the heart, heartily, Id.:—in Trag. always κέαρ.
that which is cried by a herald, a proclamation, public notice, Hdt., attic
a reward offered by proclamation, Xen., Aeschin.
the office of herald or crier, Hdt., Plat.
a herald's wand, Lat. caduceus, Hdt., Thuc.
a proclamation, message, Aesch.
to be a herald or crier, fulfil the office of one, Plat.
trans. to proclaim, notify, τί τινι Aesch., Eur.
of heralds, Plat.
the halcyon. The form κείρυλος, is a joke in Ar., the barber Sporgilos being called (from κείρω), rasor-bird.

a herald, pursuivant, marshal, public messenger, Hom., etc. In Hom. they summon the assembly, separate combatants, have charge of sacrifices, act as envoys, and their persons were sacred. After Hom., Hermes is called the κῆρυξ of the gods, Hes., etc.
at Athens, a crier, who made proclamation in the public assemblies, Ar., etc.

to be a herald, officiate as herald, Il.; λαὸν κηρύσσοντες ἀγειρόντων let them convene the people by voice of herald, Id.; κήρυσσε, κῆρυξ Aesch., etc.:—impers., κηρύσσει (sc. ὁ κῆρυξ) he gives notice, proclamation is made, Xen.
c. acc. pers. to summon by voice of herald, Hom., Ar.
to proclaim as conqueror, Xen., etc.: to extol, Eur.
to call upon, invoke, Aesch., Eur.
c. acc. rei, to proclaim, announce, τί τινι Trag.:— to proclaim or advertise for sale, Hdt.; κ. ἀποικίαν to proclaim a colony, i. e. to invite people to join as colonists, Thuc.
to proclaim or command publicly, Lat. indicere, Aesch., Soph., etc.; τὰ κηρυχθέντα the public orders, Soph.
of sea monsters, Mosch.
any sea-monster or huge fish, Hom., Hdt.
an abyss, hollow, cf. κητώεις.
killing sea-monsters, Anth.
as epith. of Lacedaemon, full of hollows or ravines, Hom.; cf. μεγακήτης.
a drone, Lat. fucus: metaph. a drone, a lazy fellow, Hes., Ar.
like a drone, Plat.
the Cephisus, a river of Phocis, Il.:—fem. λίμνη Κηφισίς Id.
the more famous river of Athens, Soph., etc.
smelling as of incense, fragrant, Il.
to adulterate coin, Ar., etc.
metaph. to palm off, Eur.
adulteration, trickery, dishonesty, Ar.
adulterated, spurious, base, of coin, Theogn., Eur.
metaph. base, false, spurious, fraudulent, of men, Theogn., Eur.; of oracles, deceitful, Hdt.; ἐν κιβδήλῳ Eur.
a pouch, wallet, Hes.
a wooden box, chest, coffer, Ar.
to wag the tail:—metaph. to change constantly, Theogn.

the latticed gates in the law-courts or council-chamber, through which the members passed, Ar.; metaph., means waitings at the bar, the law's delays, Plut.; in sg., ἐντὸς τῆς κιγκλίδος διατρίβειν to live in court, Luc.
prob. a kind of wagtail, Theogn.

entry.etym: pass., only in pres. and imperf.
entry.sense: to be spread abroad or over, of the dawning day, Il.; ὕπνος ἐπ’ ὄσσοις κ. Eur.
the Lat. cithara (whence guitar), a kind of lyre or lute, Hhymn., Hdt., attic: —it was of triangular shape, with seven strings, Eur. Cf. κῐθᾰρίζω

to play the cithara, φόρμιγγι κιθάριζε Il., Hes.; λύρῃ ἐρατὸν κιθαρίζων Hhymn. (so that there can have been no great difference between the κιθάρα, λύρα, and φόρμιγξ); κιθαρίζειν οὐκ ἐπίσταται, of an uneducated person, Ar.
a playing on the cithara, Plat.
that which is played on the cithara, a piece of music for it, Plat.
= κιθάρα, Hom., etc.
= κιθαριστύς, Id.
a player on the cithara, Hes., attic
skilled in harp-playing, Plat.: ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) = κῐθᾰριστύς, Id.
the art of playing the cithara, Il.
to sing to the cithara, Plat.
a singing to the cithara, Plat.
of or for harp-playing, Ar.
ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) = κιθαρῳδία, Plat.
one who plays and sings to the cithara, a harper, Hdt., Plat., etc.
a ringlet, Lat. cincinnus, Ar., Theocr.
the castor berry, Hdt.
onomatop., a cry in imitation of the screechowl's note, toowhit, toowhoo, Ar.
to call, summon, Hom.
to call on, invoke, implore, Il., Aesch., etc.
to accost, address, Il.
to name, call by name, Id., Aesch., Eur.: —Pass., νῆσός τις Συρίη κικλήσκεται there is an island called Syros, Od.; cf. κλῄζω II.
Cicynna, an Attic deme: Κικυννεύς, ὁ, a Cicynnian, attic; pl. Κικυννῆς, Ar.; Κικυννόθεν, from Cicynna, Id.
strength, vigour, Od., Hhymn.

entry.etym: a verb only found in doric aor1 ἔκιξα
entry.sense: = ἤνεγκα Anth.:—in Ar. we have ἀπ-έκιξαν, sent away, shook off.
a Cilician, Il.: fem. Κίλισσα, Aesch.: —adj. Κιλίκιος, η, ον Cilician, Id.; ἡ Κιλικία, (sc. γῆ), Cilicia, Hdt.
in pl. κιλλίβαντες, a three-legged stand for supporting any thing, κιλλίβαντες ἀσπίδος a shield- stand, Ar.
a niggard, Arist.
Cimmerian, K. ἰσθμός the Crimea, Aesch.; Κιμμέριος, η, ον, Hdt.
the Cimmerians, a people dwelling beyond the Ocean in perpetual darkness, Od.: in later geography, a people about the Palus Maeotis, Hdt.
sc. γῆ, Cimolian earth, a white clay, from Cimolus in the Cyclades, which was used by way of soap in the baths, Ar.
the rank smell of a he-goat, Luc.
to smell like a goat, Ar.
a fox: hence of a cunning rogue, Soph., Ar., etc.:—in Theocr. the voc. κίναδε implies a masc. form κίναδος, ου.
motion, rustling, as of wings, Aesch.
lust, Aeschin., Luc.
Lat. cinaedus, a lewd fellow, Plat.
a risk, hazard, venture, bold enterprise, Soph., Eur.
one must venture, Eur.
a daring, venturesome person, Thuc.
adventurous, Arist.
to be daring, to make a venture, take the risk, do a daring thing, Hdt., Ar., etc.: to be in danger, Thuc.

that in respect of which danger is incurred in dat., κ. τῶι σώματι, τῆι ψυχῆι Hdt.; κ. πάσηι τῆι Ἑλλάδι to run a risk with all Greece, i. e. endanger it all, Id., etc.; so, κ. περὶ τῆς ψυχῆς Ar., etc.
c. acc. cogn. to venture, hazard, κινδύνευμα Plat.; μάχην Aeschin.:—Pass. to be risked or hazarded, μεταβολὴ κινδυνεύεται there is risk of change, Thuc.; τὰ μέγιστα κινδυνεύεται are endangered, Dem.

c. inf. to run the risk of doing or being, Hdt., Thuc., etc.:— then, implying a chance of success, κινδυνεύω (c. inf.) is used to express what may possibly or probably happen, κινδυνεύουσι οἱ ἄνθρωποι γόητες εἶναι they run a risk of being reputed conjurors, Hdt.; κινδυνεύσεις ἐπιδεῖξαι χρηστὸς εἶναι you will have a chance of showing your worth, Xen.; κινδυνεύει ἀγαθὸν γεγονέναι it is very likely to prove good, Plat.:—then impers., κινδυνεύει it may be, possibly, Id.
Pass. to be endangered or imperilled, Thuc., Dem.

a danger, risk, hazard, venture, enterprise, Lat. periculum, Pind., Ar., etc.; κίνδυνον ἀναρρίπτειν to run a risk, Hdt., etc.; κίνδυνον or κινδύνους ἀναλαβέσθαι, ὑποδύεσθαι, αἴρεσθαι, ὑπομεῖναι, etc., attic
pf to set in motion, to move, Hom., attic

to move or remove a thing from its place, Hdt.; κ. τὰ ἀκίνητα to meddle with things sacred, Id., Soph.; κ. τὰ χρήματα ἐς ἄλλο τι to apply them to an alien purpose, Hdt.;— κ. τὸ στρατόπεδον, Lat. castra movere, Xen.:— to change, innovate, τὰ νόμαια Hdt.
to rouse, disturb, of a wasps' nest, Il.: to stir up, arouse, urge on, Trag., etc.
to set agoing, cause, call forth, Soph., etc.:—proverb., κ. πᾶν χρῆμα to turn every stone, try every way, Hdt.
Pass. to be put in motion, to be moved, move, stir, Il., Hdt., attic
to move forward, of soldiers, Soph., Xen., etc.
motion, Pind.
a motion, movement, Plut.
movement, motion, Plat., etc.: a dance, Luc.
movement, in a political sense, Thuc.; of the Peloponn. war, Id.
to be moved, Plat.
κινητέον, one must call into play, Id.
one that sets agoing, an author, Ar.
of or for putting in motion, Xen.
cinnamon, a word borrowed from the Phoenicians, Hdt.
anything moved about, αἰθέριον κ. a sport for the winds of heaven, Aesch.
Dep., to go, move, ἐς πόλεμον κίνυντο (epic imperf.) they were marching to battle, Il.; κινυμένοιο as he moved, Id.
Dep. to utter a plaintive sound, lament, wail, Ar.:—c. acc. cogn., χαλινοὶ κινύρονται φόνον the bridles ring or clash murderously, Aesch.
wailing, plaintive, Il.
Pass. = κινέομαι, to sway backwards and forwards, Aesch.
the capital of a column, Xen.
Circe, an enchantress, dwelling in the island Aea, who changed Ulysses' companions into swine, Od.
a kind of hawk or falcon, so called from its wheeling flight, ἵρηξ κίρκος (where ἵρηξ is the generic term, κίρκος the specific, like βοῦς τοῦρος) , Od.
a ring, circle, mostly in form κρίκος.
to hoop round, secure with rings, Aesch.
to mix wine with water, in 3rd sg. imperf. ἐκίρνα and κίρνη, part. κιρνάς, Od.; in Hdt., 3rd sg. pres. κιρνᾶι, 1st pl. κίρναμεν.
the pumice-stone, Lat. pumex, Arist., Luc.
a worm in wood or in corn, the weevil, Lat. curculio, Pind.
a chattering, greedy bird, the jay or magpie, Ar.
to crave for strange food, of pregnant women: metaph., κ. τῆς εἰρήνης Ar.; c. inf. to long to do a thing, Id.
ivy-clad, Soph.
of ivy, Eur.
of or from Cissia in southern Persia, Hdt.; Κισσία ἰηλεμίστρια a Cissian mourner, Aesch.
ivy-crowned, Hhymn.
made of ivy, Luc.
ivy, Lat. hedera, Soph., Eur., etc.
ivy-crowned, Anth.
to be decked with ivy, Anth.
ivy-wreathed, Pind.: luxuriant with ivy, Eur.
to wreathe with ivy, Eur.
a rustic drinking-cup, prob. with an ivy-wreath carved on it, Od.
decked with ivy, Anth.
a box, chest, Lat. cista, Od., Ar.
a writing-case, desk, Ar.
carrying a chest in mystic processions, Dem.

to reach, hit, or light upon, meet with, find, Hom.:— to overtake, Il.: to reach, arrive at, Id.; σε δουρὶ κιχήσομαι shall reach thee, Id.; τέλος θανάτοιο κιχήμενον death that is sure to reach one, inevitable, Id.
rarely c. gen., like τυγχάνω, Soph.
a thrush, Lat. turdus, Od., Ar.
to chirp like a thrush: hence, to titter, giggle, or to eat κίχλαι, to live luxuriously, Ar.
to lend.
a pillar, Lat. columna, Od.: a flogging-post, Soph., Aeschin.; proverb., ἔσθιε τοὺς Μεγακλέους κίονας eat the pillars of his hall, for being a spendthrift, he had nothing else left to give, Ar.
in pl. the pillars guarded by Atlas, which keep heaven and earth asunder, Od.; whereas in Hdt. Mount Atlas is ὁ κίων τοῦ οὐρανοῦ.
a columnar grave-stone, Anth.
to go, Hom., Aesch.
of hounds, to give tongue, only in pres., Aesch., Xen.
with a clang, noise, din, Il.

any sharp sound, such as the twang of a bow, Il.; the scream of cranes, Hom.; the grunting of swine, Od.; the hissing of serpents, Aesch.; the barking of dogs, Xen.:—also of song, Soph.; κλ. δύσφατος, of Cassandra-prophecies, Aesch.
screaming, of cranes, Anth.
a young slip or shoot broken off: esp. an olive-branch wound round with wool and presented by suppliants, Hdt., Aesch., Soph.

to make a sharp piercing sound, of birds, to scream, screech, Il., Soph., etc.; of dogs, to bark, bay, Od., Ar.; of things, as of arrows in the quiver, to clash, rattle, Il.; of the wind, to whistle, Od.; of wheels, to creak, Aesch.; c. acc. cogn., κλάζουσι φόβον ring forth terror, Id.

of men, to shout, scream, Il.:—the nearest approach to articulate sound is in Aesch., μάντις ἔκλαγξεν ἄλλο μῆχαρ shrieked forth another remedy; Ζῆνα ἐπινίκια κλάζων sounding loudly the victory-song of Zeus, Id.

to weep, lament, wail, Hom., etc.; αὐτὸν κλαίοντα ἀφήσω I shall send him home weeping, i. e. well beaten, Il.; hence κλαύσεται he shall weep, i. e. he shall repent it, Ar.; κλαύσει μακρά Id.; κλάων to your sorrow, at your peril, Soph., Eur.; κλάειν σε λέγω or κελεύω, Lat. plorare te jubeo, Ar.
trans. to weep for, lament, Hom.:—in Pass. to be lamented, Aesch.: impers., μάτην ἐμοὶ κεκλαύσεται I shall mourn in vain, Ar.
Mid. to bewail oneself, weep aloud, Aesch.; so perf. part. pass., κεκλαυμένος bathed in tears, all tears, Id., Soph.
trans. to bewail to oneself, Soph.
mutilated, Hippiatr.
breaking clods, Anth.
a breaking, NTest.
that which is broken off, a fragment, morsel, NTest., Plut.
to dress vines: metaph. κλ. τινά to give him a dressing, Ar.
broken in pieces, Anth.
a weeping, Hom., Hdt., Aesch.
to make to weep:—Pass. to weep, Plat.
a crying like a child, Plut.
a weeping, wailing, Aesch.
a trouble, misfortune, Soph., Ar.
Desiderat. of κλαίω, to wish to weep, τὸ θύριον φθεγγόμενον ἄλλως κλαυσιᾷ the door is like to weep (i. e. shall suffer) for creaking without cause, Ar.
smiles mixed with tears, Xen.
rue-the-fight, a parody on the name of La-machus (ready-for-fight), Ar.
wept, bewailed: to be bewailed, mournful, Aesch., Soph.
to break, break off, Hom., etc.
a little key, Ar.
to have charge of the keys, κλ. θεᾶς to be her priestess, Eur.
Pass. to be closely watched kept in check, Id.
holding the keys, having charge of a place, Eur.; of Aeacus, as judge of the dead, Anth.
a keyhole; or, generally, a cleft, chink, Luc.
a bar for closing a door, Hhymn.:—mostly in pl., like Lat. claustra, Trag., etc.
famous, renowned, illustrious, Solon., Pind., Trag.; καὶ τοῦτο κλεινὸν αὐτοῦ is well known of him, Luc.
that which serves for closing:
a bar or bolt, drawn or undrawn by a latch or thong (ἱμάς), Hom.
a key, or rather a kind of catch or hook, by which the bar (ὀχεύς) was shot or unshot from the outside, Id.
a key (unknown to Hom.), Aesch., Eur.
metaph., Ἁσυχία βουλᾶν τε καὶ πολέμων κλαῖδας ἔχοισα Pind.; κλῇς ἐπὶ γλώσσῃ βέβηκε, of enforced silence, Soph.; so, καθαρὰν ἀνοῖξαι κλῇδα φρενῶν Eur.
the hook or tongue of a clasp, Od.
the collar-bone, so called because it locks the neck and breast together Il., Soph., etc.
a rowing bench, which locked the sides of the ship together, Od.
a narrow pass, "the key" of a country, Hdt.; a strait, Eur.
that can be shut or closed, Od., Thuc.
= κλεῖθρον, Lat. claustrum, Luc.
to shut, close, bar, κλήισεν δὲ θύρας barred the doors, Od.; ἐκλήισεν ὀχῆας shot the bars, so as to close the door, Id.; κλῄειν στόμα Eur.
to shut up, close, block, Βόσπορον κλήισαι Aesch.; κληίσειν τοὺς ἔσπλους ναυσί Thuc.:—Pass. to be shut up, Hdt.
to confine, Eur.
to celebrate.
Clio, one of the Muses, Hes. etc.; esp. the Muse of epic Poetry and History.
a theft, Eur., Ar.
a stratagem in war, Thuc.: a fraud, Dem., Aeschin.

a rumour, report, news, Lat. fama, Hom.; σὸν κλέος news of thee, Od.; c. gen., κλέος Ἀχαιῶν the report of their coming, Il.:— a mere report, opp. to certainty, κλέος οἶον ἀκούομεν, οὐδέ τι ἴδμεν we hear a rumour only, but know naught, Id.

good report, fame, glory, Hom.; κλέος οὐρανὸν ἵκει Od.; κλ. ἑλέσθαι, εὑρέσθαι Pind.; λαβεῖν Soph.; κλ. καταθέσθαι to lay up store of glory, Hdt., etc.: —in pl., ἄειδε κλέα ἀνδρῶν (shortd. from κλέεα), was singing the lays of their achievements, Il.

in bad sense, δύσφημον κλέος ill repute, Pind.; αἰσχρὸν κλ. Eur.;—both senses combined in Thuc., ἧς ἂν ἐπ’ ἐλάχιστον ἀρετῆς πέρι ἢ ψόγου κλέος ᾖ of whom there is least talk either for praise or blame.
one must conceal, Soph.
a thief, Il., Aesch., etc.: generally, a cheat, knave, Soph.
thieving, Plat.
the most arrant thief, Ar.
to steal, filch, purloin, Hom., etc.; τῆς γενεῆς ἔκλεψε from that breed Anchises stole, i. e. stole foals of that breed, Il.; σῶμα κλ. to let it down secretly, Eur.
in part. act. thievish, κλέπτον βλέπει he has a thief's look, Ar.
to cozen, cheat, deceive, beguile, Il., Hes., etc.:—Pass., προβαίνει κλεπτόμενος he goes on blindfold, Hdt.
like κρύπτω, to conceal, keep secret, disguise, Pind., Soph., Eur., etc.
to do secretly or treacherously, κλ. σφαγάς to perpetrate slaughter secretly, Soph.; κλ. μύθους to whisper malicious rumours, Id.; κλέπτων ἢ βιαζόμενος by fraud or force, Plat.
to seize or occupy secretly, Xen.
deceiving, dissembling, Hhymn.
a water-clock, like our sand-glasses, used to time speeches in the lawcourts, Ar.
name of an ebbing well in the Acropolis at Athens, Id.

entry.etym: Pass., epic 2nd sg. imperf. ἔκλεο (for ἐκλέεο）
entry.sense: to tell of, celebrate, Od., Hes., Eur.:—Pass. to be famous, Od., Pind.; ἔνθ’ ἀγοραὶ κλέονται where are held the famous meetings, Soph.
by name, Il.
an omen or presage contained in a word or sound, Od., Hdt., Aesch.
a rumour, tidings, report, Hdt., Trag.; κληηδὼν πατρός news of my father, Od.
glory, repute, Trag.
a calling on, appeal, πατρῷαι κληδόνες Aesch.
a name, appellation, Id.
to make famous, to celebrate in song, laud, Hhymn., Pind., Eur.:—Pass. to be spoken of, talked of, Aesch., Eur.
to name, call, Soph.:— Pass., ἔνθα κληίζεται οὑμός Κιθαιρών where is Cithaeron called mine, Id.; cf. κικλήσκω fin.
in late writers for κλείω, κλῄω, to shut.
the alder, prob. alnus, still called κλέθρα in Greece, Od.
a vine-twig, vine-branch, Lat. palmes, Ar., Plat.: generally, a cutting, slip, Xen.: —metaph., ἀνατέμνειν τὰ κλ. τὰ τοῦ δήμου Dem.:— the vine-switch of the Roman centurions, Lat. vitis, Plut.
of vine-twigs, Theogn.
Dim. of κλῆμα:—in pl. brush-wood, fagot-wood, Thuc.
to receive a share of an inheritance, to inherit a portion of property, c. gen., Dem.:—also c. acc. rei, to inherit, Luc.
to be an inheritor or heir, τινός of a person, Id.: also c. acc. to succeed one, Plut., Anth.
an inheritance, Luc.
an inheritance, Dem.:—generally, κλ. λαμβάνειν τινός to take possession of . . , Arist.
one who receives a portion of an inheritance, an inheritor, heir, Dem., etc.
distributed by shaking the lots, Hhymn.
a lot; in Hom., each man marks his own lot, and they are thrown into a helmet, and the first which came out was the winning lot.
a casting lots, drawing lots, Eur.; many officers at Athens obtained their offices by lot, as opp. to election (χειροτονία, αἵρεσις), Xen., Arist.; cf. κύαμος II.
an allotment of land assigned to citizens (cf. κληρουχία), Hdt., Thuc., etc.
any piece of land, a portion, farm, Hom., etc.
in Eccl. the clergy, as opp. to the laity.
to obtain by allotment, to have allotted to one, esp. of lands divided among conquerors, Hdt., etc.
the allotment of land to citizens in a foreign country, Arist.

collectively, = οἱ κληροῦχοι, the body of citizens who receive such allotments, Thuc., Plut.—An Athenian κληρουχία differed from a colony (ἀποικία), in that the κληροῦχοι were still citizens of the mother country, instead of forming an independent state.
of or for a κληρουχία, γῆ κλ. land for allotment, Ar.; τὰ κληρουχικά (sc. χρήματα) Dem.
one who held an allotment of land, esp. to citizens in a foreign country (v. κληρουχία), an allottee, Hdt., Thuc., etc.:—metaph., μητέρα πολλῶν ἐτῶν κληροῦχον having old age for her lot, Soph.
to appoint to an office by lot, opp. to αἱρεῖσθαι or χειροτονεῖν, Hdt., attic:—of the lot, to fall on, Lat. designare, Eur.:— Pass. to be appointed by lot, Dem., etc.
to cast lots, draw lots, Plat.;—so in Mid., Aesch., Dem.
in Mid. also, κληροῦσθαί τι to have allotted one, obtain by lot, Eur., Aeschin.; also c. gen., Dem.
to allot, assign, Pind., Thuc.
κλ. ὀμφάν to deliver an oracle, Eur.
appointed by lot, opp. to αἱρετός and κεχειροτονημένος (elected), Plat., etc.
a calling, call, Xen., etc.
a calling into court, legal summons, prosecution, Ar., Xen., etc.
an invitation to a feast, Xen., Dem.
a name, appellation, Plat.
a shutting up, closing, Thuc.
to be called, named, Plat.
κλητέον, one must call, Id.
to summon into court or give evidence that a summons has been served (v. κλητήρ), Ar.
one who calls, a summoner, or rather a witness who gave evidence that the legal summons had been served (cf. Horace's licet antestari), Ar., Dem.
generally, = κῆρυξ, Aesch.
called, invited, welcome, Od.
called out, chosen, Il.
the round of a ladder, Eur.
a ladder or staircase (because of its leaning aslant), Od., etc.:— a scaling-ladder, Thuc., Xen.; κλίμακος προσαμβάσεις Aesch.:— a ship's ladder, Eur., Theocr.
a frame with cross-bars, on which persons to be tortured were tied, Ar.
in Soph., κλίμακες ἀμφίπλεκτοι intertwining ladders, to express the entanglement of the limbs of wrestlers.
a climax, i. e. a gradual ascent from weaker expressions to stronger, Lat. gradatio, as Cicero's abiit, evasit, erupit.
an inclination, slope:—esp. the supposed slope of the earth towards the pole: hence a region or zone of the earth, clime, Plut., Anth.
of or for beds, Dem.
that on which one lies, a couch or bed, Hdt., Ar., etc.:—also, a bier, Thuc.
bed-ridden, Lat. lecto affixus, Plut.
Lat. clinicus, a physician that visits his patients in their beds, Anth.
bed-ridden, Xen.
making beds or bedsteads, an upholsterer, Plat., Dem.
a couch, sofa, Od., Theocr.
to make to bend, slope, or slant, Lat. inclinare, κλίνειν τάλαντα to incline or turn the scale, Il.; Τρῶας ἔκλιναν made them give way, Id.; ἔκλινε μάχην turned the tide of war, Id.
to make one thing lean against another, i. e. σάκε’ ὤμοισι κλίναντες, i. e. raising their shields so that the upper rim rested on their shoulders, Id.
to turn aside, ὄσσε πάλιν κλίνασα having turned back her eyes, Id.
to make to recline, ἐν κλίνηι κλ. τινά to make him lie down at table, Hdt.:—metaph., ἡμέρα κλίνει ἅπαντα puts to rest, lays low all things, Soph.
Pass. to be bent, bend, ἐκλίνθη he bent aside, swerved, Il.; of a pan, ἂψ ἑτέρως’ ἐκλίθη it was tipped over to the other side, Od.
to lean or stay oneself upon or against a thing, c. dat., Hom.; so in Mid., κλινάμενος Od.:—also, κεκλιμένος ἐπάλξεσιν seeking safety in them, Il.
to lie down, lie, Hom., etc.; to lie on a couch at meals, Hdt., etc.
of Places (in perf.), to lie sloping towards the sea, ἁλὶ κεκλιμένη Od.; νῆσοι, αἵθ’ ἁλὶ κεκλίαται (epic for κέκλινται), Id.
to wander from the right course, Theogn.
Mid. to decline, of the day, Hdt.; so, intr. in Act., ἡ ἡμέρα ἤρξατο κλίνειν NTest.:—metaph., κλ. ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον to fall off, degenerate, Xen.
folding doors or gates, Plut.: —metaph. a means of entrance, access, Hdt.
a place for lying down, hence

a hut, cot, cabin, such as besiegers lived in during long sieges, Il.:—that they were not tents, but wooden huts, appears from Il. 24.448 sq.; and when an army broke up, it burnt them on the spot, Od. 8.501
a couch or easy chair, Od., Pind.
a bed, nuptial bed, Eur.
a company of people sitting at meals, NTest.
a reclining or lying, Plut.
out of or from a hut, Il.
into or to the hut, Il.
the outbuildings round a herdman's cot, Od.
a bending, inclination, τοῦ τραχήλου Plut.
a lying down, lying, Eur.
a couch, Hom.
a clime, Anth.
a slope, hill-side, Lat. clivus, Hom., Soph.
a dog-collar, esp. a large wooden collar, put on mischievous dogs, Ar., Xen.
a sort of pillory, Eur.
χρύσεος κλ. a collar of gold, Id., Anth.
to drive in confusion, drive before one, Il., Hes.
generally, to ruffle, Soph., Ar.
Pass. to be driven in confusion, rush wildly, Il., Pind.
to be beaten by the waves, Soph.
any confused motion, the press of battle, battle-rout, turmoil, Il.; κλόνοι ἱππιόχαρμαι throngs of fighting horsemen, Aesch.
stolen, Aesch., Eur.
a thief, stealer, Soph.
generally, a secret doer, perpetrator, Id.
theft, Lat. furtum, Aesch., Eur.
a secret act, fraud, Eur., Aeschin.; κλοπῇ by stealth or fraud, Soph.; ποδοῖν κλοπὰν ἀρέσθαι, i. e. to steal away, Id.
the surprise of a military post, Xen.
thievish, artful, μῦθοι Od.
a thief, Hhymn.
to deal subtly, to spin out time by false pretences, Il.;—it seems to be a lengthd. form of κλέπτω, κλωπεύω.
Pass. to be tossed like waves, NTest.
a little wave, ripple, Eur.; generally, a wave, Aesch.:—as collective noun, the surf, Thuc.
metaph., κλ. χολῆς Aesch.
a wave, billow, and collectively surf Od., Trag.
metaph., κλ. κακῶν a sea of troubles, Aesch.; κλ. ξυμφορᾶς Soph.; κλ. ἔφιππος a flood of horsemen, Id., etc.
to dash over, of a wave, Hhymn.: to dash like a wave, Aesch.:—Pass. to be dashed up, of the sea, Hom.; to rise in waves, Hes.
to wash off or away, Eur.
to wash or rinse out, Xen.
εἰς ὦτα κλ. to put water into the ears and so cleanse them, Eur.
κεκλυσμένος καρῶι washed over or coated with wax, Theocr.
famous, Theocr.
a liquid used for washing out: esp. a clyster, drench, Hdt.
a place washed by the waves, the sea-beach, Plut., Luc.
a clyster-pipe, syringe, Hdt.
the queen of Agamemnon, Il.
famous for trees, Anth.
famous for work, Od., Anth.
glorious with fruit, Pind.
famous for skill, Hhymn.
famous for toils, Anth.
famous for wisdom, Anth.
with famous children, Anth.
with noble steeds, Il.
heard of, i. e. famous, renowned, glorious, of persons, Hom.
of things, noble, splendid, beauteous, Id., etc.
famous for his art, renowned artist, Hom.
famous for the bow, renowned archer, Hom.
to hear, Hom., etc.; κλύειν τί τινος to hear a thing from a person, Il., etc.; then, κλύειν τινος to hear him, Id.; κλ. τι to hear it, Od., etc.:—c. gen. objecti, to hear of a person or thing, Soph.
to perceive generally, know, Od., Hes.

to give ear to, attend to, τινός Hom., etc.; the imperat. is esp. used in prayers, give ear to me, hear me, κλῦθί μευ, Ἀργυρότοξε Il.; κέκλυτέ μευ, θεοί Id.:—also c. dat. to listen to, obey, Hes., etc.
in Trag. like ἀκούω V. to be called or spoken of so and so, with an adv., εὖ or κακῶς κλύειν.
a bird-cage, Anth.
the clucking of hens: the clucking sound by which we urge on a horse, Xen.
to croak, of jackdaws:—then, in sign of disapprobation, to hoot, Dem.
the spinners, a name of the Parcae or goddesses of fate, Od.
spinster, one of the three Μοῖραι or Parcae, who spins the thread of life, Hes.; Lachesis had charge of the past, Clotho of the present, Atropos of the future, Plat., Luc.
to twist by spinning, spin, Hdt., Luc.:—Pass., τὰ κλωσθέντα one's destiny, Plat.
stony, rocky, Il.
a heap of stones,
a twig, spray, Soph., Eur.
to steal, Xen.
thievish, clandestine, Eur.
to cluck like a hen.
a spindle, Theocr.
a thread, yarn, line, Ar.; λίνου κλ. the flaxen thread, i. e. the net, Aesch.
a web, Eur.
a thief, Hdt., Eur., Xen.
to card or dress cloth, (which was done either with a prickly plant, the teasel, or with a comb):—of torture, to card, lacerate, Aesch., Soph.
a fuller's shop, Hdt.
a fuller, i. e. a cloth-dresser, clothes-cleaner, Hdt., Ar.
to clean cloth, Ar.
the prickly teasel, a plant used by fullers to dress cloth.
a carding-comb, also used as an instrument of torture, Hdt.
to scrape or grate, Lat. radere, Il.; τὸν κηρὸν κνᾶν to scrape it off, Hdt.
to scratch:— Mid. to scratch oneself, Plat.
to tickle, Id.; Mid., κνᾶσθαι τὰ ὦτα to tickle one's ears, Luc.
to cloud over, obscure, Aesch.
dark, dusky, Aesch., Eur.
in the dark, early in the morning, Ar.
darkness, evening dusk, twilight, Il., Aesch.; also, τὸ κατὰ γῆς κν. Eur.
later, the morning twilight or dawn, Lat. diluculum, κνέφᾳ at dawn, Xen.
to scratch, tickle:—Pass. to itch, NTest.
pale yellow, tawny, Theocr., Anth.: hence the goat is called κνάκων, ὁ, Theocr.; and the wolf κνηκίας, Babr.
white-legged, Theocr.
the part between the knee and ankle, the leg, Lat. tibia, Hom., Hdt., Eur., etc.
wearing greaves, Hdt.

a greave or piece of armour from knee to ankle, Lat. ocrea, περὶ κνήμῃσιν ἔθηκεν Il.; the κνημῖδες were fastened at the ankle with clasps (ἐπισφύρια) : βόειαι κνημῖδες are ox-hide leggings, used by labourers, Od.
the projecting limb or (as we say) shoulder of a mountain, Hom.
Desiderat. of κνάω, to wish to scratch, to feel an itching, to itch, Plat.
scraping or gnawing gold, Anth.
a sting, bite, Xen.
an itching, irritation, Plut.
a knife for scraping cheese, Il.
a nettle, Lat. urtica, Theocr., Anth.
of or from Cnidos; οἱ Κνίδιοι the Cnidians, Hdt.

to scrape or grate: to tickle: metaph., of love, to nettle, chafe, irritate, Hdt., Eur.; of satiety, Pind.; of anxiety, Hdt., etc.; οὐ κνίσω τὸ ῥῆμ’ ἕκαστον will not attack every word, Ar.:—Pass., κνίζεσθαί τινος to be stung (with love) for one, Theocr.
κν. ὀργάν to provoke anger, Pind.
niggardly, Anth.
Lat. nidor, the steam and odour which exhales from roasting meat, the savour and steam of burnt sacrifice, which ascends up to heaven as a gift to the gods, Hom.
that which caused this smell and steam, i. e. the fat, in which the flesh of the victim was wrapped and burnt, μηρούς τ’ ἐξέταμον κατά τε κνίσῃ ἐκάλυψαν Il.
to fill with the steam or savour of burnt sacrifice, Eur., Ar.
full of the steam of burnt sacrifice, steamy, Od.
in pl. scrapings, Plat.
scratches, Anth.: quarrels, Id.
an itching of the skin, tickling, Ar.
to reduce to vapour, Luc.
steaming, of a sacrifice, Aesch.
like σκνίψ, a small insect which gnaws figs, Ar.
Dep. properly of a dog, to whine, whimper, Soph., Ar.
a whining, whimpering, Od.
= κνυζηθμός of infants, Lat. vagitus, Hdt.
to disfigure the eyes, make dim and dark Od.
any dangerous animal, from a lion to a serpent or worm, a monster, beast, Od., Hes., Trag.: —of persons, as a term of reproach, ὦ παντομισῆ κνώδαλα Aesch.
in pl. κνώδοντες, two projecting teeth on the blade of a hunting spear, Xen.; ξίφους διπλοῖ κνώδοντες, i. e. a two-edged sword, Soph.: also κνώδων alone for a sword, Id.
to slumber, sleep, Od., Pind.
a stupid fellow, booby, Ar.
Comic word, to express the croaking of frogs, βρεκεκεκὲξ κοὰξ κοάξ Ar.
a knavish trick, Ar.
an impudent rogue, arrant knave, Ar.: —Κόβαλοι were mischievous goblins, invoked by rogues, Id. II. as adj. κόβαλα, knavish tricks, rogues, Id.
as adj. κόβαλα, knavish tricks,
a mussel or cockle, Lat. concha, Xen.
the case round a seal attached to diplomas or documents, Ar.
full of shells, λίθος κογχ. shelly marble, Xen.
a small kind of mussel or cockle, Arist.
its shell, any bivalve-shell, Hdt.
the Lat. quadrans, = 1/4 of an as, NTest.
to mark, perceive, hear, Anacr.

Lat. cothurnus, a buskin or high boot, reaching to the middle of the leg, Hdt., etc. The κόθορνος was worn by tragic actors, its heels serving to add height to the figure: thus it became the emblem of Tragedy, as the soccus of Comedy.
since the buskins might be worn on either foot, ὁ Κόθορνος was a nickname for a trimmer or timeserver, such as Theramenes, Xen.
of drones, dock-tailed, i. e. without a sting, Hes.
entry.etym: Prob. from κοθώ an old word for βλάβη, and οὐρά tail.

entry.sense: to cry κοΐ, squeak like a young pig, Ar.

entry.etym: ionic for ποίᾳ, dat. sg. of ποῖος, ionic κοῖος
entry.sense: used as adv. how? in what way? in what respect? Hdt.
to make hollow, scoop out, Hdt.; κ. χῶμα, i. e. to dig a grave, Theocr.
a hollow, deep valley, Anth.

entry.etym: fem. of κοῖλος, name of a δῆμος in Attica, Hdt.

entry.sense: the large cavity of the body, the belly, Lat. venter, Hdt., Ar., etc.
the intestines, bowels, Hdt.; κ. ὑεία pig's tripe, Ar.; in pl. tripe and puddings, Id.
a tripe-seller, Ar.
hollow-bellied, hungry, Aesch.: metaph. a hollow shield, Id.
lying in a hollow, Pind.

hollow, hollowed, epith. of ships, which in early times were hollowed out of trees, Hom.; later, κοίλη ναῦς was the hold of the ship, Hdt., Xen.; so, ἡ κοίλη alone, Theocr.:—of the Trojan horse, κ. λόχος, κ. δόρυ Od.; κ. κάπετος, of a grave, Il.; κ. δέμνια, of the bed when no one is in it, Soph.

of Places, lying in a hollow or forming a hollow, κοίλη Λακεδαίμων the vale of L., Od.; κ. Θεσσαλία Hdt.; κ. Ἄργος Soph.; τὰ Κοῖλα τῆς Εὐβοίας Hdt.; ἡ Κοιλή the valley of the Ilissus, Id.:— κ. λιμήν of a harbour lying between high cliffs, Od.; κ. αἰγιαλός an embayed beach, Id.:— κ. ὁδός a hollow way, Il.:— κ. ποταμός a river nearly empty of water, Thuc. (so Virgil, cava flumina): metaph. of the voice, hollow, μυκάσατο κοῖλον Theocr.; φθέγγεσθαι κοῖλον Luc.
as Subst. κοῖλον, ου, τό, a hollow, cavity, ravine, Plat.; like κοιλία, of the cavities in the body, τὰ κ. γαστρός Eur.; also, ἐν τῷ κοίλῳ καὶ μυχῷ τοῦ λιμένος Thuc.
hollow-eyed, Xen.
hollow-rimmed, Anth.
hollow-like, cavernous, φάραγξ Babr.
a hollow, cavity, Babr., etc.
hollow-eyed: fem. κοιλῶπις, ιδος, Anth.
hollow to look at: hollow, Eur.
to lull or hush to sleep, put to sleep, Hom.
metaph. to lull to rest, still, calm, ἀνέμους, κύματα Id.; ὀδύνας Il.; κοίμησον εὔφημον στόμα lay thy tongue asleep in silence, Aesch.
Mid. and Pass. to fall asleep, go or lie abed, Hom., Hdt., etc.
of the sleep of death, κοιμήσατο χάλκεον ὕπνον he slept an iron sleep, Il.: absol. to fall asleep, die, Soph., NTest.
to keep watch at night, Lat. excubare, Aesch., Xen.
sleep, κοιμήματα αὐτογέννητα intercourse of the mother with her own child, Soph.
a lying down to sleep, Plat., NTest.

to put to sleep, Eur.; ἄημα ἐκοίμισε πόντον, i. e. the winds suffer the sea to rest— by ceasing (cf. Virg. straverunt aequora venti), Soph.: metaph., μεγαληγορίαν κ. to lay pride asleep, Eur.; so, κ. τὰς λύπας Xen.:—Pass., παῖς κοιμίζεται Eur.
of the sleep of death, Soph., Eur.; also in Mid., Eur.
one who puts to bed, Anth.

entry.etym: dat. fem. of κοινός, used as adv., v. κοινός B. II.

entry.sense: to deliberate in common, Xen.
having a common bed, a bedfellow, consort, Aesch.
a paramour, Soph.
to commune or take counsel with, τινι Hdt., attic; πρός τινα Thuc.
sailing in common, Soph.
of common foot, κ. παρουσία, i. e. the arrival of persons all together, Soph.
common, shared in common, opp. to ἴδιος, Hes., attic; proverb., κοινὸν τύχη Aesch.; κοινὰ τὰ τῶν φίλων Eur.
c. dat., κ. τινι common to or with another, Aesch.; also c. gen., πάντων κ. φάος Id.
common to all the people, common, public, general, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
τὸ κοινόν the state, Lat. respublica, Hdt., attic
the government, public authorities, Thuc., Xen.; ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ by public authority, Hdt.; ἄνευ τοῦ τῶν πάντων κοινοῦ without consent of the league, Thuc.
the public treasury, Hdt., Thuc.
τὰ κοινά public affairs, Oratt.; πρὸς τὰ κοινὰ προσελθεῖν, προσιέναι to enter public life, Dem., etc.; also the public money, Ar.
common, ordinary, usual, Plat., etc.
of Persons, of common origin or kindred, esp. of brothers and sisters, Pind., Soph.
like κοινωνός, a partner, Soph., Ar.
lending a ready ear to all, impartial, Thuc., Plat.:— courteous, affable, Xen.
of events, κοινότεραι τύχαι more impartial (i. e. more equal) chances, Thuc.
of meats, common, profane, NTest.
adv. κοινῶς, in common, jointly, opp. to ἰδίᾳ, Eur., etc.
publicly, Thuc., etc.
sociably, like other citizens, Arist., Plut.
in common language or fashion, Plut.
so fem. dat. κοινῇ, in common, by common consent, in concert, Hdt., Soph., Eur.
publicly, Xen.
so with Preps., ἐς κοινόν in common, Aesch.; εἰς τὸ κ. for common use, Plat.
a sharing in common, community, partnership, Plat., etc.
affability, Xen.
of or from common parents, ἐλπίδες κ. hopes in one born of the same parents, i. e. a brother, Soph.
loving in common, Aesch.
like-minded with, τινί Eur.
to make common, communicate, impart a thing to another, κ. τί τινι Aesch., Eur., etc.; τι ἔς τινα Eur.
to make common, to defile, profane, NTest.: —Mid. to deem or pronounce profane, Id.
Mid. to communicate one to another, Aesch., Soph.
to cause to be communicated, τί τινι Plat.
to take counsel with, τινι Xen.
to be partner or partaker, τινος of a thing, Eur.
c. acc. rei, to take part or share in, Id., Thuc.
Pass. to have intercourse with, Eur.
to have or do in common with, have a share of or take part in a thing with another, τινός τινι Xen.
κ. τινός to have a share of or take part in a thing, Trag., Xen.
κ. τινι to have dealings with or intercourse, Ar., Plat.
rarely c. acc. rei, κ. φόνον τινι to commit murder in common with him, Eur.
absol. to share in an opinion, to agree, Plat.:— to form a community, Arist.
in pl. acts of communion, communications, dealings between man and man, Plat.
one must give a share, Plat.
communion, association, partnership, fellowship, Pind., Thuc., etc.
c. gen. objecti, communion with, partnership in, Eur., etc.; τίς θαλάσσης βουκόλοις κ.; what communion have herdsmen with the sea? Id.
a common gift, contribution, alms, NTest.
held in common, social, Arist.
giving a share, τινος of a thing, Luc.
a companion, partner, τινος in a thing, Aesch., etc.; ὁ τοῦ κακοῦ κ. accomplice in the evil, Soph.; also, τινι in a thing, Eur.
absol. a partner, fellow, Plat., Dem.
as adj. = κοινός, Eur.
Comic word, to express the squeaking of young pigs, Ar.
to be lord or master, to rule, command, Hom.
c. gen. to be lord of, Hes., Aesch.; also, c. dat., Aesch.
sovereignty, Anth.
a ruler, commander, Hom., Trag.
to put to bed:—Mid., doric aor1 ἐκοιταξάμην, to go to bed, sleep, Pind.
in bed, ap. Dem.
as Subst., κοιταῖον, ου, τό, the lair of a wild beast, Plut.
the marriage-bed, Soph., Eur.
the lair of a beast, nest of a bird, Eur.
the act of going to bed, τῆς κοίτης ὥρη bed- time, Hdt.; τραπέζῃ καὶ κοίτῃ δέκεσθαι to entertain "at bed and board, " Id.
ἔχειν κοίτην ἔκ τινος to be pregnant by a man, NTest.:—in bad sense, chambering, lasciviousness, Id.
a place to lie on, bed, Od.
sleep, Id., Hes.
a bed-chamber, ὁ ἐπὶ τοῦ κοιτῶνος a chamberlain, praefectus cubiculi, NTest.
scarlet, Lat. coccineus, Plut., NTest.
a grain, seed, Hhymn., Hdt.
the kermesberry, used to dye scarlet, Theophr.
to cry cuckoo, Hes.; of the cock, to crow, Theocr.
to cry like a cuckoo, give a signal by such cry, Ar.

a cuckoo, so called from its cry κόκκυ, Lat. cuculus, Hes., Ar., etc.; ἐχειροτόνησάν με κόκκυγές γε τρεῖς I was elected by three cuckoo-voices, i. e. by three who gave their votes over and over again, Ar.
properly cuckoo! the bird's cry, used as an exclamation, now! quick! κόκκυ, πεδίονδε Ar.; κόκκυ, μεθεῖτε quick— let go, Id.
a pomegranate-seed, Solon.
ancestors, Anth.

entry.etym: Prob. from κόλος, akin to κολούω
entry.sense: Properly, to curtail, dock, prune: then, like Lat. castigare, to keep within bounds, check, correct, Plat.:—perf. pass. part. chastened, Arist.
to chastise, punish, Soph., Eur., etc.:—Mid. to get a person punished, Ar., Plat.:—Pass. to be punished, Xen.
flattery, fawning, Plat., Aeschin.
a piece of flattery, Xen.
to be flattered, Luc.
disposed to flatter, flattering, fawning, Luc.: ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) = κολακεία, Plat.
to flatter, Ar., Xen., etc.:— Pass. to be flattered, be open to flattery, Dem.
parasite-named, Comic distortion of the name Κλε-ώνυμος, Ar.
a flatterer, fawner, Ar., Plat., etc.
a chisel, Luc.
of birds, to peck at, Luc., Anth.:—of Pegasus, to strike the ground with his hoof, Anth.
to carve or chisel, Id.
chastisement, correction, punishment, Plat., etc.
chastisement, Xen.
to be chastised, Plat.
κολαστέον, one must chastised, Id.
a house of correction, Luc.
= κόλασμα, κόλασις, Xen.
a chastiser, punisher, Trag.
corrective, Plat.
to buffet, NTest.
a sheath, scabbard of a sword, Lat. culeus, Hom., attic
to trample on, τινα Ar.
= κόλλοψ, Luc.
a kind of cake or roll, Ar.
glue, Lat. gluten, Hdt.
to glue, cement, Ar., Plat.
to join one metal to another, κ. χρυσὸν ἐλέφαντά τε, i. e. to make [a crown] inlaid with gold and ivory, Pind.

generally, to join fast together:— Pass. to cleave to, κεκόλληται πρὸς ἄτᾳ is indissolubly bound to woe, Aesch.; so, of persons, κ. τινι to cleave to another, NTest.; and of things, ὁ κονιορτὸς ὁ κολληθείς τινι Id.
to put together, build, Pind.
a glueing or welding, κ. σιδήρου a welding of iron, Lat. ferruminatio, or perhaps the art of inlaying or damasking iron, Hdt., Theophr.
glued together, closely joined, well-framed, Hom., Eur., etc.
ὑποκρητηρίδιον κολλητόν a stand welded to the κρητήρ, Hdt.
roll-eating, Ar.
a roll or loaf of coarse bread.
the peg or screw by which the strings of the lyre were tightened, Od., Plat.:—metaph., τῆς ὀργῆς τὸν κόλλοπ’ ἀνιέναι to let down the strings of your passion, Ar.
a small money-changer, NTest.
a small coin, κολλύβου for a doit, Ar.
in pl. κόλλυβα, τά, small round cakes, Id.
eye-salve, Lat. collyrium.
a fine clay, in which a seal can be impressed, Luc.
docked, curtailed, c. gen., κολοβὸς κεράτων, Lat. truncus pedum, Plat.; κ. χειρῶν Anth.
absol. maimed, mutilated, Xen.
to dock, curtail, shorten, NTest.
a chief of jackdaws, jackdaw-general, Ar.
a jackdaw, daw, Lat. graculus, Il., Pind., Ar.: proverbs: κολοιὸς ποτὶ κολοιόν "birds of a feather flock together, " Arist.; κολοιὸς ἀλλοτρίοις πτεροῖς ἀγάλλεται a jackdaw "in borrowed plumes, " Luc.
a large heavy wave before it breaks (κόλον κῦμα), the swell that foreruns a storm, Ar.
a pumpkin, Lat. cucurbita.
made from pumpkins, Anth.
made from pumpkins, πλοῖα Luc.
the colon or lower intestine, Ar.
docked, curtal, Lat. curtus, Il.;of oxen, stump-horned or hornless, Hdt.; so, ὦ κόλε, addressed to a he-goat, Theocr.

a colossus, of the huge statues in the Egypt. temples, Hdt.: generally a statue, Aesch., Theocr. The most famous Colossus was that of Apollo at Rhodes, 70 cubits high, made in the time of Demetrius Poliorcetes, Luc.
poet. word, a noisy rabble, Il., Ar.
dock-tailed, Plut.
a docking, cutting short, Arist.
to cut short, dock, curtail, Hdt.

metaph. to cut off, disappoint, τὸ μὲν τελέει, τὸ δὲ κολούει part he brings to pass, part he cuts off, of the threats of Achilles, Il.; μηδὲ τὰ δῶρα κολούετε curtail them not, Od.:—of persons, τὰ ὑπερέχοντα κ. to cut down, degrade, those who are exalted above others, Hdt.:—Pass. to be cut short or abridged, Aesch.; ἐπειδὰν κολουθῶσι when they suffer abatement, Thuc.
a summit, top, finishing, κολοφῶνα ἐπιτιθέναι, to put the finishing stroke to a thing, Plat.
swelling in folds, Aesch.
Lat. sinus:
the bosom, Il.
the womb, Eur.

the fold formed by a loose garment, as it fell over the girdle, Il.:—this fold sometimes served for a pocket, Od., Hdt.; κόλπον ἀνιεμένη letting down her robe so as to form a fold, i. e. baring her breast, Il.; κόλπῳ πεπλώματος under the deep-folded robe, Aesch.; ἐπὶ σφυρὰ κόλπον ἀνεῖσαι having let their folded robes fall down to their ankles, Theocr.
any hollow, as
of the sea, first, in a half-literal sense, Θέτις ὑπεδέξατο κόλπῳ received him in her bosom, Il.; then, of the deep hollow between waves, Hom.
a bay or gulf of the sea, Il., Aesch.
a vale, κ. Ἀργεῖος Pind.; Ἐλευσινίας Δηοῦς ἐν κόλποις Soph.

to form into a swelling fold; esp. to make a sail belly or swell, Lat. sinuare, ἄνεμος κ. τὴν ὀθόνην Luc.; χιτῶνας κολπώσαντες τῷ ἀνέμῳ, καθάπερ ἱστία Id.:—Pass. to bosom or swell out, of a sail, Mosch.; κολποῦται Ζέφυρος εἰς ὀθόνας Anth.; of a bay, to curve, Polyb.
embosomed, embayed, Eur.
a folded garment, Plut.
to plunge into the sea, NTest.
a swimming-bath, Plat.
a diver, Thuc., Plat., etc.
a sea-bird, a diver, Ar.
a diver, Ar.
a Colchian, Hdt., etc.:—adj. Κολχικός, ή, όν, Colchian, Id.:—fem. Κολχίς, ίδος, and as Subst. Κολχίς ( sub. γῆ), Eur.
to brawl, scold, Il.
from the deme Κολωνός (q. v.), Dem.
a hill, mound, Il.: esp. a sepulchral mound, barrow, Lat. tumulus, Soph.
the Lat. colonia, NTest.
a hill, Hhymn., Hdt.; κ. λίθων a heap of stones, Hdt.
Colonus, a deme of Attica lying on a hill, about a mile NW. of Athens, immortalised by Sophocles, who was a native of it, in his Oed. Col.
a brawling, wrangling, Il.
the strawberry-tree, arbutus, Ar.
eating the fruit of the arbutus, Ar.

to let the hair grow long, wear long hair, Il.; κομέειν τὴν κεφαλήν Hdt. In early times the Greeks wore their hair long, whence κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοί in Hom. At Sparta the fashion continued. At Athens it was so worn by youths up to the 18th year, when they offered their long locks to some deity; and to wear long hair was considered as a sign of aristocratic habits: hence

κομᾶν meant to plume oneself, give oneself airs, be proud or haughty, like Lat. cristam tollere, Ar.; οὗτος ἐκόμησε ἐπὶ τυραννίδι he aimed at the monarchy, Hdt.; ἐπὶ τῷ κομᾷς; on what do you plume yourself? Ar.
of horses, χρυσέῃσιν ἐθείρῃσιν κομόωντε decked with golden manes, Il.
metaph. of trees, plants, foliage, Hhymn., etc.
to take care of, attend to, tend, Hom.

the hair, hair of the head, Lat. coma, Hom., etc.; also in pl., Id.: —κόμην τρέφειν to let the hair grow long, Hdt.; κόμην κείρεσθαι to shave off the hair, in mourning, Od., etc.; κόμαι πρόσθετοι false hair, a wig, Xen.
metaph. the foliage, leaves of trees, Od.
Comic adaptation of the name ὁ Αμψνιας, coxcomb-Amynias (cf. κομάω), Ar.
wearing long hair, long-haired, ap. Hdt., Ar.
metaph., ἰὸς κ. a feathered arrow, Soph.; λειμὼν κ. a grassy meadow, Eur.
as Subst. a comet, Arist.
attendance, care, in Il., always of care bestowed on horses; in Od., of care bestowed on men, by means of baths, etc.; also, care bestowed on a garden, Od.
provision, supplies, Id.
carriage, conveyance, importation, Thuc.: a gathering in of harvest, Xen.
(from Mid. also) a carrying away for oneself, a recovery, Hdt.:— the recovery of a debt, payment, Dem.
(from Pass.) a going or coming, Hdt.: an escape, safe return, Id.
exactly, just, Plat., Dem.
like πάνυ, absolutely, altogether, quite, Plat.; οὐ κομιδῇ not at all, Plut.
in answers, κομιδῇ μὲν οὖν just so, yes certainly, Ar., Plat.
to take care of, provide for, Hom.:— to receive hospitably, to entertain, Thuc.; more commonly in Mid., Hom.
of things, to mind, attend to, give heed to, Id., etc.; ἔξω κομίζειν πηλοῦ πόδα to keep one's foot out of the mud, Aesch.
to carry away so as to preserve, carry home, carry safe away, Il., etc.; simply, to save, rescue, τινὰ ἐκ θανάτου Pind.; but, νεκρὸν κ. to carry out to burial, Soph., Eur.
to carry off as a prize or as booty, Il., Pind.:—Mid. to get for oneself, receive in full, acquire, gain, Soph., etc.
to carry, convey, bear, Hom., etc.:—Pass. to be conveyed, to journey, travel, Hdt.; εἴσω κομίζου get thee in, Aesch.; so in fut. and aor1 mid., κομιεύμεθα ἐς Σίριν Hdt., etc.
to bring to a place, bring hither, bring in, καρπὸν κ. to gather in corn, Id., etc.:—so in Mid., Id., Soph.; and perf. pass. in mid. sense, τοὺς καρποὺς κεκόμισθε you have reaped the fruits, Dem.
to conduct, escort, Soph., Plat., etc.; κ. ναῦς Thuc.
to get back, recover, Pind., Eur., Plat., etc.:—Mid. to get back for oneself, recover, Eur., Thuc.; κομίζεσθαι χρήματα to recover a debt, Dem.:—Pass. to come or go back, return, Hdt., attic
like Lat. affero, to bring, give, Aesch.
to be taken care of, to be gathered in, Aesch.
κομιστέον, one must bring, Plat.
one who takes care of, Eur.
a bringer, conductor, Id.
in pl., like σῶστρα, reward for saving, Aesch.
reward for bringing, Eur.
the stamp or impression of a coin, Ar.: proverb., πονηροῦ κόμματος of bad stamp, Id.
= νόμισμα, coin, coinage, Id.
a short clause of a sentence, Lat. comma, Cic.
consisting of short clauses, μικρὰ καὶ κ. ἐρωτήματα Luc.
gum, Lat. gummi, Hdt.
a striking: esp. like Lat. planctus (from plango), a beating of the breast in lamentation, ἔκοψα κομμὸν Ἄριον I lamented with Median lamentation, Aesch.
in attic Drama, a wild lament, sung alternately by an actor and the chorus, such as Aesch. Ag. 1072-1185.
to beautify, Arist.
a beautifier, embellisher, Luc.
of or for embellishment:— ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη), the art of embellishment, Plat.
a dresser, tirewoman, Ar., Plat.
to vaunt, boast, brag, Trag.; c. acc. cogn., κ. λόγον to speak big words, Aesch.

to boast of, κ. γέρας to boast one's office, Id.:—Pass. to be renowned, Eur.; φόβος κομπάζεται fear is loudly spoken, Aesch.; τινὸς δὲ παῖς πατρὸς κομπάζεται; of what father is he said to be the son? Eur.
Com. word, one of the Κόμποσ- deme, a bragsman, Ar.
in pl. boasts, braggart words, Aesch., Ar.
a braggart, Plut.
to ring, clash, κόμπει χαλκός Il.
metaph., like κομπάζω, to speak big, boast, brag, vaunt, Hdt., Eur.; c. acc. cogn., κ. μῦθον to speak a boastful speech, Soph.
c. acc. to boast of, Aesch.:—Pass., to be boasted of, Thuc.
to talk big, be an empty braggart, Ar.
a noise, din, clash, as of a boar's tusks when he whets them, Il.; the stamping of dancers' feet, Od.
metaph. a boast, vaunt, Hdt., Aesch., etc.
rarely in good sense, praise, Pind.
pomp-bundle-worded, derisive epith. of Aeschylus in Ar.
boastful, vainglorious, Thuc.; τὸ κομπῶδες boastfulness, Id.
refinement, esp. of language, Plat.
with Euripides-prettinesses (shortened from κομψευριπιδικῶς), Ar.
to refine upon, quibble upon, κόμψευε νῦν τὴν δόξαν aye, quibble on the word δόξα (referring to the previous line), Soph.:—Mid. to deal in refinements or subtleties, Plat.
dainty-seeming, Ar.
well-dressed, Lat. comptus; hence, a pretty fellow, Lat. bellus homo, Ar.

accomplished, elegant, exquisite, refined, dainty, clever, witty, of persons or their words and acts, Id.; κ. περί τι clever about a thing, Plat.; of a dog's instinct, exquisite, acute, Id.; in a sneering sense, of Sophists who refine overmuch, studied, affected, Eur., etc.
adv. κομψῶς, elegantly, prettily, daintily, Ar., Plat., etc.
κομψότερον ἔχειν to be better in health, NTest.
to resound, clash, ring, reecho, Hom., Hes.
with a noise, clash, din, Anth.
a ringing, clashing, din, Od., Hes.
a knuckle, κονδύλοις πατάξαι, opp. to ἐπὶ κόρρης (a slap in the face), Dem.: proverb., κολλύραν καὶ κόνδυλον ὄψον ἐπ’ αὐτῇ a roll and knuckle- sauce to it, i. e. a good thrashing, Ar.
to raise dust: to hasten, Anth.
dust, a cloud of dust, stirred up by men's feet, Il.; also in pl., like Lat. arenae, Hom., etc.
sand or soil (v. ὑπερέπτω) Il.
ashes, in pl. like Lat. cineres, Od.
a fine powder, sprinkled over wrestlers' bodies after being oiled, to make them more easily grasped by the opponent:—this powder was also used in the bath, Ar.
entry.etym: ῑ in κονίῃσιν, in other cases ῑ usually.

entry.sense: plastered or pitched, Xen.
to plaster or whiten over, Lat. dealbare, Dem.:—Pass. to be whitened, NTest.
dust stirred up, a cloud of dust, such as is made by troops, Hdt., Ar., etc.; κ. τῆς ὕλης νεωστὶ κεκαυμένης, i. e. a cloud of woodashes, Thuc.
metaph. a dirty fellow, Dem.
a cloud of dust, Il.
Lat. cinis, dust, Il., etc.;—of the grave, Pind., Soph.
ashes, Hom.
= κονία II, Luc.: metaph. of toil, Id.
to make dusty, cover with clouds of dust, Il.:—Pass., φεῦγον κεκονιμένοι all dusty fled they, Virgil's pulverulenta fuga dant terga, Id.; hence, to be in great haste, Ar., etc.
Pass. to be sprinkled as with dust, Theocr.
intr., κονίοντες πεδίοιο galloping o'er the dusty plain, Hom.
a drunken flute-player; Κόννου ὁ ψῆφος, proverb. of a worthless opinion, Ar.
a pole, punting-pole, boat-hook, Lat. contus, Od., Hdt., attic: the shaft of a pike, Luc.
carrying a pole or pike, Luc.
a strong-smelling plant, fleabane, pulicaria, poet. κνύζα, Theocr.
to grow weary: of the wind, to abate, Hdt., NTest.
a chisel, Luc.
a cutting in pieces, slaughter, NTest.
to be tired, grow weary, Ar., NTest.
to work hard, toil, NTest.
a prater, liar, wrangler, Eur.
a chopper, cleaver, a broad curved knife, somewhat like our bill, Eur., Xen.
a striking, beating, Aesch., Eur.
toil, trouble, suffering, Aesch., Soph.
weariness, fatigue, Eur., Ar.
a letter of the ancient Greek alphabet (#4), retained as a numeral = 90, between π ( 80 ) and this shews that it was the same as the Hebr. (koph) and Lat. Q; cf. σταῦ, σάμπι.
branded with the letter koppa, as a mark, ἵππος κ. Ar.; cf. σαμφόρας.
full of dung, filthy, Ar.
a dunghill: also = κόπρος, NTest.
to dung, manure, Od.
a dung-gatherer, a dirty fellow, Ar.
dung, ordure, manure, Hom., Hdt., etc.
a farm-yard, home-stead, Hom.
to cover with dung or dirt, Ar.
carrying dung; κόφινος κ. a dung- basket, Xen.
a place for dung, privy, Dem.
chopped small: κοπτή, ἡ, a cake of pounded sesame, Anth.
to strike, smite, knock down, Od.; κόψε μιν παρήιον smote him on the cheek Il.

to cut off, chop off, Hom., etc.; κ. δένδρα to fell trees, Thuc., etc.; κ. τὴν χώραν to cut down the trees in it, to lay it waste, Xen.:—Pass., of ships, to be shattered or disabled by the enemy, Thuc.:—metaph., φρενῶν κεκομμένος stricken in mind, Aesch.
to hammer, forge, Hom.: to stamp metal, coin money, Hdt.:— Mid. to coin oneself money, order to be coined, Id.: Pass., of the money, to be stamped or coined, Ar.
to knock at the door, Lat. pulsare, Id., etc.
to cut small, chop up or pound in a mortar, Hdt.
of a horse, to jolt or shake his rider, Xen.
metaph. to tire out, weary, Dem.
Mid. κόπτομαι, to beat one's breast through grief, Lat. plangere, Il., Hdt., Plat.
κόπτεσθαί τινα to mourn for any one, Lat. plangere aliquem, Eur., etc.
a young raven, Ar.

Lat. corvus, a raven or carrion-crow, Aesch., etc.; in imprecations, ἐς κόρακας "pasce corvos," "go to the dogs," "go and be hanged," Ar.; βάλλ’ ἐς κόρακας Id.; οὐκ ἐς κόρακας ἀποφθερεῖ; Id.; ἐς κόρακας οἰχήσεται Id.
anything like a raven's beak, an engine for grappling ships, Polyb.
a hooked handle of a door, Anth.
and instrument of torture, Luc.
a girl, maiden, Anth., NTest.
a barbarism for κόρη, Ar.
a gift or votive offering for the service of God, NTest.:—hence κορβανᾶς, ὁ, the treasury of the temple at Jerusalem, Id.
like the dance κόρδαξ: hence, tripping, running, ῥυθμὸς κ., of trochaic metres, Arist.
the dancing of the κόρδαξ, Dem.
the cordax, a dance of the old Comedy, κόρδακα ἑλκύσαι to dance the κόρδαξ, prob. from its slow, trailing movement, Ar.

entry.etym: κεκορηώς, epic part. perf. act. with pass. sense
entry.sense: to sate, satiate, satisfy, τινα Theogn., Aesch.: to fill one with a thing, c. dat., Il.; also c. gen. rei, to fill full of, Soph.:—Mid. to satisfy oneself, have one's fill, c. gen., ἐκορέσσατο φορβῆς Il., etc.; c. part., κλαίουσα κορέσσατο she had her fill of weeping, Od.: —Pass. to be satiated, Hes.; rarely c. dat. rei, πλούτωι κεκορημένος Theogn.; ὕβρι Hdt.
= κορεία, maidenhood, Eur., in pl.
Pass. to be a maid, grow up to maidenhood, Eur.
to sweep, sweep out, Od.; κ. τὴν Ἑλλάδα to sweep Greece clean, depopulate her, Ar.
a besom, broom, Ar.
fem. of κόρος, κοῦρος
a maiden, maid, damsel, Lat. puella, Il., Soph., etc.
a bride, young wife, Hom., Eur.
a daughter, κοῦραι Διός Il.; κ. Διός, of Athene, Aesch.:—in voc., κούρα my daughter, Id., Soph.
the pupil of the eye, Lat. pupula, because a little image appears therein, Eur., Ar.
a long sleeve reaching over the hand, Xen.
Κόρη, doric Κόρα, ionic Κούρη, ἡ, Cora, the Daughter (of Demeter), name under which Persephone (Proserpine) was worshipped in Attica, τῇ Μητρὶ καὶ τῇ Κούρῃ Hdt., etc.; Δημήτηρ καὶ Κόρη Xen., etc.
to lift up, raise, Ζεὺς κόρθυνεν ἑὸν μένος raised high his wrath, Hes.:—Pass., κῦμα κορθύεται waxes high, rears its crest, Il.
in Theocr., κόρθυος ἁ τομά the swathe of mown corn.
coriander, Ar.
Dep. to fondle, caress, coax, Ar.
Corinthian, Hdt., etc.:—also Κορινθιακός, ή, όν, Xen.; Κορινθικός, Anth.

Corinth, the city and country, Il., Hdt., attic; famed for its luxury, whence the proverb οὐ παντὸς ἀνδρὸς εἰς Κόρινθον ἐσθ’ ὁ πλοῦς; — with a masc. adj., ὀφρυόεντα K. Orac. ap. Hdt.:—proverb., Διὸς Κόρινθος, used of persons who are always repeating the same old story, Ar., etc.
adv. Κορινθόθι, at Corinth, Il.
a bug, Lat. cimex, Ar.
the rumbling of the empty bowels: generally, any hollow noise, a din, tumult, Aesch., Ar.
the trunk of a tree (with the boughs lopped off), Od., Eur.; κορμοὶ ξύλων logs of timber, Hdt.; κ. ναυτικοί, i. e. oars, Eur.
one's fill, satiety, surfeit, Hom., etc.; πάντων μὲν κόρος ἔστι, καὶ ὕπνου one may have one's fill of all things, even of sleep, etc., Il.; κ. ἔχειν τινός to have one's fill of a thing, Eur.
the consequence of satiety, insolence, Pind.; πρὸς κόρον insolently, Aesch.
a boy, lad, stripling, Hom., etc.: κοῦροι young men, warriors, Il.; also servants, like Lat. pueri, Hom.
with gen. of prop. names, a son, Od.; Θησέως κ. Soph., etc.
entry.etym: Prob. from κείρω, one who has cut his hair short on emerging from boyhood.

entry.sense: the Hebrew cor, a dry measure containing 10 attic medimni, about 120 gallons, NTest.
one of the temples, the side of the forehead, Il.;—so in attic, ἐπὶ κόρρης πατάσσειν to box on the ear, Dem.; cf. κόνδυλος.
the hair on the temples, which is the first to turn gray, Aesch.
Corybantian, Anth.
to be filled with Corybantic frenzy, Plat.:—in Ar., comically, of a drowsy person suddenly starting up.
to purify or consecrate by Corybantic rites, Ar.
a Corybant, priest of Cybele in Phrygia; in pl. Κορύβαντες, Eur., etc.
enthusiasm, Luc.
the crested lark, Ar.
a running at the nose, Lat. pituita, Luc.: —metaph. drivelling, stupidity, Id.
to run at the nose, Plat.
helmet-shaking, i. e. with waving plume, Il.
with glancing helm, Il.
the uppermost point, head, end, νηῶν ἄκρα κόρυμβα high-pointed sterns of ships, Il.; in pl. of a single ship, Aesch.
the top of a hill, Hdt., Aesch.
= κρωβύλος, Anth.
a cluster of fruit or flowers, Mosch., Anth.
a club, mace, Il., Hdt.:— a shepherd's staff, Theocr.
entry.etym: ῠ in Hom.; ῡ in Eur.

entry.sense: a club-bearer, mace-bearer, Il.
club-bearing: κορυνοφόροι, οἱ, club-bearers, the body-guard of Peisistratus, Hdt.
one that butts with the head, Theocr.
to butt with the head, Theocr.
a helmet, helm, casque, Hom.
the head, Eur.
to furnish with a helmet, and, generally, to fit out, equip, marshal, Il., Hes.:—Pass. and Mid. to equip or arm oneself, Il.
to make crested, κόρυσσε κῦμα he reared his crested wave, Id.:—Pass. to rear its head, of a wave, Id.; of Rumour, Id.; of clouds, Theocr.
a helmed man, an armed warrior, Il.
the head-stall of a bridle, Xen.
the upper rim of a hunting-net, Xen.
the head man, chief man, leader, Hdt., etc.:—in the attic Drama, the leader of the chorus, Dem.; κ. ἑστηκώς standing at the head of the row, Ar.
as adj. at the top, ὁ κ. πῖλος the apex, of the Roman flamen, Plut.
the head, top, highest point; hence,
the crown or top of the head, Il., Hdt., attic
the top or peak of a mountain, Il., Hdt., Aesch.
metaph. the highest point, Lat. summa, παντὸς ἔχει κορυφάν is the best of all, Pind.; κορυφὰ λόγων προτέρων the sum and substance of ancient legends, Id.
the height or excellence of a thing, i. e. the choicest, noblest, best, Id.
to bring to a head:— Pass., [κῦμα] κορυφοῦται rises with arching crest, Il.; τὸ ἔσχατον κορυφοῦται βασιλεῦσι kings are on the highest pinnacle, Pind.
to bring to an end, finish, Plut.:—Pass., κορυφούμενος being summed up, Anth.
old as a crow or Hecuba, Anth.
κορώνεως συκῆ, ἡ, a fig of raven-gray colour, Ar.
Lat. cornix, the chough or sea-crow, a small kind with red legs and bill, Od.
= κόραξ, the carrion-crow, Hes., Ar.
anything hooked or curved, like a crow's bill,
the handle on a door, Od.
the tip of a bow, on which the bowstring was hooked, Hom.:—metaph., βιῷ κορώνην ἐπιθεῖναι to put a finish to life, Luc.
to arch the neck, Anth.
crook-beaked, curved, of ships, from the outline of the prow and stern, Hom.
of kine, with crumpled horns, Theocr.
as Subst. a curved line, a flourish with the pen at the end of a book, Anth.:—metaph. an end, finish, ἐπιθεῖναι κορωνίδα τινί Luc.
shooting crows: κορωνοβόλον, τό, a sling or bow for crow-shooting, Etc.; Anth.
curved, crooked: with crumpled horns, Archil.
like, as in a sieve, Luc.
a diviner by a sieve, Theocr.
a sieve, Ar., Plat.
shreds of leather; in Ar., of the scraps of flattery offered by the tanner Cleon to his patron Δῆμος.
to order, arrange, Hom., etc.: esp. to set an army in array, marshal it, Il.:— Mid., κοσμησάμενος πολιήτας having arranged his men, Id.
generally, to arrange, prepare, δόρπον Od.; ἔργα Hes., etc.
to dispose, order, rule, govern, Hdt., Soph., etc.; τὰ κοσμούμενα orderly institutions, set order, Soph.
in Crete, to be Cosmos (κόσμος ΙΙΙ), rule as such, Arist.
to deck, adorn, equip, furnish, dress, esp. of women, Hhymn., Hes., etc.: Mid., κοσμέεσθαι τὰς κεφαλάς to adorn their heads, Hdt., etc.
metaph. to adorn, embellish, Eur., Thuc., etc.
to honour, pay honour to, Soph., Eur., etc.
in Pass. to be assigned or ascribed to, ἐς τὸν Αἰγύπτιον νόμον αὗται [αἱ πόλεις] ἐκεκοσμέατο Hdt.
an ornament, decoration, Xen.
an ordering, disposition, arrangement, adornment, Plat.
an orderer, director, Epigr. ap. Aeschin.
an adorner, Xen.
skilled in arranging: ἡ -κή (sc, τέχνη) , the art of dress and ornament, Plat.
well-ordered, trim, Od.
one who marshals an army, a commander, Hom.
of the world or universe, Luc.
of this world, earthly, NTest.
well-ordered, regular, moderate, δαπάνη Plat.:— κόσμιόν ἐστι, c. inf., 'tis a regular practice, Ar.
of persons, orderly, well-behaved, regular, discreet, quiet, Id., Plat., etc.: —τὸ κ. decorum, decency, order, Soph.:—adv. κοσμίως, regularly, decently, Ar., etc.; κοσμίως ἔχειν to be orderly, Plat.
propriety, decorum, orderly behaviour, Ar., Plat.
dressing the hair, Anth.
lord of the world, NTest.
holding the world together, Anth.
order, κόσμῳ and κατὰ κόσμον in order, duly, Il., etc.; μὰψ ἀτὰρ οὐ κατὰ κόσμον Id.; οὐδενὶ κόσμῳ in no sort of order, Hdt., attic
good order, good behaviour, decency, Aesch., Dem.
the form, fashion of a thing, Od., Hdt.
of states, order, government, Hdt., Thuc.
an ornament, decoration, embellishment, dress, Il., etc.; esp. of women, Lat. mundus muliebris, Id., Hes., etc.:—in pl. ornaments, Aesch., etc.
metaph. honour, credit, Hdt., Soph., etc.
a regulator, title of the chief magistrate in Crete, Arist.
the world or universe, from its perfect order, Lat. mundus, Plat., etc.
mankind, as we use "the world," NTest.
destroying the world, Anth.
to bear a grudge against, c. gen., ἀπάτης κοτέων angry at the trick, Il.: absol. to be angry, Hom.
wrathful, jealous, Il.
producing wild olive-trees, Mosch.
the wild olive-tree, Lat. oleaster, Ar.
eating wild olive-berries, Ar.
a grudge, rancour, wrath, Hom., Aesch.
to play at the cottabus, Ar.
the prize of the game κότταβος, Arist.

the cottabus, a Sicilian game, much in vogue at Athens. Each person threw the wine left in his cup, so as to fall in a metal basin; if the whole fell with a clear sound, it was a good sign. But the game was played in various ways.
any cup-shaped hollow:
in pl. the suckers on the arms (πλεκτάναι) of the polypus, Od., in epic dat. pl. κοτυληδονόφιν.
= κοτύλη 2, the socket of the hip-joint, Ar.
a cup, Hom.
the cup or socket of a joint, esp. of the hip-joint, Il.
a liquid measure, containing 6 κύαθοι, i. e. nearly half a pint, Ar., Thuc.
that can be drawn in cups, i. e. flowing copiously, streaming, Il.
nickname of a toper, Plut.
a shearing or cropping of the hair, tonsure, Hdt., Eur.
a lock cut off, Aesch.
a barber's shop, Ar.
a barber, hair-cutter, Lat. tonsor, Plat., Anth., etc.
youthful, Hhymn.
young men, esp. young warriors, Il.
Κουρῆτες, οἱ, the Curetes oldest inhabitants of Pleuron in Aetolia, Il.
one with short hair, Luc.
of hair, to need clipping, Luc.

wedded, of the husband (κουρίδιος πόσις) or the wife (κουριδίη ἄλοχος), Hom.: esp. a lawful, wedded wife, as opp. to a concubine, Id., Hdt.:—hence, λέχος κουρίδιον our lawful marriage, bed, Il.; κ. δῶμα a husband's house.
later, nuptial, bridal, Ar., Anth.
intr. to be a youth, Od.
trans. to bring up from boyhood, Hes.
of, for cutting hair, Eur.
pass. shorn off, Aesch., Eur.
shorn, κρᾶτα Eur.
by the hair, Od.
devouring children, Aesch.
youth, youthful prime, Anth.: mirthfulness, Theocr.
youthful, Anth.
younger, more youthful, Hom.; used much like a positive.
bearing boy-children, Eur.
rearing boys; ἀγαθὴ κ. good nursing-mother, of Ithaca, Od.; so, κ. Ἑλλάς Eur.
the Lat. custodia, NTest.
intr. to be light, Hes., Eur.: of pain, to be alleviated, assuaged, Soph.
trans. to make light: hence to lift up, raise, Id.; ἅλμα κουφιεῖν to make a light leap, Id.; κ. πήδημα Eur.:—Pass. to be lifted up, soar, Plat.

c. gen., ὄχλου κ. χθόνα, to lighten, earth of a multitude, Eur.: —absol. to lighten ships of their cargo, Thuc.: to relieve persons from burthens, Xen.:—Pass. to be relieved, νόσου from disease, Eur.; κουφισθήσομαι ψυχήν Id.; metaph. to feel one's burthens lightened, Thuc.
c. acc. rei, to lighten, assuage, συμφοράς Dem.; ἔρωτα, Theocr.
a lightening, alleviation, relief, Thuc.
light talking, Thuc.
light-minded, thoughtless, Aesch., Soph.
light, nimble, Trag.; used by Hom. only in neut. pl. as. adv. κοῦφα προβιβάς stepping lightly on, Il.:—metaph., κουφότεραι φρένες too buoyant, Pind.
metaph. also light, easy, Aesch., Xen.
empty, unsubstantial, vain, Soph., Thuc.
light in point of weight, opp. to βαρύς, Plat., etc.; κούφα σοι χθὼν ἐπάνωθε πέσοι may earth lie lightly on thee, sit tibi terra levis, Eur.; of soldiers, ὡπλισμένοι κουφοτέροις ὅπλοις Xen.
adv. -φως, lightly, nimbly, Aesch.; κ. ἐσκευασμένοι, of soldiers, Thuc., Xen.
metaph. lightly, with light heart, κουφότερόν μετεφώνεε Od.; κούφως φέρειν to bear lightly, Eur.; ὡς κουφότατα φέρειν Hdt.
lightly, with ease, Aesch.
a basket, Ar., Xen.; in later times used specially by Jews, NTest.; being apparently smaller than the σπυρίς.
a snail with a spiral shell, Lat. cochlea, Theocr.
a small snail, Batr.
a shell-fish with a spiral shell, used for dying purple, Lat. murex, Arist., Anth.; used as a trumpet, like Lat. concha, Eur., Theocr., etc.
to stream forth copiously, Theocr.
the posteriors, dual τὰ κοχώνᾱ Ar.
a blackbird, Ar.
a couch, bed, Lat. grabatus, NTest.
to swing, wave, brandish, Eur., Ar.: to shake, agitate, Aesch.:—Pass., αἰχμὴ κραδαινομένη κατὰ γαίης quivering in the ground, Il.
metaph. to agitate, Plut.
to shake, brandish, only in part., κραδάων δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος Hom.
the quivering spray at the end of a branch, Hes., Ar.:—generally, a fig-tree, Ar.
to croak, of frogs, Ar.: generally, to scream, shriek, cry aloud, Aesch., Ar.; κέκραχθι Ar.; κραγὸν κεκράξεται will bawl aloud, Id. (κραγόν being aor2 part. used adverbially).
c. acc. rei, to clamour for a thing, Id.
to accomplish, fulfil, bring to pass, Hom., Trag.:—Pass., with fut. mid., to be accomplished or brought to pass, Il., Eur.; v. ἐπικραίνω.
to finish the tale of . . , c. acc., Hhymn.
absol. to exercise sway, to reign, c. acc. cogn. κρ. σκῆπτρα to sway the staff of rule, Soph.
c. gen. to reign over, govern, τοῦ στρατοῦ, τῆς χώρας Id.
intr. to fulfil one's course, Aesch.
only in pres., to have a sick head-ache, consequent upon a debauch, Ar., Plat.
a drunken head-ache, Lat. crapula, ἐκ κραιπάλης after a drunken bout, Ar.
rambling in drunken revelry, Ar.
rapid, rushing, of strong winds, Hom.; of swift feet, Id.:—metaph. hasty, rash, Il.
adv., quickly, hastily, Hom.; also neut. pl. as adv., Id.
swift-rushing, Aesch.
swift-bearing, αὖραι Aesch.
cabbage, kail, Eupol., etc.
loud, ringing, Ar.
cabbage-eater, Batr.
with hard rocky soil, Hhymn.
rocky, rugged, of Ithaca, Hom.; of Athens, Pind.; hence Athens was called Κραναὰ πόλις or αἱ Κρανααί Id.; Κραναοί the people of Attica, Hdt.; and Κραναός a mythical king of Athens, Aesch.
the cornel-tree, dog-wood, Lat. cornus, its wood was used for shafts and bows, Hom.
made of cornel-wood, Lat. corneus, τόξα Hdt., Xen.
the upper part of the head, the skull, Il., Pind., Eur.
Lat. cornus, Theophr.
to make helmets: in Ar. of one who talks big and warlike.
a helmet-maker, Ar.
a helmet, Hdt., Aesch.
one that accomplishes: a ruler, sovereign, fem. κράντειρα, Anth.

entry.etym: shortened for κράνος as δῶ, for δῶμα, Anth.

entry.sense: a mixing, blending, compounding, Aesch., Plat.
the temperature of the air, Lat. temperies, Plat.
metaph. combination, union, Id.
in Gramm., crasis i. e. the combination of two syllables into one long vowel or diphthong, e. g. τοὔνομα for τὸ ὄνομα, ἁνήρ for ὁ ἀνήρ.

the edge, border, skirt or hem of a thing, esp. of cloth, Theocr.; mostly in pl., Eur., Ar.: —metaph., also in pl., the skirts of a mountain, Xen.; πρὸς κρασπέδοισι στρατοπέδου on the skirts of the army, Eur.
Pass. to be bordered, or edged, Eur.

entry.etym: κρᾶτα, as nom. and acc., Soph.
In Hom. also we have a lengthd. gen. and dat., κράᾰτος, κράᾰτι, pl. nom. κράᾰτα
entry.sense: the head, Hom., Trag.; ἐπὶ κρατὸς λιμένος at the head or far end of the bay, Od.
an old gen. κρῆθεν is used in the phrase κατὰ κρῆθεν, down from the head, from the top, Id., Hes.: hence, like penitus, from head to foot, entirely, Τρῶας κατὰ κρῆθεν λάβε πένθος Il.
hurled with violence, Eur.
with strong plates, Il.
mighty force, Od.
of hard stones, rocky, Aesch., Eur.
strong, mighty, resistless, Hom., Trag.
with hard ground or soil, Od.
stout-footed, epic:— καρταίπους is used absol. for ταῦρος in Pind.
hard-shelled, Orac. ap. Hdt.
mighty with the spear, poet. καρτ-, Pind.
strong-necked, Plat.
strong, stout, mighty, Hom.
of things, conditions, etc., strong, mighty, cruel, Id., Hes.
of passions, strong, vehement, mighty, Hom.; κρ. μῦθος a harsh, rough speech, Id.
adv. -ρῶς, strongly, stoutly, roughly, Id.
stout-hearted, dauntless, Hom., Hes.
stout of hand, Anth.
strong-hoofed, solid-hoofed, Hom.:— strong-clawed, of wolves, Od.
the forked stand or frame on which a spit turns, Il.
to be strong, mighty, powerful: hence,
absol. to rule, hold sway, be sovereign, Hom., Trag.; ἡ κρατοῦσα the lady of the house, Aesch.
c. dat. to rule among, κρατέεις νεκύεσσιν Od.
c. gen. to be lord or master of, ruler over, πάντων Hom.; δωμάτων Aesch., etc.

to conquer, prevail, get the upper hand, Hdt., attic; κρ. γνώμηι to prevail in opinion, Hdt.; τῆι μάχηι Eur., etc.;—also c. acc. cogn., κρ. τὸν ἀγῶνα Dem.:— οἱ κρατοῦντες the conquerors, Xen.:—of reports, etc., to prevail, become current, Soph., Thuc.
impers., κατθανεῖν κρατεῖ 'tis better to die, Aesch.; κρατεῖ ἀπολέσθαι Eur.
c. gen. to prevail over, Aesch.; ὁ λόγος τοῦ ἔργου ἐκράτει surpassed, went beyond it, Thuc.
c. acc. to conquer, master, outdo, surpass, Pind., attic:—Pass. to be conquered, Hdt., attic
to become master of, get possession of τῆς ἀρχῆς Hdt.; τῆς γῆς Thuc.
to lay hold of, τῆς χειρός NTest.
c. acc. rei, to seize, hold fast, θρόνους Soph., Xen.
to control, command, Aesch.
to drink from a bowl of wine, Dem.

a mixing vessel, esp. a large bowl, in which the wine was mixed with water, and from which the cups were filled, Hom., etc.; οἶνον δ’ ἐκ κρητῆρος ἀφυσσάμενοι δεπάεσσιν ἔκχεον Il.; πίνοντες κρητῆρας drinking bowls of wine, Id.; κρητῆρα στήσασθαι ἐλεύθερον to give a bowl of wine to be drunk in honour of the deliverance, Id.; ἐπιστέψασθαι ποτοῖο, v. ἐπιστέφω.
metaph., κρατῆρα πλήσας κακῶν having filled a bowl full of woes, Aesch.
any cup-shaped hollow, a basin in a rock, Soph., Plat.
conquering in the fight, Pind.
victorious in the foot-race, Pind.
victorious in the race, Pind.
to be mightiest, best, most excellent, Soph.
to gain the upper hand, τινί or ἔν τινι in a thing, Xen.
strongest, mightiest, Il., etc.; Λημνίων τὸ κρ. the best of their men, Thuc.:—of things, καρτίστη μάχη the fiercest fight, Il.
generally, best, most excellent, as Sup. of ἀγαθός, Pind., Soph., etc.
οἱ κράτιστοι, like οἱ βέλτιστοι, of the aristocracy, Xen.
neut. pl. κράτιστα as adv., best, Id. —The comp. in use is κρείσσων, q. v.
strength, might, Hom., attic; κατὰ κράτος with all one's might or strength, by open force, by storm, Thuc., Xen., etc.
personified, Strength, Might, Aesch.
generally, might, power, Hom.: rule, sway, sovereignty, Hdt., attic
c. gen. power over, Hdt., attic; in pl., ἀστραπᾶν κράτη νέμων Soph.
of persons, a power, an authority, Aesch.
mastery, victory, Hom., attic; κρ. ἀριστείας the meed of highest valour, Soph.
to strengthen, Hdt., Thuc.:—Mid., ἐκαρτύναντο φάλαγγας they strengthened their ranks, Il., so in Thuc.:—Pass. to wax strong, Hdt.
to harden, τοὺς πόδας Xen.
= κρατέω, to rule, govern, c. gen., Soph., Eur.; also c. acc., Aesch.; absol., Id., Soph., etc.
to become master, get possession of, c. gen., Soph.:— c. acc., βασιληίδα τιμὰν κρ. to hold, exercise, Eur.
καρτύνειν βέλεα to ply or throw them stoutly, Pind.
strong, mighty, Hom.
to bay, of dogs, Poeta ap. Plat.; of men, to cry aloud, scream, Dem., NTest.
as a Patronym. son of a croaker, Batr.
a crying, screaming, shrieking, shouting, Lat. clamor, Eur., Xen.
a flesh-hook, to take meat out of the pot, Ar.
a morsel of meat, slice of meat, Ar., Xen.
to distribute flesh, to divide the flesh of a victim among the guests, Luc.:—Mid. to divide among themselves, Theocr.
a distribution of flesh, Luc., etc.
one who distributes the flesh of victims, a carver, Eur.
flesh, meat, a piece of meat, Od., etc.; τρία κρέα ἢ καὶ πλέα Xen.; also in collective sense, dressed meat, meat, flesh, Hom., etc.
a body, person, ὦ δεξιώτατον κρέας Ar.
containing flesh, Anth.
a meat-tray, dresser, Il.
dearer than children, Aesch.
stronger, mightier, more powerful, Il., etc.
in sense often as comp. of ἀγαθός, better, οἱ κρέσσονες one's betters, Pind.; so, τὰ κρείσσω Eur.: —τὰ κρείσσονα one's advantages, Thuc.
