c. inf., οὔτις κρείσσων δόμεναι no one has a better right to give, Od.: —κρεῖσσόν ἐστι, c. inf., 'tis better to . . , κρεῖσσόν ἐστι θανεῖν ἢ πάσχειν κακῶς Aesch.:—also κρείσσων εἰμί, c. part., κρείσσων ἦσθα μηκέτ’ ὢν ἢ ζῶν τυφλός thou wert better not alive, than living blind, Soph.
too great for, ὕψος κρεῖσσον ἐκπηδήματος too great for leaping out of, Aesch.; κρείσσον’ ἀγχόνης too bad for hanging, Soph.; ἐλπίδος κρ. worse than one expected, Thuc.
having power over, master of, γαστρός Xen.; κρ. χρημάτων superior to bribes, Thuc.
in attic Prose in moral sense, better, more excellent, Ar.
a ruler, lord, master, Hom.; ὕπατε κρειόντων, of Zeus, Il.; as a general title of honour, Od.:—fem. κρείουσα, lady, mistress, Il., Hes.:—after Hom. in the form κρέων, Pind.
a kind of tapestry, Ar.
struck so as to sound, of stringed instruments: generally, played, sung, Aesch.
to strike the web with the κερκίς, to weave, Eur.
to strike the lyre with the plectron, Anth.:—generally, to play on an instrument, Ar.
of any sharp noise, βοὴν πτεροῖς κρ. Id.
a net or basket to hang things up in, Ar.

to hang, hang up, Il.; κρεμόω ποτὶ ναόν will bring them to the temple and hang them up there, Il.; κρ. τινά τινος to hang one up by a thing, Ar.; κρεμάσας τὰ νόημα, in allusion to Socrates in his basket, Id.; —κρεμάσαι τὴν ἀσπίδα to hang up one's shield, i. e. have done with war, Id.:—so in Mid., πηδάλιον κρεμάσασθαι to hang up one's rudder, i. e. give up the sea, Hes.

Pass. to be hung up, suspended, ὅτε τ’ ἐκρέμω(2 imperf.) when thou wert hanging, Il.: to be hung up as a votive offering, Pind., Hdt.; εἴπερ ἐκ ποδῶν κρέμαιτο Ar.:—metaph., μῶμος κρέματαί τινι censure hangs over him, Pind.; ὁ ἐκ τοῦ σώματος κρεμάμενος depending on the body, Xen.
to be hung, of persons, Eur.
metaph. to be in suspense, Arist.
hung, hung up, hanging, κρ. αὐχένος hung by the neck, Soph.; c. gen., also, hung from or on a thing, Eur.: —κρεμαστὴ ἀρτάνη, i. e. a halter, Soph.; so, βρόχοι κρ. Eur.
rattling instruments, like our castanets.
a rattling as with castanets, Hhymn.
Lat. crex, the corn-crake, land-rail, Ar.
a distributor of flesh, carver at a public meal, Lat. dispensator, Plut.
to cut in pieces, Aesch., Eur.
to cut up meat like a butcher (κρεουργός), to butcher, Luc.
like a butcher, in pieces, Hdt.
working, i. e. cutting up meat, κρεουργὸν ἦμαρ a day of feasting, Aesch.
eating flesh, carnivorous, Hdt.
good, agreeable, Il.: of persons, good, serviceable, Plat.
true, real, εἴπατέ μοι τὸ κρήγυον, Theocr.: adv. in good earnest, Anth.
a veil or mantilla with lappets, passing over the head and hanging down on each side, Hom.
metaph. in pl. the battlements which crown a city's walls, Id., Eur.
the cover of a wine-jar, Od.
Pass. κρήμναμαι, to hang, be suspended, Eur.: to float in air, Aesch.
a haunter of steeps, Anth.
speaking crags, i. e. using big, rugged words, Ar.
an overhanging bank, as the steep bank of a river, edge of a trench, Il.: later, a beetling cliff, crag, Hdt., Ar.; κατὰ τῶν κρημνῶν down from the cliffs of Epipolae, Thuc.
precipitous, Thuc.
of, from a spring or fountain, Νύμφαι κρηναῖαι = Κρηνιάδες, Od.; κρ. ὕδωρ spring water, Hdt.; κρ. ποτόν Soph., etc.
from a well or spring, Anth.
to a well or spring, Od.
a well, spring, fountain, Lat. fons, Hom., etc.; opp. to φρέαρ (a tank), Hdt., Thuc.: —Poets use it in pl. for water, Soph.
spring-nymphs, Theocr.; so Κρᾱνίδες Mosch.
a half-boot, Xen.:— κρηπῖδες soldiers' boots, i. e. soldiers themselves, Theocr.

generally, a groundwork, foundation, basement of a temple or altar, Hdt., Soph., etc.:—metaph., κρηπὶς σοφῶν ἐπέων Pind.; οὐδέπω κρηπὶς κακῶν ὕπεστι we have not yet got to the bottom of misery, Aesch.; ἡ ἐγκράτεια ἀρετῆς κρηπίς self-control is the foundation of virtue, Xen.
the walled edge of a river, a quay, Lat. crepido, Hdt.
a Cretan, Hom., etc.; fem. Κρῆσσα, ης, Aesch.
as adj. Cretan, Soph.; also Κρήσιος, η, ον, Id., Eur.
a place of refuge, retreat, resort, Hdt.
entry.etym: The first part of the word, κρησ-, is uncertain.

entry.sense: from Crete, Il.
to Crete, Od.
Crete, now Candia, Hom.; epic gen. pl. Κρητάων εὐρειάων Od.
to play the Cretan, NTest., Plut.
of or from the island of Crete, Cretan, Aesch., Thuc.
Κρητικόν (sc. ἱμάτιον), a short garment, used at sacred rites, Ar.
Κρητικός (sc. ποῦς), a Cretic, a metrical foot [\h\ \v\ \h\][–⏑–], e. g. Ἀντιφῶν, called also amphimacer (ἀμφίμακρος).
Cretan behaviour, i. e. lying, Plut.
baked in a pan (κρίβανος), ὁ κρ. (sc. ἄρτος), a loaf so baked, Ar.; hence, comically, βοῦς κρ. Id.
an earthen vessel, a pan, wider at bottom than at top, wherein bread was baked by putting hot embers round it, Hdt., Ar.
to creak, Lat. stridere, Il.
of persons, to screech, Ar.
of a horse, to be barley-fed, to wax wanton, Aesch.
barley-corns, barley (cf. κρῖ), the meal being ἄλφιτα, Hom., Ar., etc.; οἶνος ἐκ κριθέων πεποιημένος a kind of beer (cf. κρίθινος), Hdt.
a disease of horses, a kind of surfeit caused by over-feeding with barley, Xen.
to feed with barley, Babr.
made of or from barley, Xen., etc.
barley-eating, Ar.
a ring on a horse's breast-band, to fasten it to the peg (ἕστωρ) at the end of the carriage-pole, Il.
an eyelet-hole in sails, through which the reefing-ropes were drawn, Hdt.
a decision, judgment, NTest.: sentence, condemnation, Id.
a matter for judgment, law-suit, Id.
coarse meal or a coarse loaf, Anth.
a lily, Hdt., Ar., etc.
Lat. cerno, to separate, part, put asunder, distinguish, Il., Xen.
to pick out, choose, Hom., Hdt., attic:—Mid. to pick out for oneself, choose, Hom., etc.: —Pass. to be chosen, Il.; perf. and aor1 part. κεκριμένος, κρινθείς picked out, chosen, Hom.

to decide disputes, Id., Hdt., etc.; σκολιὰς κρίνειν θέμιστας to judge crooked judgments, i. e. to judge unjustly, Il.; κρίνουσι βόηι καὶ οὐ ψήφωι they decide the question by shouting, not by voting, Thuc.; to decide a contest for a prize, Soph., etc.; κρ. τὰς θεάς to decide their contest, i. e. judge them, Eur.:—Pass. and Mid., of persons, to have a contest decided, come to issue, Hom., etc.
to adjudge, κράτος τινί Soph.
to judge of, estimate, πρὸς ἐμαυτὸν κρίνων [αὐτόν] judging of him by myself, Dem.:—Pass., ἴσον παρ’ ἐμοὶ κέκριται Hdt.
to expound, interpret dreams, Id., Aesch., etc.: so in Mid., Il.
c. acc. et inf. to decide or judge that, Hdt., attic
c. inf. only, to determine to do a thing, NTest.
to question, Soph.
to bring to trial, accuse, Xen., etc.:—Pass. to be brought to trial, Thuc., etc.
to pass sentence upon, to condemn, Soph., Dem.
ram-faced, Hdt.
a ram, Lat. aries, Hom., Hdt., etc.
a battering-ram, Lat. aries, Xen.
barley, Hom.
Crisa, a city in Phocis, near Delphi, Il.:—adj. Κρισαῖος, η, ον Crisaean, Id., Hdt.
decisive, critical, Anth.
a separating, power of distinguishing, Arist.: choice, selection, Id.
a decision, judgment, Hdt., Aesch.; κρ. οὐκ ἀληθής no certain means of judging, Soph.
in legal sense, a trial, Ar., Thuc., etc.:— the result of a trial, condemnation, Xen.
a trial of skill, τόξου in archery, Soph.
a dispute, περί τινος Hdt.
the event or issue of a thing, κρίσιν ἔχειν to be decided, of a war, Thuc.
to be decided or judged: —κριτέον one must decide or judge, Plat.
a means for judging or trying, a criterion, standard, test, Plat.
a court of judgment, tribunal, Id.
a decider, judge, umpire, Hdt., Thuc.:—at Athens, of the judges in the poetic contests, Ar.
κρ. ἐνυπνίων an interpreter of dreams, Aesch.
able to discern, critical, Arist.
of or for judging, Id.
picked out, chosen, Hom.
choice, excellent, Pind., Soph.
of a horse, to stamp, strike with the hoof, Il.
a pebble, shingle, Anth.
saffron-coloured, Pind., Eur.

entry.etym: also (as if from a nom. *κρόξ) heterocl. acc. κρόκα, nom. pl. κρόκες Anth.:
entry.sense: the thread which is passed between the threads of the warp (στήμων, tela), the woof or weft, Lat. subtemen, Hes., Hdt., etc.
κροκύς, the flock or nap of woollen cloth, cloth with curly nap, Ar.: in pl., μαλακαῖς κρόκαις with cloths of soft wool, Pind.; κρόκαισι with flocks of wool, Soph.
of saffron, Anth.
saffron-dyed, Aesch.
metaph., ἐπὶ δὲ καρδίαν ἔδραμε κρ. σταγών to my heart ran the sallow, sickly blood-drop (that precedes death), Aesch.
a lizard, properly an ionic word, Hdt.
the Nile-lizard, crocodile, Id.
saffron-coloured, Eur., etc.
with yellow veil, Il., Hes.
the crocus, Il., Soph.
saffron (which is made from its stigmas), Aesch., etc.
to crown with yellow ivy, Anth.
the flock or nap on woollen cloth, Hdt., Luc., etc.
saffron-dyed, saffron-coloured, Pind.
as Subst., κροκωτός (sc. χιτών), a saffron-coloured frock, worn by Bacchus, Ar.
a belch of onions and vinegar, Ar.
an onion, Hom.:—later κρόμμυον, Hdt., Ar.
patronym., son of Cronus, i. e. Zeus, Hom.
= Κρόνιος, Κρ. ἀστήρ the planet Saturn, Anth.
in contemptuous sense, old-fashioned, out of date, Ar.
Saturnian, of Cronus or Saturn, Aesch., etc.
Κρόνια (sc. ἱερά), τά, his festival celebrated on the twelfth of Hecatombaeon, Dem.:—later, τὰ Κρόνια were the Roman Saturnalia; hence, αἱ Κρονιάδες ἡμέραι the time of the Saturnalia, Plut.
Κρόνιον (sc. ὄρος), the hill of Cronus or Saturn, Pind.
like Κρονικός, in contemptuous sense, Κρονίων ὄζειν to smell of the dark ages, Ar.
an old dotard, Ar.
patronym., son of Cronus, i. e. Zeus, Hom.

Cronus, identified with the Lat. Saturnus, son of Uranos and Gaia, husband of Rhea, father of Zeus, Poseidon, Hades, Hera, Demeter and Hestia, Hes.: he reigned in heaven until his sons banished him to Tartarus, Il., Aesch.; his time was the golden age, Hes.
a name at Athens, a superannuated old dotard, old fool, Ar.
battlements on walls, Il.; of the steps by which the Pyramids rose to a point, Hdt.
to use rattles or castanets, Hdt.:—generally, ἵπποι ὄχεα κροτάλιζον were rattling them along, Il.
a rattle, castanet, used in the worship of Cybele, or Dionysus, Hdt., Eur.
metaph. a rattling fellow, a rattle, Ar.
the side of the forehead (v. κόρση), in pl. the temples, Lat. tempora, Il., etc.
of a mountain, its side, Aesch., Anth.
to make to rattle, of horses, ὄχεα κροτέοντες rattling them along, Il.
to knock, strike, smite, Hdt., Eur.; κροτεῖν τὰς χεῖρας or τὼ χεῖρε to clap the hands, Hdt., Xen.: absol. to clap, applaud, Xen., etc.
of a smith, to hammer or weld together, Plat.:—Pass. to be wrought by the hammer; metaph., ἐξ ἀπάτας κεκροταμένος one mass of trickery, Theocr.
intr. to make a rattling noise, Arist., Luc.
work wrought by the hammer:— metaph. of Ulysses, a hardened knave, Eur.
a clapping, τινὶ χειρῶν Plat.
stricken, sounding with blows, Aesch.: rattling, Soph.
a striking, the sound made by striking, κρ. ποδῶν the beat of the feet in dancing, Eur.; κρ. χειρῶν a clapping of hands, applause, Ar., Xen.
a stroke: a sound made by striking stringed instruments with the plectron, a note, Plat.
of or for playing on a stringed instrument, Anth.
to send forth a stream,
a gush or stream, Anth.
a spring, well-head, whence the streams (πηγαί) issue, Il., Soph.; so, κρουνοὶ Ἡφαίστου streams of lava from Etna, Pind.: metaph. a torrent of words, Ar.
a pourer forth of washy twaddle, Ar.
a striking, smiting, Plut.
a tapping of earthen vessels, to see whether they ring sound: metaph. deception, cheatery, Ar.
a playing on a stringed instrument, Plut.
fit for striking the ears, impressive, Arist.:—metaph. of a speaker, Ar.
to strike, smite: to strike one against another, κρ. χεῖρας to clap hands, Eur.; κρ. τὰ ὅπλα πρὸς ἄλληλα Thuc., etc.:— κρ. τὸν πόδα (i. e. κρ. τὴν γῆν τῶι ποδί) in dancing, Eur.
κέραμον κρούειν to tap an earthen vessel, to try whether it rings sound: hence to examine, prove, Plat.
to strike a lyre with the plectron, Id.
κρούειν τὴν θύραν to knock at the door on the outside, Xen., etc.
as a nautical term, in Mid., κρούεσθαι πρύμναν, like ἀνακρούεσθαι, to back a ship, Thuc.
without the knowledge of, κρύβδα Διός, Lat. clam Jove, Il.
absol., like κρύβδην, secretly, Pind.
secretly, Od., Ar.
c. gen., like κρύβδα, κρύβδαν πατρός Pind.
icy, chilling, in Hom. only metaph., κρυεροῖο γόοιο, κρυεροῖο φόβοιο; so κρυερὰ πάθεα Ar.
icy-cold, Id.
icy cold, frost, Hdt., Eur.
icy-cold, frozen, icy, Anth.
chilling, Il., Hes.
icy-cold, Anth.
icy cold, chill, frost, Hes.: metaph., καρδίαν περιπίτνει κρύος Aesch.
secret, clandestine, Il., Aesch.: neut. pl. as adv., Il.
a secret commission on which young Spartans were obliged to serve, watching the country and enduring hardships, Plat.

entry.etym: verb. adj. of κρύπτω, Soph., Anth.

entry.sense: to conceal, hide, Eur.
intrans, to hide oneself, lie concealed, Xen.
Pass. to be ensnared, Eur.
hidden, secret, Il., Hdt., etc.; κρυπτὴ τάφρος a trench covered and concealed by planks and earth, Hdt.; τὸ κρ. τῆς πολιτείας the secret character of [the Spartan] institutions, Thuc.
to hide, cover, cloak, Hom., attic:—Mid., κάρα κρυψάμενος having cloaked his head, Soph., etc.:—Pass. to hide oneself, lie hidden, of setting stars, Hes., Eur.
to cover in the earth, bury, Hes., Hdt., attic
to hide, conceal, keep secret, Od., Soph.: —Pass., perf. part. κεκρυμμένος secret, Od., Soph.
c. dupl. acc. to conceal something from one, μή με κρύψηις τοῦτο Aesch., etc.
intr. (sub. ἑαυτόν) to hide oneself, lie hidden, Soph.
to be clear as crystal, NTest.
of crystal, crystalline, Anth.
congealed to ice, frozen, Eur.
clear ice, ice, Lat. glacies, Hom., Hdt., attic
crystal, rock-crystal, Anth.
hidden, Pind., Trag.
secret, clandestine, Aesch.:—adv. -ως, Id.
without the knowledge of, c. gen., Thuc.: absol. secretly, Id.
hidden, concealed, Soph., etc.
secret, clandestine, Hes., Soph., etc.
κρυφὸν θέμεν to throw a cloud over, Pind.
hiding one's thoughts, dissembling, Xen.
a hiding, concealment, Eur.: — the art of concealing, Arist.
a roll or knot of hair on the crown of the head, Thuc., Anth.:—also a tuft of hair on a helmet, Xen.
a nickname of the orator Hegesippus, Aeschin.
the cawing of a crow, Anth.
to cry like a crow, caw, Lat. crocitare, Hes., Ar.:—also of other birds, as cranes, Ar.; of young halcyons, Luc.:—of a wagon, to creak, groan, Babr.
a water-pail, pitcher, jar, Eur.
a cinerary urn, Mosch., Anth.
a murderer, Anth.
in pres., imperf., fut. and aor1:
to procure for oneself, to get, gain, acquire, Hom.; κτήσασθαι βίον ἀπό τινος to get one's living from a thing, Hdt.; κ. χάριν to win favour, Soph.; κ. φίλους, ἑταίρους Id.
of evils, to bring upon oneself, incur, Id., Eur., etc.: —κ. τινὰ πολέμιον to make him so, Xen.
to procure or get for another, ἐμοὶ ἐκτήσατο κεῖνος Od.

in perf. and plup. with fut. κεκτήσομαι, to have acquired, i. e. to possess, have, hold, Il., Hdt., etc.; κεκτ. τινὰ σύμμαχον Eur.; of evils, κεκτ. κακά Soph., Eur.; ὁ κεκτημένος an owner, master, as a Subst., ὁ ἐμοῦ κ. Soph.; of a woman's lord and master, Eur.
aor1 pass. ἐκτήθην in pass. sense, to be gotten, Id., Thuc.
= κτῆμα, Pind.
mostly in pl. κτέανα, possessions, property, Hes., Aesch., etc.
κόσμων κτ. thou that hast put us in possession of honours, Aesch.
to get, gain, win, Hom.:—Mid., with perf. pass., to get for oneself, acquire, Hhymn., Theocr.
gotten, acquired, Anth.

to kill, slay, Hom., etc.; of animals, to slaughter, Id.; Οὖτις με κτείνει δόλωι seeks to kill me (the force of the pres. tense), Od.; ὁ κτανών the slayer, murderer, Aesch.; οἱ κτανόντες Id.:— to put to death by law, Thuc., Plat.—In attic θνήσκω or ἀποθνήσκω is used for the Pass.
a comb, Lat. pecten: esp.,
the comb in the loom, which separates the threads of the warp, Anth.
a rake, Id.
in pl. the fingers, which branch like the teeth of a comb, Aesch.
to comb, curry horses, Eur.:— Mid., κτενίζεσθαι τὰς κόμας to comb one's hair, Hdt.
a small comb, Luc.
a combing, Eur.
a possession, Il.
funeral gifts, burnt with the dead, funeral honours, Hom.
c. acc. pers. to bury with due honours, Il.
c. acc. cogn., κτέρεα κτερεΐξαι to pay funeral honours, Od.
= κτερεΐζω 1, Il., Soph.
c. acc. cogn., κτέρεα κτ., like κτερεΐζω 2, Hom.
anything gotten, a piece of property, a possession, Od., attic:—of a slave, παλαιὸν οἴκων κτ. Eur.
in pl. possessions, property, wealth, Hom.; ἔρως, ὃς ἐν κτήμασι πίπτεις who fallest on wealth, i. e. on the wealthy, Soph.
like beasts, Hdt.
flocks and herds, which in ancient times constituted wealth, Hhymn., Hdt.
in sg. a single beast, as an ox or sheep, Hdt., Xen.: a beast for riding, Lat. jumentum, NTest.
cattle-keeping, Plut.
belonging to property, χρήματα κτ. property, Aesch.; κτ. βοτόν a sheep of one's own flock, Soph.
belonging to one's house, Ζεὺς κτήσιος the protector of property, Aesch.; κτ. βωμός the altar of Ζεὺς κτήσιος, Id.
acquisition, Thuc., Plat.; κατ’ ἔργου κτῆσιν according to success in the work, Soph.
(from perf.) possession, Id., Thuc., etc.
as collective, = κτήματα, possessions, property, Hom.; in pl., Hdt., Plat., etc.
to be gotten, Plat.
neut. one must get, Id.
acquisitive: —ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) the art of getting property, Plat.
that may be gotten, Il., Eur.
worth getting, desirable, Plat.
acquired: κτητή a female slave, Hes.
a possessor, owner, NTest., Anth.
of a marten-cat, κτιδέη κυνέη a marten-skin helmet, Il.
to people a country, build houses and cities in it, colonise, Il., Hdt., etc.
of a city, to found, plant, build, Od., Hdt., etc.:—Pass. to be founded, Σμύρνην τὴν ἀπὸ Κολοφῶνος κτισθεῖσαν founded by emigrants from Colophon, Hdt.
κτ. ἄλσος to plant a grove, Pind.; κτ. βωμόν to set up an altar, Id.; τὸν Κύρνον κτίσαι to establish his worship, Hdt.
to create, bring into being, bring about, Aesch.; τὸν χαλινὸν κτίσας having invented it, Soph.
to make so and so, ἐλεύθερον κτ. τινά Aesch., etc.
to perpetrate a deed, Soph.
tame, docile, gentle, Pind.
as Subst., κτίλος, ὁ, a ram, Il.
to tame:—Mid., ἐκτιλώσαντο τὰς λοιπὰς τῶν Ἀμαζόνων got them tamed, Hdt.
a founding, foundation, ἀποικιῶν Isocr., etc.
loosely, = πρᾶξις, a doing, an act, Pind.
a creating, the creation of the universe, NTest.
that which was created, the creation, Id.
an authority created or ordained, Id.
anything created, a creature, NTest.
a founder, Lat. conditor, Luc.: a restorer, Plut.
generally, an inhabitant, Eur.
to crash, of trees falling, Il.; of thunder, Hom., Soph.
to ring, resound, echo, Il., etc.
Causal, to make to ring or resound, χθόνα; c. dupl. acc., κτύπησε κρᾶτα πλαγάν made the head ring with a blow, Eur.: —hence again in Pass. to ring, resound, Ar.
any loud noise, a crash of thunder, Il., Aesch.; of the trampling of feet, Hom.; of a storm, Aesch.; battle- din, clash of arms, Id.
a cup, for drawing wine out of the κρατήρ or bowl, Xen., etc.
a cupping-glass, Ar.
chosen by beans, i. e. by lot, Xen.
Pass. to be so elected, Dem.
a bean, Lat. faba, Il.

the lot by which public officers were elected at Athens (because those who drew white beans were chosen), ὁ τῷ κυάμῳ λαχών an officer chosen by lot, Hdt.; βουλὴ ἡ ἀπὸ τοῦ κυάμου Thuc.; ἄρχοντας ἀπὸ κυάμου καθιστάναι Xen.
bean-eater, Ar.
the eating of beans, bean-diet, Luc.
she of the dark Aegis, Pind.
with dark edge, Theocr.
dark-gleaming, Eur., Ar.

Κ. νῆσοι or πέτραι, αἱ, dark rocks, two islands at the entrance of the Euxine, Hdt.; —mythically supposed to close and crush passing ships, hence called Συμπληγάδες; the sea near being Κυάνεα πελάγη, Soph.
properly, dark-blue, glossy-blue, of a serpent's iridescent hues, Il., Hes.; of the swallow, Simon.; of the deep sea, Eur.
generally, dark, black, of the mourning veil of Thetis, Il.; of clouds, Hom.; of hair, Il.; κυανέη κάπετος a deep dark trench, Id.; κυάνεαι φάλαγγες dark masses of warriors, Id., etc.
dark-eyed, Anth.
dark-blue, deep-blue, Eur.
dark-haired, Anth.
with feet of κύανος, Il.
dark-veiled, Hhymn.
with dark-blue prow, dark-prowed, of ships, Hom.
with blue-black feathers, dark-winged, Hes., Eur.
cyanus, a dark-blue substance, used in the Heroic Age to adorn works in metal, perh. blue steel, Hom.
as fem. the blue corn-flower, Anth.
as adj. = κυάνεος, with comp. and Sup. κυανώτερος, -ώτατος, Anacreont.
dark-robed, Bion.
dark-browed, Theocr.
dark-haired, of Poseidon, perh. in reference to the dark blue of the sea, Hom.; of a horse, dark-maned, Il., Hes.:—epic nom. κυανοχαῖτα (like ἱππότα for ἱππότης), Il.; so in voc., Hhymn.
dark-coloured, dark-looking, Eur.; so κυανό-χρως, ωτος, ὁ, ἡ, Id.
dark-eyed, fem.
Od.: generally, dark-looking, νῆες κυανώπιδες Aesch.
dark-looking, Anth.
dice-playing, dicing, Xen., etc.: metaph. sleight of hand, trickery, NTest.
a gaming-house, Aeschin.
Cybele, a Phrygian goddess, Eur., Ar.; cf. Κυβήβη.
Lat. gubernare, to steer, Od., etc.: absol. to act as pilot or helmsman, Ar.
metaph. to guide, govern, Pind., Soph.
sc. ἱερά a festival at Athens in memory of the steersman of Theseus, Plut.
steering, pilotage, Plat.
metaph. government, Pind.
a steersman, helmsman, pilot, Lat. gubernator, Hom., etc.: ionic acc. κυβερνήτεα Hdt.
metaph. a guide, governor, Eur., Plat.
good at steering, Plat.; comp. -ώτερος, Id.; Sup. -ώτατος, Xen.:— ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) the pilot's art, Plat.
a dicer, gambler, Xen.
of or for dice-playing, Aeschin.
skilled in dice-playing, Plat.
to play at dice, Ar., etc.
metaph. to run a risk or hazard, Xen., etc.; c. acc. to hazard, venture on, Eur.:—Pass. to be set upon a stake, Anth.
to tumble head foremost, tumble, Il., Xen., etc.
a summerset, Luc.
a summerset, Luc.
a tumbler, Hom.
a diver, Il. 3. one who pitches headlong, Eur.

Lat. cubus, a cube: a cubical die, marked on all 6 sides (whereas the ἀστράγαλος was marked only on four sides), in pl., dice, Hdt., etc.; the Greeks threw with three dice, so that τρὶς ἕξ, three sixes, was the highest throw, Aesch., Plat.; κρίνειν τι ἐν κύβοις to decide it by the dice, by chance, Aesch.
also of the single pips on the dice, βέβληκ’ Ἀχιλλεὺς δύο κύβω καὶ τέσσαρα he has thrown two aces and a four, Aesch. ap. Ar.
a cubic number, i. e. a number multiplied twice into itself, as 27 is the cube of 3, Plat.
to revile:—Pass. to be reviled, Soph.
to give or do honour to, glorify, Hom.
to gladden by marks of honour, Id.
in bad sense, to flatter, fawn upon, Hes.
glorious, renowned, famous, Hom.
to hold in honour, Il.
to vaunt, boast, Id.
glorious, Anth.
glorifying or ennobling men, bringing them glory or renown, Il.
pass. famous for men, Anth.
to bear oneself proudly, go proudly along, exult, Il.

entry.etym: Sup. of κυδρός, formed from κῦδος, as αἴσχιστος, sup. of αἰσχρός, from αἶσχος
entry.sense: most glorious, most honoured, noblest, Hom.
comp.
nobler: τί μοι ζῆν δῆτα κύδιον; what boots it me to live? Eur.
to make a hubbub, Ar.
to make an uproar, spread alarm, Il.
trans. to drive in confusion, Id.
the din of battle, uproar, hubbub, Il., Ar.
glory, renown, esp. in war, Il.: of a single person, κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν glory of the Achaians, like Lat. decus, Hom.
glorious, illustrious, noble, Hom., Hes.; of a horse, proud, stately, Xen. (For the irreg. comp. and Sup., v. κύδιστος.）
Cydonian: μῆλον Κ. a quince, Stesich., etc.
metaph. swelling like a quince, round and plump, Ar.
like κύω, to bear in the womb, to be pregnant with a child, Lat. gestare, Il., Plat.
absol. to be pregnant, be with child, Hdt.
an island and town on the coast of Mysia, Hdt.:—hence Κυζῐκηνός, ή, όν of or from Cyzicus: ὁ Κυζικηνός (with or without στατήρ), a gold coin, Xen.
that which is conceived, an embryo, foetus, Plat.
pregnant, Hesych.
conception, Plat.
Cythereia, surname of Aphrodite, Od.:— also Κυθέρη, and Κυθηριάς, άδος, Anth.
an island, now Cerigo, to the south of Laconia, Hom.
Cytherean, Il., etc.; ἡ Κυθηρία (sc. γῆ) Xen.
a Spartan magistrate sent annually to govern the island of Cythera, Thuc.
from Cythera, Il.
Pass. to conceive, become pregnant, Hdt., Plat.
to stir up and mix, beat up, Hom., Ar.: Mid. in Act. sense, Ar.

like ταράσσω, to stir up, to throw into confusion or disorder, confound, Aesch., Ar., Plat., etc.:—Pass. to be confounded, panic-stricken, Il.; of waves, Hom.; ὑπ’ ἀνδρὸς τοξότου κυκώμενος hustled by him, Ar.
mixed drink, a potion, tankard, made of barley-meal, grated cheese and wine, Hom.
metaph. of any mixture, medley, Luc.
a ladle for stirring: metaph. an agitator, Ar.
a stirring up, mixing up, Plat.
mixed with ashes, Ar.
round, circular; and of Time, revolving, Eur.; αἱ Κυκλάδες (sc. νῆσοι), the Cyclades, islands in the Aegaean sea, which encircle Delos, attic
to move round and round, wheel along, c. acc., Il.
to move round or in a circle, Soph.; βάσιν κυκλεῖν, metaph. from dogs questing about for the scent, Id.; κ. πρόσωπον to turn the face round, look round, Eur.
Mid. and Pass. to form a circle round, to surround, encompass, encircle, Hdt., Soph.
to go round and round, revolve, Plat.
round, Anth.
circular: οἱ κυκλικοί, Epic poets whose writings formed a cycle or series of legends down to the death of Ulysses, Anth.
a teacher of the dithyrambic chorus (v. κύκλιος II), Ar.
round, circular, ὕδωρ κύκλιον, of the Delian lake (cf. τροχοειδής), Eur.
κύκλιος χορός, οῦ, a chorus danced in a ring round an altar, a dithyrambic chorus, Ar., etc.:— κύκλια μέλη dithyrambic songs, Ar.
to brawl like the torrent Cycloborus, Ar.
Cycloborus, a torrent in Attica, Ar.
driven in a circle, Anth.
from all around, NTest.
a round lead-pencil, Anth.
in or into a circle or round, Il.
to drive round in a circle, whirl round, Ar.
a ring, circle, round, Hom.; ἀσπίδος κύκλος the round shield, Aesch.
Adverbial usages, κύκλῳ in a circle or ring, round about, Od., Hdt., attic; c. gen., κ. τοῦ στρατοπέδου Xen., etc.
any circular body:
a wheel, Il.
a place of assembly, the ἀγορά, Id., attic:—then, like Lat. corona, a ring or circle of people, Soph., Xen.
the vault of the sky, Hdt., Soph., etc.
the orb or disk of the sun and moon, Hdt., Trag.
the wall round a city, esp. round Athens, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
a round shield, v. supr. 1. 1.
in pl. the eye-balls, eyes, Soph.:—rarely in sg., the eye, Id.
any circular motion, an orbit of the heavenly bodies, revolution of the seasons, cycle of events, Hdt., Eur.
a circular dance, Ar.
made round by turning (as in a lathe), Hdt.: then, generally, round, circular, Hom., etc.; κυκλοτερὲς τόξον ἔτεινεν stretched it into a circle, Il.
to encircle, surround, Eur.:—so in Mid., Hdt., Aesch., etc.:—Pass. to be surrounded, Aesch., Thuc.
to move in a circle, whirl round, Pind., Eur.:—Pass. or Mid. to go in a circle, go round, Xen.; metaph., Aesch.
to form into a circle, τόξα Anth.:— Pass., of a bow, to form a circle, Eur.; cf. κυκλοτερής.
Cyclopean, commonly used of the architecture attributed to the Cyclopes, (also called Πελασγικός), Eur.
like the Cyclopes, Κ. ζῆν to live a savage unsocial life, Arist.
little Cyclops, Eur.
ἡ K. γῆ, i. e. Mycenae, Id.:—fem. Κυκλωπίς, ίδος, Id.
a surrounding, in a battle, Xen.; τὴν πλέονα κύκλωσιν σφῶν the larger body that was endeavouring to surround them, Thuc.
rounded, round, Aesch.

a Cyclops, properly Round-eye.— The Cyclopes appear in Od. as savage giants, dwelling in Sicily; in sg. of Polyphemus:— they were builders of the walls of Mycenae, etc., τὰ Κυκλώπων βάθρα, i. e. Mycenae, Eur.
of a swan, Anth.
swan-shaped, Aesch.
swan-plumed, Eur.
a swan, Il., etc.:—metaph., from the legends of the swan's dying song (Aesch., Plat.), a minstrel, Anth.
swan-like, Anth.
a rolling, wallowing, Plut.
a roller, cylinder, Plut.
to roll, roll along or down, Od., Soph., etc.: metaph., πῆμα θεὸς Δαναοῖσι κυλίνδει rolls down calamity upon one, Il.
to roll away, Anth.
Pass. to be rolled, roll along, roll, Hom.: to toss about like a ship at sea, Pind.: to be whirled round on a wheel, of Ixion, Id.
of persons, κυλίνδεσθαι κατὰ κόπρον to roll or wallow in the dirt (in sign of grief), Hom.: to roam to and fro, wander about, Xen.
of Time, to roll by, Pind.
of words, to be tost from man to man, i. e. be much talked of, Lat. jactari, Ar.
a cup, drinking-cup, wine-cup, Lat. calix, Hdt., Pind., etc.; περιελαύνειν τὰς κ. to push round the cup, Xen.
a rolling, wallowing, or a wallowing place, NTest.
a place for horses to roll in, Xen.
later form of κυλίνδω, to roll along, Theocr., Luc.
Aegyptian bread, Hdt.
Cyllene, a mountain in Arcadia, Il.; whence Hermes was called Κυλλήνιος, Hom.
crook-footed, halting, of Vulcan, Il.; voc. Κυλλοπόδῑον Id.
crooked, crippled, properly of legs bent outwards by disease, Ar.:— ἔμβαλε κυλλῇ (sc. χειρί) put into a crooked hand, i. e. with the fingers crooked like a beggar's, Id.
to have a swelling below the eye, from a blow or from sleepless nights, Ar., Theocr.
to rise in waves or billows, to swell, Hom., Plat.
metaph. of passion, to swell, seethe, Pind., Aesch.
trans. to agitate, Luc., Anth.:—Pass., Plut.
anything swollen (as if pregnant):—hence,
the swell of the sea, a wave, billow, Hom., etc.; collectively, ὡς τὸ κῦμα ἔστρωτο when the swell abated, Hdt.
metaph. of a flood of men, Aesch.:—metaph., κ. ἄτης, κακῶν, συμφορᾶς Id., Eur.
the foetus in the womb, embryo, Aesch.; of the earth, Id.
surging, billowy, κ. ὁ ποταμὸς ἐγένετο Hdt.
act. causing waves, stormy, ἄνεμος Id.
breaking like waves, Soph.
wave-stiller, a Nereid, Hes.
wave-beaten, Soph.
to cover with waves, Plut.
Pass. to be raised or to rise in waves, of the sea, Thuc.
a place where the waves break, the beach, Hdt.
on which the waves break, Plut.
a cymbal, Xen.
head-foremost, Lat. pronus, Il.
as Subst. the crown of a helmet, Id.
a bird, perh. the night-jar, Il.
to strew with cummin, Luc.
cummin, attic, NTest.
a cummin-splitter, i. e. a skinflint, niggard, Arist.
a cummin-splitting-cress-scraper, Ar.
meeting the waves, Eur.
wave-receiver, a Nereid, Il.
wave-swift, a Nereid, Il., Hes.
wave-walker, Hes.
wavy, a Nereid, Hes.
a dog's collar, Anth.
a hound-leader, i. e. a huntsman, Aesch., Soph.
a leader of hounds, huntsman, Xen.
a fox-dog, mongrel between dog and fox, nickname of Cleon, Ar.
dog-fly, i. e. shameless fly, abusive epithet of impudent women, Il.
a little dog, whelp, Xen., etc.
fem. adj. of a dog: as Subst. (sub. θρίξ), dog's hair, of a bad fleece, Theocr.
to play the Cynic, Luc.

entry.etym: properly fem. of κύνεος, sub. δορά
entry.sense: a dog's skin: then, a leathern cap, not necessarily of dog's skin, for we find κ. ταυρείη, κτιδέη, etc., Hom.
of, belonging to a dog, Ar.; κ. θάνατος a dog's death, Id.; τὰ κύνεια (sub. κρέα) dog's flesh, Id.
metaph. shameless, unabashed, Il., Hes.
to kiss, Hom., Eur., etc.
= προσκυνέω, Eur.

entry.etym: later form for κῠνηγέσιον (signf. II), Plut.

entry.sense: a hunting-establishment, huntsmen and hounds, a pack of hounds, Hdt., Xen.
a hunt, chase, pursuit, Xen.; so in pl., Eur.
that which is taken in hunting, the game, Xen.
to hunt, Ar., Xen., etc.:—metaph. to persecute, harass, Aesch.
to quest about, like a hound, Soph.
a hunter, huntsman, Od., Eur., etc.; κυναγέτας ἀμφὶ πάλᾳ one who seeks the prize in wrestling, Pind.:—fem. κυνηγέτις, doric κῠναγέτις, ιδος a huntress, Anth.
of or for hunting, fond of the chase, Plat.:— ὁ κυνηγετικός [λόγος] name of Xenophon's work on Hunting.
to hunt, chase, later form of κυνηγετέω, Plut.
hunt, chase, hunting, Trag.
the hunt, chase, Plut.
like a dog, Ar.
Cynthus, a mountain in Delos, birth-place of Apollo and Artemis, Hhymn.:—hence Apollo is called Κύνθιος, and Κυνθο-γενής, born on Cynthus, Ar., Anth.
a puppy (cf. λαγιδεύς, λυκιδεύς) , Theocr.
a little dog, whelp, puppy, Ar., Plat., etc.
to play the dog: metaph. to live like a Cynic, belong to their sect, Luc.
dog-like, Lat. caninus, Xen.
Κυνικός, οῦ, a Cynic, as the followers of the philosopher Antisthenes were called, Plut.
a bitch-puppy, Ar.
a young dog, puppy, Hdt.
metaph. a little Cynic, Luc.
Cynical philosophy or conduct, Luc.
a canine tooth, Xen., etc.
to run with dogs, Xen.
impudent as a dog, Theocr.
dog-headed; οἱ Κυνοκέφαλοι, dog-heads, the name of a people, Hdt.
the dogfaced baboon, Plat., Luc. [κυνοκεφάλλῳ in Ar.]
dog-stealing, Ar.
to beat like a dog, Ar.
dog-faced, Luc.
Cynosarges, a gymnasium outside Athens, for the use of those who were not pure Athenians, Hdt., Dem., etc.
dog-thorn or dog-rose, Theocr.
dog's-tail, the Cynosure, a name for the constellation Ursa Minor, Arat.
torn by dogs, Soph.
a dog-holder, dog-leash, Anth.
a dog-skin sack, used in hunting, Xen.
dog-minded, shameless, Aesch.
more dog-like, i. e. more shameless, more audacious, Hom.; more horrible, κύντερον ἄλλο ποτ’ ἔτλης Od.
Sup. κύντατος, η, ον most audacious, Il., Hhymn.
a she-dog:—as prop. n. Κυνώ, Hdt.
the dog-eyed, i. e. shameless one, Il.:—so fem.κῠνῶπις, ιδος, Hom.
to be pregnant, Luc.
of cypress-wood, Od., Thuc.
a cypress, Od., Hdt., etc.
a short frock, Anth.
a sweet-smelling marsh-plant, perh. galingale, used to feed horses, Hom.
at which they fight with cups (cf. Horace pugnare scyphis), Anth.
a big-bellied drinking vessel, a beaker, goblet, cup, Hom.
carrying cups, Anth.
like Cypris, i. e. lovely, tender, Anth.
of Cyprus, Cyprian, Hdt., etc.
Κύπρια, τά, an Epic poem introductory to the Il., Id.
Cypris, a name of Aphrodite, from the island of Cyprus, where she was most worshipped, Il., Trag., etc.
as appellat. love, passion, Eur., etc.
Cyprus-born, of Aphrodite, Hhymn., etc.:—fem. Κυπρο-γένεια, ἡ, Pind.
from Cyprus, Anth.
to Cyprus, Il.
Cyprus, a Greek island on the S. coast of Asia Minor, Hom., etc.:—the Romans got from it the best copper, Lat. cyprium.
to keep stooping, to go poking about, potter about a thing, Ar., Plat.

to bend forward, stoop down, Hom., Hdt., etc.; θέει κύψας runs with the head down, i. e. at full speed, Ar.; κύψας ἐσθίει eats stooping, i. e. greedily, Id.; κέρεα κεκυφότα ἐς τὸ ἔμπροσθεν horns bent forward, of certain African oxen, Hdt.
to hang the head from shame, Ar.
to bow down under a burden, Dem.
a Persian bonnet or hat, with a peaked crown, prob. much like the τιάρα, Hdt.: the King alone wore it upright, Ar.

entry.etym: shortd. form of Κορύβας, q. v.

entry.sense: triangular tablets, fitted at the angles so as to form a pyramid of three sides, and having the earliest laws written on the sides, Ar., Plat.
in sg. metaph. of a pettifogging lawyer, Ar.
of Cyrus, Xen.
followed by a case, to hit, light upon:
c. dat. to light upon, meet with, fall in with, strike against, Il., Hes.:—of things, κυρεῖν τινι to befall or be granted to him, Soph., Eur.
c. gen. to hit the mark, like τυγχάνω, Aesch.:— to reach to or as far as, Hhymn.: to meet with, find, Aesch., Soph.
to attain to, be master of, obtain, Lat. potiri, Hdt., Trag.
c. acc., like Lat. potiri, to obtain, reach, find, Aesch., Eur.
without a case, to happen, come to pass, Trag.
to be right, hit the exact truth, Soph.

as auxil. Verb, like τυγχάνω with partic., to turn out, prove to be so and so, σεσωσμένος κυρεῖ Aesch.; ζῶν κυρεῖ Soph.; ἐχθρὸς ὢν κυρεῖ Eur.; with partic. omitted, it acts merely as the copula, to be, Trag.
to butt with the horns: metaph., τὸ σκέλος κυρηβάσει he shall come butt against my leg, or my leg shall butt him, kick him, Ar.
husks, bran:—a bran-shop, Ar.
Cyrene, a Greek colony in Africa, Hdt.: —the people were called Κυρηναῖοι, and the country ἡ Κυρηναία, Id.

of or for a lord or master: esp. belonging to the Lord (Christ); Κ. δεῖπνον the Lord's Supper, ἡ κυριακὴ ἡμέρα the LORD'S day, dies Dominica, NTest. (Assumed to be original of the Teutonic kirk, kirche, church; but how this Greek name came to be adopted by the Northern nations, rather than the Roman name ecclesia, has not been satisfactorily explained.)
to be lord or master of people orof a country, c. gen., Xen.
to have legal power to do, c. inf., ap. Aeschin.

of persons, having power or authority over, lord or master of, c. gen., Pind., attic:— κύριός εἰμι, c. inf., I have authority to do, am entitled to do, Aesch., etc.; κυριώτεροι δοῦναι better able to give, Thuc.
absol. having authority, authoritative, supreme, κ. εἶναι to have authority, Plat.; τὸ κύριον the ruling power in a state, τὰ κύρια the authorities, Soph., Dem.
not of persons, authoritative, decisive, dominant, supreme, δίκαι Eur.; μῦθος κυριώτερος of more authority, Id., etc.
opp. to ἄκυρος, authorised, ratified, valid, νόμοι, δόγματα Dem.; κ. θέσθαι or ποιεῖσθαί τι to appoint by authority, Soph., Dem.

of times, etc., fixed, ordained, appointed, Hdt., Eur., etc.;—so, τὸ κύριον the appointed time, Aesch.:—at Athens, κυρία ἐκκλησία a regular or ordinary assembly, opp. to σύγκλητος ἐκκλησία (one specially summoned), Ar.
legitimate, regular, proper, Aesch.
of words, authorised, vernacular, Lat. proprius, Arist.
as Subst.,
a lord, master, Lat. dominus, of gods, Pind., Soph., etc.: the head of a family, master of a house, Aesch., etc.:—later, κύριε was a form of respectful address, like our sir, NTest.
κυρία, ἡ, mistress or lady of the house, Lat. domina, Menand., etc.
ὁ Κύριος, the Lord, = Hebr. Jehovah, Lxx.; in NTest. esp. of Christ.
dominion, NTest.
to butt with the horns, Plat.:—metaph. of floating corpses knocking against the shore, Aesch.
like a lord or master, authoritatively, Aesch.
regularly, legitimately, properly, κ. ἔχειν to be fixed, hold good, Id.; κ. αἰτεῖσθαι, suo jure, Soph., etc.
of words, in their proper sense, Arist.
that which one meets with or finds, i. e. booty, prey, spoil, Hom.
of a person, one who gets booty, a swindler, Ar.
Cyrnus, old name of Corsica, Hdt.: οἱ Κύρνιοι Id.
supreme power, authority, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
confirmation, validity, certainty, Soph.
Cyrus:
ὁ πρότερος, the elder Cyrus, Hdt.
ὁ νεώτερος, the brother of Artaxerxes, Xen.

to make valid, confirm, ratify, determine, Lat. ratum facere, Hdt., Aesch., etc.:—Mid. to accomplish one's end, Plat.:—Pass. to be ratified, Hdt., attic:—generally, κεκύρωται τέλος the end hath been fixed or determined, Aesch.; πρὶν κεκυρῶσθαι σφαγάς before it has been accomplished, Eur.:—impers. c. inf., ἐκεκύρωτο συμβάλλειν it had been decided to fight, Hdt.; ἐκυρώθη ναυμαχέειν Id.
κ. δίκην to decide it, Aesch.
one that fishes with the κύρτη, Anth.
a fishing-basket, Lat. nassa, Hdt.; κυρτός, ὁ, =κυρτευτής, Plat.
a bird-cage, Lat. cavea, Anth.
curved, arched, of a wave breaking, Il.; ὤμω κυρτώ round, humped, Id.; κ. τροχός Eur.
to curve or bend into an arch, κυρτῶν νῶτα, of a bull preparing to charge, Eur.; κ. λαίφεα Anth.:—Pass. to form a curve or arch, of a wave breaking, Od., Xen.
a ratification, Thuc., Plat.
the bladder, Il., Ar.
cytisus, a kind of clover, Theocr.
a kind of plaster, Luc.
with capacious belly, Anth.
the hollow of a shield or breastplate, Aesch., Ar.
any vessel, a vase, jar, urn, Aesch., Soph., etc.; πλεκτὸν κ. a basket, Eur.
anything that contains the body, Soph.
the cell of a comb of bees or wasps, Ar.
metaph., τοὐρανοῦ τὸν κ. the concave vault of heaven, Id.
with neck arched and head low, of a horse, Xen.
bent forwards, bent, stooping, hump-backed, Od., Ar.
the bent yoke of the plough, Theogn.
a sort of pillory in which criminals were fastened by the neck, Ar.
one who has had his neck in the pillory, a knave, Lat. furcifer, Luc.
any hollow vessel: a chest, box, Hdt., Ar.
descendants of Cypselus, Theogn.
a dog or bitch, Hom., etc.; most commonly of hounds, Id., etc.; the Laconian breed was famous, Soph.;— νή or μὰ τὸν κύνα was the favourite oath of Socrates, Plat.: cf. τραπεζεύς.
as a word of reproach, to denote shamelessness or audacity in women, rashness, recklessness in men, Hom.
at Athens a nickname of the Cynics, Arist., Anth.
the Trag. apply the term to the ministers of the gods; the eagle is Διὸς πτηνὸς κύων Aesch.; the griffins Ζηνὸς ἀκραγεῖς κύνες Id.; the Bacchantes Λύσσης κ. Eur., etc.
a sea-dog, mentioned as a fish in Od.
the dog-star, i. e. the dog of Orion, placed among the stars with its master, Il.
in pres. and imperf., of females, to conceive, Orac. ap. Hdt., Theogn., etc.
rarely c. acc. to be pregnant with a child, Xen.
in aor1 ἔκῡσα, Causal, of the male, to impregnate, and mid. ἐκῡσάμην, of the female, to conceive, Hes.
a fleece, used as bedding, Hom., Hdt.
a fish of the gudgeon kind, Plat., etc.
the head, Il.
a sheepskin, fleece, used for bedding, Ar., Plat.
to prove by ringing, of money, Ar.
ringing, jingling, as with bells, Eur.
with bells on his horses' trappings, Ar.
to carry the bell round, to visit the sentinels, Ar.:—Pass., ἅπαντα κωδωνοφορεῖται everywhere the bell goes round, i. e. the sentinels are being visited, Id.

a bell, Aesch., Eur.:—in fortified towns an officer went round at night with a bell to challenge the sentries, and see that they were awake, Thuc.; ὡς κώδωνα ἐξαψάμενος like one with an alarm-bell in his hand, Dem.
a Laconian drinking-vessel, Ar.
a shriek, wail, Aesch., Soph.
a shrieking, wailing, Il., Trag.
Κωκῡτός, οῦ, ὁ, Cocytus, river of wailing (cf. Ἀχέρων), one of the rivers of hell, Od., etc.
to shriek, cry, wail, mostly of women, Hom.
to wail over one dead, Od., Aesch., Soph.

collector of the pieces at a sacrifice, name of a magistrate at Athens, who had charge of the public table in the Prytaneion, and paid the dicasts, Ar.; κωλαγρέτου γάλα, comically for the μισθὸς δικαστικός, Id.
the thigh-bone with the flesh on it, the ham, esp. of a swine, Ar., Xen.
the hollow of the knees, Lat. poples, Il.
Colias, a promontory of Attica, with a temple of Aphrodite there, Hdt., Ar.
a limb, esp. the leg, Trag.
of plants, a limb or arm, Anth.
a member of anything, as,
a member of a building, as the side or front, Hdt.
one limb or half of the race-course (δίαυλος), Aesch.
a member or clause of a sentence, Lat. membrum, Arist.
a hindrance, impediment, Eur., Thuc.
a defence against a thing, precaution, Thuc.
= κώλυμα, ἐπὶ κωλύμῃ for the purpose ofhindering, Thuc.
one must hinder, Xen.
a hinderer, Thuc.
preventive, Xen.
to let, hinder, check, prevent:

c. acc. et inf. to hinder or prevent one from doing, Hdt., Soph., etc.; with a negative added, κ. τινὰ μὴ θανεῖν Eur., etc.:—Pass. to be hindered, τοῦ ὕδατος πιεῖν from drinking of the water, Plat.; κωλυόμεσθα μὴ μαθεῖν Eur.; rarely with part., μὴ κωλύωνται περαιούμενοι Thuc.
c. gen. rei, κ. τινά τινος to let or hinder one from a thing, Xen.; so, κ. τινα ἀπό τινος Id.
c. acc. rei, to hinder, prevent, impede, Eur., Thuc.:—Pass., μηδὲ δαπάνηι κεκωλύσθω and let there be no hindrance by reason of expense, Thuc.
absol., ὁ κωλύσων one to hinder, Soph.; τὸ κωλῦον a hindrance, Xen.
often in 3 pers., οὐδὲν κωλύει there is nothing to hinder, c. acc. et inf., Hdt., Ar.:— οὐδὲν κωλύει, absol., as a form of assent, nothing hinders, be it so, Ar.
to go about with a party of revellers, to revel, make merry, Lat. comissari, Hes., Theogn., Eur., etc.
to go in festal procession, Pind., Dem.
to celebrate a κῶμος in honour of the victor at the games, to join in festivities, Pind.; c. acc. cogn., ἑορτὰν κ. Id.
c. dat. pers. to approach with a κῶμος, sing in his honour, Id.
c. acc. pers. to honour or celebrate him in or with the κῶμος, Id.
to break in upon in the manner of revellers, κ. ποτὶ τὰν Ἀμαρυλλίδα Theocr.:—generally, to burst in, Anth.
deep sleep, slumber, Lat. sopor, Hom., Hes.
the head man of a village, Xen.
a reveller, Plat., Xen.
epith. of Bacchus, the jolly god, Ar.

= Lat. vicus, a village or country town, opp. to a fortified city; properly a doric word, = attic δῆμος, Hes., Hdt.; κατοικῆσθαι κατὰ κώμας to live in separate villages (not in walled towns), of the Medes, Hdt.; so, of a country, κατὰ κώμας οἰκεῖσθαι to have its people distributed into villages, Thuc.
a villager, countryman, Plat., Xen.
in a city, one of the same quarter, Lat. vicinus, Ar.; more loosely, χθονὸς κωμῆται dwellers in a land, Eur.
Lat. comicus, = κωμῳδικός, Aeschin.
a village-town, i. e. a place not entitled to be called a πόλις, NTest.

properly a village festival: a revel, carousal, merry-making, Lat. comissatio, Hhymn., Theogn., etc.: it ended in the party parading the streets crowned, bearing torches, singing, dancing, and playing frolics, Ar.
a band of revellers, a jovial troop, Eur.:—metaph. a rout, band, κ. Ἐρινύων Aesch.; of an army, Eur., etc.
the ode sung at one of these festive processions, Pind.
a bundle of hay, Lat. manipulus, Theocr.
to represent in a comedy, to satirise, lampoon, libel, Ar., Plat.:—Pass. to be so satirised, Ar.
κωμωιδεῖν τὰ δίκαια = κωμωιδοῦντα εἰπεῖν τὰ δ., Id.
to write comedies, Luc.

a comedy, Ar., etc.:—Two derivs. are suggested: one from κῶμος, ᾠδή, the revel-song; the other from κώμη, ᾠδή, the village-song. There were three periods of Attic Comedy, Old, Middle, New, — παλαιά, μέση, νέα. The Old Comedy was used to attack by name the most powerful persons of the day, ending B. C. 393; the Middle Comedy lost the chorus, but still attacked notabilities under assumed characters, ending B. C. 337; the New was our Comedy of Manners, and may be best understood from Plautus and Terence.
of comedy, comic, Ar.
the comic poet's art, Ar.
a comic poet, because he had to train the actors and chorus, Ar.
to play the parasite and buffoon, Ar.
a maker of comedies, comic poet, Plat.
a comedian, i. e.,
a comic actor, Xen., Aeschin.
a comic poet, Plat.
hemlock, Lat. cicuta:—hemlock-juice, by which criminals were put to death at Athens, Ar., etc.
a small cone, Anth.
extracted from pine-cones, Anth.
the fruit of the πεύκη, a pine-cone, Theocr., etc.
a cone, Lat. conus, in Mathematics, Arist.
the cone of a helmet, Anth.
to make a conic section, Anth.
bearing a cone, Anth.
an Egyptian couch with mosquito-curtains; conopium in Hor.
a gnat, mosquito, Lat. culex, Hdt., Aesch., etc.
of, from the island Cos, Coan, Hdt.
as Subst., Κῷος (sc. βόλος), the highest throw with the ἀστράγαλοι, v. Χῖος.
of or near Copae (in Boeotia), ἡ Κ. λίμνη lake Copais Strab.
ἐγχέλεις Κωπαΐδες eels from lake Copais, Ar.
only in pl. κωπέες, attic κωπῆς, pieces of wood fit for making oars, oar-spars, Hdt., Ar., etc.
to propel with oars, Anth.
hilted, Il.
to pull an oar: metaph. of any similar motion forwards and backwards, as of a carpenter using an auger, Eur.
a rower, Polyb.
any handle:

the handle of an oar, and generally an oar, Od., Pind., attic; νερτέρᾳ προσήμενος κώπῃ, = θαλαμίτης, metaph. of a man of low rank, Aesch.; παραπέμπειν ἐφ’ ἕνδεκα κώπαις, a proverb of dub. origin, meaning "to escort with all the honours, " Ar.:—poet. to express ships, σὺν κώπᾳ χιλιοναύτᾳ, of Agamemnon's fleet, Eur.
the handle of a sword, the haft, hilt, Lat. capulus, Hom., Soph.
the handle of a key, Od.
the haft of a torch, Eur.
furnished with oars, Aesch., Eur., Thuc.
holding the oar, χείρ Eur.
a leathern sack or wallet for provisions, Od.
in the gymnasium, a large leathern sack hung up, filled with fig-grains (κεγχραμίδες), flour, or sand, for the athletes to strike, Arist.
doric Dim. of κούρα, a little girl, Ar.
Corycian (from the Corycian cave in Mt. Parnassus), Soph.; κορυφαὶ Κ. the peaks of Parnassus, Eur.; also Κωρυκὶς, πέτρα Aesch.
a promontory of Cilicia, Hhymn., Thuc.
the island Cos, opposite Caria, Hom.:— Κόωνδε to Cos, Il.
to prattle, chatter, Lat. garrire, mostly with notion of wheedling, Hes., Theogn., etc.
trans. to talk over, attempt to wheedle, Theogn., Soph.
of a swallow, twittering, Anacr., etc.: of persons, chattering, prattling, babbling, Lat. garrulus, Theogn., Theocr.
metaph. lively, expressive, Theocr., Anth.
radical sense, blunt, dull, obtuse, κωφὸν βέλος the blunt, dull shaft, opp. to ὀξύ, Il.
metaph.:

dumb, mute, κύματι κωφῷ with dumb wave, before it breaks, Id.; κωφὴν γαῖαν ἀεικίζει dishonours the dumb, senseless earth, Id.; τὰ μὲν ἄλλα ἔσκε κωφά the other parts of the ground sounded dull, opp. to the ringing of the hollow parts, Hdt.; ὁ κ. λιμήν, prob. the bay of Munychia, as opp. to the noisy Peiraeus, Xen.
after Hom., of men, dumb, Orac. ap. Hdt.: deaf and dumb, Id.
deaf, Lat. surdus, Hhymn., Aesch., etc.
of the mind, dull, stupid, Lat. fatuus, Soph.; also senseless, unmeaning, κ. καὶ παλαί’ ἔπη Id.
deafness, Plat., Dem., etc.

entry.etym: a gen. λάου in Soph. as if λᾶας was of first decl.
entry.sense: Lat. lapis, a stone, Hom., etc.
the part intended for grasping, a handle, haft, Dem.; λαβαὶ ἀμφίστομοι of a cup, Soph.
as a pugilistic term, a grip or hold, ὥσπερ ἀθλητὴς λαβὴν ζητεῖν Plut.:—metaph. a handle, occasion, opportunity, λαβὴν διδόναι, Lat. ausam praebere, Ar.; so, λ. παραδιδόναι, παρέχειν Id., Plat.
a bold, rash talker, braggart, Il.
a ravenous sea-fish, perh. the bass, Ar.
Dep. to talk rashly, brag, Il.
rapid of foot, rushing, Anth.
to drink hard, Anth.
Hom. of wind, rain, etc., furious, boisterous, Hdt.; λ. πῦρ, κύματα, πόντος, etc., Eur.
after Hom., of men, boisterous, turbulent, violent, Theogn., Soph., etc.
greedy, Pind., Eur.
adv. λάβρως, violently, furiously, Theogn.
greedily, Aesch.
violence, greed, Anth.
rushing furiously, Aesch.
a labyrinth or maze, a building consisting of halls connected by tortuous passages, Hdt.
any spiral body, as a snail, Anth.; ἐκ σχοίνων λαβ. a bow-net of rushes, Theocr.
Pass. to be slack or gaunt through hunger, to starve, Ar.; λᾰγᾰρόομαι, Pass. to be or become slack: of frozen water, to be in the act of thawing, Anth.
slack, hollow, sunken, of the flanks, Xen.:— κατὰ τὸ λαγαρώτατον in the least defensible part, Plut.
slack, loose, pliant, Xen.
leader of the people, Pind.
of the hare, Aesch.
a leveret, Xen.
lasciviousness, lust, Xen.
lascivious, lustful, Arist.
hare-devourer, Aesch.
a hare-hunter, Anth.
to kill hares, Anth.
a flask, flagon, Lat. lagena, Anth., etc.

c.acc. to obtain by lot, by fate, by the will of the gods, Hom.; with inf. added, ἔλαχον πολιὴν ἅλα ναιέμεν I had the sea for my portion to dwell in, says Poseidon, Il.; ἔλαχ’ ἄναξ δούλην σ’ ἔχειν Eur.:—of the genius presiding over one's life, ἐμὲ μὲν Κὴρ λάχε Il.; esp. in perf. to be the tutelary deity of a place, to protect it, θεοῖσιν, οἳ Περσίδα γῆν λελόγχασι Hdt.:—absol., πρὸς Θύμβρης ἔλαχον Λύκιοι had their post assigned near Thymbra, Il.

of public officers, to obtain an office by lot (v. κύαμος ΙΙ); ἀρχὴν λαχεῖν, opp. to χειροτονηθῆναι (to be elected), Ar.; so, c. inf., ὁ λαχὼν πολεμαρχέειν he who had the lot to be polemarch, Hdt.; οἱ λαχόντες βουλευταί (sc. εἶναι), Oratt.; and absol., οἱ λαχόντες those on whom the lot fell, Thuc.
as attic law-term, λαγχάνειν δίκην to obtain leave to bring on a suit, Plat., Oratt.; and (without δίκην) λαγχάνειν τινι to bring an action against one, Oratt.
c. gen. partit. to get one's share of, become possessed of, Hom., attic
absol. to draw (i. e. obtain) the lot, Od.: cast lots, NTest.
Causal epic redupl. aor. λέλαχον, to put in possession of a thing, πυρὸς λελαχεῖν τινα to grant one the right of funeral fire, Il.
intr. to fall to one's lot or share, Od., Eur.
a leveret, Ar.
the hollow on each side below the ribs, the flank, Eur.; in pl. the flanks, Id., Ar.
metaph. any hollow, Anth., Plut.
of the hare, Ar.:— τὰ λαγῷα (sc. κρέα), hare's flesh, and, generally, dainties, delicacies, ζῆν ἐν πᾶσι λαγῴοις Id.
a hare, Lat. lepus, Hom., Aesch., etc.
a killing of hares, Anth.
an aromatic gum, gum mastich, Hdt.
a kind of ant: as pr. n. the father of Ulysses, Od.; also Λαέρτιος, ου, Λάρτιος, Soph.
to take, seize, grasp, Il.; ὀδὰξ λαζοίατο γαῖαν may they bite the dust, Id.; metaph., πάλιν δ’ ὅ γε λάζετο μῦθον he took back, i. e. altered his speech, Hom.
the form λάζυμαι occurs in Hhymn. and Eur.
likely to escape notice, Arist.
banishing care, Il., Anth.
forgetful of sorrow, Soph.; βίοτος ὀδυνᾶν λ. a life forgetful of pain, Id.
robbing of voice, Hes.
secret, covert, clandestine, furtive, Aesch., Soph.; λ. ὡδί one born in secret child-birth, Eur.:— adv. -ως, Aesch., etc.
secretly, covertly, by stealth, treacherously, Hom.; λάθρῃ γυῖα βαρύνεται imperceptibly, Il.; so in attic, Soph., etc.
c. gen. without the knowledge of, unknown to, λάθρῃ Λαομέδοντος Il.; λάθρῃ τῶν στρατηγῶν Hdt.; so in attic.
neut.pl. as adv., treacherously, Id.
hitting secretly, δόναξ Anth.
biting secretly, Anth.
stealthy-paced, Anth.
a kind of pulse: pl. λάθυρα Babr.
a small stone, pebble, Od.
biting secretly, i. e. without barking, of a dog, Ar.
fut. άσομαι, to wench, Ar.
a wencher, Ar.:—fem. λαικάστρια, a wench, harlot, Id.
a tempest, furious storm, hurricane, Hom.

entry.etym: perh. the same as λαιμός, Ar.

entry.sense: gluttony, Plat.
very greedy, gluttonous, Arist.
throat-biting, Anth.
a dog-collar, Anth.
a springe for catching birds, Id.
gushing from the throat, Eur.
the throat, gullet, Hom., Eur.
with the throat severed, Eur.
with the throat cut, severed by the throat, Eur.; Γοργοῦς λαιμότομοι σταλαγμοί the blood dripping from the Gorgon's severed head, Id.
throat-cutting, Eur., Anth.
proparox.
= χλαῖνα, Lat. laena, Strab.
of stone or marble, Hom., etc.; λάϊνον ἕσσο χιτῶνα thou hadst put on a coat of stone, i. e. thou hadst been stoned to death, Il.
metaph. stony-hearted, Theocr.
Lat. laevus, left, λαιᾶς χειρός on the left hand, Aesch.; πρὸς λαιᾷ χερί Eur.
to reap corn, Theocr.
a kind of shield or target, lighter than the ἀσπίς, covered with raw hides, Il., Hdt.
the depth or gulf of the sea, μέγα λαῖτμα θαλάσσης, ἁλὸς λ. Hom.; alone, λαῖτμα μέγ’ ἐκπερόωσι Od.
a tattered garment, rags, in sg. and pl., Od.
a piece of cloth or canvas, a sail, Aesch.; in pl., Soph.
light, nimble, swift, Il., Pind., Eur.:—neut. pl. as adv. swiftly, Eur.
to shout, howl, Aesch.
Lacaena, a Laconian woman, Theogn., etc.
as fem. adj. = Λακωνική, Hdt., Eur., etc.
very lascivious, Ar.
Lacedaemon, the capital of Laconia, and Laconia itself, Hom., Hdt., etc.
as adj., Hdt., Eur.; but regul. adj. Λακεδαιμόνιος, α, ον, of persons, Hdt., etc.

entry.etym: from λᾰκεῖν, aor2 inf. of λάσκω
entry.sense: one that screams or cries, λ. κορώνη a cawing crow, Hes.; λ. κύων a yelping dog, ap. Plat.
to tear, Anth.
in pl. tatters, Eur.
a rent, rending, Aesch.; in pl., Id.; λακίδες πέπλων tatters, Ar.
torn, μόρος λ. death by rending, Luc.
pit-wealth, Comic nickname of Callias, who found a buried treasure, Plut.
a pond for water-fowl, Lat. vivarium, Hdt., Dem.
a pit, reservoir, Hdt., Xen.
trampled on, Soph.

to kick with the heel or foot, kick at, spurn, Od.; φλὸξ αἰθέρα λακτίζοισα flames lashing heaven, Pind.; κραδία φόβωι φρένα λακτίζει my heart "knocks at my ribs" for fear, Aesch.; τὸν πεσόντα λακτίσαι to trample on the fallen, Id.; τὴν θύραν λ. to kick at the door, Ar.:—Pass., ὑπὸ ἵππου λακτισθείς Xen.
absol. to kick, struggle, of one dying, Od.: proverb., λ. πρὸς κέντρα to kick against the pricks, Pind., Aesch., etc.
a trampling on, c. gen., Aesch.; λακτιστής, οῦ, one who kicks, ἵπποι λ. kicking horses, Xen.; λ. ληνοῦ a treader of the wine-press, Anth.
to imitate the Lacedaemonians, Plat., Xen., etc.
to be in the Lacedaemonian interest, to Laconize, Xen.
Laconian, Ar., etc.
as Subst.,
ἡ Λακωνική (sub. γῆ), Laconia, Ar., etc.
Λακωνικαί (sub. ἐμβάδες), αἱ, Laconian shoes, used by men, Id.
τὸ Λακωνικόν the state of Lacedaemon, Hdt.
imitation of Lacedaemonian manners, Cic.
a being in the Lacedaemonian interest, Laconism, Xen.
one who imitates the Lacedaemonians, Plut.
one who takes part with them, a Laconizer, Xen.
to have a Laconomania, Ar.
a Laconian or Lacedaemonian, of men, as Λάκαινα of women, Pind., Ar., etc.
as adj. Laconian, Anth.
to prattle, to babble, Pind.: of birds and grasshoppers, to chirrup, chirp, Theocr.
prattle, babbling, Anth.
to talk, chat, prattle, babble, Ar., etc.:—generally, to talk, say, Soph.
c. acc. to talk of, Theocr.
in late Gr., just like λέγω, to speak, NTest., Thuc.:—Pass., λαληθήσεταί σοι it shall be told thee, NTest.
the proper sense, to chatter, is sometimes opp. to articulate speech, as of monkeys, λαλοῦσι μὲν φράζουσι δὲ οὔ Plut.; of locusts, to chirp, Theocr.
of musical sounds, αὐλῶι λαλεῖν Id.
talkative, Anth.
talk, prattle, Mosch.
a prater, Soph., Eur.
to be talked of, Anth.
given to babbling, Ar.
a talker, prattler, Anth.
talking, talk, chat, Ar., Anth.
speech, conversation, NTest.; talkativeness, loquacity, Aeschin.
a form of speech, dialect, NTest.
pebbles, from their prattling in the stream, Theocr.
talkative, babbling, loquacious, Eur., Plat., etc.:—metaph., λάλοι πτέρυγες Anth.:—irr. comp. λαλίστερος Ar.: Sup. λαλίστατος Eur.
Hebr. words, what? why? NTest.
little jockey-Lamachus, Ar.
eager-for-fight, a well-known Athenian general, Ar., Thuc.
The orig. sense of the word is two-fold, one (more active) to take, and the other (more passive) to receive
to take:

to take hold of, grasp, seize, Hom., etc.; the part seized in gen., the whole in acc., τὴν πτέρυγος λάβεν caught her by the wing, Il.; γούνων λάβε κούρην Od., etc.:—then, with gen. of part only, ποδῶν, γούνων, κόρυθος λάβεν took hold of the feet, etc., Il.
to take by violence, seize, carry off as prize or booty, Hom.
λ. δίκην, ποινάς, Lat. sumere poenas, to exact punishment, Eur., etc.; v. infr. II. 3.
of passions, feelings, etc., to seize, Hom., etc.; of fever and sudden illnesses, to attack, Hdt., attic
of a deity, to seize, possess, τινά Hdt.: of darkness, and the like, to occupy, possess, Aesch.

to catch, come upon, overtake, as an enemy, Hom., Hdt.: to catch, find, come upon, λ. τινὰ μοῦνον Hdt., etc.: also, to catch, find out, detect, Lat. deprehendo, Id.: so Pass., ἐπ’ αὐτοφώρωι εἰλημμένος caught in the act, Ar.
λ. τινὰ ὁρκίοισι to bind him by oaths, Hdt.
to take as an assistant, Soph.
τὴν Ἴδην λαβὼν ἐς ἀριστερὴν χέρα taking, keeping Ida to your left; so, λ. ἐν δεξιᾶι Thuc.
λ. Ἑλληνίδα ἐσθῆτα to assume it, Hdt.

to apprehend by the senses, Soph., Plat.:— to seize with the mind, apprehend, comprehend, Hdt., etc.:— to take, i. e. understand, a thing so and so, e. g. a passage of an author, Lat. accipere, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
to take in hand, undertake, Hdt.
the part. λαβών is almost pleon., as, λαβὼν κύσε χεῖρα took and kissed, Od.; so in attic
to receive:
to have given one, to get, gain, win, Hom., etc.:—also in bad sense, λ. ὄνειδος Soph.; θάνατον Eur., etc.
to receive in marriage, Hdt., Xen.
λ. δίκην to receive, i. e. suffer, punishment, as we say, to catch it, Lat. dare poenas, Hdt., Eur.: —an unusual sense, v. supr. I. 2.
λ. ὅρκον to accept an oath as a test, Arist.; λ. λόγον to demand an account, Xen.
to conceive, Aesch.
to receive as produce or profit, Ar., Plat.; to purchase Ar.
to admit of, Pind.

of persons subject to feelings, passions, and the like, λ. θυμόν to take heart, Od.; so, periphr., λ. φόβον = φοβεῖσθαι, Soph., etc.; so, λ. ὕψος = ὑψοῦσθαι, Thuc.; λ. νόσον (as we say) "to take a cold, " Plat.; so, αἱ οἰκίαι ἐπάλξεις λαμβάνουσαι receiving battlements, having battlements added, Thuc.
Mid. to take hold of, lay hold on, c. gen., σχεδίης Od., Hdt., etc.
of place, λ. τῶν ὀρῶν to take to the mountains, reach, gain them, Thuc.
Λ, λ, λάμβδα λάβδα, τό, indecl., eleventh letter of the Gr. Alphabet: as a numeral λʹ = 30, but ͵λ = 30,000.
attic λ is sometimes represented by π, as κλίβανος κρίβανος, γλώσσαλγος γλώσσαργος, ναύκραρος ναύκληρος, ἀλκ-ή ἀρκ-εῖν: so, ὁλᾷς Θέωλος κόλαξ were lisping pronunc. for ὁρᾷς Θέωρος κόραξ, Ar.
doric λ becomes ν, as, ἦνθον φίντατος for ἦλθον φίλτατος; whereas attic λ sometimes replaces ν, as, λίτρον πλεύμων for νίτρον πνεύμων.
initial λ is dropt, as εἴβω for λείβω, αἰψηρὸς ἀφύσσω ἄχνη for λαιψηρὸς λαφύσσω λάχνη.
epic Poets double λ, metri grat., esp. after the augment, as, ἔλλαβε ἐλλιτάνευε; and in compds., as in τρίλλιστος:—and Homer omits λ, where two come together, metri grat., as Ἀχιλεύς.
δ sometimes becomes λ, cf. δέλτα, II. 5.
γ and λ are interchanged in μόγις μόλις.
ν before λ becomes λ, as in συλλαμβάνω ἐλλείπω.
a monster said to feed on man's flesh, a bugbear to frighten children with, Ar.
the superintendence of the λαμπαδηδρομία, a branch of the Gymnasiarchia, Arist.

the torch-race, an Athenian ceremony at the festivals of the fire-gods Prometheus, Hephaestus, and Athena, in which the runners carried lighted torches, from the joint altar of these gods in the outer Cerameicus to the Acropolis; after the Persian war Pan received a like honour, Hdt.
a torch-bearer, Aesch.
a small torch, Plat.
a bandage for wounds, Ar.
torch-carrying, bright-beaming, Eur.
a torch, Aesch., Soph., etc.: a beacon-light, Aesch.:—later, an oil-lamp, NTest., Anth.
metaph. of the sun, Soph., Eur., etc.; ἡ ἐπιοῦσα λ. the coming light, i. e. the next day, Eur.
the torch-race, like λαμπαδηδρομία, Hdt.; λαμπάδα δραμεῖν to run the race, Ar.
gleaming with torches, Soph.
to shine, only in epic part. λαμπετόων, shining, ὄσσε δέ οἱ πυρὶ λαμπετόωντι ἐΐκτην Hom.
lustre, Plut.
a torch, Aesch.: light, Id.
one of the horses of Aurora, bright, Od.
as a dog's name, firetail, Theocr.
bright, brilliant, radiant, of the sun and stars, the eyes, etc., Il., attic
of white objects, bright, Od., Hdt.
of water, bright, limpid, Aesch., etc.; of the air, Eur.
of the voice, clear, sonorous, distinct, Lat. clarus, Dem.; so, λαμπρὰ κηρύσσειν Eur.

metaph. of vigorous action, λ. ἄνεμος a fresh keen wind, Hdt.; λ. καὶ μέγας καθιείς swooping down like a fresh and mighty breeze, Ar.; λαμπρὸς φανήσεται he will come vigorously forth, Eur.:—so adv., λαμπρῶς vigorously, Thuc.
metaph. also, clear, manifest, decisive, Aesch., Thuc.: —so adv., λαμπρῶς κοὐδὲν αἰνικτηρίως Aesch.; λελυμένων λ. τῶν σπονδῶν Thuc.; λαμπρῶς ἐλέγετο it was said without concealment, Id.
of persons, well-known, illustrious, Hdt., Dem.: also magnificent, munificent, Lat. splendidus, clarus, Dem., etc.
bright, joyous, Soph.
of outward appearance, splendid, brilliant, Xen.; of youthful bloom, Thuc.: —so of dress, etc., Ar., etc.:—adv., λαμπρότατα most splendidly, Xen.
brilliancy, splendour, Hdt., attic: —in pl. distinctions, Thuc.
splendid conduct, munificence, Dem.
clearness and loudness of voice, Hdt.
clear-voiced, Dem.

to make bright or brilliant, Xen.:—Mid., ἐλαμπρύνοντο τὰς ἀσπίδας polished their shields, Id.:— Pass., ὄμμασιν λαμπρύνεται is made clear -sighted, Aesch.; λελάμπρυνται κόρας Soph. ap. Ar.:—also to be or become clear or notorious, Eur.
Mid. to make oneself splendid, pride oneself on a thing, distinguish oneself in, c. dat., Id., Thuc.
a holding of torches, watchfire, Aesch.
a stand or grate for pine and other wood used for lighting rooms, Od.; ὧ χαῖρε, λ. νυκτός thou that lightest up the night, of the beacon-fire, Aesch.; ἕσπεροι λαμπτῆρες the evening watch-fires, Soph.
generally, = λαμπάς1 Eur., Xen.
to give light, shine, beam, be bright, brilliant, radiant, of the gleam of arms, Il.; of the eyes, Id.; of fire, Soph.:—Mid. or Pass., λαμπομένης κόρυθος Il., etc.
of sound, to be clear, ring loud and clear, Soph.
metaph. to shine forth, to be famous or conspicuous, Aesch., Eur., etc.
of persons, φαιδρὸς λάμποντι μετώπωι with beaming face, Ar.: to shine, gain glory, Id.
trans. to make to shine, light up, Eur., Anth.
audacity, impudence, Plut.
gluttonous, greedy, Theocr.
metaph. bold, wanton, impudent, Xen., Plut.
in most of the act. tenses, to escape notice, to be unknown, unseen, unnoticed:
c. acc. pers., λ. τινά only, to escape his notice, Lat. latere aliquem, Hom., attic; impers., σὲ λέληθε it has escaped your notice, Plat.
most often with a part. added, in which case we usually translate the part. by a Verb, and express λανθάνω by an Adverb, unawares, without being observed, unseen, unknown; and this, either,
with an acc. pers., ἄλλον τινὰ λήθω μαρνάμενος I am unseen by others while fighting, i. e. I fight unseen by them, Il.; μὴ λάθηι με προσπεσών lest he come on unseen by me, Soph.

without an acc., μὴ διαφθαρεὶς λάθηι lest he perish without himself knowing it, Id.; δουλεύων λέληθας you are a slave without knowing it, Ar.—This construct. is reversed, as in our idiom, ἀπὸ τείχεος ἆλτο λαθών (for ἔλαθεν ἁλόμενος) Il.; λήθουσά μ’ ἐξέπινες Soph.

the compd. Verbs ἐκληθάνω, ἐπιλήθω (v. sub vocc.), take a Causal sense, to make one forget a thing, c. gen. rei: so in redupl. aor2 λέλαθον, ὄφρα λελάθηι ὀδυνάων that he may cause him to forget his pains, Il.
Mid. and Pass. to let a thing escape one, to forget:
to forget, absol. or c. gen. rei, Hom.; so in redupl. aor., οὐδέ σέθεν θεοὶ λελάθοντο Il., etc.; and in perf. pass., ἐμεῖο λελασμένος Id.; κείνου λελῆσθαι Soph.
to forget purposely, to pass over, ἢ λάθετ’ ἢ οὐκ ἐνόησεν either he chose to forget it or perceived it not, Il.
hewn out of the rock, NTest.
to hew in stone, Lxx.
an allotment of land, Hdt.
with the foot, Hom., Aesch.; λὰξ πατεῖσθαι to be trodden under foot, Aesch.
man-taming: in Hom. as prop. name.
receiving the people: in Hom. as prop. name Λαόδοκος.
ruler of the people: in Hom. as prop. n.
suffered by the people, Aesch.
serving as a passage for the people, man-conveying, λ. μηχαναί, i. e. a bridge, Aesch.
worshipped by the people, Pind.
ionic ληός, attic λεώς: —, the people, both in sg. and pl., i. e.
in the warlike language of Il., the people or men of the army, soldiers; also a land-army, opp. to a fleet; the common men, opp. to their leaders
in the peaceful Od., men, people; so, ναυτικὸς λεώς seafaring folk, Aesch.; ὁ γεωργικὸς λεώς Ar.; ἀκούετε, λεῴ hear o people! the usual way of beginning proclamations at Athens, like our oyez! Id.
in NTest. of Jews, and later of Christians, as opp. to heathens.
（σεύω) rousing or stirring nations, Hom.
λαοσσόοι ἀγῶνες assemblies to which the people flock, Pind.
（σώζω) preserving the people or nations, Anth.
a stone-worker, Anth.
stirred by a stone, Anth.
nourishing or tending the people, Pind.; τιμὴ λ. an office useful to the people, Id.
cutting stones, σμίλη Anth.
as Subst. a stone-cutter, statuary, Id.
ruining the people, destructive, c. gen., Theogn.
slaying the people, Theocr.
bearing people, λαοφόρος ὁδός a highway, thoroughfare, Il.; ὑπὲρ τῶν μάλιστα λεωφόρων πυλέων over the gates of greatest thoroughfare, Hdt.
the soft part of the body between the ribs and hip, the flank, Il., Hdt., etc.; in pl. the flanks, Lat. ilia, Hdt.
slack, loose, Arist.
insep. Prefix with intensive force, as in λά-μαχος very warlike, λα-κατάρατος much accursed.
the scum, filth, Aesch.
to lap with the tongue, of wolves, Il.
to drink greedily, suck in, Luc.
fatted, fat, Ar.; metaph., Id.
Larissaean, of or from Larissa, Thuc., etc.; ionic Ληρισσ- Hdt.
as Subst., a kind of kettle or pot, first made at Larissa, Arist.
Larissa, a name of many old Greek cities, Il., etc.:—orig. it denoted a citadel, such as the Larissa of Argos.
a charcoal-basket, Ar.
a coffer, box, chest, Il., Hdt.
a cinerary urn or coffin, Il., Thuc.
an ark, in which children were exposed, Simon.
pleasant to the taste, dainty, sweet, Hom.: —epic Sup., λᾱρώτατος οἶνος (metri grat. for λᾱρότατος) Od.: comp. λαρότερον as adv., Anth.
pleasant to the smell, Mosch., Anth.
pleasant to the eye, lovely, Anth.
pleasant to the ear, sweet to hear, Id.
a ravenous sea-bird, perh. a cormorant, described as dashing down into the sea and then floating on the waves, Od.: metaph. of demagogues, Ar.
a singing bird, Anth.
to shout lustily, bellow, bawl, Dem.
trans. to outdo in shouting, λαρυγγιῶ τοὺς ῥήτορας Ar.
the larynx or upper part of the windpipe, Arist.:—in Poets the throat, Eur., Ar.
always in pl., a trivet or stand for a pot; also a gridiron, Ar.
mockery, insult, Hdt.
with rough, shaggy neck, Hom., Ar., etc.
hairy, rough, shaggy, woolly, Hom., Soph., etc.
shaggy with brushwood, bushy, Xen., Theocr.; τὰ λάσια bushes, Xen.
hairy-breasted, Anth.
to ring, rattle, crash, λάκε χαλκός Il.; λάκε δ’ ὀστέα the bones cracked, broke with a crash, Id.
of animals, to shriek, scream, of the falcon, ὀξὺ λεληκώς Id.; of the nightingale in the falcon's talons, τί λέληκας; Hes.; also of dogs, to howl, bay, Od.
of men, to shout, scream, cry aloud, Aesch., Soph., etc.; τί λέλᾱκας; Ar.; μή νυν λακήσηις Id.:—hence of Oracles, to noise abroad, Aesch., etc.: also, to sing, πρὸς αὐλόν Eur.
c. acc. cogn. to shriek forth, utter aloud, Trag.
to crack or burst asunder, NTest.
in pl., like Lat. lautumiae, quarries, Anth.
the state of a hired workman, service, servitude, Trag.
λ. τοῦ θεοῦ, θεῶν service to the gods, divine worship, Plat.; absol., NTest.
in pl. service for hire, πόνων λατρεύματα painful service, Soph.
service paid to the gods, worship, Eur.
= λάτρις, a slave, Id.
to work for hire or pay, to be in servitude, serve, Xen.
λ. τινί to be bound or enslaved to, Soph., Eur., etc.; c. acc. pers. to serve, Eur.:—metaph., λατρ. πέτρᾳ, of Prometheus, Aesch.; μόχθοις λατρ. Soph.; λ. νόμοις to obey, Xen.
to serve the gods, λ. Φοίβῳ Eur.: c. acc. cogn., πόνον λ. to render them due service, Id.
of a servant or service, Pind.; παραδιδόναι τινὰ λάτριον to give him into slavery, Id.
a workman for hire, hired servant, and in fem. a handmaid, Theogn., Soph.
pay, hire, Aesch. in pl.
the throat, Il.
an alley, lane, passage, Lat. angiportus, Od., Hdt.: a sewer, drain, privy, Ar.
a mountain in the S. of Attica, famous for its silver-mines, Hdt., Thuc.
of Mt. Lauri_um, Ar.
gluttony, Ar.
spoils taken in war, Lat. spolia, Trag., Xen.
to sell booty, Xen.
a seller of booty, one who has bought up booty to retail, Lat. sector, Xen.
to swallow greedily, gulp down, devour, Il.; metaph. of fire, to consume, Anth.
gluttonous, Hdt., Anth.
to dig, Mosch.
gathering vegetables, Anth.
a gathering of vegetables, Thuc.
mostly in pl. garden-herbs, potherbs, vegetables, greens, Lat. olera, Plat., etc.
in pl. also, the vegetable-market, green-market, Ar.
vegetable-winged, Luc.
one who sells vegetables, a green-grocer; fem. λᾰχᾰνόπωλις, ιδος, Ar.
fem. adj. well-tilled, fertile, Od.:—others read ἐλάχεια, from ἐλαχύς, small.
Lachesis, disposer of lots, one of the three Fates, Hes., Pind.; v. Κλωθώ.
λάχεσις, ιος, as appellative, lot, destiny, ap. Hdt.
allotment, τάφων πατρῴων λαχαί a share in their fathers' tombs, Aesch.
hairy, shaggy, Il., Pind.
soft hair, down, Lat. lanugo, of a young man's beard, Od., Pind.; of the thin hair on Thersites' head, Il.; of the nap or pile on cloth, Id.; of sheep's wool, Soph.
with shaggy limbs, Eur.
Pass. to grow downy, of a youth's chin, Solon., Anth.
wool, Od.
downy, Eur.
an allotted portion, Lat. sors:
one's special lot, portion, destiny, Theogn., Soph.: one's appointed office, Aesch.
a portion obtained by lot, a lot, share, portion, Id., Xen.
= βλέπω, to behold, look upon, c. acc., Od.; ὀξὺ λάων quick of sight, Hhymn.

entry.etym: an old Doric Verb, found only in pres.
λῶ, λῆις, λῆι, λῶμες, λῆτε, λῶντι:— subj., 2 and 3rd sg. λῆις, λῆι: opt. 3rd sg. λώιη: inf. λῆν: part. τῶι λῶντι.
entry.sense: =θέλω, to wish, desire
popular, Lat. popularis, Plut.
a lioness, Hdt., Aesch.
to smooth or polish, Hom.; ἵπποισι κέλευθον λειανέω I will smooth the way, Il.
to rub smooth, pound in a mortar, Lat. levigare, Hdt.; to grind with the teeth, Xen.:— generally, to crush, extirpate, Hdt.
to smooth away wrinkles, Plat.:—metaph. to smooth or soften down harsh words, Hdt.
fem. adj. smoothing, polishing, Anth.
a kettle or caldron of copper, Hom., etc.
a basin in which the purifying water (χέρνιψ) was handed to the guests before meals, Od.; also a pan for washing the feet, Id.: a bath, Aesch.
a cymbal, Hdt.
a cinerary urn, Aesch., Soph.:—generally, a casket, Soph.
the Lat. legio, NTest., Plut.

entry.etym: Pass. is only found in 3rd sg. epic aor2
entry.sense: part. to lay asleep, lull to sleep, λέξον με Il.; ἔλεξα Διὸς νόον Id.: —Pass. and Mid. to lie asleep, to lie, Hom.
to gather, pick up, Lat. lego, colligo, Hom., Pind.; αἱμασιὰς λέγων picking out stones for building walls, Od.:—Mid. to gather for oneself, Il.
Mid. to choose for oneself, pick out, Hom.:—Pass. to be chosen, Il.
to count, tell, reckon up, Od.; μετὰ τοῖσιν ἐλέγμην I reckoned myself among them, Id.; λέκτο δ’ ἀριθμόν he told him over the number, Id.:—Pass., μετὰ τοῖσιν ἐλέχθην I was counted among these, Il.
so in attic, λ. ἐν ἐχθροῖς to count among one's enemies, count as a foe, Aesch.; λ. τινὰ οὐδαμοῦ to count him as naught, nullo in numero habere, Soph.
to recount, tell over, Od., Aesch., etc.:—Mid., τί σὲ χρὴ ταῦτα λέγεσθαι; why need'st thou tell the tale thereof? Il.; μηκέτι ταῦτα λεγώμεθα Id.
to say, speak, Hdt., Trag., etc.; λέγε say on, Hdt.; so, λέγοις ἄν Plat.: of oracles, to say, declare, Hdt.
λέγειν τινά τι to say something of another, esp., κακὰ λ. τινά to speak ill of him, abuse, revile him, Id.; ἀγαθὰ λ. τινά Ar.;—also, εὖ or κακῶς λ. τινά Aesch., etc.
to call by name, Soph.:— to call so and so, οὔτοι γυναῖκας ἀλλὰ Γοργόνας λέγω Aesch.
λ. τινὰ or τινὶ ποιεῖν τι to tell one to do, Soph., Xen., etc.

λ. τι to say something, i. e. to speak to the point or purpose, Soph.; λέγω τι; am I right? Id.; opp. to οὐδὲν λέγει, has no meaning, no authority, Ar.; but οὐδὲν λέγειν, also, to say what is not, to lie, Id., Plat., etc.

like Lat. dicere, to mean, τί τοῦτο λέγει; what does this mean? Ar., Plat.; πῶς λέγεις; how mean you? Plat.:—to explain more fully, εἴσω κομίζου σύ, Κασάνδραν λέγω get thee in—thou, I mean Cassandra, Aesch.; ποταμός Ἀχελῶιον λέγω Soph.

Pass., λέγεται, like Lat. dicitur, it is said, on dit, Hdt., attic; also λέγονται εἶναι they are said to be, Xen.:— τὸ λεγόμενον, absol., as the saying goes, Thuc., etc.:— ὁ λεγόμενος the so-called, οἱ λ. αὐτόνομοι εἶναι Xen.
of orators, to speak (emphatically), λέγειν δεινός Soph.; λ. τε καὶ πράσσειν δυνατώτατος Thuc.
to boast of, tell of, Xen.: to recite what is written, λαβὲ τὸ βιβλίον καὶ λέγε Plat., etc.:—but the sense of Lat. lego, to read, only occurs in compds., ἀναλέγομαι, ἐπιλέγομαι.
a making of booty, robbery, Xen.
to drive away cattle as booty, to make booty, Soph., Xen.
c. acc. loci, to plunder, despoil, Hdt.

entry.note: λεία, ionic ληίη, doric λαία, ἡ,
entry.sense: booty, plunder, Hdt., Soph., Eur., etc.:—generally, pillageable property, Thuc., Xen.; λείαν ποιεῖσθαι χώραν = λεηλατεῖν χώραν, Thuc.:— Μυσῶν λεία, of anything that may be plundered with impunity, from the effeminate character of the Mysians, Dem.
plunder (as an act), ζῆν ἀπὸ ληίης Hdt.
to pour, pour forth, οἶνον λείβειν to make a libation of wine, Hom.; also λείβειν (without οἶνον) Il.; λείβειν θεοῖς Od.

like εἴβω, to let flow, shed, δάκρυα λ. Hom., Trag.: —Pass., of the tears, to be shed, pour forth, Eur., Xen.; of persons, λείβεσθαι δακρύοις κόρας to have one's eyes running with tears, Eur.: metaph. of sound, Pind.
in Pass., also, to melt or pine away, Ar.
a meadow, Eur., Anth.
τοῦ παιδὸς τὰ λείμματα what was left of him, his remains, Hdt.
of a meadow, Lat. pratensis, Aesch., Theocr.
from a meadow, Il.; also λειμωνόθε, Theocr.
any moist, grassy place, a meadow, mead, holm, Lat. pratum, Hom., Aesch., etc.
smooth-chinned, Hdt.
having low waves, Luc.
smoothing the warp, Anth.
a lion's skin, Anth.
a lion-fighter, Theocr.
a wrestler with a lion, Anth.
Lat. levis, smooth, Il., Plat., etc.:—of cloths, smooth, plain, not embroidered, Thuc.
smooth, level, flat, of land, Hom.; λεῖα δ’ ἐποίησεν [θεμείλια] levelled them with the ground, Il.:—c. gen., χῶρος λεῖος πετράων smooth (i. e. free) from rocks, Od.
smooth-skinned, beardless, Theocr.
metaph. smooth, soft, of wind, Ar.; of words, Aesch.
smoothness, Aesch., Xen., etc.
one must leave or abandon, Eur., Plat., etc.
trans.,
to leave, quit, Hom., etc.
to leave behind, leave at home, Id., etc.; esp. of dying men, to leave (as a legacy), Il., etc.:— so in Mid. to leave behind one, as a memorial, Hdt., etc.
to leave, forsake, abandon, desert, leave in the lurch, Il., etc.; λ. ἐράνους to fail in paying . . , Dem.; so, λ. δασμόν, φοράν Xen.:—conversely, λίπον ἰοὶ ἄνακτα the arrows failed him, Od.
intr. to be gone, to be wanting, cease, be missing, Lat. deficio, Soph., Eur., etc.
Pass. to be left, left behind, Hom., etc.
to remain, remain over and above, Il., Hdt., etc.
to remain alive, Od.
c. gen. to be left without, to be forsaken of, σοῦ λελειμμένη Soph.;— but, λελειμμένος δορός left by the spear, i. e. not slain, Aesch.

to be left behind in a race, Il.; λελειμμένος οἰῶν lingering behind the sheep, Od.; ἐς δίσκουρα λέλειπτο he had been left behind as much as a quoit's throw, Il.; τοῦ κήρυκος μὴ λείπεσθαι not to be behind the herald, Thuc.
to come short of, be inferior, worse, weaker or less than, τινος Hdt., attic; λέλειψαι τῶν ἐμῶν βουλευμάτων you come short of, understand not my plans, Eur.
λείπεσθαι ἀπό τινος to keep aloof from one, Il.; λ. βασιλέος or ἀπὸ βασιλέος to desert the king, Hdt.:—absol. to keep aloof, be absent, Id.
to be wanting or lacking in a thing, ὀδυρμάτων ἐλείπετ’ οὐδέν Soph., etc.
properly, like a lily: metaph., χρὼς λειριόεις lily skin, Il.; of the cicadae, ὂψ λειριόεσσα their delicate voice, Id.
a lily, esp. the white lily, Hhymn.
of or for the people, public.
at Athens, to serve public offices at one's own cost, Oratt.; τὰ λελειτουργημένα the services performed, Dem.
generally, to perform public duties, to serve the people or state, τῇ πόλει Xen.; so, λ. τοῖς σώμασι to serve in one's own person, Dem.
more generally, to serve a master, c. dat., Arist.
to perform religious service, minister, NTest.
the performance of a λειτουργία, Plut.

at Athens, a liturgy, i. e. a public duty, which the richer citizens discharged at their own expense.—The ordinary liturgies (ἐγκύκλιοι) were the γυμνασιαρχία, χορηγία, and ἑστίασις: the extraordinary, such as the τριηραρχία, were reserved for special occasions.
generally, any service or ministration, help, NTest.
the public service of the gods, Arist.:— the service or ministry of priests, NTest.: hence our word liturgy.
ministering, NTest.
at Athens, one who performed a λειτουργία (q. v.).
a public servant, the Roman lictor, Plut.: metaph., λ. τῆς χρείας ἐμῆς ministering to my need, NTest.
in religious sense, a minister, Id.
a tree-moss, lichen, then, a lichenlike eruption, canker, scurvy, blight, Aesch.
lick-man, name of a mouse, Batr.: so also λειχο-μύλη, ἡ, Lick-meal, Id.:
lick-platter, Id.
to lick up, Hdt., Aesch., Ar.
irreg. part. perf., γλώσσηισι λελειχμότες playing with their tongues, Hes.
gathering remnants, Anth.
a piece left, wreck, remnant, relic, Eur.
in pl., remains, remnants, Lat. reliquiae, of the dead, Soph., Plat.;—but, ἀγαθῶν ἀνδρῶν λ. are their deeds, good name, Eur.; λείψανα, remnants of youth, Ar.
a waterless district near mount Parnes in Attica, Hdt.
smooth; as pr. n. in Hom.
a hod, Id.
Dim. of λεκᾰ́νη, Ar., Xen.
a peasepudding-seller, Ar.
pulse-porridge, peasepudding, Ar.
a dish, plate, pot, pan, Hippon.
to be said or spoken, Plat.
λεκτέον, one must speak, Id.
able to speak, Xen.
suited for speaking, Dem.
（λέγω2) gathered, chosen, picked out, Aesch., Soph., etc.
（λέγω3) capable of being spoken, to be spoken, Soph., Eur., etc.
a couch, bed, Lat. lectus, in sg. and pl., Hom.; λέκτρονδε to bed, Od.
pl. the marriage-bed, Pind., Trag.; ἀλλότρια, νόθα, λέκτρα, of illicit connexions, Eur.

entry.etym: adverb from part. perf. of λανθάνω,
entry.sense: imperceptibly, Plat.
to strive eagerly, in part. λελῐημένος, Il.; as a mere adj. eager, in haste, Id.: later 3rd sg. plup., Theocr.
according to calculation, Hdt., Eur.
a boat, Lat. lembus, a ship's cock-boat, Dem.
a fishing-boat, Theocr.
that which is peeled off, peel, husk, skin, scale, Ar.
Lat. linteum, a cloth, napkin, NTest.
a speaking, saying, speech, Plat.
a way of speaking, diction, style, Id., etc.
κατὰ λέξιν as the phrase goes, Anth.
(sub. δορά ) a lion's skin, Hdt., Ar.
of a lion, Theocr.
fed on by lions, Strab.
in chariot drawn by lions, Anth.
lion-headed, Luc.
lion-killing, Anth.
bearing the figure of a lion, Luc.
of lion nature, Eur.
clad in a lion's skin, Anth.
lion-like, Plat., etc.

a broad leather strap fastening the yoke (ζυγόν) to the neck, and passing between the fore-legs to the girth (μασχαλιστήρ), mostly in pl., Il., Aesch.: so metaph., ἀνάγκης δῦναι λέπαδνον to put on the halter of necessity, Aesch.
rocky, rugged, Eur.
with white coat, Theocr.
a limpet, from its clinging to the rock (λέπας), Ar.
a bare rock, scaur, crag, Aesch., Eur., etc.
a limpet-shaped drinking-cup, Ar.
Pass. to be covered with scales.
scaly, covered with scales, of the crocodile, Hdt.; of scale-armour, Id.
as Subst., a fish of the Nile with large scales, Id.
a scale, husk, λ. ᾠοῦ an egg- shell, Ar.; the cup of a filbert, Anth.
collectively, the scales of fish, Hdt.
leprosy, Hdt.
scaly, scabby, rough, leprous, Ar.
fine, delicate, Il., Anth.
thin-upon-thin, i. e. thin as thin can be, Anth.
of thin, poor soil, Thuc.
written small or neat, Luc.
written small or neat, Luc.
slightly framed, slight, Aesch.
to talk subtly, to chop logic, quibble, Ar.; λ. τι to discuss in quibbling fashion, Luc.:—so as Dep. λεπτολογέομαι, Id.
speaking subtly, subtle, quibbling, Ar.
of fine threads, Eur., Anth.
sc. νόμισμα a very small coin, a mite, NTest.
peeled, husked, threshed out, Il.
fine, small, of dust, ashes, etc., Id., Soph., Ar.
