thin, fine, delicate, of cloth, thread, etc., Hom., Eur.
of the human figure, thin, lean, meagre, Ar., Xen.: also slender, taper, Plat.
of space, like στενός, strait, narrow, Od.; ἐπὶ λεπτόν in a thin line, Xen.
generally, small, weak, impotent, μῆτις Il.; ἐλπίς Ar.; λ. ἴχνη faint traces, Xen.; τὰ λεπτὰ τῶν προβάτων small cattle, i. e. sheep and goats, Hdt.; λ. πλοῖα small craft, Id., etc.
light, slight, of sounds, Aesch.; λ. πνοαί light breezes, Eur.
of wine, light, Luc.
metaph. fine, subtle, refined, νοῦς, μῦθος Eur., etc.:— so adv., λεπτῶς μεριμνᾶν Plat.
thinness: fineness, delicacy, leanness, Plat.
metaph. subtlety, Ar.
to cut small, mince, Strab.
to do fine work, of joiners and turners, Plut.
metaph. = λεπτολογέω, Eur.
finely worked, Hhymn.
to make small or fine: to thresh out, winnow, Anth.:—Pass. to be reduced, grow lean, Arist.; τοὺς ὤμους λεπτύνεσθαι Xen.
consisting of coats or layers, like the onion, Arist.
to strip off the rind or husks, to peel, bark, περὶ γάρ ῥά ἑ χαλκὸς ἔλεψεν φύλλα τε καὶ φλοιόν Il.
metaph. in Com. poets, to hide, i. e. thrash.
Lerna, in Argolis, the abode of the Hydra, Eur.:—adj. Λερναῖος, η, ον or ος, ον, Hes., Eur.
to imitate Sappho (the Lesbian poetry), Ar.
Lesbian, of Lesbos, Hdt., etc.
a Lesbian woman, Il.; so Λεσβιάς, άδος, Anth.
from Lesbos, Il.
Lesbos, an island on the W. coast of Asia Minor, Hom., etc.
to prate, chatter, Theogn.
gossip, Plat.
to chat or converse with, τινί App.; in Mid. to chat, converse, cf. προ-λεσχηνεύομαι.
a place where people assembled to talk and hear news, a lounge, club-room, Od., etc.: —also a council-hall, council, Aesch., Soph.
talk or gossip, such as went on in the λέσχαι, Eur.:— in good sense, conversation, discussion, Hdt., Soph.
in sad or sorry plight, wretched, pitiful, dismal, Od.:—adv., so, λευγαλέως χωρεῖν to go in ill plight, Il.
a Levite, NTest.
to make white, whiten, Od., Eur., etc.
to make bright or light, ἠὼς λευκαίνει φῶς morn brightens up her light, Eur.
white-blossoming; generally, blanched, white, Pind.; v. χνοάζω.
to have white blossoms: generally, to be white or made white, Hdt., Babr.
of or with white clay, Strab.
white-shielded, Il., Xen.:—in Trag. the Argives are λευκάσπιδες.
poet. fem. of λευκός, Eur.
white leprosy, Hdt., etc.
the white poplar, Lat. populus alba, Ar., Dem.
with white oars, Eur.
white, blanched, Aesch.
daughters of Leucippus, nymphs worshipped at Sparta, Eur.
riding or driving white horses, Pind., Soph.; λ. ἀγυιαί streets thronged with white horses, Pind.
to paint in white on a coloured ground, Arist.
the white goddess, under which name Ino was worshipped as a sea-goddess, Od.
λευκότρῐχος, ον, white-haired, white, Eur., Ar.
with white cuirass, Xen.
made of λευκόϊον, Anth.
for λευκὸν ἴον, literally white-violet, but used for
the wall-flower, Theocr., etc.
a bulbous plant, the snow-flake, Anth.
white with surf, Eur.
white flax for ropes and rigging, Hdt.
white-crested, Ar.:—as Subst. λευκόλοφον, τό, a white hill, Anth.
white, as a colour, τὸ λ. οἶδεν knows black from white, Ar.
a white dress, λευκὸν ἀμπέχει are dressed in white, Id.
with white fruit, Anth.
fair-cheeked, Anth.
a white rock, Polyb.
gen. εως, white-armed, Eur.
white-footed, bare-footed, Eur.
white-winged, of a ship, Eur.:—generally, white, Aesch., Eur.
with white horses, Trag.
light, bright, brilliant, of sun light, Hom., Soph.; and of metallic surfaces, λέβης Il.; also, λ. γαλήνη a glassy calm, Od.; of water, generally, bright, limpid, Hom., Eur.
metaph. clear, plain, distinct, of authors, Anth.
of colour, white, Hom., etc.; λ. ἅρμα = λεύκιππον, Eur.

of the skin, white, fair, Hom., Trag.; with a notion of bare, πούς Eur., cf. λευκόπους:—later, as a mark of effeminacy, blanched, white, pale, Ar., Xen.:— λευκαὶ φρένες in Pind. may be pale with envy, envious.
λ. χρυσός, pale gold, i. e. gold alloyed with silver (prob. the same as ἤλεκτρον), opp. to χρυσὸς ἄπεφθος, Hdt.
λευκὸν ἦμαρ νυκτὸς ἐκ μελαγχίμου a bright day after a night of mourning, Aesch.
grizzled, Eur.
white-ankled, Theocr.
white-growing, Ar.
white-gleaming, Eur.
white-robed, Anth.
white-browed, Orac. ap. Hdt.
white-coated, Batr.
of white complexion: heterocl. acc. λευκόχροα κόμαν Eur.
white-skinned, Theocr.
to make white: λ. πόδα to bare the foot, Anth.:—Mid., λευκοῦσθαι τὰ ὅπλα to whiten their shields, Xen.:—Pass. to be or become white, Pind.
white-armed, Hom., Hes.
a tablet covered with gypsum to write on, a notice-board, register, Lat. album, Oratt.
smooth, level, even, Od., Aesch., Eur.
smooth, polished, Pind.
stoning, Eur.; λ. καταφθοραί or θάνατος death by stoning, Id.; λ. ἀραί curses that will end in stoning, Aesch.
a stoning, Aesch.
to look or gaze upon, see, behold, Il., Trag.
absol. to look, gaze, Hom., Soph., etc.:— ὁ μὴ λεύσσων he that sees no more, i. e. is dead, Soph.; so, εἰ λεύσσει φάος if he still sees the light, Eur.
c. acc. cogn., λεύσσειν δέργμα δράκοντος to look the look of a dragon, Aesch.; λ. φόνον to look murder, Theocr.
one who stones, a stoner, Eur.: —in Orac. ap. Hdt., λευστήρ is prob. one deserving to be stoned.
as adj., λευστὴρ μόρος death by stoning, Aesch.
to stone, Thuc., Eur.:—Pass., λευσθῆναι πέτροις Soph.
in bed, τέκνα λεχαῖα nestlings, Aesch.
grown with grass fit to make a bed, i. e. grassy, meadowy, Il., Hhymn.
of the river Asopus, from its grassy banks, Il., Orac. ap. Hdt.
bed-ridden, Eur.
to bed, Hom.
a couch, bed, Hom., etc.
a kind of state-bed or bier, Il., etc.
a marriage-bed, and generally marriage, Od., Trag.; so in pl. τὰ νυμφικὰ λ. Soph.; γῆμαι μείζω λέχη to make a great marriage, Eur., etc.:—also for the concrete, σὰ λέχεα thy spouse, Id.
a bird's nest, Aesch., Soph.
slanting, slantwise, crosswise, Lat. obliquus, Soph., Eur.:—metaph., πάντα γὰρ λ. τἀν χεροῖν all the business in hand is cross, Soph.
crosswise, Lat. oblique.
of or belonging to child-bed, δῶρα λεχ. presents made at the birth, Anth.
a woman in childbed, or one who has just given birth, Lat. puerpera, Eur.
the temple of the daughters of Leos, Thuc.
Lat. leo, a lion, Hom.; of Artemis, Ζεύς σε λέοντα γυναιξὶ θῆκε Zeus made thee a lion toward women, because she was supposed to cause their sudden death, Il.; οἴκοι λέοντες, ἐν μάχῃ δ’ ἀλώπεκες Ar.
= λεοντῆ, a lion's skin, Luc.
one who will do anything, i. e. audacious, villainous, a knave, Aesch.; λεωργότατος Xen.
entirely, wholly, λ. οὐδέν nothing at all, Archil.; cf. λεωργός.
one of their own people, a fellow-citizen, Hdt.
to stay, abate, like παύω, Il.:—c. gen., χεῖρας λήγειν φόνοιο to stay hands from murder, Od.
intr. to leave off, cease, come to an end, Il., Hdt., attic: c. gen. to stop or cease from a thing, χόλοιο, φόνοιο, etc., Il., attic: c. part to cease doing, λήγειν ἀείδων Il., etc.
a shrub, the mastich, on which the gum λάδανον is found, cistus creticus.
a light summer dress, Alcman.
of or from Lethe, Lethean, Anth.
drowsy, Anth.
forgetful: c. gen. forgetful of, Anth.,
as Subst. lethargy, Arist.
causing forgetfulness, Luc.
a forgetting, forgetfulness, Lat. oblivio, Il., attic; λ. παρέχειν, ἐμποιεῖν Plat.; εἰς λήθην ἐμβάλλειν τινά Aeschin., etc.
after Hom., a place of oblivion in the lower world, Simon., etc.
taken prisoner, captive, Il.
crop-consuming, crop destroying: fem., σῦς ληιβότειρα, Od.
taken as booty, captive, Anth.
Dep.:
to seize as booty, to carry off as prey, Hom., Hdt.:—generally, to get by force, to gain, get, Hes.
to plunder, despoil, esp. by raids or forays, ἀλλήλους Thuc., Xen.
absol. to plunder, Hdt.
perf. λέλῃσμαι in pass. sense, to be carried off, taken as booty, Eur.
dwelling in the country, Anth.
a crop, Lat. seges, ὡς δ’ ὅτε κινήσῃ Ζέφυρος βαθὺ λήιον Il.; so Hes., Hdt.
a corn-field, field, Theocr., Babr.
booty, spoil, Hom., etc.; mostly of cattle, Il.; and without notion of plunder, cattle, stock, Hes., Theocr.
a robber, esp. a pirate, rover, Od.
to be carried off as booty, to be won by force, Il.; also (with the vowel shortd.) λεϊστός Id.
plundering, ionic form in Hdt.
= ληιστήρ, Od.
as adj. plundering, Anth.
she who makes or dispenses booty, Il.
Achaean name for the town-hall or council-room, = Athen. πρυτανεῖον, Hdt., Plut.
doric λᾱκέω, to sound, Theocr.
to adorn rhetorically, amplify, Strab.
a small oil-flask, Ar.
an oil-flask, oil-bottle, Od., Ar.: a casket for unguents, Ar.
in pl. tropes, tragic phrases, Lat. ampullae, Cicero.
making oil-flasks, Plut.
will, desire, resolve, purpose, mind, Aesch., Eur.
temper of mind, spirit, whether,
good, courage, resolution, Hdt., Pind., attic; or,
bad, insolence, arrogance, audacity, Soph.
to be high-spirited, resolute, Ar.
to be blear-eyed or purblind, λημᾶν κολοκύνταις to have one's eyes running pumpkins, Ar.: metaph., λημᾶν τὰς φρένας Id.

a humour that gathers in the corner of the eye, gum, rheum:—metaph., Pericles called Aegina ἡ τοῦ Πειραιέως λ. the eyesore of Peiraeeus, Arist., Plut.; λῆμαι Κρονικαί old prejudices that dim the eyes, Ar.

anything received, income, Aesch.; λ. καὶ ἀνάλωμα receipt and expense, Plat.: generally, gain, profit, Lat. lucrum, Soph., etc.; παντὸς ἥττων λήμματος unable to resist any temptation of gain, Dem.; often in pl., Id.
Lemnian, v. Λῆμνος.
a woollen fillet or riband, Lat. taenia, Plut., etc.
from Lemnos, Pind.
Lemnos, an island in the Aegaean sea, sacred to Hephaestus, Hom., etc.:—from the volcanic nature of the island, the Λήμνιον πῦρ became proverbial, Soph.
of or belonging to the Λήναια, Anth.
belonging to the wine-press:
epith. of Bacchus as god of the wine-press, Diod.
Λήναια (sc. ἱερά), τά, the Lenaea, an Athenian festival held in the month Ληναιών in honour of Bacchus, at which there were contests of the Comic Poets, Ar.
Λήναιον, ου, τό, the Lenaeum, or place at Athens where the Lenaea were held, Id., Plat.
ionic name of the seventh attic month ὁ, Γαμηλιών, in which the Lenaea were held ( v. Διονύσια ) the latter part of Jan. and former of Feb., Hes.
Bacchanals, Theocr.
like Lat. lacus, alveus, a tub or trough; esp.,
a wine-vat, Theocr.
a trough for watering cattle, Hhymn.
Lat. lana, wool, Aesch.
belonging to the ληξίαρχος·—τὸ λ. γραμματεῖον the register of each Athenian deme, Dem.
the officer at Athens who entered young citizens on the list of their deme when they came of age.
a portion assigned by lot, an allotment, Plat.; cf. λάξις.
as law-term, λ. δίκης or λ. alone, a written complaint lodged with the Archon, as the first step to a lawsuit, Id., Aeschin.
cessation, Aesch.
to be taken or accepted, Plat.
neut. ληπτέον, one must take hold, Ar.: one must undertake, Xen.; one must take or choose, Id.
one must take, receive, Id.
disposed to accept, Arist.
to be apprehended, Plat., Anth.
to be foolish or silly, speak or act foolishly, Lat. nugari, Soph., Ar.
silly talk, nonsense, Plat.
silly talk, nonsense, trumpery, Ar.:—of persons, nonsense, a trifler, Plat.; λῆροι λεπτότατοι, of sophists, Ar.; as an exclamation, λῆρος, nonsense! humbug! Id.
a poor trinket, Anth.
frivolous, silly, Plat., Arist.
taking men unawares, a thief, Hhymn.
forgetfulness, Hes., Soph.
a captain of robbers, Plut.
a robber's life, robbery, piracy, buccaneering, Lat. latrocinium, Thuc., Xen.
to be a robber: to carry on a piratical war, to practise piracy, Lat. latrocinari, Dem.
c. acc. to spoil, plunder, Thuc.
a band of robbers, Xen., Aeschin.:— a retreat or nest of robbers, Strab.
robbery, in pl., Luc.
a robber, plunderer, Soph., Eur., Xen.; esp. by sea, a pirate, rover, buccaneer, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
inclined to rob, piratical, buccaneering, Thuc., Dem.:— τὸ λῃστικόν piracy, Thuc.; also a band of robbers, Id.
adv. -κῶς, in the manner of pirates; comp. -κώτερον, Id.
λῆστιν ἴσχειν = ἐπιλανθάνεσθαι, to forget, Soph.
slaying robbers, Anth.
piratical, Thuc., etc.
ναῦς λ. a pirate vessel, Dem., etc.
born of Leto, epith. of Apollo and Artemis, Eur.: pecul. fem. Λατογένεια, Aesch.
son of Leto, i. e. Apollo, Hhymn., Hes.
of or born from Leto, Soph.; doric Λατῴα, Anth.: fem. also Λητωίς, ίδος, Id.
Leto, Lat. Latona, mother of Apollo and Artemis, Hom.
a taking hold, seizing, catching, seizure, Thuc.
an accepting, receiving, Plat.; in pl. receipts, Id.
epic Dep to bend, incline:

mostly of persons, to go aside, withdraw, recoil, shrink back, Il.; δεῦρο λιάσθης hither has thou retired, Id.; παρὰ κληῖδα λιάσθη, of a vision, slipped away by the key-hole, Od.; ἐλιάσθην πρός σε I came away to thee, Eur.
to sink, fall, πρηνὴς ἐλιάσθη, λιαζόμενος προτὶ γαίῃ Il.
of things, λιάζετο κῦμα retired, drew back, Id.; πτερὰ λίασθεν (for ἐλιάσθησαν) the dying bird's wings dropped, Id.

very, exceedingly, Hom.; οὐδέ τι λ. οὕτω not so very much, Od.; with a Verb, very much, overmuch, exceedingly, Hom.; strengthd. καὶ λίην, as, aye truly, verily, Id.; λίην πιστεύειν to believe implicitly, Hdt.; κόμπος λίαν εἰρημένος verily, truly, Aesch.; ἡ λίαν φιλότης his too great love, Id.
warm, Hom.; οὖρος λ. a warm soft wind, Od.; ὕπνος λ. balmy sleep, Il.
a small stream, Strab.
=λείβω, to let fall in drops:— Mid. to run out in drops, trickle, Anth.
the frankincense-tree, producing λιβανωτός, Hdt., etc.
= λιβανωτός, in which sense it is fem., Eur., etc.
frankincense coloured, Strab.
to fumigate with frankincense, Strab.
frankincense, the gum of the tree λίβανος, Hdt., Ar., etc.
a censer, Lat. thuribulum, NTest.
bearing frankincense, Hdt.
anything that drops or trickles, a spring, stream, Soph., Eur.: standing water, Babr.: —in pl. streams, pools, Aesch., Eur.
the Lat. libertinus, a freedman, NTest.
= λιβάς: λ. αἵματος a drop or fleck of blood, Aesch.: pl. λίβη tears, Id.
dripping, wet, Anth.
from Libya, Theocr.
Libya, the north part of Africa west of Egypt, Od., Hdt.; in later writers also for the whole Continent
Libyan, Hdt., etc.
Liburnian; Λιβυρνικόν (sc. πλοῖον), a light vessel like a galley or felucca, such as was used by the Λιβυρνοί, Plut.; also Λιβυρνίς, ίδος, sc. ναῦς, Id.
the Liburnians, a people on the Adriatic below Istria, Strab.
a Libyan, Hdt., etc.; and as adj. = Λιβυκός, Eur.; fem. Λίβυσσα, Pind.; also Λιβυστικός, ή, όν, Aesch.
a Liby-Phoenician, i. e. Carthaginian, Polyb.

entry.etym: poetic verb, only in pres. and imperf.
entry.sense: to cry aloud, of heralds, Il.; of mourners, Aesch.; also, σύριγγι λ. to produce clear sounds on the pipe, to play on it, Anth.; c. acc. cogn., μέλος λ. Bion, Mosch.
trans. to sing of, Anth.
in loud clear tone, Hom.
only in epic aor1, λίγξε βιός the bow twanged, Il.
just scraping, grazing, Lat. strictim, Od.
thick smoke mixed with flame, a murky flame, Aesch., Soph., Ar.; λιγνὺς πρόσεδρος in Soph. is the smoky flame hanging round Hercules.
a name borne by Mimnermus, Solon.
clear-sounding, κιθάρη Anth.
clear-singing, Hhymn.
clear-speaking, Anth.
shrill-blowing, whistling, Od.
chirping with the wings, of the cicada, Anth.

clear, whistling, of winds, Il.; of a whip, Id.; λιγυρὰ ἄχεα griefs which vent themselves in shrill wailings, Eur.:—also clear-voiced, sweet-toned, Hom., etc.:—neut. pl. as adv., λιγυρὰ ἀείδειν Theogn.; λιγυρῶς Theocr.
pliant, flexible, of dogs' tails, Xen.
clear, whistling, of winds, Hom.: of a clear, sweet sound, clear-toned, Id.; of the nightingale, Aesch.
adv. shrilly, Hom.; clearly, Il.:—neut. as adv., λιγὺ μέλπεσθαι Hes., Aesch.
a Ligurian, Hdt., Thuc., etc.:— adj. Λῐγυστικός, ή, όν Ligurian, Strab.
clear-voiced, of heralds, Hom.; of the nightingale, Ar.
clear-voiced, loud-voiced, screaming, Il.; also of sweet sounds, Hes., Theocr.
to fling stones, Strab.
trans. to stone a man, NTest.
stony, Od.
as fem. Subst., = λίθος, a grave-stone, Anth.; of the pumice-stone, Id.
collectively in sg., a shower of stones, Aesch.
a sort of fine stone or marble for building, Strab.
a precious stone, Id.
of stone, Hom.
built of stones, Anth.
to suffer from stone, Plat.
a pebble, Plat.
of stone, Hdt., Plat., etc.; λ. θάνατος stony death, caused by seeing the Gorgon's head, Pind.; στῆναι λίθινος, of a statue, Hdt.
stone-throwing, pelting, Anth.
set with stones, Id.
to pelt with stones, stone, NTest.
proparox. λιθόβολος, ον, pass. struck with stones, stoned, Eur.
throwing stones, pelting with stones: λιθοβόλοι, οἱ, stone-throwers, Thuc., etc.
λιθοβόλος, an engine for hurling stones, Polyb., etc.
a sculptor, Luc.
petrifying with a glance, Anth.
stone-built, Anth.
building with stones, a mason, Xen.
turning to stone, Anth.
set with precious stones, Theophr., Plut.:— λ. στόμιον a bit set with stones (to make it sharper), Soph.
τὸ λ. inlaid work, mosaic, Strab.
a stone-cutter, Dem.
death by stoning, Anth.
stoned with stones: λ. Ἄρης death by stoning, Soph.
a stone-building, Xen.
one who builds with stones picked out to fit their places, not cut square; then, generally = λιθοδόμος, a mason, Thuc., etc.
a stone or marble-mason, Anth., Luc.
turning to stone, Luc.
with stony skin, Hhymn.
a chasm made by tearing out stones, Soph.
a stone, Hom., etc.: a precious stone, Hdt.: marble, Id.:—proverb., λίθον ἕψειν to boil a stone, i. e. "to lose one's labour," Ar.;— of stupidity, λίθοι blocks, stones, Id.
stone as a substance, opp. to wood, flesh, etc, Il., etc.
also fem., Hom., Theocr.;—but the fem. was mostly used of some special stone, as the magnet, Eur., Plat.; of a touchstone, Plat.; ἡ διαφανὴς λ. a piece of crystal used for a burning glass, Ar.
at Athens, λίθος (masc.) was a name for various blocks of stone used for rostra or tribunes, as,
the Bema of the Pnyx, Ar.
another in the ἀγορά used by the κήρυκες, Plut.
an altar in the ἀγορά, Dem.
a piece on a draughtboard, Theocr.
paved with stones, Soph.:— λιθόστρωτον, τό, a tesselated pavement, NTest.
a place where stone is cut, a quarry; mostly in pl., quarries, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
a stone-cutter, Xen.
to turn into stone, petrify, Anth.
a worker in stone, stone-mason, Ar., Thuc.
as adj., σιδήρια λιθουργά a stonemason's tools, Thuc.
to carry stones, Thuc.
carrying stones:—as Subst., = λιθοβόλος, Polyb.
like stone, stony, Hdt., Xen.
presiding over winnowing, Anth.
to part the grain from the chaff, to winnow, Il., Xen.:— metaph. to scatter like chaff, NTest.
a winnower of corn, Il.
a winnowing, Anth.
a winnowing-fan, i. e. a broad basket, in which the corn was placed after threshing, and then thrown against the wind:—it was sacred to Bacchus, cf. Virgil's mystica vannus Iacchi, Soph., Anth.
the infant Bacchus was carried in it: hence a cradle, Hhymn., etc.
carrying the sacred λίκνον in procession, Dem.
crosswise, sideways, Hom.; cf. λέχριος

entry.etym: Mid., only in pres. and imperf.
entry.sense: to long or desire earnestly, Il.; metaph. of a lance, λιλαιομένη χροὸς ἆσαι longing to taste flesh, Id.; λιλαιομένη πόσιν εἶναι longing for him to be her husband, Od.: —also c. gen. to long for, λιλαιόμενοι πολέμοιο Il., etc.:—also, φόωσδε λιλαίεσθαι to struggle to the light of day, Od.
to suffer from hunger, Hdt.
god of the harbour, Anth.: fem. λιμενῖτις, ιδος, Id.
tarrying in the harbour, Anth.
watching the harbour, Anth.

a harbour, haven, creek, whereas ὅρμος is properly the inner part of the harbour, the landing-place, Hom., etc.; in pl., Od., Soph., etc.; —also c. gen. objecti, λιμένες θαλάσσης havens of refuge from the sea, Od.
metaph. a haven, retreat, refuge, Theogn.; ἑταιρείας λ. a haven of friendship, Soph.; λ. τῶν ἐμῶν βουλευμάτων Eur.; c. gen. objecti, χείματος λ. a harbour of refuge from the storm, Id.

a place of resort, receptacle, πλούτου λ. Aesch.; παντὸς οἰωνοῦ λ. Soph.; in O. T. 420, the sense seems to be—how will Cithaeron not be filled with thy cries (λιμὴν ἔσται τῆς σῆς βοῆς) ? how will it not reecho them?
hungry, causing hunger, Theocr., Anth.
furnished with a good harbour, Thuc.
of or from the marsh or mere, ὄρνιθας χερσαίους τε καὶ λ. both land-fowl and water fowl, Hdt., Ar.

entry.etym: poet. fem. of λιμναῖος, Theocr., Babr.

entry.sense: a pool of standing water left by the sea or a river, Il.: then, a marshy lake, mere, Lat. palus, Id., Hdt., attic:—also, a large pool or basin (artificial), Hdt.
in Hom. and other Poets, the sea.
Λίμναι, ῶν, αἱ, a quarter of Athens (once prob. marshy), near the Acropolis, in which stood the Lenaeum, Ar., Thuc., etc.
laker, name of a frog, Batr.
living in marshes, Theocr.
epith. of Artemis, dat. Λιμνᾶτι shortd. for Λιμνάτιδι, Anth.
one who works in λίμναι, a fisherman, Plut.
marsh-born, Anth.
grace of the marsh, or -χαρής, love-marsh, name of a frog, Batr.
like a marsh, marshy: τὸ λιμνῶδες τοῦ Στρυμόνος the marshy ground at the mouth of the Strymon, Thuc.
dying of hunger, Aesch.
to kill by hunger, starve, Plat.
a killing by hunger or by abstinence from food, Plat.
hunger, famine, Hom., etc.:— proverb., ἀπολεῖτε λιμῷ Μηλίῳ, referring to the siege of Melos, Ar.:—metaph., of the mind, Eur.
causing hunger, Anth.
a cutaneous disease, scurvy, Polyb.
to be famished, hungry, Strab., Anth.
of flax, flaxen, linen, Lat. lineus, Hdt., Plat., etc.
bound with flaxen cords, Eur.; λινόδετος τοῦ ποδός tied by the foot, Ar.
one who uses nets, Anth.
wearing a linen cuirass, Il., Xen.
spinning flax, Anth.
flax-woven, Eur.
anything made of flax:

a cord, fishing-line, Il.: the thread spun from a distaff, Eur., etc.; and in pl., Id.:—metaph. the thread of destiny spun by the Fates, Hom., Theocr.:—proverb., λίνον λίνῳ συνάπτειν, i. e. to join like with like, to deal with matters of like kind, Plat.
a fishing-net, Il.:— a hunting-net, Theocr.
linen, linen-cloth, Hom.: sail-cloth, Ar.
flax for spinning, Id.
the plant that produces flax, Lat. linum, Hdt., etc.; λίνου σπέρμα lint-seed, Thuc.
on λίνον ἄειδεν, v. Λίνος II.
with linen robe, Anth.
sail-wafting, Eur.
Dep. to watch nets, see whether anything is caught, Ar.
sail-winged, of ships, Aesch.
one who watches nets to see whether anything is caught, Arist.
Linos, a mythical minstrel, son of Apollo and Urania (Calliope), teacher of Orpheus, Theocr., etc.

as appellat., the song or lay of Linos, sung by a boy to the cithara while the vintagers are at work, Λίνον ὑπὸ καλὸν ἄειδεν sang the lovely lay of Linos in accompaniment, Il.:—cf. αἴλινος which is a mournful song.
a laying of nets: the nets laid, Anth.
a weaver, Strab.
linen-wasting, Aesch.
to oil, anoint: Mid. to anoint oneself, Anth.
of rivers, to make fat, enrich, Eur.
to be in want of men, Strab.; λῐπ-ανδρία, want of men, Id.

adv. unctuously, richly, ἀλεῖψαι or ἀλείψασθαι λίπ’ ἐλαίῳ to anoint or cause to be anointed richly with oil, Il.; so, χρῖσαι or χρίσασθαι λίπ’ ἐλαίῳ Id.; only once without ἐλαίῳ, λοέσσατο καὶ λίπ’ ἄλειψεν Od. In all these places, the final vowel is uncertain; but we have λίπα ἀλείψασθαι, -εσθαι in Thuc., etc.
with bright tiara, Pind.
the largest of the Aeolian islands, Thuc., etc.:—adj. Λῐπᾰραῖος, η, ον of Lipara, αἱ Λ. νῆσοι the group of these islands, Polyb.

to persist, persevere, hold out, Hdt.; so in part., διάγειν λιπαρέοντας to continue to hold out, Id.; also, reversely, λιπαρέετε μένοντες persist in holding your ground, Id.; so, c. dat., λ. τῇ πόσει to keep on drinking, Id.
of persistent entreaty,
absol. to persist in intreating, to be importunate, Id., Aesch., etc.
c. acc. et inf. to importune one to do a thing, Aesch., Soph.
c. acc., λιπαρεῖν αὐτόν entreat earnestly for him, Dem.
persisting or persevering in a thing, earnest, indefatigable, Plat.
of things, Ar., Luc.
earnest in begging or praying, importunate, λ. χείρ a hand instant in prayer, Soph.:— τὸ λιπαρές importunity, Luc.; πρὸς τὸ λ. = λιπαρῶς, Soph.
adv. -ρῶς, earnestly, importunately, Plat.
entry.etym: Deriv. uncertain: the first syll. seems to be from λι-, λίαν.

entry.sense: one must be importunate, Xen.
importunity, persistence, Hdt.
bright-girdled, Eur.
bright-throned, Aesch.
with bright head-band, Il.
with glossy locks, Il.
oily, shiny with oil, acc. to the custom of oiling the skin in the palaestra, Od., Ar., etc.
oily, greasy, Ar.
of the skin, shining, sleek, Lat. nitidus, λιπαροὶ πόδες bright, smooth feet, without a wrinkle, Il.; λιπαρώτεροι ἐγένοντο Hdt.; λ. στῆθος Ar., etc.
of condition, rich, comfortable, easy, Lat. nitidus, lautus, Od., Pind.; so, λιπαρῶς γηράσκειν Od.
of things, bright, brilliant, costly, splendid, Hom.
of soil, fat, rich, fruitful, Lat. pinguis, Hhymn., Theogn.; λιπαραὶ Ἀθῆναι, a favourite epith. with the Athenians, prob. with allusion to the Attic olive, Pind., Ar.
with shining skin, Theocr.
deserted by light, blind, Anth.
to be fat and sleek, epic part. λιπόων Anth.
desolate, forlorn, homeless, outcast, Archil.
having abandoned her marriage ties, of Helen, Eur.
wanting a limb, maimed, Anth.
λῐπο-μαρτῠρίου δίκη, an action against a witness for non-appearance, Dem.
motherless, Anth.
deserting the fleet, Aesch.
leaving the sailors, Theocr.
causing to forget one's country, of the lotos, Anth.
deserter of one's father, Eur.
left by breath, breathless, dead, Anth.
wanting flesh, Anth.
fat, βεβρῶτες αἵματος λίπος gorged with fat and blood, Soph.
falling from the wreath, Anth.
desertion of the army, refusal to serve, Hdt., Thuc.
a leaving one's post, desertion, Dem.
λῐπο-ταξίου γραφή, ἡ, an indictment for desertion, Plat., Dem.
having lost one's hair, Anth.
to leave life, swoon, Thuc., Xen.
to lack spirit, fail in courage, Hdt.
Dep., with perf. pass. λέλιμμαι, to be eager, Aesch.:—c. gen. to be eager for, long for, Id.
a lion, Il., Hes., Theocr.
smooth, Od.
as masc. Subst., only in dat. λιτί and acc. λῖτα, smooth cloth, linen cloth: others take λῖτα to be acc. pl. neut. linen cloths:—in Anth., we have λίτα [ῐ] πολυδαίδαλα, embroidered stuffs.
smooth, polished, Ar.
as Subst. λίσπαι, ῶν, αἱ, dice cut in two by friends (ξένοι), each of whom kept half as tallies (σύμβολα), Plat.
smooth, bare, Eur., Theocr.
as Subst. a bare, smooth cliff, Plut.

to beg, pray, entreat, beseech, either absol. or c. acc. pers., Hom.; that by which one prays, in gen., λ. τινα γούνων Il.; λ. Ζηνός Od.:—an inf. is often added, οὐδέ σ’ ἔγωγε λίσσομαι μένειν I do not pray thee to remain, Il.
c. acc. rei, to beg or pray for, οἷ αὐτῶι θάνατον λιτέσθαι Id.: c. dupl. acc. pers. et rei, ταῦτα μὲν οὐχ ὑμέας ἔτι λίσσομαι this I beg of you no more, Od.
smooth, λισσὴ αἰπεῖά τε εἰς ἅλα πέτρη a smooth rock running sheer into the sea, Od.; λισσὴ δ’ ἀναδέδρομε πέτρη Id.
to be moved by prayer, ap. Plat.
to dig round a plant, Od.
a tool for levelling or smoothing, a spade, a kind of shovel, Od., Mosch.

to pray, entreat, esp. for protection, either absol. or c. acc. pers., Hom.; that by which one prays in gen., γούνων λιτανεύειν Od.; also, γούνων ἁψάμενοι λιτανεύσομεν (epic for -ωμεν), Il.; c. inf., Id.
praying, suppliant, μέλη Aesch.: —as Subst., λιτανά, τά, = λιταί, ἀμφὶ λιτᾰνὰ ἔχεσθαι to be engaged in prayer, Id.
to slip away, Ar.
a prayer, entreaty, mostly in pl., Od., Hdt., Trag.
Λιταί, Prayers of sorrow and repentance, personified in Il. 9. 502 sq.
living plainly or sparingly, Strab.
suppliant, supplicatory, Pind.
smooth, plain: of style, simple, unadorned, Arist.: of persons, simple, frugal, Polyb.: adv. λιτῶς, Anth.
paltry, petty, Id.
plainness, simplicity, Plut.
weighing or worth a λίτρα, Anth.
a silver coin of Sicily, Lat. libra:—as a weight, 12 ounces, a pound, Anth.:—metaph., λίτρᾰν ἐτῶν ζήσας having lived a pound of years, i. e. 72 (for a pound of gold was coined into 72 pieces), Id.

entry.etym: older form for νίτρον, Hdt., Plat.

entry.sense: Lityerses, a son of Midas: a reaper's song named after him, Theocr.
the Roman lituus, Plut.
the fore-finger, from its use in licking up, Luc.
= λιχμάω, Hes.
trans. to lick, ionic 3rd sg. imperf. λιχμάζεσκε Mosch.
to lick with the tongue, of snakes, Eur.:—Mid., ἐλιχμῶντο περὶ τὴν κεφαλήν played like serpents round the head, Ar.
daintiness, greediness, Xen., Plat.
to lick, Luc.
to lick up:— metaph. to desire greedily, covet, δόξαν Plut.
nice in eating, dainty, Anth.
dainty, lickerish, greedy, Xen., Plat.
metaph. curious, Eur.

entry.etym: from λείβω, because it brought wet
entry.sense: the SW. wind, Lat. Africus, Hdt., Theocr.

entry.etym: only in gen. and acc. λιβάς or λίβος being used as nom.
entry.sense: a stream, Aesch.: a draught, Id.
desire of making water, natural needs, Aesch.
the lobe of the ear, Il.
the lobe of the liver, Aesch., Eur.: generally, the liver, Aesch.
by picking out, of stones for building, Thuc.; of soldiers, Plut.
λ. δύστηνα wretched petty speeches, Dem.
gathered, picked, chosen, of picked men, Hdt., Eur., etc.
λ. λίθοι unhewn stones, taken just as they were picked, cf. λογάδην.
properly a speaking-place: in the attic theatre, the part of the stage occupied by the speakers, Lat. pulpitum, Plut., etc.
a collection for the poor, NTest.
a little fable or story, Ar.

to count, reckon, calculate, compute, Hdt.; λ. ἀπὸ χειρός to calculate off hand, Ar.:—c. acc. rei, λ. τοὺς τόκους to calculate the interest, Id.; τρεῖς μνᾶς ἀναλώσας λογίσασθαι δώδεκα to spend 3 minae and set down 12, Id.
c. acc. et inf. to reckon or calculate that, Hdt., Dem.
λ. τί τινι to set down to one's account, charge to one, Lat. imputare, Dem., NTest.
λογ. ἀπό . . to deduct from . . , Dem.
without reference to numbers, to take into account, calculate, consider, Hdt., attic; λ. περί τινος to form calculations about . . , Hdt., Xen.

c. acc. et inf. to count, deem, consider that . . , Hdt., attic; with the inf. omitted, to reckon or account so and so, τὸν καθ’ ἡμέραν βίον λογίζου σόν Eur.; μίαν ἄμφω τὰς ἡμέρας λ. to count both days as one, Xen.
c. inf. fut. to count or reckon upon doing, to calculate or expect that . . , Hdt., Xen.;—c. acc. only, to count upon, Soph.
to conclude by reasoning, infer that a thing is, Plat., Xen.
the aor1 ἐλογίσθην and sometimes perf. λελόγισμαι are used in pass. sense, to be counted or calculated, Xen.
worth mention, notable, remarkable, famous, Hdt.
an announcement, oracle, Hdt.; in pl. oracles, Id., Eur., etc.
versed in tales or stories (λόγος IV): as Subst. a chronicler, annalist, Hdt.
generally learned, erudite, Arist., etc.
skilled in words, eloquent, Eur., Plut.
a counting, reckoning, calculation, computation, Thuc., Plat.:—in pl. arithmetic, Xen., Plat.
an account, bill, Dem.
without reference to number, calculation, consideration, reasoning, Thuc., Dem.
an argument, conclusion, Xen.
reasoning power, reason, Id.
one must calculate or subtract, Dem.
the place at Athens where the λογισταί met, Oratt.
a calculator, teacher of arithmetic, Plat.
a calculator, reasoner, Ar., Dem.
in pl. auditors, at Athens, ten members of the βουλή, to whom magistrates going out of office submitted their accounts, Dem., etc.
skilled or practised in calculating, Xen., Plat.:— ἡ λογιστική (sc. τέχνη), arithmetic, Plat.
endued with reason, rational, Arist.:— τὸ λ. the reasoning faculty, Plat.
using one's reason, reasonable, Xen.
to write speeches, Plut.
a writing of speeches, and, generally, of prose, Plat.
of or for writing speeches or prose, Plat.
a prose-writer:—the early Greek chroniclers are so called by Thuc.
like λογοποιός II, a speech-writer, one who lived by writing speeches for others to deliver, Plat., etc.
a prater, Anth.
to war about words, NTest.
a war about words, NTest.
to invent stories, to write, compose, Plat.
to fabricate tales, of newsmongers, Thuc., Dem., etc.
to write speeches (v. λογοποιός II), Plat.
tale-telling, news-mongering, Theophr.
of or like a λογοποιός: ἡ -κὴ τέχνη, = λογογραφική, Plat.
a prose-writer, esp. an historian, chronicler, Plat., etc.
a writer of fables, Hdt., Plut.
= λογογράφος II, Plat.
a tale-teller, newsmonger, Dem.
(A) the word or that by which the inward thought is expressed, Lat. oratio; and, (B) the inward thought itself, Lat. ratio.
Lat. vox, oratio, that which is said or spoken:
a word, pl. words, i. e. language, talk, Hom., etc.; λόγου ἕνεκα, Lat. dicis causa, merely for talking's sake, Plat.; λόγῳ in word, in pretence, opp. to ἔργῳ (in deed, in reality), Hdt., attic
a word, saying, statement, Thuc.: an oracle, Pind., Plat.:— a saying, maxim, proverb, Pind., Aesch.
an assertion, promise, Soph.
a resolution, κοινῷ λ. by common consent, Hdt.
a condition, ἐπὶ λόγῳ τοιῷδε Id.
a command, Aesch.
speech, discourse, conversation, εἰς λόγους ἐλθεῖν, συνελθεῖν, ἀφικέσθαι τινί Hdt., attic; λόγου μεῖζον, κρεῖσσον beyond expression, Hdt., Thuc.; λόγου ἄξιον worth mention, Hdt.
right of speech, power to speak, λόγον αἰτεῖσθαι Thuc.; διδόναι Xen.
talk about one, report, repute, Lat. fama, λόγος, Hdt., attic; λόγος ἐστί, λόγος ἔχει, κατέχει, φέρεται, c. acc. et inf., so the story goes, Lat. fama fert, Hdt., attic
speech, language, Plat.
a saying, tale, story, opp. on the one hand to mere fable (μῦθος), on the other, to regular history (ἱστορία), Hdt., Thuc., etc.: then, a fictitious story, fable, like those of Aesop, Hdt., Plat.
a narrative, and in pl. histories, history, Hdt.: in sg. one part of such a work, Id.
generally, prose-writing, prose, Xen., etc.
a speech, oration, Oratt.
like ῥῆμα, the thing spoken of, the subject or matter of the λόγος, Hdt., attic
that which is stated, a proposition, position, principle, Plat.: also = ὁρισμός, a definition, Id.
Lat. ratio, thought, reason, οὐκ ἔχει λόγον admits not of reason, Soph.; ὀρθὸς λ. Plat.; ὡς ἔχει λόγον, = ὡς ἔοικεν, Dem.:— κατὰ λόγον agreeably to reason, Plat.; μετὰ λόγου Id.
an opinion, expectation, Hdt.
a reason, ground, plea, Soph., etc.; ἐκ τίνος λόγου; on what ground? Aesch.; ἐξ οὐδενὸς λ. Soph., etc.
ὁ λόγος αἱρέει, c. acc. et inf., it stands to reason that . . , Lat. ratio evincit, Hdt.

account, consideration, esteem, regard, λόγον βροτῶν οὐκ ἔσχεν οὐδένα Aesch.; Μαρδονίου λόγος οὐδεὶς γίγνεται Hdt.; λόγου οὐδενὸς γενέσθαι to be of no account, Id.; λόγου ποιεῖσθαί τινα or τι, to make account of a person or thing, Id.;—so, ἐν οὐδενὶ λόγῳ ποιεῖσθαι Id.;— ἐν ἀνδρὸς λόγῳ εἶναι to be reckoned as a man, Id.

an account, λόγον διδόναι τινός to give an account of a thing, Id., attic; so, λόγον παρέχειν Plat.; λ. λαμβάνειν παρά τινος Dem.; λ. ἀπαιτεῖν Id.; ὑπέχειν Plat., Dem., etc.; ἐγγράφειν Dem., etc.; ἀποφέρειν Aeschin.; cf. λογιστής.
due relation, proportion, analogy, κατὰ λόγον τινός or τινί Hdt., attic
Ὁ ΛΟΓ́ΟΣ, the Logos or Word, comprising both senses of Thought and Word, NTest.
to pierce with a spear, Anth.
a spear-head, javelin-head, Lat. spiculum, Hdt., attic; in pl. of a single spear, the point with its barbs, τὸ ξυστὸν τῇσι λόγχῃσι ὁμοίως the shaft alike with the spear-head, Hdt.
a lance, spear, javelin, Lat. lancea, Pind., Soph., etc.
a troop of spearmen, "a plump of spears, " Soph., Eur.
armed with a spear, Eur.
of a spear, κλόνοι λ. the clash of spears, Aesch.
Pass. to be furnished with a point, Arist.
making spears, Eur.
spear-bearing, Eur.: as Subst. a spear-man, pike-man, Ar., Xen., etc.
lance-headed, Eur., Anth.
a cup for pouring libations, Plut.
a drink-offering, Lat. libatio, Hom.; opt. in pl., Pind., Soph.
pestilent, deadly, fatal, Il.
ruin, havoc, of death by plague, Il.; by war, Id.; of the destruction of the ships, Id.
to abuse, revile, Hdt., attic; to rebuke, Xen.:—Mid. to rail at one another, Ar.
λοιδοροῦμαι is also used as Dep., c. dat., to rail at, Id., Xen.:—c. acc. cogn., πάντα τὰ αἰσχρὰ λοιδορέονται they use all kind of foul reproaches, Hdt.
railing, abuse, an affront, Arist.
railing, abuse, Thuc., Plat.
railing, abusive, Eur.:—adv. -ρως, Strab.
a plague, pestilence, Il., Hdt., attic; of the plague at Athens, Thuc.
of persons, a plague, pest, Dem. (Prob. akin to λύμη, Lat. lues.)
like plague, pestilential, ἡ λ. νόσος the plague, Thuc.
to have the plague, Luc.

remaining, the rest, Lat. reliquus, Hdt., etc.; in attic the Art. may either be in the same case as the Noun or have the Noun in gen. dependent on it, τὴν λοιπὴν ὁδὸν πορεύεσθαι Xen.; αἱ λοιπαὶ τῶν νεῶν Thuc.; also, τὸ λοιπὸν τῆς ἡμέρας Xen.
λοιπόν [ἐστι], c. inf., it remains to shew, etc., Plat., Xen.; with Art., τὸ λ. ἐστι σκέψασθαι what remains is to consider, Plat.:— ὃ δὲ λοιπόν, quod superest, Aesch., etc.

often of Time, ὁ λ. χρόνος the future, Pind., attic; πρὸς τὸν λοιπὸν τοῦ χρόνου Dem.; τὸν λ. χρόνον for the future, Soph.; τοῦ λ. χρόνου Id.;—so in neut., τὸ λοιπόν henceforward, hereafter, Trag.; so, τὰ λοιπά Id.
τὸ λοιπόν and τὰ λοιπά the rest, Aesch.; also λοιπόν as adv., further, besides, Plat.
λοισθήιον ἄεθλον the prize for the last in the race, Il.
= λοῖσθος, Pind., Trag.:—neut. λοίσθιον, as adv. last, Soph., Eur.
left behind, last, Il., Eur.;Sup. λοισθότατος last of all, Hes.
a cloak, Anth.

the Locrians, of which there were three tribes, the Opuntian, opposite Euboea, Il.; the Epicnemidian, on Mount Cnemis on the Maliac Gulf, Thuc.; and the Ozolian, on the Corinthian Gulf, Id.:— the Epizephyrian or Zephyrian were a colony of the last on Mount Zephyrium in lower Italy, Pind., Thuc.
Locrian, fem. Λοκρίς, ίδος, Pind.; ἡ Λοκρίς ( sc. γῆ ), Ar.
epith. of Apollo, Hdt., Trag.;—either from λοξός, the ambiguous, or from λέγω, λόγος, the speaker.
going side-ways, Batr.
slanting, crosswise, aslant, Lat. obliquus, Eur.; λοξὰ βαίνειν, of a crab, Babr.; ὁ λοξὸς κύκλος the ecliptic, Arist.

of suspicious looks, λοξὸν ὁρᾶν to look askance, Lat. limis oculis, Solon.; λοξὰ βλ. Theocr.; αὐχένα λοξὸν ἔχειν to turn the neck aside, i. e. withdraw his favour, Tyrtae.; also = Horace's stare capite obstipo, Theogn.
of language, indirect, ambiguous, of oracles, Luc.
slanting direction, obliquity, Strab.
oblique-running, Anth.
obliquity, of the ecliptic, Anth., Strab.
dish-snatcher, Anth.
a platter, Ar.
a flat dish, Ar.
the shell, husk, peel, λοπὸς κρομύοιο the peel of an onion, Od.
slain in the bath, Aesch.

a bath, bathing place, Hom.; mostly in pl., θερμὰ λοετρά hot baths, Il.; attic θερμὰ λουτρά Aesch., etc.; also called λουτρὰ Ἡράκλεια Ar.; ὑδάτων λουτρά water for bathing or washing, Soph.; λοῦσαι τινα λουτρόν to give one a bath, Id.
in Poets, = σπονδαί or χοαί libations to the dead, Id., Eur.
bringing water for bathing or washing, esp. from the fountain Callirrhoe on the wedding-day: hence, λ. χλιδή the marriage-ceremony, Eur.
as Subst., λουτροφόρος, the black urn placed on the tomb of unmarried persons, Dem., Anth.
to pour water into the bath, Anth.
pouring water into the bath, the slave who did this, Od., Xen.; λ. τρίπους a three-legged kettle, in which water was warmed for bathing, Hom.
a bathing-room, bath-house, Aesch., Xen.

to wash another, properly, to wash his body (νίζω being used of the hands and feet, πλύνω of clothes), Hom.; λούσατε ἐν ποταμῶι bathe him, i. e. let him bathe, Od.:—also, λό’ ἐκ τρίποδος washed me [with water] from a caldron, Id.

Mid. and Pass. to bathe, c. gen., λελουμένος Ὠκεανοῖο (of a star just risen), fresh from Ocean's bath, Il.;so, λούεσθαι ποταμοῖο to bathe [in water] of the river, Id.; so, ἀπὸ κρήνης λούμενος Hdt.:—absol., λούσαντο Od., etc.; λελουμένος fresh-bathed, after bathing, Hdt.; ἦλθε λουσόμενος (Hor., ire lavatum), Ar.
in strict pass. sense, λοῦσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ Διός, i. e. to be washed by the rain from heaven, Hdt.
in strict mid. sense, λοέσσασθαι χρόα to wash one's body, Hes.
to have a crest (λόφος), of larks, Babr.
to be ill of a crest (i. e. to have more crest than enought), Ar.
a crest-case, Ar.: any case, Id.
crested, of a lark, Babr.
the mane on the neck and back of certain animals, the mane of horses, the bristly back of boars and hyaenas, Od., Hdt.
the back-fin of fishes, Anth.
a dweller on the hills, of Pan, Anth.
a torch of vine bark, Anth.
Pass. to be crested.
a crest-maker, Ar.

properly the back of the neck of draught-cattle, because the yoke rubs it (λέπει); of a horse, the mane, Il.; of a man, the nape of the neck, Id.; ὑπὸ ζυγῷ λόφον ἔχειν to have the neck under the yoke, i. e. to obey patiently, Soph.
the crest of a hill, a ridge, Od., Hdt., etc.
the crest of a helmet, Lat. crista, Hom., etc.
the crest on the head of birds, Lat. crista, as of the lark, Simon.; the cock's comb, Ar.
of men, the tuft of hair upon the crown, λόφους κείρεσθαι to shave so as to leave tufts, Hdt.
a being crested, ἡ λ. ἡ τῶν ὀρνέων their crests, Ar.
to lead a λόχος or company (commonly of 100 men), Xen.; c. gen., λόχου λοχηγεῖν Hdt.
the rank or office of λοχαγός, Xen.
the leader of an armed band, Soph.
esp. the captain of a company (100 men), Xen.: —but, in the Spartan army, the commander of a λόχος, Id.; in the Persian, of 24 men, Id.
clandestine, Anth.
to lie in wait for, to watch, waylay, entrap, Od., Hdt.
absol. to lie in wait or ambush, Il., Hdt.; in aor1 part. with another Verb, λοχήσας πολλοὺς διέφθειρεν Thuc.; Mid., λοχησάμενος Od.
c. acc. loci, to occupy with an ambuscade, ἐλόχησαν τὴν ὁδόν Hdt.
childbirth, childbed, Eur., Plat.
= λόχευμα I, Anth.
the place of childbirth, Eur.
an ambush, Hes.
that which is born, a child, Eur.
in pl., childbirth, Id.: metaph., κάλυκος ἐν λοχεύμασιν in the bursting of the bud, Aesch.
to bring forth, bear, Hhymn., Anth.
of the midwife, to bring to the birth. attend in childbirth, deliver, τινά Eur.:—Pass. to be delivered, bear children, Id.; λοχευθεῖσα πυρί, of Semele, Id.
Mid., just like Act., of the mother, Eur.; of the birthplace, Anth.
Pass., of the child, to be brought forth, born, Soph.; Προμᾱθεῖ λοχευθεῖσα brought to birth by Prometheus, Eur.: —metaph., generally, to lie embedded, ἐν τεύτλοισι Ar.
to lie in wait for, τινά: Pass., λοχισθέντες διεφθάρησαν they were cut to pieces by falling into an ambuscade, Thuc.
to place in ambush, Id.
to distribute men in companies (λόχοι), to put them in order of battle, Hdt., Plut.
of or belonging to childbirth, λ. νοσήματα childbed, Eur.; ὠδίνων λοχίαις ἀνάγκαις Id.
Λοχία, epith. of Artemis Εἰλείθυια, Id.
λόχια, ων, τά, childbirth, Anth.
a placing in ambush, Plut.
one of the same company, a fellow-soldier, comrade, Aesch., Xen.
of the coppice, Μοῦσα λ., of the nightingale, Ar.
a thicket, coppice, copse, Od., Pind.
overgrown with bushes, Thuc.
to ambush, for an ambuscade, Hom.
an ambush, i. e.
a place of ambush, place for lying in wait, Hom., Eur.
the act of lying in wait, λόχον εἷσαι to place an ambuscade, Hom.; λέγεσθαι ἐς λόχον to lie in ambush, Il.:—c. gen. objecti, λόχος θείοιο γέροντος the way to watch him, Od.
the men that form the ambush, Il., Eur.

any armed band, a body of troops, Od., Trag.:— a body of soldiers, a company, regiment, Xen.:—among the Spartans, a λόχος was the fourth or fifth part of a μόρα Hdt.:— ὁ ἱερὸς λ. the sacred company at Thebes, Plut.
any body of people, a union for civil purposes, Xen., etc.:—used to transl. the Rom. centuria, Plut., etc.
a lying-in, childbirth, parturition, Aesch.
Deliverer, of Bacchus, Anacreont.
shadowy, murky, gloomy, Eur.
with sobs, Soph., Anth.
of white marble, Babr., Anth.
marble-white, Anth.
white marble, Anth.
to bend or twist as one does a withe, πλευρὰν λ. of a dancer, Ar.; λ. ἀλλήλους, of wrestlers, Luc.
to throw, master, Theocr.
Pass. to bend or twist oneself like a withe, to bend aside or writhe, so as to avoid a blow, Plat., Luc.:—metaph., in perf. part. λελυγισμένος, broken, effeminate, Anth.
to turn, play, as a joint in the socket, Soph.
metaph. to be thrown or mastered, Theocr.
a bending, twisting, of wrestlers, Luc.: metaph., of the windings and twistings of a sophist, Ar.
lynx-like, Anth.
a lynx, Eur., etc.
a spasmodic affection of the throat, hiccough, hiccup, λ. κενή an ineffectual retching, nothing being thrown off the stomach, Thuc.
vitex agnus castus, a willow-like tree, withy; in pl. its withes, Lat. vimina, Hom., Eur.
made of withes, Anth.
to tie fast, Anth.
sore, baneful, mournful, Hom., Trag.: —τὰ λυγρά bane, misery, ruin, Hom., Hes.
baneful, with an act. force, φάρμακα λυγρά Od.; γαστὴρ λυγρή the stomach that cause of bane, Id.
εἵματα λυγρά sorry garments, Id.
of persons, baneful, mischievous, Id.: sorry, i. e. weak, cowardly, Hom., Soph.
adv. -ρῶς, sorely, Il.
τὰ, Λυδιακά, a history of Lydia by Xanthus.
Lydia, in Asia Minor, Hdt.
to play the Lydian, of Magnes, in reference to his play called Λυδοί, Ar.
of Lydia, Lydian, Pind., etc.: —Λυδία λίθος, a stone used to assay gold, Soph.; also, Λ. πέτρα Theocr.
in the Lydian tongue, after the Lydian fashion, Plat.: of Music, in the Lydian mode, ἡ Λ. ἁρμονία Id.
a Lydian, Pind., Hdt., etc.
to have the hiccough or hiccup, to sob violently, Ar., Anth.
dissolution: hence, faction, sedition, Pind.
defilement from blood, gore, Hom., Anth.
defiled with gore, Anth.

entry.etym: Prob. from *λύκη, βαίνω, the path of light, the sun's course.
entry.sense: a year, Od., Bion.
λῠκᾰβαντίδες, ὧραι, ῶν, αἱ, the hours that make up the year, Anth.
a she-wolf, Babr., Plut.
Lycaean, Arcadian, Epith. of Zeus, Hdt., Pind., etc.
Λύκαιον, ου, his temple, Plut.; so, Λ. σήκωμα Eur.
Mount Lycaeus in Arcadia, Theocr.
Λύκαια, sc. ἱερά, τά, the festival of Lycaean Zeus, Xen.:—also = Roman Lupercalia, Plut.
a district in the S. of Asia Minor, Xen., etc.: the people were Λυκάονες, οἱ, Id.:—adv. Λυκιστί, in Lycaonian, NTest.
of or at twilight: τὸ λυκαυγές early dawn, Luc.
a wolf-skin, Il.
the Lyceum, a gymnasium with covered walks in the Eastern suburb of Athens, named after the neighbouring temple of Apollo Λύκειος, Ar., Plat., etc.
of or belonging to a wolf, Eur.

Λύκειος, as epith. of Apollo, either as λυκοκτόνος (q. v.), or as the Lycian god (v. Λυκηγενής), or (from *λύκη) as the god of light, Aesch.; there is a play upon the doubtful meanings, Λύκει’ ἄναξ, λύκειος γενοῦ στρατῷ δαΐῳ, Lycean lord, be a very wolf to the enemy, Id.
light, a Root, whence come λυκά-βας, λύχνος, etc.
of Apollo, commonly explained Lycian-born, i. e. at Patara, Il.
president of the Lycians, Strab.
a wolf's whelp, Solon., Theocr.
from Lycia, Il.
to Lycia, Id.
of Lycian workmanship, Hdt., Dem.
the Lycians, Il., etc.
epith. of Apollo (cf. Λύκειος), Pind., Eur.
bold as a wolf, Anth.
epith. of Apollo, wolf-slayer, Soph.
wolf-worrier, Anth.

Lat. lupus, a wolf, Hom.;—proverb., λύκον ἰδεῖν to see a wolf, i. e. to be struck dumb, as was vulgarly believed of any one of whom a wolf got the first look, Plat., Theocr. (so Virg., Moerim lupi videre priores); λύκος οἶν ὑμεναιοῖ, of an impossibility, Ar.
twilight, the gloaming, Lat. diluculum.
to tear like a wolf:—Pass. to be torn by wolves, πρόβατα λελυκωμένα Xen.

to treat with indignity, to outrage, to maltreat, c. acc., Hdt., Soph., etc.; c. acc. cogn., λύμης, ἥν με ἐλυμήνω Eur.:—of things, τὰς ῥήσεις ἃς ἐλυμαίνου the speeches you used to murder (as an actor), Dem.; ὀψοποιία λ. τὰ ὄψα spoils, Xen.
c. dat. to inflict indignities or outrages upon, Hdt., Ar., etc.
absol. to cause ruin, Thuc., Xen.
sometimes as Pass., λυμανθὲν δέμας Aesch.; λελυμάνθαι Dem.
injurious, destructive, Aesch.: c. gen. destroying, ruining, Id.
a spoiler, destroyer, Xen.
as adj. ruining, c. gen., Soph.
mostly in pl. the water used in washing, washings, off-scourings, filth, Il.; λύμαθ’ ἁγνίσας ἐμά, of blood on the hands, Soph.
moral filth, defilement, in sg., Id.
= λύμη, ruin, bane, Aesch.; of a person, λῦμα Ἀχαιῶν, i. e. Hector, Eur.
a destroyer, spoiler, corrupter, Soph., Eur.
brutal outrage, maltreatment, maiming, Hdt., Aesch., etc.:—in pl. outrages, indignities, Hdt., Aesch.
= λῦμα, defilement, Polyb.
to give pain to, to pain, distress, grieve, vex, annoy, Hdt., Trag., etc.; ἡ θώραξ λ. distresses by its weight, Xen.:—absol. to cause pain or grief, Soph.
of marauders, to harass, annoy by constant attacks, Hdt., Thuc., etc.

Pass. with fut. mid. to be pained, grieved, distressed, Theogn., etc.; μὴ λυπέεο be not distressed, Hdt.:—c. acc. cogn., λύπας λυπεῖσθαι Plat.:—also c. acc. rei, to grieve about a thing, Soph.:—absol. to feel pain, Eur., etc.
pain, Soph.
pain of body, Lat. dolor, Plat.: distress, sad plight or condition, Hdt.
pain of mind, grief, Id., attic.
of things, painful, distressing, Lat. molestus, Hdt., attic
of persons,
in good sense, causing sorrow by one's departure, Eur.
in bad sense, causing pain, troublesome, vexatious, offensive, Soph., Thuc., etc.
adv. λυπηρῶς, painfully, so as to cause pain, Soph.; λυπηρῶς ἔχει it is painful, Id.
one must feel pain, Xen.
wretched, poor, sorry, of land, Od., Hdt.
of persons, causing pain, offensive, troublesome, Aesch., Eur.
of states and conditions, painful, distressing, Aesch., Eur.
adv., λυπρῶς ἔφερεν, aegre ferebat, Eur.
poverty, of land, Strab.
with poor land, Strab.
one who sings to the lyre, Anth.:— contr. λυρῳδός, Id., Plut.
Lat. lyra, a lyre, a Greek musical instrument like the κιθάρα, invented by Hermes, with seven strings, Hhymn., Eur.
to play the lyre, Anacreont.
of or for the lyre, lyric, Anacreont.
as Subst., a lyrist, Anth., Plut.
delighting in the lyre, Anth.
fitted for the lyre, lyric, Anth.
charmed by the lyre, Anth.
a striking the lyre, Anth.
ἡ -κή, sc. τέχνη, the art or craft of lyre-making, Plat.
a lyre-maker, Plat.
a festival in honour of Lysander, Plut.
ending sorrow, Ar.
dissolving marriage, Anth.
loosing the zone, epith. of Eileithyia, who assisted women in travail, Theocr.
ending evil, Theogn.
ending strife, Anth.: fem. λυσιμάχη, Ar.
limb-relaxing, of sleep, etc., Od., Hes., etc.
driving care away, Anth.
able to loose or relieve, Aesch.
pass. that can be redeemed, redeemable, Plat.
releasing, delivering, Plat.
giving a loose to play or sport, Anacreont.
delivering from love, Anth.
releasing from toil, Pind.

entry.note: λῠ́σις, gen. εως ionic ιος, ἡ,
entry.sense: a loosing, setting free, releasing, ransoming, of a slain man, Il.; λ. θανάτου deliverance from death, Od.; πενίης Theogn., etc.
absol. a means of letting loose, Soph.:— deliverance from guilt by expiatory rites, Id.; οὐδ’ ἔχει λύσιν [τὰ πήματα] admit not of atonement, Id.
a loosing, parting, λ. ψυχῆς ἀπὸ σώματος Plat.:— dissolution, πολιτείας Arist.
= δόρπου λ. a place for banqueting, Pind.

to pay what is due, and then "to pay, " i. e. to profit, avail, c. dat., λυσιτελεῖ τί τινι Ar., Plat.:—impers., λυσιτελεῖ μοι it profits me, is better for me, τεθνάναι λυσιτελεῖ ἢ ζῆν 'tis better to be dead than alive, Andoc.; λυσιτελεῖ μοι ὥσπερ ἔχω ἔχειν it is expedient for me to be as I am, Plat.
neut. part. as Subst., τὸ λυσιτελοῦν, profit, gain, advantage, Id., Dem.; τὰ λυσιτελοῦντα Thuc.
paying what is due: hence, useful, profitable, advantageous, Plat.; τὸ λυσιτελέστατον πρὸς ἀργύριον what was most profitable in point of money, Dem.
cheap, Xen.
usefully, profitably, Xen.
opening the veins, Anth.
releasing from care, Anacreont.
one who played women's characters in male attire, Plut.
to rave, τινί against one, Soph.
rage, fury, esp. martial rage, Il.
after Hom. raging madness, raving, frenzy, Trag.
canine madness, rabies, Xen.
raging mad, Eur.
to be raging in battle, Hdt.
to rave, be mad, Soph., Plat.
of dogs, Ar.; of wolves, Theocr.
a fit of madness: in pl. ravings, Eur.
one that is raging or raving mad, Il., Anth.
raging mad, Anth.
to enrage, madden, epic part. λυσσώων, Anth.
like one raging, frantic, of martial rage, Il.
of madness, Soph., Eur.
one must solve, Plat.
loosing, releasing, delivering, Aesch.:—c. gen., τῶνδ’ ἐμοὶ λυτήριος my deliverer from these things, Id.; ἐκ θανάτου λ. Eur.
= λύτρον, recompense, Pind.
one who looses, a deliverer, Eur.
an arbitrator, decider, νεικέων Aesch.
refutative, of arguments, Arist.
that may be loosed or dissolved, Plat.
of arguments, refutable, Arist.
a price paid,
for ransom, a ransom, mostly in pl. ransom-money, Hdt.; λύτρα λαβεῖν τινος to receive as ransom for . . , Thuc.; λύτρα ἀποδιδόναι, καταθεῖναι to pay ransom, Dem.
an atonement, συμφορᾶς for calamity, Pind.; in pl., Plat.; so also, λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν NTest.
generally, a recompense, Pind.
to release on receipt of ransom, to hold to ransom, Plat.:—Pass. to be ransomed, Dem.
ransoming, Plut.
one must ransom, Arist.
a ransomer, redeemer, NTest.
a place to keep lamps in, Luc.
a lamp-stand, Theocr., Luc.
a kind of fish, Luc.
lychnis, a plant with a scarlet flower, Anth.
a precious stone that emits light, prob. the ruby, Luc.
a precious stone of a red colour, Strab.
a lighting of lamps, feast of Lanterns, Hdt.
making lamps or lanterns, Ar.
city of lamps, Luc.
a dealer in lamps or lanterns, Ar.
pl. λύχνοι and λύχνα: — a portable light, a lamp, carried in the hand or set on a lamp-stand (λυχνίον), Od., Hdt., attic; περὶ λύχνων ἁφάς about lamplighting time, Hdt.
in pl. the lamp-market, Ar.
carrying a lamp, Plut.
Orig. sense, to loose:

of things, to loosen, unbind, unfasten, ζωστῆρα, θώρηκα Il.; ἀσκὸν λ. to untie a skin (used as a bottle), Od.; λ. ἡνίαν to slack the rein, Soph.; λ. γράμματα to open a letter, Eur.; στόμα λ. to open the mouth, Id.; λ. ὀφρύν to unfold the brow, Id., etc.:—Mid., ἐλύσατο ἱμάντα undid her belt, Il.; λύσασθαι τρίχα to unbind one's hair, Bion.
of living beings,
of horses, etc., to undo, unyoke, unharness, Hom.; Mid., λύεσθαι ἵππους ὑπ’ ὄχεσφι to unyoke one's horses, Il.
of men, to loose, release from bonds or prison, from difficulty or danger, Hom., Att:—Mid. to get one loosed or set free, Hes.

of prisoners, to release on receipt of ransom (ἄποινα), hold to ransom, release, Hom.; λύειν τινὰ ἀποίνων on payment of ransom, Il.:—Mid. to release by payment of ransom, to get a person released, to ransom, redeem, Hom., attic
to give up, [θρόνον] λῦσον ἄμμιν Pind.
to resolve a whole into its parts, to dissolve, break up, λ. ἀγορήν to dissolve the assembly, Hom.; also to break up the market, Xen.:— Pass., λῦτο ἀγών Il.; ἐλύθη ἡ στρατιά Xen.
to loosen, slacken, σπάρτα λέλυνται, i. e. have rotted, Il.

to loosen, i. e. weaken, relax, λῦσέ οἱ γυῖα made his limbs slack or loose, i. e. killed him, Id.; λ. μένος τινί Id.; but, καμάτωι γούνατ’ ἔλυσαν made the knees weak with toil, Od.:—so in Pass., λύντο δὲ γυῖα, as the effect of death, sleep, weariness, fear, etc., Il., etc.; γυῖα λέλυντο Hom., etc.
to undo, bring to naught, break down, destroy, Hom.: and generally, to undo, do away with, put an end to, Lat. dissolvere, Id., attic; λ. βίον, i. e. to die, Eur.
to repeal, annul, do away with, Hdt., etc.; λ. ψῆφον to rescind a vote, Dem.:— Pass., λέλυται πάντα all ties are broken, Id.
to solve a problem or difficulty, Plat.
to refute an argument, Arist.
to unravel the plot of a tragedy, Id.
to break a law or treaty, Hdt., Thuc.
to solve, fulfil, accomplish, τὰ μαντεῖα Soph.
to atone for, make up for, Lat. luere, Id., Eur.
μισθοὺς λύειν to pay wages in full, Xen.

τέλη λύειν = λυσιτελεῖν, to pay, profit, avail, ἔνθα μὴ τέλη λύει φρονοῦντι where it boots not to be wise, Soph.; also λύει alone, much like λυσιτελεῖ, λύει ἄλγος Eur.; φημὶ τοιούτους γάμους λύειν βροτοῖς Id.

to treat despitefully, to outrage, maltreat, λώβην λωβᾶσθαί τινα to do one despite, Il.: esp. to maim, mutilate, Hdt.; λ. βίον to make ruin of one's life, Soph.; λ. τοὺς νέους to corrupt the youth, Plat.:—sometimes, like λυμαίνομαι, c. dat., Ar., Plat.:—absol. to do despite, act outrageously, Il.
the perf. is used in pass. sense, λελωβημένος mutilated, Hdt., Plat.; also aor1 pass., μεγάλας λώβας λωβηθείς Plat.
to mock, make a mock of, τινά Od.
despiteful treatment, outrage, dishonour, Hom., Hdt., attic:—esp. mutilation, maiming, Hdt.
of persons, a disgrace, Lat. opprobrium, λώβην εἶναι Il.
one who treats despitefully, a foul slanderer, Il.; a destroyer, of the Furies, Soph.
pass. a worthless wretch, Il.
λ. τέχνης one who disgraces his trade, Ar.
despitefully treated, outraged, Il., Soph.
act. insulting, abusive, Soph.

more desirable, more agreeable, and (generally) better, τόδε λώιόν ἐστι Hom.; and as adv. better, Od.:—we also find a comp. λωΐτερος, ον, in neut., λωίτερον καὶ ἄμεινον Id.—In attic λῴων was used as comp. of ἀγαθός.
Sup. λῷστος, η, ον Theogn., attic; τὰ λῷστα βουλεύειν Aesch.; ὦ λῷστε my good friend, Plat.
the border of a robe:—Dim. λωμάτιον, τό, Anth.
a Macedon. month, answering to the attic βοηδρομιών, Philipp. ap. Dem.
a covering, robe, mantle, Od., Theocr.
to cover, cloak, Soph.
to steal clothes, esp. from bathers or travellers, Plat., Xen.
generally, to rob, plunder, Ar.
one who slips into another's clothes, a clothes-stealer, esp. one who steals the clothes of bathers, or strips travellers, Soph.
generally, a thief, robber, footpad, Ar., Dem.
Mid. to choose for oneself, cull the best, Aesch.
made of lotus-wood, Theocr.
a flower: metaph. the fairest, choicest, best, Eur.
overgrown with lotus, πεδία λωτεῦντα (ionic for -όεντα) lotus-plains, Il.
the lotus, name of several plants.
the Greek lotus, a plant on which horses fed, a kind of clover or trefoil, Hom.
the Cyrenean lotus, an African shrub, whose fruit was the food of certain tribes on the coast, hence called Lotophagi, Od., Hdt.
the Egyptian lotus, the lily of the Nile, Hdt.
a North-African tree; from its hard black wood flutes were made:—hence Λιβὺς λωτός is used in Poets for a flute, Eur.
producing lotus, Eur.
the Lotus-eaters, a peaceful people on the coast of Cyrenaica, Od., Hdt.
to rest from toil, take rest, Il.
c. gen. to take rest or abate from, recover from, χόλου Aesch.; πόνου Soph.; λ. ἀπὸ νόσου καὶ πολέμου Thuc.
to abate, of a disease, Id.
trans. to lighten, relieve, ὁ λωφήσων γὰρ οὐ πέφυκέ πω Aesch.
relieving, λ. ἱερά expiatory offerings, Apoll.
abatement, cessation, Thuc.
acc. μάγαδιν: — the magadis, a kind of harp, with twenty strings, Com.
the bridge of the cithara, Lat. pons.
a piece of jugglery; in pl. juggleries, deceptions, Plat.
to use charms or philtres, of Circe, Ar.:— to play tricks, Dem.
any means for charming or bewitching, a philtre.
the theology of the Magians, Plat.
a cook-shop, Lat. popina, Arist., Babr.
the place where the public cooks lived, the cooks' quarter, Theophr.
to be a cook, to cook meat, Theophr.
to be a butcher, Babr.
fit for a cook or cookery, Ar., etc.:— ἡ μαγειρικὴ τέχνη cookery, Plat.:—adv. -κῶς, in a cook-like way, like a true "artist, " Ar.
a cook, Hdt., attic
a butcher, Eur. (From ΜΑΓ, Root of μάσσω ( q. v.), because baking bread was the business of the ancient cook.)
a piece of magic art; in pl. charms, spells, Eur.
one who wipes, Anth.
to be a Magus, use magic arts, Plut.: c. acc. cogn., μέλη μ. to sing incantations, Eur.
trans. to call forth by magic arts, Anth.
fit for the Magians, Magian, Plut.
a Magnesian, a dweller in Magnesia in Thessaly, Il., etc.; or Magnesia in Lydia, Hdt., etc.: fem. Μάγνησσα, Theocr.:—adj. Μαγνητικός, ή, όν Magnesian, Aesch.; fem. Μαγνῆτις, ιδος, Pind.
Μαγνῆτις λίθος, the magnet, Plat.
a Magus, Magian, one of a Median tribe, Hdt.
one of the wise men in Persia who interpreted dreams, Id.
any enchanter or wizard, and in bad sense, a juggler, impostor, Soph., Eur., etc.;—fem., Anth.
the slaughter of the Magians, a Persian festival, Hdt.
wet, flaccid: bald, Anth.
to be flaccid: to be bald, Ar.
a barley-cake, Hdt., Hes., attic
a barley-scone, Ar.
a trencher for serving barley cakes on, Hor.
that which is learnt, a lesson, Hdt., Soph., etc.
learning, knowledge, science, oft. in pl., Ar., Thuc., etc.: esp. the mathematical sciences, Plat., etc.
disposed to learn, Plat.
mathematical:— μαθηματικός, οῦ, a mathematician, Arist.; τὰ μαθηματικά mathematics, Id.
astronomical, mathematici = Chaldaei, Juven.
learning, the getting of knowledge, Soph., Thuc., etc.
desire of learning, Soph.
education, instruction, Plat., Xen.
to be learnt, Hdt.
μαθητέον, one must learn, Ar., Xen.
to be pupil, τινί to one, Plut.
trans. to make a disciple of, instruct, NTest.
a learner, pupil, Lat. discipulus, Hdt., Plat., etc.
Desiderat. of μανθάνω, to wish to become a disciple, Ar.
= μαθητεύω, Anth.
disposed to learn, τινος Plat.
learnt, that may be learnt, Xen., Plat.
Maeander, a river of Caria, Il., Hdt.
metaph. a winding pattern, Strab.
good mother, dame, Od.
a fostermother, nurse, Eur.:—also a true mother, Aesch., Eur.
a midwife, Plat.
Maia, daughter of Atlas, mother of Hermes, Hhymn., Hes.
the product of a midwife's art, a delivery, σὸν μὲν παιδίον, ἐμὸν δὲ μαίευμα Plat.
fut. σομαι, Dep. to serve as a midwife, Luc.
c. acc. pers. to deliver a woman, Plat.
delivery of a woman in childbirth, Plat.
of or for midwifery, obstetric, Plat.: —ἡ μαιευτικὴ τέχνη or ἡ -κή alone, midwifery, — the name given by Socrates to his art of eliciting from others what was in their minds, Id.
the fifth Attic month, the end of November and beginning of December, Dem.
epith. of Zeus, the boisterous, stormy, in whose honour a festival was held at Athens in the month Μαιμακτηριών, Plut.
to be very eager, pant or quiver with eagerness, Il.; c. gen., χεῖρα μαιμῶσαν φόνου a hand eager for murder, Soph.
Mount Maenalus in Arcadia, sacred to Pan, Theocr.:—adj. Μαινάλιος, η, ον, Pind.; ἡ Μαιναλία (sc. χώρα) Thuc.
raving, frantic, Eur.
as Subst. a mad woman, Il.: esp. a Bacchante, Bacchanal, Maenad, Soph.; of the Furies, Aesch.; of Cassandra, Eur.
act. causing madness, Pind.
maena, a small sea-fish, which, like our herring, was salted, Anth.
a sprat, Ar., etc.
raving, frenzied, Sapph..

to rage, be furious, Hom.; ὁ μανείς the madman, Soph.: to be mad with wine, Od.:—of Bacchic frenzy, Il., Soph.; ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ μ. to be driven mad by the god, Hdt.; τὸ μαίνεσθαι madness, Soph.; πλεῖν ἢ μαίνομαι more than madness, Ar.:—c. acc. cogn., μεμηνὼς οὐ σμικρὰν νόσον mad with no slight disease, Aesch.
of fire, to rage, riot, Il.; so, μαινομένη ἐλπίς Orac. ap. Hdt.; ἔρις Aesch., etc.
the aor1 act. ἔμηνα, in Causal sense, to madden, enrage, Eur., Xen.
to seek:
absol. to endeavour, strive, Od., Pind., Aesch.
c. acc. to search, examine, Od.
to seek after, seek for, τι Pind.: c. inf. to seek to do, Id., Soph.
Dep. to deliver a woman, Luc., Anth.
(with or without μήν), the Lat. Maius, May, Plut., etc.:—as adj., Μάϊαι Καλάνδαι the Calends of May, Id.
the sparkler, i. e. the dog-star, Anth.
the Maeotians, a Scythian tribe to the North of the Black Sea, Hdt., Xen.
as adj.
Maeotian, ποταμὸς M. the Tanais, Hdt.:— Μαιῶτις, λίμνη the Palus Maeotis, Sea of Azof, Aesch., etc.; ἡ λίμνη ἡ Μαιῆτις (ionic) Hdt.
Μαιωτικός, ή, όν, αὐλὼν M., i. e. the Cimmerian Bosporus, Aesch.
in Scythian fashion, Theocr.
a midwife's wages, Luc.
happiness, bliss, κενὴ μ. Luc.:—euphem. for ἐς κόρακας, ἄπαγ’ ἐς μακαρίαν Ar.
to bless, to deem or pronounce happy, Lat. gratulari, Od., Hdt., attic; ironically, μακαρίσαντες ὑμῶν τὸ ἀπειρόκακον while we bless your simplicity, Thuc.
of men, blessed, happy, Pind., Eur., etc.:—in addresses, ὦ μακάριε, like ὦ θαυμάσιε, my good sir, my dear sir, Plat.:—c. gen., ὦ μ. τῆς τύχης happy you for your good fortune! Ar.
οἱ μακάριοι, like οἱ ὄλβιοι, the rich and better educated, Plat., Arist.
adv. -ίως, Eur., Ar.
happiness, bliss, Plat., Arist.;
a pronouncing happy, blessing, Plat., Arist.
deemed or to be deemed happy, enviable, Hdt., attic
like μάκαρ III, one blessed, i. e. dead, Aesch., etc.
as adj., μ. βίος, with a double meaning, Ar.
blessed, happy, of the gods, as opp. to mortal men, Il.; absol., μάκαρες the blessed ones, Od., Hes., Pind., Trag.
of men, blest, fortunate, ὦ μάκαρ Ἀτρείδη Il.; so, μάκαιρα ἑστία, etc., Pind.:— esp. wealthy, ἀνδρὸς μάκαρος κατ’ ἄρουραν Il.

μάκαρες also meant the dead, as secure from the ills of life, Hes.:— μακάρων νῆσοι the Islands of the Blest (in the ocean at the extreme West) where heroes and demi-gods enjoyed rest for ever, Id., Pind.
comp. μακάρτερος, Sup. μακάρτατος Od.
tall, taper, Od.
to be on the Macedonian side, Plut.
to speak Macedonian, Id.
in Macedonian, Id.
a Macedonian, οἱ Μακεδόνες, the Macedonians, Hdt.:—adj. Μακεδόνιος, η, ον, and -ονικός, ή, όν, Id., etc.; ἡ Μακεδονία Macedon, Id.; so, ἡ Μακεδονὶς, γῆ Id.; γῆ Μακεδών Anth.

entry.etym: μία, κέλλω, as δίκελλα from δίς, κέλλω.
entry.sense: a pick-axe with one point, Il., Aesch.
the meat-market, shambles, NTest.
long and tedious, Aesch.
to be stupid, Ar.; part. perf. μεμακκοηκώς sitting mooning, Id.
lasting long, Soph.
of persons, long-lived, aged, Id.; οἱ μακραίωνες the immortals, Id.

entry.etym: acc. fem. of μακρός used as adv.
entry.sense: a long way, far, far away, Aesch., Soph., etc.; τοὖργον οὐ μ. λέγεις the business you speak of is not far to seek, Soph.:—c. gen. far from, Eur.:—comp., μακροτέραν to a greater distance, Thuc., Xen.; Sup., ὅτι μακροτάτην as far as possible, c. gen. loci, Xen.
μακρὰν λέγειν to speak at length, Aesch., Soph.
of Time, long, μ. ζῆν, ἀναμένειν Soph.; οὐ μ. Lat. brevi, Eur.; so, οὐκ ἐς μακρήν Hdt., etc.
long-necked, long, Eur.
to speak at great length, Aesch., Eur., etc.
tediousness, Pind.
the season of long days, Hdt.
long-lived, Arist.; μακροβιώτατος Hdt.: —οἱ M., an Ethiopian people, Id.
longevity, Arist.
long, Aesch.
very old, Anth.
running long or far, Xen.
from afar, Strab.; of Time, from long since, Polyb.
to be long-suffering, NTest.; and μακροθῡμία, long-suffering, forbearance, NTest.
longsuffering, patient, Anth.: adv. -μως, NTest.
long-headed, of the Scythians, Strab.
to have long hair, Strab.
long-limbed: ἡ μ. a kind of sling, Strab.
of sentences, with long clauses, Arist.
to speak at length, use many words, Plat.; c. acc. rei, to speak long on a subject, Xen.
length of speech, Plat.
speaking at length, Plat.
with long wool, Strab.
long-breathed, long-protracted, wearisome, Eur.
to go or travel far, Strab.
a long way or journey, Strab.
long-bearded, Strab.
of Space,
in point of length, long, Hom., etc.; ἐπὶ τὰ μακρότερα towards the longer sides, i. e. lengthwise, Hdt.
in point of height, tall, Hom., e. g. μακρὸς Ὄλυμπος, μ. δένδρεα, τείχεα, etc.:—also reversely, like Lat. altus, deep, Il.

in point of distance, long, far, far distant, Id., Hdt.; τὰ μακρότατα the remotest parts, Hdt.:—often in neut. pl. as adv., μακρὰ βιβάς far-striding, Il.; also, μακρὸν ἀϋτεῖν, βοᾶν to shout so as to be heard afar, Hom.; so, μακρότερον σφενδονᾶν to sling to a greater distance, Xen.
generally, large in size or in degree, large, great, Aesch., Soph.
dat. μακρῷ is used to strengthen the comp. and Sup. by far, Lat. longe, μακρῷ πρῶτος, μ. μάλιστα Hdt.; ἀσθενεστέρα μ. Aesch., etc.
of Time, long, long-lasting, long, Od., Hdt., etc.; οὐ μακροῦ χρόνου for no long time, Soph.; τὸν μ. βίον Aesch.; μακρότερος μηνί by a month, Hdt.:—so, μακρὸν ἐέλδωρ a long-cherished wish, Od.
long, tedious, Pind., Soph.

neut. with Preps. in adverb. sense, διὰ μακροῦ (sc. χρόνου) after a long time, long delayed, Eur.; οὐ διὰ μακροῦ not long after, Thuc.:—but, διὰ μακρῶν at great length, Plat.: —οὐκ ἐς μακρόν for no long time, Pind.: —ἐπὶ μακρόν far, a long way, Xen.; ὅσον ἐπὶ μακρότατον or ὅσον μ. as far as possible, Hdt.; ἐπὶ μακρότερον yet more, Thuc.
regul. comp. μακρότερος Od., Hdt., etc.; Sup. μακρότατος Il., etc.:—irreg. comp. μάσσων, Sup. μήκιστος, v. sub vocc.
adv. μακρῶς, at great length, slowly, Polyb.
length, Ar.
far-stretching, Anth.
beyond, further, Plat., etc.
far-stretching, long drawn out, σχοῖνοι Anth.
long-necked, Anth.
long-necked, of a bottle, Anth.
a tedious prater, Anth.
long-armed, Lat. longimanus, name of Artaxerxes I. Strab., Plut.
with long hoofs, Strab.
a longhead; Μάκρωνες, οἱ, a people of Pontus, Hdt.
a kneading-trough, Ar., Xen.
soft-footed, treading softly, Theocr.
softness, delicacy, effeminacy, Hdt., Thuc.
want of patience, weakness, Arist.
calmness of the sea, Caesar.
to be softened or made effeminate, shew weakness or cowardice, Thuc., Xen.
to be softened or appeased, Thuc.
with or of soft soil, Strab.
mild of mood, Aesch.
Lat. mollis, soft, Hom., etc.; μ. νειός a fresh-ploughed fallow, Il.; μ. λειμών a soft grassy meadow, Od.; μ. παρειαί Soph.; σώματα Xen.: —adv., καθίζου μαλακῶς sit softly, i. e. on a cushion, Ar.

of things not subject to touch, soft, gentle, θάνατος, ὕπνος Hom.; μαλακῶς εὕδειν to sleep softly, Od.; μαλακὰ ἔπεα, μ. λόγοι soft, fair words, Hom.; μ. βλέμμα tender, youthful looks, Ar.; light, mild, ζημία Thuc.

in bad sense, of persons, soft, yielding, remiss, Id., Xen.:—adv., μαλακωτέρως ἀνθήπτετο attacked him somewhat feebly, Thuc.: —also faint-hearted, effeminate, cowardly, Id., Xen.; μαλακὸν οὐδὲν ἐνδιδόναι not to give in from want of spirit, not to flag a whit, Hdt., Ar.
softness, Plat., etc.
weakness, effeminacy, Plut.
soft-handed, Pind.
one that melts and moulds, Plut.
Pass., like μαλακίζομαι, to flag, Xen.
very, very much, exceedingly, Hom., etc.

strengthening the word with which it stands, μάλα πολλά very many, Id.; μάλα πάντες, μ. πᾶσαι, μ. πάντα, all together, every one, Id.; μάλ’ ἀσκηθής all unhurt, Od.; ἀβληχρὸς μάλα τοῖος so very weak, Id.:—so in attic, μάλα δὴ πρεσβύτης very old, Xen.; μ. γέ τινες ὀλίγοι Plat.:—so with Advs., πάγχυ μάλα and μάλα πάγχυ quite utterly, Il.; εὖ μάλα right well, Od.; μάλ’ αἰεί for ever and aye, Il.; ἄχρι μάλα κνέφαος until quite dark, Od.; μάλα διαμπερές right through, Il.:—so in attic, to express repeated action, μάλ’ αὖθις, μάλ’ αὖ Aesch., etc.:— with Verbs, μή με μάλ’ αἴνεε praise me not greatly, Il.; ἡ δὲ μάλ’ ἡνιόχευεν she drove carefully, Od., etc.
strengthening an assertion, εἰ μάλα μιν χόλος ἵκοι if wrath come on him ever so much, Hom.; so μάλα περ with a partic., μάλα περ μεμαώς though desiring never so much, Il.
in attic in answers, yes, certainly, exactly so, μάλα γε Plat., etc.; μ. τοι Xen., etc.; καὶ μ. δή Id.
comp. μᾶλλον, more, Hom.; μᾶλλον τοῦ δέοντος more than is right, Plat., Xen., etc.; παντὸς μᾶλλον more than anything, i. e. most certainly, Plat.
denoting increase, more and more, still more, Od.; μᾶλλον μᾶλλον, Lat. magis magisque, Eur., Ar.
sometimes joined to a second comp., ῥηίτεροι μᾶλλον Il.; μᾶλλον ἆσσον Soph., etc.
μᾶλλον δέ, much more, but rather, πολλοί, μᾶλλον δὲ πάντες Dem.

in μᾶλλον ἢ οὐ, οὐ seems redundant, ἥκει ὁ Πέρσης οὐδὲν μᾶλλον ἐπ’ ἡμέας ἢ οὐ ἐπ’ ὑμέας the Persians have come not more against us, than against you, Hdt.; in this case μᾶλλον ἢ οὐ is preceded by another negat.
τὸ μ. καὶ ἧττον, a form of argument, which we call a fortiori, Arist.

Sup. μάλιστα, most, most of all, Hom., etc.; μάλιστα μέν . . , ἔπειτα δέ . . , first and above all . . , next . . , Soph.:— τί μάλιστα; what is the precise thing that you want? Plat.; ὡς or ὅτι μ., Lat. quam maxime, Id.; ὅσον μ. Aesch.; ὡς μ. certainly, in answers, Plat.; ὡς δύναμαι μ. Id.; μακρῷ μ. Hdt.
ἐς τὰ μάλιστα for the most part, mostly, Id.; so, τὰ μάλιστα Thuc., etc.; also, ἀνὴρ δόκιμος ὁμοῖα τῷ μ. as famous as he that is most [famous], Hdt.
ἐν τοῖς μ. especially, as much as any, Thuc., Plat.
μάλιστα may be added to a Sup., ἔχθιστος μάλιστα, μάλιστα φίλτατος Il.; μ. φίλτατος Eur.
with numbers, μάλιστα means about, Thuc., Xen., etc.; so, ἐς μέσον μάλιστα about the middle, Hdt.; ἥμισυ μ. Thuc., etc.
καὶ μάλιστα is used in answers, most certainly, Lat. vel maxime, Ar.; so, μ γε Soph.; μ. πάντων Ar.

to make soft, of dressing leather, to make it soft and supple;— hence, with reference to Cleon's trade of tanner, μαλ. τινά to give one a dressing, hide him, Ar.: Pass., ἐν παγκρατίῳ μαλαχθείς worsted in it, Pind.
to soften metal or other material for working, Plat.
metaph. to soften, appease, make to relent, Eur.:—Pass. to be softened, to relent, Soph., Ar.; μ. νόσου to be relieved from disease, Soph.
mallow, Lat. malva, Hes., Ar., etc.
mighty, fierce, devouring, ravening, of fire, Il., etc.
metaph. fiery, glowing, vehement, furious, Pind., Trag.
the arm-pit, Lat. ala, only in phrase ὑπὸ μάλης, under the arm, as the place for carrying concealed weapons, Xen., Plat.:—hence ὑπὸ μάλης underhand, secretly, Lat. furtim, Dem.
Pass. to be softened, of persons, Aesch., Eur.:— to relax, give in, Plat.
one must be remiss, Plat.:—so μαλθακιστέα, Ar.
soft, Pind., attic:—adv., μαλθακῶς κατακεῖσθαι to recline on soft cushions, Ar.
metaph. faint-hearted, remiss, cowardly, Il., attic:—also weak, feeble, Ar.
in good sense, soft, gentle, mild, Theogn., attic:—adv. gently, Aesch., Soph.; neut. as adv., Aesch.
soft-voiced, Pind.
a mixture of wax and pitch for laying over writing-tablets, Dem.
to soften, soothe, Trag.:—Pass., μαλθαχθεῖς’ ὕπνῳ unnerved by sleep, Aesch.
a lock of hair, Anth.

entry.etym: Sup. of μάλα, v. μάλα III.

entry.sense: to become numb with cold, to be torpid, Hes., Xen., Dem.

entry.etym: comp. of μάλα; v. μάλα II.

entry.sense: a lock of wool, wool, Hes., Aesch., etc.: — a lock of hair, Eur.
white, Theocr.
Comic word for a blockhead, simpleton, Ar.
μαμμᾶν αἰτεῖν, to cry for the breast, to suck the breast, of babies, Ar.
mamma, mammy, a child's attempt to articulate mother, Anth.:—so ἄττα, πάππας, τάτα, τέττα, papa, for father.
a grandmother, Plut.
a Syrian deity, god of riches; Hence riches, wealth, NTest.
mandrake, a narcotic plant, Xen., Dem.
an inclosed space:
for cattle, a fold, byre, stable, Theocr., etc.
the setting of a ring, Anth.
Maneros, only son of the first king of Egypt: a national dirge named after him, Hdt.

to learn, esp. by inquiry; and in aor. to have learnt, i. e. to understand, know, Od., attic; ἀεὶ γὰρ ἡβᾶι τοῖς γέρουσιν εὖ μαθεῖν Aesch.; οἱ μανθάνοντες, learners, pupils, Xen.: —c. inf. to learn to do, learn how to do, Il., Aesch., etc.
to perceive by the senses, remark, notice, Hdt., Xen.:—with a part., μάνθανε ὤν, like ἴσθι ὤν, know that you are, Soph., etc.
to understand, comprehend, Aesch., etc.:—often in Dialogue, μανθάνεις; Lat. tenes? d'ye see?— Answ., πάνυ μανθάνω, perfectly! Ar.
in attic, τί μαθών; often begins a question, having learnt what? for what new reason? wherefore? Id., etc.
an armlet, worn of gold used by Persians and Gauls, Polyb.
madness, frenzy, Hdt., Trag., etc.
enthusiasm, inspired frenzy, Eur., Plat.
mad passion, fury, Trag.
raging, frantic, mad, Soph.; with a neut. Subst., μανιάσιν λυσσήμασι with mad ravings, Eur.
of or for madness, mad, Ar.; μανικόν τι βλέπειν to look mad, Id.
of persons, frenzied, frantic, Plat.:— mad, extravagant, Xen.: —adv., μανικῶς διακεῖσθαι Plat.
like madness, mad, Xen.
like a madman, crazy, Thuc.; τὸ μ. madness, Eur.
a Hebr. word, manna, a morsel, grain, the gum of the tamarisk; generally, food, NTest.
Lat. monile, a collar,
wearing a collar, Theocr.
Lat. rarus, loose in texture, porous, Plat., etc.
few, scanty, Xen., etc.:—adv. -νῶς, τοσούτῳ μανότερον so much the less often, Id.
looseness of texture, porousness, Arist.
fewness, scantiness, Plat.
prophesying, prophetic power, Hhymn.: mode of divination, Hdt.; αἴνιγμα μαντείας ἔδει the riddle stood in need of divination, Soph.
= μαντεῖον II, Tyrtae., Soph.

entry.note: μαντεῖον, ionic and epic -ήιον, ου, τό,
entry.sense: an oracle, i. e.,
an oracular response, Od., Hdt., attic
the seat of an oracle, Hdt., Aesch., etc.
oracular, prophetic, Pind., Aesch., etc.; μ. ἄναξ, i. e. Apollo, Eur.
an oracle, Pind., Trag.
to divine, prophesy, presage, Hom., etc.; c. acc. cogn., μαντεῖα μ. Aesch.
generally, to divine, presage, augur, forbode, surmise, of any presentiment, Plat., etc.; c. gen., μαντευσόμεσθα τἀνδρὸς ὡς ὀλωλότος Aesch.
of animals, to get scent of a thing, Theocr.
to consult an oracle, seek divinations, Hdt., attic; ταῦτα καὶ μ. this is the question I ask the oracle, Eur.
aor1 and perf. pass. in pass. sense, ἐμαντεύθη an oracle was given, Hdt.; τὰ μεμαντευμένα the words of the oracles, Id.
one must divine, Eur.
foretold by an oracle, Eur.: prescribed by an oracle, Xen.
of or for a soothsayer or his art, prophetic, oracular, Trag.
ἡ μαντικὴ τέχνη, = μαντεία, the faculty of divination, prophecy, Soph.; so, ἡ μαντική alone, Hdt., Plat.
of persons, like a prophet, oracular, Plat.:—adv. -κῶς, Ar.
to prophesy, Aesch.
frenzied, inspired, Eur.
one who divines, a seer, prophet, Hom., etc.:—as fem. a prophetess, Trag., Thuc.
metaph. a diviner, foreboder, Soph.
a kind of grasshopper, Theocr.
the art of divination, Il., Pind.
oracular, Eur.

a Particle used in strong protestations and oaths, followed by acc. of the deity or thing appealed to; in itself neither affirmative nor negative, but made so by prefixing ναί or οὐ, or by the context:—thus,
ναὶ μὰ . . , in affirmation, ναὶ μὰ τόδε σκῆπτρον yea by this sceptre, Il.; ναὶ μὰ Δία, ναὶ μὰ τὸν Δία Ar., Plat.
οὐ μὰ . . , in negation, οὐ μὰ Ζῆνα, nay, by . . , Il.; οὔ τοι μὰ τοὺς δώδεκα θεούς Ar.
in attic μά is often used alone, mostly in negat. sense μὰ τὸν Ποσειδῶ Eur.:— in answers, when the negation is expressed in the question, οὐκ αὖ μ’ ἐάσεις; Answ. μὰ Δἴ (sc. οὐκ ἐάσω) Ar.
the name of the deity was often suppressed, ναὶ μὰ τόν, οὐ μὰ τόν Plat.
shortd. doric form for μάτηρ, μᾶ γᾶ for μῆτερ γῆ, Aesch.; μᾶ, πόθεν ἅνθρωπος; Theocr.
a whip, scourge, Aesch., Eur.
fennel, Lat. marathrum, Dem.
a Marathon fighter, a Marathon-man, proverb. of a brave veteran, Ar.
Marathon, a deme on the East of Attica, prob. so called from its being overgrown with fennel, Od., Hdt., etc.
to put out or quench fire, Hhymn.:—Pass. to die away, go slowly out, of fire, Il.

metaph., ὄψεις μ. to quench the orbs of sight, Soph.; νόσος μαραίνει με makes me waste away, wears me out, Aesch.; of time, πάντα χρόνος μαραίνει Soph.: —Pass. to die away, waste away, decay, wither, Eur., Thuc.; αἷμα μαραίνεται χερός blood dies away from my hand, Aesch.; of a river, to dry up, Hdt.
μαρὰν ἀθά, Syriac phrase, = ὁ Κύριος ἥκει, NTest.
to rage furiously, Il.
a pearl, Theophr., etc.
raging, Aesch.; c. inf., μαργῶν ἱέναι madly eager to go, Eur.
Margites, i. e. a mad fellow, hero of a mock-heroic poem ascribed to Homer.
raging mad, Lat. furiosus, μάργε, madman! Od.; then in Pind., Aesch., etc.
of appetite, greedy, gluttonous, Od., Eur.
lewd, lustful, Theogn., Eur.
raging passion, Soph.
gluttony, Plat.
lust, Eur.
Marea, a town in Lower Egypt, Hdt., Thuc.
a lake near it, Strab.; more commonly called ἡ Μαρεῶτις, ( sc. λίμνη ) Id.:—also ὁ Μαρεώτης, ( sc. οἶνος ) Id.
a hand, Pind.
Μαριανδῡνοί, οἱ, a people of Bithynia, Hdt., etc.:— Μαριανδυνὸς θρηνητήρ one who utters a wild, barbaric lament, Aesch.; cf. Κίσσιος.
ὦ Μᾰρῑλάδη O son of coal-dust! comic name of an Acharnian collier, Id.
the embers of charcoal, Ar.

entry.etym: ΠΟ, Root of some tenses of πίνω
entry.sense: coal-dust-gulper, of a blacksmith, Anth.
to flash, sparkle, of arms, Il.; ὄμματα μαρμαίροντα the sparkling eyes of Aphrodite, Il.; νύκτα ἄστροισι μαρμαίρουσαν Aesch.
flashing, sparkling, glistening, gleaming, of metals, Il., Hes.; also, ἃλς μαρμαρέη the many-twinkling sea, Il.
of marble, Anth.
of marble, Theocr.
sculpture in marble, Strab.
any stone or rock of crystalline structure, which sparkles (μαρμαίρει) in the light, Hom., etc.; also, πέτρος μάρμαρος Il.
marble, Strab.: — a marble tombstone, Theocr.
a flashing, sparkling, of light, Plat.: of any quick motion, μαρμαρυγαὶ ποδῶν the quick twinkling of dancers' feet, Od.
with sparkling eyes, Eur.

entry.etym: Dep., only in pres. and imperf.
entry.sense: to fight, do battle, τινί with or against another, Il.; ἐπί τινι Id.; πρός τινα Eur.
to quarrel, wrangle with words, Il.
in Pind. to contend, struggle, strive to one's uttermost, Pind.

to catch, lay hold of, seize, τινά Hom., etc.: c. gen. partis, μ. τινὰ ποδός to catch one by the foot, Soph., Il.; ποσὶ μ. τινά to overtake, catch a fugitive, Il.: but, χθόνα μάρπτε ποδοῖιν reached ground with his feet, Id.: metaph., τὸν ὕπνος ἔμαρψε him sleep overtook, Id.; γῆρας ἔμαρψε old age got hold of him, Od.; εἴ σε μάρψει ψῆφος if the votes shall convict thee, Aesch.; ἄσκοποι πλάκες ἔμαρψαν the unseen land engulphed him, Soph.
a bag, pouch, Lat. marsupium, Xen.
sc. μήν, Lat. Martius, the month of March, Plut.

to be a witness, to bear witness, give evidence, bear testimony, Simon., etc.: c. dat. pers. to bear witness to or in favour of another, Hdt., attic; μαρτυρέει μοι τῆι γνώμηι bears witness to my opinion, Hdt.
c. acc. rei, to bear witness to a thing, testify it, Soph., etc.
c. inf. to testify that a thing is, Id.; τίς σοι μαρτυρήσει κλύειν; who will bear thee witness that he heard..? Id.
c. acc. cogn., μ. ἀκοήν to give hearsay evidence, Dem.:—so in Pass., μαρτυρίαι μαρτυρηθεῖσαι Id.
Pass. also impers., μαρτυρεῖται testimony is borne, Plat.; οἶδα μαρτυρήσεσθαι I know that testimony will be given, Xen.
testimony, Eur.
witness, testimony, evidence, often in pl., Od.; μαρτυριῶν ἀπέχεσθαι to refuse to give evidence, Ar.
a testimony, proof, Hdt., etc.; μαρτύρια παρέχεσθαι to bring forward evidence, Id.: —μαρτύριον δέ . . , followed by γάρ, here is a proof, namely . . , Id., Thuc., etc.
Mid to call to witness, attest, invoke, Soph., Eur., etc.; c. part., μαρτύρομαι τυπτόμενος I call you to witness that I am being beaten, Ar.
c. acc. rei, to call one to witness a thing, Hdt., Ar.
to protest, asseverate, μ. ὅτι . . Ar., etc.; absol., μαρτύρομαι I protest, Id., Thuc.

entry.etym: old Ep. form for μαρτυς, Hom.
