to call by a new name, αἰγίδας μετωνόμασαν called them by a new name— αἰγίδες, Hdt.:—Pass. to take or receive a new name, Id., Thuc.
of Place, from behind, backwards, back, Hom., Hes.
of Time, after, afterwards, Hom.
prep. with gen. behind, Id.
autumnal, Thuc., Xen.:—neut. as adv., Hes. [Cf. ὀπωρινός.]
late autumn, Thuc.
the space between rows of vines, Ar.
participation, partnership, communion, τινός, in a thing, Ar., Dem.
participation, communion, Hdt.

entry.note: fut. ίσω 3rd sg. epic aor1 opt. μετοχλίσσειε
entry.sense: to remove by a lever, hoist a heavy body out of the way, Od.
to push back the bar, Il.
sharing in, partaking of, c. gen., Hdt., Eur.
as Subst. a partner, accomplice in, τοῦ φόνου Eur.; absol., Thuc.
to measure in any way:
of Space, to measure, i. e. pass over, traverse, πέλαγος μέγα μετρήσασαν Od.:—Mid., ἅλα μετρήσασθαι Mosch.

in the common sense, to measure, Lat. metiri, τὴν γῆν σταδίοισι Hdt.; τῆι γαστρὶ μ. τὴν εὐδαιμονίαν to measure happiness by sensual enjoyments, Dem.:—Mid., μετρεῖσθαι ἴχνη to measure his steps by the eye, Soph.:—Pass. to be measured, Hdt., Aesch.
to count, Theocr.
to measure out, dole out, Ar., Dem.:—Mid. to have measured out to one, εὖ μετρεῖσθαι to get good measure, Hes.; τὰ ἄλφιτα μετρούμενοι Dem.
a measured distance, Eur.
a measure, allowance, dole, Id.
measuring, measurement, Hdt., Xen.
one must measure, Plat.
a measurer, Plat.
= ἀμφορεύς, a liquid measure, holding 12 χόες or 144 κοτύλαι, about 9 gallons Engl., Dem.
of or for measuring, Plat.: ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) mensuration, Id.
measurable, Eur., Plat.
to be moderate, keep measure, Soph., Thuc., etc.
trans. to moderate, regulate, control, Lat. moderari, Plat., etc.
of or for metre, metrical, Arist.: τὰ -κά and ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη), prosody, Id.
to bear reasonably with, τινί NTest.
moderating one's passions, a Peripatetic word.
a moderate drinker, Xen.
within measure, and so,
of Size, of average height, Hdt.; μ. πῆχυς the common cubit, Id.; so of Time, moderate, Plat.
of Number, few, Xen.

of Degree, holding to the mean, moderate, Hes., Eur., etc.:—of a mean or middle state, opp. to a high or low estate, Trag., etc.; τὸ μέτριον the mean, Lat. aurea mediocritas, Soph.; so, τὰ μέτρια Eur., etc.; —so, μ. φιλία a friendship not too great, Id.; μ. ἐσθῆτι χρῆσθαι common dress, Thuc.; μετρίᾳ φυλακῇ not in strict custody, Id.; οἱ μέτριοι common men, the common sort, Dem.:—also, ὅσον οἰόμεθα μέτριον εἶναι just sufficient, Plat.
moderate, tolerable, Hdt., Soph., etc.; τὰ μ. moderate terms, Thuc.
of Persons, moderate, temperate, virtuous, Theogn., Eur.; μετριώτεροι ἐς τὰ πολιτικά Thuc.; μέτρ. πρὸς δίαιταν Aeschin.
proportionate, fitting, Xen.
adv. μετρίως, moderately, within due limits, in due measure, fairly, Hdt., Thuc., etc.; μ. ἔχειν τοῦ βίου to be moderately well off, Hdt.:—comp. μετριώτερον, Sup. -ώτατα, Thuc.
enough, sufficiently, Ar., etc.
modestly, temperately, Eur., Xen.:— to fair terms, Thuc.
the neut. μέτριον and μέτρια are also used as adv., Plat.:—with Art., τὸ μέτριον Xen.; τὰ μέτρια Thuc.
moderation, Thuc., Plat.; μ. τῶν σίτων moderation in food, Xen.
a middle condition, Lat. mediocritas, Arist.
that by which anything is measured:
a measure or rule, Il.; ἄνδρα πάντων χρημάτων μ. εἶναι is a measure of all things, Plat.
a measure of content, whether solid or liquid, δῶκεν μέθυ, χίλια μέτρα Il.; εἴκοσι μέτρα ἀλφίτου Od.
measure, length, size, μέτρα κελεύθου the length of the way, Od.; μέτρον ἑξήκοντα σταδίους Thuc.; μέτρον ἥβης full measure, i. e. the prime, of youth, Il.; μέτρα μορφῆς one's size and shape, Eur.
due measure or limit, proportion, μέτρα φυλάσσεσθαι Hes.; κατὰ μέτρον Id. ὑπὲρ μέτρον Theogn.; πλέον μέτρου Plat.;— μέτρῷ μετρίως, Pind.
metre, opp. to μέλος (tune)and ῥυθμός (time), Ar., Plat.
a verse, Plat.
adv. with front-foremost; of ships, forming a close front, in line, Hdt.; opp. to ἐπὶ κέρως (in column), Thuc.
on the forehead, Anth.
the forehead, Il.
the space between the eyes, the brow, forehead, Hom., etc.
the front or face of a wall or building, Hdt.: the front of an army or fleet, Aesch., Xen.; ἐπὶ μετώπου or ἐν μετώπῳ in line, opp. to ἐπὶ κέρως or κέρας (in column), Xen.
to a given point, even so far,
before a prep. μέχρι πρός, Lat. usque ad, Plat.:—so before Advs., μ. δεῦρο τοῦ λόγου Id.; μ. τότε Thuc.
serving as a prep. c. gen. even to, as far as,
of Place, μέχρι θαλάσσης Il.; μ. τῆς πόλεως Thuc.
of Time, τέο μέχρις; i. e. τινός μέχρι χρόνου; Lat. quousque? how long? Il.; so, μέχρι οὗ; μέχρι ὅσου; Hdt.; with the Art., τὸ μ. ἐμεῦ up to my time, Id.
of Measure or Degree, μ. σοῦ δικαίου so far as consists with right, Thuc.; μ. τοῦ δυνατοῦ Plat.
with Numbers, up to, about, nearly, sometimes without altering the case of the Subst., μέχρι τριάκοντα ἔτη Aeschin.
in ionic, μέχρι οὗ is sometimes used like the simple μέχρι, μέχρι οὗ ὀκτὼ πύργων Hdt.
as a Conjunct. so long as, until, μέχρι μὲν ὥρεον, with δέ in apodosi, Id.; μ. σκότος ἐγένετο Xen.
μέχρι ἄν foll. by the subj., Id.; so without ἄν, μ. τοῦτο ἴδωμεν Hdt.
an elliptic phrase for μὴ γένοιτο, ἀλλά . . , in answers, nay but, not so but, σὲ δὲ ταῦτ’ ἀρέσκει; Answ. μἀλλὰ πλεῖν ἢ μαίνομαι Ar.

an elliptic phrase, used in emphatic denial, certainly not, where a Verb must be supplied from the foregoing passage, μὴ λεγέτω τὸ ὄνομα, Answ. μὴ γάρ (sc. λεγέτω) Plat.:—also in parenthesis, where it may be translated much less, like μὴ ὅτι, Aeschin.
in no wise, not at all, Hdt., Aesch., etc.
from no place, Xen.; μ. ἄλλοθεν from no other place, Plat.
nowhere, Luc.
nowhither, Soph.
nowhither, μ. ἄλλοσε Plat.
for μηδὲ ἀμός, only in pl. μηδαμοί (in ionic writers), none, Hdt.
nowhere, Aesch.; μ. ἄλλοθι Plat.:— metaph. μ. νομίζεται nullo in numero habetur, Aesch.

entry.etym: i. e. μηδὲ εἷς, μηδὲ μία, μηδὲ ἕν
entry.sense: and not one, related to οὐδείς as μή to οὐ, Il., etc.; —rare in Pl., Xen.

μηδὲ εἷς, which (so written) is never elided even in attic, retained the first emphatic sense not even one, and often had a Particle between, as μηδ’ ἂν εἷς, or a prep., μηδ’ ἐξ ἑνός, μηδὲ περὶ ἑνός etc., Plat.

nobody, naught, good for naught, ὁ μηδείς Soph.; pl., οὐ γὰρ ἠξίου τοὺς μηδένας Id.:— so, μηδέν or τὸ μηδέν often as Subst., naught, nothing, Id.; μηδὲν λέγειν to say what is naught, Xen.; τοῦ μηδενὸς ἄξιος Hdt.; ἐς τὸ μηδὲν ἥκειν Eur.;—and of persons, τὸ μηδέν a good for naught, τὸ μηδὲν εἶναι of an eunuch, Hdt.; τὸ μ. ὄντας Soph.
neut. μηδέν as adv. not at all, by no means, Aesch., etc.
μή δέ, Negat. Particle, (related to οὐδέ as μή to οὐ):
as Conjunct. but not or and not, nor, μή τι σὺ ταῦτα διείρεο μηδὲ μετάλλα Il.:—more rarely without a negative preceding, τεκνοῦσθαι, μηδ’ ἄπαιδα θνήσκειν Aesch.
doubled, μηδέ . . μηδέ . . , Opposing the two clauses of a sentence, Il.:— μηδέ also follows μήτε, Soph., Plat.
as adv., joined with a single word or phrase, not even, Lat. ne . . quidem, Hom., etc.
never, Ar., Plat., etc.
μηδέ ποτε and never, Hes.
nor as yet, not as yet, Aesch., etc.
never yet, Dem.
fem. prop. n., adorned-with-prudence, from μήδεσι (dat. pl. of μῆδος) and κέκασμαι, Il.
or μηδ’, ἕτερος, α ον, neither of the two, Thuc., Plat.: adv. -ρως, in neither of two ways, Arist.
to neither side, Thuc.
to be a Mede in language or habits: to side with the Medes, to Medize, Hdt., Thuc.
the war with the Medes, the name given to the great Persian war, Thuc.; ὁ Μ. πόλεμος Id.
Μηδικὴ πόα medick, a kind of clover, Ar.
a leaning towards the Medes, being in their interest, Medism, Hdt., Thuc.
sub. γυνή a Median woman, Hdt.
Mede-slaying, Anth.
to be minded, to intend, resolve, Il.; ἅσς’ ἂν μηδοίμην what counsels I should take, Od.

c. acc. rei, to plan, plot, contrive, κακὰ μήδεσθαί τινι to scheme misery for him, Il.; μήσατό μοι ὄλεθρον Od.:—also c. acc. pers. et rei, κακὰ μήσατ’ Ἀχαιούς he wrought them mischief, Hom.; so ἐπ’ ἀνδρὶ τοῦτ’ ἐμήσατο στύγος Aesch.
to invent, τέχνας Id.; τί δὲ μήσωμαι; what shall I attempt? Id.
counsels, plans, arts, schemes, Hom.; μάχης μ. plans of fight, Il.
the genitals, Od.
a Mede, Median, Hdt., etc.
counsel, prudence, Anth.
Dep., to bleat, of sheep, Hom.; of a hunted fawn or hare, to scream, shriek, Il.; of a wounded horse, Id.
a bleating, Lat. balatus, Plut.
the bleating one, of she-goats, Hom.: —later, μ. ἄρνες, = βληχάδες, Eur.
long, Anth.

entry.etym: formed from μή, ἔτι, with κ inserted
entry.sense: no more, no longer, no further, Hom., etc.

entry.etym: irr. Sup. of μακρός (formed from μῆκος, as αἴσχιστος from αἶσχος),
entry.sense: tallest, Hom.
greatest, Soph., Eur.
longest, in point of Time, Xen.:—neut. μήκιστον as adv., in the highest degree, Hhymn.; also, τί νύ μοι μήκιστα γένηται; what is to become of me in the long run, at last? Od.
farthest, ὅτι δύνᾳ μάκιστον as far as possible, Soph.; μήκιστον ἀπελαύνειν to drive as far off as possible, Xen.
length, Od.; ἐν μήκει καὶ πλάτει καὶ βάθει Plat.; μ. ὁδοῦ Hdt.; πλοῦ Thuc.: —in pl., τὰ μέγαλα μ. great distances, Plat.
of persons, height, tallness, stature, Od.
of Time, Aesch., etc.:—also μ. λόγου, μ. τῶν λόγων a long speech, Id.; ἐν μήκει λόγων Thuc.
τὸ μῆκος or μῆκος absol. as adv. in length, Hdt., etc.:— at length, in full, οὐ μῆκος ἀλλὰ σύντομα Soph.
μῆκος in height, Od.
to lengthen, prolong, extend, Xen.:—of Time, μ. χρόνον, βίον Eur.
μ. λόγον, λόγους to spin out a speech, speak at length, Hdt., Soph., etc.:—also without λόγον, to be lengthy or tedious, Hdt:—c. acc., μ. τὰ περὶ τῆς πόλεως to talk at length about them, Thuc.
μ. βοήν to raise a loud cry, Soph.
Mid., ἐμακύναντο κολοσσόν reared a tall statue, Anth.
the poppy, Il., etc.
an apple-tree, Lat. malus, Od.
of a sheep, κρέα Hdt.; μ. φόνος slaughter of sheep, Eur.
a probe, etc., Lat. specillum, Hipp., etc.
nymphs of Malis in Trachis, Soph.
an inhabitant of Malis (Μῆλις), a Malian, pl. Μηλιέες, Hdt.; in old attic Μηλιῆς, Soph., Thuc.
as adj., Μηλιεὺς κόλπος the Sinus Maliacus, Hdt.;— Μηλιακός, ή, όν, Thuc.:—fem. Μηλὶς, λίμνη = Μηλιεύς κόλπος, Soph.
from the island of Melos, Melian, Theogn., Thuc.; λιμὸς M., proverb. of famine, because of the sufferings during the siege of Melos, Ar.

entry.etym: ionic for Μᾱλίς, with or without γῆ
entry.sense: Malis in Trachis, Hdt.; cf. Μηλιεύς.
a shepherd, Il.
grazed by sheep, epith. of pastoral districts, Pind.
sheep-receiving, in sacrifice, of Apollo, Pind.
one who sacrifices sheep, a priest, Eur.; βωμὸς μ. a sacrificial altar, Id.
the cockchafer, Ar.
a sheep or goat, Od.;in pl. sheep and goats, small cattle, Lat. pecudes, opp. to βόες, Il.; with an adj. added to distinguish the gender, ἄρσενα μ. rams, wethers, Od.
Lat. ma_lum, an apple or (generally) any tree-fruit, Hom., Hes., Hdt., attic
pl., metaph. of a girl's breasts, Theocr.:—also the cheeks, Lat. malae, Anth., Luc.; cf. μηλοπάρῃος:—but in Theocr., τὰ σὰ δάκρυα μᾶλα ῥέοντι thy tears run sweet or round as apples.
a shepherd or goatherd, Eur.;—so μηλο-νομεύς, έως, Anth.
tending sheep or goats, Eur.
apple-cheeked, Theocr.
μηλο-σκόπος, κορυφή, the top of a hill from which sheep or goats (μῆλα) are watched, Hhymn.
set with fruit-trees, Eur.
sheep-protecting, Anth.
to slay sheep, ἱερὰ μ. to offer sheep in sacrifice, Soph.; absol., Ar.
sheep-feeding, Orac. ap. Hdt., Aesch.
a girdle that confines the breasts, Anth.
sheep-slaying, Aesch.
to carry apples, Theocr.
bearing apples, Eur.
a sheep-watcher, Anth.
looking like an apple, yellow, ripe, Od.:—with the gen. cf. αἴθων, -ονος.
in doric and epic μάν, a Particle used to strengthen asseverations, Lat. vero, verily, truly, Hom., etc.
after other Particles,
ἦ μήν, like ἦ μέν (μήν being only a stronger form), now verily, full surely, ἦ μὴν καὶ πόνος ἐστίν Il.;—so in attic, to introduce an oath, c. inf., ὄμνυσι δ’ ἦ μὴν λαπάξειν Aesch., etc.

καὶ μήν, to introduce something new or special, καὶ μὴν Τάνταλον εἰσεῖδον Od.: in dramatic Poets to mark the entrance of a person on the stage, and see . . , here comes . . ; so of new facts or arguments, Trag., Dem.
ἀλλὰ μήν, yet truly, Lat. verum enimvero, Aesch., Ar.
οὐ μήν, of a truth not, Il., attic

after interrogatives, it mostly takes somewhat of an objective force, τί μήν; quid vero? what then? i. e. of course, naturally so, Aesch., etc.; τί μὴν οὐ; well, why not? Eur.; πῶς μήν; well, but how . . ? Xen.
much like μέντοι, Lat. tamen, οὐ μὴν ἄτιμοι τεθνήξομεν Aesch.

a month, Hom., etc. In early times the month was divided into two parts, the beginning and the waning (μὴν ἱστάμενος and μὴν φθίνων), Od.: the Attic division was into three decads, μὴν ἱστάμενος (also ἀρχόμενος or εἰσιών), μεσῶν, and φθίνων (or ἀπιών): the last division was reckoned backwards, μηνὸς τετάρτῃ φθίνοντος on the fourth day from the end of the month, Thuc.; Μαιμακτηριῶνος δεκάτῃ ἀπιόντος, i. e. on the 21st, ap. Dem.; but sometimes forwards, as, τῇ τρίτῃ ἐπ’ εἰκάδι the three-and twentieth, etc.:— ἐκείνου τοῦ μηνός in the course of that month, Xen.:— κατὰ μῆνα monthly, Ar.; so τοῦ μηνὸς ἑκάστου Id.; or τοῦ μηνός alone, by the month, id.
= μηνίσκος, Id.
the moon, Eur.
the moon, Il., Aesch.
monthly, Strab.
wrath, Il.
a cause of wrath, μή τοί τι θεῶν μήνιμα γένωμαι lest I be the cause of bringing wrath upon thee, Hom.
guilt, blood-guiltiness, Plat.
a crescent, Lat. lunula: a covering to protect the head of statues (like the nimbus or glory of Christian Saints), Ar.
wrath, anger, of the gods, Hom., Hdt., attic

to be wroth with another, vent one's wrath on him, c. dat. pers., Il.; c. gen. rei, ἱρῶν μηνίσας wrathful because of sacred rites, Id.; πατρὶ μηνίσας φόνου Soph.; absol. to be wrathful, Hom.: so in Mid., Aesch.
crescent-shaped, Lat. lunatus, Hdt., Thuc., etc.; μηνοειδὲς ποιήσαντες τῶν νεῶν having formed them in a crescent, Hdt.:—of the sun and moon when partially eclipsed, Thuc., Xen.
an information, Thuc.
an informer, guide, Aesch.
bringing to light, μ. χρόνος Eur.
Subst. an informer, Lat. delator, Thuc.; κατά τινος against a person, Dem.
the price of information, reward, Hhymn.:—in attic only pl. μήνυτρα, Thuc., etc.

to disclose what is secret, reveal, betray, generally, to make known, declare, indicate, Hhymn., Hdt., attic:—with acc. and part., μ. τινὰ ἔχοντα to shew that he has, Hdt.; the part. is sometimes omitted, τόδ’ ἔργον σε μηνύει κακόν (sc. ὄντα) Eur.
at Athens to inform, lay public information against another, κατά τινος Oratt.:—impers. in Pass., μηνύεται information is laid, μεμήνυται it has been laid, Thuc.
in Pass. also of persons, to be informed against, to be denounced, Xen.:—also of things, μηνυθέντος τοῦ ἐπιβουλεύματος Thuc.
an elliptic phrase, μὴ [λέγε] ὅπως, followed by ἀλλ’ οὐδέ, as μὴ ὅπως ὀρχεῖσθαι, ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὀρθοῦσθαι ἐδύνασθε not only could you not dance, but not even stand upright, Xen.
= μὴ ὅπως, foll. by ἀλλά, Lat. ne dicam, as, μὴ ὅτι ἰδιώτην τινά, ἀλλὰ τὸν μέγαν βασιλέα not to say a private person, but the great king, Plat.; μὴ ὅτι θεός, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄνθρωποι οὐ φιλοῦσιν Xen.
οὐδε or καὶ οὐ followed by μὴ ὅτι, as οὐδὲ ἀναπνεῖν, μὴ ὅτι λέγειν τι δυνησόμεθα we shall not be able to breathe, much less to speak, Id.

after Verbs expressing fear or apprehension, = Lat. vereor ut, δέδοικα μὴ οὐ γένηταί τι I fear it will not be; whereas δέδοικα μὴ γένηται mean, I fear it will be. Here, μή and οὐ each retain their proper force.
with Inf.,

after Verbs of hindering, denying, avoiding, needing, when μὴ οὐ resembles Lat. quin or quominus, οὐδὲν κωλύει μὴ οὐκ ἀληθὲς εἶναι τοῦτο nihil impedit quin hoc verum sit; or with the Art., οὐδὲν ἐλλείψω τὸ μὴ οὐ πυθέσθαι nihil praetermittam quominus reperiam, Soph.
after Verbs signifying impossibility, impropriety, reluctance, μὴ οὐ has a negative translation, δεινὸν ἐδόκεε εἶναι μὴ οὐ λαβεῖν Hdt.; αἰσχύνη ἦν μὴ οὐ δυσπουδάζειν Xen.
μὴ οὐ with the Partic., only after a negat., expressed or implied, δυσάλγητος γὰρ ἂν εἤν μὴ οὐ κατοικτείρων I should be hard-hearted if I did not pity, Soph.
= εἰ μή, except πόλεις χαλεπαὶ λαβεῖν, μὴ οὐ πολιορκία Dem.
not, is the negative of thought, as οὐ of statement, i. e. μή says that one thinks a thing is not, οὐ that it is not. The same differences hold for all compds. of μή and οὐ.
μή in INDEPENDENT sentences,
with Imperat., μή μ’ ἐρέθιζε do not provoke me, Il.; μή τις ἀκουσάτω let not any one hear, Od.
with Subj. μὴ δή μ’ ἐάσῃς Il.; μὴ ἴομεν (epic for ἴωμεν) Id.; μὴ πάθωμεν Xen.

with Opt. to express a wish that a thing may not happen, ἃ μὴ κραίνοι τύχη which may fortune not bring to pass, Aesch.:—also in wishes that refer to past time and therefore cannot be fulfilled, μή ποτ’ ὤφελον λιπεῖν Soph.

in vows and oaths, where οὐ might be expected, ἴστω Ζεὺς μὴ μὲν τοῖς ἵπποισιν ἀνὴρ ἐποχήσεται ἄλλος Zeus be my witness, not another man shall ride on these horses, Il.; μὰ τὴν Ἀφροδίτην, μὴ ἐγώ σ’ ἀφήσω Ar.
with Inf., used as Imperat., μὴ δή μοι ἀπόπροθεν ἰσχέμεν ἵππους Il.
In DEPENDENT clauses:
with Final Conjunctions, ἵνα μή, ὅπως μή, ὥς μή, ὄφρα, that not, Lat. ne, Il., attic:— μή often stands alone = ἵνα μή, Hom., attic
in the protasis of conditional sentences, after εἰ (epic αἰ), εἴ κε (αἴ κε), εἰ ἄν, ἤν, ἐάν, ᾱ̓́ν, Lat. nisi, Hom., etc.;—so, ὅτε μή = εἰ μή; etc.
in relat. clauses, when they imply a condition or supposition, λέγονθ’ ἃ μὴ δεῖ such things as one ought not, Soph.; λόγοις τοιούτοις οἷς σὺ μὴ τέρψει κλύων Id.
with Inf., always except when the Inf. represents Ind. or Opt., as in oratio obliqua.

with Participle, when it can be resolved into a conditional clause, μὴ ἀπενείκας = εἰ μὴ ἀπήνεικε Hdt.; μὴ θέλων = εἰ μὴ θέλεις, Aesch.; so in a general sense, δίδασκέ μ’ ὡς μὴ εἰδότα = ut qui nihil sciam, Soph.
with abstract Nouns as with Partic., τὰ μὴ δίκαια = ἃ ἂν μὴ ᾖ δίκαια, Aesch.; τὸ μὴ καλόν Soph.; ἡ μὴ ’μπειρία = τὸ μὴ ἔχειν ἐμπειρίαν, want of experience, Ar.
after Verbs expressing fear or apprehension (cf. μὴ οὐ):
when the thing feared is fut., with pres. Subj., I fear he may persuade thee, Il.
with Opt. for Subj., according to the sequence of moods and tenses, Hom., etc.
when the action is present or past, the Ind. is used, φοβούμεθα μὴ ἡμαρτήκαμεν we fear we have made a mistake, Thuc.
without a Verb to express hesitation, perhaps, μὴ ἀγροικότερον ᾖ τὸ ἀληθὲς εἰπεῖν Plat.
In QUESTIONS:
Direct questions,

with Ind., implying a negat. answer, surely not, you don't mean to say that, Lat. num? whereas with οὐ an affirm. answer is expected, Lat. nonne? ἆρ’ οὐ τέθνηκε; surely he is dead, is he not? ἆρα μὴ τέθνηκε; surely he is not dead, is he?:—when οὐ and μή appear in consecutive clauses, each negat. retains its proper force, οὐ σῖγ’ ἀνέξει μηδὲ δειλίαν ἀρεῖς; will you not be silent, and will you be cowardly? i. e. be silent and be not cowardly, Soph.
with the Subj., when the answer is somewhat doubtful, μὴ οὕτω φῶμεν; can we say so? Plat.:—so also with Opt. and ἄν, πῶς ἄν τις μὴ λέγοι; how can a man help speaking? Id.
indirect questions with μή belong in fact to μή with Verbs of fear and apprehension, περισκοπῶ μή πού τις ἐγχρίμπτῃ Soph.
lest perchance, Lat. ne forte, Plat.
or μή ποτε
as adv. never, on no account, after ὡς, εἰ, etc., Aesch., etc.;—also with inf., in oaths, ὀμοῦμαι, μήποτε τῆς εὐνῆς ἐπιβήμεναι Il.
in prohibition or strong denial, with aor. subj., μήποτε καὶ σὺ ὀλέσσῃς Od.
perhaps, like nescio an, Arist.
as Conj. that at no time, lest ever, Lat. ne quando, Od.
lest anywhere, that nowhere, Lat. necubi, Od.: lest perchance, Hom., etc.
or μή, πω,
as adv. not yet, Lat. nondum, Od., attic
as Conj. that not yet, lest yet, Od., etc.
of past time, never yet, Soph.
or μή, πως, lest in any way, lest any how, lest perchance, Hom.
in case of doubt, or in indirect questions, whether or no, Il.
of or belonging to the thigh, Lat. femoralis, αἱ μ. the thighs, Xen.
slices cut from the thighs, Hom. It was the custom to cut out the μηρία (ἐκ μηρία τάμνον), wrap them in two folds of fat (κνίσῃ ἐκάλυψαν, δίπτυχα ποιήσαντες), and burn them upon the altar.
= μηροί, the thighs, Bion.
a cord, line, string, Il.: a fishing-line, Theocr.
the thigh, Lat. femur, in Hom.
in pl. = μηρία, Hom., Soph.
in pl. also, generally, the leg-bones, Hdt.
thigh-bred, of Bacchus, Anth.
striking the thigh, Anth.
Dep.
to draw up, furl sails, Od.: to draw up cables, etc., Anth.:— κρόκα ἐν στήμονι μηρύσασθαι to weave the woof into the warp, Hes.
Pass., κισσὸς μαρύεται περὶ χείλη ivy winds round the edge, Theocr.
an adviser, counsellor, Hom.; Ἀθηναῖοι μήστωρες ἀϋτῆς authors of the battle-din, Il.; κρατερὸν μήστωρα φόβοιο, of Diomede, Id.
and not, mostly doubled, μήτε . . μήτε . . , neither . . nor, Hom., etc.
a mother, Hom., etc.; of animals, a dam, Id.; ἀπό or ἐκ μητρός from one's mother's womb, Pind., Aesch.
also of lands, μήτηρ μήλων, θηρῶν mother of flocks, of game, Il.; of Earth, γῆ πάντων μ. Hes.; γῆ μήτηρ Aesch.; ὦ γαῖα μῆτερ Eur.:—also ἡ Μάτηρ alone for Δημήτηρ, Hdt.
of one's native land, μᾶτερ ἐμά, Θήβα Pind., etc.
poet. as the source of events, μ. ἀέθλων, of Olympia, Id.; night is the mother of day, Aesch.; the grape of wine, Id.
to meditate, deliberate, debate, Il.:—Mid., μητιάασθε consider among you, Id.
c. acc. rei, = μητίομαι, Hom.
a counsellor, as epith. of Ζεύς, all-wise! Hom.
wise in counsel, all-wise, Hhymn., Hes.
φάρμακα μητιόεντα wise, i. e. well-chosen, helpful, remedies, Od.
Dep.:— to devise, contrive, plan, Hom.: c. dupl. acc. to plan evil against one, Od.
the faculty of advising, wisdom, counsel, cunning, craft, Hom., Aesch.; μῆτιν ἀλώπηξ a fox for craft, Pind.:—of a poet's skill or craft, Id.
advice, counsel, a plan, undertaking, μῆτιν ὑφαίνειν Hom.
μή-τῐς or μή, τις, lest any one, lest anything; that no one, that nothing, Lat. ne quis, ne quid, constructed like the adv. μή, Hom., etc.
μήτι or μή τι, adv. used imperatively, Il.;—with Opt. to express a wish, ὄλοιντο μή τι πάντες Soph.
after Verbs of fear or doubt, Hom., etc.
in questions, μή τί σοι δοκῶ ταρβεῖν; do I seem to thee to fear? (i. e. I do not), Aesch.
μή τί γε, let alone, much less, Lat. nedum, ne dicam, Dem.
μή-τοι or μή, τοι, stronger form of μή, with Imperat.and Subj., μή τοι δοκεῖτε Aesch., etc.: in an oath, with inf., Id.
after Verbs implying negation, Soph.
a begging priest of Cybele, the mother of the gods:—Iphicrates gave this name to Callias, who was really her Δᾳδοῦχος, Arist.
a mother's brother or sister, uncle or aunt:—in Pind., ματραδελφεός.,
striking one's mother, a matricide, Aesch., Plat., etc.
Lat. matrix, the womb, Hdt., Plat., etc.
of a mother, Lat. maternus, Arist.
μητρίς, sc. γῆ, Cretan word in Plat.
received by the mother, Pind.
with a mother's mind, Anth.
from the mother, by the mother's side, Hdt., Pind.
from one's mother, from one's mother's hand, Aesch., Ar.
from one's mother's womb, Aesch.
a sister by the same mother, Lat. soror uterina, Aesch.
to kill one's mother, Aesch., Eur.
killing one's mother, matricidal, Aesch.; μ. μίασμα the stain of a mother's murder, Id.; so, μ. κηλίς, αἷμα Eur.
as Subst. a matricide, Aesch., Eur.
one's mother's mother, Pind.
one's mother's father, Il., Hdt.
the mother-state, in relation to colonies, as of Athens to the Ionians, Hdt., Thuc.; of Doris to the Peloponn. Dorians, Hdt., Thuc.
one's mother-city, mother-country, home, Pind., Soph.
a metropolis in our sense, capital city, Xen.
tending mothers, epith. of Eileithyia, Pind.
rejected by one's mother, Anth.
mother-murdering, Anth.
murdering one's mother, matricidal, Aesch.
as Subst. a matricide, Id.

entry.note: μητρυιά, doric ματρ-, ᾶς, ionic μητρυιή, ῆς, ἡ,
entry.sense: a step-mother, Il., etc.: the unkindness of step-mothers was proverbial (cf. Lat. injusta noverca); hence metaph., μ. νεῶν, of a dangerous coast, Aesch.

entry.etym: contr. for μητρώιος (which occurs in Od.）
entry.sense: of a mother, a mother's, maternal, Od., attic; μ. δέμας, periphr. for τὴν μητέρα, Aesch.: —τὰ μ. a mother's right. Hdt.
Μητρῷον (sc. ἱερόν), the temple of Cybele at Athens, which was the depository of the state-archives, Dem., Aeschin.

entry.etym: pl. always of the third decl., like πάτρως
entry.sense: a maternal uncle, Il., Hdt., etc.
any relation by the mother's side, Pind., Eur.
= μητροπάτωρ, Pind.
like Lat. machinari, to make by art, put together, construct, build, Il., Hdt., etc.; generally to prepare, make ready, Hdt., Aesch., etc.
to contrive, devise, by art or cunning, Hom., etc.;—also simply to cause, effect, Hdt., attic:—absol. to form designs, Od.:—c. acc. et inf. to contrive to do or that a thing may be, Xen.
Mid. to procure for oneself, Soph., Xen.

the Act. μηχανάω is used by Hom. only in epic part., ἀτάσθαλα μηχανόωντας contriving dire effects, Od., and by Soph. in inf. μηχανᾶν: but perf. μεμηχάνημαι is used in pass. sense by Hdt. and in attic; but also in act. sense, Plat., Xen.
an engine, used in sieges, Dem.
a subtle contrivance, cunning work, Trag.; of the robe in which Agamemnon was entangled, Aesch.
= Lat. machina:
an instrument, machine for lifting weights and the like, Hdt.; μ. Ποσειδῶνος, of the trident, Aesch.; λαοπόροις μ., of Xerxes' bridge of boats, Id.
an engine of war, Thuc.
a theatrical machine, by which gods were made to appear in the air, Plat.: hence proverb. of any sudden appearance, ὥσπερ ἀπὸ μηχανῆς (cf. Lat. deus ex machina), Dem.

any contrivance, for doing a thing, Hdt., etc.: in pl. μηχαναί, shifts, devices, arts, wiles, Hes., attic; μηχαναῖς Διός by the arts of Zeus, Aesch.; proverb., μηχαναὶ Σισύφου Ar.:—Phrases, μηχανήν or μηχανὰς προσφέρειν Eur.; εὑρίσκειν Aesch., etc.:—c. gen., μ. κακῶν a contrivance against ills, Eur.; but, μ. σωτηρίας a way of providing safety, Aesch.
οὐδεμία μηχανή [ἐστι] ὅπως οὐ, c. fut., Hdt.; also, μὴ οὐ, c. inf., Id.
in adverb, phrases, ἐκ μηχανῆς τινος in some way or other, Id.; μηδεμιῆι μηχανῆι by no means whatsoever, Id.
one must contrive, Plat.
full of resources, inventive, ingenious, clever, Xen.
c. gen. rei, able to procure, Id.
of or for machines, mechanical, Arist.:— ὁ μηχανικός an engineer, Plut.
inventing artifices, Ar.
ingenious, Soph.
an engineer, maker of war-engines, Plat., Xen.: a theatrical machinist, Ar.
to form crafty plans, Aesch.
craftily-dealing, soph.: c. gen., μ. κακῶν crafty workers of ill, Eur.
conveying military machines, Plut.
a means, expedient, remedy, Il.; μῆχος κακοῦ a remedy for Ill, Od., Hdt.; κακῶν Eur.
properly, to stain, dye, ἐλέφαντα φοίνικι μιαίνειν (cf. Virgil's violaverit ostro si quis ebur), Il.
to stain, defile, sully, esp. with blood, μιάνθην (epic 3rd dual for μιανθήτην) αἵματι μηροί Id.; αἵματι πεσεῖ μιανθείς Soph.; μ. τοὺς θεῶν βωμοὺς αἵματι Plat.; βορβόρωι ὕδωρ μιαίνων Aesch.

of moral stains, to taint, defile, Pind., Trag.; hence Soph. says, θεοὺς μιαίνειν οὔ τις ἀνθρώπων σθένει:— Pass. to incur such defilement, Aesch., etc.; μιαίνεσθαι τὴν ψυχήν Plat.; τῆς ἄλλης [γῆς] αὐτῶι μεμιασμένης Thuc.
to be or become blood-stained, Eur.
c. acc. to murder, Isocr., Plat.
bloodguiltiness, Dem., Diod.
pollution from eating blood, Plut.
blood-stained, bloody, Il.: defiled with blood, blood-guilty, Trag.; c. gen., μ. τέκνων stained with thy children's blood, Eur.:—comp. -ώτερος Hdt., Eur.; Sup. -ώτατος, Id.
brutality, Xen., Dem.
foul-tongued, Anth.
stained with blood, Il.: defiled with blood, Eur.
generally, defiled, polluted, unclean, Hdt.: in moral sense, Soph.; as a term of foul reproach, brutal, coarse, disgusting, Ar.; μ. φωνή a coarse, brutal voice, Id.:—adv. μιαρῶς, Id.
stain, defilement, the taint of guilt, Lat. piaculum, Trag., etc.
of persons, a defilement, pollution, Aesch., Soph.
a wretch stained with crime, a guilty wretch, a pollution, Lat. homo piacularis, Trag.
= ἀλάστωρ, an avenger, Id.
to have intercourse, Od.
mixed with, c. dat., Pind.
mixed pell-mell, Eur.
promiscuously, confusedly, Od.; c. dat., μίγδα θεοῖς among the gods, Il.
a mixture: μίγματα mixtures, medicines, NTest.
like Lat. misceo, to mix, mix up, mingle, properly of liquids, οἶνον καὶ ὕδωρ Hom.; μ. τί τινι to mix one thing with another, Id., etc.
generally, to join, bring together.
in hostile sense, μῖξαι χεῖράς τε μένος τε to join battle hand to hand, Il.; Ἄρη μίξουσιν Soph.
to bring into connexion with, make acquainted with, ἄνδρας μισγέμεναι κακότητι to bring men to misery, Od.; reversely, πότμον μῖξαί τινι to bring death upon him, Pind.

Pass. to be mixed up with, mingled among, προμάχοισιν ἐμίχθη Il.; ἐώλπει μίξεσθαι ξενίηι hoped to be bound by hospitable ties, Od.:—also, to mingle with, hold intercourse with, live with, Id., Aesch.: absol. in pl., of several persons, to hold intercourse, Od.

to be brought into contact with, κάρη κονίηισιν ἐμίχθη his head was rolled in the dust, Hom.; ἐν κονίηισι μιγῆναι Il.; κλισίηισι μιγῆναι to reach, get at them, Id.; μίσγεσθαι ἐς Ἀχαιούς to go to join them, Id.; μίσγεσθαι ὑπὲρ ποταμοῖο to cross the river, Id.; μίσγεσθαι φύλλοις, στεφάνοις to come to, i. e. win, the crown of victory, Pind.
in hostile sense, to mix in fight, Il.
to have intercourse with, to be united to, of men and women, Hom.; φιλότητι and ἐν φιλότητι μιγῆναι Id.; εὐνῆι ἔμικτο Od.
Midas, a king of Phrygia proverbial for his wealth, Tyrtae., Plat.
Mithras, the Persian Sun-god, Xen.
doing petty wrongs, Arist.
complaining of trifles, Luc.
with small furrows: χῶρος μ. a little field, Anth.
a pedlar, huckster, Babr.
exposing oneself to danger for trifles, Arist.
fut. ήσομαι, Dep. to examine minutely, treat or tell with painful minuteness, Xen.
to deal meanly or shabbily, Luc.
the character of a μικρολόγος, frivolity: pettiness, meanness, Plat., etc.
reckoning trifles; and so,
caring about petty expenses, penurious, Dem.
cavilling about trifles, captious, Plat.
a citizen of a petty town, German Kleinstadter, Ar., Xen.
wicked in small things, Arist.
the character of a μικροπρεπής, meanness, shabbiness, Arist.
petty in one's notions, mean, shabby, Arist.
small, little, in point of Size, Hom., etc.; also in point of Quantity, Hes., Ar., etc.
in Amount or Importance, little, petty, trivial, slight, Theogn., Soph., etc.; σμ. τίθησι με makes me of small account. Soph.; οὐ σμικρὸν φρονεῖ Id.
of Time, little, short, Pind., Ar., etc.; ἐν σμικρῷ (sc. χρόνῳ) shortly, Xen.
Adverbial usages,
regul. adv., σμικρῶς, but little, Sup. σμικρότατα, Id.
σμικροῦ or μικροῦ within a little, almost, Id., Dem.; in full, μικροῦ δεῖ or δεῖν, v. δεῖ II:—but μικροῦ πρίασθαι to buy for a little, cheap, Xen.
μικρῷ by a little, with the comp., Plat.
μικρόν and μικρά, a little, Xen., Plat.
with Preps.,
ἐπὶ σμικρόν but a little, Soph.
κατὰ μικρόν into small pieces, Xen.; so, κατὰ μικρὰ γενόμενοι Id.:— also little by little, κατὰ μικρὸν ἀεί Ar.
παρὰ μικρόν within a little, παρὰ μ. ἐλθεῖν, c. inf., to be within an ace of doing, Eur.
μετὰ μικρόν a little after, NTest.
besides the regul. comp. and Sup. μικρότερος, -ότατος, there are the irreg. ἐλάσσων, ἐλάχιστος, from ἐλαχύς, and μείων or μειότερος, μειότατος.
smallness: littleness, meanness, pettiness, Arist.
petty ambition, Theophr.
seeking petty distinctions, Theophr.
with little land or soil, Strab.
littleness of soul, meanness of spirit, Dem., Arist.
little of soul, mean-spirited, Dem., Arist.
mixed, blended, compound, Plat., etc.
Milesian, Μιλήσιοι, οἱ, the Milesians, Hdt.; Μιλησίη (sc. χώρα), Id.
Miletus, a Greek city in Caria, Il.
= Lat. milliarium, a mile-stone.
a copper vessel, pointed at the top and furnished with winding tubes, to boil water in, Anth. [where μῐλῐᾱριον].
a marking by milestones, Strab.
a Roman mile, milliarium, = 1000 paces,= 8 stades, = 1680 yards, i. e. 80 yards less than our mile, Polyb., etc.
a vessel for keeping μίλτος in, Anth.
red, μ. στάγμα the red mark made by the carpenter's line, Anth.
painted with μίλτος, painted red, of ships, Hdt.
red-cheeked, of ships which had their bows painted red, Hom.
red chalk, ruddle, Lat. rubrica, Hdt.
daubed with red, Anth.
to paint red:—Pass. to paint oneself red or be painted red, Hdt.; σχοινίον μεμιλτωμένον the rope covered with red chalk with which they swept loiterers out of the Agora to the Pnyx, Ar.
hare-soup or jugged hare, with the blood of the animal in it, Ar.

to mimic, imitate, represent, portray, Hhymn., Aesch., etc.; μ. τινά τι one in a thing, Hdt.; τινα κατά τι Id.; perf. part. in act. sense στύλοισι φοίνικας μεμιμημένοισι pillars made to represent palms, Id.; but also in pass. made exactly like, portrayed, Id., Plat.
of the fine arts, to represent, express by means of imitation, of an actor, Ar., Plat.; of painting and music, Plat.; of sculpture and poetry, Arist.
imitative, c. gen., Luc., Anth.
pass. imitated, copied, Plut.
anything imitated, a counterfeit, copy, Eur., Plat.
imitation, Thuc., Plat., etc.; κατὰ σὴν μ. to imitate you, Ar.
representation by means of art, Plat.: a representation, portrait, Hdt.
to be imitated, Xen.
μιμητέον, one must imitate, Eur., Xen.
an imitator, copyist, Plat., etc.
one who represents characters, Arist.
a mere actor, an impostor (cf. ὑποκριτής), Plat.
good at imitating, imitative, of the fine arts, Plat., etc.:— ἡ -κή (with or without τέχνη) the power of imitating, Id.
to be imitated or copied, Xen.
to wait, stay, Il.
to await, expect, c. acc., Hhymn.

entry.etym: μέμνημαι is used in pres. sense like Lat. memini
entry.sense: In active, Causal of μνάομαι to remind, put one in mind, Od.; τινός of a thing, Hom., etc.
to recall to memory, make famous, Pind.
Mid. and Pass., to remind oneself of a thing, call to mind, remember, c. acc., Hom., etc.:— c. gen., ἀλκῆς μνήσασθαι to bethink one of one's strength, Hom., etc.; also, περὶ πομπῆς μνησόμεθα Od.
c. inf. to remember or be minded to do a thing, Il., Ar., etc.
c. part., μέμνημαι κλύων I remember hearing, Aesch.; μ. ἐλθών I remember having come, i. e. to have come, Eur.
absol., μεμνήσομαι I will bear in mind, not forget, Hom.; perf. part. ὧδέ τις μεμνημένος μαχέσθω let him fight with good heed, let him remember to fight, Il.
to remember a thing aloud, i. e. to mention, make mention of c. gen., Hom; περί τινος Hdt., etc; ὑπέρ τινος Dem.

entry.etym: formed by redupl. from μένω ( i. e. μι-μένω, cf. γί-γνομαι, πί-πτω), and used for μένω when the first syll.was to be long; μιμνόντεσσι, Ep. dat. pl. part. for μίμνουσι.
entry.sense: to stay, stand fast, in battle Il.
to stay, tarry, Id.
of things, to remain, Od.: also to be left for one, Aesch.
c. acc. to await, wait for, Il., etc.:—impers., μίμνει παθεῖν τὸν ἔρξαντα it awaits the doer to suffer, Aesch.
Pass. to be recited like mimes, Strab.
composing or reciting μῖμοι, Anth.
an imitator, mimic: an actor, mime, Dem., Plut.
a mime, a kind of prose drama, such as Sophron wrote, Arist.
a singer of μῖμοι, Plut.
to besmear with dung, befoul, Ar.

entry.etym: ionic acc. sg. of the pron. of the 3rd pers. (v. ἵ) through all genders, for αὐτόν, αὐτήν, αὐτο
always enclitic, Hom., Hdt.; doric and attic νιν
entry.sense: Hom. joins μὶν αὐτόν himself, as a stronger form; but αὐτόν μιν is reflexive, oneself, for ἑαυτόν, Od.
rarely as 3 pers. pl. for αὐτούς, αὐτάς, αὐτά.
the Minyans, a race of nobles in Orchomenos, Hdt., etc
Minyan, Il.; epic also Μινυήϊος, Hom.

entry.etym: only used in pres. and ionic imperf. μινύθεσκον
entry.sense: to make smaller or less, lessen, curtail, Il., Hes.
to diminish in number, Od.
intr. to become smaller or less, decrease, decay, come to naught, perish, Hom., Hes.
shortlived, Hom.:—comp. μινυνθαδιώτερος Il.
a little, very little, Hom.; of Time, a short time, Id.; μίνυνθα δέ οἱ γένεθ’ ὁρμή but shortlived was his effort, Id.
to complain in a low tone, to whimper, whine, Hom.: generally, to sing in a low soft tone, to warble, hum, Ar., Plat.
a warbling, Theocr.
Dep., = μινυρίζω, of the nightingale, to warble, Soph.: to hum a tune, Aesch.
complaining in a low tone, whining, whimpering, Theocr.; μινυρὰ θρέεσθαι = μινυρίζειν, Aesch.
shortlived, Anth.
of Minos, Hhymn.
Minos, son of Zeus and Europa, king of Crete, Hom., Hes., etc.:—gen. Μίνωος Od.; acc. Μίνωα Hom.;—also gen. Μίνω Hdt.; acc. Μίνων Il., or Μίνω Hdt., etc.; dat. Μίνῳ Plat.
a mixing, mingling, Plat.; v. κρᾶσις,
intercourse with others, esp. sexual intercourse, Hdt.
half barbarian half Greek, Eur., Xen.
half-beast, Eur.
with mingled cries, Aesch.
mixed with white, Luc.
half-Lydian, Strab.
in the mixed-Lydian measure, Plat.
half-woman, Hdt., Eur.
half-Phrygian, Strab.
a hatred of good or goodness, Plut.
hating good or goodness.
hating the Athenians: Sup. μισαθηναιότατος Dem.
hating boasters, Luc.
hating Alexander, Aeschin.
hating the vine, Anth.
hatred of mankind, Plat., Dem.
hating mankind, misanthropic, Plat.
a place where mountain glens and their streams meet, a meeting of glens, Il.
a hater of the Greeks, Xen.

to hate, Pind., attic:—c. acc. et inf., μίσησεν δ’ ἄρα μιν κυσὶ κύρμα γενέσθαι, Zeus hated (would not suffer) that he should become a prey to dogs, Il.; οὐ μισοῦντα τὴν πόλιν, τὸ μὴ οὐ μεγάλην εἶναι not grudging that the city should be great, Ar.:—Pass. to be hated, Hdt., attic
an object of hate, of persons, μ. ἀνδρῶν καὶ θεῶν Aesch.; c. dat., μ. πᾶσιν Eur.
to be hated, Xen.
μισητέον, one must hate, Luc.
hateful lust, lewdness, Ar.
generally, greediness, greed, Id.
hateful, Aesch., Xen.
payment of wages, recompense, NTest.
one who pays wages, a rewarder, NTest.
a little fee, Ar.
to work or serve for hire, Plat., Dem.; μισθαρνῶν ἀνύειν τι to do a thing for pay, Soph.
a hired workman, Plut.
of or for hired work, mercenary: ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) the trade of one who takes wages or pay, Plat.
an earning of wages, Dem.
of or for hired work, mercenary, Arist.
Comic Patron., son of a placeman, Ar.
salaried, hired, Plut., NTest.
payment of wages, Thuc., Xen.
to pay wages, absol., Xen., Dem.: —c. acc. to furnish with pay, Decret. ap. Dem.
one who pays wages, a paymaster, Plat., Xen.

wages, pay, hire, Hom., etc.; μισθῷ ἐπὶ ῥητῷ for fixed wages, Il.; μισθοῖο τέλος the end of our hired service, Id.; θητεύειν ἐπὶ μισθῷ Hdt.; μισθοῦ ἕνεκα for pay or wages, Xen.; so in gen., μισθοῦ Soph., Xen.; μηνὸς μισθόν as a month's pay, Thuc.

at Athens, the pay of the soldiers and sailors, Id., etc.:—also, μ. βουλευτικός the pay of the council of 500, a drachma to each for each day of sitting; μ. δικαστικός or ἡλιαστικός the pay of a dicast (at first one obol, but from the time of Cleon three) for each day he sat on a jury; μ. συνηγορικός the fee of a public advocate, one drachma for each court-day; μ. ἐκκλησιαστικός the fee for attending the popular assembly.
a physician's fee, Arist.
generally, recompense, reward, Hom., etc.
in bad sense, payment, requital, Trag.
= ἡ τοῦ μισθοῦ φορά, receipt of wages or wages received, hire, pay, Ar., Thuc., etc.
to be a μισθοφόρος, to receive wages or pay in the public service, to serve for hire, Ar., Xen., etc.;—also c. acc. rei, to receive as pay, τρεῖς δραχμάς Ar.
of mercenary soldiers, Id., Thuc.; μισθ. τινί Xen.; μ. ἐν τοῖς ἀδυνάτοις, as if he were a pauper, Aeschin.
to bring in rent or profit, μισθοφοροῦσα οἰκία Isae.; ζεῦγος ἢ ἀνδράποδον μισθοφοροῦν Xen.:— Pass. to be let for hire, Id.
one must receive pay, Thuc.
service as a mercenary, Dem.
receiving wages or pay, serving for hire, mercenary, Plat., Dem.
as Subst., μισθοφόροι, οἱ, mercenaries, Thuc., Xen., etc.; —also, μ. τριήρεις galleys manned with mercenaries, Ar.

to let out for hire, farm out, let, Lat. locare, τί τινι Ar.: in pres. and imperf. to offer to let, μισθοῖ αὑτὸν Ὀλυνθίοις offers his services for pay to them, Dem.:—c. inf., μ. τὸν νηὸν τριηκοσίων ταλάντων ἐξεργάσασθαι to let out the building of it for 300 talents, Lat. locare aedem exstruendam, Hdt.

Mid., fut. μισθώσομαι: aor1 ἐμισθωσάμην: perf. μεμίσθωμαι:— to have let to one, to hire, Lat. conducere, Hdt., attic; μ. τινα ταλάντου to engage his services at a talent a year, Hdt.; c. inf., μ. νηὸν ἐξοικοδομῆσαι to contract for the building of the temple, Lat. conducere aedem aedificandam, Id.
Pass., aor1 ἐμισθώθην: perf. μεμίσθωμαι (v. supr. II):— to be hired for pay, Id.; ἐκ τοῦ μισθωθῆναι from the hire, Dem.: of a house, to be let on contract, Id.
the price agreed on in hiring, the contract-price, Hdt., Dem.
that which is let for hire, a hired house, NTest.
a letting for hire, δίκη μισθώσεως or δ. μισθώσεως οἴκου an action against a guardian who neglected to let his ward's house.
rent, Dem.
one who pays rent, a tenant, Dem.
of or for letting out:— ἡ μισθωτική, = μισθαρνική, a mercenary trade, Plat.
hired, Hdt., Plat.
as Subst. an hireling, hired servant, Ar.: of soldiers, in pl., mercenaries, Hdt., Thuc.
hating fraud or jugglery, Luc.
woman-hater, Strab.
hatred of democracy, Oratt.
hating the commons, Ar., Xen.
hating the gods, godless, Aesch.
hating the hunt, Xen.
hating Caesar, Plut.
a Laconian-hater, Ar.
hating Lamachus, Ar.
hatred of argument, Plat.
hating argument or dialectic, Plat.
hating bastards, Anth.
hating boys or children, Luc.
an enemy to the Persians, Xen.
hating the commonwealth, Ar.
to hate work, Plat.
hating knaves, Dem., Aeschin.
hatred of work, Luc.
hating the shield-handle (πόρπαξ), i. e. hating war, Ar., in Com. Sup. μῑσοπορπᾱκίστατος.
hating the poor, of the gout, Anth.
a Roman-hater, Plut.
hating philosophy, Plat.
hate, hatred: and so,
pass. hate borne one, a being hated, Trag., Plat.
act. hate felt against another, a grudge, Soph., etc.; μ. τινός τινι felt by one against another, Eur.
of persons, a hateful object, = μίσημα, Trag.
an enemy of Sulla, Plut.
hating children, Aeschin.
a tyrant-hater, Hdt., Aeschin.
hating arrogance, Luc.
hating Philip, Aeschin.
hating the better sort, Xen.
hating lies, Luc.
to cut up meat, Hom.
working the thread, Anth.
Mid. to ply the woof, Anth.:— φθόγγον μιτώσασθαι to let one's voice sound like a string, Id.
composed of threads, Anth.
a thread of the warp, Lat. tela, Il.;— κατὰ μίτον thread by thread, i. e. in an unbroken series, Polyb.
the string of a lyre, Anth.

entry.note: μίτρα, epic and ionic μίτρη, ἡ,
entry.sense: a belt or girdle, worn round the waist beneath the cuirass (whereas the ζωστήρ went over it), Il.
= ζώνη, the maiden-zone, Theocr., Mosch., etc.
a girdle worn by wrestlers, Anth.
a head-band worn by Greek women to tie up their hair, a snood, Eur.
the victor's chaplet at the games, Pind.; Λυδία μίτρα a Lydian garland (i. e. an ode in Lydian measure), Id.
a Persian head-dress, turban, Hdt.
the Persian Aphrodite, Hdt.
wearing a μίτρα or turban, Hdt.
bound with a μίτρα, Anth.
Lat. mutilus, curtailed, esp. hornless, Theocr.
like threads of threads, βρόχος μ. σινδόνος a halter of threads or linen, Soph.
of the weight of a μνᾶ, Xen., etc.
like μιμνήσκομαι, to be mindful of a person or thing, c. gen., Il.:— to turn one's mind to a thing, φύγαδε μνώοντο Id.
to woo for one's bride, to court, c. acc. pers., Od.
to sue for, solicit a favour or office, Lat. ambire, Hdt.
the Lat. mina,
as a weight, = 100 drachmae, = about 15.2 oz. troy.
as a sum of money, also = 100 drachmae, i. e. 4 l. s. 3 d.:—60 μναῖ made a talent.
remembrance, memory, Soph., Eur.
mention, μνείαν ποιεῖσθαί τινος or περί τινος Plat., Aeschin.
Lat. monimentum:
a memorial, remembrance, record of a person or thing, Od., Soph., etc.
a mound or building in honour of the dead, a monument, Il., Hdt., attic
a memorial dedicated to a god, Simon. ap. Thuc.
= μνήμη, memory, Theogn.

entry.note: μνημεῖον, doric μνᾱμεῖον, ionic μνημήιον, ου, τό,
entry.sense: Lat. monimentum, any memorial, remembrance, record of a person or thing, Hdt., attic
of one dead, a monument, Soph., etc.
remembering, Od., as cited by Arist.
a remembrance, memory, record of a person or thing, Theogn., Hdt., etc.; πρὸς ἃ ἔπασχον τὴν μνήμην ἐποιοῦντο made their recollection suit their sufferings, Thuc.
memory as a power of the mind, attic:— εἰπεῖν τι μνήμης ὕπο (or ἄπο) from memory, Soph.
= μνημεῖον a monument, Plat.; an epitaph, Arist.
mention of a thing, Hdt.
a record of the past, Arist.
one must remember, Plat.
of or for reminding, Plotin.
that can be or ought to be remembered, Arist.
to call to mind, remember, c. acc., Hdt., Trag.; c. gen., Plat.
to call to another's mind, mention, Lat. memorare, c. acc., Id.
Pass. to be remembered, had in memory, μνημονεύσεται χάρις Eur.; μνημονευθήσεται Dem.
of or for remembrance or memory, τὸ μνημονικόν = μνήμη, memory, Xen.; but, also, memoria technica, Plat.
of persons, having a good memory, Ar.; μνημονικώτατος Dem.
adv. -κῶς, from or by memory, Aeschin.
remembrance, memory, μνημοσύνη πυρὸς γενέσθω let us be mindful of the fire, Il.
as prop. n. Mnemosyne, mother of the Muses, Hhymn., Hes., etc.
a remembrance, memorial, record of a person or thing, Hdt.
a memorandum, reminder, μνημόσυνα γράψομαι Ar.

entry.note: μνήμων, doric μνάμων, ονος, ὁ, ἡ,
entry.sense: mindful, καὶ γὰρ μνήμων εἰμί I remember it well, Od.; μνήμοσιν δέλτοις φρενῶν Aesch.: c. gen. mindful of, giving heed to, Od.
ever-mindful, unforgetting, Aesch.
having a good memory, Ar., Plat.
as Subst. μνήμονες, οἱ, municpal officers, Recorders, Arist.
to offer public thanksgiving, Orac. ap. Dem.

to remember wrongs done one, remember past injuries, Hdt., Dem.; οὐ μν. to bear no malice, pass an act of amnesty, Ar., Thuc., etc.: c. dat. pers. et gen. rei, μ. τινί τινος to bear one a grudge for a thing, Xen.
c. acc. rei, τὴν ἡλικίαν μν. to remind one of the ills of age, Ar.
bearing malice, Arist.
reminding of misery, μν. πόνος the painful memory of woe, Aesch.
a wooing, courting, Plat.
mindful of, c. gen., Pind.
courtship, wooing, in pl., espousals, Eur.
to woo, court, seek in marriage, Od., Eur.: to woo and win, espouse, Theogn., Theocr.:—Pass., μναστευθεῖς’ ἐξ Ἐλλάνων Eur.
to promise in marriage, betroth, τὴν θυγατέρα τινί Id.:—Pass., τῇ μεμνηστευμένῃ αὐτῷ γυναικί to his betrothed wife, NTest.
to sue or canvass for a thing, Plut.

sic.seg: mnhsth/r, doric mnasthfailing on lembuf [] | /r, h=ros, o(,

entry.sense: a wooer, suitor, Od.; c. gen., παιδὸς ἐμῆς μν. Hdt.; γάμων μν. Aesch.
calling to mind, mindful of, c. gen., Pind.
remembrance, heed, οὐδέ τις ἡμῖν δόρπου μνῆστις ἔην Od.; ἴσχε κἀμοῦ μνῆστω Soph.:— οὕτω δὴ Γέλωνος μνῆστις γέγονεν then you bethought yourselves of Gelon, Hdt.
wooed and won, wedded, ἄλοχος μνηστή a wedded wife, Hom.
mindful of, τινός Aesch.
mossy, soft as moss, Anth.
of persons, toiling, wretched, Trag.
of things, toilsome, grievous, Eur.
to toil, suffer, Hom.; ἐξ ἔργων μογέοντες tired after work, Od.: the part. is nearly = μόγις, with pain or trouble, hardly, μογέων ἀποκινήσασκε Il.
in Trag. to suffer pain, be distressed, Aesch.
trans. to labour at, τι Anth.
hardly-speaking, dumb, NTest.
with toil and pain, i. e. hardly, scarcely, Hom., Hdt., attic:—cf. the post-Hom. μόλις.
toil, trouble, Il.
trouble, distress, Lat. labor, Soph.
helping women in hard childbirth, of Eileithyia, Il.; of Artemis, Theocr.
a dry measure, Lat. modius, = the sixth of a medimnus, about 2 gallons, NTest.
battle, battle-din, Il.
like a μόθων, ionic ap. Plut.
at Lacedaemon, the child of an Helot, brought up as foster-brother of a young Spartan:— since such young Helots were likely to presume, μόθων came to mean an impudent fellow, Ar.
a rude, licentious dance, Eur., Ar.
a part, portion, Hom.
a division of a people, Hdt.
a political party, Lat. partes, Id., Eur.
the part, portion, share which falls to one, in the distribution of booty, Hom.; or of a meal, Od.; ἡ τοῦ πατρὸς μοῖρα one's patrimony, ap. Dem.
in various phrases, οὐδ’ αἰδοῦς μοῖραν ἔχουσιν has no part in shame, Od.; τέσσαρας μοίρας ἔχον ἐμοί filling the place of four relations to me, Aesch.

one's portion in life, lot, fate, destiny, Hom., etc.; ἡ πεπρωμένη μ. Hdt.; μοῖρ’ ἐστι, c. inf., 'tis one's fate, Hom.; ἔσχε μοῖρ’ Ἀχιλλέα θανεῖν 'twas his fate to die, Soph.;— μ. βιότοιο one's portion or measure of life, Il.; ὑπὲρ μοῖραν (v. μόρος) Id.; ἀγαθῇ μοίρᾳ by good luck, Eur.; θείᾳ μοίρᾳ by divine providence, Xen.
like μόρος, man's appointed doom, i. e. death, Hom., Aesch.:— also the cause of death, Od.
that which is one's due, Lat. quod fas est, κατὰ μοῖραν as is meet, rightly, Hom.; opp. to παρὰ μοῖραν, Od.; μοῖραν νέμειν τινί to give one his due, Soph.
respect, esteem, ἐν οὐδεμίᾳ μοίρῃ μεγάλῃ ἄγειν τινά to hold one in no great respect, Hdt.; ἐν μείζονι μ. εἶναι Plat.
with a gen. almost periphr., μ. φρενῶν, for φρένες, Aesch.; ἀνδρὸς μοίρᾳ προσετέθη it was accounted manly, Thuc.; ἐν πολεμίου μοίρᾳ as if he were an enemy, Dem.
Μοῖρα, as prop. n., the goddess of fate, the Roman Parca, Hom.; later, there were three, Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos, Hes.
Μοῖραι, of the Furies, Aesch.
to share, divide, distribute, Luc.; Mid. to divide among themselves, Aesch.:—Pass. to be allotted, Luc.
child of destiny, Il.
allotted by destiny, destined, doomed, Lat. fatalis, μ. ἆμαρ etc., the day of doom, Pind.; μοιριδία τίσις Soph.; ἁ μοιριδία δύνασις the power of fate, Id.
ordained by destiny, Aesch.
a fine imposed on one taken in adultery, Od.
an adulteress, NTest.:as adj. adulterous, Id.
as Subst. = μοιχεία, Id.
trans., = μοιχεύω: metaph., μοιχᾶν τὴν θάλατταν to have dalliance with the sea, Xen.:—Pass., like μοιχεύομαι, to commit adultery, NTest.
adultery, Plat.
an adulteress, Plat.
to commit adultery with a woman, to debauch her, c. acc., Ar., Plat.:—Pass., of the woman, Ar.
intr. to commit adultery, Lat. moechari, Id., Xen.
born in adultery, Luc.
adulterous, μ. διαβολαί accusations of adultery, Luc.
an adulterer, paramour, debaucher, Lat. moechus, Ar., Plat.:— κεκάρθαι μοιχόν to have the head shaven, as was done to adulterers, Ar.
heavy with lead, leaded, Anth.
lead, Hom.; fem. in Anth.

entry.etym: later form for μόγις, Trag., Thuc., etc.
entry.sense: with a negat., οὐ μόλις not scarcely, i. e. quite, utterly, Aesch., Eur.
a greedy fellow, applied to a beggar, Od.
Molossian, Hdt., Aesch., etc.:—fem. Μολοσσία, ( sc. γῆ ) Pind.
to sing of, Lat. canere, Ar.
a minstrel or dancer, Anth.
like a song, Aesch.
the song and dance, a chant or song accompanied by measured movements, in honour of a god, or as an amusement, Hom.:—then, generally, play, sport, of a game at ball, Od.
singing, song, as opp. to dancing Hom., Trag.
she who sings and dances, Anth.
a piece of lead, used as the sink of a fishing-line, Il.
leaden, of lead, μ. κανών, a flexible rule that could be moulded to curves, Arist.
a leaden weight on a net, Plat.
a leaden ball, Xen.
lead, Hdt., Eur.
plumbago, vulgarly called black lead, used as a test of gold, Theogn.:— a black-lead pencil, Anth.
Pass. to get into dirty quarrels, Ar.
defilement, NTest.
to stain, sully, defile, Ar.; μ. τινά to make a beast of him, Id.; also to defile a woman, Theocr.:—Pass. to become vile, ἐν ἀμαθίᾳ μολύνεσθαι to wallow in ignorance, Plat.
blame, censure, Pind., Aesch.:— cause or ground of complaint, μομφὴν ἔχειν τινί Pind.; ἕν σοι μομφὴν ἔχω in one thing I blame thee, Eur.; μ. ξυνοῦ δορός blame as to helping spear, Soph.
consisting of units, μ. ἀριθμός abstract number, Arist.
of horses, having one frontlet, μονάμπυκες πῶλοι horses that run single, race-horses, opp. to chariots Eur.; so, μονάμπυκες alone, Id.; of a bull, having no yoke-fellow, Id.
to be sovereign, Pind., Plat.; ἐπὶ τούτου μουναρχέοντος in this monarch's time, Hdt.; c. gen., ἑκόντων μ. Arist.
the rule of one, monarchy, sovereignty, Hdt., Trag., etc.:—of a general in chief, Xen.; of the Roman Dictator, Plut.
monarchical, Plat.
of persons, inclined to monarchy:—adv. -κῶς, Plut.
one who rules alone, a monarch, sovereign, Theogn., Aesch., etc.
as adj., σκᾶπτον μ. the sovereign sceptre, Pind.
for the Roman Dictator, Plut.
alone, solitary, Eur.; as masc. of a man, Aesch.
as Subst., μονάς, άδος, a unit, Plat.
to play a solo on the flute, Plut.
a living alone, celibacy, Plat.
a player on the single flute, Ath.
in one way only, Plat.; ᾗπερ μοναχῇ in which way only, Xen.
single, solitary: as Subst. a monk, Anth.
alone, only, μ. ἐνταῦθα Plat.
in one way only, Arist.
one who rows singly, Anth.
a staying, abiding, tarrying, stay, Hdt., Eur., etc.; μονὴν ποιεῖσθαι to make delay, tarry, Thuc.: a stopping place, station, mansion, NTest.
single, solitary, Luc.
staying in one's place, stable, steadfast, Soph., Plat.; of soldiers, Lat. statarius, Xen.
of things, conditions and the like, abiding, lasting, stable, Lat. stabilis, Eur., Thuc., etc.
one who uses a single horse, a horseman, rider, Xen., etc.
walking alone: μέτρον μ. metre of but one foot, Anth.

entry.note: μονο-γενής, epic and ionic μουνο-γενής, ές
entry.sense: only-begotten, single, Hes., Hdt., etc.; μ. αἷμα one and the same blood, Eur.
one-eyed, Anth.
one-fingered, Luc.
one-eyed, Eur.
uniform in sound, Anth.
one-toothed, Aesch.
plucked from one stem, cut from one block, of a statue, Pind.
of one form or kind, uniform, Plat.
yoked alone, i. e. single, solitary, Aesch.:—so μονοζῠγής, ές, Anth.
lasting one day only, Batr.
alone, singly, Hdt.
a single horse, Anth.
with but one horn, Plut.
μονό-κλαυτος, θρῆνος, ὁ, a lament by one only, Aesch.
a bed for one only, i. e. a coffin, Anth.
with but one sandal, Pind.
with one bank of oars, Xen.
with but one leg: of buildings, of one story, Hdt.:—of sentences, consisting of one clause, Arist.:—generally, of one kind, one-sided. Id.
with one oar or one ship, Eur.
a singularly huge lion, Anth.
made out of one stone, Hdt.
a singularly huge wolf, Plut.
to fight in single combat, Eur.; τινι with one, Hdt.; of the Athenians at Marathon, μοῦνοι μουνομαχήσαντες τῷ Πέρσῃ having fought single-handed with the Persians, Id.
single combat, Hdt.
of or in single combat, Polyb.
fighting in single combat, Aesch., Eur.
μονομάχος, a gladiator, Luc.
consisting of one part, Luc.
reft of mother, Eur.
in a single night, Anth.
made from a solid trunk, Xen.
made of wood only, Plat.
an only child, Eur.
with but one sole, Anth.
wearing the tunic only, Eur.
one-footed, Anth.
to be engaged in one thing, Arist.
exclusive sale, monopoly, Arist.
with one horse, Eur.
digging with one point, Anth.
to eat once in the day, Xen.

entry.note: μόνος, epic and ionic μοῦνος, η, ον
entry.sense: alone, left alone, forsaken solitary, Lat. solus, Hom., etc.; μοῦνος ἐών Id.; μούνω ἄνευθ’ ἄλλων Od.
c. gen., μόνος σοῦ without thee, Soph.; also, μοῦνος ἀπό τινος Hhymn., Soph.
alone, only, μοῦνος παῖς υἱός an only son. Hom.; εἷς μόνος, μόνος εἷς Hdt., Soph.
c. gen., μοῦνος πάντων ἀνθρώπων alone of all men, Hdt.; μόνος ἀνδρῶν Soph., etc.
Sup. μονώτατος, the one only person, one above all others, Ar., Theocr.
adv. μόνως, only, Thuc., Xen.
the common adv. is μόνον, alone, only, Lat. solum, Hdt., attic; οὐχ ἅπαξ μ. Aesch.
only, Lat. modo, with an imperat., ἀποκρίνου μ. Plat.; μή με καταπίῃς μ. Eur.
the adj. often stands as an adv., χοίνικος μόνης ἁλῶν for a gallon of salt only, Ar.
οὐ μόνον . . , ἀλλὰ καὶ . . , Id., etc.:— μόνον, like Lat. solum, is sometimes omitted in these phrases, μὴ τοὺς ἐγγύς, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς ἀπόθεν Thuc.
μόνον οὐ, Like Lat. tantum non, all but, Ar., Dem.; μονονουχί Dem.
κατὰ μόνας, as adv. alone, Thuc.
walking alone, Aesch.
consisting of one verse, Anth.; τὰ μ. single verses, Plut.
going alone, alone, single, Eur.
carved out of a single block, Anth.
of one syllable, dealing in monosyllables, of grammarians, Anth.
with but one child, Eur.
at a solitary table, Eur.
living alone, solitary, Eur.
to eat but one kind of food, Strab.
a rearing singly, Plat.
one-eyed, Hdt.
watching alone, sole guardian, Aesch.
single in one's opinion, Aesch.
of single nature, single, Hdt.
solid-hoofed, Eur.
wearing only the tunic, Luc.
voting alone, μονόψαφον κατασχοῖσα ξίφος keeping her sword solitary of purpose, of Hypermnestra, Pind.
to make single or solitary, ἡμετέρην γενεὴν μούνωσε isolated our house, i. e. allowed but one son in each generation, Od.
Pass. to be left alone or forsaken, Hom.; ἐμουνοῦντο they were left each man by himself, Hdt.; μουνωθέντα taken apart, without witnesses, Id.
c. gen., μεμουνωμένοι συμμάχων deserted by allies, Id.; μονωθεὶς δάμαρτος Eur.; μονωθεῖσα ἀπὸ πατρός Id.
to sing a monody or solo, Ar.
a monody or solo, opp. to the song of the chorus, Ar.
separation from, τινος, Plut.
solitary, Arist.

entry.note: μον-ώψ, ionic μουνώψ, ῶπος, ὁ, ἡ,
entry.sense: one-eyed, Aesch., Eur.
a mora, one of the six regiments in which all spartans of military age were enrolled, Xen.
to make with pain and toil, Anth.

(sc. ἐλαῖαι) αἱ, the sacred olives in the Academy, prob. so called, because parted (μειρόμεναι) from the original olive-stock in the Acropolis, Ar.:— Ζεὺς Μόριος, was the guardian of these sacred olives, Soph.
a piece, portion, section, Hdt., Plat., etc.; of quarters of the glove, Hdt.; of parts of a country, Thuc.; of an army, Id.
a member of a council, Arist.
= μόρσιμος, anth.
v. μορίαι.
Dep.:
to frighten, scare, Ar., Plat.
to be afraid of, τι Plat.
hideous to behold, Ar.

entry.etym: Formed from the sound, like Lat. murmur.
entry.sense: of water, to roar and boil, Il.
a hideous she-monster, used by nurses to frighten children with, Luc.: generally, a bugbear, Ar., Xen.
as an exclamation to frighten children with, boh! μορμώ, δάκνει ἵππος Theocr.; μορμὼ τοῦ θράσους a fig for his courage! Ar.
of earrings, wrought with much pains, skilfully wrought, Hom.
= μοῖρα III, man's appointed doom, fate, destiny, μόρος [ἐστὶν] ὀλέσθαι 'tis one's doom to die, Il.; ὑπὲρ μόρον beyond one's destiny, Hom.
doom, death, Lat. fatum, Il., Hdt., Trag.
= νεκρός, a corpse, Anth.
the son of Night, Hes.
appointed by fate, destined, Lat. fatalis, Hom., Hdt., Aesch.; τὸ μόρσιμον destiny, doom, Pind., Trag.; τὰ μόρσιμα Solon.
fore-doomed to die, Hom.
to soil, stain, defile: perf. pass. part. μεμορυγμένα καπνῷ Od.
to use gesticulations, Xen.
to shape, fashion, mould, Anth.
Morpheus, god of dreams, because of the forms he calls up before the sleeper, Ovid.
formed, λίθου of stone, Anth.: esp. well-formed, shapely, Lat. formosus, Pind.

form, shape, Lat. forma, σοὶ δ’ ἐπὶ μὲν μορφὴ ἐπέων thou hast power to give shape to words, i. e. to give a colour of truth to lies, Od.; θεὸς μορφὴν ἔπεσι στέφει God adds a crown of shapeliness to his words, Id.
form, shape, figure, esp. like Lat. forma, a fine or beautiful form, Pind., Trag.
generally, form, fashion, appearance, Soph., Xen.
a form, kind, sort, Eur., Plat.
epith. of an eagle, prob. dusky, dark, Lat. furvus, Il., Hes.
to give form or shape to, Anth.
form, shape, Aesch., Eur.
form, semblance, NTest.
συῶν μ. changing men into swine, Eur.
dwellers-in-wooden-houses, a people on the Black Sea, near Colchis, Xen., etc.
a wooden house or tower, Xen.
of a calf, κρέα μόσχεια veal, Xen.; μόσχεια alone, anth.; μ. αἷμα Id.; μ. κυνοῦχος a calf-skin leash, Xen.; μόσχειον (sc. δέρμα), a calf skin, Id.
to plant a sucker: metaph. to plant or propagate men, Dem.
a young shoot, συκίδων from fig-trees, Ar.
a young calf, Theocr.
a young shoot or twig, Il.: cf. ὄσχος, ὄζος.
a calf, Eur.: a young bull, which form the god Apis was believed to assume, Hdt.: and as fem. a heifer, young cow, Eur.:—a calf was the prize of Lyric Poets, ᾄδειν ἐπὶ μόσχῳ Ar.
metaph. a boy, or as fem. a girl, maid, Lat. juvenca, Eur.
any young animal, Id.
shredded linen, lint, cf. ἔμμοτος.
singly, in single combat, Od.
Munychia, a harbour at Athens between Phalerum and Peiraeeus, Hdt., Thuc.
at Munychia, Thuc.
the 10th Attic month, in which was held the festival of Munychian Artemis, = the latter part of April and beginning of May, Ar., Aeschin.
leader of the Muses, Lat. Musagetes, of Apollo, Plat.

the Muse, in pl. the Muses, goddesses of song, music, poetry, dancing, the drama, and all fine arts, Hom.: the names of the nine were Clio, Euterpe, Thalia, Melpomene, Terpsichore, Erato, Polymnia or Polyhymnia, Urania, and Calliope, Hes.,
μοῦσα, as appellat., music, song, Pind., Trag.:—also eloquence, Eur.:—in pl. arts, accomplishments, Ar., Plat.
a temple of the Muses, seat or haunt of the Muses, Aeschin.

generally, a school of art and poetry, Id.: metaph., μουσεῖα θρηνήμασι ξυνῳδά choirs chiming in with dirges, Eur.; χελιδόνων μουσεῖα choirs of swallows (whose twittering was a type of barbarous tongues), Ar.
of or belonging to the Muses, Eur.; ἅρμα Μοισαῖον the car of poesy, Pind.; λίθος M. a monument of song, Id.
musical, Anth.
to sing of, chant, Theocr.:—Mid. in act. sense, Eur.
any art over which the Muses presided, esp. music or lyric poetry, Hdt., attic
generally, art, letters, accomplishment, Hdt., Plat.; young Athenians were taught μουσική, γράμματα, γυμναστική, Plat., Arist.
of or for music, musical, Ar., Thuc., etc.; τὰ μουσικά music, Xen.; v. μουσική.
of persons, skilled in music, musical, Id., Plat.
generally, a votary of the Muses, a man of letters and accomplishment, a scholar, Ar., Plat.:—c. inf., μουσικώτεροι λέγειν more accomplished in speaking, Eur.
adv. -κῶς, harmoniously, suitably, Plat.: Sup. μουσικώτατα Ar.
built by song, of the walls of Thebes, Anth.
Muse-inspired, Plut.
to be Muse-mad, Luc.
devoted to the Muses, Anth.
the mother of Muses and all arts, of Memory, Aesch.
Pass. to be trained in the ways of the Muses, to be educated or accomplished, Ar., Pericl.
to write poetry: to sing of, τινά Ar.
making poetry, a poet, poetess, Hdt.
singing or playing, Eur.
serving the Muses; μ. στοναχά a tuneful lament, Eur.
as Subst. a bard, minstrel, poet, Id.
musical-looking, Anth.
a singing, making poetry, Luc.
cultivating music: as Subst. a singing girl, Xen.
loving the Muses, Anth.
delighting in the Muses, Anth.

to be weary with toil, to be sore distressed, Il., Soph.:— to work hard, labour, Eur., etc.; c. acc. cogn., μ. μόχθους, πόνους to undergo hardships, or to execute painful tasks, Id.; μ. μαθήματα to toil at learning, Id.
c. acc. objecti, τέκνα ἁμόχθησα the children whom I toiled for, Id.; μ. τινά θεραπεύμασιν = θεραπεύειν, Id.; cf. μόχθος.
always in pl. toils, hardships, Trag.
bad condition, badness, Plat.
in moral sense, badness, wickedness, depravity, Ar., Plat.; τὰ πρῶτα τῆς ἐκεῖ μ. chief of the rascaldom down there (in Hades), Ar.
suffering hardship, in sore distress, miserable, wretched, Aesch., Ar., etc.; μοχθηρὰ τλῆναι to suffer hardships, Aesch.
in a bad state, in sorry plight, worthless, Ar., Plat., etc.:—adv., μοχθηρῶς διακεῖσθαι to be in a sorry plight, Plat.; so in comp., μοχθηροτέρως ἔχειν Id.; -ότερον Xen.:—Sup. -ότατα Plat.
in moral sense, wicked, knavish, rascally, Lat. pravus, Thuc., Ar., etc.
one must labour, Eur.
to suffer, ἕλκει μοχθίζοντα ὕδρου suffering by its sting, Il.; μ. δαίμονι φαύλῳ Theogn.

toil, hard work hardship, distress, trouble, Hes., Trag.: pl. toils, troubles, hardships, Trag.; τέκνων for children, Eur. -μόχθος and πόνος are both used in the sense of hardship, distress; yet this notion belongs properly to μόχθος, while πόνος is properly work, Lat. labor (from πένομαι, πένης, the poor man's lot).
one who heaves by a lever, γῆς καὶ θαλάσσης μ. he who makes earth and sea to heave, Ar.; καινῶν ἐπῶν μ. one who heaves up new words, Id.
to prise up, heave up by a lever, Hdt., Eur.
στήλας ἐμόχλεον they strove to heave them up with levers, Il.
a bar used as a lever, a crowbar, handspike, Lat, vectis, used for moving ships, Od.; for forcing doors and gates, Eur.
the stake which Ulysses ran into the Cyclops' eye, Od.
a wooden bar, placed across gates on the inside and secured by the βάλανος, Aesch., Thuc.
apostr. for με.
rarely for μοι, Hom.
a mouse-trap, Anth.
the shrew-mouse, field-mouse, Lat. mus araneus, Hdt.
a moaning, muttering, Aesch.
wet, dripping, Il., Hes., Soph.
to ooze with damp, be clammy from decay, of a corpse, Soph.; μυδῶσα κηκίς clammy moisture, Id.; μυδῶσαι σταγόνες oozing drops, Id.
to forge red-hot iron, Aesch.
forging red-hot iron, μ. μίμημα the manner of a smith smiting iron, Eur.
a mass of red-hot metal, Hdt.; μύδρους αἴρειν χεροῖν to hold red-hot iron in the hands, as an ordeal, Soph.
of marrow; = μυελόεις, Anth.
full of marrow, Od.

marrow, Lat. medulla, Il., Hom., etc.:— the brain, Soph.: metaph. of strengthening food, οἶνον καὶ ἄλφιτα, μυελὸν ἀνδρῶν Od.; πρὸς ἄκρον μ. ψυχῆς the marrow or inmost part, Eur.; Τρινακρίας μ., of Syracuse, Theocr.

to initiate into the mysteries, μυῆσαι Dem.:—in Pass. to be initiated, Hdt., Ar.; οἱ μεμυημένοι the initiated, Ar.; c. acc. cogn. to be initiated in a thing, τὰ Καβείρων ὄργια μεμύηται in the mysteries of the Cabiri, Hdt.; τὰ μέγαλα (sc. μυστήρια) μεμύησαι Plat.
generally to teach, instruct, c. inf., ἐμύησάς τινα ἰδεῖν Anth.
to murmur with closed lips, to mutter, moan, Aesch.; οἰκτισμὸν μ. to make a piteous moaning, Id.
to drink with closed lips, to suck in, Xen.

to say, speak, absol., Il.:—c. acc. et inf. to say that, Id.: c. inf. only, to order, Aesch.:—c. acc. to tell, recount, Hom.; also, to tell of, Il.:—c. acc. cogn. to say, speak, utter, Hom.; πόλιν μ. πολύχρυσον to speak of the city as rich in gold, Il.
to say over to oneself, con over, consider, Hom.
a story told, tale, Arist., Plut.
later form of μυθέομαι, Eur.:—Pass. to be spoken of, Id.; ὡς μεμύθευται βροτοῖς as is related by mortals, Id.
Dep. to recount fables, Babr.
a collection of Fables, like those of Babr.
mythic, legendary, Plat.
to write fabulous accounts, Strab.
a writing of fables, Strab.
a writer of legends, Polyb., Plut.
to tell word for word, Od.
to tell mythic tales or legends, Plat., Xen.
c. acc. to tell as a legend or mythic tale, Plat.:—Pass., οἷαι μυθολογοῦνται παλαιαὶ γενέσθαι φύσεις such as they are fabled to have been, Id.: impers., μυθολογεῖται the legend goes, Arist.
to invent like a mythical tale, μ. πολιτείαν to frame an imaginary constitution, Plat.
to tell stories, converse, Lat. confabulari, Id.
a mythical narrative, Plat., Plut.

entry.etym: verb. adj. of μυθολογέω I, Plat.

entry.sense: a telling of mythic legends, legendary lore, mythology, Plat.
a legend, story, tale, Id.
versed in legendary lore, Plat.
a teller of legends, romancer, Plat.
making mythic legends, Plat.
anything, delivered by word of mouth, word, speech, opp. to ἔργον, Hom., etc.
a speech in the public assembly, Od., Ar.
talk, conversation, mostly in pl., Od.
counsel, advice, a command, order, also a promise, Il.
the subject of speech, the thing or matter itself, Od., Eur.
a resolve, purpose, design, plan, Hom.
a saying, saw, proverb, Aesch.
the talk of men, rumour, Soph., Eur.

a tale, story, narrative, Hom.; μ. παιδός of or about him, Od.:—after Hom., μῦθος, like Lat. fabula, is a tale, legend, myth, opp. to λόγος the historic tale, Hdt., Plat., etc.: a fable, such as those of Aesop, Plat.
legendary, fabulous, Plat.: τὸ μ. the domain of fable, Thuc.; τὸ μὴ μ. αὐτῶν such part of them as is not fabulous, Id.
a fly, Lat. musca, Il.:—proverb., μυίης θάρσος, of excessive boldness, Id.
a fly-flap, of a long beard, Anth.
flapping away flies, Anth.

entry.etym: Formed from the sound, cf. βληχάομαι, μηκάομαι, βρυχάομαι, βρωμάομαι.
entry.sense: Lat. mugire, to low, bellow, roar, of oxen, Il.; of calves, Od; of Hercules in agony, Eur., etc.
of things, as of heavy gates, to grate, creak, Il.; of a shield, to ring, Id.; of meat roasting, to hiss upon the spits, Od.; of thunder, Ar.
a lowing, bellowing, of oxen, Hom.
a lowing, bellowing, roaring, of oxen, Eur.; of a lioness, Theocr.; the roar of thunder, Aesch.
Mycenaean, Hom., etc.: fem. Μυκηνίς, ίδος, Eur.
from Mycene, Il.
Mycene, Mycenae, an ancient Pelasgic or Achaean city, superseded by the Dorian Argos, Hom., etc.
a mushroom, Lat. fungus.
any thing shaped like a mushroom,
the chape or cap at the end of a scabbard, Hdt.
the snuff of a lamp-wick, supposed to forbode rain, Ar.
a bellower, of oxen, Theocr.
made of mushrooms, Luc.
to turn up the nose or sneer at:—Pass. to be mocked, NTest.
out of the nose, Anth.
sounding from the nostril, Aesch.
the nose, snout, Ar.: in pl. the nostrils, Hdt., Ar.
from the use of the nose to express ridicule, a sneerer, Anth.
of or working in a mill, Anth.
a millstone, a large round stone, Il.
a miller, Anth.
Lat. mola, a mill, a handmill turned by women, Od.
the nether millstone, Ar.; the upper being ὄνος, Id.
bruised in a mill, Od.
to grind the teeth, Hes., in epic part. μυλιόωντες.
masc. adj. of or for a mill, λίθος μ. a mill stone, Plat.
rock for millstones, Strab.
of or for a mill, λίθος NTest.
like a millstone, Lat. molaris, Il.
a millstone, Strab.
a miller who keeps slaves to work his mill, Dem.
a mill-house, Thuc.; εἰς μ. καταβαλεῖν, Lat. detrudere in pistrinum, to condemn [a slave] to work the mill, Eur.
an excuse, pretence, Od.
the discharge from the nose, Lat. pituita, Hes., etc.
the nostrils, Lat. nares, Hdt.
to catch mice, Strab.
mouse-killing, Batr.
a battle of mice, Plut.
a light vessel, chiefly used by pirates, Plut.
mouse-tailed: curtailed, Arist.
a muttering sound made with the lips, μῦ λαλεῖν to mutter, Hippon.:—to imitate the sound of sobbing, μὺ μῦ, μὺ μῦ, or rather μυμῦ, μυμῦ, Ar.
Μ, μ, μῦ, τό:—indecl., twelfth letter in the Gr. alphabet: as numerals, μʹ = 40, but ͵μ = 40,000.
μ is the labial liquid, corresponding to β:
changes:
aeolic and Lacon. into π, as πεδά for μετά.
attic and doric into ν, as νιν for μιν; so Lat. ne, num = μή, μῶν.
μ is doubled,
poet. in compds., as ἄμμορος, φιλομμειδής; and after the augm., as ἔλλαβον.
aeolic, as ἄμμες ὔμμες ἐμμί, for ἡμεῖς ὑμεῖς εἰμί.
μ is added,
at the beginning of a word, as ἴα μία, ὄσχος μόσχος.
in the middle of a word to facilitate pronunciation, as ὄμβριμος ὄβριμος, τύμπανον τύπανον, etc., esp. after redupl., as πίμπλημι for πίπλημι; after α- privat., as ἄμβροτος, ἄβροτος.
Lat. muraena, a sea-eel, lamprey, Ar.; a sea-serpent, Aesch.
to prepare unguents, Aesop.

sense.gloss: one who prepares unguents. a perfumer.

entry.sense: ten thousand times, Ar.
holding 10, 000 measures: metaph. of prodigious size, Ar.
containing 10, 000 inhabitants, Arist.
commander of 10, 000 men, Hdt.: so μῡρί-αρχος, ου, Xen.
a number of 10, 000, a myriad, Hdt., etc.; indefinitely of countless numbers, Eur.:—when μυριάς, μυριάδες are used absol. of money, δραχμῶν must be supplied, Ar.; when of corn, μεδίμνων, Dem.
adj. consisting of 10, 000, Aesch., Eur.
of 10, 000 years: of countless years, Aesch.
to rub with ointment or unguent, anoint, Ar.:—Pass., μεμυρισμένοι τὸ σῶμα having the body anointed, Hdt.
Lat. myrica, a shrub esp. thriving in marshy ground and near the sea, the tamarisk, Il.
a tamarisk bush, Anth.
a tamarisk bough, Il.
with ten thousand oxen, Anth.
with immense teeth, Anth.
with countless fruit, Soph.
many-headed, Eur.
said ten thousand times, Xen.
of countless shapes, Anth.
of countless labours, Anth.
with countless ships, Anth.
where tens of thousands die, Plut.
0, 000 times as many as, c. gen., Xen., Arist.
infinite in number, Eur.
numberless, countless, infinite, properly of Number, and commonly in pl., Hom.; in sg. with collective Nouns, μυρίον χέραδος Il.; χαλκός Pind.
of Size, measureless, immense, infinite, πένθος, ἄχος Il.; μ. κέλευθος an endless journey, Pind.; μ. χρόνος id.; μυρίη ὄψις all kinds of sights, Hdt., etc.
neut. pl. μυρία as adv., much, immensely, incessantly, κλαίειν Anth.
dat. as adv., μυρίῳ σοφώτερος infinitely wiser, Eur.; μυρίῳ βέλτιον, μ. κάλλιον Plat.

as a definite numeral, in pl. μύριοι, αι, α, ten thousand, the greatest number in Greek expressed by one word, Hes., etc.:—in sg. with collective nouns, ἵππος μυρίη 10, 000 horse, Hdt.; ἀσπὶς μυρία Xen.
the 10, 000 th, Ar.; μ. ἔτος 10, 000 years hence, Plat.
a body of ten thousand, Xen.
with ten thousand armed men, Eur.
carrying 10, 000 measures, to designate a merchant-ship of large tonnage, Thuc.
with ten thousand voices, Anth.
with countless eyes, Aesch.
Lat. formica, the ant, Hes., etc.
a beast of prey in India, Hdt.
the Myrmidons, a warlike people of Thessaly, subjects of Achilles, Hom.
anointed, Anth.
sweet juice extracted form plants, sweet-oil, unguent, balsam, Hdt., etc.
a place where unguents were sold, the perfume-market, Ar.
breathing sweet unguents, Anth.
a dealer in unguents or scented oils, a perfumer, Xen.
a perfumer's shop, Dem.
shining with unguent, Anth.
anointed with unguent, Eur.
with anointed skin, Anth.
= μύρτος, Pind., Eur.
a branch or wreath of myrtle, Hdt., Ar.
myrtle-like, Hhymn.
a myrtle-grove, Lat. myrtetum, Ar.
a myrtle-berry, Lat. myrtum, Ar.
the myrtle, Lat. myrtus, Simon., etc.
a twig or spray of myrtle, Pind., Ar.
epic Verb, to flow, run, trickle, δάκρυσι μῦρον (epic imperf.) were melting into tears, Hes.
Mid. to melt into tears, to shed tears, weep, Hom., Hes.
c. acc. to weep for, bewail, Bion., Mosch.
foul, dirty: hence, loathsome, abominable, Eur.; τὸ μ. an abomination, Hdt.
of persons, defiled, polluted, Eur.
Dep.: to feel disgust at anything loathsome, to loathe, abominate, c. acc., Eur., Xen.
a Mysian dirge, Aesch.; cf. Κίσσιος.
uncleanness of body or mind: metaph. an abomination, defilement, Lat. piaculum, Trag.
a Mysian, Aesch.:—from their effeminate character, Μυσῶν λεία came to mean a prey to all, of anything that can be plundered with impunity, Dem.
Lat. mus, a mouse, Batr.; μ. ἀρουραῖος the field-mouse, or the hamster, Hdt.; μῦς πίσσας γεύεται, proverb. of one who is tempted to eat and finds himself caught, Theocr.
a muscle of the body, Lat. musculus, Id.
to run about like a mouse, Ar.
initiation into the mysteries, Plut.
one who initiates into mysteries, a mystagogue, Plut.
doric and Lacon. word, the upper lip, the moustache, Theocr.: cf. μάσταξ.
of or for mysteries, mystic, Ar.
a mystery or secret doctrine; in pl., τὰ μ. the mysteries of the Cabiri in Samothrace, Hdt.; of Demeter at Eleusis, Aesch., etc.
any mystery or secret, Plat.
mystic implements, Eur., Ar.
in NTest. a mystery, a divine secret, something above human intelligence.
of or for the mysteries: μ. σπονδή an armistice during the Eleusinian mysteries, Aeschin.
one initiated, Eur.
as adj. mystic, Ar., Anth.
mystic, connected with the mysteries, μ. Ἴακχος the mystic chant Iacchus, Hdt.; τὰ μ. the mysteries, Thuc.:— χοιρία μ., in Ar., are prob. wretched lean pigs, such as the μύσται were wont to offer.
Dep. to sop bread in soup or gravy and eat it, Ar.: metaph., μυστιλᾶται τῶν δημοσίων he ladles out public money, Id.:—perf. part. in pass. sense, scooped out, Id.
a piece of bread used to sup up soup or gravy with, Ar.
solemnising mysteries, performing mystic rites, Anth.
as adj. mystic, Anth.
a mystagogue, Anacreont.
receiving the initiated, δόμος μ., i. e. Eleusis, Ar.
Mytilene, the chief city of Lesbos, Thuc.
to hash up, make mince-meat of, τινά Ar.
a savoury dish of cheese, honey, garlic, mashed up into a sort of paste, Lat. moretum, Ar.
to snort, jeer, Theocr.
a snorting, moaning, Eur.
inward, inmost, retired, embayed, Aesch., Luc.
= μυγμός moaning, groaning, Od.
adv. from the inmost part of the house, from the women's chambers, Aesch.
in the farthest corner, Od.
adv. to the far corner, Od.
the innermost place, inmost nook or corner, Lat. sinus, recessus, Hom., etc.
the inmost part of a house, the women's apartments, Lat. penetralia, Od., Trag.
a bay or creek running far inland, Hdt.; πόντιος μ., i. e. the Adriatic, Aesch.
full of recesses, cavernous, Eur.
a cluster of muscles, a muscle, Il.
to be shortsighted, see dimly, NTest.
intr. to close, be shut, of the eyes, Il., Eur.; so, χείλεα μεμυκώς having the lips closed, Anth.
of persons, μύσας with one's eyes shut, Soph., Ar.
metaph. to be lulled to rest, to abate, of pain, Soph.; of storms, Anth.
trans. to close, shut, Id.
to spur, prick with a spur, Xen.
Pass. (μύωψ II. 1) to be teased by flies, of a horse, Id.
contracting the eyes, as shortsighted people do, shortsighted, Arist.
as Subst., μύωψ, ωπος, ὁ, the horsefly or gadfly, Lat. tabanus, Aesch., Plat.
a goad, spur, Xen., Theophr.:—metaph. a stimulant, Luc., Anth.
the toil and moil of war, Il.; ξείνου καὶ Ἴρου μ. the struggle between Irus and the stranger, Od.
moly, mandrake, a fabulous herb of magic power, having a black root and white blossom, given by Hermes to Ulysses, as a counter-charm to the charms of Circe, Od.
Dep.: to find, fault with, blame, c. acc., Il., Aesch.:—an aor1 inf. μωμηθῆναι in pass. sense, NTest.
to be blamed, Aesch.
blame, ridicule, disgrace, μῶμον ἀνάψαι to set a brand upon one, Od.
personified Momus, the critic God, Hes.

contr. for μὴ οὖν, used like μή, in questions to which a negative answer is expected, but surely not? is it so? Lat. num? μῶν ἐστι . . ; Answ. οὐ δῆτα, Eur.: sometimes it asks doubtingly like Lat. num forte? and answered in the affirm., Id.: — μῶν οὐ . . ; requires an affirm. answer, Lat. nonne ? Trag.
with a single, i. e. uncloven, hoof, Lat. solipes, of the horse, Hom., Eur.
to be silly, foolish, Eur., Xen., etc.:—c. acc. rei, πεῖραν μωραίνειν to make a mad attempt, Aesch.
Causal, to make foolish, convict of folly, NTest.:—Pass., of salt, to become insipid, lose its savour, Id.
silliness, folly, μωρίην ἐπιφέρειν τινι to impute folly to him, Hdt.; μωρίαν ὀφλισκάνειν to be charged with it, Soph.; ἐδόκει μωρία εἶναι ταῦτα Thuc.; τῆς μωρίας! what folly! Ar.
silly talking, NTest.
speaking foolishly, Arist.
foolishly wise, a sapient fool, Luc.
dull, sluggish, stupid, Soph., etc.; τὸ- μ. folly, Eur.; μῶρα φρονεῖν, δρᾶν, λέγειν Soph., Eur.:—adv. -ρως, Xen.
an inhabitant, Simon.; as fem., Anth.
of or for the Naiads, Anth.
a Naiad, a river nymph, (as Νηρηίς is a sea-nymph), mostly in pl. Ναϊάδες, ionic Νηϊάδες, Od., Eur.:—so also ionic Νηίς, ίδος, in sg., Il., Eur.
of persons, to dwell, often in Hom. and Hes.
c. acc. loci, to dwell in, inhabit, Hom., Hes.
of places, to be situated, lie, Hom.: hence to exist, Ἰθάκης ἔτι ναιεταούσης Il.
used in strong affirmation, yea, verily, Lat. nae, Hom., attic; in Hom. mostly followed by δή.
ναὶ μά in oaths, yea by . . , ναὶ μὰ τόδε σκῆπτρον Il.; μά is sometimes omitted, ναὶ τὰν κόραν Ar.; ναὶ πρὸς θεῶν Eur.
in answers, alone, aye, yes, τοῦτ’ ἐτήτυμον; answ. ναί Aesch.; ναί, ναί Ar.

entry.etym: adverb for ναί, like οὐχί for οὐ, Soph.

entry.sense: of persons, to dwell, abide, Il., Hes., Trag.:—c. acc loci, to dwell in, inhabit, οἶκον, δῶμα, ἅλα, etc., Hom., etc.:—Pass. to be inhabited, Theocr.
of places, to lie, be situated, Soph.
Causal, in epic aor1 ἔνασσα or νάσσα,
c. acc. loci, to give one to dwell in, νάσσα πόλιν I would have given him a town for his home, Od.: also to make habitable, to build, νηὸν ἔνασσαν Hhymn.:—Pass., v. εὐναιόμενος.
c. acc. pers. to let one dwell, settle him, Pind.; Pass., epic aor1 νάσθην, to be settled, to dwell, Il.; so, aor1 mid., νάσσατο ἄγχι Ἑλικῶνος Hes.; perf. νένασται Anth.
to run over, to be full, Od.
a wooly or hairy skin, a goatskin, Od.
a fleece, Lat. vellus, Hdt., Pind., etc.
anything flowing, running water, a river, stream, Trag., Plat.
a dwarf, Ar.
of dwarfish stature, Ar.
Naxian; οἱ N. the Naxians, Hdt.; Ναξία ἀκόνα a Naxian whetstone, Pind.
of Naxian work, Ar.
Naxos, one of the Cyclades, Hhymn.
the overseer of a temple, Hes.
the dwelling of a god, a temple, Hom., Hdt., etc.
the inmost part of a temple, the cell, in which the image of the god was placed, Hdt., Xen.
the keeper of a temple, Lat. aedituus, Eur., Arist.
of a wooded vale or dell, Soph., Eur.
a wooded vale, dell, or glen, Il., Soph.

entry.etym: later form of νάπη, Soph., Eur., Xen.

entry.sense: = σίναπι; ν. βλέπειν Ar.; cf. κάρδαμον.
anointed with nard-oil, Anth.
a plant, nard, spikenard, nard-oil, Anth.
carrying a νάρθηξ, a wand-bearer, πολλοί τοι ναρθηκοφόροι, Βάκχοι δέ τε παῦροι, i. e. there are many officials, but few inspired, Plat.

a tall umbelliferous plant, Lat. ferula, with a hollow, pithy stalk, in which Prometheus conveyed fire from heaven to earth, Hes. The stalks furnished the Bacchanalian wands (θύρσοι), Eur., (cf. ναρθηκο-φόρος); they were also used for canes by schoolmasters, Xen.
a casket for unguents, Luc.
to grow stiff or numb, Lat. torpere, Il., Plat.
numbness, deadness, Lat. torpor, Ar.
a flat fish, the torpedo or electric ray, Plat.
the narcissus, Hhymn., Soph., etc.
entry.etym: From ναρκάω, because of its narcotic properties.

entry.sense: a flowing stream, a stream, Eur.
to press or squeeze close, stamp down, Od., Theocr.
close- pressed: ναστός (sc. πλακοῦς), a well-kneaded cake, cheese-cake, Ar.
to suffer shipwreck, be shipwrecked, Hdt., Xen., etc.:—metaph. of chariots, to be wrecked, Dem.
shipwreck, Hdt., Eur.
a piece of wreck, Hdt., Aesch., Thuc.: metaph., ναυάγια ἱππικά the wreck of a chariot, Soph.
= ναυαγία, Strab.
shipwrecked, stranded, Lat. naufragus, Hdt., Eur.; ναυαγοὺς ἀναιρεῖσθαι to pick up the shipwrecked men, Xen.; ν. τάφος the grave of the shipwrecked, i. e. the sea, Anth.
act. causing shipwreck, ἄνεμοι Id.
