to command a fleet, Hdt., Xen.
the command of a fleet, office of ναύαρχος, Thuc.: the period of his command, Xen.
the ship of the ναύαρχος, Polyb.
the commander of a fleet, an admiral, Hdt., Aesch., Soph.:—esp. the Spartan admiral-in-chief, whereas the Athen. admirals retained the name of στρατηγοί (generals), Thuc., Xen., etc.
a "ship-goer," a seaman, Hdt., Aesch., Soph., etc.
as adj., ν. στρατός Aesch.; στόλος Soph., etc.
a ship's cable, Eur.
to be a shipowner, Ar., Xen.
metaph., ν. πόλιν to manage, govern, Aesch., Soph.
a seafaring life, ship-owning, Arist.
poet. a voyage, Eur.:— an adventure, enterprise, Id.
a ship, Id.
the ship of a ναύκληρος, Dem.
= ναύσταθμος, Eur.
a shipowner, ship-master, Hdt., Soph., etc.
as adj., ν. χείρ the master's hand, of a charioteer (cf. ἡνίοχος I. 3), Eur.

at Athens, one of a division, of the citizens, made for financial purposes before Solon.'s time. There were 4 in each φρατρία, 12 in each of the 4 old φυλαί, in all 48, afterwards increased to 50. (Apparently an old form of ναύ-κληρος: but the connexion of the word with ναῦς ship is not explained.)
to be master of the sea, Thuc.:— Pass. to be mastered at sea, Xen.
master or mistress of the seas, Hdt.
Naucratis in Egypt, Hdt.
= ναυκράτης, Hdt., Thuc.
the master of a ship, Soph.
passage-money, the fare or freight, Xen.
the freight or cargo of ships, Dem.
to lie in a harbour or creek, esp. to lie in wait there in order to sally out on passing ships, Hdt., Eur.
c. acc. to lie in wait for, Thuc.
affording safe anchorage, of a harbour, Od., Soph.; ὦ ναύλοχα καὶ πετραῖα λουτρά ye springs by the haven and from the rock (where some take ναύλοχα as Subst.) Soph.
to fight in a ship or by sea, engage in a naval battle, Hdt., Xen.; ν. τὴν περὶ τῶν κρεῶν to be in the battle for the carcases (i. e. Arginusae), Ar.
metaph. to do battle with, κακοῖς Id.
Desid., to wish to fight by sea, Thuc.
one must fight by sea, Arist.
a sea-fight, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
of or for a sea-fight, ξυστὰ ναύμαχα boarding pikes, Il.; δόρατα Hdt.
act. fighting at sea, Anth.
a city on the north of the gulf of Corinth, Thuc.
to build ships, Ar., Plat.: —Mid., ναῦς ναυπηγέεσθαι to build oneself ships, get them built, Hdt., attic:—Pass., of ships, to be built, Thuc., Xen.
useful in shipbuilding, of wood, Hdt., Thuc.
shipbuilding, Hdt., Thuc.
skilled in shipbuilding, Luc.: ἡ ναυπηγική (sc. τέχνη) the art of shipbuilding, Arist.
a shipbuilder's-yard, dockyard, Ar.
a shipwright, Thuc., Plat.
Nauplia in Argolis, Hdt., etc.
a Nauplian, Strab. :— Ναύπλιος, or -έιος, η, ον, Eur.
of a country, ship-frequented, Aesch.
ship-speeding, of oars, Eur.
to carry by sea, Eur.:—Mid. to take with one by sea, Id.:—Pass. to go by sea, Id.
famed for ships, Od.

entry.etym: = ναυσῐπέρᾱτος, epith. of the Phaeacians, Od.

entry.sense: navigable or (perhaps) to be crossed by a ferry, Hdt.
act. ship-wafting, Eur.
traversed by ships, navigable, of a river, Xen.
act. passing in a ship, seafaring, Eur.
causing a ship to pass, of oars, Id.
lamentable to ships, Pind.
carried by ship, seafaring, Pind.

a ship, Hom., etc.; ἐν νήεσσι or ἐν νηυσίν at the ships, i. e. in the camp formed by the ships drawn up on shore, Il.; ναῦς μακραί, Lat. naves longae, ships of war, which were built long for speed, while the merchant-vessels (ναῦς στρόγγυλαι, γαῦλοι, ὁλκάδες) were round-built, Hdt., etc
a harbour, anchorage, roadstead, Lat. statio navium, Eur., Thuc., Plut.
trans. to carry or convey by sea, Eur.:—Pass., with fut. mid. -ήσομαι, to go by sea, Id.
to guide, steer, Aesch., Eur.: metaph., τὼ πτέρυγε ποῖ ναυστολεῖς; whither pliest thou thy wings? Ar.
intr. like Pass. to go by ship, sail, Soph., Eur.
generally, c. acc. loci, to travel over, Eur.
anything conveyed by ship: in pl. also = ναυστολία, πόντου ναυστολήματα Eur.
a going by sea, naval expedition, Eur.
crossing the water, Aesch.
Lat. nauta, a seaman, sailor, Hom., Hes., etc.; as adj., ν. ὅμιλος Eur.
a mate or companion by sea, ναύτην ἄγειν τινά Soph.
seasickness, qualmishness, disgust, Lat. nausea, Simon.
to be qualmish, suffer from seasickness or nausea, Ar., Plat.
seafaring, naval, ὁ ν. στρατός opp. to ὁ πεζός, Hdt.; ν. λεώς Aesch.; στόλος Soph.; ν. ἐρείπια wrecks of ships, Aesch.; ν. ἀναρχία among the seamen, Eur.:— τὸ ναυτικόν a navy, fleet, Hdt., Ar., etc.
of persons, skilled in seamanship, nautical, ναυτικοὶ ἐγένοντο became a naval power, Thuc.
ἡ ναυτική (sc. τέχνη) navigation, seamanship, Hdt.; so, τὰ ναυτικά Plat.;—but, τὰ ναυτικά, also, naval affairs naval power, Thuc., Xen.
at Athens, ναυτικόν technically meant money borrowed or lent on bottomry, Xen., etc.
sailing, seamanship, Od., Hes.
a voyage, Pind., Hdt.
a ship, Anth.
Dep. to sail, go by sea, Hdt.; rare in attic
a seaman, sailor, Hdt., Aesch., etc.
as adj., ναυτίλος, ον, of a ship, Aesch.
the nautilus, a shell-fish, furnished with a membrane which serves it for a sail, Arist.
to take on board; metaph., Anth.
collecting seamen, Strab.
shipwreck, loss of ships, Anth.
shipwrecked, ν. στολή, πέπλοι the garb of shipwrecked men, Eur.
ship-fenced, Aesch., Eur.; στρατός Ar.:— ναύφρακτον βλέπειν to look like a ship of war, Id.

entry.etym: prob. only in pres. and imperf. :
entry.sense: to flow, Hom.
newly or lately told, Aesch.
only in pres., intr. to be young or new, Aesch.; τὸ νεάζον youth, Soph.; νεάζων thinking or acting like a youth, Eur.
to be the younger of two, ὁ μὲν νεάζων Soph.
to grow young, Anth.
newly taken, Aesch.
newly-whetted, Soph.
young, fresh, Xen., Plat.
of fish, fresh, Dem.
newly caught, Hdt.
new-blown, Anth.
a youthful, i. e. a spirited or (in bad sense) a wanton act or word, Plat., etc.

Dep., to act like a hot-headed youth, to act wantonly, to brawl, swagger, Plat.; τοιοῦτον ν. to make such youthful promises, Dem.:—c. inf. to undertake with youthful spirit, Plut.:—Pass., ἐφ’ ἅπασι τοῖς ἑαυτῷ νενεανιευμένοις to all his wanton acts, Dem.
a young man, youth, with ἀνήρ, Od.; so, παῖς νεηνίης Hdt.; alone, like νεανίσκος, Soph., Eur., etc.
youthful, i. e. in good sense, impetuous, brave, active, Eur., Ar., etc.; or in bad sense, hot-headed, headstrong, Eur., Dem.
of things, new, young, fresh, Eur.
youthful, fresh, active, vigorous, Ar.; ν. κρέας a fine large piece, Id.
high-spirited, impetuous, dashing, generous, gay, τὸ νεανικώτατον the gayest, most dashing feat, Id.; so, ν. καὶ μεγαλοπρεπεῖς τὰς διανοίας Plat.; μέγα καὶ νεανικὸν φρόνημα Dem.
in bad sense, headstrong, wanton, insolent, Plat.
of things, vehement, mighty, Eur., Arist.
adv. νεανικῶς, vigorously, Ar.
violently, wantonly, τύπτειν, τωθάζειν Id.
Dep. to be in one's youth, Xen.
a youth, Hdt., attic
a young woman, girl, maiden, Il., Trag.; of a young married woman, Eur.
as adj. youthful, Id.
new, Anth.
singing youthfully, Anth.
a new city, prop. n. of several cities (like our Newtown), esp. Neapolis, Naples.
young, youthful, Il., Trag.; νεαροί youths, Aesch.;— τὸ ν. youthful spirit, Xen.
of things, new, fresh, νεαρὰ ἐξευρεῖν Pind.; ν. μυελός Aesch.
of events, new, recent, Soph.
adv. -ρῶς, youthfully, rawly, Luc.
sc. χορδή the lowest of the three strings which formed the old musical scale (the other two being ἡ μέση and ἡ ὑπάτη), Plat.

entry.etym: a poet. Sup. of νέος, as μέσατος of μέσος
entry.sense: the last, uttermost, lowest, Hom.; ὑπαὶ πόδα νείατον Ἴδης at the lowest slope of Ida, Il.:—c. gen., πόλις νεάτη Πύλου a city on the border of Pylos, Id.
of Time, latest, last, Soph.; τίς ἄρα νέατος λήξει, i. e. ὥστε νέατος γενέσθαι, Id.; νέατον as adv. for the last time, Eur.
a ploughing up of fallow land, Xen.
to plough up anew, of fallow land, Lat. agros novare, Ar.:—Pass., νεωμένη (sc. γῆ) land new-ploughed, Lat. novale, Hes.
of a fawn, Anth.
clad in fawnskin, Anth.
to wear a fawnskin at the feast of Bacchus, or, as trans., to robe in fawnskins, Dem.
a fawnskin, esp. as the dress of Bacchus and the Bacchantes, Eur.
the young of the deer, a fawn, Hom., etc.; πέδιλα νεβρῶν fawnskin brogues, Hdt.
fawn-like, of Bacchus, Anth.
new-born, just born, Od.
fresh-blown, young, Eur.
newly whetted or sharpened, Il.
newly kneaded: νεήλατα, τά, new cakes, Dem.
newly come, a new-comer, Il., Hdt.
castrated when young, Anth.
new-sounding, Hhymn.

entry.etym: irreg. fem. comp. (cf. πρέσβειρα) of νέος, as νέατος, νείατος is Sup.
entry.sense: lower, νειαίρῃ δ’ ἐν γαστρί in the lower part of the belly, Il.
one who wrangles with another, c. gen., Hes.
to quarrel or wrangle with one, c. dat., Il.:—absol., Hom.; part. νεικέων, obstinately, Hdt.
trans. to rail at, abuse, upbraid, revile, c. acc. pers., Hom.
a quarrel, wrangle, strife, Hom., Hdt., etc.
strife of words, railing, abuse, a taunt, reproach, Il., Hdt.
a strife at law, dispute before a judge, Od.
battle, fight, Hom.; ν. φυλόπιδος Od.; of dissensions between whole nations, νεῖκος πρὸς Καρχηδονίους Hdt.
cause of strife, matter of quarrel, Soph.
from the Nile, Anth.
Nile-born, Anth.
a Nilometer, a rod graduated to shew the rise and fall of the Nile, Strab.
watered by the Nile, Anth.
the Nile, first in Hes.;—in Hom. the river is called Αἴγυπτος.
situate on the Nile, Anth.
in or on the Nile:—fem., Νειλῶτις χθών the land of Nile, Aesch.
from the bottom, νειόθεν ἐκ κραδίης from the bottom of his heart, Il.
at the bottom, δάκε νειόθι θυμόν it stung him to his heart's core, Hes.: c. gen., νειόθι λίμνης Il.
to take a green crop off a field, by which it is freshened and prepared for corn, Xen.
Lat. novale, new land, i. e. land ploughed up anew after being left fallow, fallow-land, Il.; νειὸς τρίπολος a thrice-ploughed fallow, Hom.: in attic also νεός, Xen.
one who breaks up a fallow, Anth.
a heap of slain, ἐν αἰνῇσιν νεκάδεσσιν (epic dat. pl.) Il.
messenger of the dead, Luc.
to conduct the dead, Luc.
a school of the dead, Luc.
of or for the dead, Luc. adv. -κῶς, Id.
laden with the dead, Anth.
receiving the dead, Aesch.
a cemetery, mausoleum, Luc.
the cinerary urns dug out of the tombs of Corinth, Strab.
city of the dead, a suburb of Alexandria used as a burial place, Strab.
conducting the dead, of Charon, Eur., Luc.
a dead body, corpse, Hom., etc.: —in pl. the dead, as dwellers in the nether world, Od.; τοὺς ἑαυτῶν ν. their own dead, of those killed in battle, Thuc.
as adj., νεκρός, ή, όν, dead, Pind.:— comp. -ότερος Anth.
to ferry the dead, of Charon, Luc.
a corpse-bearer,
robbery of the dead, Plat.
murderer of the dead, Anth.
burying the dead, Polyb.
to make dead:—Pass. to be dead, νεκρωθείς Anth.; νενεκρωμένος NTest.
to mortify, NTest.
corpse-like, Luc.
a burial-place, Anth.
a state of death, deadness: death, NTest.
nectarous, of garments, prob., scented, fragrant, or generally, divine, beautiful, Il.:—literally, ν. σπονδαί libations of nectar, Pind.
nectar, the drink of the gods, as ambrosia was their food, Hom., etc.; poured like wine by Hebe, and mixed with water, Id.
metaph., νέκταρ μελισσᾶν, i. e. honey, Eur.: of perfumed unguent, Anth.:—Pind. calls his Ode ν. χυτόν.
a rite by which ghosts were called up and questioned, name for Od. II
an oracle of the dead, a place where ghosts were called up and questioned, Hdt.
ferrying the dead, of Charon, Anth.
bearing the dead, of a bier, Id.
a dead body, a corpse, corse, Hom., Hdt., Soph., etc.:— in pl. the spirits of the dead, Lat. Manes, inferi, in Od., Il.
as adj. dead, Soph., Anth.
Nemea, a wooded district between Argos and Corinth, Pind., etc.
Nemean, Pind.
Νέμεα, poet. Νέμεια, (sc. ἱερά), τά, the Nemean games, celebrated in the second and fourth years of each Olympiad, Id., Thuc.
Mid., νεμέθοντο the cattle were grazing, feeding, Il.
Nemean, Eur., etc.; also Νέμεος, Theocr.; Νεμειαῖος, Hes.; Νεμεαῖος, Pind.
to feel just resentment, to be wroth at undeserved good or bad fortune (cf. νέμεσις), properly of the gods, Il., Hes.; ν. τινι to be wroth with a person or at a thing, Hom.
Mid. and Pass., properly, to be displeased with oneself: to take shame to oneself, feel shame, Hom.
Mid. very much like the Act., c. dat. pers., Id.; c. acc. et inf. to be indignant at seeing, Od.; c. acc. rei, νεμεσσᾶται κακὰ ἔργα visits evil deeds upon the doers, Id.
disposed to just indignation, Arist.
causing indignation or wrath, νεμεσσητὸν δέ κεν εἴη 'twere enough to make one wroth, Il., etc.; so Soph., etc.
to be regarded with awe, awful, Il., Theocr.
epic Dep. to be wroth with another, c. dat., Hom.; c. acc. rei, to be wroth with one for a thing, Il.; c. acc. et. inf. to be angry or amazed that . . , Id.
like νεμεσάομαι, to feel shame, c. acc. et inf., Id.
to dread, θεοὺς νεμεσίζετο he stood in awe of the gods, Od.
properly, distribution of what is due; hence a righteous assignment of anger, wrath at anything unjust, just resentment, Hom.: indignation at undeserved good fortune, Arist.
of the gods, indignation, wrath, ἐκ θεοῦ ν. Hdt., Soph.
the object of just resentment, Hom.; οὐ νέμεσις [ἐστί] 'tis no cause for wrath that . . , c. inf., Id., Soph.
indignation at one's own misdeed, a sense of sin, Il.
Νέμεσις, ιος, as prop. n., voc. Νέμεσι, Nemesis, the impersonation of divine wrath, Hes.: in Trag., the goddess of retribution.
an avenger, Aesch.
a wooded pasture, glade, Lat. nemus, Il., Soph.

to deal out, distribute, dispense, of meat and drink, Hom., etc.; of the gods, νέμει ὄλβον Ὀλύμπιος ἀνθρώποισιν Od.; μοῖραν ν. τινί to pay one due respect, Aesch., etc.:—Pass., ἐπὶ τοὺς Ἕλληνας νέμεται is freely bestowed upon them, Hdt.; κρέα νενεμημένα portions of meat, Xen.
Mid. to distribute among themselves, and so, to have as one's portion, possess, enjoy, Hom., etc.
to dwell in, inhabit, Id.: absol. to dwell, Hdt.
to spend, pass, αἰῶνα, ἡμέραν Pind.
Act. much like Mid. to hold, possess, γῆν, χώραν, πόλιν Hdt., attic:—Pass., of places, to be inhabited, Hdt.; of a country, to maintain itself, be constituted, Thuc.
to hold sway, manage, Hdt., Aesch.:— ν. οἴακα to manage the helm, Aesch.; ν. ἰσχὺν ἐπὶ σκήπτροισι to support one's strength on staves, Id.; ν. γλῶσσαν to use the tongue, Id.
like νομίζω, to hold, consider as so and so, σὲ νέμω θεόν Soph.; προστάτην ν. τινά to take as one's patron, Arist.
of herdsmen, to pasture or graze their flocks, drive to pasture, tend, Lat. pascere, Od., Hdt., attic, etc.:—metaph., ν. χόλον Soph.

Mid., of cattle, to feed, i. e. go to pasture, graze, Lat. pasci, Hom., etc.: c. acc. cogn. to feed on, Hdt., etc.; of men, to eat, Soph.; of fire, to consume, devour, Il., etc.; of cancerous sores, to spread, ἐνέμετο πρόσω Hdt.
c. acc. loci, ὄρη νέμειν to graze the hills [with cattle], Xen.: Pass., [τὸ ὄρος] νέμεται βουσί Xen.
metaph., πυρὶ νέμειν πόλιν to give a city to the flames, Hdt.: Pass., πυρὶ χθὼν νέμεται the land is devoured by fire, Il.
newly watered, Il.
newly married, a young husband or wife, Hdt.; ν. νύμφη, κόρη Aesch., Eur.
new-born, Aesch., Plat.
new-born, young, Od., Theocr.

entry.etym: contr. for νεόγονος, Hdt., Aesch., etc.

entry.sense: newly painted or written, Anth.
with young limbs, Pind.
a Spartan word, newly enfranchised, Thuc.; Helots were called Νεοδαμώδεις when set free for service in war, Xen.
newly stripped off, Od.
newly flayed, βοῦς Xen.
of dramas, newly brought out, Luc.
newly tamed, πῶλος Hhymn.; γάμοι a newly formed marriage, Eur.
newly tamed, of horses: metaph. new-wedded, Eur.
new-built, Pind., Anth.
fresh-plucked, βωμοὶ ν. altars wreathed with fresh-plucked leaves, Theocr.
just having run, Babr.
newly yoked: metaph. new-married, Eur.
newly, lately, Soph.
fresh budding or sprouting, Il., Hes.
of animals, new-born, Anth.
metaph. fresh, εὐφροσύνη Hhymn.; ν. αὔξεται grows with youthful vigour, Pind.
just giving milk, Aesch.
youthful passion, Il.
newly built, Pind.
newly settled, Thuc.
whose grief is fresh, freshgrieving, Hes.
having lately inherited, Anth.
fresh spun, Theocr.
just slain, Eur.
fresh-chiselled, Ar.
new and strange, unheard of, Aesch.
entry.etym: -κοτος seems to be a mere termin.

entry.sense: newly mixed: metaph. newly made, νεοκρᾶτα φίλον Aesch.
newly founded or built, Hdt., Thuc.
lately or just killed, Pind.
a band of youths, the youth of a nation, Lat. juventus, Aesch., Theocr.
just bathed, Hhymn.
to go or come (mostly with fut. sense), πάλιν ν. to go away or back, return, Hom.; οἶκόνδε νέεσθαι Id.; of streams, to flow back, Il.
fresh-mourning, Od.
lately built or made, Anth.
fresh curdled, fresh made, Babr.
newly become rich, upstart (cf. Fr. nouveau riche), Dem., Arist.
newly washen, Od.
newly shorn, Soph.
befitting young people, youthful, extravagant, Plut.
fresh-sawn, Od.
surname of Pyrrhus, son of Achilles, new-warrior, because he came late to Troy, Soph., Eur.
newly-founded, Aesch.
fresh-reeking, Soph.
fresh-flowing, Soph., Anth.
newly drawn, Aesch.
newly arisen, new, Soph.
new and sparkling, with all the gloss on, Pind.
newly taken as booty, Anth.
newly cleaned, Il., Plut.
new-carved, Anth.
newly drawn, Aesch.
fresh-plucked, Soph.

young, youthful, Hom.; or alone, νέοι youths, Il., Hes., etc.; in attic with Art., ὁ νέος, οἱ νέοι, Ar., etc.:— τὸ νέον, = νεότης, Soph.; ἐκ νέου from a youth, from youth upwards, Plat., etc.; ἐκ νέων Arist.
suited to a youth, youthful, Lat. juvenilis, Aesch., Eur.
of things, new, fresh, Il., attic
of events, new, strange, τί νέον; Aesch.; μῶν τι βουλεύει νέον; Soph.

neut. νέον as adv. of Time, newly, lately, just, just now, Hom., attic; also with the Art., καὶ τὸ παλαιὸν καὶ τὸ νέον Hdt.: comp. adv. νεωτέρως Plat.; Sup. νεώτατα most recently, Thuc.;—also, ἐκ νέας, ionic ἐκ νέης, anew, afresh, Lat. denuo, Hdt.
for νεώτερος, νεώτατος, v. νεώτερος: the orig. comp. and Sup. were νεαρός, νέατος.
newly sown, fresh-sown, Aesch.
to hatch, Ar.
to build a nest:—Pass., ὅσα ἦν νενεοσσευμένα ὀρνίθων γένεα as many as had their nests built, Hdt.
a nest of young birds, a nest, Hdt., attic
a young bird, nestling, chick, Ar.
rearing chickens, Anth.
a young bird, nestling, chick, Il., Soph., etc.
any young animal, as a young crocodile, Hdt.; of young children, Aesch., Eur.
Pass. to be reared as in the nest, of a child, Ar.
newly twisted, νευρή Il.
fresh-slain, Soph., Eur.
newly initiated, Plat.
newly wrought, Il.
newly made, Il.
youth, Lat. juventa, Il., Eur., etc.
youthful spirit, impetuosity, Hdt.: in bad sense, rashness, petulance, Plat., etc.
collective, like νεολαία, a body of youth, the youth, Lat. juventus, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
newly cut, Theocr.
having just brought forth, Eur.
fresh cut or ploughed, Aesch.; ν. πλήγματα newly inflicted, Soph.
fresh cut off, fresh cut, ἕλιξ Eur.
to make new, renew, Anth.
new-made, Plat., Plut.
lately wounded, Il., Hes.
newly trodden, Anth.
of blood, fresh-shed, Eur.
newly planted: metaph. a new convert, neophyte, NTest.
newly imprinted, Soph.
new, Aesch., Eur., Ar.
of political innovations, νεοχμόν τι ποιέειν, = νεοχμόω, Hdt.
to make political innovations, Lat. res novas tentare, πολλὰ νεόχμωσε caused many innovations, Thuc.
with the first down or beard, Anth.
to renovate, renew, νέωσον Aesch.:—Mid., τάφους ἐνεώσατο had them renewed, Anth.
young ones, children, Od., Theocr.
entry.etym: An old word of uncertain deriv.

entry.sense: underground, anth.
the courier of the dead, Luc.
lower, nether, Lat. inferior, a comp. without any Posit. in use (νέρθε, ἔνερθε), Aesch.
mostly of the world below, Trag.; ἡ νερτέρα θεός Soph.; νέρτεροι, Lat. inferi, the dead, Aesch., etc.; also, ν. πλάκες, χθών, δώματα, of the realms below, Soph., Eur.
an unknown bird of prey, Ar.
a nod or sign, Thuc.; νεύματος ἕνεκα for a mere nod, i. e. without cause, Xen.
a string or cord of sinew, a bowstring, Hom., Hes., etc.
with sounding strings, Anth.
a sinew, tendon; in pl., the tendons of the feet, Il., Plat.
metaph. in pl., τὰ νεῦρα τῆς τραγῳδίας, of lyric odes, their sinews, vigour, Ar.; τὰ νεῦρα τῶν πραγμάτων Aeschin.
gut, cord made of sinew, for fastening the head of the arrow to the shaft, Il.: the cord of a sling, Xen.
plaited with sinews, Anth.
to stitch or mend shoes, Xen.
one who stitches with sinews, a mender of shoes, cobbler, Ar., Plat.
drawn by the string, ν. ἄτρακτος the arrow drawn and just ready to fly, Soph.
drawn by strings, moved by strings, of puppets, Hdt., Xen.
stretched by sinews, made of gut, Anth.
delighting in the bowstring or in the lyre, Anth.
to nod, of a warrior threatening his foe, Il.; of one making signs, Od.; of one fainting, Id.
one must swim, Plat.
able to swim, Plat.
to nod or beckon, as a sign, Hom.: c. inf. to beckon to one to do a thing, in token of command, Hom., Eur.
to nod or bow in token of assent, Hom., Soph.:—c. acc. et inf. to promise that, Il.:—c. acc. rei, to grant, promise, Soph., Eur.
generally, to bow the head, bend forward, of warriors charging, Il.; of ears of corn, Hes.; ν. κάτω to stoop, Eur.:—c. acc. cogn., ν. κεφαλήν Od.
to incline in any way, ν. εἴς τι to incline towards, Thuc.:—of countries, like Lat. vergere, to slope, ν. εἰς δύσιν Polyb.

entry.etym: only in nom. and in epic gen. νεφεληγερέταο
entry.sense: cloud-gatherer, cloud-compeller, of Zeus, Hom.
a cloud, Hom., etc.
metaph., νεφέλη δέ μιν ἀμφεκάλυψεν κυανέη, of death, Il.; ἄχεος ν. a cloud of sorrow, Hom.; Κενταύρου φονίᾳ νεφέλᾳ, i. e. with his blood, Soph.
a bird-net, Ar.
a cloud-centaur, Luc.
Cloud-cuckoo-town, built by the birds in Ar.
a Cloud-cuckoo-man, Ar.

entry.etym: as if from νεφελόω to form clouds
entry.sense: clouded, made of clouds, Luc.
cloud-like, Anth.
a cloud, mass or pile of clouds, Hom., etc.
metaph., θανάτου νέφος the cloud of death, Id.; so, σκότου ν., of blindness, Soph.; ν. οἰμωγῆς, στεναγμῶν Eur.; ν. ὀφρύων a cloud upon the brows, Id.
metaph. also a cloud of men or birds, Il., Hdt.; ν. πολέμοιο the cloud of battle, Il.
νεφρῖτις ( sc. νόσος) nephritis, a disease of the kidneys, Thuc.
in pl. the kidneys, Plat., etc.; so in dual, Ar.
to swim, Od., Hdt., etc.:— metaph. of shoes that are too large, ἔνεον ἐν ταῖς ἐμβάσιν I was floating in my shoes, as if they were boats, Ar.
to spin, of a spider, νεῖ νήματα Hes.: Mid., ἅσσα οἱ νήσαντο the threads which [the Fates] spun out to him, Od.:—Pass., τὰ νηθέντα Plat.
to heap, pile, heap up, πυρὰν νῆσαι to pile a funeral pyre, Hdt.; νήσαντες ξύλα Eur.:—Pass., ἀμφορῆς νενησμένοι Ar.; ἄρτοι νενημένοι Xen.
to serve a temple: ironically, to sweep clean, clean out, plunder a temple, Plat.
the office of a νεωκόρος, Anth.
the custodian of a temple, Lat. aedituus, Plat., Xen.
a title of Asiatic towns, which had built a temple in honour of their patron-god, as Ephesus was, ν. Ἀρτέμιδος NTest.
to haul a ship up on land, Lat. subducere navem, Polyb.
a ship-hauler, Arist.
newly bought, of slaves, Ar.
new, fresh, late, Lat. recens, νεώρη βόστρυχον τετμημένον a lock of hair but just cut off, Soph.; φόβος νεώρης Id.
a place were ships are taken care of, a dockyard, Ar., Thuc.; also in pl., like Lat. navalia, Eur., Thuc., etc. Cf. νεώσοικος.
a dock, Ar.:—in pl. sheds, slips, docks, in which ships might be built, repaired, or laid up, being parts of the νεώριον, Hdt., Thuc.

entry.etym: attic for ναός, as λεώς for λαός
entry.sense: a temple, Aesch., etc.

entry.etym: adverb of νέος, for νέως, as μεγαλωστί for μεγάλως
entry.sense: lately, just now, Hdt., Soph.
adv. next year, for next year, εἰς νέωτα Xen., Theocr.
youngest, Il.
most recent, Arist.
to attempt anything new, make a violent change, Thuc., Xen., etc.: ν. ἐς τὴν ἀσθένειαν to change [health] into sickness, Thuc.
to attempt political changes, make innovations or revolutionary movements, Lat. res novas tentare, Id., etc.
c. acc., ν. τὴν πολιτείαν to revolutionise the state, Id.:—Pass., ἐνεωτερίζετο τὰ περὶ τὴν ὀλιγαρχίαν Id.
innovation, revolutionary movement, Plat., etc.
an innovator, Plut.
innovation, revolution, Thuc.
innovating, revolutionary, Thuc. Arist.
younger, Il., Soph.:— οἱ νεώτεροι the younger sort, men of military age, Thuc.
too young, Od.:—c. gen., οἱ νεώτεροι τῶν πραγμάτων those who are too young to remember the events, Dem.
of events, newer, later, Pind.: metaph. later, worse, Soph.; νεώτερα alone, Lat. gravius quid, Hdt., attic; μῶν τι ν. ἀγγέλλεις; Plat.; νεώτερα βουλεύειν or ποιεῖν περί τινος Hdt., Thuc.
of political changes, νεώτερόν τι, an innovation, revolutionary movement, Hdt., Xen.
new-made, Il.
unwaking, νήγρετος ὕπνος a sleep that knows no waking, deep sleep, Od.; neut. as adv., νήγρετον εὕδειν without waking, Id.
the bowels, entrails, Il.
epith. of ὕπνος, either = ἡδύς, sweet, delightful; or
from νη-, δύνω, sleep from which one rises not, sound sleep, much like νήγρετος, Hom.
the stomach, Od., Hes., Aesch., etc.
the belly, paunch, Il., Hdt.; the womb, Il.: metaph., of earth, gremium telluris, Eur.
epic longer form of νέω D: epic aor1 νήησα: — to heap, heap or pile up, Hom.
to pile, load, [νῆας] νηήσας εὖ Il.: Mid., νῆα χρυσοῦ νηησάσθω let him pile his ship with gold, Id.
to spin, Plat.; 2nd sg. ionic imperf. νήθεσκες, Anth.
of or for a ship, δόρυ νήιον or νήιον alone, ship-timber, Hom.
unknowing of, unpractised in a thing, c. gen., Od.; absol., Il.
consisting of ships, στρατὸς ν. a fleet, Thuc.
unprofitable, Hom.
not horned, epic nom. pl. νήκεροι Hes.
incurable, neut. as adv. incurably, Hes.
not to hear, to give no heed to, disobey one, c. gen., Il.
swimming, Anth.
punishing without pity, ruthlessly punishing, Hes.
father of Nestor, Hom.:—epic adj. Νηλήιος, Il., etc.:—Patr., Νηλείδης, ου, ὁ, and Νηληιάδης, εω, or ᾱο, Hom.

pitiless, ruthless, Il.; νηλέϊ χαλκῷ with ruthless steel, Hom.; νηλέϊ ὕπνῳ relentless sleep, which exposes men without defence to ill, Od.; νηλεὲς ἦμαρ, i. e. the day of death, Hom.:— adv. νηλεῶς Aesch.
pass. unpitied, Soph.
nickname of philosophers, barefoot and looking after oil, Anth.
unshod, barefooted, Soph.
entry.etym: Commonly deriv. from νη-, ἦλιψ without shoe.

entry.sense: guiltless, harmless, Od.
that which is spun, a thread, yarn, Od., Hes., Eur.
certainty, truth, doric νᾱμέρτεια, Soph.

unerring, infallible, Od., Hes.; νημερτέα βουλήν a sure decree, i. e. one that will infallibly be enforced, Od.; νημερτέα εἰπεῖν or μυθήσασθαι to speak sure truths, Hom.; ionic adv. νημερτέως as trisyll., Od.
stillness in the air, a calm, νηνεμίης in a calm, Il.; γαλήνη ἔπλετο νηνεμίη there was a calm, a ceasing of all winds, Od.; ἐξ αἰθρίης τε καὶ νηνεμίης Hdt.
without wind, breezeless, calm, hushed, Il., Aesch., Eur.:—metaph., ν. ἔστης’ ὄχλον Eur.
a swimming, Batr.
busying oneself in a temple: a temple-keeper, Hes., Anth.
to go by sea, Anth.
bearing ships, Anth.

attic Particle of strong affirmation, like epic ναί; with acc. of the Divinity invoked, νὴ Δία (in familiar attic, νὴ Δί or νηδί), Ar.; also with the Art., νὴ τὸν Δία Id.; νὴ τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν, νὴ τὴν Ἄρτεμιν, νὴ τὸν Ποσειδῶ Id.
negat. Prefix, being a stronger form of ἀνα- privat., combined with short vowels, as in νηλεής, νήριθμος, νήκεστος, νήνεμος, or before consonants, as in νηκερδής, νηπενθής, νήποινος.
banishing pain, φάρμακον νηπενθές an opiate, Od.:— νηπενθής, as epith. of Apollo, Anth.
childhood, ἐν νηπιέῃ Il.:—in pl. childish tricks or follies, νηπιέῃσιν in childish fashion, in folly, Hom.
to be childish, play like a child, Il.
epic Dim. of νήπιος, infantine, childish, Il.
not yet speaking, Lat. infans, Hom.; νήπια τέκνα, βρέφος ν. Eur.:—also νήπια young animals, Il.
metaph. like a child, childish, silly, Hom., Hes.; without forethought, Hom., Aesch.
childhood, childishness, Plat.
of childish mind, silly, Strab.
with unbraided hair, Bion.
Lat. impune, Plat.
unavenged, Hom.:—neut. νήποινον as adv., Od.
φυτῶν νήποινος without share of fruitful trees, Pind.
Dep. to play child's tricks, Anth.
a little child, Il., Ar.
as adj. like a child, childish, Il.
Nereus, a sea-god, son of Πόντος (the sea), father of the Nereids, Hes.
a daughter of Nereus, a Nereid or Nymph of the sea, mostly in pl., Νηρηίδες, Hom.; Νηρεΐδες Hes.; attic Νηρῇδες Soph., Eur.
countless, Theocr.
countless, immense, Hes.:— hence the name of the Ithacan mountain, Νήριτον εἰνοσίφυλλον Hom.
of an island, insular, Eur.
an islet, Thuc.
to be or form an island, Polyb.
an islet, Strab.
spinning, Plat.
an islet, Hdt., Thuc.
of or belonging to an island: doric fem. νᾱσῖτις, ιδος, Anth.
an islander, Hdt., Ar., etc.
as adj. of or in an island, insular , Hdt., Eur.; νησιῶτις πέτρα an island rock, Aesch.
of or from an island, Hdt., Eur.; ὄνομα νησιωτικὸν Σαλαμῖνα θέμενον having given it the island name of Salamis, Eur.:— τὸ ν. insular situation, Thuc.
like an island, Strab.
an island-fight, Luc.
an island, Lat. insula, Hom., Hes., etc.; ἐν τᾷ μεγάλᾳ Δωρίδι νάσῳ Πέλοπος, i. e. in Peloponnese, Soph.; μακάρων νῆσοι, v. sub μάκαρ.
entry.etym: Perhaps from νέω to swim, as if floating land.

entry.sense: a fast, Hdt.
to fast, Ar.
not eating, fasting, of persons, Hom.; c. gen., νῆστις βορᾶς Eur.:—metaph., νῆστιν ἀνὰ ψάμμον over the hungry sand, Aesch.
νῆστις νόσος, λιμός hungry famine, Id.; νήστισιν αἰκίαις the pains of hunger, Id.; νήστιδες δύαι Id.
act. causing hunger, starving, πνοιαὶ νήστιδες Id.
unavenged, Anth.
heaped, piled up, Od.
a duck, Lat. anas (gen. a-nat-is), Hdt., Ar., etc.
a little duck, Ar.
breathless, Hes.
unmixed with wine, wineless, νηφ. μειλίγματα the offerings to the Eumenides, composed of water, milk, and honey, Aesch.
of persons, sober, NTest.
sober, Theogn., Soph.
to drink no wine, Theogn., Plat.; part. νήφων as adj. = νηφάλιος, Hdt., Plat.
metaph. to be sober, dispassionate, Xen.
to swim, Act. Od., Hes. also as Dep., Od., Anth.
soberness, Strab.
a pipe or whistle, used by the κελευστής to give the time in rowing, Ar.

entry.etym: the pres. νίπτω, from which the tenses are formed, only in late writers
entry.sense: to wash the hands or feet of another, Od.:—Mid., χεῖρας νίψασθαι to wash one's hands, Il., Hes.; so, νίψασθαι, absol., to wash one's hands, Od., etc.; νίψασθαι ἁλός to wash [with water] from the sea, Id.
generally to purge, cleanse, Soph., Eur.

to wash off, ἱδρῶ νίψεν ἀπὸ χρωτός washed off the sweat from the skin, Il.; αἷμα νίζ’ ὕδατι Id.:—Mid., χρόα νίζετο ἅλμην he washed the brine off his skin, Od.:—Pass., αἷμα νένιπται Il.—The word is commonly said of persons washing part of the person, while λούομαι is used of bathing, πλύνω of washing clothes.
a conqueror, Plut.

absol. to conquer, prevail, vanquish, Hom., etc.; ὁ νικήσας the conqueror, ὁ νικηθείς the conquered, Il.; ἐνίκησα καὶ δεύτερος καὶ τέταρτος ἐγενόμην I won the first prize, Thuc.; νικᾶν ἐπὶ πᾶσι κριταῖς in the opinion of all the judges, Ar.; c. acc. cogn., πάντα ἐνίκα he won all the bouts, Il.; παγκράτιον Thuc.; ν. Ὀλύμπια to be conqueror in the Ol. games, Id., etc.

of opinions, to prevail, carry the day, Hom., etc.; ἐκ τῆς νικώσης [γνώμης] according to the prevailing opinion, vote of the majority, Xen.:—impers., ἐνίκα (sc. ἡ γνώμη) it was resolved, Lat. visum est, c. inf., ἐνίκα μὴ ἐκλιπεῖν τὴν πόλιν it was carried not to leave the city, Hdt.; ἐνίκησε λοιμὸν εἰρῆσθαι it was the general opinion that λοιμός was the word, Thuc.
as law-term, ν. τὴν δίκην to win one's cause, Eur., Ar.
c. acc. pers. to conquer, vanquish, Hom., etc.; μὴ φῦναι τὸν ἅπαντα νικᾶι λόγον not to be born is best, Soph.; νίκης νικᾶν τινα to win victory over one, Od.

generally of passions, etc., to conquer, to overpower, Il.; βαρεῖαν ἡδονὴν νικᾶτέ με ye force me to grant you pleasure against my will, Soph.; c. inf., μηδ’ ἡ βία σε νικησάτω μισεῖν let not force prevail on thee to hate, Id.
Pass., νικᾶσθαί τινος, like ἡττᾶσθαι, to be inferior to, give way, yield to, Id., Eur.; ἢν τοῦτο νικηθῆις ἐμοῦ Ar.
victorious, Anth.
victory, Polyb.
victory in battle, Il., etc.; in the games, Pind., etc.:—c. gen. subjecti, νίκη φαίνεται Μενελάου plainly belongs to Menelaus, Il.; but c. gen. objecti, νίκη ἀντιπάλων victory over opponents, Ar.
generally, the upper hand, ascendancy, νίκην διασώζεσθαι to keep the fruits of victory, Xen.
as prop. n. Nike, the goddess of victory, Hes.
one must conquer, Eur.
belonging to a conqueror or to victory; ν. φίλημα a kiss as the conqueror's reward, Xen.
as Subst., νικητήριον (sc. ἆθλον), the prize of victory, Ar., Xen.; mostly in pl., Eur., Plat.
νικητήρια (sc. ἱερά), τά, the festival of victory, Xen.
likely to conquer, conducing to victory, Xen.; τὸ νικητικώτατον the most likely way to conquer, Plut.
to carry off as a prize, δάκρυα ν. to win naught but tears, Eur.
a conquering, victory, Pind.
bringing victory, Aesch.
（φέρομαι) bearing off the prize, conquering, victorious, Pind., Soph., etc.
prevailing in the council, Ar.
doric and Trag. enclit. acc. of 3rd pers. Pron., like epic and ionic μιν, for αὐτόν, αὐτήν, him, her, Pind., Trag.;—rarely for αὐτό, it, Pind., Aesch.; and for αὐτούς, -τάς (in pl.), Pind.
for dat. αὐτῷ, Id.
a washing vessel, basin, NTest.
water for washing, mostly in pl., Eur., Anth.
like νέομαι to go, go away, Hom., Pind.; c. acc. loci, to go to a place, Eur.
in Hdt. and attic λίτρον, carbonate of soda, Hdt.
snow, acc. formed from a nom. νίψ, which is not found, Hes.
a snowflake, in pl. snowflakes, Il., Hdt.; as a simile for persuasive eloquence, ἔπεα νιφάδεσσι ἐοικότα χειμερίῃσιν Il.:—the sg. in collective sense, a snowstorm, snow, Id., Pind.
generally, a shower of stones, Aesch., Eur.; ν. πολέμου the sleet of war, Pind.
as fem. adj., = νιφόεσσα, Soph.
falling snow, a snowstorm, Hom., Hdt., etc.
like snow, snowy, Polyb.

sic.seg: ni^fo-blhfailing on lembuf [] | /s, h=tos, o(, h(,

entry.sense: snow-stricken, snowclad, of mountains, Eur., Ar.
snowy, snowclad, snowcapt, Hom., Hes., etc.
piled with snow, Soph.
to snow, pers., ὅτε ὤρετο Ζεὺς νιφέμεν (epic inf.) when Zeus started to snow, Il.; ὅταν νίφηι ὁ θεός Xen.:—metaph., χρυσῶι νίφων falling in a shower of gold, Pind.
impers., νίφει it snows (cf. ὕω, συσκοτάζω), Ar.:—so in Mid., νιφάδος νιφομένας when the snow is snowing, Aesch.
Pass. to be snowed on, Hdt., Ar., etc.
intellectual, Plat., etc.

to perceive by the eyes, observe, notice, ὀφθαλμοῖς or ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς νοέειν Il.; distinguished from mere sight, τὸν δὲ ἰδὼν ἐνόησε Id.; οὐκ ἴδεν οὐδ’ ἐνόησε Hom.:—hence, θυμῶι νοέω καὶ οἶδα ἕκαστα Od., etc.: —so in Mid., Theogn., Soph.
absol. to think, suppose, Hom., Hdt., etc.; ἄλλα ν. to be of another mind, Hdt.:—part. νοέων, έουσα thoughtful, wary, discreet, Hom.
to think out, devise, contrive, purpose, intend, Od., Hdt.
c. inf. to be minded to do a thing, Il., Soph., etc.:—so in Mid., Il., Hdt.
to conceive of or deem to be so and so, ὡς μηκέτ’ ὄντα κεῖνον νόει Soph.
of words, to bear a certain sense, to mean so and so, πυθοίμεθ’ ἂν τὸν χρησμὸν ὅ τι νοεῖ Ar., Plat.
that which is perceived, a perception, thought, Hom., Hes., attic: as an emblem of swiftness, ὡσεὶ πτερὸν ἠὲ νόημα Od.
a thought, purpose, design, Hom., Ar.
like νόησις, understanding, mind, Hom.: disposition, Pind.
thoughtful, intelligent, Od.
in one's right mind, Hdt.
intelligence, thought, Plat.
intelligent, Arist.
perceptible to the mind, thinkable, opp. to visible (ὁρατός), Plat.
base-born, Eur.
birth out of wedlock, Plut.
to adulterate: Pass., aor1 inf. νοθευθῆναι Luc.
counterfeit charms, Anth.
a bastard, baseborn child, i. e. one born of a slave or concubine, opp. to γνήσιος, Lat. legitimus, Il., Hdt., attic; νόθη κούρη Il.
generally, spurious, counterfeit, supposititious, Plat.
of or for a herdsman's life, nomadic, pastoral, Arist.:—adv. -κῶς, like Nomads, Strab.
Numidian, Polyb.
customary: νόμαια, ων, τά, like νόμιμα, customs, usages, Hdt.
the chief of an Egyptian province (νομός), Hdt.
roaming about for pasture: οἱ Νομάδες roaming, pastoral tribes, Nomads, Hdt., attic; and as prop. n., Numidians, Polyb.
fem. adj. grazing, feeding, at pasture, Soph.
metaph., κρῆναι νομάδες wandering streams, Id.
that which is put to graze, i. e. a flock, Aesch.
a shepherd, herdsman, Hom., etc.
a dealer out, distributer, ἀγαθῶν Plat.
pl. νομέες, the ribs of a ship, Hdt.
to put to graze, drive afield, of the shepherd, Od.:—in Pass. of the flocks, to go to pasture, Plat.
βουσὶ νομοὺς ν. to eat down the pastures with oxen, Lat. depascere, Hhymn.
absol. to be a shepherd, tend flocks, Theocr.
a pasture, pasturage, Hdt., Soph.
fodder, food, Plat.
a feeding, grazing, of herds: metaph., νομὴ πυρός a spreading of fire, Polyb.; νομὴν ἔχειν, of a cancerous sore, to spread, NTest.
division, distribution, Hdt., Plat., etc.

to hold or own as a custom or usage, to use customarily, practise, Hdt.; ν. γλῶσσαν to have a language in common use, Id.; ν. οὔτε ἀσπίδα οὔτε δόρυ Id.:—Pass. to be the custom, be customary, Aesch.; σωφροσύνη νενόμιστο was the fashion, Ar.; —impers., ὡς νομίζεται as is the custom, Trag.:—part. νομιζόμενος, η, ον, customary, usual, Thuc.; τὰ νομιζόμενα customs, usages, Lat. instituta, Hdt., attic; τὰ νομισθέντα Eur.
to adopt a custom or usage, Ἕλληνες ἀπ’ Αἰγυπτίων ταῦτα νενομίκασι Hdt.
c. dat. to be used to a thing, νομίζουσιν Αἰγύπτιοι οὐδ’ ἥρωσιν οὐδέν, i. e. do not worship heroes, Id.: hence to make common use of, use, φωνῆι Id.; ἀγῶσι καὶ θυσίαις Thuc.

c. inf. to have a custom of doing, to be accustomed to do, Hdt.:—Pass. impers., γυμνοὺς εἰσιέναι νομίζεται it is customary for them . . , Ar.; νενόμισται καλέεσθαι it has been usual to be called, Hdt.
Pass. to be ordered and governed after old laws and customs, Id.

to own, acknowledge, consider as, τοὺς κακοὺς χρηστοὺς ν. Soph.; νομίσαι χρὴ ταῦτα μυστήρια Ar.:— θεὸν ν. τινά to hold or believe in one as a god, Plat., Xen.:—hence, νομίζειν τούτους [θεούς] to believe in these [as gods], Hdt.; οὓς ἡ πόλις νομίζει θεοὺς οὐ νομίζων not believing in the gods in which the State believes, Xen., Plat.: —but, νομίζειν θεοὺς εἶναι to believe that there are gods, Plat.; θεοὺς ν. οὐδαμοῦ Aesch.;—so that ν. τοὺς θεούς and ν. θεούς differ, the one being to believe in certain gods, the other to believe in gods generally, cf. ἡγέομαι III. 2 :—Pass., Ἕλληνες ἤρξαντο νομισθῆναι to be considered as . . , Hdt.
to esteem or hold in honour, Pind.:—Pass. to be in esteem, Plat.
c. acc. rei, to deem, hold, believe, τι περί τινος Id.
c. acc. et inf. to deem, hold, believe that, Soph., Xen.;—also, like δοκέω, c. inf. fut. to expect that . . , Soph.
Pass., with gen. of the person in possession, τοῦ θεῶν νομίζεται; whose sanctuary is it held to be? Id.
absol., νομίζοντα λέγειν to speak with full belief, Plat.
resting on law, conventional, Arist.:—adv. -κῶς, Id.
relating to the law, NTest. Plut.
learned in the law, a lawyer, NTest.
conformable to custom, usage, or law, customary, prescriptive, established, lawful, rightful, Eur.:— νόμιμόν [ἐστί] τινι ποιεῖν τι Xen.
νόμιμα, ων, τά, usages, customs, Hdt., attic
funeral rites, Lat. justa, Thuc.
adv. -μως, Plat.: comp. -ώτερον Xen.
of shepherds, pastoral, ν. θεός, i. e. Pan, Hhymn.; of Apollo, as shepherd of Admetus, Theocr.
usage, prescription, custom, ἡ ἁνθρωπεία ἐς τὸ θεῖον νόμισις the established belief about the Deity, Thuc.
anything sanctioned by usage, a custom, institution, Trag., Ar.
the current coin of a state, Hdt.
to be accounted, Plat.
Pass. to be current, Polyb.
written legislation, Strab.
（νόμος II) a composer of music, Plat.
one who explains laws, Plut.
a teacher of the law, Plut., NTest.
lawgiving, legislation, Plat.
to make law, Plat., Xen., etc.:— Mid. to make laws for oneself, frame laws, Plat.
trans. to ordain by law, τι Id., etc.:—Pass., impers., περὶ ταῦτα οὕτω σφι νενομοθέτηται it hath been so ordained by law, Hdt.
a law, ordinance, Plat.
a lawgiver, Thuc., Plat., etc.
at Athens, the Nomothetae were a committee of the dicasts charged with the revision of the laws, Dem.
to be settled by law, Plat.
trans. one must ordain by law, Arist.
of or for a lawgiver or legislation, Plat.: ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) legislation, Id.
of persons, fitted for legislation, Arist.
to pasture, Hom.

anything assigned, a usage, custom, law, ordinance, Lat. institutum, Hes.; νόμος πάντων βασιλεύς custom is lord of all, Pind. ap. Hdt.; κατὰ νόμον according to custom or law, Hes., Hdt., attic; poet. κὰν νόμον Pind.:— παρὰ νόμον contrary to law, Aesch.:—dat. νόμῳ by custom, conventionally, opp. to φύσει, Hdt., Arist.:—at Athens νόμοι were Solon.'s laws, those of Draco being called θεσμοί.
ἐν χειρῶν νόμῳ by the law of force, in the fight or scuffle, Hdt.; ἐν χειρὸς νόμῳ in actual warfare, Arist.; also, ἐς χειρῶν νόμον ἀπικέσθαι to come to blows, Hdt.
a musical mode or strain, Aesch., Plat., etc.; νόμοι κιθαρῳδικοί Ar.
a song sung in honour of some god, Hdt.; νόμοι πολεμικοί war- tunes, Thuc.
a feeding-place for cattle, pasture, Hom.; ν. ὕλης a woodland pasture, Od.
herbage, Hhymn.:—generally, food, Hes., Ar.
metaph., ἐπέων πολὺς νομός a wide range for words, Il.
an abode allotted or assigned to one, a district, province, Pind., Soph., etc.; νομὸν ἔχειν to have one's dwelling-place, Hdt., Ar.
one of the districts into which Egypt was divided, Hdt., etc.; applied also to other provinces, Id.
a guardian of the laws, Plat.
palsying the mind, Anth.
mind, perception, Hom., etc.; νόῳ heedfully, Od.; παρὲκ νόον senselessly, Il.; σὺν νόῳ wisely, Hdt.; νόῳ λαβεῖν τι to apprehend it, Id.; νόῳ ἔχειν to keep in mind, Id.
νοῦν ἔχειν means
to have sense, be sensible, Soph., Ar., etc.; περισσὰ πράσσειν οὐκ ἔχει νοῦν οὐδένα to aim too high has no sense, Soph.
to have one's mind directed to something, ἄλλος’ ὄμμα, θἀτέρᾳ δὲ νοῦν ἔχειν Id.; δεῦρο νοῦν ἔχε Eur.
the mind, heart, χαῖρε νόῳ Od.; so, νόος ἔμπεδος, ἀπηνής Hom.; ἐκ παντὸς νόου with all his heart and soul, Hdt., etc.
one's mind, purpose, τί σοι ἐν νόῳ ἐστὶ ποιεῖν; what do you intend to do? Id.; ἐν νόῳ ἔχειν, c. inf., to intend, Id.; νόον τελεῖν Il.
the sense or meaning of a word or speech, Hdt., Ar.
liable to sickness, sickly, Arist.
ν. κοίτη a bed of sickness, Id.:—adv., νοσερῶς ἔχειν τὸ σῶμα Arist.

to be sick, ill, to ail, whether in body or mind, Hdt., attic; τῆς πόλεως οὔπω νενοσηκυίας not yet having suffered from the plague, Thuc.; ν. ὀφθαλμούς to be affected in the eyes, Plat.; τὸ νοσοῦν, = νόσος, Soph.:—also of things, γῆ νοσεῖ Xen.
of passion, ν. μάτην to be mad, Soph.; θολερῷ χειμῶνι νοσήσας Id.
generally, to be in an unsound state, to suffer, νοσεῖ τὰ τῶν θεῶν Eur.; ν. τι τῶν ἀπορρήτων κακῶν Id.:—of states, to suffer from faction, be in disorder, Hdt.
care of the sick, nursing, Plut.
(from Pass.) matter discharged from a sore, Soph.
to tend a sick person, Babr.
a sickness, disease, plague, Soph., etc.
metaph. disease, affliction, Aesch., Plat.
of disorder in a state, Plat., etc.
diseased, unhealthy, Xen.
sickness, disease, malady, Hom., etc.
generally, distress, misery, suffering, sorrow, evil, Hes., Trag.
disease of mind, Trag.; θεία ν., i. e. madness, Soph.
of states, disorder, sedition, Plat.
a plague, bane, of a whirlwind, Soph.
care of the sick, Plat.
to come or go back, return, esp. to one's home or country, Hom., Soph., etc.
to return safe, to escape, Il., etc.
belonging to a return, ν. ἦμαρ the day of return, i. e. the return itself, Od.; so, ν. φάος Aesch.
able or likely to return, alive, safe, Lat. salvus, Od.
of plants, yielding a return, productive, τὸ ἐν σοι νοστιμώτατον what was most flourishing in you, Luc.
a return home or homeward, Hom.; c. gen. objecti, νόστος Ἀχαιΐδος his chance of returning to Greece, Od.; νόστον γαίης Φαιήκων thy way to the land of the Phaeacians, Id.
generally, travel, journey, ἐπὶ φορβῆς ν. a journey after (i. e. in search of) food, Soph.; ν. πρὸς Ἴλιον Eur.
to turn one's back upon a person, to turn away, shrink back, Hom.
to turn away from a person, c. gen., Od.
c. acc. to forsake, abandon, Hom., Soph.

after Hom., in Act., attic fut. νοσφιῶ: aor1 ἐνόσφισα: — to set apart or aloof, to separate, remove, Eur.:—metaph., ν. τινὰ βίου to separate him from life, i. e. kill him, Soph.; so, ν. τινά alone, Aesch.
to deprive, rob, τινά τι one of a thing, Pind.; also, τινά τινος Aesch., Eur.
Mid. to put aside for oneself, to appropriate, purloin, Xen.:— ν. ἀπὸ τῆς τιμῆς to appropriate part of the price, NTest.
but the Mid. is also just like the Act., to deprive, rob, Eur.

entry.etym: before a vowel or metri grat. -φῐν, though may also be elided
entry.sense: as adv. of Place, aloof, apart, afar, away, Hom.; ν. ἰδών having looked aside, Od.; νόσφιν ἀπό aloof from, Il.; νόσφιν ἤ . ., like πλὴν ἤ . . , besides, except, Theocr.
as prep. aloof or away from, far from, Hom., Hes.
without, forsaken or unaided by, Hom., Aesch.
of mind or disposition, νόσφιν Ἀχαιῶν βουλεύειν apart from the Achaians, i. e. of a different way of thinking, Il.; ν. Δήμητρος, Lat. clam Cerere, without her knowledge, Hhymn.
beside, except, νόσφι Ποσειδάωνος Od.; νόσφ’ Ὠκεανοῖο Il.
sickly, diseased, ailing, Plat., etc.
act. pestilential, baneful, Eur.
wet, damp, moist, Eur.; χειμὼν ν. a storm of rain, Thuc.
wet, νοτίαι εἰαριναί spring rains, Il.
to wet:—Pass. to be wetted or wet, Plat., Anth.
wet, moist, damp, Il., Aesch.:— ἐν νοτίῳ, i. e. the open sea, Od.
southern, ν. θάλασσα, i. e. the Indian ocean, Hdt.
moisture, wet, Eur.
the south or south-west wind, Lat. Auster, Od., Hdt., etc.
Notus is personified as god of the S. wind, Hes.
the south or south-west quarter, πρὸς νότον τῆς Λήμνου Hdt.; τὸ πρὸς ν. τῆς πόλεως Thuc.
choke-full of sense, clever: adv. -κῶς, Ar.
to put in mind, to admonish, warn, advise, Hdt., Aesch., etc.;—c. dupl. acc., τοιαῦτ’ ἄνολβον ἄνδρ’ ἐνουθέτει Soph.:—Pass., Id., etc.
admonition, warning, Aesch., Eur., etc.; τἀμὰ νουθετήματα given to me, Soph.
admonition, warning, Eur., Plat., etc.
to be admonished, Eur.
νουθετητέον, one must warn, Arist.
monitory, Plat., Xen.
the new moon, the first of the month, Pind., Ar.; ν. κατὰ σελήνην, to denote the true new moon, as opp. to the νουμηνία of the calendars, Hdt., Ar., etc.
good sense, discretion, Polyb.
with understanding, sensible, discreet, Polyb. adv. -χῶς, Id.
a pricking, puncture, Plut.
to watch by night, Plut.
nightly, name of Bacchus, from his nightly festivals, Anth.
one who rows by night, Anth.
fit for hunting by night, Xen.
to pass the night, Xen.: of soldiers, to keep watch by night, bivouac, Id.
nightly, Ar.
by night, nightly, Lat. nocturnus, Ar.; ν. γενέσθαι to happen by night, Id.
a bat, Lat. vespertilio, Od., Hdt., Ar.
appearing by night, Eur.
to summon by night, Eur.; so in Mid., Aesch.
a nightly summons, Eur.
covered by night, murky, Aesch.
roaring by night, Eur.
thief of the night, Anth.
the night-raven, Anth.
eating secretly by night, Anth.
nightly-sounding, Anth.
illumined by night alone, i. e. murky, dark, Simon.
nightly, Anth.
nightly-roaming-to-and-fro, Anth.
making to wander by night, rousing from bed, Aesch.; ν. εὐνή a restless, uneasy bed, Id.
roaming by night, Luc.
roaming by night, Eur.
solemnised by night, Aesch.
shining by night, Anth.
with shades dark as night, Id.
appearing by night, Aesch., Eur.
night-roaming, Aesch.
watching by night, Aesch.
a night-hunter, Xen.
to fight by night, Plut.
a night- battle, Hdt., Thuc.
roaming about by night, Ar.
to travel by night, Xen.
a night-journey, night-march, Polyb.
to keep guard by night, ν. τὰ ἔξω to watch the outer parts by night, Xen.
a night-watcher, warder, Lat. excubitor, Xen.
a temple of Night, Luc.
by night, Hes., Soph., etc.
to lead the bride to the bridegroom's house, γάμους ν. to court a marriage, Plut.
leader of the bride, Eur.
a temple of the nymphs, Plut.
of or sacred to the nymphs, Eur., Anth.
of a bride, bridal, nuptial, Pind., Eur.
as Subst.,
νυμφεῖον (sc. δῶμα), the bridechamber, Soph.
νυμφεῖα (sc. ἱερά), τά, nuptial rites, marriage, Id.
νυμφεῖα τοῦ σαυτοῦ τέκνου thine own son's bride, Id.
marriage, espousal, Soph., Eur.
in sg. the person married, καλὸν ν. τινι "a good match for him, " Eur.
nuptial, Eur.
one who escorts the bride to the bridegroom's house, negotiator of a marriage, Plat.
a bridegroom, husband, Eur.
a bride's-maid, Ar.
to lead the bride, to give in marriage, betroth, Eur.
to marry, of the woman, Lat. nubere, Soph.; but also of the man, Lat. ducere, Eur.; of both parties, νυμφεύετ’, εὖ πράσσοιτε Id.
Pass. c. fut. mid. νυμφεύσομαι; aor1 mid. et pass. ἐνυμφευσάμην, ἐνυμφεύθην:— to be given in marriage, marry, of the woman, Id.; ν. ἔκ τινος to be wedded by him, Id.
in Mid. of the man, to take to wife, Id.
epic voc. νύμφᾰ: doric νύμφᾱ:—, a young wife, bride, Lat. nupta, Il., Trag.
any married woman, Od., Eur.
a marriageable maiden, Il., Hes.
= Lat. nurus, daughter-in-law, NTest.

as prop. name, a Nymph, Hom.; θεαὶ Νύμφαι Il.; distinguished by special names, spring- nymphs being Ναϊάδες, sea- nymphs Νηρηίδες, tree- nymphs Δρυάδες, Ἁμαδρυάδες, mountain- nymphs ὀρεστιάδες, ὀρεάδες, meadow- nymphs λειμωνιάδες.
persons in a state of rapture, as seers and poets, were said to be caught by the Nymphs, νυμφόληπτοι, Lat. lymphatici.
the chrysalis, or pupa of moths, Anth.
of a bride, bridal, Eur., Ar.
a bridegroom, one lately married, Hom., etc.; in pl., τοῖς νεωστὶ νυμφίοις to the bridal pair, Eur.
bridal, Pind.
nymph-born, Anth.
to be deplored by wives, Aesch.
to dress a bride, Anth.
intr. to dress oneself as a bride, Eur.
dressing a bride:—generally, bridal, Eur.
caught by nymphs, Plat.
to escort the bride, Anth.
honouring the bride: μέλος ν. the bridal song, Aesch.
the bridechamber, NTest.
stronger form of νῦν, with pres. now, even now, Plat.
with past tenses, just now, ἃ νῦν δὴ ἐγὼ ἔλεγον Id.
familiar attic for νυνὶδέ, Id.

entry.etym: attic form of νῦν, strengthd. by -ῑ demonstr.
entry.sense: now, at this moment, Dem., Aeschin.
familiar attic for νυνὶ μέν, Ar.

now at this very time, Lat. nunc, οἳ νῦν βροτοί εἰσι mortals who now live, such as they are now, Il.; so in attic, οἱ νῦν ἄνθρωποι men of the present day; τὸ νῦν the present time, Plat.;— τὰ νῦν (often written τανῦν) used simply like νῦν, Hdt., attic
also of what is just past, just now, but now, Hom., Soph.
now, i. e. as it is, as the case now stands, Thuc.; so, καὶ νῦν even in this case, Xen.
besides the sense of Time, the enclit. νυν, νυ denotes
immediate sequence of one thing upon another, then, thereupon, thereafter, Hom.
also by way of Inference, then, therefore, Il., etc.
used to strengthen a command, δεῦρό νυν quick then! Il.; εἶά νυν, etc.; φέρε νυν, ἄγε νυν, σπεῦδέ νυν, σίγα νυν, etc., Xen.:—also to strengthen a question, τίς νυν; τί νυν; who then? what then? Id.

Lat. nox, night, i. e. either the night-season or a night, Hom., Hes., etc.; νυκτός by night, Lat. noctu, Od., attic; νυκτὸς ἔτι while it was still night, Hdt.; ν. τῆσδε Soph.; ἄκρας ν. at deadof night, Id.; also, νυκτί Hdt., Soph.;— νύκτα the night long, the livelong night, Hom.; νύκτας by nights, Id.;— μέσαι νύκτες midnight, Plat.

with Preps., ἀνὰ νύκτα by night, Il.; διὰ νύκτα Od.; εἰς νύκτα, εἰς τὴν ν. towards night, Xen.; ὑπὸ νύκτα just at night-fall, Thuc., Xen.; διὰ νυκτός in the course of the night, Plat.; ἐκ νυκτός just after night-fall, Xen.; πόρρω τῶν νυκτῶν far into the night, Id.:— ἐπὶ νυκτί by night, Il.; e)n nukti/, e)n th=| v.ἐν νυκτί, ἐν τῇ ν. Aesch., etc.
in pl., also, the watches of the night, Pind., Plat.:—the Greeks divided the night into three watches, Hom., etc.
the dark of night, Hom.
the night of death, Id.; ν. Ἄιδης τε Soph.
Νύξ as prop. n., the goddess of Night, daughter of Chaos, Il., Hes.
the quarter of night, i. e. the West, Hes.
a daughter-in-law, Hom.; in wider sense, any female connected by marriage, Il.
a bride, wife, Theocr., Anth.
Ν, ν, νῦ, τό, indecl., thirteenth letter of Greek alphabet; as numeral, νʹ = 50, but ͵ν = 50,000. ν is the dental or palatal liquid, corresponding with the mute δ. Dialectic changes,
doric, ν represents λ, v. Λ λ. 2.
attic and doric for μ, v. Μ μ. II. 2.
Euphonic changes:
into γ before the palatals γ κ χ, and before ξ, as ἔγγονος ἔγκαιρος ἐγχώριος ἐγξέω etc.
into μ before the labials β π φ, and before ψ, as σύμβιος συμπότης συμφυής ἔμψυχος; likewise before μ. as ἐμμανής.
into λ, before λ, as ἐλλείπω συλλαμβάνω.
into ρ before ρ, as συρράπτω: in compds. of ἐν ν sometimes remains, as ἔνρυθμος.
into σ before σ, as σύσσιτος πάσσοφος.

the so-called νῦ ἐφελκυστικόν is found with dat. pl. in σι, as ἀνδράσιν; 3rd pl. of verbs in σι, as εἰλήφασιν; 3rd sg.in -ε, -ι, as ἔκτανεν δείκνυσιν: the local termin. -σι, as Ἀθήνῃσι Ὀλυμπίασι; the Epic. termin. φι, as ὀστεόφιν; the numeral εἴκοσι; the Advs. νόσφι, πέρυσι; the enclit. Particles κέ and νύ. This ν was mostly used to avoid a hiatus where a vowel follows.
name of several hills sacred to Bacchus, Hhymn., etc.;—adj. Νύσιος, η, ον, Id.; Νυσήιος, Ar.
like Lat. meta, the name of two posts in the ἱππόδρομος:
the turning-post, so placed that the chariots driving up the right side of the course, turned round it, and returned by the left side (cf. καμπτήρ), Il.
the starting post, which was also the winning post, Hom.
to touch with a sharp point, to prick, spur, pierce, Il., Hes.; ἀγκῶνι νύξας having nudged him with the elbow, Od.; ν. γνώμην to prick it (and see what is in it), Ar.
to nod in sleep, to nap, slumber, Xen., Plat.
to be sleepy, napping, Lat. dormito, Ar., Plat.
to hang the head, Anth.
one that nods, nodding, Ar.
a nightly watch, Lat. pervigilium, Eur.
to watch the night through, to pass the night, Eur.
a night and a day, NTest.
nightly, i. e.
of persons, doing a thing by night, Hes., Aesch., etc.
of things, happening by night, Soph., Eur.
of places, dark as night, gloomy, Aesch., Eur.
toothless, Ar., Theocr.
ease from pain, Theocr.
an anodyne, Pind.
without pain, Pind.
act. soothing pain, anodyne, Soph.
sluggishness, dulness, Plat., etc.
sluggish, slothful, torpid, epith. of the ass, Il., Eur., etc.
of the understanding, dull, stupid, νωθέστερος somewhat dull, Hdt.
sluggish, slothful, torpid, Plat.
of or from us two, Hom.
without pause, unceasingly, continually, Hom.:—so, νωλεμέως, Il.; ν. ἐχέμεν to persevere, Id.; but, ν. κτείνοντο they were murdered without pause, i. e. one after the other, Od.
to deal out, distribute, esp. food and drink at festivals, Hom.
（νέμω III. 2) to direct, guide, control,
of weapons, to handle, wield, sway the lance, shield, rudder, Hom.; so metaph., νώμα πηδαλίῳ πόλιν was steering it, Lat. gubernabat, Pind.; πᾶν ν. ἐπὶ τέρμα Aesch.
of the limbs, to ply nimbly, γούνατα νωμᾶν Il.; πόδα ν. Soph.; ν. ὀφρύν to move the brow, Aesch.
to revolve in the mind, Od.: to observe, watch, Hdt., Trag.

entry.etym: epic for νώνῠμος, used when the penult. is to be long, Hom., Hes.

entry.sense: nameless, unknown, inglorious, Od., Aesch., Soph.
c. gen., Σαπφοῦς νώνυμος without the name of Sappho, i. e. without knowledge of her, Anth.
flashing, gleaming, of metal, Il.
with mailed back, Batr.
of the back or spine, ν. ἄρθρα the spinal vertebrae, Eur.
to turn one's back, Lat. terga dare, Eur.; c. acc. cogn., παλίσσυτον δράμημα νωτίσαι to turn about in backward course, Soph.
to cover the back of, τινά Eur.; πόντον νωτίσαι to skim the sea, Aesch.
that which covers the back, of wings, Eur.
the back, Lat. tergum, Il.; often in pl., like Lat. terga, Hom.; τὰ νῶτα ἐντρέπειν, ἐπιστρέφειν to turn the back, i. e. flee, Hdt.; νῶτα δεῖξαι Plut.; κατὰ νώτου from behind, in rear, Hdt., Thuc.
metaph. any wide surface, ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης Hom.; of plains, Pind., Eur.
the back or ridge, of a hill, Pind., Eur.; of a chariot, Eur.
carrying on the back: as Subst. a beast of burthen, Xen.
moving slowly and heavily, sluggish, Eur.
laziness, sluggishness, Il.
to comb or card wool, so as to make it fit for spinning, Od., etc.
of cloth, to full or dress it, Ar.
metaph. to dress, thrash, beat, ῥάβδοις ἔξαινον τὰ σώματα Plut.:—Pass., ξανθέν mangled, Anth.;—c. acc. cogn., ξαίνειν κατὰ τοῦ νώτου πολλὰς (sc. πληγάς) Dem.
to make yellow or brown, by roasting or frying, Ar.
Xanthias, name of a slave in Comedy, Ar.;—no doubt he had yellow hair; cf. πυρρίας.
yellow-haired, Solon., Theocr.
with yellow head, Anth.
yellow, of various shades; of golden hair, Hom.; so, ξανθαὶ ἵπποι bay or chestnut mares, Il.
Ξάνθος paroxyt., as prop. n.
a stream of the Troad, so called by gods, by men Scamander, Id.
a horse of Achilles, bayard, the other being Βαλίος, dapple, Id.
yellowness, esp. of hair, Strab.
to have yellow hair, Strab.
yellow by nature, ἕλικες Anth.
with yellow coat, Anth.
with yellow skin, Mosch.

entry.etym: ionic for ξενεῖον which is not used
entry.sense: a host's gift, given to a departing guest, Hom.; δῶρα ξεινήια Od.
one who takes charge of guests, Pind.
to be a ξεναγός, Xen., Dem.
to guide strangers, shew them the sights, Luc.: Pass., impers., ἄριστά σοι ξενάγηται your work as a guide has been done excellently, Plat.
a commander of auxiliary or mercenary troops (ξένοι), Thuc., Xen., etc. (The form is doric; but like many military terms, it was adopted in attic)
a stranger's guide, Plut.
one who cheats strangers, or who cheats his host, Eur.
aiding strangers, Pind.
at Sparta, expulsion of foreigners, an alien act, Thuc., Plat., etc.
to banish foreigners, Ar.
a female guest: a foreign woman, Aesch., etc.
(sub. γῆ), a foreign country, Soph., Xen.
the rights of a guest, hospitality, friendly entertainment or reception, Lat. hospitium, Od., Hdt., etc.

a friendly relation between two foreigners, or between an individual and a foreign state (cf. πρόξενος), ξεινίην τινὶ συντίθεσθαι, Lat. hospitium facere cum aliquo, Hdt.; κατὰ τὴν ξ. because of their friendly relations, Thuc.; πρὸς ξενίας τᾶς σᾶς by thy friendship with us, Soph.
the state or disabilities of an alien, ξενίας φεύγειν (sc. γραφήν) to be indicted as an alien, Ar.

to receive or entertain strangers, to receive as a guest, Lat. hospitio excipere, Hom., Hdt., etc.; ξ. τινὰ πολλοῖς ἀγαθοῖς to present with hospitable gifts, Xen.:—metaph., ὃν Ἄρης οὐκ ἐξένισεν, i. e. who fell not in battle, Soph.:—Pass. to be entertained as a guest, Hdt., attic
to astonish by some strange sight, Polyb.:—Pass. to be astonished, Id.
intr. to be a stranger, speak with a foreign accent, Luc.: to be strange or unusual, Id.

of or for a stranger, of foreign kind, opp. to ἀστικός, Eur.; ξενικά the taxes paid by aliens at Athens, Dem.;— τὸ ξ. the class of aliens, Arist.; τὸ ξ. (sc. δικαστήριον) the court in which aliens sued or were sued, Id.
of soldiers, hired for service, mercenary, Hdt., Xen. τὸ ξενικόν = οἱ ξένοι, a body of mercenaries, Ar., Thuc., etc.
= ξένιος, hospitable, friendly, Aeschin.:— ἡ ξενική friendly relation, as between host and guest, Arist.
foreign, alien, Hdt.; ξ. ὀνόματα foreign names, Plat.; of style, foreign, I. e. abounding in unusual words, Arist.

belonging to a friend and guest, hospitable, Ζεὺς ξένιος as protector of the rights of hospitality, Il., Aesch.:— τράπεζα ξ. the guests' table, Od.; ξένιός τινι bound to him by ties of hospitality, Hdt.

ξείνια, attic ξένια, ων, τά, friendly gifts, meat and drink, given to the guest by his host, Hom.; ξένια παρέσχε δαῖτα as a friendly gift, Aesch.; βοῦν ξένια ἔπεμψεν Xen.; ἐπὶ ξένια καλεῖν to invite any one to eat with you, Hdt., etc.; metaph., θάνατος ξένιά σοι γενήσεται Eur.
foreign, Pind., attic
the entertainment of guests, Thuc.
a living abroad, Luc.
to live abroad, Luc.
Dep. ξενιτεύομαι, to be in foreign service, Isocr.
one who murders guests, Eur.
one that devours guests or strangers, of the Cyclops, Eur.
ionic ξεινο-, to entertain guests or strangers, Hdt., Eur., etc.:—in late Gr. ξενοδοχέω, NTest.
one who receives strangers, a host, Od.
entertainment of a stranger, Xen.
a host, epith. of Bacchus, Anth.
full of strangers, Eur.
to sacrifice strangers, Strab.
to slay guests or strangers, Hdt., Eur.
to slay one's host, Eur.
slaying guests or strangers, Eur., Aeschin.
to enlist strangers, levy mercenaries, Dem., etc.
levying mercenaries, Polyb.
to have a strange feeling, feel strange or shy, Plut.
a guest-friend, I. e. any citizen of a foreign state, with whom one has a treaty of hospitality for self and heirs, confirmed by mutual presents (ξένια) and an appeal to Ζεὺς ξένιος, Hom.
of one of the parties bound by ties of hospitality, i. e. either the guest, or = ξεινοδόκος, the host, Id., Hdt., etc.
any one entitled to hospitality, a stranger, refugee, Od.
any stranger or foreigner, Hes., attic:—the term was politely used of any one whose name was unknown, and the address ὦ ξένε came to mean little more than friend, Soph.
a foreign soldier, hireling, mercenary, Thuc., Xen.
foreign, Soph., Eur., etc.
c. gen. rei, strange to a thing, ignorant of it, Soph.:—adv., ξένως ἔχω τῆς λέξεως I am a stranger to the language, Plat.
alien, strange, unusual, Aesch.
a lodging for guests or strangers, Soph.
hospitality, Od.
honouring strangers, Aesch.
to entertain strangers, to maintain mercenary troops, Thuc., Dem.
to murder strangers, Eur.
murdering strangers, Eur.
to make one's friend and guest, Aesch.
mostly in Pass., with fut. mid. ξενώσομαι: perf. ἐξένωμαι: aor1 ἐξενώθην:
to enter into a treaty of hospitality with one, Lat. hospitio jungi, c. dat., Hdt., Xen.; absol., Xen.
to take up his abode with one as a guest, to be entertained, Trag.
to be in foreign parts, to be abroad, Soph., Eur.: to go into banishment, Eur.
a guest-chamber, Eur.
a being abroad, Eur.
dry, ποτὶ ξερόν to the dry land, Od., Anth.
= Lat. sextarius, nearly a pint, NTest.
smoothed, polished, wrought, Hom., Hdt., attic; ξ. αἴθουσαι halls of polished stone, Il.
to smooth or polish by scraping, planing, filing, of a carpenter, Od., etc.
to parch up, dry up, Eur., Xen.:—Pass. to become or be dry, parched, Il., etc.
to lay dry, Lat. siccare, Thuc.
properly to rub dry with oil, without the use of the bath, Lex ap. Plut., Aeschin.
of the colour of withered vine-leaves, bright red, Juven.
( sc. γῆ) dry land, v. ξηρός III.
dry, Lat. siccus, opp. to ὑγρός, Hdt., Ar.; ξηροῖς ὄμμασι, Hor.'s siccis oculis, Aesch.
of bodily condition, withered, lean, haggard, δέμας Eur., Theocr.
like Lat. siccus, fasting, austere, harsh, Eur., Ar.; ἐν ξηροῖσιν ἐκτρέφειν Eur.
as Subst., ἡ ξηρά (sc. γῆ), dry land, Xen.; so, τὸ ξηρόν Hdt.; ναῦς ἐπὶ τοῦ ξηροῦ ποιεῖν to leave the ships aground, Thuc.
dryness, Plat., Xen.: ἡ ξ. τῶν νεῶν the dryness, i. e. soundness, of their timbers, Thuc.
to eat dry food, Anth., etc.

Ξ, ξ, ξῖ, τό, indecl., fourteenth letter of the Gk. alphabet: as numeral ξʹ = 60, but ͵ξ = 60,000: introduced in the archonship of Euclides, 403 B. C.—It is a double consonant, compounded of γς, κς, or χς. Changes

ξ in aeolic and attic appears as an aspirated form of κ, cf. ξυνός with κοινός, ξύν with cum;— or of σ, cf. ξύν with σύν, ξέστης with Lat. sextarius; and so in doric fut. of Verbs in -ζω, κομίξω κλᾳξῶ παιξῶ for κομίσω κλῄσω παίσω.
interchanged with σς, ionic διξός, τριξός for δισσός, τρισσός.
sword in hand, Eur.
sword in hand, Aesch., Eur.
a dagger, Thuc., etc.
a sword-belt, Plut.
slain by the sword, ξ. θάνατος death by the sword, Aesch.
slaying with the sword, Soph.
a sword, Hom.; distinguished from μάχαιρα, q. v.
the drawing of a sword, Plut.
drawing a sword, Aesch.
a sword-cutler, Ar.
an image carved of wood, Xen.: generally, an image, statue, Eur.
a carving of images, Luc.
a sculptor's chisel, anth.
with tawny wings, Eur.
of a colour, between ξανθός and πυρρός, yellowish, brown-yellow, tawny, epith. of the bee, Eur.; of the nightingale, Aesch., Eur., etc.
later of sound, shrill, thrilling, Babr., Anth.
a tool for scraping wood, a plane or rasp, Xen.
a sickle-shaped dagger, Id.
to carry wood, Dem.
a piece of wood, a stick, Polyb.
Mid. to gather wood, Xen.
of wood, wooden, Hdt., attic
metaph. wooden, νοῦς Anth.
to beat with a stick, cudgel, Polyb.
a cudgelling, Lat. fustuarium, Polyb.
hewing or felling wood, Xen.
wood cut and ready for use, firewood, timber, Hom.; ξύλα νήια ship- timber, Hes.; ξ. ναυπηγήσιμα Thuc.
in sg. a piece of wood, a post, Hom.: a perch, Ar.: a stick, cudgel, club, Hdt., Ar.
a collar of wood, put on the neck of the prisoner, Ar.:—also stocks, for the feet, Hdt., Ar.; cf. πεντεσύριγγος.
a plank or beam to which malefactors were bound, the Cross, NTest.
a money-changer's table, Dem.
πρῶτον ξύλον the front bench of the Athenian theatre, Ar.
of live wood, a tree, Xen.
built of wood, Strab.
to work wood, Hdt.
a working of wood, carpentry, Aesch.
eating wood, Strab.
to carry a stick, as the Cynics did, Luc.
a thicket, copse, Il.
the woodwork of a house, frame-work, Thuc.
epic for συν-είκοσι, twenty together, Od.

entry.etym: epic and ionic for ξύνειος, which does not occur
entry.sense: ξυνήια common property, common stock, Il.
a joint-owner, partner in a thing, c. gen., Hes.; ξυνάονες ἑλκέων, I. e. afflicted by sores, Pind.:—absol., ξυνάν a friend, Id.
the free, bounteous giver, Anth.

older form of κοινός, common, public, general, concerning or belonging to all in common, Il.; γαῖα ξυνὴ πάντων earth the common property of all, Id.; ξ. Ἐνυάλιος, i. e. war hath an even hand, is uncertain, Id.; ξ. πᾶσι ἀγαθόν Hdt.; ξυνὰ λέγειν to speak for the common good, Aesch.
friendly-minded, Anth.
rejoicing in common, Anth.

to shave, Hdt.: proverb. of great danger or sharp pain, ξυρεῖ ἐν χρῶι it shaves close, touches the quick, Soph.:—Mid. and Pass. to shave oneself or have oneself shaved, Hdt.; ξυρεῦνται πᾶν τὸ σῶμα they have their whole body shaved, Id.
keen as a rasor, Xen.
pass. close-shaven, Eur.; κουρᾷ ξυρήκει with close tonsure, Id.
a rasor, Hom., etc.:—proverb, ἐπὶ ξυροῦ ἵσταται ἀκμῆς ὄλεθρος ἠὲ βιῶναι death or life is balanced on a rasor's edge, Il.; ἐπὶ ξυροῦ τῆς ἀκμῆς ἔχεται ἡμῖν τὰ πράγματα Hdt.; βεβὼς ἐπὶ ξυρῷ τύχης Soph.
in pl., scrapings, Anth.
a graving tool, Lat. scalprum, Anth.
a xystis, a robe of fine material, a robe of state, Ar., Plat., etc.
spear-darting, Anth.
the polished shaft of a spear, Il., Hdt.
generally, a spear, lance, Il., Eur.
scraped, polished, Hdt.
a covered colonnade on the S. side of the gymnasium, where athletes exercised in winter, Xen., etc.: so called from its smooth and polished floor.
carrying a spear, Xen.
to scrape, plane, smooth or polish, Od.: metaph., ξῦσαι ἀπὸ γῆρας to scrape off, get rid of old age, Hhymn.:— Mid., παλτὸν ξύσασθαι to shape oneself a javelin-shaft, Xen.
to make smooth, work delicately, Il.
woe, woe! Lat. vae! Aesch.
to converse or chat with one, c. dat., Il.; ὀαριζέμεναι (epic inf.) Id.
a familiar friend, Od.
familiar converse, fond discourse, Il., Theocr.:—generally, ἡ γὰρ πολέμου ὀαριστύς such is war's intercourse, Il.
as concrete, προμάχων ὀαριστύς the company of out-fighters, Id.
familiar converse, fond discourse, chat, talk, Hhymn., Hes.
a song, lay, ditty, Pind.
a wife, in gen. pl., ὀάρων ἕνεκα σφετεράων Il.; contr. dat. pl., ἀμυνέμεναι ὤρεσσιν Id.
a name of the fertile islets in the Libyan desert, Hdt.
a small spit, Ar., Xen., etc.
a coin stamped with a spit, Plut.
the leg of a compass, Ar.
a spit, Il., Hdt., attic
ὀβ. λίθινος a pointed square pillar, obelisk, Hdt.
entry.etym: ὀβελός is prob. βέλος with ο prefixed.

entry.sense: an obol, as a weight, = 1/6th part of a δραχμή, worth rather more than three halfpence, Ar.; ἐν δυοῖν ὀβολοῖν θεωρεῖν, as we might say "to sit in the shilling gallery, " Dem.
to weigh obols: practise petty usury, Luc.
a weigher of obols, i. e. a petty usurer, Ar.
(sc. τέχνη), the trade of a petty usurer, usury, Arist.
the young of animals, Aesch., Eur.
doing deeds of violence, Il.
strong-minded, Hes.
daughter of a mighty sire, Il., Solon., etc.
strong, mighty, Il.:—neut. as adv., ὄβριμον ἐβρόντησε he thundered mightily, Hes.
entry.etym: From βρι-, βριαρός, with ο prefixed.
poetic for ὄγδοος, as τρίτατος for τρίτος
entry.sense: the eighth, Hom.
eighty, Lat. octoginta, Thuc., etc.:—ionic and doric ὀγδώκοντα, Il., Theocr.
eighty-four, NTest.
eighty years old, Luc.:— ionic and doric ὀγδωκοντα-έτης, ες, Solon.
eightieth, Thuc., etc.
eighth, Lat. octavus, Hom., etc.

ὅγε, ἥγε, τόγε, the demonstr. Pron. ὁ, ἡ, τό, made more emphatic by the addition of γε, like Lat. hicce, haecce, hocce, he, she, it, Hom., Hes., etc.:— γε may be rendered sometimes by indeed or at least, Lat. quidem.
Adverbial usages:
dat. τῇγε, of place, here, on this very spot, Il.
acc. neut. τόγε, on this account, for this very reason, Hom.
Dep. to bray, of the ass, Luc.

entry.etym: a name of Athena at Thebes, Aesch.

entry.sense: bulky, swollen:—metaph. stately, pompous, Xen.; τὸ ὀγκηρόν trouble, Arist.
a brayer, i. e. an ass. Anth.
a case for arrows and other implements, Od.
the barb of an arrow, in pl. the barbed points, Il.
entry.etym: From same Root as Lat. uncus.

entry.sense: bulk, size, mass, Lat. moles, Plat., etc.
a bulk, mass, heap, ὄ. φρυγάνων a heap of fagots, Hdt.; σμικρὸς ὄ. ἐν σμικρῷ κύτει, of a dead man's ashes, Soph.; ὅ. γαστρός, of a child in the womb, Eur.
metaph. weight, trouble, Soph.
weight, importance, dignity, pride, and in bad sense self-importance, pretension, Id., Eur., etc.
entry.etym: From Root ΕΓΚ, in ἐνεγκεῖν to bear.

entry.sense: to heap up a mound:—Pass., Anth.

metaph. to bring to honour and dignity, exalt, extol, Eur.; ὀγκῶσαι τὸ φρόνημα to puff up one's conceit, Ar.; so in Mid., Id.:—Pass. to be puffed up, inflated, Eur.: in good sense, to be honoured, Id.
Pass. to be puffed up, Ar.
swelling, rounded, Xen.
metaph. swollen, inflated, Plat.
heaped up, Anth.
to move in a straight line, properly of ploughers or mowers; metaph., ὀγμ. στίβον to trail one's weary way, of a lame man, Soph.; ὤγμευον αὐτῷ they were marching in file before him, Xen.
any straight line, a furrow in ploughing, Il.: a swathe in reaping, Id.
metaph. the path of the heavenly bodies, Hhymn.; ὄγμος ὀδόντων a row of teeth, Anth.
a pear-tree, Od.
= ἐνόδιος:—ὁδαῖα, ων, τὰ goods with which a merchant travels, his freight, Od.

by biting with the teeth, Lat. mordicus, Hom.; ὀδὰξ ἕλον οὖδας they bit the ground, of men in the agonies of death, Il.; so, γαῖαν ὀδὰξ ἑλόντες Eur.; ὀδὰξ ἐν χείλεσι φύντες biting the lips in smothered rage, Od.; διατρώξομαι ὀδὰξ τὸ δίκτυον Ar.
to feel a biting, stinging pain, feel irritation, Xen.
to export and sell; generally, to sell, Eur.:—Pass. to be carried away and sold, Id.

demonstr. Pron., this, formed by adding the enclit. -δε to the old demonstr. Pron. τό, and declined like it: epic dat. pl. τοῖσδεσσι, τοῖσδεσσιν and τοῖσδεσι; ionic τοισίδε:—ὅδε, like οὗτος opp. to ἐκεῖνος, to designate the nearer as opp. to the more remote; but ὅδε is also deictic, i. e. refersto what can be pointed out. This deictic force is more emphat. in the forms ὁδί, ἡδί, etc. [ῑ], which belong to Com. and Oratt., and are never used in Trag.:

of Place, like French voici, to point out what is before one, Ἕκτορος ἥδε γυνή here is the wife of Hector, Il., etc.:—also with Verbs, here, ὅστις ὅδε κρατέει who holds sway here, Id.; ἔγχος μὲν τόδε κεῖται here it lies, Id.:—in Trag., to indicate the entrance of a person on the stage, καὶ μὴν Ἐτεοκλῆς ὅδε χωρεῖ and see here comes . . , Eur.; ὅδ’ εἰμ’ Ὀρέστης here I am—Orestes, Id.
so also with τίς interrog., τίς ὅδε Ναυσικάᾳ ἕπεται; who is this following her.? Od.
in Trag., ὅδε and ὅδ’ ἀνήρ, emphatic for ἐγώ; so, τῇδε χερί with this hand of mine, Soph.
of Time, to indicate the immediate present, ἥδ’ ἡμέρα Id., etc.; τοῦδ’ αὐτοῦ λυκάβαντος on this very day, Od.; νυκτὸς τῆσδε in the night just past, Soph.
ἐς τόδε, elliptic c. gen., ἐς τόδ’ ἡμέρας Eur.; ἐς τόδε ἡλικίης Hdt.
in a more general sense, to indicate something before one, οὐκ ἔρανος τάδε γ’ ἐστίν these preparations which I see are not an ἔρανος, Od., ; Ἀπόλλων τάδ’ ἦν this was Apollo, Soph.
to indicate something immediately to come, ταῦτα μὲν Λακεδαιμόνιοι λέγουσι, τάδε δὲ ἐγὼ γράφω Hdt.
Adverbial usage of some cases:
fem. dat. τῇδε , of Place, here, on the spot, Lat. hac, Hom., etc.:—of Way or Manner, thus, Il., attic
acc. neut. τόδε, hither, to this spot, Hom.; δεῦρο τόδε Id.
therefore, on this account, Od.; acc. neut. pl., τάδε Id.
neut. dat. pl. τοῖσδε and τοισίδε, in or with these words, Hdt.
to go, travel, Il., Xen.
Pass. to be provided with thoroughfares, Strab.
to lead one upon his way, c. acc. pers., Aesch.; absol. to lead the way, Eur.
a guide, Plut.
belonging to a way, ὄρνις ὅδ. a bird of omen for the journey (or seen by the way), Aesch.
a road-way, Aesch.
a wayfarer, traveller, Od., Soph.; doric ὁδίτας, Theocr.
to stray from the road, wander or roam about, Ar.
straying from one road into another, wandering about, Anth.
to travel, walk, Hdt., Soph., etc.; ὁδ. τοὺς τόπους to walk over this ground, Soph.
a journey, way, Hdt., etc.
provisions for the voyage, Lat. viaticum, Od.
a wayfarer, traveller, Aesch., Soph., Ar.;—in Il., a fellow-traveller, or guide.
bearing teeth, κόσμος ὀδ. an ornament formed of strings of teeth, Anth.
sprung from the dragon's teeth, Eur.
to make or level a road, Xen.:— Pass., of roads, to be made fit for use, Id.
metaph. to reduce to a system, τι Arist.
c. dat. pers. to act as pioneer, serve as guide, Xen.:—Pass. to make one's way, advance, Lat. progredi, Plat.
a making of roads:—hence, a pioneering, preparation, Arist.
the work of a pioneer, Xen.
one who opens the way, a pioneer, Xen.
a road-surveyor, Aeschin.
a threshold, Soph., etc.
a way, path, track, road, highway: ποταμοῦ ὁδός the course of a river, Xen.; the path of the heavenly bodies, Eur.
with Preps., πρὸς ὁδοῦ further on the way, forwards, Il. (cf. φροῦδος):—κατ’ ὁδόν by the way, Hdt.;— ἐκ τῆς ὁδοῦ on his road Id.
a travelling, journeying, whether by land or water, a journey or voyage, Hom., etc.:—also an expedition, foray, Il.:—c. gen., τὴν εὐθὺς Ἀργοῦς ὁδόν the way leading straight to Argos, Eur.
metaph. a way or manner, θεσπεσία ὁδός the way or course of divination, Aesch.; ὁδ. μαντικῆς Soph.; λογίων ὁ the way, intent of the oracles, Ar.
a way of doing, speaking, etc., τριφασίας ἄλλας ὁδοὺς λόγων three other ways of telling the story, Hdt.; ὁδὸν ἥντιν’ ἰών by what course of action, Ar., etc.
a way, method, system; ὁδῷ methodically, systematically, Plat.
the Way, i. e. the Christian Faith, NTest.
a conductor, conductress, Eur.
Lat. dens, dentis, a tooth, Hom., Hes., etc.; ἕρκος ὀδόντων, v. ἕρκος 1; πρίειν ὀδόντας, v. πρίω.
a watcher of the roads, Hdt.
to lead by the right way, Aesch.; c. inf., τὸν φρονεῖν βροτοὺς ὁδώσαντα who put mortals on the way to wisdom, Id.: of things, to direct, ordain, Eur.:—Pass. to be on the right way, be conducted, Hdt.
to cause one pain or suffering, to distress, Eur., etc.:—Pass. to feel pain, suffer pain, Soph., Ar.; ἃ ὠδυνήθην the pains I suffered, Ar.
pain of body, Lat. dolor, Hom., attic
pain of mind, grief, distress, Hom., etc.; ὀδύνη τινός grief for him, Il.
painful, Pind., Ar.
painful, distressing, Eur., Ar.
killing, i. e. stilling, pain, Il.
a complaint, wailing, Trag.
a complaining, lamentation, Aesch., Eur., etc.

entry.etym: the Trag. use a form δύρομαι when required by the metre.
Dep., mostly in pres. and impf.,
entry.sense: to lament, bewail, mourn for:
c. acc. pers., Hom., Soph.; c. acc. rei, ὁ δ’ ὀδύρετο πατρίδα γαῖαν mourned for it, i. e. for the want of it, Od.; so, νόστον ὀδυρομένη Id.
c. gen. pers. to mourn for, for the sake of, Hom.
c. dat. pers. to wail or lament to or before others, Id.
absol. to wail, mourn, Id., Eur.
disposed to complain, querulous, Arist. adv. -κῶς, comp. κωτέρως, Id.
mourned for, lamentable: neut. pl. ὀδυρτά, as adv., painfully, Ar.
the Odyssey, Arist.
of Ulysses, Od.

Lat. Ulysses, Ulixes, king of Ithaca, whose adventures after the fall of Troy are told in the Odyssey: epic Ὀδῠσεύς, aeolic gen. Ὀδῠσεῦς: acc. Ὀδυσσέᾱ, but the two last syll. form one in Soph. Cf. ὀδύσσομαι.

entry.etym: Prob. from the Root δυσ- with ο) prefixed.Ὀδυσσεύς is derived from it, v. Od. 19. 407 sq.
epic verb, only in aor1 Mid.
entry.sense: to be wroth against, to hate another, c. dat., Hom., Hes.
smell, scent, Anth.
passable: practicable, Soph.
branching, Anth.
the Ozolae, a tribe of the Locrians, perhaps from the strong-smelling sulphur-springs in their country, Strab.
a bough, branch, twig, shoot, Il., Hes., etc.
metaph. an offshoot, scion, ὄζος Ἄρηος, of a famous warrior, Il.; so, τὼ Θησείδα ὄζω Ἀθηνῶν Eur.
with bad breath, Anth.

entry.etym: ὄδωδα pf. with pres. sense and and plqpf. as impf
entry.sense: to smell, whether to smell sweet or to stink, used by Hom. only in 3rd sg. plup.:—c. gen. rei, to smell of a thing, ὄζων τρυγός smelling of wine-lees, Ar.; metaph. to smell or savour of a thing, Lat. sapere aliquid, Κρονίων ὄζων smelling of musty antiquity, Id.

impers., ὄζει ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ὡσεὶ ἴων there is a smell from it as of violets, Hdt.; ὄζει ἡδὺ τῆς χρόας there is a sweet smell from the skin, Ar.;—so c. dupl. gen., ἱματίων ὀζήσει δεξιότητος there will be an odour of cleverness from your clothes, Id.
relat. adv., answering to demonstr. τόθεν and interr. πόθεν, Lat. unde, whence, from which, Hom., etc.:— also from whom, ὅθεν περ αὐτὸς ἐσπάρη from whom himself was born, Soph.
ὅθεν δή from whatever source, in what manner soever, Plat.
= ὅθι, οὗ, ὅπου, where, Il., Soph.
whence, wherefore, Eur., Plat.
relat. adv., answering to demonstr. τόθι and interr. πόθι, poet. for οὗ, Lat. ubi, where, Hom., Trag.
strange, foreign, Lat. alienus, Eur., Plat.
Dep. to care for, take heed, regard, reck, always with a negat., Hom.
fine linen, in pl., fine linen cloths, Hom.
sails, Anth.: in sg. a sail, Luc.
a piece of fine linen:— in pl. linen cloths, bandages, Ar.

entry.etym: for ὅτου ἕνεκα as οὕνεκα for οὗ ἕνεκα
entry.sense: because, Soph.
like οὕνεκα, simply for ὡς or ὅτι, that, Lat. quod, Trag.
with like hair, Il.
Mount Othrys in Thessaly, Hdt.
to steer, and so to guide, manage, Hdt., Arist.
a helmsman: metaph. a pilot, ruler, Aesch.
to steer, direct, Aesch.
the handle of the rudder, the tiller, and generally, the helm, Aesch., Eur., etc.:— metaph. the helm of government, Aesch.
in Il., οἴηκες are the rings of the yoke, through which pass the reins for guiding the mules.
a villager: Οἰᾶτις, νομός is a pasture in the Attic deme Οἴα, Soph.
to open, ὤιξα θύρας Il.: absol., ὦιξε γέροντι he opened the door to the old man, Id.; [οἶνον] ὤιξεν ταμίη she broached the wine, Od.; πρὸς φίλους οἴγειν στόμα Aesch.
to make to swell, Lat. tumefacere, Il.:— Pass. to swell, Lat. tumere, Id.
= οἰδέω, Ar.

to know, εὖ οἶδα I know well; εὖ ἴσθι be assured: often c. acc. rei, νοήματα οἶδε, μήδεα οἶδε he is versed in counsels, Hom.; with neut. Adjs., πεπνυμένα, φίλα, ἀθεμίστια εἰδώς Id.; also c. gen., τόξων εὖ εἰδώς cunning in the use of the bow; οἰωνῶν σάφα εἰδώς Od.: —χάριν εἰδέναι τινί to acknowledge a debt to another, thank him, Il., etc.:—the Imperat. in protestations, ἴστω Ζεὺς αὐτός be Zeus my witness, Id.; doric ἴττω Ζεύς, ἴττω Ar.: —εἰδώς absol. one who knows, εἰδυίηι πάντ’ ἀγορεύω Il.; ἰδυίηισι πραπίδεσσι with knowing mind, Id.
c. inf. to know how to do, Id., attic
with the part. to know that so and so is the case, ἴσθι μοι δώσων know that thou wilt give, Aesch.; τὸν Μῆδον ἴσμεν ἐλθόντα Thuc.
οὐκ οἶδα εἰ, I know not whether, expresses disbelief, like Lat. nescio an non, οὐκ οἶδ’ ἂν εἰ πείσαιμι Eur.

οἶδα or ἴσθι are often parenthetic, οἶδ’ ἐγώ Id.; οἶδ’ ὅτι, οἶσθ’ ὅτι, ἴσθ’ ὅτι, πάρειμι Soph.; so, εὖ οἶδ’ ὅτι Dem.: —in Trag. also, οἶσθ’ ὃ δρᾶσον; equivalent to δρᾶσον —οἶσθ’ ὅ; do— know'st thou what? i. e. make haste and do; οἶσθ’ ὡς ποίησον, etc.
to swell, become swollen, Lat. tumere, ὤιδεε δὲ χρόα he had his body swollen, Od.; οἰδεῖν τὰ πόδε to have swollen feet, Ar.
metaph. of inflated style, Id.; also, οἰδεόντων πρηγμάτων when times were troublous (like tument negotia in Cic.), Hdt.
a swelling, tumour, Dem.
of Oedipus, Plut.
Oedipus, i. e. the swollen footed (v. Soph. O. T. 718, Eur. Phoen. 25):—gen. Οἰδίποδος, but in Trag. Οἰδίπου (as if from Οἴδιπος), acc. Οἰδίπουν: voc. Οἰδίπους.
a swelling, swell, οἴδματι θύων raging with swollen waves, Il.; in pl., Soph.:—generally, the sea, Id., Eur.
of or from a sheep, Hdt.
of the same age, Il.
sorry, wretched, Theocr.

woful, pitiable, miserable, Hom.; of conditions, toilsome, dreary, Id.; also sorry, poor, Hdt. [Though Hom. makes ῡ, he forms the comp. and Sup., metri grat., ὀϊζῡρώτερος, -ώτατος, for -ότερος, -ότατος.]
woe, misery, distress, hardship, suffering, Hom.
entry.etym: ῡ in nom. and acc.; ῠ in trisyll. cases.

entry.sense: to wail, mourn, lament, περὶ κεῖνον ὀΐζυε (imperat.) Il.
c. acc. rei, to suffer, ὀϊζύομεν κακὰ πολλά Il.: absol. to suffer greatly, Od.
a rudder, helm, Hom.
opinion, an opinion, Plat.: self-conceit, Bion.
one must suppose, Arist.
a sheep, Theocr.
to one's home, home, homewards, Hom., etc.
= οἴκοι, at home, Xen. οἴκαδις, Doric for οἴκαδε, Ar.
one's own, Plut.
a minding one's own affair, Plat.
