in or of the house, domestic, Hes., etc.; τὰ οἰκεῖα household affairs, property, Lat. res familiaris, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
of persons, of the same family or kin, related, Lat. cognatus, Hdt., attic; οἱ ἑωυτοῦ οἰκηιότατοι his own nearest kinsmen, Hdt.; κατὰ τὸ οἰκεῖον Ἀτρεῖ because of his relationship to Atreus, Thuc.
friendly, Dem.

of things, belonging to one's house or family, one's own, Aesch., etc.; ἡ οἰκεία (sc. γῆ), ionic ἡ οἰκηίη, Hdt.; τὰ οἰκήια one's own property, Id.; οἰκεῖοι πόλεμοι wars in one's own country, Thuc.; of corn, home-grown, Id.
personal, private, opp. to δημόσιος, κοινός, Theogn., Hdt., attic; μηδὲν οἰκειοτέρᾳ τῇ ἀπολαύσει with enjoyment not more our own, Thuc.; οἰκεία ξύνεσις mother wit, Id.
proper to a thing, fitting, suitable, becoming, Hdt., Dem.
c. dat. rei, belonging to, conformable to the nature of a thing, Plat.
οἰκ. ὄνομα a word in its proper, literal sense, Arist.
the adv. οἰκείως has the same senses as the adj., familiarly, Thuc., Xen.
affectionately, dutifully, Id.
kindred, relationship, Hdt., attic: intimacy, friendliness, kindness, Thuc.:—in pl. friendly relations, Dem.
of words, the proper sense, Plut.
to make one's own:
to make a person one's friend, Thuc.; so in Mid. to win his favour or affection, conciliate, Hdt.:—Pass. to be made friendly, Thuc.: to be closely united, Plat.
Mid. also, c. acc. rei, to make one's own, claim as one's own, appropriate, Hdt., Plat.
kindred, relationship, Strab.
a taking as one's own, appropriation, Thuc.
the household, Lat. familia, Strab., Luc.
to inhabit, Eur.
a house-slave, menial, Hdt., attic; οἱ οἰκέται, Lat. familia, one's household, the women and children, Hdt., attic; opp. to οἱ δοῦλοι, Plat.
of or for the menials or household, Plat., Arist.
fem. of οἰκέτης, Eur.
the mistress of the house, Lat. matrona, Theocr.
an inmate of one's house, Hom.
a menial, servant, Od., Soph.
trans. to inhabit, occupy, Il., Hdt., attic:—Pass. to be inhabited, Il., Hdt., etc.; cf. οἰκουμένη.

Pass. to be settled, of those to whom new abodes are assigned, Il.; οἱ ἐν τῆι ἠπείρωι οἰκημένοι those who have been settled, i. e. those who dwell on the mainland, Hdt.; of cities, to be situate, to lie, Id.
to manage, direct, govern, like διοικέω, Soph., etc.
intr. to dwell, live, be settled, Hom., etc.; ἔξω τῶν κακῶν οἰκεῖν γλυκύ sweet is it to live free from cares, Soph.
of cities, in a pass. sense, to be settled, be situated, Hdt., Xen.
to conduct oneself or be conducted so and so, σωφρόνως γε οἰκοῦσα [πόλις] εὖ ἂν οἰκοῖτο a state with habits of self-control would be well governed, Plat.
any inhabited place, a dwellingplace, Pind., attic: a chamber, and in pl. a house, Hdt.
special senses,
a brothel, Hdt.: a tavern, Isae.
a cage or pen for animals, Hdt.
a temple, fane, chapel, Id.
a prison, Dem.
a storeroom, Plat., Dem.
a workshop, Plat.
a story, Lat. tabulatum, Xen.
habitable, Polyb.
the act of dwelling, habitation, Hdt., attic
management, administration, Plat.
a house, dwelling, residence, Hdt., Soph., etc.; κατασκαφὴς οἴκ. of the grave, Soph.
a dwelling-place, habitation, Eur.
inhabited, Soph.
an inhabitant, Hdt., attic; οἰκ. θεοῦ one who dwells in the temple of the god, Eur.; Ἅιδου οἰκ., of one dead, Soph.
a colonist, Thuc.
of or belonging to a house, οἱ οἰκ. one's domestics, NTest.
a building, house, dwelling, Hdt.
a household, domestic establishment, Plat.; οἰκίας δύο ᾤκει, i. e. he kept two establishments, Dem.
the household, i. e. inmates of the house, Lat. familia, Plat.
the house or family from which one is descended, Hdt., attic
a chamber, Ar.
c. acc. rei, to found as a colony or new settlement, πόλιν Hdt., Ar., etc.:— Pass., πόλις οἴκισται Hdt.
to people with new settlers, colonise, χώρην Id.; νήσους Thuc.:—Mid. ὅπη γῆς πύργον οἰκιούμεθα in what part of the world we shall make ourselves a fenced home, Eur.
c. acc. pers. to remove, transplant, Id.; metaph., τὸν μὲν ἀφ’ ὑψηλῶν βραχὺν ὤικισεν brought him from high to low estate, Eur.:—Pass. to settle in a place, Id., Plat.
in form a Dim. of οἶκος: only in pl. like Lat. aedes, a house, dwelling, abode, Hom., Hdt.
a peopling, colonisation, Thuc.
a small room, Dem.

entry.etym: poetic for οἰκιστής, Pind., Orac. ap. Hdt.

entry.sense: a coloniser, founder of a city, Hdt., Thuc.
born in the house, homebred, of slaves, Lat. verna, Plat.; of quails, Ar.
to be master of the house, to rule the household, NTest.
the master of the house, the good man of the house, NTest.
to build a house: generally, to build, οἰκίαν, γέφυραν, τεῖχος Hdt.:—Mid., οἰκοδομεῖσθαι οἴκημα to build oneself a house, have it built, Id.:—Pass. to be built, Id.
metaph. to build or found upon, ἔργα ἐπί τι Xen.; οἰκ. τέχνην ἔπεσιν Ar.
metaph., also, to build up, edify, NTest.:—Pass., οἰκοδομηθήσεται εἰς τὸ ἐσθίειν will be emboldened to eat, Id.
a building, structure, Hdt., Thuc.

entry.etym: a late form for οἰκοδόμημα, Plut., NTest.

entry.sense: the act or manner of building, Thuc.
= οἰκοδόμημα, Plat.
one must build, Plat.
fitted for building: ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) architecture, Luc.
built, Strab.
= οἰκοδόμησις, Thuc.
a building, edifice, Plat.
practised or skilful in building, Plat.: ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη), the art of building, architecture, Id.; so, τὰ οἰκοδομικά Id.
a builder, an architect, Hdt., Plat.

from one's house, from home, Il., Thuc.; οἴκοθεν οἴκαδε from house to house, proverb. of one who has two homes, Pind.; εὐθὺς οἴκ., i. e. from childhood, Arist.:—often without any sense of motion, τὰ οἴκ. domestic affairs, Eur.; στρατηγοὺς εἵλοντο ἐκ τῶν οἴκ. Xen.
from one's household stores, Il.
from one's own resources, by one's own virtues, by nature, Pind., Eur.
wholly, absolutely, Aeschin.
at home, Hom.
at home, in the house, Lat. domi, Il., Hes., etc.; τὰ οἴκοι one's domestic affairs, Xen., Plat.; so, ἡ οἴκοι δίαιτα Soph.; ἡ οἴκοι (sc. πόλις) one's own country, Id.
to manage as a house steward, to manage, order, regulate, Soph., Xen.
metaph. of an artist, to treat, handle a subject, Arist., Luc.
intr. to be a house-steward, NTest.
the management of a household or family, husbandry, thrift, Plat., etc.

practised in the management of a household or family, Plat., etc.: hence, thrifty, frugal, economical, Xen.:— ὁ οἰκ. title of a treatise on the duties of domestic life, by Xen.; and τὰ οἰκονομικά, a similar treatise by Arist.: ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη), domestic economy, Plat., Xen., etc.
one who manages a household, Xen., Plat.
generally, a manager, administrator, Arist.: οἱ Καίσαρος οἰκ. the Roman procuratores, Luc.
as fem. a housekeeper, housewife, Aesch.
the site of a house, Xen., Aeschin., etc.
the house itself, a building, Thuc.
constituting a house, οἰκ. τροφή the comforts of a house, Soph.
taking one's meals at home, living at one's own expense, unpaid, Menand.

a house, abode, dwelling, Hom., Hes., etc.:— acc. οἶκον, = οἶκόνδε, οἴκαδε, homeward, home, Od.; κατ’ οἴκους at home, within, Hdt.; κατ’ οἶκον Soph., etc: —ἐπ’ οἴκου ἀποχωρεῖν to go home wards, Thuc., etc.: ἀπ’ οἴκου from home, Id.
part of a house, a room, chamber, Od.: pl. οἶκοι for a single house, Lat. aedes, tecta, Id., attic
the house of a god, a temple, Hdt., Eur.
one's house, household goods, substance, Hom., etc.
a house, household, family, Od., etc.
ruining a family, Critias.
a slave born and bred in the house, Dem.
a domestic tyrant, Anth.

entry.etym: ionic adv. part. perf. of οἰκώς for ἐοικώς
entry.sense: reasonably, probably, Hdt.

( sc. γῆ) the inhabited world, a term used to designate the Greek world, as opp. to barbarian lands, Hdt., Dem., etc.:—so in Roman times, the Roman world, NTest.: metaph., ἡ οἰκ. ἡ μέλλουσα the world to come, i. e. the kingdom of Christ, Id.
of or from the whole world (ἡ οἰκουμένη); of Eccl. Councils, oecumenical.
a house-steward, NTest.
to watch or keep the house, Aesch., Soph.: generally to keep safe, guard, Ar.
to keep at home, as women, Soph., Plat.
ἕβδομον οἰκ. μῆνα πολιορκοῦντες they idled away seven months in the siege, Plut.
the watch or keeping of a house, Eur.; οἰκ. τῶν ξένων = οἱ οἰκουροῦντες ξένοι, Soph.
a keeping the house, staying, at home, Eur.
in concrete sense, of persons, οἰκουρήματα φθείρειν to corrupt the stay-at-homes, i. e. the women, Eur.
housekeeping, the cares of housekeeping, Eur.
a staying at home, of women, Plut.
inclined to keep at home: — τὸ -κόν, = οἰκουρία, Luc.
of or for housekeeping: hence οἰκούρια (sc. δῶρα) τά, wages, reward for keeping the house, Soph.
keeping within doors, ἑταῖραι οἰκόριαι (doric for οἰκούριαι) female house- mates, Pind.
watching the house, of a watchdog, Ar.
as Subst., οἰκουρός, ἡ, the mistress of the house, housekeeper, Eur.:—contemptuously of a man, a stay-at-home, opp. to one who goes forth to war, Aesch.; so, δίαιτα οἰκ. Plut.
to ruin a house, squander one's substance, Plat.:—Pass., aor1 οἰκοφθόρην, perf. οἰκοφθόρημαι, to be ruined, undone, Hdt.
a squandering one's substance, Plat.
one who ruins a house, a prodigal, Plat.
a house-guard, Anth.

entry.etym: Pass., only in pres. and impf.
entry.sense: to pity, feel pity for, have pity upon, c. acc., Il., Hdt., attic:— οἰκτ. τινά τινος to pity one for or because of a thing, Aesch.:—also c. acc. rei, Ar.
c. inf., οἰκτ. νιν λιπεῖν I am sorry to leave her, Soph.
to pity, have pity upon, c. acc., Aesch., Soph., etc.:— Mid. in same sense, Eur., Thuc.
in Mid. also, to bewail, lament, Eur.: absol. to express one's pity, Id.; οἶκτον οἰκτίζεσθαι to utter a wail, Aesch.
pity, compassion, Pind.:—in pl. compassionate feelings, mercies, NTest.
merciful, Theocr., NTest.
lamentation, Eur.
lamentation, Aesch., Xen., etc.

entry.etym: irreg. Sup. of οἰκτρός (cf. αἰσχρός, αἴσχιστος)
entry.sense: most pitiable, lamentable, Hom.:—neut. pl. οἴκτιστα as adv., Od.
pity, compassion, Od., Dht., attic:—c. gen. objecti, compassion for, οἶκτος τῆς πόλιος Hdt.
wailing piteously, piteous, Plat.
pitiable, in piteous plight, Il., Soph., etc.
of things, pitiable, piteous, lamentable, Hdt., Aesch., etc.

in act. sense, piteous, Od., Soph.; οἰκτρᾶς γόον ὄρνιθος, of the nightingale, Soph.;—neut. pl. as regul. adv. οἰκτρῶς, Aesch., Soph. —Besides comp. and Sup. οἰκτρότερος, -τατος, Hom. has an irreg. Sup. οἴκτιστος (q. v.).
to pour forth piteously, Ar.
profitable to a house, γυνὴ οἰκ. a wife whose prudence makes the house thrive, Theocr.
profit to a house, housewifery, Od.
Oi_leus, a Locrian chief, fatherof Ajax the Less, Il.
entry.etym: The orig. form was ϝῑλεύς, from ϝίλη (ἴλη), a troop.

entry.sense: = ὅρμημα, Lat. impetus, οἶμα λέοντος ἔχων with the spring of a lion, Il.; αἰετοῦ οἴματ’ ἔχων with the swoop of an eagle, Id.
to swoop or pounce upon its prey, of an eagle, Hom.; κίρκος οἴμησε μετὰ τρήρωνα πέλειαν swooped after a dove, Il.
absol. to dart along, Orac. ap. Hdt.
=oi)=mos: metaph. a song, lay, Od.

exclam. of pain, fright, pity, anger, grief, also of surprise, properly οἴ μοι ah me! woe's me! Theogn., Trag.:— οἴμοι is mostly absol., or is used with a nom., οἴμοι ἐγὼ τλάμων, οἴμοι τάλας etc., Soph.;—c. gen. causae, οἴμοι τῶν κακῶν, οἴμοι γέλωτος ah me for my misfortunes, for the laughter, Trag.
entry.etym: The last syll. in οἴμοι may be elided before ὡς.

entry.sense: a way, road, path, Hes., Aesch., etc.
a strip of land, tract, country, Σκύθην ἐς οἶμον Aesch.
metaph. the course or strain of song, Hhymn., Pind.
loud wailing, lamentation, Il., Hdt., Trag., etc.
a cry of lamentation, wail, Aesch., Eur.
to wail aloud, lament, Hom., Trag.
in familiar attic, οἴμωζε is a curse, plague take you, go howl! Lat. abeas in malam rem, Ar.; οἰμώζετε Id.; οἰμώξεσθ’ ἄρα Id.; οἰμώζειν λέγω σοι Id.; so, οὐκ οἰμώξεται; Id.
trans. to pity, bewail, c. acc., Tyrtae., Trag.: Pass., οἰμωχθείς bewailed, Theogn.; ὠιμωγμένος Eur.
pitiable, Ar.
the first shoot of the vine: generally, the vine, Eur., Ar.
the soft down of the young vine-leaves, Pind.
a vine-leaf, Theocr.
to strip off vine-leaves, as is done when the grapes are ripening, Ar.
weak or bad wine, Dem.
a vine-leaf, Xen.
the vine, Babr.
adj. of wine, vinous Anth.
the vine, Hes., Eur.
= οἶνος, wine, Anth.
of wine, Eur.
containing wine, Hdt., Pind.
of countries, rich in wine, Anth.
a vessel for drawing wine, Ar.
Mid. to procure wine by barter, buy wine, Il.
to be heavy with wine, Theogn.
heavy with wine, Lat. vino gravis, Il., Anth.
wine-soaked, drunken, Anth.
holding wine, Pind.
giver of wine, of Bacchus, Eur.
of or with wine.
Oenooe, name of an Attic deme, Hdt., etc.
honey mixed with wine, mead, Anth.
with soil fit to produce wine, wine-producing, Od.
οἰνόπεδον, ου, τό, as Subst. a vineyard, Il., Theogn.:—also οἰνοπέδη, ἡ, Anth.
ripe for wine-making, Anth.
wine-bewildered, Eur.
abounding in wine, Od.
wine-stricken, Anth.
to drink wine, Hom.
a wine-drinker, Od.
Lat. vinum, wine, Hom., etc.; παρ’ οἴνῳ over one's wine, Lat. inter pocula, Soph.; οἶνος ἐκ κριθῶν barley- wine, a kind of beer, Hdt.
rearing or bearing wine, Anth.
a cake or porridge of wine mixed with barley, water and oil, eaten by rowers, Ar.
meat full of wine, Luc.
drunkenness, Xen.
given to drinking, drunken, Xen., etc.
holding wine, Critias; οἰνοφόρον, (sc. σκεῦος) a wine-jar, oenophrus, in Hor.
a place in Boeotia, Thuc.
planted or grown with vines, Strab.
rejoicing in wine, Anth.
wine Charon, nickname of Philip of Macedon, because he put poison in his enemies' wine, and so, sent them over the Styx, Anth.
to pour out wine for drinking, Hom.
c. acc., νέκταρ ἐωινοχόει she was pouring out nectar for wine, Il.
a festival, at which wine is offered, Plut.
a can for ladling wine from the mixing bowl (κρατήρ) into the cups, Hes., Eur.
a wine-pourer, cupbearer, Hom., etc.
of poured wine, πῶμα οἰν. a draught of wine, Soph.
wine-coloured, wine-dark (never in nom.), ἐπὶ οἴνοπι πόντῳ Hom.; of oxen, wine-red, Id.
to intoxicate, οἰνῶσαι σῶμα ποτοῖς Critias.
Pass. οἰνόομαι to get drunk, be drunken, οἰνωθέντες Od.; perf. part., ᾠνωμένος, ionic οἰνωμένος, Hdt., Soph.
a wine-cellar, Xen.
of a fresh, ruddy complexion, Id., Theocr.
generally, dark, Id.
lonesome, Anth.
feeding alone, of cattle: metaph. of Ajax, φρενὸς οἰοβώτας = μονόφρων, Soph.
from one only, i. e. by oneself, alone, in phrase οἰόθεν οἶος all alone, Il.
to suppose, think, deem, imagine, c. acc. et inf., mostly inf. fut., Hom., etc.

c. inf. alone, when both Verbs have the same subject, as, κιχήσεσθαί σε ὀΐω I think to catch, i. e. I think I shall. . , Il.; οὐ γὰρ ὀΐω πολεμίζειν I do not think, i. e. mean, to fight, Id.; ἐν πρώτοισιν ὀΐω ἔμμεναι I expect to be, Od.
sometimes the subject of the inf. is to be supplied from the context (as in I), τρώσεσθαι ὀΐω I fear [that many] will be wounded, Il.; διωκέμεναι γὰρ ὀΐω I fear [they] are pursuing me, Od.

absol., αἰεὶ ὀΐεαι thou art ever suspecting, Il.: also, to deem, forebode, θυμὸς ὀΐσατό μοι my heart foreboded it, Od.; ὀΐσατο κατὰ θυμόν he had a presage of it in his soul, Id. :—impers., ὀΐεταί μοι ἀνὰ θυμόν there comes a boding into my heart, Id.
trans. to wait for, look for, κεῖνον ὀϊομένη looking for his return, Id.; γόον δ’ ὠίετο θυμός his soul was intent on grief, Id.
used by Hom. parenthetically, in first person, ἐν πρώτοισιν, ὀΐω, κείσεται among the first, I ween, will he be lying, Il.; ἔπειτά γ’, ὀΐω, γνώσεαι Od.

in attic this parenthetic use in confined to the contr, form οἶμαι, imperf. ὤιμην, I think, I suppose, I believe; even between a prep. and its case, ἐν οἶμαι πολλοῖς Dem.:—answering a question, expressive of positive certainty, I believe you, of course, no doubt, Ar., etc. ; οἶμαι ἔγωγε yes I think so, yes certainly, Plat.:—also in a parenthetic question, πῶς οἴει; πῶς οἴεσθε; how think you ? like πῶς δοκεῖς; also οἴει; alone, don't you think so? what think you? Id.
οἴομαι δεῖν I hold it necessary, think it my duty, like Fr. je crois devoir, Soph., Plat.
as if, Lat. quasi, tanquamsi, Arist.
（οἶος) feeding alone: hence, lone, lonely, of places, ἐπ’ οἰονόμοιο (neut.) in solitude, Anth.
（ὄϊς, οἶς) as Subst., a shepherd, Id.
adj. = οἷόν περ εἰ, as it were, Plat.
possible; οὐχ οἷόντε impossible: v. οἷος III. 2.
Pass. to be left alone, abandoned, forsaken.
entry.etym: only in 3rd sg. aor1 οἰώθη Il.

entry.sense: to tend sheep, to roam the mountains, Eur.:—c. acc. loci, to roam over, Anth.
traversed by sheep, Hom.
lonely, solitary, single, Pind.
act. tending sheep, Hhymn.
Scyth. for ἀνδρο-κτόνοι, οἰόρ, being = ἀνήρ (vir), Hdt.
of such and such a kind, Arist.

alone, lone, lonely, though it can often only be rendered by an adv. alone, only, Hom., Hes.; οἶος ἄνευθ’ ἄλλων Il. ;—with negat., οὐκ οἶος, ἅμα τῷγε. . , not alone, but. . , Id.;—neut., οἶον as adv., Id.
strengthd., εἷς οἶος, μία οἴη one alone, one only, Hom.; in dual, δύο οἴω Id.; in pl., δύο οἴαι Od.:—rare in attic

c. gen., οἴη θεῶν alone of the gods, Il.; so, οἴη ἐν ἀθανάτοισιν alone among the goddesses, Id.; οἶος μετὰ τοῖσι Od.; but, οἶος ἀπ’ ἄλλων alone from, apart from, Id.; οἶος Ἀτρειδῶν δίχα, clam Atridis, Soph.
single in its kind, unique, excellent, Il.

such as, what sort or manner of nature, kind, or temper, Lat. qualis, relat. Pronoun, correlative to the interrog. ποῖος, the indef. ποιός, and the demonstr. τοῖος, Hom., Hes., etc.; strengthd., ὅσσος ἔην οἷός τε, Lat. qualis erat quantusque, Il.: c. acc., οἷος ἀρετήν what a man for virtue, Id.; often only to be rendered by an adv., οἷος μέτεισι πόλεμόνδε how he rushes into war, Id. Usage:

οἷος in an indepent sentence expresses astonishment, strengthd. by δή, οἷον δὴ τὸν μῦθον ἐπεφράσθης ἀγορεῦσαι why, what a word it has come into thy mind to speak! Od.; so in neut., as adv., v. infr. v.
so in indirect sentences, where no antec. can be supplied, ὁρῶν ἐν οἵοις ἐσμέν Xen.

containing a Comparison, often without an antec., οἷος ἀστὴρ εἶσι like as a star wanders, Il.; οἷος καὶ Πάρις ᾔσχυνε like as Paris also dishonoured, Aesch.:—in this sense, οἷος is often attached to the case of its antec., πρὸς ἄνδρας τολμηρούς, οἵους Ἀθηναίους (for οἷοιἈθηναῖοι), Thuc.

οἷος, οἵα, οἷον, esp. in attic, often stand for ὅτι τοῖος, τοία, τοῖον, so that the relat. introduces the reason for the preceding statement, ἄνακτα χόλος λάβεν, οἷον ἄκουσεν anger seized the king, because of what he heard. Il.

but if the Comparison is general, Hom. uses οἷός τε (which must be distinguished from οἷός τε c. inf., v. infr. III. 2), οἷός τε Ἄρης some such one as Ares, Il.; also, οἷός τις the sort of person who, Hom.
when a Comparison involves Time, οἷος ὅ τε is used, like as when . . , Od.

οἷος is used in many brief attic phrases, οὐδὲν γὰρ οἷον ἀκούειν αὐτοῦ τοῦ νόμου there's nothing like hearing the words of the law, Dem.; —it adds force to the Sup., χωρίον οἷον χαλεπώτατον, = τοιοῦτον οἷόν ἐστι χαλεπώτατον, Xen.

οἷος with inf. implies Fitness or Ability to do, οἷος ἔην τελέσαι ἔργον τε ἔπος τε so ready was he to make good both deed and word, Od.; οἷος ἔην βουλευέμεν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι so good both at counsel and in fight, Od.; τὸ πρᾶγμα μέγα καὶ μὴ οἷον νεωτέρῳ βουλεύσασθαι the matter is great and not such as for a young man to advise upon, Thuc.; without an inf., ὁ δ’ οἷός ἐστιν οἰκουρὸς μόνον fit only [to be] a house-dog, Ar.

but this sense is commonly expressed by οἷός τε, c. inf., fit or able to do, λέγειν οἷός τε κἀγώ Id.; οἷός τε ἦν πείθειν Dem.: freq. in neut. sg. and pl., οἷόν τε ἐστί and οἷά τε ἐστί, οἷόν τε γίγνεται it is possible, Hdt., attic; without inf., οἷόν τε ἐστίν it is possible, οὐχ οἷόν τε ἐστίν it cannot be, Ar.; with a Sup., καλὸν ὡς οἷόν τε μάλιστα as beautiful as is possible, Plat.; ὡς οἷόν τε διὰ βραχυτάτων Id.

the relat. is in attic often repeated in the same clause, οἷ’ ἔργα δράσας οἷα λαγχάνει κακά after what deeds what sufferings are his! Soph.; οἵαν ἀνθ’ οἵων θυμάτων χάριν what thanks and for what offerings! Id.
as adv. in neut., to add force, οἷον ἐερσήεις how fresh, Il.; οἷα ἀτάσθαλα Od.:—the regul. adv. οἵως is seldom used, οἷος ὢν οἵως ἔχεις in what a state art thou for such a man! Soph.
in Comparisons, as, like as, just as, Hom., Trag.; οἷά τις ἀηδών Aesch.;— οἷον ὅτε like as when, cf. II. 4.
as, οἷον τί λέγεις; as for example, what do you mean? Plat.
like ὡς with a partic., οἷα ἀπροσδοκήτου γενομένου inasmuch as it was unexpected, Thuc.
with Numerals, about, οἷον δέκα σταδίους, etc.
with only a tunic on, lightly clad, Od.
exclam. of pain, grief, pity, astonishment, ah! woe! Lat. heu! vae! sometimes with nom., οἲ ’γώ Soph.; mostly c. dat., v. οἴμοι; c. acc., οἲ ἐμὲ δειλήν Anth.
relat. adv.
whither, Lat. quo, Trag.; οὐκ ἤκουσας οἷ προβαίνει τὸ πρᾶγμα Ar.:—c. gen., οἷ μ’ ἀτιμίας ἄγεις to what a height of dishonour you lead me, Soph.
with Verbs of rest, οἷ φθίνει τύχα where, i. e. how, in what, it ends, Eur.; so, οἷ κακίας τελευτᾷ in what state of vice he ends, Plat.
whither, Lat. quo, v. οἷ.
Lat. ovis, sheep, both ram and ewe, Hom., etc.; but the gender is sometimes marked by a word added, ὄϊν ἀρνειὸν ῥέζειν θῆλύν τε to sacrifice a male sheep and a female, Od.
to be borne, Soph.
οἰστέον one must bear, Eur.
one must get, κέρδος Soph.
an archer, Anth.
to shoot arrows, Hom.: c. gen. to shoot at, ὀϊστευσον Μενελάου Il.
arrow-shooting, Anth.
an arrow-holder, a quiver, Aesch.
an arrow, Hom., Hes., etc.
that must be borne, endurable, Thuc.
to sting, properly of the gadfly; then metaph. to sting to madness, αὐτὰς ἐκ δόμων οἴστρησα I drave them raging out of the house, Eur.:—Pass., οἰστρηθείς driven mad, Soph.
intr. like Pass. to be driven by the gadfly, driven mad, οἰστρήσασα in frenzy, frantically, Aesch.; of Menelaus, Eur.; ἡ ψυχὴ οἰστρᾶι Plat.
driven by a gadfly, Aesch.
the smart of a gadfly's sting: metaph. frenzy, Soph.
to strike as with a sting, Anth.
driven round and round by the gadfly, Aesch.
stung by a gadfly, driven wild, Trag.
the gadfly, breese, Lat. asilus, an insect which infests cattle, Od., Aesch.
metaph. a sting, anything that drives mad, Eur.: absol. the smart of pain, agony, Soph.
mad desire, insane passion, Hdt., Eur., etc.:—generally, madness, frenzy, Soph., Eur.
a tree of the osier kind.
of osier, of wicker-work, Od., Thuc., etc.
the grease extracted from sheep's wool, Hdt.
with the grease in it, greasy, Ar.
of Oeta, Soph., etc.; οἱ Οἰταῖοι the men of Oeta, Thuc.
Mount Oeta in Thessaly, Strab.
fate, doom, Hom., Soph., Eur.
name of a city in Thessaly, Il.
an Oechalian, Il.
from Oechalia, Il.

entry.etym: only in pres. and ionic imperf. οἴχνεσκον
entry.sense: to go, come, Od.; to walk, i. e. to live, Soph.
like οἴχομαι, to be gone, Id.
c. acc. pers., like προσέρχομαι, to approach, Pind.

Dep. to be gone, to have gone, Lat. abesse (not abire), in perf. sense, and imperf. ὠιχόμην in plup. sense, directly opp. to ἥκω, to have come, while ἔρχομαι, to go or come, serves as the pres. to both, Hom., etc.;—often c. part., οἴχεται φεύγων is fled and gone, Il.; ὤιχετ’ ἀποπτάμενος he hath taken flight and gone, Id.; οἴχεται θανών (v. infr. II. 1); also with an adj., οἴχεται φροῦδος he's clean gone, Ar.:—c. acc. pers. to have escaped from, Id.
Special usages,

euphem. for θνήσκω, to be gone hence, οἴχεται εἰς Ἀΐδαο Il.; in attic, οἴχεται θανών Soph., etc.:—part. οἰχόμενος for θανών, departed, dead, Trag.; but in Hom. simply absent or away, Ὀδυσῆος πόθος οἰχομένοιο desire of the absent Ulysses, Od.
to be undone, ruined, Soph.; esp. in ὤιχωκα or οἴχωκα, Lat. perii, Aesch., etc.
of things, to denote any quick, violent motion, to rush, sweep along, Il.
Dep.
to take omens from the flight and cries of birds, Lat. augurium, capere, Xen.
generally, to divine from omens, augur, c. acc. et inf., Id.
divination by the flight or cries of birds, Lat. augurium, Eur.
a place for watching the flight of birds:—an omen or token, Xen.
one who foretells from the flight and cries of birds, an augur, Il., Hes.
of or for an omen: ἡ -κή (sc.τέχνη), augury, Plat.
of the cry of birds, οἰ. γόος the wailing cry of birds, Aesch.
killing birds, Aesch.
one who takes omens from the flight and cries of birds, an augur, Eur.
one busied with the flight and cries of birds, an augur, Il., etc.
to watch the flight of birds, to take auguries, Eur.
a large bird, bird of prey, such as a vulture or eagle, and so distinguished from a common bird (ὄρνις), Hom., etc.
a bird of omen or augury, Hom., etc.:—the flight to (not from) the right, i. e. towards the East, was fortunate, and vice versa.

an omen, presage, drawn from these birds, Lat. auspicium or augurium, according as taken from seeing their flight or hearing their cry, Il., etc.; δέκομαι τὸν οἰωνόν I accept the omen, hail it as favourable, Hdt.
entry.etym: commonly deriv. from οἶος, — most birds of prey being solitary, — cf. κοινωνός from κοινός

entry.sense: a nautical word, used,
trans. of the seamen, to run [a ship] aground or on shore, Hdt., Thuc.
intr. of the ship, to run aground, Thuc., Xen.; so, metaph., Ar.
a folding-chair, camp-stool, Ar.
squatting, of a frog, Babr.

to crouch down on one's hams, to squat, Xen.: ἐς γόνυ ὀκλάσας δέχεται τῇ σαρίσσῃ τὴν ἐπέλασιν, of a soldier waiting an attack, Luc.; of a weary traveller, Soph.:—c. acc., ὀκλ. τὰ ὀπίσθια, τοὺς προσθίους to bend their hind or fore legs, Xen.

to shrink from doing, to scruple, hesitate to do a thing, c. inf., Il., etc.; ὀκνῶ προδότης καλεῖσθαι I shrink from being called, fear to be called, Soph.; ὀκνῶ ὀνομάσαι I shrink from naming, hesitate to name, Dem.; rarely c. acc., ὃν ὀκνεῖτε Soph.; ὀκνεῖν περί τινος Xen.
absol. to shrink, hesitate, hang back, Hdt., Soph., etc.
shrinking, hesitating, backward, unready, timid, Pind.; ὀκνηρὸς ἐς τὰ πολεμικά Thuc.:—adv. -ρῶς, Xen., etc.
of things, causing fear, vexatious, troublesome, Soph.
shrinking, hesitation, unreadiness, sluggishness, Il., Aesch.; ὄκνος καὶ μέλλησις Thuc.
alarm, fear, Aesch., Soph.
c. gen., τοῦ πόνου οὐκ ὄκνος [ἐστί] I grudge not labour, Soph.
c. inf., παρέσχεν ὄκνον μὴ ἐλθεῖν made them hesitate to go, Thuc.; ὄκνος ἦν ἀνίστασθαι Xen.
Pass. to be made rough or jagged: metaph. to be exasperated, πανθυμαδὸν ὀκριόωντο Od.
a kind of tribune on the stage, from which the actors declaimed, Plat.
having many points or roughnesses, rugged, jagged, Il., Aesch.
like ἄκρις, ἄκρα, a jagged point or prominence.
as adj. ὀκρίς, ίδος, = ὀκριόεις, rugged, Aesch.
chilling, horrible, Il.
consisting of eight pieces, Hes.
weighing or worth eight drachmae, Anth.
on the eighth day, NTest.
adv. eight times, Luc.
eight thousand, Hdt., Xen.; in sg., ἵππος ὀκτακισχιλίη "8000 horse, " Hdt.
eight-spoked, Il.
eight hundred, Hdt.
eight months old, Xen.
eightfold, Lat. octuplus, Ar.
eight feet long, Hes.
eight-footed, Batr., Anth.
with eight roots: of a stag's horns, with eight points, Anth.
of chariots, with eight poles, i. e. drawn by eight pairs of oxen abreast, Xen.
eight-stretched, ἕλικες ὀκτ. the eight arms of the cuttlefish, Anth.
weighing or worth 18 drachmae, Dem.
eighteen, Hdt., etc.
eighteenth: ὀκτωκαιδεκάτῃ (sc. ἡμέρᾳ) on the eighteenth day, Od.
eighteen years old, Dem., Theocr.:—fem. έτις, ιδος, Luc.
Lat. octo, eight, Hom., etc.
eight feet long, broad or high, Plat.

entry.etym: a lisping way of pronouncing ὁράω, Ar.

entry.sense: to make happy, Eur.:— to deem or pronounce happy, Aesch., Soph., etc.:—Pass. to be or be deemed happy, perf. part. ὠλβισμένοι Eur.; aor1 part. ὀλβισθείς Id.
of blessed lot, Il.
bestowing bliss, Eur.
making happy, Anth.
of persons, happy, blest, in Hom., always in reference to worldly goods, wealth, like Lat. beatus, Hom., etc.

of things, in neut. pl., θεοὶ δέ τοι ὄλβια δοῖεν may they give thee rich gifts, Od.; neut. pl. as adv., ὄλβια ζωέμεναι to live happily, Id.:—adv. -ίως, Soph.; Sup. ὀλβιώτατος Hdt.; in later Poets, ὄλβιστος.
giver of bliss, of good or wealth, like ὀλβιοδώτης, Eur.
happiness, bliss, weal, wealth, Hom., etc.
bringing bliss or wealth, Eur.
destructive, deadly, ὀλ. ἦμαρ the day of destruction, Il.; ψῆφος ὀλεθρία a vote of death, Aesch.:— ὀλέθριον as adv. fatally, Soph.
c. gen., γάμοι ὀλέθριοι φίλων bringing ruin on his friends, Aesch.
of persons, ruined, lost, undone, Soph.:— rascally, worthless, Luc.

ruin, destruction, death, Hom., Trag., etc.; ὀλέθρου πείρατα, Like θανάτου τέλος, the consummation of death, Il.:— οὐκ εἰς ὄλεθρον; as an imprecation, ruin seize thee! Soph.:— χρημάτων ὀλέθρῳ by loss of money, Thuc.; ἐπ’ ὀλέθρῳ Plat.
like Lat. pernicies and pestis, that which causes destruction, a pest, plague, curse, Hes.; of persons, Hdt.; so Oedipus calls himself τὸν ὄλεθρον μέγαν Soph.; ὄλ. Μακεδών, of Philip, Dem., etc.
epic imperf. ὄλεκον, ionic ὀλέκεσκον, like ὄλλυμι, to ruin, destroy, kill, Hom., Trag.:—Pass. to perish, die, esp. a violent death, ὀλέκοντο δὲ λαοί Il.
man-destroying, Theogn.
beast-slaying, Eur.
destroying tyrants, Anth.
a destroyer, murderer, Il.:— fem. ὀλέτειρα, Babr., Anth.
but few times, seldom, Eur., Thuc., etc.
scant of vines, Anth.
to be scant of men, Plut., etc.
scantiness of men, Strab.
scantiness of men, Thuc., Xen.
scant of men, Xen.
a scanty meal, Plut.
contented with little, Luc.
to be member of an oligarchy, Arist.:—Pass. to be governed by the few, be under an oligarchy, Thuc., Plat.
an oligarchy, government in the hands of a few families or persons, Hdt., attic
oligarchical, of, for or like oligarchy, ὀλ. κόσμος Thuc., Arist.:—adv. -χῶς, Plat., Dem.
of persons, inclined to oligarchy, Plat.
having little arable land, Anth.
from some few parts, Hdt.
in few places, Plat.
having little power, in feeble case, powerless, Od.
weak, powerless, Anth.
weakness, faintness, Od.
want of arable land, Anth.
with little corn, or with a small bread-basket, Anth.
production of few at a birth, Plat.
producing few at a birth, Hdt.

entry.etym: part. with no pres. in use
entry.sense: able to do little, feeble, powerless, Il.
of little might, feeble, Ar.
weakness, feebleness, Aesch.
fewness of years, youth, Xen.
with little wood, Anth.
of little faith, NTest.
with little flesh, Luc.
small eating, moderation in food, Arist.
of Number or Quantity, few, little, scanty, small, opp. to πολύς, Hom., etc.; the governing body in Oligarchies was called οἱ ὀλίγοι, Thuc., etc.
c. inf. too few to do a thing, Hdt., Thuc.
of Size, little, small, opp. to μέγας, Hom.; ὀλίγον ἢ οὐδέν little or nothing, Plat.

neut. ὀλίγον as adv., little, a little, slightly, Hom., Eur.; with comp. Adjs., ὀλίγον προγενέστερος Il.; ὀλ. ἧσσον Od.; so, ὀλ. τι πρότερον Hdt.; but ὀλίγῳ is more common with the comp. in Prose, Id., etc.
special phrases:
ὀλίγου δεῖν almost, ὀλίγοῦ ἐδέησε καταλαβεῖν wanted but little of overtaking, Id.:—hence ὀλίγου alone, all but, almost, Od., attic; ὀλίγου ἐς χιλίους hard upon 1000, Thuc.
δι’ ὀλίγου (sc. χώρου) at a short distance, Aesch., etc.: also, δι’ ὀλίγου (sc. χρόνου) at short notice, suddenly, Thuc.:— δι’ ὀλίγων in few words, Plat.
ἐν ὀλίγῳ (sc. χώρῳ) in a small space, within small compass, Thuc.:—also, ἐν ὀλίγῳ (sc. χρόνῳ) in a short time, suddenly, Plat., NTest.
ἐν ὀλίγοις one among few, i. e. exceedingly, remarkably, Hdt.
ἐξ ὀλίγου = δι’ ὀλίγου, of Time, Thuc.
ἐς ὀλίγον within a little, Id.
κατ’ ὀλίγον by little and little, Id.; but the adj. often takes the gender and number of its Subst., κατ’ ὀλίγους few at a time, in small parties, Hdt., Thuc.
μετ’ ὀλίγον τούτων shortly after these things, Xen.
παρ’ ὀλίγον within a little, almost, Eur.:—but, παρ’ ὀλ. ποιεῖσθαι to hold of small account, Xen.
the adv. ὀλίγως is rare, οὐκ ὀλίγως Anth.
Comparison:
the comp. is commonly supplied by μείων, ἥσσων or ἐλάσσων: the form ὀλίζων, ονος, is rare.
Sup. ὀλίγιστος, η, ον, Il., attic:— ὀλίγιστον or τὸ ὀλ., as adv., Lat. minime, Plat.; ὡς ὀλίγιστα Id.
the consisting of few lines, Anth.
one out of a few, opp. to πολλοστός, Plut.
ὀλ. χρόνον for the smallest space of Time, Soph.
of Number, fewness, Plat.
of Amount, smallness, scantiness:—of Time, shortness, Id.
fewness of friends, Arist.
lasting or living but little time, of short duration, Theogn., Hdt., etc.
faint-hearted, NTest.
to esteem little or lightly, make small account of, c. gen., Xen., Plat.:—absol. to take no heed, Thuc.:—Pass., perf. ὠλιγώρημαι, to be lightly esteemed, Dem.
an esteeming lightly, slighting, contempt, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
negligence, ap. Dem.
little-caring, lightly-esteeming, scornful, contemptuous, Hdt., Dem.:—adv., ὀλιγώρως ἔχειν to be careless, negligent, Plat., Xen.
to slip, slip and fall, Il.; ἐξ ἀντύγων ὤλισθε he slipped from the chariot, Soph.:—metaph. to make a slip, Ar.
to slip or glide along, Theocr.
slippery, Lat. lubricus, Pind., Xen.
of persons, slippery, hard to catch and keep hold of, Plat., Anth.
liable to slip, Plut.
slipperiness, Luc.
= a slip, Id.
a ship which is towed, a ship of burthen, trading vessel, merchantman, Hdt.
a drawing, dragging, tugging: a drawing on or towards a thing, attraction, force of attraction, Plat.
a bowl or basin, Plut.
drawing to oneself, attractive, Plat.
as an Instrument, a machine for hauling ships on land, a hauling-engine, Hdt., Thuc.
a strap, rein, Soph.
as an Effect, a furrow, Lat. sulcus, ὁλκὸς τοῦ ξύλου the furrow made by the wood, Xen.
periphr., ὁλκοὶ δάφνης drawings of laurels, i. e. laurel-boughs (or brooms made of them) drawn along, Eur.
Act. = Lat. perdo,
to destroy, make an end of, Hom., Trag.:—also of doing away with evil, ὤλεσεν νόσον Aesch.
to lose, θυμόν, ψυχήν, μένος, ἦτορ ὀλέσαι to lose life, Hom.; πόνον ὀλέσαντες having lost their labour, Aesch.
Mid., = Lat. pereo,

to perish, come to an end, Hom.; also c. acc. cogn., κακὸν οἶτον, κακὸν μόρον ὀλέσθαι to die by an evil death, Il.:— ὄλοιο, ὄλοισθε may'st thou, may ye, perish! an imprecation, Trag.; so, ὀλοίμην, ὄλοιτο, ὄλοιντο, Soph.
to be ruined, undone, Hom., attic
of things, to be lost, Hom.
perf. ὄλωλα, in sense of Mid., to have perished, to be undone, ruined, Il., Aesch., etc.; τῶν ὀλωλότων of the dead, Aesch.
a maker of mortars, Arist.
a round smooth stone, a roller, Il.
any round body: a mortar, Hes., Hdt.: a kneading-trough, Ar.
a destroyer, NTest.
to destroy utterly, NTest.

entry.etym: an epic form of ὀλοός, Il.

entry.sense: a rolling stone, a round stone, such as besieged people rolled down upon their assailants, Hdt., Xen.; ὀλοοίτροχος in Il. and Orac. ap. Hdt.
as adj., πέτροι ὁλοίτροχοι round stones, to which the muscles of an athlete's arm are compared, Theocr.
to bring a burnt-offering, to offer whole, Xen.
a whole burnt-offering, holocaust, NTest.
completeness or soundness in all its parts, NTest.
complete in all parts, entire, perfect, Lat. integer, Plat., etc.
any loud cry, mostly of a joyous kind (unlike Lat. ululatus), used by women invoking a god, Il., Hdt., etc.
a loud cry, mostly of joy, Eur.
a loud crying, mostly a joyous cry, in honour of the gods, Aesch., Eur.;—rarely of lamentation, Aesch.
an unknown animal, named from its note: prob. a kind of owl, Theocr.
to cry to the gods with a loud voice, cry aloud, of women crying aloud to the gods in prayer or thanksgiving, Od., Hhymn. Apoll.; so also in Aesch., Eur., etc.

whole, entire, complete, Lat. integer, οὖλος ἄρτος a whole loaf, Od.; ὅλην πόλιν a whole city, Eur.; ὅλους βοῦς Ar., etc.;— πόλεις ὅλαι are whole, entire cities, opp. to ὅλη ἡ πόλις, the whole city, the city as a whole, Plat.:—with the Art. it may either precede or follow the Subst., τῆς ἡμέρας ὅλης the whole day, δι’ ὅλης τῆς νυκτός through the whole night, Xen., etc.
whole, i. e. safe and sound, Plat.
entire, utter, ὅλον ἁμάρτημα an utter blunder, Xen.; of a person, ὅλος εἶναι πρός τινι = Lat. totus in illis, Dem.
neut. as adv., ὅλον or τὸ ὅλον, wholly, entirely, Plat.; ὅλῳ καὶ παντί Id., etc.; τῷ ὅλῳ καὶ παντί Id.;— so, κατὰ ὅλον on the whole, generally, Id.; δι’ ὅλου, καθ’ ὅλου (v. sub διόλου, καθόλου).
as Subst., τὸ ὅλον the universe, Id.
τὰ ὅλα, one's all, Dem.; τοῖς ὅλοις = ὅλως, altogether, Philipp. ap. Dem.
adv. ὅλως, wholly, altogether, Plat., etc.
on the whole, speaking generally, in short, in a word, Like ἑνὶ λόγῳ, Lat. denique, Dem.
often with a neg., οὐχ ὅλως not at all, Plat., Xen., etc.
destroying, destructive, fatal, deadly, murderous, Hom., Hes., Aesch., Eur.:— ὀλοὰ φρονεῖν to be bent on ill, design ill, Il.:—comp. ὀλοώτερος Id.; Sup. ὀλοώτατος (used as fem.) Od.
in pass. sense, lost, dead, Aesch.
meaning mischief, baleful, Il.:—in Od. always of crafty, shrewd, men, not Greeks; such men being regarded as baneful.
all-purple, Xen.
to pluck out, tear out, Anth.
mud, muddy liquor, Anth.
made of solid beaten metal, Anth.
a general survey or estimate, Strab.
whole, entire, complete, Lat. integer, Theocr.
relating to the whole, important, considerable, Polyb.:—adv. -ρῶς, entirely, utterly, Id.

a coarse rush, used in wicker-work: —hence the proverb, ἀπορράπτειν τὸ φιλίππου στόμα ὁλοσχοίνῳ ἀβρόχῳ to stop Philip's mouth with an unsoaked rush, (for rushes were soaked to make them tough), i. e. without any trouble, Aeschin.
of lamentation, lamenting, Hom.: —ὀλοφυδνά, as adv., Anth.
lamentation, Ar., Thuc., etc.
intr. to lament, wail, moan, weep, Hom., etc.
to lament or mourn for the ills of others, to feel pity, Hom.: c. gen. to have pity upon one, Il.
to beg with tears and lamentations, καί μοι δὸς τὴν χεῖρ’, ὀλοφύρομαι Id.
c. inf., πῶς ὀλοφύρεαι ἄλκιμος εἶναι; why lament that thou must be brave? Od.
c. acc. to lament over, bewail, Id., Hdt., attic
to pity, Hom.
ὀλοφύρσεις τῶν ἀπογιγνομένων lamentations for the departed, Id.
querulous, Arist.
epic adj. destructive, deadly, pernicious, Od.; ὀλοφώια εἰδώς versed in pernicious arts, Id.
entry.etym: From ΟΛ, the Root of ὄλλυμι: the term. -φώιος has not been explained.

entry.sense: a leathern oil-flask, Theocr., Anth.
to Olympia, Thuc.
Olympian, Thuc., Xen.
Ὀλυμπία (sc. χώρα), Olympia, a district of Elis round the city of Pisa, where the Olympic games were held, Hdt., etc.; or the city Pisa itself, Pind. Οὐλυμπία, Id.

Ὀλύμπια (sc. ἱερά) the Olympic games, in honour of Olympian Zeus, established by Hercules in 776 B. C., and renewed by Iphitus, and held at intervals of four years at Olympia, Hdt.; Ὀλ. ἀναιρεῖν, νικᾶν to win at the Olympic games, Id., etc.
at Olympia, Ar., etc.; cf. θύρᾱσι.
Olympian as epith. of the Muses, Il., Hes.; of the Graces, Ar.
Ὀλ. ἐλαία the olive-crown of the Olympic games, Pind.
as Subst.,
the Olympic games, Hdt., Pind.
(sub. νίκη), a victory at Olympia, Hdt.

an Olympiad, i. e. the space of four years between the celebrations of the Olympic games; used as an historical date from about 300 B. C. The 1st Olympiad began 776 B. C.; the 293rd and last in 393 A. D.
the temple of Olympian Zeus, Thuc., Plat.;—wrongly written Ὀλύμπιον.
of Olympus, Hdt.
of Olympia, Olympic, ὁ Ὀλ. ἀγών the Olympic games, Ar.
a conqueror in the Olympic games, Pind.
as adj., Ὀλ. ὕμνος Id.
Olympian, of Olympus, dwelling on Olympus, Hom., etc.; Zeus is called simple Ὀλύμπιος in Hom.; Ζεὺς πατὴρ Ὀλ. Soph.; ὁ Ζεὺς ὁ Ὀλ. Thuc.
to Olympus, Hom., etc.
Olympus, a mountain on the Macedonian frontier of Thessaly.—Hom. makes it the seat of the gods, but distinguished from heaven (οὐρανός).
the name was common to several other mountains, each apparently the highest in its own district, in Mysia, Hdt.; in Laconia, Polyb., etc.
of or relating to Olynthus (in Chalcidice), Dem.
a winter-fig which seldom ripens, an untimely fig, Lat. grossus, Hdt.
mostly in pl. ὄλυραι, a kind of grain, spelt or rye, Il., Hdt.; cf. ζειά.
to make a noise or din, of a number of people speaking at once, Od.
a noise, din, made by a number of people speaking together, Hom., Eur.; of a tempest, Il.
a noisy throng, Id.
related by blood, Pind.
of the same blood, related by blood, Lat. consanguineus, Hdt., Aesch.; φόνος ὅμ. murder by one near of kin, Aesch.
as Subst., ὅμαιμος, a brother or sister, Id., Soph.
blood-relationship, Anth.
= ὅμαιμος, Hdt., Aesch.: — ὁμαιμονέστερος more near akin, Soph.
as Subst. a brother or sister, Id.
= ὁμόγνιος (II), Aesch.
union for battle, a defensive alliance, league, Hdt., Thuc.
a fellow-fighter, an ally, Thuc.
level, τὰ ὁμαλῆ level ground, Xen.
to make even or level, Xen.
to level, equalise, Arist.
of a surface, even, level, Od., etc.; ἐν τῷ ὁμαλῷ on level ground, Thuc.; ὁμαλώτατον Id.
of circumstances, on a level, equal, ὁμαλὸς ὁ γάμος marriage with an equal, Aesch.; ὁμαλοὶ ἔρωτες Theocr.; ἀλλάλοις ὁμαλοί on a level with one another, equal, Id.
of the average sort, ὁμ. στρατιώτης an ordinary sort of soldier, Id.
adv. ὁμαλῶς, evenly, ὁμ. βαίνειν to march in an even line, Thuc.; ὁμ. προϊέναι Xen.
of all alike, Plut.
evenness of surface, Arist.; a level, Id.
equality, Plat., Arist.
to meet,
in hostile sense, to meet in fight, τὼ δ’ ἄρ’ ὁμαρτήτην Il.
to go together, βῆσαν ὁμαρτήσαντες they walked together, Od.; οὐδέ κεν ἵρηξ κίρκος ὁμαρτήσειε could not keep pace with the ship, Id.
c. dat. to walk beside, accompany, attend, τινί Hes., Trag.:—also, to pursue, chase, Aesch.
of things, to attend, Id.
in Mid. c. acc. to go after or attack jointly, Il. Hence
together, Eur.
ὁμάρτη, doric for ὁμάρτει, imperat. of ὁμαρτέω.
a fellow-soldier, Anth.
with adjoining lands, Anth.
a dwelling together, σύζυγοι ὁμ. wedded unions, Aesch.
sounding together or in concert, Soph.
to rain, μετοπωρινὸν ὀμβρήσαντος Ζηνός when Zeus sends the autumn rains, Hes.
trans. to bedew, Anth.
rainy, of rain, ὕδωρ ὄμβριον rain water, Hdt.; ὀμβρία χάλαζα Soph.; νέφος Ar.
receiving rain, Anth.
sounding with rain, Aesch.
Lat. imber, a storm of rain, a thunderstorm, Il., Hdt.: heavy rain, Hdt., Soph., etc.
generally, water, Soph.
metaph. a shower of tears, blood, etc., Aesch., Soph.
rain-bringing, Lat. imbrifer, Aesch., Ar.
a partner of the bed, consort, both of the man and woman, Anth.
playing together, a playmate, Anth.
assembled, ὁμηγερέεσσι θεοῖσι (epic dat. pl.) Il.
Dep. to assemble, call together, Od.
an assembly, meeting, company, Il., Aesch., Eur.
sameness of age, esp. of young persons; and as a collective, those of the same age, one's friends, comrades, Hom., Theogn.
addressed to a female, = ὁμῆλιξ, ὁμηλικίη δέ μοι αὐτῷ but thou art of the same age with myself, Od.
of the same age, mostly of young persons, Od., Hdt., etc.
as Subst. an equal in age, comrade, Lat. aequalis, Od., Eur.
of like stature, Luc.
a giving of hostages or securities a security, Lat. vadimonium, Thuc.
a temple of Homer, Strab.
Homeric, Hdt.: τὸ Ὁμ. the Homeric phrase, Plat.
a hostage, pledge, Plut.
to be or serve as a hostage, Aeschin.
trans. to give as a hostage, Eur.
to meet, Od.
metaph. to accord, agree, φωνῇ ὁμηρεῦσαι (ionic for ὁμηροῦσαι, part. pl. fem.) Hes.
the Homerids, a family or guild of poets in Chios, who traced their descent from Homer and recited his poems, Pind.:—generally, the imitators or the admirers of Homer, Plat.
Homeric, in Homeric manner, Plat.
Homer; the name first occurs in a Fragm. of Hes.
a pledge for the maintenance of unity, a surety, a hostage, Hdt., attic
of things, a pledge, security, τὴν γῆν ὅμηρον ἔχειν Thuc.

Ο, ο, ὂ μικρόν, little or short o, as opp. to ὂ μέγα great or long o, i. e. double o (for ω was orig. written , i. e. οο): fifteenth letter in the Greek alphabet: as numeral οʹ = 70, but ͵ο = 70,000. In early times ο represents both ο and ω; and in many words must have sounded like ου, as in βόλομαι for βούλομαι; while reversely, in ionic μοῦνος νοῦσος κοῦρος οὔνομα stand for μόνος νόσος κόρος ὄνομα. Dialect. changes: aeolic for α, as στροτός for στρατός; — for ε, Ἐρχόμενος for Ὀρχόμενος (Boeot.);—for ῠ, as ὄνυμα στύμα for ὄνομα στόμα.
doric often into οι, ἀγνοιέω πτοιέω πνοιά for ἀγνοέω ἀλοάω πτοέω.
like α, ο is often rejected or prefixed for euphony, as κέλλω ὀκέλλω, δύρομαι ὀδύρομαι.
in compd. Adjectives, ο is changed metri grat. into η, θεογενής ξιφοφόρος into θεηγενής ξιφηφόρος.
in groups or bands, in crowds, Lat. turmatim, Il.
to be in company with, consort with others, c. dat. pl., Od., attic; also, ὁμ. μετὰ Τρώεσσιν Il.; ἐνὶ πρώτοισιν ὁμιλεῖ is in company with the foremost, Id.
absol. to join in company, Od.; περὶ νεκρὸν ὁμ. to throng about the corpse, Hom.
in hostile sense, to join battle with, ὁμιλέομεν Δαναοῖσιν Id.:—absol. to join battle, Il.

of social intercourse, to hold converse with, consort with, associate with others, c. dat., Hdt., Aesch.; ἀλλήλοις, μετ’ ἀλλήλων, πρὸς ἀλλήλους Plat.:—of scholars, ὁμ. τινι to frequent a teacher's lectures, be his pupil, Xen.
absol. to be friends, Hdt.
of marriage, Soph., Xen.

of things or business which one has to do with, to attend to, busy oneself with, ὁμιλεῖν πολέμῳ Thuc.; πράγμασι καινοῖς Ar.; φιλοσοφίᾳ Plat.:—then, much like χρῆσθαι, νομίζειν, Lat. uti, ὁμ. τύχαις to be in good fortune, Pind.; εὐτυχίᾳ ὁμιλεῖν Eur.; ἐκτὸς ὁμιλεῖ (sc. τῶν ὀργῶν), i. e. wanders from his right mind, Soph.
of the things themselves, πλαγίαις φρένεσσιν ὄλβος οὐ . . ὁμ. does not consort with a crooked mind, Pind.; κυλίκων νεῖμεν ἐμοὶ τέρψιν ὁμιλεῖν gave me the delight of cups to keep me company, Soph.
to deal with a man, ταῦτα ἡ ἐμὴ νεότης ἐς τὴν Πελοποννησίων δύναμιν ὡμίλησε thus hath my youth wrought by intercourse with the power, Thuc.
of place, to come into, be in, visit, c. dat., Hdt., Aesch.
intercourse, Plat.
a disciple, scholar, Xen.
with whom one may consort, οὐχ ὁμιλητός unapproachable, Aesch.

a being together, communion, intercourse, converse, company, Lat. commercium, Aesch., etc.:— ὁμ. τινός communion or intercourse with one, Hdt.; πρός τινα Soph., etc.; τοὺς ἀξίους δὲ τῆς ἐμῆς ὁμιλίας those who are worthy of my society, Ar.; ὁμ. χθονός intercourse with a country, Eur.; πολιτεία καὶ ὁμ. public and private life, Thuc.:—also in pl., Ἑλληνικαὶ ὁμιλίαι association with Greeks, Hdt.; αἱ συγγενεῖς ὁμιλίαι intercourse with kinsfolk, Eur.
sexual intercourse, Hdt., Xen., etc.
instruction, Xen.:—later, a homily, sermon.
an association, company, Hdt., Aesch.:—in collect. sense, fellow-sojourners, Aesch.; ναὸς ὁμ. ship- mates, Soph.
any assembled crowd, a throng of people, Hom., Hdt., Aesch.: the mass of the people, the crowd, opp. to the chiefs, Il.; ὁ ψιλὸς ὅμ. the crowd of irregulars, as opp. to the ὁπλῖται, Thuc.
the throng of battle, Il.; πρώτῳ ἐν ὁμ., Lat. in prima acie, Id.: generally tumult, confusion, Hdt.
Lat. mingo, to make water, Hes.
a mist, fog, (not so thick as νέφος or νεφέλη), Il.; κονίης ὀμίχλη a cloud of dust, Id.
metaph. a mist over the eyes, Aesch.: darkness, gloom, Anth.

entry.etym: Root found in ὦμμαι, perf. pass. of ὁράω
entry.sense: the eye, Hom., etc.; κατὰ χθονὸς ὄμματα πήξας Il.; ὀρθοῖς ὄμμασιν ὁρᾶν τινα, Lat. rectis oculis aspicere, to look straight, Soph., etc.; οὐκ οἶδ’ ὄμμασιν ποίοις βλέπων πατέρα ποτ’ ἂν προσεῖδον how I could have looked him in the face, Id.; so, ὁρᾶν τινα ἐν ὄμμασι Id.; λαμπρὸς ὥσπερ ὄμματι to judge by his eyes or expression, Id.; ἐς ὄμμα τινὸς ἐλθεῖν to come within sight of him, Eur.;— κατ’ ὄμματα before one's eyes, Soph.; ἐλθεῖν κατ’ ὄμμα face to face, Eur.; but κατ’ ὄμμα, also, in point of eye-sight, Soph.:— ὡς ἀπ’ ὀμμάτων to judge by the eye, Lat. ex obtutu, Id.;— ἐν ὄμμασι, Lat. in oculis, before one's eyes, Aesch., Thuc.; —ἐξ ὀμμάτων out of sight, Eur.
that which one sees, a sight, vision, Soph.
the eye of heaven, i. e. the sun, Id., Eur.; but, ὄμμα νυκτός periphr. for νύξ (v. infr. V), Aesch., Eur.
generally, light, that which brings light, ὄμμα δόμων νομίζω δεσπότου παρουσίαν Aesch.; ὄμμα φήμης the light of glad tidings, Soph.:—hence, anything dear or precious, Aesch.
periphr. of the person, ὄμμα πελείας for πελεία, Soph.; ὄμμα νύμφας for νύμφα, Soph.; ξύναιμον ὄμμα for ξυναίμων, Id.; ὦ ταυρόμορφον ὄμμα Κηφισοῦ for ὦ ταυρόμορφε Κηφισέ, Eur.
bereft of eyes, Soph., Eur.
act. depriving of eyes, φλογμὸς ὀμμ. φυτῶν heat that robs plants of their eyes or buds, Aesch.
to furnish with eyes:—Pass., φρὴν ὠμματωμένη a mind furnished with eyes, quick of sight, Aesch.
to swear, Hom.; c. acc. cogn., ὀμνυέτω δέ τοι ὅρκον Il.; ὅ τις κ’ ἐπίορκον ὀμόσσηι whosoever swears a false oath, Id.
to swear to a thing, affirm or confirm by oath, ταῦτα δ’ ἐγὼν ἐθέλω ὀμόσαι Id.; ὄμν. τὴν εἰρήνην Dem.

foll. by inf. fut. to swear that one will . . , Il., Soph.;—often with ἦ μέν or (in attic) ἦ μήν preceding the inf., καί μοι ὄμοσσον ἦ μέν μοι ἀρήξειν Il.; so by inf. aor. and ἄν, Xen.:—foll. by inf. pres. to swear that one is doing a thing, Soph.; by inf. perf. to swear that one has done, Dem.
absol. εἰπεῖν ὀμόσας to say with an oath, Plat.

with acc. of the person or thing sworn by, to swear by, ὀμόσαι Στυγὸς ὕδωρ Il.; ὀμωμοκὼς τοὺς θεούς Dem.;—rarely c. dat., τῶι δ’ ἄρ’ ὄμνυτ’; Ar.:—Pass., ὀμώμοσται Ζεύς Zeus has been sworn by, adjured, Eur.
having a common altar, Thuc.
persons suckled with the same milk, foster-brothers or sisters, clansmen, Arist.
married to the same wife, Eur.; ὁμόγαμοι having married sisters, Id.
from the same womb, born of the same mother, Il.
an own brother, Eur.
of the same race or family, Eur.; ὁμ. μιάσματα, of bloodshed in a family, Id.:— also as Subst., ὁμογενής τινος one's congener, Id.
act. having the same wife, Soph.
one equally aged, Luc.
speaking the same tongue, Hdt.; τινι with one, Id., Xen.
of the same race: ὁμόγν. θεοί gods who protect a race or family, Lat. Dii gentilitii, Soph.; Ζεὺς ὁμ. Eur. Ar.
to be of one mind, to league together, Thuc., Xen.; ὁμ. τινί to consent to, Xen.; ὁμ. τινί τι to agree with one in a thing, Id.
of one's mind, like-minded, τινί with one, Thuc., Xen., etc.; ὁμ. τινα λαμβάνειν, ποιεῖν, ποιεῖσθαι to bring to one's own opinion, Xen.
= ὁμο-γενής, Pind.; τινι with one, Xen.
sharing one's bed, Aesch.
of the same people or race, Pind.; τινι with one, Id.
living with others, Luc.; ὁμοδίαιτα τοῖς πολλοῖς common to the generality, Id.
to be of the same opinion, agree perfectly, τινι with one, Plat.: absol. to agree together, Id.
unanimity, Plat.
of the same opinion, Luc.
a fellow-slave, Eur., Plat., etc.; ὁμ. τινος Plat.; τινι Xen.
a running together, meeting, Luc.
of the same people or race, hdt., Arist.:—generally, of the same kind, Arist.
yoked together, Plat.
of the same habits or character, Plat., Arist.
living in the same chamber with another, c. gen., Pind.
from the same place, properly a gen. (like ἐμέθεν, σέθεν, οὐρανόθεν), ἐξ ὁμόθεν Od.
as adv. from the same source, Hhymn., Hes.; τὸν ὁμόθεν a brother, Eur.; so, τὸν ὁμ. πεφυκότα Id.; ὁμ. εἶναί τινι to be from the same parents with him, Soph.
from near, hand to hand, ὁμ. μάχην ποιεῖσθαι, Lat. cominus pugnare, Xen.; ὁμόθεν διώκειν to follow close upon, Id.
sharing the same throne, Pind.
with one accord, Dem.; mostly joined with πάντες, Ar., Xen.
to be like, NTest.

entry.etym: ῑ metri grat. before a long syll.

entry.sense: ending alike, rhyming, of verses.
to have similar feelings or affections, to sympathise, τινί with another, Arist.
of things, to be subject to the same laws, to be homogeneous, Strab.
having like feelings or affections, sympathetic, τινί with another, Plat.
generally, of like nature, Id.
of like appearance with, τινι Aesch.

entry.etym: ionic and old attic ὁμοῖος, η, ον
entry.sense: like, resembling, Lat. similis, Hom., etc.; proverb., τὸν ὁμοῖον ἄγει θεὸς ὡς τὸν ὁμοῖον "birds of a feather flock together, " Od.; so, ὁ ὅμοιος τῷ ὁμοίῳ Plat.:—comp. ὁμοιότερος more like, Id.; Sup. -ότατος most like, Hdt., Soph., etc.
= ὁ αὐτός, the same, Hom.; ἓν καὶ ὅμ. one and the same, Plat.; ὁμοῖον ἡμῖν ἔσται it will be all one to us, Lat. perinde erit, Hdt.; σὺ δ’ αἰνεῖν εἴτε με ψέγειν θέλεις, ὁμοῖον Aesch.
shared alike by both, common, ὁμ. πόλεμος war in which each takes part, Hom.; γῆρας, θάνατος, μοῖρα common to all, Id.
equal in force, a match for one, Lat. par, Il., Hdt.
like in mind, at one with, agreeing with, τινι Hes.:—hence (sub. ἑαυτῷ) always the same, Id.; ὅμοιος πρὸς τοὺς αὐτοὺς κινδύνους Thuc.

τὸ ὁμοῖον ἀνταποδιδόναι to give "tit for tat," Lat. par pari referre, Hdt.; so, τὴν ὁμοίην (sc. χάριν) διδόναι or ἀποδιδόναι τινί Id.; τὴν ὁμοίην φέρεσθαι παρά τινος to have a like return made one, Id.; ἐπ’ ἴσῃ καὶ ὁμοίᾳ (v. ἴσος II.2).
ἐν ὁμοίῳ ποιεῖσθαί τι to hold a thing in like esteem, Id.
ἐκ τοῦ ὁμοίου, alike, much like ὁμοίως, Thuc.; ἐκ τῶν ὁμοίων with equal advantages, in fair fight, Aesch.
of the same rank or station, Hdt.: οἱ ὅμοιοι, the peers, Xen., Arist.
Construction:
absol., as often in Hom., etc.
the person or thing to which one is like in dat., as with Lat. similis, Hom., etc.; also in gen.: —ellipt., κόμαι Χαρίτεσσιν ὁμοῖαι, for -κόμαι ταῖς τῶν Χαρίτων ὁμοῖαι, Il.
that in which a person or thing is like another is in acc., ἀθανάτῃσι φυὴν καὶ εἶδος ὁμοίη Od.
with inf., θείειν ἀνέμοισιν ὁμοῖοι like the winds to run, Il.
foll. by καί, like Lat. perinde ac, Hdt., etc.
adv., often in the neuters, ὅμοιον and ὅμοια, ionic and old attic ὁμοῖον, ὁμοῖα, in like manner with, ὁμοῖα τοῖς μάλιστα "second to none, " Hdt.; ὁμοῖα τοῖς πρώτοισι Id.
alike, Aesch.
regul. adv. ὁμοίως, in like manner with, c. dat., Hdt., attic; ὁμ. καὶ . . Hdt.
alike, equally, Id., Aesch.
ending alike, Arist.: τὸ ὁμοιοτέλευτον the like ending of two verses.
likeness, resemblance, Plat.
likeness of manners and life, Strab.
of like manners and life, Thuc.:— adv. -πως, in like manner with another, c. dat., Id.

to make like, Lat. assimilare, τί τινι Eur., Plat.; πρὸς τὰ παρόντα τὰς ὀργὰς ὁμ. to make their feelings suitable to present circumstances, Thuc.:—Pass. to be made like, become like, Hom., Eur., etc.; in perf. ὡμοίωμαι, to be like, Plat.
to liken, compare, τί τινι Hdt., etc.; so in Mid., Id.:— in N. T. of parables.
in Mid. also to make a like return, Hdt.
a likeness, image, resemblance, counterfeit, Plat.
a becoming like, assimilation, Plat.
likeness, resemblance, NTest.
eating together, ap. Arist.
concentric with, Strab.
to call out together, Od., Soph.; ὁμ. τινι to call or shout to, whether to encourage or upbraid, threaten, Il.;—c. inf. to command loudly, call on one to do, Id.
properly of several persons, a joint call; but of single persons, μεῖναι ὁμοκλήν to bide his call, Il.; with a sense of reproof, rebuke, Hom.
generally, harmony.
one who has an equal share of an inheritance, a coheir, Pind.
one who calls out to, an upbraider, threatener, Il.
reclining on the same couch, at table, Hdt.
sharing the same bed, Eur.; but, Ζηνὸς ὁμόλεκτρον κάρα, of Tyndareus, as husband of Leda, Id.
to speak together; hence,
to speak one language, τινί with one, Hdt.:—generally, οὐδὲν ὁμ. τινί to have naught to do with, Id.
to hold the same language with, i. e. to agree with, τινί Id., Thuc.

to agree to a thing, allow, admit, confess, concede, grant, c. acc. rei, Hdt., Soph., etc.; ὁμ. τὴν εἰρήνην to agree to the terms of peace, Dem.:— without the acc. rei, ὁμολογῶ σοι I grant you, i. e. I admit it, Ar., Xen.:—c. inf. to allow, confess, grant that . . , Ar., Plat.
to agree or promise to do, c. inf., Plat.
the inf. is often omitted, ὁμολογήσαντες (sc. ἀπαλλάξεσθαι) Hdt.:—hence simply to make an agreement, come to terms, τινί with another, Id.
Mid., just like the Act., Plat., Xen.
Pass. to be agreed upon, allowed or granted by common consent, Xen.; c. inf. to be allowed or confessed to be, Plat., Xen.
absol., ὁμολογεῖται it is granted, allowed, Plat.; τὰ ὁμολογούμενα, τὰ ὡμολογημένα things granted, Lat. concessa, Id.
that which is agreed upon, taken for granted, a postulate, Plat.
agreement, Plat.
an assent, admission, concession, Id.: κατὰ τὴν ἐμὴν ὁμ. by my admission, Id.
an agreement made, compact, Id.; often in pl., Id.; esp. in war, terms of surrender, Hdt., Thuc.
agreeing, of one mind, ὁμ. γενέσθαι τινὶ περί τινος to be of one mind with one on a point, Xen.:—also of things, agreeing, correspondent, Arist.
adv. -γως, agreeably to, in unison with, Id.:—so, ἐξ ὁμολόγου confessedly, Polyb.

entry.etym: adverb from part. pres. pass. of ὁμολογέω
entry.sense: conformably with, τοῖς εἰρημένοις Xen.
by common consent, confessedly, Thuc., Plat.
a name of Zeus in Boeotia and Thessaly: —hence one of the Gates of Thebes were called πύλαι Ὁμολωίδες, Aesch., Eur.
a fellow-knave (cf. μαστιγίας) Ar.
born of the same mother, Lat. frater uterinus, Hdt., Plat.; ὁμοματρία ἀδελφή Ar.
companion in death, Luc.
to be of one mind, agree together, live in harmony, Thuc.; ὁμονοοῦσα ὀλιγαρχία a united oligarchy, Arist.
c. dat. to live in harmony with others, c. dat., Plat.
conducing to agreement, in harmony, Plat.:—adv. -ικῶς ἔχειν to be of one mind, Id.
oneness of mind or thought, unity, concord, Thuc., Plat., etc.
of one mind, Lat. concors: adv. -νόως, Xen.
of like feelings or affections, sympathetic, Arist.; c. gen., ὁμ. λύπης καὶ ἡδονῆς affected alike by pain and pleasure, Plat.
by the same father, Hdt., Aesch.
to sail together or in company, Polyb.
a sailing in company, Cic.
sailing together or in company, Anth.
from or of the same city: poet. ὁμό-πτολις, Soph.
of or with the same plumage, Plat.; ὁμόπτεροι ἐμοί my fellow-birds, birds of my feather, Ar.
metaph. of like feather, closely resembling, Aesch., Eur.; νᾶες ὁμ. consort-ships (or equally swift), Aesch.; ἀπήνη ὁμ. i. e. the two brothers, Eteocles and Polynices, Eur.
to wipe off, 3rd sg. imperf. ὠμόργαζε Hhymn.
to wipe:— Mid., δάκρυα ὠμόργνυντο were wiping away their tears, Od.; παρειάων δάκρυ’ ὀμορξαμένη were wiping the tears from their cheeks, Il.
ionic ὁμουρέω, fut. -ήσω to border upon, march with, [οἱ Κελτοὶ] ὁμουρέουσι Κυνησίοισι Hdt.
having the same borders with, marching with, bordering on, τοῖσι Δωριεῦσι, τῇ Λιβύῃ Hdt.; absol. bordering, Thuc.; πόλεμος ὅμορος a border war, Dem.
metaph. bordering on, closely resembling, Arist.
also as Subst., a neighbour, Hdt., Thuc.; κατὰ τὸ ὅμορον because of their neighbourhood, Thuc.
to row together; metaph. to agree, consent, Soph.; ὁμ. τινι to agree with him, Eur.
properly, rowing together: hence side by side, Theocr.:—so, ὁμορρόθιος, ον, Anth.

to one and the same place, Il.; ὁμός’ ἦλθε μάχη the battle came to the same spot, i. e. the armies met, Id.; ὁμόσε ἰέναι, like Lat. cominus pugnare, ὁμ. ἰέναι τοῖς ἐχθροῖς to close with the enemy, Thuc.; ὁμ. χωρεῖν; so, ὁμ. θεῖν, φέρεσθαι to run to meet, Xen.
metaph., ὁμ. ἰέναι τοῖς λόγοις to come to issue with the arguments, Eur.
of equal might, Anth.
to eat with, take one's meals with others, c. dat., Hdt.
eating together, μετά τινος Hdt.
equipped in the same way, Thuc.
to live in the same tent or house with others, c. dat., Xen.
one and the same, common, joint, Lat. communis, Hom., Hes.; ὁμὰ φρονεῖν to be of one mind, Hes.
sharing in the drink-offering, sharing the same cup, Hdt., Dem.
sown together: sprung from the same race, kindred, Hhymn., Trag.: as Subst. a brother or a sister, Trag.
ὁμ. γυνή a wife common to two (Laius and Oedipus), Soph.; of Oedipus, τοῦ πατρὸς ὁμόσπορος having the same wife with his father, Id.
in company with others, c. gen., Soph.
buried together, Aeschin.
practising the same craft with another, c. dat., Plat.:—as Subst., a fellow-workman, Hdt., Plat.
sameness of value or honour, Luc.
held in equal honour, Il.; μακάρεσσι with the gods, Theocr.; c. gen. rei, τῆς στρατηγίας ὁμ. having an equal share in the command, Plut.
οἱ ὁμότιμοι, among the Persians, nobles of equal rank, the peers of the realm, Xen.
having one common wall, separated by a party-wall, contiguous, Plat.:—metaph., of disease, γείτων ὁμ. a next-door neighbour, Aesch.
eating at the same table with another, c. dat., Hdt.; συνέστιος καὶ ὁμ. Plat.;— οἱ ὁμ., messmates, Persian name for certain courtiers, Xen.
of the same habits or life, Plat.:— as Subst., οἱ ὁμότροποί τινος one's messmates, Aeschin.
of like fashion, Hdt.
reared or bred together with another, c. dat., Hhymn.; ὁμότροφα τοῖσι ἀνθρώποισι θηρία, of domestic animals, Hdt.
absol., ὁμότρ. πεδία plains where we fed in common, Ar.
properly gen. neut. of ὁμός,
of Place, at the same place, together, Il., Soph., etc.
together, at once, ἄμφω ὁμοῦ Od.; δυοῖν ὁμοῦ Soph.; αἶγας ὁμοῦ καὶ ὄϊς both sheep and goats, Il.; λιμὸν ὁμου καὶ λοιμόν Hes., etc.
c. dat. together with, along with, κεῖσθαι ὁμοῦ νεκύεσσι Il.; οἰμωγὴ ὁμοῦ κωκύμασιν Aesch.
close at hand, hard by, Soph., Ar.: c. dat. close to, Soph., Xen.
rarely c. gen., νεὼς ὁμοῦ στείχειν to go to join my ship, Soph.
of amount, in all, εἰσὶν ὁμοῦ δισμύριοι Dem., etc.
ὁμοῦ καί just like, Xen.
going by the side of another, c. gen., Pind.

to be of the same mind, have the same thoughts, Od.; ὁμοφρονέοντε νοήμασιν in unity of purposes, Id.; πόλεμος ὁμοφρονέων a war of common consent, Hdt.:—c. dat., οὑ γὰρ ἀλλήλοισι ὁμοφρονέουσι are not agreed together, Id.
of the same growth or nature, Plat.
sameness of race or tribe, Strab.

of the same race or stock, Thuc., etc.; οἱ ὁμ. those of the same race, Xen.; φιλία ὁμόφ. friendship with those of the same stock, Eur.:— τὸ ὁμόφυλον, = ὁμοφυλία, Id.; τὸ μὴ ὁμ. a city peopled by different races, Arist.
to speak the same language with another, c. dat., Hdt.
to sound together, c. dat., ὁ. τῷ λόγῳ chimes in with the argument, Arist.
in Music, unison, Arist.
speaking the same language with others, c. dat., Hdt., Thuc., etc.
of the same sound or tone, in unison with, τινι Aesch.
sameness of colour, Xen.
the even surface of the body, the skin, Hdt.
to keep time with, τινί Luc.: absol. to keep time, Id.
having an equal right to vote with others, c. dat., Hdt.; μετά τινων Id.
to unite: aor1 pass. inf. ὁμωθῆναι Il.
of or relating to corn: hence bountiful, wealthy, ὄμπνιᾰ Anth.
made from unripe grapes: hence harsh, austere, crabbed, Ar.
with sour grapes, Anth.
having a boss, bossy, Anth.
having a navel or boss, ἀσπίδος ὀμφαλοέσσης of the shield with a central boss, Il.; ζυγὸν ὀμφαλόεν a yoke with a knob on the top, Id.
the navel, Lat. umbilicus, Il., Hdt., etc.
anything central (like a navel):
the knob or boss in the middle of the shield, Lat. umbo, Il.
a button or knob on the horse's yoke to fasten the reins to, Id.
in pl. the knobs at each end of the stick round which books were rolled, Lat. umbilici, Luc.

the centre or middle point, as the island of Calypso is the ὀμφαλός of the sea, Od.; and Delphi (or rather a round stone in the Delphic temple) was called ὀμφαλός as marking the middle point of Earth, Pind., Aesch., etc.
an unripe grape, πάροιθε δέ τ’ ὄμφακές εἰσιν Od.; ὅτ’ ὄμφακες αἰόλλονται Hes.; ὅταν δὲ τεύχῃ Ζεὺς ἀπ’ ὄμφακος οἶνον, i. e. autumn, when the unripe grapes become fit to make wine, Aesch.

the voice of a god (opp. to αὐδή, the human voice), Hom.; θείη δέ μιν ἀμφέχυτ’ ὀμφή, of the voice of the dream sent by Zeus to Agamemnon, Il.; κατ’ ὀμφὴν σήν on hearing the sound of thy name (for the name of Oedipus had something awful in it), Soph.
a sweet voice, Pind.:— a voice, sound, Eur.
a having the same name, identity, an equivocal word, Arist.
having the same name, Il., etc.; τινι with one, Thuc., etc.; τὸν ὁμ. ἐμαυτῷ my own namesake, Dem.:—as Subst., c. gen., ὁ σαυτοῦ or ὁ σὸς ὁμώνυμος your namesake, Plat.
of like kind, Id.
lodging under the same roof with another, c. dat., Dem., Babr.

entry.etym: Conj. from ὁμός but with changed accent
entry.sense: all the same, nevertheless, notwithstanding, still, Lat. tamen, Il., Soph., etc.:—often strengthened by other words, ἀλλ’ ὅμως, Lat. attamen, but still, but for all that, Ar., etc.; ὅμως μήν, ὅμως μέντοι Plat.; ὅμως γε μήν, ὅμως γε μέντοι Ar.:—used elliptically, οἴσεις οὐδὲν ὑγιές, ἀλλ’ ὅμως (sc. οἰστέον) Id.

in apodosis after καί εἰ or καὶ ἐάν, as tamen after etsi or quamquam, κεἰ τὸ μηδὲν ἐξερῶ, φράσω δ’ ὅμως even if I shall say nothing plainly, yet I will speak, Soph.;—so, κλῦθί μου νοσῶν ὅμως (i. e. εἰ νοσεῖς, ὅμως κλῦθι), Id.
to limit single words, Lat. quamvis, ἀπάλαμόν περ ὅμως helpless though he be, Hes., etc.
equally, likewise, alike, Lat. pariter, Hom., Trag.; πλῆθεν ὁμῶς ἵππων τε καὶ ἀνδρῶν was filled full both of men and horses alike, Il.; πάντες ὁμῶς all alike, Hom.
c. dat. like as, equally with, ἐχθρὸς ὁμῶς Ἀΐδαο πύλῃσι hated like the gates of hell, Il.
together with, Theogn.
holding or dwelling together, τοὺς ὁμωχέτας δαίμονας worshipped in the same temple, Thuc.
the wild ass, Strab., Babr.

entry.etym: only used in nom. and acc. sg., the other cases being supplied by ὄνειρος
entry.sense: a dream, vision in sleep, opp. to a waking vision (ὕπαρ), Od., Soph., etc.; ὥστε μηδ’ ὄναρ ἰδεῖν, to express profound sleep, Plat.
proverb. of anything fleeting or unreal, ὀλιγοχρόνιον ὥσπερ ὄναρ Theogn.; παρέρχεται ὡς ὄναρ ἥβη Theocr.
ὄναρ as adv., in a dream, in sleep, ὄναρ ὑμᾶς καλῶ Aesch.; μηδ’ ἰδὼν ὄναρ not even in my dreams, Eur., etc.; cf. ὕπαρ.
ὀνεία, (sc. δορά) ass's skin, fem. of ὄνειος, Babr.
anything that profits or helps, Il.: advantage, aid, succour, Hes., etc.
a means of strengthening, refreshment, Od., Hes.; στιβάδεσσιν ὄνειαρ good for beds, Theocr.
in pl. ὀνείᾰτα, food, victuals, Hom.; also of rich presents Il.
of persons, πᾶσιν ὄνειαρ Id.
reproachful, Hom.
dishonourable, Anth.

c. acc. rei et dat. pers. to throw a reproach upon one, cast in one's teeth, object or impute to one, Lat. objicere, exprobrare, Hom., etc.; also, ὀνειδίζειν τινὶ ὅτι . . to impute it to him that . . , Il., Plat.
omitting the acc. rei, to reproach, upbraid,
c. dat. pers., Il., Hdt.
c. acc. pers., ἔπεσίν μιν ὀνείδισον Il.; τυφλόν μ’ ὠνείδισας (sc. ὄντα) did'st reproach me with being blind, Soph.
insult, reproach, blame, Hdt.
full of reproach, Eur.
one who reproaches with a thing, c. gen. rei, Arist.
reproachful, abusive, Luc.
reproach, censure, blame, Hom.; ὄνειδος ἔχειν to be in disgrace, Hdt.; ὄνειδός [ἐστι], c. inf., Eur.; ὡς ἐν ὀνείδει by way of reproach, Plat.:—pl., ὀνείδη ἔχειν τὰ μέγιστα Id., etc.

matter of reproach, a reproach, disgrace, σοὶ, μὲν δὴ κατηφείη καὶ ὄν., Il.; c. gen., τὸ πόλεως ὄν. the reproach of the city, Aesch.; ὄν. Ἑλλάνων Soph.; so, Oedipus calls his daughters τοιαῦτ’ ὀνείδη Id.
of an ass, Ar.; ὄν. γάλα ass's milk, Dem.
dreamy, of dreams, ἐν ὀνειρείῃσι πύλῃσι at the gates of dreams, Od.
an interpreter of dreams, Theocr., Theophr.
for interpreting dreams, πινάκιον Plut.
an interpreter of dreams, Aesch.
to deal with dreams, i. e. to dream, Plat.; ὀν. τι to dream of a thing. Ar.; πολλὰ ὀνειροπολεῖ ἐν τῇ γνώμῃ "builds many such castles in the air," Dem.
to cheat by dreams, Ar.
one occupied with dreams, a dreamer, or an interpreter of dreams, Il., Hdt.

entry.etym: pl. ὄνειρα, but the metaph. form ὀνείρατα as if from ὄνειραρ was more common in nom. and acc.; so, gen. ὀνειράτων, dat. -ασι; also in sg., gen ὀνείρατος, dat. ὀνείρατι
entry.sense: a dream, Hom., etc.
as prop. n. Ὄνειρος, god of dreams, Id., Hes.; cf. ἐνύπνιον.
versed in dreams and their interpretations, Eur.
to draw up with a windlass (ὄνος III. 1), imperf. ὤνευον Thuc.
a donkey-driver, Dem.
useful, profitable, beneficial, Aesch., Soph.: aiding, succouring, Soph.
useful to the state, Simon.
use, profit, advantage, good luck, Od., Soph.:—c. gen. rei, enjoyment of a thing, profit or delight from it, Aesch., etc.; so, ὄν. εὑρεῖν ἀπό τινος Soph.
the dung of animals, Il.
a little ass, donkey, Ar.
of or for an ass: ὀνικὸς μύλος, v. ὄνος III. 2.

entry.etym: impf. act for ὀνίνημι supplied by ὠφέλουν
entry.sense: Act. to profit, benefit, help, assist, and, like Lat. juvo, to gratify, delight; absol. and c. acc. pers., Il., etc.; πολλὰ ὀν. τινα Od.; ὡς ὤνησας ὅτι ἀπεκρίνω how you pleased me by answering, Plat.

Mid. to have profit or advantage, derive benefit, have enjoyment or delight, Hom., etc.; c. gen. to have advantage from, have enjoyment of, δαιτὸς ὄνησο Od.; τί σευ ἄλλος ὀνήσεται; what good will others have of thee, i. e. what good will you have done them? Il.; so, ὄνασθαί τι ἀπό τινος Plat.
aor.2 part. ὀνήμενος, = felix, ἐσθλός μοι δοκεῖ εἶναι, ὀνήμενος he seems to me noble, favoured by the gods, Od.

aor. opt. ὀναίμην, αιο, αιτο, in protestations and wishes, ὄναιο, Lat. sis felix! Eur., etc.; and c. gen., ὄναιο τῶν φρενῶν bless thee for thy good sense, Id.; μὴ νῦν ὀναίμην may I not thrive (where βίου must be supplied), Soph.:—also in ironical sense, ὄναιο μέν τἄν you'd be the better of it! Ar.; ἁλσὶν διασμηχθεὶς ὄναιτ’ ἂν οὑτοσί he'd be very nice if he were rubbed down with salt, Id.
ass's dung, in pl., Ar.
to have a mare covered by an ass, Xen.
to name or speak of by name, call or address by name, Il., Hdt., Xen.
of things, to name, specify, Il.
ὀν. τινά τι to call one something, Hdt., attic: in Mid., παῖδά μ’ ὠνομάζετο called me his son, Soph.:—Pass., ὄνομα δ’ ὠνομάζετο Ἕλενος Id., etc.
εἶναι is often added pleon., τὰς οὐνομάζουσι εἶναι Ὑπερόχην καί . . whose names they say are Hyperoche and . . , Hdt.; σοφιστὴν ὀνομάζουσιν τὸν ἄνδρα εἶναι Plat.
to name or call after . . , ἐπί τινι Hdt., etc.; ἔκ τινος Soph.:—Pass., ἀπὸ τούτου τοῦτο οὐνομάζεται hence this saying has arisen, Hdt.
to use names or words, μάλα σεμνῶς ὀνομάζων Dem.
to name or call by name, and of things, to name, repeat, Hom.
simply, to utter, speak, Od.: c. inf. fut, to promise to do, Id.
to nominate, appoint, Il.

Dep., to blame, find fault with, throw a slur upon, treat scornfully, τι Hom.; ἦ οὔνεσθ’, ὅτι μοι Ζεὺς ἔδωκεν; do ye complain that Zeus has given? Il.; c. gen., οὐδ’ σε ἔολπα ὀνόσσεσθαι κακότητος I hope thou wilt not quarrel with thy ill-luck (i. e. deem it too light), Od.; ὀν. τινα to throw a slur upon, Hdt.
calling by name, by name, Lat. nominatim, Od.
one who announces guests by name, Lat. nomenclator, Luc.
of famous name, Il.
Lat. nomen, a name, Hom., etc.:—absol., by name, πόλις ὄνομα Καιναί Xen., etc.; also in dat., πόλις Θάψακος ὀνόματι Id.
ὄν. θεῖναί τινα to give one a name, Od.; but commonly in Mid., ὄν. θέσθαι Id., attic; and for Pass., ὄν. κεῖταί τινι Ar., etc.; ὄν. ἔχειν ἀπό τινος Hdt.
ὄνομα καλεῖν τινα to call one by name, Od., attic; so with pass. verbs. ὄν. ὠνομάζετο Ἕλενος Soph.; ὄν. κέκληται δημοκρατία Thuc.
name. fame, Ἰθάκης γε καὶ ἐς Τροίην ὄνομ’ ἵκει Od.; τὸ μέγα ὄν. τῶν Ἀθηνῶν Thuc.; ὄνομα or τὸ ὄν. ἔχειν to have a name for a thing (good or bad), 2 opt., Thuc.
a mere name, opp. to the real person or thing, Od.; opp. to ἔργον, Eur., etc.
a false name, pretence, pretext, ὀνόματι or ἐπ’ ὀνόματι under the pretence, Thuc.
ὄνομα is also used in periphr. phrases, ὄνομα τῆς σωτηρίας, for σωτηρία, Eur.; ὦ φίλτατον ὄν. Πολυνείκους Id.
a phrase, expression, Xen.: generally, a saying, speech, Dem.
in Grammar, a noun, Lat. nomen, opp. to ῥῆμα, verbum, Ar., Plat., etc.
by name, Hdt., Thuc.
named, to be named, and οὐκ ὀνομαστός not to be named or mentioned, i. e. abominable, Lat. infandus, Od.
of name or note, notable, famous, Theogn., Hdt., etc.
telling people's names, Lat. nomenclator, Plut.
to coin names, Arist.
an ass, Il., Hdt., etc.:—proverb.,
περὶ ὄνου σκιᾶς for an ass's shadow, i. e. for nothing at all, Lat. de lana caprina, Ar., Plat.
ὄνου πόκαι or πόκες, v. πόκος II.
ἀπ’ ὄνου πεσεῖν, of one who gets into a scrape by his own clumsiness, with a pun on ἀπὸ νοῦ πεσεῖν, Ar.
ὄνος ἄγων μυστήρια, of one heavily laden, Id.
ὄνου ὑβριστότερος, of brutality, Xen.
ὄνου ὦτα λαβεῖν, like Midas, Ar.
ὄνων φάτνη a luminous appearance between the ὄνοι (two stars in the breast of the Crab), Lat. praesepe, Theocr.
from the ass as a beast of burden,
a windlass, pulley, Hdt.
the upper millstone, ὄνος ἀλέτης Xen.:—so, μύλος ὀνικός NTest.
a beaker, wine-cup, Ar.
to be blamed or scorned, Il.
to blame, Hhymn., Hes.
an ass-keeper, Hdt.
existing things, the present, opp. to the past and future; but also, reality, truth, opp. to that which is not, Plat.
that which one has, property, like οὐσία, Dem.
really, verily, Eur., etc.; ὄντως τε καὶ ἀληθῶς really and truly, Plat.

Lat. unguis, in Hom. only in pl. of the eagle's talons;— of human beings, a nail, Hes., Hdt., attic:—of horses and oxen, a hoof, Xen.—Special phrases, εἰς ἄκρους τοὺς ὄνυχας ἀφίκετο (sc. ὁ οἶνος) warmed me to my fingers' ends, Eur.; ὄνυχας ἐπ’ ἄκρους στάς on tiptoe, Lat. summis digitis, Id.; ἐξ ἁπαλῶν ὀνύχων from childhood, Hor. de tenero ungui, Anth.; ὀδοῦσι καὶ ὄνυξι, i. e. in every possible way, Luc.
a veined gem, onyx, Id.
made of onyx, Plut.
a sauce of vinegar and brine, Ar.
of or for vinegar, Anth.
sharp, sour, tart, Ar.
a vinegar-cruet, Lat. acetabulum, Ar.; applied to a diminutive person, Id.
poor wine, vin-de-pays, Ar., Xen.
vinegar made therefrom, Aesch., Ar.
metaph. of a sour fellow, Theocr.
a kind of beech: a spear-shaft made from its wood, a spear, Eur.
a vinegar-saucer, then, generally, a shallow vessel, saucer, Ar.
sharp-pointed, Il.
shrill-screaming, Aesch.
sour milk, whey, Strab.
shrill-wailing, Aesch.
quick-sighted, Hdt., Luc.
sharp-sounding, Anth.
sharp-edged, sharp-pointed, Eur.
of a person, goaded to passion, infuriated, Soph.
to be quick to anger, Eur.
Pass. to be provoked, Ar.
sudden anger, Eur.
quick to anger, choleric, Eur., Ar., etc.: — sharp to punish, of the Areopagus, Aesch.: τὸ ὀξύθυμον, by crasis τοὐξύθυμον, = ὀξυθυμία, Eur.
with pointed leaves, of a pine, Anth.
wailed with shrill cries, Soph.
to seize quickly: to seize an opportunity, Xen.
glib of tongue, Ar.
quickness at learning, Strab.
keenly studied, Ar.
bringing down the quick anger (of the Erinyes), Aesch.
clear-singing, Aesch.
a sharpener, Anth.
to sharpen: metaph. to goad to anger, provoke, Soph.:—Pass., Hdt.
to sharpen, quicken, Anth.
sharp-pointed, Il.
sharp-pointed, Anth.
ravenously hungry, Cic.
sharp-pointed, Aesch.
swift-footed, Eur.
sharp-pointed, Aesch.
swift-winged:— τὰ ὀξύπτερα swift wings, Aesop.
turning quickly, of a delicate balance: metaph., ὀξ. πρὸς τὰς ὀργάς sudden and quick to anger, Plat.; ὀξ. θυμός sudden anger, Id.
sharp, keen, Hom., Hes., etc.; ἐς ὀξὺ ἀπηγμένος brought to a point, Hdt.; τὸ ὀξύ the vertex of a triangle, Id.
of feeling, sharp, keen, ὀδύναι Il.; ὀξὺς ἠέλιος the piercing sun, Hhymn.; so, χιὼν ὀξεῖα, like Hor.'s gelu acutum, Pind.; μάχη ὀξέα keenly contested, Hdt.
of the sight, neut. as adv., ὀξύτατον δέρκεσθαι to be keenest of sight, Il.; so ὀξὺ νοεῖν to notice a thing sharply, Id.; ὀξὺ ἀκούειν to be quick of hearing, Id.
of things that affect the sight, dazzling, bright, of the sun, Id.; of colours, Ar.
of sound, sharp, shrill, piercing, Il.; and of the voice, ὀξὺ βοήσας, ὀξὺ λεληκώς Id., etc.
of musical tones, sharp, high, opp. to βαρύς, Plat.
of taste, sharp, pungent, acid, Xen., etc.
of smell, ὀξύτατον ὄζειν Ar.
metaph. of mind, sharp, keen: quick to anger, hasty, passionate, Il., Soph., etc.
sharp, quick, clever, Plat.; c. inf., ὀξ. ἐπινοῆσαι Thuc.; γνῶναι ὀξύτατοι Dem.
of motion, quick, swift, Ar.; [ἡ νόσος] ὀξεῖα φοιτᾷ καὶ ταχεῖ’ ἀπέρχεται Soph.; ὀξὺς νότος Id.
regul. adv. ὀξέως, quickly, soon, Thuc., Plat.; but,
neut. ὀξύ and pl. ὀξέα as adv., v. supr.:—comp. ὀξύτερον Thuc., etc.; Sup. ὀξύτατον Il.; ὀξύτατα Plat.
sharp-toothed, sharp-fanged, Aesch.; of a gnat, Ar.:—of a sword, sharp-edged, Eur.
sharpness, pointedness, Plat.
of sound, sharpness, opp. to βαρύτης, Id.
of the mind, sharpness, cleverness, Id.
of motion, quickness, Id., Dem.
sharp-cutting, keen, Pind.
sharp-sounding, piercing, of sound, Soph.
oxytone, having the acute accent, i. e. the accent on the last syllable.
piercing, pointed, πίτυς ὀξ. the pine with its sharp spines, Anth.
sharpness of voice, Arist.
sharp-voiced, thrilling, Soph.
quick with the hands, quick to strike, Theocr.
ὀξύχειρι σὺν κτύπῳ with quick beating of the hands in lamentation, Aesch.
quick to anger, Solon., Soph.
sharp-sighted, Arist., Luc.
to follow, accompany, attend, τινί Il., Pind.
of things, ἀνεμώλια γάρ μοι ὀπηδεῖ [τόξα] useless do they go with me, Il.; ἀρετὴν σήν, ἥ σοι ὀπηδεῖ Od., etc.
attendant, Soph., Eur.: metaph., ἀοιδὰ στεφάνων ὀπαδός Pind.; πυκνοστίκτων ὀπ. ἐλάφων pursuing them, of artemis, Soph.; ἀστέρες νυκτὸς ὀπ. Theocr.
as adj. accompanying, attending, c. dat., Hhymn.

to make to follow, send with one, give as a companion, or follower, ἐπεί ῥά οἱ ὤπασα πομπόν Il.; πολὺν δέ μοι ὤπασε λαόν gave me many subjects, Id.:—Mid. to bid another follow one, take as a companion, Hom.
also of things, κῦδος ὀπάζει gives him glory to be with him, Il.; then simply, to give, grant, Hom., Pind., Aesch.
to give besides, add, ἔργῳ δ’ ἔργον ὄπαζε Hhymn.; ἔργον πρὸς ἀσπίδι ὤπασεν put a work of art on the shield, Aesch.
like διώκω, to press hard, chase, Ἕκτωρ ὤπαζε Ἀχαιούς Il.; χαλεπὸν δέ σε γῆρας ὀπάζει Id.:—Pass., χειμάρρους ὀπαζόμενος Διὸς ὄμβρῳ a torrent following, i. e. swollen with, rain, Id.
a hole in the roof, Plut.; cf. ἀνοπαῖα.
by the same father, Il.;so, ὀπάτωρ, ορος, ὁ, ἡ, Anth.
a comrade in war, an esquire, such as was Meriones to Idomeneus, Phoenix to Peleus, Il.
the, that
ὁ, ἡ, τό, is
demonstr. Pronoun.
the definite Article.

in epic, the relative Pronoun, when it is written with the accent ὅ, ἥ, τό = ὅς, ἥ, ὅ. Besides the common forms, note epic gen. sg. τοῖο for τοῦ; pl. nom. τοί, ταί; gen. fem. τάων [ᾰ], dat. τοῖσι, τῇς and τῇσι; dual gen, and dat. τοῖιν:— in Trag. we find τοὶ μέν . . , τοὶ δέ . . , for οἱ μέν . . , οἱ δέ . . ; dat. pl. also τοῖσι, ταῖσι: the dual has commonly but one gender, τώ for τά, τοῖν for ταῖν.
DEMONSTR. PRONOUN:
joined with a Subst., not as the Art., but like Lat. ille, ὁ Τυδείδης Tydeus's famous son, Il.; Νέστωρ ὁ γέρων Nestor— that aged man, Id.; τιμῆς τῆς Πριάμου for honour, namely that of Priam, Id.
without a Subst., he, she, it, ὁ γὰρ ἦλθε Id., etc.
pecul. usages,
before Relat. Pronouns, to call attention to the foregoing noun, ἐφάμην σε περὶ φρένας ἔμμεναι ἄλλων, τῶν ὅσσοι Λυκίκην ναιετάουσιν far above the rest, namely above those who . . , Id.
ὁ μέν . . , ὁ δέ . . , either in Opposition, ὁ μέν the former, ὁ δέ the latter), or in Partition, the one . . , the other . . , Lat. hic . . , ille . . .
absolute usages of single cases,
fem. dat. τῇ, there, on that spot, Hom.; τὸ μὲν τῇ, τὸ δὲ τῇ Xen.:—with a notion of motion towards, thither, Il.
of Manner, τῇπερ in this way, thus, Od.; τῇ μέν . . , τῇ δέ . . , in one way . . , in another . . , or partly . . , partly, Eur., etc.
relative, where, for ᾗ, Hom.
neut. gen. τοῦ, therefore, Id.
neut. dat. τῷ, therefore, Id., Soph.
thus, in this wise, then, if this be so, on this condition, Hom.
neut. acc. wherefore, Id., Soph.; τὸ δέ, absol., but as to this . . , Plat.
τὸ μέν . . , τὸ δέ . . , partly . . , partly . . , or on the one hand . . , on the other . . , Od., attic; τὰ μέν . . , τὰ δέ . . , Hdt., Soph., Thuc.; also, τὰ μέν τι . . , τὰ δέ τι . . , Xen.
with Prepositions, of Time, ἐκ τοῦ, epic τοῖο, ever since, Il.
πρὸ τοῦ, sometimes written προτοῦ, before this, aforetime, Hdt., Aesch.; so, ἐν τῷ προτοῦ χρόνῳ Thuc.
ἐν τοῖς is often used in Prose with Superlatives, ἐν τοῖς θειότατον one of the most marvellous things, Hdt.; ἐν τοῖς πρῶτοι among the first, Thuc.

THE DEFINITE ARTICLE, the, the indefin. being τὶς, τὶ, a or an. The use of as the Article sprung from its use as demonstr. Pron., τὸν ὀπίστατον him that was hindmost, i.e. the hindmost man, Il.; τὸν ἄριστον him that was bravest, etc.;— also with Advs. τὸ πρίν, τὸ πάρος περ, τὸ πρόσθεν, τὸ τρίτον, τὰ πρῶτα all in Il.

the true Article is first fully established in attic: it is omitted with prop. names and with appellatives which require no specification, as θεός, βασιλεύς:—but it is added to Prop. Names, when there has been previous mention of the person, as Thuc. speaks first of Πειθίας, and then refers to him as ὁ Π.; or to give pecul. emphasis, like Lat. ille, ὁ Λάϊος, ὁ Φοῖβος Soph.
with Infinitives, which thereby become Substantives, τὸ εἶναι the being; τὸ φρονεῖν good sense, etc.
in neuter, to specify any word or expression, τὸ ἄνθρωπος the word man; τὸ λέγω the word λέγω; τὸ μηδὲν ἄγαν the sentiment "ne quid nimis."
before Pronouns,
before the pers. Pron., to give them greater emphasis, but only in acc., τὸν ἐμέ, τὸν σὲ καὶ ἐμέ Plat.
before the interrog., to make the question more precise, τὸ τί; Aesch., etc.; τὰ ποῖα; Eur.
Elliptic. expressions:

before the gen. of a prop. n., to express descent, ὁ Διός (sc. παῖς) ἡ Λητοῦς (sc. θυγάτηρ) often in attic; but sometimes, as appears from the context, to denote husband, brother, friend, wife:— then before a gen. it indicates all general relations, as, τὰ τῆς πόλεως all that concerns the state; τὰ τῶν Ἀθηναίων φρονεῖν to hold with the Athenians, be on their side, Hdt.:—so with neut. of possess. Pron., τὸ ἐμόν, τὸ σόν what regards me or thee, my or thy business. But τὸ τινος is often also, a man's saying, as, τὸ τοῦ Σόλωνος Hdt.
with cases governed by Preps., οἱ ἐν τῇ πόλει, οἱ ἀπὸ (or ἐκ) τῆς πόλεως the men of the city; οἱ ἀμφί τινα, οἱ περί τινα such an one and his followers, but also periphr. for the person himself.
on μὰ τόν, v. μά IV.
