boundary, used by Hom. in three places, viz., ὅσα δίσκου οὖρα πέλονται as far as is the limit or space of a quoit's throw (cf. δίσκουρα), Il.; ὅσσον τ’ ἐπὶ οὖρα πέλονται ἡμιόνων as far as is the range of mules (in ploughing), Id.; and so, more fully ὅσσον τ’ οὖρον πέλει ἡμιόνοιϊν, τόσσον ὑπεκπροθέων Od.: —what the distance expressed by the range of mules may be is uncertain; the common explanation is the length by which mules would distance oxen in ploughing a given space in the same time.

a fair wind, Hom., etc.; ἡμῖν δ’ αὖ κατόπισθε νεὼς οὖρον ἵει Od.; πέμψω δέ τοι οὖρον ὄπισθεν Id.; ἂψ δὲ θεοὶ οὖρον στρέψαν the gods changed the wind again to a fair one, Id.; πέμπειν κατ’ οὖρον to send down (i. e. with) the wind, speed on its way, Orac. ap. Hdt.; so, metaph., ἴτω κατ’ οὖρον let it be swept before the wind to ruin, Aesch.; ταῦτα μὲν ῥείτω κατ’ οὖρον let these things drift with the wind, Soph.
οὖρός [ἐστι], like καιρός, 'tis a fair time, Id.; ἐγένετο τις οὖρος ἐκ κακῶν Eur.
a watcher, warder, guardian, Hom., Pind.
entry.etym: From the same Root as ὁράω and ὤρα cura.

entry.sense: Lat. urus, a buffalo, Anth.
a trench or channel for hauling up ships and launching them again, Il.
that which is one's own, one's substance, property, Hdt., Eur.
= τὸ εἶναι, being, existence, Plat.; τὰς ἄπαιδας οὐσίας her childless state, Soph.
the being, essence, nature of a thing, Plat., etc.

auris, the ear, Hom.; ὀρθὰ ἱστάναι τὰ ὦτα, of horses, Hdt.; βοᾷ ἐν ὠσὶ κέλαδος rings in the ear, Aesch.; φθόγγος βάλλει δι’ ὤτων Soph.; δι’ ὤτων ἦν λόγος, i. e. heard generally, Eur.; εἰς οὖς into the ear, secretly, Id.; so, εἰς ὦτα φέρειν Soph.:—metaph. of spies, Xen.; —τὰ ὦτα ἐπὶ τῶν ὤμων ἔχοντες, of persons who slink away ashamed (hanging their ears like dogs), Plat.:—athletes are described as having their ears bruised and swollen, τεθλαγμένος οὔατα πυγμαῖς Theocr.
the ear or handle, of pitchers, cups, etc., οὔατα δ’ αὐτοῦ τέσσαρ’ ἔσαν Il.

to wound, c. dupl. acc., Κυπρίδα οὔτασε χεῖρα wounded Venus on the hand, Il.; also, σάκος οὔτασε pierced the shield, Id.; c. acc. cogn., ἕλκος, ὅ με βροτὸς οὔτασεν ἀνήρ the wound which a man struck me withal, Id.

entry.etym: forms generated as if both from οὐτάω and from οὔτημι.
entry.sense: to wound, hurt, hit with any kind of weapon, οὖτα δὲ δουρί, οὐτ. ἔγχεϊ, χαλκῶι, etc., Il.; properly opp. to βάλλω, to wound by striking or thrusting, Id.; cf. οὐτάζω; κατ’ οὐταμένην ὠτειλήν by the wound inflicted, Id.; τὸ ξίφος διανταίαν [πληγήν] οὐτᾶι Aesch.
sometimes, generally, to wound, like βάλλω, Eur.
and not, Il., Hdt.

mostly repeated, οὔτε . . , οὔτε . . , neither . . , nor . . , Lat. neque . . , neque . . , Hom., etc.: —οὔτε may be foll. by a posit. clause with τε, Lat. neque . . , et . . , οὔτ’ αὐτὸς κτενέει, ἀπό τ’ ἄλλους πάντας ἐρύξει he will both not kill and will defend, Il.:—the former οὔτε is sometimes omitted, ναυσὶ δ’ οὔτε πεζός [neither] by sea nor by land, Pind.
a wounding, Zonar.
she who wounds, Anth.
of no account, worthless, Hom.
regardless, reckless, Aesch.
not, I suppose . . , surely you do not mean that . . , Pind., Soph., etc.
in no wise, Hes., Theocr.
not at all yet, Hdt.
Nobody, Noman, a name assumed by Ulysses to deceive Polyphemus, Od.
no one or nobody, Lat. nemo, nullus, neut. nothing, Lat. nihil, Hom., etc.: —οὐδείς being used in Prose.
neut. οὔτι as adv. not a whit, by no means, not at all, Il., Hdt., attic
as prop. n. with changed accent,
indeed not, Lat. non sane, Hom., Hes., etc.; in attic before oaths, οὔτοι μὰ τὴν Δήμητρα, μὰ τὸν Ἀπόλλω Ar., etc.

entry.etym: οὗτος strengthd. by the demonstr. affix -ί [ῑ]
entry.sense: this man here, Lat. hic-ce, Ar. and attic Prose: after a vowel, γ is often inserted, αὑτηγί for αὑτηΐ γε, ταυταγί for ταυταί γε, etc., Ar.
demonstr. Pron. this, Lat. hic, to designate the nearer of two things, opp. to ἐκεῖνος, the more remote (cf. ὅδε), Hom., etc.
when, of two things, one precedes and the other follows, ὅδε generally refers to what follows, οὗτος to what precedes, Soph., etc.
so also, οὗτος is used emphat., generally in contempt, while ἐκεῖνος (like Lat. ille) denotes praise, ὁ πάντ’ ἄναλκις οὗτος, i. e. Aegisthus, Id.; οὗτος ἀνήρ Plat.; τούτους τοὺς συκοφάντας Id.
in attic law-language, οὗτος is commonly applied to the opponent, whether plaintiff or defendant, whereas in Lat. hic was the client, iste the opponent, Dem.
often much like an adv., in local sense (cf. ὅδε init.), τίς δ’ οὗτος κατὰ νῆας ἔρχεαι; who art thou here that comest . . ? Il.; often in attic, τίς οὑτοσί; who's this here? Ar.
with Pron. of 2nd pers., οὗτος σύ, Lat. heus tu! ho you! you there! Soph., etc.; and then οὗτος alone like a Vocat., οὗτος, τί ποιεῖς; Aesch.; ὦ οὗτος οὗτος, Οἰδίπους Soph.
this phrase mostly implies anger, impatience, or scorn:—so, οὗτος ἀνήρ for ἐγώ, Od.
καὶ οὗτος is also added to heighten the force of a previous word, ναυτικῷ ἀγῶνι, καὶ τούτῳ πρὸς Ἀθηναίους Thuc.; v. infr. III. 5.
neut. ταῦτα in various phrases,
ταῦτ’, ὦ δέσποτα yes Sir, (i. e. ταῦτά ἐστι, etc.), Ar.; so ταῦτα δή Id.
ταῦτα μὲν δὴ ὑπάρξει so it shall be, Plat.
καὶ ταῦτα μὲν δὴ ταῦτα, Lat. haec hactenus, Id.
διὰ ταῦτα therefore, attic; πρὸς ταῦτα so then, therefore, Trag.:—also ταῦτα absol., therefore, Il.; ταῦτ’ ἄρα Ar.; ταῦτα δή Aesch.; ταῦτ’ οὖν Soph.

καὶ ταῦτα, adding a circumstance heightening the force of what has been said, and that, Lat. et hoc, ἄνδρα θανεῖν, καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς γυναικός to think that a man should die, and that by a woman's hand, Aesch., etc.
τοῦτο μέν . . , τοῦτο δέ . . , on the one hand . . , on the other . . , partly . . , partly. . , Hdt.
dat. fem. tau/th| on this spot, here, Soph., etc.
in this point, herein, Ar., etc.
in this way, thus, Trag., etc.
ἐκ τούτου or τούτων, thereupon, Xen.: therefore, Id.
ἐν τούτῳ herein, so far, Thuc., Plat., etc.
in the meantime, Thuc., Xen.
πρὸς τούτοις besides, Hdt., attic

entry.etym: strengthd. for οὕτως v. οὑτοσί, attic Prose.
adverb of οὗτος, as Lat. sic of hic
entry.sense: in this way or manner, so, thus:—properly, οὕτως is antec. to ὡς, as Lat. sic to ut, Hom., etc.; οὕτω δὴ ἔσται so it shall be, ratifying what goes before, Od., etc.:—in Prose οὕτως alone in answers, even so, just so, Xen.
in wishes or prayers, οὕτω νῦν Ζεὺς θείη (as Hor. sic te diva regat), Od.; οὕτως ὀναίμην τῶν τέκνων, μισῶ τὸν ἄνδρα (as in Engl., so help me God), Ar.; οὕτω νομιζοίμην σοφός . . Id.
beginning a story, οὕτω ποτ’ ἦν μῦς καὶ γαλῆ so once upon a time . . , Id.; ἦν οὕτω δὴ παῖς Plat.
οὕτως ἔχειν, οὕτως ἔχειν τινός, v. ἔχω B. II. 2; ἔχειν is sometimes omitted, τούτων μὲν οὕτω so much for this, Aesch.
= εἰς τοῦτο, οὕτω τάρβους to such a pitch of terror, Eur.

οὕτω, or οὕτω δή, introduces the apodosis after a protasis, ἐπειδὴ περιελήλυθε ὁ πόλεμος, οὕτω δὴ Γέλωνος μνῆστις γέγονε Hdt.:— after participles, ἐν κλιβάνῳ πνίξαντες, οὕτω τρώγουσι, i. e. ἐπειδὴ ἔπνιξαν, οὕτω . . , Id.
inferential Lat. itaque, Soph., Plat.
with an adj. or adv. so, so much, so very, καλὸς οὕτω Il.; πρυμνόθεν οὕτως so entirely, Aesch.

like αὔτως, with a diminishing power, so, merely so, simply, like Lat. sic, μὰψ οὕτως Il.; οὕτω πίνοντας πρὸς ἡδονήν (as Hor. jacentes sic temere), Plat.; also off-hand, at once, Id.; οὐ .. οὕτως ἄπει = impune, Eur.
a debtor, τινί Plat.: ὀφ. εἰμί, c. inf., I am under bond to do a thing, Soph.:—fem. ὀφειλέτις, ιδος, Eur.
that which is owed, a debt, Thuc., Plat.
a debt, NTest.:— one's due, Id.

to owe, have to pay or account for, Hom., etc.; ὀφ. τινί to be debtor to another, Ar.; absol. to be in debt, Id.:—Pass. to be owed, to be due, Hom., attic: of persons, to be liable to, θανάτωι πάντες ὀφειλόμεθα (as Horace debemur morti), Anth.
c. inf. to be bound, to be obliged to do a thing, Il., etc.:—Pass., σοι ταῦτ’ ὀφείλεται παθεῖν it is thy destiny to suffer this, Soph.; πᾶσιν κατθανεῖν ὀφείλεται Eur.
in this sense epic imperf. ὤφελλον, ὄφελλον and aor2 ὤφελον, ὄφελον are used of that which one ought to have done (ought being the pret. of owe), ὤφελεν εὔχεσθαι Il., etc.

these tenses are also used, foll. by inf., to express a wish that cannot be accomplished, τὴν ὄφελε κατακτάμεν Ἄρτεμις would that Artemis had slain her! (but she had not), Lat. utinam interfecisset! Id.; often preceded by εἴθε (epic αἴθε), αἴθ’ ὄφελες ἄγονός τ’ ἔμεναι O that thou hadst been unborn, Id.; αἴθ’ ὤφελλ’ ὁ ξεῖνος ὀλέσθαι Od.; —so with ὡς, ὡς ὄφελον ὤλέσθαι O that I had taken! Il.; ὡς ὤφελες ὀλέσθαι Id.; with negat., μηδ’ ὄφελες λίσσεσθαι would thou hadst never prayed! Id.; so in attic:—in late Greek with Ind., ὄφελον ἐβασιλεύσατε, for βασιλεῦσαι, would ye were kings, NTest.
impers. ὀφείλει, Lat. oportet, c. acc. et inf., Pind.

to increase, enlarge, strengthen, Hom.; ἲς ἀνέμου κύματ’ ὀφέλλει the force of the wind raises high the waves, Il.; μῦθον ὀφ. to multiply words, Id.; ὄφρ’ ἂν Ἀχαιοὶ υἱὸν ἐμὸν τίσωσιν, ὀφέλλωσί τέ ἑ τιμῆι and may advance him in honour, Id.: —Pass., οἶκος ὀφέλλεται it waxes great, prospers, Od.

furtherance, advantage, help, used often (like opus) as an indecl. adj., αἴ κ’ ὄφελός τι γενώμεθα whether we can be of any use, Il.; τί δῆτ’ ἂν εἴης ὄφ. ἡμῖν; what good couldst thou be to us? Ar.; c. inf., τί ὄφ. σώματι κάμνοντι σιτία διδόναι; Plat.; c. gen., τῶν ὄφελός ἐστι οὐδέν of which there is no profit, Hdt.; ὄφ. οὐδὲν γεωργοῦ ἀργοῦ Xen.;—but, ὅ τι περ ὄφελος στρατεύματος the serviceable part of the army, Id.
snake-like, Plat.
ophthalmia, Ar., Xen., etc.
to suffer from ophthalmia, Hdt., Ar.
eye-service, NTest.

entry.etym: from ΟΠ, Root of ὄψομαι, ὀφθῆναι
entry.sense: the eye, mostly in pl., Hom., etc.; ἐλθεῖν ἐς ὀφθαλμούς τινος to come before one's eyes, Il.; ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν before one's eyes, Lat. in oculis, Hom., attic; πρὸ τῶν ὀφθ. Aeschin.; ἐξ ὀφθαλμῶν out of one's sight, Hdt.; κατ’ ὀφθαλμούς to one's face, Ar.

in sg. the eye of a master or ruler, πάντα ἰδὼν Διὸς ὀφθ. Hes.; so a king is called ὀφθ. οἴκων Aesch.; and in Persia ὀφθαλμὸς βασιλέως, the king's eye, was a confidential officer, through whom he beheld his subjects, Hdt., Ar., etc.
ἑσπέρας ὀφθ., νυκτὸς ὀφθ., of the moon, Pind.
the dearest, best, as the eye is the most precious part of the body, ὀφθαλμὸς Σικελίας Id.; μέγας ὀφθαλμός a great comfort, Soph.
the eye or bud of a plant or tree, Xen.
wetting the eyes, Eur.
apparent to the eye, Strab.
tearing out the eyes, Aesch.
with serpents for legs, Luc.
a serpent, snake, Il., Hdt., Trag.:—metaph., πτηνὸν ὄφιν, of an arrow, Aesch.
entry.etym: The first syll. is sometimes made long, when it was pronounced (and perh. ought to be written) ὄπφις, v. ὀχέω.

entry.sense: a fine incurred in a lawsuit, Dem.
to owe, to be liable to pay a fine, Eur., etc.
δίκην ὀφλεῖν to be cast in a suit, lose one's cause, Ar.; so, ὀφλεῖν δίαιταν to lose in an arbitration, Dem.; τὰς εὐθύνας ὀφλεῖν to have one's accounts not passed, Aeschin.
absol. to be cast, to be the losing party, Ar., Thuc.
c. gen. criminis, ὀφλὼν κλοπῆς δίκην to be convicted in an action for theft, Aesch.; then, without δίκην, ὠφληκὼς φόνου found guilty of murder, Plat.: also c. gen. poenae, θανάτου δίκην ὀφλ. Id.

generally, of anything which one deserves or brings on oneself, αἰσχύνην, βλάβην ὀφλ. to bring infamy, loss on oneself, incur them, Eur.; ὀφλ. γέλωτα to be laughed at, Id.; δειλίην ὤφλεε πρὸς βασιλῆος he drew upon himself the reproach of cowardice from the king, Hdt.; so, μωρίαν ὀφλισκάνω Soph.
Final and Temporal Conj. in ionic and doric Poets:
Final Conj., like ἵνα, ὡς, that, in order that, to the end that, Hom., Pind.
Temporal Conj., like ἕως, Lat. donec, so long as, while, mostly with imperf., ὄφρα μὲν ἠὼς ἦν Od.
with subj., it commonly has ἄν (κε or κεν) with it, Hom.

until, ὄφρα καὶ αὐτὼ κατέκταθεν till they too were slain, Il.; with subj., of future time, ἔχει κότον, ὄφρα τελέσσηι he bears malice till he have satisfied it, Id.; —but in this case, ἄν (κε or κεν) is commonly added.
to have ridges, Strab.

entry.etym: ionic for ὀφρύς II, Hdt., Eur.

entry.sense: on the brow of a rock, beetling, Il., ap. Hdt.
metaph. majestic, Anth.

the brow, eyebrow, Lat. supercilium, mostly in pl., the brows, Hom.; ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι νεῦσε Κρονίων, i. e. ἐπένευσε ὀφρύσι, nodded assent, Il.; ἀνὰ δ’ ὀφρύσι νεῦσεν ἑκάστῳ made a sign not to do, Od.: used in phrases to denote grief, scorn, pride, τὰς ὀφρῦς ἀνασπᾶν Ar.; ὀφρῦς ἐπαίρειν Eur., etc.; τὰς ὀφρῦς συνάγειν to knit the brows, frown, Ar.:—on the other hand, καταβάλλειν, λύειν, μεθιέναι τὰς ὀφρῦς to let down or unknit the brow, Eur.
ὀφρύς alone, like Lat. supercilium, scorn, pride, Anth.
the brow of a hill, a beetling crag, Il., etc.
the holder of a shield, a bar across the hollow of the shield, through which the bearer passed his arm, Hdt.
adv., used to strengthen the Sup. ἄριστος, ὄχ’ ἄριστος far the best, Il., etc.
a covering or impregnating, of the male animal, Xen.
to conduct water by a conduit or canal, Hdt.:—Pass. to be conducted, conveyed, Id.; metaph., ὠχετεύετο φάτις Aesch.
conducting or drawing off water by a ditch or conduit, Il.: metaph., πνεῦμα ὀχ., of the flute, Anth.
a means for carrying water, a water-pipe, Hdt., Thuc., etc.: a conduit, channel, aqueduct, Arist.
in pl. streams, Pind., Eur.
metaph., ὀχετὸν παρεκτρέπειν to make a side channel or means of escape, Eur.
anything for holding or fastening:
a strap for fastening the helmet under the chin, Il.
in pl. the fastenings of the belt, Id.
a bar to fasten the door inside, Hom.
of male animals, to cover, Plat.: Pass., of the female: Mid. of both sexes, Hdt.
frequent. of ἔχω to uphold, sustain, endure, Od., Pind.; νηπιάας ὀχέειν to keep playing childish tricks, Od.; φρουρὰν ὀχήσω will maintain a watch, Aesch.
to carry, Eur., Xen.
to let another ride, to mount him, αὐτὸς βαδίζω, τοῦτον δ’ ὀχῶ Ar.; of a general, to let the men ride, Xen.
Mid. to have oneself carried, to be carried or borne, Hom., Hdt., attic
absol. (without the dat. ἵππωι or νηί), to drive, ride, sail, [ἵπποι] ἀλεγεινοὶ ὀχέεσθαι difficult to use in a chariot, Il.

of a ship, to ride at anchor, λεπτή τις ἐλπίς ἐστ’ ἐφ’ ἧς ὀχούμεθα ’tis but a slender hope on which we ride at anchor, Ar.; so, ὠχεῖσθ’ Id.; cf. Plat.; so, ἐπ’ ἀσθενοῦς ῥώμης ὀχεῖσθαι Eur. [In Pind. the first syll. is made long, when it was pronounced (and perh. ought to be written) ὀκχέω, v. ὄφις.]
anything that bears or supports, γῆς ὄχημα, stay of earth, = γαιήοχος, Eur.
a carriage, a chariot, Lat. vehiculum, Hdt., Soph., Eur.
of ships, but mostly with some addition, λινόπτερα ναυτίλων ὄχ. Aesch.; ὄχ. ναός Soph.
of animals that are ridden, ὄχημα κανθάρου a riding beetle (as we say a riding-horse), Ar.
a bearing, carrying, Plat.
(from Pass.) a being carried, ἵππων ὀχήσεις riding, Id.
to be sorely angered, to be vexed in spirit, Hom.

older form of ὄχθος, a rising ground, a bank, dyke by the side of a river, Il.: mostly in pl. the raised banks of a river, Hom.; ὄχθαι καπέτοιο the banks of the trench, Il.; also the dunes or denes along the sea (cf. θίς), Od.
hilly, Anth.
a bank, hill, Hhymn., Hdt., attic: a barrow or mound, Lat. tumulus, Aesch.
mob-oratory, Plut.
to move, disturb, ψηφῖδες ἅπασαι ὀχλεῦνται (ionic for -οῦνται) all the pebbles are rolled or swept away by the water, Il.
to trouble, importune, Hdt., Aesch.:—absol. to be troublesome or irksome, Soph.
troublesome, irksome, importunate, Hdt., Eur., Plat.
to move by a lever, to heave up, τὸν [λᾶαν] οὔ κε δύ’ ἀνέρε ὀχλίσσειαν Hom.
a mob-courtier, Polyb.; cf. δημο-κόπος.
mob-rule, the lowest grade of democracy, Polyb.
to make a riot, NTest.
a moving crowd, a throng, mob, Pind., Aesch., etc.; ὁ ὄχλος τῶν στρατιωτῶν the mass of the soldiers, Xen.; τῷ ὄχλῳ in point of numbers, Thuc.; οἱ τοιοῦτοι ὄχλοι undisciplined masses like these, Id.
in political sense, the populace, mob, Lat. turba, opp. to δῆμος, Id., Xen.
generally, a mass, multitude, ὄχλος λόγων Aesch.
like Lat. turba, annoyance, trouble, ὄχλον παρέχειν τινί to give one trouble, Hdt.; δι’ ὄχλου εἶναι, γενέσθαι to be or become troublesome, Ar., Thuc.
like a mob, and so,
turbulent, unruly, Plat.; τὸ ὀχλ. troublesomeness, Thuc.
common, vulgar, Plut.
to grip fast, Eur.; τὸν λεωργὸν ὀχμάσαι to bind him fast, Aesch.; ἵππον ὀχμάζει he makes the horse obedient to the bit, Eur.
a wild pear, Theocr.

anything which bears, a carriage, Lat. vehiculum, Hdt., Aesch., etc.; by Hom. in heterocl. neut. pl. ὄχεα, ων, τά, of a single chariot, ἐξ ὀχέων Il.; and in poet. dat. ὄχεσφι, -φιν, Id.; later in masc. pl. ἐπ’ εὐκύκλοις ὄχοις, of the Scythian waggons, Aesch.
τροχαλοὶ ὄχοι ἀπήνης the swift-running bearers of the chariot, i.e. the wheels, Eur.
anything which holds, νηῶν ὄχοι steads for ships, harbours, Od.
Dep. to make secure, fortify, Polyb.
like ἐχυρός, firm, lasting, stout, Hes., Aesch.
of places, strong, secure, Eur.: esp. of a stronghold or position, strong, tenable, Xen.
adv. -ρῶς, Eur.
to make fast and sure, fortify, Polyb.: —the Mid. just like Act., Xen.
a stronghold, fortress, Xen.
one must strengthen, Plut.

entry.note: ὀψ-ᾱμάτης, voc. -ᾶτα, doric for -αμήτης, ου, ὁ,
entry.sense: one who mows till late at even, Theocr.
one who ploughs late, Hes.
Desiderat. of ὁράω, to wish to see a thing, c. gen., Il.
after a long time, late, Lat. sero, Hom., etc.; ὀψὲ διδάσκεσθαι or μανθάνειν to be late in learning, learn too late, Aesch., Soph.
late in the day, at even, opp. to πρωί, Hom., Thuc., etc.; ὀψὲ ἦν, ὀψὲ ἐγίγνετο it was, it was getting, late, Xen.; so, ἐς ὀψέ Thuc.
c. gen., ὀψὲ τῆς ἡμέρας late in the day, Livy's serum diei, Id.; so, τῆς ὥρας ἐγίγνετο ὀψέ Dem.; ὀψὲ τῆς ἡλικίας late in life, Luc.
ὀψία (sc. ὥρα) the latter part of day, evening, opp. to ὄρθρος, often also joined with δείλη, δείλη ἦν ὀψίη Hdt.; περὶ δείλην ὀψίαν Thuc.; δείλης ὀψίας late in the evening, Dem. Cf. δείλη.
late-born, after-born, Hom.
of a son, late-born, born in one's old age, Hhymn.
later-born, i. e. younger, Hdt.: young, Theocr.
to do, go or come late, Xen.:— Pass., ὀψισθέντες belated, benighted, Id.
going late to bed, Aesch.
to learn late, Luc.
late in learning, late to learn, Hor.'s serus studiorum, Plat.:— too old to learn, c. gen., Xen.
vain of late-gotten learning, pedantic, Theophr.
late-gotten learning, Theophr.
late, slow, τέρας ὄψ. a prognostic late of fulfilment, Il.:— late in the season, Xen., NTest.
late-observing, of Epimetheus, Pind.
late, Lat. serus, Pind.: attic comp. ὀψιαίτερος, η, ον, earlier; Sup. ὀψιαίτατος, η, ον, earliest, Xen.:—neut. ὀψιαίτερον as adv., comp. of ὀψέ, Plat.; Sup. ὀψιαίτατα Id., Xen.
look, appearance, aspect of a person or thing, Lat. species oris, aspectus, Il., Soph.; εἰκάζεσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς φανερᾶς ὄψεως Thuc.:—acc. absol. in appearance, Pind., attic
the countenance, face, Eur., etc.
= θέαμα, a sight, Aesch., Eur., etc.; ἄλλην ὄψιν οἰκοδομημάτων other architectural sights, Hdt.; τῇ ὄψει from what they saw, opp. to τῇ γνώμῃ, Thuc.
a vision, apparition, Hdt., Trag.
eyesight, vision, Hom., Hdt., attic: in pl. the organs of sight, the eyes, Soph., Xen.
view, sight, Lat. conspectus, ἀπικέσθαι ἐς ὄψιν τινί to come into one's sight, i. e. presence, Hdt.; εἰς ὄψιν τινός or τινὶ ἥκειν, μολεῖν, ἐλθεῖν, περᾶν Aesch., Eur.
to be late fulfilled, Il.
properly, cooked meat, or, generally, meat, opp. to bread and other provisions, Hom., Ar.
anything eaten with bread or food, to give it flavour and relish, κρόμυον, ποτῷ ὄψον onions, a zest or relish to wine, Il.; ἐσθίουσι ἐπὶ τῷ σίτῳ ὄψον Xen.
seasoning, sauce, Plat.; κολλύραν καὶ κόνδυλον ὄψον ἐπ’ αὐτῇ pudding and knuckle- sauce withal, Ar.; λιμῷ ὅσαπερ ὄψῳ διαχρῆσθε, i. e. "hunger is the best sauce," Xen.
generally, dainty fare, in pl. dainties, Plat.
at Athens, mostly, fish, the chief dainty of the Athenians, Ar.
the fish-market, Id., Aeschin.
to eat meat or fish with bread, Xen.
of or fit for cookery: ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) the art of cookery, Arist.
cookery, esp. fine cookery, Xen., Plat.
one who cooks meat, a cook, Hdt.; distinguished from ἀρτοποιός and σιτοποιός, Xen., Plat.
dressing food elaborately, Anth.
to eat things meant to be eaten only with bread, to live daintily, Ar.
dainty living, Aeschin.
one who eats things meant to be only eaten with bread, such as fish and dainties, a dainty fellow, epicure, gourmand, Ar., Xen.:— irreg. Sup. ὀψοφαγίστατος Xen.

entry.etym: only used in obl. cases of sg. ὀπός, ὀπί, ὄπα
entry.sense: a voice, Hom., Hes., Trag.; of flutes, Theogn.
a word, Il., Soph.
to buy fish and dainties, Ar., Xen.
one who buys fish or victuals, a purveyor, Ar.
a furnishing with provisions, the supplies and pay of an army, Polyb.
provisions or provision-money, Lat. obsonium, supplies and pay for an army, Polyb.: —metaph., ὀψώνια ἁμαρτίας the wages of sin, NTest.
quite ridiculous, Plat.
mother of all, Anth.
wordiness, garrulity, Pind.
frost, Xen.; cf. πάγος II.
frosty, ice-cold, Soph.
anything that fixes or fastens, a snare, noose, trap, Hdt.: a fowling-net, Xen.
metaph. a trap, snare, Aesch.
to lay a snare for, entrap, NTest.
solid, Luc.:—adv., παγίως λέγειν, to say positively, without reservations, Plat.
= πάγη, a trap, Ar.: metaph. a trap, snare, δουρατέα π. of the Trojan horse, Anth.
ἄγκυρα παγὶς νεῶν the anchor which holds ships fast, Id.
ever renewed, ever fresh, Aesch.
utterly bad, all-unlucky, Hes.: most noxious, Id., Plat.—adv., παγκάκως ὀλέσθαι Aesch.; π. ἔχει τινί Id.
of persons, utterly bad, most evil or wicked, Theogn.: Sup. ὦ παγκάκιστε, Soph., Eur.
all beautiful, good or noble, Ar., Plat.: adv. -λως, Plat., etc.
of all kinds of fruit, Soph.: rich in every fruit, rich in fruit, Pind.
all-concealing, Soph.
all-lamented, most lamentable, Aesch., Soph.
act. all tearful, Soph.
a complete inheritance, Aesch., Eur.
held in full possession, Eur.
common to all, Soph.; θεοῦ μάστιγι παγκοίνῳ, i. e. by death, Aesch.; ἓν ἀπέχθημα π. βροτοῖς one object of hate common to all mankind, Eur.; π. στάσις all the band together, Aesch.
where all must sleep, θάλαμος παγκοίτας, i. e. the grave, Soph.; π. Ἅιδας Id.
covered all over with dust, ἄεθλα παγκ. prizes gained in all the contests, Soph.
all-powerful, all-mighty, Trag.; π. ἕδραι the imperial throne of Zeus, Aesch.:— τοῖνδε π. φονεύς their victorious slayer, Id.
to perform the exercises of the παγκράτιον, Plat.:—metaph. to sway one's arms about like a gymnast, to gesticulate violently, Aeschin.
one who practises the παγκράτιον, Plat.
of or for the παγκράτιον, ἡ παγκ. τέχνη the pancratiast's art, Plat.
skilled in the παγκράτιον, Arist.
a complete contest, an exercise which combined both wrestling and boxing (πάλη and πυγμή), Hdt., Pind., etc.
Lat. pagus, a canton, district, Plut.
that which is fixed or firmly set:
a mountain-peak, a rocky hill, Od., Hes., Trag.; ὁ Ἄρειος (ionic Ἀρήιος) πάγος the Areopagus at Athens, v. Ἄρειος II.
= παγετός, Soph.
a kind of crab, Lat. pagurus, Ar.
most difficult to deal with, Xen., Plat. adv., παγχαλέπως ἔχειν πρός τινα to be ill affected towards him, Xen.
all-brasen, all-brass, Hom., Od., Trag.
good for all work, Ar., Xen.
all-anointed: πάγχριστον (sc. φαρμακόν) seems to mean full-anointing, Soph.
all-golden, of solid gold, Il., Hes.
= πάνυ quite, wholly, entirely, altogether, Hom., Pind.; πάγχυ δοκέειν or ἐλπίζειν to think or hope fully, Hdt.
anything that befals one, a suffering, calamity, misfortune, Soph., Thuc.: mostly in pl., Hdt., attic; proverb., τὰ δέ μοι παθήματα μαθήματα γέγονε my sufferings have been my lessons, Hdt.
a passive emotion or condition, Xen., Plat.
in pl. incidents, occurrences, Plat.
a passive state, Plat.; τὰς ἐκεῖ πάθας what happened there, Soph.; πᾶσαν τὴν ἑωυτοῦ π. all that had happened to him, Hdt.
= πάθημα, Pind., Soph.; ἡ π. τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν blindness, Hdt.
subject to feeling, capable of feeling a thing, c. gen., Arist.
impassioned, pathetic, Id.:—adv., παθητικῶς λέγειν Id.
one who has suffered: subject to passion, Plut.
of the Saviour, destined to suffer, NTest.
anything that befalls one, an incident, accident, Hdt., Soph.
what one has suffered, one's experience, Aesch.; in pl., Plat.: —commonly in bad sense, a suffering, misfortune, calamity, Hdt., Aesch., etc.; ἀνήκεστον π. ἔρδειν to do an irreparable mischief, Hdt.
of the soul, a passion, emotion, such as love, hate, etc., Thuc., Plat., etc.
any passive state, a condition, state, Plat.: in pl. the incidents or changes to which things are liable, τὰ περὶ τὸν οὐρανὸν π. Id., etc.
a pathetic mode of expression, pathos, Arist.
Paean or Paeon, the physician of the gods, Il.; Παιήονος γενέθλη the sons of Paeon, i. e. physicians, Od.
after Hom., the name and office were transferred to Apollo, who was invoked by the cry ἰήιε Παιάν Aesch., Soph.; ἰὼ Παιάν Soph.
as appellat. a physician, healer, Aesch., Soph.: then, a saviour, deliverer, Eur.
παιάν, epic παιήων, a paean, i. e. a choral song, a hymn or chant, addressed to Apollo, Il., Aesch., Soph.
a song of triumph after victory, properly to Apollo, Il., Aesch.; also a war-song, Aesch., Xen.:—the phrase was, ἐξάρχειν τὸν παιᾶνα Xen.; π. ἐξάρχεσθαι, ποιεῖσθαι Id.
any solemn song or chant, esp. on beginning an undertaking, in omen of success, Thuc.; a song sung at a feast, Xen.
Aesch., by an oxymoron, joins π. Ἐρινύων, π. τοῦ θανόντος; so, π. στυγνός, of a dirge, Eur.
Κρητῶν παιήονες paean-singers, Hhymn.
in Prosody, a paeon, a foot consisting of three short and 1 long syll., in any order, Arist.
play, sport, sportive strain, Eur.
play, sport, a game, Hdt.
fond of a joke, Hdt.
a plaything, toy, Plat.
in Theocr., the Egyptians are called κακὰ παίγνια roguish playmates,
a game, a sportive poem, Anth.; of the merry chirp of the cicada, Id.
sportive, droll, Anth.
playful, sportive, Plut.: τὸ παιγνιῶδες playfulness, Xen.
the room in which the παιδαγωγοί waited for their boys, Dem.: a school, Plut.

entry.etym: fut. mid. παιδαγωγήσομαι in pass. sense
entry.sense: to attend as a παιδαγωγός, to train and teach, educate, Plat.: to watch as one does a child, Eur.
generally, to educate, Plat.
the office of a παιδαγωγός, attendance on boys, education, Plat.: generally, attendance on the sick, Eur.
suitable to a παιδαγωγός·—ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) τῶν νοσημάτων = ἡ ἰατρική, the tending of diseases, Plat.

a boy-ward; at Athens, the slave who went with a boy from home to school and back again, a kind of tutor, Hdt., Eur., etc.: —hence Phoenix is called the παιδαγωγός of Achilles, Plat.; Fabius is jeeringly called the παιδαγωγός of Hannibal, because he always followed him about, Plut.
a young, little boy, Ar.; ἐκ παιδαρίου from a child, Plat.: in pl. young children, Ar.: a young slave, Id., Xen.
childish, puerile, Plat.
the rearing of a child, Aesch.
training and teaching, education, Ar., Thuc., etc.
its result, culture, learning, accomplishments, Plat.
πλεκτὰ Αἰγύπτου παιδεία the twisted handiwork of Egypt, i. e. ropes of byblus, Eur.
youth, childhood, Theogn., Eur.
of or for a boy, Aesch.; π. τροφή the care of rearing children, a mother's cares, Soph.
to be a παιδεραστής, Plat.
a lover of boys, Ar., Plat.
that which is reared up, taught, a nursling, scholar, pupil, Eur., etc.; μῆλα, φυλλάδος Παρνασίας παιδεύματ’ Id.:—in pl. of a single object, Id.
a thing taught, subject of instruction, lesson, Xen.
education, a system of education, Hdt., Ar., etc.; τὴν ὑπ’ ἀρετῆς Ἡρακλέους παίδευσιν his education by virtue, Xen.
its result, culture, learning, accomplishments, Ar., Plat.
an instructing or priming of witnesses, Dem.
a means of educating, τὴν πόλιν τῆς Ἑλλάδος παίδευσιν εἶναι that our city is the school of Greece, Thuc.
to be educated, Plat.
παιδευτέον, one must educate, Id.
a school, Strab.
a teacher, instructor, preceptor, Plat.
a corrector, chastiser, NTest.
of or for teaching: —ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη), education, Plat.; so, τὸ παιδευτικόν Plut.
to be gained by education, Plat.
to bring up or rear a child, Soph.

mostly, opp. to τρέφω, to train, teach, educate, Id., Eur., etc.; παιδεύειν τινα μουσικῆι καὶ γυμναστικῆι Plat.; ἐν μουσικῆι Id.; π. τινὰ εἰς πρὸς ἀρετήν Id.; c. dupl. acc., π. τινά τι to teach one a thing, Id.; c. acc. et inf., π. τινὰ κιθαρίζειν Hdt.; and without inf., π. γυναῖκας σώφρονας [εἶναι] Eur.:—hence in Pass., c. acc. rei, to be taught a thing, Plat.:—absol., ὁ πεπαιδευμένος a man of education, opp. to ἀπαίδευτος or ἰδιώτης, Xen., Plat.:—Mid. to have any one taught, cause him to be educated, Plat.
to correct, discipline, Soph., Xen.: to chastise, punish, NTest.

childish play, sport, game, pastime, Xen., Plat.; π. παίζειν πρός τινα to play a game with him, Ar.; μετὰ παιδιᾶς in sport, Thuc.; ὥστε σοι τὸν νῦν χόλον παιδιὰν εἶναι δοκεῖν will seem mere child's play, Aesch.
of, for or like a child, boyish, Lat. puerilis, Plat., etc.
playful, sportive, Id., Xen.; so, adv. -κῶς, Plat.
of or for a beloved youth, π. λόγος a love- tale, Xen.
as Subst., παιδικά, ῶν, τά, a darling, favourite, Lat. deliciae, Thuc., Plat., etc.
from a child, NTest.
a little or young child, Hdt., Ar., Plat.
a slave-lad, Ar.
a young girl, maiden, Xen.
a young slave, courtesan, Hdt., Plut.
a young boy or son, Xen.
playful, Lat. ludibundus, Arist.
childish, Aesch., Anth.
παιδνός, οῦ, as Subst. a boy, lad, Od.
child-eating, μόχθοι π., said of Thyestes, Aesch.
a begetting of children, Plat.
begetting children, Ζεῦ παιδογόνε πόριος Ἰνάχου father of a child by the daughter of Inachus, Eur.
making fruitful, Theocr.
to take care of a child, Anth.
to murder children, Eur.
child-murdering, Soph., Eur.
murderer of children: fem. παιδ-ολέτειρα, murderess of children, Eur.
destroying children, Aesch.
the education of children, Arist.
the office of παιδονόμος, Id.
one of a board of magistrates in Dorian States, who superintended the education of youths, Xen., Arist.
to beget children, Eur.; πεπαιδοποίηται has been begotten, Dem.
to bear children, of the woman, Soph.
more commonly as Dep., fut. -ήσομαι: aor1 ἐπαιδοποιησάμην: perf. πεπαιδοποίημαι, in same sense as Act., Eur., Xen., etc.
procreation of children, Plat.
begetting or bearing children, Eur.
generative, Hdt.
through which a child passes, Anth.
to beget children, Plat.
begetting children, Ar.
to train as a gymnastic master: generally, to train, π. τινὰ πονηρὸν εἶναι Dem.
one who teaches boys wrestling and other exercises, a gymnastic master, Ar., Plat., etc.; ἐν παιδοτρίβου at his school, Ar.
of or for a παιδοτρίβης: ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) his art, the art of wrestling, Arist.: adv., παιδοτριβικῶς like a gymnastic master, Ar.
the rearing of children, Plat.
rearing boys, Simon.: παιδοτρόφος ἐλάα Soph.
as fem. Subst. a mother, Eur.
wounded by children, πάθεα π. wounds and death at children's hands, Aesch.
= παιδοποιία, Plat.
in Soph. = γυνὴ παιδοποιός, a mother.
to love boys, Theogn., Solon.
killing children, Il., Eur.; π. συμφορή the accident or calamity of having killed a son, Hdt.; π. αἷμα the blood of slain children, Eur.
to waft away a boy, Anth.
properly, to play like a child, to sport, play, Od., Hdt., etc.
to dance, Od., Pind.:—so in Mid., Hes.
to play [a game], σφαίρηι π. to play at ball, Od.; also, π. σφαῖραν Plut.
to play (on an instrument), Hhymn.

to sport, play, jest, joke, Hdt., Xen., etc.; π. πρός τινα to make sport of one, mock him, Eur.; π. εἴς τι to jest upon a thing, Plat.: the part. παίζων is used absol. in jest, jestingly, Id.:—Pass., ὁ λόγος πέπαισται is jocularly told, Hdt.; ταῦτα πεπαίσθω ὑμῖν enough of jest, Plat.
c. acc. to play with, Anth., Luc.
healing, like Παιώνιος, Anth.
the Paeonians, a people of Macedonia, Il.; Παίων στρατός Eur.:— Παιονία, ἡ, their land, Il.:—adj. Παιονικός, ή, όν Paeonian, Thuc.; pecul. fem. Παιονίς, ίδος, Hdt.
like παιπάλη, a piece of subtlety, of a man, Ar., Aeschin.
pollen the finest flour or meal, Lat. flos farinae, Ar.: metaph. of a subtle rogue, Id.
craggy, rugged, old epic word of uncertain origin, epith. of hills, mountain-paths, and rocky islands, Hom.
in relation to Descent, a child, whether son or daughter, Il.:— παῖς παιδός a child's child, grandchild, Id.; Ἀγήνορος παῖδες ἐκ παίδων Eur.;—of animals, Aesch.
metaph., ἀμπέλου παῖς, i. e. wine, Pind.
periphr., δυστήνων παῖδες (v. sub δύστηνος); οἱ Λυδῶν παῖδες, sons of the Lydians, i. e. the Lydians, Hdt.; π. Ἑλλήνων Aesch.; οἱ Ἀσκληπιοῦ π. i. e. physicians, Plat., etc.

in relation to Age, a child, either a boy, youth, lad, or a girl, maiden, Hom., etc.; with another Subst., παῖς συφορβός a boy- swineherd, Il.: —ἐκ παιδός from a child, Plat.; ἐκ παίδων or παίδων εὐθύς Id.; εὐθὺς ἐκ παίδων ἐξελθών Dem.
in relation to Condition, a slave, servant, man or maid, Aesch., Ar., etc.

entry.etym: redupl. from ΦΑ, Root of φαίνομαι
entry.sense: to dart or rush wildly about, Il.

to strike, smite, Hdt., Trag.; π. τινὰ ἐς τὴν γῆν Hdt.; π. τινὰ ἐς τὴν γαστέρα Ar.; εἰς τὰ στέρνα or κατὰ τὸ στέρνον Xen.; c. dupl. acc., π. τινὰ τὸ νῶτον Ar.:—also c. acc. cogn., ὀλίγας π. (sc. πληγάς) Xen.;— π. ἅλμην, of rowers, , Aesch.:—Mid., ἐπαίσατο τὸν μηρόν he smote his thigh, Xen.

c. acc. instrumenti, to strike, dash one thing against another, ναῦς ἐν νηὶ στόλον ἔπαισε one ship struck its beak against another, Aesch.; metaph., ἐν δ’ ἐμῶι κάραι θεὸς μέγα βάρος ἔπαισεν the god dashed a great weight upon my head, i. e. smote me heavily, Soph.; ἔπαισας ἐπὶ νόσωι νόσον Id.
to drive away, τοὺς σφῆκας ἀπὸ τῆς οἰκίας Ar.
to hit hard in speaking, Id.
intr. to strike or dash against, Lat. illido, πρός τινι or τι Aesch., Xen.; c. acc., παίειν ἄφαντον ἕρμα strikes on a hidden reef, Aesch.; so, στήλην παίσας, of a charioteer, Soph.
to eat, Ar.
Παιωνιὰς σοφία the healing art, medicine, Anth.
a festival of Paeon, Ar.
like a paean or song of victory, Aesch.

to chant the paean or song of triumph, Hdt., Ar., etc.; c. acc. cogn. to sing in triumph, Aesch.; of an after-dinner song, Xen.: Pass., 3rd sg. imperf. used impersonally, ἐπεπαιώνιστο αὐτοῖς the paean had been sung by them, Thuc.
belonging to Paeon, medicinal, healing, Aesch., Soph., Ar.
a healer, reliever, c. gen., Soph.
a chanting of the paean, Thuc.
to fasten, make fast, δῶμα πάκτου make fast the house, Soph.
to stop up, stop, caulk, Ar.
to bind fast, Anth.
a cake of preserved fruit, Hdt., Luc.
born long ago, full of years, ancient, Hom.; ἄνθρωποι Aesch., Eur.
to wrestle or fight, Pind.; cf. Παλαίμων.
Palaemon, i. e. wrestler, masc. prop. n., a name of Melicertes, son of Ino, who was adored as a sea-god friendly to the shipwrecked, Eur.
ancient mother, Eur.
rich from early times, Thuc.
old in years,
of persons, old, aged, ἢ νέος ἠὲ παλαιός Hom.; π. γέρων, π. γρηῦς Od.; χρόνῳ π. Soph.
of things, οἶνος Od.; νῆες Id.
of old date, ancient,
of persons, Hom.; Μίνως παλαίτατος ὧν ἀκοῇ ἴσμεν Thuc.; οἱ π. the ancients, Lat. veteres, Id.
of things, Od., Hdt., etc.: —τὸ παλαιόν, as adv. like τὸ πάλαι, anciently, formerly, Hdt., etc.; ἐκ παλαιοῦ from of old, Id.; ἐκ παλαιτέρου from older time, Id.; ἐκ παλαιτάτου Thuc.
of things, also, antiquated, obsolete, Aesch., Soph.
antiquity, obsoleteness, Eur., Plat.
old in mind, with the wisdom of age, Aesch.
to make old, mostly in Pass. (pres.) to be old or antiquated, βραχίονος π. is of long standing, Hipp.
in Pass. also, to become old, Plat.
like Lat. antiquare, to abrogate a law, NTest.

long ago, in olden time, in days of yore, in time gone by Il., Soph., etc.; πάλαι ποτέ once upon a time, Ar.:—often used with a pres. in the sense of a perf., ὁρῶ πάλαι, Lat. dudum video, I have long seen, Soph.; πάλαι ποτ’ ὄντες ye who have long ago been, Ar.;—also with the Art., τὸ πάλαι Hdt., Thuc., etc.
πάλαι is often used like an adj. with the Art. and a Noun, οἱ πάλαι φῶτες men of old, Pind.; Κάδμου τοῦ πάλαι Soph.; τὰ π. Dem.
of time just past, ἠμὲν πάλαι ἠδ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν Il.: hence πάλαι comes to mean not long ago, but now, just now, much like ἄρτι, Aesch., Plat.
a bout or fall in wrestling, Hdt.; ἓν μὲν τόδ’ ἤδη τῶν τριῶν παλαισμάτων Aesch.
any struggle, Trag.
any trick or artifice, subterfuge, Ar.; π. δικαστηρίου a trick of the courts, Aeschin.
wrestling, the wrestler's art, Hom.

entry.etym: later form of παλαστή, q. v.

entry.sense: a wrestler, Hdt., Plat., etc.
generally, a rival, adversary, Aesch., Soph.: a candidate, suitor, Aesch.
expert in wrestling, Arist., Luc.
a palaestra, wrestling-school, wherein wrestlers (παλαισταί) were trained, Hdt., Eur.
like a παλαιστής, π. θεός god of the palaestra, Babr.
spoken long ago, Od., Pind., Aesch.
having a legend attached to it, legendary, δρῦς π. an oak of ancient story, Od.
generally, primeval, ancient, olden, Pind., Soph.
that has been long in a country, an ancient inhabitant, indigenous, Aesch., Anth.
to wrestle, Il., Plat.: π. τινί to wrestle with one, Od., Pind.:—Pass., παλαισθείς beaten, Eur.
a growing old, Strab.
Dep.
to manage, execute, Xen.
like μηχανάομαι, to manage adroitly, contrive cunningly, Ar.
name of a hero, the Inventor, Ar., etc.
the palm of the hand, the hand, Hom., Pind.; πάσχειν τι ὑπ’ Ἄρηος παλαμάων by the hands of Ares, Il.:—hence a deed of force, Soph.
the hand as used in works of art, Hes.

metaph. cunning, art, a device, plan, method, Hdt., etc.; π. βιότου a device for one's livelihood, Theogn.: of the gods, θεοῦ σὺν παλάμᾳ, θεῶν παλάμαι, παλάμαις Διός by their arts, Pind.; παλάμας πλέκειν Ar.; π. πυριγενής a fire-born instrument, i. e. a sword, Eur.
one guilty of violence, a blood-guilty man, murderer, Aesch., Soph.: —ὦ παλαμναίη oh miscreant! of the fox, Babr.
= ἀλάστωρ, the avenger of blood, Eur., Xen.
to besprinkle, sully, defile, Od.; mostly in Pass., Hom.:—Mid., παλάσσετο χεῖρας he defiled his hands, Il.
Pass. also of things, to be scattered abroad, Id.
perf. pass. of lots shaken in an urn, κλήρῳ πεπαλάχθαι to determine one's fate by lot, Hom.; cf. πάλος.
the palm of the hand: as a measure of length, a palm, four fingers' breadth, a little more than three inches.
a palm long or broad, Hdt.
to catch by decoy-birds, Ar.
to be disabled, Hdt.
wrestling, Lat. lucta, Hom., Pind., etc.
generally, battle, Aesch., Eur.
a being born again, new birth; used by Cic. of his restoration after exile:— hence, in NTest.,
regeneration by baptism.
contradictory, false, Pind.
of strange or foreign tongue, Id.
to sell over again, sell wares by retail, Dem.
one who buys and sells again, a petty retailer, huckster, Ar., Dem.
of wounds, breaking out afresh: metaph. in adv., αὐτῷ παλιγκότως συνεφέρετο according to his old ill-luck fared it with him, Hdt.
of fresh outbreaks of passion, κληδόνες π. injurious, untoward reports, Aesch.; π. τύχη adverse fortune, Id.
of persons, hostile, malignant, Ar., Theocr.; παλίγκοτοι adversaries, Pind.
entry.etym: -κοτος seems to be a termin., as in ἀλλόκοτος.

entry.sense: very swift, Anth.
to say again, repeat, recapitulate, 3rd sg. plup. pass. ἐπαλιλλόγητο Hdt.
recapitulation, Arist.
retractation, recantation, Theophr.
to gather collected again, Il.
repeated.
walking back, ἱστῶν παλίμβαμοι ὁδοί, of women working at the loom, Pind.
growing again, Eur.
thrown back, reversed: hence, untrustworthy, uncertain, unstable, Plat.: τὸ παλίμβολον instability, Aeschin.
doubly long, Aesch.
falling back:—in neut. as adv., back, back again, Hom.
a patching up or cobbling of shoes, Theophr.
back-wandering, Aesch.
Pass. to wander back, only in aor. 1 part. παλιμπλαγχθείς wandering homewards, Hom.
wandering to and fro, Anth.
washed up again, vamped up; metaph. of a plagiarist, Anth.
retributive: παλίμποινα, ων, τά, retribution, repayment, Aesch.
stern-foremost, Eur.
back-speaking, recanting, π. ἀοιδά = παλινῳδία, Eur.
scraped again, βιβλίον παλ. a palimpsest, i. e. a parchment from which one writing has been erased to make room for another, Plut.
to be taken back or recalled, ἔπος οὐ παλινάγρετον an irrevocable word, Il.
growing again, Anth.
a double deserter, Xen.
a second action, a new trial, Plut.
whirling round and round, Anth.
to run back again, of a ship, Plut.
a running back or backwards, Anth.
recurring, of the tide, Strab.
running back again, Luc.
a returning calm, Anth.
rushing back, Il.
starting back, Il.:—neut. as adv. back again, Anth.; attic παλίνορρον, with a backward wrench, Ar.
recurring, inveterate, much like παλίγ-κοτος, Aesch.

of Place, back, backwards, Hom., Hes., etc.; π. χωρέειν Hdt.; π. ἔρχεσθαι Aesch., etc.; also, πάλιν δοῦναι to give back, restore, Il.:—c. gen., πάλιν τράπεθ’ υἷος ἑοῖο she turned back from her son, Id.; πάλιν κίε θυγατέρος ἧς Id.;—also πάλιν αὖτις back again, αὖτε πάλιν, ἂψ π., π. ὀπίσσω, etc.

with a notion of contradiction, πάλιν ἐρεῖν to gain say (i. e. say against), Il.; but, μῦθον πάλιν λάζεσθαι to take back one's word, unsay it, Id.; opp. to ἀληθέα εἰπεῖν, Od.: in Prose, contrariwise, Plat.: —c. gen., τὸ πάλιν νεότητος youth's opposite, Pind.; χρόνου τὸ πάλιν the change of time, Eur.
of Time, again, once more, anew, Soph., etc.; so, αὖθις πάλιν, πάλιν αὖθις, αὖ πάλιν, πάλιν αὖ, αὖ πάλιν αὖθις, αὖθις αὖ πάλιν, attic
again, in turn, Soph.
shaded over again, thick-shaded, Hhymn., etc.
a looking back again; acc. as adv. in the opposite direction, Eur.
safe again, recovered, Anth.
to speak words of ill omen, Aesch.
like ἄντιτος, requited, avenged, Od.
back-stretched, back-bending, epith. of the bow, Hom. It denotes the form of the Homeric bow, which when unstrung bent in a direction contrary to that which it took when strung.
ἡνίαι π. back-stretched reins, Ar.
rubbed again and again: hence hardened, knavish, Soph.
turned back, averted, Lat. retortus, π. ὄμματα Aesch.
turning back, Soph., Eur.
with a reverse of fortune, Aesch.
to recant an ode and so, generally, to revoke, recant, Plat.
a palinode or recantation, a name first given to an ode by Stesichorus, in which he recants his attack upon Helen, Plat.
a thorny shrub, Rhamnus paliurus, Eur., Theocr.
made of the wood of the παλίουρος, Anth.
to ebb and flow, Lat. reciprocare, Strab., Theophr.
back-rushing, refluent, Od.
the reflux of water, back-water, Hdt.:— metaph. of fortune, Polyb.
inclining backwards, π. γόνυ backward-sinking knee, Eur.
back-flowing, refluent, Eur.
metaph. recurring, returning upon one's head, Id.
roaring with ebb and flow, Aesch.
a rush backwards, back-flow, Plut.
in retribution, Soph.
rushing hurriedly back, δρόμημα π. hurried flight, Soph.; παλ. στείχειν Eur.
pursuit back again or in turn, as when fugitives rally and turn on their pursuers, Il., Hes.
a statue of Pallas, Hdt., Ar.
as Dep., π. τινα to keep as a concubine, Hdt.
as Pass. to be a concubine, Plut.
a concubine, mistress, Lat. pellex, opp. to a lawful wife (κουριδίη ἄλοχος), Hom.
entry.etym: Prob. from same Root as παλλάς = νεᾶνις.

entry.sense: Pallas, in Hom. always Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη or Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη.
entry.etym: Commonly deriv. from πάλλω, either as brandisher of the spear:—but prob. it is an old word παλλάς = νεᾶνις.

entry.sense: all-white, Aesch., Eur.
an inhabitant of Παλλήνη; fem. Παλληνίς, ίδος, Id.
a peninsula and town of Chalcidice, Hdt., etc.
an Attic deme.
to poise or sway a missile before it is thrown, Eur., Ar.
to sway other arms, not missiles, σάκος Hes.; πέλτας Eur.:—then, to toss a child, Il.; Νὺξ ὄχημ’ ἔπαλλεν she drave it furiously, Eur.

κλήρους ἐν κυνέηι πάλλον they shook the lots together in a helmet, till one leapt forth, Hom.: absol. to cast lots, Il.; ὅθ’ αὐτοὺς οἱ βραβεῖς κλήροις ἔπηλαν where the stewards ranged them by casting lots, Soph.:—Mid. to draw lots, ἔλαχον ἅλα παλλομένων I obtained the sea when we cast lots, Il.; so in Hdt., Soph.

Pass. to swing or dash oneself, ἐν ἄντυγι πάλτο he dashed himself upon the shield-rim, Il.: to quiver, leap, esp. in fear, πάλλεται ἦτορ Id.; also of the person, παλλομένη κραδίην Id.; of dying fish, to quiver, leap, Hdt.
intr., like the Pass., to leap, bound, Eur.: to quiver, Soph., Eur.

the lot cast from a shaken helmet, ἂμ πάλον θέμεν to cast the lot again, Pind.; πάλωι λαχεῖν to obtain by lot, Hdt., Aesch.; ἀρχὰς πάλωι ἄρχειν to hold public offices by lot, Hdt.; οὓς ἐκλήρωσεν πάλος Eur.
brandished, hurled, Soph.
as Subst., παλτόν, οῦ, a light spear used by the Persian cavalry, like the Moorish jereed, Xen.
to strew or sprinkle, ἄλφιτα παλύνειν Hom.
to bestrew, besprinkle, with dat. of the thing sprinkled, παλύνας ἀλφίτου ἀκτῇ Od.
of liquids, ἁ σῦριγξ εὐρῶτι παλύνεται Theocr.
to sprinkle, cover lightly, χιὼν ἐπάλυνεν ἀρούρας Il.
property, Anth.
absolute monarchy, Arist.
queen of all, Ar.
an absolute monarch, Arist.
all-subduing, Pind.
all-vain, all-useless, Aesch.
fighting with all, Aesch.: esp. = παγκρατιαστής, ready for every kind of contest, Plat., Theocr.
very great, immense, Plat.
neut. as adv., παμμέγεθες ἀναβοᾶν Aeschin.
all-black, Od.
very long, prolonged, Soph., Plat.
through all months, the live-long year, Soph.
mother of all, Aesch.
a very mother, mother indeed, τοῦδε π. νεκροῦ Soph.
all-abominable, Ar.
all-mingled, promiscuous, Aesch.
all-hapless, Soph.
very old, Plat., etc.
like πάνυ, quite, wholly, altogether, Hom., Hes., Eur.; οὐδέ τι πάμπαν not at all, by no means, Il.: with the Art., τὸ π. Eur.
all-persuasive, Pind.
like πάμπαν, entirely, Theogn., Aesch., Soph.
entire possession, the full property, Aesch., Eur.
with the whole multitude, NTest.
of or with the whole multitude, Xen.
= πάμπολυς, very numerous. multitudinous, Plat., Dem.
neut. as adv. entirely, Dem.
in which all sorts of blows are given and received, ἄεθλα Soph.
all-variegated, of rich and varied work, Hom.: all-spotted, of fawn-skins, Eur.
prevailing in all cities, universal, Soph.
very much, great, large or numerous, Ar., Xen.:—in pl. very many, Ar.
all-depraved, thoroughly knavish, Ar., Plat.: adv., παμπονήρως ἔχειν to be very ill, Luc.
all-purple, Pind.
all-venerable, Anth.
all-conspicuous, Aesch.
corrupt in Aesch. Ag.
first of all, the very first, Il.: in neut. πάμπρωτον and -τα as adv., Hom.
all-devouring, voracious, Eur.
all-shining, all-brilliant, radiant, Soph., Eur., etc.; of honey, bright, pure, Aesch.
to shine or beam brightly, of burnished metal, Il.; of a star, Id.; στήθεσι παμφαίνοντες with their breasts white-gleaming, i. e. naked, Id.

entry.etym: epic part. as if from παμφᾰνάω
entry.sense: bright-shining, beaming, of burnished metal, Il.; of the Sun, Od.
skilled in all charms or drugs, Pind.
all-destroying, Aesch.
all-blazing, Soph.
all-feeding, Anth.
all-bearing, all-productive, Lat. omnium ferax, χώρη παμφορωτέρη Hdt.; a friend is called παμφορώτατον κτῆμα by Xen.
bearing all things with it, π. χέραδος a mixed mass of rubbish, Pind.
of mingled tribes, of all sorts, Ar.
with all tones, full-toned or many-tone, Pind.: generally, expressive, Anth.
by all the votes, Anth.
with all his soul, or = πασῶν τῶν ψυχῶν, Soph.
quite or very soft, Luc.
all-hallowed, Lat. sacrosanctus, Plut.
one who catches everything, Anth.
catching all, Il.
all-wakeful, Anth.

Πᾰν-ᾰθήναια (sc. ἱερά), τά, the Panathenaea, two festivals of the Athenians, τὰ μεγάλα and τὰ μικρά, in honour of Athena, Ar., etc. The greater was celebrated in the third year of each Olympiad, the latter annually.
of or at the Panathenaea, Thuc.
all-wretched, Trag.
all-shining, Anth.
all-blazing, Il.
epith. of armour, either all-variegated, sparkling, or, quite light, easily-moved, Il.
metaph. manifold, Aesch.
utterly ugly, ugliest, Arist.
the cause of all, Aesch.
to whom all the guilt belongs, Id.
all-avenging, Anth.
all true, all too true, of a person, Aesch.
of things, absolutely true or real, Plat.
all-powerful, Aesch.
all-embracing, Aesch.
without any share in a thing, c. gen., Anth.
all-blameless, Simon.
sung by all, Anth.
all-tender, all-delicate, Od.
all-harmless, Hes., Anth.
all-hapless, Il.
all-silver, Od.
all virtuous, Luc.
best of all, Hes., Anth.
all-sufficing:—the gen. fem. παναρκέτας in Aesch. is prob. corrupt.
in Music, suited to all modes; τὸ π. (sc. ὄργανον) an instrument on which all modes can be played, Plat.
metaph. all harmonious, Id.
all-powerful, ruling all, Soph.
all-exact, infallible, Anth.
all-away from the friends of one's youth, Il.
all-imperishable, Anth.
all-inevitable, Anth.
all-leafless, Hhymn.
all the Achaians, Hom.
all-untimely, doomed to an untimely end, Il., Anth.
a complete banquet, a banquet at which nothing is wanting, Hdt., Ar.
all-tearful, Soph.
allbewept, most miserable, Trag.
the all-subduer, all-tamer, Hom., Soph.
all-dreadful, terrible, Plat.: —πάνδεινόν ἐστι it is outrageous, Dem.
clever at all things, Plat., Dem.
knavish like Pandeletus (a sycophant), Ar.
all-seeing, Anth.
with the whole people, in a mass or body, Hdt., Aesch.; π. βοηθεῖν, στρατεύειν, of a whole people going out to war, a levee en masse, Thuc.
the whole people, Plat.
πτωχὸς πανδήμιος one who begs of all people, a public beggar, Od.; π. πόλις the city with all its people, Soph.
of or belonging to all the people, public, common, Soph., Eur.; π. πόλις, στρατός the whole body of the city, of the army, Soph.
π. Ἔρως, common, vulgar love, as opp. to the spiritual sort (οὐράνιος), Plat., Xen.
Πάν-δια (sc. ἱερά) a feast of Zeus, Dem.
all righteous, Soph. adv. -κως, most justly, Aesch.; but simply = πάντως, Soph.
daughter of Pandion, i. e. the swallow, Hes.
one of the Attic tribes, Aeschin.
a house for the reception of strangers, an inn, hotel, Ar., Dem., etc.
one who receives all comers, an innkeeper, host, Plat., etc.: metaph., πάσης κακίας π. Id.
a hostess, Ar.; metaph., φάλαινα π. a sea-monster ready to take all in, Id.
to receive and entertain as a host, Hdt., Plat.: absol. to keep an inn, Theophr.
metaph. to take upon oneself, assume, Aesch.
all-receiving, common to all, Pind., Aesch.: c. gen., δόμοι π. ξένων Aesch.
absolute fame, perfect glory, Pind.
all-lamentable, all-plaintive, Trag.
the total setting of a star, Anth.
giver of all, Ar.
pass. as fem. prop. n., Pandora, i. e. the all-endowed, a beautiful female, made by Hephaestus, who received presents from all the gods, in order to win the heart of Epimetheus, Hes.
giver of all, epic Hom.
with the whole nation, Strab.
like in all points, Anth.
a temple of Pan, Strab.
entirely free, Anth.
all the Hellenes, Il., Hes., Eur.
Boeotian name of the month Μεταγειτνιών, Philipp. ap. Dem.
all-lovely, Anth.
all-surveying, Anth.
all-effecting, doric gen. -εργέτα Aesch.
all-desolate, Luc.
lasting the whole evening, Anth.
with all the household, Plut.
all the year long, Pind.
quite happy, Luc.
much strained, very active, Anth.
of metals, quite purified, Hes.
to celebrate or attend a festival, πανηγύρις π. to keep holy-days, Hdt.
fit for a public festival, ὁ λόγος ὁ π., or ὁ π. alone, a panegyric, eulogy, Isocr., Arist.
ostentatious, pompous, Plut.
a general or national assembly, esp. a festal assembly in honour of a national god, Pind., Aesch., etc.; πανηγύρις πανηγυρίζειν, ἀνάγειν, ποιεῖσθαι to hold such festivals, keep holy-days, Hdt.
any assembly, θεῶν Aesch.; φίλων Eur.:— the assembly, people assembled, Thuc.
one who attends a πανήγυρις, Luc.
all day, the livelong day, Od.
to spend the whole day in a thing, c. acc., Eur.

all day long, πανημέριοι θεὸν ἱλάσκοντο continued to appease the god all day long, Il.; ὅσσον τε πανημερίη νηῦς ἤνυσεν as much as a ship sails in a whole day, Od.:—neut. πανημέριον, as adv. = πανῆμαρ, Il.
of the whole day, Eur.
= πᾰν-ημέριος, Aesch.:—neut. πανημερόν (oxyt.) as adv., Hdt.
doric πανάμερος = πάντως τῇδε τῇ ἡμέρᾳ, Soph.
with all manner of trees, Anth.
the panther or leopard, Hdt., Xen.
in high wrath, Od.
celebrated with all kinds of sacrifices, Soph.
of or for Pan, Luc.
of fears, panic, such fears being attributed to Pan, Plut.
all-lovely, Anth.
burning with desire, Soph.
their place of meeting at Mycale, and the common temple there built, Hdt.
Πανιώνια (sc. ἱερά), τά, the festival of the united Ionians, Id.
grievously disfigured, hideous, Luc.
to celebrate a night festival, keep vigil, τῇ θεᾷ Ar.
generally, to do anything the livelong night, φλὸξ συνεχὲς π. it lasts all night long, Pind.; c. acc., π. τὴν νύκτα to spend the livelong night, Ar.
fit for a night-reveller, Anth.
all night long, εὗδον παννύχιοι Il.; π. χοροί Soph.; τὸ ἐλλύχνιον καίεται παννύχιον Hdt.:—neut. as adv., Il. παν-νῡχίς, ίδος, ἡ, (νύξ) a night-festival, vigil, Hdt., Eur., etc.
a night-watch, vigil, Soph.
= παννύχιος, Od., Hdt., attic
lasting all the night, τί πάννυχον ὕπνον ἀωτεῖς; Il.; π. σελάνα Eur.:—neut. pl. as adv., πάννυχα the livelong night, Soph.
most lamentable, Anth.
gen. υος, all-unhappy, Aesch.
with all the house, household and all, Hdt.
with all one's house, Strab.
Exclam. oh utter woe! Aesch.
truly happy, Hhymn., Theogn.
in whole troops, Aesch.
all-eyed, Anth.
just like, Anth.
sender of all ominous voices, author of all divination, Il., Anth.

the full armour of an ὁπλίτης, i. e. shield, helmet, breastplate, greaves, sword, and lance, a full suit of armour, panoply, Thuc., etc.; πανοπλίᾳ, ionic -ίῃ, in full armour, cap-à-pie, Hdt.; so, πανοπλίαν ἔχων στῆναι Ar.; τὴν π. λαβεῖν Id.:— metaph., ἡ π. τοῦ θεοῦ NTest.
a man in full armour, Tyrtae.
in full armour, full-armed, Aesch., Eur.; πάνοπλα ἀμφιβλήματα suits of full armour, Eur.
the all-seeing, of the sun, Aesch.; of the herdsman Argus, Eur.
always fit for landing in, Od.
Πάνορμος, ὁ, the ancient name of Palermo, Thuc.; Πανορμῖτις, ιδος, ἡ, its territory, Polyb.
the ancient name of Palermo, Thuc.; Πανορμῖτις, ιδος, ἡ, its territory, Polyb.
a torch, = φανός, Aesch.
to play the knave or villain, Eur., Ar.; ἃ πανουργεῖς the rogueries you are playing, Ar.; ὅσια πανουργήσασα, an oxymoron, having dared a righteous crime, Soph.
a knavish trick, villany, Soph.
knavery, roguery, villany, Lat. malitia, Aesch., Soph.: in pl. knaveries, villanies, Soph., etc.
knave-Hipparchides, Ar.
ready to do anything wicked, knavish, villanous, Aesch., etc.:—as Subst. a knave, rogue, villain, Eur., Ar.; τὰ π. the knavish sort, Soph.; but also = πανουργία, Id.:—comp. -ότερος, Sup. -ότατος, Ar.
adv. -γως, Sup. -ότατα, Id.
in a less positively bad sense, cunning, crafty, clever, smart, Plat., etc.
all-seen, in the sight of all, Il.
Pan, god of Arcadia, son of Hermes, Hhymn.; represented with goat's feet, horns, and shaggy hair. At Athens his worship began after the battle of Marathon, Hdt.:—pl. Πᾶνες in Ar., Theocr.
in full armour, Soph.
of the moon, at the full, ἡ σελήνη ἐτύγχανε οὖσα π. Thuc.; π. κύκλος the moon's full orb, Eur.
ἡ πανσέληνος (sc. ὥρα) the time of full moon, Hdt., Ar.; τὰν αὔριον π. at the next full moon, Soph.; without the Art., Aesch.
all-majestic, Luc.
all-seeing, Anth.
all-wise, Eur., Plat.
a mixture of all seeds, Luc.
composed of all sorts of seeds, Anth.
a levy of the whole army, πανστρατιᾶς γενομένης Thuc.: elsewhere only in dat. πανστρατιᾷ as adv., with the whole army, Hdt., Thuc.; cf. πανσυδίῃ.
with all speed, = πάσῃ τῇ σπουδῇ, Il.; attic πανσυδίᾳ or πασσυδίᾳ, Eur.—No nom. πανσυδία occurs, cf. πανστρατιά.
with all one's force; π. διεφθάρθαι utterly, Thuc.
swept all together, αἰὼν πάνσυρτος ἀχέων a life of accumulated woes, Soph.
all-wretched, Aesch., Eur.
all in all, altogether, wholly, absolutely, Hdt., attic; οὐ π. οὕτως ἀλόγως not so absolutely without reason, Thuc.:—with the Art., τὸ π. Id.
in replying, it affirms strongly, by all means, quite so, undoubtedly, Plat., Xen.
all-powerful, Aesch.
lord of all, Ar.
all-ruling, Soph.
adv. of Place, everywhere, Lat. ubique, ubivis, Thuc., Plat., etc.:—c. gen. loci, in every part of, π. τοῦ Ἑλλησπόντου Hdt.; π. ἄστεως Eur.
on every side, in every direction, every way, Hdt., attic
by all means, absolutely, Hdt.; οὐ κατ’ ἓν μόνον, ἀλλὰ π. in all respects, Id.; π. δρῶντες, i. e. whatever we do, Soph.
adv. from all places, from all quarters, on every side, Lat. undique, Hdt., attic
from every side, i. e. in every way, Thuc., Xen.
in every direction, any whither, every way, Lat. quovis, quoquoversus, Ar., Dem.
everywhere, Lat. ubique, ubivis, Hdt., attic:—c. gen., π. τῆς γῆς Plat.
altogether, always, absolutely, Id.
in all ways, altogether, Lat. omnino, Plat.
consummation, Polyb.
all-complete, absolute, complete, entire, Aesch., etc.; π. δάμαρ uxor legitima, the mistress of the house, Soph.; π. ἐσχάραι the whole number of sacrificial hearths, their complete tale, Id.
act. all-accomplishing, all-achieving, Aesch.
adv. παντελῶς, ionic -έως, altogether, utterly, absolutely, entirely, completely, Hdt., attic; παντελέως εἶχε it was quite finished, Hdt.; π. θανεῖν to die outright, Soph.
in answers, most certainly, παντελῶς γε, π. μὲν οὖν Id., Plat.
later, εἰς τὸ παντελές = παντελῶς, NTest.
= πανοπλία, Eur.ὅπλων πολέμιος παντευχία enemies in full array, Id.; ξὺν παντευχίᾳ in full armour, Aesch.
assistant of all arts, Aesch.
every way, on every side, Hom., Hdt., Ar.
in every way, by all means, altogether, entirely, Plat., etc.
all-honourable, Soph.
all-overpowering, Anth.
making all old, i. e. subduing all, Soph.
of every kind, of all sorts, manifold, Hhymn., Aesch., etc.:—in pl., πολλοὶ καὶ π. Hdt.:—adv. -πῶς, in all kinds of ways, Poeta ap. Arist.
παντοδαπὸς γίγνεται, = παντοῖος γίγνεται, assumes every shape, Ar.
from all quarters, from every side, Lat. undique, Il., Hdt., Trag.
everywhere, Anth.
of all sorts or kinds, manifold, Hom., Hdt., Soph.
παντοῖος γίγνεται he takes all shapes, i. e. tries every shift, turns every stone, Hdt.
adv. -ως, in all kinds of ways, Id., Plat.
almighty, NTest., Anth.
utterly short-lived, Anth.
all-daring, shameless, Aesch., Eur.
a pantomimic actor, Luc.
all-hateful, Aesch.
ready for all, reckless, Theophr.
all-inventive, opp. to ἄπορος, Soph.
a place where all things are for sale, a general market, bazaar, Plat.
every way, in all directions, Il., Xen.
adv. at all times, always, NTest.
all-devouring, Anth.
mixed all together, Aesch.
all-trembling, Aesch.
all-routed, tumultuous, Aesch.
all-nourishing, Anth.; π. πελειάς a dove that rears all her nestlings, Aesch.
altogether; in Hom., always πάντως οὐ, in nowise, by no means, not at all, Lat. omnino non: ἔδεε πάντως it was altogether necessary, Hdt.; εἰ π. ἐλεύσεσθε if ye positively will go, Id.
in affirmations, at all events, at any rate, Id., attic; ἄλλως τε πάντως καί above all . . , Aesch.
with the imperat., in command or entreaty, π. παρατίθετε only put on table, Plat.
in answers, yes by all means, Id.; so, πάντως γάρ . . Ar.; π. δήπου Plat.
eminent above all, Anth.
highest of all, Od.

altogether, entirely, Aesch., etc.; π. μανθάνω perfectly, Ar.:—with Adjs. very, exceedingly, π. πολλοί, ὀλίγοι, π. μικρός, μέγας Aesch., etc.:— with Advs., π. σφόδρα Ar.; μόλις or μόγις π. Plat.; with Nouns in adv. sense, π. σπουδῇ in very great haste, Dem.; π. ἐξ εἰκότος λόγου Plat.:—with a Part., π. ἀδικῶν if ever so criminal, Thuc.
strengthd., καὶ πάνυ Id., Xen.
οὐ πάνυ, like οὐ πάντως, Lat. omnino non, not at all, Soph., etc.
in answers, yes by all means, no doubt, certainly, Ar.; πάνυ γε, πάνυ μὲν οὖν Id., Plat.: —πάνυ καλῶς, Lat. benigne, no I thank you, Ar.
ὁ πάνυ (where κλεινός may be supplied), the excellent, the famous, οἱ πάνυ τῶν στρατιωτῶν Thuc.; ὁ πάνυ Περικλῆς Xen.
for the very last time, Soph., Eur.; so πανύστατα Eur.
last of all, Hom., Soph., Eur., Anth.
utter destruction, utter ruin: in dat., πανωλεθρίῃ ὄλλυσθαι Hdt.; πανωλεθρία ἀπώλετο Thuc.
utterly ruined, utterly destroyed, Hdt.; πανωλέθρους ὀλέσθαι Soph.; π. πίπτειν Aesch., etc.
in moral sense, utterly abandoned, Lat. perditissimus, Soph., Eur.
act. all destructive, all-ruinous, Hdt., Aesch.
= πανώλεθρος, Aesch.
in moral sense, like πανώλεθρος I. 2, Soph., Eur.
act. all-destructive, Soph.
visible to all, Anth.

entry.etym: The forms ἐπᾱσάμην, πέπᾱμαι must not be confounded with ἐπασάμην, πέπασμαι from πατέομαι, to eat.
entry.sense: to get, acquire, Lat. potior, πᾱσάμενος ἐπίτασσε when you've got slaves order them, Theocr.: chiefly in perf. πέπᾱμαι, = κέκτημαι, to possess, Pind., Eur., Ar., 3rd pl. πέπανται Xen.; inf. πεπᾶσθαι Solon, Eur.; part. πεπᾱμένος Aesch., Xen.; plup. ἐπεπάμην Xen.
Comic exaggeration of παπαῖ, ἀππαπαῖ παπαιάξ Ar.
as exclam. of surprise, Eur.
Exclam. of suffering, Lat. vae, oh! Trag.; φεῦ παπαῖ, παπαῖ μάλ’ αὖθις Soph.; also, παππαπαππαπαῖ Id.; παπαῖ, ἀπαππαπαῖ, παπαπαππαπαππαπαππαπαῖ Id.
of surprise, like Lat. papae, vah, atat, Hdt.
to call any one papa, Il.
papa, a child's word for πατήρ, father, (as μάμμα for μήτηρ) in voc., πάππᾰ φίλε Od.; in acc., πάππαν καλεῖν, like παππάζειν, Ar.
to wheedle one's father, Ar.
dear little papa, Ar.
a grandfather, Hdt., Ar.: —in pl. one's grand-parents, ancestors, Arist.
a little bird, Ar.
of or from one's grand-fathers, Ar.
a Thracian lake-fish, Hdt.
to look earnestly, gaze, Hom.; mostly with notion of alarm or caution, to look or peer around, Id.
c. acc. to look round for, look after, Il., Pind.; παπτάναις (doric aor1 part.) having set eyes on a thing, Pind.: to glare at, τινά Soph.
the papyrus, an Egyptian rush with triangular stalks: paper was made by peeling off its outer coat (βύβλος), and gluing the slips together.
anything made of it, linen, cord, etc., Anth.
like a staff, π. θεραπεύμασι with service as of a staff, Eur.
like a Bacchanal, theatrical, Plut.

entry.note: fut. -βᾰλῶ aor2 παρέβᾰλον perf. παραβέβληκα Pass., perf. -βέβλημαι: —
entry.sense: to throw beside or by, throw to one, as fodder to horses, Hom.: to hold out as a bait, Xen.
to cast in one's teeth, Lat. objicere, τί τινι Aeschin.

to expose, παρέβαλεν ἐμέ exposed me to them, Ar.:—Mid. to expose oneself or what is one's own to danger, αἰὲν ἐμὴν ψυχὴν παραβαλλόμενος πολεμίζειν risking it in war, Il.; so, παραβάλλεσθαι τὰ τέκνα Hdt.:—Pass., κύβοισι παραβεβλημένος given up to dice, Ar.

Mid. also to set what one values upon a chance, to hazard it as at play, πλείω παραβαλλόμενοι having greater interests at stake, Thuc.; so in perf. pass., Λακεδαιμονίοις πλεῖστον δὴ παραβεβλημένοι having risked far the most upon them, Id.;—also, τὸν κίνδυνον τῶν σωμάτων παραβαλλομένους Id.

to lay beside, to compare one with another, τί τινι Hdt.; τι πρός τι Xen.; τι παρά τι Plat.:—so in Mid., absol., παραβαλλόμεναι vying with one another, Eur.; —and in Pass., ἀπάτα δ’ ἀπάταις παραβαλλομένα one piece of treachery set against others, Soph.
Mid. to bring alongside, τὴν ἄκατον παραβάλλου bring your boat alongside, Ar.; and absol., παραβαλοῦ Id.

to throw, turn, bend sideways, παραβάλλειν τὸν ὀφθαλμόν or τὼ ὀφθαλμώ to cast the eyes askance, like a timid animal, Id., Plat.; so, π. τὸ ἕτερον οὖς πλάγιον to turn one's ears to listen, Xen.; π. τοὺς γομφίους to lay to one's grinders, Ar.
to deposit with one, entrust to him, Lat. committere, τί τινι Hdt.
in Mid. to deceive, betray, Id., Eur., etc.
intr. to come near, approach, Plat., Arist.; π. ἀλλήλοις to meet one another, Plat.
to go by sea, to cross over, Lat. trajicere, παρέβαλε νηυσί Hdt.; so of the ships, ναῦς Πελοποννησίων παρέβαλον εἰς Ἰωνίαν Thuc.
to turn aside, pass over, Arist.
to dye at the same time, Plut.
a going aside, deviation, Arist.
an overstepping, τῶν δικαίων Plut.:—absol. a transgression, Id.
the parabasis, a part of the old Comedy, in which the chorus came forward and addressed the audience in the Poet's name.

entry.note: παραβάτης, poet. παραιβάτης, and παρβάτης, ου, ὁ,
entry.sense: one who stands beside: properly the warrior who stood beside the charioteer, Il., Eur., Xen.
in pl. light troops (velites) who ran beside the horsemen, Plut.
（παραβαίνω II. 1) a transgressor, Aesch.
a woman who follows the reapers, Theocr.
to be overcome or overreached, Aesch., Soph.
Dep. to use violence to one, to constrain, compel him, NTest.
to grow up beside or by, Plat.
to look aside, take a side look, Ar.; π. θατέρῳ (sc. ὀφθαλμῷ) to look suspiciously with one eye, Id.
to see wrong, Luc.
thrown in by the way, παραβλήδην ἀγορεύων speaking with a side-meaning, i. e. maliciously, deceitfully, Il.; cf. παράβολος I.
that which is thrown beside or before, a curtain or screen used to cover the sides of ships, Xen.
to be compared, τινί to one, Plut.
comparable, Plut.
to go beside, for the purpose of protecting, c. dat., Il.
looking askance, squinting, Il.
help, aid, succour, Plat.
to come up to help, τινί Thuc.: —absol. to come to the rescue, Ar., Thuc.
Dep. to run hazard, NTest.
juxta-position, comparison, Plat.
a comparison, illustration, analogy, Arist.
a parable, i. e. a fictitious narrative by which some religious or moral lesson is conveyed, NTest.
a by-word, proverb, Id.
thrown in by the way, deceitful, παραίβολα = παραβλήδην, Hhymn.
exposing oneself: hence,
of persons, venturesome, reckless, Ar.
of things and actions, hazardous, perilous, Hdt.
stuffed in: pushed aside or into a corner, ἐν παραβύστῳ in a corner, Dem.
to stuff in, insert, Luc.
a command or order issued to soldiers, a charge, Xen., NTest.
the summoning one's partisans to support one in a law-suit, exertion of influence, Dem.
canvassing for public office, Lat. ambitus, Plut.
a set of rules, Arist.
to transmit as a message, as by telegraph, παραγγείλασα σέλας Aesch.; μνήμην παραγγέλλοντες ὧν ἐκύρσατε Eur.; π. τὸ σύνθημα to pass on the watchword, Xen.
generally, to give the word, give orders, of the general, Hdt., Aesch., etc.; π. τινὶ ποιεῖν τι Hdt., Xen., etc.:—Pass., τὰ παραγγελλόμενα military orders, Thuc.; so, τὰ παρηγγελμένα Xen.

to order, recommend, exhort, π. τινὶ ποιεῖν τι Soph., etc.; τί τινι Eur.; ὅπως ἂν . . , to give orders to the end that . . , Plat.:—c. acc. rei only, to order, π. παρασκευὴν σίτου to order corn to be prepared, Lat. imperare frumentum, Hdt.; π. σιτία Thuc.; στρατείαν Aeschin.
to encourage, cheer on, ἵππους Theogn.; π. εἰς ὅπλα to call to arms, Xen.
to summon to one's help, summon one's partisans, form a cabal, Dem.
π. τὴν ἀρχήν to canvass for office, Lat. magistratum ambire, Plut.; π. εἰς ὑπατείαν to be candidate for the consulship, Id.
a message transmitted by beacons, Aesch.
an order, command, ἀπὸ παραγγέλματος by word of command, Thuc.
an instruction, precept, Xen.
in war, a giving the word of command, Thuc.; ἀπὸ παραγγέλσεως πορεύεσθαι Xen.
to give just a taste of, τινός Plut.
to be superannuated, Aeschin.

entry.note: ionic and later -γίνομαι fut. γενήσομαι aor2 παρεγενόμην
entry.sense: to be beside, to be by or near, attend upon one, c. dat., Od., Plat.: c. dat. rei, π. τῇ μάχῃ to be present at . . , Plat.
π. τινι to come to one's side, come to aid, stand by, second, support, Hes., Hdt., attic
of things, to be at hand, to be gained, to accrue to one, π. τινι, Lat. contingere alicui, Thuc., Xen.:—impers., σῷ τρόπῳ παραγίγνεται εἰδέναι Plat.
to come to, τινι Theogn., Hdt.; π. ἐς τὠυτό to come to the same point, Hdt.:—absol. to arrive, come up, Id.
to come to maturity, of corn, Id.; of the horns of oxen, to be fully grown, Id.
to decide wrongly, err in their judgment, Xen.
that which is taken into the arms, a beloved one, Soph.
to set the arms a-kimbo:—Mid. to push aside with the elbows, elbow, Luc.
the cheekpiece of a helmet or tiara, Strab.
that which one writes beside, an additional clause, Dem.
anything written beside: an exception taken by the defendant to the admissibility of a suit (γραφή), a demurrer, Dem.
to write by the side, Ar.:—generally, to add a clause to a law or contract, Plat., Dem.: esp. by fraud, ἄλλου πατρὸς ἑαυτὸν παραγράφειν to enroll oneself with a wrong father's name, Dem.
Mid., with perf. pass.,
παραγράφεσθαι τὸν νόμον to have the law written in parallel columns with a decree charged with illegality, Id.: Pass., οἱ παραγεγραμμένοι νόμοι Id., Aeschin.
παραγραφὴν παραγράφεσθαι to demur to the admissibility of a suit (v. παραγραφή), Dem.
to lay bare at the side: metaph. to lay bare, disclose, τὸν πάντα λόγον Hdt.
to lead by or past a place, c. acc. loci, Hdt.
as military term, to march the men up from the side, to bring them from column into line, Xen.
to lead aside from the way, mislead, Lat. seducere, Pind., attic: —Pass., φόβῳ παρηγόμην Soph.; ἀπάτῃ Thuc.
generally, to lead to or into a thing, ἔς τι Eur.; mostly of something bad, Theogn., etc.:—Pass. to be induced, c. inf., παρηγμένος εἰργάσθαι τι Soph.
of things, to lead aside, alter the course of a thing, Hdt., Plat.
to bring and set beside others, to bring forward, introduce, ἐς μέσον Hdt.; π. εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον to bring a matter before the court, Dem.:—also to bring forward as a witness, Id.
to bring in, with a notion of secresy, Hdt.:—Pass. to come in stealthily, slip in, Soph.
intr. to pass by, pass on one's way, Xen.
to pass away, NTest.; so in Pass., Id., Plut.
a leading by or past, carrying across, Xen.
as military term, a wheeling from column into line, Id.
π. τῶν κωπῶν a sliding motion of the oars, so that they made no dash (πίτυλος) in coming out of the water, Id.
a misleading, seduction, Hdt.:— a false argument, fallacy, quibble, Dem.:—also delay, Plut.
a variation, as of language, Hdt.
a persuading, Plat.
to weep beside or with, τινί Luc.

entry.note: fut. -δαρθήσομαι aor2 παρέδαρθον epic παρέδρᾰθον inf. παραδραθέειν
entry.sense: to sleep beside another, c. dat., Hom.
a pattern or model of the thing to be executed, Lat. exemplar, an architect's plan, Hdt.; a sculptor's or painter's model, Plat.
a precedent, example, Thuc., Plat.; ἐπὶ παραδείγματος by way of example, Aeschin.
an example, i. e. a lesson or warning, π. ἔχειν τινός to take a lesson from another, Thuc.; τὸ σὸν π. ἔχων Soph.; ζῶντά τινα τοῖς λοιποῖς π. ποιεῖν Dem.
an argument, proof from example, Thuc.
the model or copy of an existing thing, Hdt.
to make an example of one, c. acc., Polyb., NTest.
characterised by examples, Arist.
to exhibit side by side: generally, to exhibit, bring forward, in Mid., Dem.
to represent as so and so, π. τινὰ οὐκ ὄντα Polyb.: also in bad sense, like παραδειγματίζω, Plut.
to exhibit and hand over, τί τινι Xen.
Pass. to go without one's dinner, Theophr.
a park, a Persian word brought in by Xen.; used for the garden of Eden, Paradise, NTest.

entry.note: παραδεκτέος, ον, verb. adj. of παραδέχομαι
entry.sense: one must admit, Plat.
to be admitted, Id.
Dep.
to receive from another, Il., Xen., etc.:—of children, to receive as inheritance, succeed to, τὴν ἀρχήν Hdt.; so, τὴν μάχην π. to take up and continue the battle, Id.
c. inf., π. τινι πράττειν τι to take upon oneself, engage to do a thing, Lat. recipere se facturum, Dem.
to admit, Plat.
to make known by a side-wind, to intimate or insinuate, Dem., Plut.
to accuse underhand, Plut.
to live with and serve another, c. dat., Ar.

to give or hand over to another, transmit, τί τινι, Lat. tradere, Hdt.; of transmission to one's successor, Id.; π. τὴν ἀρετήν to transmit, impart as a teacher, Plat.:—c. inf., π. τινὶ τοὺς νέους διδάσκειν Id.

to give a city or person into another's hands, Hdt.; esp. as an hostage, to deliver up, surrender, Lat. dedere, Id., Thuc., etc.; also, with notion of treachery, to betray, Xen.: τύχῃ αὑτὸν π. to commit oneself to fortune, Thuc.
to give up to justice, ἑωυτὸν Κροίσῳ Hdt.; τινὰ εἰς τὸν δῆμον Xen.
to hand down legends, opinions, and the like, Lat. memoriae prodere, Dem.

to grant, bestow, κῦδός τινι Pind.:—in pres. and imperf. to offer, allow, αἵρεσιν Id.: c. inf. to allow one to do, Hdt.; so, c. acc. rei, ὁ θεὸς τοῦτό γε οὐ παρεδίδου Id.:—absol., τοῦ θεοῦ παραδιδόντος if he permits, Id.
Dep. to relate by the way, Arist.
marvellousness, Strab.
to tell marvels, Strab.:—Pass., πολλὰ παραδοξολογεῖται many marvels are told, Id.
a tale of wonder, marvel, Aeschin.
contrary to opinion, incredible, paradoxical, Plat., Xen., etc.; ἐκ τοῦ παραδόξου contrary to expectation, Dem.:—adv. -ξως, Aeschin.
handed down, hereditary, Polyb.
a handing down, transmission, Thuc.
the transmission of legends and doctrines, tradition, Plat., etc.:—also that which is so handed down, a tradition, NTest.
a giving up, surrender, Thuc.
to be handed down, Plat.: παραδοτέον one must hand over, τί τινι Id.
to be given up, Id.
παραδοτέα one must give up, Thuc.
capable of being taught, Plat.
a receiving from another: also that which has been received, a hereditary custom, Eur.
acceptance, approval, Polyb.
to be at hand, to serve another, c. dat., Od.
a running beside or over, traversing, Plut.; ἐν παραδρομῇ cursorily, Arist.
that may be run through, παράδρομα gaps, Xen.
to reign with another, Thuc.

entry.note: μιδ. intr. aor2 act. παρέδυν epic inf. παραδύμεναι
entry.sense: to creep past, slink or steal past, Il.
to creep or steal in, Plat., Dem.
a creeping in beside, encroachment, Dem.
to be disposed to deliver up, Thuc.
to sing beside or to one, c. dat., Od.
to lift up beside:—Pass., aor1 παρ-ηέρθην, to hang on one side, Il.
to yoke beside, set beside, Eur.:—Pass. to be joined, coupled with another, c. dat., Dem.
yoked beside: pl. παράζυγες supernumeraries, Arist.
to gird to the side, Plat.:—Mid. to wear at the girdle, Plut.
beside the sea, lying on the sea-side, maritime, Hdt., Xen.
to comfort, cheer;— Pass., Eur.
to embolden, cheer on, encourage, Thuc., Xen.
Dep. to compare, Theophr.
to assuage, Aesch.
to heat to excess:—Pass., aor1 part. παραθερμανθείς, of a man become quarrelsome in his cups, Aeschin.
over-hot, Plut.
juxta-position, neighbourhood, Polyb.; ἐκ παραθέσεως on comparison, Id.
to run beside or alongside, Plat., Xen.
to run beyond, outrun, τινά Xen.: to run past, Id.
to touch on cursorily, Luc.
to examine a thing beside another, compare, τινὰ πρός τινα Xen.
to look slightly at, overlook, neglect, Dem.:—Pass., NTest.
anything entrusted to one, a deposit, Hdt.: of persons, a hostage, Id.
to move or stir in passing, Anth.:—metaph., θόρυβον π. to raise a shout in applause, Pind.
intr., of words, to fall by chance from a person, Id.

an exhortation, address, Hdt., attic; c. gen. pers. advice or counsel given by a person, Hdt.; c. gen. rei, advice given for or towards a thing, Thuc.; ἐπὶ γνώμης παραινέσει to recommend an opinion, Id.

entry.note: 3rd sg. imperf. παρῄνει ionic παραίνεε fut. -έσω and -έσομαι aor1 παρῄνεσα perf. παρῄνεκα Pass., perf. inf. παρῃνῆσθαι
entry.sense: to exhort, recommend, advise, π. τινὶ ποιεῖν τι Hdt., Ar., etc.; π. τί τινι Aesch.; π. τινί to advise a person, Id.
to advise or recommend publicly, παρῄνει τοιάδε Thuc.; οὐ π. to advise not to do, Id.
a taking away from beside, curtailing, τῶν προσόδων Thuc.

entry.note: fut. ήσω aor2 παρεῖλον perf. παρῄρηκα
entry.sense: to take away from beside, withdraw, remove, Eur.:— c. gen. partit. to take away part of a thing, Id., Thuc.:—Pass., παρῃρημένοι τὰ ὅπλα having their arms taken from them, Thuc.
π. ἀρὰν εἰς παῖδα to draw aside the curse on thy son's head, Eur.
Mid. to draw over to one's own side, seduce, detach, Xen., Dem.
to take away, Xen.: Mid., παραιρεῖσθαι τὴν θρασύτητα to lessen, damp it, Dem.
generally, to take away from, steal away from, τί τινος Hdt., Eur.
the edge or selvage of cloth (cut off by the tailor): generally, a band, strip, Thuc.
Dep.:— to remark or hear of by the way, τινος Xen.; absol., οὐχὶ παρῄσθευ (doric for παρῄσθου), Theocr.
of ill omen, ominous, Il.
to dart past, Il.; c. acc., ἵπποι γάρ με παρήιξαν Id.
Dep.
to beg from another, ask as a favour of him, Lat. exorare, τί τινα Eur., Plat., etc.: to obtain by entreaty, τι Hdt.
π. τινα to move by entreaty, obtain leave from, Id.: to intercede with a person, prevail upon him by supplications, Id., Eur.
c. acc. et inf. to entreat one to do or be so and so, Hdt., Xen., etc.:—also c. gen. pers. et inf. to beg of a person to do a thing, Eur.:—c. inf. only, to obtain leave to do, Hdt.
c. acc. rei, Lat. deprecari, to avert by entreaty, deprecate, τὴν ὀργήν, τὰς ζημίας Aeschin.
to decline, deprecate, χάριν Pind.
c. acc. pers. to ask him to excuse one, decline his invitation, Polyb.; absol., NTest.:—Pass., ἔχε με παρῃτημένον have me excused, Id.
π. γυναῖκα to divorce her, Luc.
c. acc. pers. to intercede for, beg off, esp. from punishment, Hdt.; π. περί τινος Xen.
earnest prayer, Plat.
a deprecating, Thuc.
an interceding for, begging off, Dem.
an intercessor, Plut.
being in part the cause of a thing, c. gen., ap. Dem.
exhorting, encouraging, Hhymn., Hes.
rebuking, Il.
persuasion, Il.
to hang up beside:—Pass. to be hung or hang beside, Hdt.:—absol., of a suppliant, to hang upon another, Plut.
Dep. to be seated beside or near another, c. dat., Ar., Thuc., etc.
Pass. to be placed by or near, Plut.
to set beside or near, Plat.
aor1 mid., παρεκαθισάμην π. τινά to make him assessor or coarbiter, Dem.
Pass. and Mid.: fut. -καθιζήσομαι: imperf. -καθιζόμην: aor1 παρεκαθισάμην:— to seat oneself or sit down beside another, c. dat., Ar., Xen.
to let down beside: inMid., πηδάλια ζεύγλαισι παρακαθίετο caused the rudder to be let down beside the rudder-bars, Eur.
to station or establish beside, Dem.
Pass. to be kept lighted beside, Hdt.
unseasonable, ill-timed, Luc.
to call to one, Xen.

to call to aid, call in, send for Lat. arcessere, Hdt., Ar., etc.; π. τινα σύμβουλον Xen.:— to call on, invoke the Gods, Id., etc.:—Pass., παρακαλούμενος καὶ ἄκλητος, "vocatus atque non vocatus, " Thuc.
to summon one's friends to attend one in a trial (cf. παράκλησις 1. 1):—Pass., παρακεκλημένοι summoned to attend at a trial, Aeschin.
to invite, ἐπὶ δαῖτα Eur.; ἐπὶ θήραν Xen.; π. τινὰ ἐπὶ τὸ βῆμα to invite him to mount the tribune, Aeschin.
to call to, exhort, cheer, encourage, τινά Aesch., Xen.
to comfort, console: in Pass., NTest.
to excite, τινὰ ἐς φόβον, ἐς δάκρυα Eur.: —of things, to foment, φλόγα Xen.
π. τινά, c. inf., to exhort one to do, Eur., Xen.
to demand, require, ὁ θάλαμος σκεύη π. Xen.
anything hung up beside or before, a covering, curtain, Plut.:—metaph. an excuse, τινος for a thing, Id.
to cover by hanging something beside, to cloak, disguise, Plut.:—Mid. to cover one's face, Plat.
to dismount beside, of horsemen who dismount to fight on foot, Polyb.
to throw down beside, Il.; ζῶμα δέ οἱ παρακάββαλεν put a waistband on him, Id.
as attic law-term, to make a special claim to property, when the claimant deposited a sum of money called παρακαταβολή, Dem.
money deposited in court by claimants, and forfeited in case of failure (v. παρακαταβάλλω II), Dem.
a deposit entrusted to one's care, Lat. fidei commissum, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
of persons entrusted to guardians, Ἀπόλλωνα παρακαταθήκην δεξαμένη Hdt.; of children, Dem.
to die beside, poet. aor2 παρακάτθανε Anth.
Pass. to lie beside another at meals, Lat. accumbere, c. dat., Xen.
to lay down beside, to put to bed with, τινά τινι Aeschin., Luc.
Pass. to sleep beside another, c. dat., Il.
to leave with one, τινά τινι Thuc.
to drive in alongside, Thuc.
Mid. to deposit one's own property with another, entrust it to his keeping, give it him in trust, Hdt., Xen., etc.
to keep back, restrain, detain, Thuc.
to make to dwell or settle beside, π. φόβον τινι to make fear his companion, Plut.
to sew on beside, patch up:—in Mid., generally, to put all in order, set straight, Ar.

entry.note: poet. πάρ-κειμαι epic 3rd sg. imperf. παρεκέσκετο
entry.sense: to lie beside or before, Hom.:—metaph., ὑμῖν παράκειται ἐναντίον ἠὲ μάχεσθαι ἢ φεύγειν the choice lies before you, to fight or to flee, Od.:—in part. close at hand, present, Pind.
an exhortation, cheering address, Eur.
a precept, maxim, Plat.
Dep.
to order one to do a thing, advise, prescribe, τί τινι Hdt., Thuc., etc.; π. ταῦτα to give this advice, Plat.;—also, π. τινι, c. inf., Id., Xen.
to exhort, τοιαῦτα παρακελευσάμενος having delivered this address, Thuc.:—absol. to encourage one another by shouting, Hdt.
παρακεκέλευστο in pass. sense, orders had been given, Id.
a calling out to, cheering on, exhorting, addressing, Thuc., Xen.
calling out to, cheering on, Plat.
summoned, of a packed audience, Thuc.
to ride by or past, τινά Ar.
a desperate venture, Thuc.
venturesome, audacious, Plat., Dem.: adv., παρακινδυνευτικῶς λέγειν Plat.
to make a rash venture, to venture, run the risk, Ar., Thuc., etc.; π. εἰς Ἰωνίαν to venture to Ionia, Thuc.
c. acc. rei, to venture, risk a thing, Ar., Plat.; τοιουτονί τι παρακεκινδυνευμένον a bold, venturous phrase, Ar.
c. inf. to have the hardihood to do a thing, Id., Xen.
to move aside, disturb, Plat.: absol. to raise troubles, enter into plots, Dem.:— Pass. to be violently incited, Luc.
intr. to be disturbed, to shift one's ground, Plat.
to be highly excited, ἐπί τινι Xen.; παρακινῶν out of his senses, Plat.
inclined to insanity: adv., παρακινητικῶς ἔχειν to shew symptoms of insanity, Plut.
to pass by, τινά Il.
to shut out, exclude, Hdt.
to steal from the side, filch underhand, Ar.
a calling to one's aid, summons, οἱ ἐκ παρακλήσεως συγκαθήμενοι a packed party in the jury, Dem.
