to prick or dot all round, περιέστιξε τοῖς μαζοῖς τὸ τεῖχος she stuck the wall all round with breasts, Hdt.; and so, περιστίξαντες κατὰ τὰ ἀγγήια τοὺς τυφλούς having set them at equal distance round the pails, Id.
to put all round, Aesch.
Mid. to surround as with toils or nets, of a besieging army, Dem.
set round in rows, Dem.
Dep. to encamp about, invest, absol. or c. acc., Xen.:—the Act. in later writers, Polyb., Plut., etc.
to whirl round, of one preparing to throw, Hom.; π. ἵππον to wheel it round, Plut.:— Pass. to be turned round, spin round, Il.; π. εἰς τἀληθῆ to come round to it, Plat.
π. τὼ χεῖρε to tie his hands behind him, Lys..
a turning or spinning round, Plat.
περιστρωφώμενος πάντα τὰ χρηστήρια going round to all the oracles, Hdt.
with pillars round the wall, surrounded with a colonnade, Hdt., Eur.
as Subst., περίστυλον, ου, τό, or περίστυλος, ὁ, a peristyle, colonnade round a temple or court-yard, Plut.
Pass., περισυλᾶσθαι τὴν οὐσίαν to be stripped of one's property, Plat.
to drag about, ἄνω καὶ κάτω Luc.
to tear away from, τί τινος Polyb.
a band for the ankle, anklet, Hdt., Anth.
to slit and tear off, Plut., Luc.
Pass., of a river, περισχίζεσθαι τὸν χῶρον to split round a piece of land, i. e. split into two branches so as to surround it, Hdt.;—so, of a stream of men, to part and go different ways, Plat.
to part off by a rope: — Mid., of the Areopagitic Council, to part itself off by a rope from the audience, Dem.
to save alive, to save from death or ruin, Xen.:—Pass. to escape with one's life, Id.
to surround with a trench, Polyb.: Pass., ἐν περιτεταφρευμένῳ on entrenched ground, Xen.
to stretch all round or over, Hdt.
to wall all round, πλίνθοις Βαβυλῶνα Ar.
to surround with a wall, so as to beleaguer, Thuc.
to build round, ὁ περιτετειχισμένος κύκλος Xen.
round the ankle, Anth.
as Subst.
circumvallation, Thuc.
a wall of circumvallation, Thuc.
to grow around, Hes.
to finish all round or completely: Pass., περὶ δ’ ἤματα μακρὰ τελέσθη Od.
to go or come round, ἂψ περιτελλομένου ἔτεος as the year came round again, Od.; περιτελλομένων ἐνιαυτῶν as years go round, Il.; so, περιτελλομέναις ὥραις Soph.
to cut or clip round about, Lat. circumcidere, οἰνὰς περιταμνέμεν to prune them, Hes.; τὴν κεφαλὴν π. κύκλῳ περὶ τὰ ὦτα Hdt.:—Mid., περιτάμνεσθαι βραχίονας to make incisions all round one's arms, Id.
of circumcision, Id.: and in Mid., περιτάμνονται τὰ αἰδοῖα they practise circumcision, Id.
to cut off the extremities, τὰ ὦτα καὶ τὴν ῥῖνα Id.:—Pass., περιτάμνεσθαι γῆν to be curtailed of certain land, Id.
to cut off and hem in all round, cut off, Lat. intercipere; hence in Mid., βοῦς περιταμνόμενος cutting off cattle for oneself, "lifting" cattle, Od.:—Pass. to be cut off, intercepted, Xen.
bounded all round, Anth.
extraordinary art or cunning, Thuc.

entry.note: fut. -θήσω aor1 περιέθηκα aor2 imperat. περίθες
entry.sense: to place round, Od.; περιτιθέναι τί τινι Hdt.:—Mid. to put round oneself, put on, Hom., Eur.
metaph., like περιβάλλω, to bestow, confer upon, π. τινὶ βασιληίην, ἐλευθερίην Hdt., Thuc.; so, π. τὴν Μηδικὴν ἀρχὴν τοῖς Ἕλλησι to put the Median yoke round their necks, Thuc.
to pluck all round, περ. θρίδακα to strip the outside leaves off a lettuce, Hdt.; so, θρίδαξ περιτετιλμένη Id.
much-honoured, Hhymn.
to stretch round about, Il.
a slice, shaving, Plat.
circumcision, NTest.
cut off all round, abrupt, steep, Lat. abruptus, Polyb.
to overshoot, outshoot, τινά Ar.
to turn and bring round, Lys., NTest., etc.
to overturn, upset, Plat.
intr. to turn or go round, Od.
Pass., περιτρέφεται κυκόωντι [the milk] forms curds as you mix it, Il.; σακέεσσι περιτρέφετο κρύσταλλος the ice froze hard upon the shields, Od.
to run round and round, run round, Theogn., Ar.
to run about, Plat.:— metaph. to be current, in vogue, Id.
c. acc. to run round, Hdt., Ar.:—metaph. to circumvent, Ar.
to tremble round about, λαοὶ περίτρεσαν the people stood trembling round, Il.
anything worn smooth by rubbing: metaph., π. δικῶν, of a pettifogger, Ar.; π. ἀγορᾶς Dem.
Mid., σάρκες περιτρομέοντο μέλεσσιν all the flesh crept on his limbs, Od.
intr., περιτροπέων ἐνιαυτός a revolving year, Il.
trans. to gather from all round, πολλὰ [μῆλα] περιτροπέοντες ἐλαύνομεν Od.; περιτροπέων φῦλ’ ἀνθρώπων driving about, perplexing them, Hhymn.
a turning round, revolution, circuit, Plat.
a turning about, changing, ἐν περιτροπῇ by turns, Hdt.
neut. pl. as adv., περιτρόχαλα κείρεσθαι to have one's hair clipt all round, Hdt.
circular, round, Il.
to gnaw round about, nibble off, purloin, Ar.:—metaph. to carp at, τινά Id.
to light upon, fall in with, meet with, a person or thing, c. dat., Thuc., etc.: absol., Id.
of events, περιτυγχάνει μοι ἡ συμφορά the accident happens to, befals me, Id.
round or at the grave, Anth.
to treat very ill, to insult wantonly, Hdt., Ar.:—Pass. to be so treated, Hdt.
Pass. to be visible all round, of mountains, etc., ὄρεος κορυφῇ περιφαινομένοιο Il.; περιφαινομένῳ ἐνὶ χώρῳ Hhymn.; so, ἐν περιφαινομένῳ (without Subst.) Od.
a being seen all round: conspicuousness, notoriety, πολλὴ π. τῆς χώρης ἐστί it is thoroughly known, Hdt.; διὰ τὴν π. τῶν ἀδικημάτων Dem.
seen all round, of a city, Thuc.
conspicuous, manifest, notable, notorious, Soph., Xen., etc.; comp. and Sup., -φανέστερος, -έστατος, Ar., Xen.:—adv. -νῶς, conspicuously, notably, manifestly, Soph., Ar., etc.; comp. -έστερον, Dem.
π. θανεῖται he will die in the sight of all, Soph.
famous, renowned, Id.
Dep. to spare and save, c. gen., Theocr.
the line round a circular body, a periphery, circumference, Arist.
the outer surface, Plut.
a round body, Id.
moving round, surrounding, c. gen., Eur.
surrounded by, c. dat., Id.
round, circular, Plat.:—of bodies, spherical, globular, Id.:—of style, rounded, Arist.
bounded by a circular line, Strab.

to carry round, Hdt.: to carry about with one, Id., Eur.:—Pass., c. acc. loci, λέοντος περιενειχθέντος τὸ τεῖχος being carried round the wall, Hdt.; absol., περιφερόμενος swinging about (in a basket), Plat.
metaph., οὔτε μέμνημαι τὸ πρᾶγμα οὔτε με περιφέρει οὐδὲν εἰδέναι τούτων nor does [my mind] carry me back to the knowledge of any of these things, Hdt.
to move round, to hand round at table, Xen.
to turn round, τὴν κεφαλήν Plut.
to carry round, publish:—Pass., περιεφέρετο τὸ ῥῆμα the saying was passed from mouth to mouth, Plat.
to carry to and fro, Plut.
to bring round, i. e. into one's own power, Id.
intr. to survive, endure, hold out, Thuc.
of periods of time, Hdt.; of argument, περιφέρεσθαι εἰς ταὐτό Plat.
to wander about, Xen.:— to be unsteady, wavering, Plut.
to flee from, escape from, c. acc., Il.; ψάμμος ἀριθμὸν π. the sand mocks thy numbering, Pind.:—absol. to escape from illness, Dem.
very burning. adv., -γῶς Plut.
to burn all round, Plut.
to scorch or char all round, of lightning, Ar.:—Pass., perf. -πέφλευσμαι, Hdt.
with bark all round, Xen.
Pass. to fear greatly, Xen.
in great fear, exceeding fearful, Thuc., Xen.; τινος of a thing, Plat.
a wandering about, Plut.
revolving, wandering, Anth.
meats carried round, Xen.
a going round, rotatory motion, circuit, revolution, Ar., Plat., etc.
the revolving vault of heaven, Plat.
metaph., ἐν ταῖς περιφοραῖς in society, Plut.
able to be carried about, portable, Hdt.
notorious, infamous, Plut.
an enclosure, Strab.
very thoughtful, very careful, Hhymn., Soph. adv. -δέως, Hom.
Mid. to think or consider about a thing, c. acc., Od.
fenced round: περίφρακτον, ου, an inclosure, Plut.
to fence all round, Plat.
to compass in thought, speculate about, τὸν ἥλιον Ar.
to overlook, to contemn, despise, Thuc.
contempt, Plut.
to guard all round, blockade closely:—Pass., Thuc.
very thoughtful, very careful, notable, of Penelope, Hom.
like ὑπέρφρων, haughty, over-weening, Aesch.
c. gen. despising a thing, Anth.

entry.note: fut. mid. -φύσομαι perf. act. περιπέφῡκα, epic -πέφῠα aor2 act. περιέφῡν inf. περιφῦναι part. -φύς and -φῠείς inf. pass. περιφῠῆναι part. pass. -φῠείς
entry.sense: Pass., to grow round about, Od.
of persons, to grow round, cling to, c. dat. or absol., Id.; so of shoes, περιέφυσαν Περσικαί τινι Ar.
to plant round about, il.
to sound round, re-echo, Plut.
to surround with a stockade, Aeschin.
exceeding joyous or glad, Hdt., Soph., etc.; τινι at a thing, Hdt., Ar.:— τὸ π. excessive joy, Thuc.
to edge round, Xen.
a bracelet, Polyb.

entry.note: fut. -χεῶ aor1 -έχεα epic περι-χεύω aor1 περίχευα
entry.sense: to pour round or over, τί τινι, properly of liquids, Hom.; of metal-workers, χρυσὸν κέρασιν περιχεύας having spread gold leaf round its horns, Il.; so in Mid., ὡς δ’ ὅτε τις χρυσὸν περιχεύεται ἀργύρῳ Od.:—Pass. to be poured around, περὶ δ’ ἀμβρόσιος κέχυθ’ ὕπνος Il.; τῶν ὀστέων περικεχυμένων heaped all round, Hdt.; of persons, περιχυθέντες crowding round, Id.
round about the earth, Anth.
to dance round, Eur., Luc.
to smear or cover over, Luc.
Mid.:— to be exceeding angry about, c. gen., Il.
to go round, Ar.
to come round to, come to in succession, π. εἰς Δαρεῖον ἡ βασιληίη Hdt.
round about a place: οἱ περίχωροι the people about, Dem., etc.:— ἡ π. (sc. γῆ) the country round about, NTest.
to wipe all round, to wipe clean, Ar.
anything wiped off, an offscouring, of a vile person, NTest.
Pass. to be made bald or bare all round, περιψιλωθῆναι τὰς σάρκας to have one's flesh all stript off, Hdt.
very cold, Plut.
excessive pain, Plat.
exceeding painful, Aesch.
suffering great pain, Dem.
to push or shove about, Dem.
to push from its place:—Pass. perf. περιέωσμαι, to be pushed away, ἐκ πάντων περιεώσμεθα Thuc.; π. ἔν τινι to lose one's place in a person's favour, Id.
a place commanding a wide view, Hom.; ἐκ περιωπῆς by a bird's-eye view, Luc.
circumspection, πολλὴν π. τινος ποιεῖσθαι to shew much caution in a thing, Thuc.

prob. ionic for περι-ούσιος, immense, countless, Solon., Anth.:—neut. as adv., περιώσιον, exceeding, beyond measure, Hom.; so pl. περιώσια, Hhymn.:—also c. gen., just like περί, περιώσιον ἄλλων far beyond the rest, Id., Pind.
a river-fish so called from its dusky colour (v. περκνός), the perch, Com.
dark coloured, of grapes or olives beginning to ripen, Anth.; cf. ἐπί-περκνος.
as Subst., name of an eagle, μόρφνον ὃν καὶ περκνὸν καλέουσι Il.
a ham, Lat. perna, Strab.

to export for sale, to sell as slaves (cf. περάω2), πέρνασχ’ ὅντιν’ ἕλεσκε πέρην ἁλὸς ἐς Σάμον Il.; περνὰς νήσων ἐπὶ τηλεδαπάων Id.: generally, τοῖς ξένοις τὰ χρήματα περνάς Eur.:—Pass., κτήματα περνάμενα goods sold or for sale, Il.; πάντα πέρναται Ar.
to pierce, pin, Il.:—Mid., χλαῖναν περονήσασθαι to buckle on one's mantle, Id.
a garment pinned or buckled on, Theocr.

anything pointed for piercing or pinning, the tongue of a buckle or brooch, the buckle or brooch itself, Lat. fibula, Hom.: also a large pin used for fastening on the outer garment or cloak (ἱμάτιον), Hdt., Soph.
the small bone of the leg, Lat. fibula, Xen.
fem. adj. fastened with a brooch, Anth.
a robe fastened on the shoulder with a brooch, Theocr.
Dep. to boast or vaunt oneself, NTest.

enclit. Particle, adding force to the word to which it is added: when this is a Noun, the part. ὤν or ἐών is added, μινυνθάδιόν περ ἐόντα all shortlived as I am, Il.; ἀγαθός περ ἐών however brave he be, Lat. quamvis fortis, Id.; ἀλόχῳ περ ἐούσῃ though she be my wife, Id.; the part. ὤν is often omitted, φράδμων περ ἀνήρ however shrewd, Id.; κρατερός περ, θεοί περ Hom.; also subjoined to other participles, ἱεμένων περ however eager, Il.; ἀχνύμενός περ grieved though he be, etc.

sometimes it simply adds force, ἐλεεινότερός περ more pitiable by far, Id.; μίνυνθά περ for a very little, ὀλίγον περ Id.:—also to strengthen a negation, οὐδέ περ no, not even, not at all, οὐδ’ ὑμῖν ποταμός περ ἐΰρροος ἀρκέσει Id.

to call attention to one or more things of a number, however, at any rate, τιμήν πέρ μοι ὄφελλεν ἐγγυαλίξαι honour however (whatever else) he owed me, Id.; τόδε πέρ μοι ἐπικρήηνον ἐέλδωρ this vow at all events, Id.
added to various Conjunctions and Relative words, with which it may form one word:
after hypothetical Conjs., v. εἴπερ.
after temporal Conjs., ὅτε περ just when, Il.; ὅταν περ Soph.
after Causal Conjs., v. ἐπείπερ, ἐπειδήπερ.
after Relatives, v. ὅσπερ, οἷός περ, ὥσπερ.
after καί, v. καίπερ.
vainglorious, braggart, Polyb.
destroyer of cities, Aesch., etc.
Persepolis, the ancient capital of Persia, Strab.
Perseus, son of Zeus and Danae, Il., Hes., etc.:—adj. Περσεῖος, α, ον, Eur.; epic Περσήιος, Theocr.:—Patron. Περσείδης, ου, epic -ηιάδης, Il.

Persephone, Proserpine, daughter of Zeus and Demeter, Il.: Hades carried her off, and as his consort she continued to reign in the lower world, see Hhymn. Cer.:— her temple is called Φερρεφάττιον, ου, τό, Dem.
sprung from Perseus, name of Alcmena, Eur.; called Περσήϊον αἷμα in Theocr.
a Persian, inhabitant of Persis, Hdt., etc.
to imitate the Persians, speak Persian, Xen.
Persian, ἡ Περσική (sc. χώρα) Persia, Hdt., etc.
Περσικαί, ῶν, αἱ, a sort of thin shoes or slippers, Ar.
Περσικός, οῦ, or Περσικόν, οῦ, the peach, Lat. malum Persicum.
Π. ὄρνις the common cock, Id.
τὰ Περσικά the Persian war, Plat., etc.; in earlier writers called τὰ Μηδικά.
a sacking, sack, π. Ἰλίου, a poem by Arctinus, Arist.
Persian, Aesch., etc.
as Subst., (.] (sub. γῆ), Persis, Persia, now Farsistan, Hdt.
(sub. γυνή), a Persian woman, Xen.
(sub. χλαῖνα), a Persian cloak, Ar.
in the Persian tongue, Hdt., Xen., etc.
chaser of the Persians, Anth.
Pass. to be governed by the Persian laws or by Persians, Aesch.
ruling Persians, Aesch.
of last year, last year's, Ar., etc.
a year ago, last year, Ar., etc.; ἡ π. κωμῳδία our last year's comedy, Id.; νῦν τε καὶ π. Xen.
name of the five officers who escorted the Hyperborean maidens to Delos, Hdt.
a fall, Soph., Eur.; τὸ οὐρανοῦ πές., i.e. the Palladium, Eur.; πεσήματα νεκρῶν dead corpses, (cf. πτῶμα) Id.
a game at draughts, Plat.
a draught-player, Plat.
fit for draught-playing (πεσσοί), skilled therein, Plat.: —πεττευτική (sc. τέχνη) = πεσσεία, Id.
to play at draughts (v. sub πεσσός), Plat., Xen.
an oval-shaped stone for playing a game like our draughts, mostly in pl., Od., Hdt., etc.
οἱ πεσσοί, the place in which the game was played, or the game itself, Eur.
to soften, ripen or change, by means of heat:
of the sun, to ripen fruit, Od.; cf. πεπαίνω.
by the action of fire, to cook, dress, bake, Hdt., Ar.:—Pass., Hdt.:—Mid., πέσσεσθαι πέμματα to cook oneself cakes, Id.
of the stomach, to digest, like Lat. concoquere, Arist.

metaph., χόλον πέσσειν to cherish or nurse one's wrath, Lat. fovere, Il.; βέλος πέσσειν to have a dart in one to nurse, Id.; but in good sense, γέρα πεσσέμεν to enjoy them, Id.; also, ἀκίνδυνον αἰῶνα πέσσειν to lead a sodden life of ease, Pind.
petalism, a mode of banishing too powerful citizens practised in Syracuse, like the ὀστρακισμός of Athens, except that the name was written upon olive-leaves.
a leaf, mostly in pl., Hom.:— poet., νεικέων πέταλα contentious votes (cf. πεταλισμός), Pind.
a leaf of metal, Luc.
broad, flat, Anth.

to spread out sails or clothes, Od.; χεῖρε πετάσσας, of one swimming, Id.: metaph., θυμὸν πετάσαι to open one's heart, Id.:—Pass., mostly in perf., to be spread on all sides, Hom.: part. spread wide, opened wide, of folding doors, πύλαι πεπταμέναι Il.; πετάσθησαν Od.
anything spread out: in pl. carpets, Aesch.
a broad-brimmed felt hat, chiefly used in Thessaly.
a perch for fowls to roost at night, Theocr.
able to fly, full fledged, of young birds, Od.:—of birds generally, able to fly, winged, Il.:—absol., πετεηνά winged fowl, Id.; so, τὰ πετεινά birds, Hdt.
to fly, of birds, bees, gnats, etc., Hom., etc.:—then, of arrows, stones, javelins, etc., Il.: also of any quick motion, to fly along, dart, rush, of men, Id., etc.

metaph. to be on the wing, flutter, Lat. volitare, of uncertain hopes, Pind., Soph.; of fickle natures, Eur.; ὄρνις πετόμενος a bird ever on the wing, Ar.; πετόμενόν τινα διώκεις "you are chasing a butterfly" Plat.
of a rock, Hes.: living on or among the rocks, Od.; Νύμφαι π. rock- Nymphs, Eur.
of rock, rocky, τάφος π. Soph.; π. δειράς, λέπας, χθών, ἄντρα, etc., Trag.
Πετραῖος, epith. of Poseidon in Thessaly, who clave the rocks of Tempe, Pind.

entry.note: πέτρα, ionic and epic πέτρη, ἡ,
entry.sense: a rock, a ledge or shelf of rock, Od.

a rock, i. e. a rocky peak or ridge, Hom.; π. σύνδρομοι, ξυμπληγάδες, of the rocky islets of the Bosporus, Pind., Eur.; π. δίλοφος, of Parnassus, Soph.—Properly, πέτρα is a fixed rock, πέτρος a stone: in Od. 9, πέτραι are masses of live rock torn up by giants.
πέτρη γλαφυρή a hollow rock, i. e. a cave, Il.; δίστομος π. a cave in the rock with a double entrance, Soph.
proverbial usages:—on οὐκ ἀπὸ δρυὸς οὐδ’ ἀπὸ πέτρης, v. δρῦς·— as a symbol of firmness, ὁ δ’ ἐστάθη ἠύτε πέτρη Od.; of hardheartedness, ἐκ πέτρας εἰργασμένος Aesch.
like rock, Luc.
rocky, Hom., Hes.
o'er-arched with rock, rockvaulted, Aesch., Eur.
of rock, rocky, Soph.
of rock, rocky, Hdt., Soph., Eur.
a stoning, Xen.
throwing stones, Xen.
as Subst., πετροβόλος, an engine for throwing stones, Lat. ballista, Polyb., etc.
with bed of rock, Anth.
a roller of rocks, Strab.
hurled from a rock, Eur.
a stone, distinguished from πέτρα (v. sub voce); in Hom., used by warriors, λάζετο πέτρον μάρμαρον ὀκριόεντα Il.; βαλὼν μυλοειδέϊ πέτρῳ Id.: —proverb., πάντα κινῆσαι πέτρον Eur.
cutting stones, Anth.
to turn into stone, petrify, Anth.
Pass. to be stoned, Eur.
like rock or stone, rocky, stony, like πετραῖος, π. κατῶρυξ, of a grave, Soph., Plat.
an inquirer, spy, Luc.

entry.etym: poet. for πυνθάνομαι, Hom., Hes., Trag.

entry.sense: tidings, news, Aesch.
ἐνὶ φρεσὶ πευκαλίμῃσι (the only phrase used by Hom.) would mean in wise, prudent, sagacious mind: cf. λευγαλέος and λυγρός.
epith. of war, = πευκήεις II, Il.
of pine or pine-wood, Eur.; πευκάενθ’ Ἥφαιστον the fire of pine-torches, Soph.
metaph. sharp, piercing, Aesch.
the pine, Il., Eur., etc.
any thing made from its wood, a torch of pine-wood, Trag.
a writing-tablet, Eur.
of or from pine or pine-wood, Soph.; π. δάκρυα tears of the pine, i. e. the resinous drops that ooze from it, Eur.
of or for inquiry, πευστηρία (sc. θυσία) a sacrifice for learning the will of the gods, Eur.

entry.etym: adverb from perf. pass. part. of φοβέω
entry.sense: timorously, Xen.

entry.etym: adverb from perf. pass. part. of φροντίζω
entry.sense: carefully, Strab.
naturally, Arist.

entry.etym: adverb from perf. pass. part. of φυλάσσω
entry.sense: cautiously, Xen., Dem.
safely, Xen.
to spring or gush forth, Anth.
c. acc. cogn. to gush forth with water, Id.
of or from a well, π. ῥέος spring-water, Aesch.; π. ἄχθος a weight of water, Eur.; π. κόραι water Nymphs, Id.
rue, Lat. ruta:—proverb., οὐδ’ ἐν σελίνῳ οὐδ’ ἐν πηγάνῳ, i. e. scarcely at the edge or beginning, because these herbs formed the borders of beds, Ar.
Πηγασὶς κρήνη, Hippocrene, Mosch.

Pegasus, a horse sprung from the blood of Medusa, and named from the springs (πηγαί) of Ocean, near which she was killed, ridden by Bellerophon when he slew Chimaera, Hes.: later poets describe him as winged, Ar.: later still, he was the favourite of the Muses, under whose hoof the fountain Hippocrene (ἵππου κρήν) sprang up on Helicon, Strab., etc.
anything congealed, hoarfrost, rime, Hes.
thick-fleeced, ἀρνειός Il.
mostly in pl. of running waters, streams, Hom., etc.; distinct from κρουνός (the spring or well-head), κρουνὼ δ’ ἵκανον καλλιρρόω, ἔνθα δὲ πηγαὶ δοιαὶ ἀναΐσσουσι Il.:—in sg., Aesch.
metaph. streams, of tears, πηγαὶ κλαυμάτων, δακρύων Id., Soph.; so, πηγαὶ γάλακτος Soph.; πόντου πηγαῖς with sea- water, Eur.; παγαὶ πυρός Pind.

= κρήνη, a fount, source, πηγαὶ ἡλίου the fount of light, i. e. the East, Aesch.:—in sg., πηγὴ ἀργύρου, of the silver-mines at Laureion, Id.; τῆς ἀκουούσης πηγῆς δι’ ὤτων, i. e. the sense of hearing, Soph.
metaph. the fount, source, origin, πηγὴ κακῶν Aesch.; ἡδονῶν, νοσημάτων Plat.
anything joined together, framework, of a ship, Anth.:—Lat. pegma, a moveable scaffold used in theatres, Juven.
metaph., π. γενναίως παγέν a bond in honour bound, Aesch.
π. τῆς χιόνος frozen snow, Polyb.

entry.etym: πέπηγα is generally used as perf. pass.
entry.sense: Radical sense, to make fast; intr. and Pass. to be solid :

to stick or fix in, ἐν δὲ μετώπωι πῆξε [τὴν αἰχμήν] Il.; π. ἐπὶ τύμβωι ἐρετμόν Od.:— to fix in the earth, plant, Soph.; σκηνὴν π. to pitch a tent, Plat.; (so Mid., σκηνὰς πήξασθαι to pitch their tents, Hdt.):—intr. perf. and Pass., δόρυ δ’ ἐν κραδίηι ἐπεπήγει the spear stuck fast in his heart, Il.; ὀϊστοὶ πῆχθεν ἐν χροΐ Id.; [ξίφος] πέπηγεν ἐν γῆι Soph.
to stick or fix on, κεφαλὴν ἀνὰ σκολόπεσσι π. to stick the head on stakes, Il., etc.: —Pass., πηχθέντας μέλη ὀβελοῖσι having their limbs fixed on spits, Eur.; παγέντες impaled, Aesch.
to fix the eyes upon an object, κατὰ χθονὸς ὄμματα π. Il.; ὄμματα πέπηγε πρός τι Plat.
to fasten together, construct, build, νῆας πῆξαι Il.; so Mid., ἄμαξαν πήξασθαι to build oneself a wagon, Hes.

to make solid, stiff, hard, of liquids, to freeze, θεὸς πήγνυσι πᾶν ῥέεθρον Aesch.; ἔπηξε (sc. ὁ θεὸς) τοὺς ποταμούς Ar.:—intr. perf. and Pass. to become solid, stiff or hard, γοῦνα πήγνυται the limbs stiffen, Il.; of liquids, to become congealed, freeze, Hdt.; ἅλες πήγνυνται the salt crystallises, Id.; κρύσταλλος ἐπεπήγει οὐ βέβαιος was not frozen strong, Thuc.

metaph. to fix, Lat. pangere foedus, intr. perf. and Pass. to be irrevocably fixed, established, εἷς ὅρος ἡμῖν παγήσεται Id.; μὴ γὰρ ὡς θεῶι νομίζετ’ ἐκείνωι τὰ παρόντα πεπηγέναι πράγματα ἀθάνατα Dem.
well put together, compact, strong, Il.; κύματι πηγῶι on the strong, big wave, Od.
frozen, icy-cold, Od.; as Subst., = παγετός, πάχνη, Anth.
a rudder or an oar used for steering, Od.; after Homer, a Greek ship commonly had two πηδάλια joined by cross-bars (ζεῦγλαι) and worked by a handle or tiller (οἴαξ).
metaph., ἱππικὰ π. of reins, Aesch.; πηδαλίῳ δικαίῳ νωμᾶν στρατόν Pind.; τὰ π. τῆς διανοίας Plat.
to leap, spring, bound, ὑψόσε ποσσὶν ἐπήδα Il.; π. ἐς σκάφος Soph.; c. acc. cogn., πήδημα πηδᾶν to take a leap, Eur.; c. acc. loci, πεδία πηδᾶν to bound over them, Soph.; π. πλάκα Eur.
metaph. of an arrow, Il.; of the heart, to leap, throb, Ar., etc.; of sudden changes, τί πηδᾶις εἰς ἄλλους τρόπους; Eur.
a leap, bound, Trag.
a beating or throbbing of the heart, τὸ μέλλον καρδία πήδημ’ ἔχει, i. e. beats with fearful presage, Eur.
a leaping, Plut.
springing, Arist., Luc.
the blade of an oar, and generally an oar, ἀναρρίπτειν ἅλα πηδῷ Od.
a net or cage set to catch birds, Ar.
cream-cheese, Theocr.

entry.note: πηκτίς, aeolic and doric πακτίς, ίδος, ἡ,
entry.sense: an ancient harp used by the Lydians, Hdt., etc.
a sort of shepherd's pipe, joined of several reeds, like Pan's pipes (σῦριγξ), Anth.
stuck in, fixed, Soph.
well put together, constructed, built, of wood-work, Hom., Hes.; τὰ πακτὰ τῶν δωμάτων the barriers of the house, Eur. ap. Ar.
congealed, curdled, γάλα Eur.
to Peleus' son, Il.

Peleus, son of Aecus, husband of Thetis, father of Achilles, prince of the Myrmidons in Thessaly, Hom.:—adj. Πήλειος, α, ον, epic Πηλήιος, η, ον, of Peleus, Il.—Patron. Πηλείδης, ου, epic εω and αο, son of Peleus, Id.; epic also Πηληιάδης, Id.; aeolic Πηλεΐδας, Pind.:—also Πηλείων, ωνος, ὁ, Il.
a helmet, casque, Il., Ar.
Pelian, of or from Mount Pelion, Anth.:—fem. Πηλιάς, άδος, Il.
how great or large? Lat. quantus? Plat.
of what age, of a certain age, Arist.
of clay, Lat. fictilis, οἱ πήλινοι clay figures, Dem.
Pelion, a mountain in Thessaly, Hom., Hes., Pind., etc.
on or at the foot of Pelion, Eur.
to build of clay, Anth.
clay-built, τοῖχοι Anth.
Pass. to wallow in mire, Luc.
a potter, Luc.
clay, earth, such as was used by the potter and modeller, Lat. lutum, Hdt., attic
sometimes for βόρβορος or ἰλύς, mud, mire, as lutum for coenum, Hdt., Ar., etc.; proverb., ἔξω κομίζειν πηλοῦ πόδα, i. e. to keep out of difficulties, Aesch.; κάσις πηλοῦ ξύνουρος, cf. σύνορος.
a worker in clay, Luc.
a town on the coast of Egypt bordering on Arabia, Hdt.:—adj., τὸ Πηλούσιον στόμα the Eastern mouth of the Nile, Id.
to carry clay, Ar.
moulded of clay, θάλαμοι π., of swallows' nests, Anth.
like clay, clayey, muddy, of places, Thuc.; of persons, Plat.

entry.etym: Mid. fut. πημᾰνοῦμαι also in pass. sense
entry.sense: to bring into misery, plunge into ruin, undo, and, in milder sense, to grieve, distress, Hom., Trag.; π. τὴν γῆν to damage it, Hdt.:—absol. to do mischief, Il.:—Pass. to suffer hurt or harm, Od., Aesch., etc.; ἴσθι πημανούμενος wilt suffer woe, Soph.
to be injured, Theogn.
suffering, misery, calamity, woe, bane, Hom., etc.; πήματα ἐπὶ πήμασι woe upon woe, Soph.; πῆμ’ ἐπὶ πήματι κεῖται, the sword forged upon the anvil, Orac. ap. Hdt.
of persons, a bane, calamity, Il., Soph.
Penelope, wife of Ulysses, Od.; Πηνελόπη, Hdt., Ar.; doric Πᾱνελόπᾱ, Anth.
entry.etym: Her name is connected with the mythic tale of the web (πήνη, πηνίον), Spinster, v. Od.

entry.note: πηνέλοψ, aeolic and doric πᾱν-, οπος, ὁ,
entry.sense: a kind of duck with purple stripes, Ar.
the thread on the spool or shuttle, the woof, and in pl. the web, Eur.
the bobbin or spool, like πηνίον, Anth.
Dep., to wind thread off a reel, Theocr.

interrog. adv., correl. to τηνίκα, ἡνίκα, properly at what point of time? at what hour? Lat. quota hora? Luc.; πηνίκα μάλιστα; about what o'clock it is? Plat.; so, πηνίκ’ ἄττα; Ar.; in full, πηνίκ’ ἐστὶ τῆς ἡμέρας; Id.
generally, for πότε; Dem.:—so, in an indirect question, Id.
the bobbin or spool on which the woof is wound, Il., Anth.
the woof on the spool, Anth.
a fixing, constructing, of woodwork, Plat.
(from Pass.) congelation, Id.
a kinsman by marriage, Lat. affinis, Hom., Hes.
interrog. Particle:
of Manner, in what way? how? Od., etc.; πῆ δή; how tell me? Id.; πῆ μάλιστα; how exactly? Plat.:—also in indirect questions, ἐκαραδόκεον τὸν πόλεμον κῆ ἀποβήσεται Hdt., etc.
to what end? wherefore? Lat. quorsum? Hom.
of Space, which way? Lat. qua? πῆ ἔβη Ἀνδρομάχη; Il., etc.; πᾶ τις τράποιτ’ ἄν; Aesch.
more rarely like ποῦ; where? Il.; πᾶ πᾶ κεῖται; Soph.:—also in indirect questions, c. gen., ἐπειρώτα, κῆ γῆς . . , Hdt.
of Manner, in some way, somehow, οὔ πη not in any way, not at all, Hom.; οὐδέ τί πη Il.; οὕτω πη in some such way, somehow so, Id.; τῇδέ πη Plat.; ἄλλῃ γέ πη Id.; εἴ πη if any way, Id.
of Space, by some way, to some place, to any place, Hom.: —c. gen., ἦ πή με πολίων ἄξεις; wilt thou carry me to some city? Il.
in some place, somewhere, anywhere, Od., attic
πῆ μέν . . , πῆ δέ . . , on one side . . , on the other . . , Plut.; partly . . , partly . . , Xen.
a leathern pouch, a wallet, scrip, Lat. pera, Od., Ar.
binding a wallet, Anth.
disabled in a limb, maimed, Lat. mancus, Il., Anth.
to lame, maim, mutilate, Ar.: —Pass., πεπηρωμένος maimed, Dem.: metaph., πεπηρωμένος πρὸς ἀρετήν incapacitated for reaching virtue, Arist.
a being maimed, mutilation, imperfection, Plat., etc.: blindness, Luc.
a cubit long, Hdt., Plat.
Mid. to take into one's arms, Anth.
the fore-arm, from the wrist to the elbow, Lat. ulna, Xen., etc.:— generally, the arm, ἀμφὶ υἱὸν ἐχεύατο πήχεε λευκώ Il., etc.
the centrepiece, which joined the two horns of the bow, Hom.
in pl., the horns or sides of the lyre, opp. to ζυγόν the bridge, Hdt.

as a measure of length, the distance from the point of the elbow to the end of the little finger, Lat. cubitus or ulna, a cubit or ell, containing 24 δάκτυλοι or 18 1/4 inches, Hdt.: the π. βασιλήιος was longer by three δάκτυλοι, = 27 δάκτυλοι or 20 1/2 inches, Id.
a cubit-rule, as we say "a foot-rule, " Ar.
to make fat, fatten, Eur.; π. χθόνα to fatten the soil, of a dead man, Aesch.:—Pass. to be or become fat, Plat., etc.
metaph.,
to increase, enlarge, πλοῦτον Pind.
to make wanton, excite, Aesch.: —Pass. to wax fat and wanton, Id.; ἔχθεσιν πιαίνεσθαι to batten on quarrels, Pind.
fat, Il.:— any fatty substance, cream, Anth.:—metaph., πῖαρ ὕπ’ οὖδας fatness is beneath the ground, Od.
metaph., also, like Lat. uber, the cream of a thing, the choicest, best, Hhymn.; π. χθονός, like οὖθαρ ἀρούρης, Anth.
that which makes fat, of a river, π. χθονί bringing fatness to the soil, Aesch.

entry.etym: doric and late attic for πίεσμα.

entry.sense: gushing, Eur.
full of springs, Plut.
a spring, fountain, Il., Hdt., Eur.
to gush forth, Anth., Plut.
to press, squeeze, press tight, Hom., attic
to press or weigh down, of a heavy weight, Pind., Ar.: metaph. to oppress, straiten, distress, Hdt., Aesch., etc.—Pass. to suffer greatly, Hdt., attic
to press hard, of a victorious army, Lat. premo, τοὺς ἐναντίους Hdt.:— Pass., εἴ πη πιέζοιντο Thuc.
to repress, stifle, Pind.
later to lay hold of, ταῦρον πιάξας τᾶς ὁπλᾶς by the hoof, Theocr.; αὐτὸν τῆς χειρός NTest.
fat, rich, of land, Hom., Pind., etc.; δαὶς πίειρα a rich, plenteous meal, Il.; of wood, resinous, unctuous, Soph.
Pieria, a district in the North of Thessaly, Hom.:
the Pierides, name of the Muses, as haunting Pieria, Hes., Pind.
from Pieria, Hes.
of Pieria, Hdt.
pressure, Anth.
a wine-cask or jar, Ar.; used for storing figs in, Dem.: hence, οἰκεῖν ἐν ταῖς πιθάκναις to live in casks, as Athenian immigrants were forced to do during the Peloponn. war, Ar.
to use probable arguments, Arist.
the use of probable arguments, as opp. to demonstration (ἀπόδειξις) Plat.
calculated to persuade; and so,
of persons, having the power of persuasion, persuasive, plausible, of popular speakers, Thuc., etc.:—c. inf., πιθανώτατος λέγειν Plat.
of arguments, Ar., Plat., etc.
of manners, persuasive, winning, Xen.
of reports, plausible, specious, probable, Hdt., Plat.
of works of art, producing illusion, true to nature, Xen.
pass. easy to persuade, credulous, Aesch.
obedient, docile, Xen.
adv. -νῶς, persuasively, comp. -ώτερον, Ρλατ.
persuasiveness, Plat., Arist.
to make probable, Arist.
a playing the ape, playing monkey's tricks, Ar.
an ape, monkey, Ar.; as fem., πίθηκος μήτηρ Babr.:—of persons, an ape, jackanapes, Ar., Dem.
to eat ape's flesh, Hdt.
carrying apes, Luc.
a wine-jar of the largest kind (cf. ἀμφορεύς), Hom., etc.; of earthenware, π. κεράμινος Hdt.; covered with a lid, Hes.
proverbs, εἰς τὸν τετρημένον πίθον ἀντλεῖν, of the task of the Danaids, i. e. labour in vain, Xen.; also ἐκ πίθω ἀντλεῖς, i. e. you have plenty of wine, "you are in clover, " Theocr.
a little ape, Babr.; of a flatterer, Pind.
a cellar, Anth.
to make sharp or bitter to the taste, NTest.
metaph. in Pass. to be exasperated, foster bitter feelings, Plat., Theocr.
bitterness, of temper, Dem., Plut.
to be or taste bitter, Strab.
miserably married, Od.
of sharp or bitter tongue, Aesch.
bearing bitter fruit, Aesch.
properly pointed, sharp, keen, ὀϊστός Il.; γλωχίς Soph.;metaph., γλώσσης πικροῖς κέντροισι Eur.
generally, sharp to the senses:
of taste, sharp, pungent, bitter, Hom., Hdt.:—so of smell, Od.
of feeling, sharp, keen, ὠδῖνες Il., Soph.
of sound, sharp, piercing, shrill, οἰμωγή, φθόγγος Soph.; γόοι Eur.
metaph.,
of things, bitter, cruel, Od., attic
of persons, bitter, malignant, Solon., Hdt., attic; πικρὸς θεοῖς hateful to the gods, Soph.; πικρὸς πολίταις Eur.
embittered, sorrowing, Soph.
comp. -ότερος, Sup. -ότατος Pind., etc.
adv. πικρῶς, bitterly, cruelly, Aesch., Soph.; π. ἔχειν τινί, πρός τινα Dem.; π. φέρειν τι Eur.
pungency, bitterness, of taste, Plat.
metaph. bitterness, cruelty, Hdt., Eur.
full of bitter bile, splenetic, Anth.
to compress wool, πιληθεὶς πέτασος a felt hat, Anth.
Pass. to be close pressed, kneaded, Id.
pileolus, Ar., Dem.
wanting the letter π, Anth.
to bring near, Hes.

Mid., to draw near to, approach, c. dat., ἅρματα χθονὶ πίλνατο the chariots went close to the ground, Il.; ἐπ’ οὔδεϊ πίλναται Id.; γαῖα καὶ οὐρανὸς πίλνατο earth and sky threatened to encounter (in the storm), Hes.
wool or hair made into felt, used as a lining for helmets, Il.; for shoes, Hes.
anything made of felt, a felt skullcap, like the modern fez, Hes.; πίλους τιήρας φορέοντες wearing turbans for caps, Hdt.; ἀντὶ τῶν πίλων μιτρηφόροι ἔσαν Id.
a felt-cloth, Xen.
a felt-cuirass, Thuc.
accustomed to wear a πῖλος, Luc.
wearing a cap, Anth.
made of felt, Strab.
soft fat, lard, Lat. adeps, Hdt., Soph.
fat, Luc., Babr.; comp. -έστερος, Luc.

entry.etym: epic for πίμπλαμαι, pass. of πίμπλημι, Il.

entry.sense: a place in Pieria, sacred to the Muses, Strab.:—adj., Πιμπληίδες, Μοῦσαι Anth.

entry.etym: ionic part. pres. fem. πιμπλεῦσαι, Hes.
in pres. and impf. formed like ἵστημι
entry.sense: to fill full of a thing, c. gen., Hom., etc.: c. dat. to fill with a thing, Eur.:—absol. to fill up, to fill, Il., attic
to fill, discharge an office, Aesch.

Mid. to fill for oneself, or what is one's own, πλήσασθαι δέπας οἴνοιο to fill oneself a cup of wine, Il.; πλ. νῆας to get ships laden, Od.; θυμὸν πλήσασθαι ἐδητύος ἠδὲ ποτῆτος to satiate one's desire with meat and drink, Id.; πεδία πίμπλασθ’ ἁρμάτων fill the plain full of your chariots, Eur.
Pass. to be filled, become or be full of, c. gen., Hom., etc.
to have enough of a thing, πλησθῆναι αἱμάτων Soph.; ἡδονῶν Plat.; —rarely c. dat., δάκρυσι πλησθείς Thuc.
to burn, burn up, πυρός with fire, Il.; πυρί Soph.; absol., Hes., Aesch.
like planks, Ar.

a small tablet, on which the δικασταί wrote their verdict, π. τιμητικόν, Lat. tabella damnatoria, Ar.;—on which a law was written, Id.; —on which the information in case of εἰσαγγελία was written, Dem.;—on which the rules for the δικασταί were written, Id.:— tablets, a memorandum book, Plat.
a tablet for painting upon, Luc.
in pl., tablets, Plut.
a picture-gallery, Strab.
one who sells small birds plucked and ranged upon a board, Ar.
a board, plank, of a ship, Od.
a tablet for writing on, Il., Plat., etc.
a trencher, platter, Od.
a panel, picture, Lat. tabula, Simon.: generally, an engraved plate, of a map, Hdt.
a register, list, Lat. album, Dem., etc.
dirty, squalid, Eur.
of Pindar, Ar.
from Mount Pindus, Pind.
the pinna, a bivalve, with a silky beard, Com.
the pinna-guard, a small crab that lives in the pinna's shell, like the hermit-crab: metaph. of a little parasitical fellow, Ar.
Pass. to be rusted, of statues, Plut.
dirt, filth, Lat. squalor, Soph., Eur.; metaph., σὺν πίνῳ χερῶν, i.e. by foul means, Aesch.
to make prudent, admonish, correct, Il., Aesch.
understanding, wisdom, Hom.
wise, prudent, discreet, understanding, Od., Solon.
of wise or understanding mind, Anth.
dirty, foul, Eur.

to drink, Hom., etc.; π. ὕδωρ Αἰσήποιο to drink its water, i. e. live on its banks, Il.;—or c. gen. partit. to drink of a thing, π. οἴνοιο (as Fr. du vin), Od.; αἵματος ὄφρα πίω Id.:—also, πίνειν κρητῆρας οἴνοιο to drink bowls of wine, Il.; π. ἀπὸ κρήνης to drink of a spring, Theogn.; δέπα, ἔνθεν ἔπινον Od.; π. ἐκ ταὐτοῦ ποτηρίου Ar.; ἐξ ἀργύρου ἢ χρυσοῦ Plat.; ἀπὸ τοῦ ποταμοῦ Xen.: —also, σκύφον ὧιπερ ἔπινον with which . . , Od.:— absol., Hom., etc.; πῖνε, πῖν’ ἐπὶ συμφοραῖς Ar.; διδόναι πιεῖν to give to drink, Hdt.; πιεῖν αἰτεῖν Xen.:— in perf. πέπωκα, to be drunk, Eur.; but, πίνοντά τε καὶ πεπωκότα drinking and having finished drinking, Plat.
metaph. to drink up, as the earth does rain, Hdt.; πιοῦσα κόνις μέλαν αἷμα Aesch., etc.
unctuous, Hdt.

Π, π, πῖ, indecl.: sixteenth letter of Gr. alphabet. As numeral πʹ = 80, but ͵π = 80,000. π is the tenuis labial mute, related to the medial β and the aspirate φ. Changes of π in the Gr. dialects, etc.
π becomes φ, βλέπ-ω βλέφ-αρον, λάπ-τω λαφ-ύσσω.

in aeolic and ionic, it stands for the asp. φ, ἀμπί for ἀμφί, πανός for φανός, ἀπικέσθαι for ἀφικ-: in ionic it was retained in apostrophe before an aspirate, ἀπ’ ἡμῶν, ἐπ’ ἡμέρην, ὑπ’ ὑμῶν, etc.: on the contrary the aspirated form was preferred in attic, ἀσφάραγος for ἀσπάραγος, σφόνδυλος for σπόνδυλος.
in ionic Prose, π becomes κ in relatives and interrogatives, κῶς ὅκως ὁκοῖος ὁκόσος for πῶς ὅπως ὁποῖος ὁπόσος.
in aeolic, π is used for μ, ὄππα for ὄμμα, πεδά for μετά.
in aeolic and doric, π for τ, πέτορες for τέσσαρες, πέμπε for πέντε.
sometimes interchanged with γ, as in λαπαρός λαγαρός, λαπάρα λαγών, λάγος lepus.
in aeolic and epic Poetry, π is often doubled in relatives, as ὅππη ὅππως ὁπποῖος for ὅπη, etc.
in Poets, τ is inserted after π, as in πτόλις, πτόλεμος for πόλις, πόλεμος.
to give to drink, πίσω σφε Δίρκας ὕδωρ I will make them drink the water of Dirce, Pind.

entry.etym: πιπράσκω shortd. from πιπεράσκω, redupl. form of περάω2
entry.sense: to sell, Dem.:— Pass. to be sold, esp. for exportation, Hdt., attic
to sell for a bribe, of political leaders, Dem.:—metaph. in Pass., πέπραμαι I am bought and sold! i. e. betrayed, ruined, undone, Soph.

to fall, fall down, Hom., etc.; πίπτειν ἐν κονίηισιν to fall in the dust, i. e. to fall and lie there, Il.; π. ἐν δεμνίοις Eur., etc.; or without ἐν, πεδίωι πίπτειν Il.; π. δεμνίοις Eur.; also, π. ἐπὶ χθονί Od.; ἐπὶ γᾶι Soph.; πρὸς πέδωι Eur.; with a Prep. of motion, π. ἐς πόντον Hes.; ἐπὶ γᾶν Aesch.; πρὸς οὖδας Eur.
Special usages:
πίπτειν ἔν τισι to fall violently upon, attack, ἐνὶ νήεσσι πέσωμεν Il.; πρὸς μῆλα καὶ ποίμνας Soph.
to throw oneself down, fall down, πρὸς βρέτη θεῶν Aesch.; ἀμφὶ γόνυ τινός Eur.
to fall in battle, πίπτε δὲ λαός Il., etc.; οἱ πεπτωκότες the fallen, Xen.; π. δορί by the spear, Eur.; —π. ὑπό τινος to fall by another's hand, Hdt.
to fall, be ruined, o( *je/rcew strato\s au)to\s u(p' e(wutou= e)/peseὁ Ξέρξεω στρατὸς αὐτὸς ὑπ’ ἑωυτοῦ ἔπεσε, Lat. mole sua corruit, Id.
to fall, sink, ἄνεμος πέσε the wind fell (so Virg. cadunt austri), Od.
to fall short, fail, Plat.; of a play, to fail, Ar.

ἐκ θυμοῦ πίπτειν τινί to fall out of his favour, Il.; so, π. ἐξ ἐλπίδων Eur.: —reversely, π. ἐς κακότητα Theogn.; εἰς νόσον Aesch.; φόβον, ἀνάγκας Eur., Thuc., etc.; also, π. ἐν φόβωι Eur.; π. δυσπραξίαις Soph.
π. εἰς ὕπνον to fall asleep, Id.; or simply ὕπνωι Aesch.
πίπτειν μετὰ ποσσὶ γυναικός to fall between her feet, i. e. to be born, Il.
of the dice, τὰ δεσποτῶν εὖ πεσόντα θήσομαι I shall count my master's throws good or lucky, Aesch.; so of lots, ὁ κλῆρος π. τινί or παρά τινα Plat.; ἐπί τινα NTest.
generally, to fall, turn out, εὖ, καλῶς πίπτειν to be lucky, Eur., etc.
to fall under, belong to a class, Arist.
of or from Pisa, Id.

entry.note: Πῖσα, or Πίση, doric Πίσα, ης, ἡ,
entry.sense: Pisa, name of a fountain at Olympia, Hdt., Pind.
a person from Pisa, Pind.
at Pisa, Anth.
made of peas, ἔτνος π. pea-soup, Ar.
meadows, Hom.
the pea, Lat. pisum, Ar.
pitch, Lat. pix, Il., Hdt., etc.: proverb., ἄρτι μῦς πίττης γεύεται, i. e. he has got the first taste of misery, Dem.
like pitch, Luc.
Mid. to remove the hair by means of a pitch-plaster, Luc.
one who pitches, Luc.
disposed to trust, confiding, Arist.: —adv., πιστευτικῶς ἔχειν τινί to rely upon one, Plat.
creating belief, Id.

to trust, trust to or in, put faith in, rely on, believe in a person or thing, c. dat., π. τινί Hdt., attic; with neut. adj., λόγοις ἐμοῖσι πίστευσον τάδε believe my words herein, Eur.:—later, π. εἰς Θεόν to believe on or in God, NTest.; π. ἐπὶ τὸν Κύριον Id.:—absol. to believe, Hdt., Thuc.:—Pass. to be trusted or believed, Plat.; πιστεύεσθαι ὑπό τινος to enjoy his confidence, Xen.; π. παρά τινι, πρός τινα Dem.; ὡς πιστευθησόμενος as if he would be believed, Id.:—Mid. to believe mutually, Id.
to comply, Soph.

c. inf. to believe that, feel sure or confident that a thing is, will be, has been, Eur., etc.; π. ποιεῖν to dare to do a thing, Dem.:—Pass., πιστεύομαι ἀληθεύσειν I am believed likely to speak truth, Xen.
c. dat. et inf., τοῖσι ἐπίστευε σιγᾶν to whom he trusted that they would keep silence, in whose secresy he confided, Hdt.
to believe, have faith, NTest.
π. τί τινι to entrust something to another, Xen., etc.:—Pass., πιστεύομαί τι I am entrusted with a thing, have it committed to me, Id.
liquid, NTest.: others refer it to πίστις, in the sense of genuine, pure.
faithful:—adv., πιστικῶς ἔχειν τινί Plut.
genuine, v. πιστικός1
trust in others, faith, Lat. fides, fiducia, Hes., Theogn., attic; c. gen. pers. faith or belief in one, Eur.:— generally, persuasion of a thing, confidence, assurance, Pind., attic
good faith, trustworthiness, faithfulness, honesty, Lat. fides, Theogn., Hdt., attic
in a commercial sense, credit, trust, πίστις τοσούτων χρημάτων ἐστί μοι παρά τινι I have credit for so much money with him, Dem.; εἰς πίστιν διδόναι τί τινι Id.
in Theol. faith, belief, as opp. to sight and knowledge, NTest.
that which gives confidence: hence,

an assurance, pledge of good faith, warrant, guarantee, Soph., Eur.; πίστιν καὶ ὅρκια ποιεῖσθαι to make a treaty by exchange of assurances and oaths, Hdt.; οὔτε π. οὔθ’ ὅρκος μένει Ar.; πίστιν διδόναι to give assurances, Hdt.; διδόναι καὶ λαμβάνειν to interchange them, Xen.:—of an oath, θεῶν πίστεις ὀμνύναι Thuc.; πίστιν ἐπιτιθέναι or προστιθέναι τινί Dem.: —φόβων π. an assurance against fears, Eur.
a means of persuasion, an argument, proof, such as used by orators, Plat., etc.
liquid medicines, opp. to βρώσιμα, Aesch.
pass. to be trusted or believed:
of persons, faithful, trusty, true, Il., Hes., attic:—in Persia οἱ πιστοί were Privy-councillors, "trusty and well-beloved, " Xen.; πιστὰ πιστῶν = πιστότατοι, Aesch.
trustworthy, worthy of credit, Thuc., etc.
of things, trustworthy, sure, of oaths, etc., Hom., etc.; οὐκέτι πιστὰ γυναιξίν no longer can one trust women, Od.; ἐλπὶς πιστὴ λόγῳ warranted by reason, Thuc.
deserving belief, credible, probable, Hdt., Plat., etc.

πιστόν, οῦ, as Subst., like πίστις II, a pledge, security, warrant, certainty, Soph., etc.; τὸ π. τῆς ἐλευθερίας Thuc.; τὸ π. ἔχοντες κἂν περιγενέσθαι feeling confidence that they should survive, Id.:—in pl., τὰ πιστὰ ποιεῖσθαι = πίστιν ποιεῖσθαι, Hdt.; πιστὰ θεῶν, of oaths, Xen.; πιστόν or πιστὰ δοῦναι καὶ λαβεῖν to give and receive pledges, to interchange pledges, Id., etc.
act. like πίσυνος, believing, trusting in, relying on, τινι Theogn., Aesch., etc.
obedient, Xen.
faithful, believing, NTest.
adv. πιστῶς, with good faith, persuasively Dem.
with disposition to believe, Id.
good faith, honesty, Hdt., Plat.
to make trustworthy, πιστοῦν τινα ὅρκοις to bind him by oaths, Thuc.
Pass. to be made trustworthy, give a pledge or warrant, ὅρκῳ πιστωθῆναί τινι to bind oneself to another by oath, Od.
to feel trust or confidence, i. e. to trust, to be persuaded, πιστωθῆναι ἐνὶ θυμῷ Id.; πιστωθεὶς ὅτι . . , feeling confidence that . . , Soph.
Mid. to give mutual pledges of fidelity, exchange troth, χεῖράς τ’ ἀλλήλων λαβέτην καὶ πιστώσαντο Il.:— πιστοῦσθαί τινα ὑφ’ ὅρκου to secure his good faith by oaths, Soph.
to confirm, prove, make good, guarantee, τι Polyb., Luc.
a drinking-trough for cattle, Eur.
an assurance, warrant, guarantee, pledge, Aesch., etc.
of persons, γηραλᾶ πιστώματα, = πιστοὶ γέροντες, Id.
to be warranted, Luc.
trusting on, relying or depending on, confiding in another, c. dat., Il., Hdt.
a place in Laconia, Hdt.
ὁ Πιτανητέων λόχος, a corps of the Spartan army, Hdt.
to spread out, ἠέρα πίτνα (epic for ἐπίτνα) Il.; πιτνὰς εἰς ἐμὲ χεῖρας stretching out his arms to me, Od.; πίτναν τ’ εἰς αἰθέρα χεῖρας (for ἐπίτναν) Pind.:—Pass., ἀμφὶ δὲ χαῖται πίτναντο Il.
to ply the plashing oar, Ar.
the measured plash of oars, Eur.; ἑνὶ πιτύλῳ with one stroke, all together, Aesch.
any quick repeated sound,
the plash of falling drops, π. δακρύων Eur.; π. σκύφου, of wine poured into a cup, Id.
the sound of repeated blows, Aesch., Eur.:—metaph., πίτυλος Ἀργείου δορός Eur.; δὶς δυοῖν πιτύλοιν twice with two strokes, Id.; also of violent frantic gestures, violence, passion, Id.
pine-bender, epith. of the robber Sinis, who killed travellers by tying them between two pine-trees bent down so as nearly to meet, and then let go again, Strab., Plut.
growing pines, Anth.
the husks of corn, bran, mostly in pl., Dem., Theocr.
the pine, stone pine, Hom.:—proverb., πίτυος τρόπον ἐκτρίβεσθαι to be destroyed like a pine, i. e. utterly, because the pine when cut down never grows again, Hdt.
pine-crowned, Anth.
abounding in pines, Strab.

entry.etym: redupl. form of ΦΑ, Root of φαίνω
entry.sense: to make manifest, declare, tell of, Hom., Aesch.: absol., πιφαύσκων Διομήδεϊ making signal to him, Il.
to set forth words, utter, μῦθον, ἔπεα Od.
c. acc. et inf. to tell one to do, Aesch.
Mid. to make manifest, Il.; to tell of, disclose, Hom., Hes.
neut. πῖον, gen. πίονος, fat, plump, Lat. pinguis, Hom.; π. δημός rich fat, Il.; of oil, Hdt.
of soil, fat, rich. Il.; also, πίονα ἔργα pingues segetes, Id.; ὀπώρας πίων ποτός, of wine, Soph.
of persons and places, rich, wealthy, Hom., Aesch.; πίονι μέτρῳ in plenteous measure, Theocr.
The comp. and Sup. are πῑότερος, πῑότατος, as if from πῖος.
to turn sideways or aside, πλ. πρὸς τοὺς ἀντίους ἀνέμους (sc. τὴν ναῦν) to beat up against adverse winds, Luc.: metaph., πλ. ἢ φωνὴν ἢ πρᾶξιν to adapt them to circumstances, Plut.
the cross-flute, as opp. to the flute-a-bec, Theocr., Bion.
placed sideways, slanting, aslant, Lat. obliquus, Thuc.

πλάγια, ων, τά, the sides, Hdt.:—in military sense, τοῖς πλαγίοις ἐπιέναι to attack the flanks, Thuc.; εἰς τὰ πλ. παράγειν or παραπέμπειν to make an army file off right and left, Xen.; πλαγίους λαβεῖν τοὺς πολεμίους to take the enemy in flank, Id.
with Preps. in adverb. sense, εἰς πλάγιον obliquely, Id.; εἰς τὰ πλάγια, opp. to εἰς τὸ ἀντίον, Thuc.; —ἐκ πλαγίου in flank, Id.; κατὰ πλάγια Xen.
metaph. not straightforward, crooked, treacherous, φρένες Pind.; πλάγια φρονεῖν Eur.
the beguiler, (or pass.) the roamer, of Bacchus, Anth.
wandering, roaming, Aesch., Eur.
metaph. wandering in mind, erring, distraught, Od., Aesch.
Πλαγκταὶ πέτραι are rocks beyond Scylla and Charybdis, affording so narrow a passage that even birds could scarcely get through, Od.; transferred by later writers to the Symplegades, Hdt., etc.
roaming, Od.
the side, old doric word.
wet, damp, Anth.
like πλανάω to make to wander or roam, Hom.
to lead astray, bewilder, Id.

Pass. to wander, rove, roam about, Od.; ἀπὸ χαλκόφι χαλκὸς ἐπλάγχθη brass glanced off from brass, Il.; c. gen. to wander from, ἁμαξιτοῦ Eur.; so, τίς πλάγχθη πολύμοχθος ἔξω; i. e. τίς ἐπλάγχθη ἔξω τοῦ πολύμοχθος εἶναι; Soph.
μέγα κῦμα πλάζ’ ὤμους the wave drove his shoulder aside, Il.:Pass., κύματι πλάζετο was driven aside by the wave, Od.
a mould in which cakes were baked, Theocr.
intr. to approach, draw near, c. dat., Soph.; c. acc., Eur.; absol., Id.
to approach, draw near, c. dat., Soph.; c. acc., Eur.; absol., Id.
an oblong figure or body, Ar.; ἰσόπλευρον πλ. a square, Xen.; of an army, ἐν πλαισίῳ τετάχθαι to be drawn up in square, Lat. agmine quadrato, as opp. to marching order, Lat. agmine longo, Thuc., Xen.
entry.etym: Prob. from same Root as πλατύς.

entry.sense: broad, Theocr.
made of planks, πλ. τρίπους a tripod with a board on it, Anth.
a flat cake, Lat. placenta, Ar.
like πλάζω, to make to wander, lead wandering about, Hdt., Aesch.:— to lead from the subject, in talking, Dem.
to lead astray, mislead, deceive, Soph., Plat.

Pass. to wander, roam about, stray, Il., Aesch.; c. acc. loci, to wander over, Lat. oberrare, Eur.; but c. acc. cogn., πολλοὺς ἑλιγμοὺς πλανᾶσθαι to wander about as in a labyrinth, Xen.:— of reports, to wander abroad, Soph.
to wander in speaking, digress, Hdt.
c. gen., πλαναθεὶς καιροῦ having missed one's opportunity, Pind.
to do a thing irregularly or at random, Hdt.; ἐνύπνια τὰ ἐς ἀνθρώπους πεπλανημένα that have visited them irregularly, Id.
to wander in mind, to be at a loss, Id., Aesch.
a wandering, Aesch., Soph.
like ἄλη, a wandering, roaming, Hdt., Aesch.
a digression, Plat.
metaph. a going astray, error, Id., etc.
a making to wander, a dispersing, τῶν νεῶν Thuc.
a wanderer, roamer, rover, Soph., Eur.
πλάνητες ἀστέρες the planets, Xen.
as adj. wandering, Plut.
one must wander, Xen.
= πλάνης, Soph., Plat.
as adj. wandering, roaming, Eur.
disposed to wander, Strab.
wandering, Plat.
going by bye-paths, wandering, Hhymn.
act. leading astray, cheating, deceiving, Theocr., Mosch.
πλάνος, = πλάνη, a wandering, roaming, straying, Soph., Eur., etc.

metaph., φροντίδος πλάνοι the wanderings of thought, Soph.; but, πλ. φρενῶν wandering of mind, madness, Eur.; πλάνοις in uncertain fits, of a disease, Soph.; κερκίδος πλάνοι, of the act of weaving, Eur.
of persons, πλάνος, a deceiver, impostor, NTest.
trodden by wanderers, Aesch.
to wander about, Ar.
a flat surface, flat land, a plain, Aesch.; πόντου πλάξ the ocean- plain, Pind.; αἰθερία πλάξ Eur.: the flat top of a hill, table-land, Soph.
a flat stone, tablet, Luc., NTest.
anything moulded, an image, figure, Ar., etc.
anything imitated, a counterfeit, forgery, Dem.
a formed style, affectation, in orators or actors, Plut.
one addicted to lying, Plut.

to form, mould, shape, Lat. fingere, properly of the artist who works in clay or wax, Hes., Hdt.; τὴν ὑδρίαν πλάσαι to mould the water-jar, Ar.; ἔπλαττεν οἰκίας made clay houses, Id.:—Pass. to be moulded, made, ὁ μὲν πλάσσεται one is a-moulding, Hdt.
generally, to mould and form by education, training, Plat.
to form in the mind, form a notion of a thing, Id.
to put in a certain form: Mid., πλασάμενος τῆι ὄψει having formed himself in face, i. e. composed his countenance, Thuc.

metaph. to make up, fabricate, forge, Soph., Dem.:— absol., πλάσας λέγειν to speak from invention, i. e. not the truth, Hdt.:—so in Mid., Xen., etc.:—Pass., οὐ πεπλασμένος ὁ κόμπος not fictitious, Aesch.
to falsify, Byz.
a moulder, modeller, Plat.
the scale of a balance, Ar.: dual, a pair of scales, Id.
a collar for horses, Eur.
a scourge, Aesch.:—In this last sense, at all events, from πλήσσω.
fit for moulding, plastic, αἱ πλ. τέχναι the plastic arts, Plat.
formed, moulded in clay or wax, Hes., Plat., etc.
metaph. fabricated, forged, counterfeit, Hdt., Eur.; πλαστός a supposititious son, Soph.
to clap, clap the hands, Theocr.; to clash, crack, Id.:—so in Mid., Anth.
to beat the breasts, Bion.; πλ. τύμπανα Anth.
a clapping, Theocr.
a rattle, Arist.
the broad petal of the poppy or anemone, which lovers laid on the left hand, and struck with the right; it was a good omen if it burst with a loud crack, Theocr.
Plataea or Plataeae in Boeotia, Hdt., etc.
at Plataeae, Thuc.
Plataeans, Hdt., etc.
of Plataea, Hdt.; τὰ -κά the events at Plataea, Id.; fem. ἡ Πλαταιὶς, γῆ, χώρα Id.
a flat stone, Hhymn.:— in pl. ledges of rock, Strab.
a grove of plane-trees, Lat. platanetum, Theogn.
the oriental plane, Lat. platanus, Ar., Plat.
entry.etym: From πλατύς, because of its broad leaves.

entry.sense: to speak or pronounce broadly, like the Dorians, Theocr.
a tablet, Polyb.
a flat surface:
the blade of an oar, an oar, Trag.; ναυτίλῳ πλάτῃ by ship, by sea, Soph.; οὐρίῳ πλάτῃ with a fair voyage, Id.
a sheet of paper, Anth.
a wife, Ar.
Pass. to be made flat like an oar-blade, Ar.
approachable, Aesch.
breadth, width, Hdt., etc.:— absol., πλάτος or τὸ πλ., in breadth, Id., Xen.
of a goose, to beat the water with its wings, to splash about:—metaph. to make a splash, to swagger, Ar.
a wide-mouthed babbler, Anth.
one must extend, Xen.
to widen, make wide, NTest.: —Mid., πλατύνεσθαι γῆν to widen one's territory, Xen.:—Pass. to grow broad, widen out, Anth.: metaph., ἡ καρδία πεπλάτυνται is opened, enlarged, NTest.
broad-backed, Batr.
broad-bottomed, πλοῖα Strab.
broad-nosed, Strab.
broad-flowing, Aesch.
ionic fem. πλατέα: — wide, broad, Il.; αἰπόλια πλατέ’ αἰγῶν broad herds, i. e. large or widespread, Hom.; π. πρόσοδοι Pind.
flat, level, Hdt., Plat.; κάρυα τὰ πλατέα, i. e. chestnuts, Xen.
of a man, broad-shouldered, Soph.
metaph., πλατὺς κατάγελως flat (i. e. downright) mockery, Ar.: neut. as adv., flatly, merely, Id.
πλατεῖα (sc. ὁδός), a street, Lat. platea, Xen.:—(sub. χείρ), the flat of the hand, Ar.
salt, brackish, Hdt.
breadth, bulk, Xen.
of Plato, Anth.; Sup. -ώτατος, Luc.: adv. -κῶς, after the manner of Plato, Strab.
adv. entwined, entangled, Anth.
plaited work, wicker-work, Plat., Xen.:—pl. wreaths, braids, Eur., NTest.
broad or long, Xen.
to run the πλέθρον; metaph. to "shoot with a long bow, " Theophr.
as measure of length, a plethron, = 100 Greek or 101 English feet, 1/6 of a stade, Hdt., Xen.
as a square measure, 10, 000 square feet (Greek) = about 37 perches, Plat., Dem.;—used to translate the Rom. jugerum, though this was about 2 roods 19 perches, Plut.
the Pleiads, seven daughters of Atlas, placed by Zeus among the stars, Hom., Hes.; only six are distinctly visible, whence the myth of the "lost Pleiad, " Ovid.
entry.etym: Prob. from πλέω, to sail, because they rose at the beginning of the sailingseason, as Ὑάδες from ὕω, with reference to the rainy season. Poets, adopting the form Πελειάδες, represented them as doves, and the ὑάδες as swine.

entry.sense: mostly, most often, very often, Xen., etc.
manifold, ἅπας πλ. χρόνος all the whole length of time, Aesch.
Dep. to count as principal author, Aesch.
throwing the most, of dicers, Anth.
crowded with people, Pind.
most, largest, also very much, very large, both of number and size, Hom., etc.; πλεῖστός εἰμι τῇ γνώμῃ I incline most to the opinion, Hdt.
with the Art., οἱ πλεῖστοι, much like οἱ πολλοί, the greatest number, Thuc., etc.; τὸ πλεῖστον τοῦ βίου the greatest part of life, Plat.; also ἡ πλ. τῆς στρατιᾶς Thuc.

Special usages: ὅσας ἂν πλείστας δύναιντο καταστρέφεσθαι the greatest number that they could possibly subdue, Hdt.; ὅτι πλ. Thuc., etc.:— εἷς ἀνὴρ πλεῖστον πόνον παρασχών the greatest of all men, Aesch.
Adverb. usages:— πλεῖστον, = μάλιστα, most, Il., attic; ὡς πλεῖστον, Lat. quam maxime, Xen.; sometimes added to a Sup., πλεῖστον ἐχθίστη, πλ. κάκιστος Soph.; so, πλεῖστα Id.:— furthest, Plat.
with the Art., τὸ πλ. for the most part, Ar.
with Preps.:
διὰ πλείστου furthest off, in point of space or time, Thuc.
εἰς πλεῖστον most, Soph.
ἐπὶ πλεῖστον over the greatest distance, to the greatest extent, in point of space or time, Hdt., Thuc.; ὡς ἐπὶ πλ. or ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πλ. for the most part. Plat.; περὶ πλείστου ποιεῖσθαι, v. περί A. IV.
ἐν τοῖς πλεῖστοι or πλεῖσται about the most, Thuc.

more, larger, both of number and size, Hom., etc.; τὸν πλείω λόγον all further speech, Soph.; πλείω τὸν πλοῦν the greater part of . . , Thuc.:—of Time, longer, πλείων χρόνος Hdt.; πλέων νύξ the greater part of night, Il.

with the Art., οἱ πλέονες the greater number, like οἱ πολλοί, the mass or crowd, Hom.; οἱ πλεῦνες Hdt., etc.; c. gen., τὰς πλεῦνας τῶν γυκαικῶν Id.:— the many, the people, opp. to the chief men, Thuc., etc.:— τὸ πλεῖον πολέμοιο the greater part of war, Hom.
pecul. usages of neut.:

as a Noun, more, πλεῦν ἔτι τούτου Hdt.; τὸ δὲ πλέον nay, what is more, Eur., Thuc.:— πλέον or τὸ πλέον τινός a higher degree of a thing, Soph.; τὸ πλ. τοῦ χρόνου Thuc.:— πλέον ἔχειν to have the best of it, win, conquer, Id.; also, like πλεονεκτέω, c. gen., Hdt., etc.; also, πλέον ποιεῖν Plat.; ἐς πλ. ποιεῖν Soph.; οὐδὲν πλ. πράσσειν, etc., Eur.:— τί πλέον; what more, i. e. what good or use is it? Ar.; so, οὐδὲν ἦν πλέον Dem.:— ἐπὶ πλέον or ἐπίπλεον, as adv., more, further, Hdt., Thuc., etc.; c. gen. beyond, ἐπὶ τὸ πλ. τινὸς ἱκέσθαι Theocr.; cf. περί A. III.
as adv. more, rather, πλέον ἔφερέ οἱ ἡ γνώμη his opinion inclined rather, Hdt.:—also, τὸ πλέον, ionic τὸ πλεῦν, for the most part, Id., etc.; τὸ πλ. = μᾶλλον, Thuc.

with Numerals, τοξότας πλ. ἢ εἴκοσι Xen.:—in this sense a contr. form πλεῖν is used by attic writers, πλεῖν ἢ τριάκονθ’ ἡμέρας Ar.; πλεῖν ἢ χιλίας (sc. δραχμάς) Id., etc.;—but ἤ is often omitted, as in Lat. quam after plus, πλεῖν ἑξακοσίας Id.; so, ἔτη γεγονὼς πλείω ἑβδομήκοντα annos plus septuaginta natus, Plat.:—Comic phrase, πλεῖν ἢ μαίνομαι more than to madness, Ar.
the pl. πλείω is also used like πλέον, Thuc., Dem.
a full period, a year, Hes.
wicker-work, Ar.
Pass. to be intertwined, πεπλεκτανημέναι δράκουσι, of the Erinyes, Aesch.
anything twined or wreathed, a coil, wreath, spire, of serpents, Aesch.; πλ. καπνοῦ a wreath of smoke, Ar.
in pl. the meshes of a spider's web, Luc.; metaph., αἱ τῶν λόγων πλεκτάναι tortuous speeches, Id.
properly fem. of πλεκτός:
a coil, wreath, Aesch.
a twisted rope, cord, string, Eur.
of plaiting, τέχναι Plat.
plaited, twisted, Hom., Hes., etc.; π. στέγαι wicker mansions, of the Scythian vans, Aesch.; πλεκτὴ Αἰγύπτου παιδεία the twisted taskwork of Egypt, i. e. ropes of biblus, Eur.
wreathed, ἄνθη Aesch.; στέφανος Eur.
to plait, twine, twist, weave, braid, Il., etc. : Med., πεῖσμα πλεξάμενος having twisted me a rope, Od.:—Pass., κράνεα πεπλεγμένα of basket-work, Hdt.; σειραὶ πεπλεγμέναι ἐξ ἱμάντων Id.
metaph. to plan, devise, contrive, like ῥάπτειν, ὑφαίνειν, mostly of tortuous means, πλ. δόλον Aesch.; μηχανάς Eur.; παντοίας παλάμας Ar.
of Poets, πλ. ὕμνον, ῥήματα Pind.; πλ. λόγους Eur.
in Pass. to twist oneself round, Aesch.
to be more, esp. to be more than enough, be superfluous, Arist.
of persons, to go beyond bounds, take or claim too much, Dem.:—c. dat. to presume upon, τῆι εὐτυχίαι Thuc.: of a writer, to be lengthy, tedious, Lat. multus sum, Strab.
πλεονάζειν τινός to have an excess of, abound in a thing, Arist.
c. acc. to state at a larger amount, Strab.:—Pass. to be exaggerated, Thuc.
more frequently, oftener, Plat.: several times, frequently, Arist.
in many points of view, Plat.
in various ways, Arist.
to have or claim more than one's due, to get or have too much, to be greedy, grasping, arrogant, Hdt., Plat.: —also to gain or have some advantage, without any bad sense, Thuc., Xen.
c. gen. rei, to have or claim more of a thing, to have or claim a larger share, Thuc., etc.
c. gen. pers. to have or gain the advantage over, τῶν ἐχθρῶν Plat.
c. acc. pers. to overreach, defraud, Menand., NTest.:— Pass. to be overreached, Thuc., Xen.
an advantage, gain, privilege, Plat., Dem.: in pl. gains, successes, Xen.
an act of overreaching, selfish trick, Dem.
one who has or claims more than his due, greedy, grasping, arrogant, Thuc., etc.:—as adj., λόγος πλ. Hdt.; Sup. πλεονεκτίστατος, Xen.
πλεονέκτης τῶν πολεμίων making gain from their losses, Id.
one must take more than one's share, Plat.
disposed to take too much, greedy, Dem., etc. adv. -κῶς, Plat.; πλ. ἔχειν Dem.
the character and conduct of a πλεονέκτης, greediness, grasping, assumption, arrogance, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
gain, advantage, Xen., etc.; ἐπὶ πλεονεξίᾳ with a view to one's own advantage, Thuc., Xen.
c. gen. pers. advantage over, Xen.
c. gen. rei, a larger share of a thing, Arist.; gain made from a thing, Dem.
a rib, Lat. costa, Hdt.: mostly in pl. the ribs, the side, Il., Hdt., attic:—in sg., also, of one side, Soph.
the side of things and places, πλευραὶ νηός Theogn.; χωρίου, ποταμοῦ Plat.; of an army, αἱ πλ. τοῦ πλαισίου Xen.
the page of a book, Anth.
from the side, Soph.
to smite the ribs, Soph.
a rib: mostly in pl. the ribs, the side, Il., Hdt., etc.;—also in sg., Soph.
of places, πλευρὸν νεῶν the side of the bay where the ships lay, Id.; τὸ δεξιὸν πλ. the right flank (of an army), Xen.
striking the sides or ribs, Anth.
like πλευρόν, in pl. the side, Aesch.
one must sail, Dem.
fit or favourable for sailing, Theocr.
to sail, go by sea, Hom., etc.; c. acc. cogn., ὑγρὰ κέλευθα πλεῖν to sail the watery ways, Od.; hence in Pass., τὸ πεπλευσμένον πέλαγος Xen.;—metaph., πλεῖν ὑφειμένηι cf. ὑφίημι 111.
of ships, Il., Hdt., etc.
of other things, to swim, float, Hom., etc.
metaph., ταύτης ἔπι πλέοντες ὀρθῆς while we keep [the ship of] our country right, Soph.; οὐδ’ ὅπως ὀρθὴ πλεύσεται (sc. ἡ πόλις) προείδετο Dem.
full of a thing, c. gen., πλεῖαι οἴνου κλισίαι Il., etc.
ῥάκη νοσηλείας πλέα rags infected with his sore, Soph.
absol. full, Il., etc.
of Time, full, complete, δέκα πλείους ἐνιαυτούς ten full years, Hes.
comp. πλειότερος Od.

a blow, stroke, Lat. plaga, Hom., etc.; πληγὴν πέπληγμαι καιρίαν Aesch.; in such phrases πληγήν or πληγάς is often omitted, πολλὰς τυπτόμενος Ar., etc.:—the person struck is said πληγὰς λαβεῖν Id.; the striker πληγὰς δοῦναι, ἐμβάλλειν, ἐντείνειν τινί Xen.
a stroke by lightning, Hes.: a blow, stroke of calamity, Aesch.; πλ. θεοῦ a blow from heaven, Soph.
a great number, a throng, crowd, multitude, Il., Hdt., etc.
τὸ πλῆθος, the greater number, the greater part, the mass, main body, Hdt., Xen., etc.:— the majority, the people, like δῆμος, Lat. plebs, Hdt., attic: —also the populace, mob, Xen.
quantity or number, Hdt., attic; πλήθει παρόντες in force, Thuc.: —absol. in acc., κόσοι πλῆθος Hdt.; πλῆθος ἀνάριθμοι Aesch.
magnitude, size or extent, ὄρος πλήθεϊ μέγιστον Hdt.; πεδίον πλῆθος ἄπειρον Id., etc.
quantity or amount, Thuc., Plat., etc.
of Time, length, Thuc., etc.
with Preps., or with ὡς, in adv. sense, ἐς πλ. in great numbers, Id.: —ὡς πλήθει upon the whole, in general, Plat.; so, ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πλ. usually, mostly, Lat. ut plurimum, Id.
Causal of πληθύω, only in pres. and imperf., to make full, increase, multiply, NTest., Hdt.
Pass. to be in the majority, to prevail, Aesch.; c. inf., ἐπαινεῖν πληθύνομαι I am led by general opinion to approve, Id.
fulness, a throng, a crowd, of people, Hom., Plut., etc.
to be or become full, τινός of a thing, Eur.:— absol., ἀγορῆς πληθυούσης, v. ἀγορά V.:—of rivers, to swell, rise, Hdt.:—so in Mid., Id.
to increase in number, multiply, Aesch.
to abound, τινί in a thing, Soph.
to be general, prevail, Lat. invalescere, of reports, Aesch., Soph.; ὁ πληθύων χρόνος increasing time, age, Soph.

entry.etym: poet. perf. πέπληθα, in pres. sense
entry.sense: to be or become full of a thing, c. gen., Il., Aesch.; χεῖρας κρεῶν πλήθοντες having them full of flesh, Aesch.; c. dat., Theocr.: absol. of rivers, to be full, brimming, Il.; so, πλήθουσα Σελήνη at her full, Id.; ἀγορᾶς πληθούσης, ἐν ἀγορᾷ πληθούσῃ, etc., v. sub ἀγορά V.
trans., like πληθύνω, Anth.
ionic word, fulness, πλ. ἀγορῆς, = ἀγορὰ πλήθουσα, Hdt.; v. ἀγορά V.
fulness, satiety, Id.
a striker, brawler, Plut.
Dep.
to bandy blows with one, c. dat., Il.
to beat one's breast for grief, Lat. plangere, Anth.
to indulge in dalliance, Strab.
anything to strike with:
an instrument for striking the lyre, plectrum, Hhymn., Eur., etc.
a spear point, π. διόβολον, of lighting, Eur.
a cock's spur, Lat. calcar, Ar.
an oar or paddle, Hdt.
a mistake in music, false note: metaph. a fault, offence, error, Plat.
to make a false note in music: metaph. to go wrong, offend, err, τι in a thing, Eur., Plat., etc.; εἴς τινα Aeschin.:—Pass., πλημμελεῖσθαι ὑπό τινος to be ill-treated by one, Plat., Dem.
a fault, trespass, Aeschin.
properly, out of tune, opp. to ἐμμελής.
metaph. in discord, faulty, erring, Plat.
of things, dissonant, discordant, unpleasant, πλημμελές τι δρᾶν, παθεῖν Eur., etc.
the flood-tide, Anth.
to rise like the flood-tide, to overflow, be redundant, Anth., Plut.
a rise of the sea, πλημμυρὶς ἐκ πόντοιο of the wave caused by the rock thrown by the Cyclops, Od.: flood-tide (cf. ῥαχία), opp. to ἄμπωτις (ebb), Hdt.
generally, a flood, deluge, Arist.; of tears, Aesch., Eur.
entry.etym: ῠ in Hom., ῡ in attic
Deriv. uncertain: perh. from πλήθω, μύρω.

entry.sense: the nave of a wheel, Il., Hes.
entry.etym: Perh. from πλήθω, the filled up or solid part of the wheel.

entry.sense: as prep. with gen., more than, and so except, save, Od., Hdt.; ὑπεγγύους πλὴν θανάτου liable to any punishment save, short of, death, Hdt.; ἐπιτρέψαι περὶ σφῶν αὐτῶν πλὴν θανάτου save in respect of death, Thuc.
as adv.:

with single words and phrases, when a negat. precedes, οὐκ οἶδα πλὴν ἕν Soph., etc.:—after πᾶς, πάντες, ἕκαστος, and the like, παντὶ δῆλον πλὴν ἐμοί Plat.; πᾶς is sometimes omitted, θνήσκουσι [πάντες] πλὴν εἷς τις Soph.; after ἄλλος, τί ἄλλο πλὴν ψευδῆ what else but lies, Id.; after a comp., like ἤ, than, ταῦτ’ ἐστὶ κρείσσω, πλὴν ὑπ’ Ἀργείοις πεσεῖν Eur.
often joined with other Particles:
πλὴν εἰ, πλὴν ἐάν, Lat. nisi si, πλὴν εἴ τις κωμῳδοποιὸς τυγχάνει ὤν Plat.; πλὴν ὅταν Aesch., etc.:—the Verb is often omitted, as with ὡσεί, ὡσπερεί, οὐδεὶς οἶδεν, πλὴν εἴ τις ὄρνις Ar.
πλὴν ἤ, much like πλὴν εἰ, οὐκ ἄλλως πλὴν ἢ Προδίκῳ Id.
πλὴν οὐ, only not, ἀπέπεμπε κήρυκας ἐς τὴν Ἑλλάδα, πλὴν οὐ ἐς Ἀθήνας Hdt.; πάντες πλὴν οὐχ οἱ τύραννοι Xen.
πλὴν ὅτι except that . . , save that, καίτοι τί διαφέρουσιν ἡμῶν ἐκεῖνοι, πλὴν ὅτι ψηφίσματ’ οὐ γράφουσιν Ar.; so, πλὴν ἢ ὅτι Hdt.
πλὴν ὅσον except or save so far as, Id.; πλὴν καθόσον εἰ Thuc.: —without a Verb, πάντων ἐρήμους, πλὴν ὅσον τὸ σὸν μέρος save so far as thou art concerned, Soph.
striking or driving horses, Il., Hes.
c. gen. full of a thing, Hdt., Trag.
filled or infected by, πλήρης ὑπ’ οἰωνῶν τε καὶ κυνῶν βορᾶς polluted by birds and dogs with meat (torn from the body of Polynices), Soph.
satiated with a thing, Id.; πλήρης ἐστὶ θηεύμενος he has gazed his fill, Hdt.
rarely c. dat. filled with, Eur.
absol. full, of a swoln stream, Hdt.; of the moon, Id.; of cups, Eur.: —esp. full of people, Ar.
full, complete, λαβεῖν τι πλῆρες Hdt., Eur.:—of number, τέσσερα ἔτεα πλήρεα four full years, Hdt.
to fulfil, NTest.
in Pass., of persons, to have full satisfaction, to be fully assured, Id.; of things, to be fully believed, Id.
fulness of assurance, certainty, NTest.
to make full:
c. gen. rei, to fill full of, Hdt., etc.:—Pass. to be filled full of, Aesch., etc.
to fill full of food, to gorge, satiate, βορᾶς ψυχὴν ἐπλήρουν Eur.; metaph., πληροῦν θυμόν to glut one's rage, animum explere, Soph., etc.
c. dat. to fill with, Eur.: Pass., πνεύμασιν πληρούμενοι filled with breath, Aesch.; πεπληρωμένος ἀδικίαι NTest.
πλ. ναῦν, τριήρη to man a ship, Hdt.; πληροῦτε θωρακεῖα man the breast-works, Aesch.; in Mid., πληροῦσθαι τὴν ναῦν to man one's ship, Xen.:—Pass., of the ships, Thuc.
of number, to make full or complete, τοὺς δέκα μῆνας Hdt.;—so in Mid., NTest.:—Pass. to be completed, Hdt., NTest.
πλ. δικαστήριον to fill it, Dem.
to fulfil, pay in full, make up, Aesch., Thuc.:—Pass., νόμοι πληρούμενοι fully observed, Aesch.
ἐς ἄγγος βακχίου μέτρημα πληρώσαντες having poured wine into the vessel till it was full, Eur.:—Pass. to crowd in to a place, Id.
intr., ἡ ὁδὸς πληροῖ ἐς τὸν ἀριθμὸν τοῦτον the length of road comes in full to this number, Hdt.
a full measure, Eur.
πλ. δαιτός the satiety of the feast, Id.; πλ. τυρῶν their fill of cheese, Id.
of ships, a full number, Hdt., Eur.; of single ships, their complement, Thuc., etc.
of number, the sum, total, Hdt., Ar.
a piece inserted to fill up, NTest.
fulness, full and perfect nature, Id.
a filling up, completing, Soph.; κυλίκων πλ. ἔχων to have the task of filling them, Eur.
fulfilment, NTest.
a filling up, filling, Plat.: often of eating and drinking, satiety, Id.
the completion of a number, Hdt.
one who completes, Dem.
to bring near, τινά τινι Xen.:—Pass. to come near, approach, τινι Eur.
intr., in sense of Pass., absol. to be near, Soph.:— to draw near to, approach, c. dat., Xen.; rarely c. gen., Id.
c. dat. pers. to be always near, to consort or associate with, τῷ ἀνδρί Soph.; γυναικί Dem.
Dius in Stob.:— an approaching, approach, Arist.
near, close to, c. gen. or dat., πλησίοι ἀλλήλων or ἀλλήλοισι Hom.:—absol. near, neighbouring, Il., Aesch., etc.:—as Subst. a neighbour, ἰδὼν ἐς πλ. ἄλλον Il., etc.
adv. πλησίον, doric πλᾱτίον, = πέλας, near, nigh, hard by, c. gen., Hom., Hdt., etc.; c. dat., Eur.
with the Art., ὁ πλησίον (sc. ὤν) one's neighbour, Theogn., Eur., etc.; so in doric, ὁ πλᾱτίον Theocr.:—also, with Substs., ὁ πλ. παράδεισος Xen.
comp. πλησιαίτερος, Sup. -αίτατος, Id.—comp. adv. πλησιαιτέρω, Hdt.; -αίτερον, Xen.; Sup. -αίτατα, Id.
near a country, bordering upon, τινι Hdt.; absol., οἱ πλ. persons who live in the next country, next neighbours, Lat. finitimi, Id., Thuc.
filling the sails, οὖρος Od., Eur.
pass. with full sails, Plut.
filling, satisfying, Plut.: τὸ πλήσμιον satiety, Id.
a filling or being filled, satiety; esp. of food, repletion, satiety, surfeit, Eur., Xen.:—c. gen., τῶν ἄλλων ἐστι πλ. Ar.

entry.etym: πέπηγα is used as pass. in late writers
the Root is ΠΛΑΓ, or ΠΛΗΓ
entry.sense: to strike, smite, Hom.; of a direct blow, as opp. to βάλλω, Hom., etc.:—c. acc. dupl. pers. et partis, τὸν πλῆξε αὐχένα struck him on the neck, Il.; πὺξ πεπληγέμεν, of boxers, Id.:—c. acc. cogn., πλῆξ’ αὐτοσχεδίην (sc. πληγήν) Id.; πεπληγὼς πληγῆισιν having driven him with blows, Id.; πέπληγον χορὸν ποσίν, like Lat. terram pede pulsare, Od.; ἵππους ἐς πόλεμον πεπληγέμεν to whip on the horses to the fray, Il.; of Zeus, to strike with lightning, Hes.:—Mid., μηρὼ πληξάμενος having smitten his thighs, Il.; πλήξασθαι τὴν κεφαλήν, in sign of grief, Hdt.:—Pass. to be struck, stricken, smitten, Hom., Trag.
with acc. of the thing set in motion, κονίσαλον ἐς οὐρανὸν ἐπέπληγον πόδες ἵππων struck the dust up to heaven, Il.
Pass. to receive a heavy blow, to be beaten, Hdt., Thuc.:— to be stricken by misfortune, Hdt.; στρατὸν τοσοῦτον πέπληγμαι, i. e. I have lost it by this blow, Aesch.
metaph. of violent emotions, to strike one from one's senses, amaze, confound, Hom.:—Pass., συμφορῆι πέπληγμαι Hdt., etc.; δώροισι πληγείς moved by bribes, Id.
to make into bricks, τὴν γῆν Hdt.:—absol. to make bricks, Ar.;—so in Mid., thuc.
to build of brick, τείχη Id.
to make in the form of a plinth or brick, Ar.
brick-fashion, i. e. in courses with the joints alternating, Hdt.
of brick, Hdt., Xen.
a small brick, Thuc., Xen.
= πλαίσιον, a rectangle or square, Plut.
a whetstone, Anth.
Mid. to build as with bricks, Anth.
to make bricks, Ar.
a brick, Hdt., Ar., etc.; πλίνθους ἑλκύσαι, εἰρύσαι, Lat. ducere lateres, to make bricks, Hdt.; ὀπτᾶν to bake them, Id.
to make bricks, Ar.
a brickmaker, Plat.
carry bricks, Ar.
carrying bricks, Ar.
brick-built, Aesch.
to cross the legs, as in trotting, πλίσσοντο πόδεσσιν they trotted, Od.; in comp., ἂν ἀπεπλίξατο would have trotted off, Ar.
producing navigation, Anth.
a skiff, boat, Ar., Xen.

a floating vessel, a ship, vessel, Hdt., Aesch., etc.; πλοῖα λεπτά small craft, Hdt., Thuc.; πλ. ἱππαγωγά transport- vessels, Hdt.; πλ. μακρά ships of war, Id.; πλ. στρογγύλα or φορτηγικά ships burthen, merchantmen, Xen.:—when opp. to ναῦς, a merchant-ship or transport, τοῖς πλοίοις καὶ ταῖς ναυσί Thuc.
a lock or braid of hair, of women, Bion.: in sg. curling hair, Theocr.
a lock or braid of hair, Aesch.: in pl. locks, properly of women, Il.:—in sg., collectively, = κόμη, Hdt.; τριχὸς πλ. Aesch.
a plaited rope, Xen.
a twining: anything woven, a web, Eur.
metaph. the complication of a plot, opp. to λύσις, Arist.
a lock of hair, a braid, curl, Trag.
a wreath or chaplet, πλόκοι σελίνων the parsley- wreath at the Isthmian games, Pind.; μυρσίνης πλόκοι Eur., etc.
a sailing, voyage, Od., Hdt., attic; πλοῦν στέλλειν, ποιεῖσθαι Soph.; μῆκός ἐστι πλόος ἡμέραι τέσσερες its length is four days' sail, Hdt.
time or tide for sailing, Hes., Soph., etc.; πλῷ χρῆσθαι to have a fair wind, Thuc.
proverb., δεύτερος πλοῦς, "the next best way" (from those who use oars when the wind fails), Plat.
health and wealth, Ar.; parox. πλουθυγιείᾱ (metri grat.) Id.
rich, wealthy, opulent, Hes., Theogn., attic
c. gen. rei, rich in a thing, Lat. dives opum, Eur., Plat.:—also c. dat., Plut.
of things, richly furnished, ample, abundant, Soph., Eur.
adv. -ίως, Hdt., Eur.

entry.etym: gen. Πλουτέως, -έος, Anth.; dat. Πλουτέϊ, -ῆι; acc. Πλουτέα Id., etc.

entry.sense: to be rich, wealthy, Hes., Theogn., Hdt., attic; πλ. ἀπὸ τῶν κοινῶν to be rich from the public purse, Ar.
c. gen. rei, to be rich in a thing, Xen.
c. dat. rei, πλ. ἐμπύροισιν Eur., Xen.
c. acc. cogn., πλ. πλοῦτον Luc.
enriching, ἔργον Xen.
one must become rich, Luc.
to make wealthy, enrich, Aesch., Xen.; ironic., πλ. τινὰ ἄταις Aesch.:—Pass., Ἅιδης γόοις πλουτίζεται Soph.; πλ. ἀπὸ βοσκημάτων, ἐκ τῆς πόλεως to gain one's wealth from . . , Xen.
adv. according to wealth, πλ. αἱρεῖσθαι τοὺς ἄρχοντας Arist.
rejoicing in riches, wealthy, Aesch.
giver of riches, Hes., Anth.
plutocracy, Xen.
wealth-creating, Plut.
wealth, riches, Hom., etc.; πλοῦτος χρυσοῦ, ἀργύρου treasure of gold, silver, Hdt.:—metaph., γᾶς πλ. ἄβυσσος, of the whole earth, Aesch.; πλοῦτος εἵματος Id.
as prop. n. Plutus, god of riches, Hes.
rich in earthly treasures, in allusion perh. to the silver mines of Laureion, Aesch.
Pluto, god of the nether world, Trag.: (prob. from πλοῦτος) the wealth-giver, as spouse of Demeter, who enriched men with the fruits of the earth.
like πλόκαμος, mostly in pl. locks, braids of hair, Il., Anth.
the tendrils of the polypus, Anth.
a trough, tank, or pit, in which dirty clothes were washed by treading, Hom.
metaph., πλυνὸν ποιεῖν τινα, = πλύνω II, Ar.
of or for washing: Πλυντήρια (sc. ἱερά), τά, a festival at Athens, in which the clothes of Athena's statue were washed, Xen., etc.
to wash, clean, properly of linen and clothes, (opp. to λούομαι to bathe, νίζω to wash the hands or feet), Hom., attic
to wash off dirt, Od.
as a slang term, πλύνειν τινά (as we say) "to give him a dressing," Ar., Dem.
a washing, Plat.
ionic imperf. πλωίζεσκον:— to sail on the sea, Hes.; οἱ Ἕλληνες μᾶλλον ἐπλώιζον began to use ships or practise navigation, Thuc.:—as Dep. πλωίζομαι, Strab., Luc.
fit for sailing:
of a ship, fit for sea, seaworthy, Thuc.
of navigation, πλωιμωτέρων γενομένων or ὄντων as navigation advanced, as circumstances became favourable for navigation, Id.
navigable, πέλαγος Soph.
Pass. to be navigated, of the sea, to navigate, Polyb.
a sailor, seaman, Ar., Plat.; including rowers and navigators, Arist.
skilled in seamanship, a seaman, Plat., Plut.; also a shipowner, Plut.
floating, Od., Hdt.; πλωτοί swimmers, i. e. fish, Anth.
navigable, Hdt.
of seasons, fit for navigation, Polyb.
a blowing, πνεύματα ἀνέμων Hdt., Aesch.: alone, a wind, blast, Trag., etc.
metaph., θαλερωτέρῳ πν. with more genial breeze or influence, Aesch.; λύσσης πν. μάργῳ Id.; πν. ταὐτὸν οὔποτ’ ἐν ἀνδράσιν φίλοις βέβηκεν the wind is constantly changing even among friends, Soph.

like Lat. spiritus or anima, breathed air, breath, Aesch.; πν. βίου the breath of life, Id.; πν. ἀθροίζειν to collect breath, Eur.; πν. ἀφιέναι, ἀνιέναι, μεθιέναι to give up the ghost, Id.; πνεύματος διαρροαί the wind-pipe, Id.
that is breathed forth, odour, scent, Id.
spirit, Lat. afflatus, Anth.: inspiration, NTest.
the spirit of man, Id.
a spirit; in NTest. of the Holy Spirit, τὸ Πνεῦμα, Πν. ἅγιον:— also of angels, Id.:—of evil spirits, Id.
of spirit, spiritual, NTest.

entry.note: πνεύμων, in later attic πλεύμων, ονος, ὁ,
entry.sense: the organ of breathing, the lungs, Lat. pulmo, Il., Plat.: mostly in pl., Trag.; πνεῦμ’ ἀνεὶς ἐκ πλευμόνων Eur.
to breathe hard, pant, Arist.; epic part. πνευστιόων, Anth.

entry.etym: Like other dissyl. Verbs in -έω, this Verb only contracts εε, εει
entry.sense: to blow, of wind and air, Od., Hdt., attic; ἡ πνέουσα (sc. αὔρα) the breeze, NTest.
to breathe, send forth an odour, Od.:—c. gen. to breathe or smell of a thing, Anth.
of animals, to breathe hard, pant, gasp, Il., Aesch.
generally, to draw breath, breathe, and so to live, Hom.; οἱ πνέοντες = οἱ ζῶντες, Soph.

metaph., c. acc. cogn. to breathe forth, breathe, μένεα πνείοντες breathing spirit, of warriors, Il.; so, πῦρ πν. Hes.; φόνον, κότον, Ἄρη Aesch.; so, πνέοντας δόρυ καὶ λόγχας Ar.; Ἀλφειὸν πνέων, of a swift runner, Id.
μέγα πνεῖν to be of a high spirit, give oneself airs, Eur.; τόσονδ’ ἔπνευσας Id.:—also, with a nom., as if it were the wind, μέγας πνέων Id.; πολὺς ἔπνει καὶ λαμπρὸς ἦν Dem.
an oven, heated by hot coals put inside it, like our brick ovens, Ar.
choking, stifling, Ar.
a choking or being choked, Xen.
stifling heat, Ar., Thuc.
to choke, throttle, strangle, Plat.; proverb., ὅταν τὸ ὕδωρ πνίγηι, τί δεῖ ἐπιπίνειν; if water chokes, why should one drink more? Arist.:—Pass. to be choked, stifled, Ar.: to be drowned, Xen.
metaph. to vex, torment, Luc.
to cook in a close-covered vessel, to stew, Hdt., Ar.
strangled, NTest.
a blowing, blast, breeze, Hom.: ἅμα πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο along with, i. e. swift as, blasts of wind, Id.; μετὰ πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο Id., etc.:— the blast of bellows, Thuc.
of animals, a breathing hard, of horses, Il., Soph.
generally, breath, ἔμπνους ἔτ’ εἰμὶ καὶ πνοὰς πνέω Eur.:—metaph., πνοιὴ Ἡφαίστοιο the breath of Hephaestus, i. e. flame, Il.; θεοῦ πνοαῖσιν ἐμμανεῖς Eur.
a breathing odour, a vapour, exhalation, σποδὸς προπέμπει πλούτου πνοάς, of a burning city, Aesch.
the breath of a wind-instrument, Pind., Eur.

the Pnyx, the place at Athens where the ἐκκλησίαι were held, Ar.; ἐν πυκνὶ ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ Dem. It was cut out of the side of a little hill west of the Acropolis, being of a semicircular form like a theatre.
of ground, produce grass, Strab.
grass, herb, Hom., etc.; ποία Μηδική, Lat. herba Medica, sainfoin or lucerne, Ar.
the grass, i. e. a grassy place, plat., Xen.
in Poets, of Time, τέσσαρας πόας four grasses, i. e. summers, Anth.
tenderfooted, Orac. ap. Hdt.
a trap for the feet, Xen., Anth.
gout in the feet, opp. to χειράγρα.
to have gout in the feet, Ar.
liable to gout, gouty, Plut.
a vessel for washing the feet in, a footpan, Hdt.
water for washing the feet in, in pl., Od.
from what country? Lat. cujas? generally, whence? where born? Hdt., Trag.; τίς καὶ π.; Plat.
generally, of what sort? ποδαπός; οἷος μὴ δάκνειν . . , of what sort? one that will not bite, Dem.
entry.etym: As in ἀλλοδαπός, ἡμεδαπός, ὑμεδαπός, τηλεδαπός, -δαπος is a termin. of uncertain origin.

entry.sense: swiftfooted or whitefooted:— Πόδαργος, ὁ, swiftfoot or whitefoot, a horse, Il.; fem. Ποδάργη, a Harpy, Id.

sufficient with the feet, swiftfooted, of Achilles, Il.; ποδάρκης ἁμέρα a day of swiftness, i. e. on which swift runners contended, Pind.; ποδαρκέων δρόμων τέμενος the field of swift courses, i. e. the Pythian racecourse, Id.
drawn over the feet, Aesch.
in pl., the ragged ends in the skins of animals, formed by the feet and tail, δέρμα λέοντος ἀφημμένον ἄκρων ἐκ ποδεώνων a lion's skin hung round one's neck by the paws, Theocr.
in sg. the neck or mouth of a wineskin, formed by one of these ends, the others being sewn up, Hdt.
generally any narrow end, a strip of land, Id.
the lower corner of a sail, the sheet, Luc.
a guide, attendant, Soph., Eur.
reaching to the feet, Il., Hdt.
windswift, of Iris, Il.

reaching to the feet, πέπλος, χιτὼν π. a frock that falls over the feet, as in the archaic Greek statues, Eur., Xen.; π. ἀσπίς the large shield which covered the body quite down to the feet, Xen.; στῦλος π. a straight, firm pillar, Aesch.
τὰ ποδήρη the parts about the feet, the feet, Id.
a foot long, broad, or high, Xen.
to tie the feet:— Pass. to have the feet tied, or to be tied by the foot, of horses, Xen.
welded to the feet, Anth.
foot-entangling, of a long robe, Aesch.
a foottrap, Anth.
ποδο-κάκη, also written ποδοκάκκη, properly, foot plague, a kind of stocks, Dem., etc.
a stamping with the feet, Strab.
bursting forth at a stamp of the foot, Anth.
a snare or trap to catch the feet, Xen.
a footwiper, footcloth, Aesch.
swiftness of foot, Il., Eur.,
swiftfooted, of Achilles, Il.; π. ἄνθρωπος Thuc.; λαγώς Xen.
generally, swift, quick, ὄμμα Aesch.; θεῶν π. βλάβαι Soph.
to eat grass, Hdt.
eating grass or herbs.

longed for, desired, much desired, esp. if absent or lost (v. πόθος), Trag.; ποθεινὸς ἦλθες Eur.; π. δάκρυα tears of regret, Id.; π. τοῖς φίλοις Ar.:—adv., ποθεινοτέρως ἔχειν τινός to long greatly for a thing, Xen.
enclit, adv. from some place or other, εἴ ποθεν Il.; εἰ καί π. ἄλλοθεν ἔλθοι Od.
interrog. adv. whence?
of place, ἠρώτα, τίς εἴη καὶ π. ἔλθοι Od.; ποῖ δὴ καὶ πόθεν; Plat.;—c. gen., τίς πόθεν εἶς ἀνδρῶν; who and from what country art thou? Il.; πόθεν γῆς; Eur.
of origin, πόθεν γένος εὔχεται εἶναι; from what source does he boast that his race is? Od.
in speaking, π. ἄρξωμαι; Aesch.
of the cause, whence? wherefore? Id.; alone, πόθεν; how can it be? impossible! Eur., Ar.

to long for, yearn after what is absent, to miss or regret what is lost, Lat. desiderare, Hom., etc.; ποθεῖς τὸν οὐ παρόντα Ar.; π. τὰς ἐν τῆι νεότητι ἡδονάς Plat.:—Pass., ὦ ποθουμένη (sc. Εἰρήνη) Ar.
of things, to require, ποθεῖ ἡ ἀπόκρισις ἐρώτησιν τοιάνδε Plat.
c. inf. to be anxious to do, Eur.; τὸ νοσοῦν ποθεῖ σε ξυμπαραστάτην λαβεῖν my sickness needs to take thee as an assistant, Soph.
absol., τὸ ποθοῦν one's desiring, one's longing, Id.
as Dep., ποθουμένη φρήν the longing soul, Id.
fond desire for one, ἐμεῖο ποθὴν ἀπεόντος ἔχουσιν Il.; σῇ ποθῇ from longing after thee, Id.
want of a thing, c. gen., Od.
enclit, adv., poet. for του, anywhere or somewhere, Il., Soph.
