of Time, αἴ κέ ποθι Ζεὺς δῷσι if ever Zeus grant, Il.: at length, Od.
indefinite, soever, haply, probably, Hom.
interrog. adv. where? Od., Soph.;—c. gen., πόθι Νύσας; in what part of Nysa? Eur.
for ποῖ; whither? Anth.
love-stricken, Anth.
a longing, yearning, fond desire or regret (for something absent or lost), Lat. desiderium, Hom., etc.
c. gen. desire or regret for a person or thing, Id.; so, δὸς π. yearning after thee, Od.; τοὐμῷ πόθῳ Soph.
love, desire, Hes., etc.

entry.etym: Att. Poets often use the penult. short, as ποιῶ, ποιεῖν, etc., which are often written ποῶ, ποεῖν, etc., as in Lat. poeta, poesis.
the perfect passive is also used in middle sense
entry.sense: Used in two general senses, to make and to do.

to make, produce, create, in Hom. often of building, π. δῶμα, τεῖχος, etc.; of smith's work, π. σάκος Il.; of works of art, Id., etc.; ποιεῖν τι ἀπὸ ξύλου to make something of wood, Hdt.; π. πλοῖα ἐξ ἀκάνθης Id.; so, c. gen., π. νηὸν λίθου Id.; φοίνικος αἱ θύραι πεποιημέναι Xen.:—Mid., οἰκία ποιήσασθαι to build them houses, Il.; also, to have a thing made, get it made, Hdt., Dem.
to make, create, ἕτερον φίλιππον ποιήσετε Dem.

of Poets, to compose, write, (old English to make), Lat. carmina facere, Hdt., attic:—also, to make or represent in poetry, Ὅμηρος Ἀχιλλέα πεποίηκε ἀμείνω Ὀδυσσέως Plat.: to describe in verse, Id.: to put into verse, Id.
to bring to pass, bring about, cause, Hom., etc.: c. acc. et inf. to cause or bring about that . . , Od., etc.

of sacrifices, and the like, π. ἱρά, like ἕρδειν, Lat. sacra facere, Hdt., Xen., Thuc., etc.; π. Ἴσθμια to hold the Isthmian games, Xen.; π. ἐκκλησίαν (as we say, to make a house), Thuc.:—Mid. in same sense, but implying indirect action, ἀγορὴν ποιήσατο Il.

of war and peace, πόλεμον ποιεῖν to cause a war, but, π. ποιεῖσθαι to make war (on one's own part), Xen.;—so, εἰρήνην π. to bring about a peace (for others); but, εἰρήνην ποιεῖσθαι to make peace (for oneself), etc.

the Mid. is often used periphr. with Nouns, ποιεῖσθαι ὁδοιπορίην for ὁδοιπορεῖν, π. πλόον for πλέειν, θαῦμα π. for θαυμάζειν, ὀργὴν π. for ὀργίζεσθαι, Hdt. etc.:— π. λόγον τινός to make account of . . , Id.; but, τοὺς λόγους π. to hold a conference, Thuc.

with an adj. as predic. to make so and so, ποιεῖν τινα ἄφρονα to make one senseless, Od.; δῶρα ὄλβια ποιεῖν to make them blest, i. e. prosper them, Id.; π. τοὺς Μήδους ἀσθενεῖς Xen.:—so with a Subst., ποιεῖν τινα βασιλῆα Od.; Ἀθηναῖον π. τινα Thuc.:—Mid., ποιεῖσθαί τινα ἄλοχον or ἄκοιτιν to take her to oneself as wife, Il.; ποιεῖσθαί τινα υἱόν to make him one's son, i. e. to adopt him as son (cf. εἰσποιέω), Id., attic:—also, ἑωυτοῦ ποιεῖσθαί τι to make a thing one's own, Hdt.
to put, π. τι ἐνὶ φρεσί τινι Hom.; π. τι ἐπὶ νόον τινί Hdt.
in war, π. τινας ὑπό τινι to bring under the power of . . , Dem.:—Mid., ποιεῖσθαι ὑπ’ ἑωυτῶι Hdt.; ποιεῖσθαί τινας ἐς τὸ συμμαχικόν Id., etc.

in Mid. to hold, deem, consider, reckon, esteem a thing as . . , συμφορὴν ποιεῖσθαί τι to take it for a visitation, Id.; δεινὸν ποιεῖσθαί τι, Lat. aegre ferre, Id.; μέγα π., c. inf., to deem it a great matter that . . , Id.; οὐκ ἀνάσχετον π. τι Thuc., etc.:—often with Preps., δι’ οὐδενὸς π. τι to hold as naught, Soph.;—ἐν ἐλαφρῶι, ἐν ὁμοίωι π. Hdt.; ἐν σμικρῶι, ἐν ὀργῆι Dem.;—παρ’ ὀλίγον, παρ’ οὐδὲν π. τι Xen.;—περὶ πολλοῦ, περὶ πλείονος, περὶ πλείστου ποιεῖσθαί τι attic
to put the case assume, that . . , Hdt., Xen.:—Pass., οἱ φιλοσοφώτατοι ποιούμενοι those who are reputed . . , Plat.
of Time, οὐ π. χρόνον to make no long time, i. e. not to delay, Dem.; τὴν νύκτα ἐφ’ ὅπλοις ποιεῖσθαι to spend it under arms, Thuc.
to do, much like πράσσω, Hom., etc.; οὐδὲν ἂν ὧν νυνὶ πεποίηκεν ἔπραξεν Dem.; Σπαρτιητικὰ ποιέειν to act like a Spartan, Hdt.; προσταχθὲν π. Soph., etc.
c. acc. dupl. to do something to another, κακά or ἀγαθὰ ποιεῖν τινά Hdt., etc.; also εὖ, κακῶς π. τινά Xen., etc.:—also c. dat. pers., ἵππωι τἀναντία π. Id.; so in Mid., φίλα ποιεῖσθαί τινι Hdt.

with an adv., ὧδε ποίησον do thus, Id.; ποίει ὅπως βούλει Xen.;—so with a partic., εὖ ἐποίησας ἀπικόμενος Hdt., etc.:— καλῶς ποιῶν is sometimes almost Adverbial, καλῶς ποιοῦντες πράττετε Dem.; εὖ ποιοῦν fortunately, Id.

absol. to be doing, to do or act, ποιέειν ἢ παθέειν to do or have done to one, Hdt.:—of medicine, to work, operate, Plat.; so, ἡ εὔνοια παρὰ πολὺ ἐποίει ἐς τοὺς Λακεδαιμονίους good-will made greatly for the Lacedaemonians, Thuc.; so impers., ἐπὶ πολὺ ἐποίει τῆς δόξης τοῖς μὲν ἠπειρώταις εἶναι it was the general character of the one to be landsmen, etc., Id.
grassy, rich in grass, Hom., Soph.: neut. pl. contr. ποιᾶντα Pind.
anything made or done; hence,
a work, Hdt., Plat.
a poetical work, poem, Plat.
a deed, act, Id.
a making, fabrication, creation, production, opp. to πρᾶξις (action), Hdt., attic
of poetry, ἡ π. τῆς τραγῳδίας, etc., Plat.: absol. poetic faculty, poesy, art of poetry, Hdt., Ar., etc.
a poetic composition, poem, Thuc., Plat.
= εἰσποίησις, adoption, Dem.
to be made or done, Hdt., attic; τὸ ποιητέον what must be done, Thuc.
one who makes, a maker, Xen., etc.
the maker of a poem, a poet, Hdt., etc.
generally, a writer, Plat.
capable of making, creative, productive, Arist.
fitted for a poet, poetical, Plat.;— ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη), the art of poetry, poetry, Id.:—adv. -κῶς, Id.
made, in the sense of εὖ ποιητός, well-made, δόμοις ἐνὶ ποιητοῖσι Hom.:— made, created, opp. to self-existent, Theogn.
made into something, esp. made into a son, adopted, Plat.; π. πολῖται factitious citizens, not so born, Arist.
made by oneself, i. e. invented, feigned, Pind., Eur.
a poetess, Luc.
with broidered reins, Pind.
with spangled garb, νὺξ π., in reference to the stars, Aesch.
a marking with various colours, embroidering, embroidery, Plat.: in pl. pieces of broidery, Xen.
varied aspect, diversity, Plat.
versatility, subtlety, craft, Dem.
to work in various colours, to broider, work in embroidery, Eur.; χορὸν ποίκιλλε he wrought a χορός of cunning workmanship, Il.
to embroider a robe, Pind., Plat., etc.
generally, to diversify, vary, Eur., Plat.:—of style, to embellish, Pind.:— to speak as in riddles, Soph.
a broidered stuff, brocade, Aesch.
broidered work, broidery, Hom.
generally, a variety, diversity, Plat.
of changeful counsel, wily-minded, Hes., Anth.

entry.note: ποικῐλό-γηρυς, doric ποικῐλό-γᾱρυς, υος, ὁ, ἡ,
entry.sense: of varied voice, many-toned, Pind.
with variegated neck, Anth.
with pied skin, Eur.
with spotted hair, dappled, Eur.
on rich-worked throne, Sapph.
full of various wiles, wily-minded, Hom.
full of various devices, Anth.
of varied form, variegated, Ar.
of various discourse, Anth.
with back of various hues, Pind., Eur.
with wings of changeful hue, Eur.
many-coloured, spotted, mottled, pied, dappled, of leopards, fawns, Hom., etc.
of robes, wrought in various colours, broidered, Il., etc.; ἐν ποικίλοις κάλλεσιν, of a rich carpet, Aesch.; so, τὰ ποικίλα Id.
of metal work, τεύχεα π. χαλκῷ in-wrought with brass, Il., etc.: but, π. δεσμός intricate, Od.
ἡ στοὰ ἡ ποικίλη, the Poecile or great hall at Athens adorned with paintings of the battle of Marathon by Polygnotus, Aeschin., etc.
metaph. changeful, various, diversified, manifold, Aesch., Plat.;— π. μῆνες the changing months, Pind.
of Art, π. ὕμνος a song of changeful strain or full of diverse art, Id.; so, ποικίλον κιθαρίζων Id.
intricate, complex, Hdt., Soph., etc.: —adv., ποικίλως αὐδώμενος speaking in double sense, Soph.
of abstruse knowledge, intricate, subtle, ποικίλον τι εἰδέναι Eur.; οὐδὲν π. nothing abstruse or difficult, Plat.:—so, of persons, subtle, wily, Aesch.; π. γὰρ ἁνήρ Ar.
changeable, changeful, unstable, Arist.:— ποικίλως ἔχειν to be different, Xen.
of a ship, with variegated prow, Soph.
delighting by variety, Anth.
manifold, Anth.
twittering in various notes, Theocr.
accompanied by the various notes of the lyre, Pind.
one must work in embroidery, Plat.
a broiderer, Aeschin.
of perplexed and juggling song, Soph.
to be shepherd, ἐπ’ ὄεσσι over the sheep, Il.: c. acc. to tend a flock, Od., Eur., etc.; absol., Theocr.:—Pass., like νέμομαι, to roam the pastures, of flocks, Il., Eur.
in Aesch., πᾶς πεποίμανται τόπος every place has been traversed (as by a shepherd seeking after stray sheep).
metaph. to tend, cherish, mind, Pind., Aesch.
like βουκολέω, to beguile, Theocr.: generally, to deceive, Eur.
a herd: metaph. an army, Aesch.
of or for a shepherd, Theocr.: —ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη), Plat.
voc. ποιμήν, a herdsman or shepherd, Hom.: after Hom. always a shepherd, Eur., Plat., etc.
metaph. a shepherd of the people, of Agamemnon, Hom., etc.; generally, a captain, chief, Soph., Eur.
of a flock or herd, Il., Hes.
a flock, Od.; properly of sheep (cf. ποιμήν), Hes., Hdt.; of a ram, Eur.
metaph. of persons, Aesch.
syncop. for ποιμένιον, = ποίμνη, a flock, Hdt., Soph., etc.
metaph. of disciples, NTest.
ὑμέναιος π. a shepherd's marriage song, Eur.
punishing, avenging, Anth.
an avenger, punisher, Aesch.
to avenge, punish:—Mid. to avenge oneself on another, c. acc., Eur.

quit-money for blood spilt, paid by the slayer to the kinsmen of the slain, (old Engl. were-gild); c. gen. pers., δῶχ’ υἷος ποινήν gave ransom or were-gild for the son, Il., etc.:—generally, a price paid, satisfaction, retribution, requital, penalty, Lat. poena, ἀπετίσατο ποινὴν ἑτάρων exacted penalty for his comrades, Od.; δυώδεκα κούρους, ποινὴν Πατρόκλοιο in retribution for the death of Patroclus, Il.; τῶν ποινήν in return for these things, Id.; ποινὴν τῖσαι Ξέρξῃ τῶν κηρύκων ἀπολομένων to give Xerxes satisfaction for the death of his heralds, Hdt.; in attic the pl. is more common; ποινὰς τῖσαι, δοῦναι to pay penalties, Lat. dare poenas, Aesch., etc.; ποινὰς λαβεῖν to exact them, Lat. sumere poenas, Eur.
in good sense, recompense, reward for a thing, τινος Pind.
as the result of the quit-money, redemption, release, Id.
personified, the goddess of Vengeance, Aesch., etc.
avenging, Anth.
avenging, punishing, Soph.
in good sense, bringing return or recompense, Pind.
to gather corn into sheaves, Theocr.
feeding on grass or herbs, Aesch.
Indef. adj., of a certain nature, kind or quality, Plat.

of what nature? of what sort? Lat. qualis? used in questions:—in Hom. expressing surprise and anger, ποῖον τὸν μῦθον ἔειπες what manner of speech hast thou spoken! ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων! ποῖον ἔειπες! etc.
ποῖος οὐ; interrog., equiv. to ἕκαστος affirm., Hdt., Soph.
in attic, often with Art., τὸ ποῖον φάρμακον; Aesch.; τὰ ποῖα τρύχη; Ar.; τὸ ποῖον; Plat., etc.
ποῖός τις; makes the question less definite, κοῖόν μέ τινα νομίζουσιν εἶναι; Hdt.; ποῖ’ ἄττα; Plat.; τὰ τοῖ’ ἄττα; Xen.
ποίᾳ, ionic κοίῃ, as Adv., = πῶς; Lat. quomodo? Hdt., Ar.
like ὁποῖος, in indirect questions, διδάξω ποῖα χρὴ λέγειν Aesch. etc. (ποῖος, πόσος must be referred to a primitive *πός, as the correlat. Adjs. οἷος, ὅσος to ὅς.）
quality, Plat., Arist.
enclit. adv. somewhither, Soph., Ar., etc.

entry.etym: υ of pres. long before a long syll., short before a short syll
entry.sense: to be out of breath from haste, to puff or bustle about, Lat. satagere, exert oneself, be busy, Hom.; aor1 part. with another Verb. δῶμα κορήσατε ποιπνύσασαι make haste and sweep the house, Od.
interrog. adv. whether? Lat. quo? theogn., etc.
c. gen., ποῖ χθονός; ποῖ γῆς; to what spot of earth? Aesch.; ποῖ φροντίδος; ποῖ φρενῶν; ποῖ γνώμης; Soph.
to what end? in what point? ποῖ τελευτᾷ; Aesch.
a blowing, snorting, Aesch.
to blow, snort: c. acc. to puff out, Anth.
like grass, Hdt.
to shear wool: Mid. to shear for oneself, τρίχας ἐποκίξατο (doric aor1) Theocr.
Pass. to be clothed with wool, Anth.
wool in its raw state, a fleece, Il., Eur., etc.: a lock or tuft of wool, Soph.
proverb. in heterocl. acc. of 3rd decl., εἰς ὄνου πόκας to an ass shearing, i. e. to no-place, Ar.
of or belonging to the Polemarch; —τὸ πολεμάρχειον his residence, Xen.
to be Polemarch, Hdt., Xen.
one who begins or leads the war, a leader, chieftain, Aesch.
a Polemarch,
at Athens, the third archon, who presided in the court in which the causes of the μέτοικοι were tried, Ar.;—in earlier times he was general-in-chief, as at Marathon, Hdt.
at Sparta, a kind of brigadier, Id., Thuc., etc.
at Thebes officers of chief rank after the Boeotarchs, Xen.
similarly at Mantineia, and in other states, Thuc.
to be at war or go to war, make war, τινί with one, Hdt., etc.; ἐπί τινα, πρός τινα Xen.
to fight, do battle, ἀπὸ τῶν ἵππων Plat.; ἀπὸ καμήλων Xen.
generally, to quarrel, wrangle, dispute with one, Soph., etc.
c. acc. to make war upon: Pass. to have war made upon one, to be treated as enemies, Thuc., Xen.
c. acc. cogn., πόλεμον πολ. Plat.:—Pass., ὁ πόλεμος οὕτως ἐπολεμήθη Xen.; so, ὅσα ἐπολεμήθη whatever hostilities passed, Id.
war-sustaining, Pind.

entry.etym: ionic adj.,for no attic form in -ειος exists
entry.sense: warlike, πολεμήια ἔργα Il.; τεύχεα Id.; πολεμήια= πολέμια, ων, τά, Hdt.
one must go to war, Arist.:—pl. πολεμητέα, Thuc.
epic πτολεμίζω, fut. ίξω, poet. form of πολεμέω, to wage war, make war, fight, τινί with one, Hom.; π. ἄντα τινός, ἐναντίβιόν τινος Il.:—also in Mid., Pind.
to fight with, absol. ῥηίτεροι πολεμίζειν Il.
of or for war, Thuc.; ἀσπὶς πολεμικωτάτη most fit for service, Xen.
ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη), the art of war, war, Plat.: —τὰ πολεμικά warlike exercises, Thuc., Xen.
τὸ πολεμικόν the signal for battle, Xen.
the military class, opp. to the civilian, Arist.
of persons, skilled in war, warlike, Thuc., etc.
like an enemy, stirring up hostility, Xen.:—adv., πολεμικῶς ἔχειν to be hostile, Id.
of or belonging to war, Pind., Aesch., etc.: —τὰ πολέμια whatever belongs to war, war and its business, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
of or like an enemy, hostile, Pind., Trag., etc.: —π. τινι hostile to one, Hdt., etc.:—as Subst. an enemy, Hdt., attic; οἱ π. the enemy, Thuc.: —τὸ π. hostility, Id.
generally, opposed, adverse, Hdt., Plat.
of or from the enemy, Aesch., Thuc.; πολέμια, ων, τά, enemy's wares, contraband, Ar.: —ἡ πολεμία (sc. γῆ, χώρα), the enemy's country, Xen.
adv. -ίως, in hostile manner, Thuc.
of or for a warrior, Hdt.; βοή, θώραξ π. Ar.; π. ἅρματα war- chariots, Hdt.; ἐλᾶν τὰ πολεμιστήρια to drive the war-chariots, a military game, Ar.
τὰ πολεμιστήρια, = τὰ πολεμικά, Xen.
a warrior, combatant, Il., Pind., etc.
π. ἵππος a war-horse, charger, Theocr.
raising the din of war, Batr.
finishing war, Aesch.

entry.etym: a compd. of πόλεμος, Λάμαχος, Ἀχαϊκός
entry.sense: a very Lamachus in war, Ar.
to the war, into the fight, Il.
to stir up war, Xen.
engaging in war, Arist.

battle, fight, war, Hom., etc.; πόλεμον αἴρεσθαί τινι to levy war against another, Aesch.; π. θέσθαι τινί Eur.; π. ἀναιρεῖσθαι, κινεῖν, ἐγείρειν, καθιστάναι, ἐπάγειν to begin a war; π. ποιεῖσθαι to make war, — opp. to π. ἀναπαύειν, καταλύεσθαι to put an end to it, make peace, all in attic
wasting by war, Aesch.
to make hostile, make an enemy of, τινά:—Mid., πῶς οὐ πολεμώσεσθε αὐτούς; surely you will make them your enemies, Thuc.:— Pass. to be made an enemy of, become an enemy, Id.

entry.etym: πολεύω like πολέω, only in pres.
entry.sense: intr. to turn about, Lat. versari, κατὰ ἄστυ π. to go about the city, i. e. live therein, Od.
trans. to turn up the soil with the plough, Soph.

entry.etym: πολέω like πολεύω, only in pres.
entry.sense: to go about, range over, νῆσον Αἴαντος πολεῖ Aesch.; τί σὺ τῆιδε πολεῖς; Eur.:—so in Mid., Aesch.
trans. to turn up the earth with the plough, to plough, Hes.
Pass. to grow white, Aesch.
grayness of hair, Menand.
ruler of a city, Pind., Eur.
guardian of the city, epith. of Athena in her oldest temple on the Acropolis of Athens, as distinguished from Ἀθ. Παρθένος, Hdt., Soph.
to build a city, to build, Il.:—Pass., Ἴλιος πεπόλιστο (epic 3rd sg. plup.) Id.; so Hdt.
χωρίον πολίζειν to colonise a country by building a city, Xen.
a citizen, Il., Hdt., Aesch.; a fellow-citizen, countryman, Hdt.
as adj., ψάμαθοι πολιήτιδος ἀκτᾶς sands on my country's shore, Eur.
into or to the city, Il.
grayhaired, Strab.
with gray hair on the temples, i.e. just beginning to be gray, Il., Hes.
to hem in a city, blockade, beleaguer, besiege, Hdt., attic:—Pass. to be besieged, in a state of siege, Hdt.; of Scamander, to be dammed back, Plat.
metaph. to be besieged, pestered, Xen.
to be besieged, Xen.
taker of cities, name of Demetrius son of Antigonus, Plut.
of or for besieging, Polyb.
a besieging, siege, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
metaph. a besieging, pestering, Plut.
gray, grizzled, grisly, of wolves, of iron, of the sea, Il.

mostly of hair, gray or hoary from age, Hom.; πολιοί gray-haired men, Od., Soph., etc.:—absol., αἱ πολιαί (sc. τρίχες) Pind.; ἅμα ταῖς πολιαῖς κατιούσαις as the gray hairs come down (i.e. from the temples to the beard), Ar.; π. δάκρυον ἐμβαλών an old man's tear, Eur.
metaph. hoary, venerable, Id.
like λευκός, bright, clear, serene, Hes., Eur.
protecting a city, Eur.:—mostly like Πολιεύς, Πολιάς, of the guardian deity of a city, Hdt., Aesch.
white-coloured, white, Eur.
a city, town, Hdt., attic
the community, Soph.

entry.etym: gen. πόλεως dissyll. in attic Poets
ionic and doric πόλιος dissyll. in Il.
entry.sense: doric πολίεσι:—acc. πόλεις, πόλιας:— a city, Hom., Hes., etc.; πόλις ἄκρη and ἀκροτάτη, = ἀκρόπολις, the citadel, Il.: this at Athens was often called simply πόλις, while the rest of the city was called ἄστυ, Thuc., etc.:—the name of the city was often added in gen., Ἰλίου π., Ἄργους π. the city of . . , Aesch., etc.; also in appos., ἡ Μένδη π. Thuc.
one's city or country, Od., etc.
when πόλις and ἄστυ are joined, the former is the body of citizens, the latter their dwellings, Il.; ὧν πόλις ἀνάριθμος ὄλλυται, where πόλις = a number of citizens, Soph.:—hence,
the state (πολιτεία), Hes., Pind., attic: esp. a free state, republic, Soph., Xen., etc.
the right of citizenship, like Lat. civitas, Ar., Dem.
managing or ruling a city, Aesch.; π. βιοτά a life of social order, Id.
guarding cities, Hhymn.
poetic for πολιοῦχος, Aesch.
dwelling in the city, Id.
a civic magistrate, at Thessalonica, NTest.
the condition and rights of a citizen, citizenship, Lat. civitas, Hdt., Thuc., etc.; πολιτείαν δοῦναί τινι Xen.
the life of a citizen, civic life, Dem.
as a concrete, the body of citizens, Arist.
the life and business of a statesman, government, administration, Ar., Thuc., etc.:—in a collective sense, the measures of a government, Dem.
civil polity, the condition or constitution of a state, Thuc., etc.:— a form of government, Plat., etc.
a republic, commonwealth, Xen., etc.
the business of government, an act of administration, Dem.; ἔν τε τοῖς κατὰ τὴν πόλιν πολιτεύμασι καὶ ἐν τοῖς Ἑλληνικοῖς both in my home and foreign policy, Id.
the government, Arist.
= πολιτεία III, Id.
to live as a citizen or freeman, live in a free state, Thuc., etc.
to have a certain form of polity, conduct the government, Id.:—Pass., of the state, to be governed, Plat., Xen., etc.; τὰ αὐτοῖς πεπολιτευμένα the measures of their administration, Dem.
Dep. like the Act. to be a free citizen, live as such, Xen., etc.
to take part in the government, Thuc., Dem.: to meddle with politics, Plat.

c. acc. to administer or govern, Dem.; π. πόλεμον ἐκ πολέμου to make perpetual war the principle of government, Aeschin.: absol. to conduct the government, Ar., Dem.; οἱ πολιτευόμενοι the ministers, Dem.
to have a certain form of government, Plat., Aeschin.
a member of a city or state (πόλις), a citizen, freeman, Lat. civis, Hom., etc.
like Lat. civis, a fellow-citizen, Hdt., Aesch., etc.
θεοὶ πολῖται = πολιοῦχοι, Aesch.
of, for, or relating to citizens, Plat., etc.

befitting a citizen, like a citizen, civic, civil, Lat. civilis, Thuc.; πολιτικωτέρα ἐγένετο ἡ ὀλιγαρχία more constitutional, Arist.:— adv., πολιτικῶς like a citizen, in a constitutional manner, Lat. civiliter, Dem.
consisting of citizens, τὸ πολιτικόν, = οἱ πολῖται, the community, Hdt., Thuc.: the civic force, opp. to οἱ σύμμαχοι, Xen., etc.
living in a community, Arist.
of or befitting a statesman, statesmanlike, Xen., Plat.

belonging to the state or its administration, political, Lat. publicus, Thuc.: —ἡ πολιτική (sub. τέχνη), the art of government, ἡ π. ἐπιστήμη or ἡ π. alone, the science of politics, Plat.: —τὰ πολιτικά, state-affairs, public matters, government, Thuc., etc.
civil, municipal, opp. to natural or general, Dem.
generally, of or for public life, public, opp. to κατ’ ἰδίας, Thuc., Xen.

entry.etym: fem. of πολίτης, Soph., Eur., etc.

entry.sense: one who watches citizens; οἱ π., in Larissa, the chief magistrates, Arist.
a small town, Plut.
grayish, whitish, Luc.
of Time, many times, often, oft, Il., etc.; c. gen., π. τοῦ μηνός often in the month, Xen.
of Degree and Number, π. μύριοι many tens of thousands, Plat.
τὸ π. mostly, for the most part, Pind.: very much, altogether, Theocr.
in attic, after εἰ, ἐάν, ἄν, perhaps, perchance, Lat. si forte, Ar., Plat.; so, μὴ πολλάκις, Lat. ne forte, Thuc., etc.
many times as many, many times more or larger, Hdt.
πολλ. ἢ . . , or ἤπερ . . , many times as many as . . , many times more or larger than . . , Id., Plat.; so c. gen., Hdt., Thuc., etc.:— neut. pl. as adv., Xen.
to multiply, Plat.
multiplication, Plat.
manifold, many times as long, Plat.; ὄνομα πολλαπλοῦν multicompound, opp. to ἁπλοῦν, Arist.
metaph., ἀνὴρ π. not simple and straightforward, Plat.
many times, often, Hdt., Xen.
in divers manners, Hdt., Soph., etc.
from many places or sides, Thuc., etc.
from or for many reasons, Id.
in many places, Xen.
towards many sides, into many parts or quarters, Thuc.; c. gen., π. τῆς Ἀρκαδίας Xen.
in many places, Eur., Plat.
c. gen., π. τῆς γῆς Plat.
= πολλαχῆ, many times, often, Hdt., etc.
in many ways, Dem., etc.
many tens of times, Ar.
many times smaller, Arist.
one of many, Lat. unus e multis, i.e. the smallest, least, Thuc., etc.:— adv., δευτέρως καὶ πολλοστῶς in a very small degree, Arist.
of Time, πολλοστῷ χρόνῳ after a very long time, Ar., Dem.
a pivot, hinge, axis:
the axis of the globe, Plat., etc.
the sphere which revolves on this axis, i. e. the vault of heaven, the sky or firmament, Lat. polus, Aesch., Eur.
the orbit of a star, Anth.
land turned up with the plough, Xen.
a concave dial (called πόλος from being shaped like the vault of heaven), Hdt., Anth.
catching much game, Anth.
conquering in many contests, Luc.
abounding in goats, Anth.
much-praised, or full of wise speech and lore, Hom., Eur.
much-rushing, impetuous, furious, Hom.; κάματος π. weariness caused by much fighting, Il.
to be full of men, to be populous, Thuc.
of places, with many men, full of men, Aesch.
of persons, numerous, Id.
much-blossoming, blooming, Od.
a large population, multitude of people, Xen.
full of people, populous, Thuc., etc.
much-frequented, crowded, Luc.
numerous, Polyb.
with many men, much-frequented, Eur., Ar.
γυνὴ π. wife of many husbands, Aesch.
rich in silver, Hdt.
much-desired, Od.
much-helpful, supplying many wants, Hdt.: —τὸ π. durability, Luc.
with many chariots, Soph.
many-toned, Plat.
with many lambs or sheep, rich in flocks, heterocl. dat. πολύαρνι, Il.
the government of many, Thuc., Xen.
with many joints, Anth.
with many stars, starry, Eur.
with many furrows, Anth.
with many necks, Anth.
much-dipped, Aesch.
very deep, Hom.
much-nourishing, Pind.
much or all nourishing, Hom., Hes., in epic form πουλυβότειρα.
much-nourishing, Aesch.
abounding in grapes, Eur.
much-counselling, Hom.
rich in oxen, Il.
with many nooses, Eur.
with much milk; poet. Sup. πουλυγαλακτοτάτη Anth.
much-cheering, delightful, gladsome, Il., Hes.
abounding in new wine, Anth.
many-tongued, δρῦς π. the vocal (oracular) oak of Dodona, Soph.; π. βοή an oft-repeated or loud-voiced cry, Id.
much-bent, much-twisting, Pind.: curling, frizzled, σέλινον Theocr.
very sagacious, Plat.
well-known, Pind.
well-bolted, νῆες Hes.
Pass. to multiply, Luc.
fecundity, Plat.
producing many at a birth, prolific, Hdt., etc.
much wrought, richly dight, of metal work, Hom.; of embroidery, Hes.
act. working with much art, very skilful, Il.
of or with many tears: hence,
much-wept, tearful, Il., Aesch.
of persons, much-weeping, Eur., Ar.
much wept or lamented, Il.
very lamentable, tearful, Od., Aesch.
act. much-weeping, Eur.
causing great expense, Hdt., Xen.
of a person, extravagant, Xen.
with many ridges, Il.
the all-receiver, i. e. Hades, Hhymn.
with many trees, abounding in trees, heterocl. dat. pl. πολυδένδρεσσι Eur.
much-seeing, Hes.
fastened with many bonds, Od.
Pollux, one of the Dioscuri, son of Leda, brother of Castor, Hom.
Com. Dim. of Πολυδεύκης, Luc.
having many lawsuits, litigious, Strab.
much-whirling, Anth.
very thirsty, Il.
much-driven, Aesch.
having various opinions, Anth.
open-handedness, Xen.
richly dowered, Hom.
polyhedral, Plut.
of many kinds, Thuc., Plat.
diversity of kind, Plat.
yielding much oil, Xen.
much convoluted, πολ. ἁδονά the pleasure of the mazy dance, Eur.
much-praised, Xen.
much-speaking, Aesch.
much-loved, Xen.
much-working, Theocr., Anth.
of many years, full of years, Eur.
much-wished-for, much-desired, Orac. ap. Hdt., Aesch.
full of jealousy and rivalry, Soph.
much-desired, longed-for, loved, Id.
much envied, Eur.
many-benched, νηῦς Il.
much-speaking, Anth.
having heard much, much-learned, Plat.
of many days, Plut.
much-loved, very lovely, Od.
many-toned, of the nightingale's voice, Od.: much or loud sounding, Il.
loud-sounding, Eur.
much-confident, Hom.
having seen much, c. gen., Plat.
of or belonging to many gods, Aesch.
very warm or hot, Plut.
abounding in wild beasts, Eur.
feeding many, Aesch.
lamentable, Anth.
much-wailing, Aesch.
with much hair, Anth.
with much noise, clamorous, Aesch.
much-spoken-of, well known, notorious, Plat.
with many doors or openings, Luc.
with many leaves, of tablets, Eur.
abounding in sacrifices, Pind., etc.
much knowledge or wisdom, in pl., νόου πολυϊδρείῃσι Od.
of much knowledge, wisdom, shrewdness, Od., Ar.
rich in horses, Il.
very learned, Anth.
abounding in fish, Strab.: also πολυ-ίχθυος, Hhymn.
drying or parching exceedingly, δίψαι Il.
very dry, Anth.
much-burning, Anth.
the government of many emperors at once, Plut.
very miserable, Anth.
much bent, Anth.
much-slaughtering, θυσίαι π. βοτῶν slaughter of many beasts, Aesch.
with much smoke, smoky, Eur.
many-headed, Anth.
abundance of fruit, Xen.
rich in fruit, Od., Hdt., attic
great craft, πολυκερδείῃσιν Od.
very crafty or wily, Od.
many-horned, π. φόνος the slaughter of much horned cattle, Soph.
well-stitched, Il.
many-headed, Plat.
full of care, grievous, Od.
very deadly, Anth.
full of monsters, Theocr.
much lamented, Aesch., Eur.
act. much lamenting, Mosch.
far-famed, Pind.
far-famed, Anth.
with many benches of rowers, in dat., νηὶ πολυκλήιδι, νηυσὶ πολυκλήισι Hom.; acc. νῆα πολυκλήιδα Hes.
of a large lot, with a large portion of land, Od., Theocr.
called from many a land, of the Trojan allies, Il.
much-dashing, Od. Hes.
pass. washed by many a wave, Hes.
much-wrought, wrought with much toil, epith. of iron, as distinguished from copper, Il.; π. θάλαμος Od.
laborious, τέχνη Anth.
with many mountain-spurs, mountainous, Il.
common to many or to all, Pind., Soph.
the rule of many, Il.
wide-ruling, Aesch. ap. Ar.
oft-diving, μέλη π., of the frogs, Ar.
many-headed, Eur.
of or belonging to Polycrates, Arist.
very mighty, Aesch.
loud-ringing, Hhymn.
with many springs, Anth.
with many possessions, exceeding rich, Il., Soph.; c. gen., π. βίου Eur.
of large possessions, wealthy, Eur.
much-slaying, murderous, Aesch., Eur.
much-praised, very glorious, Anth.
swelling with many waves, Solon.
much-lamenting, Theogn.

entry.etym: the ionic declension πολλός, ή, όν is retained by the attic in all cases, except the nom. and acc. masc. and neut. Hom. uses both ionic and attic forms.
entry.sense: of Number, many, opp. to ὀλίγος, Hom., etc.;— with nouns of multitude, πουλὺς ὅμιλος Od.; πολλὸν πλῆθος Hdt., etc.:—also of anything often repeated, πολλὸν ἦν τοῦτο τὸ ἔπος Id.; πολλὸς αἰνεόμενος Id.; τούτῳ πολλῷ χρήσεται τῷ λόγῳ often, Dem.

of Size, Degree, Force, much, mighty, great, Il., etc.; π. ὕπνος deep sleep, Od.; π. ὑμέναιος a loud song, Il., etc.:—rarely of a single person, μέγας καὶ πολλὸς ἐγένεο Hdt.; ἢν πολλῇ ῥυῇ if she flow with full stream, metaph. from a river, Eur.; πολλῷ ῥέοντι Dem.; from the wind, πολὺς ἔπνει was blowing strong, Id.; often with a Partic., πολλὸς ἦν λισσόμενος he was all intreaties, Lat. multus erat in precando, Hdt.; so, π. ἦν ἐν τοῖσι λόγοισι Id., etc.
of Value or Worth, πολέος or πολλοῦ ἄξιος Hom.; πολλοῦ and περὶ πολλοῦ ποιεῖσθαί τι, Lat. magni facere, cf. περί A.IV; ἐπὶ πολλῷ at a high price, Dem.
of Space, large, wide, wide-stretched, π. χώρη, πεδίον Il., Hes., etc.; πόντος, πέλαγος Hes., etc.;— πολλὸς ἔκειτο he lay outstretched, Il.;— π. κέλευθος a far way, Aesch., etc.
of Time, long, πολὺν χρόνον Hom., etc.; πολλοῦ χρόνου Ar.; ἐκ πολλοῦ Thuc.; ἔτι πολλῆς νυκτός, Lat. multa nocte, while still quite night, Id.
Special usages:
partitive c. gen., e. g. πολλοὶ Τρώων for πολλοὶ Τρῶες, Il.; πολλὸν σαρκός for πολλὴ σάρξ, Od.; in Prose, the adj. generally takes the gender of the gen., τῆς γῆς οὐ πολλήν Thuc.
joined to another adj. by καί, πολέες τε καὶ ἐσθλοί many men and good, Il.; π. καὶ πονηρά Xen.; μεγάλα καὶ π. Dem.

with the Art., of persons or things well known, Ἑλένα μία τὰς πολλὰς ψυχὰς ὀλέσας’ those many lives, Aesch.; ὡς ὁ πολλὸς λόγος the common report, Hdt.:—esp. οἱ πολλοί the many, i. e. the greater number, Thuc.; hence, like τὸ πλῆθος, the people, the commonalty, Id.; εἷς τῶν πολλῶν one of the multitude, Dem.
τὺ πολύ, c. gen., τῆς στρατιῆς τὸ πολλόν Hdt.; τῶν λογάδων τὸ πολύ Thuc.; but also, ὁ στρατὸς ὁ πολλός Hdt.
τὰ πολλά the most, Od., etc.
the pl. πολλά is used with Verbs in the sense of very much, too much, πολλὰ πράσσειν = πολυπραγμονεῖν, Eur., Ar.; π. ἔρξαι τινά to do one much harm, Aesch.
πολλάς with Verbs of beating, the Subst. πληγάς being omitted, v. πληγή 1.
Adverbial usages:

neut. πολύ (ionic πολλόν), πολλά, much, very, Hom., etc.; μάλα πολλά Id.; πάνυ πολύ Plat.:—also of repetition, many times, ofttimes, often, much, Hom., etc.:—also with the Art., τὸ πολύ for the most part, Plat.; ὡς τὸ π. Xen.; so, τὰ πολλά, ὡς τὰ π. Thuc.
of Degree, far, very much, Hdt.; so absol. gen. πολλοῦ, very, θρασὺς εἶ πολλοῦ Ar.; πολλοῦ πολύς, πολλοῦ πολλή, πολλοῦ πολύ, much too much, Id.
of Space, a great way, far, οὐ πολλόν Hdt., etc.
of Time, long, Id.
πολύ is often joined with Adjs. and Advs.,
with a comp. to increase its compar. force, πολὺ κάλλιον, μεῖζον, πολλὸν ἀμείνων, παυρότεροι much, far more beautiful, etc., Hom., etc.:—so dat. πολλῷ by far, Hdt., etc.
with a Sup., πολὺ πρῶτος, πολλὸν ἄριστος far the first, etc., Il., etc.:—also, πολλῷ πλεῖστοι Hdt.
in attic with a Positive, ὦ πολλὰ μὲν τάλαινα, πολλὰ δ’ αὖ σοφή Aesch.
with Preps.,
διὰ πολλοῦ at a great distance, V. διά A. II. 2.
ἐκ πολλοῦ from a great distance, Thuc.; for a long time, v. ἐκ II. 1.
ἐπὶ πολύ,
over a great space, far, οὐκ ἐπὶ πολλόν Hdt.
for a long time, long, Thuc.
to a great extent, Plat.; so, ὡς ἐπὶ π. very generally, Thuc.; ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ π. for the most part, Id.
παρὰ πολύ, by far, v. παρά C. I. 5.
περὶ πολλοῦ, v. supr. I. 3.
for comp. πλείων, πλέων; Sup. πλεῖστος, v. sub vocc.
very fruitful, Eur.
rich in grapes, Il., Soph.
rich in ears of corn, Theocr.
with many stories, Strab.
with many stems, Anth.
causing many groans, Anth.
decked with many a wreath, Aesch.; c. gen. wreathed with, δάφνης Soph.
a number of lines, Anth.
in many rows, Strab.
much-sighing, mournful, Od., Aesch.
of things, causing many sighs, mournful, Il., Trag.
convolution, Anth.
much-twisted, Anth.
with many columns, Strab., Plut.
polysyllabic, Luc.
of many shapes, varied in form, Strab.
many-branching, κέλευθα Soph., Arist., Strab.
rich in heaps of corn, Anth.
worth many talents, Luc.
possessing many talents, Id.
much-frightened, Anth.
abundance of children, Arist.
with many children, prolific, Aesch.
extravagance, Hdt., Thuc.
very expensive, very costly, opp. to εὐτελής, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
of persons, spending much, lavish, extravagant, Menand., etc.: —adv. -λῶς, Xen.; Sup. -λέστατα, in the costliest manner, Hdt.
much-delighting, Anth.
skilled in divers arts, Solon.
skill in many arts, Plat.
skilled in many arts, Strab.
highly honoured, most honoured, Ar., Plat.
very costly, Ar.
very costly, Anth., Babr.
worthy of high honour, ap. Hdt.
having borne much, much-enduring, epith. of Ulysses, Hom., Soph.
much-enduring, Hom., Ar.
having borne much, miserable, Od.
much-lacerated, παρειά Anth.
abounding in doves, Il.
much-pierced, full of holes, porous, Od.; of a flute, Anth.
abounding in tripods, Anth.
versatility, craft, Hdt.
much-turned, i. e. much-travelled, much-wandering, Lat. multum jactatus, of Ulysses, Od.
turning many ways, of the polypus, Theogn.
metaph. shifty, versatile, wily, of Hermes, Hhymn., Plat.; τὸ π. τῆς γνώμης their versatility of mind, Thuc.
various, manifold, Thuc.:—of diseases and war, changeful, complicated, Plut.:—adv. -πως in many manners, NTest.
well-fed, Plut.
much-famed in song, Pind.
much sung of, famous, Eur., Ar.
knowing many drugs or charms, Hom.
much-spoken-of, very famous, excellent, Pind.
abounding in songs and legends, Od., Pind.
many-voiced, wordy, Od.; ἐς πολύφημον ἐξενεῖκαι to bring it forth to the many-voiced, i. e. the agora (the "parliament"), Orac. ap. Hdt.
pass. utterly destroyed, Soph.
destroying many, deathful, rife with death or ruin, Pind., Aesch.
abundance of friends, Arist.
dear to many, Pind.
suffering from many love-charms, love-sick, Theocr.
loud-roaring, θάλασσα Hom., etc.
murderous, Eur.
feeding many, bountiful, Il., Hes.
productiveness, Xen.
bearing much, Plat.
that will bear much water, of strong wine: metaph., πολυφόρῳ δαίμονι συγκεκρᾶσθαι to have a fortune that wants tempering, Ar.
very eloquent or wise, Hes.
much-thinking, thoughtful, Anth.
fulness of understanding, great shrewdness, Theogn., Hdt.
much-thinking, thoughtful, ingenious, inventive, Hom.
much-talking, loquacious, Luc.
abounding in copper or brass Hom.
wrought of brass, all-brasen, Id.
wide-yawning, Theocr.
a multitude of hands, i. e. workmen or assistants, Thuc., Xen.
with many hands, many handed, Soph.
with many men, Aesch.
the use of many strings in the lyre, Plat.
many-stringed, Theocr.: many-toned, of the flute, Plat.; also, π. ᾠδαί Eur.; π. γῆρυς the sound of many strings, Id.
to abound in money, Strab.
greatness of wealth, Xen.
useful for many purposes, Arist.
long-existing, of olden time, ancient, Hhymn., Hdt., Xen.
lasting for long, Arist.:—comp. -ώτερος, Plat.; Sup. -ώτατος, Xen.
rich in gold, Hom.; of Aphrodite, Lat. aurea Venus, Hes.
widely diffused, Plut.
spacious, extensive, Luc.
high-heaped, Aesch.
number or diversity of votes, Thuc.
with many pebbles, pebbly, of a river-bed, Orac. ap. Hdt.
with many votes, Luc.
very painful, Theocr.
pass. suffering great pain, Anth.
having many names, Plat.:— worshipped under many names, Hhymn., Soph.
of great name, famous, Hhymn., Hes.
with many meshes, δίκτυον Od., Anth.
to be very careful, opp. to ὀλιγωρέω, Aeschin., Arist.
very useful, useful in many ways, Arist. adv. -λῶς, Sup. -ωφελέστατα, Xen.
escorting, conveying, Eur.; π. οὖρος a fair wind, Pind.
of Hermes, who escorted the souls of the dead, Aesch., Soph.
a leading in procession, Polyb.
jeering, ribaldry, such as was allowed to those who took part in the processions at the festivals of Bacchus and Demeter, Dem.
any vessel employed in solemn processions, Dem.
at Athens, a storehouse for such vessels, Id.
one who attends or escorts, a conductor, guide, Od.; of favourable winds, οὖροι πομπῆες νηῶν Id.
one who attends a procession, Thuc.
to conduct, escort, e. g. as a guide, Od.; Ἑρμοῦ τέχνην π. to use the escorting art of Hermes, Soph.
to lead a procession, π. πομπήν, Lat. pompam ducere, ap. Dem.:—Pass. to be led in triumph (at Rome), Plut.
absol. to march in a procession, Dem., Theocr.
to abuse with ribald jests (cf. πομπεία II), Dem.
conduct, escort, guidance, Hom., etc.; οὐρία π. the conduct of a fair wind, Eur.
concrete, an escort, Aesch., Eur.
a sending away, a sending home, Od.
a sending, mission, Hdt., Plat.: simply, a sending, ξύλων Thuc.
a solemn procession, Lat. pompa, ὑπὸ πομπῆς, σὺν πομπῇ in procession, Hdt.; μήλων κνισάεσσα πομπή the flesh of sheep for sacrifice carried in procession, Pind.; τὰς πομπὰς πέμπουσιν Dem.
τείνειν π. to lead a long procession, of a military expedition, Aesch., Eur.
of or for a solemn procession, π. ἵππος a horse of state, Xen.:—metaph. pompous, showy, Plut.
conducting, escorting, guiding, Trag.:—c. gen., π. χώρα φίλων a land that lends escort to friends, Eur.; νόστου πόμπιμον τέλος the home-sending end of one's return, i. e. one's safe return, Pind.
pass. sent, conveyed, Soph., Eur.
a conductor, escort, guide, Hom., Hdt.; of Hermes (cf. πομπαῖος), Soph.; πομποί attendants, guards, Id.: also πομπός, a conductress, Od.
c. gen. rei, τῆσδε προστροπῆς π. conveyor, carrier of these suppliant offerings, Aesch.
a messenger, one who is sent for a person or thing, Soph.
as adj., π. ἀρχαί the conducting chiefs, Aesch.; πῦρ πομπόν the missive fire, Id.
to lead in procession, Strab.
the noise made by bubbles rising, Ar.
to bubble up, gush forth, Pind.
a bubble, Plat.
in early Greek only as Dep.
absol. to work hard, do work, suffer toil, Hom.; περὶ δόρπα πονέοντο were busied about their supper, Il.; so, πεπόνητο καθ’ ἵππους was busy with the horses, of a charioteer, Id.
metaph. to be in distress, to distress oneself, Id.:— to suffer, be sick, Thuc.
c. acc. to work hard at, to make or do with pains or care, Hom., Hes.
after Hom., the act. form prevails
intr. to toil, labour, Theogn., Hdt., attic; μάτην π. to labour in vain, Soph.; c. acc., τὰ μηδὲν ὠφελοῦντα μὴ πόνει do not labour at things that profit not, Aesch.
c. acc. cogn., π. πόνον, μόχθους to go through, suffer them, Trag.; also c. acc. partis, πονεῖν τὰ σκέλη Ar.
absol. to labour, be hard-pressed, suffer, Thuc., Xen.: to be worn out, spoilt, Dem.
Pass., impers., οὐκ ἄλλως αὐτοῖς πεπόνηται = πεπονήκασι, Plat.
trans.,
c. acc. pers. to afflict, distress, Pind.:—Pass. to be worn out, to suffer greatly, Soph., Thuc.
Pass., also, to be trained or educated, Arist., Theocr.
c. acc. rei, like ἐκπονεῖν, to gain by toil or labour, χρήματα Xen.: Pass. to be won or achieved by toil, Pind.
that which is wrought out, work, Eur.: a work, book, Anth.
a knavish trick, in pl., Dem.
Dep. to be evil, act wickedly, play the rogue, Arist.; οἱ πεπονηρευμένοι Dem.
a bad state or condition, badness, Plat.
in moral sense, wickedness, vice, knavery, Lat. pravitas, Id., Xen.: in pl. knavish tricks, rogueries, Dem.
baseness, cowardice, Eur.
teaching wickedness, Strab.
Pass. to be governed by the bad, Arist.
government of the bad, Arist.
toilsome, painful, grievous, Theogn., Ar.
in bad case, in sorry plight, useless, good-for-nothing, Ar., Plat., etc.:—adv., πονηρῶς ἔχειν to be in bad case, Thuc.
in moral sense, bad, worthless, knavish, Lat. pravus, improbus, Aesch., Eur.; πονηρὸς κἀκ πονηρῶν rogue and son of rogues, Ar.; πόνῳ πονηρός laboriously wicked, Id.:— ὁ π. the evil one, NTest.
base, cowardly, Soph.; π. χρώματα the coward's hue, Xen.
fond of bad men, Arist.
one must toil, Plat.

work, esp. hard work, toil, Lat. labor, in Hom. mostly of war, μάχης π. the toil of battle, and π. alone = μάχη, πόνον ἔχειν, = μάχεσθαι, Il.; ὁ Μηδικὸς π. battle with the Medes, Hdt.; οἱ Τρωικοὶ πόνοι Id.
generally, toil, labour, Il., etc.
bodily exertion, exercise, Eur., Xen.; ἐνάλιος π., i. e. fishing, Pind.
a work, task, business, ἐπεὶ π. ἄλλος ἔπειγεν Od., Soph.
implements for labour, stock in trade, Theocr.; πόνος ἐντὶ θάλασσα the sea is their workshop, Mosch.
the consequence of toil, distress, trouble, suffering, pain, Il., etc.
anything produced by work, a work, τρητὸς μελισσᾶν π., of honey, Pind.; τοὺς ἡμετέρους π. the fruits of our labour, Xen.
Πόνος a mythol. person, son of Eris, Hes.

entry.etym: poet. fem. of πόντιος, Pind., Eur.

entry.sense: to plunge in the sea, Aesch.
from Pontus, Pontic, Il. δένδρεον, prob., the bird-cherry, Hdt.
of the sea, of Poseidon, Hhymn., Soph.; π. δάκη sea monsters, Aesch.; π. κύματα Id.; ᾅδης πόντος, i. e. death by drowning, Id.
by the sea, of places, Pind., Aesch.
in the sea, of islands, Pind.; of ships, Aesch., etc.
of persons, δέχεσθαι ποντίους from the sea, Eur.; ἀφιέναι πόντιον into the sea, Id.
brought by sea or from beyond sea, of iron, Aesch.
that which is cast into the sea, esp. as an offering, Eur.
from or out of the sea, Il.
one who fishes in the sea, Anth.
lord of the sea, Pind., Aesch., etc.
into the sea, Od.
a Nereid, Sea-traverser, Hes.
to pass over the sea, epic inf. -έμεναι Od.; part. ποντοπορεύων sea-traversing, Id.
to pass the sea, νῆυς ποντοποροῦσα sea-sailing, Od.
passing over the sea, seafaring, of ships, Hom., Soph.
Sea-Poseidon, Ar.
the sea, esp. the open sea, Hom., etc.

of special seas, π. Ἰκάριος, Θρηίκιος Il.; ὁ Αἰγαῖος π. Hdt.; Ἰόνιος, Σαρωνικός, Σικελός, Eur.:—but most commonly π. Εὔξεινος Id.; ὁ Εὔξεινος π. Hdt.; generally called simply ὁ Πόντος or Πόντος, Id., attic
like πέμμα, a round cake, used at sacrifices, Ar.
like πόποι, an exclamation, Aesch.
exclam. of surprise, anger or pain, ὦ πόποι oh strange! oh shame! Hom., Trag.
cry of the hoopoe, Ar.
to whistle, cheep or chirp, Ar.
of an inarticulate sound, commonly used by the Greeks in case of thunder, as a sort of charm, Id.
in bad sense, to play ill on the flute, let the breath be heard in playing, Theocr.
a whistling, Xen.
a walking, mode of walking or running, gait, Plat.
a going, a journey, way, passage, Aesch., Plat.
a march, Thuc., Xen.
a crossing of water, passage, Aesch.
a place in which one walks, βροτῶν πορεύματα their haunts, Aesch.
that may be crossed, passable, Xen.:—of a road, possible to pass, Eur.
to be traversed, Soph., Xen.
πορευτέον, one must go, Soph., Eur.
gone over, passed, passable, Polyb.; καιρὸς π. the season for travelling, Id.
act. going, travelling, Aesch.
Act. to make to go, carry, convey, Pind., Soph.:—c. dupl. acc. to carry or ferry over, Νέσσος ποταμὸν βροτοὺς ἐπόρευσε Soph.; γυναῖκ’ λίμναν πορεύσας Eur.
of things, to bring, furnish, bestow, find, Id.
Pass. and Mid. to be driven or carried, Soph.
to go, walk, march, Hdt., attic; to go across, pass, Hdt., etc.; c. acc. loci, to enter, π. στέγας Soph., etc.; c. acc. cogn., μακρὰν ὁδὸν π. Xen.:—c. acc. loci, to go over, traverse, Id.
to walk, i. e. live, Soph.
collat. form of πέρθω, to destroy, ravage, waste, plunder, Hom., Hdt., Trag.
in pres. and imperf. to endeavour to destroy, to besiege a town, Hdt.:—to destroy, despoil, ruin, Aesch.:—in Pass. to be ruined, undone, Eur.
the sack of a town, Dem.
a destroyer, ravager, Eur.
a place for crossing, a passage over, ferry, Hdt.
a passage-boat, ferry-boat, Id., Xen.
the fare of the ferry, ferryman's fee, Luc.
a passage, ferry, ὠκύπορον π. ἀχέων, of the river Acheron, Aesch.
ionic ῆος, ὁ, a ferryman, Lat. portitor, Od., etc.; π. νεκύων, of Charon, Eur.
generally, a boatman, seaman, Hdt., Theocr.
engaged as a ferryman, Arist.

to carry or ferry over a strait, river, Lat. trajicere, Eur.; π. τινὰς εἰς Σαλαμῖνα Aeschin.: then, generally, to carry, bring, Trag.:— Pass. to be carried or ferried over, to pass from place to place, Hdt., Eur.; c. acc. loci, to pass through, Eur.
the Act. is also used intr., like Lat. trajicere, to pass over, Anth.
a ship, boat, Eur.
a ferry or a place crossed by a ferry, a strait, firth, Od.; of the straits of Salamis, Hdt.; π. Ἕλλας the Hellespont, Aesch.; ὁ εἰς Ἅιδου π. the Styx, Eur.
a crossing by a ferry, passage, Soph., Eur.; π. χθονός a passage to it, Eur.

Properly, like πορεύω, to carry: to bring about, to furnish, provide, supply, procure, cause, Ar., Plat.; absol., θεοῦ πορίζοντος καλῶς Eur.:—often with a notion of contriving or inventing, Id., etc.:—Mid. to furnish oneself with, to provide, procure, Lat. sibi comparare, Ar., Thuc.:— Pass. to be provided, Thuc., etc.
πορίζεταί τινι, impers., it is in one's power to do, c. inf., Xen.
able to provide, full of resources, inventive, contriving, Ar.:—c. acc., ἄπορα πόριμος making possible the impossible, Aesch.
pass. practicable, Luc.
well-provided, Thuc.
a providing, procuring, Polyb.: — a means of getting, Plut.: means of gain, NTest.
one who supplies or provides, Thuc.
at Athens the πορισταί were a financial board appointed to raise extraordinary supplies, Procurators, Ar.
the name used by robbers of themselves, conveyancers, Arist.
able to furnish, Xen.
a ping or hoop, passed round the joint of the spearhead and shaft, Il.
fornication, prostitution, Dem.
a house of ill-fame, brothel, Ar.
to prostitute:—Pass., of a woman, to be or become a prostitute, Hdt., Dem., etc.
intr. in Act., = Pass., Luc.
a harlot, prostitute, Ar.
of or for harlots, π. τέλος the tax paid by brothel-keepers, Aeschin.
to keep a brothel, Ar.
the trade of a brothel-keeper, Aeschin.
a brothel-keeper, Aeschin., Dem.
loving harlots, Anth.
a means of passing a river, a ford, ferry, Lat. vadum, Il., Hdt., etc.; Πλούτωνος π. the Stygian ferry, Aesch.
a narrow sea, strait, firth, Lat. fretum, Hes., Aesch.; Ἰόνιος π. the Ionian sea which is the passage-way from Greece to Italy, Pind.:— ἐν πόρῳ in the passage-way (of ships), in the "fair-way" Hdt.
periphr., πόροι ἁλός the paths of the sea, i. e. the sea, Od.; ἐνάλιοι π. Aesch., etc.; so, of rivers, πόρος Ἀλφεοῦ, Σκαμάνδρου, i. e. the Alpheus, etc., Pind.
a way over a river, a bridge, Hdt.
generally a pathway, way, Aesch., Soph.; πόρος οἰωνῶν their pathway, Aesch.
a passage through the skin, οἱ πόροι the pores, Plat.

c. gen. rei, a way or means of achieving, accomplishing, οὐκ ἐδύνατο π. οὐδένα ἀνευρεῖν Hdt.; π. ὁδοῦ a means of performing the journey, Ar.; π. κακῶν a means of averting evils, Eur.:—c. inf., πόρος τις τίσασθαι Id.
absol. a means of providing, contrivance, device, resource, Aesch., Ar.
at Athens, π. χρημάτων a way of getting or raising money, Xen., Dem.: in pl., "ways and means, " resources, revenue, Dem.
a going, journey, voyage, Aesch., Eur.
a garment fastened with a πόρπη, in pl., Eur.
the handle of a shield, Soph., Eur., etc.; ἔχουσι πόρπακας [αἱ ἀσπίδες], i. e. they are ready for use, Ar.
part of a horse's headgear, Eur.
to fasten with a buckle, to buckle or pin down, Aesch.
a buckle-pin, Eur.;—in pl. a buckle or brooch, Il., Eur.
from a more distant point, Isocr.
of Time, from long, long ago, Eur., Plat., etc.
Dep. to buy besides, Xen., Dem.
to offer, present what one has prepared, in Hom. of the wife preparing her husband's bed.
generally, to make ready, prepare, provide, Soph., Eur., etc.:—Mid. to provide for oneself, get ready, Aesch.
of evils, ἐχθροῖς π. ἐχθρά Id.; π. τοῖς πολεμίοις κακά Xen.:—Pass., ἐπορσύνθη κακά Aesch.
to arrange, adjust, manage, π. τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ Hdt.; τάδε Soph., etc.
to treat with care, tend, Pind., etc.
a calf, Il.
a calf, young heifer, Il., Soph.:— a young cow, Theocr., Mosch.
nourishing calves, Hhymn.
the purple-fish, Lat. murex, Aesch.
purple dye, purple, Hdt.
= πορφυρίς, purple raiment, Aesch.
Homeric usage
of the swoln sea, darkgleaming, dark; so, π. νεφέλη.
of blood, Il.; π. θάνατος, of death in battle, Id.
of stuff, cloths, etc., dark, russet.
of the rainbow, prob. bright, lustrous; and of serpents glittering.— Hom. seems not to have known the πορφύρα, so that the word does not imply any definite colour.
after Hom. (from πορφύρα) dark red, purple or crimson, Pind., Hdt., Trag.
purple-clad, in purple, Luc.
a fisher for purple fish, Hdt.
of or for a purple-dyer, Eur.
a purple garment or covering, Xen.
a red-coloured bird, Ar.
the water-hen, Ar.
purple-like, purply, Eur.
a dealer in purple, fem. πορφῠρό-πωλις, ιδος, NTest.
spread with purple cloth, Aesch.
properly of the sea, ὡς ὅτε πορφύρῃ πέλαγος μέγα κύματι κωφῷ as when the huge sea gleams darkly with dumb swell (i. e. with waves that do not break), Il.
metaph., πολλὰ δέ οἱ κραδίη πόρφυρε much was his heart troubled, Hom.
after Hom., when the purple-fish (πορφύρα) and its dye became known, to grow purple or red, Bion., Anth.:—so in Mid., εὔδια μέν Anth.

entry.etym: πόρω assumed as pres. to the aor2 ἔπορον and perfect πέπρωται.
entry.sense: to furnish, offer, present, give, Hom., Hes.; εὖχος π. to fulfil a wish, Od.; ὅρκον π. to offer to take an oath, Aesch.:—c. inf. to grant that . . , πόρε κούρηισιν ἕπεσθαι τιμάς (for ὥστε ἕπεσθαι) Il.; σοὶ θεοὶ πόροιεν, ὡς ( = οἷα) ἐγὼ θέλω Soph.
= πορεύω, to bring, εἴ τις δεῦρο Θησέα πόροι Id.

perf. only in 3rd sg. πέπρωται, plup. πέπρωτο, it has or had been (is or was) fated, foredoomed, c. acc. pers. et inf., ἄμφω πέπρωται γαῖαν ἐρεῦσαι it is fated that both should redden earth, Il.; τί γὰρ πέπρωται Ζηνὶ πλὴν ἀεὶ κρατεῖν; Aesch.; so, πεπρωμένον ἔστι = πέπρωται, Id., Xen.

part. as adj., πεπρωμένος, η, ον, allotted, fated to one, Il.; of persons, destined to a thing, αἴσηι Id.:—absol. destined, Pind.; πεπρ. βίος one's natural life (as in Lat. mors fatalis is a natural death), Id.; so in Trag. and Xen.: ἡ πεπρωμένη (sc. μοῖρα), an appointed lot, fate, destiny, Hdt., Trag.

who, Pron., traced in the interrog. forms, ποῦ,ποῖ, πῆ, πῶς, πω, πόθι, πόθεν, πότε, πότερος, πόστος,ποῖος, πόσος, to each of which there is a correspondingenclitic form, που, ποι, πη, πως, etc.;—in these forms π in ionic Gr. is represented by κ, as κοῦ, κοῖ, etc.
how many times? how often? Lat. quoties? epic Plat.
how many times multiplied? how many fold? Lat. quotuplex? Plat.
c. gen. what multiple of . . ? Id.
the sixth month of the Athen. year, = latter half of December and former of January.
sacred to Poseidon, Eur.:—poet. Ποσειδαώνιος, and -όνιος, Soph., Anth.: doric Ποσειδᾱ́νιος, Pind.
Ποσειδώνιον, (sc. ἱερόν) τό, the temple of Poseidon, Thuc.
Ποσειδώνια, τά, his festival, Strab.
Poseidon, Lat. Neptunus, son of Cronos and Rhea, brother of Zeus, god of the sea, husband of Amphitrite, Hom., etc.
membrum virile, Ar.
comic word for a little boy, Ar.
sacred to Poseidon, Il.
Ποσῐδήιον, ου, τό, ionic for Ποσίδειον, the temple of Poseidon, Od.
how many times? π. παίζειν = ἀρτιάζειν, Xen.
a husband, spouse, mate, Hom., etc.; κρυπτὸς π., of a paramour, Eur.

entry.etym: ΠΟ, Root of some tenses of πίνω
entry.sense: a drinking, drink, beverage, Hom.; συγγίνεσθαι ἐς πόσιν to meet for a carousal, Hdt.; παρὰ τὴν πόσιν, Lat. inter pocula, over their cups, Id.; πόσιος ἐν βάθει Theocr.
a draught, Aesch.
indef. adj. of a certain quantity or magnitude, Lat. aliquantus, Id., etc.

entry.note: πόσος;, ionic and aeolic κόσος, η, ον
entry.sense: interrog. adj. corresponding to the relat. ὅσος and demonstr. τόσος, Lat. quantus? of what quantity? opp. to πηλίκος (which refers to bulk), often with τις added:
of Number, how many? Hdt., attic: with sg. Nouns, how great? how much? π. τι πλῆθος; Aesch.
of Distance, how far? Xen.
of Time, how long? Soph., etc.
of Value, how much? Ar.; πόσου; for how much? at what price? Lat. quanti? Id.; so, ἐπὶ πόσῳ; Plat.
to reckon up, count, τὰς ψήφους Theophr.
struck with the foot in dancing, Orac. ap. Hdt.
in how many days? Lat. quota die? Xen.
which of a number? Lat. quotus? πόστον δὴ ἔτος ἐστὶν ὅτε ξείνισσας ἐκεῖνον; how many years is it since . . ? Od.:—in indirect questions, πόστῳ μέρει with how small a part, Xen.
fresh, new, Lat. recens, Pind., Aesch.
metaph. new, unexpected, unheard of, Aesch., Soph.
adv. like a river, Luc.
of or from a river, Aesch., Eur.; οἱ ἵπποι οἱ π., v. ἱπποπόταμος.
washed by a river, Strab.
to or towards a river, Hom.

entry.etym: ΠΟ, Root of some tenses of πίνω
entry.sense: a river, stream, Hom., etc.:—proverb., ἄνω ποταμῶν χωροῦσι παγαί, of extraordinary events, Eur.:—of rivers of fire or lava, Pind.
as a person, Ποταμός, a river-god, Il.
carried away by a river, NTest.
deposited by a river, Strab.

winged, flying, furnished with wings, Pind., Eur.; ἐν ποτανοῖς among fowls, Pind.:—metaph., ποτανὸς ἐν Μοίσαισι, i. e. soaring in the arts of the Muses, Id.; ποτανᾷ μαχανᾷ by soaring art, i. e. by poesy, Id.
to fly about, Hom.; κεραυνοὶ ποτέοντο Hes.: simply = πέτομαι, to fly, Aesch., Eur.; τὰ ποτήμενα συλλαβεῖν, of vain pursuits, Theocr.:—perf. (with pres. sense), to be upon the wing, Hom.
metaph. to hover, Aesch.
to be on the wing, be fluttered, Eur., Ar.
ποτέον, one must drink, Plat.
enclit. Particle:
at some time or other, at some time, Hom., etc.

at any time, ever, Soph., etc.; often after relat. words, ὅστις ποτέ, ὅστις δήποτε, ὅστις δηποτοῦν, v. δήποτε; also after πω, v. πώποτε; and after negatives, when it often becomes one word with the negat., οὔποτε, μήποτε, οὐδέποτε, μηδέποτε.
in correl. clauses it stands first, with accent, ποτὲ μέν . . , ποτὲ δέ . . , at one time . . , at another . . , Lat. modo . . , modo . . , Plat.
of some unknown point of time,
the past, once, erst, Il., Trag.; in telling a story, once upon a time, Ar.
the future, at some time, Il., etc.:—with imperat., Lat. tandem aliquando, Soph.
in questions, τίς ποτε; Lat. qui tandem? who in the world? Aesch., etc.; v. τίποτε; τίπτε.
interrog. Particle used in direct and indirect questions, corresponding to the relat. ὅτε, ὁπότε and demonstr. τότε, when? at what time? Hom.; πότ’, εἰ μὴ νῦν Aesch.; also, ἐς πότε λήξει; Soph.
whether of the two? Lat. uter? both in direct and indirect questions, ὁπότερος being the relat. form., Il., Hdt., attic

neut. πότερον, πότερα, as adv. at the beginning of an interrog. sentence containing two alternative propositions, πότερον . . , ἤ . . , Lat. utrum . . , an . . , whether . . or . . , τίνες κατῆρξαν, πότερον Ἕλληνες ἢ παῖς ἐμός; Aesch.; πότερ’ ἄκων ἢ ἑκών; Dem.
sometimes a third clause (with ἤ) is inaccurately added, πότερα παρὰ δήμου ἢ ὀλιγαρχίης ἢ μουνάρχου; Hdt.
the second alternative is sometimes left to be supplied, πότερα δὴ κερτομῶν λέγεις τάδε [ἢ μή . .]; Soph.
without interrog., like ἅτερος, either of the two, Lat. alteruter, Plat.
on whether of the two sides? on which side (of two)? Xen., etc.
in which of two ways? Lat. utro modo? Xen., etc.
in indirect questions, διορίσαι π. λέγεις to define which you mean, Plat.
a flight, Aesch.
flight, Od.

entry.etym: ΠΟ, Root of some tenses of πίνω
entry.sense: a drinking-cup, wine-cup, Hdt., attic

entry.etym: ΠΟ, Root of some tenses of πίνω
entry.sense: a drinking-cup, wine-cup, Eur.

entry.etym: ΠΟ, Root of some tenses of πίνω
entry.sense: a drinker, tippler, toper:—metaph., πότης λύχνος a tippling lamp, i. e. that consumes much oil, Ar.: Comic Sup., ποτίστατος, Id.

entry.etym: ΠΟ, Root of some tenses of πίνω
entry.sense: a drinking, drink, Hom.
flying, winged: ποτητά, τά, fowls, birds, Od.
doric city named after Poseidon (doric Ποτῑδάν), Ar., etc.
a Potidaean, Hdt., etc.
Potidaen, Thuc.

entry.etym: doric form used by Hom., the common form προσδόρπιος not in use
entry.sense: of or serving for supper, ὄβριμον ἄχθος ὕλης ἵνα οἱ ποτιδόρπιον εἴη that it might serve to dress his supper, Od.
to give to drink, c. dupl. acc., τοὺς ἵππους νέκταρ ἐπότισε gave them nectar to drink, Plat.; ποτήριον π. τινά NTest.
to water the ground, Xen.; to water cattle, Theocr.
fond of drinking, Plut.: adv., ποτικῶς ἔχειν to be given to drinking, Id.
a cushion, Theocr.
of water, drinkable, fresh, Hdt., Xen., etc.
metaph. fresh, sweet, pleasant, Plat.:—of persons, mild, gentle, Theocr.

entry.etym: doric for προσπτήσσω, which is not in use
entry.sense: to crouch or cower towards, c. gen., ἀκταὶ λιμένος ποτιπεπτηυῖαι (epic perf. part. fem. for προσπεπτηκυῖαι) verging towards it, so as to shut it in, Od.
that which befals one, one's lot, destiny: commonly of evil destiny, death, of the killer, πότμον ἐφεῖναι, or of the killed, πότμον ἐπισπεῖν, Hom.;—also in Pind. and Trag.
without a sense of evil, π. συγγενής one's natural gifts, Pind.; εὐτυχεῖ πότμῳ Aesch.; π. ξυνήθης πατρός my father's customary fortune, Soph.
πότνα θεά Od.; πότνα θεάων Hhymn.; πότνα θεῶν Eur.
an ancient Boeot. town, Strab.
Dep. to cry or lament aloud, shriek, howl, Plut., Luc.

entry.etym: from same Root as πόσις, δεσπότης
entry.sense: a poet. title of honour, used chiefly in addressing goddesses or ladies:

= δέσποινα, mistress, queen, c. gen., πότνια θηρῶν (nom.) queen of wild beasts, Lat. potens ferarum, Il.; po/tnia bel/ewnπότνια βέλεων Pind.: absol., πότνι’ Ἐρινύς Aesch.; often in voc., ὦ πότνι’ Ἥρα Id.; ὦ πότνια (sc. Ἀθηναία) Ar.:—in pl. of the Eumenides, Hdt., Soph.; also of Demeter and Proserpine, Soph., etc.
as adj. revered, august, Hom.
lamentation, Strab.
Potnian, Ποτνιάδες ἵπποι Boeotian mares, noted for their hot temper, hence raging, furious, Eur.

entry.etym: ΠΟ, Root of some tenses of πίνω
entry.sense: drunk, fit for drinking, Aesch., Eur.
as Subst., poto/n, ou=, to/, that which one drinks, drink, esp. of wine, Hom., Hdt., attic; σῖτα καὶ ποτά meat and drink, Hdt.
πάτριον π. drink of my sires, Aesch.; π. κρηναῖον Soph.

entry.etym: ΠΟ, Root of some tenses of πίνω.
entry.sense: drinking, a drinking-bout, carousal, Xen.; παρὰ πότον, Lat. inter pocula, Id.; ἐν τοῖς πότοις Aeschin.

anywhere, somewhere, Hom., etc.; often with other Advs. of Place, οὐχ ἑκάς που somewhere not far off, Soph.; πέλας που Id.; ἄλλοθί που Dem.:—c. gen., ἀλλά που αὐτοῦ ἀγρῶν in some part there of the fields, Od.; εἴ που τῆς χώρας τοῦτο συνέβη Dem.

also without reference to Place, in some degree, καί πού τι Thuc.:—often to qualify an expression, anyway, possibly, perhaps, I suppose, I ween, Hom., etc.; εἴ που, ἐάν που, εἰ μή που Xen.; τί που . . ; what in the world? Aesch.;with numerals, δέκα κου about ten, Hdt.:— οὔ τί που denies with indignation or wonder, surely it cannot be, Soph., etc.; whereas οὐ δήπου adds a suspicion that it is so, οὐ δήπου Στράτων; Ar.

interrog. adv., in direct or indirect questions, corresponding to the relat. ὅπου, where? Lat. ubi? Hom., etc.:—c. gen. loci, ποῦ γῆς; ποῦ χθονός; where in theworld? Lat. ubinam terrarum? Aesch., etc.; so, ποῦ ποτ’ εἶ φρενῶν; Soph.; ποῦ γνώμης εἶ; Id=Soph..; ποῦ τύχης; at what point of fortune? Id=Soph.

of manner, how? Eur.; to express an inference very strongly, κοῦ γε δὴ . . οὐκ ἂν χωσθείη κόλπος . . ; how then would it not . . ? i. e. it certainly would . . , Hdt.; also in Trag., in indignant questions, how? by what right? ποῦ σὺ μάντις εἰ σοφός; Soph.

a foot, Lat. pes, pedis, Hom., etc.; in pl., also, a bird's talons, Od.; the arms of a polypus, Hes.; ξύλινος π., of an artificial foot, Hdt.: phrases in respect to the footrace, περιγιγνόμεθ’ ἄλλων πόδεσσιν, to be better than others in running, Od.; ποσὶν ἐρίζειν to race on foot, Il.; ποσὶ νικᾶν, ἀέθλια ποσσὶν ἄροντο Hom.:—the dat. ποσί is added to all kinds of Verbs denoting motion, ποσὶ βῆναι, δραμεῖν, ὀρχεῖσθαι, etc.; for πόδα βαίνειν, v. βαίνω A. II. 3:—metaph., νόστιμον ναῦς ἐκίνησεν πόδα started on its homeward way, Eur.

as a mark of close proximity, πρόσθεν ποδός or ποδῶν, προπάροιθε ποδῶν just before one, Hom.; πὰρ ποδί close at hand, Pind.; but, παρά or πὰρ ποδός off-hand, at once, Theogn.:—so, παρὰ πόδα in a moment, Soph.; παρὰ πόδας Plut.:— ἐν ποσί, like ἐμποδών, close at hand, Hdt., attic; τὰ πρὸς ποσί Soph.:—these phrases are opp. to ἐκ ποδῶν, out of the way, far off, Hdt. (cf. ἐκποδών).
to denote close pursuit, κατὰ πόδας on the track, Lat. e vestigio, Id., attic; c. gen. pers., κατὰ πόδας τινος ἔρχεσθαι, ἰέναι to come close at his heels, Hdt.
various phrases: ἐπὶ πόδα backwards, facing the enemy, ἐπὶ π. ἀναχωρεῖν, ἀνάγειν, ἀναχάζεσθαι to retire leisurely, Lat. pedetentim, Xen.
περὶ πόδα, properly of a shoe, round the foot, i. e. fitting exactly, Theophr., Luc.
ὡς ποδῶν ἔχει as he is off for feet, i. e. as quick as he can, Hdt.
ἔξω τινὸς πόδα ἔχειν to have one's foot out of a thing, i. e. be clear of it, ἔξω κομίζου πηλοῦ πόδα Aesch.; πημάτων ἔξω πόδα ἔχειν Id.:—opp. to εἰς ἄντλον ἐμβῆσαι πόδα, Eur.
to denote energetic action, ἀμφοῖν ποδοῖν, Ar.; βοηθεῖν ποδὶ καὶ χειρὶ καὶ πάσῃ δυνάμει Aeschin.; for ὀρθῷ ποδί, v. ὀρθός II.
πούς τινος, periphr. for a person, σὺν πατρὸς μολὼν ποδί, i. e. σὺν πατρί, Eur.; παρθένου δέχου πόδα Id.:—also, ἐξ ἑνὸς ποδός, i. e. μόνος ὤν, Soph.; οἱ ἀφ’ ἡσύχου π., i. e. οἱ ἡσύχως ζῶντες, Eur.
metaph. of things, the foot or lowest part, esp. the foot of a hill, Lat. pes montis, Il., etc.

in a ship, πόδες are the lower corners of the sail or the ropes fastened thereto, the sheets, Od.; χαλᾶν πόδα to slack away or ease off the sheet, Eur.; τοῦ ποδὸς παριέναι to let go hold of it, Ar.; ἐκπετάσαι πόδα (with reference to the sail), Eur.: —opp. to τείνειν πόδα, to haul it tight, Soph.; ναῦς ἐνταθεῖσα ποδί a ship with her sheet close hauled, Eur.
a foot, as a measure of length, 4 palms (παλασταί) or 6 fingers, about 1/8 of an inch longer than our foot, Hdt., etc.
a foot in Prosody, Ar., Plat.
like grass, grassy, Hdt., etc.

that which has been done, a deed, act, Lat. facinus, Hdt., attic; τῶν πραγμάτων πλέον more than facts, Eur.; τὸ σὸν τί ἐστι τὸ πρ.; what is your work in life? Plat.; γύναιον πρ. ποιεῖν to do a woman's work, Dem.
like Lat. res, a thing, matter, affair, Hdt., attic; σφισί τε καὶ Ἀθηναίοις εἶναι οὐδὲν πρ. they had no thing in common, Hdt.
anything necessary or expedient, πρῆγμά ἐστι, c. inf., it is necessary, expedient to do, 'tis my duty or business to do, like Lat. opus est, Hdt.

a thing of consequence or importance, πρ. ποιεῖσθαί τι Id.; of a person, ἦν μέγιστον πρ. Δημοκήδης παρὰ βασιλέϊ he was made much of by the king, Id.; ἄμαχον πρ., of a woman, Xen.; ἀσταθμητότατον πρ. ὁ δῆμος Dem.
used of a battle, as we say an action, affair, Xen.
euphem. for something bad or disgraceful, the thing, the business, Thuc.; Εὐρυβάτου πρᾶγμα, οὐ πόλεως ἔργον his job, Dem.
in pl., πράγματα,

circumstances, affairs, Hdt., attic; τοῖς πράγμασιν τέθνηκα τοῖς δ’ ἔργοισι δ’ οὔ by circumstances, not by acts, Eur.; ἀπηλλάχθαι πραγμάτων to be quit of the business of life, Plat.; ἀποτυγχάνειν τῶν πρ. to fail in success, Xen.

state-affairs, Eur., etc.; τὰ πολιτικὰ πρ. Plat.:—also, τὰ Περσικὰ πρ. the Persian power, Hdt.; ἐν ταῖς ναυσὶ τῶν Ἑλλήνων τὰ πρ. ἐγένετο Thuc.; καταλαμβάνειν τὰ πρ. to seize the government, Lat. rerum potiri, Id.; ἔχειν, κατέχειν τὰ πρ. Id.; οἱ ἐν τοῖς πράγμασι, like οἱ ἐν τέλει, those who are in power or office, the ministers, Id.; οἱ ἐπὶ τοῖς πρ. ὄντες, οἱ ἐπὶ τῶν πρ., Dem.:— νεώτερα πρ. innovations, Lat. res novae, Oratt.
one's private affairs or circumstances, Hdt., attic

in bad sense, troublesome business, trouble, annoyance, Ar.; πράγματα ἔχειν, c. part., to have trouble about a thing, Hdt.; πρ. παρέχειν τινί to cause one trouble, Id.; c. inf., to cause one the trouble of doing, Plat.
the careful prosecution of an affair, diligent study, hard work, Plat., Dem., etc.
occupation, business, Plat., Aeschin.:—in pl. affairs in general, dealings, Plat., etc.
the treatment of a subject, Id.; a treatise, Arist.; an historical work, systematic history, Polyb., Luc.
Dep. to busy or exert oneself, take trouble, Hdt., Xen., Plat.
to be engaged in business, spend one's time in business, Xen., etc.
c. acc. rei, to take in hand, treat laboriously, undertake, Plat.:—of authors, to elaborate a work, Ar., Plat.
of historians, to treat systematically, Polyb.; οἱ πραγματευόμενοι systematic historians, Id.
perf. πεπραγμάτευμαι also in pass. sense, to be laboured at, worked out, Plat., Aeschin.
to be laboured at, Arist.
fit for business, active, business-like; οἱ πραγματικοί men of action, Polyb.
in Roman writers, pragmaticus was a kind of attorney, Cic.
of history, systematic, Polyb.: of a speech, conduct, etc., able, prudent, Id.:—adv. -κῶς, Id.
a trifling matter, petty lawsuit, Ar.
one who hunts after lawsuits, a pettifogger, Ar.
laborious, troublesome: adv. -δως, comp. -έστερον Dem.
poetic for πρᾶγμα, Pind., Aesch., Soph., Ar.
= πράγματα, state-affairs, Aesch.
= Lat. Praetorium, the residence of the Governor, Government-house, NTest.:—at Rome, the Castra Praetoriana, Id.
to be done, Plat., etc.
πρακτέον, one must do, Soph., Plat.

sic.seg: prakth/r, ionic prhkthfailing on lembuf [] | /r, h=ros, o(,

entry.sense: one that does, a doer, Il.
a trader, Lat. negotiator, Od.
fit for action, fit for business, business-like, practical, Xen., Plat.; αἱ πρ. ἀρχαί the principles of action, Arist.
active, effective, Polyb.; πρ. παρά τινος carrying one's point with another, Xen.
c. gen. able to effect a thing, etc., Arist.
of things, active, vigorous, Ar., Plat.
τὰ πρακτά things to be done, points of moral action, Arist.
one who does or executes, an accomplisher, Soph.; with a fem. Subst., Id.
one who exacts payment, a tax-gatherer, Dem., etc.
in Poets also, one who exacts punishment, a punisher, avenger, Aesch., Soph.:—so as adj., with a fem. Subst., avenging, Aesch.
πράμνειος οἶνος, ὁ, Pramnian wine, Hom.; also Πράμνιος, Ar.:—so named from Pramne, prob. a hill in the island of Icaria.
aforetime, erst, Theocr.
to take by surprise or treachery, Polyb.:— to overreach, outwit, τινά Id.
a doing, transaction, business, πλεῖν κατὰ πρῆξιν on a trading voyage, Od.; πρῆξις δ’ ἥδ’ ἰδίη, οὐ δήμιος a private, not a public affair, Id.
the result or issue of a business, οὐ γάρ τις πρ. πέλεται γόοιο no good comes of weeping, Il.; so, ὄυ τις πρ. ἐγίγνετο μυρομένοισιν Od.; πρ. οὐρίαν θέλων Aesch.; χρησμῶν πρ. their issue, Id.
an acting, transacting, doing, κακότητος Theogn.; πρ. πολεμική, ποιητική, πολιτική Plat.:— action, opp. to πάθος, Id.; ἐν ταῖς πράξεσι in actual life, Id.
action, exercise, χειρῶν, σκελῶν Id.
an action, act, Soph., etc.
like τὸ εὖ or κακῶς πράσσειν, a doing well or ill, faring so and so, one's fortune, state, condition, Hdt., Aesch., etc.
practical ability, dexterity, Polyb.:— also, practice, trickery, Id.
the exaction of money, recovery of outstanding debts or arrears, πρ. συμβολαίων Plat., Dem.:—hence, the exaction of vengeance, retribution, Eur.
in pl. public or political life, Dem.
temperately, Ar.

entry.etym: the declension varies between the two forms πρᾶος and πρᾱύς—the attic sg. is from πρᾶος, except that the fem. is πραεῖα: poet. sg. from πραΰς
entry.sense: Mild, soft, gentle, meek, Hhymn., Pind., Plat.:—of a horse, gentle, Xen.; of other animals, tame, Id.
of actions, feelings, mild, Plat.
making mild, taming, Pind.

adv. πράως, ( from πρᾶος) mildly, gently, Plat.; πράως ἔχειν πρός τι Id.; πράως λέγειν τὸ πάθος to speak lightly of it, Xen.; πράως διακεῖσθαι, opp. to ὀργίζεσθαι, Dem.;—comp., Plat.;—Sup., πραότατα Id.
mildness, gentleness, Plat., etc.
poet. word,
properly = φρένες, the midriff, diaphragm, Il.: then
like φρένες, the wits, understanding, mind, heart, Id.:—sg. πραπίς, ίδος, Pind., Eur.
properly a bed of leeks: generally, a garden-plot, Od.:—metaph., πρασιαὶ πρασιαί in companies or groups, NTest.
for sale, Lat. venalis, Xen.
a selling, sale, ὠνῇ τε καὶ πρήσι (ionic dat.) χρέονται Hdt.; ἐπὶ πρήσι for sale, Id.; πρᾶσιν ποιεῖσθαι Aeschin.
a leek-slice, Anth.
a leek, Lat. porrum, Ar.
leek-green, name of a frog, Batr.
leek-eater, name of a frog, Batr.
to pass over, ἅλα πρήσσοντες Od.; πρ. κέλευθον to accomplish a journey, Hom.; also c. gen., ἵνα πρήσσωμεν ὁδοῖο Il.

to achieve, bring about, effect, accomplish, Id.; οὔτι πρ. to avail naught, Id.; πρ. δεσμόν to cause one's bondage, bring it on oneself, Pind.; πρ. ὥστε, Lat. efficere ut, Aesch.: —Pass., πέπρακται τοὖργον Id.; τὰ πεπραγμένα, Lat. acta, Pind., attic
absol. to effect an object, be successful, Hom.
to make so and so (cf. ποιέω III), Νηρηίδων τινὰ πρ. ἄκοιτιν Pind.
to have to do, be busy with, τὰ ἑαυτοῦ πράττειν to mind one's own business, Soph., etc.
πράττειν τὰ πολιτικά, τὰ τῆς πόλεως to manage state-affairs, take part in the government, Plat.:—then, absol., without any addition, ἱκανὸς πράττειν, of a statesman, Xen.

generally, to transact, negotiate, manage, πρ. Θηβαίοις τὰ πράγματα to manage matters for their interest, Dem.; and in Pass., τῶι Ἱπποκράτει τὰ πράγματα ἐπράττετο matters were negotiated with him, Thuc.;—but τὰ πράγματα may be omitted, οἱ πράσσοντες αὐτῶι those who were treating with him, Id.; so, πράσσειν πρός τινα Id.; ἔς τινα Id.; also, πρ. περὶ εἰρήνης Xen.; οἱ πράσσοντες the traitors, Thuc.; also, πρ. ὅπως πόλεμος γένηται Id.; c. acc. et inf., τὴν ναῦν μὴ δεῦρο πλεῖν ἔπραττεν Dem.:—Pass., of secret practices, εἰ μή τι σὺν ἀργύρωι ἐπράσσετο unless some bribery was a-practising, Soph.; ἐπράσσετο προδόσιος πέρι Thuc.
to practise, Lat. agere, ἀρετάς Pind.; δίκαια ἢ ἄδικα Plat.: absol. to act, Id., etc.

intr. to be in a certain state or condition, to do or fare so and so, ὁ στόλος οὕτω ἔπρηξε Hdt., etc.; εὖ or κακῶς πράττειν to do or fare well or ill, Id., etc.; πρ. καλῶς Aesch.; εὐτυχῶς Soph.; πρ. ὡς ἄριστα καὶ κάλλιστα Thuc.; the perf. 2 πέπρᾱγα is mostly used in this sense, Hdt., Ar., etc.
c. dupl. acc. pers. et rei, πράττειν τινά τι to do something to one, Eur., etc.

πράττειν τινὰ ἀργύριον to exact money from one, Hdt.: often in attic, of state officers, who collected the taxes (cf. εἰσπράσσω, ἐκπράσσω III), Plat., etc.; also, πρ. τι παρά τινος to obtain or demand from another, Hdt.:—metaph., φόνον πρ. to exact punishment for murder, to avenge, punish, Aesch.:—Pass., πεπραγμένος τὸν φόρον called on to pay up the tribute, Thuc.:—Mid., πράξασθαί τινα ἀργύριον, χρήματα, μισθόν, τόκους to exact for oneself, Hdt., etc.; φόρους πράσσεσθαι ἀπό or ἐκ τῶν πόλεων Thuc.:—perf. and plup. pass. are used in mid. sense, εἰ μὲν ἐπεπράγμην τοῦτον τὴν δίκην if I had exacted from him the full amount, Dem.
to be sold, for sale, Lat. venalis, Plat.
a place for selling, a market, Hdt.
a dealer, Plat., Dem.

entry.etym: doric for πρῶτος (contr. from πρόατος) Ar., Theocr.

entry.sense: sold, Soph.
softly-smiling, Anth.
of gentle counsel, gracious, Pind.
of gentle mind, Anth.
a softening, appeasing, Arist.
fit for appeasing, Arist.

to make soft, mild or gentle, to soften, soothe, calm, Hes., etc.; πρ. ἕλκος to soothe a raging sore, Soph.; πρ. τινὰ λόγοις Aesch.:—Pass. to become soft or gentle, grow milder, Hdt.; of passion, to abate, Id.
to tame wild animals, Hes., Xen.
with tamed neck, Anth.
from the stump, i. e. root and branch, utterly, Aesch.
the bottom of the trunk of a tree, the stump: generally, the stem, trunk, Lat. codex, caudex, Hhymn., Xen., etc.
the root or bottom of anything, πρέμνον πράγματος Ar.
in fit manner, meetly, beseemingly, gracefully, Pind., Aesch.
c. dat. in a manner befitting, suitably to, Plat.; also c. gen., like ἀξίως, Id.
distinguished, renowned, Aesch.
fit, becoming, suitable, proper, Ar.; c. dat., Xen., etc.
of impressions on the senses,

on the eye, to be clearly seen, to be conspicuous, ὁ δ’ ἔπρεπε καὶ διὰ πάντων Il.; c. dat. rei, to be distinguished in or by a thing, Aesch., Eur.:—absol. to shine forth, shew itself, appear, Pind., Aesch.; with a part., to be clearly seen as doing or being, Aesch.
on the ear, βοὰ πρέπει the cry sounds loud and clear, Pind., Aesch.
on the smell, to be strong or rank, Aesch.
to be conspicuously like, to be like, to resemble, c. dat., Pind., Eur.
c. inf., δράμημα φωτὸς Περσικὸν πρέπει μαθεῖν his running is like Persian to behold, i. e. one may see it is Persian, Aesch.; so, πρέπει ὡς τύραννος εἰσορᾶν Soph.
to be conspicuously fit, to become, beseem, suit, c. dat. pers., θνατὰ θνατοῖσι πρέπει Pind., etc.

often in part., πρέπον ἐστί or ἦν for πρέπει or ἔπρεπε, Thuc., etc.; rarely c. gen., πρ. ἦν δαίμονος τοὐμοῦ τόδε Soph.:—part. neut. τὸ πρέπον, οντος, that which is seemly, fitness, propriety, Lat. decorum, Plat.
rarely with a person as the subject, πρέπων ἔφυς φωνεῖν art the fit person to speak, Soph.

impers. πρέπει, Lat. decet, it is fitting, it beseems, suits, becomes, c. dat. pers. et inf., οὐ πρέπει ἄμμιν λύειν τείχη Theogn.; ὡς πρέπει δούλοις λέγειν Eur.:—also c. acc. pers. et inf., τὸν πρέπει τυγχανέμεν ὕμνων Pind., etc.:—c. inf. only, πρέπει γαρυέμεν Id.:—when an acc. alone follows, an inf. must be supplied, τίσασθαι ὡς ἐκείνους πρέπει (sc. τίσασθαι) Hdt.
epic fem. of πρέσβυς, the august, honoured, mostly of Hera, Ἥρη, πρέσβα θεά Il.
age, seniority, κατὰ πρεσβείαν Aesch.
rank, dignity, Plat.
an embassy, embassage, Thuc., Plat.
the body of ambassadors, as we say, the Embassy, Ar., Thuc.:— the ambassadors, of early times were elders.
a gift of honour, such as was offered to elders, Il.
the privilege of age, and generally, a privilege, Plat., etc.
the right of the eldest, his share of the inheritance, Dem.

entry.etym: fem. of πρέσβυς, = πρέσβα, Hhymn., Eur.

entry.sense: an ambassador, embassy, in pl., Eur.
#an embassage, Thuc.
an ambassador, Thuc., Plat., etc.
an agent or commissioner, Dem.
properly of age,
intr. to be the elder or eldest, Soph.; τῶν προτέρων ἐπρέσβευε he was the eldest of the former children, Hdt.; πρ. ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ to be his eldest son, Thuc.
to take the first place, be best, Soph.:—c. gen. to rank before, take precedence of others, πρ. τῶν πολλῶν Plat.; to rule over, Ὀλύμπου πρ. Soph.

trans. to place as eldest or first, to put first in rank, to pay honour or worship to, Aesch., Soph.:—Pass. to be put in the first rank, hold the first place, Lat. antiquior sum, Aesch.; c. gen., πρεσβεύεται κακῶν is most notable of mischiefs, Id.
to be an ambassador or go as one, serve or negociate as one, Hdt., Eur., etc.; v. πρεσβεία fin.
c. acc. objecti, πρ. τὴν εἰρήνην to negotiate peace, Dem.; so, πρ. ὑπὲρ τουτωνί Id.
Mid. to send ambassadors, Thuc.:—also to go as ambassador, Id.
Pass., τὰ ἑαυτῶι πεπρεσβευμένα his negotiations, Dem.
πρεσβηὶς τιμή the highest or most ancient honour, Hhymn.
age, κατὰ πρέσβιν according to age, Hhymn., Plat.
eldest, most august, most honoured, Hhymn., Aesch.
an object of reverence, Aesch.; πρ. Ἀργείων august assembly of Argives, Id.
seniority of birth, Hdt.
eldest-born, first-born, Il., Eur.
οἱ πρεσβυγενεῖς the senators, Plut.

an old man, Lat. senex, (the prose form is πρεσβύτης), Soph., Eur.:— ὁ πρέσβυς is used much like ὁ πρεσβύτερος, the elder, Aesch.:—pl. πρέσβεις, elders, always implying dignity, chiefs, princes, Id.; epic πρέσβηες Hes.

Hom. uses only the comp. and Sup., comp. πρεσβύτερος, α, ον, elder, older, Il., Hdt., Pind., attic; ἐνιαυτῷ by a year, Ar.; βουλαὶ πρεσβύτεραι the wise councils of age, Pind.;—Sup. πρεσβύτατος, η, ον, eldest, Il., Hes., etc.: —the comp. and Sup. were used of things, πρεσβύτερόν τι (or οὐδὲν) ἔχειν = Lat. aliquid (or nihil) antiquius habere, to deem higher, more important, τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πρεσβύτερα ποιεῖσθαι ἢ τὰ τῶν ἀνδρῶν Hdt.; πρεσβύτατον κρίνειν τι Thuc.; πρεσβυτέρως γυμναστικὴν μουσικῆς τετιμηκέναι more highly than . . , Plat.: —hence, merely of magnitude, πρεσβύτερον κακὸν κακοῦ one evil greater than another, Soph.
like πρεσβευτής, an ambassador, Aesch., Ar.;—pl. πρέσβεις is more used than πρεσβευταί, Ar., Xen., etc.
a chief, president: comp. πρεσβύτερος, an elder of the Jewish Council, NTest., etc.: an elder of the Church, presbyter, Id.
a council of elders, NTest.
like an old man, elderly, Lat. senilis, ὄχλος Ar.; κακὰ πρ. the evils of age, Id.
old-fashioned, antiquated, Id.:—adv. -κῶς, Plut.
an aged woman, Aesch.
gentleness of temper, graciousness, Eur.
poet. adj. gentle of mood, friendly, gracious, favourable, Aesch., Eur.:—adv. -νῶς, Aesch.
propitiatory, Id.
the crop of birds, Ar.
entry.etym: From πρό, ἀγείρω, because birds collect their food there before it passes into the second stomach.

entry.sense: to blow up, swell out by blowing, ἔπρησεν δ’ ἄνεμος μέσον ἱστίον Od.
to blow out, drive out by blowing, τὸ δ’ [αἷμα] ἀνὰ στόμα πρῆσε he blew a shower of blood through his mouth, Il.
to blow hard, Ar.
with the face downwards, head-foremost, Lat. pronus, opp. to ὕπτιος (Lat. supinus), Il., Hes.
of the sides of hills, πρὸς κατὰ πρανοῦς down hill, Xen.; κατὰ τὰ πρανῆ Id.
to throw headlong:—Pass. to fall headlong, πρηνιχθείς Anth.
a hurricane, Hes., Hdt.

entry.etym: note the aorist infinitive is πρίασθαι not πριάσθαι
entry.sense: to have a thing sold to one, to buy, purchase, Hom., attic; c. dat. pretii, πρ. κτεάτεσσιν ἑοῖσιν to buy with one's money, Od.; c. gen., πρ. θανάτοιο to purchase by his death, Pind.; πρ. τι ταλάντου Xen.; π. πολλοῦ Id.; metaph., οὐδενὸς λόγου πρίασθαι to buy at no price, Soph.; πρ. τι παρά τινος Hdt.:—πρ. τίμιον τοὔλαιον to buy it dear, Ar.
to farm a tax, Xen.
Patronymic, son of Priam Il.
of or like Priam, Arist., Eur.
Priam, Il., etc.; prob. a chief, king,

entry.note: Πρίᾱπος, ionic Πρίηπος, ὁ, πρῐ́ν, adv.
entry.sense: Priapus, the god of gardens and vineyards, and generally of country life, Luc.:— adj. Πρῑάπειος, η, ον, Anth.
made from the πρῖνος, Lat. iligneus, Hes., Ar.:—metaph. oaken, i. e. tough, sturdy, Ar.
the evergreen oak, ilex, or the scarlet oak, quercus coccifera, Hes., Ar., etc.
formed with a comparative force from πρό:
adv. of Time, before,
of future time, before that time, sooner, with fut. Ind. or Subj. = fut., Hom.: with Opt. and κεν, Od.

of past time, aforetime, formerly, once, erst, Hom.; so with the Art., τὸ πρίν γε . . , νῦν δὲ . . ; νῦν δὲ . . τὸ πρίν γε Il.:—with the Art. the Part. ὤν is omitted, τὰ πρὶν πελώρια (sc. ὄντα) the giants of old, Aesch.; ἐν τῷ πρὶν χρόνῳ Soph.; ἐν τοῖς πρὶν λόγοις Thuc.

πρὶν ἤ, as Conjunction, before that, before, ere, priusquam, Hom.; but ἤ is often omitted, so that πρίν becomes a Conjunction: the antecedent clause also has πρίν (or πρότερον, πρόσθεν, πάρος), so that πρίν the Conjunction is relat. to πρίν the adv., especially after a negat.:—it is constructed with Inf., ναῖε δὲ Πήδαιον, πρὶν ἐλθεῖν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν Il.; οὐδὲ παύσεται χόλου, πρὶν κατασκῆψαί τινα Eur.
with a finite Verb:
with Ind., in which case Hom. uses πρίν γ’ ὅτε, πρίν γ’ ὅτε δή, until, μάχη τέτατο, πρίν γ’ ὅτε δὴ Ζεὺς κῦδος Ἕκτορι δῶκε Il.; so, οὐκ ἦν ἀλέξημ’ οὐδέν, πρίν γ’ ἐγὼ σφίσιν ἔδειξα Aesch.

with Subj. only after negatives or equiv. of neg., οὐ καταδυσόμεθ’, πρὶν μόρσιμον ἦμαρ ἐπέλθῃ we will not go down, till the day of death come on, Od.;—in attic πρὶν ἄν is regular, οὐδέν ἐστι τέρμα μοι μόχθων, πρὶν ἂν Ζεὺς ἐκπέσῃ τυραννίδος Aesch.; but ἄν is sometimes omitted, μὴ στέναζε, πρὶν μάθῃς Soph.; as always with πρὶν ἤ, πρὶν ἢ ἀνορθώσωσι Hdt.
with Opt., after historical tenses, οὐκ ἔθελεν φεύγειν πρὶν πειρήσαιτ’ Ἀχιλῆος Il.; ἔδοξέ μοι μὴ ποιεῖσθαι, πρὶν φράσαιμί σοι Soph.
tough as oak, Ar.
like a saw, Anth.
a saw: πριστῆρες ὀδόντες the incisors, Anth.
sawn, Od.
a sawyer, Ar.
a saw, Soph.; πρίων ὀδόντων a saw of teeth, i. e. a jagged row, Anth.; v. πρίων2.
entry.etym: ῑ, attic; but ῐ in later Poets.

entry.sense: a comic Noun, formed from πρίω, imperat. of ἐπριάμην, with a pun upon πρίων, a saw, ὁ πρ. ἀπῆν that rasping word "buy" was unknown, Ar.
to saw, πρ. δίχα to saw asunder, Thuc.: Pass. to be cut in pieces, Eur.
πρίειν τοὺς ὀδόντας to grind or gnash the teeth, Ar.:—metaph. in Pass. to be irritated, Anth.
to seize as with the teeth, bind fast, ζωστῆρι πρισθεὶς ἱππικῶν ἐξ ἀντύγων Soph.
a forewarning, early intimation, Thuc.
to break before, Od.
a stating beforehand, Arist., Plut.

entry.note: aor1 -ηγόρευσα perf. -ηγόρευκα the attic fut. is προερῶ attic fut. προερῶ aor. προεῖπον perf. προείρηκα mid. -εύσομαι Pass. -εύσομαι in mid. form perf. -ηγόρευμαι
entry.sense: to tell beforehand, Thuc.: c. inf. to tell or declare beforehand that . . , Hdt., etc.; so, πρ. ὅτι . . , Xen.
to foretell, prophesy, τὸ μέλλον Id.
to speak before all, to state, declare or proclaim publicly, Hdt., Thuc.; to have a thing proclaimed by herald, Hdt.
c. inf. to order publicly, πρ. ὑμῖν παρεῖναι Id.; πρ. τοῖς πολίταις μὴ κινεῖν to forbid them to move, Plat.:—Pass., γυμνάζεσθαι προαγορεύεται ἅπασι Xen.; τὰ προηγορευμένα Id.
to give notice, notify, Plat.

entry.note: fut. άξω perf. -ῆχα aor2 -ήγᾰγον Pass., aor1 -ήχθην perf. -ῆγμαι
entry.sense: to lead forward, on, onward, Hdt., etc.: to escort on their way, Id., Xen.
to bring forward in public, Plat.

to lead on, induce, Hdt., Thuc.; c. inf., πρ. τινὰ κινδυνεύειν Thuc.; with Preps., πρ. θυμὸν ἐς ἀμπλακίην Theogn.; τινὰ εἰς φιλοποσίαν, εἰς μῖσος Xen.; ἐπ’ ἀρετήν Id.:—so in Mid., ἐς γέλωτα προαγαγέσθαι τινά to move one to laughter, Hdt.; εἰς ἀνάγκην Dem.
to carry on or forward, πρ. τὴν πόλιν to lead it on to power, Thuc.; μέχρι πόρρω προήγαγον τὴν ἔχθραν carried it so far, Dem.:—Pass. to increase, wax, Id.
