comp. προὐργιαίτερος, α, ον, more serviceable, πρ. ποιεῖσθαί τι to deem of more consequence, Thuc.; πρ. γίγνεται, Plat.
to maltreat, insult, only in two passages, ὁρῶν ἐμαυτὸν ὦδε προυσελούμενον Aesch.; οὓς μὲν ἴσμεν εὐγενεῖς προυσελοῦμεν we insult those whom we know to be noble, Ar.
to filch beforehand, πρ. τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, i. e. get it held (without notice) before the expected time, Aeschin.

entry.note: fut. -φᾰνῶ aor1 -έφηνα Pass., aor2 προὐφάνην part. προφᾰνείς 3rd pl. perf. προπέφανται
entry.sense: to bring forth, bring to light, shew forth, manifest, display, Soph.: metaph., Ἀχιλεὺς Αἰγίναν πρ. brought it into light, made it illustrious, Pind.:—Pass. to be shewn forth, come to light, appear, Hom., Soph.; impers., οὐδὲ προὐφαίνετ’ ἰδέσθαι nor was there light enough for us to see, Od.:—aor2 pass. part. προφᾰνείς, εῖσα, coming forward, appearing, Id.
to indicate or declare before, Soph., Dem.
= προτίθημι I. 5, to propose, ἆθλα Xen.
Pass., metaph. of sound, to be plainly heard, προὐφάνη κτύπος Soph.
to shew beforehand, foreshew, of oracles, Hdt., Soph.; ὅκως στρατίην πέμψεις, οὐ προφαίνεις holdest out no hope that thou wilt send, Hdt.: —Pass. or Mid. to shew itself or appear before, Xen.
seeminly intr. (the cognate acc. φάος or φῶς being understood), to give forth light, shine forth, οὐδὲ σελήνη προὔφαινε Od.; of a torch, Plut.; ὁ προφαίνων a torch-bearer, Id.
shewing itself or seen beforehand, Arist.
seen clearly or plainly, conspicuous, Xen.
metaph. quite plain or clear, Plat.; ἀπὸ or ἐκ τοῦ προφανοῦς openly, Thuc.:—adv. -νῶς, Polyb.
far seen, hence far-famed, Pind.
foreshewn, as by an oracle, Hdt., Soph.; πρόφαντα δέ σφι ἐγίνετο oracles were delivered to them, Hdt.

entry.note: imperf. προὐφασιζόμην fut. attic προφασιοῦμαι aor1 προὐφασισάμην
entry.sense: Dep.:

to set up as a pretext or excuse, allege by way of excuse, plead in excuse, c. acc., Theogn., Thuc., etc.; c. inf. to allege as an excuse that . . , Dem.:—absol. to make excuses, Thuc.:—aor1 προφασισθῆναι in pass. sense, to be used as a pretext, Id.
to allege (by way of accusation) that, Plat.
that which is alleged as the cause, an allegation, plea, καὶ ἐπὶ μεγάλῃ καὶ ἐπὶ βραχείᾳ ὁμοίως προφάσει to great or small plea alike, Thuc.; πρ. ἀληθεστάτη Id.

mostly in bad sense, a mere pretext, a pretence, excuse, Hdt., etc.; opp. to the true cause (αἰτία), Thuc.: c. gen. the pretext or pretence for a thing, Hdt., etc.:—absol. in acc., πρόφασιν in pretence, Il., attic; πρόφασιν μέν, opp. to τὸ δ’ ἀληθές, Thuc.; so in dat., προφάσει Id.: — ἀπὸ προφάσιος τοιῆσδε from or on some such pretext as this, Hdt., etc.:— προφάσιος εἵνεκεν Id.:— ἐπὶ προφάσει by way of excuse, Theogn., Thuc.; so, ἐπὶ προφάσιος Hdt.; κατὰ πρόφασιν Id.:—foll. by an inf., αὕτη ἦν σοι πρ. ἐκβαλεῖν ἐμέ for casting me out, Soph.; πρόφασιν ἔχει τοῖς δειλαίοις μὴ ἰέναι gives them an excuse for not going, Plat.

phrases, πρόφασιν διδόναι, ἐνδιδόναι to give occasion, make an excuse, Dem.; πρ. ἐνδοῦναί τινι Thuc.; πρ. προτείνειν, προΐσχεσθαι to put forward an excuse, Hdt.; παρέχειν Ar.; προφάσιας ἕλκειν to keep making pretences, Hdt., etc.; elliptically, μή μοι πρόφασιν (sc. πάρεχε) no excuse, no shuffling, Ar.
Pind. personifies Πρόφασις, as daughter of Epimetheus (Afterthought).
in Soph. it must mean suggestion.

carried before, placed before, excelling, c. gen., Hes.:—comp., more excellent, superior, surpassing, τῶν ἄλλων προφερέστερος Od.; c. inf., [ἡμίονοι] βοῶν προφερέστεραί εἰσιν ἑλκέμεναι are better than oxen in drawing, Il.:—Sup. προφερέστατος Id., Hes.:—also comp. and Sup., προφέρτερος, προφέρτατος Soph.
looking older than one is, well-grown, precocious, Plat., Aeschin.

entry.note: fut. -οίσω aor1 -ήνεγκα aor2 -ήνεγκον —epic 3rd sg. pres. subj. προφέρῃσι
entry.sense: to bring before one, bring to, present, offer, Il., Thuc.
of words, πρ. ὀνείδεά τινι to throw reproaches in his teeth, Il.: and so, πρ. τινί to throw in one's teeth, bring forward, allege, Lat. objicere, μή μοι δῶρα πρόφερε Ἀφροδίτης Id.
simply, to utter, αὐδάν, μῦθον Eur.; πρ. Αἴγιναν πάτραν to proclaim it as their country, Pind.
to bring forward, cite, Thuc.; προφέρων Ἄρτεμιν pleading Artemis as authority, Aesch.
of an oracle, to propose as a task, Hdt.:—Pass., προὐνεχθέντος τινί (gen. absol.) if it were commanded one to do so, Aesch.

to bring forward, display, Il.; ἔριδα πρ. to shew, i. e. engage in, rivalry, Od.; πόλεμόν τινι πρ. to declare war against one, Hdt.:—Mid., ξεινοδόκῳ ἔριδα προφέρεσθαι to offer quarrel to one's host, Od.
to bear on or away, to carry off, sweep away, of a storm, Hom.
to move forward, πόδα Eur.:—then, to promote, further, assist, ἠὼς προφέρει ὁδοῦ morning furthers one on the road, Hes.; πρ. εἴς τι to conduce, help towards gaining an object, Thuc.
intr. to surpass, excel another, c. gen., Hdt., Thuc.
to flee forwards, flee away, Il.
c. acc. to flee from, shun, avoid, Hom.
the gift of interpreting the will of the gods, Orac. ap. Luc.
in NTest., the gift of expounding scripture, of speaking and preaching.
to be an interpreter of the gods, μαντεύεο, Μοῖσα, προφατεύσω δ’ ἐγώ Pind.; τίς προφητεύει θεοῦ who is his interpreter? Eur.; ὅστις σοι προφητεύσει τάδε who will give thee this oracular advice, Id.
in NTest. to expound scripture, to speak and preach under the influence of the Holy Spirit.

one who speaks for a God and interprets his will to man, a prophet; so Teiresias is πρ. Διός, Jove's interpreter, Pind.; and of Apollo, Διὸς προφήτης ἐστὶ Λοξίας πατρός Aesch.; while the Pythia, in turn, became the προφῆτις of Apollo, Hdt.; so Poets are called οἱ τῶν Μουσῶν προφῆται interpreters of the Muses, Plat.
generally, an interpreter, declarer, ἐγὼ πρ. σοι λόγων γενήσομαι Eur.; so, the bowl is called κώμου προφάτης, Pind.
in NTest.,
one who possesses the gift of προφητεία, an inspired preacher and teacher.
the revealer of God's counsel for the future, a prophet (in the modern sense of the word), a predicter of future events.
oracular, Luc.
of the Pythia, Eur.
to outrun, anticipate, c. acc., Aesch., Plat.
absol. to be beforehand, Eur.
dead or killed before, Anth.
Pass. to fear beforehand, fear at the thought of, Xen.
apt to fear beforehand, Arist.
Mid., in weaving, to carry on the web by passing the weft across the warp: metaph., τὴν ὁδὸν προφορεῖσθαι to run to and fro, Ar.
to foretell, Hdt.: perf. pass. part. προπεφραδμένα ἆθλα Hes.
kindly, gracious, Hom.
with forward mind, hence zealous, willing, ready, glad to do a thing, Hom., etc.
of acts, efforts, earnest, zealous, Id.
epic adv. προφρονέως, readily, earnestly, zealously, Il.; later προφρόνως Theogn., attic
a guard in front; in pl. outposts, videttes, piquets, Xen.; in sg., ἡ πρ. αὐτοῦ his advanced guard, Id.; διὰ προφυλακῆς with an advanced guard, Thuc.
προφῠλᾰκὶς, ναῦς, ἡ, a look-out ship, Thuc.
an advanced guard: οἱ προφύλακες

to keep guard before, to guard a place or house, c. acc., Hhymn. (in the epic 2nd pl. imperat. προφύλαχθε, for προφυλάσσετε), Xen.; προφυλάσσειν ἐπί τινι to keep guard over a person or place, Hdt.:—absol. to be on guard, keep watch, ἡ προφυλάσσουσα (sc. ναῦς) = προφυλακίς, Id.: —Mid. to guard oneself, to be on one's guard, take precautions, Id., Thuc.:—c. acc. to be on one's guard or take precautions against, Lat. cavere, Hdt., Xen.
to mix up or knead beforehand: metaph. in Pass., προπεφύραται λόγος the speech is all ready concocted or brewed, Ar.
to plant before: metaph. to engender, Soph.
to utter beforehand, Aesch.; προφωνεῖ τόνδε λόγον gives this order beforehand, Id.
to order beforehand or publicly, c. dat. et inf., καί σοι προφωνῶ τόνδε μὴ θάπτειν Soph.; with inf. omitted, ὑμῖν προφωνῶ τάδε Id.
to rejoice beforehand, Plat.
in 3rd sg. imperat. προχαιρέτω, far be it from me! away with it! Aesch.
to forge beforehand, Aesch.
with prominent lips, Strab.
to put into the hand, have ready at hand, Polyb.:—Pass., in perf. part., taken in hand, undertaken, Plat., Dem.
as Dep. προχειρίζομαι, fut. attic -χειριοῦμαι: — to take into one's hand, prepare for oneself, Dem.
to choose, elect, Id.
c. inf. to determine to do, Polyb.
at hand, ready, Aesch., Soph.; of a drawn sword or knife, Soph., Eur.; λίθοις καὶ . . ἀκοντίοις, ὡς ἕκαστός τι πρόχειρον εἶχε Thuc.; ὃ προχειρότατον ἔχω εἰπεῖν Dem.
πρόχειρόν [ἐστι] it is easy, c. inf., Plat., etc.
of persons, ready to do, c. inf., Soph.; c. dat., πρ. τῇ φυγῇ ready for flight, Eur.
adv. -ρως, off-hand, readily, Plat.
to choose or elect before, Plat., Aeschin.
to give a previous vote, Dem.
to pour forth or forward, Il., Pind.; σπονδὰς προχέαι Hdt.:—metaph., ὄπα γλυκεῖαν Pind.:—Pass., metaph. of large bodies of men pouring over a plain, Il.
with the knees forward, i. e. kneeling, on one's knees, Il.; metaph., ὥς κεν ἀπόλωνται πρόχνυ that they may perish on their knees, i. e. may be brought low and perish, Id.; so, πρόχνυ ὀλέσθαι Od.
mostly in pl., the outpouring, i. e. the mouth, of a river, Hom., Pind., etc.; sg. in Hes.
a chamberpot, Xen.
a vessel for pouring out, a ewer for pouring water on the hands of guests, Hom., Soph.;— a wine-jug from which the cupbearer pours into the cups, Od.
to dance before in a chorus, πρ. κῶμον to lead a κῶμος or festive band, Eur.
to smear before, πρ. τί τινι to smear or rub with a thing, Soph.
of former time, Luc.
a pouring out, πρ. τῆς γῆς a deposition of mud by a river, Lat. alluvies, Hdt.: —in οὐλὰς κριθῶν πρόχυσιν ἐποιέετο (cf. προχύται), πρόχυσιν ἐποιέετο must be taken as a simple Verb = προέχεε, Id.
(sc. κριθαί) αἱ = οὐλο-χύται, Eur.
an urn for libations, Eur.
poured out in front:— Προχύτη νῆσος the island of Procida, formed by eruption from Vesuvius, Strab.
very lame or halt, Luc.
to go or come forward, advance, πρὸς ἐμὴν χεῖρα as my hand guides thee, Soph.; of troops, Thuc.:—of Time, to go on, Xen.

metaph. of States, wars, enterprises, etc., to proceed, advance, go on, often with some word to denote a good or bad issue, εὖ προχωρῆσαι Eur.; προχωρησάντων ἐπὶ μέγα τῶν πραγμάτων Thuc.; τούτων προκεχωρηκότων ὡς ἐβούλοντο Xen.:—absol. to go on well, prosper, Hdt., etc.

impers., προχωρεῖ μοι it goes on well for me, I have success, ὡς οἱ δόλῳ οὐ προεχώρεε when he could not succeed by craft, Id.; c. inf., ἢν μὴ προχωρήσῃ ἀπελθεῖν if it be not possible to depart, Thuc.:—absol. in part., προκεχωρηκότων when things went on well, Xen.
later, of persons, to advance, Luc.
to push forward, push or urge on, Plat.; πρ. αὑτόν to rush on, Xen.
ruined beforehand, Dem.
before the time, untimely, Anth.
men-at-arms, foot-soldiers, opp. to chiefs fighting from chariots, Il.
of a ship-stern, Anth.

(sub. ναῦς) the hindmost part of a ship, the stern, poop, Lat. puppis, Hom., etc.; he sometimes has it in full, νηὶ πάρα πρύμνῃ, ἐπὶ πρύμνῃ νηί, νηὶ ἐνὶ πρ., and in pl., νηυσὶν ἔπι πρύμνῃσι; though he also has πρύμνη νηός Od.:— ἐπὶ πρύμνην ἀνακρούεσθαι to back a ship (v. ἀνακρούω II); so, χωρεῖν πρύμναν to retire, draw back, Eur.; ἐπείγει κατὰ πρύμναν, of a fair wind, Soph.; κατὰ πρ. ἵσταται τὸ πνεῦμα Thuc.—Ships were fastened or drawn up on land by the stern, Il.: hence, πρύμνας λῦσαι Eur.; cf. πρυμνήσιος.
metaph. of the vessel of the State, Aesch.
generally the bottom, πρ. Ὄσσας the foot of mount Ossa, Eur.
steersman, name of a Phaeacian, Od.
from the stern, Il., Aesch., Eur.
of or from a ship's stern, κάλως Eur.:—neut. pl. πρυμνήσια (sc. δεσμά) stern-cables, Lat. retinacula navis, Hom.
the steersman:—metaph., χώρας πρ. ἄναξ "the pilot" of the State, Aesch.
as masc. adj. = πρυμνήσιος, πρ. κάλως Eur.
from the bottom, hence like Lat. funditus, utterly, root and branch, Aesch.
the lower part, end, Il.; πρυμνοῖς ἀγορᾶς ἔπι at the far end of the agora, Pind.

the hindmost, undermost, end-most: in Hom. always of the end of the limb next the body, the root, πρυμνὸς βραχίων, πρυμνὴ γλῶσσα, etc.; so, πρυμνὴν ὕλην ἐκτάμνειν to cut off the wood at the root, Il.; δόρυ πρυμνόν the part of a spear-head where it joins the shaft, Id.; λᾶας πρυμνὸς παχύς a stone broad at base, opp. to ὕπερθεν ὀξύς (which follows), Id.; Sup. πρυμνότατος Od.:—for πρύμνη ναῦς, v. πρύμνα.
holding the ship's stern, Anth.
detaining the ships (because they were anchored by the stern), Αὖλις Eur.
the foot of a mountain, Il.

the prytany or presidency, at Athens a period of 35 or 36 days, about 1/10 of a year, during which the prytanes of each φυλή in turn presided in the βουλή and ἐκκλησία, Oratt.; ἑνδεκάτῃ τῆς πρυτανείας (sc. τῆς Πανδιονίδος) on the 11th of the presidency of the Tribe Pandionis, Dem.
any public office held by rotation, πρ. τῆς ἡμέρης the chief command for the day, held by each general in turn, Hdt.

the presidents' hall, town-hall, Lat. curia, Hdt., Thuc., etc.; consecrated to Hestia or Vesta, to whom a perpetual fire was kept burning in it, which in Colonies was brought from the Prytaneion of the mother-city: at Athens the Prytanes had their meals there, and there they entertained foreign ambassadors, Ar., Dem.: citizens also of high merit, and the children of those who had fallen in battle, were rewarded by a seat at this public table, ἐν πρυτανείῳ δειπνεῖν, σιτεῖσθαι Ar., Plat.
a law-court at Athens, Dem., Plut.

πρυτανεῖα, τά, a sum of money deposited by each party to a lawsuit before the suit began, Ar., etc.; τιθέναι πρυτανεῖά τινι, i. e. bring an action against, Id.; ἵν’ αἱ θέσεις γίγνοιντο τῇ νουμηνίᾳ (sc. τῶν πρυτανείων) Id.; δέχεσθαι τὰ πρ. to receive this deposit, i. e. to allow the action to be brought, Id.
to be πρύτανις or president, to hold sway, Hhymn.
at Athens, to hold office as Prytanis, properly used of the presiding φυλή (v. πρύτανις II), ἔτυχεν ἡ φυλὴ Ἀκαμαντὶς πρυτανεύουσα Plat., etc.
πρ. περὶ εἰρήνης to put the question on a motion for peace, this being the duty of the Prytanes, Ar., etc.
generally, to manage, regulate, Dem.:—Pass., πρυτανεύεσθαι παρά τινος to suffer oneself to be guided by one, Id.
a prince, ruler, lord, chief, of Hiero, Pind.; of Zeus, Id., Aesch.

at Athens, a Prytanis or President: the πρυτάνεις were a committee of 50, chosen by lot from each of the 10 φυλαί, so that each set formed 1/10 part of the βουλή or Council of 500; out of these 50 πρυτάνεις one was chosen by lot as chief-president (ἐπιστάτης); he chose 9 πρόεδροι; and the real business was in the hands of this smaller body, with a secretary (γραμματεύς) added.—The φυλή which first entered office every year was determined by lot; and their term of office (πρυτανεία) was about five weeks. During this time all treaties and public acts ran in their name, in this form: Ἀκαμαντὶς [φυλὴ] ἐπρυτάνευε, Φαίνιππος ἐγραμμάτευε, Νικιάδης ἐπεστάτει the Tribe Acamantis were the Presidency, Phaenippus the Secretary, Niciades the Chief-president, Thuc.
lately, just now, Lat. nuper, Il., etc.
the day before yesterday, οὐ χθές, ἀλλὰ πρ. Thuc.; πρώην τε καὶ χθές till yesterday or the day before, i. e. till very lately, Hdt.; so, χθές τε καὶ πρώην Ar.; πρώην καὶ χθές Dem.
in the prime of youth, Hom.; fem. πρωθήβη Od.
neut. pl. πρωιζά was used as adv., just like πρώην, χθιζά τε καὶ πρωιζά yesterday or the day before, Il.
οὕτω δὴ πρ. κατέδραθες so very early, Theocr.
early, of fruits, Xen.
early,
early in the day, at early morn, Il.; also, περὶ δείλην πρωίην (cf. δείλη) Hdt.:— πρωία used alone as Subst., ἦν δὲ πρωία, πρωίας γενομένης NTest.
early in the year, πρώιος [ὁ στρατὸς] συνελέγετο Hdt.; πρῷα τῶν καρπίμων early fruits, Ar.
early in the day, early, at morn, Il.; c. gen., πρωὶ ἔτι τῆς ἡμέρης Hdt.; ἑκάστης ἡμέρας τὸ πρῷ Xen.; πρῷ τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ early next morning, Id.; ἅμα πρωί, ἀπὸ πρωί NTest.
generally, betimes, early, in good time, Lat. mature, tempestive, Hes., Ar., etc.; c. gen., πρῲ τῆς ὥρας Thuc.

= πρὸ καιροῦ, too soon, too early, πρῷ γε στενάζεις Aesch.; πρῲ ἐσβαλόντες, καὶ τοῦ σίτου ἔτι χλωροῦ ὄντος Thuc. —πρωί takes its degrees of comparison from its deriv. adj. πρώιος, comp. πρωιαίτερον, Sup. πρωιαίτατα, attic πρῳαίτερον, πρῳαίτατα, Thuc., etc.
the anus, generally, the hinder parts, tail, Ar.

entry.etym: gen. and dat. πρῶνος, πρῶνι, not πρωνός, πρωνί for it is contr. from πρεών
entry.sense: a foreland, headland, Lat. promontorium, Il.; the pl. is πρώονες from the lengthd. form πρώων, Id.:—in Aesch. Pers. 132, ἀμφοτέρας πρῶνα κοινὸν αἴας the foreland common to both continents is perh. the Chersonese; and Id. 879, πρὼν ἅλιος the peninsula of Asia Minor.
a dewdrop, Theocr.

entry.etym: ionic -ηθεν, in Poets before a consonant
entry.sense: from the ship's head, from the front, Pind., Thuc., etc.:—it is an old gen., and is so used ἐκ πρῴραθεν, by Theocr.

entry.etym: not πρώρα, for it is contr. from πρώειρα
entry.sense: the forepart of a ship, a ship's head, prow, bow, Lat. prora, Od., etc.; πνεῦμα τοὐκ πρῴρας a contrary wind, opp. to κατὰ πρύμναν, Soph.
metaph., πρῷρα βιότου the prow of life's vessel, i. e. early youth, Eur.; πάροιθεν πρῴρας καρδίας before my heart's prow, in front of my heart, Aesch.
to be a πρῳράτης, Ar.
the officer in command at the bow, the look-out man, Xen., etc.
announcing first, c. gen., Anth.
the first fruits of the chase: mostly in pl., Anth.
to be πρωταγωνιστής, Plut.:— metaph. to play first fiddle, to take the lead, Arist.
one who plays the first part, the chief actor, Lat. primarum partium actor, Arist.
first-beginning, primal, πρ. ἄτα Aesch.
the chief rank, first place, Dem.:—mostly in pl. the first prize, first part or place, Plat., Dem.
monument of Protesilaus, Strab.
Protesilaus, first-of-the-people, name of the hero who first leaped ashore at Troy, Il.
to be the first, hold the first place, Plat., etc.:— to be first in a thing, καρτερίᾳ Xen.; βδελυρίᾳ Aeschin.; περὶ κακίαν Id.
c. gen. pers. to be first of or among, τῶν ῥητόρων Id.
the earliest plougher, Hes.
the very first, first of the first, Hom.; πολὺ πρώτιστος Id.: neut. πρώτιστον as adv. first of all, Od., Ar., etc.: —so πρώτιστα, Hom., attic; —τὸ πρώτιστον Eur.; τὰ πρώτιστα Od.
first struck, Eur.
first-born, firstling, Il., Hes.; φοῖνιξ πρ. first-created, Eur.
of rank, πρ. οἶκοι high-born houses, Soph.
first-ordained, Luc.
newly wedded, Anth.
the first seat, NTest.
the first seat at table, NTest.
committing the first murder, the first homicide, of Ixion, Aesch.
first dog, i. e. chief of the Cynics, Anth.
the first spoils in war, the firstfruits; τῶν σῶν γονάτων πρωτόλεια as the first act of my supplication, Eur.
the first prophet or seer, Aesch.
dying or dead first, Aesch.
first cause of ill, Aesch.
going to sea for the first time, Od., Eur.; πρ. πλάτα the firstplied oar (of the ship Argo), Eur.
sailing first or foremost, Xen.
the advanced guard, vanguard, Polyb.
one who stands first, on the right, the right-hand man, Thuc.; but οἱ πρ. the front-rank men, Xen.
metaph. the leader of a party, NTest.
the rights of the first-born, birthright, NTest.
bearing her first-born, Il., Theocr.
pass. first-born, Anth., NTest.
first cut, Anth.

entry.etym: the pres. in use was the Dep. πτάρνυμαι
entry.sense: to sneeze, μέγ’ ἔπτᾰρε he sneezed aloud, Od., Ar.; "Ζεῦ σῶσον," ἐὰν πτάρῃ, as we say "God bless you, " Anth.:—of a lamp, to sputter, Id.
a stumble, trip, false step, Theogn.
a failure, misfortune, defeat, Hdt., Dem., etc.
trans. to make to stumble or fall, τινὰ πρός τινι Pind.:—Pass., τὰ πταισθέντα failures, Luc.

intr. to stumble, trip, fall, Soph., etc.; πτ. πρός τινι to stumble against, fall over, Aesch., Plat.; πρός τι Xen.; also, μὴ περὶ Μαρδονίωι πταίσηι ἡ Ἑλλάς lest Hellas should get a fall over him, i.e. be defeated by him, Hdt.
metaph. to make a false step, to fail, Thuc., Dem.; so, ἐλάχιστα, τὰ πλείω πτ. Thuc. etc.
a sneezing, Ar., Thuc., etc.
to sneeze, (v. *πταίρω), Xen.
the elm, Lat. ulmus, Il.
made of feathers, πτ. κύκλος a feather- fan, Eur.; πτ. ῥιπίς Anth.
feathered, winged, Ar.
the heel, Il.: the under part of the heel, Aesch.
a ham, Batr.
ham-scraper, Batr.
ham-nibbler, Batr.
ham-eater, Batr.
moved by flapping wings: metaph. high-soaring, Ar.
feathered, winged, ὀϊστοί, ἰοί Il.; πέδιλα Hes., etc.
feather-like, light, λαισήια Il.
metaph., ἔπεα πτερόεντα winged words, Hom., Hes.; so, πτ. ὕμνος Pind.; also, φυγὴ πτερόεσσα Eur.
mostly in pl. feathers, Od., Hdt., etc.; in sg. a feather, Ar.

= πτέρυξ, a bird's wing, in pl. wings, Hom., Aesch.; Παλλάδος ὑπὸ πτεροῖς ὄντας, metaph. from chickens under the hen's wings, Aesch.: —τῷ πτερὰ γίγνετο he got as it were wings, i. e. spirit, courage, Il.
the wings of a bat (v. πτίλον II), Hdt.
any winged creature, as the Sphinx, Eur.; a beetle, Ar.
like οἰωνός, Lat. avis, an augury, omen, Pind., Soph.
anything like wings: as
a ship's wings, i. e. oars (cf. πτερόω), ἐρετμά, τά τε πτερὰ νηυσὶ πέλονται Od.; νηὸς πτερά Hes., Eur.:— hence birds are said πτεροῖς ἐρέσσειν, Eur.
ἀέθλων πτερά, i. e. the wings of victory, which lift the Poet to heaven, Pind.
a feathered arrow, Eur.
τοῦ πώγωνος τὰ πτερά the points of the beard, Luc.
in Architecture, of the rows of columns along the sides of Greek temples, v. ἄπτερος.
motley-feathered, Ar.
wing-footed, of Hermes, Anth.
to shed the feathers, moult, Ar.: metaph. to be plucked, fleeced, plundered, Id.
feathered, winged, Aesch., Eur.; πτ. φῦλα the feathered tribes, Ar.:—metaph., πτ. Διὸς βέλος the winged bolt of Zeus, Id.
to grow feathers, Plat.
feather-producing, Plat.
to furnish with feathers or wings, feather, τινά Ar.; πτεροῦν βιβλίον to tie a paper to a feathered arrow, Hdt.:—Pass. to be or become feathered, to be fledged, Ar., Plat.
to furnish a ship with oars: metaph. in Pass., σκάφος τάρσῳ ἐπτερωμένον winged with oars, Eur.
metaph. to set on the wing, excite (cf. ἀναπτερόω), Ar.:—Pass. to be excited, Luc.
to flutter with the wings, like young birds trying to fly, Ar.: to flap the wings like a cock crowing, Id.:—in Ar. Eq. the word alludes to a play by Magnes called Ὄρνιθες.
the wing of a building, a turret or pinnacle, NTest.
having wings, winged, Ar.
the wing of a bird, Il.; in pl. wings, Hom., etc.
a winged creature, a bird, Anth.
anything like a wing, the flap or skirt of a coat of armour, Xen.; also of the doric χιτών, Ar.
the broad edge of a knife or spear, Plut.
anything that covers or protects like wings, πτ. πέπλων Eur.; Εὐβοίης πτέρυξ, i. e. Aulis, Id.
metaph., πτέρυγες γόων the wings, i. e. the flight or flow, of grief, Soph.; πτ. Πιερίδων Pind.
attic -ττομαι, fut. ξομαι, Dep. to clap the wings like a cock crowing, Babr., Luc.
that which is feathered, e. g. a feathered arrow, Aesch.
plumage, Plat.
plumage, Ar.
feathered, Hdt., Eur., etc.
winged, Hdt., Trag.; so, πτ. φθόγγος, a sound as of wings, Ar.
πτερωτοί (sc. ὄρνιθες) feathered fowl, birds, Eur.
bird-killing, Anth.
feathered, winged, Trag., etc.; Διὸς πτ. κύνες, i. e. eagles, Aesch.
τὰ πτηνά winged creatures, fowls, birds, Id., Trag.; πτηνὸν ὀρνίθων γένος Ar.; πταναὶ θῆραι chase of winged game, Soph.
metaph., πτηνοὶ μῦθοι, like Homer's ἔπεα πτερόεντα, Eur.; πτ. ὄνειροι fleeting dreams, Id.
a flying, flight, Aesch.
to frighten, scare, alarm, Lat. terrere, Il., Theogn.
intr. to crouch or cower down for fear (cf. πτώσσω), properly of animals, Soph.; of men, Pind., attic; πτ. βωμὸν ὕπο Eur.; also c. acc. loci, πτ. βωμόν to flee cowering to the altar, Id.
to crouch like a wild beast ready to spring, Id.;—so of men in ambush, ὑπὸ τεύχεσι πεπτηῶτες Od.
c. acc. rei, to crouch for fear of, ἀπειλάς Aesch.
used properly of the soft feathers or down under the true feathers, a piece of down, a plumelet, Ar.; cf. πτιλωτός.
a wing-like membrane in a kind of serpent, Hdt.
with feathered back, Anth.
with membranous wings, opp. to πτερωτός, Arist.
peeled barley: a drink made thereof, barley-water, a ptisan, Ar.
to winnow: to peel or to bray in a mortar, Hdt.
one who shells or pounds, Anth.
abject fear, terror, Polyb.
to terrify, scare, Anth.:—Pass. to be scared, dismayed, φρένες ἐπτοίηθεν Od.; ἐπτοημένος Aesch., Eur.

metaph. to flutter, excite by any passion, τό μοι καρδίαν ἐπτόασεν Sapph.:—Pass. to be in a flutter, be passionately excited, Theogn.; ἐπτοημένοι φρένας Aesch.; ὡς ἐπτόηται Eur.:—generally, μέθ’ ὁμήλικας ἐπτοίηται he gapes like one distraught after his fellows, Hes.; τὸ πτοηθέν distraction, Eur.
passionate excitement, Plat.
of or from Ptolemy, Strab.
name of several cities, esp. of one in Phoenicia, now Acre, Strab.
sacking or wasting cities, Il., Pind.

entry.etym: epic for πόλις, Hom., Aesch., Eur.

entry.sense: a young branch, shoot, sucker, sapling, Od., Eur., etc.;— πτ. μέγας, of Hercules' club, Anth.
a sprouting, budding, Hes.
anything folded, πέπλοιο πτύγμα a folded mantle, Il.
folded, πτ. πίναξ folding tablets, Il.

entry.etym: not in nom., πτυχή being used instead
entry.sense: a fold, leaf, plate, mostly in pl., πτύχες σάκεος plates of metal or leather used to form a shield, Il.: the folds of a garment, Hhymn., Eur.; of the entrails, Eur.:—of writing tablets (cf. πτυκτός), Trag.

in pl. of the sides of a hill (which viewed from a distance appears to be in folds), a cleft, glen, corrie, combe, Hom., etc.; also in sg., Il., Soph.:—so also of the sky with its cloud-clefts, Eur.:—metaph., ὕμνων πτυχαί varied turns of poesy, Pind.
a winnowing-shovel or fan, Lat. vannus, with which corn after threshing was thrown up against the wind to clear it of the chaff, Il. (in poet. gen. πτυόφιν), Theocr.
Pass.:— to be scared or frightened, properly of horses, Plut.
timorous, Strab.

to fold, χιτῶνα, εἵματα πτύξαι to fold up garments, and put them by, Od.; χεῖρας πτύξαι ἐπί τινι to fold one's arms over or round another, Soph.; βιβλίον πτ. to fold up or close a book, NTest.:—Pass. to be folded, doubled up, Il.; Mid. to fold round oneself, wrap round one, Ar.
to spit out or up, Il.: absol. to spit, Hdt., Xen.
of the sea, to disgorge, Anth.:—absol., ἐπ’ ἀϊόνι πτύοντα, of waves, Theocr.; πτύσας with a splash, Anth.
metaph., πτύσας in token of abhorrence or loathing, Soph.; πτύσας προσώπωι with loathing in his face, Id.
εἰς κόλπον πτύειν, Lat. in sinum spuere, done three times to avert a bad omen, Theocr.
cowering, timorous, epic Hom.: πτωκάδες in Soph. seem to be timorous creatures, birds.
a fall, πεσεῖν πτώματ’ οὐκ ἀνασχετά Aesch.; πίπτουσι πτώματ’ αἰσχρά Soph.
metaph. a fall, calamity, Lat. casus, Eur.
of persons, a fallen body, corpse, carcase, πτῶμα Ἑλένης, Ἐτεοκλέους Id.; also πτώματα alone, Aesch.
the cowering animal, i. e. the hare, Il., Theocr.; also, πτῶκα λαγῷον (the two Substs. being joined, as in ἴρηξ κίρκος, σῦς κάπρος), Il.
having fallen, Aesch.
a falling, fall, Plat.
Lat. casus, the case of a noun, Arist.

to crouch or cower from fear, properly of animals (cf. πτάξ, πτώξ, πτωκάς), Od.; πτώσσουσι καθ’ ὕδωρ flee cowering into the water, Id.; of men, Id.; πτ. ὑφ’ Ἕκτορι fly cowering before Hector, Id.; so, εἰς ἐρημίαν πτ. Eur.
to go cowering or cringing about, like a beggar, Od., Hes.
c. acc. pers., οὐδ’ ἔτι ἀλλήλους πτώσσοιμεν let us no longer flee from one another, Il.; ποῖ καί με φυγᾷ πτώσσουσι; whither have they fled for fear of me? Eur.
beggary, mendacity, Hdt., Ar.
to be a beggar, go begging, beg, Od., Ar., etc.
trans. to get by begging, δαῖτα Od.
c. acc. pers. to beg or ask an alms of, Theogn.
of or fit for a beggar, beggarly, Eur., Plat., etc.
a beggar-poet, Gorg. ap. Arist.
drawing beggarly characters, of a poet, Ar.
making poor, Plut.
one who crouches or cringes, a beggar (v. πτώσσω 1. 2), Od., Hes., etc.; πτωχὸς ἀνήρ a beggar-man, Od., etc.; πτωχή a beggar-woman, Soph., NTest.
as adj. beggarly, like πτωχικός, Soph., NTest.: c. gen., poor in a thing, Anth.
comp. πτωχότερος, irreg. πτωχίστερος, Ar.: Sup. πτωχότατος, Anth.
adv. -χῶς, poorly, scantily, Babr.
(sc. ἱερά), the Pyanepsia, an Athenian festival in the month Πυανεψιών, in honour of Apollo; said to be so called from the custom of cooking beans at the feast (πύανον ἕψειν), Plut.
the fourth month of the attic year,so named from the festival Πυανέψια, = latter part ofOctober and former of November, Theophr.
a kind of bean.
of or on the rump: τὸ πυγαῖον = ἡ πυγή, the rump, Hdt.
white-rump, the name of a kind of antelope, Hdt.
the white-tailed eagle, the erne, Soph., etc.
the rump, buttocks, Ar., etc.
a thin rump, Ar.
a πυγμή long or tall: of men, dwarfish, Hdt.:— Πυγμαῖοι, οἱ, the Pygmies, a race of dwarfs on the upper Nile, said to have been warred on and destroyed by cranes, Il.
to practise boxing, be a boxer, Inscr. in Hdt., Anth.
boxing, Lat. pugilatus, Il., Pind.
one who fights with the fist, a boxer, Lat. pugil, Od., Pind., etc.
a fist, Lat. pugnus, πυγμῇ νικήσαντα having conquered with the fist, in boxing, Il.; later, πυγμὴν νικᾶν Eur.; πυγμᾶς ἄεθλα Pind.
πυγμῇ νίψασθαι in NTest., is interpr. = πύκα, diligently; or = πυκνά, often, with; cf. πυκνός B. II. and III.
a measure of length, the distance from the elbow to the knuckles, = 18 δάκτυλοι, about 13 1/2 inches.
with sweeping train, Hes.
of the length of a πυγών, Od.
the distance from the elbows to the first joint of the fingers, = 20 δάκτυλοι or 5 παλαισταί, rather more than 15 inches, Hdt., Xen.
an oblong trough, for feeding animals, Od.: a bathing-tub, Ar.:— a vat, kitchen-boiler, Id.
the philosopher Pythagoras, Hdt., etc.
of Pythagoras, Arist.
to be a disciple of Pythagoras, Arist., etc.
a name of Apollo at Delphi
one who consults Apollo's oracle, Strab.
(sc. ἱερά), the Pythian games, celebrated every four years (prob. in the 3rd Olympian year) at Pytho or Delphi in honour of Pythian Apollo, Pind., etc.
(sc. ἱέρεια), the Pythia, priestess of Pythian Apollo at Delphi, Hdt., etc.
(sub. ἱέρεια), = ἡ Πυθία, the Pythian priestess, Aesch.
(sub. ἑορτή), the celebration of the Pythian games, Pind.
(sub. πομπή), a sacred mission from Athens to Pytho or Delphi, Strab.
of or for Pytho, Pythian, Trag., etc.
a conqueror in the Pythian games, Pind.
of or a belonging to a Pythian victory, Pind.
the temple of Pythian Apollo, Thuc.
Pythian, i. e. Delphian, of Apollo, Hhymn., Pind., attic; Π. alone, Eur.; ἐν Πυθίου in his temple, Thuc.
= Πυθικός, Pind., Soph., etc.
οἱ Πύθιοι, Lacon. Ποίθιοι, at Sparta, four persons whose office it was to consult the Delphic oracle on affairs of state, Hdt., Xen.
the hollow bottom or stand of a cup, Lat. fundus, Il., Hes., etc.
of the sea, the bottom, depth, Hes., Solon., etc.
the bottom or foundation of a thing, in pl., χθόνα ἐκ πυθμένων κραδαίνειν Aesch.; ἐκ π. ἔκλινε κλῇθρα Soph.; δίκας π. the anvil-stand on which is forged the sword of retribution, Id.
the bottom, stock, root of a tree, Od., Solon.:—metaph. the stem or stock of a family, Aesch.; σμικροῦ γένοιτ’ ἂν σπέρματος π. μέγας, i. e. great things might come from small, Id.
at Pytho or Delphi, Pind., Xen., etc.
to Pytho or Delphi, Plut.
confirmed by the Pythian god: τὰ Πυθόκραντα the Pythian oracles, Aesch.
the Pythian prophet, Aesch., —Π. ἑστία the prophetic seat at Pytho, Soph.
sent by the Pythian oracle, Aesch.
delivered by the Pythian god, Aesch., Xen.
= Πυθοχρήστης, Eur.
to Pytho, Od., Soph., Ar., etc.
from Pytho, Pind.
the serpent Python, slain by Apollo.
πνεῦμα Πύθωνος a spirit of divination, NTest.: ventriloquists (ἐγγαστρίμυθοι) were called Πύθωνες, Plut.
Pytho, older name of that part of Phocis at the foot of Parnassus, in which lay the city of Delphi, Hom., etc.
to make rot, to rot, Il., Hes.:—Pass. to become rotten, to decay, Hom.
vehement, Aesch.

to make close, cover or wrap up, enwrap, Il.; π. νῆα λίθοισι to surround a ship with stones, so as to protect it when laid up, Hes.:— to cover thickly, of a youth's chin, Od.; πυκ. στεφάνοις to cover thick with crowns, Eur., Theocr.; so in Mid., στεφάνοις κεφαλὰς πυκασώμεθα Anth.; also without στεφάνοις, to crown, deck with garlands, Eur.:—Pass., στέμμασι πυκασθείς Hdt.; δάφνῃ πυκασθείς Eur.; perf. part. πεπυκασμένος, thickly covered, ὄρος πεπυκασμένον a hill well-clothed with wood, Hes.:—Mid., πυκάζου cover thyself, Eur.
metaph., Ἕκτορα ἄχος πύκασε φρένας threw a shadow over his heart, Il.:—Pass., νόον πεπυκασμένος, close, cautious of mind, Hes.
to close, shut, shut up, ἐντὸς πυκάζειν σφέας αὐτούς to shut themselves close up within, Od.; πύκαζε (sc. τὸ δῶμα) shut it close, Soph.
poet. adv., v. πυκνός B. III.
of close or cautious mind, shrewd, Hom.
assembled in the Pnyx, Ar.; cf. πνύξ.
thick-feathered, π. ἀηδόνες, where it seems to be a poet. periphr. for πυκναί, multitudinous, Soph.
thick with berries, Anth.
close, compact: and so,
of consistency, close, firm, solid, opp. to what is loose and porous (μανός, ἀραιός), Hom.; πυκινὸν λέχος a well-stuffed bed, Id.
close-packed, crowded, thick, close, dense, Id.; of the plumage of a sea-bird, Id.; of foliage, Id.; of a shower of darts or stones, Id., Hdt.; of hair, Aesch., etc.
frequent, many, Lat. creber, Id., Eur., etc.
well put together, compact, fast, strong, Il.
close, concealed, δόλος Id.
generally, strong of its kind, great, sore, excessive, ἄτη Id.
metaph. of the mind, sagacious, shrewd, wise, Hom.; πυκινοί the wise, Soph.; of a fox, Ar.
adv. πυκινῶς, and after Hom. πυκνῶς, θύραι or σανίδες πυκινῶς ἀραρυῖαι close or fast shut, Hom.
very much, constantly, sorely, greatly, Id.
sagaciously, shrewdly, craftily, Id.
Hom. also uses neuters πυκνόν and πυκνά, πυκινόν and πυκινά as adv., much, often; so also in attic; comp. πυκνότερον, πυκνότερα; Sup. πυκνότατα.
poet. adv. πύκα (q. v.), as if from πύκος, strongly, Hom.
πύκα βάλλετο with thick-falling darts, Il.
carefully, diligently, Id.
thick-spotted, dappled, ἔλαφοι Soph.
closeness, thickness, denseness, Ar., Thuc., etc.
frequency, Isocr., etc.
metaph. sagacity, shrewdness, craft, Ar.

to make close or solid, to pack close, π. ἑαυτούς to close their ranks, Hdt.; σαυτὸν στρόβει πυκνώσας spin yourself round and concentrate your thoughts, Ar.:—Pass. to be compressed, πυκνουμένῳ πνεύματι, i. e. without taking breath, Plut.
Pass. to be thickly covered, Xen.
close order or array, Plut.
in pl. combined notes, or recurrent notes, in music, Plat.
to practise boxing, box, spar, Xen., etc.; εἰς κρᾶτα π. to strike with the fist on the head, Eur.
a boxer, pugilist, Pind., Soph.
skilled in boxing, Plat.: —ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) the art of boxing, Id.
of or for boxers, Id.
a writing tablet, Anth.
prob. an unknown animal, perh. the beaver, Ar.
to be or act as a Πυλαγόρας, Dem.
one sent as a deputy to Pylae, where the Amphictyonic Council was held, the deputy of a Greek State to that Council, Dem., Aeschin.
(sc. σύνοδος), the autumn-meeting of the Amphictyons at Pylae, Hdt.; then, generally, the Amphictyonic Council, Id.
the right of sending deputies to this Council, Dem.
a promiscuous crowd, such as was found at these meetings, Plut.: then, idle jesting, trifling, Id.
jesting, silly, Plut.
fighting at the gates, or at Pylos, Ar.
at Pylae, Anth.
gate-fastener, he that keeps the gates of hell, Hom.
at the gates, Soph.
keeping the gate, a gate-keeper, Il. (Altered, to suit the epic metre, from πυλαορός, cf. τιμάορος, τιμωρός, and v. οὖρος custos.)
watching at the door, of Hermes, Hhymn.
one wing of a pair of double gates, Hdt.: mostly in pl. the gates of a town, opp. to θύρα (a house-door), Il., attic
in Trag., sometimes, of the house-door.
Ἀΐδαο πύλαι, periphr. for the nether world, hell, Hom., Aesch., etc.
generally, an entrance, of the liver, π. καὶ δοχαὶ χολῆς the orifice and receptacle of gall, Eur.

an entrance into a country through mountains, a mountain-pass, Hdt.: esp. Πύλαι, ῶν, αἱ, the common name for Θερμοπύλαι, the pass round the mountains from Thessaly to Locris, considered the gates of Greece, Id.; so, of the pass from Syria into Cilicia, Xen., etc.
also of narrow straits, by which one enters a broad sea, ἐπ’ αὐταῖς λίμνης π., of the Thracian Bosporus, Aesch.; ἐν πύλαις, of the Euripus, Eur.
a postern, Hdt., Thuc.
from Pylos, Od.
sprung from Pylos, Il.
to or towards Pylos, Hom.
Pylos, a town and district of Triphylia in Peloponnesus, where Nestor ruled, Hom. Two towns of the same name, in Elis and Messenia, are often confounded with Triphylian Pylos.
to furnish with gates, Xen.:— Pass. to be so furnished, Ar.
a gate, gateway, Aesch., Eur.
a gateway, gate-house, Polyb., etc.
to be a πυλωρός, keep the gate, Luc., etc.
a gate-keeper, warder, porter (v. πυλαωρός), Aesch., Eur.; also as fem., ἡ π. δωμάτων γυνή Eur.:—metaph., τοῖον πυλωρὸν φύλακα τροφῆς such a watchful guardian of thy life, Soph.
last-speaking, ἠχώ Anth.
hindmost, last, Il.:— also outermost, Id.:— nethermost, φάρος Plat.; π. Ταρτάρου βάθη Luc.
of Time, last, Hom.:—neut. πύματον and πύματα as adv., at the last, for the last time, Hom.
of Degree, ὅ τι πύματον whatever is the last, worst fate, Soph.
the bottom of a vessel, Theophr.
to learn by hearsay or by inquiry, Hdt.:
πυνθ. τί τινος to learn something from a person, Hom., etc.; τι ἀπό τινος Aesch.; ἔκ τινος Soph.; παρά τινος Hdt.
c. acc. rei only, to hear or learn a thing, Od., attic
c. gen. to hear of, hear tell of, hear news of, Od., etc.
π. τινά τινος to inquire about one person of or from another, Ar.; so, π. περί τινος Hdt., attic

c. part., πυθόμην ὁρμαίνοντα ὁδόν I heard that he was starting, Od.; π. τὸ Πλημμύριον ἑαλωκός to hear that Plemmyrium had been taken, Thuc.:—so, οὔπω πυθέσθην Πατρόκλοιο θανόντος they had not yet heard of his being dead, Il.
c. inf. to hear or learn that, Soph., etc.
made of box-wood, Il., Theocr.
a tablet of box-wood, Luc.
a box of box-wood, Luc.
the box-tree or box-wood, Lat. buxus.
with clenched fist, πὺξ ἀγαθὸς Πολυδεύκης good at the fist, i. e. at boxing, Hom., etc.; πὺξ μάχεσθαι with the fists, Il.; πὺξ πατάσσειν, παίειν Ar.
the first milk after the birth, beestings, Lat. colostrum, Ar.
an exclamation of surprise, bravo! Plat.
a pair of fire-tongs, Hom.
serving for tongues, Anth.
to turn in the fire, to harden in the fire, char, Od.
a pyramid, Hdt.
a cake of wheat and honey, given as a prize, Ar.
watch-fires, mostly in acc., καίωμεν πυρὰ πολλά Il.; πυρὰ ἐκκαίειν Hdt.:— beacon-fires, Thuc.: — ἄτιμος ἐν πυροῖσι, of sacrificial fires, Aesch.
entry.etym: The accent, as well as the dat. πυροῖς, shews that it does not belong to πῦρ.

entry.sense: fiery bright, Hhymn., Anth.
like a tower:—of soldiers, in columns, in close array, Il.: v. πύργος II.
Pass. to be shut up as in a tower, to be beleaguered, Aesch., Eur.
of a place, fortified, ap. Paus.
tower-like, Aesch.
destroying towers, Aesch.
to assault a tower, Xen.
a tower, Il., Hdt., etc.:—in pl. the city walls with towers, Il.; so, collectively, in sg., Od., Eur.
a movable tower for storming towns, Xen.
metaph. a tower of defence, as Ajax is called πύργος Ἀχαιοῖς, Od.; παῖς ἄρσην πατέρ’ ἔχει πύργον μέγαν Eur.; θανάτων π. a tower of defence from deaths, Soph.
the highest part of any building, where the women lived, Il.
troops drawn up in close order, a column, Id.; cf. πυργηδόν.
to bear a tower or towers, Luc.
bearing a tower, of Cybele, Anth.
a tower-guard, warder, Aesch.
to gird or fence with towers, Od., Eur.:—Mid. to build towers, Xen.:—Pass., πυργωθείς furnished with a tower, of an elephant, Anth.

metaph. to raise up to a towering height, πυργῶσαι ῥήματα σεμνά "to build the lofty rhyme," Ar.; so, ἀοιδὰς ἐπύργωσε Eur.:—hence, to exalt, lift up, Id.; so, π. χάριν to exalt, exaggerate it, Id.:—Pass. to exalt oneself, Aesch.; πεπύργωσαι θράσει, λόγοις Eur.
like a tower, Soph.
that which is furnished with towers, a fenced city, Orac. ap. Hdt., Eur.:—in pl. fenced walls, Aesch., Eur.
fem. adj. towering, Aesch.
burning with fire, incendiary, Aesch.
mostly in pl. pieces of wood, rubbed one against another to produce fire, Hhymn., Soph., etc.
to be ill of a fever, Eur., Ar.
burning heat, fiery heat, Il.
feverish heat, a fever, Ar., etc.
a fire-proof vessel, Anth.
fanning fire, Anth.
the stone of stone-fruit, as of the olive, Hdt.

entry.note: πῠρή, ῆς, ionic πῠρή, ῆς, ἡ,
entry.sense: any place where fire is kindled,
a funeral-pyre, Lat. bustum, Il., Hdt., etc.
a mound raised on the place of the pyre, Soph., Eur.
an altar for burnt sacrifice, Hdt., Eur.:—also the fire burning thereon, Hdt.
producing fire, Anth.

entry.etym: πυρός, πέφαται 3rd sg. perf. pass. of *φένω
entry.sense: π. λάτρις Δήμητρος the wheat-slaying servant of Demeter, i. e. a millstone, Anth.
wheat-bearing, Od.
beestings-pudding, Ar.
a vapour-bath, made by throwing scented substances on hot embers confined under a cloth, Hdt.
a vapour-bath, heated by a furnace underneath, Plut.
fire-wrought, Aesch.
born in fire: of instruments, wrought by fire, Eur.
producing fire, Plut.
devoured by fire, Aesch.
with fiery point, Od.
heated in the fire, Anth.
or -καυτος, burnt in fire, Il.
wherein fire lies asleep, νάρθηξ π., of the cane of Prometheus, Anth.
bright with fire, Plut.
seized by fire, volcanic, Strab.
to break out into a furious blaze, Plut.
of wheat, wheaten, Xen., etc.
of fire, fiery, hot, Anth.

entry.etym: πῠρι-πνέων, ουσα, ον, part. with no Verb in use
entry.sense: firebreathing, Eur.
fire-breathing, fiery, Anth.
roaring with fire, Theocr.
sowing fire, inflaming, Anth.
fire-streaming, Eur.
of or in fire, Luc.
cherishing fire, of billows.
fire-blazing: as Subst., Pyriphlegethon, one of the rivers of hell, Od.
flaming with fire, blazing, Eur., Xen.
blazing with fire, Eur.
fire-coloured, Alcidam. ap. Arist.

entry.note: πυρ-καϊά, epic and ionic ιή, ἡ,
entry.sense: any place where fire is kindled, a funeral pyre, Il.
a fire, conflagration, Hdt.: arson, Lex ap. Dem.
metaph. the flame of love, Anth.
fit for eating, Theocr.
wheaten bread, Od.
giving forth fire:— τὰ πυροβόλα bolts or arrows tipped with fire, Plut.
made from wheat, Anth.
fiery, Anth.
ὁ Πυρόεις the planet Mars, from his fiery colour, Arist.
a theft of fire, Anth.
reaping wheat, Anth.
to deal in wheat, Dem.
bursting in the fire, fire-flawed, cracked, Ar.
wheat, Hom.; also in pl., Od., etc.
wheat-bearing, Il., Eur.

to burn with fire, burn up, Hdt., Soph.: to burn as a burnt sacrifice, Aesch., Eur.; π. Κύκλωπος ὄψιν to burn out his eye, Eur.:—Mid., παῖδα πυρωσαμένη having placed one's son on the pyre, Anth.:—Pass. to set on fire, to be burnt, Pind., Eur.
metaph. in Pass. to be inflamed or excited, Aesch.
Pass. also, of gold, to be proved or tested by fire, NTest.
to fumigate, Theocr.
to play tricks with fire, play mischievous tricks, Hhom.
wrought from fire, of a thunderbolt, Pind.
firebreathing, Τυφών Aesch., Eur.
fire, Hom., etc.; πῦρ καίειν or δαίειν to kindle fire, Id.; πῦρ ἀνακαίειν, ἅπτειν, ἐξάπτειν, αἴθειν, ἐναύειν, v. sub vocc.; πῦρ ἐμβάλλειν νηυσί Il.
the funeral-fire (cf. πυρά), Id.
the fire of the hearth, πυρὶ δέχεσθαί τινα Eur.; π. ἄσβεστον or ἀθάνατον the fire of Vesta in the Prytaneion, Plut.

as a symbol of things irresistible or terrible, μάρναντο δέμας πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο they were fighting like burning fire, Il.; κρεῖσσον ἀμαιμακέτου πυρός Soph.; διὰ πυρὸς ἰέναι (as we say) to go through fire and water, Xen.; but, διὰ πυρὸς ἦλθε ἑτέρῳ λέκτρῳ she raged furiously against the other partner of the bed, Eur.:—of persons, ὦ πῦρ σύ Soph.:—rarely as an image of warmth and comfort, Aesch.
to light and keep up a fire, watch a fire, Od., Xen.; π. τοὺς ἄνθρακας to stir up the fire, Ar.
to waste with fire, burn and destroy, Id.;—Mid., πυρπολέεσθαι πᾶσαν τὴν Ἀττικήν to cause it to be burnt with fire, Hdt.
a watchfire, beacon, Eur.
wasting with fire, burning, κεραυνός Eur.
to be fiery red, of the sky, NTest.
named after Pyrrhus, Theocr.
(sc. ὄρχησις), the pyrrhic dance, a kind of war-dance, Ar., Xen.;—attributed to one Πύρριχος the inventor.
generally, δειναὶ π. strange contortions, Eur.:—proverb., πυρρίχην βλέπειν "to look daggers, " Ar.
to dance the pyrrhic dance, Luc.
of or belonging to the pyrrhic dance, Luc.
ποὺς π. a pyrrhic, i. e. a foot consisting of two short syllables, used in the πυρρίχη or war-song.
a dancer of the πυρρίχη: οἱ π. the chorus of Pyrrhic dancers, Lys., Isae.
red, Theocr.
red-bearded, Anth.
red-haired, Solon.
a crow with a red beak, Plin.
Pass. to become red, Arist.
one that ogles young boys with a play upon πῡρο-πίπης, ogling wheat (i. e. dinner in the Prytaneium), Ar.
flame-coloured, yellowish-red: of persons with red hair, like the Scythians, Lat. rufus, Hdt.; of the colour of the first beard, Aesch., Eur.
generally, red, tawny, Lat. fulvus, λέων Eur., Xen.
of persons also, red with blushes, Ar.; but, κύων πυρς’ ἔχουσα δέργματα glaring with red eyes, Eur.
to make red, tinge with red, Eur.
to light up, kindle, πυρσεύσας σέλας Εὐβοίαν having lit up Euboea with beacon-fires (σέλας combining with the notion of the Verb), Eur.

to make signals by torches or beacon-fires, Xen.: metaph., πυρσεύετε κραυγὴν ἀγῶνος give a shout in signal of battle, Eur.:—Pass., δόξα ὥσπερ ἀπὸ σκοπῆς πυρσεύεται Plut.: impers., πυρσεύεται fire-signals are made, Luc.
shooting forth fire, Anth.
red-backed, Eur.
a firebrand, torch, Il., Eur.:—in pl. fires, Anth.:—metaph., πυρσὸς ὕμνων Pind.; pl. the fires of love, Theocr.
a beacon or signal-fire, bale-fire, Hdt.
pl. πύρσα, watch-fires, Eur.
fire-producing, π. λίθος a flint, Anth.
like a firebrand, Eur.
to be a πυρφόρος, to carry a torch, Eur.
to set on fire, Aesch.
fire-bearing, Aesch.; of lightning, Pind., Aesch.:— πυρφόροι ὀϊστοί arrows with combustibles tied to them, Thuc.
in special senses,

epith. of Zeus in reference to his lightnings, Soph.; of Demeter, in reference to the torches used by her worshippers, Eur.; of Artemis, Soph.; —but θεὸς πυρφόρος the fire-bearing god, the god who produces plague or fever, Id.
ὁ πυρφόρος, in the Lacedaemonian army, was the priest who kept the sacrificial fire, which was never allowed to go out, Xen.; hence proverb. of a total defeat, ἔδεε δὲ μηδὲ πυρφόρον περιγενέσθαι Hdt.
like fire, fiery, Ar., etc.
fiery-eyed, fiery, Aesch.
enquiry, τὰς πύστεις ἐρωτῶντες, εἰ . . introducing the questions whether . . , Thuc.
that which is learnt by asking, tidings, Aesch., Eur.; κατὰ πύστιν ᾗ χωροίη according as they learnt which way he was gone, Thuc.; πύστει τῶν προγενομένων by hearing of what was done before, Id.
plaited with osier, πτερὰ πυτιναῖα are given to Diitrephes, because he had grown rich by his trade of a basket-maker, Ar.

sense.gloss: a flask covered with plaited osier.

entry.sense: wearing a beard, Anth.
the beard, Hdt., Ar., etc.:—metaph., πώγων πυρός a beard or tail of fire, Aesch.
a breeding of foals, stud, breed, Xen.
of a foal, χαίτη Suid.
to go up and down, go to and fro, Lat. versari in loco: hence, to go or come frequently, εἰς ἀγορὴν πωλέσκετο Il.; εἰς ἡμέτερον [δῶμα] πωλεύμενοι Od.
horsebreaking, Xen.
to break in a young horse, Xen.

to exchange or barter goods, to sell or offer for sale, Hdt., attic; c. gen. pretii, ἐς Σάρδις χρημάτων μεγάλων π. to sell at a high price for exportation to Sardis, Hdt.; ἐπώλεε οὐδενὸς χρήματος refused to sell it at any price, Id.; ἐρέσθαι ὁπόσου πωλεῖ to ask what he wants for it, Xen.; absol., π. πρός τινα to deal with one, Ar.
π. τέλη to let out the taxes, Lat. locare, Aeschin.
to sell, i. e. give up, betray, Dem.:—of persons, to be bought and sold, Ar.
a selling, sale, Xen.
a seller, dealer, Ar.
a place where wares are sold, an auction-room, shop, Xen.
the office of the πωληταί, Dem.
one who sells; at Athens, the πωληταί were ten officers, who let out (locabant) the taxes and revenues to the highest bidders, Dem.
of foals, fillies, or young horses, ἀπήνη π. a chariot drawn by horses, Soph., Eur.; π. διώγματα pursuit in chariot drawn by horses, Eur.
of any young animal, π. ἑδώλια the girls' apartments, Aesch.
a pony, Ar.
to break young horses, Eur., Xen.
metaph. to train up, Soph.
a horsebreaker, Xen.
fighting on horseback or in a chariot, Anth.
a foal, young horse, whether colt or filly, Hom.: in Poets generally for ἵππος, Soph., etc.
a young animal, a puppy, Anth.
in Poets, in fem., a young girl, maiden, like δάμαλις, μόσχος, πόρτις, Lat. juvenca, Eur.:—more rarely masc., a young man, Aesch.
rearing young horses, Anth.
a lid, cover, Hom.

entry.etym: ΠΟ, Root of some tenses of πίνω
entry.sense: a drink, a draught, Trag., Plat., etc.
to furnish with a lid, cover up, Babr.
up to this time, yet, almost always with a negat. (like Lat. -dum in nondum), with which it forms one word, οὔπω, μήπω.
after Hom., with questions which imply a negative, Soph., Thuc.
ever yet, mostly with negat., οὐ πώποτε, μὴ πώποτε, Hom., etc.
πῶ μάλα; or πώμαλα; where in the world? how in the name of fortune? i. e. not a whit, Ar., Dem.
Lat. tophus, Ital. tufa, a porous stone; the πώρινος λίθος of Hdt.
to petrify, turn into stone: metaph. in Pass. to become hardened, of the heart, NTest.
petrifaction: metaph. hardness, NTest.
in a certain way, opp. to ἁπλῶς, Arist.
in any way, at all, by any means, Hom.; ὧδέ πως somehow so, Xen.; ἄλλως πως in some other way, Id.:—after hypothet. Particles, εἴπως, ἐάν or ἤν πως, Lat. si qua, si forte, Od., etc.

interrog. adv. of manner, how? in what way or manner? Lat. qui? quomodo? used in direct questions, as ὅπως in indirect, Hom., etc.:—with a second interrog. in the same clause, πῶς ἐκ τίνος νεὼς . . ἥκετε; how and by what ship came ye? Eur.:—c. gen., πῶς ἀγῶνος ἥκομεν; how are we come off in it? Id.
with Verbs of selling, how? at what price? πῶς ὁ σῖτος ὤνιος; Ar.
πῶς δοκεῖς; v. δοκέω 1. 2.

with other Particles, πῶς ἂν. . ; epic πῶς κε or κεν . . ; how possibly . . ? Hom., Eur.: —in Trag., πῶς ἄν with opt. expresses a wish, O how might it be? i. e. would that it were . . ! Lat. O si . . ! O utinam . . ! πῶς ἂν θάνοιμι; πῶς ἂν ὀλοίμην, etc.
πῶς ἄρα . . ; in reply, how then . . ? Hom.
πῶς γὰρ . . ; also in reply, as if something had gone before, [that cannot be], for how can . . ? Id., Soph.
πῶς δή; how in the world? Il., etc.:—also, πῶς γὰρ δή; Od.; πῶς δῆτα . . ; Aesch., etc.
καὶ πῶς . . ; to introduce an objection, yet how can it be? attic
πῶς οὐ . . ; how not so . . ; ? i. e. surely it is so . . , Thuc., etc.
πῶς οὖν. . ; like πῶς ἄρα . . ; Aesch., etc.
πῶς ποτε . . ; how ever . . ? Soph.
to fly about, Il., Hapoll.

entry.note: πῶυ, ος, εος, pl. πώεα, ων, τά,
entry.sense: a flock, of sheep, opp. to ἀγέλη (a herd of oxen), Hom., Hes.
o my master, Hebr. words in NTest.
a little rod, a wand, Babr.
a fighting with a staff or foil, Plut.
to sit as umpire, Soph.
holding a rod or wand; hence, like ῥαβδοῦχος, of the Rom. lictors, Plut.
a rod, wand, stick, switch, Lat. virga, Hom., Xen.
a magic wand, as that of Circe or Hermes, Hom.
a fishing-rod, Od.:—also a limed twig, for catching birds, Ar.
a spear-staff or shaft, Xen.
a staff of office, like the earlier σκῆπτρον, Pind.
the wand borne by the ῥαψῳδός: hence, κατὰ ῥάβδον ἐπέων according to the measure of his (Homer's) verses, Pind.
a rod for chastisement, Plat.; αἱ ῥάβδοι the fasces of the Roman lictors, Plut.
a stripe or strip, Il.
to carry a rod or wand, as a badge of office:—Pass., at Rome, to have the fasces borne before one, Plut.
at Rome, the fasces, Plut.
one who carries a rod or staff of office:
a judge, umpire at a contest, Plat.
a magistrate's attendant, a beadle, Ar.:—so, at Rome, of the lictors who carried the fasces, Polyb., etc.
to carry a wand or stick, Strab.
the fluting of columns, Arist.
striped, Xen.
a rent, chink, Anth.
tearing, furious, Plut., Luc.
to gather grapes, Theocr.
gathering berries, Anth.
the Persian name for a black strong smelling petroleum, Hdt.
slender, taper, Il., Theogn., etc.
of the limbs or body, taper, slim, Hes., Theogn.
generally, tender or mobile, ὄσσε Aesch.

easy, ready, easy to make or do, opp. to χαλεπός, Hom., etc.; ῥηίδιόν τοι ἔπος a word easy for thee to understand, Od.:—c. inf., τάφρος ῥηιδίη περῆσαι easy to pass over, Il.; ῥηίτεροι πολεμίζειν easier to fight with, Id.
ῥᾴδιόν ἐστι it is easy to do a thing, c. inf., Pind., Thuc.; c. acc. et inf., τύραννον εὐσεβεῖν οὐ ῥᾴδιον Soph.; also, ῥᾷστοί εἰσιν ἀμύνεσθαι = ῥᾴδιόν ἐστιν αὐτοὺς ἀμύνεσθαι, Thuc.
also, ῥᾴδιόν ἐστι it is a light matter, you think little of doing, παρ’ ὑμῖν ῥ. ξενοκτονεῖν Eur.
of persons, easy, complaisant, Lat. facilis, commodus, Dem.:—in bad sense, reckless, Luc.
adv. ῥᾳδίως, epic and ionic ῥηιδίως, easily, lightly, readily, willingly, Hom., etc.; ῥᾳδίως φέρειν to bear lightly, make light of a thing, Eur., etc.
in bad sense, lightly, recklessly, rashly, Thuc.; ῥᾳδίως οὕτω in this easy, thoughtless way, Plat.
comp., ῥᾷον φέρειν Thuc.
Sup. ῥᾷστα, esp. in phrases, ῥᾷστα φέρειν Soph.; ὡς ῥᾷστα φέρειν Aesch.
to do things with ease or off-hand, Luc.
to live an easy, lazy life, take things easily, Xen.
to act thoughtlessly or recklessly, to do wrong, misbehave, Id.
a reckless act, crime, Plut.
ease in doing, facility, Xen.
easiness, laziness, sloth, Id.
recklessness, want of principle, wickedness, lewdness, Id.: fraud, Plut.
properly, doing things easily; in bad sense, unscrupulous, reckless, Arist.
of things, impure, Xen.
a drop, Il., Hes.
of solids, a grain, bit, Il.
to give one a slap on the buttocks, Ar.
to leave off work, to be remiss, Xen.
easiness of temper, a taking things easily, Thuc.
recreation, relaxation, amusement, Eur.
in bad sense, indifference, sluggishness, laziness, Xen., etc.; ῥ. κτήσασθαι to get a name for laziness, Eur.
heedlessness, rashness, Plat.
taking things easy, indifferent, lazy, sluggish, Lat. socors, Soph., etc.
of things, easy, Lat. securus, Isocr., Plat.:—adv. -μως, Plat.
adv. also, like ῥᾳδίως, lightly, with equanimity, Id.; comp. -ότερον, Isocr.; -οτέρως, Arist.
with crooked head, Anth.
crook-legged, Anth.
crooked, bent, Arist.
to grow easier, find relief, recover from illness, Plat., Dem.:— to take one's rest, Xen.
to sprinkle, besprinkle, ῥάσσατε (sc. δῶμα ὕδατι) Od.; αἵματι βωμόν Eur.:—Pass., πύργοι αἵματι ἐρράδατ’ Il.; αἵματι δ’ ἐρράδαται τοῖχοι Od.:—of dust, ἵπποι ῥαίνοντο κονίηι Il.
metaph., ῥ. τινὰ ὕμνωι Pind.
to sprinkle, with acc. of the thing sprinkled, ῥαίνειν ἐς τὰ βλέφαρα to sprinkle (vinegar) in their eyes, Ar.
a hammer, Il., Aesch.
to break, shiver, shatter, wreck, Od.;— Pass., ῥαιόμενος one shipwrecked, Id.; φάσγανον ἐρραίσθη was shivered, Il.
to crush, destroy, in Pass., Aesch., Soph.
Hebr. word expressive of utter contempt, NTest.
a rag, in pl. rags, Ar.
a rag-stitcher, Ar.
ragged, Eur.
ragged, torn, tattered, Anth.
wrinkled, Id.
a ragged garment, a rag, Od., Ar.: in pl. ῥάκεα, attic ῥάκη, rags, tatters, Od., Hdt., etc.
generally, a strip of cloth, Hdt.: a strip of flesh, Aesch.
in pl. rents in the face, wrinkles, Ar.
metaph. a rag, remnant, Anon. ap. Arist.; of an old seaman, ἁλίοιο βίου ῥάκος Anth.
to tear in strips, Plut.
in pl., = ῥάκη, rags, Ar.
a beak, bill, neb, Ar.
a drop, Eur.; a rain-drop, Ar.
of or for sprinkling:—in Aesch., it seems to be bedabbled, reeking.
= ῥαίνω, NTest.
of the effect, to purify, Id.
a sprinkling, NTest.
a grape, Lat. racemus, Plat.
to strike with a stick, to cudgel, flog, bastinado, Hdt., Dem.
to slap in the face, NTest.
a stroke, a slap on the face, Luc.
stitched, patched, Od.
metaph. strung together, continuous, of verses, Pind.
worked with the needle: ῥαπτόν, οῦ, an embroidered carpet, Xen.; ῥαπτὴ σφαῖρα a stitched ball, of divers colours, Anth.

to sew or stitch together, stich, Il., Ar.:— Mid., ῥάπτεσθαι ὀχετὸν δερμάτων to make oneself a pipe of leather, Hdt.; ῥαψάμενος τουτί (sc. τὸ προσκεφάλαιον) having got it stitched, Ar.; but also, to sew on or to one, Id.:—Pass., ἐρράφθαι τὸ χεῖλος to have one's lip sewed up, Dem.
metaph. to devise, contrive, plot, Hom., etc.; proverb., τὸ ὑπόδημα ἔρραψας μὲν σύ, ὑπεδήσατο δὲ Ἀρισταγόρης you made the shoe, but Aristagoras put it on, Hdt.
enclit. Particle, Hom., and in lyric passages of Trag.
τὸ Ρ̓άριον (sc. πεδίον) the field of Rarus, sacred to Demeter, where tillage was first practised, Hhymn.
Raros, father of Triptolemus.
to be idle, listless, Xen.
easiness or an easy way of doing anything, Plat.; ῥᾳστώνῃ or μετὰ ῥᾳστώνης with ease, easily, lightly, Id.; ῥᾳστώνην φυγῆς παρέχειν to provide an easy way of escape, Plut.
easiness of temper, good nature, kindness, Lat. facilitas, τινός to or towards a person, Hdt.

relief or recovery from, τῆς πόσεως from the effects of drinking, Plat.: absol. rest leisure, ease, Id.; διὰ ῥᾳστώνην for the sake of resting, Xen.: —also luxurious ease, indolence, carelessness, Thuc., Dem.
to thrust a radish up the fundament, a punishment of adulterers in Athens, Ar.
the radish, Lat. raphanus, Ar.
a stitcher, patcher: metaph., ῥ. φόνου a planner of murder, Aesch.
a seam, Lat. sutura, Od.
the suture of the skull, Hdt.; so, ῥαφαὶ ὀστέων Eur.
a needle, Anth.
the sea breaking on the shore, esp. the flood-tide, opp. to ἄμπωτις, Hdt.
a rocky shore or beach, Aesch., Thuc.
to cut through the spine, to cleave in twain, Aesch., Soph.
the lower part of the back, the chine, Il.: then, the spine or backbone, ὑπὸ ῥάχιν παγῆναι to be impaled, Aesch.
anything ridged like the backbone, a mountain-ridge, Hdt.
with surf, Strab.
a thorn-bush, briar, Xen.:— collectively, a thorn-hedge, a wattled fence, Hdt.
to recite epic poems, Plat.
in contemptuous sense, to repeat by heart or rote, to declaim, Dem., Luc.; c. inf. to keep saying that . . , Dem.
recitation of epic poetry, Plat.
epic composition, opp. to lyric (κιθαρῳδία), Id.
a portion of an epic poem fit for recitation at one time, e. g. a book of the Iliad or Odyssey, a lay, canto, Plut., Luc.
of or for a rhapsodist: ἡ -κή (with and without τέχνη), the rhapsodist's art, Plat.

properly one who stitches or strings songs together; esp. a person who recited epic poems, a rhapsodist, applied to Homer, Plat.; but ῥαψῳδοί commonly meant a class of persons who got their living by reciting the poems of Homer, Hdt., Plat.; v. ῥαψῳδία II.
Soph. calls the Sphinx ῥαψῳδὸς κύων, because she proposed her riddle publicly, as the rhapsodists did their lays.
Rhea, daughter of Uranus and Gaia, wife of Cronus, mother of the gods, Hom., etc.
easily, lightly, Il.
entry.etym: Sometimes used as one long syll.

entry.sense: to snore, Lat. sterto, Aesch., Ar.; of horses, to snort, Eur.
to do, act, deal, Od.:—absol., Hom.:—c. acc. rei, to do, accomplish, make, Id., etc.: —Pass., μῆχος ῥεχθέντος κακοῦ a remedy for mischief once done, Il.

c. dupl. acc. pers. et rei, to do something to one, κακὸν ῥέζειν τινά Hom.; ἀγαθὰ ῥ. τινά Id.; also more rarely c. dat. pers., μηκέτι μοι κακὰ ῥέζετε do me no more mischiefs, Od.; ὅσα βροτοῖς ἔρεξας κακά Eur.
with strengthd. signf., εἴ τι ῥέξει if it shall avail aught, be of any service, Il.
in spec. sense, to perform sacrifices, Hom., Soph.; absol. to do sacrifice, Lat. operari, facere, ῥέζειν θεῶι Hom.:—sometimes with the victim in acc., ῥέξω βοῦν ἦνιν will sacrifice it, Id.
a limb, in pl. the limbs, body, Il.
in sg. the face, countenance, Soph., Eur.
easily, lightly, Hom.; θεοὶ ῥεῖα ζώοντες the gods who live at ease, Lat. securum agentes aevom, Id.; strengthd. ῥεῖα μάλ’ Il.
that which flows, a river, stream, mostly in pl., ποταμοῖο ῥέεθρα Il.; Στυγὸς ὕδατος αἰπὰ ῥ. Id.; streams of blood, Aesch.:—sg., Hdt., Aesch.
the bed or channel of a river, Il., Hdt.
a worker, doer, Hes.
active, Plut.
Dep. to roam, rove, roll about, Plut.: metaph. to be unsteady, act at random, Id.
roving, rolling, Plut.
a stream, Aesch.

properly of the descending scale, to incline downwards, to sink, fall, Lat. vergere, inclinare, Il., Ar.:—of things, to incline one way or the other, to be always shifting, Pind.; ὕπνος ἐπὶ βλεφάροις ῥέπων sleep falling upon the eyes, Id.
of one of two contending parties, to preponderate, prevail, Hdt., Plat.
of persons, εὖ ῥέπει θεός is favourably inclined, Aesch.; ῥέπειν ἐπί τι to incline towards a thing, Dem.; εἴς or πρός τι Plat., Arist.; εἴς τινα Luc.
of duties, ῥ. εἴς τινα to fall or devolve upon one, Aesch., Soph.
of events, to fall, happen in a certain way, Soph.; r(. εἴς τι to turn or come to something, Aesch., Ar.
that which flows, a flow, stream, current, Aesch., Soph., etc.
the stream of a river, mostly in pl., Hdt., Eur.; a stream of lava, Thuc.: metaph. a stream or flood of men, Trag., Soph.
a flood, Thuc.
a discharge from the body, a flux, rheum, Luc.
Pass. to flow as a current, Strab.
a rivulet, Plut.
flowing, liquid, Plut.

to flow, run, stream, gush, Hom., etc.:—with dat. of that which flows, πηγὴ ῥέει ὕδατι the fountain runs with water, Il.; ῥέεν αἵματι γαῖα Id.; ῥεῖ γάλακτι πέδον Eur.; of a river, μέγας ῥεῖ runs with full stream, Hdt.; so, πολὺς ῥεῖ, metaph. of men, Aesch.; of a river, also, ῥ. ἀπὸ χιόνος to derive its stream from melted snow, Hdt.:—proverb., ἄνω ῥέειν to flow backwards, of impossibilities, Eur.

metaph. of things, ἐκ χειρῶν βέλεα ῥέον from their hands rained darts, Il.; of a flow of words, ἀπὸ γλώσσης μέλιτος γλυκίων ῥέεν αὐδή Id.; absol., of the tongue, to run glibly, Aesch. (cf. Hor., salso multoque fluenti): of words or sentiments, to be current, Soph.
to fall, drop off, e. g. of hair, Od., Theocr.: then, generally, to flow or melt away, perish, Soph., Plat.
of persons, ῥ. ἐπί or εἴς τι to be inclined, given to a thing, Isocr., Plat.
very rarely trans. to let flow, pour, ἔρρει χοάς Eur.
c. acc. cogn., ῥείτω γάλα, μέλι let the land run milk, honey, Theocr.; οἶνον ῥέων Luc.
a breakage, fracture, Dem.
the sea breaking on the beach, the line of breakers, surf, Hom.; ἐπὶ or παρὰ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης by the edge of the sea, Id.
to break, break asunder or in pieces, rend, shiver, shatter, Hom., etc.:—to rend garments, in sign of grief, Aesch.:—Mid. to break for oneself, get broken, Il.
to break a line of battle or body of men, Id., Hdt.; in Mid., ῥήξασθαι φάλαγγας, στίχας to break oneself a way through the lines, Il.; absol., ῥήξασθαι to break or force one's way, Id.
to let break loose, let loose, Id.
ῥῆξαι φωνήν to let loose the voice, of children and persons who have been dumb breaking into speech, Hdt.: then to speak freely, speak out (like rumpere vocem, Virgil), Id., Ar., etc.
δακρύων ῥήξασα νάματα having let loose floods of tears, Soph.; so, ῥ. κλαυθμόν Plut.
absol. in the form ῥήσσω, to beat the ground, dance, Il.
later, as a term of fighters, to fell, knock down, Dem.
Pass., mostly used in aor2 ἐρράγην [α], to break, burst, of waves, Il.; of clouds, Ar.
to break asunder, be rent, of the earth in an earthquake, Plat.; of garments, Xen.
to burst forth, like lightning, Ar.
of ships, to be wrecked, Dem.: metaph. of hopes, Aesch.
intr., like Pass., to break forth, of a river, to break its bounds, Hdt.:—metaph. of sudden misfortunes, bursts of passion, Soph.
in this intr. sense the perf. ἔρρωγα is commonly used of tears, Id.; metaph., κακῶν πέλαγος ἔρρωγεν Aesch., etc.
a rug, blanket, used as the covering of a bed or seat, Hom.; or as a garment, Od.
that can be broken or rent, penetrable, Il.
that which is said or spoken, a word, saying, Theogn., Hdt., etc.; κατὰ ῥῆμα word for word, Aeschin.
a phrase, opp. to ὄνομα (a single word), Plat.
the subject of speech, a thing, NTest.
in Gramm., a verb, opp. to ὄνομα (a noun), ῥήματα καὶ ὀνόματα Plat.
a pet phrase, phrasicle, Ar.
clad in sheepskin, Anth.

sense.gloss: might to break through armed ranks

entry.sense: breaking through armed ranks, Hom.
opening a path, of Apollo, Anth.
breaking the spirit, of Bacchus, Anth.
a breaking, bursting, ῥήξεις broken flames, a bad omen, Eur.
a saying, speaking, speech, Od., Hdt., etc.; ἡ ἀπὸ Σκυθῶν ῥῆσις the Scythian phrase, Hdt.
a resolution, declaration, Id.
a tale, legend, Pind.
a phrase or passage, a speech in a play, Ar.
one must mention, Plat.
a speaker, Il.
skill in public speaking, eloquence, oratory, rhetoric, Plat.
a piece of oratory, set speech, Isocr.
to speak in public, to use or practise oratory, Plat.:—Pass., of the speech, to be spoken, Isocr.
to teach oratory, Strab.
oratorical, rhetorical, ἡ ῥητορική (sc. τέχνη) rhetoric, the art of speaking, Plat.; ῥητορικὴ δειλία an orator's timidity, Aeschin.:— adv. -κῶς, Plat.
of persons, skilled in speaking, fit to be an orator, Id., etc.

stated, specified, Il.; ἐς χρόνον ῥητόν at a set or stated time, Hdt.; ἡμέραι ῥ. Thuc.; ἐπὶ ῥητοῖς γέρασι with fixed prerogatives, Id.; ῥ. ἀργύριον a stated sum, Id.; ἐπὶ ῥητοῖς on stated terms, on certain conditions, Hdt., Eur.:—adv. ῥητῶς, expressly, distinctly, NTest.
spoken of, known, famous, Hes.
that may be spoken or told, Aesch., Soph.; ῥητὸν ἄρρητόν τ’ ἔπος, Lat. fas nefasque, Soph.
in Mathem., ῥητά are rational quantities, opp. to surds (ἄλογα), Plat.
a verbal agreement, bargain, covenant, Od.; παρὰ τὴν ῥήτραν Xen.
the unwritten laws of Lycurgus were called ῥῆτραι, Lex ap. Plut.: generally, a decree, ordinance, Tyrtae., Xen.
speech, a word, Luc.
a public speaker, pleader, Lat. orator, Eur., etc.
making one shudder with cold, chilling: metaph., ῥιγεδανὴ Ἑλένη Helen at whose name one shudders, horrible, Il.
to shiver or shudder with cold: metaph. to shudder with fear or horror, Il., Soph.:—c. inf. to shudder to do, shrink from doing, Il.; also, ῥ. μὴ . . , Od.
to cool or slacken in zeal, Pind.
to bristle with arms, Theocr.
trans. to shudder at anything, Il.
making to shiver, chilling, Hes.

entry.etym: neut. comp. adj. formed from ῥῖγος
entry.sense: more frosty, colder, Od.:—metaph. more horrible, Hom.

entry.etym: Sup. adj. formed from ῥῖγος (as ku=/distosκύδιστος from κῦδος）
entry.sense: coldest: most horrible, Il.
fighting with cold, Anth.
frost, cold, Lat. frigus, Od., etc.

entry.etym: this word, like ἱδρόω, has an irreg. contr. into ω, ωι, for ου, οι,
entry.sense: to be cold, shiver from cold, Od., Hdt.
a root, Od., attic: in pl. the roots, Hom.
metaph. the roots of the eye, Od.; the roots or foundations of the earth, Hes., Aesch., etc.
ἐκ ῥιζῶν, Lat. radicitus, Plut.
anything that grows like a root from one stem, whence Pindar calls Libya the τρίτη ῥίζα χθονός, considering the earth as divided into three continents.
metaph. the root or stock from which a family springs, Lat. stirps, Pind., Aesch., etc.; and so a race, family, Aesch., Eur., etc.
a little root, Ar.
to strike root, Anth.
by, from the roots, Luc.
one who cuts roots, Luc.
to eat roots, Strab.; ῥ. τὰ σπέρματα to destroy them by nibbling the roots, Id.
eating roots, Arist.
to make to strike root: metaph. to root in the ground, plant, Od.; ἐρρίζωσε τὴν τυραννίδα Hdt.: —Pass. to take root, strike root, Xen.: metaph. to be rooted, firmly fixed, Soph., NTest.
Pass. also of land, to be planted with trees, Od.
a root: metaph. a stem, race Aesch.
root-grubbing, of grammarians, Anth.
a taking root, beginning life, Plut.
shrivelled with cold: generally, shrivelled, crooked, Hhymn., Anth.
adv. lightly, swiftly, fleetly, Il., Aesch.
of a swift chariot, Pind.; ῥ. ἁμίλλαις with the swift racing of chariots, Soph.
to file, Anth.
with a nose reaching to the chin, Anth.
to track by scent, Aesch.
one who tracks by scent, of hounds.
a file or rasp, Xen.
emitted through the nose, of a snorting sound, Anth.
the rhinoceros or nosehorn, Strab.
a hide, Il.
= ῥινός II. 2, a shield, Od.
snub-nosed, Luc.
the skin of a man, Hom.
the hide of a beast, esp. an ox-hide, Id.
an ox-hide shield, Id.
shield-piercing, Il., Hes.
a sewer, Lat. cloaca, Strab.
any jutting part of a mountain,
the peak, Hom.
a headland, foreland, Od., Thuc.

the swing or force with which anything is thrown, Lat. impetus, αἰγανέης ῥιπή the flight of a javelin, Il.; ῥιπὴ Βορέαο the sweep or rush of the N. wind, Id.; ῥιπὴ Διόθεν, of a storm, Aesch.; ἐννυχιᾶν ἀπὸ ῥιπᾶν prob. means from the quarter of the night storms, i.e. from the North, Soph.; ῥ. πυρός the rush of fire, Il.

ῥ. πτερύγων a flapping of wings, Aesch.; of the buzz of a gnat's wing, Id.; of quivering light, ῥιπαὶ ἄστρων Soph.; of any rapid movement, ῥ. ποδῶν Eur.; ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ in the twinkling of an eye, NTest.
to fan the flame, Lat. conflare, Ar.:—Pass. to be blown about, NTest.
a fan for raising the fire, Ar.
a lady's fan, Anth.
to throw to and fro, toss about, Lat. jactare, Il.; ὀφρύσι ῥιπτάζειν to move the eyebrows up and down, Hhymn.:—Pass. to be tossed about, Plut.
thrown, ῥ.μόρος death by being thrown down (a precipice), Soph.
to throw, cast, hurl, Hom., etc.; ῥ. χθονί to throw on the ground, Soph.:— to cast a net, Pass., ἔρριπται ὁ βόλος the cast has been made, Orac. ap. Hdt.:— to throw or toss about, πλοκάμους Eur.
to cast out of house or land, Soph.:— Pass., μὴ ῥιφθῶ κυσίν Id.
to throw off or away, of arms, clothes, Eur., etc.
ῥ. λόγους to cast them forth, hurl them, Aesch., Eur.:—but also, to throw them away, waste them, Aesch., Eur.: Pass., οἴχεται ταῦτ’ ἐρριμμένα Soph.
to cast lots or dice, Eur., Plat.
ῥ. ἑαυτόν to throw or cast oneself down, Xen.;—then absol. to fling oneself, ἐς πόντον Theogn.; ἐς τάφρον Eur.
the nose, Lat. nasus, Hom., Hdt., etc.
in pl. the nostrils, nose, Lat. nares, Il., etc.
a pipe or conduit.
throwing away his shield in battle, a recreant, Ar.
a throwing, casting, hurling, Plat.
a casting about of the eyes, Plut.
a being thrown or hurled, Plat.
running needless risks, fool-hardy, reckless, Xen.
throwing away one's arms, Aesch.
plaited work, wicker-work, a mat, Lat. crates, Od., etc.
ionic and epic ῥοιή, a pomegranate-tree, Od.
the fruit, a pomegranate, Hhymn., Ar.
a knob shaped like a pomegranate, Hdt.
the woof or weft, Batr.
waving, flickering, Il.
of roses, Eur.
like a rose, rosy, Anth.
a rose-tree, rose-bush, Archil.
Rhodian, of Rhodes, Strab.: —also Ῥόδιος, η, ον, Il., Xen.
rosy-fingered, of Aurora, Hom.
rose-like, rosy, Anth.
of roses, Il., Eur.
rose-coloured, Anth.
a rose-apple: metaph. of a rosy cheek, Theocr.
the rose, Lat. rosa, Hhymn., Theogn., etc.; aeolic βρόδον, Sapph.:—metaph., ῥόδα μ’ εἴρηκας you've spoken roses of me, have said all things sweet and lovely, Ar.
rosy-armed, Hhymn., Hes., etc.
the isle of Rhodes, Il., etc.
a rose-bed, garden of roses, Lat. rosarium, Dem., etc.
a river, stream, flood, Hom., etc.; mostly in pl., ἐπ’ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων Il.; ἀμπέλου ῥοαί the juice of the grape, Eur.:—metaph. the stream of song or poesy, Pind.; also, ῥοαί the tide of affairs, Id.

to make a rushing noise, to dash, of waves or the stroke of oars: hence, of any confused noise, ταῦτα ἐρρόθουν ἐμοί such clamours they raised against me, Soph.; λόγοι ἐρρόθουν there was a noise of words, Id.
of pigs, to make a guttling noise, Ar.
dashing, Aesch.
rushing, roaring, dashing, of waves, Od.; of oars, Eur.
as Subst. ῥόθια, τά, waves dashing on the beach, breakers, waves, Soph., etc.;—collectively in sg. the surf, surge, Aesch., Eur.
a shout of applause, Ar.; generally, a tumult, riot, Eur.
a rushing noise, dash of waves or of oars, ἐξ ἑνὸς ῥόθου with one stroke, i. e. all at once, Aesch.
of any confused, inarticulate sound, Περσίδος γλώσσης ῥ. the noise of the Persian (i. e. barbarian) tongue, Id.
to swallow with a noise, suck down, of Charybdis, Od.; cf. ἀναρροιβδέω.
like ῥοιζέω, to move with a rustling sound, make to rustle, Aesch.
a whistling, piping, Eur.
any rushing noise, πτερῶν ῥ. the whirring of wings, Soph.; ἀνέμου ῥ. whistling of the wind, Ar.
to whistle, Lat. stridere, Il.; of a snake, to hiss, Hes.:—Pass. to rush through the air, ἐρροίζητο (3rd sg. plup.) Anth.
a rushing, whirring noise or motion, as of birds, Ar.
the whistling or whizzing of an arrow, Il.:—any whistling or piping sound, as of a shepherd, Od.
rushing motion, a rush, swing, Plut.
crooked, Theocr.
spun round like a top, Anth.
rhomboidal, Strab.; ῥ. σχῆμα a rhomboid, a four-sided figure with the opposite sides and angles equal.
a spinning-top or wheel, Lat. turbo, Eur., Anth.
a magic wheel, used by sorcerers to aid their spells, Theocr., Hor.
a spinning, whirling motion, of a top or wheel, ἱέντα ῥόμβον ἀκόντων shooting forth whirling darts, Pind.; ῥ. αἰετοῦ the eagle's swoop, Id.
a rhomb, lozenge, i. e. a four-sided figure with all the sides, but only the opposite angles, equal, Euclid.
a fish, the turbot, brill.
lozenge-shaped, Anth.
a large sword, scymitar, used by the Thracians, Plut., NTest.
a stream, flow, current, Hom., etc.; ποταμοὺς ἔτρεψε νέεσθαι κὰρ ῥόον to flow in their own bed, Il.; κατὰ ῥόον down stream, Od., Hdt., etc.; πρὸς ῥόον against stream, Il.:— a current at sea, Thuc.
a club, cudgel, thicker at the buttend; used to cudgel an ass, Il.; to walk with, Od., etc.:— a war-club or mace, shod with metal, Id., Hdt.
= ῥόπτρον III, Xen.
inclination downwards, the sinking of the scale, Aesch.; διαφέρειν τὴν ῥ. to disturb the balance, Plut.

metaph. the turn of the scale, the critical moment, Lat. momentum, ἔχεται ῥοπᾶς (sc. ἡ πόλις) is at a crisis of her fortunes, Alcae. ap. Ar.; ῥ. Δίκας the balance or critical turn of Justice, Aesch.; σμικρὰ παλαιὰ σώματ’ εὐνάζει ῥοπή a slight turn of the scale lays aged bodies to rest, Soph.; ἐπὶ σμικρᾶς ῥοπῆς dependent on a slight turn of the scale, of one dying, Eur.; ἐπὶ ῥοπῆς μιᾶς ὄντες depending on a single turn of the scale, Thuc.; ῥ. βίου the turning point of life, i. e. death, Soph.
metaph. influence, Dem.
the wood in a mouse-trap which springs up when touched, Archil.; metaph., δίκης ῥόπτρον Eur.
a tambourine or kettledrum, Luc., Anth.
the knocker on a housedoor, Eur.
reddish, Lat. russus, Anth.
to sup greedily up, gulp down, Aesch., Ar.
to drain dry, empty, Ar.; so, ῥ. ἀρτηρίας, of the poison on the robe of Hercules, Soph.
drawing in, absorbing, Strab.
that can be or is supped up, Strab.
to dash with a roaring sound, of the sea, Od.
a roaring of the sea.
with a strong stream, of a sea in which there are strong currents, Thuc.: of rocks, exposed to such seas, Strab.
a rushing stream, a torrent, Thuc.; ὁ ῥ. τοῦ πυρός, of a stream of lava, Id.
a snout, muzzle, of swine, Stesich.; of dogs, Theocr.: of birds, a beak, neb, Ar.
flowingly, abundantly, Plut.
abundantly, Od.
to growl, snarl, ῥύζει ἐπίκλαυτον νόμον snarls its melancholy ditty, Ar.

to bring into measure or proportion: generally, to order, to educate, train, Xen., etc.:—metaph., ῥ. λύπην ὅπου to define the place of grief, Soph.:—Mid., ῥ. πλόκαμον to arrange one's hair, Eur.:—Pass., νηλεῶς ὧδ’ ἐρρύθμισμαι thus ruthlessly am I brought to order, Aesch.
measured motion, time, rhythm, Lat. numerus, Ar., Plat., etc.: —ἐν ῥυθμῷ in time, Virgil's in numerum, Xen.; μετὰ ῥυθμοῦ Thuc.; θάττονα ῥυθμὸν ἐπάγειν to play in quicker time, Xen.
proportion or symmetry of parts, Plat.
generally, arrangement, order, Eur.
the state or condition of the soul, temper, disposition, Theogn., etc.
the form or shape of a thing, Hdt.; of a breastplate, Xen.
the wise, manner or fashion of a thing, Eur.; τίς ῥ. φόνου; what kind of slaughter? Id.
a plane, Anth.
that which is drawn:
τόξου ῥῦμα, i. e. the Persian archers, opp. to λόγχης ἰσχύς, i. e. the Greek spearmen, Aesch.; ἐκ τόξου ῥύματος from the distance of a bow- shot, Xen.
a towing-line, Polyb.
（ῥύομαι) a defence, protection, Eur.; πύργου ῥ. a tower of defence, Soph.

the force, swing, rush of a body in motion, Lat. impetus, ῥύμῃ with a swing, Thuc.; πτερύγων ῥύμη the rush of wings, Ar.; ἡ ῥ. τῶν ἵππων Xen.:—metaph., εὐτυχεῖ ῥύμῃ θεοῦ Eur.; ἡ ῥ. τῆς ὀργῆς the vehemence of passion, Dem.
absol. a rush, charge, of soldiers, Thuc., Xen.
a street, Lat. vicus, Polyb., NTest.
anything for washing, soap, Plat.
the pole of a carriage, Il., Hdt.; ἐν πρώτῳ ῥυμῷ at the end of the pole, Il.
to tow, Polyb., etc.

to draw to oneself, i. e. draw out of danger, to rescue, save, deliver, Hom., Hes., etc.; ῥ. τινα ὑπὲκ θανάτου, ὑπὲκ κακοῦ to save from . . , Hom.;—so c. gen., ῥ. τινα τοῦ μὴ κατακαυθῆναι Hdt.; or c. inf. alone, ῥ. τινα θανεῖν or μὴ κατθανεῖν Eur.: also, to save from an illness, cure, Hdt.: to set free, redeem, Il.; ἐκ δουλοσύνης Hdt.
generally, to shield, guard, protect, of guardian gods, chiefs, etc., Il. etc.:—of defensive armour, Id.
Soph. has ῥῦσαι in a double sense, ῥῦσαι σεαυτὸν . . , ῥῦσαι δὲ μίασμα τοῦ τεθνηκότος deliver thyself,—and deliver us from the pollution; so, ῥ. τὰς αἰτίας to remove the charges, Thuc.
to draw back, to hold back, check, Od., Pind.
to keep off, Pind.
to defile, disfigure, disparage, Arist.:—Pass. to be or become foul, Xen.
dirt, filth: sordidness, Critias, Plut.
foul, filthy, dirty:—metaph. dirty, sordid, Arist.:—adv. -ρῶς, Anth.
to be foul, filthy, dirty, Od.; imperf. ἐρρύπων, Ar.
Pass. to be foul, perf. part. ῥερῠπωμένος, epic for ἐρρυπωμένοι, fouled, soiled, Od.
dirt, filth, dirtiness, uncleanness, heterocl. pl. ῥύπα, Od.; in sg., Plat., etc.
a cry of the Athenian rowers, like ὠόπ, yoho! Ar.; hence, τὸ ῥυππαπαί one's messmates, Id.
to remove dirt from garments, to wash, Arist.:—Pass. to wash oneself, ἐξ ὅτου ἐγὼ ῥύπτομαι ever since I began to wash, i. e. from childhood, Ar.
Pass. to be wrinkled, Anth.
to seize as a pledge, to drag away, Eur.:—Pass. to be so dragged away, Id.
defending altars, Aesch.
preserving the chariot, Pind.
that which is dragged away:
booty, prey, ῥύσια ἐλαύνεσθαι, of cattle, Il.; τοῦ ῥυσίου θ’ ἥμαρτε, i. e. Helen., Aesch.
that which is seized as a pledge, a pledge, surety, ῥύσια δοῦναι Solon.; ῥύσιον τιθέναι Soph.
that which is seized by way of reprisal, φόνον φόνου ῥύσιον τῖσαι to suffer death in reprisal for death, Id.
in pl. offerings for deliverance, Anth.
delivering, saving, Aesch., Anth.
saving the city, Aesch.
setting free from trouble, Anth.
a flowing, flow, Plat.
the course of a river, stream, Polyb.

entry.etym: = ῥύομαι· ῥύσκευ, epic 2nd sg. imperf., Il.

entry.sense: drawn up, shrivelled, wrinkled, Il., Eur., etc.; ῥ. ἐπισκύνιον, of a frown, Anth.
wrinkledness, wrinkles, Plut.
to drag about, πολλὰ ῥυστάζεσκεν (3rd sg. ionic imperf.) περὶ σῆμα he dragged it many times round the grave of Patroclus, Il.; δμωὰς ῥυστάζειν κατὰ δώματα, Od.
a dragging about, maltreatment, Od.
the rope of a horse's halter, Xen.
one who draws or stretches, ῥ. βιοῦ, ὀϊστῶν drawer of the bow, of arrows, Od.
like ἱμάς, the strap by which a horse draws, a trace, Il.:—also a rein, Id.; ἀπὸ ῥυτῆρος with loose rein, Lat. immissis habenis, at full galop:—used as a strap to flog with, Dem., Aeschin.
（ῥύομαι) a saver, guard, defender, Od.
with shrivelled rind, σῦκον Anth.
to make wrinkled:—Pass. to be so, perf. part. ἐρρυτιδωμένος Luc.
a fold or pucker in the face, a wrinkle, Lat. ruga, Ar., Plat.
a rein, Hes.
（ῥέω) a drinking-cup, running to a point with a small hole, through which the wine ran, Dem.
dragged along, ῥυτοὶ λάες stones dragged along, i. e. too large to carry, Od.
flowing, running, fluid, liquid, Trag.
a saviour, deliverer, Aesch., Anth.; τινός from a thing, Id.
whence ἐρύω, to draw
broken, cleft, rent, torn, Hom.
ragged, Babr.; ῥ. πέτρα a cloven rock, Theocr.
the nose: in pl. the nostrils, Strab.
Roman, a Roman, Polyb., etc.; adv. -κῶς, in Latin, Anth.
in Latin, Plut.
strong of body, Plat.
of things, mighty, strong, Hdt.
bodily strength, strength, might, Hdt., Trag., etc.; οὐ μιᾷ ῥώμῃ not single-handed, Soph.
a force, i. e. army, Xen.
to strengthen, make strong and mighty, Plut.
mostly in perf. pass. (with pres. sense) ἔρρωμαι, and plup. ἐρρώμην (as imperf.):— to put forth strength, have strength or might, Eur., Thuc.:—c. inf. to have strength to do, be eager to do, Thuc.
often in imperat., ἔρρωσο, farewell, Lat. vale, Xen.; also, φράζειν τινὶ ἐρρῶσθαι, Lat. valere jubere, Plat.
part. ἐρρωμένος, = ῥωμαλέος, v. sub voce.
a cleft: in Od., ῥῶγες μεγάροιο are narrow passages leading to the hall.

to move with speed or violence, to dart, rush, rush on, Hom.; ῥ. περὶ πυρήν Od.; ἀμφ’ Ἀχελώιον ἐρρώσαντο danced about Achelous, Il.; χορὸν ἐρρώσαντο plied the lusty dance, Hhymn.; ὑπὸ ῥώοντο ἄνακτι lustily they moved under the king's weight, Il.; so, γούνατα ἐρρώσαντο Od.; also of the hair, ἐρρώοντο μετὰ πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο it waved streaming in the wind, Il.
Ρ, ρ, ῥῶ, τό, indecl., seventeenth letter of Gr. Alphabet, as numeral ρʹ = 100, but ͵ρ = 100,000. Dialectic and other changes:
aeolic, at the end of words σ passed into ρ, as οὗτορ, ἵππορ for οὗτος, ἵππος; cf. Lat. arbor arbos, honor honos.
in attic, ρρ replaced the ionic and old attic ρς, as ἄρρην, θάρρος for ἄρσην, θάρσος.
in some words ρ is transposed, as κάρτος epic for κράτος, ἀταρπός for ἀτραπός, κραδίη for καρδία:—mostly in Poets.
ρ at the beginning of a word was pronounced so as to make a short vowel at the end of the word before long by position, as, ψυχρὴ ὑπὸ ῥιπῆς Il.
by reason of this pronunc., ρ was doubled after a prep. or α privat. , and after the augment, as ἀπορρίπτω, ἄρρωστος, ἔρριψα.
if ρ begins a word, it takes the rough breathing, except in aeolic
brushes, brushwood, Il.
of or for petty wares, trumpery, worthless, Plut.; ῥωπικὰ γράψασθαι to paint poorly, coarsely, Anth.
petty wares, Aesch., Dem.
