a cleft, ῥωχμὸς γαίης a gutter scooped out by heavy rains, Il.
a shrub, bush: only pl. bushes, underwood, brushwood, Od. Od.
a Phyrgian deity, identified with Bacchus, Ar.:— τὰ Σαβάζια Bacchic orgies, Strab.
shattered; metaph. enervated, Anth.
a shatterer, destroyer, of a goblin who broke pots, epic Hom.
a Chaldaean phrase, hast thou forsaken me? NTest.
hosts, armies, NTest.
to keep the Sabbath, Lxx.
a keeping of days of rest, NTest.
the Hebrew sabbath, i. e. rest, NTest.; also in pl. of the single day, heterocl. dat. pl. σάββασι (as if from σάββας), Id.
a period of seven days, a week, μία τῶν σαββάτων the first day of the week, Id.
a cry at the feast of Sabazios, Dem.
a single edged axe or bill, a weapon used by the Scythian tribes, Hdt., Xen.
of or for a drag-net, Anth.
one who fishes with a drag-net, of a comb, τριχῶν σαγ. Anth., Plut.
to take fish with a drag-net (σαγήνη), Luc.
metaph. to sweep as with a drag-net, i. e. to sweep the population off the face of a country by forming a line and marching over it, a Persian practice, Hdt., etc.: Pass., σαγηνευθεὶς ὑπ’ ἔρωτι Anth.
a large drag-net for taking fish, a seine, Ital. sagena, Luc., NTest.
one who casts a drag-net, a fisherman, Anth.
attached to a drag-net, Anth.
a man's pack, baggage, αὐτόφορτος οἰκείᾳ σαγῇ, i. e. carrying his own baggage, Aesch.: generally, harness, equipment, Id., Eur.
= σάγμα II, a pack-saddle, Babr.
to wear a cloak, Strab.
mostly in pl. covering: the covering of a shield, Eur., Ar.: a large cloak, Ar.
a pack-saddle, Strab., Plut.
a pile, ὅπλων Plut.
a coarse cloak, used by the Gauls, Polyb.
Sadducees, name of a Jewish sect, NTest.
rotten, decayed, unsound, cracked, Plat., Dem.—adv., σαθρῶς ἱδρυμένος built on unsound foundations, Arist.
metaph., πρίν τι καὶ σαθρὸν ἐγγίνεσθαί σφι before any unsound thought comes into their heads, i. e. before they prove traitors, Hdt.; σ. λόγοι Eur.
of dogs, to wag the tail, fawn, Od.; οὐρῆι ἔσηνε, of the dog Argus, Id.
metaph. to fawn, cringe, Pind., Aesch.
c. acc. pers. to fawn upon, Ar.: to pay court to, greet, Pind., Soph.; σα. μόρον to deprecate, shrink from death, Aesch.:—Pass., σαίνομαι ὑπ’ ἐλπίδος Id.
to beguile, cozen, deceive, Id.
in NTest., σαίνεσθαι ἐν ταῖς θλίψεσι seems to mean to be moved, disturbed.

in perf. to draw back the lips and shew the teeth, to grin like a dog, Lat. ringi, σεσαρυῖα (epic for σεσηρυῖα) Hes.; σεσηρώς Ar.:—in good sense, smiling, Theocr.:—the neut. is used in adv. sense, σεσᾱρὸς γελᾶν to laugh with open mouth, Theocr.; σεσηρὸς αἰκάλλειν, of a fox, Babr.
in pres. and aor1, to sweep a floor, Eur.
c. acc. rei, to sweep up or away, Soph.
wielding a shield, Il.
shield-bearing, Soph., Eur.
a small bag, Xen.
sackcloth, mourning, Menand.
cherishing a huge beard, Anth.
a coarse hair-cloth, sackcloth, Lat. cilicium, NTest.
anything made of this cloth, a sack, bag, Hdt., Ar.
a coarse beard, Ar.

a shield, Hom., etc. The earliest shields were of wicker-work or of wood, covered with ox-hides, and sometimes with metal-plates, (that of Ajax had seven hides and an eighth layer of metal); it was concave, so as to hold liquid, Aesch.
a sack, Ar.
a packer, Ἅιδου σάκτωρ who crowds the nether world (with dead men), Aesch.
one who weaves sackcloth, a sailmaker, Dem.
a word of uncertain origin, denoting a swaggerer, Arist.
betrayer of Salamis, Solon.
Salaminian, of or from Salamis, Hdt.
Σαλαμινία (sub. ναῦς), ἡ, one of the Athen. sacred ships, Ar., Thuc.; v. πάραλος III.
Salamis, an island opposite Athens, Il., etc.
a town of Cyprus founded by Teucer of Salamis, Hhymn., Hdt.
to overload, cram full, σεσαλαγμένος Anth.
to cause to rock, make to oscillate, shake to and fro, Eur., Anth.; σα. τοὺς ὄχλους to stir them up, NTest.:—Pass. to be shaken to and fro, totter, reel, χθὼν σεσάλευται Aesch.
intr. to move up and down, to roll, toss, as on the sea, Xen.:—metaph. to toss like a ship at sea, to be tempest-tost, be in sore distress, Soph., Eur.
of a ship also, to ride at anchor: metaph., σα. ἐπί τινι to ride at anchor on one's friend, depend upon him, Plut.
any unsteady, tossing motion, of an earthquake, Eur.: the tossing or rolling swell of the sea, Id.; so in pl., πόντιοι σάλοι Id.
of ships or persons in them, a tossing on the sea, Soph.: —metaph. of the ship of the state, tempest-tossing, Id.; σάλον ἔχειν to be in distress, Plut.
lancer-whiskered-trumpeters, Ar.
a trumpeter, Thuc., Xen.
a war-trumpet, trump, Il., Trag., etc.:—metaph., Πιερικὰ σ., of Pindar, Anth.
a trumpet-call, ap. Arist.

to sound the trumpet, give signal by trumpet, Xen.: c. acc. cogn., σα. ῥυθμούς Id.; cf. ἀνακλητικός: metaph., ἀμφὶ δὲ σάλπιγξεν οὐρανός heaven trumpeted around, of thunder as if a signal for battle, Il.:—impers., ἐπεὶ ἐσάλπιγξε (sc. ὁ σαλπιγκτής) when the trumpet sounded, Xen.
a ship of Samian build, Plut.
Samaria, a city of Palestine
a Samaritan, NTest., etc.;fem. -εῖτις, ιδος, Id.
a triangular musical instrument with four strings, Lat. sambuca, Arist.
an engine of like form used in sieges, Plut.
a player on the sambuca:—fem. σαμβῡκίστρια, Plut.
Samothrace, an island near Thrace, the seat of the mysteries of the Cabiri, Hdt.:—the inhabitants were Σαμοθρήικες, Id.; adj. Σᾰμοθρᾴκιος, η, ον, ionic -θρηίκιος, η, ον, Id.
Samos, the name of several Greek islands:
an old name for Κεφαλληνία, Hom.
Σάμος Θρηικίη, = Σαμοθρᾴκη, Il.
Samos, the large island over against Ephesus, Hhymn., etc.: hence adj. Σάμιος, η, ον, Hdt.
a horse branded with the letter σάν (v. sub Σ, σ), Ar.; cf. κοππατίας.
a wooden sole, bound by straps round the instep and ankle, mostly in pl. sandals, Hhymn., etc.
red or orange-coloured mineral, Arist.
of orange colour, Hdt.
a pit whence σανδαράκη is dug, Strab.
a bright red colour, also called ἀρμένιον, Strab.
a small trencher, Ar.
like πινάκιον, a tablet, Aeschin.
a planking, framework, Polyb.
a board, plank, Anth., etc.
anything made of planks:
a door, in pl. folding doors, Lat. fores, Hom.:—rare in sg., Eur.
a wooden platform, scaffold or stage, Od.: a ship's deck, Eur.
in pl. wooden tablets for writing on, Id.:—at Athens, tablets on which were written public notices, Ar., etc.
a plank to which offenders were bound or nailed, Hdt.; so perh. in Od. 22. 174.

entry.etym: as Posit., found only in the contr. form σῶς, σᾶ

entry.sense: rotten, putrid, Theogn., Ar.; of fish, stale, rancid, τάριχος Ar.
generally, stale, worn out, Lat. obsoletus, Id.:—of persons, Id.
of wine, in good sense, mellow, Id.
rottenness, putridity, Plat.
a blue gem, the sapphire, or (as others think) lapis lazuli.
a plait, braid, Aesch.
a basket, NTest.

used of bitter or scornful laughter, σαρδάνιον γελᾶν (sc. γέλωτα); μείδησε σαρδάνιον he laughed a bitter laugh, Od.; so, ἀνεκάγχασε σαρδάνιον Plat.; ridere γέλωτα σαρδάνιον Cic.—Others write Σαρδόνιον, deriving it from Σαρδώ, because such laughter resembled the effect produced by a Sardinian plant, which screwed up the face of the eater, Plut.: (hence our form sardonic).
Sardes, the capital of Lydia, dat. Σάρδεσι, Aesch.:—adj. Σαρδιᾱνός, ionic -ηνός, ή, όν, Hdt.; and Σαρδιᾱνικός, ή, όν, Ar.
the Sardian stone, carnelian, Plat.
the rope sustaining the upper-edge of a hunting-net, Xen.
the sardonyx, Anth.
Sardinia, Hdt., Ar.; the obl. cases are sometimes Σαρδόνος, -όνι, -όνα (as if from Σαρδών), Polyb.:—adj. Σαρδόνιος, η, ον, and Σαρδονικός, ή, όν, Hdt.
the sarissa, a long pike used in the Macedonian phalanx, Polyb.
to tear flesh like dogs, Ar.
to strip off the flesh, scrape it out, Hdt.
fleshly, sensual, Anth.
of flesh, in the flesh, Theocr.
= σαρκικός, opp. to πνευματικός, NTest.
fleshy, corpulent, Plat.
forsaken by flesh, lean, Anth.
compact of flesh, Anth.
eating flesh, carnivorous, Arist.
λίθος σ. a limestone found at Assos in Troas, remarkable for consuming the flesh of corpses laid in it; coffins were made of it, and such a coffin was called a σαρκοφάγος, Juven.
to make to look like flesh, of a sculptor, Anth.
fleshy, Xen., etc.; θεοὶ ἔναιμοι καὶ σαρκώδεες gods of flesh and blood, Hdt.

flesh, Lat. caro, Hom., etc.: in pl. the flesh or muscles of the body, ἔγκατά τε σάρκας τε καὶ ὀστέα Hom.; so in Hes., Aesch., etc.:—so sometimes in sg., the flesh, the body, γέροντα τὸν νοῦν, σάρκα δ’ ἡβῶσαν φέρει Aesch.
the flesh, as opp. to the spirit, NTest.; also for man's nature generally, Id.; πᾶσα σάρξ all human kind, Id.
a broom, besom, Anth.
to sweep clean, NTest.:— Pass., perf. part. σεσαρωμένος Id.
Σαρπεδον.
Satan, i. e. an adversary, enemy: name for the Devil, NTest.
a war-chariot, chariot, car, Hhymn., Eur.
a Hebrew measure, 1/30 of a κόρος, = about 1 1/2 modii or 24 sextarii, NTest.
a satrapy, the office or province of a satrap, Hdt., Xen.
to be a satrap, exercise the authority of one, Xen.
c. gen. to rule as a satrap, σ. τῆς χώρας Id.;—also c. acc., Id.
a satrap, viceroy, Lat. satrapa, Xen.
gold, Ar.

entry.etym: The Root is ΣΑΓ, as in perf. pass., σάγμα, σάγος, σάγη.
entry.sense: to pack or load, properly of putting the packsaddle on beasts of burthen: hence,
of warriors, in Pass. to be fully armed, Hdt.; χαλκῶι σεσαγμένοι Theocr.
to furnish with all things needful, σάξαντες ὕδατι [τὴν ἐσβολήν] having furnished the entrance (into Egypt) with water, Hdt.

generally, to load heavily, fill quite full of a thing: Pass., c. gen., πημάτων σεσαγμένος laden with woes, Aesch.; τριήρης σεσαγμένη ἀνθρώπων Xen.:—also c. dat. to fill full with a thing, Luc.; so in Mid., χρυσῶι σαξάμενος πήρην Id.:—Pass., σεσαγμένος πλούτου τὴν ψυχήν having his fill of riches, Xen.
to pack close, press down, Id.
like a Satyr, Plut.
of or resembling the Satyric drama, Plat., Arist.:— σατυρικόν, οῦ, a Satyric drama, Xen.

a Satyr, companion of Bacchus, Hes., etc.: the Satyrs were represented with pointed ears, snub nose, goat's tail, and budding horns: later, goats' legs were added. They differed from Pan and Fauns by the want of real horns.

a play in which the chorus consisted of Satyrs, the Satyric drama (not to be confounded with the Rom. Satura or Satira), Ar. It formed the fourth piece of a Tragic tetralogy: the only Satyric drama extant is the Cyclops of Eur.
Pass. to swagger, dance affectedly, Eur.
to walk in a swaggering way, Ar.
swaggering, straddling, Hhymn., etc.
a javelin, Menand., Strab.
a lizard, Lat. lacerta, Hdt.
lizard-killer, epith. of Apollo, Plin.
a Sarmatian, Hdt.:—fem. Σαυρομάτις, Id.
= σαύρα, Lat. lacertus, Hdt.
a spike at the butt-end of a spear, by which it was stuck into the ground, Il., Hdt.

clearly, plainly, assuredly, of a surety, with Verbs of knowing, σάφα οἶδα, σάφα εἰδώς, Hom.; also in Trag., σάφ’ οἶδα, σάφ’ ἴσθι, etc.; σάφ’ ἴσθι, ὅτι . . Ar.; also withVerbs of speaking, σάφα εἰπεῖν Hom., Pind.
speaking clearly or truly, Anth.
distinctness, perspicuity, Plat., etc.
to tell distinctly, Aesch.
τὸ σαφανές the plain truth, Pind. adv. -νῶς, Theogn., Aesch.; ionic -νέως, Hdt.
to make clear or plain, point out clearly, explain, Aesch., Xen.
explanatory, τινος of a thing, Luc.
clear, plain, distinct, manifest, Hhymn., Aesch., etc.; τὸ σαφές the clear truth, Eur., etc.
of persons, Aesch., Eur.: of oracles and prophets, as in Virgil certus Apollo, sure, unerring, Soph.
adv. σᾰφῶς, ionic -έως, plainly, distinctly, well, σ. φράσαι, δεικνύναι, εἰδέναι, Hdt., attic:— certainly, manifestly, Aesch., etc.; ἦν σ. was manifest, Id.:—comp. -έστερον, Sup. -έστατα, Id., etc.
to sift, bolt, Hdt., in 3rd pl. σῶσι.
to quench, put out, Lat. extinguere, Hdt., Pind.
generally, to quench, quell, check, σβ. χόλον, μένος Il.; ὕβριν Simon.; κύματα Ar., etc.
Pass. σβέννυμαι (with intr. tenses of Act., v. supr.), to be quenched, go out, Lat. extingui, of fire, Il.: metaph. of men, to become extinct, die, Anth.
generally, to be quelled or lulled, of wind, Od.
serving to quench fire, Thuc.

of thyself, only in gen., dat. and acc. sg., masc. and fem., Hdt., attic; ἐν σαυτῷ γενοῦ contain thyself, Soph.:—in pl. separated, ὑμῶν αὐτῶν, etc.: and orig. it was separated in sg., as in Hom., who always says σοὶ αὐτῷ, σ’ αὐτόν.
to be afraid of, τι Il.
an object of awe or worship, NTest.

entry.etym: only in nom., acc., and voc. sg.
entry.sense: reverential awe, a feeling of awe, Hom., etc.:—generally, reverence, worship, Trag.; c. gen. objecti, Διὸς σέβας reverence for Jove, Aesch.
the object of awe, holiness, majesty, Eur.: periphr. for persons, σ. κηρύκων, i. e. Hermes, Aesch.
an object of wonder, a wonder, Hhymn., Soph.: an honour conferred on one, as the arms of Achilles on Ulysses, Soph.
= Lat. Augusta, the Empress, Anth.
reverenced, august: used to render the imperial name Augustus, Strab., NTest.

fut. attic σεβιῶ: aor1 ἐσέβισα:—like σεβάζομαι, to worship, honour, Lat. revereor, Pind., Trag.; καινὰ λέχη σ. to devote oneself to a new wife, Eur.: —also in Mid., οὐδὲν σεβίζει ἀράς standest not in awe of curses, Aesch.; aor1 pass. part., ἁγὼ σεβισθείς Soph.
Dep.
to feel awe or fear before God, to feel religious awe, feel shame, Il., Ar.; σεφθεῖσα awe-stricken, Plat.: c. inf. to dread or fear to do a thing, Aesch., Plat.
c. acc. pers. to honour with pious awe, to worship, Lat. veneror, Pind., Hdt., etc.:—then, to do homage to, pay honour or respect to, Trag.

entry.etym: used only in pres. and imperf.
entry.sense: to worship, honour, Pind., attic; εὖ σέβειν τινά for εὐσεβεῖν εἴς τινα, Eur.:—c. inf., ὑβρίζειν οὐ σέβω, i. e. τὸ ὑβρίζειν, I do not respect, approve of insolence, Aesch.; τὸ μὴ ἀδικεῖν σέβοντες Id.—then, σέβομαι as Pass. to be reverenced, Soph.
absol. to worship, be religious, Aesch., Soph.
Silenus, companion of Bacchus, Hdt.; father of the Satyrs, Eur.
like Silenus, Plat.
joined by a cord or band, ἵππος σ. = σειραφόρος, Soph.
of cord, twisted, βρόχοι Eur.
a cord, rope, string, band, Hom.; σ. χρυσείη a cord or chain of gold, Il.
a cord with a noose, like the lasso, used by the Sagartians and Sarmatians to entangle and drag away their enemies, Hdt.
led by a rope, Hdt.

σειραφόρος (sc. ἵππος), a horse which draws by the trace only (being harnessed by the side of the yoke-horses, ζύγιοι), a trace-horse, outrigger: metaph., sometimes a yoke-mate, coadjutor, Aesch.; sometimes for one who has light work, Id.

a Siren: in pl. Σειρῆνες, αἱ, the Sirens, mythical sisters on the south coast of Italy, who enticed seamen by their songs, and then slew them, Od. Hom. only knows of two, whence epic dual. gen. Σειρήνοιιν.
metaph. a Siren, deceitful woman, Eur.: the Siren charm of eloquence, Aeschin.
scorched by the sun or dog-star, Anth.
the scorcher, name of the dog-star, Lat. Sirius, which marks the season of greatest heat, i. e. Aug. 24 to Sept. 24, Hes., Eur.; called Σείριος κύων Aesch.; Σείριος ἀστήρ Hes.
a knotted scourge, Eccl., Byz.
a shaking off of burdens, Plut.: a name for the disburdening ordinance of Solon., by which all debts were lowered, Id.
earth-shaker, epith. of Poseidon, Pind.
of earthquakes, σεισμ. τάφος a burial in the ruins caused by an earthquake, Plut.
a shaking, shock, γῆς, χθονὸς σ. an earthquake, Eur.; absol., Hdt., attic
generally, a shock, agitation, commotion, Plat., NTest.
shaken, Ar.
to shake, move to and fro, Hom.; σε. ἔγχος, μελίην to shake the poised spear, Il.; κάρα σει., in sign of discontent, Soph.:—also, σείειν τῆι οὐρᾶι Xen.
of earthquakes, which were attributed to Poseidon, Hdt.; absol., σείσας by an earthquake, Ar.: impers., σείει there is an earthquake, Thuc., Xen.
metaph. to shake, agitate, disturb, Pind., Soph.
in attic, to accuse falsely or spitefully, so as to extort hush-money, Ar.; cf. Lat. concutio.
Pass. to shake, heave, quake, of the earth, Il., Hdt.:—metaph. to be shaken to its foundation, τὸ τερπνὸν πίτνει σεσεισμένον Pind.; οἷς ἂν σεισθῆι θεόθεν δόμος Soph.
generally, to move to and fro, Il.: Pass., ὀδόντες ἐσείοντο his teeth were loosened, Hdt.; σεισθῆναι σάλωι Eur.
Mid. to shake something of one's own, Theocr., Anth.
like Pass. to shake oneself, to shake, Il.
to enlighten, illume:—Pass. to beam brightly, Ar.
father of light, Anth.
a bright flame, blaze, light, σ. πυρός Il.; alone, Id.:— lightning, a flash of lightning, Id., Hdt., etc.:— a torch, Hhymn.:— the flash of an angry eye, Aesch.: metaph., ἔρωτος σ. Theocr.
light-bringing, Aesch.
a cup, named after Seleucus, Plut.

entry.etym: poetic for σελήνη, Ar.; doric σελαναία Eur.

entry.sense: lighted by the moon, σ. νύξ a moonlight night, Orac. ap. Hdt., Anth.

the moon, Lat. luna, Hom.; σ. πλήθουσα the full- moon, Il.; νουμηνία κατὰ σελήνην, i. e. by the lunar month, Thuc.; πρὸς τὴν σελήνην by moonlight, Xen.; so, εἰς τὴν σ. Aeschin.:— τὴν σ. καθαιρεῖν, Hor.'s lunam deducere, of witches, Ar.; δεκάτῃ σελήνῃ in the tenth moon (i. e. month), Eur.
as fem. prop. n., Selene, the goddess of the moon, Hes., etc.
Dep. to be moonstruck, i. e. epileptic, NTest.
of or for the moon, lunar, Plut.
devouring leaves of books, of a bookworm, Anth.

parsley, Lat. apium, Hom., etc.:—with its leaves victors at the Isthmian and Nemean games were crowned, Pind.:—from its being planted in garden borders came the prov., οὐδ’ ἐν σελίνῳ οὐδ’ ἐν πηγάνῳ "tis scarcely begun yet, " Ar.
a plank: metaph. a leaf of papyrus: — generally, the page of a book, Anth.
the Selli, guardians of the oracle of Zeus at Dodona, bound to live a rough, austere life, Il., Soph.,
the deck of a ship, Hhymn., Eur.
in pl. σέλματα, rowing-benches, Lat. transtra, Trag.
generally, a seat, throne, Aesch.
σέλματα πύργων scaffolds behind the parapet, on which the defenders of the wall stood, Id.
logs of building timber, Strab.
the finest wheaten flour, Lat. simila, similago, Ar.
to speak gravely and solemnly, Aeschin.:—also as Dep. σεμνολογέομαι, to talk in solemn phrases, Dem.
a grave or solemn talker, Dem.
a grave and reverend seer, Soph.
to make august, to magnify, Strab.
to assume a grave, solemn countenance, Ar.
revered, august, holy, awful:
properly of certain gods; at Athens esp. of the Furies, σεμναὶ θεαί or Σεμναί, Trag.; σ. τέλη their rites, Id.
then of things divine, Hhymn., Trag.; σ. βίος a life devoted to the gods, Eur.; σεμνὰ φθέγγεσθαι = εὔφημα, Aesch.; τὸ σ. holiness, Dem.
of human beings, reverend, august, solemn, stately, majestic, Hdt., attic
of things, Aesch., etc.; οὐδὲν σ. nothing very wonderful, Arist.; σεμνόν ἐστι, c. inf., 'tis a noble, fine thing to . . , Plat.

in bad sense, proud, haughty, Trag.: —in contempt or irony, solemn, pompous, grand, Aesch., etc.; σεμνὸν βλέπειν to look grave and solemn, Eur.; ὡς σ. οὑπίτριπτος how grand the rascal is! Ar.; ὡς σ. ὁ κατάρατος Id.
adv. -νῶς, Eur., etc.: comp. -ότερον, Xen.
solemnly spoken, Aesch.
gravity, solemnity, dignity, majesty, Eur., Xen.
in bad sense, solemnity, pompousness, Luc.; of a girl, prudery, Eur.
reverenced with awe, Aesch.
to make solemn or grand, to exalt, magnify, embellish, Hdt.
= σεμνόω to exalt, magnify, Hdt., attic:—Pass. to be in high repute, Plat.
Mid. to be grave, solemn, to affect a grave and solemn air, Eur., Ar.; σ.ε ἐπί τινι to be proud of a thing, to pique oneself on it, Dem.; ἔν τινι Id.
adverbial Suffix, denoting motion towards, e. g. ἄλλοσε to some other place.
august, Aesch.
a kind of endive or chicory, Anth.
a kind of gnat or winged ant, Ar.

entry.etym: adverb from part. perf. pass. of σοφίζομαι
entry.sense: cunningly, Xen.

entry.etym: ionic and late attic for τεῦτλον.
note that we have ἐσσύμενος not ἐσσυμένος.
entry.sense: to put in quick motion: to drive, hunt, chase away, Hom.; so in Mid., Il.
to set on, let loose at, κύνας σε. ἐπὶ συΐ Id.:—c. inf. to urge on, Od.
of things, to throw, hurl, Il.
Pass. and Mid. to run, rush, dart or shoot along, Hom., Trag.:—c. inf. to hasten, speed to do a thing, Il.
metaph. to be eager, have longings, Od.; v. ἐσσύμενος.
to shut up in a pen: Pass., σήκασθεν (for ἐσηκάσθησαν) κατὰ Ἴλιον were cooped up in Ilium, Il.; ἐν αὐλίῳ σηκασθέντες Xen.
a housekeeper, porteress, Ar.
kept in the fold, sucking, of a lamb, Theocr.
cleaning a byre or pen, a herdsman, Od.
a pen, fold, for lambs, kids, calves, Hom., Hes.; σ. δράκοντος the dragon's den, Eur.
a sacred enclosure, chapel, shrine, Soph., Eur.
a sepulchre, burial-place, Simon.
the trunk of an old olive-tree, Lys.
to weigh, balance, Plut.
in the balance, σμικρὸν τὸ σὸν σ. προστίθης slight is the weight that you throw into the scale, Eur.
= σηκός II, a sacred enclosure, Id.
a standard, Polyb.:— a band under one standard, the Roman manipulus, Id.
to shew by a sign, indicate, make known, point out, Hom., etc.
absol. to give signs, make signals, Il., Trag.

to give a sign or signal to do a thing, Il.; c. inf., Hdt., etc.; μὴ σημήναντός σου without any order from you, Plat.:—c. gen. to bear command over, τινός or ἐπί τισι Hom.: absol. to give orders, Id.; σημαίνων = σημάντωρ, Soph.

in war, to give the signal of attack, Thuc.; ση. τῆι σάλπιγγι Xen.; ση. ἀναχώρησιν to make signal for retreat, Thuc.:—impers., σημαίνει (sc. ὁ σαλπιγκτής) signal is given, τοῖς Ἕλλησι ὡς ἐσήμηνε when signal was given for the Greeks to attack, Hdt.; ἐσήμαινε πάντα παραρτέεσθαι signal was given to make all ready, Id.
to signify, indicate, announce, declare, Eur., Hdt., attic
generally, to signify, interpret, explain, Hdt., Aesch.; absol., σήμαινε tell, Soph.
= σφραγίζω, to stamp with a sign or mark, to seal, Lat. obsignare, mostly in Mid., Xen.:—Pass., εὖ σεσημάνθαι to be well sealed up, Ar.; τὰ σεσημασμέναι, opp. to τὰ ἀσήμαντα, Dem.
Mid. σημαίνομαι, like τεκμαίρομαι, to give oneself a token, i. e. conclude from signs, conjecture, Soph.
to mark for oneself, σημαίνεσθαι βύβλωι (sc. βοῦν), i. e. by sealing a strip of byblus round his horn, Hdt.
Lat. signifer, a standard-bearer, Polyb.
a mark or seal upon anything to be kept, Aesch.
σημαντρὶς γῆ, clay used for sealing, like our wax, Hdt.
a seal, Hdt., Eur.; metaph., δεινοῖς σημάντροισιν ἐσφραγισμένοι, i. e. wounded, Eur.
one who gives a signal, a leader, commander, Hom.; of a horse, a driver; of a herd, a herdsman, Il.: a subordinate officer, Hdt.
an informer, guide, indicator, Anth.
a sign, mark, token, Hom., etc.; the star on a horse's forehead, Il.
a sign from heaven, an omen, portent, Hom., etc.
generally, a sign to do or begin something, Od.; a watchword, Eur.; a battle-sign, signal, Id.
the sign by which a grave is known, a mound, cairn, barrow, Lat. tumulus, Hom., etc.:—generally, a grave, tomb, Hdt., attic

a token by which any one's identity was certified: the σήματα λυγρά of Bellerophon were pictorial, not written, tokens (v. γράφω init.), Il.:— the mark on the lot of Ajax, Id.: the device or bearing on a shield, Aesch.; the seal impressed on a letter, Soph.
a constellation, Il., Eur.
full of tombs, Anth.
one who makes devices for shields, Aesch.
a shorthand writer, Plut.
a sign, a mark, token, Hdt., attic
a sign from the gods, an omen, Soph., Plat.: esp. of the constellations, Eur.
a sign or signal to do a thing made by flags, Hdt.; αἴρειν, κατασπᾶν τὸ σ. to make or take down the signal for battle, Thuc.; τὰ σημεῖα ἤρθη the signals agreed upon were made, Id.
an ensign or flag, on the admiral's ship, Hdt.; on the general's tent, Xen.:—then, generally, a standard, ensign, Eur.: hence, a boundary, limit, Dem.
a device upon a shield, Hdt., Eur.; upon ships, a figure-head, Ar.
a signal, watchword, Thuc.
in reasoning, a sign or proof, Ar., Thuc., etc.:— σημεῖον δέ: or σημεῖον γάρ: (to introduce an argument) this is a proof of it, Dem., etc.
to mark (by milestones), Polyb.
Mid. to interpret as a sign, Strab.
marked, remarkable, Strab.
to-day, Hom., Pind.:—the common attic form was τήμερον, Ar., etc.; εἰς τήμερον Plat.; ἡ τ. ἡμέρα Dem.
the Lat. semicinctium, an apron or kerchief, NTest.
having a mark set or affixed, Anth.
rottenness, putrefaction, Plat.
the cuttle-fish, which when pursued darkens the water by ejecting a liquid, Ar.
to make rotten or putrid, make to fester, of a serpent's poison, Aesch.
metaph. to corrupt, waste, Plat.
Pass., the perf. σέσηπα being used in pres. sense for σήπομαι: aor2 ἐσάπην [short ᾰ]:— to be or become rotten, to rot, moulder, of dead bodies, Il.; of timber, Hdt., Il.
of live flesh, to mortify, Hdt., Plat.
a hollow rock, cave, Plat.; of a lion's den, Theocr.
Seric, silken, Luc.:—Subst., σηρικόν, or σιρικόν, οῦ, a silken robe, silk, NTest.
the Seres, an Indian people from whom the ancients got silk, Strab.
made of sesame, Luc.
a sesame pudding, Ar.
sesame, a plant, from the fruit of which (σήσαμον) an oil was pressed.
made of sesame, Xen.
of sesame:—as Subst. (contr.) σησαμοῦς, a sesame-cake, Ar.
the seed or fruit of the sesame-plant (σησάμη), Hdt., Ar.
= σησάμη, Ar., Xen.
a mess of sesame and cheese, Batr.
a moth which eats woollen stuff, Lat. tinea, Ar.:—metaph. for a bookworm, Anth.
Sestos, a town on the European side of the Hellespont, over against Abydos, Il.
eaten by moths, NTest.

an ancient ending of 2 pers. sg. act., in Hom. and other Poets, mostly in subj., as ἐθέλῃσθα, ἔχῃσθα, εἴπῃσθα, rarely in opt. as κλαίοισθα. In attic it was retained in some irreg. Verbs, ἦσθα, οἶσθα, ᾔδησθα.
strong, mighty, Il., Eur.:—comp. σθεναρώτερος Soph.

strength, might, Il., Pind.:—c. inf., σθ. πολεμίζειν strength to war, Il.; σθ. ὥστε καθελεῖν Eur.; σθένει by force, Soph.; λόγῳ τε καὶ σθένει both by right and might, Id.; so, ὑπὸ σθένους Eur.; παντὶ σθένει with all one's might, Thuc.
strength, might, of all kinds moral as well as physical, σθένος τῆς ἀληθείας Soph.; ἀγγέλων σθ. their might or authority, Aesch.
a force of men, like δύναμις, Il., Soph.
metaph., like Lat. vis for copia, a quantity, profusion, Pind.
periphr., like βίη, ἴς, μένος, as σθένος Ἰδομενῆος, Ὠρίωνος, for Idomeneus, Orion, themselves, Il., Hes.

to have strength or might, be strong or mighty, Soph., Eur.; σθ. χερί, ποσί to be strong in hand, in foot, Soph., Eur.; σθένοντος ἐν πλούτῳ Soph.; τοσοῦτον σθένει Id.; ὅσονπερ ἂν σθένῃ Id.; οἱ κάτω σθένοντες they who have power below, Eur.
c. inf. to have strength or power to do, be able, Soph., Eur.
the jawbone, jaw, Soph.
spittle, saliva, Xen., etc.
a fat hog, with or without σῦς, Hom.
a Sibyl, prophetess, Ar., Plat.
Sibylline, Plut.
to play the Sibyl: metaph. to be like an old Sibyl, old womanish, Ar.
a believer in the Sibyl, a seer, diviner, Plut.
a hunting spear, a spear, pike, Anth.
to bid one be silent, τινά Xen.
silent, still, Anth.
glossy, glittering, shining, splendid, Hom.
entry.etym: From σίαλος, with γ inserted, and ι made long metri grat.

entry.sense: silently, σῖγα ἔχειν to be silent, Soph.; κάθησο σῖγα Ar.; alone, σῖγα hush! be still! Aesch.:—the public crier proclaiming silence said σῖγα πᾶς (sc. ἔστω) Ar.
under one's breath, in a whisper, secretly, Aesch., Soph.
silent, Aesch.
to be silent or still, to keep silence, Hdt., attic; σίγα, hush! be still! Hom.:—Pass., τί σεσίγηται δόμος; why is the house hushed? Eur.
trans. to hold silent, to keep secret, Hdt., Aesch., etc.:—Pass. to be kept silent or secret, Lat. taceri, Hdt., Eur., etc.; ἐσιγήθη σιωπή silence was kept, Eur.
disposed to silence, silent, mute, Soph.; τὰ σιγηλά silence, Eur.
silence, σιγὴν ἔχειν to keep silence, Hdt.; σιγὴν ποιεῖσθαι to make silence, Id.; σιγὴν φυλάσσειν Eur.:—in pl., σιγαὶ ἀνέμων Id.
σιγῇ, as adv. in silence, Hom.; also like σῖγα, as an exclam., σιγῇ νυν (sc. ἔστε) be silent now! Od.;also, in an under tone, in a whisper, Hdt.; σιγῇ βουλεύεσθαι Xen.
secretly, σιγῇ ἔχειν τι to keep it secret, like σιωπᾶν, Hdt.; σιγᾷ καλύψαι, στέγειν, κεύθειν Pind., Soph.
c. gen., σιγῇ τινος unknown to him, Hdt., Eur.
one must be silent, Eur.
the Hebr. shekel, a weightand coin, = 4 attic δραχμαί, NTest.
the Persian σ. was = 7 1/2 attic ὀβολοί, Xen.
Σ, σ, σῖγμα, τό, indecl., a semi-vowel, eighteenth letter of the Gr. Alph.: as numeral σʹ = 200, but ͵σ = 200,000.

beside the form Σ, it was written as a semicircle Ϲ. In the written character, final σ became ς: from which must be distinguished the character ϛʹ = 6. There was also a Doric name σάν [ᾰ] (cf. σαμ-φόρας), which appeared at the end of the alphabet as σαμπί or σαμπῖ, ϡ, = 900.
dialectic and other changes:
aeolic and ionic into δ, as ὀδμή ἴδμεν for ὀσμή ἴσμεν.

aeolic and doric into τ, τύ ἴττω Ποτίδαν ποτί φατί for σύ ἴστω Ποσειδῶν πρός φησί:—so in later attic, as μέταυλος τήμερον for μέσαυλος σήμερον:—in later attic, also σσ passed into ττ, πράττω τάττω for πράσσω τάσσω, θάλαττα ἥττων for θάλασσα ἥσσων.
in aeolic and doric, and in Poets, σ was often doubled, as ὅσσος μέσσος ὀπίσσω for ὅσος μέσος ὀπίσω, and in fut. and aor. 1 forms, as δαμάσσω ὀλέσσω, etc. for δαμάσω ὀλέσω, etc.
σ sometimes passed into πτ or vice versa, as πέσσω and πέπτω, ὄψομαι (*ὄπτω) and ὄσσομαι, ἐνίσσω and ἐνίπτω.

doric into ξ, in fut. and aor1 of Verbs, with their deriv. Nouns, as ἐργάξομαι χείριξις for ἐργάσομαι χείρισις:—so in ionic, διξός τριξός for δισσός τρισσός; and in old attic, the prep. σύν, with all its Compds., was written ξύν.
attic σ and σσ sometimes passed into ψ, cf. Ψ ψ III.
in aeolic, as in Lat., σ represents the aspirate, Σαλμυδησσός Ἁλμυδησσός, σῦς (Lat. sus) ὗς, ἅλς sal, ἕξ sex, ἑπτά septem, ἕρπω serpo, ὕλη sylva.
prefixed to words beginning with μ and τ, μύραινα σμύραινα, μικρός σμικρός, τέγος στέγω, Lat. tego; more rarely before κ and φ, σκίδναμαι κίδναμαι, σφάλλω fallo, σφενδόνη funda.
σ was inserted in the middle of words before θ, esp. by Poets in the 1 pers. pl. pass. and mid., as τυπτόμεσθα for τυπτόμεθα; so ὄπισθεν for ὄπιθεν.
conversely, the Lacon. used to throw out σ between two vowels, writing Μῶα for Μοῦσα.
σ changed into ρ, doric and attic, when another ρ goes before, as ἄρρην for ἄρσην, θάρρος for θάρσος.
Lacon., σ is substituted for θ, as σιός Ἀσάνα παρσένος for θεός Ἀθήνη παρθένος.
doric, σδ for ζ, as μασδός τράπεσδα for μαζός τράπεζα.
ς is appended to οὕτω ἄχρι μέχρι before a vowel.
the letter sigma, v. sub Σ, σ.
Cyprian word for a spear, Hdt.
σιγύνης among the Ligyes near Marseilles was used for κάπηλος, Id.
the Σιγῦναι were a people on the Middle Danube, Id.
a working in iron, Xen.
iron-works, iron-mines, Arist.

entry.note: σῐδήρεος, α, ionic η, ον, epic σιδήρειος, η, ον
entry.sense: made of iron or steel, iron, Lat. ferreus, Hom., etc.; χεὶρ σιδηρᾶ a grappling-iron, Thuc.:— σιδήρειος ὀρυμαγδός, i. e. the clang of arms, Il.; σιδήρεος οὐρανός the iron sky, the firmament, which the ancients held to be of metal, Od.

metaph., σιδήρεος ἐν φρεσὶ θυμός a soul of iron, i. e. hard as iron, Hom.; οἱ κραδίη σιδηρέη Od.; σοί γε σιδήρεα πάντα τέτυκται thou art iron all! Id.:—of Hercules, the ironside, Simon.; ὦ σιδήρεοι O ye ironhearted! Aeschin.
σιδάρεοι, οἱ, a Byzantine iron coin, always in doric form, Ar.
a worker in iron, a smith, Xen.
an implement or tool of iron, σιδηρίων ἐπαΐειν to feel iron, not to be proof against it, Hdt.; θερμὰ σιδήρια hot irons, Id.
of iron, σ. πόλεμος iron war, Pind.
ἡ σιδηρῖτις λίθος the loadstone, Strab.
iron-eating, Soph.
iron-fingered, Anth.
iron-bound, ἐν ξύλῳ σιδηροδέτῳ, i. e. in the stocks, Hdt.

sic.seg: si^dhro-kmhfailing on lembuf [] | /s, h=tos, o(, h(,

entry.sense: slain by iron, i. e. by the sword, used with the neut. dat. βοτοῖς, Soph.
mother of iron, Aesch.
distributing with iron, i. e. with the sword, Aesch.
iron-backed, Eur.
moulded of iron, Luc.
smitten by iron, Aesch.
sown or produced by iron, Luc.

iron, Lat. ferrum, Hom., etc.: iron was the last of the metals brought into common use by the Greeks: hence it is πολύκμητος, wrought with much toil, Hom.: and was of high value, pieces of it being given as prizes, Il. It mostly came from the north and east of the Euxine, Σκύθης σ. Aesch.
like Lat. ferrum, anything made of iron, an iron tool or weapon, a sword or knife, an axe-head, etc., Hom., etc.
a place for selling iron, a smithy, a cutler's shop, Xen.
a worker in iron, Aesch.
producing iron, Anth.
to cut or cleave with iron, Anth.
iron-works, Strab.
to bear iron, wear arms, go armed, Thuc.:—Mid., Id.
Mid. to go with an armed escort, Plut.
bearing arms or tools, Anth.
of iron heart, Aesch., Eur.
of iron and copper, τομή Luc.
fighting (or perhaps exulting) in iron, epith. of war-horses, Pind.
to overlay with iron, Luc.: —Pass., ἐσεσιδήρωτο ἐπὶ μέγα καὶ τοῦ ἄλλου ξύλου iron had been laid over a great part of the rest of the wood, Thuc.
pomegranate-peel, Ar.
men of Sidon, Il.; also Σιδόνιοι Od.
from Sidon, Il.
Sidon, one of the oldest cities of Phoenicia, Od., Hdt.: hence adj. Σῑδόνιος, η, ον, Il., Aesch.; Σιδονίη (sc. γῆ) Od.; Σιδόνιοι men of Sidon, Od.; Σιδώνιος, Hdt., attic; fem. Σιδωνιάς, άδος, Eur.
to hiss, of hot metal plunged into water, to which is compared the hissing of the Cyclops' eye when the burnt stake was thrust into it, Od.; so, of a pot boiling, Ar.; of fish frying, Id.
Sithonia, a part of Thrace, Hdt.
Sicania, i. e. the part of Sicily near Agrigentum: also = Σικελία, Od.
a Sicanian, Thuc.: adj. Σικανικός, ή, όν, Id.
the Lat. sicarius, an assassin, NTest.
Sicily, Hdt., etc.
Sicilian, Theocr.
Sicilian, Ar., etc.
a Sicilian Greek, as distinguished from a native Σικελός, Thuc.
Sicilian, of or from Sicily, Lat. Siculus, Od., Eur., etc.
Σικελοί, οἱ, the Siceli, the old inhabitants of Sicily, Od., Hdt.
a fermented liquor, NTest.
the Sicinnis, a dance of Satyrs used in the Satyrical drama, Eur., Luc.
a fruit like the cucumber or gourd, perh. the melon, Arist.
a cupping-glass, because it was shaped like the gourd, cucurbita, Id.
a cucumber or gourd, Ar.
(sc. ὑποδήματα) τά, Sicyonians, a kind of women's shoes, Luc.
of or from Sicyon, Pind.
Sicyon, Il.; also Xen.;—as adj., γῆ Σ. Anth.:—regul. adj. Σῐκυώνιος, η, ον Sicyonian, Thuc.
= κρότων or κίκι, called in Hdt. σιλλικύπριον, τό.
to insult, mock, jeer, banter, Luc.
squint-eyed, Luc.
a satirical poem or lampoon in hexam. verse, such as those written by Timon of Phlius, who was called ὁ σιλλο-γράφος.
a parchment-label (Lat. index) appended to the outside of a book, Cic.
a large river fish, Lat. silurus, perh. the sheat? Juvenal.
an insect, blatta, Luc.: also = tinea, a book-worm, Id., Anth.
Lat. laserpitium, a plant, used in food and medicine, assafoetida, Solon., Hdt.
bearing silphium, Strab.
intr. to grow in a hive, of honey, Anth.
of or from the hive: fem. σιμβληίς, ίδος, Anth.
a beehive, Hes., Theocr.
metaph. any store or hoard, Ar.
the river Simois, Il.; contr. Σῐμοῦς, οῦντος, Hes.; adj. Σιμοέντιος, contr. Σιμούντιος, α, ον, or ος, ον, Eur.; poet. fem. Σιμοεντίς, ίδος, Id.; also Σιμοείσιος, ον, Strab.

snub-nosed, flat-nosed, like the Tartars (or Scythians, as the Ancients called them), Hdt., etc.: —of the nose, snub, flat, opp. to γρυπός, Xen.;—as this kind of nose gives a pert expression, σιμά as adv. means sneeringly, Anth.
metaph. bent upwards, up-hill, πρὸς τὸ σιμὸν διώκειν to pursue uphill, Xen.:—generally, hollow, concave, Id.
masc. prop. n. flat-nose, Anth.
the shape of a snub nose, snubbiness, Xen.
metaph., τὴν σ. τῶν ὀδόντων the upward curve of a boar's tusks, Id.
to turn up the nose, and generally, to bend upwards.
the upturned bow of a ship, Plut.
to ravage or destroy wantonly, Hdt.:—Pass. to be treated wantonly, Ar.
mischievousness, Arist.
mischievous, c. gen. rei, τῶν ἑωυτοῦ σ. ruining his own affairs, Hdt.
mustard, NTest.
sindon, a fine cloth, a kind of cambric or muslin, (prob. derived from Ἰνδός, Sind), Hdt.; σινδὼν βυσσίνη, used for mummy-cloth, Id.: generally, fine linen, Soph., Thuc.
a muslin garment, Luc.
= σήθω, to sift, winnow, NTest.
a ravager, plunderer, Aesch.:—as adj. destroying, σ. ἀνήρ as an example of a γλῶσσα, Poeta ap. Arist.
as prop. n., Σίνις, the destroyer, a famous robber of the Isthmus of Corinth, called ὁ Πιτυοκάμπτης, Eur., Xen.
to do one harm or mischief, to plunder, Od.; to destroy, Id.; to pillage or waste a country, to waste or destroy the crops, Hdt.
generally, to hurt, harm, damage, Hes., Hdt.: in war, to injure, harass, Hdt., Xen.
hurt, harm, mischief, injury, Hdt.
of things, a mischief, bane, plague, Aesch.
destructive, ravenous, of wild beasts, Il.
the Sintians, early inhabitants of Lemnos, who were pirates, Hom.
Sinon, i. e. the Mischievous, the Greek who persuaded the Trojans to receive the wooden horse, Soph.
an inhabitant of Sinope, Xen., etc.
Sinope, a town of Paphlagonia on the Black Sea, Hdt.
the country of Sinope, Strab.
the water-parsnep or marsh-wort, Theocr.
a meal-tub, meal-jar, flour bin, Ar.
new wine boiled down, Lat. defrutum, Ar.
silk, v. σηρικός.
a pit or vessel for keeping corn, Dem.
mint or thyme, Ar., Anth.
a cloak of goats-hair, which served as a garment by day and a coverlet by night, Ar.
a plant of the Iris kind, Theophr.
a garment of skin, Hdt.
wearing a coat of skin, Hdt.
Sisyphian, Eur., etc.; fem. Σισυφίς, Theocr.

entry.etym: Prob. a redupl. form of σοφός (with aeolic υ for ο the crafty.)
entry.sense: a king of Corinth, noted as the craftiest of men, punished in the shades below, Hom., etc.
to convey corn, Luc.
conveyance of corn, Luc.
conveying or transporting corn, σ. πλοῖα provision-ships, Hdt.; σ. ναῦς Thuc.
to take food, eat, Od., Hdt.
c. acc. to feed on, eat, Hdt.: metaph., σ. ἐλπίδας Aesch.; τὴν σοφίαν Ar.
fed up, fatted, Xen., NTest.
to feed, fatten, Hdt.:—Pass. to feed on, to eat, Plut.
= σιταγωγέω, to convey or transport corn, Dem.: to import corn, παρὰ τινος Id.
the conveyance or importation of corn, Dem.
provisions, victuals, esp. of soldiers' provision-money, Xen., Dem.:—at Rome, σιτ. ἔμμηνον a monthly allowance of grain to the poorer citizens, Lat. tessera frumentaria, Plut.
of corn, μέτρα σ. corn-measures, Arist.
an eating, feeding, ἐπὶ σιτήσει for home consumption, Hdt.; σ. ἐν Πρυτανείῳ public maintenance in the Prytaneum, Ar., Plat.
food, Hdt.
to feed, nourish, fatten, Hdt., Ar.:—Pass. = σιτέομαι, to eat, Theocr.
of wheat or corn, σ. τροφή Strab.; ὁ σ. νόμος lex frumentaria, Plut.
grain, corn: food made from grain, bread, ποιεῖσθαι σιτία ἀπὸ ὀλυρέων to feed off spelt, Hdt.
generally, food, victuals, provisions, Id.; σιτία ἡμερῶν τριῶν three days' provision, of soldiers, Ar.; σιτία καὶ ποτά meat and drink, Plat., Xen.
τἀν Πρυτανείῳ σιτία public maintenance in the Prytaneum, Ar.; cf. σίτησις.
rarely food for dogs, Xen.

entry.etym: verb. adj. of σιτίζω, = σιτευτός, NTest.

entry.sense: want of corn or food, Hdt., Thuc.
holding food, Anth.
to furnish with provisions:—Pass. to be provisioned or victualled, Thuc.
to collect corn, to forage, Polyb.
a collecting of corn, a foraging, Plut.
a collector of corn or provisions.
one who measures out corn: a magistrate who had to inspect the corn measures, Arist.
the office of σιτομέτρης, Plut.
a measured portion of corn, NTest.
dealing out corn or food, σ. ἐλπίς the hope of getting food, Soph.
to prepare corn for food, to make bread, Eur.; σ. τινί to give victuals to any one, Xen.:—Mid. to prepare food for oneself, take food, Id.
breadmaking, the preparation of food, Xen.
for breadmaking, Xen.
σ. ἀνάγκη the task of grinding and baking, Eur.
as Subst. one that ground the corn in the handmill, Thuc.; mostly fem. a baking-woman, Hdt.; γυναῖκες σ. Id., Thuc.
the conveyance or convoy of corn, Dem.

entry.note: σῖτος, heterog. pl. σῖτα, ων, τά,
entry.sense: corn, grain, comprehending both wheat (πυρός) and barley (κριθή), Od., Thuc.; σ. ἀληλεσμένος ground corn, Hdt., Thuc.
food made from grain, bread, as opp. to flesh-meat, Od., Hdt.; σῖτον ἔδοντες, a general epith. of men as opp. to beasts, Od.; hence of savages, who eat flesh only, οὐδέ τι σῖτον ἤσθιον Hes.
in wider sense, meat, as opp. to drink, σῖτος ἠδὲ ποτής Hom.; σῖτα καὶ ποτά Hdt., etc.
rarely of beasts, food, fodder, Hes., Eur.
in attic Law, the public allowance of grain made to widows and orphans, Dem.
eating corn or bread, Od., Hdt.
carrying corn or provisions, Hdt.
corn-inspectors, Athenian officers, originally three in number, but afterwards ten in the City and five in Peiraeeus, who registered imports of corn, and saw that the corn-measures were right, Dem.
a cry of drovers to their flocks; when ἀπό follows, to call them off; sht! chit! when πρός, to lead them on, Theocr.
a buyer of corn, a commissary for buying it, Dem.
purchase of corn, the office of σιτώνης, Dem.
crippled, maimed, Lat. mancus.
to maim, cripple, bring to misery, Il.
Siphnian, Hdt.
Siphnos, one of the Cyclades, Hdt.
a tube, pipe, siphon, used for drawing wine out of the cask, Hippon.:— a service-pipe for water in houses, Strab.
to be silent or still, keep silence, Hdt., attic; φησὶν σιωπῶν, i. e. his silence gives consent, Eur.
trans. to hold silent, keep secret, not to speak of, Xen., etc.:—Pass. to be kept silent or secret, σιγῶς’ ὧν σιωπᾶσθαι χρεών keeping secret things which ought to be kept secret, Eur.
silent, still, quiet, Eur.
silence, Soph., Eur., etc.; σιωπὴν ποιεῖν Xen.; ἦν σ. there was a hush or calm, Soph.
the habit of silence, Dem.
dat. σιωπῇ as adv., in silence, Hom., attic
to be passed over in silence, Luc.
σιωπητέον, one must pass over in silence, Id.
to limp, halt, Il.: metaph., σκ. πρὸς τὴν θεραπείαν Luc.
ὁ σκάζων, also χωλίαμβος, the iambic verse of Hippon., being a regular senarius, with a spondee or trochee in the last place, Anth.
Lat. scaevus, left, on the left hand or side, σκαιῇ (sc. χειρί) with the left hand, Il.; χειρὶ σκαιῇ Hes.
western, westward, for the Greek auspex turned his face northward, and so had the west on his left; hence, Σκαιαὶ πύλαι the west gate of Troy, Il.; σκαιὸν ῥίον the western headland, Od.
unlucky, ill-omened, mischievous (because birds of ill omen appeared on the left or in the west, birds of good omen on the right or in the East), Hdt., Soph.
metaph. of persons, like French gauche, lefthanded, awkward, clumsy, Hdt., Eur., etc.
lefthandedness, awkwardness, Hdt., Soph., etc.
to behave amiss, Ar.
to skip, frisk, Hom.
a petty quibble, Ar.
a hoer, Xen.
to stir, poke, ἄνθρακας Ar., Luc.
uneven, unequal, ἀριθμὸς σκ. an odd number, Plat.; τρίγωνον σκ. a triangle with unequal sides, Arist.; of a path, uneven, Anth.
to stir up, hoe, Hdt.
the pin or thole to which the Greek oar was fastened by a thong (τροπωτήρ), Aesch., Eur.
the digger, i. e. the mole, Ar.
Scamandrian, Id., Soph., etc.
the Scamander, the famous river of Troy, ὃν Ξάνθον καλέουσι θεοί, ἄνδρες δὲ Σκάμανδρον Il.

the stick in a trap on which the bait is placed, and which, when touched by the animal, springs up and shuts the trap, the trap-spring: metaph., σκανδάληθρ’ ἱστὰς ἐπῶν setting word- traps, i. e. words which one's adversary will catch at, and be caught himself, Ar.
to make to stumble, give offence to any one, τινά NTest.:—Pass. to take offence, Id.
a trap or snare laid for an enemy, NTest.:—metaph. a stumbling-block, offence, scandal, Id.
chervil (i. e. chaerophyllum), Ar.
a digging tool, mattock, Theocr., Anth.
the act of digging, Anth.
a digger, delver, Hom. ap. Arist.
dug: that may be dug: —Σκαπτὴ ὕλη a district in Thrace, Hdt.
to dig, delve, μοχθεῖν καὶ σκ. Ar.; proverb., σκάπτειν οὐκ ἐπίσταμαι Id.
c. acc.,
to dig the ground, Xen., Luc.
to dig about, φυτὰ σκ. (as we say to hoe turnips), Hhymn.: metaph. to dig up, Eur.
σκ. τάφρον to dig a trench, Thuc.:—Pass., τὰ ἐσκαμμένα scores to mark a leap, metaph., ὑπὲρ τὰ ἐσκαμμένα ἅλλεσθαι to overleap the mark, Plat.
to blink, wink, Eur., Xen.
a scratching up, σκαριφισμοὶ λήρων small criticisms, petty quibbles, Ar.
eating dirt, Ar.
a digger, delver, ditcher, Eur.
anything dug or scooped out,
a trough or tub, basin or bowl, Hdt.
a light boat, skiff, Ar.
proverb., τὴν σκάφην σκάφην λέγειν "to call a spade a spade, " to call things by their right names, Luc.
a small skiff, Strab.
Dim. of σκάφη: esp.
a bowl, milk-pail, Od.:— a pot for honey, Theocr.
a small boat, skiff, canoe, Anth.
a shovel, Id.
a digging, hoeing, σκάφος οἰνέων the time for hoeing vines, Hes.
the hull of a ship, Lat. alveus, Hdt., Trag.:—generally, a ship, Aesch., Ar., etc.
= σκαφίς II, Anth.
to scatter, disperse, Hom.
Pass. to be scattered, to disperse, of men, Hdt., Thuc.; of the rays of the sun, Aesch.; of a report, to be spread abroad, Hdt.
a scattering, Od.
exact, careful: adv., -ῶς Aesch.
dried up, withered: as Subst. σκελετός, οῦ, a dried body, mummy, Anth., Plut.
like a mummy, Luc.
to dry, dry up, make dry, parch, Il.
Pass., σκέλλομαι, with intr. perf. act. ἔσκληκα, to be parched, lean, dry, v. κατασκέλλομαι.

the leg from the hip downwards, Hdt., etc.; πρυμνὸν σκέλος the ham or buttock, Il.:—as a military phrase, ἐπὶ σκέλος πάλιν χωρεῖν, ἀνάγειν to retreat with the face towards the enemy, Lat. pedetentim, Eur., Ar.
metaph., τὰ σκέλη the legs, i. e. the two long walls between Athens and Peiraeus, Strab.; τὰ μακρὰ σκ. Plut.
a subject for speculation, a question, Plat.
speculation, Id.
to cover, shelter, Xen.
a covering, Anth.
sheltered or sheltering, Anth.
a carpenter's axe or adze, used for smoothing the trunks of trees, different from the πέλεκυς, Od.
a covering, shelter, Plat.
a covering, shelter, ἐπὶ σκέπας in or under shelter, Od.; σκέπας ἀνέμοιο shelter from the wind, Id.; nom. and acc. pl. σκέπᾰ, Hes.
to cover, shelter, ἀνέμων σκεπόωσι κῦμα (epic for σκεπάουσι) they ward off (provide shelter against) the sea raised by the wind, Od.; κόρυν σκεπάουσιν ἔθειραι Theocr.
a covering, shelter, protection, Xen.:—c. gen., ἐν σκέπῃ τοῦ πολέμου under shelter from war, Hdt.; ὑπὸ τὴν Ῥωμαίων σκέπην under their protection, Polyb.
one must reflect or consider, Ar., Thuc., etc.
σκεπτέος, η, ον, to be considered, examined, Antipho.
reflective: οἱ σκεπτικοί, the Sceptics or philosophers who asserted nothing, but only opined, Cic. opinatores, Luc.

entry.etym: in Att. σκοπῶ or σκοποῦμαι are used in the present
entry.sense: to look about, look carefully, followed by prep. εἰς, Od., Eur.:—c. acc. to look after, watch, Il., Hdt., attic:—absol. to look out, reconnoitre, Hdt.; σκέψαι look, Aesch.; σκέψασθε look out, Ar.
of the mind, to look to, view, examine, consider, think on, Soph., Thuc., etc.:—σκέψασθε δέ: only consider, Thuc.
to think of beforehand, premeditate, Dem.
perf. also in pass. sense, ἐσκεμμένα things well-considered, Thuc.; σκοπεῖτε οὖν. Answ. ἔσκεπται Plat.; so 3 fut. pass. ἐσκέψεται Id.
to scold, abuse, σκ. πονηρά to use foul abuse, Ar.
to carry away goods and chattels, Dem., Aeschin.
conveying goods:— τὰ σκ. baggage-wagons, Plut.; transport vessels, Strab.
as Subst. a baggage-master, Xen.
to prepare, make ready, esp. to prepare or dress food, Hdt., Ar.; σκ. ἔκ τινος περικόμματα to make mincemeat of him, Ar.:—Mid. to prepare for oneself, Eur., Plat.
generally to make ready, Hhymn.; σκ. ἡδονάς to provide, procure, Plat.:—Mid., like μηχανάομαι, to contrive, bring about, Hdt.
of persons, to furnish, supply:—Pass., σιτίοισι εὖ ἐσκευασμένος Id.; ποταμοῖσι Σκύθαι ἐσκευάδαται Id.
to dress up, dress out, Id., Ar., etc.:— Pass., ἐσκευασμένοι fully accoutred, Thuc.; of things, τὰ προπύλαια τύποισι ἐσκευάδαται are decorated with figures, Hdt.
a small vessel or utensil, Ar.:—implements of gaming, Aeschin.
a preparing, dressing, Plat.
one must prepare to do a thing, c. inf., Ar.
prepared by art, artificial, Plat.
equipment, attire, apparel, dress, Lat. apparatus, Hdt., Soph., etc.
a fashion, style of dress or equipment, Hdt., Thuc.
tackle, as of a net, Pind.
a tool-chest, arms-chest, Aeschin.
to fabricate, Plut.
in pl. the dress of a tragic actor, Plut.
a maker of masks and other stage-properties, Ar.

a vessel or implement of any kind, Ar., Thuc., etc.:—pl. in collective sense, furniture, house-gear, utensils, chattels, Ar.:—esp. of military accoutrements, equipment, Thuc., Xen.: baggage, luggage, Lat. impedimenta, Ar., Xen.:— the tackling or gear of ships, Xen., NTest.
an inanimate object, a thing, Plat.
metaph., τὸ σκεῦος, the body, as the vessel of the soul, NTest.; σκεῦος ἐκλογῆς a chosen vessel, of St. Paul, Id.
to carry baggage, Xen.:—Pass. to have one's baggage carried, Plut.
of or for baggage-carrying, Xen.; βάρος σκ. the load for one animal, a beast's load, Id.
carrying σκεύη, αἱ σκ. κάμηλοι the baggage- camels, Hdt.; τὰ σκ. (sc. κτήνη) the beasts of burden in an army, Thuc., etc.
as Subst., of persons, a baggage-carrier, porter, Ar.; οἱ σκ. the sutlers, camp-followers, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
to watch the baggage, Plut.
Dep.
to look after the baggage (τὰ σκεύη) : hence, generally, to examine throughly, ransack it, Plut.
to fabricate, make up, Dem.; with a sense of fraud or intrigue, Id.:—absol. to act knavishly, Id.
a fabrication, fraud, Dem.
attention to baggage: hence, generally, great care, excessive care, Arist.
fabrication, knavery, intrigue, Dem.
a viewing, perception by the senses, Plat.
speculation, consideration, Id.; νέμειν σκέψιν to take thought of a thing, Eur.; ἐνθεὶς τῇ τέχνῃ σκέψιν Ar.; σκ. περί τινος or τι inquiry into, speculation on a thing, Plat.
hesitation, doubt (v. σκεπτικός), Anth.
= σκηνέω, Xen.
σκηνάομαι Dep., with perf. and plup. pass., to dwell, live, Plat.; ἐσκηνημένοι in covered carriages (v. σκήνη III), Ar.; ἱερά, ἐν οἷς ἐσκήνηντο in which they found harbourage, Thuc.
c. acc., σκηνησάμενος καλύβην having built him a hut or cottage, Id.

to be or dwell in a tent, to be encamped, Xen.: generally, to be quartered or billeted, ἐν οἰκίαις Thuc.; ἐν κώμαις, κατὰ τὰς κώμας Xen.; σκ. εἰς τὰς κώμας to go to the villages and quarter themselves there, Id.
a dwelling-place, Xen.: in pl. a nest, Aesch.
a covered place, a tent, Hdt., Soph., etc.: —in pl. a camp, Lat. castra, Aesch., Xen.
generally, a dwelling-place, house, temple, Eur.

a wooden stage for actors, Plat.:—in the regular theatre, the σκηνή was a wall at the back of the stage, with doors for entrance and exit; the stage (in our sense) was προσκήνιον or λογεῖον, the sides or wings παρασκήνια, and the wall under the stage, fronting the orchestra, ὑποσκήνια.
οἱ ἀπὸ σκηνῆς, the actors, players, Dem.
τὸ ἐπὶ σκηνῆς μέρος that which is actually represented on the stage, Arist.; τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς σκηνῆς (sc. ᾄσματα), odes sung on the stage, Id.
metaph. stage-effect, unreality, σκηνὴ πᾶς ὁ βίος "all the world's a stage, " Anth.
the tented cover, tilt of a wagon, Aesch., Xen.: also a bed-tester, Dem.
an entertainment given in tents, a banquet, Xen.
a dweller in tents, Strab.: metaph. a low fellow, Isocr.
to bring on the stage, Strab.
scene-painting, Arist.
for or in the manner of scene-painting, Strab.
a setting up of tents: the Feast of Tents or Tabernacles, NTest.
a pitching of tents, Polyb.
tent-making:—as Subst. a tentmaker, NTest.
metaph. the body (as the tabernacle of the soul), NTest.
a watcher in a tent, Xen.
to pitch tents, encamp, Xen.
= σκηνέω, to dwell in a tent, Id.: generally, to settle, take up one's abode, Id.:—in perf. pass. to live or be, Plat.
to occupy with tents, Plut.
quarters, Xen.
metaph. the body, NTest.
a thunder-bolt, Soph., Xen.:— metaph. of pestilence, Aesch.; of war, Eur., Dem.
the bearing a staff or sceptre as the badge of command, military command, Aesch.:— generally, command, power, Anth.
bearing a staff or sceptre as the badge of command, σκ. βασιλεύς a sceptred king, Hom.
as Subst. a wand-bearer, an officer in the Persian court, Xen.
a staff or stick to lean upon, a walking-stick, Hom., Aesch.: metaph. of the daughters of Oedipus, σκῆπτρα φωτός his staffs or supports, Soph.

a staff, as the badge of command, a sceptre: in Hom. borne by chiefs, and transmitted from father to son, whence the passage in Il. 2 is called ἡ τοῦ σκήπτρου παράδοσις, Thuc.:—also borne by judges, by heralds, by speakers, who on rising to speak received it from the herald, Hom.
the sceptre, i. e. royalty, kingly power, rule, Il., Trag.
to rule over, c. gen., Anth.
bearing a sceptre, kingly, Anth.
to prop, stay one thing against or upon another: Pass. and Mid. to lean upon a staff, Hom.: metaph. to lean upon a person or thing, Dem.
c. acc. rei, to put forward by way of support, allege in excuse, Eur.:—in Mid. to allege on one's own behalf, Hdt., Thuc.; c. inf. to pretend to be, Ar., Dem.
to hurl, dart, Aesch.; metaph., σκ. ἀλάστορα εἴς τινα Eur.
intr. to fall heavily, Aesch., Soph.
Mid., to support oneself, Od.; σκηριπτόμενος χερσίν τε ποσίν τε pressing with hands and feet, Id.
a pretext, plea, excuse, pretence, Trag.; c. gen., κατὰ φόνου τινὰ σκῆψιν on some pretence of murder, Hdt.; σκ. τοῦ μὴ ποιεῖν a plea, excuse for not doing, Dem.
to draw with gradations of light and shade: to sketch out, Lat. adumbrare:—Pass., τὰ ἐσκιαγραφημένα Plat.
a mere sketch, Plat.
a sketch or rough painting, such as to produce an effect at a distance, scene-painting, Plat.

sense.gloss: drawing in light and shade, sketching.

entry.sense: a sunshade, parasol, Ar.
to overshadow, shade, Il., Eur.
generally, to overshadow, cover, Hes., Hdt.:—Pass., Eur.
to shade in painting, Luc.
to fight in the shade, i. e. in the school (for practice): to fight with a shadow, to fight in vain, Plat.
shade-footed, a fabulous people in Libya, with immense feet which they used as sunshades, Ar.

entry.note: σκια, ᾶς, ionic σκιή, ῆς, ἡ,
entry.sense: a shadow, Od.; σκιὰ ἀντίστοιχος ὥς like the shadow that is one's double, Eur.
the shade of one who is dead, a phantom, Od., Trag.; so of one worn to a shadow, Aesch.:—in proverbs of man's mortal estate, σκιᾶς ὄναρ ἄνθρωπος Pind.; εἴδωλον σκιᾶς Aesch., etc.
the shade of trees, etc., πετραίη σκιή the shade of a rock, Hes.; ἐν σκιῇ Id.; ὑπὸ σκιῇ Hdt.; ὑπὸ σκιᾶς Eur.; σκιὰν Σειρίου κυνός shade from it's heat, Aesch.
with shading leaves, Eur.
any thing serving as a shade, a canopy, pavilion, Theocr., Plut.
a being brought up in the shade, a sedentary, effeminate life, Plut.
to rear in the shade:—Pass. to keep in the shade, shun heat and labour, Hdt., Xen.
intr. in Act. to wear a shade, cover one's head, Hdt.; ἐσκιατροφηκώς, of an effeminate man, Plat.
to overshadow:—Pass. to be shaded or become dark, σκιόωντο ἀγυιαί (epic 3rd pl. imperf.) Od.

to disperse:— Pass. σκίδναμαι, only in pres. and imperf. to be scattered, to disperse, of a crowd, Hom.; of foam or spray, of a cloud of dust, Il.; σκιδναμένης Δημήτερος when the corn is being scattered, i. e. at seedtime, Orac. ap. Hdt.; ἅμα ἡλίῳ σκιδναμένῳ as the sun begins to spread his light, i. e. soon after sunrise, Id.
shady, giving shade, Hom., Pind., etc.
shady, shaded, Hes., Pind.
dark-coloured, Anth.
a squill, sea-onion, Theogn., Theocr.
to jeer at, flout, τινά Ar.
a small couch, low bed, Ar., Xen.
to allege, Pind.
a splinter, Lat. scindula:—metaph., λόγων σχινδάλαμοι straw-splittings, quibbles, Ar.
a straw-splitter, Anth.
fleeting like a shadow, shadowy, Ar., Plat.
shady, shadowy, οὔρεα σκιόεντα i. e. thickly wooded, Hom.; σκ. μέγαρα dark chambers, Od.
act., νέφεα σκ. overshadowing clouds, Hom.
shadowy, unsubstantial, Anth.
a staff, Hdt., Eur., etc.
the festival of Athena Σκιράς, held in the month Pyanepsion, Ar.; different from the Σκιροφόρια, which fell in Scirophorion.
name of Athena, Strab.
a gambling-house, Isocr.
a dice-box:—metaph. trickery, cheating, Hippon.

the Scirites, a division of the Spartan army, consisting of 600 foot: they fought on the left wing near the king, and were (originally at least) περίοικοι, from the Arcadian district Σκιρῖτις, Thuc., Xen.
the hard rind of cheese, cheese-parings, Ar.
the white sunshade which was borne from the Acropolis, in the festivals of Athena Σκιράς (τὰ Σκίρα), Plut.
stucco: any hard covering, v. σκῖρον.
Scirophorion, the 12th Attic month, the latter part of June and former of July, so called from the festival Σκιροφόρια, Antipho., etc.
to spring, leap, bound, Il., Eur., etc.:—metaph. of gusts of wind, Aesch.
a bound, leap, Aesch., Eur.
a bounding, leaping, Plut.
a leaper, Mosch.
spring-footed, Anth.
leaper, name of a Satyr, Anth.
the wind which blew from the Scironian rocks in the Isthmus, Strab.

a robber who haunted the rocks between Attica and Megara, killed by Theseus, Xen.; Σκείρωνος ἀκταί the coast near these rocks, Eur.; the adjacent sea was Σκιρωνικὸν, οἶδμα θαλάσσης Simon. in Anth.; the rocks themselves Σκιρωνίδες πέτραι Eur.; Σκιρωνὶς ὁδός the road from Athens to Megara, Hdt.
invoked as the powers of impudence, Ar.
shady, Eur.
to bring up hardy, Luc.
hardness of heart, NTest.
hard, Lat. durus, Theogn., Aesch., etc.
of sound, hard, harsh, crashing, Lat. aridus, Hes., Hdt.
hard, stiff, unyielding, Lat. rigidus, Ar., Xen.:—of boys who look old for their age, stiff, sturdy, Plut., Luc.
metaph. of things, hard, austere, severe, Soph., Eur.; σκληρὰ μαλθακῶς λέγων Soph.
adv., σκληρῶς καθῆσθαι, i. e. on a hard seat, Ar.
hardness, Plat.
of persons, hardness, harshness, austerity, Id.
stiff-necked, NTest.
to harden:—metaph. to harden the heart, NTest.
slender, slight, thin, Plat.
dark, σκν. ὁδίτης a wanderer in the twilight, Theocr.
with curled hair or leaves, Anth.

a song which went round at banquets, sung to the lyre by the guests, Ar.; so called from its zigzag course— each guest who sung holding a myrtle-branch (μυρρίνη), which he passed across the table to any one he chose.

curved, winding, twisted, tangled, Lat. obliquus, Hdt., Eur., etc.:— bent sideways, δουλείη κεφαλὴ σκολιή (Hor. stat capite obstipo) Theogn.: metaph. crooked, i. e. unjust, unrighteous, Il., Hes., etc.; σκολιὰ πράττειν, εἰπεῖν Plat.:—so adv. σκολιῶς, Hes.
crookedness, Plut.: in pl. the windings of a stream, etc., Strab.
a bend, curve, Strab.
to impale.
an eatable kind of thistle, an artichoke, Hes.
a sea-fish, a kind of tunny, Ar.
the chief scout, the leader of a reconnoitring party, Xen.
running over rocks, Anth.
a look-out place, a peak, headland or promontory, Lat. scopulus, Hom., etc.

entry.etym: later form for σκοπέω, Strab., etc.
used by Att. writers only in pres. and impf., the other tenses being supplied by σκέπτομαι.
entry.sense: to look at or after a thing: to behold, contemplate, Pind., Soph., etc.:—absol. to look out, watch, Soph., etc.
metaph. to look to, consider, examine, Hdt., attic; σκ. τι Thuc., etc.; σκ. περί τινος or τι Plat.: absol., ὀρθῶς σκοπεῖν Eur., etc.
to look out for, c. acc., Xen., etc.
Mid., used just like Act., Soph., Eur.
Pass., σκοπῶν καὶ σκοπούμενος considering and being considered, Plat.

entry.etym: = σκοπιά I, in pl., Aesch., Xen.

entry.sense: to look about one, spy from a high place or watchtower, Il.: to spy, explore, Od.
trans. to spy out, search out, discover, c. acc., Il., Anth., etc.:—so in Mid. to look out for, Theocr.
a lookout-place, a mountain-peak, Hom.: of the Trojan acropolis, Eur.: cf. σκόπελος.
metaph. the height or highest point of anything, Pind.
a watchtower, Lat. specula, Hdt., Plat.
a look-out, watch, σκοπιὴν ἔχειν to keep watch, Od., Hdt.
a highlander, of Pan, Anth.
Dep. to look out for, watch, Ar.
a watcher.
one that watches, one that looks after things, Hom.; of gods and kings, a guardian, protector, Ὀλύμπου σκ. Pind.
a lookout-man, watchman, stationed on a σκοπιά, Lat. speculator, Hom., Xen.: one who marks game, Xen.
a spy, scout, Il., Trag.
the object on which one fixes the eye, a mark, Lat. scopus, Od.; ἀπὸ σκοποῦ away from the mark, Id.; so, παρὰ σκοπόν Pind.; σκοποῦ τυχεῖν to hit the mark, Id.; ἐπὶ σκοπὸν βάλλειν Xen.
metaph. an aim, end, object, Plat.
to dismiss contemptuously, Luc.:—Pass. to be treated contemptuously, Dem.
Dep. to stretch one's limbs, yawn, gape, Ar.
a sauce of brine and garlic, Ar.
to prime game-cocks with garlic before fighting, Ar.:—Pass., ἐσκοροδισμένος primed with garlic, Id.
garlic-fighters, Luc.
garlic, Lat. allium, the root of which consists of several separate cloves (γελγῖθες), and is thus distinguished from the onion (κρόμμυον), and leek (πράσον), Hdt.; in pl., Ar.
to scatter, disperse, Strab., NTest.
a scorpion, Plat., Dem.
an engine of war for discharging arrows, Plut.
in the dark, i.e. before daybreak or after nightfall, Xen.
of things, dark, obscure, Plut.
dark, Aesch., Eur., etc.; ἀνὰ τὸ σκοτεινόν in the darkness, Thuc.
of a person, darkling, blind, Soph., Eur.
metaph. dark, obscure, Eur., Plat.:—so adv. -νῶς, Plat.
darkness, gloom, Anth.
to make dark:—Pass. to be darkened, NTest.
dark,
of persons, in the dark, darkling, σκότιον δέ ἑ γείνατο μήτηρ, i. e. not in open wedlock, Il.; so, σκότιοι παῖδες Eur.; σκ. εὐναί clandestine Loves, Id., etc.
of things and places, dark, Id.
metaph., like σκοτεινός, dark, obscure, Ar.
dark with shaggy thick hair, κυνῆ σκ., of a "cap of darkness, " Ar.
to suffer from dizziness or vertigo, Ar., Plat.
dark-looking, Plat.
dark, Hes.
dark and moonless, Od.
darkness, gloom, Od., attic
the darkness of death, Il., Eur.
of blindness, σκότον βλέπειν Soph.; σκότον δεδορκώς Eur.
metaph., σκότῳ κρύπτειν, like Hor.'s nocte premere, to hide in darkness, Soph.; so, διὰ σκότους ἐστί it is dark and uncertain, Xen.; κατὰ σκότον, ὑπὸ σκότου Soph., etc.
to make dark, to blind:—Pass. to be in darkness: also to suffer from vertigo, Plat.
dark, Plat.
dung, filth, refuse, Anth.
to be angry, τινί with one, Il.
to be angry or wroth with one, τινί Hom.: absol. to be wroth, Il.
a Scythian: proverb., Σκυθῶν ἐρημία, as we might say "the desert of Africa, " Ar.: —fem. Σκύθαινᾰ.
as adj. Scythian, Aesch.
at Athens, a policeman, one of the city-guard, which was mostly composed of Scythian slaves, Ar.
to behave like a Scythian: hence, from the Scythian practice of scalping slain enemies, to shave the head, ἐσκυθισμένος ξυρῶι Eur.
to behave like a Scythian: hence, from the Scythian practice of scalping slain enemies, to shave the head, ἐσκυθισμένος ξυρῷ Eur.
Scythian, Aesch., etc.:— ἡ Σκυθική (sc. γῆ) Hdt., etc.:—fem. Σκυθίς, ίδος, acc. ίν, Aeschin.
adv. -κῶς, Strab., Plut.
in the Scythian tongue, Hdt.
a Scythian bowman, Xen.
to be angry, peevish, Eur.
angry, sullen, Menand.
to look angry or sullen, be of a sad countenance, Ar., Xen., etc.
angry-looking, of sad countenance, sullen, Eur., Aesch., etc.:— τὸ σκυθρωπόν, = σκυλάκαινα, Eur.—adv., σκυθρωπῶς ἔχειν Xen.
of things, gloomy, sad, melancholy, Eur.
a breeding of dogs, Plut.
a whelp, cub, Anth.
to pair dogs for breeding, Xen.
Pass. to be suckled, Strab.
like a young dog: τὸ σκυλακῶδες the nature of puppies, Xen.
a young dog, whelp, puppy, Lat. catulus, Od., Hes.:—generally, a dog, Soph., etc.
= σκύμνος, Eur.
mostly in pl. the arms stript off a slain enemy, spoils, Eur., Thuc.
to strip or despoil a slain enemy of his arms, Hes., Hdt.; c. acc. pers. et rei, Κύκνον σκυλεύσαντες ἀπ’ ὤμων τεύχεα having stript the arms of Cycnus from his shoulders, Hes.
c. acc. rei et gen. pers. to strip the arms off an enemy, Xen.; so, ἀπὸ τῶν νεκρῶν σκ. ψέλια Hdt.
Scylla, a monster barking like a dog, who inhabited a cavern in the Straits, of Sicily, and rent unwary mariners, Od.
to rend, mangle:—Pass., Aesch.
metaph. to trouble, annoy, Lat. vexare, NTest.:—Pass. or Mid., μὴ σκύλλου trouble not thyself, Id.; ἐσκυλμένοι troubled, distressed, Id.
to tan hides, Ar.
a tanner of hides, Ar.:—so σκῠλό-δεψος, ὁ, Dem.
mostly in pl. σκῦλα, the arms stript off a slain enemy, spoils, Soph., Thuc.; εἰς σκῦλα γράφειν to write one's name on arms taken as spoil, Eur.: —rarely in sg., booty, spoil, prey, Id.
a skin, hide, Theocr., Anth.
receiving the spoil, Anth.
delighting in spoils, Anth.
a cub, whelp, esp. a lion's whelp, Il., Hdt., attic; of other animals, Eur., Plut.; in poets also of men, Ἀχίλλειος σκ. Eur.
the isle of Scyros, one of the Sporades, not far from Euboea, Hom.:—adj. Σκύριος, a Scyrian, Hdt.:—adv., Σκῡρόθεν from Scyros, Il.
a staff, cudgel, club, Anth.

at Sparta, a staff or baton, used as a cypher for writing dispatches:—a strip of leather was rolled slantwise round it, on which the dispatches were written lengthwise, so that when unrolled they were unintelligible: commanders abroad had a staff of like thickness, round which they rolled these papers, and so were able to read the dispatches:—hence σκυτάλη came to mean a Spartan dispatch, Thuc., Xen.; and generally a message, Pind.
to carry a club, Strab.
carrying a club, Strab.
a stick, Hdt.
to be a shoemaker, Xen.
skilled in shoemaking:— ἡ -κή (sub. τέχνη) = σκυτοτομία, Plat.
leathern, made of leather, Hdt., Ar.
metaph. skinny, gaunt, Anth.
a leather-dresser, currier, Theophr.: so, σκῡτόδεψος, ὁ, Plat., Luc.
a skin, hide, esp. a dressed or tanned hide, Od., Ar., etc.
a leather thong, a whip, Dem.; σκύτη βλέπειν to look whips, i. e. as if one was going to be whipt, Ar.
to cut leather for shoes, to be a shoemaker, Ar., Plat.
shoemaking, Plat.
of or for a shoemaker, Ar.; ὁ σκ. = ὁ σκυτοτόμος, Plat.: ἡ-κή (sc. τέχνη) = σκυτοτομία, Id.
a leather-cutter, a worker in leather, Il., Xen., etc.: esp. a shoemaker, cobbler, Ar.
to gnaw leather, Luc.
a cup, can, Od., Eur., etc.: a milk-pail, Theocr.
eaten of worms, NTest.
a worm, Lat. lumbricus, Il.
of the grubs, of insects, Ar., etc.
like σκόλοψ, a pointed stake, Il.
a jest, joke, gibe, scoff, Ar.; ἐν σκώμματος μέρει by way of a joke, Aeschin.; σκ. παρὰ γράμμα a pun, Arist.
mocking, jesting, Plut., Luc.
a mocker, jester, Ar.
to hoot, mock, jeer, scoff at, τινά Ar.; also, σκ. εἰς τὰ ῥάκια to jest at his rags, Id.; εἴς τινα Aeschin.
in good sense, to joke with, τινά Hdt.
absol. to jest, joke, be funny, Ar., Xen., etc.
the dross of metal, slag, scoria, Strab.
dung, Ar.
a small kind of owl, Od., Theocr.
of smaragdus, NTest.
Lat. smaragdus, a precious stone of a green colour, a name given to the emerald and to malachite, Hdt.
to crash, as thunder, Il.; of the sea, to roar, Id.; of cranes, to scream, Id.
to wipe or cleanse with soap or unguent; (but the Act. is mostly found in compds. δια-, ἐκ-, ἐπι-σμάω): — Mid., σμᾶσθαι τὴν κεφαλήν to wash or anoint one's head, Hdt.
terrible to look on, fearful, aweful, direful, Hom.
terrible to hear, in neut. as adv., terribly, Id.; so in pl. σμερδαλέα, Il.
Il., Aesch.:—as adv., σμερδνόν Il.
soap or unguent, Plut.
holding a swarm of bees, Anth.

entry.note: σμῆνος, doric σμᾶνος, ος, εος, τό,
entry.sense: a beehive, Hes., Plat.
a swarm of bees, Aesch., etc.; of wasps, Ar.:—metaph., of clouds, Id., etc.
to wipe off by help of soap or unguent, to wash off, Od.
to wipe clean, Babr.: proverb., Αἰθίοπα σμ. "to wash a black man white," Luc.: —Mid., σμηχομένα κρόταφον wiping her brow clean, Anth.

entry.etym: ionic and old attic for μικρός.

entry.sense: Lat. taxus, the yew, Plat.
the convolvulus, or perh. bryony, Trag., Ar.
a piece of carved work: metaph., σμιλεύματα ἔργων finely carved works, Ar.
cut, carved, Anth.
a knife for cutting, carving or pruning, Plat., etc.: a graving tool, chisel, Anth.
Dim. of σμίλη, Lat. scalpellum, Luc.
name of Apollo (from Σμίνθος or Σμίνθη a town in Troas), the Sminthian, Il.
a mouse (a Cretan word), Anth.
a two-pronged hoe or mattock, Lat. bidens, Ar., Plat.
with pain, painful, Soph. adv. -ρῶς, Id.
of Smyrna, Pind.
of myrrh, Anth.
Smyrna, in Ionia, Hdt., etc.
like μύρρα, myrrh, the resinous gum of an Arabian tree, used for embalming the dead, Hdt.; called σμύρνης ἱδρώς by Eur.; also used for anointing, Ar.; and a salve, Hdt.
to flavour or drug with myrrh: Pass., οἶνος ἐσμυρνισμένος NTest.
bearing myrrh, Strab.
to burn in a mouldering fire:— Pass. to smoulder away, Il., Mosch.
a weal, swollen bruise, caused by a blow, Il.
to rub down, grind down, Ar.
properly, scaring birds away: — and so,
rushing, rapid, Ar.:—adv. -ρῶς, Id.
swaggering, pompous, haughty, Id.; of a horse, Xen.:—adv. -ρῶς, Plut.; also neut. as adv., Theocr.
of things, Ar.
to scare away birds, Ar., etc.
generally, to drive away, clear away, Xen.
to move rapidly, πόδα σοβεῖν, of dancing, Ar.:—metaph. in Pass. to be much agitated, vehemently excited, Anth., Plut.
intr. to strut, swagger, bustle, Dem., Plut.; σόβει ἐς Ἄργος bustle off to Argos, Luc.
to speak incorrectly, commit a solecism, φωνῇ Σκυθικῇ σολ. to speak bad Scythian, Hdt.
incorrectness in the use of language, a solecism, Luc.
one who speaks incorrectly, Luc.
speaking incorrectly, using provincialisms, Anacr., etc.
metaph. erring against good manners, awkward, clumsy, Xen., Arist.
entry.etym: Said to come from the corruption of the Attic dialect by the Athenian colonists of Σόλοι in Cilicia.

entry.sense: a mass or lump of iron, used in throwing, Il.; distinguished from the flat δίσκος or quoit.

entry.etym: epic and ionic form of σῶος, σῶς: v. σῶς.

entry.sense: a coffin-maker, Ar., Anth.
a vessel for holding anything, esp. a cinerary urn, Il.:— a coffin, Hdt., Ar.
as nickname of an old man or woman, Ar.

entry.etym: possessive adj. of pers. Pron. σύ, the earlier form being τεός
entry.sense: thy, thine, of thee, Lat. tuus, tua, tuum, Hom., etc.; epic gen. σοῖο; — in attic often with the Art., δέμας τὸ σόν, τὸ σὸν κάρα:—σὸν ἔργον, c. inf., 'tis thy business to . . , Soph.; so, σόν [ἐστι] alone, Aesch.:— οἱ σοί thy kinsfolk, people, Soph.:— τὸ σόν what concerns thee, thy interest, words, purpose, Id.:— τὰ σά thy property, Od.; thy interests, Soph.
with a gen. added, τὰ σ’ αὐτῆς ἔργα Il.; σὸν μόνης δώρημα Soph.
objective, for thee, σῇ ποθῇ Il.; σός τε πόθος σά τε μήδεα Od.; σῇ προμηθίᾳ Soph.
the Lat. suda_rium, a kerchief, NTest.
worshipped at Sunium, Ar.
hawk-of-sunium, Ar.
a man of Sunium, Decret. ap. Dem.
Sunium, the southern headland of Attica, Od., etc.:—adj., Σουνιακός, ή, όν, Hdt.:—
σοῦ, σοῦ, shoo! shoo!, a cry to scare away birds, Ar.
born at Susa, Aesch.
a man of Susa, Xen.
= Σοῦς Aesch.; but Σ. γυνή a woman of Susa, Xen.
the lily, a Phoen. word.
Σοῦσα, τά, Susa, in the province of Susiana or Shushan, winter residence of the King of Persia, Hdt., Xen.
skill in handicraft and art, Il., Xen., etc.:— σ. τινός or περί τινος knowledge of, acquaintance with a thing, Plat.
sound judgment, intelligence, practical wisdom, such as was attributed to the Seven Wise men, Theogn., Hdt.; in not so good a sense, cunning, shrewdness, craft, like δεινότης, Hdt.
wisdom, philosophy, Theogn., attic
to make wise, instruct, NTest.
Pass. to be clever or skilled in a thing, c. gen., ναυτιλίης σεσοφισμένος skilled in seamanship, Hes.:—absol. to pursue wisdom, be well instructed, Xen.
Mid. to teach oneself, learn, τι Id.

σοφίζομαι, as Dep., with aor1 mid. and perf. pass. to play subtle tricks, deal subtly, Theogn., Eur., etc.; οὐδὲν σοφιζόμεσθα τοῖσι δαίμοσι we argue not subtly about the gods, Eur.:—in speaking, to use sophistical arguments, to quibble, περί τι Plat.; καίπερ οὕτω τούτου σεσοφισμένου though this man has dealt thus craftily, Dem.

c. acc. rei, to devise cleverly or skilfully, Hdt., Ar.; ἀλλότρια σ. to meddle with other men's craft, Ar.; τὸ τοῦτο δεῖ σοφισθῆναι this one must gain by craft, Soph.:—perf. part. σεσοφισμένος in pass. sense, craftily devised, NTest.
c. acc. pers. to deceive, Anth.
any skilful act, the skilful dressing of food, Xen.
a clever device, contrivance, Hdt., Trag.
in less good sense, a sly trick, artifice, Eur., Thuc.; a stage-trick, claptrap, Ar.
a captious argument, a quibble, fallacy, sophism, Plat., etc.
verb. adj. one must contrive, Arist.
to play the sophist, argue as one, Dem.
to give lectures, of the Sophists, Plut.
a master of one's craft or art, an adept, of a diviner, Hdt.; of poets, Pind.; of the Creator, Plat.; metaph., σ. πημάτων an adept in misery, Eur.
like φρόνιμος, one who is clever in matters of life, a wise man, in which sense the seven Sages are called σοφισταί, Hdt.; of Prometheus, Aesch.

at Athens, a Sophist, i. e. a professor of grammar, rhetoric, politics, mathematics, such as Prodicus, Gorgias, Protagoras, Thuc., Plat., etc. At first the Sophists were held in honour; but from their loose principles they fell into ill repute, and the word came to mean,
a sophist (in bad sense), a quibbler, cheat, Ar., Dem., etc.
of or for a sophist, Plat.
like a sophist, sophistical, Xen., etc. adv. -κῶς, Plat.
Sophocles, Ar., etc.
wise-minded, Luc.
properly, skilled in any handicraft or art, cunning in his craft, Theogn., etc; of a charioteer, Pind.; of poets and musicians, Id.; of a soothsayer, Soph., etc.

clever in matters of common life, wise, prudent, shrewd, σ. ἄνδρες Θεσσαλοί shrewd fellows, the Thessalians! Hdt.; πολλὰ σοφός Aesch.; μείζω σοφίαν σοφός Plat., etc.; τῶν σοφῶν κρείσσω better than all craft, Soph.; σοφόν [ἐστι] c. inf., Eur.
skilled in the sciences, learned, profound, wise, Id., Plat., etc.; hence, ironically, abstruse, obscure, Ar., etc.
pass., of things, cleverly devised, wise, Hdt., etc.; σοφώτερ’ ἢ κατ’ ἄνδρα συμβαλεῖν things too clever for man to understand, Eur.
adv. σοφῶς, cleverly, wisely, Soph., Eur., etc.:—comp. -ώτερον, Eur.: Sup. -ώτατα, Id.
to preserve, save, deliver, 2nd sg. subj. σόῃς, 3rd sg. and pl. σόῃ, σόωσι, Il.
entry.etym: rare epic Verb for σαόω, σώζω

entry.sense: to draw off, Hdt.
an eunuch, Lat. spado, Plut.

in weaving, to strike home the woof with the σπάθη; metaph., λίαν σπαθᾶν to go too fast, a cant phrase for throwing away money, Ar.; so, σπ. τὰ χρήματα Plut.:—Pass., ἐσπαθᾶτο ταῦτα these were the prodigalities indulged in, Dem.
a flat blade used by weavers in the upright loom (instead of the comb (κτείς) used in the horizontal), for striking the threads of the woof home, so as to make the web close, Aesch.
to gasp, of dying fish, Anth.; cf. ἀσπαίρω.
of things, to be rare, scarce, scanty, Pind., Ar.
of persons, to lack or be in want of, τινός Hdt., Aesch., etc.;—so in Pass., ἐσπανίσμεθ’ ἀρωγῶν Aesch.: absol. to be in want, Eur.

rare, scarce, scanty, Hdt., Eur.; σπάνιον ἑαυτὸν παρέχειν, Lat. difficiles aditus habere, Plat.; ὕδατι σπανίῳ χρώμενοι having a scanty supply of water, Thuc.; c. inf., σπ. ἰδεῖν rare to behold, Xen.: of persons in an adv. sense, σπάνιος ἐπιφοιτᾷ he seldom visits, Hdt.:— σπάνιόν ἐστι, c. inf., it is seldom that . . , Xen.:— τὸ σπάνιον = σπάνις, Aeschin.
comp. σπανιώτερος, Hdt., Thuc.: —Sup. -ώτατος, attic
adv. -ίως, seldom, Xen.; so σπανίᾳ, Plat.: comp. -ιώτερον, Thuc.
lack of a thing, Isocr.
scarcity, rareness, dearth, lack of a thing, Eur., Dem.:— οὐ σπάνις [ἐστι] = οὐ σπάνιον, there is no lack, no difficulty, Eur.
of things, scanty, Soph.
lack of corn or food, Xen.
a piece torn off, a piece, shred, fragment, ὅσων σπαράγματα all whose mangled corpses, Soph.; σπάραγμα κόμας Eur.
= σπαραγμός, a tearing, rending, Id.
a tearing, rending, mangling, Eur.
a convulsion, spasm, Soph.
to tear, rend in pieces, mangle, Lat. lacerare, Eur., Ar.:—Mid., σπαράσσεσθαι κόμας to tear one's hair, Eur.
to rend asunder, Aesch.
metaph. to pull to pieces, attack, Lat. conviciis lacerare, Ar., Plat.
a child in swaddling-clothes, Hhymn.
a swathing band, and in pl. swaddling-clothes, Hhymn., Pind.; παῖς ἔτ’ ὢν ἐν σπαργάνοις Aesch.; tokens by which a person is identified, Lat. monumenta, crepundia, Soph., Ar.
to wrap in swaddling-clothes, swathe, Eur.:—Pass., perf. part. ἐσπαργανωμένος NTest.
to be full to bursting, to swell, be ripe, Eur.
metaph., like Lat. turgere, to swell with passion, Plat.:—absol. to wax wanton, be insolent, Plut.
entry.etym: Prob. from same Root as σφρῑγάω.

entry.sense: of Spartacus, Plut.
from Sparta, Od.
to Sparta, Id.
Sparta, Hom., etc.
a Spartan, Eur., Thuc.
(sub. γυνή) a Spartan woman, Eur., etc.; (sub. χώρα) Laconia, Plut.; also as adj., Σπ. γυνή, χθών, γῆ Eur.
a small cord, Ar.
a rope, cable, Il., etc.; (prob. akin to σπεῖρα).
a rope made from broom (σπάρτος).
sown, grown from seed: metaph., σπαρτῶν γένος children of men, Aesch.
at Thebes, Σπαρτοί, οἱ, the sown-men, those who claimed descent from the dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus, the Cadmeans, Thebans, Pind., Eur.; λόγχη σπαρτός the Theban spear, Eur.
scattered, of the limbs of a corpse, Anth.
Spanish broom, esparto, Xen., etc.
bearing broom, Strab.
a spasm, convulsion, τῶν ὑστερῶν Arist.
a piece torn off, shred, Plut.
a convulsion, spasm, Hdt., Soph.
to live lewdly, to run riot, NTest.
lewdness, wantonness, riot, luxury, Anth.
excrement, Ar.
of a sword, to draw, Eur.;—mostly in Mid., Hom.:—Pass. to be drawn, Il.; ἐσπασμένοι τὰ ξίφη having their swords drawn, Xen.
πάλον σπᾶν to draw a lot (out of a helmet), Aesch.
absol., σπᾶτ’ ἀνδρείως pull, hoist away, like men.
of violent actions, to pluck off or out, κόμην Soph.
like σπαράσσω, to tear, rend, of beasts, Id.
to wrench, sprain:—Pass., τὸν μηρὸν σπασθῆναι Hdt.
to snatch, tear or drag away, Eur.
metaph. to carry away, draw aside, Soph., Plat.
Pass. to be convulsed, Soph.
to draw in, suck in, quaff, Aesch., Eur.
to draw tight, pull the reins, Xen.
of angling: hence, proverb., οὐκ ἔσπασεν ταύτηι γε "he took nothing by his motion," Ar.
to adopt, appropriate, Anth.
a coil, spire, convolution, Aesch.: αἰῶνος σπ. a period, cycle, Anth.
Pass. to be coiled or folded round.
Lat. spira, anything wound or coiled: in pl. the coils or spires of a serpent, Eur.; also σπείραις δικτυοκλώστοις with the net's meshy folds, Soph.
σπεῖραι βόειαι thongs or straps of ox-hide bound round a boxer's fist, the caestus, Theocr.
a body of men-at-arms, the Roman manipulus, = two centuries, Polyb.:—also a cohort, NTest.
in coils or spires, spirally, Anth.
（σπεῖρα II) of troops, in maniples, Polyb.
a light, summer-garment, Xen.
a piece of cloth, εἴλυμα σπείρων a wrapping cloth, Od.; κακὰ σπεῖρα sorry wraps, Id.; ἄτερ σπείρου without a shroud, Id.; also a sail, Id.
forming a circle, Anth.
to sow:
to sow seed, Hes., attic
to sow children, to engender, beget them, Soph.:—Pass. to be born, Id., Eur.
to scatter like seed, strew, throw about, χρυσὸν καὶ ἄργυρον Hdt.; δρόσον Eur.:—to spread abroad, as Virgil spargere voces, Soph.:—Pass. to be scattered, dispersed, Eur., Thuc.
to sow a field, Hes., Hdt., etc.: Pass., ἡ σπειρομένη Αἴγυπτος the arable part of Egypt, Hdt.
proverb., πόντον σπείρειν, of lost labour, Theogn.
Latin speculator, one of the body-guard, NTest.

to pour or make a drink-offering before drinking, Lat. libare, Hom.:—σπ. οἶνον to pour wine, Hom.; λοιβάς Soph.; σπονδάς, χοάς Eur.; ellipt., σπ. ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος (sc. σπονδήν) to pour a libation in honour of the good genius, Ar.:—rarely c. dat. rei, ὕδατι σπ. to make a drink-offering with water, Od.:—in NTest. the Pass. is used metaph. of a person, σπένδομαι ἐπὶ τῆι θυσίαι I am offered (as a drink-offering) over the sacrifice.
without any religious sense, to pour, Hdt., Xen., etc.

Mid. to pour libations one with another, and, as this was the custom in making treaties, to make a treaty, make peace, Hdt., Ar., etc.; σπένδεσθαί τινι to make peace with one, Eur., etc.; so, σπ. πρός τινα Thuc., etc.:— σπένδεσθαι τῆι πρεσβείαι to give it pledges of safe conduct, Aeschin.: c. acc., εἰρήνην σπεισάμενοι Λακεδαιμονίοισι having concluded a peace with them, Hdt.; ἐσπεῖσθαι νεῖκος to make up a quarrel, Eur.; σπ. ἀναίρεσιν τοῖς νεκροῖς to make a truce for taking up the dead, Thuc.:—Pass., of a treaty, to be concluded, Id.
a cave, cavern, grotto, Hom.: of the form σπέος, Hom. uses only nom. and acc. sg., with epic dat. σπῆι; of the form σπεῖος, acc. sg., gen. σπείους, dat. pl. σπέσσι and σπήεσσι; gen. pl. σπείων Hhymn.
to sow with seed: to beget, Hes.
that which is sown:
the seed of plants, Hes., Hdt., attic:—also of animals, Pind., Eur.
metaph. of the germ, origin, element of anything, σπ. πυρός Od.; φλογός Pind.; κακῶν Dem.
seed, offspring, issue, Trag., etc.
race, origin, descent, Id.
babbling, gossip, Plut.
picking up seeds, of granivorous birds, Plut.
metaph. one who picks up scraps of knowledge, a babbler, Dem., NTest.
bearing seed, Anth.
the Spercheius, i. e. rapid (from σπέρχω), a river of Thessaly, Il.
hasty, rapid, hurried, Hes., Aesch.

to set in rapid motion:—Pass. to be in haste to do a thing, c. inf., Il.; σπ. ἐρετμοῖς to hasten with oars, to ply them rapidly, Od.: part. σπερχόμενος as adv., in haste, hastily, hurriedly, Hom., Eur.
metaph. to be hasty and angry, Il., Hdt.; μὴ σπέρχου be not hasty, Eur.
intr. = Pass., ὅτε σπέρχωσιν ἄελλαι when storms are driven rapidly, Hom.

trans. to set a-going, to urge on, hasten, quicken, Hom., etc.:—also, to seek eagerly, strive after, Theogn.; promote zealously, to press or urge on, Soph., etc.; so in Mid., Aesch.:—Pass., to be urged on, Hdt.
c. acc. et inf., σπεύσατε Τεῦκρον μολεῖν urge him to come, Soph.
intr. to press on, hasten, to exert oneself, strive eagerly or anxiously, Il., attic; ὡς σὺ σπεύδεις as you urge, contend, Plat.: part. σπεύδων as adv. in haste, eagerly, Il., Aesch.
c. inf. to be eager to do a thing, Hes., Hdt., etc.; so in Mid., σπευδόμεναι ἀφελεῖν Aesch.
c. acc. rei et inf. to be anxious that . . , Hdt., Xen.
a grotto, cave, cavern, Plat.
cavern-like, Plat.
wide, broad, διὰ σπιδέος πεδίοιο Il.
the space one can span with the thumb and little finger, a span, Lat. dodrans, about 7 1/2 inches, Hdt., Plat.
