rock-like: rocky, Strab.
a rock over which the sea dashes, a ledge of rock, Od.:—generally, a slab, Soph.
a spot, stain, blemish, NTest.
to stain, soil, NTest.:—Pass., perf. part. ἐσπιλωμένος Id.
a spark, Hhymn.
a spark, Lat. scintilla, Il., Ar.
a bird of the finch kind, the siskin, Ar.
to eat the inwards (σπλάγχνα) of a victim after a sacrifice, Ar.
to prophesy from the inwards, Strab.
Dep. to feel compassion, mercy, NTest.

mostly in pl. σπλάγχνα, the inward parts, esp. the viscera thoracis, i. e. heart, lungs, liver, kidneys, which in sacrifices were reserved to be eaten by the sacrificers, Hom., etc.:—hence the sacrificial feast, Lat. visceratio, Ar.:—also as used in divination, Aesch., etc.
any part of the inwards, the womb, Pind., Soph.: so in sg., Aesch.
metaph., like our heart, the seat of the feelings and affections, Id., Eur., etc.:—so in sg., Soph., Eur.; ἀνδρὸς σπλάγχνον ἐκμαθεῖν to learn a man's inward nature, Eur.
the milt, spleen, Hdt.
a sponge, Ar.
to wipe with a sponge, Dem.
a sponge, Hom., etc.
lying on ashes, Anth.
to pound, smite, crush, Ar.:—Pass., σποδούμενος νιφάδι pelted by the storm, Eur.; πρὸς πέτρας σπ. dashed against the rocks, Id.; absol., στρατὸς κακῶς σπ. handled roughly, in sorry plight, Aesch.
a heap of ashes, ashes, Od., Eur.
metaph., = σποδός III, Anth.
to roast or bake in the ashes, burn to ashes, Ar., Plat.
Pass. to be burnt to ashes, Anth.
wood-ashes, embers, and generally, ashes, Od., Hdt., attic: the ashes of the dead, Aesch., Soph., etc.
dust, Hdt.
metaph., σπ. κυλίκων, of a bibulous old woman, "a sponge, " Anth.
a leathern garment, buff-jerkin, Ar., Xen.
the beginning of the libation, the right of beginning it, Hdt.
used at a libation:— σπονδεῖος (sc. πούς), in metre, a spondee, a foot consisting of two long syllables, being the metre proper to the slow melodies used at σπονδαί (a treaty).
a drink-offering, i. e. the wine poured out to the gods before drinking, Lat. libatio, Hes., Hdt.; σπονδὰς θεοῖς λείβειν, σπένδειν Aesch., Eur.

in pl., σπονδαί was a solemn treaty or truce, (because solemn drink-offerings were made on concluding them); σπονδαὶ ἄκρητοι the truce made by pouring unmixed wine, Il.; αἱ Λακεδαιμονίων σπ. the truce with them. Thuc.; σπονδὰς παραδιδόναι Ar.; δέχεσθαι Thuc.; τυχεῖν Xen.; σπ. ποιεῖσθαί τινι to make a truce with one, Hdt.; πρός τινα Ar.; σπ. τέμνειν (like ὅρκια τέμνειν) Eur.; σπ. ἄγειν πρός τινας Thuc.
αἱ Ὀλυμπικαὶ σπ. the solemn truce or armistice during the Olympic games, Id.
the treaty itself, εἴρηται ἐν ταῖς σπ. Id.
making a σπονδή, Anth.
one who brings proposals for a truce or treaty of peace (σπονδαί), Ar.
a herald or officer who published the sacred σπονδαί of the Olympic and other games, Pind., etc.
scatteredly, here and there, Lat. sparsim, Thuc., Plat.: casually, Anth.
scattered, τὰ σπ. ζῷα, opp. to τὰ ἀγελαῖα (gregarious), Arist.
σποραῖα, ων, τά seeds, Babr.
a sowing of seed, Plat.: of children, origin, birth, Aesch., Soph.
seed-time, Eur.
the seed sown, Id.:—of persons, seed, offspring, Soph.: generally, θηλὺς σπ. the female race, Eur. Hence.

mostly in pl. scattered, dispersed, Hdt., Thuc.; of men, σποράδες ᾤκουν, i. e. not in communities, Arist.; αἱ Σποράδες (sc. νῆσοι) the islands off the west coast of Asia Minor, opp. to αἱ Κυκλάδες, Strab.
sown corn, growing corn, Aesch.
a sowing of corn, Xen.
sown, to be sown, fit for sowing, Xen., Theocr.; τὰ σπόριμα the corn-fields, NTest.; μέτρον σπ. a measure of seed-corn, Anth.
a sowing, Hdt., Xen., etc.
seed-time, Xen., Theocr.
seed, Theocr.
produce, fruit, harvest, crop, Hdt., Soph.
intr. to make haste,
of things, to be busy, eager, zealous, earnest to do a thing, c. inf., Soph., etc.; also, σπ. περί τινος or τι Xen., Plat.; εἴς or πρός τι Dem.; ἐπί τινι Xen.
of persons, σπ. πρός τινα to be busy with him, Plat.; σπ. περί τινα to be anxious for his success, canvass for him, Xen.; ὑπέρ τινος Dem.
absol. to be serious or earnest, Ar., etc.; ἐσπουδακότι προσώπωι with a grave face, Xen.
trans.,
c. acc. rei, to do anything hastily or earnestly, Eur., Plat., etc.:—Pass. to be zealously pursued, Eur., etc.:—esp. in perf. part., serious, Plat., etc.
Pass., also, of persons, to be treated with respect, to be courted, Arist., etc.
to speak seriously, talk on serious subjects, Xen.; so in Mid., Id.:—Pass., to be treated seriously, Id.
of persons, earnest, serious, Xen.; active, zealous, Plut.
good, excellent, Hdt., Plat.; σπουδαῖος τὴν τέχνην Xen.
of men of character and importance, Id.
in moral sense, good, opp. to πονηρός, Id.
of things, worth one's serious attention, serious, weighty, Theogn., Hdt., attic
good of its kind, excellent, Hdt., etc.
adv. σπουδαίως, seriously, earnestly, well, Xen., etc.:—comp., -ότερον, Id.; Sup. -ότατα, most carefully, in the best way, Hdt.—There are also irreg. comp. and Sup. σπουδαι-έστερος, -έστατος.
one who canvasses for office, a place-man, Xen.
canvassing for office, Lat. ambitus, Plut.
to canvass for office, Arist.
comic Patronymic of σπουδάρχης, son of placeman, Ar.
a thing or work done with zeal, a pursuit, Plat.
to be sought for zealously, Xen.
σπουδαστέον, one must bestir oneself, be earnest or anxious, Eur., etc.
one who wishes well to another, a supporter, partisan, Lat. fautor, Plut.
zealous, earnest, serious, Plat.
that deserves to be sought or tried zealously, Plat.
haste, speed, Hdt., etc.; ὅκως σπουδῆς ἔχει τις according as one makes speed, Id.

zeal, pains, exertion, trouble, Od., attic: —σπουδὴν ποιεῖσθαι, c. inf., to take pains to do a thing, Hdt.; c. gen., σπουδήν τινος ποιήσασθαι to make much ado about a thing, Id.; so, σπ. ἔχειν τινός or εἴς τι Eur.; σπουδῇ ὅπλων with great attention to the arms, Thuc.:—in pl. zealous exertions, Hdt., Eur.; also party feelings, rivalries, Hdt., Ar.
zeal, earnestness, seriousness, Eur., etc.
an object of attention, a serious engagement, Eur.
σπουδῇ, as adv. in haste, hastily, Od., Hdt., attic
with great exertion, with difficulty, hardly, scarcely, Hom.
earnestly, seriously, urgently, Eur., etc.; πολλῇ σπ. very busily, Hdt., etc.; so with Preps., ἀπὸ σπουδῆς in earnest, seriously, Il.; μετὰ σπουδῆς Xen.
in Scythian, an eye, Hdt.
a ball of dung, as that of sheep or goats: pl. sheeps' or goats' dung, Ar.
a large basket, a creel (v. κόφινος), Hdt., Ar., etc.
a Stagyrite, of Aristotle.
a city in Macedonia, Hdt., etc.
a drop, distilment, Aesch.
a drop, Trag.
standing erect or upright, Aesch.; στ. ἔγχη pikes for close fight, opp. to missiles (cf. στάδιος 1), Id.
a measuring by stades, Strab.
to run in the stadium, Dem.
one who runs the stadium, one who runs for a prize, Simon., Aeschin.

entry.etym: pl. στάδια and στάδιοι, but never στάδιος in sg.
entry.sense: a fixed standard of length, a stade, = 100 ὀργυιαί or 6 πλέθρα, i. e. 600 Greek or 606 3/4 English feet, about 1/8 of a Roman mile, Polyb.: —ἑκατὸν σταδίοισιν ἄριστος "best by a hundred miles, " Ar.; πλεῖν ἢ σταδίῳ λαλίστερος more loquacious than a mile and more, Id.
a race-course (that of Olympia being a stade long), Pind., etc.; ἀγωνίζεσθαι στ. to run a race, Hdt.; στ. νικᾶν to win one, Xen.
standing firm, σταδίη ὑσμίνη close fight, Lat. pugna stataria, Il.; ἐν σταδίῃ (sc. ὑσμίνῃ) Id.
firm, strong, Pind.
of persons,
c. acc. rei, to drop, let fall or shed drop by drop, Il., Aesch., etc.
c. dat. rei, αἵματι στ. to drip with blood, Aesch.; στάζων ἱδρῶτι Soph.;—rarely c. gen., Id.
intr. of things, to drop, fall in drops, drip, trickle, Hdt., Soph., Eur.; metaph., στάζει ἐν ὕπνωι πόνος Aesch.
standing fast, steadfast, ἡ σταθερή (sc. γῆ), terra firma, Anth.;—of the sea, calm, still, Id.
στ. μεσημβρία high noon, when the sun seems to stand still in the meridian, Plat.
metaph. steady, deliberate, Anth.
scorched, burnt, Aesch.
to scorch, roast, fry, Ar.
to measure by rule, Eur.: —Pass., with fut. mid. -ήσομαι, to be measured, estimated, Ar.
as Dep. (v. σταθμόω), to estimate distance or size, without actual measurement, Hdt., Plat.: metaph. to estimate one thing by another, τί τινι Plat.; absol. to conjecture, Soph.
to attach weight to a thing, value it, Plat.

a carpenter's line, Hom., Theogn.; —properly a line rubbed with chalk, distinguished from the rule (κανών) Xen., etc.:—proverb., παρὰ στάθμην by the rule, Lat. ad amussim, Theogn.; but in Aesch., παρὰ στ. beside the line, beyond measure; κατὰ στ. νοεῖν to guess aright, Theocr.
the plummet or the plumbline, Anth.
the line which bounds the racecourse, the goal, Lat. meta, Pind., Eur.
metaph. a law, rule, Ὑλλίδος στάθμας ἐν νόμοις, i. e. according to laws of Dorian rule, Pind.
to be measured, Plat.
to the stall, homewards, Od.
a standing place for animals, Lat. stabulum, a stable, fold, Il.: a stye, Od.: of men, a dwelling, abode, Hes., Soph.
quarters, lodgings for travellers or soldiers, Lat. statio, Xen.
in Persia, σταθμοί were stations on the royal road, where the king rested, Hdt.: hence a day's journey, day's march, averaging about 5 parasangs or 15 miles, Id., Xen.
like Lat. statio, a station for ships, Eur.
an upright post, the bearing pillar of the roof, Od.: a door-post, esp. in pl., Hom., attic
the balance, Ar., Il.; ἱστᾶν σταθμῷ τι πρός τι to weigh one thing against another, Hdt.
weight, σταθμὸν ἔχειν τάλαντον to weigh a talent, Id.; absol. in acc., ἴσα σταθμόν equal in weight, Id.; ἡμιπλίνθια σταθμὸν διτάλαντα two talents in or by weight, Id.:—in pl. weights, Eur., etc.

entry.etym: the aor1 mid. σταθμώσασθαι is = σταθμήσασθαι
entry.sense: to form an estimate, to judge or conclude by or from a thing, Hdt.
flour of spelt mixed and made into dough, Hdt.
of flour or dough of spelt, Hdt., Plut.
oozing out in drops, trickling, dropping, distilling, Ar.
that which drops, a drop, Aesch., Soph.
a dropping, dripping, Aesch., Eur.; στ. εἰρήνης the least drop of peace, Ar.
to let drop, δάκρυ Eur.
intr. of things, to drop, drip, Id.; c. acc. cogn., στ. φόνον to drop blood, Id.
to drop, let fall, δάκρυ Anth.
a stake to which nets are fastened, Xen., Theocr.
furnished with a στήλη or gravestone, Anth.
the ribs of a ship, which stand up from the keel, Lat. statumina, Od.
a wine-jar, Ar.
an earthen jar for racking off wine, Ar.: cf. ἀμφορεύς.
intr. to rebel, revolt, rise in rebellion, τινί against one, Hdt., Xen., etc.; πρός τινα Xen.
in the Greek states, to form a party or faction, be at odds, quarrel, Hdt., etc.
of the states themselves, to be at discord, be distracted by factions, Ar., Thuc., etc.
trans. to revolutionise, throw into confusion, τὴν πόλιν Lys., etc.
seditious, factious, Plat., etc.: Adv., στασιαστικῶς ἔχειν to be factious, Dem.
standing, stationary; of water, stagnant, Xen.
stable, steadfast, steady, firm, Plat.:—of men, steadfast, steady, solid, Lat. constans, Id.:—of music, Arist.
στάσιμον (with or without μέλος), in Tragedy, a regular song of the chorus, prob. so named because it was not sung till the chorus had taken its stand in the orchestra.
a standing, the posture of standing, Aesch., Plat.
a position, posture. post, station, Hdt., Eur.; τῆς στάσεως παρασύρων τὰς δρῦς tearing the oaks from their ground, Ar.
a point of the compass, ἡ στ. τῆς μεσαμβρίης Hdt.
the position, state or condition of a person, Lat. status, Plat.
a party, company, band, Aesch.: a sect of philosophers, Plut.
esp. a party formed for seditious purposes, a faction, Solon., Hdt., attic
sedition, discord, Hdt., attic; στάσιν ποιεῖσθαι Isocr.; πόλιν εἰς στάσιν ἐμβάλλειν Xen.
factious, Arist.: quarrelsome, Xen.
watcher of the station or fold, Eur.
a state of faction, Plat.
mostly in pl. the members of a party or faction, partisans, Hdt., attic
factious, seditious, Thuc.
one must appoint, Plat.
a weight, = λίτρα: then a coin of various values:
the gold stater best known at Athens was the Persian, called στατὴρ Δαρεικός or simply Δαρεικός, Daric, from Darius Hystaspes, worth about 1 l. 2s., Hdt., Thuc.
later a silver stater was in use, = τετράδραχμον, NTest., Xen.
to place: Pass. = ἵσταμαι, to stand, Eur.:—so also intr. in Act., Id.
placed, standing, στατὸς ἵππος a stalled horse, Il., Soph.: —στατὸς χιτών a tunic reaching to the feet, Plut.
an upright pale or stake, Hom., etc.: of piles driven in to serve as a foundation, Hdt., Thuc.
the Cross, NTest.: its form was represented by the Greek letter Τ, Luc.
bearing the cross, Anth.
to fence with pales, impalisade, Thuc.
to crucify, Polyb., NTest.
a palisade or stockade, Lat. vallum, Thuc., Xen.
a palisading, Thuc.
a bunch of grapes, Hom., Theocr.
parox. σταφυλή, the plummet of a level, ἵπποι σταφυλῇ ἐπὶ νῶτον ἔϊσαι horses matched in height by the level, matched to a nicety, Il.
a bunch of grapes, Theocr.
a grape-stealer, Anth.
cutting ears of corn, Anth.
nourishing ears of corn, Anth.
mother of ears of corn, Anth.
crowned with ears of corn, Anth.
an ear of corn, Lat. spica, Il., Hes., etc.:—metaph., στ. ἄτης Aesch.; of the Theban Σπαρτοί, Eur.
generally, a scion, child, progeny, Anth.

entry.etym: prob. from ΣΤΑ, Root of ἵστημι
entry.sense: stiff fat, tallow, suet, Lat. sebum, opp. to πιμελή (Lat. adeps, soft fat), Od., Xen.
to cover, Xen.: metaph., ὕπνος στ. τινά covers, embraces one, Soph.:—Pass., πλοῖον ἐστεγασμένον a decked vessel, Antipho.
a covering, Anth.
covering so as to keep out water, water-tight, waterproof, Xen., Anth.
generally, covering, enclosing, confining, of a net, Aesch.
closely covered, λευκῆς χιόνος πτέρυγι στεγανός, of Polynices, represented as an eagle, covered by his white Argive shield (v. λεύκασπις), Soph.; of a building, roofed, Thuc.
metaph., τὸ οὐ στεγανόν leakiness, Plat.
adv. -νῶς, confinedly, through a tube, Thuc.
master of the house, Hdt.
anything which covers, a covering, Xen.:— a roof, Lat. tectum, Plat.
one must cover, Xen.
covered, sheltered, Strab.
that serves for covering, Hdt.
a covering, cover, wrapper, Aesch., Plut.
a roof, Lat. tectum, Hdt., Aesch., Xen., etc.
a roofed place, a chamber, room, Hdt., Xen., etc.; ἑρκεῖος στ., of a tent, Soph.; ἐκ κατώρυχος στέγη, of the grave, Id.
often in pl., like Lat. tecta, a house, dwelling, Aesch.; κατὰ στέγας at home, Soph.
waterproof, Hdt.; στεγνὰ οἰκήματα, of a cave, Eur.
as Subst., στεγνόν, οῦ, a covered dwelling, Xen.
of thick nature, Anth.
a roof: then, like στέγη, a house, mansion, Aesch., Soph., etc.:—of an urn containing ashes, Soph.
to cover closely, so as to keep water either out or in:
to keep water out, νῆες οὐδὲν στέγουσαι not watertight, Thuc.:—so in Mid., στέγεσθαι ὄμβρους to keep off rain from oneself, Pind.; ναῦς οὐκ ἐστέξατο κῦμα Anth.
generally, to keep off, fend off weapons, etc., δόρυ στέγειν Aesch.; στ. τὰς πληγάς Ar.
later, to bear up against, endure, Polyb., NTest.:—absol. to contain oneself, hold out, NTest.
with acc. of the thing covered, to cover, shelter, protect, Soph., Xen.
to cover, conceal, keep hidden, Soph., Eur.:—Pass. to be kept secret, Thuc.; παρ’ ὑμῶν εὖ στεγοίμεθ’ let my counsel be kept secret by you, Soph.
to keep water in, hold water, keep in, Eur., Plat.
generally, to contain, hold, Soph., Eur.
to tread on, tread under foot, Hom.
c. acc. cogn. to tread or walk on a path, Eur.; also, χοροὺς στείβειν to tread measures, Id.
absol. to tread, Id.
to stamp down, in Pass., Theocr.; αἱ στειβόμεναι ὁδοί the beaten roads, Xen.
the hole for the handle of an axe, Od.
the handle or helve of an axe, Od.
narrow-necked, Anth.
a narrow, strait, confined space, Hom.; στεῖνος ὁδοῦ Il.
generally, pressure, straits, distress, Hhymn.; σωφρονεῖν ὑπὸ στένει to learn wisdom by suffering, Aesch.
to straiten: Pass. to become strait, to be narrowed, Od.; of persons, to be straitened for room, Il.

to be or become full, be thronged, c. gen., στείνοντο δὲ σηκοὶ ἀρνῶν the folds were crowded with lambs, Od.; c. dat., ποταμὸς στεινόμενος νεκύεσσι Il.:—metaph., ἀρνειὸς λάχνῳ στεινόμενος burdened with its wool, Od.
a ship's keel, esp. the curved part of it, cutwater, Lat. carina, Hom.
a cow that has not calved, Od.: of a woman, barren, NTest., Anth.
barren, Lat. sterilis, Eur.
to walk, march, go or come, Od., Hdt., Trag.:—c. acc. loci, to go to, approach, Trag.
to go after one another, go in line or order (whence στίχος, στίχες, στοῖχος), Il., Hdt.
c. acc. cogn., στ. ὁδόν Aesch., Soph.
a handle, Babr., Anth.
to furnish with a handle, Anth.
cutting stems, Anth.
Pass. to grow into a stem, Strab.
the crown of the root, stump, whence the trunk springs, Lat. codex, Pind., Dem.

to set in order, to arrange, array, equip, make ready, Hom., Hdt., attic:—also, στέλλειν τινὰ ἐσθῆτι to furnish with a garment, Hdt.; so c. dupl. acc., στολὴν στ. τινά Eur.:—Mid., στείλασθαι πέπλους to put on robes, Id.; metaph., ἐπὶ θήρας πόθον ἐστέλλου didst set thy heart upon the chase, Id.:—Pass. to fit oneself out, get ready, Il., Hdt.; στολὴν ἐσταλμένος equipt in a dress, Hdt.; ἐστ. ἐπὶ πόλεμον Xen.; metaph., ἐπὶ τυραννίδ’ ἐστάλης Ar.

to despatch on an expedition, and, generally, to despatch, send, Aesch., Soph.:—Pass. to get ready for an expedition, to start, set out, Hdt.; and in aor2 pass. to have set out, to be on one's way, Id.; c. acc. cogn., ὁδὸν στέλλεσθαι Soph.; στέλλου begone! Aesch.

in attic the Act. has sometimes the intr. sense of the Pass., like Lat. trajicere, to prepare to go, start, set forth, where στόλον may be supplied, ἔστελλε ἐς ἀποικίην Hdt., etc.:—reversely, ἡ ὁδὸς εἰς Κόρινθον στέλλει leads to Corinth, Luc.
Mid. in sense of μεταπέμπομαι, to send for one, Soph.: also to fetch, bring a person to a place, Id.
to bring together, gather up, ἱστία στεῖλαν took in, furled the sails, Od.: and in Mid., ἱστία μὲν στείλαντο they furled their sails, Il.; χιτῶνας ἐστάλατο they girded up their clothes to work, Hes.
in Mid. also to check, repress, λόγον στέλλεσθαι to draw in one's words, i. e. not speak out the whole truth, Eur.
also in Mid. to shrink from a thing, avoid it, NTest.
broad belts put round dogs when used to hunt wild beasts, Xen.
to shake, agitate, Aesch.
a wreath, garland, wound by suppliants round a staff or olive branch, Il., Soph.; sometimes worn on the head, Hdt.
a mass of olives from which the oil has been pressed, olive-cake, Ar.
a sigh, groan, moan, Soph., Eur.
a sighing, groaning, moaning, Trag.
to sigh often, sigh deeply, generally, to sigh, groan, moan, Trag.; τί ἐστέναξας τοῦτο; why utterdst thou this moan? Eur.; c. acc. cogn., παιᾶνα στ. Id.
trans. to bemoan, bewail, Soph., etc.
one must bewail, Eur.
to be mourned, giving cause for grief, Soph., Eur.
mournful, Eur.
only in pres. and imperf. to sigh, groan, wail, Hom.:—so in Mid., Il.
trans. to bewail, lament, Od.
to sigh, groan, wail, Hom.: so in Mid., Il., Aesch., Soph.:—metaph. of the roar of torrents, Il.; the loud breathing of horses galloping, Id.; στοᾶς στεναχούσης groaning from being overcrowded, Ar.
trans. to bewail, lament, Il., Aesch.; so in Mid., Od.
to talk subtly, quibble, Ar.
at or on a strait, Eur.
a narrow way or pass, Xen.
with a narrow pass or outlet, Hdt., Aesch., Eur.
as Subst. στενόπορα, ionic στειν-, τά, narrow passes, defiles, Hdt., Thuc.: —in sg. στενόπορον, ου, a strait, narrow, Xen.
narrow, strait, Hdt., Eur., etc.; ἐν στενῷ, ionic στεινῷ, in a narrow compass, Hdt., Aesch.
as Subst., τὰ στενά the straits, of a pass, Hdt.; of a sea, Thuc.; also, ἡ στενή a narrow strip of land, Id.
metaph. narrow, close, confined, ἀπειληθῆναι ἐς στεινόν to be driven into a corner, Hdt.; εἰς στ. καταστῆναι Dem.
scanty, little, petty, Plat.—From old ionic forms στεινότερος, -ότατος, come irr. attic στενότερος, -ότατος: but reg. στενώτερος also occurs.
narrow-mouthed, Strab.
narrowness, straitness, Hdt., Thuc.
to straiten for room, Luc.:—Pass. to be crowded together: metaph. to be straitened, NTest.
narrowness of space: want of room, Thuc., etc.:—metaph., ἡ στ. τοῦ ποταμοῦ the difficulty of passing the river, Xen.
to straiten:—in Pass., Anth.
Stentorian, with a voice like Stentor's, Arist.
Stentor, a Greek at Troy, famous for his loud voice, Il.
to moan, sigh, groan, Hom., Trag.; so in Mid., Aesch., Eur.
c. gen. to moan or sigh for, Eur.; ὑπέρ τινος Aesch.; τινί or ἐπί τινι Eur.; c. acc. cogn., πένθος οἰκεῖον στ. Soph.:—Mid., Aesch.
c. acc. to bewail, lament, Id., etc.; στένειν τινὰ τῆς τύχης to pity him for his ill fortune, Id.: so in Mid., στένεσθαί τινα Eur.
narrow-looking, narrow, strait, confined, Il.
as Subst., στενωπός (sc. ὁδός), a narrow passage or way, strait, Od., etc.
crowned, Anth.
a love-charm, love, affection, in sg. and pl., Aesch., Eur.
a love-charm, τινος to influence him, Soph.

to love, of the mutual love of parents and children, Soph., Eur., etc.; of king and people, Hdt., Soph.; of a country and her colonies, Thuc.; of brothers and sisters, Eur.; of friends, Soph.; of husband and wife, Hdt., Soph.
generally, to be fond of, shew liking for, Theogn., Soph., etc.:—also of things, to accept gladly, Hdt., etc.
to be content or satisfied, acquiesce, Soph., Dem.; στέρξον oblige me, do me the favour, Soph.

c. acc. to be content with, acquiesce in, submit to, bear with, Hdt.; στ. τὴν τυραννίδα bear with it, Aesch.; στ. κακά Soph.:—also c. dat., στ. τοῖσι σοῖς Eur.; τῆι ἐμῆι τύχηι Plat.:—c. part., πῶς ἂν στέρξαιμι κακὸν τόδε λεύσσων Soph.; στ. ξυμφορᾶι νικώμενοι Eur.:—rarely c. inf., οὐκ ἔστεργέ σοι ὅμοιος εἶναι Id.
to entreat one to do, Ἀπόλλω στέργω μολεῖν Soph.
stiff, stark, firm, solid, Hom., etc.; αἰχμὴ στερεὴ πᾶσα χρυσέη all of solid gold, Hdt.:—adv. -εῶς, firmly, fast, Hom.
metaph. stiff, stubborn, harsh, Id., etc.: so in adv., Id.
στ. ἀριθμός a cubic number, Arist.
stubborn-hearted, Soph.
to make firm or solid, Xen.:— to strengthen, NTest.:—Pass. to be made strong, Xen.
a solid body, foundation: metaph. steadfastness, NTest.
to deprive, bereave, rob of anything, c. acc. pers. et gen. rei, Od., Trag., etc.:—Pass. to be deprived, bereaved or robbed of anything, c. gen., Hdt., attic
c. acc. rei, to take away, Anth.:—Pass. to have taken from one, βίον στερείς Eur.
deprivation, privation, of a thing, Thuc.: absol. negation, privation, Arist.
to deprive of a thing, Thuc.:—Pass. to be deprived of a thing, Hdt., attic
firm, solid, Thuc.
= στεῖρος, Lat. sterilis, barren, Plat.
to be loved, amiable, loved, Soph.
the breast, chest, both in sg. and pl., Hom., Trag.
the breast as the seat of the affections, the heart, Trag.
of or from beaten breasts, Eur., Anth.
a beating of the breast for grief, Luc.
broad-swelling, of a plain, Soph.
to be wanting in, to lack, want, Lat. carere, c. gen., Hes., Hdt., attic:—absol. to suffer loss, Soph., Xen.
either (from ἀγείρω, cf. νεφεληγερέτα) he who gathers the lightning, or (from ἐγείρω) who rouses the lightning, Il.
a flash of lightning, Il., Hes., etc.:—generally flash, gleam, sheen, Hom.
lightner, name of one of the three Cyclopes, Hes.
flashing, Soph.
with strong limbs, Anth.
stiff, firm, solid, strong, Eur.: stiff with age, Ar.
hard, rugged, uneasy, λέκτρα Eur.
metaph. stubborn, obdurate, hard, Aesch., Eur., etc.:—adv., στερρῶς, stiffly, obstinately, Xen.

entry.etym: used by Hom. only in 3rd sg. pres. and imperf. στεῦται, στεῦτο, and once by Aesch. in 3rd pl. στεῦνται
entry.sense: Dep., to make as if one would, to promise or threaten that one will, Il.; also with aor. inf., στεῦται ἀκοῦσαι Od.; so, στεῦται ἀμφιβαλεῖν Aesch.: —absol., στεῦτο he made eager efforts, Od.
a place where wreaths are plaited or sold, Anth.
plaiting wreaths, Plut.
anything that encircles the head, for defence or ornament:
the brim of the helmet, projecting behind as well as before, Il.
part of a woman's head-dress, a diadem, coronal, Id., Hes., etc.:—metaph., of a city, ἀπὸ στεφάναν κέκαρσαι πύργων thou hast been shorn of thy coronal of towers, Eur.
the brim or edge of anything, the brow of a hill, edge of a cliff, Il.; of a basket, Mosch.
to wear a wreath, Eur., Dem.
the wearing a wreath, esp. of victory, Pind., Eur.
the right of wearing a crown, Dem.
wearing a crown or wreath, crowned, Eur.; στ. ἀγών = στεφανίτης ἀγών, Hdt.
the title of certain magistrates who had the right of wearing crowns, as the Archons, Aeschin.
to crown, Ar.
of a crown: στ. ἀγών acontest in which the prize was a crown, Xen., Dem.
properly, that which surrounds, στ. πολέμοιο the circling crowd of fight, Il.; of the wall round a town, Pind.; καλλίπαις στ. a circle of fair children, Eur.

a crown, wreath, garland, chaplet, Hes., etc.: esp. at the public games, a crown of victory, Pind., Hdt., etc.:— these prize-crowns were mostly of leaves, of κότινος at the Olympic games, δάφνη at the Pythian, σέλινον at the Nemean, κισσός or πίτυς at the Isthmian.
generally, the meed of victory, the prize, victory, like Lat. palma, Soph.; στέφανον προτιθέναι to propose a prize, Thuc.
generally, a crown of glory, an honour, glory, Inscr. ap. Hdt.:— a crown as a badge of office or distinction, Dem.

used by Hom. in Pass., to be put round, Lat. circumdari, ἢν περὶ μὲν φόβος ἐστεφάνωται round about which (the shield) is Terror wreathed, Il.; ἀμφὶ δέ μιν νέφος ἐστεφάνωτο all round about him was a cloud, Id.; περὶ νῆσον πόντος ἐστεφάνωται the sea lies round about the island, Od.
to be surrounded, Lat. cingi, ἐστεφανωμένος τιήρην μυρσίνηι having his tiara wreathed with myrtle, Hdt.

Act. to crown, wreathe, χαίτην Pind.; στ. τινά Eur., etc.: c. dupl. acc., εὐαγγέλια στεφανοῦν τινά to crown one for good tidings, Ar.:—Pass. to be crowned or rewarded with a crown, Hdt., Pind.:—Mid. to crown oneself, στεφανοῦσθε κισσῶι Eur., Ar.
in Mid. to win a crown, of the victor at the games, Pind.
to crown as an honour or reward, Eur., Lys.:—to crown or honour with libations, Eur.
Pass. to wear a crown as a badge of office, Xen., Dem.
like a wreath, wreathed, Eur.
that which surrounds, a crown or wreath, Theogn., Pind.; στ. πύργων [the city's] coronal of towers, Soph.
a crown as the prize of victory, Pind.
an honour, glory, Id.
a crown, wreath, garland, Eur.; pl. στέφη, = στέμματα, Aesch., Soph.
of libations, Aesch.
to put round, Lat. circumdare, ἀμφὶ κεφαλῆι νέφος ἔστεφε δῖα θεάων Il.; θεὸς μορφὴν ἔπεσι στέφει Od.:—Mid. to put round one's head, Anth.
to surround, crown, wreath, τινὰ ἄνθεσι Hes.; μυρσίνης κλάδοις Eur.:—Mid., στέφου κάρα crown thy head, Id.:—Pass. to be crowned, Aesch.
to crown with libations, Soph.
the breast, Lat. pectus, Hom., Xen.
metaph. the breast as the seat of feeling, the heart, Hom. (always in pl.), Aesch.

entry.etym: late pres. formed from ἕστηκα perf. of ἵστημι
entry.sense: to stand, NTest.
a block of stone used as a prop or buttress to a wall, Il.: a block of rockcrystal, in which the Egyptian mummies were cased, Hdt.
a block or slab, bearing an inscription; and so,
a gravestone, Hom., attic

a block or slab, inscribed with record of victories, dedications, treaties, decrees, etc., Hdt., attic; γράφειν τινὰ εἰς στήλην, ἀναγράφειν ἐν στήλῃ, whether for honour, or for infamy, Hdt., Dem.:—also the record itself, a contract, agreement, κατὰ τὴν στήλην according to agreement, Ar.; στῆλαι αἱ πρὸς Θηβαίους Dem.
a boundary post, Xen.:— the turning-post at the end of the racecourse, Lat. meta, Soph., Xen.
for Στῆλαι Ἡρακλήιαι, v. Ἡράκλειος.
of or like a στήλη, Luc., Anth.
inscribed on a στήλη, posted or placarded as infamous, στηλίτην τινὰ ἀναγράφειν, ποιεῖν Isocr., Dem.
to set up as a monument, Anth.

entry.etym: Dim. of στήμων signf. I, Arist.

entry.sense: intr. to be torn to shreds, Aesch.
the warp in the ancient upright loom, Hes., Plat.
a thread, Batr.
a support, Eur.
= στῆριγξ 2, Plut.
a propping, supporting; and (in pass. sense) fixedness, steadfastness, NTest.
a support, prop, stay, Xen.
the fork with which the pole of a two-wheeled chariot was propped, Lat. furca, Lys.
to make fast, prop, fix, set, Il.; λίθον κατὰ χθονὸς ἐστ. he set the stone fast in the ground, Hes.:—Mid. to fix for oneself, Anth.
metaph. to confirm, establish, NTest.
intr. = Pass., στηρίξαι ποσὶν ἔμπεδον Od.; κῦμα οὐρανῶι στηρίζον a wave rising up to heaven, Eur.; and metaph., κλέος οὐρανῶι στηρίζον Id.
of diseases, to fix, settle, determine to a particular part, ὁπότε εἰς τὴν καρδίαν στηρίξαι (sc. ἡ νόσος) Thuc.

Pass. and Mid. to be firmly set or fixed, to stand fast or steady, στηρίξασθαι to get a firm footing, Il.; δώματα πρὸς οὐρανὸν ἐστήρικται the house is lifted up to heaven, Hes.; so, ὀρθὴ δ’ ἐς ὀρθὴν αἰθέρ’ ἐστηρίξατο Eur.
metaph., ὅπου στηρίζει ποτέ wheresoever thou art tarrying, art settled, Soph.
Ζεὺς Στ. Jupiter Stator, Plut.
the Lyric poet Stesichorus, whose real name was Tisias, Simon.
to sleep on litter, Polyb.
compact, strong, stout, sturdy, Hom., Hes.
a bed of straw, rushes, or leaves, Eur., Theocr.
a mattress, pallet, Hdt., Ar.
to tread, traverse: Pass., πᾶν ἐστίβηται πλευρόν every side has been traversed, Soph.
frozen dew, rime, hoar frost, Od.
Mid. or Pass. to paint one's eyelids and eyebrows with black paint (στίβι), Strab.
Lat. stibium, = στίμμι.
a trodden way, track, path, Hhymn., Soph., etc.
a track, footstep, Hdt., Aesch., etc.; κατὰ στίβον on the track or trail, Hdt.; στίβοι φιλάνορες traces of her who had lain in the bed, Aesch.
a going, gait, Soph.
one who tattooes, a tattooer, Hdt.
the mark of a pointed instrument, a tattoo-mark, brand, Hdt., NTest.
to bear tattoo-marks, Luc.
one who bears tattoo-marks, a branded culprit, runaway slave, Xen., etc.
a spot, point, Arist.:— metaph. a jot, tittle, Dem.; ἐν στ. χρόνου in a moment, NTest.

entry.etym: the Root is ΣΤΙΓ, cf. ἔστιγμαι, στιγμή, etc.
entry.sense: to mark with a pointed instrument, to tattoo, Hdt., Xen.
to brand, as a mark of disgrace, Hdt., Ar.; ἔστιζον στίγματα βασιλήια branded them with the royal brand-marks, Hdt.; esp. of runaways, δραπέτης ἐστιγμένος Ar.
c. dupl. acc., στίγματα στίζειν τινά to brand one with a mark, Hdt.
metaph., βακτηρίαι στ. to beat black and blue, Ar.
to mark with a full stop, Lat. interpungere, Anth.
punctured, Anth.:—generally, spotted, dappled, Soph., Eur.; στικτὰ ὄμματα, of the hundred eyes of Argus, Eur.
to glisten, Hom., Eur.; c. acc. cogn., στ. ἀστραπάς to flash lightning, Eur.:—metaph. to shine, be bright, Id.
a drop, Lat. stilla: metaph. a little bit, a moment, Ar.
glittering, glistening, Il.

entry.etym: the other cases are taken from στίχος
entry.sense: a row, line, rank or file, esp. of soldiers, Il., Aesch., etc.:—metaph., ἐπέων στίχες verses, lays, Pind.
trodden down, close-pressed, Lat. stipatus, Soph.; στιπτοὶ γέροντες tough, sturdy old fellows, Ar.
a close-pressed or compact body: a body of men in close array, a column, mass, Hdt., Aesch.; νεῶν στῖφος the close array of ships, Aesch.
firm, solid, Xen.
one who sings verses, a poet, Anth.
Dep. to march in rows or ranks, esp. of soldiers, Il.; of ships in line, Id.; of shepherds with their herds, Id.: later, we have epic 3rd pl. στιχόωσι in same sense, Mosch.
of lines or verses, στ. θάνατος of one who was rhymed to death, Anth.
writing verse, Anth.
a row or file of soldiers, Xen.
a line of poetry, a verse, Ar.
a scraper, to remove the oil and dirt (γλοίος) from the skin in the bath, Plat., etc.
a tiara, Xen.
a roofed colonnade, piazza, cloister, Lat. porticus, Hdt., Xen.
at Athens this name was given to various public buildings:
a storehouse, magazine, warehouse for corn, Ar.
ἡ βασίλειος or ἡ τοῦ βασιλέως στοά the court where the ἄρχων βασιλεύς sat, Id., Plat.
the Poecile or Painted Chamber, in which Zeno of Citium taught, and so his school was called οἱ ἐκ τῆς στοᾶς or Στωικοί, Luc.
a shed to protect besiegers, Polyb.
to pile up, pack together, Luc.
a plant used for stuffing or padding; and metaph. " padding, " an expletive, Ar.
in rows:— αἱ Στοιχάδες (sc. νῆσοι) a row of islands off Marseilles, now les Isles d' Hieres, Strab.
properly, one of a row: hence,
in the sun-dial, the shadow of the gnomon, Ar.
generally, one of a series, an elementary sound of the voice, a letter, Plat.:— κατὰ στοιχεῖον in the order of the letters, alphabetically, Anth.
in pl. the elements, Plat., etc.
the elements of knowledge, rudiments, ἀρξάμενοι ἀπὸ τῶν στ. Xen.
to go in a line or row: to go in battle-order, Xen.
c. dat. to be in line with, walk by rule or principle, c. dat., NTest.
to tell in regular order, Aesch.
to set a row of poles with nets to drive the game into, Xen.
to order or arrange in system, Aesch.
a row, στοῖχοι τῶν ἀναβαθμῶν, of a flight of steps, Hdt.; κατὰ στοῖχον in a row, Thuc.: of ships, a column, ἐν στοίχοις τρισί Aesch.; of soldiers, a file, Thuc.
a line of poles supporting hunting-nets, Xen.
moving in close array, Eur.
an equipment, armament, Aesch.
equipment, raiment, apparel, Hdt., Trag.
a piece of dress, a garment, robe, Soph., Eur., etc.; στ. θηρός, of the lion's skin which Hercules wore, Eur.
Mid. to dress oneself in a garment, c. acc., Eur.
στ. χιτών a tunic hanging in folds, Xen.
to put in trim, στολίσας νηὸς πτερά having trimmed the sails, Hes.
to equip, dress:—Pass., ἐστολισμένος δορί armed with spear, Eur.
metaph. to deck, adorn, Anth.
a scanty garment, Anth.
a garment, mantle, Eur.
a garment, robe, Eur., etc.; νεβρῶν στολίδες, i. e. fawnskins worn as garments, Id.
νηῶν στολίδες sails, Anth.
in pl. folds in a garment, Eur.
an equipment for warlike purposes, an expedition by land or sea, Hdt., Trag., etc.; τεθριπποβάμων στ. an equipage with four horses, Eur.
generally, a journey or voyage, Soph., etc.; ἰδίῳ στόλῳ in a journey on one's own account, opp. to δημοσίῳ or κοινῷ στ. (on behalf of the state), Hdt., Thuc.
the purpose or cause of a journey, a mission, errand, Soph., Ar.
an armament, army, or, a sea-force, fleet, attic; οὐ πολλῷ στόλῳ, i. e. in one ship, Soph.; πρόπας στόλος all the host, Id.
παγκρατίου στ., periphr. for παγκράτιον, Pind.
= ἔμβολον, a ship's beak, Id., Aesch.
a salt-water lake, estuary, Strab.: so, στομάλιμνον, ου, τό, Theocr.
the mouth, Lat. os, Hom., etc.

the mouth as the organ of speech, δέκα μὲν γλῶσσαι, δέκα δὲ στόματ’ Il.; στ. τὸ δῖον the mouth of Jove, Aesch.; Μοισᾶν στόμα their mouthpiece, Theocr.;—with Preps., ἀνὰ στόμα ἔχειν to have always in one's mouth, Eur.: ἀπὸ στόματος by word of mouth, Xen., etc.: διὰ στόμα was in every one's mouth, Aesch.; πᾶσι διὰ στόματος 'tis the common talk, Theocr.: ἐξ ἑνὸς στ. with one voice, Ar.; κατὰ στόμα face to face, Hdt., attic

στ. ποταμοῦ the mouth of a river, Lat. ostia, Hom., etc.; so, ἠιόνος στ. μακρόν the wide mouth of the bay, Il.; στ. τοῦ Πόντου, Lat. fauces Ponti, Hdt.:—also, a chasm or cleft in the earth with a stream gushing out, Id.; τὸ ἄνω, τὸ κάτω στόμα τοῦ ὀρύγματος the opening or width of the trench at top, at bottom, Id.
any outlet or entrance, Od., Xen.
the foremost part, face, front:
of weapons, the point, Il.; the edge of a sword, NTest.:—also like Lat. acies, the front, στόμα πολέμοιο, ὑσμίνης Il.; so alone, Xen.
generally, ἄκρον στ. πύργων the top of the towers, Eur.; τὸ στόμα τοῦ βίου the verge of life, Xen.
busy with the tongue, loud-tongued, Aesch., Soph.; στ. γλωσσαλγία wearisome wordiness, Eur.
word-making, Ar.
properly, a mouth, opening: hence,
the throat, gullet, Il.
in late Gr. the orifice of the stomach, the stomach.
the mouth of a cave, Soph.: a cave, vault, Aesch.: the socket of a bolt, Anth.
a bridle-bit, bit, Hdt., Trag.; metaph., στ. Τροίας a bit or curb for Troy, i. e. the Greek army, Aesch.
to muzzle or gag, Hdt.
（στόμα II) to furnish with an edge: metaph. to steel, harden, train for anything, Ar.:—Pass., Plut.
to fringe, fence, Id.; Pass., [δράκαινα] ἐχίδναις ἐστομωμένη Eur.
to mouth, rant, vaunt, Ar.
a mouther, ranter, Ar.
a mouth, entrance, Aesch.
a furnishing with a sharp edge: metaph., πολλὴν στόμωσιν ἔχειν to have a sharp edge, Soph.
to groan, sigh, Il.
trans. to sigh, groan over or for, τινά Soph., Mosch.
a groaning, wailing, Hom., Eur.; in pl. groans, sighs, Il., Soph.
causing groans or sighs, Hom., Aesch., etc.
generally, mournful, sad, wretched, Hom., Soph.; neut. as adv., Aesch.
a sighing, groaning, lamentation, Hom.; of the sea, Soph.
any sharp point, as of a rock, Eur.: a pen-knife, Anth.
love, affection, of parents and children, Antipho.
to spread the clothes over a bed, λέχος στορέσαι, Lat. lectum sternere, to make up a bed, Il.; κλίνην ἔστρωσαν Hdt.; absol. to make a bed, χαμάδις στορέσας Od.
generally to spread, strew, ἀνθρακιὴν στ. Il.; στιβάδας NTest.
to spread smooth, level, πόντον στ., Lat. sternere aequor, Od.:—metaph. to calm, soothe, στορέσας ὀργήν Aesch.
to level, lay low a tree, Anth.: metaph., λῆμα στ., Eur.; φρόνημα Thuc.
ὁδὸν στ. to pave a road, Lat. viam sternere:—Pass., ἐστρωμένη ὁδός Hdt.
to strew or spread with a thing, μυρσίνηισι τὴν ὁδόν Id.:—Pass., of a room, to be ready furnished, NTest.; cf. στρῶμα.
a point, the tyne of a deer's horn, Anth.
to aim or shoot at, c. gen., τοῦ σκοποῦ Plat., etc.
metaph. to aim at, endeavour after, Id.; στ. φίλων κριτῶν to aim at having friends as judges, Xen.
to endeavour to make out, to guess at a thing, c. gen., Isocr.:— absol. to make guesses, conjecture, Soph., Xen.
the thing aimed, a javelin, Eur.
one must aim at, τοῦ μέσου Arist.
skilful in aiming at, able to hit, c. gen., Arist.
able to guess, sagacious, Plat.: adv., στοχαστικῶς ἔχειν to be sagacious, Arist.
an aim, shot, Eur.
to strangle, Strab.
Mid. to squeeze oneself up, twist oneself, metaph. to keep loitering about, Ar.
retention of the urine, strangury, Ar.
that which is squeezed out, a drop, Anth.
to lighten, Soph.
the general of an army, Hdt.

entry.etym: assumed as pres. of the epic 3rd pl. imperf. ἐστρατόωντο
entry.sense: they were encamped, Il.

an expedition, campaign, στρατηίην or -είαν ποιεῖσθαι Hdt., Thuc.; ἀπὸ στρατείας coming from war, after service done, Aesch.; κατὰ τὴν Σιτάλκου στρατείαν about the time of his expedition, Thuc.; ἐπὶ στρατείας or ἐν στρατείᾳ εἶναι to be on foreign service, Plat., Xen.: pl. military service, warfare, Plat.
στρ. ἡ ἐν τοῖς μέρεσιν, an expedition for special service, to train the young soldiers next after serving as περίπολοι, Aeschin.
an expedition, campaign, Hdt., attic
an armament, army, Hdt., attic:—also a naval armament, Soph., Thuc.
= στρατός, the host, people, Eur.
fit for service, serviceable, Xen.
an expedition, Hdt.
one must make an expedition, Xen.
to serve in war, serve as a soldier, do military service, take the field, march, Hdt., attic; c. acc. cogn., στρ. στρατείαν Eur.
Dep. στρατεύομαι, fut. -εύσομαι: aor1 ἐστρατευσάμην and ἐστρατεύθην: perf. ἐστράτευμαι:—to serve, take the field, Lat. militari, Hdt.; ἐστρατευμένος having been a soldier, Ar.
to lead an army, march, Hdt., attic

to be general, Hdt., attic:—c. gen. to be general of an army, Hdt., attic:—to lead as general, c. dat., ἐστρατήγησε Λακεδαιμονίοισι Hdt.; c. acc. cogn., στρ. πόλεμον to conduct war, Dem.: with neut. adj., to do a thing as general, τοῦτο Xen.; πάντα Dem.:—Pass. to be conducted, Plat., Dem.
metaph., ποῦ σὺ στρατηγεῖς τοῦδε; how claim'st thou to command this man? Soph.
the office, dignity, or post of general, command, Hdt., attic; of naval command, Xen.
the office of στρατηγός at Athens, a sort of war-minister, Ar., Plat.:—at Rome the Praetorship, Plut.
a period of command, campaign, Xen.
the qualities or skill of a general, generalship, Id.
to wish to be a general, wish to make war, Xen., Dem.
of or for a general, Plat.:— ἡ -κή (sc. τέχνη) = στρατηγία II, Id.;so, τὰ στρ. Xen.
of persons, fitted for command, versed in generalship, Id., etc.:—adv. -κῶς, εὖ καὶ στρ. Ar.
at Rome, praetorian, Strab.
the general's tent, Lat. praetorium, Soph., Dem.
at Athens, the place where the στρατηγοί held their sittings, Aeschin.
of the general, πύλαι στρ. the entrance of the general s tent, Soph.; ναῦς στρ. the admiral's ship, flag-ship, Thuc.; so, ἡ στρ. alone, Hdt.: at Rome, σπεῖρα στρ. the praetorian cohort, Plut.
the leader or commander of an army, a general, Hdt., attic: generally, a commander, governor, Soph.

at Athens, the title of 10 officers elected yearly to command the army and navy, and conduct the war-department, with the Polemarch at their head, Hdt., Thuc., etc.; when distinguished from ναύαρχος and ἵππαρχος the στρατηγός is commander of the infantry, Dem.
one of the chief magistrates of several Greek cities, Hdt., Polyb.
στρ. ὕπατος, or στρατηγός alone, the Roman Consul, Polyb.; στρ. ἑξαπέλεκυς the Praetor, Id.:—also one of the duumviri or chief magistrates of Roman colonies, NTest.
an officer who had the custody of the Temple at Jerusalem, Id.
an expedition, campaign, Hdt.
the army itself, Id.
to lead an army into the field, Hdt., Aesch., etc.
c. gen. to be commander of, to command, Eur.; c. dat., Id.
a leader of an army, a general, commander, Soph., Eur., etc.; of an admiral, στρ. νεῶν Aesch.
an army, Aesch., Thuc., etc.: absol. a land force, as distinguished from a fleet, Hdt.
generally, a host, company, band, Pind.
= στρατεία, an expedition, Ar., Thuc.
warlike, Hdt.
a citizen bound to military service; generally, a soldier, Hdt., attic; collectively, ὁ στρατιώτης the soldiers, Thuc.
of or for soldiers, Xen., etc.:— τὸ στρ. (sc. ἀργύριον) the pay of the forces, Dem.; but, τὸ στρ. (sc. πλῆθος) the soldiery, Thuc.; τὰ στρατιωτικά (sc. πράγματα) military affairs, Xen.
fit for a soldier, military, στρ. ἡλικία the military age, Id.
warlike, soldierlike, γένη Arist.
adv. like a soldier, Isocr.:—of ships, στρατιωτικώτερον παρεσκευασμένοι equipped rather as troop-ships than for battle, Thuc.
as adj., στρ. ἀρωγά the martial aid, Aesch.
στρ. (sc. ναῦς), a troop-ship, transport, Thuc., Xen.
to levy soldiers: Pass., Plut.
prophet to the army, Aesch.
a military commander, Lat. tribunus legionis, Luc.
an encamping, Xen.
an encampment, the position of an army, Id.
of an encampment, Polyb.
to encamp, bivouac, take up a position, Xen.:
as Dep. στρατοπεδεύομαι, Hdt., Thuc., etc.; perf. ἐστρατοπεδεῦσθαι to be in camp, Xen.: of a fleet, to be stationed, Hdt.
the ground on which soldiers are encamped, a camp, encampment, Hdt., Aesch.:— hence, a camp, encamped army, Hdt., Thuc.
generally, an army, Hdt.; also, a squadron of ships, Id., Thuc.
the Roman legion, Polyb.
an encamped army, generally, an army, host, ἀνὰ στρατόν or κατὰ στρ. throughout the army, Hom.; epic gen. στρατόφι Il.; of a naval force, Aesch., etc.
the soldiery, people, exclusive of the chiefs, Hom.: so, the commons, people, Pind., Aesch.
any band or body of men, Pind.
a commanding officer, Strab.
to lead to war; only found in aor1 pass. part. στρατωθέν (sc. στόμιον) the curb formed by the army, Aesch.: v. στρατάω.
Comic patronymic, son of the army, Ar.
twisted, crooked, Arist.; of the brows, knit, wrinkled, Anth.: metaph., στρεβλοῖσι παλαίσμασι by cunning dodges in wrestling, Ar.
crookedness, Plut.
to twist or strain tight, στρ. τὰ ὅπλα ὄνοισι to draw the cables taut with windlasses, Hdt.: to screw up the strings of an instrument, Plat.
to twist or wrench a dislocated limb, with a view to setting it, Hdt.
to stretch on the wheel or rack, to rack, torture, Ar.:—Pass., στρεβλοῦσθαι ἐπὶ τροχοῦ Id.
metaph. to pervert or distort words, NTest.
a wrench, strain, sprain, Dem.
whirling-bright, Ar.
flexible, pliant: στρεπτὸς χιτών a shirt of chain-armour, Lat. lorica annulata, Il.; στρεπταὶ λύγοι pliant withs, Eur.: twined, wreathed, Anth.
στρεπτός, οῦ, a collar of twisted or linked metal, Lat. torques, Hdt., Xen., etc.
of pastry, a twist or roll, Dem.
metaph. to be bent or turned, στρεπτοὶ καὶ θεοὶ αὐτοί the gods themselves may be turned (by prayer), Il.; στρ. γλῶσσα a glib, pliant tongue, Id.
bent, curved, of a pick-axe, Eur.; of a bow, Theocr.
wearing a collar, Lat. torquatus, Hdt.
Pass. to be squeezed out in drops: metaph. to be drained of one's strength, exhausted, Hom.
to spin or whirl something round: Pass., ὄσσε οἱ στρεφεδίνηθεν (for -νήθησαν) his eyes span round, of one stunned by a blow on the nape of the neck, Il.
to turn about or aside, turn, Hom., etc.; στρ. ἵππους to turn or guide horses, Il.; στρ. σάκος to sway the shield, Soph.
ἄνω καὶ κάτω στρ. to turn upside down, Aesch., Plat.; so, κάτω στρ. Soph.; so, στρέφειν alone, to overturn, upset, Eur.
to twist a rope, Xen.
metaph. of pain, to twist, torture, Ar., Plat.
to twist, plait, ἐστραμμένα Xen.: to spin, Luc.
metaph. to turn a thing over in one's mind, τί στρέφω τάδε; Eur., Dem.
to turn from the right course, divert, embezzle, Lys.
Pass. and Mid. to turn oneself, to turn round or about, turn to and fro, Il.; ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα στρέφεσθαι, of one tossing in bed, Id.
to turn to or from an object, to turn back, return, Id., Soph.; στραφέντες ἔφευγον Xen.
of the heavenly bodies, to revolve, Od.; of the distaff, Plat.

to twist about, like a wrestler trying to elude his adversary; so, in argument, to twist and turn, shuffle, τί ταῦτα στρέφει; why d'ye shuffle so? Ar.; τί δῆτα ἔχων στρέφει; why then do you keep shuffling, Plat.; πάσας στροφὰς στρέφεσθαι to twist every way, Id.
to turn and change, Soph.; τοῦ δὲ σοῦ ψόφου οὐκ ἂν στραφείην I would not turn for any noise of thine, Id.
to twist oneself up with a thing, stick close to it, Od.:—then, like Lat. versari, to be always engaged, Plat.
generally, to be at large, go about Soph.
ἐστραμμένος, η, ον, of places, ἐστρ. ἐπὶ τόπον turned towards, Polyb.
in strict Mid. sense, to turn about with oneself, take back, Soph.
intr. in Act., like Pass. to turn about, Il.; of soldiers, to wheel about, Xen.
to twist justice, Ar.
cunning in the perversion of justice, Ar.
strong, hard, rough, harsh: neut. as adv., Anth.
to run riot, wax wanton, NTest.
wantonness, NTest.
Comic word, οὐδ’ ἂν στριβιλικίγξ not the least, not a fraction, Ar.
to twist, twirl or whirl about, Ar.:—metaph. to make dizzy, distract, Aesch.: —Pass. to whirl about, Id.
to twist about, Anth.
conical, Strab.
spinning, whirling, Anth.
anything twisted or whirled: a top, Plat.
a whirlpool, whirlwind, Luc.
a whirling dance, pirouette, Ar.
a twisting or whirling round, of the effect of a whirlwind, Aesch.
to twirl, spin, Anth.
round, spherical, Hdt., Ar., etc.; λίθοι στρ. pebbles, Xen.
circular, Plat.
round, compactly formed, Xen.
of ships, στρ. ναῦς, στρ. πλοῖον, a merchant-ship, from its round shape, as opp. to the long narrow ship-of-war (μακρὰ ναῦς), Hdt., Thuc., etc.
metaph. of phrases, well-rounded, compact, pithy, terse, Ar., Plat.:—adv., στρογγυλώτατα as tersely as possible, Arist.
roundness, Plat.
like a top, whirling, Anth.
a body rounded or spun round: hence,
a top, Lat. turbo, Il.
a whirlwind, Aesch.
a snail, Theocr.
στρούθειον μῆλον, ου, τό, a kind of quince, Anth.
an ostrich, from its camel-like neck, Strab.
the sparrow, Il., etc.

ὁ μέγας στρ. the large bird, i. e. the ostrich, Struthio, Xen.: also called στρουθὸς κατάγαιος (i. e. the bird that runs on the ground, does not fly), Hdt.; also simply στρουθός, like στρουθοκάμηλος, Ar.
feeding on birds, Strab.
epith. of Hermes, standing as porter at the door-hinges, with a play on the sense of twisty, shifty, Ar.
a whirl, eddy, Hom.:—metaph., στρ. μάχης Anth.
ἠλάκατα στρ. to turn the spindle, Od.
turning round, Ἄρκτου στροφάδες κέλευθοι the Bear's revolving path, Soph.
Στροφάδες (sc. νῆσοι) αἱ, the drifting isles, a group not far from Zacynthus, supposed to have been once floating.
a twisted noose, cord, Xen.
a windlass, capstan, on which a cable runs, Luc.
the socket in which the pivot of a door (ὁ στρόφιγξ) moved, Ar.
to have the colic (v. στρόφος II), Ar.
a turning, e.g. of a horse, Xen.; ἐν στροφαῖσιν ὀμμάτων with rolling of the eyes, Eur.
a twist, such as wrestlers make to elude their adversary, Plat.:—metaph. a trick, dodge, Ar.
the turning of the Chorus as they danced from right to left of the ὀρχήστρα: the strain sung during this evolution, the strophe, to which the ἀντιστροφή answers.
the pivot, axle or pin on which a body turns, Eur.
στρόφιγγες were pivots working in sockets, at top and bottom of a door, which served instead of hinges, Plut.
metaph., στρ. γλώττης, of a well-hung tongue, Ar.
a band worn by women round the breast, Ar.
a headband worn by priests, Plut.
a twisting, slippery fellow, Ar.
Pass. to wheel eddying round, of vultures wheeling round their nest, Aesch.
a twisted band or cord, used as a sword-belt, Od.: generally, a cord, rope, Hdt.
= στρόφιον, a maiden-zone, Aesch.
a swathing-cloth, swaddling-band, Hhymn.
a twisting of the bowels, colic, Lat. tormina, Ar.
(sc. ἄνεμος), a wind blowing from the Strymon, i. e. a NNE. wind, Hdt.
the Strymon, a river of Thrace, Hes., Hdt.:—adj. Στρυμόνιος, η, ον of the Strymon, Aesch., Eur.; and Στρυμονικός, ή, όν, Strab.
of a taste which draws up the mouth, rough, harsh, astringent, Xen., Anth.
metaph. of temper or manner, harsh, austere, Ar., Xen.
a rough, harsh taste: metaph. harshness of temper, Plut.
anything spread or laid out for lying or sitting upon, a mattress, bed, Lat. stragulum, vestis stragula, Theogn.:—in pl. the bedclothes, the coverings of a dinner-couch, Ar., etc.
a horsecloth, horse-trappings, Xen.
a leathern or linen sack in which slaves had to tie up the bedclothes (στρώματα), Xen., Aeschin.
one who has the care of the bedding, Plut.
a bed spread or prepared; generally, a bed, couch, Pind., Aesch., etc.: a mattress, bedding, Xen.; στρ. ἄφθιτος, of the golden fleece, Pind.
one that gets couches ready, Plut.
spread, laid, covered, Hes., Eur.; στρωτὰ φάρη bed clothes, Soph.

Frequent. of στρέφω, as τρωπάω of τρέπω, to turn constantly, στρ. ἠλάκατα to keep turning the spindle, i. e. spin, Od.:—Pass. to keep turning, so as to face the enemy, Il.: to roam about, wander, Id.; στρ. ἀνὰ τὴν πόλιν Hdt.; hence, like Lat. versari in loco, to move freely in a place, live there, Il.; ἐν λέχει στρωφώμενος, i. e. claiming a husband's rights, Aesch.
hating a man or the male sex, Aesch.
poet. adj. hated, abominated, loathed, or hateful, abominable, loathsome, Hom., Trag.:—c. dat. bearing hatred or malice towards one, στυγερὸς δέ οἱ ἔπλετο θυμῷ Il.
hateful, wretched, miserable, Soph., Ar.
adv. -ρῶς, to one's sorrow, miserably, Hom., Soph.
of hateful look, horrible, Hes.

to hate, abominate, abhor, stronger than μισέω, Hom., Trag.:—c. inf. to hate or fear to do a thing, Il., Soph.:—Pass. to be abhorred, detested, Aesch.; τί δ’ ἐστι πρός γ’ ἐμοῦ στυγούμενον; what is the horrid thing that I have done? Soph.
in aor1, to make hateful, Od.
an abomination, Eur.
hated, abominated, hateful, Aesch., NTest.
Stygian, Aesch., Soph.
= στυγητός, hateful, abominable, Eur.
to look gloomy, be sorrowful, NTest.; of weather, to be gloomy, lowering, Id.
hated, abhorred, hateful, Aesch., Soph.:—c. dat. hateful or hostile to one, Aesch., Soph.
gloomy, sullen, Lat. tristis, Aesch., Eur.; ὁρᾶν στυγνός gloomy to behold, Xen.;— στυγνὸς εἴκων yielding sullenly, with an ill grace, Soph.; neut. as adv., Id.
gloominess, sullenness, Plut.
to make gloomy:—Pass. to be gloomy, Anth.
hating marriage, Anth.
hatred, as expressed in looks, sullenness, gloom, Aesch.
an object of hatred, an abomination, Id.; of persons, δεσπότου στ. thy hated lord, Id.; στύγη θεῶν, of the Erinyes, Id.:— a deed of horror, Id.
a staff or rod, Strab.
a mast to carry a sail at the stern, as in a yawl, Plut.
a pillar with figures on it, Anth.
a pillar, as a support or bearing, Hdt., etc.
to prop with pillars; metaph. in Mid., ζωὴν στυλώσασθαι to support one's life (by means of children), Anth.
a city and mountain of Arcadia, Il.:—adj. Στυμφάλιος, η, ον, ionic -ήλιος, η, ον, Hdt., etc.; fem. Στυμφᾱλίς, ίδος, Strab.
the Styx, i. e. the hateful, a river of the nether world, by which the gods in Homer swore their most sacred oaths, Il.
the coarse fibre of flax or hemp, tow, oakum, Lat. stuppa, Hdt., Xen., etc.
a dealer in oakum, Ar.
an astringent earth, alum or vitriol, Hdt.
made of the wood of the tree στύραξ, Strab.
storax, a fragrant gum, Arist.
ἡ στ., the tree producing this gum, Hdt.
the spike at the lower end of a spear-shaft, Xen., Plat.
ill-usage, abuse, Ar.
to strike hard, smite, Il.; of the wind, to drive away clouds, Id.; ἐξ ἑδέων στυφελίξαι to thrust him from his seat, Id.
generally, to treat roughly, misuse, maltreat, Hom.
hard, rough, Aesch.
metaph. harsh, severe, cruel, Id.
striking with a stick; used, like ὀρτυγοκόπος, of a game, in which they put quails in a ring, and hit them with little sticks; if a quail ran out of the ring, it was beaten, Ar.
to draw together: Pass., χείλεα στυφθείς having his lips drawn up by the taste, Anth.
of a colonnade or piazza:— hence, Stoic, of or belonging to the Stoics (because Zeno taught in the στοὰ Ποικίλη), NTest.; cf. Στοϊκός.
wordiness, Ar.: small talk, Anth.
a gossip-gleaner, Ar.

entry.etym: from στωμύλος, as στρογγύλλω from στρογγύλος
entry.sense: to be talkative, to chatter, babble, Ar.:—so as Dep. στωμύλλομαι, fut. στωμυλοῦμαι, aor1 ἐστωμυλάμην, Id.
mouthy, wordy, talkative, chattering, glib, Ar., Theocr.; τὰ στ. ταῦτα this nonsense, Anth.
a boar-hunt, Anth.
to live like a Sybarite, Ar.
Sybaris, a city of Magna Graecia, on a river of the same name, noted for luxury, Hdt., etc.
a Sybarite, Hdt., Ar.:—fem. Συβαρῖτις, ιδος, Ar.; and as adj., Theocr.
of Sybaris: λόγοι Σ. a class of fables among the Greeks, Ar.
a herd of swine, Hom.
swine-pastures, name of some islets near Corcyra, Thuc.
a swineherd, Od., Hdt.
united in wedlock, married, ἄλλῳ to another, Eur.:—generally, connected by marriage, Id.
ξύγγαμός σοι Ζεύς sharing thy marriage-bed, of Amphitryon, Id.: pl. the rival wives of one man, Id.
bordering, neighbouring, Eur.
sameness of descent or family, relationship, kin, Eur., etc.: c. gen. kin, relationship with or to another, ἡ ξ. τοῦ θεοῦ Plat.; also, ἡ πρὸς τοὺς παῖδας σ. Isocr.
ties of kindred, family connexion, influence, Plat.
one's kin, kinsfolk, kinsmen, Eur.; in pl. families, Dem.
born with, congenital, natural, in-born, Pind., Aesch.; συγγενεῖς μῆνες the months of my natural life, Soph.:—so in adv., συγγενῶς δύστηνος miserable from my birth, Eur.

of the same kin, descent or family with another, akin to him, τινι Hdt., attic:—absol. akin, cognate, Trag., etc.:—as Subst. a kinsman, relative, τινος of another, Ar., Plat.:—in pl., οἱ συγγενεῖς kinsfolk, kinsmen, Hdt., etc.:— τὸ συγγενές, = συγγένεια, Aesch., etc.; εἰ τούτῳ προσήκει Λαΐῳ τι σ. if this man had any connexion with Laius, Soph.
metaph. akin, cognate, of like kind, Ar., Plat.
at the Persian court, συγγενής was a title bestowed by the king as a mark of honour (like Cousin), Xen.
congenital, hereditary, Plut.
of or for kinsmen, σ. φιλία between kinsfolk, Arist.: —adv. -κῶς, like kinsfolk, Dem.
a co-mate in old age, Babr.
to be a fellow-labourer, Isae.
a fellow-labourer, Ar.
to rejoice with, τινί Eur.
to grow old together with, τινί Hdt.; absol., Aesch.
growing old together, Anth.
Dep.
to be with any one, hold converse or communication with, associate or keep company with, τινί Hdt., attic; so, also, σ. ἐς λόγους τινί Ar.
of disciples or pupils, to hold converse with a master, consult him, Id., etc.
to come to assist, τινί or πρός τινα Aesch.; absol., Soph.
to come together, meet, Hdt., etc.; οἱ συγγιγνόμενοι comrades, Xen.
to think with, agree with, τινί Xen.; c. acc., τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ξυνέγνωσαν shared the error, Thuc.:—absol. to consent, agree, Hdt., Thuc.; so in Mid., Hdt.
σ. ἑαυτῷ to be conscious, καὶ αὐτοὶ ξυνέγνωσαν σφίσιν ὡς ἠδικηκότες Lys.:—so in Mid., συνεγινώσκετο ἑωυτῷ οὐκέτι εἶναι δυνατός Hdt.
to allow, acknowledge, own, confess, τι Id., attic; c. acc. et inf., Hdt.; c. part., ξυγγνοῖμεν ἂν ἡμαρτηκότες Soph.:—absol. to confess one's error, in Act. and Mid., Id.
to have a fellow-feeling with another: and so, to make allowance for him, excuse, pardon, forgive, τινί Id., etc.; σ. τινὶ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, Lat. ignoscere alicui culpam, Eur.; also c. gen. rei, Plut.
acknowledgment, confession, συγγνώμην ἔχειν, ὅτι . . to acknowledge that . . , Hdt.
a fellow-feeling with another, a lenient judgment, allowance, Ar., NTest.

pardon, forgiveness, συγγνώμην ἔχειν to pardon, τινί Hdt., attic; τινός for a thing, Hdt., attic:—opp. to συγγνώμης τυγχάνειν, to obtain forgiveness, Xen., etc.; ξυγγνώμην λήψονται, will be pardoned, Thuc.
of acts, συγγνώμην ἔχει admit of excuse, are excusable, Soph.; ἔχειν τι ξυγγνώμης Thuc.
inclined to pardon, indulgent, Arist.
of things, pardonable, Id.
disposed to pardon, indulgent, Xen.; σ. εἶναί τινος to be disposed to forgive a thing, Eur.
pass. pardoned, deserving pardon or indulgence, allowable, Thuc.
one must pardon, indulge, τινί Plat.
to be pardoned, pardonable, allowable, Eur., etc.:— συγγνωστόν or συγγνωστά ἐστι, c. inf., Id.
to fasten together with nails, Plut.
poet. adj. = συγγενής, born with, congenital, inborn, natural, Pind., Aesch.
connected by blood, akin, Lat. cognatus, Pind., Eur.:— as Subst. a brother, sister, Eur.; σύγγονοι kinsfolk, cousins, Pind.
a writing, a written paper, Hdt., Plat., etc.:— a written composition, book, work, Xen., etc.; esp. a prose work, treatise, a written speech, Id., Isocr.
a clause of a law, Aeschin.
a physician's prescription, Xen.
one who collects and writes down historic facts, an historian, Xen.: generally, an author, a prose-writer, Ar., Plat.
συγγραφεῖς, οἱ, at Athens (in the 21st year of Pelop. war) commissioners appointed to draw up measures for altering the constitution, Thuc.
a writing or noting down, Hdt.
that which is written, a writing, book: a history, narrative, Thuc., etc.
a written contract, a covenant, bond, Lat. syngrapha, Id.; συγγ. ναυτικαί a bond to secure money lent on bottomry, Dem.; ἀνδριάντα ἐκδεδωκὼς κατὰ συγγραφήν having contracted for its execution, Id.
given to writing, esp. in prose, Luc. adv., συγγραφικῶς ἐρεῖν to speak like a book, i. e. with great precision, Plat.
to write or note down, Lat. conscribere, Xen.;—so in Mid. to have a thing written down, take care that it is written down, Hdt.
to describe, Id.
to compose a writing or a work in writing, Lat. conscribere, πόλεμον ξ. to write the history of the war, Thuc.:—esp. to write in prose, Plat.
to compose a speech to be delivered by another, Isocr., Plat.:—Mid. to get speeches composed, Plat.

to compile, draw up, τοὺς πατρίους νόμους Xen.:—Mid., συγγράφεσθαί τι to draw up a contract or bond, Id.; συγγράφεσθαι εἰρήνην πρός τινα to make a treaty of peace with another, Isocr.; absol. to sign a treaty, Thuc.:— πατέρες συγγεγραμμένοι = the Rom. Patres conscripti, Plut.
to draw up a form of motion to be submitted to vote, Xen.: so in Mid., Plat.
to paint by contract, Ar.
to exercise together:—Pass. to exercise oneself with or together, Plat.
a companion in bodily exercises, Plat., Xen.
to burn up together, Plut.

entry.note: ionic συγκατ fut. ήσω aor2 συγκαθεῖλον
entry.sense: to put down together, to join in putting down, τὸν βάρβαρον Thuc.
to accomplish a thing with any one, τί τινι Hdt.
to join in composing the limbs of a dead man, to join in preparing for burial, Soph.
to sit down together, Plat.
to shut up with another, τινά τινι Xen., etc.:—Pass. to be shut up with, τινί Aeschin.
to drag down together:—fut. pass. συγκαθελκυσθήσεται Aesch.
to sleep with, τινί Aesch.
to be seated or sit with or by the side of, Hdt., Eur.: of a number of persons, to sit together, sit in conclave, Ar., Thuc.
to join in dedicating, Plut.
to make to sit together:—Mid. or Pass. to sit in conclave, meet for deliberation, Xen.
intr., = Mid. to sit with one, Luc.

to let down with or together, to deposit together, Eur.:— σ. ἑαυτόν to let oneself down, lower oneself, εἴς τι Plat.; and absol. (sub. ἑαυτόν) to stoop, condescend, accommodate oneself to others, c. dat., Id.
to bring into place together, ap. Dem.
to join in setting up, Lat. constituere, τὴν τυραννίδα Aesch., etc.:—of settling disturbed countries, Thuc.:— to help in arranging, managing, treating, Eur.
set on fire with or at once, burn up, Lat. comburere, Plat.
to partake in sufferings, NTest.
Pass. to endure adversity with another, τινι NTest.
to call to council, convoke, convene, Il., Hdt., attic:—so in Mid., Hdt., NTest.
to invite with others to a feast, Xen.
to be veiled, concealed, Aesch.
wrapped up, Aesch.
to cover or veil completely, Od., Eur.: Pass., συγκεκαλυμμένη muffled up, Plut.:— Mid. to wrap oneself up, cover one's face, Xen.
to labour or suffer with, sympathise with, τινί Aesch., Eur.
to work, toil or travail with another, τινί Soph., Eur.: absol. to join in labour, Soph.
a bight, joint, Xen.
to bend together, bend the knee, Plat.: Pass., συγκεκαμμένῳ τῷ σκέλει, of a person mounting a horse, Xen.: of the action of sitting down, ξυγκαμφθεὶς κάθημαι Plat.
an own sister, Eur.
an own brother or sister, Eur.
to go or come down with, τινί Eur.
to go down together, esp. to the sea-side, Thuc.
to come down to one's aid, Aesch.
to come down to, agree to, Polyb.
to throw down along with, ἑαυτόν τινι Plut.
to grow old together with, τινί Hdt.
to join in bringing back, τὸν δῆμον Aeschin.
to pursue with or together, Thuc.
to join in enslaving, τινά τινι Thuc.; so in Mid., Id.
to sink or set together with, Theocr.
a sinking together, Strab.
to yoke together, join in marriage, τινά τινι Plut.:—Pass., ἄτῃ συγκατέζευκται has become a yoke-fellow with misery, Soph.
to bury along with, Hdt.
approval, agreement, concord, NTest.
submission, Plut.
to make an inroad with another, Xen.
to die along with, τινί Mosch.
to burn together, Soph.
to agree with, favour, τινί Xen.
c. acc. rei, to sanction, approve, Plut.
to come to land together, Plut.
to burn together or also, τὰς σκηνάς Xen.:—Pass. to be burnt with, τινί Hdt.
Pass. to lie with or together, Plat.
to shut in or enclose with or together, Hdt.
to make to lie with: — Pass. to lie together, Ar.
Pass., also, to lie on the same couch with another at table, Id.
to cut up together:—Pass., Plut.
Dep. to join with another in acquiring, σ. Φιλίππῳ τὴν ἀρχήν Dem.
to slay together, Soph., Eur.
to seize, take possession of together, Xen.: to occupy at the same time, in a military sense, Thuc.
to leave together, σ. φρουράν to leave a joint garrison in a place, Thuc.
to join or help in undoing or putting down, τὸν δῆμον Thuc., etc.
to mix in with, mingle, blend with, Χάριτας Μούσαις συγκαταμιγνύς Eur.:—Pass. to be absorbed in a thing, Xen.
to be quite closed up, Anth.
to assist in conquering by sea, τινά Aeschin.
to assign also:—Mid. to divide jointly among themselves, τὴν γῆν Thuc.
to consent to a thing, τινί Polyb.
to infect likewise, Antipho.
to intertwine or intermix with, τί τινι Plut.
to join in accomplishing, Act. and Mid., Dem.
to throw down together, Luc.
to demolish with another or altogether, Eur.
Mid. to pour over at the same time, Xen.
to help in establishing or framing, Thuc., etc.; σ. τὸν πόλεμον to join in promoting the war, Dem.
to bring into one dwelling with others, Xen.
to dart down together, Plut.
to pull down with oneself, Luc.:—Pass., τὰ φρούρια τὰ εἰς τὴν Σύρων ἐπικράτειαν συγκατασπασθέντα which were at the same time brought under their dominion, Xen.
to gulp down together, Luc.
to help in stirring up, Plut.
to bring to an end together, Plut.
Mid. to conquer together or at the same time, Thuc., etc.
to arrange or draw up together, Xen.
to deposit together or at the same time: Mid., σ. τινι τὴν αὐτὴν δόξαν to deliver the same opinion with another, Plat.:—then, with dat. only, to agree with, assent to, Philipp. ap. Dem.
to eat at the same time, Plut.
to burn with or together, Luc.
Dep. to join in a lie against, τινός Aeschin.
Dep.
to condemn with or together, Plut.
Pass. to be reckoned along with others, NTest.
Dep.
to help or assist any one in accomplishing a work, τί τινι Hdt., Eur.: c. dat. only, to cooperate with, Hdt.
to help to conquer a country, Plut.
to join in murdering, Eur.
Dep. with aor. and perf. act., to come back together, return from exile together, Lys., etc.
to eat up, devour with or together, Plut.
Dep. to join in praying for a thing, Soph.
to join in accusing, τινός Dem.
to dwell with one, τινί Soph.
to colonise jointly, join in colonising, Hdt., Thuc.
to plant in a place along with others, Eur.
metaph. to establish jointly, Thuc.
Mid. to lament with or together, Soph.
to help in righting, Isocr.
to bury with, τί τινι Plut.
to patch up, cobble, of leather-workers: Pass., θώραξ ἐκ δερμάτων συγκεκαττυμένος Luc.
Pass. to lie together, Soph.
as Pass. of συντίθημι, to be composed or compounded, ἔκ τινων of certain parts, Plat., etc.
of written works, to be composed, Thuc., Plat., etc.
to be contrived, concocted, Eur., etc.
to be agreed on by two parties, Thuc.: in part. agreed on, arranged, αἱ συγκείμεναι ἡμέραι Hdt.; κατὰ τὰ συγκείμενα according to the terms agreed on, Id.; ἐκ τῶν ξυγκειμένων Thuc.
impers. σύγκειται, it has been or is agreed on, Hdt., Thuc., etc.; so, συγκειμένου σφι, c. inf., since they had agreed to . . , Hdt.

entry.etym: adverb from perf. pass. part. of συγκροτέω
entry.sense: in a finished way, Luc.
to join in ordering, Eur., Thuc.
to pierce together, to stab at once, Lat. telis confodere, Hdt.:—Pass., ἔμελλε συγκεντηθήσεσθαι Id.

entry.note: or -ύω fut. -κεράσω perf. -κέκρᾱκα Pass., fut. -κρᾱθήσομαι aor1 -εκράθην ionic -εκρήθην perf. -κεκρᾱμαι
entry.sense: to mix up with, commingle or blend with, temper by mixing with, τί τινι Plat.
to mix together, commingle, πολλά Id.; ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων ξ. to make a mixture of both, Id.
to attemper, compose, NTest.
Pass. to be commingled, blended together, Aesch., Eur., etc.
of friendships, to be formed by close union, Hdt.:—Mid., συγκεράσασθαι φιλίαν to form a close friendship, Id.
of persons, to be closely attached to, τινι Xen.: to become involved in misfortune, Soph., etc.; οἴκτῳ συγκεκραμένη deeply affected by . . , Id.
to strike with or as with a thunderbolt, shiver in pieces, Eur.
to bring together under one head, to sum up, Xen.:—Pass. to be brought under one head, summed up, Aeschin.; of business, to be summarily done, Xen.

entry.etym: adverb from perf. pass. part. of συγχέω
entry.sense: confusedly, indiscriminately, Arist.
to incur danger along with, τινί Thuc., etc.;—absol. to be partners in danger, Xen., Dem., etc.
to stir up together, NTest.
to weep with, τινί Anth.
to break off:—Pass. to be cramped, Plat.
a shutting up, closing up (of a line of battle), Thuc.
a narrow pass, defile, Plut.

entry.note: fut. -κλείσω ionic -κληίω fut. -κληίσω attic ξυγ-κλῄω fut. -κλῄσω Pass., aor1 συνεκλείσθην old attic ξυνεκλῄσθην perf. συγκέκλειμαι or -εισμαι attic ξυνκέκλῃμαι, ionic συνκεκλήιμαι
entry.sense: to shut or coop up, hem in, enclose, Hdt.; ἐς τόπον Thuc.; ξυνέκλῃε διὰ μέσου shut off and intercepted them, Id.:— Pass., λίμνη συγκεκληιμένη οὔρεσι Hdt.; συγκεκλῃμένη muffled, Eur.
to set together to fight as in the lists, Id.
to shut close, to close, ὄμμα Id.; τὰς πύλας Thuc.: absol., σύγκλειε shut the doors, Ar.
σ. τὰς ἀσπίδας to lock their shields, Xen.: absol. to close up the ranks of an army, Thuc.: Pass., τὸ οὐ ξυγκλῃσθέν the part that was not closed up, of a gap in the line, Id.
Pass. to be well linked, Eur.
to steal along with, Antipho.
a joint-heir with, τινός NTest.
having portions that join, bordering, neighbouring, Eur.
to embrace in one lot, choose by lot, Plut.
to assign by the same lot, τί τινι Dem.: to couple with one, τινά τινι Aeschin.
of senatorial rank, Lat. senatorius, Plut.
called together, summoned, Soph.
σ. ἐκκλησία at Athens, an assembly specially summoned by the στρατηγός (opp. to the ordinary meetings, αἱ κυρίαι), Decret. ap. Dem.:—generally, σύγκλητος (sc. ἐκκλησία), a legislative body, Arist.
the meeting-line at the foot of two mountain slopes, Plut.
to lay together:—Pass. to lie with another, c. dat., Hdt., Eur.
to dash together, confound utterly, Il.
washed together by the waves; metaph., ἄνθρωποι σύγκλυδες a promiscuous crowd, a mob, rabble, Lat. colluvies hominum, Thuc.; so σύγκλυδες alone, Plat.
to sleep with, lie with another, c. dat., Hdt., Trag.
partner of one's bed, in pl., Eur.
a sleeping together, Plat.
to join in wedlock, τινά τινι Ar.
Mid. to communicate, impart, τί τινι Thuc.
to have a joint share of a thing, c. gen., Dem.
c. dat. to take part in, have fellowship with, NTest.
partaking jointly of a thing, c. gen., NTest.
a bedfellow, partner, Pind.
to glue or cement together, Ar., Plat.
one who glues together, a fabricator, Ar.
glued together: adv., συγκόλλως ἔχειν to fit exactly, Aesch.
a gathering in of harvest, Thuc., Xen.
in pass. sense, a being gathered together, crowding into a place, Thuc.

to carry or bring together, collect, Hdt.:—Mid., with perf. pass., to bring together to oneself, collect, Id., Xen.; σ. πρὸς ἑαυτόν to claim as one's own, Xen.:—Pass. to be heaped together, Hdt.; metaph., ταῦτα συγκομίζεται are gained both at once, Soph.
of the harvest, to gather in, store up, house it, in Act. and Mid., Xen.:—Pass., of the harvest, ὀργᾷ συγκομίζεσθαι it is ripe for carrying, Hdt.
to help in burying, Soph.
a cutting short: in Gramm. syncope, i. e. a cutting a word short by striking out one or more letters, Plut.
to break up, cut up, Hdt., Xen.
to thrash soundly, pound well, Xen.;—Pass., perf. inf. συγκεκόφθαι Ar.; part. συγκεκομμένος Eur.
to confer honour on, to be an ornament to, Xen.
to help to lighten, help to keep above water, Luc.
a mixing together, commixture, blending, tempering, Thuc., Plat., etc.
to keep troops together, Plut.
mixed together, closely united, Eur.
to compound, Plat.
to compare, τι πρός τι Arist., etc.: to measure, estimate, Anth.
a compounding, Plat., etc.
a comparing, comparison, Arist., etc.
one must compare, Arist.
to strike together; σ. τὼ χεῖρε to clap the hands for joy, Xen.; but also to smite them together in grief, Luc.:—Pass. to be applauded, Xen.
to hammer or weld together, Ar.: hence, to weld a number of men into one body, i. e. organise them, Dem., etc.:—perf. pass. part. συγκεκροτημένος well-trained, in good discipline, Xen., Dem.
collision: a conflict, Plut.
to strike together, Lat. collido, σ. τὼ χεῖρε to clap the hands, Ar.
metaph. to bring into collision, Dem.; σ. τινὰς ἀλλήλοις to wear out by collision, Thuc.
intr. to clash together, come into collision, Id., etc.
to cover up or completely, Eur.:— to conceal utterly, Id., Xen., etc.
Dep. to win or gain along with another, c. dat., Thuc.; τὴν ὅλην χώραν συγκτήσασθαι to have gained joint possession of it, Arist.
to join with another in founding or colonising, Hdt., Thuc.
Pass., perf. part. συνεκτισμένος well-cultivated.
a joint-founder or coloniser, Hdt.
a fellow-gamester, Aeschin.
to play at dice with, τινί Hdt.
to confound utterly, Ar.
Pass. to roll about or wallow together, Xen.

entry.note: συγ-κῠνηγός, doric and attic συγ-κῠνᾱγός, οῦ, ὁ
entry.sense: a fellow-hunter, Eur.; fem. a fellow-huntress, Id.

to bend forwards, stoop and lay heads together, Ar.:—metaph., συγκύψαντες ποιοῦσι they do it in concert, in conspiracy, Hdt.; ἐς ἓν συγκεκυφέναι to be acting in concert, Ar.:—generally, to draw together, of the wings of an army, Xen.
to come together by chance, Il., Hdt.: to meet with an accident, συγκύρσαι τύχῃ Soph.; εἰς ἓν μοίρας ξυνέκυρσας art involved in one and the same fate, Eur.
c. part., like τυγχάνω, συνεκύρησε παραπεσοῦσα νηῦς fell in the way by chance, Hdt.
of events and accidents, like συμβαίνω, to happen, occur, Id., Eur.: —impers., c. inf., συνεκύρησε γενέσθαι it came to pass that . . , Hdt.:—so, in Pass., τὸ ἐς Λακεδαιμονίους συγκεκυρημένον Id.
of places, to be contiguous to, τινί Polyb.
coincidence, κατὰ συγκυρίαν by chance, NTest.
with limbs close together, Xen.
to march together in a κῶμος or band of revellers, Pind.
a fellow-reveller, Eur., Ar.
to satirise as in a comedy, Luc.
to rejoice with, take part in joy, Aesch., Ar.; τινί with another, Arist.
to wish one joy, congratulate, σ. τινὶ τῶν γεγενημένων to wish one joy of the events, Dem.
Mid. to go through the winters with one, Ar.
to put hand to a thing together, to accomplish, Isae.

entry.note: fut. -χεῶ, εῖς, εῖ aor1 -έχεα epic -έχευα inf. -χεῦαι Pass., aor1 -εχύθην epic3 sg. aor2 σύγχῠτο
entry.sense: to pour together, commingle, confound, Il., Dem., etc.:—Pass. to be in confusion, Il.
like συγχώννυμι, to make ruinous, destroy, obliterate, demolish, Hdt., Eur.
of the mind, to confound, trouble, Hom., Hdt., etc.:—Pass., Eur.
to confound, make of none effect, frustrate, Il., Hdt., attic
a companion in a dance, Xen.
to join in the dance, Ar.:— to be of the same chorus, Arist.
to furnish as supplies, Plut.
to contribute towards a thing, c. dat., Id.
a fellow-choragus: generally, sharing with a partner in the expense, Dem.
with the grass joining, i. e. bordering upon, c. gen., Eur.; Φαρσαλίας σύγχορτα πεδία i. e. the marches or boundaries of Pharsalia, Id.
Dep.
to make joint use of, avail oneself of, c. dat., Polyb.: generally to have dealings with, τινι NTest.
to borrow jointly, τί τινος something from another, Polyb.
of like colour or look, Polyb.
to confound, NTest.
a commixture, confusion, Eur.; σ. ἔχειν to be confounded, Id.
of contracts and treaties, a violation, Thuc., etc.
to melt down, Dem.

entry.note: -ύω συγχόω inf. συγχοῦν fut. -χώσω perf. pass. -κέχωσμαι
entry.sense: to heap all together, to heap with earth, cover with a mound, bank up, Hdt.
to make into ruinous heaps, demolish, Id.
generally, to confound, Aesch.
to come together, meet, πέτραι συγχωροῦσαι the Symplegades, Eur.; συγχωρεῖν λόγοις to meet in argument, Id.

to make way, give place, yield or defer to, Lat. concedere, τινί Ar., etc.; Συρηκοσίοισι τῆς ἡγεμονίης συγχ. to make concessions to them about the command, Hdt.; in bad sense, to be in collusion with, connive at, τοῖς πονηροῖς Dem.; ξ. πρός τινας to come to terms with them, Thuc.

to accede or agree, assent to, acquiesce in another's opinion, Hdt., attic:—absol. to agree, acquiesce, consent, assent, Soph.; τὸ συγκεχωρηκὸς τῆς εὐσεβείας a yielding, unexacting temper of piety, Dem.
c. acc. rei, to concede, give up, yield, Hdt., attic:—Pass., τὰ συγχωρηθέντα χρήματα Dem.
to concede or grant in argument, Plat.; c. acc. et inf. to grant that, Id.
impers. συγχωρεῖ, it is agreed, it may be done, ὅπῃ ἂν ξυγχωρῇ as may be agreed, Thuc.
a concession, Plut.
to be conceded, Luc.
neut., συγχωρητέον one must concede, Plat.: so in pl. συγχωρητέα, Soph.
impetuously, hurriedly, Aesch.
of swine, Lat. suillus, Xen., Luc.
to live with another, c. dat., Dem., etc.; c. dat. rei, σ. φιλοπραγμοσύνῃ to pass one's life in meddling, Id.:—absol. to live together, Arist.

to yoke together, couple or pair together, Hdt., Zen.: esp. in marriage, Eur., etc.:— Mid. to yoke for oneself, Xen.:—Pass. to be yoked or coupled with, τινί Eur.: absol., συζυγέντες ὁμιλοῦσι they live in close familiarity, Xen.
a being yoked together, esp. of wedded union, Plat.:—of things, close union, combination, Id.
to search or examine together with another, c. dat., Plat.
σ. τινί or πρός τινα to dispute with a person, NTest.
a joint inquirer: a disputer, NTest.
to darken utterly, Anth.
= σύζευξις, Eur.
a yoke of animals, a pair, Id., Plat.
joined, united, Eur.
yoked together, paired, σ. ὁμαυλίαι wedded union, Aesch.
as fem. Subst. a wife, Eur.; masc. a yoke-fellow, comrade, Id., Ar.

entry.etym: = σύζυγος, of a wedded pair, Eur.

entry.sense: to quicken together with, τινά τινι NTest.
to pluck ripe figs, Ar., Xen.
the fruit of the συκάμινος, a mulberry, Lat. morum, Arist.
the mulberry-tree, Lat. morus, Theophr.
= συκόμορος, NTest.
the fig-tree, Lat. ficus (the fruit being σῦκον), Od.
= σῦκον I, a fig, Ar.
to fatten with figs, Anth.
of the fig-tree, σ. ξύλον fig wood, Ar.:—the wood of the fig was spongy and useless (Horace's inutile lignum), Plat.:—hence,
metaph., σύκινοι ἄνδρες worthless, good-for-nothing fellows, Theocr.; σ. σύζυγος a false, treacherous comrade, with a play on συκοφαντικός, Ar.
a slip or cutting from a fig-tree, a young fig-tree, Ar.
to gather figs, Ar.
the fruit of the συκόμορος, Strab.
the fig-mulberry, an Egyptian kind that bears its fruit on the branches, called also συκάμινος ἡ Αἰγυπτία, Theophr.
the fruit of the συκῆ, a fig, Lat. ficus, Od., etc.: proverb., σῦκα αἰτεῖν, i. e. to be dainty, Ar.
a wart on the eyelid, Id.
Pass. to be fed with figs, Anth.
to eat figs, Theophr.
c. acc. pers. to accuse falsely, slander, calumniate, Ar., Plat.:— Pass. to be falsely accused, Xen., etc.
c. acc. rei, to misrepresent, Dem.:—but also, to extort by false accusations, Lys., NTest.
absol. to deal in false accusations, Ar., Plat.: generally, to deal falsely, to give false counsel, Dem.
a sycophant's trick, false accusation, calumny, Aeschin.

a false accuser, slanderer, Ar., etc.; (never used in the modern sense of sycophant, i. e. κόλαξ):—generally, a false adviser, Dem. (Commonly derived from σῦκον, φαίνω, one who informed against persons exporting figs from Attica: better perh. a fig-shewer, i. e. one who brings figs to light by shaking the tree (the figs having been hidden in the thick foliage); and then, metaph., one who makes rich men yield up their fruit by false accusations).
false accusation, slander, calumny, Xen., etc.
a sophism, Arist.
the Sycophant-wind (cf. καικίας) Ar.
slanderous, calumnious, Dem.: adv. -κῶς, Isocr.

entry.etym: used metri grat. for συκοφαντία, Anth.

entry.sense: to carry figs, Anth.
fig-bearing, Strab.
to carry off as booty, lead captive, NTest.

to strip off, esp. to strip off the arms of a slain enemy: c. acc. pers. et rei, to strip off from another, strip him of his arms, Il., Eur.:—Pass., c. acc. rei, to be stript, robbed, deprived of a thing, Trag.
c. acc. pers. only, to strip a man of his arms, to strip bare, pillage, plunder, Il., Hdt., etc.
c. acc. rei only, to strip off, τεύχεα ἐσύλα Il.:—also to take off or out, ἐσύλα τόξον took out the bow [from its case], Id.; σύλα πῶμα φαρέτρης took the lid off the quiver, Id.
to carry off, seize as spoil or booty, Hdt., attic:—Pass. to be carried off as spoil, Hdt.; to be taken away, Eur.; c. gen. rei, τίς σε συλᾷ πάτρας; who carries thee away from this country? Id.

entry.etym: epic for συλάω, used in pres. and imperf.
entry.sense: to despoil of arms, Il.: also, to despoil secretly, to trick, cheat, Id.
sula/w:—Mid. to steal for oneself, κηρίον ἐκ σίμβλων συλεύμενος (doric for -ούμενος) Theocr.

the right of seizing the ship or cargo of a foreign merchant, to cover losses received through him: generally, the right of seizure, right of reprisal, mostly in pl. σῦλαι or σῦλα; σύλας διδόναι τινὶ κατά τινος Dem.; ὅπου σῦλαι μὴ ὦσιν Ἀθηναίοις where the Athenians have [to fear] no right of seizure, ap. Dem.; σῦλα ποιεῖσθαι to exercise this right, Lys.
a robber, Eur.
that which holds together, Aesch.
Pass. that which is held together, of several letters taken together, so as to form one sound, a syllable, Id., Plat., etc.
to join letters into syllables, to pronounce letters together, Luc.
to be chosen by lot with others, Plut.
to talk or converse with another, NTest.

entry.note: fut. -λήψομαι perf. συνείληφα pass. -είλημμαι aor1 συνέλᾰβον inf. συλλᾰβεῖν Pass., fut. -ληφθήσομαι
entry.sense: to collect, gather together, esp. to rally scattered troops, Hdt., Xen., etc.
simply, to take with one, take up and carry off, Soph., Ar.: to buy up, Ar.
to put together, close the mouth of a corpse, Plat.; σ. αὐτοῦ τὸ στόμα to shut his mouth, Ar.
in speaking, to comprehend, comprise, Hdt., Plat.

to lay hold of, seize, grasp, c. acc., Hdt., Soph.; c. gen., σ. τῶν σχοινίων to lay hold of them, Ar.; absol. in part., ξυλλαβών quickly, in a hurry, Id.:—also in Mid., c. gen., ξυλλαβέσθαι τοῦ ξύλου Id.
to apprehend, arrest, Hdt., attic:— Pass., πρὶν ξυλληφθῆναι before they were arrested, Thuc.
of the mind, to comprehend, understand, Hdt., Pind.
to receive at the same time, enjoy together, Hdt.
of females, to conceive, Luc.
c. dat. pers. to take part with, assist, Hdt., attic:—absol. to assist, Aesch., etc.
c. dat. pers. et c. gen. rei, to take part with one in a thing, Eur., Ar.:—so in Mid., συνελάβετο τοῦ στρατεύματος Hdt.; νόσου συλλαβέσθαι Soph.: to contribute towards a thing, Thuc.

entry.note: fut. -λέξω aor1 συνέλεξα perf. -είλοχα Mid., fut. -λέξομαι aor1 -ελεξάμην Pass., fut. -λεγήσομαι aor1 -ελέχθην aor2 -ελέγην perf. -είλεγμαι
entry.sense: to collect, gather, Il., Hdt., attic: —σ. μέλη to compile, scrape together tunes, Ar.; σ. ὕβρεις αὐτοῦ to compile a list of them, Dem.:—Mid. to collect for oneself, for one's own use, Il., etc.
σ. σθένος to collect one's powers, make a rally, Eur.:—Pass. to be collected, of the mind, Plat.
Pass. to come together, become customary, Xen.
