sometimes c. part., ἐτόλμα βαλλόμενος he submitted to be struck, Od.; τόλμα ἐρῶσα Eur.
c. acc., τολμᾶν πόλεμον to undertake, venture on it, Od.; τοιαῦτα, πάντα τ. Trag.; also, τ. τὰ βέλτιστα Thuc.: Pass., οἷ’ ἐτολμήθη πατήρ such things as my father had dared (or done) against him, Eur.
an adventure, enterprise, deed of daring, Eur., etc.
τὸ τολμηρόν τινος his hardihood, Id.; adv. -ρῶς, Id.; comp. -ότερον, Id.
one must venture, Eur.
a bold, venturous man, Thuc.
to be ventured; ἔστ’ ἐκείνῳ πάντα τολμητά all things are within the compass of his daring, Soph.; ἐλπὶς τ. Eur.
for the rest, for the future:—better divisim τὸ λοιπόν.

properly, to wind off wool into a clew for spinning: metaph. to wind off, achieve, accomplish, ἐγὼ δὲ δόλους τολυπεύω, of Penelope's web (where there is a play on the literal sense), Od.; τ. πόλεμον Hom.
a clew or ball of wool, Lat. glomus, Ar., Anth.
cut, cut off, Aesch., Eur.
cut in pieces, cut or shredded ready for use, Aesch.
to need cutting, πρὸς τομῶντι πήματι for a disease that needs the knife, Soph.
one that cuts, a shoemaker's knife, Plat.: the edge of a knife, Xen.

the end left after cutting, the stump of a tree, Il.; δοκοῦ τ. the end of a beam, Thuc.; λίθοι ἐν τομῇ ἐγγώνιοι stones cut square, Id.; so, τομῇ προσθεῖσα βόστρυχον having fitted the lock to the place from which it was cut, Aesch.
a cutting, hewing, cleaving, ἐν τομᾷ σιδήρου by stroke of iron, Soph.; φασγάνου τομαί Eur.:—as a surgical operation, τομῇ χρῆσθαι Plat.; διὰ καύσεών τε καὶ τομῶν by cautery and the knife, Id.
a victim cut up for sacrifice; τὰ τόμια the parts of the victim, Dem.
cutting, ἕστηκεν ᾗ τομώτατος is placed as it will cut sharpest, Soph.
a cut, slice, Batr., Ar.
part of a book, a tome, volume,
a pitch-pipe, Plut.
to speak inarticulately, mutter, babble, Ar.
that by which a thing is stretched, a rope, cord, brace, οἱ τόνοι τῶν κλινέων the cords of beds, Hdt.; ἐκ τριῶν τόνων of three plies or strands, of ropes, Xen.:—in machines, straining-cords, Plut.
a stretching, tightening, straining, strain, tension, Hdt.
of sounds, a straining, raising of the voice, Aeschin., Dem.:— the pitch of the voice, Plat., etc.
measure, metre, Hdt.
in Music, τόνοι were modes or keys differing in pitch, of which in early Greek music there were three, the Dorian, Lydian, and Phrygian.
exertion of force, mental exertion, energy, Luc.:— generally, force, strength, intensity, Plut.
metaph. the tenour of one's way, a course, Pind., Plut.
for the present, v. νῦν 1.
Dep. to shoot with a bow, Od.; c. gen. to shoot at, Id.
mighty with the bow, Anth.
lord of the bow, bowman, archer, Aesch.
captain of the archers, Thuc.

that which is shot, an arrow, Hdt., Eur., etc.; ὅσον τ. ἐξικνέεται the distance of a bowshot, Hdt.; πρὶν τ. ἐξικνεῖσθαι before an arrow reached them, Xen.; ἐντὸς τοξεύματος within bow-shot, Id.; ἔξω τοξεύματος Thuc.:—metaph., καρδίας τοξεύματα Soph.
collective in pl. for οἱ τοξόται, the archery, Hdt.
struck by an arrow, Soph.
to shoot with the bow, τινός at a mark, Il., Soph.; εἴς τινα Hdt.:—metaph. to aim at, c. gen., Eur.:—absol. to use the bow, Hdt., Thuc., etc.; καθ’ ὑπερβολὰν τοξεύσας having shot too high, Soph.
c. acc. to shoot or hit with an arrow, τινά Eur., Xen.:—Pass. to be struck by an arrow, Thuc.
c. acc. rei, to shoot from a bow: metaph., to discharge, send forth, ὕμνους Pind.; ταῦτα ἐτόξευσεν μάτην hath shot these arrows in vain, Eur.: —Pass., πᾶν τετόξευται βέλος Aesch.
furnished with the bow, Eur.
= τοξικός, Id.; τ. ψαλμός the twang of the bowstring, Id.
of or for the bow, Aesch.:— ἡ τοξική (sc. τέχνη) archery, Plat.
of persons, skilled in the use of the bow, τοξικώτατος Xen.
shooting with the bow, Anth.
subduing with the bow, τ. Ἄρης the war of archers, i. e. the Persians, Aesch.; τ. Ἄρτεμις Eur.

a bow, Hom.; often in pl., because the ancient bow was of two pieces of horn joined by the πῆχυς in the middle; τόξα τιταίνειν or ἕλκειν to draw the bow, Il.:—as the bow was specially the Oriental weapon, τόξου ῥῦμα meant the Persians, opp. to λόγχης ἰσχύς (the Greek spearmen), Aesch.: —metaph., τόξῳ by guess, Id.
in pl. also, bow and arrows, Hom., Hdt., etc.
metaph., τόξα ἡλίου its rays, Eur.
to make like a bow, to arch, τ. τὰς ὀφρῦς, of a supercilious person, Ar.
bowmanship, archery, Il., Eur.
a bowman, archer, Il., Hdt., Trag., etc.
the Archer, Sagittarius, a sign in the Zodiac, Luc.
at Athens, οἱ τοξόται were the city-guard, also called Σκύθαι, because they were slaves bought from the parts north of Greece, Ar., etc.
drawing the bow, Aesch.
αἰχμὴ τ. the bowstretching arrow, Id.
to bear a bow, of Eros, Anth.
bow-bearing, Il., Eur., etc.: — ὁ τοξοφόρος = τοξότης, Hdt.
the topaz, Anth.
to aim at, guess, Aesch., Ar.
better written divisim τὸ πάλαι, τὸ παλαιόν, etc.
ruling over a place, γυνὴ τ. the mistress, Aesch.
concerning τόποι or common-places, Arist.
to determine the site, Strab.
to mark the site of a place, Strab.
to wage war by holding strong positions, Plut.

a place, Lat. locus, Aesch., etc.; periphr., χθονὸς πᾶς τόπος, i. e. the whole earth, Id.; Πέλοπος ἐν τόποις in Peloponnesus, Id., etc.; ὁ τόπος τῆς χώρας the local circumstances of the district, Dem.
place, position, Aeschin.
a place or passage in an author, NTest., etc.
a topic, Aeschin.: a common-place in Rhetoric, Arist.
metaph. a place, occasion, opportunity, Thuc.
better written divisim τὸ πρίν, etc.
a carving in relief, Plut.
a borer, piercer, Anth.
worked in relief: metaph. elaborate, Anth.
to work in relief, Strab.:—c. acc. to represent in this manner, Anth.
to bore through, pierce, Il.
metaph. to proclaim in shrill piercing tones, in redupl. fut. τετορήσω, Ar.: cf. τορός.
like τορνεύω, to work, shape, Anth.
any hole or socket, in which a pin or peg is stuck, Hdt.
lyre-turner and shield-maker, Ar.
to work with a lathe-chisel: metaph. of verses, to turn neatly, to round off, Ar.
to turn round, as an auger, Eur.

Dep. to mark off with the τόρνος, to make round, τορνώσαντο σῆμα they rounded off the barrow, Il.; ὅσσον τίς τ’ ἔδαφος νηὸς τορνώσεται large as the bottom of a ship which a man shall round off, with allusion to the round shape of a merchant-vessel (cf. γαυλός), Od.
a carpenter's tool for drawing a circle, compasses, Theogn., Hdt., Eur.
piercing:
of the voice, piercing, thrilling, Luc.; so in adv., τορῶς γεγωνεῖν Eur.:—metaph., τ. φόβος thrilling fear, Aesch.
metaph. clear, distinct, plain, Id.:—so in adv., τορῶς τεκμαίρειν, λέγειν Id., etc.
of persons, sharp, ready, smart, Xen.:—so in adv., ἐπερείδεσθαι τορῶς Ar.
imitation of a bird's note, Ar.
a stirrer, ladle, Ar.
to stir, stir up or about, Ar.
so many times, so often, Il.
to-day, Bion.
c. inf. so strong, so able, to do a thing, Od.
neut. τοσόνδε, epic τοσσόνδε, as adv. so very, so much, Hom., etc.; of Time, so long, Aesch.
as Subst., τοσόνδ’ ἔχεις τόλμης Soph.

antecedent to relat. ὅσος; Lat. tantus: of Size, Space, Quantity, so great, so vast: of Time, so long: of Number, in pl., so many: of Sound, so loud: of Degree, so much, so very:— often in Hom. and Hes., οὔτι τόσος γε ὅσος Αἴας not so huge as Ajax, Il.: absol. just so much or just so many, Od.; τρὶς τόσσα δῶρα thrice as many gifts, Il.; δὶς τόσα κακά Soph.
used for ὅσος, Lat. quantus, Pind.
τόσον and τόσσον as adv., so much, so far, so very, Lat. tantum, τ. πλέες so many more, Il., etc.
ἐκ τόσου so long since, Hdt.
τόσῳ with a comp., and by so much more, Thuc.
regul. adv., δὶς τόσως Eur.
of so large a number, Aesch.
later attic for τοσοῦτος, with a stronger demonstr. force, Ar., Plat., etc.

= τόσος in all senses, but with a stronger demonstr. force, Hom., etc.; of persons, so large, so tall, καί σε τοσοῦτον ἔθηκα Il.; so great in rank, skill,or character, Soph., etc.:—in pl. so many, Hom.,etc.:—also τοσοῦτος μέγαθος so large, Hdt.; τοσοῦτος τὸ βάθος so deep, Xen.:—with numeral Advs., δὶς τ.,πολλάκις τ., etc., Thuc., etc.; ἕτερον τοσοῦτο as large again, Hdt.

neut. as Subst., so much, thus much, τοσσοῦτον ὀνήσιος Od.; τοσαῦτ’ ἔλεξε Aesch.; —with Preps., διὰ τοσούτου at so small a distance, Thuc.;— ἐς τοσοῦτο so far, Lat. hactenus, eatenus, Hdt., etc.;— ἐκ τ. from so far, so far off, Xen.;— ἐν τοσούτῳ in the meantime, Ar.;— ἐπὶ τοσοῦτο so far, Hdt.;— κατὰ τοσοῦτον so far, Plat.;— μέχρι τοσούτου so far, so long, Thuc.;— παρὰ τοσοῦτον κινδύνου into such imminent danger, Id.
neut. also as adv., so much, so far, Od., Soph., etc.
so much, Hom., Thuc., etc.:—but τοσούτῳ is more common with Comparatives, Hdt., etc.

entry.etym: aor1 part. of an unknown pres.
entry.sense: to happen to be, Pind.
so great, much, Anth.: in pl. so many, Id.
better written divisim τὸ τελευταῖον, etc.
at times, now and then, τοτὲ μὲν . . , τοτὲ δὲ . . , at one time . . , at another . . , Od., Aesch., etc.; τοτ’ ἄλλος, ἄλλοθ’ ἅτερος Soph.; τοτὲ μὲν . . , αὖθις δὲ . . , Plat.
at that time, then, Lat. tunc, Antec. to Relat. ὅτε or ὁπότε, opp. to νῦν, Il., Hom., etc.:—also in indef. sense, in those times, formerly, Soph., etc.; τότ’ ἢ τότε at one time or other, Aesch., Eur.
joined with other Particles, καὶ τότε δή Hom.; καὶ τότ’ ἔπειτα Il.; τότε δή ῥα Od., etc.; τότ’ ἤδη then at length, Hes.
with the Article, οἱ τότε the men of that time, Il., etc.; οἱ τότε ἄνθρωποι Hdt.; τῇ τόθ’ ἡμέρᾳ Soph.; ἐν τῷ τότε (sc. χρόνῳ) Thuc.
εἰς τότε until then, Dem.; ἐκ τότε or ἐκτότε since then, Plut.
imitation of a bird's note, Ar.
an exclam., Aesch.; τοτοτοῖ, Soph.
better written divisim τὸ τρίτον.
for that reason, therefore, Hom., etc.
interrog., for τίνος ἕνεκα; wherefore? Anth.
hence, thence, Theocr.
demonstr. adv. of Time, up to or during that time, so long, antecedent to relat. ὄφρα, Il.
absol. meanwhile, Hom.
of or from the Epirotic city Τραγασαί, Strab.:—of swine, Τραγασαῖα in Tragasaean fashion, with a play on τραγεῖν, Ar.; Τραγασαίου πατρός, with a play on τράγος, Id.
of or from a he-goat: ὁ τραγείη (sc. δορά) a goat's skin, Theocr.
the goat-stag, as the Greeks called a fantastic animal, represented on Eastern carpets and the like, Ar.
properly that which is eaten for eating's sake, mostly in pl., dried fruits or sweetmeats, eaten as dessert, Lat. bellaria, Ar., Xen.
to eat sweetmeats, Arist.: so Mid., τραγηματίζομαι, Theophr.
of or like a goat, goatish, Plut., etc.
of or for tragedy, tragic (cf. τραγῳδία), Hdt., Xen., etc.; τρ. λῆρος tragic trumpery, Ar.
generally, tragic, stately, majestic, Id., Plat.
in bad sense, in tragic style, plaintive, Dem.
adv. -κῶς, in tragic style or fashion, Plat.
οἰκεῖν τρ. to live in splendour, Plut.
of a he-goat, Anth.
a young he-goat, Theocr., Anth.
for shearing he-goats, Luc.
of slaughtered goats, Eur.
with armpits smelling like a he-goat, Ar.
goat-footed, Anth.
goat-shanked, Hdt., Luc.
a he-goat, Lat. hircus, Od., etc.
to eat he-goats, Strab.
to act a tragedy, Ar.
c. acc. objecti, to represent in tragedy, Luc.:—Pass. to be the subject of a tragedy, Isocr., etc.
metaph. to tell in tragic phrase, to declaim, Dem.

a tragedy, invented by the Dorians, and at first of lyric character (τραγικοὶ χοροί Hdt.); then transplanted to Athens, where it assumed its dramatic form, Ar., etc. Its proper sense is goat-song, because in early times a goat was the prize, or because the actors were clothed in goat-skins.
generally, any grave, serious poetry, Plat.
befitting tragedy, χοροί Hdt., Ar.; τραγῳδικὸν βλέπειν to look tragic, Ar.; ὠδυνήθην τραγῳδικόν suffered a tragic woe, Id.
writing tragedies, Polyb.
a tragic poet, who trained his own chorus and actors, Ar.
a maker of tragedies, a tragic poet, tragedian, Ar., Plat., etc.

properly, a goat-singer (v. τραγῳδία), i. e. a tragic poet and singer, these characters being orig. one, Ar.:—later, when the poets ceased to act, the term meant a tragedian or tragic actor, the tragic poet being called τραγῳδοποιός or τραγῳδοδιδάσκαλος.
of members of the tragic chorus, Ar.
the pl. is often used = τραγῳδία, ἐν τοῖσι τραγῳδοῖς in tragedy, Id., Dem., etc.
Trallians, Thracian barbarians, Plut.
piercing: metaph. clear, distinct:—adv., τρανῶς εἰδέναι, μανθάνειν Aesch., Eur.; comp. τρανότερον, Anth.
to make clear, plain, distinct, Anth.

four-legged a table, esp. a dining-table, Hom., Hdt., etc.; ξενίη τρ. the hospitable board, Od.; τραπέζῃ καὶ κοίτῃ δέκεσθαι to entertain at bed and board, Hdt.; Περσικὴν τράπεζαν παρετίθετο he kept a table in the Persian fashion, Thuc.; εἰς ἀλλοτρίαν τράπεζαν βλέπειν to live at other men's table, Xen.
a table, as implying what is upon it, a dinner, meal, Hdt., etc.; Συρακοσία τρ., proverb. of luxurious living, Hor. Siculae dapes, Plat.
a money-changer's table, a bank, Lat. mensa argentaria, Id., etc.; ἡ ἐγγύη ἡ ἐπὶ τὴν τρ. security given to the bank, Dem.; οἱ ἐπὶ ταῖς τραπέζαις bankers, Isocr.
at, of a table, κύνες τραπεζῆες (ionic for τραπεζεῖς) dogs fed from their master's table, Hom.
to be engaged in banking, Dem.
one who keeps a bank, a banker, Lat. argentarius, Dem.
of or for the banker, Isocr.
table-making, Strab.
to tread grapes, Od., Hes.
one must turn, Luc.
a crate, whereon to dry figs, Ar.
to lisp, Lat. balbutire, as Alcibiades made r into l, Ar.; of children, Id.
lisping, Lat. balbus, esp. of children, Hdt.
of the swallow, twittering, Anth.
a lisping, Plut.

entry.note: τραῦμα, ionic and doric τρῶμα, ατος, τό,
entry.sense: a wound, hurt, Hdt., attic; τραῦμα λαβεῖν ὑπό τινος Dem.; λαβεῖν καὶ δοῦναι Plut.
of things, a hurt, damage, as of ships, Hdt.
in war, a blow, defeat, Id.
ἡ τραύματος γραφή an indictment for wounding (with intent to murder), Aeschin.
to wound, Hdt., attic
a wounded man, οἱ τρ. the wounded of an army, Hdt., Thuc.
properly, well-fed, οἱ τραφεροί or τὰ τραφερά the fat ones, i.e. fishes, Theocr.
τραφερή (sub. γῆ), as Subst. the dry land, land, ἐπὶ τραφερήν τε καὶ ὑγρήν Hom.
of, on, or from the neck, Strab.
scraps of meat and gristle about the neck, scraps, offal, Ar.
of wrestlers, to bend the neck back, and so to overpower, Theophr.:—Pass. to have one's neck bent back so that the throat gapes when cut: hence, to be laid open, NTest.
chaining the neck, Anth.
the neck, throat, Hdt., Eur., etc.

Trachis, in Thessaly, named from the ruggedness (τραχύτης) of the district, Il., etc.:—adj. Τρᾱχῑ́νιος, η, ον, ionic Τρηχ-, Hdt., etc.; also ος, ον, Theocr.:— οἱ Τραχίνιοι the people of Trachis, Hdt., etc.:— ἡ Τραχινία the country, Id., Soph., etc.; also called Τραχίς, Thuc.
to make rough, rugged, uneven, Plat.:—Pass. to become rough, Id.; τρ. τῇ φωνῇ to use rough harsh tones, Plut.
in Aesch. Theb., τράχυνε refers to τραχύς γε μέντοι δῆμος (just before) call them rough, I care not.
metaph. in Pass. to be exasperated, Plat.
intr. to be rough, Plut.
rugged, rough, Lat. asper, Hom., etc.; as epith. of Ithaca, Od.; cf. Τραχίς:—also, rough, shaggy, Xen.:—of a bit, rough, sharp, Id.: of the voice of boys, when it breaks, Plut.
rough, harsh, savage, Pind., Aesch., etc.
adv. τρᾱχέως, ionic τρηχέως, roughly, Hdt.; τραχέως ἔχειν to be rough, Isocr.; τρ. φέρειν, Lat. aegre ferre, Plut.
of rough speech or pronunciation, Strab.
roughness, ruggedness, Xen.; sharpness, of a bit, Id.
of persons, roughness, harshness, ὀργῆς Aesch.
a rugged, stony tract, Luc.; so Τραχωνῖτις, ιδος, NTest., etc.
thirteen, Hdt., attic; also written divisim, gen. τριῶν καὶ δέκα, dat. τρισὶ καὶ δέκα, etc.:—an indecl. form τρισκαίδεκα occurs, in all genders and cases, Hom., Ar., etc.
Lat. tres, tria, three, Hom., etc.
Lat. tremo, to tremble, quake, quiver, Il., Eur.:—c. inf. to tremble or fear to do, Aesch., Soph.: —c. acc. to tremble at, fear, Soph., Eur., etc.
one must turn, Ar.
to turn or direct towards a thing, Hom., etc.; mostly followed by a prep., τρ. τινὰ εἰς εὐνήν to shew him to bed, Od.; τρ. πόλεις ἐς ὕβριν Thuc.; τρ. κεφαλὴν πρὸς ἠέλιον Od.
Pass. to turn one's steps, turn in a certain direction, τραφθῆναι ἀν’ Ἑλλάδα to roam up and down Greece, Od.; c. acc. cogn., τρέπεσθαι ὁδόν to take a course, Hdt.
Pass. also to turn or betake oneself, εἰς ἀοιδήν Od.; ἐπὶ ἔργα Il.; ἐφ’ ἁρπαγήν Thuc.; πρὸς ληιστείαν Id.
Pass. and Mid., of places, to be turned or look in a certain direction, πρὸς ζόφον Od.; πρὸς ἄρκτον, πρὸς νότον Hdt., etc.

to turn, i. e. turn about, τρέπειν ἵππους Il.; τὰ καλὰ τρ. ἔζω to turn the best side outmost, Pind.:—Pass., αἰχμὴ τράπετο the point bent back, Il.; of the solstice, ἐπειδὰν ἐν χειμῶνι τράπηται ἥλιος (v. τροπή I) Xen.
τρ. τὴν αἰτίαν, τὴν ὀργὴν εἴς τινα to divert the blame, the anger upon another, Isae., Dem.:—Pass., in imprecations, ἐς κεφαλὴν τρέποιτο ἐμοί on my head be it! Ar.
to turn another way, to alter, change, νόον, φρένας Hom., etc.; ἐς γέλων τρ. τὸ πρᾶγμα Ar.:—Pass. to be changed, change, Hom., etc.; c. acc. cogn., τρεπόμενος τροπάς undergoing changes, Aeschin.

to turn or put to flight, rout, defeat, Il., Hdt., etc.; τρ. φύγαδε, Lat. convertere in fugam, Il.; τρ. ἐς φυγήν Eur.;—so, in aor1 mid., to put an enemy to flight, Xen.:—Pass. to be put to flight, turn and flee, Aesch., Xen., etc.; so in Mid., ἐς φυγὴν τραπέσθαι Hdt., Thuc.:—also intr. in Act., φύγαδ’ ἔτραπε Il.
to turn away, keep off, hinder, τρ. τινὰ ἀπὸ τείχεος Id.; βέλος ἔτραπεν ἄλληι Id.
to overturn, like ἀνατρέπω, Aesch.
to turn, apply, τρ. τι ἐς ἄλλο τι Hdt.; ποῦ τέτροφας τὰς ἐμβάδας; what have you made of your shoes? Ar.:—Pass., ποῖ τρέπεται τὰ χρήματα; Id.
to thicken or congeal a liquid, γάλα θρέψαι to curdle it. Od.; τυρὸν τρέφειν Theocr.:—Pass., with intr. perf. act. τέτροφα, to become firm, περὶ χροῒ τέτροφεν ἄλκη Od.

to make to grow or increase, to bring up, breed, rear, Hom., etc.; c. acc. cogn., τρ. τινὰ τροφήν τινα to bring up in a certain way, Hdt.:—Mid. to rear for oneself, Od., etc.:—Pass. to reared, grow up, Hom.; κάρτιστοι τράφεν ἄνδρες grew up the strongest men, Il.; ἐξ ὅτου ’τράφην ἐγώ from the time when I left the nursery, Ar.; μιᾶς τρέφει πρὸς νυκτός, i. e. art a child of night, Soph.

of slaves, horses, dogs and the like, to rear and keep them, Hom., etc.; τρ. παιδαγωγούς Aeschin.; τρ. γυναῖκα Eur.;—metaph., αἰγιαλὸν ἔνδον τρέφει he keeps quite a sea-beach in the house, Ar.:—Pass. to bred, reared, Soph.
to let grow, cherish, foster, χαίτην τρέφε Il.; τρ. ὑπήνην Ar.; τρ. κόμην = κομᾶν, Hdt.;—also, τάδ’ ὕεσσι τρέφει ἀλοιφήν this is what puts fat on swine, Od.
of earth and sea, to produce, teem with, χθὼν τρέφει φάρμακα Id.; θάλασσα τρέφουσα πορφύραν Aesch.

to have within oneself, to contain, keep, have, ὅ τι πόλις τέτροφεν ἄφιλον Soph.; τρέφειν τὴν γλῶσσαν ἡσυχωτέραν to keep his tongue more quiet, Id.; νόσον τρ. Id.; οἵας λατρείας τρέφει what services she constantly performs, Id.
maintain, support, τρ. Ἥλιος χθονὸς φύσιν Aesch.; τρ. τὸν πατέρα Aeschin.: esp. to maintain an army or navy, Thuc., Xen.
aor2 act. in intr. sense, ἔτραφον = pass. ἐτράφην, ὃς ἔτραφ’ ἄριστος Il.; τραφέμεν (ionic for τραφεῖν) Hom.
so perf. τέτροφα, v. supr. I.
a twig, Anth.
a twig, Anth.

entry.etym: δραμοῦμαι and ἔδραμον from Root ΔΡΕΜ or ΔΡΑΜ
entry.sense: to run, Lat. curro, Hom., etc.:—of horses, Il.:—of things, to run, move quickly, Hom., etc.
c. acc. loci, to run over, Eur., Xen.

c. acc. cogn., τρ. δρόμον, ἀγῶνα to run a course, a heat, Eur., etc.: often metaph., ἀγῶνα δρ. to run a risk, Id.; πολλοὺς ἀγῶνας δραμεῖν περὶ σφέων αὐτέων to run many risks for their lives, Hdt.:—sometimes the acc. is omitted, τρ. περὶ ἑωυτοῦ to run the risk of his life, Id.; τρ. περὶ τῆς νίκης Xen.
παρ’ ἓν πάλαισμα ἔδραμε νικᾶν he was within one bout of carrying off the victory, Hdt.

entry.etym: this Verb is never contracted, except when the contraction is into ει
entry.sense: to flee from fear, flee away, Il.; μὴ τρέσας without fear, Aesch.; οὐδὲν τρέσας Plat.:— τρέσας is used like a Subst., a runaway, coward, Il.; Ἀριστόδημος ὁ τρέσας Hdt.
trans. to flee from, fear, dread, be afraid of, c. acc., Il., Trag., Xen.
a perforation, hole, aperture, orifice, Lat. foramen, Ar., Plat.
porous, Anth.
timorous, shy, Hom.

perforated, with a hole in it, Od.; τρητὰ λέχεα, prob. inlaid bedsteads, or having holes through which the cords that supported the bedding were drawn:— τρητὸς μελισσῶν πόνος, i. e. the honeycomb, Pind.; τρ. λίθαξ pumice-stone, Anth.
a trident, the badge of Poseidon, Hom.
to heave with the trident: generally, to heave or prise up, overthrow, Eur.
τρ. τὴν γῆν δικέλλῃ to break it up with a mattock, Ar.
the number thirty, Aesch.
the thirtieth day of the month, Hes.: hence, a month, containing 30 days, Luc.

sense.gloss: a political division, containing thirty families.

entry.sense: with or of thirty knots, Xen.
of thirty days, Hdt.
thirty years old, Plat.; in contr. form, οἱ τριακοντοῦται the men of thirty years, Id.; fem. τριακοντοῦτις Isae.
τριακονταέτης, ες, of or for thirty years, Thuc.;—in fem. form, σπονδαὶ τριηκοντουτίδες Hdt.; αἱ τριακοντούτιδες σπονδαί Ar.
with thirty benches, Theocr.
thirty times, Plut.

entry.etym: indecl., with a gen. τριηκόντων in Hes.; dat. τριηκόντεσσιν Anth.
entry.sense: thirty, Lat. triginta, Hom., etc.
οἱ τριάκοντα,
at Sparta, the council of thirty, assigned to the kings, Xen.
at Athens, the Thirty, commonly called the thirty tyrants, appointed on the taking of Athens (B C. 404), Plat., etc.
the rule of the Thirty, at Athens, Xen.
producing thirtyfold, Strab.
(sc. ναῦς), a thirty-oared ship, Thuc., Xen.; in Hdt. written τριηκόντερος.,
of thirty fathoms, Xen.
three hundred, Hom., Hdt., etc.; also with collective noun in sg., ἵππος τρ. Xen.
οἱ τρ. at Athens, the richest members of the συμμορίαι, who managed their affairs, Dem.
the Three Hundred, who fell at Thermopylae, Hdt.
those whose property produced 300 medimni, i. e. the Ἱππεῖς.
bearing three hundredfold, Strab.
the thirtieth, Hdt., etc.
τριακοστή, a duty of one-thirtieth, Dem.
a victor, Aesch.
to vanquish, of a wrestler, who did not win until he had conquered in three bouts (παλαίσματα).
with three sails or masts, Luc.
the number three, a triad, Plat.
rubbed, worn, Anth., Luc.
the Triballi, a people on the borders of Thrace; as a Comic name for barbarian gods, Ar.:—adj. Τριβαλλικός, ή, όν, Hdt.
three-pointed, Anth.
a rubbing or wearing away, wasting, Aesch.
practice, as opp. to theory, Xen.: also mere practice, routine, as opp. to true art, Plat.
that about which one is busied, an object of care, Lat. cura, Aesch.
of Time, a spending, Soph., Plat.; ἀξίαν τριβὴν ἔχει 'tis time well spend, Aesch.; βίος οὐκ ἄχαρις ἐς τὴν τριβήν a life pleasant enough in the spending, Ar.
delay, putting off, ἐς τριβὰς ἐλᾶν to seek delays, Soph.; τριβὰς πορίζειν Ar.; and with the Verb omitted, μὴ τριβὰς ἔτι no more delays, Soph.
in Ar. τριβολεκτράπελα στωμύλλειν to deal in coarse rude jests.
as Subst. a caltrop, i. e. a three-spiked implement, formed so that one of the spikes must point upwards, used to lame the enemy's horses, Plut.
a prickly plant, a burr, thistle, NTest.
τρίβολοι, οἱ, a threshing-machine, boards with sharp stones fixed in the bottom, Anth.
a worn or beaten track, the high road, highway, Hdt., Eur.: a footpath, Xen.
rubbing, attrition, Aesch.
metaph. delay, Id.
like a τρίβων, cloak-wise, Ar.
as adj. practised or skilled in a thing, c. gen., Hdt., Eur., etc.
absol., a hackneyed, crafty fellow, rogue, Ar.

to rub: to rub or thresh corn, Il.; μοχλὸν τρῖψαι ἐν ὀφθαλμῶι to work round the stake in his eye, Od.; χρυσὸν βασάνωι τρ. to rub it on a touchstone, so as to test its purity (cf. παρατρίβω), Theogn.:—Mid., χρηστηρίοις ἐν τοῖσδε τρίβεσθαι μύσος to rub one's pollution upon these shrines, pollute them with it, Aesch.
to rub down, grind, pound, Ar., etc.
to crush, βότρυν Id.
to wear out by rubbing: Pass., of a road, to wear or tread it smooth, ἀτραπὸς τετριμμένη Id.
of Time, to wear away, spend, Lat. terere vitam, Soph., Eur.:— absol. to waste time, tarry, Aesch.
to waste or ravage a country, Eur.
metaph.,
of persons, to wear out, Hes.: Pass. to be worn out, Il., Thuc.:—Mid., τρίψεσθαι αὐτὴν περὶ αὑτήν to wear itself out by internal struggles, Id.:—Pass., τριβόμενος ληός an oppressed people, Hdt.
of money and property, to waste, squander it, Id.
to use constantly, Ar.
Pass. to be much busied or engrossed with a thing, Hdt.
a third generation, Strab.
triply old, τρ. μῦθος τάδε φωνεῖ 'tis a thrice-told tale, Aesch.
a triple (i. e. huge) giant, Orph.
with three pupils: then, of earrings, with three bright drops, Hom.
the red mullet: also τρίγλᾰ, Anth.
bearing mullets, τρ. χιτών a net for catching them, Anth.
in Doric architecture, the triglyph, a three-grooved tablet placed at equal distances along the frieze, Eur.:—also τρίγλυφον, ου, τό, Arist.
three-barbed, Il.
a scream, squeak, Plut.
the third generation, Dem.
thrice-born: in pl. simply = τρεῖς, three, Eur.
triangular-shaped, Polyb.
three-cornered, triangular, Aesch.
as Subst., τρίγωνον, ου, a triangle, Plat.: name of a musical instrument, Id.
a slave through three generations, thrice a slave, Soph.
worth or weighing three drachms, Ar.
thrice coiled, Orac. ap. Hdt., Anth.
like three ships' beaks, Ar.
(sc. ἑορτή) a triennial festival, Hdt., Eur.
(sub. περίοδος), a period of three years, Hhymn., Arist.
of or for three years, Hdt., Theocr.: netut. τριέτες as adv. for three years, Od.
and τρίζυξ, three yoked, three in union, of the Graces, Eur., Anth.
of animals, to utter a shrill cry, to scream, cry, of young birds, Il.; of bats, Od.; of ghosts (which, in Shaksp., "squeak and gibber"), Hom., etc.
of other sounds, νῶτα τετρίγει (epic plup.) the wrestlers' backs cracked, Il.; τρ. τοὺς ὀδόντας to gnash the teeth, NTest.; of a musical string, to twang, Anth.
a length of three half-feet, a foot and a-half, Xen.
to be a τριήραρχος, to command a trireme, Hdt., Thuc.: c. gen., τρ. νηός Hdt.

at Athens, to be trierarch, i. e. fit out a trireme for the public service, Ar.; Pass., τριηραρχοῦσιν οἱ πλούσιοι, ὁ δὲ δῆμος τριηραρχεῖται the rich find trierarchs, the people has trierarchs found it, Xen.
the trierarch's crew, Dem.
the command of a trireme, Arist.
at Athens, the fitting out of a trireme for the public service, a trierarchy, Xen.
of or for the trierarchy, Dem.
the captain of a trireme, Hdt., attic
at Athens, a trierarch, who had to fit out a trireme for the public service, Ar., Thuc.
the flute-player, who gave the time to the rowers in the trireme, Dem.
Lat. triremis, a galley with three banks of oars, the common form of the Greek ship-of-war, Hdt., etc.: first built by the Corinthians, Thuc.:—cf. θαλάμιος, ζυγίτης, θρανίτης.
of or for a trireme, Dem.
a trireme-man, Hdt., Thuc.
building triremes, Dem.
touching on or connected with three seas, Strab.
the Three-headed, a satirical attack on three cities, Sparta, Athens, Thebes, Luc.
three-headed, Hes., Hdt.
three-headed, Luc.
with three couches: as Subst., τρίκλινος (sub. οἶκος), a dining-room with three couches, the Roman triclinium.
thrice-spun, three-twisted, Anth.
three-hilled, Orac. in Strab.

entry.note: τρῐ-κόρῠθος, ον; and τρί-κορυς, ῠθος, ὁ,
entry.sense: with triple plume, Eur.
three-topped, Strab.
thrice a crow's age, Anth.
three-headed, of Cerberus, Soph., Eur.
the third wave, a huge wave, for the third was supposed to be the largest (as in Lat. the fluctus decumanus), Plat.:—metaph., τρ. κακῶν Aesch.
thrice (i. e. often or earnestly) prayed for, Il.
a trilogy, v. τετραλογία.
a triple crest, Ar.
thrice-blest, Anth.

of verses, consisting of three metres; i. e. in iambics, trochaics, and anapaestics, of three syzygies (of two feet each); but in dactylics of three single feet: τρ. ἴαμβος an iambic verse of three metres or six feet, versus senarius, Hdt.; so τόνος τρίμετρος trimeter verse, Id.; τρίμετρον, ου, Ar.
of three months, Soph.; so, ἡ τρίμηνος a period of three months, Hdt.
that which is rubbed: metaph., like τρίβων II. 2, a practised knave, Ar.
a beaten road, Xen.
a triple portion, triple pay, Xen.
threefold, triple, Aesch.
three-formed:—in pl. = τρεῖς, Μοῖραι τρ. the three fates, Aesch.
Sicily, a later form of Θρινακίη, Thuc.
a trident or three-pronged mattock, Anth.
a meeting of three roads, Lat. trivium, Theogn., Eur., etc.
Hecate, Lat. Trivia, ἁ θεὸς ἐν τριόδοισι Theocr.; οἷος ἐκ τριόδου i. e. vulgar, Luc.
with three teeth, three-pronged: as Subst., a trident, Pind.
a headland of Caria, on which was a temple consecrated to Apollo, τὸ Τριοπικὸν ἱρόν, ὁ Τριόπιος Ἀπολλών Hdt.
a kind of hawk, perh. the buzzard, Ar.
a sound imitative of a bird's voice, Ar.
having three children, Plut.
long long ago, Ar.
three hands broad, long, etc., Hdt.
thrice-brandished; metaph. threefold, manifold, Aesch.
triply-base, an arch-rogue, Anth.
thrice-fattened, thrice-gorged, Aesch.
Prefix, from τρίς or τρίᾰ, in compds. three times, thrice, Lat. ter.
three-leafed, Hhymn.
three cubits long or tall, Hdt., attic
thrice or thoroughly apish, Anth.
triple, threefold, Lat. triplex, Il.
to triple, take three times, Plut.
thrice as many, thrice as much, thrice as great as, c. gen., Ar., Plat., etc.: —absol., τριπλασίαν δύναμιν εἶχε (sc. τῆς προτέρας) Xen.
τριπλάσιον as adv., τριπλάσιον thrice as much, Ar.
three πλέθρα wide, Xen.
triple, threefold, ἐν τριπλαῖς ἀμαξιτοῖς = ἐν τριόδῳ, Soph.; ὄνομα τρ. compounded of three, Arist.:—attic neut. pl. τριπλᾶ, Aesch.:—dat. fem. τριπλῇ as adv., Il., Luc.
three feet long, Hes.
to bring a tripod, offer it as a sign of victory, Strab.
thrice (i. e. much)longed for, Bion., Mosch.
with three cities, Pind.
thrice-repeated, Soph.
thrice ploughed, Hom., Hes.
τρῐπόνητος, ἔρις, ἡ, a contest between three labouring women, Anth.
thrice-wasted, Anth.
three-footed, of or with three feet: and so
measuring three feet, Hdt., Plat.
going on three feet, of an old man who leans on a staff, Hes.; so, τρίποδας ὁδοὺς στείχει Aesch.
with three feet, three-legged:
a tripod, a three-footed brass kettle or caldron, Hom.: —from a tripod of this kind (Lat. cortina) the Delphic Priestess delivered her oracles, Eur., Ar.
a three-legged table, Xen.
the vat into which the oil runs when pressed out: metaph., τρ. δικῶν a vat to receive the juice of law-suits, Ar.
a rubber, shampooer, Plut.
threefold, Lat. triplex, Il., Eur.
of or with three horses: τρ. ἅρμα δαιμόνων, of the three goddesses on Mount Ida, Eur.
with three poles, i. e. with four horses abreast, Aesch.
thrice-unhappy, Soph., etc.
thrice-tormented, Anth.
thrice-numbered, Orac. ap. Luc.
thrice-pleased, most willing, Xen.
thrice-untimely, Anth.
(sc. ἡμέρα) άδος, the third ninth day in a month; i. e. the ninth day (ἡ ἐννεάς) of the third decad, the 29th, Hes.
thrice an ἔπαρχος, i. e. Praetor, Anth.
thrice-happy, Luc.
thirteen cubits high, ἀνὴρ τρ., of a long lazy loon, Theocr.
of thirteen times the value of silver, Hdt.
thirteenth, Hom., etc.; ἡ τρισκαιδεκάτη (sc. ἡμέρα) the 13 th day, Od.
fruiting thirteen times, Luc.
thirteen years old, Lys.
thrice unlucky, Ar.
with three oarpins; but νᾶες αἱ τρ. are simply = τριήρεις, Aesch.
thrice-accursed, Dem.
three-legged, ξόανον Theocr.
thrice-kneaded, Batr.
thrice-blest, Od., Ar., etc.
thrice ten thousand, 30, 000, Hdt., Ar., etc.:—in sg. with a collective Subst., τρισμυρία ἵππος thirty thousand horse, Aesch.
thirty thousand times long-ago, Ar.
thrice happy or fortunate, Anth.
thrice victorious at Olympia, Pind.
three spans long, Hes., Xen.
thrice-poured, τρ. χοαί a triple drink-offering, of honey, milk, and wine, Soph.

thrice, three times, Lat. ter, Hom., etc.; τρὶς τόσος thrice as much or many, Il., etc.; ἐς τρίς up to three times, even thrice, Hdt., attic: —used to add force to a word in compds., such as τρισάθλιος, τρίσμακαρ, like Lat. ter beatus, thrice blest: — proverb., τρὶς ἓξ βάλλειν to throw thrice six, i. e. the highest throw (there being three dice), Aesch.
from three sides, Anth.
threefold, Lat. triplex, Eur., etc.:—adv. -ῶς, Anth.
in pl., = τρεῖς, Pind., Soph., etc.
of or with three stories: τὸ τρ. (sc. οἴκημα) the third story, NTest.
in three rows, Il., Hes.
in three rows, Od.:— threefold, Anth.
three-edged or -pointed, Anth.
trisyllabic, Luc.
three thousand, Il., etc.
the three-thousandth, Plat.
three-bodied, Lat. tricorpor, Aesch.
to be a τριταγωνιστής, Dem.
on the stage, the player who took the third part, a third-rate actor, Dem.

on the third day, used with Verbs so as to agree with the subject, τριταῖοι ἐγένοντο ἐν τῇ Ἀττικῇ Hdt.; ἐσβεβληκὼς τριταῖος ἐς Μηλιέας having invaded Melis three days before, Id.; τρ. γενόμενος after being three days dead, Id.:— τριταῖος (sc. πυρετός), a tertian fever, Plat.
of events, lasting three days, Eur.
generally for τρίτος, Id.
of three talents, Ar.
worth three talents, Isae.
thrice-wretched, Eur., Anth.
thrice-stretched, very long, Anth.
forming a third part of, c. gen., Hdt.
as Subst., τριτημόριον, ου, a third part, a third, Id., Thuc., etc.
forming a third foot, Eur.
Trito-born, a name of Athena, Hom., Hes., Hhymn., Orac. ap. Hdt.
entry.etym: From the Lake Τριτωνίς in Libya, near which the goddess was born, Eur. Others interpret τριτογένεια born on the third day of the month, or the third child after Apollo and Artemis.

entry.sense: bearing three times or three at a time, Anth.
τρ. αἰών a life in which one has poured the third libation (to Ζεὺς Σωτήρ), i. e. complete felicity, Aesch.
sown for the third time, τρ. γονή the third generation, Aesch.

the third, Lat. tertius, Hom., etc.; τρίτος ἦλθε he came himself the third, i. e. with two others, Od.; so, τρίτος αὐτός, attic:— the third often appears as completing the tale, τρίτην ἐπενδίδωμι (sub. πληγήν) the third and finishing stroke, Aesch.; cf. σωτήρ I. 2.
τρίτη, with or without ἡμέρα, the day after to-morrow, ἐς τρίτην ἡμέραν Ar.; τῇ τρίτῃ Xen.;—but, χθὲς καὶ τρ. ἡμέραν yesterday and the day before, Id.
τρίτον as adv., thirdly, Soph., Eur., etc.; also, τὸ τρίτον Hom., attic
τρίτα, ων, τά,
(sub. ἱερά) a sacrifice to the dead, offered the third day after the funeral, Isae.
τὰ τρίτα λέγειν τινί to play the third part to any one, Dem.
the number three, Lat. ternio: esp. a sacrifice of three animals, a boar, goat, and ram, Ar.
at Athens, a third of the φυλή, Dem., Aeschin.
Τρῑτωνιὰς λίμνη, ἡ, the Libyan lake Tritonis, Eur.
Tritonis, a lake in Libya famous for old Greek legends, Pind., Hdt.; cf. Τριτογένεια.
Triton, a sea-god, son of Poseidon and Amphitrite, Hes.:—pl. Τρίτωνες, Tritons, a lower race of sea-gods, Mosch.
the god of the Libyan lake Tritonis, Hdt.
a river in Libya, joining the lake Tritonis with the sea, Id., Aesch.
threefold, Lat. triplex, Hdt.:—in pl., much the same as τρεῖς, Id.
thrice-beloved, Theocr.
a plant, tre-foil, clover, Hdt.
of three tribes, τριφύλους ποιέειν to divide into three tribes, Hdt.
the threefold people, i. e. the Dorians, so called from their three tribes, Od.
very angry, Anth.
a coin worth three χαλκοῖ, Theophr.
cloven in three, Aesch.
threefold, in three parts, Lat. trifariam, Hom.; c. gen., τρ. νυκτὸς ἔην 'twas in the third watch of the night, Od.; τρίχα σχίζειν τι Hdt.
in or into three parts, Hdt., Xen.
in three ways, triply, Plat.
in or into three parts, Hom.
of hair, Xen.
a kind of anchovy full of small hair-like bones, Ar.
eating hair: hence τριχόβρωτες, = σῆτες or θρῖπες, moths, Ar.
holding or measuring three χοίνικες, Xen.: Comic phrase, τρ. ἔπος a most capacious word, Ar.
thrice-detested, Anth.
hair-fleeced, Anth.
Pass. to be furnished with hair, Arist.
to shed the hair, Ar.
in three places, Hdt.
τρῐχό-φοιτος ἴουλος, the first down of youth just passing into hair, Anth.
a growth of hair, hair, Hdt., Xen.; ἐν γενείου συλλογῇ τριχώματος, i. e. just at the age of manhood, Aesch.
to waste the day, Lat. terere tempus, Ar.
rubbing, friction, Plat., etc.
resistance to the touch when rubbed, firmness, Hdt.
τρίψεις potted meats, Anth.
a three-obol-piece, a half-drachma, at Athens, the pay of the dicasts for a day's sitting, first given by Pericles, Ar.
the pay of the marine soldiery (ἐπιβάται), Thuc.
of three stories or floors, Hdt.
of three fathoms, Xen.
from Troy, Od.; ἀπὸ Τροίηθε Il.; doric Τρωίᾱθεν Pind.
to Troy, Il., etc.; doric Τρῴανδε Pind.
Troy, whether of the city, "Troytown, " Hom., etc.; or the country, the Troad, Il.:— also Τροΐα, as trisyll., Soph.; doric Τρωία, Pind., Aesch.; contr. Τρῴα, Pind.

entry.note: Τροιζήνιος, η, ον, Eur.; fem. Τροιζηνίς, ίδος,
entry.sense: of Troezen, οἱ Τροιζήνιοι the people of Troezen, Hdt.
Troezen in Argolis, Il., Hdt., etc.
trembling, Eur.: trembling for fear, quaking, Id.
fearful, Id.
to tremble, quake, quiver, esp. from fear, Il.:—c. inf. to fear to do, Theocr.
c. acc. to tremble before or at a person, to stand in awe of, Hom.
entry.etym: In each sense Hom. uses both Act. and Mid., but only in pres. and imperf.; epic and ionic τρομεοίατο for τρομέοιντο, Il.; ionic part. τρομεύμενος Solon.

entry.sense: a trembling, quaking, quivering, esp. from fear, Il., Aesch.
from cold, Plat.
(sc. πνοή), an alternating wind:—metaph., λήματος, φρενὸς τροπαία a change in the spirit of one's mind, Aesch.; τρ. κακῶν a release from evils, Id.

a trophy, Lat. tropaeum, Trag., etc.; i. e. a monument of the enemy's defeat (τροπή II), consisting of arms taken from the enemy, hung on trees or posts; the common phrase was στῆσαι or στήσασθαι τρ. to set up trophies, Eur., Thuc.; ἱδρῦσαι Eur.; c. gen. pers., τροπαῖα τῶν πολεμίων a trophy won from the enemy, Id.; so, τροπαῖ’ ἔστησε τῶν ἐμῶν χερῶν Soph.; and, στῆσαι τροπαῖα κατὰ or ἀπὸ τῶν πολεμίων, Lat. triumphare de aliquo, Oratt.
of or for defeat (τροπή II), ἐχθρῶν θύειν τροπαῖα (sc. ἱερά) a sacrifice for their defeat, Eur.; Ζεὺς Τρ., as giver of victory, Soph.
causing rout, Ἕκτορος ὄμμασι τροπαῖοι, i. e. terrible to the eyes of Hector, Eur.
like ἀποτρόπαιος, averting, Lat. averruncus, Ζεύς Soph.
bearing trophies, Plut.
a bundle, bunch, σκορόδων τρ. a bunch of garlic, Ar.
to turn, Il.
a turn, turning:

τροπαὶ ἠελίοιο the tropics or solstices, i. e. midsummer and midwinter, Lat. solstitium and bruma, when the sun appears to turn his course and cross the ecliptic. Hom. speaks of τροπαὶ ἠελίοιο as denoting a point in the heavens, prob. to the westward, Od.; τροπαὶ θεριναί and χειμεριναί, Hdt., attic:—when τροπαί is used alone, it mostly refers to the winter solstice, περὶ ἡλίου τροπάς (sc. χειμερινάς) Thuc.
a turn, change, = μεταβολή, Aeschin., Plut.
τροπαὶ λέξεως a change of speech by figures or tropes (τρόποι), Luc.

the turning of the enemy, putting him to flight, a rout, τροπήν (or τροπάς) τινος ποιεῖν or ποιεῖσθαι to put one to flight, Hdt., Ar., etc.; τροπὴ γίγνεται Hdt.; ἐν τροπῇ δορός in the rout caused by the spear, Soph.
of the solstice, ὁ τροπικός (sc. κύκλος) the tropic or solstice, Arist.; αἱ τρ. ἡμέραι Id.
in Rhetoric, tropical, figurative.
a ship's keel, Od., Hdt.; τρόπεις θέσθαι to lay the keel, Plut.; and metaph., λέγε τὴν τρόπιν τοῦ πράγματος Ar.
a turn, direction, course, way, Hdt.

a way, manner, fashion, τρόπῳ τοιῷδε in such wise, Hdt.; τίνι τρόπῳ; Lat. quomodo? how? Aesch., etc.; ποίῳ τρ.; Id.; ἑνί γε τῷ τρ. in one way or other, Ar.; παντὶ τρόπῳ by all means, Aesch.; οὐδενὶ τρ., μηδενὶ τρ. in no wise, by no means, on no account, Hdt., etc.:—so in pl., τρόποισι ποίοις; Soph.; ναυκλήρου τρόποις Id.

absol. in acc., τίνα τρόπον; how? Ar.; τρ. τινά in a manner, Eur.; οὐδένα, μηδένα τρ. Xen.; πίτυος τρόπον after the manner of a pine, Hdt.; in pl., κεχώρισται τοὺς τρόπους in its ways, Id.; πάντας τρόπους in all ways, Plat.
with Preps., γυναικὸς ἐν τρόποις, ἐν τρ. Ἰξίονος Aesch.:— ἐς ὄρνιθος τρ. Luc.; κατὰ πάντα τρ. Ar., etc.; κατὰ πάντας τρόπους Id.:— κατὰ τρόπον, absol., fitly, duly, Lat. rite, Isocr.

of persons, a way of life, habit, custom, Pind.; μῶν ἡλιαστά; Answ. μἀλλὰ θατέρου τρ. are you a Heliast?—No, but of the other sort, Ar.:—a man's character, temper, τρόπου ἡσυχίου of a quiet temper, Hdt.; οὐ τοὐμοῦ τρόπου not to my taste, Ar.; πρὸς τοῦ Κύρου τρόπου Xen.; so in pl. ways, habits, σκληρὸς τοὺς τρόπους Ar.; ὑπηρετεῖν τοῖς τρόποις τινός Id.
in Music, τρ. Λύδιος Pind.; ᾠδῆς τρόπος Plat.
in speaking or writing, manner, style, Isocr.:—but in Rhetoric, tropes, figures, Cic.
a twisted leathern thong, with which the oar was fastened to the thole, Od.
to bear with, τινά NTest.
to furnish the oar with its thong: Mid., τροποῦτο κώπην ἀμφὶ σκαλμόν fastened his oar by its thong round the thole, Aesch.:—Pass., of the oar, to be furnished with its thong, Ar.
a piece of cheese, Ar.
pay for bringing up, the wages of a nurse or rearer, Aesch., etc.
βίου τροφεῖα one's living, food, Soph.; τροφεῖα ματρός mother's milk, Eur.

one who rears or brings up, a foster-father, Soph., Eur.; of a woman, a nurse, Aesch.:—metaph. of the plains and fountains of Troy, χαίρετ’ ὦ τροφῆς ἐμοί ye who reared me, Soph.; πάσης κακίας τρ. one who fosters all wickedness, Plat.
nourishment, food, victuals, Hdt., Soph., etc.; ἡ καθ’ ἡμέραν τρ. one's daily bread, Thuc.; τροφὴν παρέχειν to furnish provisions, forage, Id.
βίου τροφή or τροφαί a way of life, livelihood, living, Soph.; so, τροφή alone, δουλίαν ἕξειν τροφήν Id.; then, simply, a mode of life, life, Plat.
that which provides sustenance, as the bow of Philoctetes, Soph.
nurture, rearing, bringing up, Hdt., Trag.; in pl., ἐν τροφαῖσιν while in the nursery, Aesch., etc.
education, Eur., etc.
sometimes, in Poets, a brood, νέα τροφή, of young people, Soph.; ἀρνῶν τροφαί, i. e. young lambs, Eur.
brought up in the house, stall-fed, Plut.
nourishing: c. gen., γᾶ τρόφιμε τῶν ἐμῶν τέκνων Eur.
as Subst., τρόφιμος, the master of the house, ἡ τροφίμη the mistress, Anth.
pass. nourished and reared up, a nursling, foster-child, Eur.; οἱ τρόφιμοι our nurslings, pupils, Plat., Xen.
well-fed, stout, large, τρόφι κῦμα a huge, swollen wave, Il.; of men, ἐπεὰν γένωνται τρόφιες οἱ παῖδες when the children grow big, Hdt.
well-fed: hence large, big, of waves, Hom.
a feeder, rearer, nurse, Od., Hdt., attic: metaph., of a city, Pind., Aesch.
to bring one nourishment, maintain, sustain, NTest.
the builder of the temple of Apollo at Delphi, Hhymn., Hdt.; καταβαίνων ὥσπερ ἐς Τροφωνίου (sc. ἄντρον) Ar.
to run like a wheel, to run along, run quickly, Hdt., Xen., etc.; τρ. ἵπποις, of a charioteer, Eur.
running, tripping, Anth.
τροχαῖος (sc. πούς), a trochee or foot consisting of a long and short syllable, used in quick time, Plat., Arist.
running, τροχαλόν τινα τιθέναι to make one run quick, Hes.; τρ. ὄχοι swift-rolling, Eur.
running, tripping, Arist.
to drive a chariot: to drive about, drive round and round, Eur.
one who guides wheels, i. e. a charioteer, Soph., Eur.
driven on wheels, wheel-drawn, Aesch., Soph.
dragged by or at the wheels, Eur.
metaph. hurried along like a wheel or chariot, Id.; μανία τρ. whirling madness, Id.
the round of a wheel, Anth.
to turn round on the wheel, torture, Arist.
the sheaf of a pulley, roller of a windlass, and the like, Lat. trochlea, Ar.
a small bird, the sandpiper, said to pick leeches out of the crocodile's throat, Hdt.
round, Anth.
a runner, messenger, Aesch.
Pass. to whirl or roll round, Aesch.
round as a wheel, circular, Theogn., Hdt.
round as a wheel, round, Anth.
to make wheels, Ar.
anything that runs round:
a round cake, Od.
a wheel, Il., Soph.; τροχοὺς μιμεῖσθαι to imitate wheels, of one who bends back so as to form a wheel, Xen.
a potter's wheel, Il.
the wheel of a stage-machine, Ar.
the wheel of torture, ἐπὶ τοῦ τροχοῦ στρεβλοῦσθαι Id., etc.; τῷ τροχῷ τινα προσδεῖν Luc.
a boy's hoop, the Graecus trochus of Hor.
τροχοὶ γῆς, θαλάσσης circles or zones of land, sea, Plat.
a ring on the bit of a bridle, Xen.
τρόχος, a running, course, μὴ πολλοὺς τρόχους ἁμιλλητῆρας ἡλίου not many racing courses of the sun, i. e. not many days, Soph.; παῖδες ἐκ τρόχων πεπαυμένοι Eur.
a race-course, Id.
a cup, bowl, Ar.

with acc. of the fruit or crop, to gather in, Lat. vindemiare, ἑτέρας [σταφυλὰς] τρυγόωσιν Od.; καρπόν Hdt.:—metaph., τρυγήσομεν αὐτήν (sc. Εἰρήνην) Ar.:—Pass., τετρυγημένοι καθ’ ὥραν gathered in due season, Luc.
absol., Ar.
with acc. of the trees or ground, ὅτε τρυγόῳεν ἀλωήν (epic opt. for τρυγῷεν) when they gathered fruit off the vineyard, Il.
proverb., ἐρήμας τρυγᾶν (sc. ἀμπέλους) to strip unwatched vines, i. e. to be bold where there is nothing to fear, Ar.
ripe fruit, a grain-crop, corn, οὐδὲ τρύγην οἴσεις Hhymn.
the vintage, Anth.
one who gathers grapes, Lat. vindemiator, Hes. [with ῡ].
a vintage, harvest, Plut., Luc.
the time thereof, the harvest or vintage, Thuc.
bearing fruits, esp. wine, Hhymn.
of lees, = κωμῳδικός, Ar.
Com. word for τρυγῳδός, with a play on κακοδαίμων, a poor-devil poet, Ar.
a straining-cloth for wine, Ar.
a lees-singer, = κωμῳδός, because the singers smeared their faces with lees (peruncti faecibus ora, Hor.), Ar.
the turtle-dove, Ar.
a hole, ἡ τρ. τῆς ῥαφίδος the eye of the needle, NTest.
a hole: metaph. a sharp fellow, sly knave, Ar.
new wine not yet fermented, wine with the lees in it, must, Lat. mustum, Hdt., Ar.
the lees of wine, Lat. faex, Hdt., Ar.:—metaph. of an old man or woman, Ar.
a carpenter's tool, a borer, auger, Lat. terebra, worked by a thong, Od., Eur.
to bore, pierce through, Od.:—Pass., τὰ ὦτα τετρυπημένος having one's ears pierced for earrings, Xen.; ψῆφος τετρυπημένη the pebble of condemnation which had a hole in it, Aeschin.
τρ. τῷ ποδὶ τὴν βελόνην to force the point through the foot, Anth.
a hole, τρ. νεώς, i. e. one of the holes through which the oars worked, Ar.: like τρυμαλιά, the eye of a needle, NTest.
a hole, Anth.
wearying a man, Soph.
wearing out life, Ar.
the tongue of a balance, and generally, a balance, pair of scales, Lat. trutina, Ar., Dem.
a helmet, Il.
to live softly, delicately, luxuriously, to fare sumptuously, Eur.:—part. τρυφῶν as adj. delicate, effeminate, luxurious, voluptuous, Ar., Plat.; τὸ τρυφῶν, as Subst., effeminacy, Ar.
to be licentious, revel, run riot, wax wanton, Eur., etc.; to be extravagant, Arist.
to give oneself airs, be fastidious, Eur., Plat.
Pass. to be fastidious, τρυφερανθείς with a coxcomb's airs, Ar.
delicate, dainty, Eur., Anth.

of persons, effeminate, luxurious, voluptuous, Ar., etc.:— τὸ τρυφερόν effeminacy, ἐς τὸ τρυφερώτερον to more effeminate habits, Thuc.:—neut. as adv., τρυφερόν voluptuously, Ar.; τρ. λαλεῖν to speak softly, Theocr.

entry.etym: rare poet. form of τρυφερός, Anth.

entry.sense: that in which one takes pride, a pride, Eur.
softness, delicacy, daintiness, Eur., Plat., etc.:—in pl. luxuries, daintinesses, Lat. deliciae, Eur.
luxuriousness, wantonness, Plat.
daintiness, insolence, fastidiousness, Id.
that which is broken off, a piece, morsel, lump, Od., Hdt.
ragged, tattered, Eur.
nightshade, used as a symbol of sweet forgetfulness, Theocr.
to be worn out, perf. part. τετρυχωμένος Thuc.
a worn out garment, a rag, shred, Eur.;—in pl. rags, tatters, Id.

to wear out, waste, consume, Od., Hes.; πτωχὸν τρύξοντά ἑ αὐτόν a beggar to eat him out of house and home, Od.; τρύχει ψυχάν distresses, afflicts the soul, Soph.; τρ. στρατείαις τὴν πόλιν Xen.:—Pass. to be worn out, Od., Soph., etc.:— τρύχεσθαί τινος to pine away for some one, Eur.

to wear out, waste, consume, Od., Hes.; πτωχὸν τρύξοντά ἑ αὐτόν a beggar to eat him out of house and home, Od.; τρύχει ψυχάν distresses, afflicts the soul, Soph.; τρ. στρατείαις τὴν πόλιν Xen.:—Pass. to be worn out, Od., Soph., etc.:— τρύχεσθαί τινος to pine away for some one, Eur.
to rub down, wear out, Aesch.:—Pass. to be worn out, τετρῦσθαι ἐς τὸ ἔσχατον κακοῦ Hdt.; τετρυμένος ταλαιπωρίηισι Id.
Trojan, Od.; Τρωιάδες γυναῖκες, or alone, Τρωιάδες Il.
γῆ Τρῳάς the Troad, Soph.; so ἡ Τρωάς Hdt.
fruits eaten at dessert, figs, nuts, sweetmeats, Ar.
a hole formed by gnawing, a mouse's hole, Batr., Babr.
one who creeps into holes:— Τρωγλοδύται, ῶν, οἱ, Troglodytes, cave-men, an Aethiopian tribe, Hdt.

entry.etym: part. with no ind. in use
entry.sense: creeping into a hole, of a mouse, Batr.
to gnaw, nibble, munch, of herbivorous animals, as mules, Od.; of swine, Ar.; of cattle, Theocr.
of men, to eat vegetables or fruit, Hdt., Ar.
from Troy, Pind.
Trojan, Il., Soph., etc.; τὰ Τρωικά the times of Troy, Hdt.
of Tros, Il.
Trojan, Id.
a gnawer, nibbler: Phoenician traffickers are called τρῶκται, greedy knaves, Od.; so, τρῶκται χεῖρες greedy hands, Anth.
to be eaten raw: eatable, Hdt.
τρωκτά, τά, = τρωγάλια, Id.
bread-gnawer, Batr.
a biting, τῶν ὀνύχων Arist.
destructive to the Trojans or to Troy, Anth.
to turn constantly, change its notes, of the nightingale, Od.:—Mid. to turn oneself, turn about, Hom.
Tros, the mythic founder of Troy, Il.
pl. Τρῶες, Τρώων, οἱ, Trojans, Hom., etc.
to be wounded, vulnerable, Il., attic
to run fast, gallop, Hom.

to hit, esp. to hit a mark with an arrow, Hom., etc.: he mostly constructs it with acc., when the object hit is alive, with gen. when it is lifeless; so, τ. τοῦ σκοποῦ Xen.;—a prep. is sometimes added, κατὰ κληῖδα, κατὰ ζωστῆρα τυχήσας [τινά] Il.;—absol., ἤμβροτες οὐδ’ ἔτυχες Id.; the part. τυχών is often joined with βάλλειν, οὐτᾶν, etc., Id.
to hit upon, light upon:

to meet by chance, meet with, fall in with a person, absol., Od.; c. gen., Aesch., etc.:—aor2 part. ὁ τυχών, the first one meets, any one, Lat. quivis, Hes., Plat., etc.; οἱ τυχόντες every-day men, the vulgar, Xen.; so, τὸ τυχόν any chance thing, Plat.

to meet with, hit, reach, gain, get, obtain a thing, and in the past tenses (like κέκτημαι), to be in possession of, to have, c. gen., Od., etc.:—after Hom. also c. acc., τ. μισθόν Hdt.; τὰ πρόσφορα Aesch., etc.:—gen. pers. added, to obtain a thing from a person, τ. τί τινος Soph.; τινὸς παρά τινος Od.
also in bad sense, βίης τυχεῖν to meet with, suffer violence, Hdt.; τ. κακῶν Eur.
absol. to hit the mark, to make a hit, Il., attic; so, τυχόντες καλῶς Aesch.
to have the lot or fate, ὅς κε τύχηι whoever draws the lot (to die), Il.
intr. to happen to be at a place, εἴπερ τύχηισι μάλα σχεδόν if by chance she be quite near, Il. etc.
of events, and things generally, to happen to one, befal one, fall to one's lot, c. dat. pers., Id., attic; also to turn out well, Od.
impers., ὅπως ἐτύγχανεν as it chanced, i. e. without any rule, indefinitely, Eur.; ὡς or ὥσπερ ἔτυχεν Xen.; ὁπότε τύχοι when it chanced, sometimes, Plat.

joined with a part., τὰ νοέων τυγχάνω which I have just now in my mind, Hdt.; ὃ τυγχάνω μαθών which I have just learnt, Soph.; ἔτυχον στρατευόμενοι they were just then engaged in an expedition, Thuc.;—in phrase τυγχάνω ὤν, simply = εἰμί, Aesch., Soph., etc.

the part. is often omitted, ἔνδον γὰρ ἄρτι τυγχάνει (sc. ὤν) Soph.; εἰ σὺ τυγχάνεις ἐπιστήμων Plat.:—sometimes indeed τυγχάνειν is used very much like εἶναι, τ. ἐν ἐμπύροις to be engaged in sacrifice, Eur.; ὡς ἕκαστοι ἐτύγχανον just as they all were, Xen.
in many phrases it is easy to supply a part., ὅ τι ἂν τύχωσι, τοῦτο λέγουσι they say whatever comes uppermost (i. e. ὅ τι ἂν τύχωσι λέγοντες), Plat.
neut. part. τυχόν, absol. like παρόν, since it so befel, Luc.
as adv. perchance, perhaps, Xen., Plat.
the hero Tydeus, one of the Seven against Thebes, Hom.
here, Theocr.
for δεῦρο, with Verbs of motion, Id.
mason's work, Eur.
to work stones, Ar.
a working of stones: in pl., κανόνων τυκίσματα, i. e. walls of stone worked by rule, opp. to the rude Cyclopean building, Eur.
an instrument for working stones with, a mason's hammer or pick, Eur.
a battle-axe, Hdt.
a Persian word (tacht), which Hdt. translates by τέλειον δεῖπνον βασιλήιον.
τυκτὸν κακόν created to be an evil, a born plague, Il.; τυκτὴ κρήνη a fountain made by man's hand, Od.: then, like εὔτυκτος, well-made, well-wrought, Hom.
like τύλος,any callous lump: a porter's shoulder, which has grown callous from carrying weights, Ar.
a cushion, bolster, Anth.
to twist up: to bend: aor1 pass. ἐτυλίχθη Theocr.
a knot or callus, Xen.; esp. inside the hands, Luc.
a knob or knot; a knobbed bolt, a ship-bolt, trenail, Ar.
to make knobby:—Pass., ῥόπαλα σιδήρῳ τετυλωμένα clubs knobbed with iron, Hdt.
to make callous, Xen.:—Pass. to be callous, Theocr.
ῥόπαλα τυλωτά, knobbed clubs, like τετυλωμένα, Hdt.
a tomb, grave, Soph.
that which is or is to be buried, a body, Eur.
to bury, entomb, Soph., Eur.
χοὰς τυμβεῦσαί τινι to pour libations on one's grave, Soph.
intr. to dwell entombed, Id.
entombed, Soph.
grave-like, sepulchral, Id.
in or at the grave, Anth.
a sepulchral mound, cairn, barrow, Lat. tumulus, Hom., Hdt., attic
generally, a tomb, grave, Aesch.; ὥσπερ ἀπὸ τύμβου πεσών like an old grave-man, Ar.
also the tombstone with the figure of the dead, Eur.
of an old man, Eur., Ar.
sepulchral, Anth.
grave-murdering, disturbing the dead, Anth.
to throw up a cairn or barrow, Hdt.
the throwing up a cairn, Il.
throwing up a cairn or barrow, Anth.
τ. χειρώματα cairns thrown up by work of hand, Aesch.
heaped up into a cairn, high-heaped, Soph.
grave-robbing, Anth.
one who digs up graves, a grave-robber, Ar.
a blow, Aesch., Theocr.
to beat a drum:—Pass., τυμπανίζεσθαι κατὰ τὰς ἐξόδους to march out to the sound of drums, Strab.
Pass. to be beaten to death, bastinadoed, NTest.
of a priestess of Cybele, Dem.
a kettledrum, such as was used esp. in the worship of Cybele, Hdt., Eur.
a drum-stick: generally, a staff, cudgel, Ar.
in Virgil tympana are wheels of solid wood.
Tyndareos or Tyndarus, husband of Leda, Od., Eur.: attic
so small, so little, Lat. tantillus, Theocr.
tantillus, Ar.; with ι demonstr., τυννουτοσί, -ονί, Id.; gen. and dat. τυννουτουί, -ῳί, Id.
to work in the mud: hence, to grub round the roots of a vine, Ar.
a drum, Hhymn., Eur.
a blow, wound, in pl., Il.
a blow, Orac. ap. Hdt.
the effect of a blow, the print or impress of a seal, Eur.; στίβου τύπος the print of a footstep, Soph.:— τύποι marks, letters, Plat.:— ὁ τ. τῶν ἵππων the sound of their tread, Xen.
anything wrought of metal or stone, in pl. figures worked in relief, Hdt., Eur.:—then, simply, a figure, image, statue, Hdt., Eur.
τύπος τινός a man's form, i. e. himself, Ἱππομέδοντος τ. Aesch.; βραχιόνων τ. = βραχίονες, Eur.
general form or character, the type or model of a thing, Plat.:— an example, NTest.
an outline, sketch, draught, Plat.; so, τύπῳ, ἐν τύπῳ in outline, in general, Id.
to form, mould, model, Plat.: so in Mid., Anth.
to beat, strike, smite, Il., etc.; ἅλα τύπτον ἐρετμοῖς Od.; ἴχνια τύπτειν to tread in his very track, Il.:—absol., Ζέφυρος λαίλαπι τύπτων the west wind beating, lashing with fury, Id.
metaph., ἄχος κατὰ φρένα τύψε sharp grief smote him to the heart, Id.; ἡ ἀληθηίη ἔτυψε Καμβύσεα Hdt., etc.
Mid., like κόπτομαι, Lat. plangor, to beat one's breast for grief, Id.; c. acc. pers. to mourn for a person, Id.
Pass. to be beaten, struck or wounded, Hom., etc.; to be stung, Xen.
c. acc. cogn. to receive blows or wounds, ἕλκεα, ὅσς’ ἐτύπη Il.; τύπτομαι πολλάς (sc. πληγάς) I get many blows, Ar.; so c. dat., καιρίηι (sc. πληγῆι) τετύφθαι Hdt.
like an outline:—adv. -δῶς, summarily, Strab.
that which is moulded, τ. χαλκόπλευρον, of a brazen urn, Soph.: a figure, outline, Eur.
a mould, model, Plut.

entry.etym: τυραννεύω always in Hdt.; both in attic Poets, as the metre required.
Pass., fut. mid. τυραννήσομαι in pass. sense
entry.sense: to be a τύραννος, an absolute sovereign or despot, and in aor. to become such, Hdt., etc.: to be a prince or princess, Eur.
c. gen. to be despotic ruler of a people or place, Solon, Hdt., attic
c. acc. to govern, Luc.:—Pass. to be governed despotically, Hdt., Thuc.
to be tyrannical, imperious, Plat.
to take the part of tyrants, Dem.
of or for a despotic ruler, royal, princely, Trag.; κύκλος τ. the circle or assembly of kings, Soph.

befitting a tyrant, despotic, imperious, τυραννικὰ φρονεῖν Ar.; τ. ξυνωμοσία in favour of tyranny, Thuc.; τὰ τυραννικά the times of despotic government, Arist.:—adv. -κῶς, Plat.; comp. -ώτερον, Arist.
kingly power, sovereignty, Pind., Trag.
absolute power, despotic rule, Hdt., attic; τ. ὑμῶν lordship over you, Dem.
pl., αἱ τυραννίδες, = οἱ τύραννοι, Hdt.
to slay a tyrant, Luc.:—Pass. to be slain as a tyrant, Id.
the slaying of a tyrant, Luc.
slayer of a tyrant, Luc.
a maker of tyrants, Plat.

an absolute sovereign, unlimited by law or constitution, Hdt., Aesch., etc.: not applied to old hereditary sovereignties (βασιλεῖαι) such as those of Hom. or of Sparta; for the term rather regards the irregular way in which the power was gained, than the way in which it was exercised, being applied to the mild Pisistratus, but not to the despotic kings of Persia. However, the word soon came to imply reproach, like our tyrant, Plat., etc.
in a wider sense, the tyrant's son, or any member of his family, Soph.:—so, ἡ τύραννος was both the queen herself or a princess, Eur.
τύραννος, ον, as adj. kingly, royal, Trag.
imperious, despotic, Thuc.; τύραννα δρᾶν Soph.
entry.etym: τύραννος is prob. from same Root as κύριος, κοίρανος.

entry.sense: slaying tyrants, Anth.
to trouble, stir up, Lat. turbare, Ar.: —Pass., τ. περί τι to be troubled about a thing, Id.
disorder, tumult, Lat. turba, Xen.
that which is curdled, cheese, Eur.
one who makes cheese, of Hermes as god of goatherds, Anth.
to make cheese:—metaph. to make a mess of anything, Dem.
of Tyre, Tyrian, Hdt., etc.
cheese-scooper, a mouse, Batr.
like cheese: τυρόεις (sc. πλακοῦς), a cheese, Theocr.
a cheese-scraper, cheese-grater, Ar.
cheese-backed, spread with cheese, Ar.
to make cheese, Strab.
to sell like cheese, Ar.
a cheesemonger, Ar.
Tyre, in Phoenicia, Hdt., etc.
cheese, Hom., Ar., etc.
cheese-eater, name of a mouse in Batr.
with cheese on it, Anth.
destroyer of Tyrrhenians, Anth.
Tyrrhenian, Etruscan, Hes., Hdt., Trag.:—also, Τυρσηνικός, ή, όν, Aesch.
a tower, Lat. turris, Pind., Xen.
little, small, of children, Hom., Aesch.; τ. θηρίον of a bee, Theocr., etc.
τυτθόν, as adv. a little, a bit, Hom.; τ. ἔτι ζώων breathing yet a little, Il.; τ. ἐδεύησεν it wanted a little, Od.:—of the voice, softly, gently, Il.
by a little, scarcely, hardly, Lat. vix; Id.; so neut. pl., Aesch.
τυτθὰ διατμῆξαι, κεάσσαι to cut small, Od.
one with cloudy wits, a stupid fellow, dullard, Ar.
a plant used for stuffing beds.
made from τύφη, Anth.
with blind foot, of Oedipus, Eur.
blind, Il., etc.:—c. gen., τ. τινος blind to a thing, Xen.:— τὰ τυφλὰ τοῦ σώματος, i. e. one's back, Id.:—of the limbs of the blind, τ. πούς, χείρ Eur.; cf. τυφλόπους.
of things, blind, dark, obscure, Aesch., Soph.; τ. σπιλάδες blind rocks, Anth.
of channels, blind, i. e. closed, choked with mud, Plut.
adv., τυφλῶς ἔχειν πρός τι to be blind to it, Plat.
with blind mouth, of rivers, Strab.
blindness, Plat.
to blind, make blind, Hdt., Eur.:— Pass. to be or become blind, Hdt., Eur.
metaph. in Pass., μόχθος τετύφλωται is baffled, Pind.; τῶν μελλόντων τετύφλωνται φραδαί wisdom is blind as to the future, Id.
a making blind, blinding, Isocr.
to be blind, Luc.
an old man dim and dull with age, a dullard, dotard, Ar.
smoke, vapour, Anth.:—metaph. conceit, vanity, Plut.
to wrap in smoke; metaph. in perf. pass. τετύφωμαι, to be in the clouds, to be crazed, demented, Plat., Dem.
Typhoeus or Typhos, a giant buried by Zeus in Cilicia, Il., Pind.
tempestuous, NTest.
like a whirlwind, Strab.
Typhon, son of Typhoeus and father of the Winds, Hes.
to raise a smoke, καπνὸν τ. Hdt.:—absol. to smoke, Soph.
trans. to smoke out, τοὺς σφῆκας Ar.
metaph., καπνῶι τ. πόλιν to fill the town with smoke, Id.
to consume in smoke, to burn slowly, Eur.:—Pass. to smoulder, Id.:—metaph., τυφόμενος πόλεμος smouldering, but not yet broken out, Plut.; so of concealed love, Anth.
a whirlwind, typhoon, Aesch., etc.
Τῡφώς, ῶ, ὁ contr. for Τῦφωεύς, q. v.
as appellat. τῡφώς, gen. τυφῶ, dat. τυφῶι, a whirlwind, typhoon, Aesch., etc.
accidental, chance, Plut.

the good which man obtains (τυγχάνει) by the favour of the gods, good fortune, luck, success, Theogn., Hdt., etc.; σὺν τύχῃ Soph.; θείᾳ τύχῃ, Lat. divinitus, Hdt., etc.:— hence Τύχη was deified, like Lat. Fortuna, Τύχη Σώτειρα Pind.; T. Σωτήρ Aesch.
generally, fortune, chance, good or bad, in sg. and pl., Hdt., attic
rarely of positive ill fortune, ἢν χρήσωνται τύχῃ, i. e. if they are killed, Eur.; τύχῃ by ill-luck, Antipho.

esp., ἀγαθὴ τ. Aesch., etc.; in dat. ἀγαθῇ τύχῃ "in God's name, " Dem., etc.; by crasis, τύχἀγαθῇ Ar.;—this formula was also introduced into treaties, like Lat. quod felix faustumque sit, Λάχης εἶπε, τύχῃ ἀγαθῇ τῶν Ἀθηναίων ποιεῖσθαι τὴν ἐκεχειρίαν Decret. in Thuc.:—so ἐπ’ ἀγαθῇ τύχῃ Ar., etc.
Adverbial usages, τύχῃ by chance, Lat. forte, forte fortuna, Soph., etc.; ἀπὸ τύχης Arist.; ἐκ τύχης Plat.; διὰ τύχην Isocr., etc.; κατὰ τύχην Thuc., etc.
a chance, hap, accident, Aesch., Soph., etc.; τῆς τύχης, τὸ ἐμὲ τυχεῖν . . ! what a piece of ill-luck, that . . ! Xen.; mostly of mishaps, misfortunes, Aesch., etc.
lucky, fortunate, Aesch.:—adv. -ρῶς, Ar.

entry.etym: adverb from aor2 part. of τυγχάνω
entry.sense: by chance, Arist.
to mock, scoff or jeer at, flout, Hdt., Ar.: —Pass. to be jeered, Plat.
absol. to jeer, Ar.
scoffing, jeering, Arist.

entry.etym: dat. sg. neut. of ὁ, ἡ, τό, used absol.
entry.sense: therefore, in this wise, thereupon, Hom.
τῷ; for τίνι; dat. sg. of τίς; who?
τῳ, enclit. for τινί, dat. sg. of τις, some one.
demonstr. adv., so, in this wise, Hom., Hes., Aesch.
doric = οὗ, where, Theocr.
the Hyades, seven stars in the head of the bull, which threatened rain when they rose with the sun, Il., Hes.
entry.etym: Commonly deriv. from ὕω, cf. Lat. Pluviae: but the genuine Lat. name was suculae, piglings, as if ὗς were the root; and this agrees with the quantity, υ being short in ὑάδες, long in ὕω: Eur. however has ὑάδες with ῡ.

entry.sense: the hyaena, an animal of the dog kind, with a bristly mane like a hog (whence the name), Hdt.
(sc. ἱερά), τά, a Lacedaemonian festival in honour of Hyacinthus, held in the month Hecatombaeon, Hdt., Thuc., etc.
dyed hyacinth-colour, Xen.
hyacinthine, Od., Eur.

the hyacinth, Il., etc.;—a flower said to have sprung up from the blood of Hyacinthus or of Ajax; and the petals were thought to bear the letters αἰ, or αἰαι, Mosch.; hence the epithet γραπτά in Theocr. The hyacinth seems to have comprehended several dark blue flowers: Hom. speaks of dark hair as ὑακινθίνῳ ἄνθει ὁμοῖαι, and Theocr. calls it black.
a precious stone, of blue colour, not (prob.) our jacinth, but the sapphire, NTest.
Hyacinthus, a Laconian youth, beloved by Apollo, who killed him by a cast of the discus, Eur.
of glass, Anth.: —contr. ὑαλοῦς, ᾶ, οῦν, of glass, Strab., Luc.
of crystal or glass, Ar.: also ὑέλινος, η, ον, Anth.
a clear, transparent stone, used by the Egyptians to enclose their mummies in, oriental alabaster, Hdt.
a convex lens of crystal, used as a burning-glass, Ar.
glass, Lat. vitrum, Plat.: glass itself existed in the time of Hdt., but was not called ὕαλος till Plato's time.
entry.etym: The word is said to be Egyptian. Others refer it to ὕω, as if the orig. sense were raindrop.

entry.sense: glass-coloured, Anth.
hump-backed, Theocr.
to wax wanton, run riot, Od., Aesch., etc.; opp. to σωφρονεῖν, Xen.
of over-fed horses or asses, to neigh or bray and prance about, Lat. lascivire, Hdt., Xen.
metaph. of a rapid rushing river, Hdt.

in dealing with other persons, ὑβρ. τινά to treat him despitefully, to outrage, insult, affront, maltreat, Il., Aesch.; more commonly, ὑβρ. εἴς τινα to commit an outrage upon or towards him, Eur., Plat.; ὑβρ. ἐπί τινα to exult over a fallen foe, Eur.

c. acc. cogn., ὑβρ. ὕβριν Aesch., Eur., etc.: —with a neut. adj., ὑβρ. τάδε to commit these outrages, Hdt.; so, τῶν ἀδικημάτων τῶν ἐς Ἀθηναίους ὕβρισαν Id.; and with double acc., ὕβριν ὑβρίζειν τινά Eur.:— hence in Pass., ὕβριν ὑβρισθῆναι Id., Dem.

at Athens in legal sense, to do one a personal outrage, to maltreat, assault, Oratt.:—Pass., γυναῖκες καὶ παῖδες ὑβρίζονται Thuc.; ὑβριζόμενος ἀποθνήσκει he dies of ill-treatment, Xen.;—and of acts, τὰ ὑβρισμένα outrages, Lys.
perf. pass. part., of things, arrogant, ostentatious, σημεῖ’ ἔχων ὑβρισμένα Eur.; στολὴ ὑβρισμένη Xen.
a wanton or insolent act, an outrage, Hdt., Eur., etc.; τόδ’ ὕβρισμ’ ἐς ἡμᾶς ἠξίωσεν ὑβρίσαι Eur., Xen.; τὰ τούτων ὑβρίσματα εἰς ἐμέ Dem.
an object of insolence, ὕβρισμα θέσθαι τινά = ὑβρίζειν, Eur.
= ὑβριστής, Id.

wantonness, wanton violence or insolence, Od., Hdt., etc.; of actions, ἆρ’ οὐχ ὕβρις τάδ’; Soph.; ταῦτ’ οὐχ ὕβρις ἐστί; Ar.:—adv. usages, ὕβρει in wantonness or insolence, Soph.; ἐφ’ ὕβρει Eur.; δι’ ὕβριν Dem.
of lewdness, opp. to σωφροσύνη. Theogn., Xen.
of over-fed horses, riotousness, restiveness, Hdt., Pind.

= ὕβρισμα, Hom.; sometimes like ὑβρίζω, foll. by a prep., Ἥρας μητέρ’ εἰς ἐμὴν ὕβρις her outrage towards . . , Eur.; ἡ κατ’ Ἀργείους ὕ. Soph.; ἡ πρὸς τοὺς δημότας ὕ. Hdt.; also c. gen. objecti, ὕ. τινός towards him, Id., etc.:—in pl. wanton acts, outrages, Hes., Eur., etc.
an outrage on the person, violation, Pind., attic

in attic law, ὕβρις comprehended all the more serious injuries done to the person, grievous assault, the slighter kind being αἰκία [ῑ]: hence ὕβρις was remedied by public indictment (γραφή), αἰκία by private action (δίκη).
a loss, damage, NTest.
as masc. = ὑβριστής, a violent, overbearing man, ὕβριν ἀνέρα Hes.
that may be insulted, Dem.
a violent, overbearing person, a wanton, insolent man, Hom., Hdt., attic
opp. to σώφρων, lustful, lewd, Ar., Xen.
of animals, wanton, restive, unruly, Eur., Xen.
of natural forces, ὑβριστὴς ἄνεμος Hes.; ὑβριστὴς ποταμός Aesch.
given to wantonness, wanton, insolent, outrageous, Plat., etc.:— τὸ ὑβριστικόν an insolent disposition, Xen.:—adv. -κῶς, Plat.; comp. -ώτερον, Dem.
wanton, insolent, outrageous: — hence comp. ὑβριστότερος, Hdt., Xen.; Sup. ὑβριστότατος, Ar., Xen.
Pass. to become healthy, get well, Arist.
to be sound, healthy or in health, Lat. bene valere, Hdt., Ar., etc.
to be sound of mind, Theogn., Ar., etc.; τὰς φρένας ὑγ. Hdt.
of soundness in political or religious opinion, τὸ ὑγιαῖνον τῆς Ἑλλάδος Id.
to be sound, healthy or in health, Lat. bene valere, Hdt., Ar., etc.
to be sound of mind, Theogn., Ar., etc.; τὰς φρένας ὑγ. Hdt.
of soundness in political or religious opinion, τὸ ὑγιαῖνον τῆς Ἑλλάδος Id.
health, soundness of body, Lat. salus, Hdt., attic:—pl. ὑγίειαι, healthy states or conditions, Plat.
of the mind, ὑ. φρενῶν soundness of mind, Aesch.
good for the health, wholesome, sound, healthy, Xen., etc.
of persons, healthy, sound, Lat. sanus, Plat.; τὸ ὑγ. health, Arist.
adv., ὑγιεινῶς ἔχειν, = ὑγιαίνειν, Plat.: —comp. ὑγιεινοτέρως and -ρον, Sup. -ότατα, Xen.
good for the health, wholesome, Pind.
of persons, healthy, hearty, sound, Lat. sanus, Hdt.

comp. and Sup. ὑγιέστερος, -ατος:— sound, healthy, hearty, sound in body, Lat. sanus, ὑγιέα ἀποδέξαι or ποιεῖν τινα to restore him to health, make him sound, Hdt.; ὑγιὴς τὸ δῆγμα cured of the bite, Xen.
of condition, σῶς καὶ ὑγιής safe and sound, in good case, Hdt., Thuc.
sound in mind, sound-minded, Eur., Plat.
of words, opinions, and the like, sound, wholesome, wise, Il., Thuc., Plat.: often with a negat., λόγος οὐχ ὑγ. Hdt.; μηδὲν ὑγιὲς φρονῶν Soph.; οὐδὲν ὑγ. λέγειν Eur., etc.
adv. ὑγιῶς, healthily, soundly, κρίνειν, Plat., Dem.
to wet, moisten, Eur., Xen.: of a river, to water a country, Eur.
with supple, soft limbs, Xen.
to go through the water, Anth.

wet, moist, running, fluid, Hom., etc.; ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον, i. e. olive-oil, as opp. to fat, Id.; ὑγρὸν ὕδωρ running water, Od.; ἄνεμοι ὑγρὸν ἀέντες winds blowing moist or rainy, as opp. to dry, parching, Id.
ἡ ὑγρά, ionic ὑγρή, the moist, i. e. the sea, Hom.; so, ὑγρὰ κέλευθα the watery ways, i. e. the sea, Id.; and ὑγρά alone, opp. to ἀπείρων γαῖα, Id.
τὸ ὑγρόν and τὰ ὑγρά wet, moisture, water, Hdt.
μέτρα ὑγρὰ καὶ ξηρά liquid and dry measure, Plat.
θῆρες ὑγροί water- animals, opp. to πεζοί, Anth.

soft, pliant, supple, lithe, Lat. mollis, of the eagle's back, Pind.; of youthful limbs, Plat.; ὑγρὰ ἔχειν τὰ σκέλη, of a horse, Xen.; so of colts, γόνατα ὑγρῶς κάμπτειν, ὑγρῶς τοῖς σκέλεσι χρῆσθαι (cf. Virgil's mollia crura reponit), Id.; so, ὑ. ἄκανθος ( Virg. mollis acanthus), Theocr.
languid, feeble, of one dying, Soph., Eur.
of the eyes, swimming, melting, languishing, ὄμμασιν ὑγρὰ δεδορκώς Anth., etc.
metaph. of persons, facile, soft-tempered, pliant, easy, Plut.: luxurious, ὑ. πρὸς τὴν διαίταν Id.
wetness, moisture, Plat.
pliancy, suppleness, Xen.: of a flame, flickering motion, lambency, Eur.
languor, Plut.
making a gurgling sound, Anth.
to make wet, moisten, Aesch.
of wine, mixed with too much water, watery, washy, Xen.:—metaph. washy, feeble, languid, Aesch., Arist.
water-proof, Anth.
of water, watery, ὑδ. νάρκισσος that loves the water, Anth.
like ὑγρός II, pliant, supple, Id.
a rivulet, Plat.
watery, like water, Anth.
transparent as water, thin, fine, Id.
a drinking of water, Luc.
to drink water, Luc.
growing in or by the water, Od.
to make watery:—Pass. to be liquid, watery, Anth.
dropsy, Arist.
to water the earth, of a river, Eur.; ὑδρ. τινά to wash, sprinkle with water, Id.:—Mid. to wash oneself, bathe, ὑδρηναμένη Od.; λουτρὰ ὑδράνασθαι χροΐ to pour water over one's body, Eur.
ὑδραίνειν χοάς τινι to pour libations to one, Id.
a hydra, water-serpent, of the Lernaean hydra, Hes., Soph.; ὕδραν τέμνειν, proverb. of labour in vain, because two heads sprang up for every one which was cut off, Plat.
a drawing water, fetching water, Thuc., etc.
a watering-place, Plut.
a water-bucket, well-bucket, Hdt.
a water-tank, Strab.
to draw, fetch or carry water, Od., Theogn.:—Mid. to draw water for oneself, fetch water, πολῖται Od., Hdt., attic
watery, wet, Od., Aesch.; κρωσσοὶ ὕδρ. water pots, Eur.
a water-pot, pitcher, urn, Ar.:— proverb., ἐπὶ θύραις τὴν ὑδρίαν to break the pitcher at the door, = "there's many a slip 'twixt cup and lip, " Arist.
a vessel of any kind, a pot of money, Ar.
the balloting urn in the law-courts, Isocr., Dem.
a cinerary urn, Ar., Luc.
of the water, Anth.
like water, watery, Eur.
fond of the water, Eur.
water-ruler, name of a frog in Batr.
water-drinking, Xen., etc.
to drink water, Hdt., Xen., etc.
a water-drinker, Xen.: in Comic phrase, a thin-blooded, mean-spirited fellow, Anth.
a water-course, whether on the ground, a conduit, canal, sluice, Ar.; or on the roof, a gutter, spout, Id.
a water-snake, Il., Hdt.
to carry water, Xen.
a water-carrying, a festival of Apollo, Luc.
carrying water, Plut.
as Subst., ὑδρ., a water-carrier, Hdt., Xen.
the water-pourer, name of the constellation Aquarius, Anth.
gushing with water, Eur.
dropsical: metaph., ναῦς ὑδρ. Anth.

entry.etym: epic also ὕδει as if from ὕδος
entry.sense: water, of any kind, but in Hom. rarely of sea-water (which he calls ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ); — also in pl., ὕδατ’ αἰενάοντα Od.; ὕδατα Καφίσια the waters of Cephisos, Pind.:— ὕδωρ κατὰ χειρός water for washing the hands, Ar.; ὕ. ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἔχευαν Hom.—Proverbs., γράφειν τι εἰς ὕδωρ of anything untrustworthy, Soph.; ἐν ὕδατι γρ. Plat.; ὅταν τὸ ὕδωρ πνίγῃ, τί δεῖ ἐπιπίνειν; if water chokes, what more can be done? of a desperate case, Arist.
rain-water, rain, Il., Hdt., attic;—more definitely, ὕδωρ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ Thuc., etc.; Ζεὺς ὕδωρ ὕει, ὁ θεὸς ὕδωρ ποιεῖ Ar.
for the phrase ἐν ὕδατι βρέχεσθαι, Hdt., v. βρέχω.

in attic law-phrase, τὸ ὕδωρ was the water of the water-clock (κλεψύδρα), Dem.; ἐν τῷ ἐμῷ ὕδατι, ἐπὶ τοῦ ἐμοῦ ὕδατος in the time allowed me, Id.; οὐκ ἐνδέχεται πρὸς τὸ αὐτὸ ὕ. εἰπεῖν one cannot say (all) in one speech, Id.; ἐπίλαβε τὸ ὕ. stop the water (which was done while the speech was interrupted by the calling of evidence and reading of documents), Id.; ἀποδιδόναι τινὶ τὸ ὕ. to give him the turn of speaking, Aeschin.
of or belonging to swine, ὑεία κοιλία pig's tripe, Ar.:— θηρίον ὕ., as a type of brutish ignorance, Plat.
Velia in Lower Italy, Hdt.
rainy, Anth.
rain, Lat. pluvius, Il., Hes., Ar.:— esp. a heavy shower, Lat. nimbus, whereas ὄμβρος, Lat. imber, is a lasting rain, and ψεκάς or ψακάς a drizzling rain, Xen., etc.
as adj. in Sup. ἄνεμοι ὑετώτατοι the rainiest winds, Hdt.
swinishness, swinish stupidity, Ar.
swinish, Plat.
epith. of Ζεὺς ὄμβριος, and of Bacchus:—to which of these the cry of Ὕης ἄττης in Dem. should be referred, is doubtful.
to talk nonsense, trifle, prate, Lat. nugari, Ar.
idle talk, nonsense, Plat., Dem.; in pl., ὕθλους λέγειν, like Lat. nugae, Plat.
Dim. of ὗς, Xen.
Dim. of υἱός, Ar.
a grandson, Xen., Dem.
of or for swine, ὑϊκόν τι πάσχειν to have something of the swine's nature, Xen.
adoption as a son, NTest.
etc. A son, Lat. filius, Hom., etc.; υἱὸν ποιεῖσθαί τινα to adopt him as a son, Aeschin.; υἱεῖς ἄνδρες grown up sons, Dem.:—rarely of animals, NTest.
periphr., υἷες Ἀχαιῶν, for Ἀχαιοί, Il.; cf. παῖς.
entry.etym: Hom. sometimes makes the 1st syll. short, as if it were ὑός.

entry.sense: a grandson, Hom., Plut.
the bark of a dog, Eur.: metaph., νηπίοις ὑλάγμασιν with idle snarlings, Aesch.
a barking, baying, Il., Xen.
to carry wood, Dem.
of the forest, savage, Theocr.
a barking, howling, Anth., Plut.
always barking, still howling or yelling, Od.
to bark, bay, howl, of dogs, Il., Ar.; of hounds, to give tongue, Xen.
metaph., κραδίη ὑλακτεῖ howls for rage, Od.; c. acc. cogn. to yell forth bold and shameless words, Soph.; ἄμους’ ὑλακτῶν howling his uncouth songs, Eur.
trans. to bark at, τινά Ar., Isocr.
a barker, Anth.
to howl, bark, bay, of dogs, Od.: so in Mid., κύνες οὐχ ὑλάοντο Id.
trans. to bark or bay at, τινά Od., Theocr.
a forester, Anth.
woody, wooded, Hom., Soph., Eur.; ἀταρπὸς ὑλ. a path through the wood, Anth.
dwelling in the woods, Id.
one who lodges in the wood, Hes.
Lat. sylva, a wood, forest, woodland, Hom., Hdt., etc.; τὰ δένδρα καὶ ὕλη fruit-trees and forest-trees, Thuc.: copse, brushwood, opp. to timber-trees, Xen.
wood cut down, firewood, fuel, Hom., etc.
like Lat. materia, stuff of which a thing is made, the raw material, wood, timber, Od., Hdt.
in Philosophy, matter, Arist.
subject matter, Id.
watching the wood, Anth.
to filter, strain: v. διυλίζω.
one who haunts the woods, Anth.
thick grown with wood, Eur.
watching over woods, Anth.
to cut or fell wood, Hes.
the cutting or felling of wood, Arist.
cutting or felling wood, Il.:— as Subst. ὑλοτόμος, a wood-cutter, woodman, Id., Soph.
pass. cut in the wood: τὸ ὑλότομον a plant used as a charm, Hhymn.
working wood: as Subst. ὑλουργός, ὁ, a carpenter or woodman, Eur.
feeding in the woods, Hes.
feeding in the woods, Eur.
a wood-carrier, Anth.
woody, wooded, Thuc.; τὰ ὑλώδη wooded ground, Xen.
turbid, muddy, Plut.
a forester, Arist.
hymenaeus, the wedding or bridal song, sung by the bride's attendants as they led her to the bridegroom's house, Il., Trag.
a wedding, Soph., Eur.; and in pl., Soph., Eur.
= Ὑμήν, Hymen, the god of marriage, addressed in wedding-songs, Ὑμὴν ὦ Ὑμέναι’ ἄναξ Eur.; doric Ὑμὰν ὦ Ὑμέναιε Theocr.
to sing the wedding-song, Aesch.
to wed, take to wife, Theocr.; proverb., πρίν κεν λύκος οἶν ὑμεναιοῖ Ar.
epith. of Bacchus, Anth.
membrane-winged, Luc.

your, yours, Lat. vester, Hom., etc.; with a Pron. added in gen., ὑμέτερος ἑκάστου θυμός the courage of each of you, Il.; ὑμέτερος αὐτῶν θυμός your own mind, Od.;— ὑμέτερόνδε to your house, Il.:— τὸ ὑμέτερον your part, your business, Hdt.; τὸ δ’ ὑμ. πρᾶξαι your character is to do so and so, Thuc.:—with the Article, αἱ ὑμέτεραι ἐλπίδες hopes raised by you, Id.; τῇ ὑμ. παρακελεύσει for the purpose of advising you, Plat.
a thin skin, membrane, Arist.
Hymen, the god of marriages, v. Ὑμέναιος.
entry.etym: ῡ, whereas in Ὑμέναιος, υ is short.

entry.sense: a singer of hymns, Anth.

with acc. to sing, laud, sing of, Lat. canere, c. acc., Hes., Trag.:—also in Prose, to celebrate, commemorate, Hdt., Xen.;—c. dupl. acc., ἃ τὴν πόλιν ὕμνησα the points wherein I praised our city, Thuc.:—Pass. to be sung of, Ἀργεῖοι ὑμνέαται (ionic for -ηνται) have been praised, Hdt.; ὑμνηθήσεται πόλις Eur.; αἱ ὑμνούμεναι φιλίαι the famous friendships, Arist.
c. acc. cogn. to sing, Aesch., Eur.

to tell over and over and over again, to repeat, recite, rehearse, Lat. decantare, Plat.; ὑμνήσεις κακά wilt sing continually of thy ills, Soph.; τὰν ἐμὰν ὑμνεῦσαι (ionic for -οῦσαι) ἀπιστοσύναν ever singing of my want of faith, Eur.:—Pass., βαί’, ἀεὶ δ’ ὑμνούμενα few words, but such as oft repeated, Soph.
intr. to sing, chant, Thuc., Xen.
in a pass. sense, φῆμαι ὑμνήσουσι περὶ τὰ ὦτα will ring in their ears, Plat. [In Eur. sometimes υ.]
one must praise, Plat., Luc.
a singer, praiser, Plat.
sung of, praised, lauded, Pind.
a composer of hymns, a lyric poet, Theocr., Anth.
making hymns: as Subst., ὑμν., ὁ, a minstrel, Eur.
busied with songs of praise: as Subst., ὑμν., ὁ, a poet, minstrel, Anth.
a hymn, festive song or ode, in praise of gods or heroes, Od.; ὕμνος θεῶν to or in honour of the gods, Aesch.; τιμῶν θεὸν ὕμνοισιν Eur.:—in Trag. also of mournful songs, Aesch., etc.
to sing a hymn or song of praise: generally, to sing, ὑμν. θρῆνον Aesch.
= χρησμῳδέω, Eur. [ῠ in Aesch.]
the singing of a hymn, hymning, Eur.
= χρησμῳδία, a prophetic strain, Id.
singing hymns, ὑμν. κόραι the minstrel maids, Eur.
your, Hom., Hes.
in Pind. also for σός.
a ploughshare, Babr., Plut.
swine's music, swinish taste in music, Ar.
of a ship, having a beak turned up like a swine's snout, Plut.
hen-bane, hyoscyamus, Xen.
a herd of swine, Strab.
summoned by messenger, Aesch.
to clasp in the arms, embrace, Eur.:—Pass., γένος ὑπηγκαλισμένη having them clasped in her arms, Id.
that which is clasped in the arms, a beloved one, Soph., Eur.
to dictate, Lat. praeire verbis, Xen., Dem.
to suggest, Plut.
trans. to lead or bring under, ὕπαγε ζυγὸν ἵππους bring them under the yoke, Il.; simply, ὑπάγειν ἡμιόνους Od.
metaph. to bring under one's power, Hdt., Luc.:—Mid. to bring under one's own power, reduce, Thuc.
to bring a person before the judgment-seat (the ὑπό refers to his being set beneath the judge's seat), Hdt.; ὑπ. τινὰ εἰς δίκην Thuc.; ὑπ. τινὰ θανάτου on a capital charge, Xen.

to lead slowly on, to lead on by degrees, τὰς κύνας Id.:— to lead on by art or deceit, Hdt., Xen.; ὑπ. τινὰ εἰς ἐλπίδα Eur.:—so in Mid., Xen.; ὑπ. τοὺς Θηβαίους to win them, Dem.:—in Mid. also to suggest a thing so as to lead a person on, Eur., Xen.
to take away from under, withdraw, Il.: Pass., ὑπαγομένου τοῦ χώματος Thuc.
to draw off, τὸ στράτευμα Id.
intr., of an army, to draw off or retire slowly, Hdt., Thuc.
to go slowly forwards, draw on, ὕπαγ’ ὦ, ὕπαγ’ ὦ on with you ! Eur.; ὕπαγε, τί μέλλεις; Ar.:—of an army, to come gradually on, Xen.
a leading on gradually, Xen.
(from ὑπάγω intr.) a retreat, withdrawal, Thuc.
to sing by way of accompaniment, in tmesi, Λίνον δ’ ὑπὸ καλὸν ἄειδεν Il.; ὑπ. μέλος Ar.; ὑπ. τινί to accompany with the voice, Id.

entry.etym: epic for ὑποδέδοικα, perf. of ὑποδείδω

entry.sense: to shew some respect for, τινα Xen.
out under, slipping away, Il.
prep. with gen. under, at the side of, Id.
under the sky, in the open air, a-field, ὑπ. κατακοιμηθῆναι, of an army, Hdt., Thuc.; ὑπ. δρόσοι Aesch.
as Subst., ἐν ὑπαίθρῳ, sub Dio, in the open air, Xen.
τὰ ὕπαιθρα, the field, the open country, Polyb.
to set on fire below or secretly, Soph.
Dep. to intimate darkly, hint at, Dem., Plut.
to dart beneath, c. acc., Il.
to dart from under, c. gen., Id.:—also, ὑπᾴξας διὰ θυρῶν Soph.
Pass. to be somewhat ashamed, τινά τι of a thing before a person, Plat.
under accusation, called to account, responsible, τινος or ὑπέρ τινος for a thing, Antipho; τινι to a person, Xen.; ὑπαίτιόν ἐστί τί τινι a charge is made against one, Id.
obedience, NTest.
absol. to listen, hearken, give ear, Hom., Eur.
to make answer when called, Od., Theocr.
foll. by a case, to listen or hearken to, give ear to, attend to, τινός Ar., etc.; also, ὑπ. τινί Thuc., etc.
Special senses:
of porters, to answer a knock at the door, ὑπ. τινί Plat., Theophr.; ὁ ὑπακούσας the porter, Xen.
of a judge, to listen to a complainant, τινί Id.:—but of accused persons, to answer to a charge, Dem.

of dependents and subjects, to submit to, τινός Hdt., Xen.; τινί Ar., Thuc.: also to yield to, comply with, τινί Plat.:—c. gen. rei, to give ear to, Xen.; ὑπ. τῷ ξυμφόρῳ τινός to comply with his interest, Thuc.:—absol. to give way, submit, comply, Hdt.
to answer one's expectations, to succeed, Luc.
metaph., αὐγαῖς ἡλίου ὑπ. to be subject to the sun's rays, Pind.
to lay thinly on, to spread like salve; in Mid., ὑπαλείφεσθαι φάρμακον Plat.
to anoint, τὼ ὀφθαλμώ Ar.:—in Mid. to anoint oneself, Id.; ὑπ. τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς to anoint one's eyes, Xen.:— Pass. of the eyes, ὑπαληλιμμένοι Id.
epic Dep. ὑπαλευάμενος θάνατον Od.; ὑπαλεύεο φήμην (imperat.) Hes.
