to stake, hazard, venture, Plat.; ὑποθεὶς τὸν ἴδιον κίνδυνον at his own risk, Dem.
Mid. as law-term, much like ἀντιτιμάομαι to propose a less penalty for oneself, Xen.
to sound in answer, echo, Aesch.
to murmur in an under-tone, Luc.
τινά Thuc.; c. acc. et inf., Id.
to suspect, surmise, Thuc.; c. acc. et inf., Id.
c. acc. pers. to suspect him, Id.
so as Dep. ὑποτοπέομαι to suspect a thing, Hdt., Ar.; c. acc. et inf. to suspect that . . , Hdt., Ar.
to lisp a little, Luc.
to tremble a little, Plat.
to bring up secretly:—Mid. to cherish secretly, Xen., Luc.:—Pass. to grow up in succession, Lat. subnasci, Plat.
to run in under, ὑπέδραμε καὶ λάβε γούνων she ran in under the sword and clasped his knees, Od.; ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας τοῦ ἵππου ὑπέδραμε κύων Hdt.: hence to trip up, Ar.
to run or stretch away under, Hhymn.
to run in between, intercept, Ar., Xen.
to insinuate oneself into any one's good graces, flatter or deceive, Eur., Plat.
to tremble a little, to shrink back, give ground, Il.: c. acc. to flee before, Id.
to rub down the ingredients of a dish, Cratin.
a dish compounded of various ingredients, pounded up together, Lat. moretum, Com.
to tremble under one, of a man's limbs, Il.
somewhat afraid or timid, Aeschin., Luc.
a turning back, repulse, Plut.
a relapse, recurrence, Id.
returning, Hom., Eur.
rallying from the effect of a blow, Theocr.
to murmur, hum in an undertone, Anth.
to eat by way of preparation, Xen.
to sketch out, Lat. adumbrare, Arist.

to strike or push down, κοντῷ ὑπ. ἐς λίμνην to poke down into the lake with a pole, Hdt.; ὑποτύπτουσα φιάλῃ ἐς τὴν θήκην dipping with a cup into the chest, Id.; ὑποτύψας τούτῳ (sc. τῷ κηλωνηίῳ) ἀντλέει he draws it dipping with the bucket into the water, Id.; ὑπ. τοῖν ποδοῖν Ar.
an outline, pattern, NTest.
Pass. to burn with a smouldering fire, burn secretly, Plut., Luc.
somewhat arrogant, Plut.
under the udder, sucking, Anth.

of wounds, festering under the scar: metaph. with festering sores underneath, unsound beneath, Plat., etc.; ὕπ. αὐτονομία a hollow independence, Thuc.; κάλλος κακῶν ὕπουλον a fair outside skinning over ills below, Soph.:—adv., ὑπούλως ἀκροᾶσθαι to render a hollow obedience, Plut.
under heaven, under the sky, Il.
reaching up to heaven, Hom.

to render service or help to one, to serve, assist, succour, τινί Hdt., etc.; χρηστὰ ὑπ. (sc. τοῖς Ἀθηναίοισι) to do them good service, Hdt., etc.; ὑπ. χάριν τινί Aesch.:—Pass., τὰ ὑπουργημένα services done or rendered, Hdt.
a service done or rendered, Hdt., Xen.
one must be kind to, Luc.
service rendered, Soph., Arist.
rendering service, serviceable, promoting, conducive to a thing, c. dat., Xen.
to bring to light from under, θρῆνυν ὑπέφηνε τραπέζης he drew the stool from under the table, Od.
to shew a little, just shew, Dem.
Pass. to be seen under, ὑπὸ τὰς πύλας πόδες ὑποφαίνονται Thuc.
to just shew oneself, be half seen, Xen.
Act. used intr. of the dawn of day, ὑποφαίνει ἡμέρα day just begins to break, Id.; so, ὑποφαίνει ἔαρ Id.:—metaph., τὰ νῦν ὑποφαίνοντα the difficulties now dawning upon us, Plat.
a light shewing through a small hole: a narrow opening, Hdt.
Dep. to spare a little, Xen.
somewhat sparingly, rarely, Plut.

entry.note: fut. ὑπ-οίσω aor1 ὑπήνεγκα aor2 ὑπήνεγκον
entry.sense: to carry away under, esp. to bear out of danger, Il.
to bear or carry by being under, to bear a burden, Xen.: metaph. to support, bear, endure, submit to, πόνους καὶ κινδύνους Isocr.; γῆρας καὶ πενίαν Aeschin., etc.
to hold out, suggest, proffer, Soph.; to pretend, allege, Xen.
to carry down:—Pass. to be borne down by a stream, Plut.: metaph. to slip or sink down, decay, Id.
to flee from under, shun, Il., Eur.: to withdraw from, endeavour to evade, Thuc.
absol. to retire a little, withdraw, Hdt., Thuc.
to hold the office of ὑποφήτης, Luc.
a suggester, interpreter, a priest who declares an oracle, Il.; Μουσάων ὑποφῆται, i. e. poets, Theocr.

entry.note: aor2 ὑπ-έφθην inf. ὑπο-φθῆναι part. -φθάς mid. part. -φθάμενος
entry.sense: to haste before, be or get beforehand, Il.; ὑποφθάμενος κτεῖνεν Od.
c. acc. to be beforehand with one, Plut.; Mid., τὸν ὑποφθαμένη φάτο μῦθον Od.
Dep.
to speak in an undertone, of a ventriloquist, Plat.
to reply, Plut.
to feel secret envy at, τινί Xen.
somewhat jealous: adv., ὑποφθόνως ἔχειν to behave somewhat jealously, Xen.
to heat from below, Anth.
murdering secretly, Soph.
a holding under, putting forward, by way of excuse, Xen.
suggestion, counsel, Hes.
to shudder slightly, Luc.
to make to grow up, Il.
to lie hidden under, τινί Anth.
to call out in answer, Plut.: to sing in answer, Mosch.
Dep.:— to give way gradually or a little, Il.
under the bridle:— ἡ ὑποχαλινιδία (sc. ἡνία), a chin-strap attached to the bit, Xen.
containing a mixture of copper, Plat.
to engrave under, Plut.
somewhat bright-eyed, Xen.
to gape a little, Ar., Xen.
under the hand, in hand, Od.
of persons, under any one's hand, under command, subject, τινι Hdt., etc.; λαβεῖν τινα ὑποχείριον to get into one's power, Eur.; ἔχειν τινὰ ὑπ. Thuc.

entry.note: fut. -χεῶ aor1 ὑπ-έχεα epic -έχευα Pass. perf. ὑπο-κέχυμαι
entry.sense: to pour into a cup placed under, to pour out; of dry things, to strew or spread under, Hom.: Pass., φύλλα ὑποκεχυμένα ὑπὸ τοῖς ποσί leaves scattered under the feet, Hdt.:—metaph., ἀπιστίη ὑπεκέχυτο αὐτῷ distrust was poured secretly into him, i. e. stole over him, Id.
under the earth, subterranean, Hes., Eur., Anth.
Pass. to be rolled beneath, Il.
to supply, Strab.
a supplying, succour, Strab.
subject, τινι Xen.; βασιλῆς βασιλέως ὕποχοι king's subjects or officers, of the great king, Aesch.
= ἔνοχος, liable to, τινος Dem.
indebted, in debt, Ar.; ὑπ. τινος his debtor, Plut.
of property, involved, Lat. obaeratus, Dem.
c. gen., ὑπ. φιλίας bound by ties of friendship, Plut.
to smear under or upon, τί τινι Hdt.; ὑπ. τινί to paint his face under the eyes, Xen.:—Mid., ὑποχρίεσθαι τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς to paint one's own eyes underneath, Id.
containing a mixture or proportion of gold: metaph. of persons, Plat.
to go back, retire, recoil, Il., Thuc.; often in part., ὑποχωρήσας φεύγει Dem.
c. gen. to retire from a place, Hdt., Xen.; ὑπ. τινὶ τοῦ θρόνου to withdraw from one's seat in honour of another, give it up to him, Ar.; and, ὑπ. τινι to give way to another, Thuc.
c. acc. to avoid, shun, Id., Plat.
to go on in succession, Pind.
a downward evacuation, Theophr.
a going back, retirement, retreat, Polyb.
a retiring-place, retreat, Luc.
having sand under, γῆ ὑποψαμμοτέρη somewhat sandy, Hdt.
somewhat dappled, ἵππος Strab.
suspicion, jealousy, ὑποψίην ἔχειν ἔς τινα Hdt., attic; πρός τινα Dem.; ἐν ὑπ. ποιεῖσθαι Aeschin.
of the object, ἔχειν ὑπ. to admit of suspicion, Plat.; ὑπ. παρέχειν Thuc.
viewed from beneath the brows; ὑπόψιος ἄλλων viewed with suspicion among others, Il.
to underbid in the purchase of victuals or to buy up underhand, Ar.
to bend oneself back, to carry one's head high, Aeschin.:—Pass., κάρα ὑπτιάζεται his head lies supine, Soph.
that which is laid back, ὑπτιάσματα χερῶν supplication with hands upstretched, Lat. supinis manibus, Aesch.; ὑπτίασμα κειμένου πατρός his father's body as it lies supine, Id.
a laying oneself backwards, Luc.
one must throw back, ἑαυτόν Xen.
Pass. to be upset, Aesch.

entry.etym: from ὑπό, as Lat. supinus from sub
entry.sense: laid back, laid on one's back, πέσεν ὕπτιος he fell backwards, opp. to πρηνής, Il.; of a quadruped, ὀρθοῦ ἑστεῶτος καὶ ὑπτίου rearing upright and falling backwards, Hdt.

generally with the under side uppermost, χείρ ὑπτία the hollow of the hand, Plut.; ἐξ ὑπτίου κράνους from the upturned helmet, with the hollow uppermost, Aesch.; so, παράθες ὑπτίαν (τὴν ἀσπίδα) Ar.; ἀψὶς ὑπτία a half-wheel with the concave side uppermost, Hdt.; ὑπτίοις σέλμασιν ναυτίλλεται he sails with the bottom uppermost, i. e. suffers shipwreck, Soph.; ἐξ ὑπτίας νεῖν to swim on the back (in metaph. sense), Plat.
of land, sloping evenly, of Egypt, Hdt.
to push or thrust away, Il.
under the elbow, Theocr.
an oath taken to delay proceedings (v. ὑπόμνυμι II), an application for postponement of a trial, Dem.
an oath taken by the prosecutor in a γραφὴ παρανόμων (v. παράνομος 2), with the effect of suspending the proposed decree, Id.
to strike one under the eye:—Pass. to have a black eye, ὑπωπιασμένος Ar.
metaph. to bruise, mortify, NTest.: also, to annoy greatly, wear out, Id.
the part of the face under the eyes: generally the face, countenance, Il.
a blow in the face, a black eye, Ar.
the foot of a mountain, the skirts of a mountain range, Il., Hdt.
under the roof, in the house, Il., Pind., Ar.
Eur.: of a swallow's nest, under the eaves, Anth.
pale yellow, sallow, Luc.
a jar, for pickles, Ar.
a shrub from which the dye ὕσγινον is derived.
dyed scarlet, Xen., Luc.
a dye from the shrub ὕσγη, scarlet, Anth.
a fight, battle, combat, Il.; metaplast. epic dat. ὑσμῖνι as if from ὑσμίν or ὑσμίς, Id.
the wild swine, whether boar (hog) or sow, Hom., etc.; σῦς ἄγριος Il.; also σῦς κάπριος or κάπρος, v. sub vocc.
the domestic pig, Hom., etc.
a rope drawn across the racecourse, let down when the runners were to start, the starting-line, Plat., Anth.
the snare or gin of a birdcatcher, Theocr.
a javelin, the Roman pilum, Polyb., etc.
hyssop, prob. the caper-plant, NTest.

entry.etym: poetic for ὕστατος, as μεσσάτιος for μέσσος, Hom.
entry.sense: neut. as adv. at last, Il.

on the day after, the next day (cf. προτεραῖος); τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ (ionic -αίῃ) ἡμέρᾳ on the following day, next day, Lat. postridie, Hdt.; often without ἡμέρᾳ, Id., attic; also, ἐς τὴν ὑστεραίην Hdt.; ἐν τῇ ὑστ. Plat.:—c. gen., τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ τῆς μάχης on the day after the battle, Id.
= ὕστερος, later, subsequent, Hdt., Xen.
the womb, mostly in pl. ὑστέραι, etc.
to be behind or later, come late, Hdt., attic

c. gen. rei, to come later than, come too late for, ὑστέρησαν ἡμέρῃ μιῇ τῆς συγκειμένης came one day after the appointed day, Hdt.; τῆς Μυτιλήνης ὑστερήκει had come too late to save Mytilene, Thuc.; ὑστ. τῆς πατρίδος to fail to assist it, Xen.
c. gen. pers. to come after him, Id.; also c. dat. to come too late for him, Thuc.
metaph. to come short of, be inferior to, τινός Plat., etc.
to come short of, fail to obtain:—so in Mid., ὑστερεῖσθαί τινος NTest.
absol. to be in want, Id.
of things, to fail, be wanting, Lat. deficere, Id.
deficiency, need, want, NTest.
to come after, come later or too late, Thuc., Xen.
c. gen. rei, to come short of, come too late for, Dem.; to lag behind, Xen.
metaph. to come short of, be inferior to any one, c. gen., Id.:—absol., ὑστ. τὸ εἰδέναι he falls short in knowledge, Id.
avenging after the act, late-avenging, Aesch.
coming late, Anth.
latter, last, comp. and Sup. without any Posit. adj. in use.
ὕστερος, η, ον latter,
of Place, latter, coming after, following, Eur., Xen.:—c. gen., ὕστεροι ἡμῶν behind us, Plat.; ὑστέρα νεώς behind (slower than) a ship, Aesch.
of Time, next, Il.; τῷ ὑστέρῳ ἔτει in the next year, Xen.; ὑστέρῳ χρόνῳ in after time, Aesch., etc.:—c. gen. pers. later than, after, Il., Plat.; also ὑστέρῳ χρόνῳ τούτων Hdt.
later, too late, Il., Soph.
c. gen. rei, too late for, Hdt., Ar.
as Subst. οἱ ὕστεροι =Lat. posteri, Eur.
of inferiority in Age, Worth, or Quality, γένει ὕστερος, i. e. younger, Il.:— c. gen., οὐδενὸς ὕστ. second to none, Soph., Thuc.; ὕστερος τῶν νόμων below the laws, Aeschin.
neut. ὕστερον as adv. behind, c. gen., Xen.
of Time, later, afterwards, Hom., etc.; also ὕστερα Od.: —c. gen., ὕστερον τούτων later than these things, after them, Hdt.; πολλῷ ὕστ. τῶν Τρωικῶν Thuc.
in adv. sense with Preps., ἐς ὕστερον Od., Hdt., etc.: — ἐν ὑστέρῳ Thuc.:— ἐξ ὑστέρης Hdt.
ὕστατος, η, ον last,
of Place, πρῶτοί τε καὶ ὕστατοι Il.

of Time, τίνα πρῶτον, τίνα δ’ ὕστατον ἐξενάριξεν; Id.; πρὸς ὕστ. φῶς Aesch.: ἡ ὑστάτη (sc. ἡμέρα) τῆς ὁρτῆς the last day of the feast, Hdt.; οὐκ ἐν ὑστάτοις not among the last, Eur.; οἱ ὕστατοι εἰπόντες Dem., etc.:—c. gen., ὕστατος ἁλώσιος all too late for . . , Pind.
the neut. sg. and pl. as adv., πύματόν τε καὶ ὕστατον Od.; ὕστατα καὶ πύματα Il.; νῦν ὕστατα Id.; ὕστατα Hdt., etc.
in adv. sense with Preps., ἐν ὑστάτοις at last, Plat.
late-destroying, Soph.
sounding after, echoing, Anth.
the porcupine, Hdt.
a whip for punishing slaves, Ar.
suffused with blood, blood-shot, Dem.
of temperament, sanguine, Plat.
to weave, ἱστὸν ὑφαίνειν to weave a web, Hom.; ἱμάτιον Plat., etc.:—absol. to weave, ply the loom, Hdt.:—Mid., ἱμάτιον ὑφαίνεσθαι to weave oneself a cloak, Plat.
to contrive, plan, invent, Lat. texere, δόλον ὑφαίνειν Il.; μῆτιν ὑφ. Od.
generally, to create, construct, Pind.
a taking away from under, a purloining, ap. Dem.

entry.note: fut. ήσω aor2 ὑφεῖλον ionic ὑπ-αιρέω
entry.sense: to seize underneath or inwardly, Hom.
to draw or take away from under a thing, c. gen., Il., Plat.:—also τὴν χεῖρα ὑφῄρει tried to draw it away, Ar.

to take away underhand, filch away, Thuc.; ὑφ. τῆς ὑποψίας gradually to take away part of . . , Id.:—Pass., ὑπαραιρημένος (ionic perf. part.) put secretly away, made away with, Hdt.:—so in Mid. to take away underhand, filch away, purloin, Id., Ar., etc.
in Mid. also c. acc. pers., ὑφ. τινά τινος to rob him of a thing, Aeschin.
under the sea, ὕφ. Ἔρεβος the darkness of the deep, Soph.; τὸ ὕφαλον the lower waters, Strab.
a weaver, Plat.
skilled in weaving, Plat.: adv. -κῶς, in weaver-like fashion, Id.
ἡ ὑφαντική (sc. τέχνη), the art of weaving, Id.
woven by the flight of the shuttle, Ar.
woven, Od., Trag.; ὅσα ὑφαντά τε καὶ λεῖα brocaded and plain stuffs, Thuc.
to set on fire from underneath, Hdt., Eur., etc.
metaph. to inflame unperceived, Xen.
to snatch away from under, Xen.
to take away underhand, filch away, Lat. surripere, Ar.
ὑφ. λόγον to snatch away a word just when one is going to speak it, take the word out of one's mouth, Hdt.: to snap up, Ar.
a woven robe, web, Od.
remissly, less violently, Lat. submisse, Xen.
I placed under or secretly, ὑπείσας ἄνδρας having set them in ambush, Hdt.
one must submit to, Plat.
one must draw away, τῶν δᾳδίων some of the torches, Ar.
to draw away gently, ὑφ. τινὰ ποδοῖιν to draw one away by the two feet, Il.: — to draw away by undermining, Thuc.
to creep on secretly, Lat. subrepere, ὑφεῖρπε γὰρ πολύ the report was spreading far, Soph.
like ὑπέρχομαι II, of involuntary feelings, to steal upon, come over, Lat. subire animum, χαρά μ’ ὑφέρπει, τρόμος μ’ ὑφ. Aesch.
Dep.
to go just before, to guide, lead, τινι Eur., Plat., etc.:— absol. to go first, lead the way, Soph., Thuc., Plat.; κατὰ τὸν ὑφηγημένον τρόπον according to the normal plan, Arist.
c. acc. cogn., ὑφ. τὴν ὁδόν to shew the way, Plut.
c. acc. rei, to shew the way to, instruct in, Xen., Plat.
to lead to a thing, indicate that it is so, Aesch.
a guiding, guidance, Dem.
one who leads the way, a guide, leader, Soph.; ὡς ὑφηγητοῦ τινος (sc. ὄντος) as if led by some (invisible) guide, Id.
a teacher, master, Plut.
to be a ὑφηνίοχος, Luc.:—Pass. to drive after or behind, of chariots, Dem.
the charioteer, as subordinate to the warrior in his chariot, Il.
a web, in pl., Aesch., Eur.
somewhat less or smaller, Hes.
to crouch beneath, c. dat., Eur.
a settling or sinking, Strab.
to sit down, crouch, Eur.
to let down, ὑφ. ἱστόν to lower the mast, Il.; ὑφ. ἱστία, Lat. submittere vela, Hhymn.
to put under, τί τινι Hom.; τι ὑπό τι Xen.:— to put a young one under its dam, put it to suck, Od., Theocr.; in Mid., of the mother, ὑφίεσθαι μαστοῖς to put it to her breast, to suckle it, Eur.
ὑφ. τινά to engage any one secretly, to prepare him to play a part, to suborn, Soph.: Pass., ὡς ἔχιδν’ ὑφειμένη like a snake secretly introduced, slipped in, Id.
to give up, surrender, Xen.

intr. to slacken, relax or abate from a thing, c. gen., ὑπεὶς τῆς ὀργῆς Hdt.; absol. to give in, abate, οὐδὲν ὑπιέντες Id.:—so too in Mid., Id.; so of things, τὸ ὕδωρ ὑπίεται τοῦ ψυχροῦ abates from its chill, Id.; τοῦ στόματός γε ὑφ. I give way as to it, Xen.; c. dat. to yield, give way to any one, τοῖς πολεμίοις Id.
in Mid. and Pass. to lower one's sails, Ar.; mostly in part. perf., πλεῖν ὑφειμένῃ δοκεῖ μοι methinks I should run with lowered sails, i. e. to lower my tone, Soph.
σώζω νεοσσοὺς ὄρνις ὣς ὑφειμένη, like a cowering hen, —or perhaps with my nestlings under me, Eur.
generally, to submit, Xen.; c. inf., κατθανεῖν ὑφειμένη submissively prepared to die, Eur.
to steal over one, Il.

in these tenses Causal, to place or set under, τί τινι Hdt., Pind.; τρεῖς σταυροὺς ὑπίστησι plants three piles in the lake to support a house, Hdt.:—metaph., γνώμας ὑποστήσας σοφάς having laid them as a foundation, Soph.
to post secretly or in ambush, Hdt., Xen.
Causal also in fut. and aor1 mid. to substitute, τί τινι one thing for another, Xen.
Pass., with aor2 act. ὑπ-έστην, perf. ὑφ-έστηκα, ionic part. ὑπ-εστεώς:— to stand under as a support, c. dat., Hdt.
to sink to the bottom, settle, τὸ ὑφιστάμενον the milk, opp. to τὸ ἐφιστάμενον (the cream), Id.

to place oneself under an engagement, engage or promise to do, c. inf. fut., ὅσς’ Ἀχιλῆι ὑπέστημεν δώσειν Il., etc.; c. inf. aor., οὔ τίς με ὑπέστη σαῶσαι Id.; c. inf. pres., Hdt.:—absol., after promise given, Od.; ὥσπερ ὑπέστη as he promised, Thuc.:—when foll. by acc., an inf. may be supplied, τρίποδας οὕς οἱ ὑπέστη (sc. δώσειν) Il.; ἐκτελέουσιν ὑπόσχεσιν ἥνπερ ὑπέσταν Id.
to submit to any one, τινι Id.

c. acc. rei, to submit to, consent to, ὁ τὸ ἐλάχιστον ὑπιστάμενος who offers to take the least, Hdt.; ὑφ. τὸν πλοῦν to undertake it unwillingly, Thuc.; so, ὑφ. τὸν κίνδυνον Id.: —rarely c. dat., ὑφ. ξυμφοραῖς ταῖς μεγίσταις Id.
to undertake an office, Xen.
to lie concealed or in ambush, Hdt., Eur., etc.
to support an attack, to resist, withstand, c. dat., Aesch.; c. acc., Eur., Thuc.:—absol. to stand one's ground, face the enemy, Lat. subsistere, Eur., Thuc.

entry.note: fut. ὑπ-όψομαι aor2 ὑπ-εῖδον and mid. -ειδόμην
entry.sense: to look at from below, view with suspicion or jealousy, suspect, τινά Thuc., etc.
to lie secretly at anchor, Polyb.
Pass. and Mid., to come to anchor secretly or under a place, Thuc., Plut.
an anchorage, Strab.
under water, of a diver, Thuc.
a big talker, boaster, braggart, Od.
to carry the neck high, shew off, Anth.
carrying the neck high, ἵππος Plat.:—metaph. stately, towering, Eur.
high-roofed, high-vaulted, Hom., Ar.
talking big, grandiloquent, vaunting, Aesch.
a carrying the neck high, Xen.
with lofty cliffs, Aesch.
Dep. to talk high, speak proudly, Plat.
high-minded: τὸ ὑψηλόνουν Plat.
high, lofty, high-raised, Lat. altus, sublimis, Hom., Hdt., Trag., etc.; of a highland country, χώρη ὀρεινὴ καὶ ὑψηλή Hdt.; ὑψηλὰ χωρία Thuc.
metaph. high, lofty, stately, Pind., Plat.; ὑψηλὰ κομπεῖν to talk loftily, Soph.; πνεῦμα ὑψηλὸν αἴρειν Eur.
to be high-minded, NTest.
high-minded, high-spirited, haughty, Eur., Plat.
high-sounding, ἵπποι ὑψηχέες loud-neighing, Il.
set on high, high-placed, Pind., Soph.
loud-shouter, name of a frog, Batr.
high-thundering, Hom.
born on high, ἐλαίας ὑψιγέννητος κλάδος its topmost shoot, Aesch.
with high limbs, high-stemmed, Pind.
of a rower, sitting high on the benches; of Zeus, high-throned, Il., Hes.
high-throned, Pind.
high-topped, Hhymn.
wandering on high, Anth.
high-horned, Od., Soph.: —also metapl. acc. ἱψικέρᾱτα πέτραν a high-peaked rock, Pind. ap. Ar.
with lofty foliage, towering, Hom., Hes., Eur.
high boasting, arrogant: adv., Soph.
with high crags, of a mountain, Hom. Epigram.
of towns, built on a high crag, Aesch.

Υ, υ, τό, indecl., twentieth letter of Gr. alphabet: as numeral υʹ = 400, but ͵υ = 400,000. Called ὑψιλόν, because the orig. sound was broad, like ου, and afterwards was thin like French u. The Gr. υ, like Lat. v, was originally both a vowel (u) and a semi-vowel (v), v. infr. II.
Interchanges of υ with other vowels,
aeolic for ο, as ὄνυμα στύμα ὔρνις for ὄνομα στόμα ὄρνις; also πίσυρες for πέτορες (τέσσαρες), cf. νύξ, Lat. nox.
aeolic, the diphth. ου became οι, Μοῖσα for Μοῦσα, λέγοισα for λέγουσα.
ῡ sometimes replaces οι, as κοινός ξυνός, κοίρανος κύριος.
Boeot. ῡ for ω, as χελύνη for χελώνη.

υ as a semivowel represented vau (ϝ), the digamma, sometimes it formed the diphth. αυ, as αὐέρυσαν for ἀνϝέρυσαν (v. αὐερύω), αὐίαχοι for ἀνϝίαχοι, αὐάτα for ἀϝάτα (ἄτη), καλαῦροψ for καλάϝροψ, ταλαύρινος for ταλάϝρινος, ταναύποδες for ταναϝόποδες; sometimes the dipth. ευ, as εὔαδεν for ἔϝαδεν.
high-crested, Pind.
ruling on high, Hes., Ar.
metaph. towering, Pind.
high-built, Hhymn.
dwelling high in the clouds, Pind.
high-built, towering, Anth.
on high, aloft, Hom.: on the high sea, out at sea, Od.
with high ground, high-placed, Pind.
with high foliage, towering, Hom.
high-flying, soaring, Hom., Ar.: generally lofty, Eur.
high or honoured in one's city, Soph.
high-footed, i. e. high-reared, lofty, Soph.
with high stern, Strab.
with high prow, Strab.
with high gates, Il., Eur.
high-towered, Aesch., Soph.

entry.etym: Sup. without any Posit. in use
entry.sense: highest, loftiest, Aesch., Soph., etc.; ἐν τοῖς ὑψίστοις, i. e. in heaven above, NTest.
loftier, Theocr.
high-shining, far-seen, Anth.
high-minded, haughty, Pind.
long-haired, Pind.
from on high, from aloft, from above, Lat. desuper, Il., Hes.
like ὑψοῦ, high, aloft, on high, Anth.
c. gen. above, over, Pind.
aloft, on high, Il.
high-roofed, high-ceiled, Hom.
aloft, on high, up high, Hom.; ὑψός’ ἔχοντες high reaching, Il.
height, Hdt., attic; ὕ. ἔχειν, λαμβάνειν to rise to some height, Thuc.:—absol. ὕψος, in height, opp. to μῆκος or εὖρος, Hdt.
metaph. the top, summit, crown, Plat.
aloft, on high, Hom.; τῆς πόλιος ἐκκεχωσμένης ὑψοῦ having the soil raised to a great height, Hdt.:—metaph., ὑψοῦ ἐξᾶραί τι to praise it highly, Id.; ὑψοῦ αἴρειν θυμόν Soph.
to lift high, raise up, Batr., Anth.: Mid. to raise for oneself, Anth.
metaph. to elevate, exalt, NTest.

to send rain, to rain, Ζεὺς ὗε Hom., etc.; ὁ θεὸς ὕει Hdt.:—then, the nom. being omitted, ὕει used impers., Lat. pluit, it rains, Hes., Hdt.; ὕοντος when it is raining, Ar.; ὕοντος πολλῷ as it was raining heavily, Xen.

c. acc. loci, ἑπτὰ ἐτέων οὐκ ὗε τὴν Θήρην for seven years it did not rain on Thera, Hdt.:—hence in Pass., with fut. mid. to be rained on, Od.; ὕσθησαν αἱ Θῆβαι Thebes was rained upon, i. e. it rained there, Hdt.; ἡ χώρη ὕεται, i. e. it rains in the country, Id.
c. acc. cogn., ὗσε χρυσόν it rained gold, Pind.; καινὸν ἀεὶ Ζεὺς ὕει ὕδωρ Ar.
brightest, Od.
brighter, Anth.

entry.etym: no pres. in use, used as aor2 of ἐσθίω
entry.sense: to eat, devour, φαγέμεν καὶ πιέμεν Od.; φαγεῖν τε καὶ πιεῖν Ar., etc.; c. gen. to eat of a thing, Od.
to eat up, devour, squander, Id.
in NTest. occurs a fut. φάγομαι, 2nd sg. φάγεσαι.
a glutton, NTest.
shining, Anth.
to shine, only found in part. φαέθων, beaming, radiant, Hom., Soph., Eur.; absol., πάννυχα καὶ φαέθοντα nights and days, Soph.
as a prop. n.
φαέθων, ὁ, shiner, one of the steeds of Eos, Od.
son of Helios or Apollo, famous for his unlucky driving of the sun-chariot, Eur.
the planet Jupiter, Cic.

entry.note: φαεινός, doric and attic φαεννόσος, η, ον
entry.sense: shining, beaming, radiant, Hom., Pind., Trag.
of the voice, clear, distinct, far-sounding, Pind.
generally, splendid, brilliant, Id.
bringing light to mortals, Hom., Eur.
light-bringing, Aesch., Eur.
ionic Φαίηξ, ηκος, a Phaeacian: they were the Homeric inhabitants of the island of Scheria (i. e. Corcyra, now Corfu), Od.
shining, of men's limbs, prob. in reference to the common use of oil, Od., Hes., Pind.
of heroes, famous, glorious, Hom., Aesch.
with bright, joyous mind, Aesch.
Pass. to beam with joy, Xen.
bright, beaming, Aesch.: sparkling, of water, Anth.
metaph. beaming with joy, bright, joyous, jocund, Solon., Trag., Xen.:—adv. -δρῶς, joyously, cheerily, Xen.; neut. pl. φαιδρά as adv., Soph.
brightness: joyousness, Isocr.
a cleanser, washer:—fem. φαιδρύντρια, Aesch.
to make bright, to cleanse, Aesch.; θεαὶ μορφὰν ἐφαίδρυναν gave me a bright form, Eur.: —in Mid., χρόα φαιδρύνεσθαι to wash one's skin clean, Hes.
metaph. to cheer, Aesch.:—Pass. to beam or brighten up with joy, Xen.
with bright, joyous look, Aesch., Eur.
a white shoe, Anth.
formed from the Lat. paenula, a thick upper garment, a cloak, NTest.
light-bringing, Hhymn.
a planet, shiner, our Saturn, Cic.
Act. to bring to light, make to appear, Hom., etc.:—Mid. to exhibit as one's own, Soph.
to shew forth, make known, reveal, disclose, shew, Od., Soph. etc.: γόνον Ἑλένηι φ. to shew her a child, i. e. grant her to bear one, Od.
of sound, to make it clear to the ear, make it ring clear, Id., Aesch.
to make clear, explain, expound, Hdt.
in attic to inform against one, to indict, impeach, Ar.:— to inform of a thing as contraband, Id.: Pass., τὰ φανθέντα articles informed against as contraband, Dem.
absol. to give information, Xen.
φαίνειν φρουράν at Sparta, to proclaim a levy, call out the array, Id.
absol. to give light, Od.; so of the sun, moon, etc., φ. τινί Ar., Theocr.; so of the Dioscuri shining in mid-air, Eur.; ἀγανὴ φαίνους’ ἐλπίς soft shining hope, Aesch.
Hom. uses the ionic aor. φάνεσκε really intr., appeared:— also perf. 2 πέφηνα is intr., Hdt., Soph., Dem.
Pass. to come to light, be seen, appear, Hom.; of fire, to shine brightly, Id.:—often of the rising of heavenly bodies, Il., Hes.; of daybreak, φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς Hom.

of persons, to come into being, φανεὶς δύστηνος born to misery, Soph.; δοῦλος φανείς shewn to be, having become, a slave, Id.:—also of events, τέλος πέφανται Il.; τὸ φανθέν what has once come to light, Soph., etc.

to appear to be so and so, c. inf., ἥτις ἀρίστη φαίνεται εἶναι Od.; τοῦτό μοι θειότατον φαίνεται γενέσθαι Hdt.:—inf. omitted, ὅστις φαίνηται ἄριστος Od., etc.:—also c. part., but φαίνεσθαι c. inf. indicates that a thing appears to be so and so, φαίνεσθαι c. part. states the fact that it manifestly is so and so, ἐμοὶ σὺ πλουτέειν φαίνεαι you appear to me to be rich, Hdt.; but, εὔνοος ἐφαίνετο ἐών he was manifestly well-inclined, Id.; φαίνεται ὁ νόμος βλάπτων the law manifestly harms, but, φαίνεται ὁ νόμος ἡμᾶς βλάψειν it appears likely to harm us, Dem.:—with the part. omitted, Κᾶρες ἐφάνησαν (sc. ὄντες) they were manifest Carians, Thuc.; τί φαίνομαι (sc. ὤν); what do I look like? Eur.
in dialogue, φαίνεταί σοι ταῦτα; does this appear so? is not this so? Answ. φαίνεται, yes, Plat.; [τοῦτο] φῆις εἶναι; Answ. φαίνομαι (sc. λέγειν) Xen.
οὐδαμοῦ φανῆναι nullo in loco haberi, Plat.
dusky, dun, gray, Lat. fuscus, Plat.
dark-robed, Aesch.
entry.etym: second syll. long, quasi φαιοκχίτων; v. X χ fin.

entry.sense: a bundle, fagot, Lat. fasciculus, Hdt., Eur.; ὕλης φάκελοι fascines, Thuc.
a dish of lentils (φακοί), lentil-soup, Ar.
lentil, and its fruit, Hdt., etc.
in phalanxes, Il., Polyb.
to fight in a phalanx; generally, to fight in the ranks, Xen.
one who fights in the phalanx, Anth.
a line of battle, battle-array, Il.; mostly in pl. the ranks, Id., Hes.

the phalanx, i. e. the heavy infantry (ὁπλῖται) in battle-order, Xen., etc.: the formation of the phalanx differed; the Spartan line at Tegea was eight deep, Thuc.: the Theban at Delium twenty-five, Id.; the phalanx was brought to perfection by Philip of Macedon.
for the main body, centre, as opp. to the wings (κέρατα), Xen.
a camp, Id.
a round piece of wood, a trunk, log, Hdt.
a venomous spider (cf. φαλάγγιον), Ar.
Pass. to become bald, Hdt.
baldheaded, bald, Hdt., Plat., etc.; πρόσωπον φαλακρόν Eur.
bald in front, Anth.
a bald man, Luc.
bosses on the sides of the helmet, to which the chin-straps were attached, Il.: —the sg., φάλαρον τιάρας, part of the headdress of the old Persian kings, Aesch.
bosses or discs of metal, used to adorn the head-gear of horses, Lat. phalerae, Hdt., Soph., etc.
the coot, so called from its bald white head, Ar.
having a patch of white, ὁ κύων ὁ φάλαρος the dog with a white spot, Theocr.
a Phalerian, Hdt.
to be patched with white, κύματα φαληριόωντα waves crested with white foam, Il.
of or from Phalerum, Ar.
from Phalerum, Plat.
at Phalerum, Xen.
to Phalerum, Thuc.
Phalerum, the western harbour of Athens
Phales, associated with the worship of Bacchus, Ar.
a whale, Lat. ba_laena, Babr.:—hence of any monster, Lat. bellua, Ar.
of or for the φαλλός·—τὸ φαλλικόν (sc. μέλος) the phallic song, Ar.
membrum virile, phallus, a figure borne in procession in the Bacchic orgies, as an emblem of the generative power in nature, Hdt., Ar.

a part of the helmet worn by the Homeric heroes, either a metal ridge in which the plume (λόφος) was fixed, or (rather) the peak of the helmet: then, an ἀμφίφαλος κυνέη would be one that had a peak behind as well as before.
giving or bringing light, Eur.
openly hating, Arist.
open to sight, visible, manifest, evident, Hdt., attic:— φανερός εἰμι, c. part., φανεροί εἰσι ἀπικόμενοι they are known to have come, Hdt.; so, φανεροὶ γιγνόμενοι ὅτι ποιοῦσιν Xen.
open, of a road, Hdt.
φ. οὐσία real property, opp. to money (ἀφανής 6), Dem., etc.
of votes, φ. ψήφῳ by open vote, opp. to κρύβδην (ballot), Thuc., etc.

adv. -ρῶς, openly, manifestly, Hdt., attic: comp. φανερώτερον Thuc.:— τὸ φανερόν is often joined with Preps. in adverb. sense, ἐκ τοῦ φανεροῦ openly, Hdt., etc.; so, ἐν τῷ φανερῷ Xen.; ἐστὸ φανερόν Thuc.
of gods, known, acknowledged, Hdt.; of persons, conspicuous, Soph., Thuc.
openly loving, an open friend, Arist.
to make manifest, NTest.
to make known or famous:—Pass. to become so, Hdt.
a torch:—a torch-procession, such as took place in the Bacchic orgies, Eur.
light, bright, Xen.:— τὸ φανόν brightness, light, Plat.
of garments, washed clean, Ar.
metaph. bright, joyous, Aesch., Plat.
conspicuous, Plat.
adv. -νῶς perspicuously; Sup. φανότατα, Luc.
a torch of vine-twigs, Xen.; cf. πᾱνός.,
to become visible, appear, shew oneself, Hdt., Eur.
to make a show, exalt oneself, Lat. se ostentare, Hdt.
φαντάζεσθαί τινι to make oneself like some one, Aesch.
in Ar., = συκοφαντεῖσθαι, to be informed against.
imagination, the power by which an object is presented (φαίνεται) to the mind (the object presented being φάντασμα), Plat., Arist.
an appearance, phantasm, phantom, Aesch., Eur.:— a vision, dream, Theocr.
in Philosophy, v. φαντασία.
a mere image, unreality, Plat.

entry.etym: epic nom. and acc. pl. φάεα [ᾱ metri grat.]
entry.sense: light, daylight, Hom., etc.:—in Poets, of life, ζώειν καὶ ὁρᾶν φάος ἠελίοιο Id.; λείπειν φάος ἠελίοιο Hes.; πέμπειν τινὰ ἐς φῶς Aesch.; πρὸς φῶς ἀνελθεῖν Soph.
of day-light, ἐν φάει Od.; φῶς γίγνεται it is becoming light, i. e. day is breaking, Plat.; ἕως ἔτι φῶς ἐστι while there is still light, Id.
the light of a torch, lamp, fire, a light, Od., Aesch.
the light of the eyes, Pind.; pl. φάεα the eyes, Lat. lumina, Od.
light, as a metaph. for deliverance, happiness, victory, Il.: also in addressing persons, γλυκερὸν φάος dear light of my life, Od.; ὦ φίλτατον φῶς Soph.
a cleft or chasm in a mountain, a ravine, gully, Aesch., Eur.
a quiver for arrows, Lat. pharetra, Hom.
a Pharisee, Separatist (from pharash, to distinguish), one of a sect who separated themselves from other Jews as affecting superior holiness.
to suffer from the effect of poison, to be ill or distraught, Dem.
the use of drugs, potions, spells, Plat.
poisoning, witchcraft, Lat. veneficium, Dem.
remedy, cure, Arist.
a poisoner, sorcerer, Soph.
to administer a drug, Plat.
to use enchantments, φαρμακεύειν τι ἐς τὸν ποταμόν to use it as a charm to calm the river, Hdt.
c. acc. pers. to drug, give him a poisonous or stupefying drug, Eur.
a sorceress, witch, Lat. venefica, Ar., Dem.

a drug, medicine, Hom., etc.: the φάρμακα applied outwardly were χριστά, ἔγχριστα, ἐπίχριστα (ointments), and παστά, ἐπίπαστα, καταπλαστά (plasters), Theocr., Ar.; those taken inwardly βρώσιμα, and πότιμα, ποτά, πιστά, Aesch., Eur., etc.:—c. gen., φ. νόσου a medicine for it, remedy against it, Aesch.; φ. κεφαλῆς for a head-ache, Plat.
in bad sense, an enchanted potion, philtre, so a charm, spell, enchantment, Od., Theocr.:—also a drug, poison, Soph., Eur.
a remedy, cure, Hes.; φ. πραΰ, of a bridle, Pind.; c. gen. a remedy against, βλάβης Aesch.; πόνων, λύπης Eur.
c. gen., also, a means of producing, σωτηρίας Id.; σοφίας Plat.
a dye, paint, colour, Hdt., etc.
a drinking of medicine, Xen., Plat.
a drinking of poison, Luc.
a dealer in drugs, Ar.
a poisoner, sorcerer, magician, NTest.
one who is sacrificed as an atonement for others, a scape-goat, Ar.; and, since worthless fellows were reserved for this fate, φαρμακός became a general name of reproach, Id., Dem.
one who grinds drugs or colours, Dem.
to endue with healing power, Pind.
of the nature of a φάρμακον, medicinal, Arist.
poisonous, Plut.
to treat by using φάρμακα, of a metal-worker, who hardens iron by plunging it in water, Od.
to heal or relieve by medicine, Plat.
to bewitch by potions or philtres: hence to bewitch by flattery, Id.: metaph. in Pass. of a lamp, as φαρμασσομένη χρίματος παρηγορίαις Aesch.
Pharos, an island in the bay of Alexandria, Od., Thuc., etc.; famous for its lighthouse, Strab.: then, as appell., φάρος, a lighthouse, Anth.
a large piece of cloth, a web, Hom., Eur.
like χλαῖνα, a cloak or mantle, worn over the χιτών, Hom., etc.:—used as a shroud or pall, Id., Soph.; also as a coverlet, Soph.
a part, portion, φάρσεα πόλιος the quarters of a city, Hdt.
the throat, gullet, Od., Eur., etc.
a sword, Hom., Soph.
forging swords, Aesch.
a sort of bean, Ar.
hence Lat. phas[e]lus, a light boat, skiff, from its likeness in shape to a bean-pod, Catull., Hor.
from the river Phasis (v. Φᾶσις): — ὁ φ. (sc. ὄρνις), the Phasian bird, pheasant, Ar.:—so Φασιανικὸς, ὄρνις, with a play on συκοφάντης, Id.
an accusation, Dem.
an assertion, Arist.
the river Phasis in Colchis, being the boundary of Europe and Asia, Hes., Hdt., etc.

entry.etym: used as imperf. of φημί. the inf. and part. pres. of φημί are also supplied by φάσκω: besides this we find attic, imperat. φάσκε
entry.sense: to say, affirm, assert, often with a notion of alleging or pretending, Od., Hdt., attic; ὡς ἔφασκεν as he said, as he alleged, Soph.
to think, deem, expect, Hom., Soph.
to promise, c. inf. fut., Od., Thuc.
an apparition, phantom, Hdt., Aesch., etc.; φ. ἀνδρός the spectral appearance of a man, Hdt.:— a vision in a dream, Aesch., etc.
a sign from heaven, portent, omen, Hdt., Trag.
a monster, prodigy, Hdt.; periphr., φάσμα ταύρου a monster of a bull, Soph.
a wild pigeon, ringdove, Ar.
dove-killing, Il.
οὔτι φατειός un- utterable, un- speakable, Hes.
one must say, Plat.
to say, speak, report, ἐφάτισαν [τὰ γράμματα] Φοινικήια κεκλῆσθαι they spoke of them by the name of Phoenician, Hdt.:—Pass., τὸ φατιζόμενον as the saying is, Soph.
to promise, engage, betroth, τὴν παῖδά τινι Eur.:— Pass., ἐμὴ φατισθεῖσα my promised bride, Id.
like φήμη, a voice from heaven, the voice of an oracle, an oracle, Aesch., Soph.

a saying among men, common talk, rumour, report, Lat. fama, Od., Trag.; κατὰ φάτιν as report goes, Hdt.; ὡς φ. κρατεῖ Aesch.; ὥσπερ ἡ φ. Soph.; φ. [ἐστί] 'tis said that . . , Pind.; ἡ φ. μιν ἔχει the report goes of him, Hdt.
the subject of a saying, a theme, Pind.
speech, words, of a single person, Soph.: speech, language, Aesch.
a manger, crib, feeding-trough, Hom., Hdt., attic
that may be spoken, οὐ φατός un- speakable, un- utterable, in- effable, Hes., Pind.
metaph. named, famous, notable, Hes.
bad upon bad, bad as bad can be, Anth.
to hold cheap, to depreciate, disparage, Xen.
of things, easy, slight, Eur., Ar., etc.: adv., φαύλως κρίνειν to estimate lightly, Aesch.; φ. ἀποδιδράσκειν to get off easily, Ar.; Sup., φαυλότατα καὶ ῥᾷστα Id.
trivial, paltry, petty, sorry, poor, Thuc., etc.; φαῦλα ἐπιφέρειν to bring paltry charges, Hdt.: adv., οὔτι φαύλως with no trivial force, Eur.
of persons, low in rank, mean, common, οἱ φαυλότατοι the commonest sort (of soldiers), Thuc., etc.: also in point of education opp. to σοφός, Eur., etc.; c. inf., φαῦλος μάχεσθαι Id.; φ. λέγειν Plat.
careless, thoughtless, indifferent, Lat. securus, Eur.;—adv., φαύλως εὕδειν Id.; φ. λογίσασθαι to estimate off-hand, roughly, Ar.; φ. εἰπεῖν, Lat. strictim dicere, carelessly, roughly, Plat.
in good sense, simple, unaffected, Id.: adv., φαύλως παιδεύειν τινα Xen.
meanness, paltriness, pettiness, badness, of persons and things, Xen., etc.; ἡ φ. τῶν στρατηγῶν their want of skill, Dem.; lack of judgment, Xen.
in good sense, plainness, simplicity, Id.
to give light, shine (like φαίνω II), Od.
Pass. to be put to flight, flee affrighted, Hom.
light, splendour, lustre, Hhymn., Pind., Trag.; esp. like φάος, φῶς, daylight, Trag.; δεκάτῳ φέγγει ἔτους in the tenth year's light, i. e. in the tenth year, Aesch.:—also moonlight, Xen.
of men, φ. ἰδεῖν to see the light, come into the world, Pind.; λιπεῖν φ. Eur.
the light of torches or fire, Aesch.:— a light, torch, Ar.; pl. φέγγη watchfires, Plut.
the light of the eyes, Eur., Theocr.; τυφλὸν φ., i. e. blindness, Eur.
light, as a metaph. for glory, pride, joy, Pind., Aesch., etc.
to make bright:—Pass. to shine, gleam, Ar.
Dep. to spare, Lat. parcere:
to spare persons and things in war, i. e. not destroy them, c. gen., Hom., attic:—absol. to spare, be merciful, Thuc.

to spare in using, to refrain from using, use sparingly, ἵππων φειδόμενος, i. e. taking care of them, Il.; μὴ φείδεο σίτου Hes.; φείδεο τῶν νηῶν Hdt.; τι φειδόμεσθα τῶν λίθων; why refrain from using them? Ar.; φ. μήτε χρημάτων μήτε πόνων Plat.
absol. to be sparing, be thrifty, live thriftily, Theogn.; οἱ γεωργοῦντες καὶ φειδόμενος Dem.:—this part is used as adj. = φειδωλός, Ar.:— adv. φειδομένως sparingly, NTest., Plut.
to draw back from, τοῦ κινδύνου Xen.; φείδου μηδὲν ὧνπερ ἐννοεῖς shrink not at all from that thou hast in mind, Soph.:—also c. inf. to spare or cease to do, forbear from doing, Eur.
sparing, thrifty, and as Subst. a niggard, miser, Ar., Plat.; φ. γλῶσσα a niggard tongue, Hes.:—c. gen., φ. χρημάτων Plat.; τὸ φειδωλόν = φειδώ, Id.:—adv. -λῶς, Id.
an oil-can with a narrow neck, that lets only a little run out, Theophr.
as pr. n. Φείδων, name of an old man in Com. Poets, Thrifty: — hence patron. Φειδωνίδης, ου, ὁ, Thrifty-son, Ar.
a sparing, νεκύων Il.
absol. thrift, parsimony, Od., Hes.: thrift in exposing oneself to danger, Thuc.
one must spare, Isocr.
stony ground: as pr. n., Ar.
made of cork, Luc.
cork-footed, Luc.
the cork-tree, Lat. quercus suber:—its bark, cork, Lat. cortex, Pind., Aesch.
Cork-land, Luc.
false hair, a wig, Luc.
to play the φέναξ, cheat, lie, Ar., Dem.
trans. to cheat, trick, τινά Ar., Dem.:—Pass. to be cheated, Ar., Dem.
cheatery, quackery, imposition, Ar., Dem.
a cheat, quack, impostor, Ar.

entry.etym: forms such as πέφαται and πεφήσεαι from root ΦΑ
entry.sense: to slay, Hom., Soph.
flower-bringing, Anth.
shield-bearing, Hhymn., Aesch.

entry.etym: only in pres. and imperf., with plup. ἐπεφόρβειν.
entry.sense: to feed, nourish, Pind., Eur.; c. gen. to feed oxen on a thing, Hhymn.
= σώζω, to preserve, Hes.
Pass. to be fed, feed upon a thing, Lat. pasci, vesci, παρέξω δαῖθ’ ὑφ’ ὧν ἐφερβόμην I shall make food for those by whom I feed myself, Soph.
to eat, feed on, c. acc., Lat. depasci, Eur.
to enjoy, have, νόον Pind.
bringing light, Anth.

giving surety:—generally, to be depended upon, trusty, sure, Aesch.:—c. inf. capable, sufficient, οὐ φ. εἰμι παρασχεῖν Hdt.; λιμὴν φ. διασῶσαι τὰς νέας Id.:—c. gen. rei, warrant for a thing, able to answer for, Soph.; so, φερεγγυώτατος πρὸς τὰ δεινά Thuc.
inured to toil or hardship, Polyb.
yielding fruit, Anth.
carrying off victory, Pind.
carrying one's house with one, of the Scythians, Hdt.:—as Subst. the house-carrier, i. e. snail, Hes.
bringing toil and trouble, Pind.
life-giving, γαῖα Hhymn., Hes.
shield-bearing, Hes.
yielding bunches of grapes, Anth.
Pass. to be carried on a litter, Plut.
a bier, litter, Polyb.:—contr. φέρτρον Il.
that which is borne, the fruit of the womb (cf. bairn from bear), Aesch.

that which is brought by the wife (cf. ἕδνον), a dowry, portion, Lat. dos, Hdt., Eur.; also in pl. of a dower, as consisting of divers presents, Eur.; but, φερναὶ πολέμου, of a wife won in battle, Id.:—in pl., also, bridal gifts, Id.
a temple of Persephonée, Dem.
bravest, best, Hom.:—of things, κακῶν φέρτατον the best, i. e. least bad, of two evils, Il.
in form φέριστος, Id.; mostly in voc. φέριστε, Id., Aesch., Soph.
comp., φέρτερος, η, ον, braver, better, Hom.:— πολὺ φέρτερόν ἐστιν 'tis much better, Id.;— τέττιγος φέρτερον ᾄδεις, as adv., Theocr.
entry.etym: The posit. occurs in προφερής: perh. the Root is φέρεσθαι, so that the orig. sense would be quick in action, vigorous.
verb. adj. of φέρω, endurable, Eur.
from Root ἘΝΕΚ or ἘΝΕΓΚ come ἤνεγκον and ἤνεικα
entry.sense: Radic. sense, to bear, Lat. fero:
to bear or carry a load, Hom., attic; of a woman with child, Aesch., Soph.
to bear, bear along, implying motion, πόδες φέρον Il.; horses are said ἅρμα φέρειν Id.; of a wind, Hom.; ὁ βορέας εἰς τὴν Ἑλλάδα φέρει is fair for Greece, Xen.

to bear, endure, suffer, Od., etc.; of wine, τὰ τρία φέρων bearing three parts of water, instead of ἴσον ἴσωι, Ar.:—often with Advs., βαρέως, δεινῶς, χαλεπῶς φέρειν τι, like Lat. aegre, graviter ferre, to bear impatiently, take ill or amiss, opp. to κούφως, ῥαιδίως φέρειν, Lat. leviter ferre, to bear patiently, take easily, Hdt., attic:—such phrases are constructed mostly c. acc. rei; sometimes, c. dat. only, βαρέως φέρειν τοῖς παροῦσι Xen.
to bring, fetch, Hom., attic:—Mid. to bring with one, or for one's own use, Od., etc.
to bring, offer, present, δῶρα Id.; χάριν τινὶ φ. to grant any one a favour, do him a kindness, Hom., attic
to bring, produce, work, cause, Hom.; φ. κακόν, πῆμα, ἄλγεα to work one woe, Id.:— to produce, bring forward, cite, Dem.
to bring one word, to tell, announce, Aesch., etc.:—so in Mid., λόγους φ. Eur.; but also, ἔπος φέρεσθαι to have word brought one, receive, Id.
to pay something due or owing, φόρον φέρειν to pay as tax or tribute, Thuc.; μισθὸν φ. Xen. (but also to receive pay, Ar., Thuc.):—of property, to bring in, yield as rent, Isae.
ψῆφον φ. to give one's vote, Lat. ferre suffragium, Aesch.; ψῆφος καθ’ ἡμῶν οἴσεται (as Pass.) Eur.:—hence φέρειν τινά, to appoint to an office, Dem.
to bear, bring forth, produce, of the earth or of trees, Od., Hdt., etc.:—absol. to bear, bear fruit, be fruitful, Hdt.
to carry off or away, Il.: of stormy winds, Od.; of a river, Hdt.:—Mid. to carry off with one, Od., Xen., etc.
to carry off as booty or plunder, Il., etc.:—often in the phrase φέρειν καὶ ἄγειν, v. ἄγω I. 3:— φέρειν alone, to rob, plunder, θεῶν ἱερά Eur.; ἀλλήλους Thuc.:—Mid. in same sense, Hom.

to carry off, gain, win, achieve, Il., Soph., etc.; μισθὸν φέρειν (v. supr. IV. 5):—so in Mid. to win for oneself, Il., attic:—metaph., τὰ πρῶτα, τὰ δεύτερα φέρεσθαι to win and hold the first, the second rank, Hdt.; πλέον or πλεῖον φέρεσθαι to gain the advantage over any one, τινος Id., etc.;—the Mid. being used of that which one gets for one's own use, esp. to take home, Id.
absol., of roads, to lead to a place, ἡ ὁδὸς φέρει εἰς . . , like Lat. via fert or ducit ad . . , Id., Thuc., etc.
of a tract of country, to stretch, extend to or towards, like Lat. vergere or spectare ad . . , φέρειν ἐπί or ἐς θάλασσαν Hdt., etc.
metaph. to lead to, be conducive to, ἐς αἰσχύνην φέρει Id.; ἐς βλάβην φέρον Soph.

to aim at a thing, hint or point at, refer to it, εἰς or πρός τι Hdt., Plat.; so, τοῦ δήμου φέρει γνώμη, ὡς . . , the people's opinion inclines to this, that . . , Hdt.; τῶν ἡ γνώμη ἔφερε συμβάλλειν their opinion inclined to giving battle, Id.
impers. much like συμφέρει, it tends (to one's interest), is conducive, φέρει σοι ταῦτα ποιεῖν; Id. d. intr., v. B. I. 2.

to carry in the mouth, i. e. to speak much of, Aeschin.: Pass., εὖ, πονηρῶς φέρεσθαι to be well or ill spoken of, Xen.: also absol. φέρεται, like Lat. fertur, [the report] is carried about, i. e. it is said, τοιόνδε φέρεται πρῆγμα γίγνεσθαι Hdt.
imperat. φέρε, like ἄγε, used as adv. come, now, well, φέρ’ εἰπὲ δή μοι Soph.; so, before 1 pers. sg. or pl. subj. used imperatively, φέρε ἀκούσω Hdt.; φ. δὴ ἴδωμεν, φ. δὴ σκεψώμεθα Plat.
before a question, φέρε τροπαῖα πῶς ἄρα στήσεις; well then, how wilt thou erect trophies? Eur.
part. neut. τὸ φέρον, as Subst. fortune, fate, τὸ φέρον ἐκ θεοῦ φέρειν χρή ye must bear what heaven bears to you, awards you, Soph.
Pass. is used in most of the above senses, esp.,
to be borne along by waves or winds, to be swept away, Od.; ἧκε φέρεσθαι he sent him flying, Il.; ἧκα πόδας καὶ χεῖρε φέρεσθαι I let go my hands and feet, let them swing free [in the leap], Od.

often in part. with another Verb of motion, φερόμενοι ἐσέπιπτον they fell on them with a rush, Hdt.; ὠιχόμην φερόμενος Plat.;—so, in part. act. used intr., φέρουσα ἐνέβαλε νηί she bore down upon the ship and struck it, Hdt.; φέρων hurriedly, in haste, Aeschin.
of voluntary motion, ἰθὺς φέρεται Il.; ὁμόσε τινὶ φέρεσθαι to come to blows with him, Xen., etc.

metaph., εὖ, κακῶς φέρεσθαι to turn out well or ill, succeed or fail, νόμοι οὐ καλῶς φέρονται Soph.; τὰ πράγματα κακῶς φέρεται Xen.; ἐᾶν ταῦτα φέρεσθαι to let these things take their course, Dem.:—of persons, εὖ φερόμενος ἐν στρατηγίαις being successful in his commands, Thuc.

entry.etym: perfect passive participle πεφυγμένος has active meaning.
entry.sense: to flee, take flight, run away, Il.;—with Preps., φ. ἀπό or ἔκ τινος Hom., etc.; rarely c. gen. only, πεφυγμένος ἦεν ἀέθλων Od.:—c. acc. cogn., φεύγειν φυγήν Eur.; (so, φυγῆι φ. Plat.); φ. τὴν παρὰ θάλασσαν (sc. ὁδόν) to flee toward the sea, Hdt.

the pres. and imperf. properly express the endeavour to flee: hence the part. φεύγων is added to the compd. Verbs ἀποφεύγω, ἐκφεύγω, προφεύγω, to distinguish the attempt from the accomplishment, βέλτερον, ὡς φεύγων προφύγηι κακὸν ἠὲ ἁλώηι it is better that one should flee and escape than stay and be caught, Il.; φεύγων ἐκφ. Hdt., etc.
φ. εἰς . . to have recourse to .. , take refuge in . . , Eur.
c. inf. to be shy of doing, shrink from doing, Hdt., Plat.; and with the inf. omitted, to shrink back, Soph.

c. acc. to flee from, to shun, avoid, Hom., etc.; φ. φόνον to flee the consequences of the murder, Eur.:—the part. perf. pass. also retains the acc. in Hom., who joins it with εἶναι or γενέσθαι = πεφευγέναι, e. g. μοῖραν δ’ οὔτινά φημι πεφυγμένον ἔμμεναι I say that no man can escape his doom, Il.; πεφυγμένον ἄμμε γενέσθαι Id.
of things, ἡνίοχον φύγον ἡνία the reins escaped from his hands, Id.
to flee one's country for a crime, Hom.; οἱ φεύγοντες the exiles, Thuc.; φ. πατρίδα Od.
φ. ὑπό τινος to be banished by him, Hdt., Xen.:—absol. to go into exile, be an exile, Lat. exulare, Hdt.

as attic law-term, to be accused or prosecuted: ὁ φεύγων the accused, defendant, Lat. reus, opp. to ὁ διώκων the accuser, prosecutor, Ar., Oratt.; c. acc., φ. γραφήν or δίκην to be put on one's trial for something, Ar., Plat.; the crime being added in gen., φ. φόνου (sub. δίκην) to be charged with murder, Lys., etc.; φ. ἀσεβείας ὑπό τινος is accused of impiety by some one, Plat.
to cry φεῦ, cry woe, only found once, τί τοῦτ’ ἔφευξας; Aesch.
one must flee, Eur.
to be shunned or avoided, Arist.
that can be avoided, Soph.
to wish to escape, Eur.
exclamation of grief or anger, ah! alas! woe! like Lat. vah, vae,, Trag.; φεῦ τάλας Soph. etc.: c. ge., φεῦ τοῦ ὄρνιθος alas for the omen! aesch.
of astonishment or admiration, ah! oh! Eur. etc.; c. gen. φεῦ τοῦ ἀνδρός oh what a man! Xen.: c. acc., φεῦ τὸ καὶ λαβεῖν πρόσφεγμα τοιοῦδ’ ἀνδρός oh but to get the speech of such a man! Soph.
Pass. to be burnt to ashes, Aesch.
a spark, piece of the embers, Ar.; ἀσπὶς ἐν τῷ φεψάλῳ κρεμήσεται, i. e. will be hung in the chimney, of things laid by and unused, Id.
oaken, Il.
a kind of oak, bearing an esculent acorn, quercus esculus, (not the Lat. fagus, our beech, though the names are identical), sacred to Ζεύς, Il., Soph.
the acorn of the same tree, Ar.
a wild fig (prob. from φῆλος, deceitful, because it seems ripe when it is not really so), Ar.
to cheat, deceive, Hhymn.
a knave, thief, Hes., etc.
to cheat, deceive, Aesch.: Pass., φηλούμενοι Eur.

doric φάμα, Lat. fama: (φημί):— a voice from heaven, a prophetic voice, Od.; so, when Ulysses prays to Zeus, φήμην τίς μοι φάσθω, he is answered by thunder, Id.; hence an oracle, divination, omen, Hdt., Soph., etc.
saying or report spread among men, rumour, Hes., Aeschin.; ὑποδεεστέρα τῆς φήμης inferior to the report of them, i. e. exaggerated, Thuc.
the talk or report of a man's character, Hes., etc.:—esp. good report, fame, Hdt., Pind.; also, φ. πονηραί Aesch., etc.
φᾶμαι songs of praise, Pind.
any voice or words, a speech, saying, Aesch.:—esp. a common saying, a tradition, legend, Eur., Plat.
a message, Trag.
to utter a voice, φήμην φημίζειν Aesch.
to spread a report, Hes.: to prophesy, Aesch.:—Mid. to express in words, Id.
in Mid. also to promise, τί τινι Eur.

entry.etym: the imperf. act. should be ἔφην, like the aor2, but ἔφασκον was generally used instead.
entry.sense: Radical sense: to declare, make known; and so, to say, affirm, assert, either absol., or foll. by inf. or by acc.; the inf. is often omitted, σὲ κακὸν καὶ ἀνάλκιδα φήσει (sc. εἶναι) Il.; but also, Κορινθίους τί φῶμεν; what shall we say of them? Xen.:—then, since what one says commonly expresses a belief or opinion, to think, deem, suppose, Il.; φαίης κε ζάκοτόν τέ τιν’ ἔμμεναι ἄφρονά τε you would say, would think, he was . . , Id.; μὴ φαθὶ λεύσσειν think not that you see, Theocr.
Special Phrases:
φασί, they say, it is said, Hom., attic; but in Prose also φησί, like French on dit, Dem.; (so Lat. inquit, ait).
φημί is sometimes joined with a synon. Verb. e.g. ἔφη λέγων, ἔφησε λέγων Hdt.; λέγει οὐδὲν φαμένη Id.
in repeating dialogues, the Verb commonly goes before its subject, ἔφην ἐγώ, ἔφη ὁ Σωκράτης said I, said Socrates; but the order is sometimes inverted, ἐγὼ ἔφην, ὁ Σωκράτης ἔφη I said, Socrates said.

in a more definite sense, like κατάφημι, to say yes, affirm, Hom., attic; καὶ τοὺς φάναι and they said yes, Hdt.; καί φημι κἀπόφημι Soph.; whereas οὔ φημι means to say no, deny, refuse, ἡ Πυθίη οὐκ ἔφη χρήσειν said she would not answer, Hdt.; ἐὰν μὴ φῆι if he say no, Ar.; φάθι ἢ μή say yes or no, Plat.
speech, talk, Hom.; δήμου φ. the voice or judgment of the people, Od.;— but δήμοιο φῆμις (Od. 15. 468) seems to be the place where the people talk, the place of assembly (ἀγορά).
fame, reputation, Id.
prob. = ἁλιαίετος, the sea-eagle, Od., Ar.
game-mad, madly fond of wild animals, epith. of Bacchus, Anth.
Lat. fera, Pind.: pl. φῆρες, of the Centaurs, Il.

entry.etym: φθανω always in attic; φθᾱνω twice in Il.
entry.sense: to come or do first or before others:
c. acc. pers. to be beforehand with, overtake, outstrip, anticipate, Il., Hdt., attic; so, ἔφθησαν τὸν χειμῶνα Hdt.:—Pass. to be overtaken, Anth.
absol. to come first, Eur., etc.; τοῦ φθάσαντος ἁρπαγή the prey of the first comer, Aesch.:—with Preps. to come or arrive first, ἐς τὸν Ἑλλήσποντον Thuc., etc.

the action in which one outstrips another is expressed by the part. agreeing with the subject, [Ἄτη] φθάνει βλάπτουσα is beforehand in doing mischief, Il.; φθῆ μιν Τηλέμαχος βαλών Telemachus was beforehand with him in striking, Od.:—in translation, the part. often becomes the chief Verb and φθάνειν is rendered by an adv., quicker, sooner, first, before, beforehand, ἔφθησαν ἀπικόμενοι arrived first, Hdt.; so with part. pass. εἴ κε φθήηι τυπείς should he be wounded first, Il.; φθάνω εὐεργετῶν I am the first to shew a kindness, Xen.:— these clauses, being compar. in sense, are sometimes foll. by a gen., φθὰν ἱππήων κοσμηθέντες they were marshalled before the horsemen, Il.; or by πρὶν . . , πρὶν ἢ . . , ἔφθη ὀρεξάμενος, πρὶν οὐτάσαι Id.; ἔφθησαν ἀναβάντες πρὶν ἢ . . Hdt.

part. φθάς or φθάσας, epic φθάμενος, used like an adv., ὅς μ’ ἔβαλε φθάμενος, for ὅς μ’ ἔφθη βαλών, Il.; οὐκ ἄλλος φθὰς ἐμεῦ κατήγορος ἔσται no other shall be an accuser before me, Hdt.; ἀνέωιξάς με φθάσας you opened the door before me, Ar.

rarely with the inf., like Lat. occuro, μόλις φθάνει θρόνοισιν ἐμπεσοῦσα μὴ χαμαὶ πεσεῖν hardly escapes falling on the ground by falling first on the seat, Eur.; φθάνει ἐλθεῖν he is first to come, Ar.

φθάνω with οὐ and part., followed by καί, like Lat. simul ac, denotes two actions following close on each other, οὐ φθάνειν χρὴ συσκιάζοντας γένυν, καὶ ὁρμᾶν you must no sooner get your beard, than you march, Id.; οὐκ ἔφθη μοι συμβᾶσα ἡ ἀτυχία καὶ εὐθὺς ἐπεχείρησαν no sooner had misfortune befallen me, when they attempted, Dem.

οὐκ ἂν φθάνοις, οὐκ ἂν φθάνοιτε, with part. pres., denote impatience, οὐκ ἂν φθάνοιτε ἀπαλλασσόμενοι you could not be too quick in departing, i. e. make haste and be off, Hdt.; οὐκ ἂν φθάνοιτε τοῦτο πράττοντε Ar.; οὐκ ἂν φθάνοις λέγων Plat.:—so, the part. φθάσας is used with imperat., λέγε φθάσας speak quickly, τρέχε φθάσας, etc.
in answers, οὐκ ἂν φθάνοιμι I could not be too quick, i. e. I will begin directly, Plat.
destructive of, τινος Arist.
perishable, Arist.
to utter a sound or voice, esp. to speak loud and clear, speak, Hom., etc.
of animals, as a horse, to neigh, whinny, Hdt.; of an eagle, to scream, Xen.; of a fawn, to cry, Theocr.
of inanimate things, of a door, to creak, Ar.; of thunder, to sound, Xen.; of musical instruments, Il.
= ὀνομάζω, to name, call by name, Plat.
c. acc. pers. to celebrate one aloud, extol, Pind.
the sound of the voice, a voice, Pind., Aesch., etc.: of a person, ὦ φθέγμ’ ἀναιδές, for ὦ φθεγξάμενε ἀναιδῆ, Soph.
language, speech, Id.
a saying, word, Id.
of other sounds, as of birds, cries, Id., Eur.; of a bull, roaring, Eur.; φθ. θυείας the grinding of the mortar, Ar.; of the nightingale's song, Id.
the morbus pedicularis, Plut.
to have morbus pedicularis, Plut.
to eat fir-cones, Hdt.
a louse, Lat. pediculus, Hdt., Ar.
a worm in vegetables, Luc.
to ruin, waste, spoil, destroy, Lat. perdere, Od., Hdt., etc.:—Pass. to go to ruin, perish, Trag., etc.

Pass., (.] φθείρεσθε (as a curse) may ye perish! ruin seize ye! Il.; φθείρου plague take thee! away with thee! Lat. abi in malam rem! Ar.; so, εἰ μὴ φθερεῖ if thou depart not . . , Eur.; c. gen., φθείρεσθε τῆσδε off from her! i. e. unhand her, let her go, Id.; φθείρεσθαι πρός . . to run headlong to . . , Dem.
to have suffered loss from shipwreck, Eur.
of women, χερσοὺς φθαρῆναι to pine away in barrenness, Soph.
destroying the race, Aesch.
Phthia in Thessaly, the home of Achilles, Hom.
at Phthia, Il.
as if from φθινάζω, a declining, sinking, Aesch.
intr. waning, Eur.
act. causing to decline, wasting, Soph.
having lost fruitfulness, Pind.
autumnal, Pind.
late autumn, the fall of the year, Hdt., Thuc.

entry.etym: poetic for φθίνω, only in present and imperfect
entry.sense: trans. to waste, consume, Od.; φθ. κῆρ cause it to pine away, Id.
intr. to waste or pine away, decay, of men, Hom.
nickname for a thin or delicate woman, starveling, Ar.
destroying or killing men, Il., Hes.
for φθισίβροτος, destroying men, Il., Od.
a perishing, decay, Pind.:—of the moon, a waning, Arist.

entry.etym: Trag. word, only used in pl. φθιτοί always without the Art.
entry.sense: the dead, Aesch., Eur.
liable to perish, Arist.

entry.etym: there is no diff. of sense in Act. and Pass.
entry.sense: to decay, wane, dwindle, of Time, πρίν κεν νὺξ φθῖτο (aor2 pass. opt.) first would the night be come to an end, Od.; so, τῆς νῦν φθιμένης νυκτός Soph.; φθίνουσιν νύκτες τε καὶ ἤματα they wane or pass away, Od.; μηδέ σοι αἰὼν φθινέτω let not thy life be wasted, Id.:— so, in the monthly reckoning, μηνῶν φθινόντων in the moon's wane, i. e. towards the month's end, Id.:— μὴν φθίνων the ending of the month, v. ἵστημι B. III. 3.
of the stars, to decline, set, Aesch.

of men, to waste away, pine, perish, Hom., Eur.;—of things, to fade away, disappear, Soph.:—so in Pass., αὐτὸς φθίεται Il.; ἤδη φθίσονται Hom.:—often in part. φθίμενος, slain, dead, Id.; φθίμενοι the dead, φθιμένοισι μετείην Od., Trag.
Causal, in fut. φθίσω [ῑ], aor1 ἔφθῑσα, to make to decay or pine away, to consume, destroy, Hom.; once in Aesch. φθίσας [ι].
a man of Phthia, Hdt., etc.
Φθιῶτις, γῆ the land of Phthia, Eur., etc.; so Φθιάς, άδος, Id.
any clear, distinct sound, esp. the voice of men, Hom., attic; also of animals, Soph., Eur.
generally, a sound, as distinguished from a voice (φωνή), Plat.:—of musical sounds, Eur.
a kind of cake, Ar.
envious, jealous, grudging, of persons, Theogn., attic:—adv., φθονερῶς ἔχειν to be enviously disposed, Plat., Xen., etc.

to bear ill-will or malice, bear a grudge, be envious or jealous, Il., Xen., etc.:—c. dat. pers., πτωχὸς πτωχῷ φθονέει Hes.; φθ. τινὶ εὖ πρήσσοντι to envy him for his good fortune, Hdt.; also c. dat. rei, to feel envy at a thing, Isocr.; ἐπί τινι Xen.:—c. dat. pers. et gen. rei, οὔ τοι ἡμιόνων φθονέω I bear thee no grudge for the mules, Od.; μή μοι φθονήσῃς τοῦ μαθήματος Plat.:—c. gen. rei only, to be grudging of a thing, ἀλλοτρίων φθονέειν Od.

to refuse to do a thing from envy or ill-will, to grudge doing, c. inf., Id., Eur., etc.; μὴ φθονήσῃς do not refuse, Lat. ne graveris, μὴ φθ. διδάξαι Plat.:—also c. acc. et inf., ἐφθόνησαν [οἱ θεοὶ] ἕνα ἄνδρα βασιλεῦσαι Hdt.;—also c. dat. et inf., τῇ δ’ οὐκ ἂν φθονέοιμι ἅψασθαι; Od.
Pass. to be envied or begrudged, Lat. invideor, Hdt., Eur., etc.
a jealous refusal, Soph.

ill-will, envy, jealousy, Lat. invidia, Hdt., etc.; φθόνον ἔχειν to feel envy or jealousy, Aesch.; but, also, to incur envy or dislike, Pind.; so, φθόνον ἀλφάνειν Eur., etc.:—c. gen. objecti, envy for, jealousy of, τῶν Ἑλλήνων φθόνῳ Hdt., etc.; but c. gen. subjecti, envy or jealousy felt by another, Eur., etc.:— in pl. envyings, jealousies, heartburnings, Isocr.
jealousy was ascribed to the gods, τὸν φθόνον πρόσκυσον deprecate their jealousy, Soph.
refusal from ill-will or envy, οὐδεὶς φθόνος, c. inf., said when you grant a request willingly, Plat.; so, ἀποκτείνειν φθόνος [ἐστί] 'tis invidious, I dare not tell, Eur.
destruction, ruin, perdition, Hdt., Trag., etc.; and of men, mortality, death, esp. by pestilence, Thuc.
the decay of matter, Plat.
the seduction, Lex ap. Aeschin.
ἴτ’ ἐς φθόρον = φθείρεσθε (v. φθείρω II. 1) a common form of cursing, Aesch.; οὐκ ἐς φθόρον; Id.
like ὄλεθρος, a pestilent fellow, Ar., Dem.
a broad, flat vessel, a bowl, used to boil liquids in, Il.; used as a cinerary urn, Id.
after Hom. a broad, flat bowl for drinking or pouring libations, Lat. patera, Hdt., attic
to undertake, set about a thing, Ar.
shining, bright, Theocr.
a kind of early fig, called from Φίβαλις, a district of Attica or Megaris:—pl., nom. φιβάλεῳ, acc. φιβάλεως Ar.
wilfully unadvised, Anth.
loving splendour, Pind., Anth.
fond of the country, Anth.
fond of the chase, a hunter, Babr.:—fem. φιλ-αγρέτις, ιδος, Anth.
fond of waking, wakeful, Anth.
loving the games, Anth.
brotherly love, NTest.
loving one's brother or sister, brotherly, sisterly, Soph., Xen.
fond of the games, Anth.
fond of the Athenians, Ar.
loving modesty, Anth.
bloodthirsty, Aesch., Eur.

entry.etym: irreg. comp. and Sup. of φίλος

entry.sense: fond of accusing, censorious, Xen., Dem.:— τὸ φ. censoriousness, Plut.
liable to blame or attack, Dem.
readily following, Ar.
fond of sheer wine, Anth.
a friend of Alexander, Strab.
loving truth, Arist.
loving the vine, Ar.
to love the vine, Tzetz.
fond of reading, Plut.
fond of spending, prodigal of, c. gen. rei, Plat.
love for the male sex, Eur.
love for a husband, Luc., Anth.
loving men, Aesch.
loving one's husband, NTest.
friend of colliers, Ar.
a humane act, Plut.
Dep. to act humanely, πρός τινα Dem.
to treat humanely, Polyb.
humanity, benevolence, kindliness, Plat., Xen., etc.:—in pl. acts of kindness, kindnesses, courtesies, Dem.
of God, love to man, NTest.
of things, ἡ τοῦ ὀνόματος φιλ. its humanity, kindliness, mildness, Dem.; ἡ φ. τῆς τέχνης, speaking of agriculture, Xen.
loving mankind, humane, benevolent, kindly, Aesch., Xen., etc.:—of dogs and horses loving men, gentle, Xen.
of things, humane, humanising, Id., etc.
adv., φιλανθρώπως τινὶ χρῆσθαι Dem.
fond of one's husband, conjugal, Aesch.
fond of singing, Theocr., Anth.
fondness for making enemies, quarrelsomeness, Isocr., Dem.
fond of making enemies, quarrelsome, Isocr., Dem. adv., φιλαπεχθημόνως ἔχειν to be quarrelsome, Plat.
fond of simplicity, Luc.
fond of travelling, Xen.
love of money, covetousness, Isocr., etc.
fond of money, covetous, Soph., Xen., etc.; Sup. φιλαργυρώτατος, Xen.:— τὸ φιλάργυρον = φιλαργυρία, Plat.
fond of virtue, Arist.
a friend of Aristides, Anth.
fond of the chariot-race, Pind., Eur.
love of rule, lust of power, Theophr., Plut.
fond of power, ambitious, Plat.
fond of playing at ἀστράγαλοι, Anth.
fond of the flute, Soph., Eur., etc.
loving oneself, Arist.
readily giving security or bail, Strab.
attached to the hair, Anth.
fond of learning, Strab.
fond of the Hellenes, Hdt., Plat.
a censorious person, Isocr.
fond of a lover, or fond of having lovers, Plat., Arist.
devotion to a lover, Plat.
love of labour, industry, Xen., Dem.
loving work, industrious, Dem.
fond of wool-spinning, Theocr., Anth.
prone to love, full of love, Anth.
fond of evening, Anth.
attachment to one's comrades, Xen.
fond of one's comrades or partisans, true to them, Thuc., Xen., etc.:—adv. -ρως, Aeschin.
loving the cry of εὐοῖ, of Bacchus, Anth.
to love, regard with affection, Lat. diligere, Hom., etc.; φ. τινὰ φιλότητα to feel affection for him, Od.; to love and cherish as one's wife, Hom.:—the epic aor1 mid. in act. sense, Il.
to treat affectionately or kindly, to welcome a guest, Hom.:—Pass., παρ’ ἄμμι φιλήσεαι welcome shalt thou be in our house, Od.
to kiss, Aesch., etc.; c. dupl. acc., τὸ φίλαμα, τὸ τὸν Ἄδωνιν φίλασεν the kiss wherewith she kissed him, Mosch.:—Mid. to kiss one another, Hdt.
of things, to love, like, approve, Od., Soph.
c. inf. to love to do, be fond of doing, and so to be wont or used to do, Hdt., Trag.

of things, events, αὔρα φιλέει πνέειν Hdt.; φιλεῖ μέγαλα στρατόπεδα ἐκπλήγνυσθαι great armies are apt to be seized with panic, Thuc.; πάντα ἀνθρώποισι φιλέει γίγνεσθαι everything comes to man by experience, Hdt.; and without γίγνεσθαι, οἷα δὴ φιλεῖ as is wont, Plat.; also impers., ὡς δὴ φιλεῖ as it is usual, Lat. ut solet, Plut.
to find pleasure in, take delight in a thing, c. dat., Ar.
fond of pleasure, Arist.
delight, Ar.
fond of pleasure, Luc., etc.
wont to bring delight, Anth.
to be attentive, Polyb.
fondness for hearing or listening to, c. gen., Isocr.
fond of hearing discussions, Plat.
fond of the spindle, Anth.
fond of the sun, Telesilla.
one who delights in the trials of the court Heliaea, Ar.
a kiss, Eur., Xen., etc.
friendliness, affection, Theogn.
loving wind: of a flute, played by the breath, Anth.
following the rein, tractable, Aesch.
loving the oar, Od.
a feeling of affection, Arist.
one must love, Soph.
disposed to love, τινος Arist.: absol. loving, affectionate, Id.
to be loved, worthy of love, Arist.; τὸ φ. the object of love, Id.
a lover, Aesch.

friendly love, affection, friendship, distinct from ἔρως, as Lat. amicitia from amor, Hdt., Eur., etc.; φ. ποιεῖσθαι πρός τινα Xen.; with gen., διὰ φιλίαν αὐτοῦ through friendship for him, Thuc.; ἡμετέρη φ. friendship with us, Theogn.; φιλία ἡ ἐμή Xen., etc.
fondness for a thing, Plat.
of or for a friend, befitting a friend, friendly, Xen., etc.:— φιλικά proofs or marks of friendship, Id. adv. -κῶς, in a friendly way, Plat., etc.; φ. ἔχειν to be kindly disposed, Xen.
prop. n. used as a term of affection, darling, Ar.
act. of or from a friend, friendly, Hdt., Trag., etc.; φ. τριήρης a friendly ship, Thuc.; ἡ φιλία (sc. γῆ, χώρα) a friendly country, opp. to ἡ πολεμία, Xen.
Ζεὺς φίλιος Zeus as god of friendship, Plat.; ναὶ τὸν φίλιον (sub. Δία) Ar.; πρὸς φιλίου Plat.
pass., beloved, dear, Trag.
adv. -ίως, Thuc., etc.
to be on Philip's side or party, to Philippize, Dem., Aeschin.
of or against Philip, Dem.
fond of horses, horse-loving, Pind., Eur., etc.:—Sup. φιλιππότατος, Xen.
the common meals or public tables at Sparta, Arist.
the common hall in which the public table was kept, Xen., Plut.:—others read φιδίτιον or φειδίτιον -ια, (as if from φείδομαι) a frugal table, cheap dinner.
loving Bacchus or wine, Anth.
loving monarchy, Plut.
a friend to the king, Plut.
loving the earth, Anth.
longing for marriage, Eur.
one who loves his belly, a glutton, Anth.
fond of the ludicrous, Arist.
laughter-loving, Plat., Arist.
fondness for a country life, Xen.
fond of a country life, Xen.
loving mirth, mirthful, Aesch.
to love books, Plut.
loving books, Plut., etc.
to love gymnastic exercises, Plat.
fondness for gymnastic exercises, Plat.
of or for a φιλογυμναστής, Plat.
fond of women, pl. φιλογύναικες Plat.
fond of trees or the wood, Anth.
loving one's lord or master, ἀνδράποδα φ. slaves that hug their chains, Hdt.; δῆμος φ. Theogn.
a friend of the δῆμος, the commons' friend, Ar.:— φ. ἔργον a popular act, Id.
loving the right, loving justice, Arist.
to be fond of litigation, Thuc.
fond of lawsuits, litigious, Lys., Dem.
a friend of travellers, Anth.
to love fame, seek honour, ἐπί τινι for or in a thing, Arist.
love of honour or glory, Polyb.
loving honour or glory, Plat.: τὸ φιλόδοξον, = φιλοδοξία, Luc.
loving noise, Anth.
fondness for giving, bounteousness, Luc.
fond of giving, bountiful, Xen.
of things, munificent, Dem.
fond of work, industrious, Anth.
loving the west wind, Anth.
fond of one's life, Arist.
fond of animals, Xen.
fond of seeing, fond of shows, plays or spectacles, Plat.; c. gen., φ. τῆς ἀληθείας Id.
loving God, pious, Arist., etc.
love of hunting, love of the chase, Xen.
fond of hunting, Xen., etc.: Sup. φιλοθηρότατος, Id.
fond of Thucydides, Anth.
ὄργια φιλόθυτα, rites offered by zealous worshippers, Aesch.
fond of sacrifices, Ar.
a friend of priests, Io_damasc.
loving one's relations, Arist.
fond of building, Xen.
prone to pity, Eur., Plat.
moving pity, ἀπ’ ὄμματος βέλει φιλοίκτῳ with piteous glance shot from her eyes, Aesch.
love of wine, Hdt.
fond of wine, Plat., etc.
loving novelty or innovation: τὸ φιλόκαινον love of novelty, Luc.
to cultivate a taste for the beautiful, Thuc.
to be eager, c. inf., Plut.
loving the beautiful, Plat., Xen., etc.: — fond of effect and elegance, Xen.
fond of honour, seeking honour, Id.
easily bending, lithe, Anth.
bearing fruit abundantly, Anth.
love of gain, greed, Xen.
to be greedy of gain, Xen.
greedy of gain, Theogn., etc.
fond of jeering, Od., Theocr.
fond of one's relatives, Xen.
fond of danger, adventurous, Xen., Dem.; πρὸς τὰ θηρία φιλοκινδυνότατος Xen.:—adv. -νως, eagerly, Id.
in bad sense, fool-hardy, Dem.
fond of wearing ivy, Eur.
fond of pinching, prurient, Anth.
fond of society, Anth.
fond of flatterers, Arist.
love of ornament or show, Plut.
loving ornament, Plut.
loving steep rocks, Anth.
loving rattles, Anth.
loving noise, Hhymn.
loving possessions, greedy of gain, covetous, Sup. φιλοκτεανώτατος, Il.
fond of dice, Ar.
loving glory, Hhymn.
loving the chase, Plut.
fond of dogs, Plat.
fond of the Laconians, Plut.
loving booty, Hhymn.
to love learning, to study, Plut.
love of learning, studiousness, Isocr.
fond of speaking, Plat.
fond of learning, literary, Lat. studiosus, Arist.
fond of reviling, abusive, Dem.
love of learning, Plat.
to be fond of learning, Plat.
fond of learning, eager after knowledge, Plat.; Sup. φιλομαθέστατος, Xen.; τὸ φιλομαθές = φιλομάθεια, Plat.
c. gen. rei, eager after a thing, Id., Xen.
one who takes note of divinations or omens, Luc.
loving the breast, Aesch.
to be eager to fight, Plut.
loving the fight, warlike, Aesch.
rain-loving, Anth.
the nightingale, because, acc. to the legend, Philomela was changed into this bird, Dem.
fond of Homer, Strab.
loving one's mother, Plut.
laughter-loving, epith. of Aphrodite, Hom., Hes.
loving dance and song, Pind.
love of the Muses, Luc.
loving the Muses, generally, loving music and the arts, Ar., Plat., etc.
to be fond of fables, Strab.
a love of fables, Strab.
fond of legends or fables, Arist.
fond of talking, Id.
loving sailors, Anth.

to be fond of strife, engage in eager rivalry, be contentious, φιλονεικῶν out of contentiousness or party spirit, Thuc., Plat.; φ. πρός τινα Lys.:—c. acc., φ. τὸ ἐμὲ εἶναι τὸν ἀποκρινόμενον to be eager that I should be the answerer, Plat.; τὰ χείρω φ. to be so obstinate as to choose the worst, Thuc.
in good sense, to struggle emulously, φ. περὶ τῶν καλλίστων Isocr.
love of strife, eager rivalry, contentiousness, party-spirit, Thuc., etc.
in good sense, emulation, Xen.; διὰ φιλονεικίαν eagerly, Id.
fond of strife, eager for strife, contentious, Pind., Plat.
in good sense, emulous, of spirited horses, Xen.: τὸ φιλόνεικον = φιλονεικία, Id.:—adv. -κως, in eager rivalry, Id., Plat., etc.
loving the bridegroom or bride, Anth.
hospitality, Theogn.
loving strangers, hospitable, Od., Aesch.; παθεῖν φιλόξενον ἔργον to meet with an act of hospitality, Pind.
fond of play, playful, sportive, Od., Ar.
loving its young, χελιδών Anth.
fond of daring, venturous, Plut.
love of one's country, patriotism, Ar.
loving one's country, Polyb., Luc.
loving one's father, Eur.
to be fond of inquiry, Polyb.
usually braided, Anth.
loving arms, Anth.
fond of sailing, Anth.
love of riches, Plut.
loving riches, φ. ἅμιλλα eager pursuit of wealth, the race for riches, Eur.
Mid. to make one's friend, attach to oneself, τινα Polyb.
a friend of poets, Plat.
loving the flock, Theocr.
making friends, Plut.
fond of war, warlike, Il., Plut.: adv. -μως, Isocr.
loving the city, Aesch.
loving one's city, patriotic, Ar., Thuc.; τὸ φιλόπολι patriotism, Thuc.
loving one's fellow-citizens, Plut.
to love labour, work hard, be laborious or industrious, Xen., Plat.
a love of bad men and actions, Theophr.
a friend to bad men, Plut.
love of labour, laboriousness, industry, Plat.; φ. τινός laborious practice of a thing, Dem.
loving labour, laborious, industrious, diligent, Soph., Plat.:—Sup. -ώτατος, Isocr.:—adv., φιλοπόνως ἔχειν to be diligent, Xen.
of things, toilsome, laborious, πόλεμος Id.
love of drinking, Xen., Plat.
a lover of drinking, fond of wine, Hdt., Ar.
a busy disposition, meddlesomeness, restless habits of life, Plat., Dem.
fond of business: in bad sense, a meddlesome fellow, busybody, Isae.
easiness of address, Isocr.
easy of address, affable, Isocr.
to strive to be first, NTest.
fond of being first: τὸ φιλόπρωτον eagerness to be first, Plut.
loving wheat, Anth.
loving autumn-fruits, Anth.
fond of orgies, Anth.
loving what is straight or right, Anth.
she who loves the harbour, Anth.
fondness for birds, Ar.
fond of birds, Plut.
loved or haunted by birds, Aesch.
attached to the nose, Anth.
loving grapes, Anth.
fond of quails, Plat.
fond of corn, occupied about it, Xen.
fond of food, fond of eating, Plat.
sceptred, Anth.
loving a staff, of Pan, Anth.
loving rocks, Anth.
fond of scoffing or jesting, Hdt.
to love knowledge, pursue it, philosophise, Lat. philosophari, Hdt., Thuc., etc.; φιλοσοφοῦντά με δεῖ ζῆν, says Socrates, Plat.
to teach philosophy, Isocr.
c. acc. to discuss philosophically, to investigate, study, Lat. meditari, Isocr.; φιλοσοφίαν φιλοσοφεῖν to pursue philosophy, Xen.
generally, to study a thing, Isocr.
one must pursue wisdom, Plat., etc.
love of knowledge and wisdom, pursuit thereof, speculation, study, Plat., etc.
the systematic treatment of a subject, investigation, Isocr.
philosophy, the investigation of truth and nature, Plat., etc.
a lover of wisdom, first used by Pythagoras, who called himself φιλόσοφος a lover of wisdom, not σοφός, a sage, Cic.: then in a wide sense of scientific men, learned men, Plat., etc.
a philosopher, i. e. one who speculates on the nature of things and truth, Ar., etc.; defined as ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας φιλοθεάμων, Plat.
as adj. loving knowledge, philosophic, Id.: of arguments, etc., scientific, philosophic, Id.; τὸ φιλόσοφον = φιλοσοφία, Id.
adv., φιλοσόφως διακεῖσθαι Isocr.; φ. ἔχειν Plat.
fond of grottoes, Anth.
used in drink-offerings, Aesch.

entry.etym: ι short: but voc. φίλε with ῑ in Hom.
entry.sense: pass. loved, beloved, dear, Lat. amicus, carus, Hom., etc.; c. dat. dear to one, Id.; voc. φίλε may be used with neut. nouns, φίλε τέκνον Od.; a gen. was sometimes added to the voc., φίλ’ ἀνδρῶν Theocr.; ὦ φίλα γυναικῶν Eur.:—often as Subst., φίλος, a friend, Hom.:—proverb., ἔστιν ὁ φ. ἄλλος αὐτός a friend is another self, Arist.; κοινὰ τὰ τῶν φίλων Plat.:—so in fem. φίλη, a dear one, friend, Lat. amica, Hom., attic:— φίλον, ου, an object of love, Soph.; τὰ φίλτατα one's nearest and dearest, such as wife and children, Trag.

of things, dear, pleasant, welcome, Hom.:—as predic., φίλον ἐστί or γίγνεταί μοι 'tis dear to me, pleases me, Lat. cordi est, Id., Hdt., etc.; εἰ τόδ’ αὐτῷ φίλον κεκλημένῳ if it please him to be so called, Aesch.

in Poets, φίλος is used of one's own limbs, life, etc., φίλον δ’ ἐξαίνυτο θυμόν he took away dear life, Il.; φίλον ἦτορ, φίλα γούνατα, πατὴρ φίλος, φίλη ἄλοχος Hom.; φίλην ἄγεσθαι to take as his own wife, Il.
in act. sense, like φίλιος, loving, friendly, Hom.; c. gen., φίλαν ξένων ἄρουραν friendly to strangers, Pind.; φίλα φρονέειν τινί to feel kindly, Il.; φ. ποιεῖσθαί τινι to make friends with one, Hdt.
adv. φίλως, φίλως χ’ ὁρόῳτε ye would fain see it, Il.; φ. ἐμοί in a manner dear or pleasing to me, Aesch.; φ. δέχεσθαί τινα Xen.
φίλος has several forms of comparison:
comp. φιλίων [ῐ], ον, Od.
comp. φίλτερος, Sup. φίλτατος, v. sub vocc.
comp. φιλαίτερος, Sup. φιλαίτατος, Xen., Theocr.
in attic μᾶλλον φίλος Aesch., etc.; Sup. μάλιστα φ. Xen.
loving crowns, garlanded, Hhymn.
loving sighs, piteous: adv. -νως, Aesch.
tender love, affectionateness, Xen.
loving tenderly, affectionate, of the love of parents and children, brothers and sisters, Xen., Theocr., etc.; τὸ φιλόστοργον = φιλοστοργία, Xen.:—adv. φιλοστόργως, Plut.
the soldier's friend, Xen.
loving the body, Plat.
loving one's children or offspring, Hdt., Eur.
to love art, practise an art, Plat.
fond of art, artistic, Plat.: τὸ φιλότεχνον ingenuity, Plut.
of friendship or love, promoting it, Od., Soph.
ἡ φιλοτησία or -ήσιος (with or without κύλιξ), the cup sacred to friendship, the loving-cup, Theogn., Ar.; φιλοτησίας προπίνειν (where φιλοτησίας is prob. acc. pl.), to drink healths, Dem.
friendship, love, affection, Hom., etc.; φ. τινός friendship with, affection for, Od.; διὰ τὴν λίαν φιλότητα βροτῶν by his over great love for men, Aesch.; ὦ φιλότης, = ὦ φίλε, my friend, Plat.

to love or seek after honour, to be ambitious, emulous, jealous, Ar., etc.; φ. ὅτι . . to be jealous because . . , Xen.:—the object of ambition is added with a prep., φιλ. ἐπί τινι to pride oneself upon it, Id., etc.; ἔν τινι Plat.;— with neut. adj., ἀεί τι φιλοτιμούμενος pursuing some object of ambition, Xen.
c. inf. to strive eagerly and emulously to do a thing, endeavour earnestly, aspire, Id.:—c. acc. et inf. to be anxious that . . , Id.
an act of ambition or magnificence, Plut.
rivalry, Luc.

the character of the φιλότιμος, love of distinction, ambition, Eur., Thuc., etc.;—in good sense, Xen.: c. gen. objecti, φ. τινός emulous desire for a thing, Plat., etc.; φ. πρός τινα ambitious rivalry with him, Isocr.
ambitious pertinacity, obstinacy, Hdt.
ambitious display, prodigality, Dem., Aeschin.
the object coveted, honour, distinction, credit, Dem.

loving honour, covetous of honour, ambitious, emulous, Eur., Plat., etc.; in good sense, Xen., Isocr.:—with abstr. Nouns (in both senses), εὐχά Aesch.; ἦθος Eur.; σοφίαι Ar.; φ. ἐπί τινι eager to be honoured for a thing, covetous of distinction in . . , ἐπὶ σοφίᾳ, ἐπ’ ἀρετῇ Plat.
emulously prodigal, lavish, Dem.
in pass. sense, = πολυτίμητος, august, Aesch.
adv. -μως, ambitiously, emulously, φ. ἔχειν to vie emulously, Plat.; φ. ἔχειν πρός τι to strive, exert oneself eagerly after a thing, Xen.
fond of such and such things, Arist.
friend of tyranny, Plut.
loving noise, noisy, Anth.
loving one's friends, Arist.
to treat affectionately, to shew kindness to, τινα Hdt., Plat.; φ. τινα τῆι δικέλληι to entertain him with a blow of the mattock, Luc.

c. dat., φιλοφρονήσασθαί τινι to shew a favour to one, Xen.:—aor1 pass. φιλοφρονηθῆναι, in a reciprocal sense, to shew kindness one to another, to greet one another, Id.; so φιλοφρονήσασθαι ἀλλήλους Id.
absol. to be of a kindly, cheerful temper, Id.
friendliness, kindliness, Il.; τινός towards one, Hdt.; πρός τινα Plat.: pl. friendly greetings, Pind.
cheerfulness, Xen.
kindly minded, kindly, friendly, affable, Pind., Aesch., etc.: adv., φιλοφρόνως ἀσπάζεσθαι to greet kindly, Hdt.; φ. ἔχειν πρός τινα to be kindly minded towards one, Xen.
friend of the choral dance, Ar.
loving the choir or choral dance, Aesch.
to love money, Plat.
love of money, Plat.
fond of money-making, Plat.
loving money, fond of money, Plat., etc.: τὸ φιλοχρήματον = φιλοχρηματία, Id.; Sup. -ώτατος, Diod. adv., φιλοχρημάτως ἔχειν = φιλοχρηματεῖν, Isocr.
loving goodness or honesty, Xen.
fond of gold, Luc., Anth.
to be fond of a place, to abide there always, haunt it, Hdt.
fondness for a place, love of one's haunts, local attachment, Ar.
fond of lies or lying, Il., Plat.
fond of blame, censorious, Eur., Plat.
to love one's life: to be cowardly or faint-hearted, Tyrtae., Eur.
one must love life, Plat.
love of life, Hdt., Plat.
loving one's life, cowardly, dastardly, faint-hearted, Eur.

entry.etym: irreg. Sup. of φίλος, Hom., Trag.
irreg. comp. of φίλος, Hom., Hes.

entry.sense: charmer, name of a mouse, Batr.
a love-charm, (cf. Shakspeare's "medicines to make me love him"), ἐστὶν φίλτρα μοι θελκτήρια ἔρωτος Eur.; of the robe of Nessus by which Deianira hoped to win back the love of Hercules, Soph.

generally, a charm, spell, as a means of winning or influencing others, hence the bit is called φ. ἵππειον, Pind.; Apollo's oracles are φίλτρα τόλμης spells to produce boldness, Aesch.; children are a φίλτρον of love to their parents, Eur., etc.
in pl. love, affection, Id.
loving moisture, Anth.
the lime or linden tree, Lat. tilia, Hdt.
of the lime or linden tree, light as linden wood, Ar.
a lover of mountains, Anth.
a muzzle, Lat. capistrum, Luc.
the nose-band of a horse's bridle, fitted with pipes through which the horses' breath made a whistling sound, Aesch.
a kind of cup, used as a dice-box, Lat. fritillus, Aeschin.
to muzzle, shut up as with a muzzle, φ. τῷ ξύλῳ τὸν αὐχένα to make fast his neck in the pillory, Ar.: metaph. to muzzle, put to silence, NTest.: Pass., aor1 imperat. φιμώθητι be thou silenced, Id.
-φι, -φιν, an old term. of dat. for -ῃ, ας, ᾖφι βίῃφι πεποιθώς; for -ῳ, as θεόφιν ἀτάλαντος; also pl., as, ; ναῦφι for ναυσί.
of gen., for -ης, as, ἐξ εὐνῆφι; for -ου, as, ἐκ θεόφιν, for -ος, κράτεσφι for κρᾱτός, of the head.
φ, φῖ, τό, indecl., twenty-first letter of the Gr.
changes of Φ:

in aeolic, doric and ionic the aspirate was often dropped, and φ became π, as in ἀσπάραγος σπόγγος σπυράς for ἀσφάραγος σφόγγος σφυράς, whereas the attic sometimes used φ for π, as φανός φάτρα for πανός πάτρα.
in aeolic, doric, and ionic φ is sometimes put for θ, as φήρ φλάω for θήρ θλάω.
older Poets sometimes treated φ as a double consonant, so that a short vowel before it becomes long by position, as in ὄφις, Ζεφύριος quasi ὄπφις, Ζεπφύριος.
a block of wood, log, Hom.
a shoot, scion, of a son, Aesch.
a tender of plants, gardener, Aesch.

entry.etym: poet. for φῠτεύω, when the 1st syll. is to be long
entry.sense: to sow, plant, beget, call into being, Trag.:—Mid. of the woman, to produce, bear, Hes.; epic 2nd sg. fut. φιτύσεαι Mosch.
to be rent with a noise, Aesch.
Comic words in Ar., meant to ridicule a bombastic style— "sound without sense."
petty, paltry, trivial, Solon., Pind., Hdt.
paltry, sorry, indifferent, bad, Aesch., Soph.; φλαῦρον ἐργάζεσθαί τινα to do one a mischief, Ar.; φλαῦρον εἰπεῖν τινα to speak disparagingly of him, Id.
useless, Soph.
of persons, οὐ φλαυροτάτους τιμωρούς not the meanest or weakest avengers, Hdt.; τῆς στρατιῆς τὸ φλαυρότατον the least serviceable part, Id.
shabby, plain, of personal appearance, Id.
bad, opp. to χρηστός, Eur.
